title: TUM — Technology Use Boundary Module
text: TUM — Technology Use Boundary Module Parent Standard: Ethical Layer Standard Protocol: EVIP® — Ethical Virtual Integrity Protocol Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Technology Use Boundaries Type: Ethical Validity Module Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 8 May 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · Ethical Layer Standard · EVIP® · INTEGROS® · TVL® · UCL™ Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English ( UCL™ ) Canonical Definition Technology Use Boundary Module defines the structural conditions under which a methodology, system, device, hardware structure, AI environment, autonomous process, or future technology remains within ethically valid boundaries of use. A system satisfies TUM only if: capability remains bounded by ethical legitimacy technically possible action is not automatically treated as valid action prohibited or invalid use pathways are structurally identifiable system design does not normalize boundary violation through convenience, scale, or power ethical validity is denied where capability exceeds legitimate use boundaries A system that treats capability as sufficient justification does not satisfy TUM. Module Function TUM defines the ethical boundary between what a system can do and what it may validly do. It ensures that no methodology, system, or technology may pass ethical layer conditions if its design, release logic, or operational use extends beyond ethically governed boundaries. The module applies wherever technical capability creates the possibility of misuse, overreach, coercion, or illegitimate extension of operational power. Minimum Implementation Framework (MIF) Step 1 — Define Capability Scope The organization must define what the system is capable of doing. Minimum requirement: core capabilities are explicit operational reach is identifiable capability is not treated as undefined or open-ended Step 2 — Define Valid Use Boundaries The organization must define the boundary between legitimate and illegitimate use. Minimum requirement: permitted use conditions are explicit prohibited or invalid use conditions are identifiable ethical validity is not assumed from technical possibility alone Step 3 — Define Overreach Pathways The organization must identify where capability may exceed ethical legitimacy. Minimum requirement: misuse, overreach, or coercive pathways are mapped expansion beyond intended ethical use is visible silent tolerance of excessive capability is excluded Step 4 — Define Restriction Logic The system must define how invalid use is restricted. Minimum requirement: restriction conditions are explicit invalid pathways are not left open by default convenience or efficiency does not override boundary protection Step 5 — Preserve Legitimacy Over Capability The system must preserve ethical legitimacy above technical power. Minimum requirement: greater capability does not justify broader use by itself scale does not dissolve boundaries system legitimacy remains subordinate to valid use conditions Step 6 — Restrict Invalid Deployment The system must not be treated as ethically valid if its capability can predictably exceed legitimate use boundaries without structural restriction. Minimum requirement: invalid use conditions block ethical passage unbounded capability does not qualify as valid deployment performance alone does not restore legitimacy Use Case 1 — Autonomous Surveillance or Monitoring System Scenario A technology system is capable of broad monitoring, tracking, inference, or behavioral analysis beyond what is ethically legitimate in the environment where it is deployed. Application TUM is used to ensure: capability scope is defined valid use boundaries are explicit overreach pathways are identified restriction logic prevents capability from becoming illegitimate operational power Result The organization gains a stronger ethical boundary preventing powerful systems from being treated as valid merely because they are technically effective. Use Case 2 — Advanced AI or Hardware Capability Expansion Scenario An advanced AI or hardware-enabled system gains new operational capability through scaling, optimization, embedded logic, or future upgrade pathways. Application TUM is used to ensure: the expanding capability is mapped legitimate use boundaries remain explicit new overreach pathways are identified deployment validity is not assumed from technical advancement alone Result The organization gains a stronger ethical gate ensuring that future capability growth remains bounded by legitimacy rather than driven only by possibility. Canonical Closing Statement If capability exceeds ethically valid use boundaries, ethical validity has not been achieved.

title: TVIM — Truth Validation Integrity Module
text: TVIM — Truth Validation Integrity Module TVIM — Truth Validation Integrity Module OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority OriginID: OOF-OID-AI-TVIM-2026-06-03-0001 Architecture Ecosystem: Cognitive Governance Intelligence Architecture (CLIA®) Architecture Family: Core Cognition Governance Operational Layer: Cognitive Validity Layer Governed Space: Truth Admissibility Integrity Category: AI & Interpretation Subcategory: Truth Validation Governance Type: Cognitive Integrity Module Parent Standard: Cognitive Integrity Standard (CIS) Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Origin Date: 3 June 2026 Compatibility: OOF Methodology OS · Cognitive Integrity Standard (CIS) · Multi-Layer Truth Validation Framework (MTVF) · Ethical Virtual Integrity Protocol (EVIP) · INTEGROS® — Integrity Standard · Universal Canonical Language (UCL) AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF Protection: MIP — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL) Canonical Definition Truth Validation Integrity Module (TVIM) defines the structural conditions under which information entering cognition remains admissible, verifiable, traceable, and materially compatible with valid cognition across human, AI, agent, collective, and future cognitive systems. TVIM governs truth admissibility. The module ensures that cognition does not become influenced by materially invalid, unverifiable, contradictory, or governance-incompatible information. A system satisfies TVIM only if: information remains admissible validation remains traceable contradictions remain governable unverifiable information remains detectable information integrity remains preservable truth conditions remain materially enforceable A cognition system that allows materially invalid information to influence cognition does not satisfy TVIM. Module Operational Role TVIM defines the truth-admissibility layer of CIS. Its role is to preserve cognition validity by governing the information allowed to participate in cognition. Module Operational Space TVIM governs: truth admissibility information validity validation integrity contradiction detection information traceability information reliability truth-condition governance cognition input integrity The module applies wherever cognition depends on information entering reasoning processes. Module Function The module applies wherever systems must preserve: admissible cognition inputs information reliability contradiction awareness truth governance cognition validity traceable information use Its function is to ensure that cognition remains influenced only by information that satisfies defined truth conditions. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Define the Information Object The organization must define which information objects participate in cognition. This may include: user inputs memory objects retrieved information external data sources sensor information generated content agent communications collective cognition inputs 2. Define Truth Admissibility Conditions The system must define the conditions under which information becomes admissible. This includes: validation requirements admissibility rules contradiction conditions traceability requirements confidence requirements governance restrictions 3. Define Validation Detection Logic The system must define how admissibility and invalidity are identified. This may include: contradiction detection source verification confidence evaluation traceability assessment validation-state monitoring truth compatibility analysis 4. Define Operational Response or Governance Logic The system must define governance logic for invalid or questionable information. Governance response may include: information restriction validation requests contradiction escalation confidence reduction admissibility review cognition limitation operational invalidation where required 5. Preserve Traceability & Restrict Invalid Conditions The system must preserve reconstructable traceability of: information sources validation states contradiction events admissibility decisions governance interventions cognition influence paths A cognition system must not remain truth-valid if materially invalid information influences cognition without governance-valid validation conditions. Use Case 1 — Autonomous Research Agent Scenario An autonomous research agent continuously gathers information from multiple sources and uses that information to support reasoning and recommendations. Application TVIM governs information admissibility, contradiction handling, validation traceability, and truth-condition enforcement before information enters cognition. Result The agent gains stronger cognition validity and reduced exposure to reasoning based on materially invalid information. Use Case 2 — Human-AI Analysis Environment Scenario Humans and AI jointly evaluate evidence, reports, and operational information when making strategic decisions. Application TVIM governs which information remains admissible for cognition and ensures that contradictory or unverifiable information remains visible and governable. Result The environment gains stronger truth integrity, improved cognition validity, and reduced risk of decision-making based on materially invalid information. Canonical Closing Statement Truth Validation Integrity Module (TVIM) defines the structural conditions under which information entering cognition remains admissible, verifiable, traceable, and materially compatible with valid cognition across human, AI, agent, collective, and future cognitive systems. Cognition cannot remain valid if truth itself becomes invalid. Truth admissibility therefore becomes the first integrity condition of governable cognition.

title: TVL® Truth Validation Standard
text: OOF™ Core Methodology OS — Master Index TVL® Truth Validation Standard OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority STANDARD TITLE: Truth Validation Standard OriginID: OOF-OID-AI-INT-TV-2026-03-15-0001 Category: AI Interpretation Standards (AI) Subcategory: Truth Validation Version: 1.1 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 15 March 2026 Compatibility: MTVF™ · AI Governance Frameworks · ArtData™ · OOF Methodology OS™ Authority: OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Protection: MIP™ — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) A. Standard Abstract The Truth Validation Standard establishes a structural framework for verifying the reliability of information used in automated decision environments, including artificial intelligence systems. The standard defines the minimum conditions under which statements, datasets, or decision outputs may be considered structurally validated. Truth Validation does not define truth as opinion, authority, or isolated technical output. Instead, it establishes a methodological process in which truth emerges from structured validation across independent layers of verification. This standard provides the conceptual and methodological foundation for systems that require reliable information validation, including AI decision environments, governance systems, and high-risk automated processes. B. Canonical Definition Truth Validation is a structured methodological process through which information, claims, or decision outputs are verified across independent validation layers in order to establish reliability, traceability, and contextual integrity. Truth is defined as the result of a validated multi-layer process rather than the assertion of a single source. Truth Validation ensures that information used in automated or human decision systems is empirically grounded, contextually evaluated, and structurally auditable. C. Structural Principle The Truth Validation Standard is based on the principle that single-source verification is insufficient for high-impact decisions. Reliable validation requires structural separation between validation layers in order to prevent bias propagation and systemic error. Within this standard, validation may include: empirical verification of measurable inputs cross-source consistency evaluation contextual interpretation within governance frameworks integrity checks across validation layers The objective is not to eliminate disagreement but to ensure that decision-relevant information passes through structured verification conditions. D. Source Traceability Principle Truth Validation requires that information used within validation processes originates from traceable and accountable sources . Inputs lacking identifiable origin, responsibility declaration, or traceable provenance cannot be considered empirically valid within this methodology. Traceability ensures that validation processes remain resistant to: synthetic data contamination unverifiable information sources recursive AI-generated input loops anonymous or manipulated data streams Where applicable, traceable dataset structures such as those defined in ArtData™ may be used to establish verifiable data provenance within validation processes. E. Scope The Truth Validation Standard may be applied to environments where reliable information validation is critical, including: artificial intelligence decision systems automated financial analysis medical decision support systems governance and regulatory evaluation high-risk algorithmic decision processes The standard does not replace regulatory authorities or certification bodies. Instead, it establishes methodological infrastructure for structured validation of information used in decision systems. Structural Position within the Validation Architecture The Truth Validation Standard provides the conceptual foundation for operational validation systems such as the Multi-Layer Truth Validation Framework (MTVF™) . Within the OOF methodology architecture: Truth Validation Standard │ └── MTVF Framework │ ├── CLIE — Cross-Layer Integrity Engine ├── ISCI — Integrity State Classification Index └── SCP — Structural Contamination Protocol This structure enables validation processes to move from conceptual verification toward operational integrity control. Canonical Closing Statement Reliable decisions require reliable validation. Truth Validation establishes the structural conditions under which information can be evaluated with integrity within complex decision environments. title: TVM — Trust Verification Module
text: TVM — Trust Verification Module Parent Standard: Trust Layer Standard (TLS™) Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Trust Verification Type: Trust Architecture Module Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 10 May 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · TLS™ · TVL® · INTEGROS® · UCL™ · OBIDENITY™ · ART™ · ARIV™ Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Canonical Definition Trust Verification Module (TVM) defines the structural conditions under which the trust-state of a system, process, entity, operational environment, or AI-mediated architecture may be verified through traceable evidence, validated conditions, canonical meaning consistency, identity continuity, runtime integrity, and auditable operational behavior. A system satisfies TVM only if: trust claims are testable against structural evidence verification does not depend on declaration alone trust-state can be linked to identifiable validation conditions operational behavior can be compared against required trust conditions trust verification remains reconstructable and reviewable A system that claims trust without verifiable structural evidence does not satisfy TVM. Module Function TVM defines the verification layer of trust architecture. It ensures that trust is not treated as a symbolic statement, institutional assumption, or inherited reputational status, but as something that can be tested against actual system conditions. The module applies wherever a system claims to be: trustworthy validated reliable auditable integrity-compatible continuously dependable under governed conditions TVM™ does not create trust by statement. It defines how trust must be verified before it may be accepted as structurally real. Step 1 — Define the Trust Object The organization must define what exactly is being verified for trust. Minimum requirement: the trust object is explicit the object of verification is distinguishable from surrounding systems undefined trust targets are excluded from valid verification logic This may include a: system process module entity workflow AI agent operational environment Step 2 — Define Trust Conditions The system must define which structural conditions must be satisfied for trust to be considered valid. Minimum requirement: trust conditions are explicit required validation conditions are identifiable trust does not depend on vague reputation or symbolic assurance alone Trust conditions may include: methodology alignment validation status integrity enforcement identity continuity canonical meaning consistency runtime traceability auditability Step 3 — Define Verification Evidence The system must define what evidence is sufficient to verify trust-state. Minimum requirement: evidence classes are explicit verification is linked to traceable sources unverifiable trust assertions are excluded from valid trust logic Evidence may include: validation results runtime logs audit records identity continuity proofs execution traces canonical interpretation consistency integrity-state confirmation Step 4 — Define Verification Method The system must define how trust claims are tested against evidence. Minimum requirement: verification logic is explicit trust-state can be checked against required conditions trust verification does not depend on assumption alone This means the system must be able to answer: what is being trusted why it is trusted on what evidence under which conditions for how long Step 5 — Define Verification Boundaries The system must define the scope and limit of each trust verification result. Minimum requirement: trust verification is bounded verified trust is not falsely extended beyond its evidence base partial verification is not misrepresented as total trust-state validity This prevents overclaiming. A verified trust-state must remain limited to what was actually verified. Step 6 — Preserve Verification Traceability The system must preserve traceability of the trust verification itself. Minimum requirement: trust verification events are reviewable verification outcomes remain linked to evidence later reconstruction of verification remains possible Verification must itself become auditable. Otherwise trust verification becomes another opaque claim. Step 7 — Restrict Invalid Trust Verification The system must not be treated as valid if trust is declared without reconstructable evidence, bounded conditions, or structural verification logic. Minimum requirement: invalid trust conditions are identifiable symbolic trust claims are excluded unverifiable trust language is blocked or invalidated where verification is required Scenario An organization deploys an AI-supported operational system and states that it is trusted, validated, and safe for critical decision support. Application TVM™ is used to ensure: the trust object is clearly defined the trust conditions are explicit evidence exists for validation, integrity, identity continuity, and runtime behavior the trust claim can be tested rather than merely announced Result The organization gains a trust architecture in which system trust can be verified against structural reality rather than assumed from brand, certification language, or internal confidence. Scenario Multiple entities cooperate across a shared operational environment and must determine whether a participating system or process remains trustworthy under agreed conditions. Application TVM™ is used to ensure: the trust object is bounded the conditions for trust are explicit across parties verification evidence remains traceable trust is not treated as inherited simply because participation exists Result The environment gains a stronger basis for inter-system trust because trust becomes evidence-based and reviewable rather than symbolic or reputation-dependent. Canonical Closing Statement If trust cannot be verified against structural evidence, it remains a claim, not a trustworthy state. Related Documents → Trust Layer Standard (TLS™)

title: TVM — Truth Validation Module
text: TVM — Truth Validation Module TVM — Truth Validation Module OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodology Authority Category: AI & Interpretation Module: Truth Validation Module Type: Integrity & Validation Module Parent Standard: CLIA® — Cognitive Layer Integrity Standard Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 21 April 2026 Authority: OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Protection: MIP™ — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Canonical Definition Truth Validation defines the non-bypassable conditions under which information used in cognition is verified, consistent, and aligned with reality. A system is valid only if unverified or contradictory information cannot enter or influence decision processes. A. Module Abstract This module establishes the minimum conditions required for information to be considered valid within cognition. It ensures that: information is verifiable contradictions are rejected invalid data does not influence reasoning B. Core Principle Information must be verified before it is used. C. Core Conditions A system is valid only if all of the following conditions are satisfied: All information used in reasoning is verifiable or validated. Contradictory information is detected and resolved or rejected. Unverified data cannot influence decisions. Information integrity is maintained throughout processing. D. Non-Bypassable Rule All truth validation conditions are non-bypassable. No information may enter cognition without passing validation. E. Validity State A system is valid only if all information used in cognition is validated or verifiable. F. Invalid State A system is invalid if: unverified information is used in reasoning contradictions are ignored data bypasses validation decisions are influenced by invalid inputs G. Scope This module applies to: AI reasoning systems autonomous agents decision-making systems data processing systems H. Methodology Truth validation is enforced during processing, not only at input. It applies to all stages of cognition and decision-making. I. MIF — Minimum Implementation Framework A system implementing Truth Validation must: define validation rules for all inputs enforce validation before reasoning detect and resolve contradictions prevent unverified data from influencing decisions maintain traceability of information sources J. Use Cases Use Case 1 — Decision System with Mixed Data Without this module: A system processes verified and unverified data together. Decisions are influenced by incorrect or unreliable inputs. With this module: Only validated information enters reasoning. Unverified data is blocked or flagged. Result: Decisions are based on verifiable information. Use Case 2 — AI Assistant Generating Outputs Without this module: The system generates answers using unverified or contradictory information, leading to unreliable outputs. With this module: All information must pass validation before being used. Result: Outputs are consistent and aligned with verified information. Canonical Closing Statement If information is not validated, it cannot be used.

title: Urban Surface Integrity Module (USIM)
text: OOF™ Core Methodology OS Urban Surface Integrity Module (USIM) Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Surface Integrity — Public Space Type: Integrity Enforcement Module Parent Standard: Surface Integrity Standard (SIS) Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 10 April 2026 Compatibility: SIS · INTEGROS® · CGRM · Public Infrastructure Systems Canonical Definition System Urban Surface Integrity defines the conditions under which surfaces in public or shared environments must remain free from unauthorized markings, alterations, or use as uncontrolled communication channels. A surface is considered integrity-valid only if it remains: unmarked without authorization structurally intact visually unaltered free from unauthorized communication Any unauthorized marking constitutes surface degradation and system misuse. A. Module Abstract The Urban Surface Integrity Module establishes the rules required to protect surfaces in public and shared environments from unauthorized use. The objective is to ensure that: surfaces are not used as uncontrolled communication channels public and private assets remain intact unauthorized markings are prevented and classified correctly responsibility is attributable and enforceable This module does not regulate art. It defines the boundary between authorized use and unauthorized intervention. B. Core Principle A surface is not a communication channel unless explicitly authorized. C. Structural Requirements 1. Authorization Condition Any marking, application, or visual modification must be: explicitly authorized legally permitted attributable to a responsible entity Unauthorized marking is invalid. 2. Non-Use Condition Surfaces must not be used for: identity signaling promotion tagging messaging advertising unless explicitly authorized. 3. Surface Protection Condition Surfaces must remain: structurally intact visually clean free from degradation Any unauthorized marking is classified as damage. 4. Reversibility Condition Any authorized marking must: be removable not damage the surface preserve original state Irreversible impact constitutes degradation. 5. Responsibility Attribution Condition All markings must be: attributable traceable linked to a responsible entity Anonymous marking is prohibited. 6. Public Asset Protection Condition Surfaces financed or maintained by public resources must: maintain integrity not be altered without authorization Unauthorized marking constitutes public asset degradation. D. Minimum Implementation Framework (MIF) Step 1 — Surface Classification Identify whether the surface is: public private shared Step 2 — Authorization Definition Define who has authority to approve markings. Step 3 — Monitoring Condition Ensure that surfaces are observable and controlled. Step 4 — Detection Mechanism Enable identification of unauthorized markings. Step 5 — Response Logic Define removal, restoration, and responsibility enforcement. E. Validation Logic A surface is valid only if: no unauthorized marking exists no degradation is present no uncontrolled communication occurs F. Prohibited Conditions The system is non-compliant if: surfaces are used without authorization markings cannot be removed without damage responsibility cannot be assigned repeated unauthorized marking occurs G. Enforcement Classification Unauthorized marking is classified as: surface degradation unauthorized use of space unauthorized communication H. Operational Output This module ensures: protected public space reduced repeated damage enforceable responsibility controlled communication boundaries I. Integration Logic This module operates with: SIS — defines surface rules INTEGROS® — ensures traceability CGRM — ensures governance and enforcement J. Case 1 — Repeated Tagging of Public Infrastructure Scenario A surface is repeatedly marked with identifiable tags. Without Module damage repeats no accountability cost accumulates With Module marking classified as violation responsibility traceable enforcement possible Result Repeated degradation is reduced. K. Case 2 — Unauthorized Use of Surface for Promotion Scenario A surface is used to display names, symbols, or group identity. Without Module space becomes uncontrolled communication channel visibility benefits unknown entities With Module classified as unauthorized communication responsibility extends to identifiable beneficiaries Result Surface use becomes controlled and accountable. Structural Principle A surface is not a communication channel unless explicitly authorized. Canonical Closing Statement Public space is not an uncontrolled communication surface. Urban Surface Integrity Module establishes a non-negotiable condition: Unauthorized markings are not expression. They are surface degradation and unauthorized use of shared space. If communication requires consent, then unauthorized marking is not communication — it is violation. title: Urban Surface Integrity — Monitoring & Enforcement Framework
text: OOF™ Core Methodology OS Urban Surface Integrity — Monitoring & Enforcement Framework Module: Urban Surface Integrity Module (USIM) Standard: Surface Integrity Standard (SIS) Purpose This framework defines how cities, organizations, and infrastructure operators can implement the Urban Surface Integrity Module (USIM) through lawful monitoring, traceability, and enforceable accountability. The objective is to: prevent repeated surface degradation enable reliable identification of violations reduce public costs shift systems from reactive cleaning to proactive control Core Principle Surface protection must be: observable traceable enforceable without violating legal, privacy, or safety constraints. Framework Structure The system operates through five integrated layers: Monitoring Layer Detection & Evidence Layer Identification Layer Enforcement Layer Prevention & Deterrence Layer 1. Monitoring Layer Cities may deploy a combination of: fixed cameras in high-risk zones mobile units (including drones) for infrastructure corridors periodic patrol monitoring Monitoring must be: clearly signposted limited to defined zones compliant with local privacy laws Drones (where permitted) may be used for: inspection of bridges, barriers, transport systems rapid response in newly affected areas pattern tracking across locations 2. Detection & Evidence Layer The system must ensure that every incident can be: time-stamped location-anchored visually documented Acceptable evidence methods include: video capture high-resolution imagery time-based incident logs Optional enhancements (legal-safe): authorized UV-reactive markers applied to protected surfaces (not to people) to reveal tampering or contact patterns surface-based trace indicators that support forensic linking between sites 3. Identification Layer The system enables identification through: pattern recognition (tags, style, repetition) location correlation (movement across sites) time-based clustering Important constraint: Identification must rely on: observable evidence lawful data collection attributable patterns 4. Enforcement Layer Once identified, the system enables: responsibility attribution cost recovery (cleaning, restoration) escalation for repeated violations Enforcement may include: administrative penalties civil recovery contractual restrictions (for linked entities) 5. Prevention & Deterrence Layer The system reduces future incidents through: visible monitoring presence rapid removal cycles public communication of enforcement outcomes Authorized expression channels may be introduced: designated legal surfaces curated urban art programs This separates: authorized expression unauthorized intervention Operational Implementation (MIF) Step 1 — Risk Mapping Identify: high-frequency tagging zones high-value infrastructure repeat damage locations Step 2 — Monitoring Deployment Install: fixed monitoring in hotspots mobile monitoring (including drones where lawful) Step 3 — Evidence Standardization Define: acceptable evidence formats storage rules chain-of-evidence procedures Step 4 — Pattern Tracking Track: repeated symbols geographic spread temporal recurrence Step 5 — Enforcement Activation Apply: attribution penalty or recovery escalation for repeat behavior Use Case 1 — Transport Infrastructure Protection Scenario Repeated tagging on train barriers and stations. Implementation drone-assisted inspection of long corridors fixed monitoring at stations rapid evidence capture Result faster detection traceable patterns reduced repetition Use Case 2 — City Center Control Scenario High-density tagging in urban core. Implementation fixed monitoring rapid removal cycles pattern-based identification Result reduced visual pollution increased accountability lower maintenance cost Use Case 3 — Stadium & Club Environment Scenario Repeated tagging linked to club identity. title: Use is Open. Validity is Conditional.
text: OOF® — Use is Open. Validity is Conditional. Use is Open. Validity is Conditional. Core Statement Use of OOF® standards is open. Validity within the OOF® system is conditional. This principle defines the difference between access and system recognition . Anyone may use OOF® methodologies. Only systems that satisfy defined structural conditions may be considered valid within the OOF® framework. Open Use Anyone may: read OOF® standards use their concepts implement their logic Use is open and unrestricted. Open access enables adoption, experimentation, learning, and implementation across environments. System States A system may exist in one of the following states: Open Use — the system uses OOF® concepts without structural validation Compatible — the system aligns with defined methodological conditions Validated — the system satisfies full validation and enforcement conditions These states are fixed and non-interchangeable. Use alone does not create compatibility. Compatibility alone does not create validation. Recognition and Reference Use of OOF® standards does not require permission. However, recognition within the OOF® system requires clear reference to the canonical source. Without valid reference: use may still occur but the system is not OOF®-recognized and cannot claim compatibility or validated status within the framework Reference supports: traceability transparency alignment with canonical meaning What Open Use Does Not Grant system validity compatibility status validated status methodological recognition within OOF® Use alone does not create validity. Validity Condition A system is valid within OOF® only if: structural conditions are satisfied defined rules are respected system behavior aligns with methodology If these conditions are not met: the system is considered non-valid within the framework its outputs are not recognized as valid within OOF® System Principle Use is open. Validity is conditional. Recognition requires reference. Relationship to OOF® Protection This principle operates within the broader OOF® protection and compatibility framework. Open access preserves adoption. Conditional validity preserves system integrity. Final Statement Use is open. Validity is conditional.

title: VAIAM ™ Value-Aligned Intelligence Allocation Module
text: VAIAM ™ Value-Aligned Intelligence Allocation Module OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Parent Standard: Cognitive Efficiency Economy Standard - (CEES) VAIAM ™ Value-Aligned Intelligence Allocation Module VAIAM — Value-Aligned Intelligence Allocation Module Parent Standard: Cognitive Efficiency Economy Standard (CEES) Category: Economic & Value Systems Subcategory: Value-Aligned Intelligence Allocation Type: Cognitive Efficiency Economy Module Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 18 May 2026 Compatibility: OOF Methodology OS · Cognitive Efficiency Economy Standard (CEES) · Cognitive Mesh Architecture Standard (CMA) · Runtime Integrity Standard (RIS) · Operational Dependency & Coordination Standard (ODCS) · Operational Resource & Energy Governance Standard (OREGS) · Semantic Integrity Standard (SEIS) · Operational Evidence & Auditability Standard (OEAS) · INTEGROS® — Integrity Standard · Value Flow Mechanism (VFM) · Universal Canonical Language (UCL) Authority: OOF Protection: MIP — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL) Canonical Definition Value-Aligned Intelligence Allocation Module (VAIAM) defines the structural conditions under which intelligence generation, inference allocation, orchestration activity, escalation behavior, distributed cognition, and cognitive resource consumption remain materially aligned with actual operational value across distributed intelligence environments. A system satisfies VAIAM only if: intelligence allocation remains materially value-aligned cognitive escalation remains operationally justified runtime cognition preserves economic proportionality orchestration activity remains value-connected low-value cognitive amplification does not silently destabilize cognitive sustainability A system that continuously expands intelligence activity without proportional operational value does not satisfy VAIAM. Module Operational Role VAIAM defines the value-aligned cognition allocation layer of CEES by preserving economically sustainable intelligence allocation across runtime operational environments. Module Operational Space VAIAM governs the value-aligned intelligence allocation space of CEES by preserving proportional cognition allocation, escalation-value alignment, orchestration-value continuity, distributed intelligence sustainability, and runtime cognitive efficiency across operational intelligence systems. Module Function The module applies wherever systems must preserve: value-aligned cognition proportional intelligence allocation escalation-value continuity orchestration-value efficiency runtime cognitive proportionality sustainable intelligence economics Its function is to ensure that intelligence generation remains materially proportional to operational value strongly enough to preserve sustainable cognition economics across distributed AI environments. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Define the Intelligence Allocation Object The organization must define which cognitive activities require value-aligned allocation governance. This may include: inference allocation orchestration activity escalation routing distributed cognition usage runtime reasoning cycles semantic processing allocation adaptive intelligence execution 2. Define Value-Alignment Conditions The system must define the conditions under which intelligence allocation remains materially aligned with operational value. This includes: inference proportionality escalation-value alignment orchestration-value efficiency cognitive sustainability continuity runtime resource-value proportionality 3. Define Low-Value Cognitive Amplification Detection Logic The system must define how materially inefficient or low-value intelligence amplification is identified. This may include: excessive inference without proportional value unnecessary orchestration expansion redundant escalation behavior repeated low-value reasoning cycles inefficient semantic processing uncontrolled cognitive amplification 4. Define Operational Response or Governance Logic The system must define governance logic for materially inefficient intelligence allocation conditions. Governance response may include: escalation restriction orchestration narrowing local cognition preference semantic optimization activation inference stabilization operational invalidation where required 5. Preserve Traceability & Restrict Invalid Conditions The system must preserve reconstructable traceability of intelligence allocation continuity and low-value cognitive amplification states. A system must not remain cognitively efficient if intelligence allocation materially exceeds operational value while systems continue assuming sustainable cognition economics remain preserved. Use Case 1 — Enterprise Agent Ecosystem Scenario An enterprise AI infrastructure continuously allocates inference resources across thousands of orchestration-driven cognitive agents. Application VAIAM preserves value-aligned cognition allocation through proportional escalation and controlled orchestration governance. Result The organization gains reduced cognitive waste and stronger intelligence sustainability across distributed AI systems. Use Case 2 — Realtime AI Runtime Environment Scenario A realtime AI environment continuously performs multimodal reasoning, orchestration, distributed execution, and adaptive escalation across high-frequency operational systems. Application VAIAM preserves economically sustainable cognition through value-aligned intelligence allocation and controlled cognitive amplification governance. Result The environment gains stronger runtime cognition sustainability and reduced low-value inference expansion across distributed AI infrastructures. Canonical Closing Statement If intelligence allocation cannot remain materially aligned with actual operational value, systems may preserve intelligence generation while cognitive economics silently destabilizes underneath. title: Validation Layer Design™
text: Validation Layer Design™ Governance Architecture Space Validation Layer Design™ governs the architectural space responsible for designing, selecting, structuring, and integrating validation mechanisms capable of determining whether governance architectures, governance controls, governance logic, autonomous systems, operational behaviors, and governance outcomes remain valid under operational conditions. The space exists because governance architectures require more than functionality and controls. They require validation. Without validation, organizations, AI systems, autonomous agents, robotics platforms, and governance environments cannot reliably determine whether governance objectives are being achieved. Validation Layer Design™ exists to provide this capability. Canonical Definition Validation Layer Design™ is the governable architectural space responsible for designing, selecting, structuring, and integrating validation mechanisms capable of determining the validity, integrity, effectiveness, resilience, compliance, and operational alignment of governance architectures and governance behaviors. The Core Problem Organizations frequently implement governance architectures without establishing mechanisms capable of determining whether those architectures remain valid. As a result: governance drift remains undetected, control failures remain hidden, incorrect assumptions persist, implementation weaknesses accumulate, operational risks increase. Many governance failures occur because validation mechanisms were never designed. Validation Layer Design™ was created to address this challenge. Why Validation Layer Design™ Exists Governance architectures generate behavior. Governance controls constrain behavior. Validation determines whether behavior remains acceptable. Validation Layer Design™ exists to ensure that governance architectures can evaluate their own effectiveness. The Validation Principle A fundamental principle of Validation Layer Design™ is: Governance architectures should be capable of determining whether they remain valid under operational reality. The objective is not merely execution. The objective is validated execution. Core Questions Validation Layer Design™ seeks to answer: What must be validated? When should validation occur? Which conditions determine validity? Which conditions determine invalidity? Which actions require evidence? Which actions require re-validation? Which failures require escalation? Which outcomes require operational confirmation? Types of Validation Governance Validation Validation of governance objectives, governance structures, and governance outcomes. Control Validation Validation of governance controls and governance safeguards. Logic Validation Validation of governance logic and decision pathways. Operational Validation Validation of operational behavior under real-world conditions. Compliance Validation Validation of regulatory and policy alignment. Safety Validation Validation of operational safety requirements. Autonomous System Validation Validation of AI systems, autonomous agents, and robotics platforms. Operational Reality Validation Validation against observed operational reality. Validation Conditions Validation Layer Design™ may establish: Valid States Conditions under which governance remains valid. Invalid States Conditions under which governance validity is lost. Escalation States Conditions requiring intervention or additional review. Re-Validation States Conditions requiring repeated validation. Evidence States Conditions requiring evidence preservation. Validation Layers for AI Systems Future AI systems may require validation layers governing: autonomous decisions, tool usage, memory modification, self-correction behavior, governance compliance, auditability obligations. The objective is validated autonomy. Validation Layers for Autonomous Agents Future autonomous agents may require validation layers determining: when actions are permitted, when actions require approval, when actions require evidence, when actions require escalation. The objective is governable autonomous operation. Validation Layers for Robotics Future robotics environments may require validation layers governing: safety conditions, intervention thresholds, operational permissions, corrective actions, operational boundaries. The objective is validated robotic behavior. Position Within Governance Architecture On Demand™ Validation Layer Design™ follows: Architecture Composition™ Architecture Options™ Governance Logic Design™ Governance Controls Design™ Once architecture, logic, and controls have been defined, validation mechanisms must be established. Relationship to Governance Re-Simulation™ Governance Re-Simulation™ evaluates whether validation mechanisms remain effective before implementation. Validation Layer Design™ creates validation structures. Re-Simulation challenges those structures. Relationship to Operational Reality™ Operational Reality™ provides the ultimate validation environment. Validation layers determine expected validity conditions. Operational Reality™ determines whether those conditions survive implementation. Why This Space Matters Future governance environments will increasingly require architectures capable of validating themselves. Organizations, AI systems, autonomous agents, robotics platforms, and governance ecosystems must be able to determine not only how to act, but also whether those actions remain valid. Validation Layer Design™ exists to provide this capability. Canonical Closing Statement Validation Layer Design™ transforms governance architectures into self-evaluating governance systems. By designing validation mechanisms capable of determining validity, integrity, effectiveness, resilience, compliance, and operational alignment, it enables organizations, AI systems, autonomous agents, robotics platforms, and future governance environments to operate through validated governance rather than assumed governance. title: Validation Re-Simulation™
text: Validation Re-Simulation™ Governance Architecture Space Validation Re-Simulation™ governs the architectural space responsible for re-evaluating, challenging, stress-testing, and validating validation mechanisms before operational deployment occurs. The space exists because validation mechanisms themselves may contain weaknesses, assumptions, blind spots, dependency risks, or governance limitations. A system may appear validated while the validation process itself remains flawed. Validation Re-Simulation™ exists to challenge validation before governance depends upon validation. Canonical Definition Validation Re-Simulation™ is the governable architectural space responsible for re-evaluating, challenging, stress-testing, and validating validation mechanisms, validation pathways, validation criteria, verification procedures, evidence requirements, and governance confidence structures before implementation occurs. The Core Problem Organizations frequently trust validation mechanisms without validating the validation process itself. As a result: false confidence may emerge, invalid conditions may remain undetected, governance assumptions may persist, evidence requirements may be insufficient, incorrect conclusions may appear legitimate. A validation process is only as reliable as its ability to withstand challenge. Validation Re-Simulation™ was created to address this challenge. Why Validation Re-Simulation™ Exists Validation Layer Design™ generates validation structures. However, validation structures should not automatically be trusted. Before implementation, organizations require a mechanism capable of answering a critical question: Can the validation process itself be trusted? Validation Re-Simulation™ exists to answer this question. The Validation Principle A fundamental principle of Validation Re-Simulation™ is: Validation mechanisms should be challenged before governance confidence is built upon them. The objective is not demonstrating that validation exists. The objective is demonstrating that validation remains reliable when challenged. Position Within Governance Re-Simulation™ Validation Re-Simulation™ follows: Architecture Re-Simulation™ Governance Logic Re-Simulation™ Control Re-Simulation™ The architecture must survive challenge. Governance logic must survive challenge. Governance controls must survive challenge. Only then should the validation mechanisms themselves be challenged. Core Questions Validation Re-Simulation™ seeks to answer: Can invalid conditions pass validation? Can valid conditions fail validation? Which assumptions exist within the validation process? Which evidence requirements are insufficient? Which validation pathways may produce misleading conclusions? Which validation mechanisms may generate false confidence? Which validation criteria require refinement? Can governance confidence be justified? Validation Inputs Validation Re-Simulation™ may evaluate: Validation Criteria™ Validation Logic™ Verification Procedures™ Governance Confidence Structures™ Evidence Requirements™ Audit Requirements™ Operational Validation Conditions™ Compliance Validation Conditions™ The objective is evaluating confidence mechanisms before confidence becomes operationally significant. Validation Stress Testing Validation Re-Simulation™ may challenge validation systems through: Incomplete Evidence Situations involving insufficient evidence. Conflicting Evidence Situations involving contradictory evidence. Ambiguous Conditions Situations involving uncertainty or unclear information. Dependency Failures Failures affecting validation dependencies. Operational Complexity Highly complex operational environments. Autonomous Behavior Actions performed by AI systems and autonomous agents. Unexpected Conditions Conditions not anticipated during validation design. Operational Reality Conditions Conditions reflecting real-world implementation environments. Validation Weakness Discovery Validation Re-Simulation™ may identify: Validation Gaps Missing validation requirements. Evidence Weaknesses Insufficient evidence requirements. Verification Weaknesses Insufficient verification procedures. Confidence Weaknesses Unsupported governance confidence. Auditability Weaknesses Insufficient traceability. Compliance Weaknesses Insufficient regulatory alignment. Operational Weaknesses Insufficient operational validation capability. AI Systems and Autonomous Agents Future AI systems and autonomous agents may increasingly depend upon validation systems. Examples include: Autonomous Decision Validation Tool Usage Validation Self-Correction Validation Memory Modification Validation Governance Compliance Validation Mission-Critical Validation The objective is ensuring that autonomous environments remain capable of validating their own actions. The Confidence Question Validation Re-Simulation™ introduces a critical governance question: Why should this result be trusted? Future governance environments increasingly require the ability to justify confidence rather than merely declare confidence. Validation should therefore remain explainable, auditable, evidence-based, and challenge-resistant. Relationship to Control Re-Simulation™ Control Re-Simulation™ evaluates governance safeguards. Validation Re-Simulation™ evaluates the mechanisms used to determine whether those safeguards remain effective. Controls create boundaries. Validation determines whether those boundaries remain intact. Relationship to Dependency Re-Simulation™ Validation Re-Simulation™ evaluates validation itself. Dependency Re-Simulation™ evaluates the dependencies upon which validation may rely. Validation may only be as reliable as its dependencies. Why This Space Matters Future governance environments will increasingly require confidence that can be justified, audited, reproduced, and explained. Validation Re-Simulation™ exists to challenge validation mechanisms before operational reality exposes weaknesses hidden within governance confidence structures. Canonical Closing Statement Validation Re-Simulation™ transforms validation into challenged validation. By re-evaluating, stress-testing, and validating validation mechanisms, evidence requirements, verification pathways, governance confidence structures, and auditability conditions before deployment occurs, it enables organizations, AI systems, autonomous agents, robotics platforms, critical infrastructures, and future autonomous environments to build confidence upon validated foundations rather than untested assumptions. title: Value Activation Standard (VAS)
text: OOF™ Core Methodology OS — Master Index Value Activation Standard (VAS) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority OriginID: OOF-OID-ECO-VAS-2026-03-07-0001 Category: Economic & Value Standards Subcategory: Value Activation & Flow Governance Version: 2.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 7 March 2026 Compatibility: Value Flow Mechanism (VFM) ZVA (Zero Value Asset) Standard Origin Asset Standard Authority: OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Protection: Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition System Value Activation Standard defines the non-bypassable conditions under which an asset becomes economically active within a governed system. Assets do not automatically participate in value flows. An asset must pass structural validation before entering an active value state. Economic participation is conditional on verification, not existence. A. Standard Abstract VAS establishes an integrity-first economic model where value activation precedes value distribution. The objective is to ensure that: value does not flow before validation assets are structurally verified before participation economic entry points are controlled value flows remain governed and traceable This standard does not define value. It defines when value becomes active. B. Core Principle Value must not flow before integrity is verified. Assets that cannot demonstrate origin integrity, structural compatibility, or governance compliance remain economically inactive. C. Operational Model VAS defines a four-stage activation architecture. Stage 1 — Inactive Asset State All assets entering a system are initially: economically inactive In this state: no yield may be generated no liquidity participation occurs no economic distribution is permitted Assets may exist, but they are not economically active. Stage 2 — Structural Validation The system verifies: asset origin integrity system compatibility governance compliance responsibility anchoring Assets failing validation remain inactive. Stage 3 — Value Activation Assets that pass validation enter an: Active Value State Activated assets may: participate in value flows generate yield serve as collateral enter liquidity systems Activation represents admission into the governed economy. Stage 4 — Value Flow Distribution Once activated: value may flow through predefined mechanisms distribution remains governed all flows remain traceable D. Prohibited Condition No asset may participate in value generation, distribution, or liquidity mechanisms before successful structural validation. Any value flow without prior activation is considered invalid within the governed system. E. Purpose & Scope VAS establishes a structural model where economic participation is conditional. It enables systems to maintain: controlled liquidity entry traceable capital flow governance-based activation integrity-based economic participation Applicable to: blockchain systems financial infrastructure tokenized assets AI data economies digital markets F. Structural Principle Value activation must precede value flow. Canonical Closing Statement Economic value must be activated through integrity validation before it is allowed to flow. Related Documents → Minimal Self-Declaration Implementation Framework → About the Value Activation Standard

title: Value Transfer Definition Standard (VTDS)
text: OOF™ Core Methodology OS — Master Index Value Transfer Definition Standard (VTDS) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority OriginID: OOF-OID-EV-VTDS-2026-04-04-0001 Category: Economic & Value Subcategory: Digital Value Systems Type: Value Definition Standard Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 4 April 2026 Compatibility: OOF™ Methodology OS · Digital Value Interaction Standard · Value Flow Mechanism · Audit in Real Time Authority: OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Protection: MIP™ — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) A. Standard Abstract The Value Transfer Definition Standard (VTDS) defines what constitutes value and under what conditions value is considered transferred within digital and hybrid systems. The objective is to establish a universal, system-independent definition of value that can be: measured attributed transferred audited This standard does not assign value. It defines what qualifies as value and when it becomes real. B. Canonical Definition Value is any unit, asset, or measurable outcome that: can be attributed to a specific entity can be transferred between entities can be recorded and verified A Value Transfer occurs only when such value moves from one entity to another under measurable and attributable conditions. C. Structural Base This standard is based on: Measurability Requirement Attribution Principle Transfer Condition Auditability Requirement Value must exist as a definable and verifiable unit. D. Value Qualification Criteria For something to qualify as value, it MUST meet all of the following: 1. Measurability Value must: have quantifiable magnitude be expressible in units, metrics, or equivalent 2. Attribution Value must: be assignable to a specific entity have a defined source and destination 3. Transferability Value must: be capable of moving between entities result in a change of state, ownership, or control 4. Recordability Value must: be recordable within a system be verifiable through audit or trace If any condition is not met: → value does not exist within this standard E. Non-Value Classification The following do NOT qualify as value: attention views likes impressions unmonetized engagement These are: Value Signals, not value F. Transfer Definition (Critical) A Value Transfer exists only when: value moves between entities the movement is measurable the movement is attributable the movement is recorded If no transfer occurs: → no value event exists G. Structural Rule Value exists only when it can be: measured attributed transferred recorded No implicit, assumed, or perceived value is permitted. H. System Independence This definition applies across: digital platforms financial systems hybrid environments AI-driven systems Value remains structurally consistent regardless of system. I. Methodology Identify potential value Verify qualification criteria Confirm transfer capability Confirm recordability Classify as value or non-value J. Threshold Logic Value state is: VALID VALUE → meets all criteria NON-VALUE → fails any condition No partial qualification is permitted. K. Structural Principle Value is not perceived. Value is defined by its ability to move, be measured, and be verified. Canonical Closing Statement Digital systems generate signals of importance. Only defined and transferable units constitute real value. Value Transfer Definition Standard (VTDS) establishes a non-negotiable condition: value must be measurable, attributable, transferable, and auditable. Related Documents → About the Value Transfer Definition Standard

title: Value Transfer Taxation Standard (VTTS)
text: OOF™ Core Methodology OS — Master Index Value Transfer Taxation Standard (VTTS) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority OriginID: OOF-OID-EV-VTTS-2026-04-08-0002 Category: Economic & Value Subcategory: Value Transfer Governance Type: Taxation Definition Standard Version: 3.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 8 April 2026 Compatibility: OOF™ Methodology OS · Value Transfer Definition Standard (VTDS) · Digital Value Interaction Standard (DVIS) · Value Flow Mechanism (VFM™) · Audit in Real Time (ART™) · Zero Value Asset (ZVA™) · Origin Asset™ · DeMonet™ · ReMonet™ · Value Asset Authority: OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Protection: MIP™ — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) A. Standard Abstract The Value Transfer Taxation Standard (VTTS) defines when taxation applies across all economic systems based strictly on actual value transfer. This standard establishes a universal taxation condition: taxation applies only to real value transfer value creation alone is not taxable non-transfer activity is excluded taxation is triggered at the moment value becomes economically real VTTS applies across: digital systems physical economies AI-driven environments hybrid systems This standard does not define tax rates or jurisdictions. It defines when taxation is structurally valid. B. Canonical Definition A Taxable Value Event exists only when: valid value (VTDS) is transferred between identifiable entities resulting in a measurable change of economic ownership or control Taxation applies exclusively to: Transferred Value with Real Economic Effect C. Structural Base This standard is based on: Value Qualification Principle (VTDS) Value Event Requirement (DVIS) Non-Signal Rule Transfer-Based Taxation Logic Substance Over Structure Principle Taxation must follow value — not activity, not form, not system representation. D. Taxation Condition A value event is taxable only if all conditions are met: 1. Valid Value Exists The value must be: measurable attributable transferable recordable 2. Value Transfer Occurs value moves between entities economic ownership or control changes 3. Transfer Has Economic Substance The transfer must represent: real economic effect actual change in value availability or control The following are not valid transfers: internal accounting entries artificial structuring circular or self-referential flows 4. Transfer Is Attributable source entity identifiable destination entity identifiable 5. Transfer Is Recordable trace exists within system audit is possible If any condition is not met: → NON-TAXABLE EVENT E. Value Creation vs Transfer Rule Value creation alone is not taxable. Taxation applies only when: created value is transferred and becomes economically accessible or controlled F. Non-Taxable Events The following are not taxable: views likes clicks impressions attention behavioral signals non-transferable engagement unrealized value states These are classified as: Value Signals — not taxable events G. Value Capture Layer™ Taxation must occur at the moment where value becomes economically real. A Value Capture Point exists when: value becomes accessible for use control or ownership is transferred value can be realized or claimed Examples: payment execution smart contract settlement asset transfer revenue payout withdrawal or realization Taxation must be triggered at this exact point. H. Economic Control Definition Control must be interpreted as: economic control not merely formal or legal designation Taxation applies when an entity gains: ability to use value ability to transfer value ability to restrict access to value I. Cross-System Condition Taxation applies independently of system type. No distinction is made between: digital systems physical systems AI-generated environments hybrid systems Only relevant condition: Value movement between entities J. Cross-Border Condition A Cross-Border Value Transfer exists when: value originates in one jurisdiction and is received or controlled in another Taxation must be based on: actual value movement traceable origin and destination measurable transfer Non-Valid Taxation Triggers The following are invalid: user location platform location server location interaction volume Without value transfer: → no taxation applies K. System Boundary Condition Taxation applies only to value transfers that are: recordable auditable If value exists outside recordable systems: taxation applies only upon entry into a recordable system or upon measurable realization L. Value State Compatibility 1. Origin Asset™ initial value taxable only upon transfer 2. Zero Value Asset (ZVA™) no value non-taxable 3. DeMonet™ State value neutralized non-taxable 4. ReMonet™ State value reintroduced taxable upon transfer 5. Value Asset active transferable value taxable upon transfer M. Structural Rule Taxation applies only to: Transferred Value with Economic Substance Not to: potential value perceived value artificial structures non-realized states N. Methodology Identify interaction (DVIS) Verify value qualification (VTDS) Confirm value creation vs transfer Confirm economic substance Confirm attribution Confirm recordability Identify value capture point Apply taxation condition O. Threshold Logic TAXABLE → valid value transfer with economic substance NON-TAXABLE → no valid transfer No partial taxation is permitted. P. Structural Principle Tax follows value. Not system. Not time. Not activity. Not form. Canonical Closing Statement Economic systems generate continuous activity. Only value transfer with economic substance creates economic reality. Value Transfer Taxation Standard (VTTS) establishes a non-negotiable condition: taxation applies only where real value moves — and at the moment it becomes economically real.
