title: Validation Criteria Standard
text: Validation Criteria Standard Validation Criteria Standard Standard ID: VCRS OriginID: OOF-OID-AI-VALIDOS-VCRS-2026-08-08-0003 Architecture: VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture Category: AI & Interpretation Subcategory: Validation Governance Type: Parent Standard Governed Space: Validation Criteria Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 8 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · OBIDENITY® · INTEGROS® · ORA™ · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Canonical Definition Validation Criteria Standard (VCRS) defines the governance conditions under which the criteria, requirements, thresholds, acceptance conditions, rejection conditions, evaluation references, and decision boundaries used to determine validity are formally established, justified, structured, maintained, and controlled before validation methodology and execution are applied. Canonical Definition Extension A Validation Object may be precisely established. Its Validation Purpose and Scope may be clearly defined. Neither determines what conditions the object must satisfy in order to support a validation determination. Validation requires explicit criteria. Without governed criteria, validation risks becoming dependent upon implicit expectations, changing thresholds, subjective interpretation, post-hoc reasoning, or standards selected after results are already known. Validation Criteria Standard therefore governs the transformation of an approved Validation Mandate into a formally defined Validation Criteria Framework. The standard establishes the governance conditions necessary to determine: what properties or conditions must be evaluated, which requirements are relevant to the Validation Purpose, which criteria are mandatory or conditional, which thresholds distinguish acceptable from unacceptable conditions, what constitutes satisfaction or non-satisfaction, how criteria relate to different parts of Validation Scope, which external references may legitimately inform criteria, how conflicts between criteria are governed, and when criteria must be changed or reassessed. VCRS does not determine which technical procedure should be used to evaluate a criterion. It does not determine whether available evidence is sufficient. It does not execute validation. It does not issue the final Validation Determination. VCRS establishes the governed conditions against which validity can later be meaningfully evaluated. Core Question Against which explicit, justified, and governable conditions should the Validation Object be evaluated in order to determine whether the Validation Purpose has been satisfied? Purpose The purpose of Validation Criteria Standard is to ensure that validation judgments are based upon criteria established before conclusions are reached. The standard prevents validity from being determined through: undefined expectations, implicit requirements, arbitrary thresholds, moving evaluation targets, selective criteria, post-hoc criteria creation, incompatible criteria, or criteria unrelated to the approved Validation Purpose and Scope. VCRS creates the evaluation foundation upon which subsequent validation methodology, evidence, execution, and determination depend. Governance Objective VCRS establishes a governed Validation Criteria Framework capable of supporting consistent, explainable, traceable, and reproducible validation determinations. The standard seeks to ensure that: validation criteria are explicit, criteria are relevant to the Validation Purpose, criteria correspond to the approved Validation Scope, criteria sources are identifiable, criteria are sufficiently precise for evaluation, thresholds are justified, acceptance and rejection conditions are distinguishable, mandatory and conditional criteria remain distinguishable, criteria conflicts are governed, criteria changes remain traceable, and subsequent validation activity can be evaluated against a stable reference. Operational Role Validation Criteria Standard serves as the evaluation-reference stage of the VALIDOS® validation governance lifecycle. It receives: Validation Object + Validation Mandate and establishes: Validation Criteria Framework capable of guiding subsequent validation methodology and execution. Its architectural role is to answer the question that follows Validation Purpose & Scope: Now that we know what is being validated and why, against what conditions should validity be judged? The Validation Criteria Framework becomes the governed reference against which later evidence and validation results can be interpreted. Governance Scope Validation Criteria Standard governs: validation criteria, validation requirements, criterion relevance, criterion applicability, criterion structure, criterion hierarchy, mandatory criteria, conditional criteria, acceptance conditions, rejection conditions, validation thresholds, threshold justification, evaluation references, criterion dependencies, criterion conflicts, criterion stability, criterion change, criterion traceability, and Validation Criteria Framework integrity. Validation Criteria Governance Model VCRS establishes the following progression: Validation Mandate → Requirement Identification → Criterion Definition → Threshold Establishment → Acceptance & Rejection Conditions → Criteria Alignment → Criteria Integrity → Validation Criteria Framework This progression converts the purpose and scope of validation into explicit conditions against which the Validation Object can subsequently be evaluated. Validation Requirement Identification Criteria must originate from identifiable validation requirements. Relevant requirements may arise from: the approved Validation Purpose, intended use, Validation Scope, operational requirements, safety requirements, performance requirements, integrity requirements, governance requirements, contractual requirements, regulatory requirements, legal requirements, domain standards, scientific knowledge, technical specifications, risk conditions, or other legitimate validation references. The existence of a requirement does not automatically make it an appropriate validation criterion. VCRS requires its relevance to the Validation Purpose and Scope to be established. Criterion Definition Each material validation criterion should be sufficiently precise to allow subsequent validation activity to determine whether the relevant condition has been satisfied. Where appropriate, a criterion should identify: the characteristic being evaluated, the requirement being tested, the relevant Validation Scope element, the applicable condition, the expected state, the evaluation boundary, and the basis upon which satisfaction can later be determined. Criteria should not depend upon undefined concepts where those concepts materially affect the validation determination. Criteria Classification Validation criteria may require different governance treatment. VCRS may distinguish, where applicable: Mandatory Criteria Conditions that must be satisfied for a defined validation outcome to be possible. Conditional Criteria Conditions that apply only when specified circumstances, uses, environments, configurations, populations, or dependencies exist. Supporting Criteria Criteria providing additional validation information without independently determining the primary validation outcome. Exclusionary Criteria Conditions whose occurrence may prevent a specified validation outcome regardless of performance against other criteria. Composite Criteria Criteria whose determination depends upon multiple subordinate conditions or measurements. Classification prevents materially different criteria from being treated as equivalent. Validation Thresholds Where a criterion requires a measurable or classifiable boundary, VCRS governs the establishment of an appropriate validation threshold. Thresholds may represent: minimum acceptable values, maximum permitted values, ranges, tolerances, confidence levels, error boundaries, performance levels, evidence thresholds, categorical conditions, binary conditions, or other governable decision boundaries. A threshold should have an identifiable methodological basis. Thresholds should not be modified after results are known merely to produce a preferred validation outcome. Acceptance Conditions Acceptance conditions establish what must be demonstrated for a criterion to be treated as sufficiently satisfied. Acceptance may be: complete, conditional, threshold-based, multi-factor, evidence-dependent, context-dependent, or otherwise governed according to the nature of the criterion. Acceptance of one criterion does not automatically establish validity of the complete Validation Object. The relationship between individual criterion results and the final Validation Determination belongs to later VALIDOS® governance. Rejection Conditions Rejection conditions establish circumstances under which a criterion cannot be considered satisfied. These may include: threshold failure, prohibited conditions, insufficient required performance, incompatible states, unacceptable uncertainty, missing mandatory requirements, or other predefined failure conditions. VCRS requires rejection conditions to remain distinguishable from: missing evidence, incomplete validation, unresolved uncertainty, and inability to execute a required validation activity. These conditions may have different methodological meanings and should not automatically be collapsed into criterion failure. Criteria Alignment The Validation Criteria Framework must remain aligned with: Validation Object → Validation Purpose → Validation Scope → Validation Depth → Validation Applicability → Validation Criteria A criterion unrelated to the approved Validation Mandate should not influence the validation determination without explicit governance justification. Likewise, a material dimension required by the Validation Mandate should not remain without adequate criteria merely because suitable evaluation is difficult. Criteria Completeness VCRS evaluates whether the Validation Criteria Framework sufficiently represents the conditions necessary to answer the approved Validation Purpose. Criteria completeness does not require every conceivable characteristic of the Validation Object to receive a criterion. It requires the criteria set to cover the material conditions necessary for the governed validation. Where material criterion gaps remain, validation should not proceed under the assumption that the Validation Mandate can be completely satisfied. Criteria Conflict Governance Validation criteria may conflict. For example: one criterion may optimize performance while another limits risk, different regulatory requirements may establish incompatible thresholds, operational objectives may conflict with safety conditions, domain standards may use different definitions, or multiple evidence references may support different evaluation boundaries. VCRS requires material criteria conflicts to be identified and governed before they are allowed to influence validation conclusions. Criteria conflict must not be silently resolved through arbitrary selection. Criteria Hierarchy Where criteria have different authority, significance, or dependency relationships, a governed hierarchy may be established. A hierarchy may identify: overriding criteria, mandatory baseline criteria, conditional criteria, subordinate criteria, composite criteria, or supporting criteria. Criteria hierarchy must be justified and documented. The hierarchy must not be altered merely because a different ordering would produce a preferred validation outcome. Criteria Stability Validation requires sufficiently stable evaluation conditions. Criteria should therefore remain controlled during the validation process. Stability does not mean criteria can never change. It means that material criteria changes must be recognized as governance events. Where criteria change after validation activity has begun, the impact upon: methodology, evidence requirements, execution, previous results, determination, and reliance must be assessed. Criteria Change Governance Material criteria change may arise from: changed Validation Purpose, changed Validation Scope, new regulatory requirements, new scientific knowledge, changed operating conditions, newly identified risks, changed object characteristics, revised external standards, or discovery that an existing criterion is methodologically inadequate. VCRS requires material changes to be: identified, justified, versioned, documented, propagated to affected validation activities, and traceable to the resulting validation record. Criteria Versioning A Validation Determination must remain associated with the criteria under which it was produced. Where the Validation Criteria Framework materially changes, previous determinations should not automatically be interpreted as having been produced under the revised criteria. Criteria versioning therefore provides the historical reference necessary to determine: Which criteria governed this validation determination? Validation Criteria and Method Separation VCRS establishes another important VALIDOS® distinction: Criteria define what must be demonstrated. Method defines how it will be examined. A criterion such as a required accuracy threshold does not itself determine which statistical test, experimental design, dataset, benchmark, simulation, expert assessment, or other method must be used to evaluate it. Keeping these responsibilities separate prevents validation criteria from becoming unnecessarily tied to one implementation technique. Validation Criteria and Evidence Separation VCRS also distinguishes criteria from evidence. Criterion: the condition against which validity is evaluated. Evidence: the information used to determine whether that condition has been satisfied. Strong evidence cannot compensate for a criterion that was never properly defined. Likewise, well-defined criteria cannot produce a reliable determination without sufficient evidence. These responsibilities therefore remain governed separately within VALIDOS®. Governance Boundary Validation Criteria Standard begins when: a Validation Object has been sufficiently established, a Validation Purpose has been identified, Validation Scope has been defined, required Validation Depth has been calibrated, and sufficient applicability and limitation conditions exist to establish evaluation requirements. It ends when a sufficiently complete, justified, stable, and traceable Validation Criteria Framework exists to support selection of validation methodology. VCRS does not determine: Validation Object identity or boundary, Validation Purpose, Validation Scope, Validation Depth, technical validation methodology, evidence fitness, source reliability, validation execution, final Validation Determination, Validation State, reliance authorization, or revalidation requirements. These responsibilities belong to other VALIDOS® Parent Standards. Minimum Governance Requirements A conforming implementation of VCRS should establish: 1. identifiable validation requirements, 2. explicit validation criteria, 3. traceable relationships between criteria and the Validation Mandate, 4. defined thresholds where required, 5. identifiable acceptance conditions, 6. identifiable rejection conditions, 7. classification of materially different criterion types where necessary, 8. governance of material criterion dependencies and conflicts, 9. criteria versioning and change control, 10. and a persistent Validation Criteria Framework capable of supporting subsequent validation methodology and execution. Governance Outputs VCRS may produce: Validation Criteria Framework, Validation Requirement Record, Validation Criterion Record, Criteria Applicability Map, Criteria Classification Record, Validation Threshold Record, Acceptance Condition Record, Rejection Condition Record, Criteria Dependency Map, Criteria Conflict Record, Criteria Completeness Determination, Criteria Version Record, Criteria Change Record. These outputs provide the evaluation reference required by subsequent VALIDOS® governance. Operational Applications Validation Criteria Standard may be applied across: artificial intelligence, autonomous systems, machine learning models, data and analytics, predictions and simulations, enterprise systems, financial services, healthcare, industrial operations, regulatory compliance, critical infrastructure, digital assets, digital identities, operational governance, public-sector systems, scientific and analytical environments, multi-system environments, and any governed environment requiring explicit validation criteria. Relationship to Other OOF Architectures Validation Criteria Standard interoperates with: GOA™ OBIDENITY® INTEGROS® ORA™ AGA™ AIG® CLIA® MGIA™ ASGA™ RIS™ by providing the canonical validation-governance methodology through which relevant governance, integrity, operational, accountability, identity, risk, cognitive, memory, autonomous-system, and other requirements may be translated into explicit validation criteria where appropriate. VCRS does not replace the substantive governance responsibilities of these architectures. It determines how relevant requirements become governed validation conditions against which a Validation Object can subsequently be evaluated. Foundational Principle Validity cannot be governed against criteria that were never explicitly established. Canonical Closing Statement Validation Criteria Standard establishes the canonical evaluation-reference layer of VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture. By governing requirement identification, criterion definition, thresholds, acceptance and rejection conditions, classification, completeness, conflicts, hierarchy, stability, versioning, and change, VCRS ensures that validity is evaluated against explicit and traceable conditions established before validation conclusions are reached, creating the methodological foundation required for consistent, explainable, and governable validation. Validation Criteria Standard Architecture: VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture Category: AI & Interpretation · Subcategory: Validation Governance Canonical Definition: Validation Criteria Standard (VCRS) defines the governance conditions under which the criteria, requirements, thresholds, acceptance conditions, rejection conditions, evaluation references, and decision boundaries used to determine validity are formally established, justified, structured, maintained, and controlled before validation methodology and execution are applied. title: About Validation Determination Standard
text: About Validation Determination Standard About Validation Determination Standard Governing the Difference Between Validation Results and What Those Results Legitimately Demonstrate Validation produces results. Results produce information. But information does not automatically produce a legitimate validation conclusion. A validation process may generate thousands of measurements, observations, tests, comparisons, simulations, expert assessments, statistical outputs, and system responses. The methodological question remains: What do those results actually demonstrate? Validation Determination Standard (VDTS) is the eighth Parent Standard of VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture, governing the transformation of the complete governed validation record into a bounded, traceable, and methodologically legitimate Validation Determination. VDTS addresses one fundamental question: What does the governed validation record legitimately demonstrate about the Validation Object? Why Validation Determination Standard Exists Validation conclusions are often treated as if they emerge automatically from validation results. They do not. Between: Result and: Conclusion there is an interpretive governance layer. A test may produce a number. A simulation may produce a scenario. An expert may produce an assessment. An AI system may produce a classification. A measurement may cross a threshold. Several tests may contradict each other. Some criteria may pass. Some may fail. Some may remain impossible to determine. The validation process must establish how these different findings become a legitimate conclusion. VDTS governs that transition. Results Are Not Determinations VALIDOS® deliberately separates: Validation Result from: Validation Determination A Validation Result is an output produced during validation execution. A Validation Determination is a governed conclusion derived from the legitimate validation record. Therefore: Validation Result ≠ Validation Determination This distinction prevents raw outputs from being treated as self-interpreting proof. The Determination Layer The preceding VALIDOS® Parent Standards establish the validation basis and execute the validation process. The lifecycle has reached: Validation Object ↓ Validation Purpose & Scope ↓ Validation Criteria ↓ Validation Method ↓ Validation Evidence Fitness ↓ Validation Source Reliability ↓ Validation Execution ↓ Validation Determination VDTS is the point where VALIDOS® asks what the completed validation process has actually established. Determination Begins With Governed Execution VDTS does not interpret every result generated during validation. It begins from execution that has already passed through execution governance. The preceding Validation Execution Standard establishes whether execution was: complete, conditionally complete, incomplete, conformant, conditionally conformant, non-conformant, invalid, Determination Ready, or Determination Blocked. This prevents VDTS from constructing certainty from execution that cannot legitimately support it. Determination Must Remain Connected to the Validation Object Every determination must remain attached to the exact Validation Object examined. This may include: object identity, version, configuration, state, release, population, environment, time, or other material boundaries. A conclusion about: Object Version 3.2 does not automatically become a conclusion about: Object Version 4.0 Validation Determination therefore remains object-bound. Determination Must Remain Purpose-Bound The meaning of a validation result depends partly upon why validation was performed. A validation designed to determine: technical performance does not automatically establish: safety regulatory compliance ethical acceptability or: operational suitability unless those questions were included within the governed Validation Purpose and Criteria. Therefore: Validated for Purpose A ≠ Validated for Purpose B Determination Cannot Exceed Validation Scope One of the most important VDTS boundaries is: Determination Scope ≤ Legitimately Executed Validation Scope If validation examined: one population, one jurisdiction, one environment, one system version, one operating range, or one defined use case, the resulting determination should not silently expand beyond those boundaries. Validation Depth Matters Not all validation provides the same level of assurance. An exploratory validation and a high-assurance validation may examine similar questions but support different strengths of conclusion. VDTS therefore preserves the relationship between: Validation Depth and: Determination Strength A conclusion cannot legitimately claim greater methodological assurance than the validation process achieved. Criterion-Level Determination Comes First VDTS does not jump immediately from execution outputs to an overall label. It first asks what the governed record demonstrates relative to each applicable Validation Criterion. A criterion may be: Satisfied Conditionally Satisfied Not Satisfied or: Not Determinable This creates a structured determination layer beneath any overall conclusion. Criterion Satisfied A criterion is Satisfied where the governed validation record provides sufficient legitimate basis to demonstrate that the required condition has been met within the applicable scope and conditions. The conclusion remains traceable to: criterion, method, evidence, sources, execution, outputs, thresholds, and limitations. Criterion Not Satisfied A criterion is Not Satisfied where the governed validation record sufficiently demonstrates that the required condition has not been met. This is fundamentally different from missing information. VALIDOS® therefore establishes: No Evidence of Satisfaction ≠ Evidence of Non-Satisfaction Criterion Not Determinable Sometimes the correct methodological conclusion is: We cannot determine this. This may occur because of: insufficient evidence, incomplete execution, unresolved conflict, excessive uncertainty, execution limitations, source limitations, or another methodological constraint. VALIDOS® treats Not Determinable as a legitimate governed outcome. It prevents uncertainty from being artificially converted into success or failure. Conditional Satisfaction Reality is often conditional. A Validation Object may satisfy a criterion: only within a defined operating range, only for a specific population, only in a specific environment, only while a control remains active, only for a specific system version, or only subject to another explicit condition. VDTS preserves those conditions. Therefore: Conditionally Satisfied ≠ Unconditionally Satisfied Critical Criteria Cannot Disappear Into Averages Suppose a system satisfies 99 criteria but fails one criterion governing catastrophic failure. A simple numerical average might suggest: 99% validated. Methodologically, that conclusion may be meaningless. VDTS therefore preserves the governance significance of critical and mandatory criteria. A critical failure cannot automatically be neutralized by many low-consequence successes. Aggregation Is a Governance Problem Multiple criterion outcomes eventually need to be interpreted together. But VALIDOS® establishes: Aggregation ≠ Averaging Criteria may be: mandatory, critical, supporting, hierarchical, conditional, exclusionary, dependent, or independently required. VDTS therefore governs how criterion outcomes may legitimately contribute to an overall Validation Determination. Weights Must Not Be Invented After Results Are Known Some validation systems legitimately use weighted criteria. But weighting creates methodological risk if weights are changed after results become visible. A validator could otherwise increase the importance of favorable results and reduce the importance of unfavorable ones. VDTS therefore requires weighting structures, where used, to remain methodologically justified and traceable. Contradictory Results Must Remain Visible Real validation rarely produces perfectly uniform evidence. One test may support satisfaction. Another may suggest failure. Different environments may produce different results. Different sources may conflict. Repeated measurements may vary. VDTS does not permit contradiction to disappear merely because one conclusion is more convenient. Instead, contradiction becomes a governed determination condition. Determination Conflict A Determination Conflict exists where legitimate validation findings support materially incompatible conclusions. The appropriate response may include: additional analysis, additional validation, method comparison, evidence reassessment, source reassessment, scope separation, conditional determination, or an Indeterminate Validation Determination. VALIDOS® does not require every conflict to be forcibly resolved. Sometimes the existence of unresolved conflict is itself the correct methodological finding. Uncertainty Must Survive Determination Validation cannot always eliminate uncertainty. Uncertainty may originate from: measurement, evidence, sources, sampling, methodology, execution, object variability, environmental variability, statistical uncertainty, or conflicting findings. VDTS ensures that material uncertainty survives the transition from results to conclusion. Uncertainty Does Not Mean Validation Failure A legitimate determination may contain uncertainty. The governance question is: Is the remaining uncertainty compatible with the Validation Purpose, Criteria, Depth, consequence, and intended determination? Low-consequence validation may tolerate uncertainty that would be unacceptable in a high-consequence environment. Evidence Conditions Propagate Forward Evidence qualified earlier under VALIDOS® may carry limitations. For example: Conditionally Fit Evidence should not silently become: Unrestricted Determination Evidence when VDTS begins. The limitations of evidence remain attached to the conclusions that depend upon it. Source Conditions Also Propagate Forward The same principle applies to sources. A source classified as usable only with: Independent Corroboration cannot legitimately become the sole unrestricted basis for a Validation Determination unless that condition was resolved. Therefore: Source Reliability Conditions → Determination Conditions where materially relevant. Execution Limitations Propagate Forward The Validation Execution Standard may permit determination while preserving residual limitations. VDTS consumes those limitations. It does not erase them. For example: If one execution portion is valid only within a reduced scope, the determination supported by that portion must remain within that scope. Positive Validation Determination A Positive Validation Determination means that the governed validation record sufficiently demonstrates satisfaction of the required Validation Criteria for the defined scope and conditions. It does not mean: The object is universally valid. It does not mean: The object will remain valid forever. It does not mean: Every possible use is authorized. It means that the governed validation event supports a positive conclusion within its legitimate boundaries. Conditional Validation Determination A Conditional Validation Determination means that the validation record supports a positive conclusion only under explicit conditions, restrictions, assumptions, or scope boundaries. These conditions are part of the determination. Removing them changes the meaning of the conclusion. Negative Validation Determination A Negative Validation Determination means that the governed validation record sufficiently demonstrates non-satisfaction of one or more criteria whose governance significance prevents a positive determination for the applicable scope. Negative determination must remain evidence-based. It cannot be inferred merely from missing information. Indeterminate Validation Determination An Indeterminate Validation Determination means that VALIDOS® does not possess sufficient governed basis to establish either a positive or negative overall conclusion. This is not methodological weakness. In some situations it is the most accurate possible conclusion. Therefore: Indeterminate ≠ Failed It means: The governed evidence does not justify certainty. Partial Validation Determination Complex systems do not always produce one uniform validation conclusion. A system may be: positively determined for one subsystem, conditionally determined for another, negatively determined for another, and indeterminate for another. Where those boundaries can be reliably separated, VDTS supports Partial Validation Determination. This preserves reality rather than forcing complexity into one misleading label. Hierarchical Determination Large systems may require determination across several levels. For example: Criterion → Component → Subsystem → System or: Test → Capability → Domain → Overall Object VDTS permits hierarchical determination where each level remains traceable to the level beneath it. A Positive Determination Is Not a Validation State This is one of the most important architectural boundaries. VDTS answers: What did this governed validation process demonstrate? The next Parent Standard asks: What formal Validation State should the Validation Object now hold? Those are different questions. A determination is a conclusion from a validation event. A state is a governed lifecycle condition associated with the object. Therefore: Validation Determination ≠ Validation State A Positive Determination Is Also Not Reliance Authorization Even a strong Positive Validation Determination does not automatically authorize operational reliance. An organization may still need to consider: risk, jurisdiction, operational context, authority, deployment conditions, time, system change, intended use, or revalidation requirements. Therefore: Positive Validation Determination ≠ Authorization to Rely Reliance belongs to the final VALIDOS® governance layer. Determination Authority Matters Some validation contexts require an identifiable authority to issue or approve the formal determination. That authority may be: human, institutional, delegated, automated under governed rules, or hybrid. VDTS does not create external legal authority. It governs the methodological authority relationship used to transform validation findings into a formal determination. Human Determination Human judgment may be necessary where: evidence is complex, criteria interact, uncertainty is material, findings conflict, or contextual interpretation is required. Human involvement does not remove the need for traceability. A human determination should still remain connected to its governed basis. Automated Determination Some validation contexts permit deterministic or automated determination. For example: If A, B, and C are satisfied and no exclusion condition exists → Positive Determination Automation can improve consistency. But the determination logic itself must remain governed. A machine should not silently create new aggregation rules during determination. AI-Assisted Determination AI may assist with: evidence synthesis, criterion mapping, conflict detection, uncertainty identification, comparison, traceability, and determination preparation. But AI assistance must remain bounded by the governed Validation Determination framework. AI should not transform methodological interpretation into an untraceable black box. Determination Must Be Reconstructable A qualified reviewer should be able to move backward from: Overall Validation Determination to: Criterion Determinations to: Execution Outputs to: Execution Activities to: Evidence and Sources to: Validation Method to: Validation Criteria to: Validation Purpose & Scope to: Validation Object This creates the conclusion traceability chain of VALIDOS®. Determination Records Matter The formal Validation Determination Record should preserve sufficient information to establish: What was concluded? About what? Against which criteria? Within which scope? From which execution? Using which evidence and sources? With which uncertainty? With which conflicts? Under which limitations? Under which conditions? By what determination authority? This prevents a later statement such as: “The system was validated.” from existing without methodological meaning. “Validated” Is Not Enough One of the central problems VALIDOS® addresses is the compression of complex validation into one word: Validated That word may conceal: what was validated, for what purpose, against what criteria, with what method, using what evidence, under which conditions, at what depth, with what uncertainty, for which version, and for how long. VDTS therefore replaces ambiguous validation claims with governed determination structure. Determination Can Change A Validation Determination is based upon the governed information available at a particular point in time. New information may emerge. For example: previously missing execution records, newly discovered deviations, evidence integrity problems, source reliability changes, methodological errors, incorrect criterion interpretation, or new information about the Validation Object. VDTS therefore allows determination reassessment. Reassessment Must Preserve History When a determination changes, the previous determination should not simply disappear. VALIDOS® preserves: Original Determination → New Information → Reassessment → Revised Determination This creates methodological history. Determination Suspension Where serious new uncertainty emerges before reassessment is complete, a determination may require suspension. Suspension means that the previous conclusion should not continue to be represented as fully current while its basis is materially uncertain. Determination Withdrawal Where the methodological basis of a determination is fundamentally destroyed, the determination may require withdrawal. Examples may include: wrong Validation Object, invalid execution, compromised critical evidence, major source failure, or fundamental methodological error. Withdrawal protects the validation record from continuing to communicate a conclusion that can no longer be defended. Position Within VALIDOS® Validation Determination Standard is the eighth Parent Standard of VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture. Its architectural position is: Validation Object → Validation Purpose & Scope → Validation Criteria → Validation Method → Validation Evidence Fitness → Validation Source Reliability → Validation Execution → Validation Determination → Validation State → Validation Reliance & Revalidation The first seven Parent Standards establish what was validated and whether the validation process was legitimate. VDTS establishes: What that legitimate validation process demonstrated. The next Parent Standard can then govern: What formal validation condition the Validation Object should hold as a result. Relationship to Other OOF® Architectures VDTS operates alongside complementary OOF® governance architectures. GOA™ may establish authority, delegation, scope, and governance conditions relevant to determination. OBIDENITY® may preserve Validation Object identity, origin, ownership, provenance, and continuity. INTEGROS® may provide integrity conditions affecting evidence, execution records, and determination artifacts. ORA™ may establish operational-reality conditions relevant to interpretation. AGA™ may establish accountability for determination roles and decisions. RIS™ may inform the strength and assurance required for high-consequence determinations. AIG®, CLIA®, MGIA™, and ASGA™ may provide specialized criteria and governance conditions where AI behavior, cognition, memory, or autonomy forms part of the Validation Object. VDTS does not replace these architectures. It consumes their relevant governed information where necessary and answers one validation-specific question: What can the governed validation record legitimately conclude? Why It Matters The weakest point of many validation processes is not necessarily testing. It is interpretation. Organizations can perform extensive testing and still produce weak conclusions if: unfavorable results are discounted, missing results are treated as success, averages hide critical failures, uncertainty disappears, conditions are omitted, scope expands during reporting, conflicting evidence is selectively resolved, or a narrow validation becomes a broad claim of validity. VDTS governs precisely this transition. From Results to Governed Knowledge VALIDOS® progressively transforms validation information. The progression is: Validation Object → what is being examined Validation Criteria → what must be demonstrated Validation Method → how it will be examined Validation Evidence & Sources → what information may support the process Validation Execution → what actually happened Validation Determination → what the governed process demonstrated This is the point where validation results become governed validation knowledge. The Determination Boundary VDTS deliberately ends before Validation State. Its final output is not: The object is permanently valid. Its output is: Given this Validation Object, Purpose, Scope, Criteria, Method, Evidence, Sources, Execution, conditions, limitations, conflicts, and uncertainty, this is what the governed validation record legitimately demonstrates. That boundary protects VALIDOS® from collapsing validation conclusion, lifecycle status, and operational reliance into one ambiguous concept. Foundational Principle Validation results become a legitimate determination only when the conclusion remains bounded by what the governed validation record can actually demonstrate. Canonical Closing Statement Validation Determination Standard establishes the formal interpretive conclusion layer of VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture by governing the transformation of determination-ready validation results into criterion-level and overall Validation Determinations. Through result qualification, criterion satisfaction and non-satisfaction, conditionality, non-determinability, critical and mandatory criterion treatment, cross-criterion interpretation, conflict, uncertainty, aggregation, scope, depth, evidence and source-condition propagation, execution limitations, partial and hierarchical determination, authority, traceability, reassessment, suspension, withdrawal, and historical continuity, VDTS ensures that no validation conclusion can legitimately claim more than the complete governed validation record is capable of demonstrating. title: Overall Validation Determination Module (OVDM)
text: Overall Validation Determination Module (OVDM) Overall Validation Determination Module (OVDM) Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Validation Determination Standard (VDTS) Operational Layer: Validation Determination Governance Layer Category: AI & Interpretation Subcategory: Validation Governance Type: Parent Standard Module Governed Space: Overall Validation Determination Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 11 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · OBIDENITY® · INTEGROS® · ORA™ · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Governed Space Overall Validation Determination Canonical Definition Overall Validation Determination Module (OVDM) defines the governance framework for transforming the complete governed Validation Determination Basis, criterion-level determinations, conflict and uncertainty conditions, cross-criterion integration structure, scope boundaries, Validation Depth, methodological limitations, and determination constraints into a formal, bounded, traceable, and methodologically defensible Overall Validation Determination. It establishes the final conclusion stage of the Validation Determination Standard and determines what the complete governed validation event legitimately demonstrates about the Validation Object. Operational Role OVDM serves as the fifth and final internal governance space of the Validation Determination Standard. The preceding modules establish: VDBRQM — Which results may legitimately participate in determination? VCDM — What does the qualified result set demonstrate about each Validation Criterion? VDCUGM — Which conflicts, uncertainties, and Determination Constraints remain? VCCIM — How should criterion outcomes be integrated according to their governance significance and relationships? OVDM asks: What Overall Validation Determination does the complete governed validation record legitimately support? The governed progression is: Qualified Determination Basis → Criterion Determinations → Conflict & Uncertainty Conditions → Cross-Criterion Integration Structure → Overall Determination Assessment → Determination Classification → Formal Validation Determination Record OVDM closes Validation Determination. It does not assign the persistent Validation State of the Validation Object. Module Operational Space OVDM governs: Overall Validation Determination, determination classification, positive determination, conditional determination, negative determination, indeterminate determination, partial determination, hierarchical determination, determination scope, determination depth, determination conditions, determination restrictions, determination limitations, determination uncertainty, determination conflict effects, determination authority, determination rationale, determination transparency, determination traceability, determination effective point, determination versioning, determination change, determination correction, determination reassessment, determination suspension, determination withdrawal, determination supersession, determination continuity, and transition to Validation State governance. Module Function OVDM applies after the cross-criterion determination structure has been sufficiently established. Its function is to prevent: criterion outcomes remaining unintegrated while a global validation claim is issued, positive determination being inferred from majority satisfaction alone, critical failures being diluted, Not Determinable criteria being treated as neutral where they are materially significant, unresolved conflict being erased at conclusion, uncertainty disappearing, conditional findings becoming unconditional, partial validation becoming universal validation, executed scope being expanded during reporting, Validation Depth being overstated, determination authority remaining unclear, and a phrase such as “validated” being issued without a reconstructable methodological meaning. Overall Validation Determination An Overall Validation Determination is the formal conclusion supported by the complete governed validation event. It describes what the validation record legitimately demonstrates about the Validation Object within: the validated object version, Validation Purpose, actual Validation Scope, achieved Validation Depth, applicable Validation Criteria, approved methodological structure, evidence conditions, source conditions, execution conditions, conflict state, uncertainty state, and applicable limitations. It is a bounded methodological conclusion. Determination Is an Event-Level Conclusion OVDM governs the conclusion produced by a particular governed validation event. This is important because the same Validation Object may later undergo: modification, new validation, revalidation, expanded validation, reduced-scope validation, or validation under different conditions. The Overall Validation Determination therefore remains linked to the validation event that produced it. Determination Classification OVDM may establish the following canonical Overall Validation Determination classes: Positive Validation Determination The complete governed validation record sufficiently demonstrates satisfaction of the criteria required for a positive conclusion within the defined scope, depth, and conditions. Conditional Validation Determination The validation record supports a positive conclusion only under explicit conditions, restrictions, limitations, assumptions, reduced scope, or other governed boundaries. Negative Validation Determination The validation record sufficiently demonstrates non-satisfaction of one or more criteria whose governance significance prevents a positive conclusion for the defined determination scope. Indeterminate Validation Determination The governed validation record does not provide sufficient legitimate basis to establish either a positive or negative overall conclusion. Partial Validation Determination Distinct parts of the Validation Object, Validation Scope, criterion structure, population, environment, or operational domain legitimately support different determination outcomes. These classes must remain distinct. Positive Validation Determination A Positive Validation Determination requires more than many favorable results. OVDM asks whether the complete integration structure permits a positive outcome. This may require: all mandatory criteria satisfied, no disqualifying critical failures, required prerequisites satisfied, no exclusionary conditions triggered, required Determination Constraints resolved, uncertainty remaining within acceptable bounds, and sufficient scope and depth for the intended positive conclusion. Positive Does Not Mean Universal VALIDOS® establishes: Positive Validation Determination ≠ Universal Validity A positive determination may apply only to: a specific version, specific population, specific environment, specific configuration, specific operational state, specific jurisdiction, specific time, or another bounded condition. The determination must preserve those boundaries. Conditional Validation Determination A Conditional Validation Determination is not a weaker wording for a Positive Determination. It is a distinct governed conclusion. The object is positively determined only if the relevant conditions remain satisfied. Conditions may include: continued control, specific operating environment, restricted scope, specific configuration, limited population, monitoring requirement, corroboration requirement, specific evidence condition, limited duration, or another methodological restriction. Conditionality Must Be Operationally Meaningful A condition should be sufficiently precise to allow later governance to determine whether it remains satisfied. Statements such as: “Valid if used appropriately” are too vague unless “appropriately” is governed elsewhere. Conditions should be operationally referenceable where possible. Negative Validation Determination A Negative Validation Determination exists where the governed record sufficiently demonstrates that the requirements for a positive determination are not met because of actual non-satisfaction of one or more materially significant criteria. Negative determination must remain grounded in positive evidence of non-satisfaction. It should not be produced merely because: validation was incomplete, evidence was missing, uncertainty was high, or execution failed. Those conditions may produce indeterminacy instead. Indeterminate Validation Determination An Indeterminate Validation Determination is appropriate where the governed validation process cannot legitimately establish either positive or negative determination. Possible causes include: mandatory criterion Not Determinable, unresolved critical conflict, determination-blocking uncertainty, insufficient determinant results, incompatible scopes, unresolved cross-criterion integration conflict, or another methodological limitation. VALIDOS® establishes: Indeterminate is an outcome, not an omission. Partial Validation Determination Partial Determination preserves structural truth where one global outcome would be misleading. For example: Subsystem A: Positive Subsystem B: Conditional Subsystem C: Negative Subsystem D: Indeterminate or: Adult Population: Positive Pediatric Population: Indeterminate or: Normal Operation: Positive Degraded Operation: Negative OVDM may represent these outcomes within one structured determination rather than forcing one universal label. Hierarchical Validation Determination For complex Validation Objects, OVDM may produce a hierarchical conclusion structure. For example: Criterion Determinations ↓ Capability Determinations ↓ Subsystem Determinations ↓ Domain Determinations ↓ Overall Validation Determination Each higher-level conclusion should remain traceable to the lower-level determinations supporting it. Overall Determination Scope OVDM establishes the exact scope to which the Overall Validation Determination applies. The determination scope must not exceed: legitimately executed scope, supported criterion scope, applicable evidence scope, reliable source scope, applicable object version, and conditions surviving cross-criterion integration. Scope Intersection Where required criteria support different scopes, the permissible overall positive scope may be constrained to the common supported region. Conceptually: Positive Determination Scope ≤ Common Supported Scope of Required Criteria Where no coherent common scope exists, Partial Determination may be required. Scope Exclusion Specific areas may need explicit exclusion. For example: Positive Validation Determination excluding high-altitude operation. Positive Validation Determination excluding pediatric use. Conditional Validation Determination excluding autonomous operation without human supervision. Exclusions should remain part of the determination record. Determination Depth The determination should preserve the Validation Depth actually achieved. Possible architecture implementations may distinguish: preliminary validation, standard validation, enhanced validation, high-assurance validation, or other governed depth levels. The determination must not imply a deeper assurance level than the validation performed. Determination Strength Is Not Determination Type A Positive Validation Determination may be supported at different strengths or depths. Therefore: Positive at Preliminary Depth is not methodologically equivalent to: Positive at High-Assurance Depth OVDM preserves this distinction. Determination Conditions OVDM collects and consolidates material conditions propagated from: criterion determinations, Evidence Fitness, Source Reliability, Execution Conformity, conflict governance, uncertainty governance, cross-criterion integration, and scope constraints. Conditions should not disappear merely because an overall conclusion has been reached. Determination Restrictions Restrictions may specify what the determination must not be used to imply. Examples include: not applicable outside tested environment, not valid for another system version, not sufficient for regulatory approval, not sufficient for autonomous deployment, not valid after specified modification, or not transferable to another population. Restrictions help prevent conclusion overreach. Determination Limitations Limitations describe known weaknesses or boundaries of the validation conclusion. These may include: limited long-term evidence, limited rare-event coverage, incomplete external validation, constrained population representation, limited operational duration, unresolved low-frequency uncertainty, or other known limitations. A positive determination may coexist with limitations. Determination Uncertainty OVDM preserves residual uncertainty remaining after VDCUGM and VCCIM. The final determination should therefore be uncertainty-aware. Where appropriate, uncertainty may be represented as: acceptable, conditionally acceptable, material but bounded, determination-limiting, or determination-blocking. Determination Conflict Effects A conflict may remain unresolved without completely preventing determination. For example: The conflict may be localized to one subsystem outside the positive determination scope. OVDM therefore considers the actual effect of remaining conflict. Determination Constraint Compliance Before issuing the Overall Validation Determination, OVDM verifies whether applicable Determination Constraints produced earlier have been respected. Examples include: required reduced scope, prohibition on unconditional positive determination, additional validation requirement, no aggregation across defined criteria, or mandatory Partial Determination. Overall Determination Logic OVDM should preserve the logic connecting: Criterion Outcomes → Integration Rules → Constraints → Overall Determination This logic must remain reconstructable. A global conclusion should not appear as an unexplained final label. Determination Rationale A Validation Determination should include or reference sufficient rationale to explain: why the conclusion was selected, which criteria controlled it, which conflicts affected it, which uncertainty remained, which conditions apply, and why alternative determination classes were not selected where material. Determination Authority Where a formal determination requires identifiable authority, OVDM may govern: determination issuer, approval authority, delegated authority, decision system, required independence, required competence, authority scope, and authorization conditions. OVDM does not create legal authority externally. It governs the authority used within the methodology. Single Determination Authority One authorized evaluator or system may issue the final determination. Where this occurs, the determination must still remain traceable to the governed validation record rather than personal preference. Multi-Party Determination Some validation environments may require multiple parties. Possible structures include: validator + reviewer, technical evaluator + governance authority, automated determination + human approval, independent assessor + regulator, or other governed arrangements. Determination Disagreement Where authorized determination actors disagree, OVDM does not automatically use majority vote unless the governance structure explicitly defines that mechanism. Disagreement may require: escalation, additional review, preserved dissent, or Indeterminate Determination. Human Overall Determination Human determination may be appropriate where integration involves substantial context, uncertainty, or judgment. The governing requirement is that the human conclusion remains constrained by: criteria, results, integration rules, conflict conditions, uncertainty, scope, and methodological record. Automated Overall Determination Where determination logic is sufficiently explicit, OVDM may be automated. Automated rules may implement: mandatory-criteria logic, critical-condition logic, hierarchical integration, exclusion rules, threshold structures, conditionality, and Determination Constraints. The rule set should remain versioned and auditable. AI-Assisted Overall Determination AI may assist with: synthesis, rationale preparation, traceability reconstruction, condition extraction, inconsistency detection, scope checking, or explanation generation. However: AI Assistance ≠ Authority to Invent Determination Logic The final determination must remain grounded in governed rules and records. Determination Effective Point The Overall Validation Determination should have an identifiable effective point. This may include: issuance date, approval date, validation completion date, or another governed reference. This is important because the next Parent Standard must determine the Validation State of the object over time. Determination Is Not Necessarily Permanent A determination reflects a governed conclusion at a specific point based upon a specific Validation Object and validation basis. It may later change because of: new evidence, source reassessment, execution correction, object modification, method error, discovered conflict, or revalidation. Validation Determination Record A formal Overall Validation Determination Record should preserve, where applicable: Validation Determination Identifier, Validation Object, object version, Validation Purpose, determination scope, achieved Validation Depth, Validation Criteria, criterion-level determinations, cross-criterion integration structure, mandatory criteria status, critical criteria status, conflicts, uncertainty, Determination Constraints, conditions, restrictions, limitations, Overall Validation Determination, determination rationale, determination authority, effective point, basis version, and sufficient lifecycle traceability. Determination Statement A formal determination statement should be capable of communicating more than: “Validated.” A governed statement should conceptually communicate: What object what version for what purpose within what scope at what depth against what criteria with what outcome subject to what conditions with what limitations at what effective point This creates validation meaning. Determination Traceability OVDM preserves the complete determination chain: Validation Object ↓ Validation Purpose & Scope ↓ Validation Criteria ↓ Validation Method ↓ Validation Evidence Fitness ↓ Validation Source Reliability ↓ Validation Execution ↓ Qualified Results ↓ Criterion Determinations ↓ Conflict & Uncertainty Governance ↓ Cross-Criterion Integration ↓ Overall Validation Determination This becomes the primary conclusion lineage of VALIDOS®. Determination Transparency A qualified reviewer should be able to understand the methodological basis of the Overall Validation Determination. Transparency may include: criteria outcome map, integration logic, conditions, limitations, conflict status, uncertainty status, and determination rationale. Transparency does not require publication of confidential technical information beyond applicable governance obligations. Determination Versioning Materially revised determinations should remain distinguishable. Possible representations may include: Determination 1.0 Determination 1.1 Determination 2.0 The exact implementation can vary. Historical determination states must remain available. Determination Correction A correction applies where the original determination contained an error but the underlying validation event can still support a corrected determination. The record should preserve: Original Determination → Error → Correction → Corrected Determination Determination Reassessment Reassessment may occur when new information materially affects the original conclusion. Possible triggers include: corrected result, newly identified execution deviation, evidence reassessment, Source Reliability reassessment, conflict resolution, new uncertainty, or methodological correction. Determination Change Possible determination transitions may include: Positive → Conditional Positive → Negative Positive → Indeterminate Conditional → Positive Conditional → Negative Negative → Positive Indeterminate → Positive or other governed transitions. Change does not erase historical conclusions. Determination Suspension A determination may be suspended where serious new information creates material doubt before reassessment is complete. Suspension means the determination should not continue to be represented as an unrestricted current conclusion. Determination Withdrawal A determination may be withdrawn where its methodological foundation is materially destroyed. Possible causes include: wrong Validation Object, invalid critical execution, compromised decisive evidence, fundamental source unreliability, incorrect criterion architecture, or determination fraud. Determination Supersession A later governed validation event may produce a new determination superseding an earlier one. The relationship should be explicit: Determination A → Superseded by Determination B Supersession does not delete Determination A. Determination Continuity OVDM preserves determination history across: object versions, revalidation, corrections, updates, scope changes, and lifecycle transitions. This enables the next VALIDOS® Parent Standard to reason about the current Validation State rather than relying on one isolated conclusion. Determination vs Validation State This boundary is fundamental. OVDM answers: What did this validation event demonstrate? The next Parent Standard must answer: Given the relevant determinations and current lifecycle conditions, what Validation State does the object now hold? Therefore: Overall Validation Determination ≠ Validation State Determination vs Reliance OVDM also does not authorize reliance. A Positive Validation Determination may exist while: deployment is prohibited, usage is restricted, regulatory approval is absent, revalidation is due, or the determination is unsuitable for a specific relying party. Therefore: Positive Validation Determination ≠ Reliance Authorization Determination Handoff to Validation State OVDM closes the eighth Parent Standard by handing forward: Overall Validation Determination, scope, depth, conditions, restrictions, limitations, uncertainty, conflicts, effective point, determination version, and determination continuity references. The next VALIDOS® Parent Standard can then determine how these elements become a formal Validation State. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Verify Cross-Criterion Integration Confirm that the criterion integration structure is sufficiently complete and consistent. 2. Identify Controlling Criterion Conditions Identify: mandatory criteria, critical criteria, exclusion conditions, unresolved Not Determinable criteria, and other controlling factors. 3. Verify Determination Constraints Ensure all material conflict, uncertainty, and integration constraints have been respected. 4. Establish Permissible Determination Scope Define the maximum scope legitimately supported by the validation record. 5. Establish Determination Depth Preserve the Validation Depth actually achieved. 6. Consolidate Conditions, Restrictions, and Limitations Carry forward all material boundaries from the complete VALIDOS® validation record. 7. Establish Overall Validation Determination Classify the result as: Positive Validation Determination, Conditional Validation Determination, Negative Validation Determination, Indeterminate Validation Determination, or Partial Validation Determination. 8. Establish Determination Rationale & Authority Preserve why the conclusion was reached and by whom or what it was formally issued where applicable. 9. Establish Effective Point Record when the determination becomes methodologically effective. 10. Create Overall Validation Determination Record Preserve the complete conclusion basis. 11. Preserve Change & Continuity Governance Maintain: corrections, reassessments, suspensions, withdrawals, supersession, versions, and historical continuity. Governance Outputs OVDM may produce: Overall Validation Determination, Positive Validation Determination Record, Conditional Validation Determination Record, Negative Validation Determination Record, Indeterminate Validation Determination Record, Partial Validation Determination Record, Hierarchical Validation Determination, Determination Scope Record, Determination Depth Record, Determination Condition Register, Determination Restriction Record, Determination Limitation Record, Determination Uncertainty Record, Determination Conflict Effect Record, Determination Constraint Compliance Record, Overall Determination Logic Record, Validation Determination Rationale, Validation Determination Authority Record, Validation Determination Effective Point, Overall Validation Determination Record, Validation Determination Traceability Map, Determination Transparency Record, Validation Determination Version, Determination Correction Record, Determination Reassessment Record, Determination Suspension Record, Determination Withdrawal Record, Determination Supersession Record, and Determination Continuity Reference. Use Case 1 — Autonomous AI System Scenario An autonomous AI system satisfies all mandatory performance criteria. One critical safety criterion is Conditionally Satisfied only where human override remains continuously available. Application VCCIM propagates the safety condition into the integrated criterion structure. OVDM cannot issue an unrestricted Positive Validation Determination. Result The system receives: Conditional Validation Determination limited to operation under continuous human override availability. The condition becomes part of the formal determination rather than an informal footnote. Use Case 2 — Healthcare AI Scenario A diagnostic AI system is positively determined across the adult validation population. Pediatric validation remains Not Determinable because the evidence basis is insufficient. Application OVDM limits the determination scope to the validated adult population. Result The system may receive: Positive Validation Determination — Adult Population together with an explicit exclusion of pediatric use from the positive determination scope. It is not represented as universally validated. Use Case 3 — Industrial Autonomous System Scenario An industrial system satisfies all normal-operation criteria but fails one critical recovery criterion during degraded operation. Application The cross-criterion integration structure identifies the recovery criterion as non-compensatory and critical. Result OVDM may establish: Negative Validation Determination for the intended unrestricted operational scope while preserving any separately valid positive determination for a narrower operational mode if that scope can be methodologically isolated. Architectural Position Overall Validation Determination is the fifth and final internal governance space of the Validation Determination Standard (VDTS). The complete VDTS progression is: Validation Determination Basis & Result Qualification → Validation Criterion Determination → Validation Determination Conflict & Uncertainty Governance → Validation Cross-Criterion Integration → Overall Validation Determination Together, these five governed spaces transform validation execution results into a formal and bounded validation conclusion. The progression is: Execution Outputs ↓ Qualified Determination Basis ↓ Criterion Determinations ↓ Governed Conflict & Uncertainty ↓ Cross-Criterion Integration ↓ Overall Validation Determination The next VALIDOS® governance question becomes fundamentally different: What formal Validation State should the Validation Object now hold as a result of the applicable determination and current lifecycle conditions? Foundational Principle A Validation Determination is legitimate only when its scope, strength, conditions, and conclusion do not exceed what the complete governed validation record is capable of demonstrating. Canonical Closing Statement Overall Validation Determination Module completes the formal conclusion lifecycle of the Validation Determination Standard within VALIDOS® by transforming qualified results, criterion-level determinations, conflicts, uncertainty, integration logic, scope, Validation Depth, conditions, restrictions, limitations, and Determination Constraints into a formal Overall Validation Determination. OVDM ensures that validation conclusions remain explicit, bounded, traceable, versioned, revisable, and methodologically defensible while preserving the critical architectural separation between what a validation event demonstrates, what Validation State an object subsequently holds, and whether any person, system, or organization may ultimately rely upon that state.
