title: Validation Determination Conflict & Uncertainty Governance Module (VDCUGM)
text: Validation Determination Conflict & Uncertainty Governance Module (VDCUGM) Validation Determination Conflict & Uncertainty Governance Module (VDCUGM) Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Validation Determination Standard (VDTS) Operational Layer: Validation Determination Governance Layer Category: AI & Interpretation Subcategory: Validation Governance Type: Parent Standard Module Governed Space: Validation Determination Conflict & Uncertainty Governance Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 11 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · OBIDENITY® · INTEGROS® · ORA™ · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Governed Space Validation Determination Conflict & Uncertainty Governance Canonical Definition Validation Determination Conflict & Uncertainty Governance Module (VDCUGM) defines the governance framework for identifying, classifying, preserving, analyzing, contextualizing, escalating, constraining, and where methodologically possible resolving material conflicts, contradictory findings, incompatible criterion signals, uncertainty, ambiguity, incomplete knowledge, and determination instability arising within the governed Validation Determination Basis. It establishes the conditions under which disagreement and uncertainty become explicit determination-governance inputs rather than hidden, averaged, discarded, or prematurely converted into certainty. Operational Role VDCUGM serves as the third internal governance space of the Validation Determination Standard. The preceding modules establish: VDBRQM — Which results may legitimately participate in determination? VCDM — What does the qualified result set demonstrate about each individual Validation Criterion? VDCUGM asks: Where do legitimate findings conflict, where does uncertainty materially affect interpretation, and what must happen before criterion outcomes can be integrated into an overall Validation Determination? The governed progression is: Criterion Determinations & Conflict Signals → Conflict Identification → Conflict Classification → Uncertainty Identification → Materiality Assessment → Cause & Scope Analysis → Resolution or Preservation → Determination Constraint → Conflict & Uncertainty Record VDCUGM does not perform final cross-criterion aggregation. It governs the interpretive instability that must be understood before aggregation can legitimately occur. Module Operational Space VDCUGM governs: determination conflict, criterion conflict, result conflict, evidence conflict, source-related determination conflict, method-related determination conflict, execution-related determination conflict, scope conflict, threshold conflict, temporal conflict, contextual conflict, contradiction, inconsistency, unresolved disagreement, determination uncertainty, measurement uncertainty, methodological uncertainty, evidentiary uncertainty, source uncertainty, execution uncertainty, sampling uncertainty, contextual uncertainty, model uncertainty, object-state uncertainty, uncertainty materiality, uncertainty propagation, conflict materiality, conflict causation, conflict localization, conflict escalation, conflict resolution, unresolved conflict preservation, conditional determination constraints, indeterminacy triggers, and conflict-and-uncertainty traceability. Module Function VDCUGM applies after criterion-level determinations and material conflict signals have been established. Its function is to prevent: contradictory findings being silently averaged, unfavorable evidence being discarded as noise, uncertainty being hidden behind point estimates, disagreements between methods being resolved by preference, disagreements between sources being resolved by reputation alone, scope differences being mistaken for factual contradiction, temporal changes being treated as inconsistent evidence, missing information being converted into certainty, one dominant criterion result suppressing legitimate contrary evidence, and overall determination being constructed before material conflict and uncertainty are governably understood. Conflict Is Not Automatically Error VALIDOS® establishes: Conflict ≠ Methodological Failure Two legitimate results may disagree because they describe: different operating conditions, different populations, different times, different system states, different methodological sensitivities, or genuinely unstable object behavior. Conflict may therefore contain important validation information. The first governance task is not to eliminate conflict. It is to understand what the conflict represents. Validation Determination Conflict A Validation Determination Conflict exists where two or more legitimate findings, criterion outcomes, or interpretive pathways support materially incompatible conclusions within an overlapping determination space. The overlap requirement matters. Two different conclusions are not necessarily conflicting if they apply to different valid scopes. Result Conflict A Result Conflict exists where qualified Validation Results materially disagree about the same validation-relevant condition. Examples include: repeated measurements producing incompatible values, two tests producing different classifications, simulation and operational testing diverging, or different time periods showing materially different behavior. Criterion Conflict A Criterion Conflict exists where one criterion-level determination contains legitimate internal inconsistency or where materially related criteria support incompatible implications. For example: Criterion A: Satisfied while: Criterion B: Not Satisfied may or may not constitute a conflict. It becomes a determination conflict only if the approved criteria structure expects those outcomes to be mutually compatible or causally related. Evidence Conflict Evidence Conflict occurs where legitimate evidence supports materially different interpretations. This may arise from: different datasets, different populations, different observations, different time periods, or different environments. Evidence Conflict is not automatically Source Conflict. Source-Related Determination Conflict Two sufficiently reliable sources may disagree. VDCUGM preserves the disagreement and examines whether it arises from: different source roles, different observations, different access, different time periods, different methodologies, or genuine factual incompatibility. A more authoritative source should not automatically win merely because of status. Method-Related Determination Conflict Different suitable Validation Methods may produce materially different findings. This may reveal: different sensitivity, different assumptions, different scope, hidden methodological limitations, or object behavior that varies by measurement method. Method conflict may require methodological comparison rather than numerical averaging. Execution-Related Conflict Execution differences may explain apparent determination conflict. For example: Two valid test results may differ because: one occurred under nominal operation, one under degraded operation, one used a different configuration, or one followed a different sequence. VDCUGM distinguishes factual disagreement from execution-context difference. Scope Conflict A Scope Conflict exists where two determinations appear contradictory but actually apply to materially different scopes. For example: Satisfied for Population A and: Not Satisfied for Population B are not necessarily contradictory. The conflict may disappear once scope is correctly represented. Temporal Conflict A Validation Object may change over time. A criterion may be satisfied at Time 1 and not satisfied at Time 2. This is not necessarily inconsistent validation. It may represent: State Change Drift Degradation Improvement or: Context Change VDCUGM preserves time as part of conflict interpretation. Contextual Conflict A system may behave differently across: jurisdictions, languages, environments, user groups, hardware, software configurations, or operating modes. Contextual differences must not be compressed into one universal conclusion if the underlying behavior is genuinely conditional. Threshold Conflict Different thresholds may produce apparently conflicting conclusions. VDCUGM identifies whether: different criterion versions were used, different jurisdictions apply different thresholds, different Validation Depths use different acceptance levels, or an unauthorized threshold change occurred. Threshold differences must remain explicit. Conflict Classification A material conflict may be classified as: Apparent Conflict The disagreement disappears when scope, time, context, or definition is clarified. Resolvable Conflict The conflict can be methodologically resolved using existing governed information. Conditionally Resolvable Conflict The conflict can be resolved only under explicit assumptions, boundaries, or additional controls. Unresolved Conflict Legitimate incompatible findings remain after reasonable governance analysis. Critical Conflict The unresolved conflict materially prevents a reliable criterion or overall determination. These classifications support downstream determination governance. Conflict Materiality Not every disagreement matters equally. Conflict materiality may depend upon: affected criterion, mandatory or critical status, Validation Purpose, Validation Depth, scope, consequence of error, persistence, strength of competing findings, and whether the conflict can change the overall determination. Conflict Localization VDCUGM seeks to determine where the conflict actually exists. Possible localization levels include: one result, one criterion, one subgroup, one environment, one time period, one subsystem, one object state, or the complete Validation Object. Localization prevents narrow conflicts from unnecessarily contaminating the entire determination. Conflict Cause Analysis Possible causes may include: measurement variation, evidence limitations, source differences, method differences, execution differences, sampling effects, data drift, object instability, context dependence, threshold mismatch, hidden dependency, or genuine unresolved reality. Cause analysis informs whether conflict can be resolved, bounded, or must remain explicit. Conflict Resolution Where methodologically justified, conflict may be resolved through: scope clarification, corrected threshold application, removal of ineligible result, corrected result qualification, method comparison, additional analysis, additional validation, source clarification, evidence clarification, temporal separation, contextual separation, or another governed mechanism. Resolution Must Not Mean Preference VALIDOS® establishes: Conflict Resolution ≠ Choosing the Preferred Result Resolution must be based upon governed methodological reasons. A favorable conclusion does not gain priority merely because it supports deployment, approval, reputation, or business objectives. Unresolved Conflict An unresolved conflict is a legitimate determination condition. Possible downstream effects include: Criterion Not Determinable, Conditional Determination, Partial Determination, reduced determination scope, additional validation requirement, or Indeterminate Validation Determination. Conflict Preservation Where conflict cannot be legitimately resolved, both sides of the conflict should remain traceable. The record should preserve: conflicting findings, their basis, relevant scope, evidence, sources, methods, uncertainty, and reason resolution was not possible. Uncertainty Governance Validation uncertainty represents the degree to which available governed information leaves material doubt concerning interpretation or determination. Uncertainty is not one single phenomenon. VDCUGM separates uncertainty by source and function. Measurement Uncertainty Measurement uncertainty concerns uncertainty inherent in observed or measured values. This may include: instrument tolerance, noise, repeatability, precision, resolution, or another measurement limitation. Methodological Uncertainty Methodological uncertainty concerns uncertainty arising from: method assumptions, model choice, analytical design, simulation limitations, sampling method, or methodological approximation. Evidentiary Uncertainty Evidentiary uncertainty concerns: incomplete evidence, limited representativeness, sparse observations, missing scenarios, temporal limitations, or Evidence Fitness restrictions. Source Uncertainty Source uncertainty concerns unresolved conditions involving: identity, provenance, capability, competence, independence, conflicts, or reliability. Execution Uncertainty Execution uncertainty concerns uncertainty about: what happened, whether a procedure was followed, whether a control remained active, whether object state changed, or whether critical execution details can be reconstructed. Sampling Uncertainty Sampling may produce uncertainty concerning whether observed results represent the wider population, environment, or state space. Contextual Uncertainty Contextual uncertainty arises where applicability across: environments, populations, jurisdictions, languages, system states, or operating conditions cannot be fully established. Object-State Uncertainty The Validation Object itself may exhibit: stochastic behavior, adaptive behavior, dynamic behavior, drift, emergent behavior, or poorly understood state transitions. This may create uncertainty that is not reducible to measurement error. Uncertainty Is Not Ignorance Some uncertainty can be characterized quantitatively or qualitatively. Other uncertainty reflects lack of knowledge. VDCUGM permits distinctions such as: Known Quantified Uncertainty Known Qualitative Uncertainty Known Unknown and: Uncharacterized Uncertainty where useful. Uncertainty Materiality Uncertainty becomes material where it can reasonably affect: criterion status, determination scope, determination conditions, overall Validation Determination, or later reliance. Not every uncertainty requires the same governance response. Uncertainty Tolerance The acceptable degree of uncertainty may depend upon: Validation Purpose, Validation Depth, criterion criticality, risk, reversibility, consequence of error, and intended reliance. A research context may tolerate uncertainty unacceptable in high-consequence autonomous deployment. Uncertainty-Compatible Determination A determination may remain legitimate where uncertainty is sufficiently bounded and compatible with the applicable governance requirements. Perfect certainty is not required. Uncertainty-Driven Conditionality Where uncertainty restricts applicability but does not prevent a conclusion, downstream determination may become conditional. For example: Positive only within tested operating conditions. Uncertainty-Driven Indeterminacy Where uncertainty prevents legitimate distinction between satisfaction and non-satisfaction, the correct outcome is indeterminacy. VALIDOS® establishes: When uncertainty materially prevents knowing, the architecture should preserve not knowing. Uncertainty Propagation Uncertainty should remain attached to the findings that depend upon it. The conceptual chain may be: Evidence Uncertainty → Result Uncertainty → Criterion Uncertainty → Overall Determination Constraint This prevents uncertainty from disappearing during aggregation. Uncertainty Amplification Several individually modest uncertainties may combine into a larger determination problem. For example: moderate evidence uncertainty, moderate source uncertainty, and moderate execution uncertainty may collectively create substantial criterion uncertainty. VDCUGM therefore considers cumulative uncertainty. Uncertainty Reduction Uncertainty may be reduced through: additional evidence, additional validation, better measurement, independent corroboration, narrower scope, improved source qualification, repeated testing, or clearer methodological boundaries. Uncertainty reduction should remain traceable. Residual Uncertainty Uncertainty remaining after reasonable reduction efforts becomes Residual Uncertainty. Residual Uncertainty must propagate into later determination governance where material. Conflict and Uncertainty Interaction Conflict and uncertainty often interact. A conflict may increase uncertainty. Uncertainty may make apparent conflict impossible to resolve. VDCUGM therefore governs them together while preserving their conceptual distinction. Conflict Without High Uncertainty Two strong findings may genuinely conflict. In such cases, the conflict may be clear even though each finding is individually well-supported. High Uncertainty Without Conflict A single criterion may have no contradictory result but still remain highly uncertain because the evidence basis is weak. Therefore: Conflict ≠ Uncertainty and: Uncertainty ≠ Conflict Determination Constraint VDCUGM may create a formal Determination Constraint. A Determination Constraint defines how identified conflict or uncertainty must affect later cross-criterion integration. Possible constraints include: reduced scope, conditional interpretation, no aggregation across specified results, additional validation required, criterion remains Not Determinable, partial determination only, or overall indeterminacy required. Critical Determination Constraint A critical conflict or uncertainty may prevent legitimate overall determination. Such a condition may create: Overall Determination Blocked by Conflict or: Overall Determination Blocked by Uncertainty where appropriate. Conflict Escalation Material conflicts may require escalation where resolution exceeds the authority or capability of the current determination process. Escalation may involve: methodology review, independent review, specialized expert review, governance authority, additional validation, or another defined pathway. Uncertainty Escalation High-consequence uncertainty may likewise require: deeper Validation Depth, additional evidence, broader testing, more reliable sources, or independent confirmation. Conflict Status VDCUGM may establish: Conflict Resolved Conflict Conditionally Resolved Conflict Bounded Conflict Unresolved Critical Conflict or: Conflict Status Undetermined Uncertainty Status Uncertainty may be characterized as: Uncertainty Acceptable Uncertainty Conditionally Acceptable Uncertainty Material Uncertainty Determination-Limiting Uncertainty Determination-Blocking or: Uncertainty Undetermined These statuses inform later integration rather than becoming Validation States. Conflict & Uncertainty Record A formal record may preserve: Conflict or Uncertainty Identifier, affected Validation Object, affected criteria, affected results, scope, time, context, evidence, sources, methods, execution references, materiality, cause, uncertainty type, competing interpretations, analysis, resolution attempt, resolution status, residual uncertainty, Determination Constraints, escalation, and sufficient traceability. Human Conflict Resolution Human expert judgment may assist conflict resolution where interpretation is complex. Where used, it should remain: attributable, bounded, competence-aware, conflict-of-interest aware, evidence-based, and traceable. Automated Conflict Detection Automated systems may identify: inconsistent results, threshold disagreement, cross-method divergence, duplicate contradictions, or statistical anomalies. Detection can be automated even where resolution requires human or governed methodological review. AI-Assisted Conflict & Uncertainty Analysis AI may assist with: clustering conflicting findings, tracing sources, identifying contextual differences, mapping uncertainty, detecting hidden assumptions, and proposing resolution pathways. AI assistance should not silently resolve a material conflict by preference or opaque reasoning. Conflict Reassessment Conflict status may change when: new results appear, evidence is corrected, scope is clarified, source reliability changes, a method error is identified, or additional validation is performed. Uncertainty Reassessment Uncertainty may change because of: new evidence, additional observation, improved measurement, model change, environmental change, or improved methodological understanding. Historical uncertainty assessments should remain visible. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Identify Material Conflicts Detect incompatible findings, criterion signals, or interpretations within overlapping determination scope. 2. Classify Conflict Type Determine whether conflict is: result-based, criterion-based, evidence-based, source-related, method-related, execution-related, scope-related, temporal, contextual, or threshold-related. 3. Identify Uncertainty Map relevant uncertainty sources affecting criterion or overall interpretation. 4. Assess Materiality Determine whether conflict or uncertainty is: immaterial, tolerable, material, determination-limiting, or determination-blocking. 5. Analyze Cause and Scope Determine whether the issue reflects: actual contradiction, scope difference, time difference, context difference, methodological limitation, source difference, execution difference, or genuine object instability. 6. Attempt Governed Resolution Where Legitimate Use methodologically defensible resolution pathways. 7. Preserve Unresolved Conflict and Residual Uncertainty Do not force closure where the governed basis does not support it. 8. Establish Determination Constraints Define how conflict and uncertainty must affect later cross-criterion integration. 9. Establish Escalation Where Required Trigger additional review or validation where materiality demands it. 10. Preserve Lifecycle Traceability Maintain: conflict records, uncertainty records, affected criteria, affected results, evidence, sources, methods, execution references, scope, context, time, materiality, cause, analysis, resolution status, residual uncertainty, Determination Constraints, reassessment triggers, changes, and sufficient lifecycle continuity. Governance Outputs VDCUGM may produce: Validation Determination Conflict Register, Result Conflict Record, Criterion Conflict Record, Evidence Conflict Record, Source-Related Conflict Record, Method-Related Conflict Record, Execution-Related Conflict Record, Scope Conflict Record, Temporal Conflict Record, Contextual Conflict Record, Threshold Conflict Record, Conflict Classification, Conflict Materiality Assessment, Conflict Cause Assessment, Conflict Localization Record, Conflict Resolution Record, Unresolved Conflict Record, Validation Uncertainty Register, Measurement Uncertainty Record, Methodological Uncertainty Record, Evidentiary Uncertainty Record, Source Uncertainty Record, Execution Uncertainty Record, Sampling Uncertainty Record, Contextual Uncertainty Record, Object-State Uncertainty Record, Residual Uncertainty Record, Cumulative Uncertainty Assessment, Determination Constraint, Critical Determination Constraint, Conflict Escalation Record, Uncertainty Escalation Record, Conflict Status, Uncertainty Status, and Conflict & Uncertainty Reassessment Record. Use Case 1 — AI Model Validation Scenario An AI model satisfies a safety criterion in simulation but produces materially different behavior during controlled real-world testing. Both validation methods were suitable and both executions were conformant. Application VDCUGM does not select the more favorable result. It examines: method differences, environmental differences, scope, execution conditions, object state, and remaining uncertainty. Result The conflict may be localized to simulation-to-reality transfer and produce a Determination Constraint preventing unrestricted criterion satisfaction until the divergence is resolved or bounded. Use Case 2 — Healthcare AI Scenario A diagnostic AI system meets the required performance threshold across the overall validation population but shows materially lower performance in a small subgroup with limited sample size. Application VDCUGM distinguishes: subgroup conflict, sampling uncertainty, population scope, and evidence limitations. Result Rather than averaging the subgroup away, the module may preserve conditionality or require the subgroup criterion to remain Not Determinable pending additional validation. Use Case 3 — Autonomous System Scenario Repeated validation of an autonomous system produces stable results under normal conditions but inconsistent outcomes under a rare degraded-state scenario. Application VDCUGM determines whether the inconsistency reflects: stochastic system behavior, insufficient sample size, environment variation, execution differences, or genuine unstable behavior. Result Where the conflict cannot be resolved, the residual uncertainty remains attached to the affected criterion and may constrain later overall determination. Architectural Position Validation Determination Conflict & Uncertainty Governance is the third internal governance space of the Validation Determination Standard (VDTS). The progression now becomes: Determination Basis & Result Qualification → Criterion Determination → Conflict & Uncertainty Governance VDBRQM establishes: Which results may participate? VCDM establishes: What does each qualified result set demonstrate about each criterion? VDCUGM establishes: Where do those findings conflict, where does uncertainty remain, and what interpretive constraints must survive? The next VDTS governance stage can then ask: How should the now-governed criterion outcomes be combined across mandatory, critical, dependent, conditional, and hierarchical criteria? The VDTS progression therefore continues: Determination Basis & Result Qualification → Criterion Determination → Conflict & Uncertainty Governance → Cross-Criterion Integration → Overall Validation Determination Foundational Principle Conflict and uncertainty should not be eliminated for the sake of a cleaner conclusion; they should remain visible until the validation record legitimately supports resolution, limitation, or indeterminacy. Canonical Closing Statement Validation Determination Conflict & Uncertainty Governance Module establishes the interpretive stability layer of VALIDOS® by governing contradictory findings, criterion conflict, evidence and source disagreement, method and execution divergence, scope and temporal differences, uncertainty, materiality, causation, localization, resolution, residual uncertainty, escalation, and Determination Constraints. VDCUGM ensures that cross-criterion integration cannot convert unresolved disagreement, methodological ambiguity, or incomplete knowledge into artificial certainty and that every later Validation Determination remains bounded by the conflicts and uncertainties the governed validation record is actually capable of resolving. title: Validation Determination Standard
text: Validation Determination Standard Validation Determination Standard Standard ID: VDTS OriginID: OOF-OID-AI-VALIDOS-VDTS-2026-08-11-0008 Architecture: VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture Category: AI & Interpretation Subcategory: Validation Governance Type: Parent Standard Governed Space: Validation Determination Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 11 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · OBIDENITY® · INTEGROS® · ORA™ · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Canonical Definition Validation Determination Standard (VDTS) defines the governance conditions under which the complete governed validation record is evaluated, integrated, interpreted, bounded, and transformed into a formal Validation Determination establishing what the executed validation legitimately demonstrates about the Validation Object relative to the applicable Validation Criteria, thresholds, conditions, evidence, methodological limitations, execution conformity, uncertainty, conflicts, and approved Validation Scope. Canonical Definition Extension Validation execution produces results. Results alone do not create a legitimate validation conclusion. A validation process may generate: measurements, test outputs, statistical findings, expert assessments, observations, simulations, criterion outcomes, contradictory findings, unresolved uncertainty, execution limitations, and residual deviations. These elements must be interpreted within the governed structure established by VALIDOS®. Validation Determination Standard therefore governs the transformation: Governed Validation Record → Validation Finding → Criterion Determination → Integrated Validation Determination VDTS establishes the conditions necessary to determine: which execution results may legitimately participate in determination, which Validation Criteria have sufficient determination basis, whether individual criteria are satisfied, not satisfied, conditionally satisfied, or not determinable, how multiple criterion outcomes interact, how mandatory and non-mandatory criteria differ, how contradictory findings are treated, how uncertainty affects determination, how residual execution limitations propagate, whether evidence and source conditions constrain interpretation, whether determination must be scoped or conditional, whether sufficient basis exists for an overall determination, and what the governed validation record actually demonstrates. VDTS does not create a permanent Validation State. It does not authorize operational reliance. It determines the validation conclusion supported by the governed validation record. Core Question What does the complete governed validation record legitimately demonstrate about the Validation Object relative to the applicable Validation Criteria and governed validation conditions? Purpose The purpose of Validation Determination Standard is to prevent validation conclusions from being reduced to: raw test scores, simple pass/fail labels, majority voting, selective evidence, favorable averages, ungoverned expert opinion, arbitrary weighting, or conclusions broader than the validation process can legitimately support. VDTS creates the interpretive governance layer between: Validation Execution and: Validation State It ensures that a validation conclusion represents what the governed validation process actually demonstrates—not what stakeholders hoped it would demonstrate. Governance Objective VDTS establishes a governed Validation Determination framework capable of producing conclusions that are: criterion-grounded, evidence-aware, source-aware, execution-aware, scope-bounded, uncertainty-aware, conflict-aware, limitation-aware, methodologically proportionate, traceable, and suitable for later Validation State assignment. The standard seeks to ensure that: only determination-ready execution enters conclusion formation, criterion outcomes remain distinguishable, critical criteria retain appropriate significance, missing information is not converted into failure or success, contradictory results remain visible, uncertainty is preserved, conditional findings remain conditional, determination scope cannot exceed executed scope, invalid execution portions do not silently contribute, aggregation remains methodologically justified, and every Validation Determination can be reconstructed from the validation record supporting it. Operational Role Validation Determination Standard serves as the formal conclusion layer of the VALIDOS® validation lifecycle. The preceding standards establish: Validation Object → Validation Purpose & Scope → Validation Criteria → Validation Method → Validation Evidence Fitness → Validation Source Reliability → Validation Execution VDTS then asks: What does that complete governed validation record actually demonstrate? Its structural progression is: Determination-Ready Execution → Result Qualification → Criterion Determination → Conflict & Uncertainty Integration → Cross-Criterion Interpretation → Overall Determination → Validation Determination Record The resulting determination can then progress into Validation State governance. Governance Scope Validation Determination Standard governs: validation-result qualification, determination basis, criterion-level determination, criterion satisfaction, criterion non-satisfaction, conditional satisfaction, non-determinability, mandatory criterion treatment, critical criterion treatment, cross-criterion interpretation, determination aggregation, determination hierarchy, contradictory findings, determination conflict, uncertainty integration, limitation integration, residual execution impact, evidence-condition propagation, source-condition propagation, determination scope, partial determination, conditional determination, negative determination, indeterminate determination, overall Validation Determination, determination authority where applicable, determination traceability, determination change, and determination reassessment. Validation Determination Basis A Validation Determination should be derived from a sufficiently governed determination basis. This may include: Validation Object reference, Validation Purpose, actual Validation Scope, Validation Depth, Validation Criteria, applicable thresholds, acceptance and rejection conditions, Validation Method Framework, Evidence Fitness information, Source Reliability information, Validation Execution Record, Execution Completeness status, Execution Conformity status, execution outputs, residual deviations, unresolved exceptions, limitations, conflicts, uncertainty, and Determination Readiness. The determination basis defines what information may legitimately support the validation conclusion. Determination-Ready Execution VDTS should consume only execution that is sufficiently ready for determination. This may include: Determination Ready or: Determination Conditionally Ready execution. Where execution is: Determination Not Ready or: Determination Blocked VDTS should not manufacture a substantive validation conclusion unsupported by the execution basis. Execution Quality and Object Outcome Are Different VALIDOS® maintains: Execution Conformity ≠ Validation Success A perfectly conformant validation may demonstrate that the Validation Object fails. Conversely: Execution Invalidity ≠ Object Invalidity Invalid execution may prevent VALIDOS® from knowing whether the object satisfies the Validation Criteria. VDTS therefore interprets object outcomes only from execution capable of legitimately supporting them. Validation Result Qualification Not every result generated during execution should automatically contribute to determination. A result may be: valid for determination, conditionally usable, limited in scope, superseded, affected by deviation, affected by unreliable source conditions, methodologically incomparable, or unusable. VDTS governs which execution results form the legitimate determination basis. Criterion Determination Every applicable Validation Criterion should receive an explicit determination where sufficient basis exists. Possible criterion-level outcomes may include: Criterion Satisfied The governed validation record sufficiently demonstrates satisfaction of the criterion under the applicable conditions. Criterion Conditionally Satisfied The criterion is satisfied only within explicit limitations, assumptions, boundaries, operating conditions, or other governed restrictions. Criterion Not Satisfied The governed validation record sufficiently demonstrates that the required criterion condition has not been satisfied. Criterion Not Determinable The governed validation record does not provide sufficient legitimate basis to determine whether the criterion is satisfied or not satisfied. These outcomes remain distinct. Not Determinable Is a Legitimate Outcome VALIDOS® establishes: Insufficient basis for determination ≠ Criterion failure and: Insufficient basis for determination ≠ Criterion satisfaction Where the validation record cannot legitimately answer the criterion question, the correct outcome is: Criterion Not Determinable This prevents uncertainty from being converted into false certainty. Criterion Satisfaction Criterion Satisfaction must remain connected to: the exact criterion, threshold where applicable, acceptance conditions, actual execution outputs, evidence, applicable source conditions, scope, object version, and relevant limitations. A satisfied criterion should therefore be reconstructable rather than asserted. Criterion Non-Satisfaction A criterion should be classified as Not Satisfied only where the governed validation record provides sufficient basis to demonstrate non-satisfaction. Absence of evidence is not automatically evidence of failure. Therefore: No Proof of Satisfaction ≠ Proof of Non-Satisfaction Conditional Criterion Determination A criterion may be satisfied only under conditions such as: defined operating range, limited population, specific system version, restricted environment, continued mitigation, additional monitoring, limited time period, or another governed boundary. Conditional determination must preserve those conditions. Mandatory Criteria Some Validation Criteria may be designated mandatory. Where a mandatory criterion is: Not Satisfied or in some validation contexts: Not Determinable the overall Validation Determination may be constrained regardless of favorable results elsewhere. The exact consequence must be established through the Validation Criteria governance structure. VDTS does not invent mandatory status retrospectively. Critical Criteria Certain criteria may be critical because failure has disproportionate consequence. A critical criterion should not be neutralized merely through favorable performance across many less important criteria. VALIDOS® therefore rejects blind averaging where materiality differs. Criterion Weighting Some validation frameworks may legitimately assign different significance to different criteria. Where weighting is used, VDTS requires that weighting be: established before outcome interpretation where reasonably possible, justified, traceable, methodologically relevant, and resistant to post-hoc manipulation. Weighting should not be altered merely because the resulting conclusion is inconvenient. Aggregation Is Not Averaging VALIDOS® establishes: Cross-Criterion Determination ≠ Arithmetic Average Different criteria may represent: mandatory conditions, critical conditions, supporting conditions, independent conditions, hierarchical conditions, conditional conditions, or exclusionary conditions. Aggregation must preserve their governance meaning. Cross-Criterion Interpretation VDTS determines how multiple criterion outcomes collectively contribute to the overall Validation Determination. Relevant questions may include: Are all mandatory criteria satisfied? Are any critical criteria not satisfied? Are material criteria not determinable? Do conditional outcomes restrict scope? Do criterion conflicts remain? Can partial validation be legitimately separated? Does one exclusionary condition override otherwise favorable findings? Determination Hierarchy Complex Validation Objects may require hierarchical determination. For example: Module Determination → Subsystem Determination → System Determination or: Criterion → Criterion Group → Validation Domain → Overall Determination VDTS permits hierarchical structure where the relationships remain explicit and methodologically justified. Partial Determination A Validation Object may support a legitimate conclusion for part of its Validation Scope while another part remains undetermined or fails. Where boundaries can be reliably separated, VDTS may permit: Partial Positive Determination Partial Negative Determination Partial Conditional Determination or: Partial Indeterminate Determination This prevents unnecessary all-or-nothing conclusions. Determination Scope Every Validation Determination must remain bounded to the scope actually supported by validation. The determination should not extend beyond: validated object version, tested population, evaluated environment, executed scenarios, applicable operational state, validated jurisdiction, or another material boundary. VALIDOS® establishes: Determination Scope ≤ Legitimately Executed Validation Scope Determination and Validation Depth The strength of a determination depends partly upon the Validation Depth achieved. A conclusion supported by exploratory validation should not automatically be represented as equivalent to one supported by high-assurance validation. VDTS therefore preserves the relationship between determination and achieved Validation Depth. Contradictory Findings Different execution results may support conflicting interpretations. VDTS requires material contradiction to remain visible. Contradiction may arise from: different methods, different environments, different populations, different object states, different evidence, different sources, measurement variation, or genuine object instability. Determination Conflict A Determination Conflict exists where legitimate validation findings support materially incompatible criterion or overall conclusions. Conflict may require: additional analysis, additional validation, method comparison, evidence review, source review, scope separation, conditional determination, or an indeterminate result. Conflict should not be resolved merely by selecting the preferred outcome. Uncertainty Integration Validation results may contain uncertainty arising from: evidence, measurement, methodology, source conditions, execution, sampling, population variability, object behavior, or unresolved conflict. VDTS integrates uncertainty into determination rather than hiding it. Uncertainty Does Not Automatically Block Determination Some uncertainty is compatible with legitimate validation. The relevant question is whether remaining uncertainty is acceptable for the applicable Validation Criterion, Purpose, Depth, and determination type. VDTS therefore supports proportionate uncertainty governance. Material Uncertainty Where uncertainty can reasonably change the criterion or overall conclusion, it becomes material. Material uncertainty may require: conditional determination, indeterminate determination, additional validation, narrower scope, or explicit limitation. Residual Execution Limitations Execution may be Determination Ready while carrying residual limitations. VDTS must preserve these limitations when interpreting results. A limitation cannot disappear merely because execution was allowed to proceed. Evidence Condition Propagation Evidence determined: Conditionally Fit may create corresponding limitations upon Validation Determination. The determination should not claim more than the evidence basis can support. Source Condition Propagation Similarly, Source Reliability restrictions may constrain how evidence is interpreted. For example: A source usable only with corroboration cannot become the sole unrestricted basis for a determination unless that condition was legitimately resolved. Determination Conditions An overall Validation Determination may be conditional. Conditions may include: restricted use, specific configuration, specific population, defined operating range, continued control, continued monitoring, limited time, supplementary validation, or another boundary. These conditions become important inputs to Validation State governance. Overall Validation Determination VDTS may establish overall determination classes such as: Positive Validation Determination The governed validation record sufficiently demonstrates satisfaction of the required Validation Criteria for the defined scope and conditions. Conditional Validation Determination The governed validation record supports a positive determination only within explicit conditions, limitations, restrictions, or reduced scope. Negative Validation Determination The governed validation record sufficiently demonstrates non-satisfaction of one or more criteria whose governance significance prevents a positive determination for the defined scope. Indeterminate Validation Determination The governed validation record does not provide sufficient legitimate basis to establish either a positive or negative overall determination. Partial Validation Determination Different governed portions of the Validation Object, criteria set, or Validation Scope legitimately support different determination outcomes. These classifications represent the validation conclusion. They are not yet the persistent Validation State. Positive Determination Is Not Reliance Authorization VALIDOS® establishes: Positive Validation Determination ≠ Authorization to Rely A system may receive a positive determination while reliance remains restricted because of: time, operational context, regulatory authority, risk, changed environment, or other governance conditions. Reliance belongs to the tenth Parent Standard. Negative Determination Is Not Universal Invalidity A Negative Validation Determination applies to the Validation Object, scope, criteria, version, and conditions actually assessed. It should not automatically be generalized to every use or future version. Indeterminate Determination Is Not Failure An Indeterminate Validation Determination means: VALIDOS® does not possess sufficient governed basis to establish the required conclusion. It does not automatically mean the object is valid. It does not automatically mean the object is invalid. This is a legitimate methodological outcome. Partial Determination A Partial Validation Determination may be necessary where: some criteria are satisfied, some criteria fail, some are indeterminate, some scope areas were not executed, or distinct components legitimately support different outcomes. Partial determination should preserve those boundaries explicitly. Determination Authority Where formal determination requires an identifiable authority, VDTS may govern: who or what may issue the determination, scope of determination authority, required independence, required competence, and authority conditions. VDTS does not create legal or regulatory authority where none exists. Human Determination A human may perform or approve a Validation Determination. Where material, relevant considerations may include: competence, assigned authority, independence, evidence access, methodological understanding, and conflict conditions. Automated Determination A Validation Determination may be partially or fully automated where governance permits. Automated determination may require: deterministic rules, governed aggregation logic, explicit criterion mapping, controlled thresholds, system identity, versioning, exception handling, and human escalation where required. Automation must not make determination logic opaque. AI-Assisted Determination AI may assist in: evidence synthesis, conflict detection, uncertainty identification, criterion mapping, traceability analysis, or determination drafting. However, the governing determination structure must remain reconstructable. AI-generated reasoning should not silently replace the approved determination logic. Determination Traceability A formal Validation Determination should be traceable through: Validation Object ↓ Validation Criteria ↓ Validation Method ↓ Evidence ↓ Sources ↓ Execution Activities ↓ Execution Outputs ↓ Criterion Determinations ↓ Overall Validation Determination This creates the conclusion chain of VALIDOS®. Validation Determination Record A formal Validation Determination Record may preserve: Determination Identifier, Validation Object, object version, Validation Purpose, actual Validation Scope, achieved Validation Depth, applicable Validation Criteria, criterion-level outcomes, mandatory criterion status, critical criterion status, execution basis, evidence basis, source conditions, conflicts, uncertainty, residual limitations, determination conditions, overall Validation Determination, determination authority where applicable, effective date, and sufficient traceability. Determination Basis Transparency The determination should permit a qualified reviewer to understand why the conclusion was reached. This does not require exposing confidential intellectual property or unrestricted internal reasoning. It requires sufficient methodological transparency to reconstruct the governed basis of the conclusion. Determination Change Governance A Validation Determination may require reassessment when: execution records change, evidence changes, Source Reliability changes, a previously unknown deviation is discovered, criterion interpretation is corrected, methodological error is identified, or another material validation fact changes. Determination Reassessment Possible outcomes may include: Determination Maintained Determination Modified Determination Restricted Determination Suspended Determination Reversed or: Determination Withdrawn Changes should not erase the historical determination. Determination Correction Where a determination error is identified, the correction should preserve: Original Determination → Identified Error → Corrected Determination → Reason This supports methodological accountability. Determination Suspension A determination may require temporary suspension where material uncertainty arises but final reassessment has not yet been completed. Suspension prevents continued representation of a potentially outdated conclusion as current. Determination Withdrawal A determination may be withdrawn where its methodological basis is materially destroyed. Possible triggers include: invalid execution, compromised evidence, major source failure, critical methodological error, wrong Validation Object, or another fundamental defect. Withdrawal concerns the determination. It does not by itself establish the object's current Validation State after reassessment. Determination Continuity Validation Determinations should remain historically connected across: corrections, revisions, revalidations, system updates, object versions, and later Validation States. This preserves the evolution of validation knowledge rather than presenting only the latest conclusion. Determination Is Not Validation State This boundary is fundamental. Validation Determination answers: What does this governed validation event demonstrate? Validation State answers: What formal validation condition does the Validation Object currently hold after considering the applicable determination, validity conditions, lifecycle status, and change? The eighth and ninth Parent Standards must therefore remain separate. Determination Is Not Reliance Similarly: Validation Determination ≠ Reliance Decision A valid determination can exist while no party is authorized to rely upon it operationally. Reliance depends upon: purpose, risk, authority, time, environment, conditions, intended use, and revalidation rules. Governance Boundary Validation Determination Standard begins when a sufficiently complete and conformant Validation Execution Record is ready for determination. It ends when the governed validation record has been interpreted into criterion-level findings and an overall Validation Determination with explicit scope, conditions, limitations, conflicts, uncertainty, and traceability. VDTS does not determine: persistent Validation State, Validation State expiration, operational reliance authorization, reliance transfer, revalidation triggers, or post-determination lifecycle governance. These responsibilities belong to subsequent VALIDOS® Parent Standards. Minimum Governance Requirements A conforming implementation of VDTS should establish: 1. an identifiable Validation Determination Basis, 2. determination-ready execution, 3. qualified execution results, 4. explicit criterion-level determinations, 5. treatment of mandatory and critical criteria, 6. explicit treatment of non-determinability, 7. governed aggregation or cross-criterion interpretation, 8. contradiction and conflict handling, 9. uncertainty integration, 10. propagation of material evidence, source, and execution limitations, 11. a bounded determination scope, 12. determination conditions and restrictions, 13. an overall Validation Determination, 14. determination traceability, 15. and a persistent Validation Determination Record. Governance Outputs VDTS may produce: Validation Determination Basis, Determination-Ready Result Set, Validation Result Qualification Record, Criterion Determination Record, Criterion Satisfaction Map, Criterion Non-Satisfaction Record, Conditional Criterion Determination, Criterion Not Determinable Record, Mandatory Criteria Determination, Critical Criteria Determination, Determination Conflict Record, Validation Uncertainty Record, Cross-Criterion Interpretation Record, Determination Aggregation Record, Partial Determination Record, Determination Scope Record, Determination Condition Record, Validation Determination, Validation Determination Record, Validation Determination Traceability Map, Determination Reassessment Trigger, Determination Change Record, Determination Suspension Record, Determination Withdrawal Record, and Determination Continuity Reference. Operational Applications Validation Determination Standard may be applied across: artificial intelligence, machine learning, autonomous systems, AI-generated outputs, software systems, datasets, predictions, simulations, scientific validation, healthcare, financial services, industrial systems, cybersecurity, critical infrastructure, regulatory environments, digital identities, operational governance, public-sector systems, and any governed environment requiring a formal validation conclusion. Relationship to Other OOF Architectures Validation Determination Standard interoperates with: GOA™ OBIDENITY® INTEGROS® ORA™ AGA™ AIG® CLIA® MGIA™ ASGA™ RIS™ by providing the canonical validation-governance methodology through which the complete governed validation record is transformed into a bounded and traceable Validation Determination. GOA™ may provide relevant determination authority and governance conditions. OBIDENITY® may preserve the identity and continuity of the Validation Object and related records. INTEGROS® may provide integrity conditions affecting evidence, records, and determination continuity. ORA™ may provide operational-reality context relevant to interpretation. AGA™ may establish accountability for determination roles and decisions. RIS™ may influence the strength of determination required for high-consequence validation. Specialized AI, cognition, memory, and autonomous-system architectures may provide domain-specific criteria and conditions consumed by VDTS. VDTS does not replace those architectures. It governs specifically what the completed validation process can legitimately conclude. Foundational Principle Validation results become a legitimate determination only when the conclusion remains bounded by what the governed validation record can actually demonstrate. Canonical Closing Statement Validation Determination Standard establishes the formal conclusion layer of VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture by transforming determination-ready execution results into criterion-level and overall Validation Determinations. Through governance of result qualification, criterion satisfaction, non-satisfaction, conditionality, non-determinability, mandatory and critical criteria, cross-criterion interpretation, conflict, uncertainty, aggregation, scope, limitations, partial determination, authority, traceability, reassessment, suspension, and withdrawal, VDTS ensures that validation conclusions cannot exceed the methodological strength, evidentiary basis, execution quality, or operational boundaries of the validation process from which they are derived. Validation Determination Standard Architecture: VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture Category: AI & Interpretation · Subcategory: Validation Governance Canonical Definition: Validation Determination Standard (VDTS) defines the governance conditions under which the complete governed validation record is evaluated, integrated, interpreted, bounded, and transformed into a formal Validation Determination establishing what the executed validation legitimately demonstrates about the Validation Object relative to the applicable Validation Criteria, thresholds, conditions, evidence, methodological limitations, execution conformity, uncertainty, conflicts, and approved Validation Scope. Governed Space: Validation Determination Validation results become a legitimate determination only when the conclusion remains bounded by what the governed validation record can actually demonstrate. → View Standard Module Architecture → Validation Determination Basis & Result Qualification Module (VDBRQM) → Validation Criterion Determination Module (VCDM) → Validation Determination Conflict & Uncertainty Governance Module (VDCUGM) → Validation Cross-Criterion Integration Module (VCCIM) → Overall Validation Determination Module (OVDM) Parent Resources → VALIDOS® Architecture Map → VALIDOS® Complete Standards & Modules Index → VALIDOS® — Four-Layer Validation Protocol™ Standards Compatibility → Validation Criteria Standard Operational compatibility within the governed validation lifecycle. → Validation Evidence Fitness Standard Operational compatibility within the governed validation lifecycle. → Validation Execution Standard Operational compatibility within the governed validation lifecycle. → Validation State Governance Standard Operational compatibility within the governed validation lifecycle. → Validation Reliance & Revalidation Standard Operational compatibility within the governed validation lifecycle. title: About Validation Evidence Fitness Standard
text: About Validation Evidence Fitness Standard About Validation Evidence Fitness Standard Governing Whether Evidence Is Fit for Validation Evidence exists everywhere. Data exists. Measurements exist. Documents exist. Observations exist. Test results exist. But the existence of evidence does not establish that the evidence is fit for validation. Validation Evidence Fitness Standard (VEFS) is the fifth Parent Standard of VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture, governing the conditions under which evidence becomes sufficiently relevant, applicable, complete, representative, timely, precise, and methodologically usable for a specific validation purpose. VEFS addresses one fundamental question: Is the available evidence actually fit for the validation question it is expected to answer? Why Validation Evidence Fitness Standard Exists Validation frequently relies upon evidence. However, evidence may be: accurate but irrelevant, relevant but incomplete, extensive but unrepresentative, precise but outdated, technically valid but contextually inapplicable, statistically significant but operationally insignificant, authoritative but incapable of answering the relevant Validation Criterion, or abundant while critical evidence remains missing. This creates an important distinction: Evidence Availability ≠ Evidence Fitness VEFS exists to govern that difference. Evidence After Method VALIDOS® establishes a deliberate architectural progression: Validation Object → Validation Purpose & Scope → Validation Criteria → Validation Method → Validation Evidence Fitness This sequence matters. Before determining whether evidence is fit, VALIDOS® must already know: what is being validated, why it is being validated, within which boundaries, against which criteria, and through which methodological approach. Only then can the architecture meaningfully ask: What evidence is required, and is the available evidence capable of supporting that validation? Evidence Must Answer a Validation Question Evidence does not become useful merely because it concerns the same general subject. A validation question creates an evidentiary requirement. The governing relationship is: Validation Criterion → Evidence Requirement → Candidate Evidence → Evidence Fitness For example, evidence showing that an AI model performs well under normal conditions does not necessarily answer a criterion concerning behavior under infrastructure failure. Likewise, evidence about one system version does not automatically validate another version. VEFS keeps evidence attached to the question it can legitimately answer. Evidence Fitness Is Contextual There is no universal category of permanently "good evidence." Evidence fitness depends upon its relationship to: the Validation Object, Validation Purpose, Validation Scope, Validation Criteria, Validation Method, Validation Depth, operational context, temporal conditions, and intended downstream reliance. The same evidence may therefore be highly fit for one validation and unusable for another. Relevance Before Volume Large evidence volumes can create an appearance of validation strength. But volume alone says little about whether the evidence addresses the actual Validation Criteria. One thousand irrelevant observations do not necessarily provide stronger validation than ten highly relevant observations. VALIDOS® therefore rejects the assumption: More Evidence = Stronger Validation VEFS instead asks whether additional evidence materially improves: criterion coverage, representativeness, precision, uncertainty reduction, contextual applicability, or evidentiary completeness. Evidence Applicability Relevant evidence may still be inapplicable. Evidence generated from: another population, another system configuration, another environment, another jurisdiction, another model version, another operating condition, another lifecycle stage, or another period cannot automatically be transferred to the current Validation Object. VEFS therefore governs the boundaries within which evidence can legitimately support validation. Evidence Completeness Evidence completeness does not mean collecting everything that can possibly be collected. It means that the material evidentiary requirements created by the Validation Criteria and Method Framework have been sufficiently addressed. A validation may contain thousands of evidence items and still contain a critical Evidence Gap. VEFS makes such gaps visible. Evidence Representativeness Evidence can be technically correct while systematically representing only favorable conditions. For example, an AI system may perform strongly across a large dataset while: important populations remain absent, rare conditions remain untested, difficult scenarios remain excluded, edge cases remain invisible, or deployment conditions differ materially from the evidence environment. VEFS therefore distinguishes evidence quantity from evidence representativeness. Evidence Across Time Evidence can age. A validation based upon evidence collected before: a model update, system modification, environmental change, operational drift, infrastructure change, new failure discovery, or significant contextual change may no longer support the same validation conclusion. VEFS therefore treats temporal applicability as a governed evidentiary condition. Precision and Resolution Matter Evidence may be too aggregated to reveal what matters. An average system-performance score may appear acceptable while concealing: subgroup failures, local instability, extreme events, temporal degradation, rare catastrophic behavior, or boundary-condition failures. VEFS asks whether evidence possesses sufficient precision and resolution for the Validation Criterion being examined. Contradictory Evidence Must Survive Validation becomes methodologically weak when unfavorable evidence disappears from the process. VEFS therefore requires material contradictory evidence to remain visible. Contradiction does not automatically invalidate the Validation Object. It may indicate: uncertainty, contextual differences, measurement differences, operational variability, methodological disagreement, or a genuine unresolved problem. The role of VEFS is not to force agreement. Its role is to ensure that relevant evidence is not removed simply because it complicates the conclusion. Evidence Gaps Are Governance Information Missing evidence is itself meaningful. An Evidence Gap may reveal that: a criterion cannot yet be evaluated, an important population has not been examined, a failure condition remains unknown, operational evidence is unavailable, historical records are incomplete, or required Validation Depth has not been achieved. VALIDOS® therefore does not automatically convert missing evidence into either validity or invalidity. It preserves the gap as a governed condition. Evidence Sufficiency Depends on Purpose Evidence sufficient for one decision may be insufficient for another. For example: Research Exploration may tolerate greater uncertainty than: Operational Deployment and operational deployment may require less evidence than: High-Consequence Autonomous Authorization where the consequences of error are materially greater. VEFS therefore connects evidence sufficiency to the Validation Purpose, Scope, Depth, and intended reliance. Evidence Fitness Is Not Source Reliability This is one of the most important architectural separations within VALIDOS®. Evidence Fitness asks: Can this evidence legitimately help answer the validation question? Source Reliability asks: Can the source from which that evidence originates be sufficiently trusted? These are different governance questions. A highly trustworthy source can provide evidence irrelevant to a particular validation. A highly relevant piece of evidence can originate from a source whose reliability remains uncertain. VALIDOS® therefore governs these spaces separately. Evidence Fitness Is Not Truth Validation VEFS does not determine whether every informational statement contained within evidence represents truth. Truth-oriented validation may exist as a specialized validation methodology or reference capability. VEFS performs a different architectural function. It determines whether evidence is fit for a governed validation role. This keeps VALIDOS® from collapsing validation governance into truth verification alone. Evidence Fitness Is Not Validation Determination Fit evidence does not mean that the Validation Object is valid. Evidence fitness establishes only that the evidence may legitimately contribute to the validation process. The later Validation Determination must evaluate what the complete governed validation record actually demonstrates. Therefore: Evidence Fit ≠ Object Validated Evidence Fitness Is Not Execution VEFS also does not determine whether evidence was actually collected, generated, processed, or evaluated according to the approved methodology. That belongs to Validation Execution governance. This allows VALIDOS® to ask two separate questions: Was the evidence appropriate? and: Was the validation process actually performed correctly using that evidence? Both conditions matter. Evidence Fitness States VEFS allows the evidence basis to be distinguished through governed conditions such as: Evidence Fit Evidence Conditionally Fit Evidence Fitness Undetermined Evidence Insufficient Evidence Unfit These conditions describe the evidentiary basis. They do not describe the Validation State of the Validation Object. This distinction prevents an evidence assessment from prematurely becoming a validity conclusion. Evidence Fitness Can Change Evidence fitness is not necessarily permanent. A previously fit evidence basis may require reassessment when: the Validation Object changes, the system version changes, Validation Criteria change, Validation Scope expands, Validation Depth increases, the operating environment changes, new contradictory evidence appears, evidence becomes outdated, or previously unknown limitations are discovered. VEFS therefore treats evidence fitness as a lifecycle condition. Position Within VALIDOS® Validation Evidence Fitness Standard is the fifth Parent Standard of VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture. Its architectural position is: Validation Object → Validation Purpose & Scope → Validation Criteria → Validation Method → Validation Evidence Fitness → Validation Source Reliability → Validation Execution → Validation Determination → Validation State → Validation Reliance & Revalidation The first four Parent Standards establish the validation question and methodological structure. VEFS establishes whether the evidentiary basis is capable of supporting that structure. The next Parent Standard can then ask whether the sources producing or providing that evidence are sufficiently reliable. Relationship to Other OOF® Architectures VEFS operates alongside complementary OOF® architectures. GOA™ may establish governance conditions affecting evidentiary authority and responsibility. OBIDENITY® may establish origin, identity, ownership, and provenance relationships. INTEGROS® may establish integrity conditions applicable to evidence. ORA™ may establish whether evidence corresponds to operational reality. AGA™ may establish accountability for evidence creation, handling, review, and use. AIG®, CLIA®, MGIA™, and ASGA™ may generate specialized evidence requirements for AI behavior, cognition, memory, and autonomous operation. RIS™ may influence required evidence depth according to risk and consequence. VEFS does not replace these architectures. It determines whether relevant evidence can legitimately perform its assigned role within validation. Why It Matters Without Evidence Fitness governance, validation can appear rigorous while relying upon evidence that does not actually support the conclusion. An organization may possess: large datasets, extensive testing, sophisticated analytics, expert reports, simulation results, audit records, and operational measurements and still lack evidence for one critical Validation Criterion. VEFS makes that difference visible. It transforms the question from: "Do we have evidence?" into: "Do we have the evidence required to legitimately answer this validation question?" That is a substantially stronger governance question. From Evidence Collection to Evidence Governance Traditional processes may focus heavily on collecting evidence. VALIDOS® adds another layer: Evidence must be governed before it can be relied upon for validation. This creates a structured transition: Evidence Requirement → Evidence Identification → Evidence Qualification → Evidence Coverage → Evidence Gap Analysis → Evidence Fitness Determination The result is not merely an evidence repository. It is a governed evidentiary basis. Foundational Principle Evidence is not validation evidence merely because it exists; it becomes validation evidence when it is fit for the question it is expected to answer. Canonical Closing Statement Validation Evidence Fitness Standard establishes the evidence-qualification layer of VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture. By distinguishing evidence availability from evidence fitness and governing relevance, applicability, completeness, representativeness, timeliness, precision, contradiction, sufficiency, limitations, gaps, change, and traceability, VEFS ensures that validation cannot derive legitimacy merely from the existence, quantity, or apparent authority of evidence. Evidence becomes methodologically usable within VALIDOS® only when it is demonstrably fit for the specific validation question it is expected to answer.
