title: Validation Evidence Relevance Module (VERM)
text: Validation Evidence Relevance Module (VERM) Validation Evidence Relevance Module (VERM) Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Validation Evidence Fitness Standard (VEFS) Operational Layer: Validation Evidence Fitness Governance Layer Category: AI & Interpretation Subcategory: Validation Governance Type: Parent Standard Module Governed Space: Validation Evidence Relevance Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 9 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · OBIDENITY® · INTEGROS® · ORA™ · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Governed Space Validation Evidence Relevance Canonical Definition Validation Evidence Relevance Module (VERM) defines the governance framework for determining whether candidate evidence possesses a sufficiently direct, meaningful, and methodologically defensible relationship to the specific Validation Object, Validation Criterion, evidence requirement, Validation Method, Validation Purpose, and Validation Scope for which it is intended to provide validation support. It establishes the conditions under which available information may be recognized as Relevant Validation Evidence rather than merely information associated with the general subject of validation. Operational Role VERM serves as the first evidence-qualification gate within the Validation Evidence Fitness Standard. Its primary question is: Does this evidence actually address the validation question for which it is being considered? The governed progression is: Evidence Requirement → Candidate Evidence → Relevance Relationship → Relevance Assessment → Relevant Validation Evidence VERM does not determine whether the evidence is sufficient, complete, representative, timely, or reliable. It determines whether the evidence has a legitimate reason to participate in the validation at all. Module Operational Space VERM governs: evidence relevance, evidence-to-object relevance, evidence-to-criterion relevance, evidence-to-requirement relevance, evidence-to-method relevance, evidence-to-purpose relevance, evidence-to-scope relevance, direct relevance, indirect relevance, supporting relevance, contextual relevance, relevance strength, relevance boundaries, relevance conditions, relevance limitations, relevance conflicts, irrelevant evidence exclusion, relevance change, and relevance traceability. Module Function VERM applies when evidence has been identified as potentially useful to a governed validation. Its function is to prevent: evidence being included merely because it concerns the same general topic, large evidence volumes creating artificial validation confidence, technically sophisticated evidence being assumed relevant, authoritative documents being treated as evidence for questions they do not answer, evidence supporting one criterion being silently transferred to another, evidence about one Validation Object being attributed to another, contextual association being mistaken for direct evidentiary support, supporting evidence being represented as determinative evidence, and irrelevant evidence obscuring material Evidence Gaps. Candidate Evidence A Candidate Evidence Item is any information, observation, measurement, record, dataset, result, document, trace, analysis, or other material proposed for use within validation. Candidate status does not establish relevance. The evidence must first be connected to an identifiable validation requirement. The governing relationship is: Validation Criterion → Evidence Requirement → Candidate Evidence Only then can relevance be meaningfully assessed. Evidence-to-Object Relevance Evidence must relate to the Validation Object established within VALIDOS®. VERM examines whether the evidence concerns: the actual object, the relevant object component, the applicable object version, the appropriate configuration, the relevant operational state, or another materially connected representation. Evidence about a similar object does not automatically constitute evidence about the Validation Object. Evidence-to-Criterion Relevance The strongest relevance relationship exists when evidence directly contributes to examination of a defined Validation Criterion. VERM asks: Which criterion does this evidence support? What characteristic does it reveal? What validation condition does it help examine? What would be lost if this evidence were removed? Does it materially affect the ability to evaluate the criterion? Evidence without an identifiable criterion relationship should not automatically enter the qualified evidence basis. Evidence-to-Requirement Relevance A Validation Criterion may create several specific evidence requirements. Evidence may therefore be relevant not merely to the criterion generally, but to a particular evidentiary need. For example: Criterion: System remains stable under infrastructure degradation. Possible evidence requirements may include: degraded-network observations, failover logs, recovery-time measurements, operational-state transitions, or failure-response records. A normal-operation performance report may concern the same system but remain irrelevant to these specific requirements. Evidence-to-Method Relevance Evidence must also be usable by, produced through, or interpretable within the applicable Validation Method where required. A method may require: quantitative measurements, observational records, structured datasets, controlled experimental results, simulation outputs, expert findings, or another evidence form. Evidence may therefore be relevant to the criterion but unusable within the selected methodological pathway. VERM keeps this relationship visible. Evidence-to-Purpose Relevance Evidence relevance can change according to Validation Purpose. Evidence suitable for: research exploration may not provide meaningful support for: deployment authorization. Likewise, evidence useful for: performance comparison may be irrelevant to: safety validation. VERM therefore evaluates relevance relative to the actual reason validation is being performed. Evidence-to-Scope Relevance Validation Scope establishes where the validation conclusion is intended to apply. VERM determines whether evidence falls within or legitimately contributes to that scope. Evidence outside the approved scope may still provide contextual information. However, contextual usefulness must not automatically be represented as direct validation support. Direct Evidence Relevance Evidence has Direct Relevance when it directly observes, measures, demonstrates, tests, or otherwise informs the condition represented by a Validation Criterion. Examples may include: measured system behavior, direct test results, operational observations, controlled experimental outcomes, or records directly documenting the condition under examination. Direct relevance does not automatically establish evidence sufficiency or reliability. Indirect Evidence Relevance Evidence has Indirect Relevance when it contributes to understanding a Validation Criterion through an inferential relationship rather than direct observation. Indirect evidence may be legitimate. However, the inferential relationship must remain visible. Indirect evidence must not silently be represented as direct evidence. Supporting Evidence Some evidence does not independently establish a validation condition but strengthens interpretation of other evidence. Supporting evidence may: provide context, explain an observation, corroborate a relationship, identify environmental conditions, establish chronology, or support methodological interpretation. VERM allows supporting evidence while preserving its actual role. Contextual Evidence Contextual evidence may be important without directly supporting a Validation Criterion. For example, information concerning: operating environment, organizational conditions, external events, system dependencies, or regulatory circumstances may help explain validation evidence. VERM distinguishes: Evidence that validates from: Evidence that helps interpret validation. This prevents contextual information from artificially increasing perceived evidentiary strength. Relevance Strength Where useful, evidence relevance may be characterized according to the strength of its relationship to the validation requirement. Possible classifications may include: Directly Relevant Materially Relevant Supporting Contextual Marginal Irrelevant These classifications do not represent evidence quality. They describe the nature and strength of the relevance relationship. Relevance Boundaries Relevant evidence should remain bounded to the condition it can legitimately support. For example: Evidence demonstrating system performance at temperatures between 10°C and 30°C may be relevant within that operating range. It should not automatically support conclusions concerning operation at −20°C. VERM therefore prevents relevance from expanding beyond the conditions represented by the evidence. Relevance Transfer Evidence may sometimes be transferred between: versions, configurations, environments, populations, jurisdictions, or related Validation Objects. Transfer requires an identifiable methodological basis. Similarity alone does not establish transferable relevance. Where material differences exist, evidence may become: conditionally relevant, contextually relevant, or irrelevant. Relevance and Correlation Evidence may correlate with a Validation Criterion without directly demonstrating it. VERM therefore distinguishes correlation from evidentiary relevance sufficient for a specific inference. For example: A system's historical reliability may be relevant to a reliability assessment. It does not necessarily prove future reliability under materially changed operating conditions. The inference boundary must remain visible. Relevance Conflict Different evaluators or methodologies may disagree about whether evidence is relevant. VERM requires material relevance disagreement to remain visible. A relevance conflict may require: methodological review, criterion clarification, scope clarification, additional evidence, or later governance escalation. Evidence should not be silently excluded merely because its implications are inconvenient. Irrelevant Evidence Exclusion Evidence determined to be irrelevant should not contribute to validation confidence. However, exclusion should remain traceable where the evidence was materially considered. This allows later review to determine: what was excluded, why it was excluded, which criterion was considered, and whether the exclusion remained justified. Evidence Volume and Relevance VERM establishes: Evidence volume cannot compensate for lack of relevance. One hundred irrelevant evidence items do not collectively become relevant. Likewise, repeated evidence supporting one criterion does not compensate for missing evidence supporting another material criterion. This principle protects validation from evidentiary inflation. Relevance Before Sufficiency VERM establishes an important sequencing rule: Relevance should be established before evidence sufficiency is assessed. It is methodologically weak to ask: Do we have enough evidence? before determining: Does this evidence actually answer the validation question? Only relevant evidence should contribute meaningfully to later sufficiency and completeness assessments. Relevance Status Candidate evidence may receive a relevance classification such as: Relevant The evidence possesses a sufficiently meaningful relationship to the defined validation requirement. Conditionally Relevant The evidence is relevant only under specified assumptions, contexts, boundaries, or inferential conditions. Relevance Undetermined Available information is insufficient to establish relevance. Irrelevant The evidence does not materially contribute to the defined validation requirement. These statuses remain attached to the specific evidence-to-validation relationship. Relevance Is Relationship-Specific VALIDOS® establishes: Evidence relevance is not a universal property of evidence. The same evidence item may be: Relevant to Criterion A, Supporting to Criterion B, and: Irrelevant to Criterion C. Relevance must therefore be represented as a relationship rather than a permanent label attached to the evidence itself. Relevance Change Governance Evidence relevance may change when: the Validation Object changes, Validation Criteria change, Validation Purpose changes, Validation Scope changes, Validation Method changes, object configuration changes, new contextual information emerges, or the evidentiary relationship is better understood. Material relevance changes must remain traceable. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Establish Evidence Requirement Identify the specific Validation Criterion and evidentiary requirement the candidate evidence is expected to support. 2. Identify Candidate Evidence Establish the evidence item or evidence body proposed for validation use. 3. Establish Relevance Relationship Determine its relationship to: Validation Object, Validation Criterion, evidence requirement, Validation Method, Validation Purpose, and Validation Scope. 4. Classify Relevance Type Where applicable, distinguish: direct, indirect, supporting, contextual, conditional, or irrelevant evidence. 5. Establish Relevance Boundary Determine the conditions within which the evidence remains relevant and prevent unsupported transfer beyond those conditions. 6. Establish Relevance Status Classify the evidence as: Relevant, Conditionally Relevant, Relevance Undetermined, or Irrelevant. 7. Preserve Relevance Traceability Maintain: Evidence Identifier, Validation Object reference, Validation Criterion reference, evidence requirement, relevance type, relevance rationale, applicable boundaries, conditions, limitations, conflicts, relevance status, version, changes, and sufficient lifecycle traceability. Relevance Output VERM may produce: Evidence Relevance Record, Evidence-to-Criterion Map, Evidence Requirement Link, Relevance Classification, Relevance Boundary, Conditional Relevance Record, Relevance Conflict Record, Irrelevant Evidence Exclusion Record, and Evidence Relevance Determination. These outputs become inputs into subsequent Evidence Fitness governance. Use Case 1 — AI Safety Validation Scenario An organization provides extensive benchmark-performance results as evidence that an AI system is safe for autonomous operation. Application VERM maps the benchmark evidence against the Validation Criteria. The results are directly relevant to performance criteria but provide only limited or no direct relevance to several autonomous safety criteria. Result The benchmark evidence remains valid evidence for the conditions it actually addresses, but it cannot be used to create artificial coverage of unrelated safety requirements. Use Case 2 — Healthcare AI Scenario A diagnostic AI system is intended for deployment across multiple patient populations. Evidence comes primarily from one population. Application VERM determines that the evidence is directly relevant to performance within the represented population but only conditionally relevant to other materially different populations. Result The evidence cannot silently be generalized across the complete Validation Scope. Architectural Position Validation Evidence Relevance is the first internal governance space of the Validation Evidence Fitness Standard (VEFS). It establishes the first transformation: Available Information → Candidate Evidence → Relevant Validation Evidence Subsequent Evidence Fitness governance can then determine whether that relevant evidence is sufficiently applicable, complete, representative, timely, and otherwise fit for the governed validation role. Foundational Principle Evidence cannot support a validation question that it does not meaningfully address. Canonical Closing Statement Validation Evidence Relevance Module establishes the first evidence-qualification gate within VALIDOS® by governing the relationship between candidate evidence and the validation question it is expected to support. By governing object relevance, criterion relevance, requirement relevance, methodological relevance, purpose and scope alignment, direct and indirect support, contextual contribution, relevance boundaries, transfer, conflict, exclusion, change, and traceability, VERM ensures that evidence enters validation because it meaningfully addresses a governed validation requirement—not merely because it exists, appears authoritative, or concerns the same general subject. title: Validation Evidence Fitness Standard
text: Validation Evidence Fitness Standard Validation Evidence Fitness Standard Standard ID: VEFS OriginID: OOF-OID-AI-VALIDOS-VEFS-2026-08-09-0005 Architecture: VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture Category: AI & Interpretation Subcategory: Validation Governance Type: Parent Standard Governed Space: Validation Evidence Fitness Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 9 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · OBIDENITY® · INTEGROS® · ORA™ · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Canonical Definition Validation Evidence Fitness Standard (VEFS) defines the governance conditions under which evidence intended to support validation is identified, qualified, assessed, bounded, and determined to be sufficiently relevant, applicable, complete, representative, timely, precise, and methodologically usable for the specific Validation Object, Validation Criteria, Validation Method, Validation Purpose, Validation Scope, and required Validation Depth. Canonical Definition Extension Validation cannot legitimately progress from methodology toward determination merely because evidence exists. Evidence may be authentic yet irrelevant. Evidence may be accurate yet incomplete. Evidence may be extensive yet unrepresentative. Evidence may be technically valid yet outdated. Evidence may be reliable within one environment yet inapplicable to another. Evidence may support one Validation Criterion while providing no meaningful support for another. Evidence existence therefore does not establish evidence fitness. Validation Evidence Fitness Standard governs the methodological relationship between available evidence and the validation question that evidence is expected to support. The standard establishes the conditions necessary to determine: what evidence is required, what evidence is available, which Validation Criteria the evidence can legitimately support, whether the evidence is relevant, whether it is applicable to the Validation Object, whether its temporal state remains appropriate, whether its coverage is sufficient, whether it is representative of the governed conditions, whether its precision and resolution are adequate, whether material evidence gaps remain, whether contradictory evidence exists, whether the evidence is methodologically usable, and whether the complete evidence basis is sufficiently fit to progress within validation. VEFS does not determine whether the originating source is trustworthy. It does not determine whether validation was correctly executed. It does not determine the final validity of the Validation Object. VEFS determines whether the evidence itself is fit for the validation role it is expected to perform. Core Question Is the available evidence sufficiently relevant, applicable, complete, representative, timely, precise, and methodologically usable to support the governed validation question? Purpose The purpose of Validation Evidence Fitness Standard is to prevent the existence, quantity, authority, technical sophistication, or apparent strength of evidence from being confused with its fitness for a particular validation. The standard prevents validation from relying upon: irrelevant evidence, insufficient evidence, incomplete evidence, outdated evidence, unrepresentative evidence, contextually inapplicable evidence, excessively aggregated evidence, selectively chosen evidence, evidence incapable of supporting the relevant Validation Criterion, or evidence whose limitations are materially inconsistent with the intended Validation Determination. VEFS establishes the evidence-quality governance layer required before evidence can legitimately support subsequent validation execution and determination. Governance Objective VEFS establishes a governed Validation Evidence Fitness Framework capable of determining whether evidence is sufficiently fit for its intended validation role. The standard seeks to ensure that: evidence requirements are explicit, evidence remains connected to Validation Criteria, evidence relevance is assessable, evidence applicability is bounded, evidence coverage is visible, evidence completeness is assessable, representativeness is governed, temporal validity is considered, precision and resolution are proportionate, contradictory evidence remains visible, evidence gaps remain explicit, evidence limitations remain traceable, evidence fitness can be determined, and evidence is not used beyond the conditions it can legitimately support. Operational Role Validation Evidence Fitness Standard serves as the evidence qualification stage of the VALIDOS® validation governance lifecycle. The preceding standards establish: Validation Object → Validation Purpose & Scope → Validation Criteria → Validation Method VEFS establishes: What evidence is sufficiently fit to support those governed validation conditions and methods? Its architectural progression is: Validation Method Framework → Evidence Requirements → Evidence Identification → Evidence Fitness Assessment → Evidence Gap Analysis → Evidence Fitness Determination → Qualified Validation Evidence The resulting qualified evidence basis can then progress into subsequent source-reliability and execution governance. Governance Scope Validation Evidence Fitness Standard governs: validation evidence requirements, evidence identification, evidence relevance, evidence applicability, evidence coverage, evidence completeness, evidence representativeness, evidence timeliness, evidence recency, evidence precision, evidence resolution, evidence granularity, evidence consistency, contradictory evidence visibility, evidence sufficiency, evidence limitations, evidence gaps, evidence fitness, evidence fitness conditions, evidence fitness change, and evidence-fitness traceability. Validation Evidence Governance Model VEFS establishes the following structural progression: Validation Requirement → Evidence Requirement → Candidate Evidence → Evidence Qualification → Evidence Coverage → Evidence Gap Analysis → Evidence Fitness Determination → Qualified Validation Evidence This progression separates the existence of information from its legitimate use as validation evidence. Validation Evidence For the purposes of VALIDOS®, Validation Evidence may include information, observations, measurements, records, test results, datasets, documents, operational traces, experimental results, simulation outputs, expert findings, audit records, system logs, physical observations, statistical results, or other evidentiary material capable of contributing to examination of a Validation Criterion. Evidence type alone does not establish fitness. The relationship between the evidence and the governed validation question must be established. Evidence Requirements Evidence requirements originate from the Validation Criteria Framework and Validation Method Framework. They may specify: required evidence type, required observation, required measurement, required population, required environment, required temporal period, required resolution, required precision, required coverage, required quantity, required diversity, required independence, or another material evidentiary condition. Evidence collection without an identifiable evidentiary requirement may produce information without producing useful validation evidence. Evidence-to-Criterion Alignment Every material item or body of Validation Evidence should have an identifiable relationship to one or more Validation Criteria. The governed relationship is: Validation Criterion → Evidence Requirement → Validation Evidence VEFS prevents evidence from being treated as supportive merely because it appears relevant to the general subject. Evidence must contribute meaningfully to the actual condition being evaluated. Evidence Relevance Evidence is relevant where it materially contributes to examination of a defined Validation Criterion or validation condition. Relevance may depend upon: the characteristic examined, the Validation Object, the Validation Purpose, the Validation Scope, the applicable criterion, and the methodological role of the evidence. Evidence that does not materially inform the governed validation question should not increase validation confidence merely because it is extensive or technically sophisticated. Evidence Applicability Evidence may be relevant but not applicable. Applicability asks whether evidence generated under one set of conditions can legitimately support conclusions about the actual Validation Object and governed validation context. Material applicability dimensions may include: object version, system configuration, population, operating environment, jurisdiction, language, lifecycle stage, deployment context, scale, and temporal conditions. Evidence transfer across materially different conditions requires justification. Evidence Completeness Evidence completeness concerns whether the evidence basis sufficiently addresses the evidentiary requirements established for the validation. Completeness does not require unlimited evidence. It requires sufficient coverage of material evidentiary needs relative to the Validation Purpose, Scope, Depth, Criteria, and Method. A large evidence volume can remain incomplete if a critical validation condition lacks evidence. Evidence Representativeness Evidence may be extensive but systematically unrepresentative. VEFS therefore governs whether evidence sufficiently represents the conditions about which validation conclusions are expected to apply. Representativeness may concern: populations, operating environments, scenarios, user groups, geographic conditions, temporal conditions, system states, failure conditions, edge cases, or other validation-relevant dimensions. Representativeness requirements must correspond to the approved Validation Scope. Evidence Timeliness Evidence may lose fitness over time. VEFS assesses whether evidence remains sufficiently current for the Validation Object and validation purpose. Timeliness may depend upon: object change, model updates, environmental change, regulatory change, operational drift, new data, infrastructure change, or elapsed time. Older evidence is not automatically invalid. Its continuing applicability must be governable. Evidence Precision and Resolution Some validation questions require evidence at a particular degree of precision or granularity. Highly aggregated evidence may conceal: subgroup failures, rare events, local deviations, temporal instability, boundary conditions, or other material differences. VEFS determines whether evidence resolution is proportionate to the condition being validated. Evidence Quantity and Evidence Quality VALIDOS® rejects the assumption: More Evidence = Stronger Validation Evidence quantity may improve validation only where additional evidence contributes meaningful: coverage, representativeness, precision, uncertainty reduction, independence, or corroboration. Duplicated, redundant, irrelevant, or highly correlated evidence should not artificially increase validation confidence. Evidence Consistency Multiple evidence items may support different interpretations. VEFS requires material inconsistency to remain visible. Evidence inconsistency may arise from: different operating conditions, different populations, different methods, measurement variation, temporal change, object change, data quality differences, or genuine uncertainty. Inconsistency is not automatically evidence failure. It may itself be validation-relevant information. Contradictory Evidence Evidence contradicting a favorable validation conclusion must not be silently excluded solely because other evidence appears stronger. Material contradictory evidence should remain identifiable and traceable into subsequent validation governance. VEFS does not determine which conflicting evidence ultimately governs the Validation Determination. It ensures that relevant contradiction survives the evidence qualification process. Evidence Gaps An Evidence Gap exists where a material evidentiary requirement cannot be sufficiently supported by available qualified evidence. Evidence gaps may concern: missing observations, missing populations, missing operating conditions, insufficient temporal coverage, missing failure scenarios, insufficient precision, unavailable historical records, or another required evidentiary condition. A gap must not be concealed by unrelated evidence volume. Evidence Sufficiency Evidence sufficiency is contextual. Evidence sufficient for: preliminary validation may be insufficient for: high-consequence operational reliance. VEFS therefore assesses sufficiency relative to: Validation Purpose, Validation Scope, Validation Depth, Validation Criteria, Validation Method, risk and consequence where applicable, and intended downstream reliance. Evidence Limitations Qualified evidence may still contain limitations. Examples include: limited population coverage, restricted operational range, low sample size, limited observation period, incomplete edge-case coverage, measurement uncertainty, insufficient granularity, or constrained transferability. Material limitations must remain connected to the evidence throughout subsequent VALIDOS® governance. Evidence Fitness Determination VEFS may establish evidence fitness conditions such as: Evidence Fit The evidence is sufficiently fit for the defined validation role. Evidence Conditionally Fit The evidence may support validation only under explicit conditions, limitations, or bounded applicability. Evidence Fitness Undetermined Available information is insufficient to determine whether the evidence is fit. Evidence Insufficient Material evidence requirements remain unsupported. Evidence Unfit The evidence cannot legitimately perform the proposed validation role. These conditions apply to the evidence basis. They do not represent the Validation State of the Validation Object. Evidence Fitness Is Role-Specific Evidence fitness is not a permanent universal property. The same evidence may be: Fit for one Validation Criterion, Conditionally Fit for another, and: Unfit for a third. Evidence fitness must therefore remain connected to its specific validation role. Evidence Fitness and Source Reliability VALIDOS® maintains a strict architectural separation: Evidence Fitness ≠ Source Reliability Evidence Fitness asks: Is this evidence suitable for answering this validation question? Source Reliability asks: Can the origin, provenance, independence, authenticity, and reliability of the source providing or producing that evidence be sufficiently trusted? Evidence can be highly relevant but originate from an unreliable source. Evidence can also originate from an authoritative source while being irrelevant to the validation question. Both governance spaces are therefore required. Evidence Fitness and Validation Method VALIDOS® also distinguishes: Method = How the condition is examined. Evidence = What informational basis supports that examination. A suitable method applied to unfit evidence can produce weak validation. Fit evidence processed through an unsuitable method can also produce weak validation. VALIDOS® governs these conditions separately so that one cannot silently compensate for failure in the other. Evidence Fitness and Execution VEFS does not establish whether evidence was actually collected, generated, processed, or interpreted according to the approved Validation Method Framework. That responsibility belongs to subsequent Validation Execution governance. VEFS establishes the conditions under which evidence is capable of legitimate validation use. Evidence Change Governance Evidence fitness may change because of: Validation Object change, new object version, changed Validation Scope, changed criteria, changed method, new evidence, contradictory evidence, changed operating environment, elapsed time, discovered evidence limitation, or improved evidentiary understanding. Material changes require proportionate evidence-fitness reassessment. Evidence Traceability Qualified Validation Evidence should remain traceable to: the Validation Object, Validation Criterion, evidence requirement, Validation Method where applicable, evidence type, applicability conditions, temporal conditions, material limitations, fitness determination, and subsequent use. This creates the evidentiary continuity necessary for reconstructable validation. Governance Boundary Validation Evidence Fitness Standard begins when established Validation Criteria and Validation Methods create identifiable evidence requirements. It ends when the relevant evidence basis has been sufficiently identified, qualified, assessed, bounded, and classified for fitness to support subsequent VALIDOS® governance. VEFS does not determine: Validation Object identity, Validation Purpose or Scope, Validation Criteria, Validation Method suitability, source trustworthiness, source provenance, validation execution conformity, final Validation Determination, Validation State, reliance authorization, or revalidation requirements. These responsibilities belong to other VALIDOS® Parent Standards or interoperating governance architectures. Minimum Governance Requirements A conforming implementation of VEFS should establish: 1. identifiable evidence requirements, 2. traceable relationships between Validation Criteria and evidence, 3. evidence relevance assessment, 4. evidence applicability assessment, 5. evidence coverage and completeness assessment, 6. representativeness assessment where applicable, 7. temporal fitness assessment, 8. sufficient precision and resolution, 9. explicit material evidence limitations, 10. explicit evidence gaps, 11. visibility of material contradictory evidence, 12. an Evidence Fitness Determination, 13. and sufficient evidence-fitness traceability throughout the validation lifecycle. Governance Outputs VEFS may produce: Validation Evidence Requirements Record, Validation Evidence Register, Criteria-to-Evidence Map, Evidence Relevance Assessment, Evidence Applicability Assessment, Evidence Coverage Map, Evidence Completeness Assessment, Evidence Representativeness Assessment, Evidence Timeliness Assessment, Evidence Precision Assessment, Evidence Limitation Record, Evidence Contradiction Record, Evidence Gap Register, Evidence Sufficiency Assessment, Evidence Fitness Determination, Qualified Validation Evidence Record, Evidence Fitness Change Record. These outputs provide the governed evidentiary basis required for subsequent VALIDOS® validation governance. Operational Applications Validation Evidence Fitness Standard may be applied across: artificial intelligence, machine learning, autonomous systems, AI-generated outputs, claims and information, datasets, predictions, simulations, analytical systems, decision systems, scientific validation, enterprise systems, financial services, healthcare, industrial operations, regulatory compliance, critical infrastructure, digital assets, digital identities, operational governance, and any governed environment requiring evidence-based validation. Relationship to Other OOF Architectures Validation Evidence Fitness Standard interoperates with: GOA™ OBIDENITY® INTEGROS® ORA™ AGA™ AIG® CLIA® MGIA™ ASGA™ RIS™ by providing the canonical validation-governance methodology for determining whether evidence originating from or relating to complementary governance spaces is sufficiently fit for the validation role it is expected to perform. VEFS does not replace evidence provenance, identity, integrity, accountability, operational reality, risk, audit, or domain- specific evidentiary requirements. It governs the methodological fitness of evidence for validation. Foundational Principle Evidence is not validation evidence merely because it exists; it becomes validation evidence when it is fit for the question it is expected to answer. Canonical Closing Statement Validation Evidence Fitness Standard establishes the canonical evidence-qualification layer of VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture. By governing evidence requirements, relevance, applicability, coverage, completeness, representativeness, timeliness, precision, consistency, contradiction, sufficiency, limitations, gaps, fitness, change, and traceability, VEFS ensures that validation conclusions cannot derive legitimacy merely from the existence or volume of evidence, but only from evidence demonstrably fit for the specific Validation Object, Criteria, Method, Purpose, Scope, and required Validation Depth to which it is applied. Validation Evidence Fitness Standard Architecture: VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture Category: AI & Interpretation · Subcategory: Validation Governance Canonical Definition: Validation Evidence Fitness Standard (VEFS) defines the governance conditions under which evidence intended to support validation is identified, qualified, assessed, bounded, and determined to be sufficiently relevant, applicable, complete, representative, timely, precise, and methodologically usable for the specific Validation Object, Validation Criteria, Validation Method, Validation Purpose, Validation Scope, and required Validation Depth. title: About Validation Execution Standard
text: About Validation Execution Standard About Validation Execution Standard Governing the Difference Between Validation Designed and Validation Actually Performed A validation methodology can be excellent. The criteria can be precise. The evidence can be fit. The sources can be reliable. And the validation can still fail methodologically if the required validation process was not actually performed as governed. Validation Execution Standard (VEXS) is the seventh Parent Standard of VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture, governing the operational transition from an approved validation design to demonstrable validation activity. VEXS addresses one fundamental question: Was the approved validation process actually performed as governed? Why Validation Execution Standard Exists Validation does not occur because a methodology exists. It occurs when that methodology is applied to a specific Validation Object under actual operational conditions. Between: What should happen and: What actually happened there may be substantial differences. A validation process may: skip required steps, examine the wrong object version, use different evidence, operate outside the approved scope, substitute instruments, change environmental conditions, alter sequencing, experience interruptions, introduce manual interventions, or fail to preserve sufficient execution records. Without execution governance, a later validation result may appear methodologically legitimate even though the process producing it materially departed from the approved validation structure. VEXS exists to make that difference governable. Validation Design Is Not Validation Execution VALIDOS® deliberately separates: Validation Method from: Validation Execution Validation Method asks: How should validation be performed? Validation Execution asks: What was actually performed? This distinction is fundamental. A method is a governed design. Execution is its operational realization. Therefore: Approved Method ≠ Executed Validation From Methodology to Operational Reality Before VEXS, VALIDOS® has established: Validation Object Validation Purpose & Scope Validation Criteria Validation Method Validation Evidence Fitness Validation Source Reliability Together, these define the governed validation basis. VEXS moves that structure into operational reality. The lifecycle becomes: Validation Design → Execution Basis → Execution Authorization → Execution Instance → Actual Validation Activity → Execution Record Only after this transition can VALIDOS® legitimately ask what the validation demonstrated. The Correct Object Must Be Executed Against Validation must remain attached to the object it was designed to examine. If validation was approved for: Object Version 3.2 but execution occurs against: Object Version 3.4 the difference may be material. Likewise, changes in: configuration, system state, dependencies, environment, operating mode, or object boundaries may change what was actually validated. VEXS therefore preserves Validation Object continuity throughout execution. Scope Must Survive Execution A Validation Scope defined during planning can change during actual execution. Some areas may become unavailable. Tests may be omitted. Additional areas may be examined. Conditions may force narrower coverage. VEXS makes these changes explicit. A later Validation Determination should never claim a scope broader than the validation activity actually performed. Criteria Must Become Activities Validation Criteria are not operationally meaningful merely because they appear in a validation document. They must be connected to actual validation activities. VEXS therefore asks: Which criteria were actually evaluated? Through which activities? Using which evidence? Under which conditions? Were any criteria omitted? VEXS does not yet decide whether those criteria were satisfied. It establishes that the required evaluation actually occurred. Planned Execution and Actual Execution VALIDOS® creates an explicit distinction between: Planned Execution and: Actual Execution This allows the validation process to compare: Expected Activity → Actual Activity rather than assuming they are identical. Where material differences exist, they become governed Execution Deviations. Execution Conditions Matter Validation does not occur in abstraction. It occurs under conditions. These may include: physical environment, digital environment, system configuration, network conditions, operational load, population, geographic context, human involvement, available tools, simulation settings, or system state. If those conditions materially differ from those required by the Validation Method, the difference may affect execution legitimacy. VEXS therefore makes execution conditions part of the validation record. Sequence Can Matter Some validation procedures depend upon order. A test performed after a system has already been modified may not establish the same thing as the same test performed before modification. Likewise, one validation activity may depend upon another being completed first. VEXS therefore governs sequence where sequence has methodological significance. Evidence Must Survive the Transition Into Execution Evidence that was previously qualified by VALIDOS® should not lose its governance conditions once execution begins. VEXS preserves relationships to: Evidence Fitness, evidence version, evidence limitations, evidence restrictions, Source Reliability, source conditions, and applicable corroboration requirements. This prevents execution from silently substituting governed evidence with materially different evidence. Reliable Sources Can Still Be Used Incorrectly Source Reliability does not guarantee correct execution. A reliable source may be: used outside its approved role, used beyond its reliability boundary, interpreted incorrectly, substituted, or used without required corroboration. Therefore: Reliable Source ≠ Correct Execution VEXS governs how source conditions are actually respected during validation activity. Execution Can Be Human, Automated, or Hybrid Modern validation may involve people, software, AI systems, autonomous agents, instruments, or combinations of them. VEXS is execution-model neutral. Human Execution A person may: perform tests, make observations, interpret evidence, operate instruments, review outputs, or intervene in the validation process. Automated Execution A system may: execute tests, monitor behavior, process evidence, run simulations, generate measurements, or evaluate defined conditions. Hybrid Execution Humans and machines may divide responsibility across the same validation process. VEXS governs the actual execution structure regardless of who or what performs it. Execution Deviations Are Governance Events Real-world validation rarely proceeds exactly as planned. Deviation itself does not automatically invalidate validation. The important questions are: What changed? Why did it change? Was it authorized? What did it affect? Was the effect material? Were compensating controls required? VEXS transforms deviation from an undocumented irregularity into a governed validation event. Not Every Deviation Has Equal Importance VALIDOS® may distinguish: Immaterial Deviation Minor Deviation Material Deviation Critical Deviation Execution-Invalidating Deviation This prevents two opposite errors: treating every deviation as catastrophic, and: ignoring deviations that materially undermine validation. Authorization Does Not Erase Methodological Effect A deviation may be formally authorized and still materially affect validation. Therefore: Authorized Deviation ≠ Methodologically Harmless Deviation Authorization establishes that the change was governed. Its methodological consequences must still remain visible. Substitution Must Be Visible Real validation processes may substitute: evidence, sources, instruments, datasets, models, personnel, environments, procedures, or controls. Substitution may be entirely legitimate. But equivalence should not be assumed merely because the substitute appears similar. VEXS requires material substitutions to remain identifiable. Interruptions Matter Validation may be interrupted by: system failure, infrastructure outage, missing evidence, safety conditions, human intervention, environmental change, resource failure, or unexpected system behavior. The governance question becomes: Can execution continue? Must part of it be repeated? Must it restart entirely? Can the interruption be accepted conditionally? VEXS provides the execution layer in which those questions can be answered. Failure to Validate Is Not Validation Failure This is one of the most important distinctions in VEXS. Suppose a required test cannot be completed because the testing environment fails. That does not demonstrate that the Validation Object failed the criterion. It demonstrates that validation could not establish the required result. VALIDOS® therefore establishes: Failure to Validate ≠ Validation Failure of the Object This prevents methodological failure from being incorrectly transformed into an object-level conclusion. Execution Completeness VEXS asks whether all materially required validation activities were actually performed. Execution may therefore be: Complete Conditionally Complete Partially Complete Incomplete or: Completeness Undetermined Completeness concerns the validation process. It does not indicate whether the object passed or failed. Execution Conformity VEXS separately asks whether actual execution sufficiently corresponded to the approved validation basis. Possible conditions may include: Execution Conformant Execution Conditionally Conformant Execution Conformity Undetermined Execution Non-Conformant Execution Invalid This creates a formal governance gate before Validation Determination. A Perfectly Executed Validation Can Produce a Negative Result This distinction is essential. A validation process may be: complete, perfectly conformant, fully documented, and methodologically strong and demonstrate that the Validation Object fails. That is not failed validation execution. It is successful execution producing a negative validation finding. Therefore: Execution Conformant ≠ Validation Object Valid An Apparently Valid Object Does Not Repair Invalid Execution The opposite is equally important. An object may in reality satisfy all required conditions. But if the validation process used to establish that conclusion was materially invalid, VALIDOS® should not manufacture methodological confidence from the likely correctness of the result. Therefore: Probable Correctness ≠ Governed Validation Execution Must Be Reconstructable A strong validation process should allow a later reviewer to reconstruct materially: What was validated? Which version? Against which criteria? Using which method? Using which evidence and sources? Who or what performed the activities? Under which conditions? In what sequence? What deviations occurred? What outputs were generated? This reconstruction creates the bridge between validation activity and auditability. Execution Records Become Methodological Evidence The execution process itself creates evidence. This may include: logs, observations, test outputs, measurements, timestamps, system records, operator records, simulation outputs, deviation records, interruption records, and other execution artifacts. Together these form the Validation Execution Record. The record establishes what the validation process can actually demonstrate was performed. Execution Can Be Repeated A failed or materially deficient execution does not necessarily end validation. VEXS allows governance of: Re-Execution and where methodologically defensible: Partial Re-Execution This permits affected validation activities to be repeated without automatically discarding unaffected valid execution. Historical Execution Must Remain Visible Repeated execution should not overwrite earlier validation history. Where validation is repeated after: failure, deviation, system change, evidence change, or corrective action, the relationship between executions should remain traceable. This creates validation execution continuity. Determination Readiness VEXS ultimately asks whether execution has reached a state where a legitimate Validation Determination can begin. This requires sufficient understanding of: object continuity, scope conformity, criteria execution, method conformity, evidence continuity, source conditions, deviations, completeness, conformity, and execution traceability. Where those conditions are sufficiently established, execution can progress. Where they are not, VEXS can prevent premature determination. Determination Block A critical execution deficiency may create a Determination Block. This means VALIDOS® does not permit methodological uncertainty about execution to disappear merely because an organization wants a final answer. Possible blocking conditions include: wrong Validation Object, critical missing activity, invalid method substitution, critical scope deviation, irrecoverable evidence discontinuity, critical execution failure, or insufficient execution traceability. The validation process must first resolve the execution problem or explicitly preserve the inability to determine. Position Within VALIDOS® Validation Execution Standard is the seventh Parent Standard of VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture. Its architectural position is: Validation Object → Validation Purpose & Scope → Validation Criteria → Validation Method → Validation Evidence Fitness → Validation Source Reliability → Validation Execution → Validation Determination → Validation State → Validation Reliance & Revalidation The first six Parent Standards establish the governed basis upon which validation can operate. VEXS establishes whether that basis was actually transformed into a legitimate validation execution. Only then does VALIDOS® move to the next question: What does the governed validation record actually demonstrate about the Validation Object? Relationship to Other OOF® Architectures VEXS operates alongside complementary OOF® architectures. GOA™ may establish authority, delegation, and governance responsibilities affecting validation execution. OBIDENITY® may preserve identity, origin, ownership, provenance, and continuity relationships. INTEGROS® may provide integrity conditions affecting validation activities and execution records. ORA™ may establish complementary operational-reality conditions. AGA™ may establish accountability for execution activities, deviations, interventions, and decisions. AIG®, CLIA®, MGIA™, and ASGA™ may provide specialized governance conditions where AI behavior, cognition, memory, or autonomous execution materially affects validation. RIS™ may inform the depth, strength, and control requirements appropriate to the consequence of validation failure. VEXS does not duplicate these architectures. It consumes relevant governed information and answers one validation-specific question: Was the validation process actually executed with sufficient conformity, completeness, control, continuity, and traceability to support a legitimate Validation Determination? Why It Matters Validation is often documented more strongly than it is executed. Policies describe ideal processes. Methodologies define required procedures. Testing plans specify controlled conditions. Standards define expectations. But operational reality may differ. VALIDOS® therefore refuses to infer execution from documentation. It requires the distinction: Designed Validation versus: Executed Validation to remain visible. From Validation Procedure to Validation Proof Traditional validation may ask: Was the procedure defined? VEXS adds: Was it actually performed? Against the correct object? Within the correct scope? Under the required conditions? Using the governed evidence? With the required sequence? What changed during execution? Can we reconstruct what happened? Is the execution sufficiently conformant to support determination? This transforms execution from an assumed procedural step into an independently governable validation layer. Foundational Principle A validation method has no operational validity until its required validation activities are actually performed. Canonical Closing Statement Validation Execution Standard establishes the operational performance layer of VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture by separating validation design from validation actually performed. Through governance of execution authorization, instantiation, object continuity, scope conformity, criteria execution, method conformity, evidence and source continuity, conditions, participants, sequencing, deviations, substitutions, interruptions, failures, completeness, conformity, reconstruction, repetition, and traceability, VEXS ensures that Validation Determination rests upon demonstrable execution rather than methodological intention, procedural assumption, or undocumented operational activity. title: Validation Execution Basis & Authorization Module (VEBAM)
text: Validation Execution Basis & Authorization Module (VEBAM) Validation Execution Basis & Authorization Module (VEBAM) Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Validation Execution Standard (VEXS) Operational Layer: Validation Execution Governance Layer Category: AI & Interpretation Subcategory: Validation Governance Type: Parent Standard Module Governed Space: Validation Execution Basis & Authorization Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 11 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · OBIDENITY® · INTEGROS® · ORA™ · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Governed Space Validation Execution Basis & Authorization Canonical Definition Validation Execution Basis & Authorization Module (VEBAM) defines the governance framework for assembling, verifying, freezing, authorizing, and preserving the complete governed basis from which a specific Validation Execution may legitimately begin. It establishes the conditions under which the outputs of preceding VALIDOS® governance stages become an identifiable, versioned, execution-ready, and authorized Validation Execution Basis. Operational Role VEBAM serves as the first internal governance space of the Validation Execution Standard. The preceding VALIDOS® Parent Standards establish: Validation Object Validation Purpose & Scope Validation Criteria Validation Method Validation Evidence Fitness and: Validation Source Reliability VEBAM asks: Are the required validation components sufficiently established, mutually connected, current, and authorized for this specific Validation Execution to begin? The governed progression is: Governed Validation Components → Execution Prerequisite Review → Basis Assembly → Basis Consistency Check → Execution Instance Definition → Authorization Assessment → Basis Freeze → Authorized Validation Execution Basis VEBAM does not perform the validation. It establishes the governed starting condition from which validation may be performed. Module Operational Space VEBAM governs: Validation Execution Basis, execution prerequisites, execution readiness, execution authorization, execution instance identity, Validation Object reference, object-version reference, Validation Purpose reference, Validation Scope reference, Validation Depth reference, Validation Criteria references, Validation Method reference, Validation Evidence references, Validation Source references, Source Reliability conditions, execution-role requirements, resource readiness, instrument readiness, system readiness, environment prerequisites, authorization authority, authorization scope, authorization conditions, basis completeness, basis consistency, basis versioning, basis freeze, basis change, authorization change, authorization withdrawal, and execution-basis traceability. Module Function VEBAM applies immediately before operational validation execution begins. Its function is to prevent: execution beginning against an undefined Validation Object, execution using the wrong object version, obsolete Validation Criteria being used, unapproved methods entering execution, Validation Scope remaining ambiguous, insufficient Validation Depth being silently accepted, unqualified evidence entering execution, Source Reliability conditions being lost, execution beginning before required prerequisites exist, incompatible validation components being assembled, execution roles remaining undefined, unavailable resources being assumed available, unauthorized validation activity being represented as governed validation, and the validation basis changing silently after execution begins. Validation Execution Basis The Validation Execution Basis is the governed collection of validation components upon which a specific execution instance depends. It may contain: Validation Object reference, object version or state, Validation Purpose, Validation Scope, Validation Depth, applicable Validation Criteria, approved Validation Method, qualified Validation Evidence, Source Reliability information, source conditions, execution requirements, participant requirements, system requirements, instrument requirements, environmental requirements, execution controls, restrictions, and authorization conditions. The Validation Execution Basis creates the methodological starting state for execution. Execution Basis Is Not a Validation Plan A Validation Execution Basis and a validation plan are related but not identical. A plan may describe intended activities. The Execution Basis establishes the governed methodological conditions that authorize those activities to begin. VALIDOS® therefore distinguishes: Execution Plan → What is intended to occur from: Validation Execution Basis → What governed validation structure permits execution to occur A plan cannot override the governed Validation Execution Basis. Execution Instance Identity Each material Validation Execution should be sufficiently identifiable as a distinct execution instance. An Execution Instance may be associated with: an identifier, Validation Object, object version, Validation Method version, execution date or period, responsible execution entity, environment, or another distinguishing attribute. This allows multiple executions of the same Validation Object to remain distinguishable. Object Reference VEBAM requires the Execution Basis to identify the exact Validation Object against which execution is authorized. The reference should remain connected to the object established under the Validation Object Standard. Where object identity cannot be sufficiently established, execution should not silently proceed. Object Version & State Reference Where validation depends upon version, configuration, release, state, or temporal condition, the relevant object instance must be explicit. VALIDOS® establishes: Authorization to validate one object state does not automatically authorize validation of another materially different state. Purpose Continuity The Validation Purpose established earlier must remain connected to execution. Execution activity should not silently drift toward a different purpose. For example: Validation authorized to determine: functional performance should not silently become validation of: regulatory compliance unless the required governance basis for that purpose has also been established. Scope Continuity The authorized Validation Scope establishes what execution may legitimately cover. VEBAM therefore identifies: included scope, excluded scope, applicable boundaries, temporal boundaries, system boundaries, population boundaries, or other relevant limits. This creates the baseline against which later execution deviations can be assessed. Validation Depth Continuity Validation Depth affects how extensively the Validation Object must be examined. VEBAM ensures that the required depth remains attached to execution. Execution should not silently substitute: limited validation for: deep validation while preserving the appearance of the original validation objective. Criteria Set The applicable Validation Criteria must be sufficiently established before execution begins. VEBAM creates an identifiable criteria set connecting the Execution Basis to the criteria that execution is expected to evaluate. The criteria set may include: mandatory criteria, conditional criteria, optional supporting criteria, criterion priority, criterion applicability, or other governed relationships. Criteria Version Where Validation Criteria change over time, the applicable criteria version must remain explicit. This prevents a later criteria revision from being incorrectly represented as the basis under which an earlier execution occurred. Method Reference The Validation Execution Basis must identify the approved Validation Method. Where multiple methods exist, the exact: method, version, configuration, procedure, test protocol, analytical process, or other relevant methodological instance should be sufficiently identifiable. Method Eligibility Continuity Where the Validation Method Standard established eligibility conditions, those conditions must remain satisfied when execution begins. A method that was previously eligible may become inappropriate if: the Validation Object changes, the Validation Scope changes, evidence availability changes, environmental conditions change, or required systems become unavailable. VEBAM therefore checks that the methodological basis remains current. Validation Evidence Reference Evidence intended for execution should remain connected to the evidence objects qualified under Validation Evidence Fitness governance. The Execution Basis may identify: required evidence, supporting evidence, optional evidence, evidence versions, evidence limitations, evidence validity periods, and Evidence Fitness conditions. This prevents unqualified evidence from entering execution without visibility. Source Reliability Reference Where evidence depends upon Validation Sources, VEBAM preserves the relevant Source Reliability conditions. These may include: Source Reliability Status, source-role restrictions, required corroboration, reliability limitations, independence conditions, source version, source validity period, or reassessment requirements. Prerequisite Governance Before execution begins, VEBAM determines whether material prerequisites have been sufficiently established. Prerequisites may include: approved method, qualified evidence, reliable or conditionally reliable sources, available instruments, required systems, required data, competent participants, required access, environmental conditions, authorization, or another validation-specific requirement. Prerequisite Status A prerequisite may be classified as: Satisfied Conditionally Satisfied Unsatisfied or: Undetermined A critical Unsatisfied or Undetermined prerequisite may prevent authorization. Resource Readiness Validation execution may require resources such as: personnel, compute, laboratories, testing environments, datasets, instruments, infrastructure, time, or external services. VEBAM determines whether required resources are sufficiently available for the intended execution. Resource availability does not itself establish methodological validity. It establishes execution readiness. Instrument Readiness Where instruments materially affect validation, readiness may require: correct instrument identity, calibration, required configuration, operating range, maintenance status, software version, or another applicable condition. An instrument that exists but is not ready should not be assumed execution-ready. System Readiness Validation may depend upon: software, testing platforms, AI systems, simulation environments, data pipelines, monitoring systems, or infrastructure. VEBAM may establish whether required systems are available in the correct state and configuration. Environment Readiness Some Validation Methods require defined environmental conditions. These may include: physical conditions, network conditions, operational state, simulation settings, controlled access, geographic conditions, or another relevant environment. VEBAM establishes whether the required environment is sufficiently available before execution begins. Participant Readiness Where human or machine participants perform material validation roles, VEBAM may establish: required role, identity, authority, competence requirement, availability, system permission, or another prerequisite. Participant readiness does not replace Source Capability or accountability governance. It ensures that required execution roles can actually be performed. Basis Completeness A Validation Execution Basis should contain sufficient information for execution to begin without relying upon material unstated assumptions. Possible completeness conditions include: Basis Complete Basis Conditionally Complete Basis Partially Complete Basis Incomplete Basis Completeness Undetermined Completeness requirements should remain proportionate to validation consequence. Basis Consistency A complete basis may still contain contradictions. VEBAM therefore assesses whether its components are materially consistent. Examples of inconsistency include: criteria requiring evidence not available, method incompatible with object type, Validation Depth inconsistent with method capability, evidence version inconsistent with object version, Source Reliability restriction incompatible with intended source role, or scope broader than authorized execution capability. Material inconsistencies must remain visible. Basis Conflict A Basis Conflict exists where two or more governed execution components impose materially incompatible requirements. A conflict may require: correction, escalation, method revision, scope revision, evidence replacement, source reassessment, or another governance action. Execution should not resolve material Basis Conflicts silently. Execution Readiness VEBAM may establish an Execution Readiness condition such as: Execution Ready All material prerequisites and basis requirements are sufficiently established. Execution Conditionally Ready Execution may proceed only under explicit conditions. Execution Readiness Undetermined Available information is insufficient to establish readiness. Execution Not Ready Material prerequisites remain unsatisfied. Readiness does not itself authorize execution where separate authorization is required. Execution Authorization Execution Authorization establishes that a defined Validation Execution Instance may legitimately proceed under the approved Validation Execution Basis. Authorization should identify, where applicable: authorization authority, authorized Validation Object, authorized scope, authorized method, applicable conditions, restrictions, effective period, and authorization status. Authorization Authority The entity granting authorization must possess sufficient authority for the relevant validation context. Authority may derive from: governance structure, organizational role, contractual authority, regulatory authority, methodological governance, delegated authority, or another legitimate basis. VEBAM does not create external legal authority. It records and governs the authority relationship used to initiate validation execution. Authorization Scope Authorization should be bounded. It may authorize: one Validation Object, one object version, one Validation Scope, one Validation Method, one execution environment, one execution period, or another defined set of conditions. Authorization should not silently extend beyond its governed scope. Conditional Authorization Execution may be authorized subject to conditions. Examples include: specific evidence must remain available, a source requires independent corroboration, execution must occur within a defined environment, a specified participant must be present, or a particular control must remain active. Conditional authorization remains valid only while its material conditions remain satisfied. Authorization Status VEBAM may establish: Authorized Conditionally Authorized Authorization Pending Authorization Denied Authorization Suspended or: Authorization Withdrawn These statuses govern permission to execute. They do not represent Validation State. Basis Freeze Immediately before execution begins, the material Validation Execution Basis should be sufficiently frozen or version-fixed. A Basis Freeze establishes the exact governed configuration under which execution began. This may include: object version, criteria version, method version, evidence set, source conditions, execution requirements, and authorization conditions. Freeze does not prohibit change. It makes subsequent change visible. Why Basis Freeze Matters Without a Basis Freeze, a validation process may change its methodological foundation during execution while later presenting the final configuration as if it had governed the complete process. VEBAM prevents this. VALIDOS® establishes: Execution history must preserve the basis that actually governed execution at the time it occurred. Basis Versioning Materially different Execution Bases should remain distinguishable. For example: Execution Basis 1.0 Execution Basis 1.1 Execution Basis 2.0 The versioning structure may vary by implementation. The governance requirement is that material basis changes remain reconstructable. Basis Change After Basis Freeze, a material change may involve: Validation Object, scope, criteria, method, evidence, source, environment, participant, instrument, system, or authorization condition. Such change becomes an execution-governance event. Depending upon materiality, it may require: updated authorization, controlled deviation, new Basis version, execution restart, partial re-execution, or complete revalidation. Authorization Change Authorization may change because of: scope expansion, scope reduction, new authority, changed method, object change, source change, environmental change, or another material condition. Authorization changes should remain historically traceable. Authorization Suspension Execution authorization may be temporarily suspended where a material condition arises that requires review. Examples include: prerequisite failure, instrument issue, source reliability concern, unexpected object change, safety concern, or governance conflict. Suspension does not automatically terminate the validation. It pauses authorization until the relevant condition is resolved. Authorization Withdrawal Authorization may be withdrawn where the basis for legitimate execution no longer exists. Withdrawal may require: stopping execution, preserving existing records, assessing already performed activities, and determining whether reauthorization or new execution is necessary. Unauthorized Execution Validation activity performed without required authorization may still produce factual observations. However, it should not automatically be represented as a governed VALIDOS® Validation Execution. VALIDOS® therefore distinguishes: Activity Occurred from: Governed Validation Execution Authorized Authorization Does Not Guarantee Valid Execution Authorization establishes permission to begin. It does not prove that execution will later be: complete, conformant, correctly sequenced, deviation-free, or methodologically valid. Therefore: Authorized Execution ≠ Conformant Execution Subsequent VEXS modules govern actual execution behavior. Basis Traceability VEBAM creates traceability between: Validation Object → Purpose & Scope → Criteria → Method → Evidence → Sources → Execution Requirements → Authorization → Execution Instance This becomes the baseline against which actual execution can later be compared. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Identify Validation Execution Instance Create a distinguishable reference for the intended execution. 2. Assemble Validation Execution Basis Connect the relevant: Validation Object, Purpose, Scope, Depth, Criteria, Method, Evidence, Sources, conditions, and restrictions. 3. Verify Prerequisites Determine whether required execution prerequisites are satisfied. 4. Assess Basis Completeness Determine whether the basis contains sufficient information for execution. 5. Assess Basis Consistency Identify contradictions, incompatibilities, or Basis Conflicts. 6. Determine Execution Readiness Establish whether execution is Ready, Conditionally Ready, Undetermined, or Not Ready. 7. Establish Execution Authorization Determine whether the defined execution instance may legitimately begin. 8. Freeze and Version the Basis Preserve the exact governed basis applicable at execution start. 9. Preserve Lifecycle Traceability Maintain: Execution Instance reference, Validation Object reference, object version, Purpose, Scope, Depth, Criteria set, Method reference, Evidence references, Source Reliability references, prerequisites, readiness status, authorization, conditions, restrictions, Basis version, Basis Freeze, changes, suspensions, withdrawals, and sufficient lifecycle traceability. Governance Outputs VEBAM may produce: Validation Execution Instance Identifier, Validation Execution Basis, Validation Execution Basis Record, Execution Prerequisite Register, Execution Prerequisite Status, Execution Resource Readiness Record, Instrument Readiness Record, System Readiness Record, Environment Readiness Record, Participant Readiness Record, Basis Completeness Assessment, Basis Consistency Assessment, Basis Conflict Record, Execution Readiness Status, Validation Execution Authorization, Authorization Scope, Authorization Condition Record, Authorization Status, Validation Execution Basis Version, Basis Freeze Record, Basis Change Record, Authorization Change Record, Authorization Suspension Record, Authorization Withdrawal Record, and Execution Basis Traceability Record. Use Case 1 — AI Model Validation Scenario An organization intends to validate a new AI model release. The validation methodology has already been approved. Application VEBAM establishes that: the Validation Object is Model Version 4.2, the approved criteria apply to Version 4.2, the correct benchmark evidence is available, source-reliability conditions remain current, the required testing environment is ready, and the approved method version is identifiable. The complete basis is frozen as Execution Basis 1.0 and authorized. Result Validation begins against a reconstructable methodological baseline rather than a loosely defined testing plan. Use Case 2 — Industrial Equipment Validation Scenario A validation is scheduled for an industrial component. The required measurement instrument exists, but its calibration expired before execution. Application VEBAM identifies the calibration requirement as an unsatisfied execution prerequisite. Result The validation remains: Execution Not Ready until the instrument condition is resolved. The existence of the instrument is not mistaken for instrument readiness. Use Case 3 — Healthcare Validation Scenario A healthcare validation has an approved method, qualified evidence, and competent participants. However, one critical evidence source has become subject to a newly identified Source Reliability restriction requiring independent corroboration. Application VEBAM propagates the new source condition into the Execution Basis. Result Execution may become: Conditionally Ready and: Conditionally Authorized subject to the required corroboration. The earlier source assessment is not silently treated as permanently valid. Architectural Position Validation Execution Basis & Authorization is the first internal governance space of the Validation Execution Standard (VEXS). It establishes the transition: Governed Validation Design → Authorized Validation Execution Basis The next execution-governance stage can then ask: How is that authorized basis instantiated into actual validation activity against the Validation Object under real execution conditions? The VEXS internal progression therefore begins: Execution Basis & Authorization → Execution Instantiation & Control → Execution Observation & Traceability → Deviation & Exception Governance → Execution Completeness & Conformity Foundational Principle Validation execution should not begin until the basis governing what may be executed is identifiable, internally coherent, sufficiently ready, and appropriately authorized. Canonical Closing Statement Validation Execution Basis & Authorization Module establishes the governed starting condition for operational validation within VALIDOS® by transforming previously established Validation Object, Purpose, Scope, Criteria, Method, Evidence, and Source Reliability information into an identifiable, consistent, versioned, execution-ready, and authorized Validation Execution Basis. Through prerequisite governance, readiness assessment, authorization, basis freezing, version control, change governance, and lifecycle traceability, VEBAM ensures that validation execution begins from a reconstructable methodological foundation rather than from procedural assumption, incomplete preparation, or undefined authority.
