Autonomous systems require more than policies surrounding them. They require governance structures capable of interacting with their operation. Autonomy increases the need for executable governance. Methodology in the AI Era Generative AI fundamentally changes the economics of knowledge production. Documents can be generated quickly. Policies can be drafted quickly. Frameworks can be proposed quickly. Standards-like structures can be produced quickly. The scarce capability therefore begins to shift. The critical questions become: What governance space does the methodology legitimately govern? Where does that space begin and end? What is outside its authority? What establishes its methodological provenance? How does it interact with other governance spaces? Can its application be validated? Can its evolution be traced? Can independent systems reference the same methodological object? Can applicable governance logic be operationalized consistently? Producing more text does not solve these questions. Methodology infrastructure does. Governance Must Become Interoperable Future intelligent ecosystems will not consist of one model, one organization, one jurisdiction, or one governance framework. Models will interact with agents. Agents will interact with other agents. Organizations will interact through automated systems. Digital systems will increasingly interact with physical infrastructure. Governance therefore cannot depend entirely on isolated interpretations implemented independently inside every system. A methodological infrastructure must make it possible for different systems to recognize defined governance structures while preserving boundaries, provenance, authority, and context. This is why interoperability is not merely a software problem. It is a methodological problem. Governance Must Remain Governable Making standards executable introduces its own governance requirements. Executable governance cannot become an invisible layer of automated authority. Its methodological origin must remain identifiable. Its applicable scope must remain bounded. Its evolution must remain traceable. Its interactions must remain examinable. Its determinations must remain capable of validation. And its authority must never silently expand simply because software is capable of executing it. Executable governance must itself remain governed. A New Infrastructure Layer The internet created infrastructure for information. Cloud computing created infrastructure for computation. AI is creating infrastructure for intelligence. Increasingly autonomous intelligence creates another requirement: methodological infrastructure for governance. OOF® is being developed within this emerging space. Not as a universal decision-maker. Not as a replacement for regulators, institutions, organizations, or legitimate authorities. But as methodological infrastructure through which governable spaces can be identified, structured, bounded, connected, referenced, and progressively operationalized. The OOF® Infrastructure Direction Human Governance Knowledge ↓ Structured Methodology ↓ Governance Architectures ↓ Standards & Modules ↓ Machine-Interpretable Governance ↓ Executable Governance Components ↓ Architecture Composition ↓ Governance Runtime ↓ Operational Governance Infrastructure The destination is not a larger library of documents. It is an infrastructure in which methodologies can progressively become referenceable, interoperable, composable, testable, traceable, and executable while preserving the boundaries that make them legitimate. Evolution Comes With Governance Intelligence will evolve. Autonomy will evolve. Operational systems will evolve. The relationships between humans, organizations, machines, and intelligent agents will evolve. Every material expansion of capability can create new governance questions and previously unidentified governance spaces. Governance infrastructure must therefore be capable of evolving with the systems it governs. Evolution comes with governance. And as intelligence becomes executable, governance must increasingly become executable too. OOF® Canonical Principle Intelligence can generate decisions. Methodology determines the governed path through which those decisions become legitimate, traceable, and operationally usable. OOF® — Methodological Reference Authority & Methodology Infrastructure Organization

title: OOF™ About Reality Representation Standard - (RRS)
text: OOF™ About Reality Representation Standard - (RRS) About Reality Representation Standard - (RRS) Governing How Reality Becomes Represented Inside a Simulation Represented Inside a Simulation A simulation never contains reality itself. It contains a representation of selected reality. That representation may simplify physical systems, abstract human behavior, approximate environments, compress complex interactions, or reproduce only those parts of reality considered relevant to the simulation purpose. Reality Representation Standard (RRS) governs this transformation. Its purpose is to ensure that organizations can distinguish between: what exists in reality and: what the simulation actually represents. Canonical Definition Reality Representation Standard (RRS) defines the governance conditions under which the aspects of reality relevant to a governed Simulation Object, Purpose, Scope, Applicability Context, and required Simulation Depth & Precision are selected, abstracted, represented, resolved, simplified, bounded, and documented within a simulation so that the simulated representation remains explicitly distinguishable from the reality it claims to represent. Why RRS Exists Every simulation must make choices. It must decide: which real-world characteristics matter, which behaviors must be represented, which interactions require detail, which elements may be simplified, which phenomena require approximation, and which real-world conditions cannot be represented sufficiently. Without explicit governance, these choices can disappear inside the model. The simulation may then appear more realistic, complete, or broadly applicable than the representation actually supports. RRS prevents that. Governed Space Simulation Reality Representation RRS governs the methodological bridge between: relevant reality and: its simulated representation. It does not determine what reality actually is. That remains within the Operational Reality governance space. RRS determines how the selected reality relevant to the simulation inquiry is translated into representable form. Governance Flow Governed Simulation Inquiry → Reality Selection → Reality Abstraction → Representation Fidelity → Representation Resolution → Simplification & Approximation → Representation Limitations → Governed Reality Representation This representation basis then supports: Simulation Assumptions → Model & Environment → Inputs & Data → Scenario Design → Simulation Execution What RRS Establishes RRS helps an organization determine: Reality Selection — which real-world characteristics actually need to appear in the simulation. Abstraction — which complexity may be reduced without destroying material behavior. Fidelity — how faithfully relevant reality must be represented. Resolution — how finely the simulation must distinguish relevant states, events, spaces, times, and interactions. Simplification — which real-world complexity may legitimately be reduced. Approximation — where direct representation is impossible or unnecessary. Representation Limitations — where the simulated reality differs materially from the reality it is intended to represent. Reality Is Not the Model One of the most important distinctions in SIMULOS® is: Reality ≠ Simulation Representation and: Simulation Representation ≠ Simulation Model Reality is the external or intended world. Reality Representation defines which characteristics of that world must enter simulation. The model is the technical mechanism later used to implement that representation. This distinction allows organizations to change models or simulation technologies without losing the underlying representation requirements. Fidelity Must Follow Purpose Higher fidelity is not automatically better. A simulation used for early design exploration may require relatively simple representations. A simulation supporting high-consequence autonomous deployment may require significantly stronger representation of: system behavior, interactions, environmental variation, failure conditions, timing, dependencies, and operational states. RRS therefore does not ask: How realistic can we make the simulation? It asks: How faithfully must the relevant reality be represented for this particular simulation purpose? Simplification Is Legitimate Simulation necessarily simplifies reality. RRS does not attempt to eliminate simplification. It makes simplification explicit and governable. An organization may simplify: geometry, environmental variation, human behavior, component detail, system interactions, or physical processes where those simplifications do not remove characteristics material to the simulation inquiry. The key principle is: Simplification must not silently remove the reality the simulation is intended to examine. Representation Limitations No representation is complete. RRS therefore requires material representation limitations to remain visible. Examples may include: incomplete human behavioral representation, simplified environmental dynamics, proxy data, incomplete physical models, limited failure behavior, uncertain system interactions, simplified network conditions, or static representation of a dynamic system. These limitations become important when organizations interpret simulation outputs later. Business Value For organizations investing heavily in simulation, RRS provides a structured way to answer a difficult but fundamental question: Does the simulated world contain enough of the real world to support the question we are asking? This helps organizations identify: unnecessary simulation complexity, missing material reality, hidden simplifications, insufficient fidelity, inappropriate abstraction, simulation gaps, and situations where high numerical precision creates false confidence. It also improves communication between: engineering teams, simulation teams, decision-makers, safety teams, auditors, validators, and operational users because all parties can refer to the same governed Reality Representation Basis. Relationship to Operational Reality The boundary with ORA™ is explicit. ORA™ asks: What is actually happening in Operational Reality? RRS asks: How must the relevant parts of that reality be represented inside this simulation? RRS therefore does not duplicate Operational Reality governance. It creates the simulation-specific representation layer between actual reality and the simulation architecture. Relationship to Validation RRS also does not determine that a simulation is valid. A simulation may possess a carefully governed Reality Representation and still require formal validation. VALIDOS® governs whether the relevant simulation, simulation output, evidence, or claim can legitimately satisfy a validation purpose. RRS provides one important part of the simulation basis that such validation may later examine. Practical Governance Test Before model construction proceeds, an organization should be able to answer: Which aspects of reality must this simulation represent? Which aspects may be abstracted? Which elements require high fidelity? Which elements may use lower fidelity? What resolution is actually necessary? What has been simplified or approximated? Which important parts of reality cannot currently be represented sufficiently? Could any of those limitations materially change the meaning of the simulation outputs? If those questions cannot be answered, simulation complexity alone cannot establish representation quality. Architectural Position RRS is the third Parent Standard of SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture. The architectural progression is: Simulation Object ↓ Simulation Purpose & Scope ↓ Reality Representation SOS establishes: What exactly are we simulating? SPSS establishes: Why are we simulating it and what must the inquiry cover? RRS establishes: Which aspects of reality must now be represented and how must that representation remain bounded by abstraction, fidelity, resolution, simplification, approximation, and known limitations? The next governance question becomes: Which assumptions are necessary to make this representation and the resulting simulation possible? Foundational Principle A simulation can legitimately represent reality only to the extent that the reality elements material to its purpose are explicitly selected, appropriately abstracted, sufficiently represented, and bounded by their known representational limitations. Canonical Closing Statement Reality Representation Standard (RRS) governs the transformation from relevant reality into simulated representation by defining what must be represented, what may be abstracted or simplified, how much fidelity and resolution are required, and which limitations must remain visible throughout the simulation lifecycle. By separating reality from its simulated representation, RRS prevents technical detail, numerical precision, or model complexity from being mistaken for real-world equivalence and establishes the governed reality basis upon which assumptions, models, environments, inputs, scenarios, execution, outputs, and later simulation-to-reality correlation can be constructed.

title: OOF™ About Simulation Assumption Standard - (SAS)
text: OOF™ About Simulation Assumption Standard - (SAS) About Simulation Assumption Standard - (SAS) Make Simulation Possible Every simulation depends on assumptions. Some are obvious. Others are embedded inside: models, default settings, environmental conditions, parameter choices, behavioral rules, dependencies, failure conditions, or expected future states. A simulation may appear technically complete while materially depending on premises that were never explicitly identified. Simulation Assumption Standard (SAS) governs those premises. Canonical Definition Simulation Assumption Standard (SAS) defines the governance conditions under which assumptions necessary to construct, configure, execute, or interpret a simulation are explicitly identified, justified, bounded, connected to their supporting basis and dependencies, assessed for uncertainty and limitations, and preserved as traceable components of the simulation lifecycle. Why SAS Exists Assumptions are not inherently a weakness. Simulation would often be impossible without them. The governance problem begins when assumptions become: hidden, unsupported, overgeneralized, mutually inconsistent, treated as facts, reused outside their original context, or disconnected from the outputs that materially depend upon them. SAS makes assumptions visible before they become invisible inside model behavior. Governed Space Simulation Assumptions SAS governs the methodological layer between: Reality Representation and: Simulation Model & Environment construction. The preceding Reality Representation Standard establishes what reality must be represented and how. SAS then establishes what must still be presumed in order to make that representation operational inside the simulation. Governance Flow Reality Representation Basis → Assumption Need → Assumption Identification → Assumption Basis → Assumption Dependency → Assumption Uncertainty → Assumption Limitation → Assumption Consequence → Governed Simulation Assumption Basis This governed basis then supports: Simulation Model & Environment → Inputs & Data → Scenario Design → Simulation Execution What SAS Establishes SAS helps an organization establish: Assumption Identification — which premises materially affect the simulation. Assumption Basis — why those assumptions are being used and what supports them. Assumption Dependencies — which assumptions depend on other conditions, systems, evidence, or assumptions. Assumption Uncertainty — how uncertain the assumed condition remains. Assumption Limitations — where the assumption stops being suitable. Assumption Consequences — what happens if the assumption is materially wrong. Assumption Traceability — which model elements, scenarios, executions, outputs, or conclusions depend upon it. Assumption Is Not Fact One of the most important SAS distinctions is: Assumption ≠ Established Fact Repeatedly using an assumption does not make it true. Embedding an assumption in software does not make it true. Producing successful simulation outputs does not independently prove the assumption. This distinction protects simulation from circular reasoning. Assumptions Must Remain Connected to Their Basis An assumption may be based on: operational observations, scientific evidence, engineering knowledge, historical data, expert judgment, design specifications, domain conventions, prior simulation, or conservative estimation. But not all assumption bases have equal strength. SAS therefore allows organizations to distinguish between assumptions that are: Strongly Supported Conditionally Supported Weakly Supported or: Necessary but Uncertain This creates a much clearer picture of where the simulation is structurally strong and where it remains dependent on uncertainty. Assumption Dependencies Matter Assumptions rarely exist in isolation. A simulation may depend on: Network availability which affects: sensor access which affects: autonomous decision behavior which affects: system output. SAS makes these relationships governable. This matters because one weak upstream assumption can influence many downstream simulation outcomes. Assumption Interaction Two reasonable assumptions may become problematic when combined. For example: Human response remains within expected range and: network latency remains within expected range may each appear acceptable. But if both move toward adverse conditions simultaneously, system behavior may materially change. SAS therefore governs not only individual assumptions but also material assumption interaction and accumulation. Uncertainty Must Remain Visible Not every assumption can be verified completely before simulation. SAS does not force artificial certainty. It allows assumptions to be represented through: ranges, probability distributions, conditional states, scenario-specific premises, uncertainty bands, or explicit unresolved status. This is often methodologically stronger than pretending one uncertain value is exact. Business Value For organizations using simulation in engineering, AI, autonomous systems, aerospace, infrastructure, healthcare, finance, safety, or decision support, SAS provides a direct way to answer: What are we assuming, and how much of the result depends on those assumptions? This helps organizations identify: hidden model dependencies, weak premises, brittle conclusions, unrealistic defaults, untested environmental expectations, critical assumptions, sensitivity to assumption failure, and situations where apparently strong outputs are actually assumption-dependent. It also makes simulations easier to: audit, compare, update, explain, challenge, re-run, and validate. Critical Assumptions Some assumptions matter much more than others. SAS allows a Critical Simulation Assumption to be identified where its failure could materially change a major simulation conclusion. This enables organizations to focus attention on the assumptions capable of creating the largest methodological consequences. Critical assumptions may require stronger: evidence, sensitivity analysis, scenario testing, monitoring, or downstream validation. Assumption Sensitivity A useful simulation-governance question is: If this assumption changes within a plausible range, does the simulation conclusion change? If the answer is no, the result may be relatively robust to that assumption. If the answer is yes, the assumption becomes materially important to interpretation. SAS therefore helps distinguish: assumption-dependent results from: more robust simulation results. Assumption Failure An assumption may later prove wrong. That does not automatically mean the entire simulation becomes useless. The relevant question is: What depended upon that assumption? The effect may be: local, scenario-specific, output-specific, model-wide, or critical. SAS preserves this dependency so that affected simulation elements can be reassessed instead of automatically discarding or blindly retaining the entire simulation. Relationship to Validation SAS governs assumptions inside the simulation. It does not universally determine whether those assumptions are valid. That is a separate validation question. Where formal validation is required: VALIDOS® may validate: the assumption, its evidence basis, the simulation, the resulting output, or a claim based upon it. The boundary is therefore clear: SIMULOS® governs the role of assumptions in simulation. VALIDOS® governs formal validation of the relevant Validation Object. Relationship to Operational Reality ORA™ governs actual Operational Reality. SAS governs what the simulation presumes about conditions that may be incomplete, uncertain, expected, or simplified relative to that reality. A later mismatch between an assumption and operational reality may become a trigger for reassessment or resimulation. Relationship to Integrity INTEGROS® may govern the integrity of: assumption records, source records, change history, traceability, or related artifacts. SAS governs the specific simulation methodology surrounding assumption identification, basis, dependency, uncertainty, limitation, and consequence. Practical Governance Test Before model construction proceeds, an organization should be able to answer: What are we assuming? Why are we assuming it? What supports the assumption? What depends upon it? How uncertain is it? What happens if it is wrong? Where does the assumption stop applying? Which simulation outputs materially depend upon it? If these questions cannot be answered for material assumptions, the simulation contains hidden methodological dependencies. Architectural Position SAS is the fourth Parent Standard of SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture. The architectural progression is: Simulation Object ↓ Simulation Purpose & Scope ↓ Reality Representation ↓ Simulation Assumptions SOS establishes: What exactly is being simulated? SPSS establishes: Why is it being simulated and what must it cover? RRS establishes: Which parts of reality must be represented and how? SAS establishes: Which premises are required to make that representation usable as a simulation, and what uncertainty, dependency, and limitation do those premises introduce? The next governance question becomes: How must the simulation model and simulation environment be constructed, configured, bounded, parameterized, and version-controlled? Foundational Principle A simulation may rely upon assumptions, but no material simulation conclusion should become stronger than the assumptions upon which that conclusion materially depends. Canonical Closing Statement Simulation Assumption Standard (SAS) governs the premises that make simulation possible by ensuring that material assumptions remain explicit, supported where possible, dependency-aware, uncertainty-aware, bounded, and traceable throughout the simulation lifecycle. By separating assumptions from facts, exposing hidden premises, governing assumption interaction and sensitivity, and preserving the consequences of assumption failure, SAS prevents simulation outputs from appearing stronger than the assumptions that materially shape them and provides the governed assumption basis required for construction of the Simulation Model & Environment.

title: OOF™ About Simulation Execution Standard - (SES)
text: OOF™ About Simulation Execution Standard - (SES) About Simulation Execution Standard - (SES) About Simulation Execution Standard (SES) Architecture: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Parent Standard: Simulation Execution Standard (SES) Governed Space: Simulation Execution Operational Space: Simulation Execution Governance Governance Flow Position: 8 of 12 — Simulation Scenario → Simulation Execution → Simulation Output Governance Canonical Definition Simulation Execution Standard (SES) defines the governance conditions under which a governed simulation is instantiated, executed, controlled, observed, repeated where required, and documented so that the actual execution remains traceable to the Simulation Object, model, environment, scenario, inputs, parameters, configuration, runtime conditions, interventions, deviations, and outputs that formed the execution event. SES governs the point at which a designed simulation becomes an actual simulation execution. It ensures that organizations can distinguish between: what was intended to run and: what actually ran. Why SES Matters Modern organizations may execute thousands or millions of simulations across AI systems, autonomous systems, robotics, digital twins, engineering environments, and mission systems. The challenge is therefore not only whether simulation capability exists. The governance question becomes: Can the organization reconstruct exactly what happened during a materially relevant simulation execution? SES provides the structure for answering: Which configuration actually ran? Which model and environment versions were used? Which scenario, inputs, and parameters were instantiated? What happened during execution? Were there interventions, interruptions, failures, or deviations? Was the simulation repeated under comparable conditions? Can the resulting outputs be traced to the execution that produced them? What SES Governs SES governs five connected execution spaces: Simulation Instantiation Establishes the exact executable simulation instance and binds it to its relevant configuration. Simulation Execution Control Governs how execution is initiated, progressed, controlled, interrupted, modified where permitted, terminated, and completed. Simulation Observation Preserves materially relevant states, events, transitions, anomalies, interventions, and runtime conditions. Simulation Repetition Governs repeated runs, randomization, repeatability, reproducibility conditions, execution variance, and comparability. Simulation Execution Documentation Creates the traceable record needed to reconstruct what actually occurred. Governance Flow Governed Scenario & Simulation Configuration ↓ Simulation Instantiation ↓ Execution Control ↓ Simulation Observation ↓ Simulation Repetition ↓ Execution Documentation ↓ Governed Simulation Execution Record ↓ Simulation Output Governance What SES Does Not Determine SES does not determine whether: the Simulation Object was correctly selected, the representation perfectly reflects reality, the simulation assumptions are universally valid, the simulation output is correct, an inference from the output is justified, the simulated system is safe, or the system should be deployed. Those questions belong to other SIMULOS® spaces or compatible OOF® architectures. SES governs specifically: the execution event and its reconstructability. Enterprise Application SES can operate above an organization's existing simulation infrastructure. A company does not need to replace its: simulation engine, robotics simulator, digital twin, Monte Carlo environment, HPC infrastructure, AI evaluation environment, engineering simulator, or proprietary simulation platform. SES provides a governance layer for examining whether simulation execution remains identifiable, controlled, observable, repeatable where required, documented, and traceable. This makes SES applicable both as an execution governance framework and as a diagnostic structure for identifying execution-governance gaps in existing simulation environments. Use Case 1 — Autonomous System SimulationScenario A company performs thousands of simulations before deploying an autonomous robotic system. Several runs show unexpected collision-avoidance behavior, but engineers cannot reliably determine whether the difference originated from: model version, environment configuration, sensor inputs, randomization, parameter changes, runtime intervention, or actual autonomous behavior. SES Application SES binds each material execution to its: Execution ID → Model → Environment → Scenario → Inputs → Parameters → Runtime Conditions → Observations → Outputs Repeated runs remain distinguishable, while material execution deviations and interventions remain visible. Result The organization can reconstruct the simulation conditions associated with the anomalous behavior and determine which executions are legitimately comparable before downstream interpretation or validation begins. Use Case 2 — Space Mission Simulation CampaignScenario A space organization executes a large mission-simulation campaign covering combinations of: navigation uncertainty, communication loss, sensor degradation, power limitations, subsystem failures, autonomous recovery, and changing environmental conditions. A critical mission decision depends upon results generated across a very large population of simulation runs. SES Application SES establishes execution and campaign traceability so that materially relevant results remain connected to: Scenario → Configuration → Execution Conditions → Runtime Events → Repetition → Completion Status → Output Interrupted, failed, modified, or anomalous runs remain visible rather than disappearing from the analytical record. Result Decision-makers can determine not merely that simulations were performed, but which configurations actually executed, under which conditions, whether execution remained complete and controlled, and which exact executions produced the outputs being relied upon. Business Value SES can help organizations identify potential governance gaps such as: Execution Traceability Gaps Configuration-to-Run Gaps Observation Gaps Intervention Traceability Gaps Execution Drift Repetition Comparability Gaps Failed-Run Visibility Gaps Execution-to-Output Lineage Gaps These findings can then be investigated before conclusions are drawn about simulation quality, validity, safety, or operational readiness. Relationship to Adjacent SIMULOS® Standards Simulation Scenario Standard (SSS) asks: What scenarios must be simulated? Simulation Execution Standard (SES) asks: What actually happened when those simulations were executed? Simulation Output Governance Standard (SOGS) then asks: What exactly did those executions produce, and what may legitimately be inferred from those outputs? The architectural transition is therefore: Scenario → Execution → Output Foundational Principle A simulation result cannot be fully understood from its output alone; it must remain connected to the execution conditions and execution history that produced it. Canonical Closing Statement Simulation Execution Standard (SES) provides the governance structure through which simulation intent becomes traceable simulation activity. By governing instantiation, execution control, observation, repetition, and execution documentation, SES enables organizations to reconstruct what actually ran, distinguish intended configuration from executed configuration, preserve material deviations and failures, compare repeated executions appropriately, and maintain lineage between simulation executions and the outputs they produce.

title: OOF™ About Simulation Input & Data Standard - (SIDS)
text: OOF™ About Simulation Input & Data Standard - (SIDS) About Simulation Input & Data Standard - (SIDS) Simulation Every simulation depends on inputs. Those inputs may come from sensors, historical records, operational systems, scientific measurements, external models, human operators, AI systems, synthetic generators, or previous simulations. But information does not become suitable simulation input merely because it exists or because a simulation can technically ingest it. Simulation Input & Data Standard (SIDS) governs the conditions under which information may legitimately enter and influence a simulation. Canonical Definition Simulation Input & Data Standard (SIDS) defines the governance conditions under which data, values, signals, measurements, states, distributions, synthetic inputs, and other information may enter a simulation and influence its behavior, requiring material inputs to remain sufficiently identifiable, representative, transformation-governed, temporally appropriate, uncertainty-aware, and traceable to their simulation use. Why SIDS Exists A strong simulation model can still produce weak or misleading results when the information entering it is: unrepresentative, stale, temporally misaligned, transformed incorrectly, based on the wrong population, missing important variation, synthetically generated without disclosure, uncertain, incomplete, or incompatible with the simulation context. SIDS therefore separates: Data Availability from: Simulation Input Suitability The key question is not: Do we have data? It is: Is this the right information to enter this simulation under these conditions? Governed Space Simulation Inputs & Data SIDS governs data specifically at the point where it becomes capable of influencing simulation behavior. It does not attempt to govern the entire organizational data lifecycle. Its focus is the simulation-input boundary. Governance Flow Governed Simulation Model & Environment ↓ Input Need ↓ Simulation Input Identification ↓ Representativeness Assessment ↓ Transformation Governance ↓ Temporal Qualification ↓ Input Uncertainty ↓ Acceptance / Restriction / Exclusion ↓ Governed Simulation Input & Data Basis ↓ Simulation Scenario Design What SIDS Governs SIDS establishes whether material Simulation Inputs are: Identifiable — what exactly entered the simulation? Representative — do the inputs sufficiently represent the conditions the simulation is intended to model? Transformation-Governed — what happened to the data before simulation use? Temporally Appropriate — does the data represent the right point, sequence, period, or system state? Uncertainty-Aware — what measurement, estimation, sampling, transformation, or representativeness uncertainty remains? Traceable — which inputs influenced which simulation configuration and execution? Representativeness Matters Data can be accurate and still be inappropriate for a simulation. For example: data collected during normal operation may accurately describe normal behavior while being unsuitable for a simulation of emergency failure. Likewise: data from one population, climate, geographic region, system generation, or operating state may not represent another. SIDS therefore treats representativeness as a simulation-specific governance question. Representative for what? must always remain connected to: Simulation Object + Purpose + Scope + Reality Representation + Scenario Context Transformation Must Remain Visible Simulation inputs are frequently transformed before use. They may be: normalized, aggregated, filtered, interpolated, extrapolated, encoded, converted, cleaned, derived, imputed, or synthetically generated. These transformations may materially change the information entering the simulation. SIDS therefore preserves the chain: Source Data → Transformation → Simulation Input A transformed input should not silently be represented as identical to the original source information. Synthetic Inputs Synthetic data can be essential to simulation. It may enable testing of: rare failures, extreme environments, unavailable populations, hypothetical systems, future conditions, edge cases, or dangerous scenarios that cannot reasonably be reproduced in reality. SIDS does not treat synthetic data as inferior by default. It requires one essential distinction: Synthetic Input ≠ Observed Reality The synthetic origin and the conditions under which that input may be used must remain visible. Temporal Context Matters Simulation data always has a relationship to time. SIDS therefore asks: When was this information observed? Which period does it represent? Is it sufficiently current for this simulation? Do multiple inputs represent the same point in time? Does sequence matter? Has temporal aggregation hidden material events? This becomes especially important for fast-changing systems such as: AI, autonomous systems, financial systems, infrastructure, transportation, digital twins, or live operational simulations. Uncertainty Must Travel With the Input Measured or estimated inputs are rarely perfectly certain. A sensor may have tolerance. Historical data may have sampling limitations. Synthetic data may depend upon generation assumptions. Interpolated values may not have been directly observed. SIDS requires material uncertainty to remain connected to the input rather than disappearing when the data enters the simulation. The simulation therefore should not imply greater certainty than its input basis supports. Missing Data Missing information is itself a governance condition. SIDS prevents missing values from silently becoming: zero average default or: synthetic replacement without an identifiable treatment. Possible responses may include substitution, imputation, scenario restriction, conditional use, or exclusion. The important requirement is visibility. Conflicting Inputs Different sources may disagree. For example: Sensor A = 50 while: Sensor B = 75 SIDS requires material conflict to remain identifiable and the treatment of that conflict to remain governable. A simulation should not simply choose the more convenient value without preserving why that choice was made. Input Sets A simulation execution rarely depends on one input. It consumes a complete Simulation Input Set. SIDS allows each execution to remain connected to the exact set of materially relevant information that entered it. This enables later reconstruction: Which inputs produced this result? Which were measured? Which were synthetic? Which had been transformed? Which were estimated or uncertain? Which represented an older system state? Business Value For organizations using simulation, SIDS provides direct operational value. It helps detect situations where expensive simulation capability is being fed with information that is unsuitable for the question being simulated. This may reveal: weak datasets, hidden population gaps, temporal mismatch, synthetic-data dependence, transformation loss, stale inputs, incompatible data sources, missing information, and outputs that appear precise despite uncertain input conditions. SIDS therefore improves the ability to: compare simulation runs, explain outputs, reproduce results, challenge simulation conclusions, update simulations, trace failures, and prepare simulation outputs for downstream validation. Relationship to Simulation Assumptions SAS governs what the simulation assumes. SIDS governs what information the simulation consumes. An assumption may influence how an input is interpreted, but the two remain distinct. For example: Assumption: Weather remains stable. Input: Measured temperature at simulation start. Relationship to Model & Environment SMES establishes the controlled model and environment. SIDS determines what information may enter that governed structure. The relationship is: Model & Environment → Input Requirements → Governed Input & Data Basis Relationship to Scenario Design SIDS does not determine which scenarios should be run. It determines which information is available and suitable to support those scenarios. The next Parent Standard, Simulation Scenario Standard (SSS), governs: Which combinations of conditions, variations, edge cases, stresses, and alternatives should actually be simulated? Relationship to VALIDOS® SIDS does not perform universal data validation. VALIDOS® may separately validate: an input dataset, a source, an evidence object, a simulation output, or the simulation itself. The boundary is: SIDS governs whether information may function as simulation input. VALIDOS® governs formal validation of the relevant Validation Object. Relationship to ORA™ ORA™ governs actual Operational Reality. Simulation Inputs may originate from that reality. SIDS governs the transformation from: Operational information into: governed simulation input without redefining Operational Reality itself. Relationship to INTEGROS® and ADIT® INTEGROS® may govern integrity of input objects, records, transformations, and preserved states. ADIT® may preserve evidence of input acquisition, transformation, substitution, and execution use. SIDS remains focused on the simulation-specific suitability and use of the input. Architectural Position SIDS is the sixth Parent Standard of SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture. The progression is: Simulation Object ↓ Simulation Purpose & Scope ↓ Reality Representation ↓ Simulation Assumptions ↓ Simulation Model & Environment ↓ Simulation Inputs & Data ↓ Simulation Scenario Design SIDS therefore marks a critical transition. Before SIDS, SIMULOS® establishes: what the simulation is, what it represents, what it assumes, and through which structure it will operate. SIDS then establishes: what information may legitimately enter that structure. Only after that foundation exists can scenario governance meaningfully determine what conditions the simulation should be asked to explore. Foundational Principle Information becomes legitimate simulation input only when what it represents, how it was transformed, when it applies, what uncertainty it carries, and where it may influence the simulation remain sufficiently governed. Canonical Closing Statement Simulation Input & Data Standard (SIDS) governs the information boundary of SIMULOS® by ensuring that material inputs remain identifiable, sufficiently representative, transformation-governed, temporally appropriate, uncertainty-aware, and traceable to the simulation activity they influence. By distinguishing technical ingestibility from methodological suitability, observed information from synthetic input, current information from temporally mismatched data, and raw information from transformed input, SIDS provides the governed Input & Data Basis required before simulation conditions can be intentionally organized into scenarios and executed.

title: OOF™ About Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Standard - (SLRS)
text: OOF™ About Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Standard - (SLRS) About Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Standard - (SLRS) About Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Standard (SLRS) Architecture: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Parent Standard: Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Standard (SLRS) Governed Space: Simulation Lifecycle, Drift & Resimulation Canonical Definition Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Standard (SLRS) governs how the continuing relevance of a simulation is monitored after its creation and use, how material divergence between the governed simulation basis and changing reality is recognized, and when change requires simulation update, resimulation, replacement, or retirement. SLRS addresses a fundamental lifecycle problem: A simulation that was appropriate when created may become progressively less representative as the object, environment, assumptions, data, operational conditions, or reality itself changes. The Standard prevents historical simulation results from retaining unchanged authority after the conditions that gave them meaning have materially changed. Why SLRS Matters Simulation governance does not end when a simulation campaign finishes. Systems evolve. Environments change. New operational data appears. Previously unknown failure modes emerge. Models improve. Assumptions become obsolete. Inputs shift. New scenarios become relevant. SLRS establishes a governed mechanism for asking: Is this simulation still relevant to the reality for which it is being relied upon? Where the answer changes materially, SLRS determines whether the appropriate response is: continued use → review → update → partial resimulation → broader resimulation → replacement → retirement. Governance Flow Governed Simulation Evidence & Reliance Basis → Lifecycle Monitoring → Simulation Drift Recognition → Resimulation Trigger → Resimulation Scope Determination → Resimulation / Replacement / Retirement → Updated Governed Simulation Lifecycle This creates the recursive lifecycle: Simulation → Operational Use → Reality Change → Simulation Drift → Resimulation Trigger → Resimulation / Replacement / Retirement What SLRS Helps Organizations Govern SLRS helps organizations prevent simulation results from becoming methodologically stale while remaining operationally influential. It provides a structured basis for monitoring changes in: the Simulation Object; object configuration and version; represented reality; environmental conditions; assumptions; models; inputs and data; scenarios; observed operational behavior; simulation-to-reality correlation; evidence relevance; known limitations. Not every change requires complete resimulation. SLRS exists partly to determine which changes are material enough to require action and how much of the simulation lifecycle must be reopened. Use Case 1 — Space Mission: Mission Reality Changes After Simulation A space mission has undergone extensive simulation covering trajectory, spacecraft behavior, navigation, landing conditions, environmental effects, system failures, crew procedures, and mission contingencies. Months later, new information becomes available. The spacecraft configuration has changed. Updated environmental observations alter expected surface conditions. A component behaves differently during physical testing. New mission constraints modify the landing profile. The original simulations may still be technically correct representations of the conditions under which they were executed. But those conditions are no longer identical to the mission now being prepared. The critical governance question becomes: Which previous simulation results remain relevant, which have materially drifted from the current mission basis, and what must be simulated again? SLRS provides the lifecycle mechanism for identifying those changes, determining their materiality, activating appropriate resimulation triggers, and defining whether resimulation must cover one affected scenario, one subsystem, a scenario family, or a much larger part of the mission simulation campaign. This prevents two opposite failures: continuing to rely on obsolete simulations and unnecessarily repeating an entire simulation program whenever anything changes. Resimulation should follow material change, not merely the passage of time. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Vehicle or Robot: Operational Reality Evolves An autonomous vehicle or robot is developed through millions of simulated scenarios and subsequently enters real-world operation. Operational experience begins producing conditions that were absent or materially different in the original simulation environment. New road layouts appear. Sensor hardware changes. Software behavior evolves. Human interaction patterns differ from those represented during development. Previously rare edge cases become observable. Weather, lighting, surfaces, obstacles, or environmental distributions change. The original simulation campaign does not suddenly become useless. But neither should its relevance be assumed to remain unchanged. SLRS establishes continuous lifecycle governance between: the simulation basis that existed when evidence was produced and the operational reality that exists now. Material differences become Simulation Drift Candidates. Where drift becomes significant, SLRS can trigger targeted resimulation of the affected conditions rather than automatically rebuilding the entire simulation campaign. If the underlying model or representation has become fundamentally unsuitable, the appropriate outcome may instead be replacement or retirement. This creates a feedback loop: Real-World Operation → New Reality Evidence → Drift Recognition → Resimulation → Updated Simulation Basis The simulation therefore becomes a governed evolving representation rather than a static artifact frozen at development time. A simulation should not remain authoritative merely because it was once representative. Enterprise Value SLRS enables organizations to maintain simulation relevance across long operational lifecycles without treating every change as either irrelevant or grounds for complete resimulation. It supports: change-sensitive simulation governance → proportionate resimulation → preserved relevance → controlled retirement. For organizations operating large simulation programs, this can reduce unnecessary computational and engineering repetition while making material simulation drift visible before outdated simulation evidence continues influencing important decisions. Foundational Principle A simulation remains governably relevant only while the conditions that support its meaning remain materially applicable; when those conditions change, continued reliance requires governed reassessment.

title: OOF™ About Simulation Model & Environment Standard - (SMES)
text: OOF™ About Simulation Model & Environment Standard - (SMES) About Simulation Model & Environment Standard - (SMES) About Simulation Model & Environment Standard (SMES) Simulation Model & Environment Standard (SMES) is the fifth Parent Standard of SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture. It governs the point at which a defined Reality Representation and governed Simulation Assumptions are transformed into the actual model and environment through which simulation activity can occur. Canonical Definition Simulation Model & Environment Standard (SMES) defines the governance conditions under which a simulation model and its simulation environment are constructed, structured, configured, parameterized, bounded, versioned, controlled, and maintained as an identifiable execution context capable of supporting governed simulation activity. Why This Standard Exists A simulation can have a clearly defined object, purpose, representation of reality, and assumptions and still produce misleading results if the model or environment implementing them is incorrectly structured or configured. SMES therefore creates a governed bridge between: what the simulation intends to represent and: the executable structure through which that representation is simulated. It makes model structure, environment configuration, parameters, boundaries, dependencies, versions, and material changes visible and governable rather than leaving them as hidden technical implementation details. What SMES Governs SMES governs the simulation-specific relationship between: Simulation Model → Simulation Environment → Boundaries → Parameters → Configuration → Versions → Controlled Execution Context It establishes whether the model and environment being used are actually the governed model and environment intended for the simulation. This includes governance of model structure, environment configuration, boundary interactions, parameterization, model-environment compatibility, configuration control, version continuity, material changes, configuration drift, and reconstruction. Governance Flow Governed Reality Representation ↓ Governed Simulation Assumptions ↓ Simulation Model Structure ↓ Simulation Environment Configuration ↓ Boundary & Interaction Definition ↓ Parameterization ↓ Model–Environment Compatibility ↓ Configuration & Version Binding ↓ Controlled Simulation Execution Context Governance Boundary SMES begins when the governed Reality Representation and Simulation Assumptions must be converted into an executable simulation structure. It ends when the model, environment, parameters, boundaries, configuration, and versions are sufficiently established and controlled for the next stage of the SIMULOS® lifecycle. It does not determine whether the resulting simulation is universally valid, whether its outputs justify operational reliance, or whether the simulated environment is equivalent to actual Operational Reality. Architectural Position Within the 12-Parent-Standard SIMULOS® lifecycle: Simulation Object → Simulation Purpose & Scope → Reality Representation → Simulation Assumptions → [Simulation Model & Environment] → downstream simulation governance SMES therefore occupies the transition between conceptual simulation design and the controlled technical structure required for simulation execution. Relationship to Other OOF® Architectures ORA™ governs actual Operational Reality; SMES governs the constructed simulation environment. VALIDOS® governs validation questions and resulting validation claims; SMES governs how the simulation model and environment themselves are established and controlled. INTEGROS® governs integrity as a distinct governance space; SMES does not duplicate general integrity governance. ADIT® may provide evidence and audit governance for model, configuration, version, and change records. Why It Matters Two simulations can appear to test the same problem while actually using different models, environments, parameter sets, boundaries, or versions. Without explicit governance of those differences, their outputs may appear comparable even when their underlying execution contexts are materially different. SMES makes those differences governable and traceable. A simulation becomes structurally governable only when the model and environment through which it operates remain identifiable, bounded, configured, parameterized, versioned, controlled, and traceably connected to the reality representation and assumptions they implement.

title: OOF™ About Simulation Object Standard - (SOS)
text: OOF™ About Simulation Object Standard - (SOS) About Simulation Object Standard - (SOS) Defining What the Simulation Actually Represents Actually Represents Every simulation begins with an object. That object may be a machine, system, process, environment, behavior, population, mission, infrastructure, autonomous system, AI-enabled system, or another target intended to be represented through simulation. Before anything can be simulated, one question must be answered: What exactly are we simulating? Simulation Object Standard (SOS) establishes the governance conditions required to answer that question consistently. SOS is the first Parent Standard of SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture. It governs the Simulation Object before simulation purpose, representation, assumptions, models, scenarios, execution, outputs, or reality correlation begin. Why SOS Exists Simulation can produce highly precise outputs while still representing the wrong object. This may occur when: the object is poorly defined, the wrong version is simulated, configurations are mixed, important components are excluded, system boundaries are unclear, a proxy is treated as the real target, or the object changes while the simulation continues to rely on an older definition. SOS prevents these problems by establishing a stable object foundation for the complete simulation lifecycle. What Is a Simulation Object? A Simulation Object is the governed target that a simulation intends to represent. It defines: what belongs to the simulation target, what remains outside it, which version applies, which configuration applies, which state applies, and: which object the resulting simulation outputs actually concern. A Simulation Object may be simple or highly complex. It may represent one component or an entire system-of-systems. The key requirement is that its identity and boundaries remain explicit. Object Before Representation SOS separates the real or intended simulation target from the mechanisms used to simulate it. Simulation Object ≠ Simulation Model Simulation Object ≠ Simulation Representation Simulation Object ≠ Simulation Environment The Simulation Object is what is being simulated. The model, representation, and environment are mechanisms through which the object is later represented and examined. This distinction prevents simulation technology from redefining the object merely because a particular model is easier to construct. Object Identity and Boundary A governed Simulation Object must be sufficiently distinguishable from materially different objects. Depending on the context, this may require identification of: system identity, version, configuration, relevant components, operational state, dependencies, temporal condition, and object boundaries. The object boundary establishes what the simulation claim can legitimately refer to. If only part of a system is included, the resulting simulation must not be represented as though the entire system was simulated. Versions, Configurations, and Change Simulation relevance may depend on the exact object version and configuration. A simulation of: Version A does not automatically apply to: Version B. A simulation of: Configuration X does not automatically apply to: Configuration Y. SOS therefore keeps simulation results connected to the object state they actually represent. When the object materially changes, that change must remain visible to downstream SIMULOS® governance. Complex Simulation Objects SIMULOS® may govern simulations involving: autonomous vehicles, aircraft, spacecraft, robot fleets, AI systems, industrial facilities, digital twins, infrastructure networks, organizations, populations, environmental systems, and complete system-of-systems environments. SOS allows complex objects to be decomposed into identifiable components while preserving their relationship to the overall Simulation Object. This makes it possible to understand whether a simulation conclusion applies to: a component, a subsystem, a complete system, or: an interconnected operational environment. Preventing Object Inflation One of the central functions of SOS is to prevent a narrow simulation from becoming a broader claim than the object definition supports. SOS therefore protects against: component → whole-system inflation single-version → product-family inflation single-configuration → all-configurations inflation and: proxy-object → target-object substitution The simulation claim must remain anchored to the object actually simulated. Governance Flow SOS progresses through: Candidate Simulation Target → Simulation Object Identification → Object Boundary → Object Structure → Object Version → Object Configuration → Object State → Object Documentation → Governed Simulation Object Once the Simulation Object is sufficiently established, SIMULOS® can proceed to the next question: Why is this object being simulated, and what must the simulation cover? Relationship to SIMULOS® SOS establishes the first governance foundation of the complete SIMULOS® lifecycle. The architecture then progresses into: Simulation Purpose & Scope → Reality Representation → Assumptions → Model & Environment → Inputs & Data → Scenario Design → Execution → Output Governance → Simulation-to-Reality Correlation → Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary → Lifecycle & Resimulation Every downstream stage depends upon the object established by SOS. Relationship to Other OOF® Architectures SOS governs specifically the Simulation Object. ORA™ governs operational reality. OBIDENITY® may govern broader identity, origin, ownership, provenance, and authority. INTEGROS® governs integrity. VALIDOS® governs validation. ADIT® governs continuous audit and evidence. These architectures may interact with SOS, but they do not replace its simulation-specific function. Why It Matters A sophisticated simulation cannot compensate for an incorrectly defined object. If the object is wrong, outdated, incomplete, or ambiguous, downstream simulation precision may create only precise answers about the wrong target. SOS therefore establishes a simple but fundamental rule: Define the object before simulating the object. Foundational Principle A simulation cannot legitimately claim to represent an object more precisely than that object has been identified, bounded, versioned, configured, and documented. Canonical Closing Statement Simulation Object Standard (SOS) establishes the object foundation of SIMULOS® by ensuring that every simulation begins with a clearly identified, bounded, versioned, configured, state-aware, and traceable Simulation Object. By separating the simulation target from its model, representation, and environment, SOS ensures that every downstream simulation activity remains connected to the exact object it claims to represent.

title: OOF™ About Simulation Output Governance Standard - (SOGS)
text: OOF™ About Simulation Output Governance Standard - (SOGS) About Simulation Output Governance Standard - (SOGS) Simulation Results Actually Mean A simulation may produce enormous amounts of data. But producing an output is not the same as understanding what that output legitimately establishes. A Simulation Output may be: direct, derived, aggregated, statistical, execution-specific, scenario-specific, or generated across millions of repeated runs. The output may also be transformed, filtered, summarized, compared, or interpreted before someone eventually uses it to support a decision. Simulation Output Governance Standard (SOGS) governs this transition. Canonical Definition Simulation Output Governance Standard (SOGS) defines the governance conditions under which outputs produced by Simulation Execution are identified, classified, bounded, interpreted, limitation-aware, documented, and connected to the execution basis that produced them so that direct Simulation Outputs remain distinguishable from derived results, aggregation, subsequent inference, and claims extending beyond the simulation itself. Why SOGS Exists Simulation programs often focus heavily on: building the model and: running the simulation. But a critical governance problem begins after execution: What exactly does the result mean? For example: 18 failures occurred in 250,000 simulation runs. That is an output. From that output, someone may conclude: The system has a failure probability of 0.0072%. That may already involve aggregation and interpretation. Another person may then conclude: The real system is 99.9928% reliable. That is a much stronger claim. These three statements are not methodologically equivalent. SOGS exists to keep them separate. Governed Space Simulation Output Governance SOGS governs Simulation Outputs after governed execution and before claims about Operational Reality, validation, or operational reliance are made. The central question is: What did the simulation actually produce, and how far may interpretation legitimately extend from that result? Governance Flow Governed Simulation Execution ↓ Simulation Output ↓ Output Identification ↓ Output Classification ↓ Execution & Scenario Binding ↓ Simulation Inference ↓ Output Limitations ↓ Output Documentation ↓ Governed Simulation Output ↓ Reality Correlation Output Is Not Inference One of the most important distinctions in SOGS is: Simulation Output ≠ Simulation Inference For example: Output: The simulated spacecraft entered Safe Mode in 14 executions. Inference: Safe Mode activation appears associated with a specific simulated power and communication condition. The inference may be supported by the output. But it is still an inference. SOGS keeps that interpretive step visible. Simulation Inference Is Not Operational Reality An even more important boundary is: Simulation Inference ≠ Real-World Fact A simulation may demonstrate: Under these modeled conditions, this behavior occurred. That does not automatically establish: The real system will behave the same way. SOGS therefore prevents a direct methodological leap from: simulated behavior to: Operational Reality. That next step requires downstream Reality Correlation and, where applicable, VALIDOS®. Direct and Derived Outputs SOGS distinguishes between: Direct Simulation Output and: Derived Simulation Output. A Direct Output may include: state reached, event occurred, trajectory produced, action selected, temperature exceeded, collision occurred, system recovered, or failure occurred. A Derived Output may include: average, percentile, failure rate, distribution, ranking, comparison, aggregated metric, or post-processed result. Derived Outputs remain legitimate. But their relationship to the original executions must remain visible. Aggregation Must Not Hide the Story Large simulation programs often reduce millions of executions into a small set of numbers. For example: Mission Success Rate: 99.98% That figure may be useful. But SOGS asks: Which executions were included? Which failed? Which were excluded? Which Scenario Space was represented? Did one rare but critical failure mode disappear inside the aggregate? Was the output produced from nominal scenarios, stress scenarios, or the complete governed Scenario Set? This protects organizations from allowing a convenient aggregate to conceal the conditions that produced it. Outputs Must Remain Connected to Execution A Simulation Output should remain traceable to: Simulation Object ↓ Model & Environment ↓ Inputs ↓ Scenario ↓ Execution ↓ Output Without this relationship, a result may later be interpreted outside the conditions under which it was generated. SOGS therefore works directly with the execution lineage produced under SES. Limitations Travel With the Output A Simulation Output may inherit limitations from: assumptions, abstraction, fidelity, Input Data, scenario coverage, execution conditions, observation limitations, repetition sufficiency, model boundaries, or unresolved uncertainty. These limitations do not disappear when an attractive chart or precise percentage is generated. SOGS establishes: Output processing does not erase upstream limitations. Precision Does Not Equal Certainty Simulation systems can produce extremely precise numbers. For example: 0.00481763 The numerical precision may be mathematically correct. But the result may depend upon: uncertain inputs, incomplete scenario coverage, simplified reality representation, assumptions, or limited execution conditions. SOGS therefore distinguishes: Computational Precision from: Strength of Interpretation. Unexpected Outputs Matter Simulation Outputs do not always confirm what was expected. Unexpected behavior may reveal: a new interaction, a hidden dependency, an Edge Case, a Scenario Coverage Gap, an unstable model region, an execution anomaly, or a new simulation question. SOGS therefore does not treat unexpected outputs as disposable noise by default. They may create a feedback path: Unexpected Output ↓ New Question ↓ Scenario Reassessment ↓ Additional Simulation Output Classification Classification helps downstream users understand what type of result they are seeing. A Simulation Output may be: Direct Derived Aggregated Intermediate Final Deterministic Stochastic Execution-Specific Repetition-Based Scenario-Level Campaign-Level or another governed class. This becomes especially important when simulation outputs move between engineering teams, management, regulators, customers, or external partners. Output Population Matters An output should identify what population it represents. For example: Failure rate = 0.2% means little unless it is known whether that represents: one scenario, one system configuration, one environment, one Repetition Set, an entire Scenario Set, or a complete simulation campaign. SOGS keeps that population boundary visible. Inference Boundary A Simulation Inference should remain bounded by the simulation conditions that support it. If a simulation examined: Environment A the output should not silently become evidence about: Environments A, B, C, and D. If a simulation represented: one software version the inference should not automatically extend to: all future versions. If the Scenario Set covered: normal and moderate stress conditions the conclusion should not automatically extend to: extreme failure conditions. Business Value SOGS helps organizations answer questions that often become difficult after large simulation programs produce enormous amounts of results: Which result came from which execution? What is direct output and what is interpretation? Which executions contributed to this aggregate? Which results were excluded? What limitations remain attached? What can legitimately be claimed? Where does the simulation stop and a reality claim begin? This makes SOGS useful as both: a Simulation Output governance framework and: a diagnostic layer for existing simulation programs. Use Case 1 — Space Mission Simulation OutputScenario A space organization runs millions of simulations for autonomous spacecraft recovery. The resulting dashboard reports: Mission Recovery Success: 99.96%. Application SOGS separates: Direct Outputs — individual recovery outcomes. Aggregated Output — 99.96% simulated recovery success. Inference — recovery performs strongly across the simulated campaign. The standard also preserves: which scenarios contributed, which runs failed, which executions were excluded, applicable power and communication conditions, scenario coverage limitations, and the execution lineage behind the aggregate. Result The organization can legitimately state what the simulation campaign demonstrated without converting: 99.96% simulated recovery success into an unsupported claim that: the real spacecraft has a 99.96% recovery probability. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Vehicle Safety SimulationScenario An autonomous vehicle simulation reports: 99.99% successful collision avoidance across a large simulation campaign. Application SOGS examines whether the result represents: all Scenario Families, only nominal traffic, Edge Cases, degraded perception, adverse weather, combined conditions, and stress scenarios. It also separates: Observed Simulation Performance from: Inference about system safety. Result The organization may conclude: The system achieved 99.99% collision avoidance within the defined governed simulation population. It may not automatically conclude: The autonomous vehicle is 99.99% safe in Operational Reality. That stronger claim requires downstream correlation and validation. Relationship to SES SES — Simulation Execution Standard governs what actually ran. SOGS governs what those executions produced. The handoff is: Governed Simulation Execution Record ↓ Governed Simulation Output Relationship to SSS SSS — Simulation Scenario Standard establishes the Scenario Space and Scenario Coverage. SOGS ensures that output interpretation remains bounded by the scenarios actually represented. Therefore: Broad Output Volume ≠ Broad Scenario Meaning. Relationship to Reality Correlation SOGS deliberately stops before establishing whether simulated behavior corresponds to Operational Reality. That next governance question is: How strongly does the governed Simulation Output correlate with actual reality? This belongs to the next SIMULOS® lifecycle space. Relationship to VALIDOS® VALIDOS® may subsequently evaluate whether a Simulation Output, Simulation Inference, reality-correlation claim, or simulation process can support a formal validation conclusion. SOGS prepares the Simulation Output for that downstream assessment. Relationship to INTEGROS® SOGS deliberately does not create a separate Simulation Output Integrity governance space. General integrity remains governed under INTEGROS®. SOGS focuses specifically on: Output Identification Output Classification Inference Output Limitations and: Output Documentation. Architectural Position SOGS is the ninth Parent Standard of SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture. The progression is: Simulation Scenario Design ↓ Simulation Execution ↓ Simulation Output Governance ↓ Reality Correlation SOGS therefore marks the transition from: what happened inside the simulation to: what that result may legitimately support as an interpretation. Why It Matters Modern organizations increasingly have no shortage of Simulation Outputs. They may have: millions of runs, enormous datasets, dashboards, distributions, AI-generated summaries, automated anomaly detection, and highly precise numerical results. The real bottleneck can become: meaning. SOGS provides a governance layer for determining: what the simulation actually produced, what was subsequently inferred, what remains limited, and where the claim must stop. Foundational Principle A Simulation Output becomes governable only when what the simulation directly produced remains distinguishable from how that output was processed, interpreted, limited, aggregated, and ultimately used to support claims beyond the execution that produced it. Canonical Closing Statement Simulation Output Governance Standard (SOGS) governs the transition from executed simulation to interpretable simulation result by ensuring that Simulation Outputs remain identifiable, classified, execution-bound, inference-bounded, limitation-aware, and documented. By separating direct output from derived output, aggregation from individual execution behavior, computational precision from interpretive certainty, and simulated behavior from claims about Operational Reality, SOGS enables organizations to use large and complex simulation outputs without allowing the meaning of those outputs to exceed the simulation conditions that actually produced them.

title: OOF™ About Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard - (SPSS)
text: OOF™ About Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard - (SPSS) About Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard - (SPSS) Governing Why a Simulation Exists Before Deciding How It Should Represent Reality Simulation Exists Before Deciding How It Should Represent Reality A simulation may be technically sophisticated and still be unsuitable for the question it is being used to answer. Before models, environments, assumptions, scenarios, inputs, or execution methods are selected, the simulation must establish why it is being performed and what it is legitimately intended to cover. Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard (SPSS) provides this governance layer within SIMULOS®. Canonical Definition Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard (SPSS) defines the governance conditions under which the reason for performing a simulation, the questions it is intended to address, its governed scope, material inclusions and exclusions, applicability context, required simulation depth, and appropriate simulation precision are formally established before downstream simulation representation begins. Why SPSS Exists Organizations use simulations for different purposes: system design, engineering analysis, safety assessment, operational planning, autonomous-system testing, AI evaluation, infrastructure planning, scenario exploration, scientific investigation, training, decision support, and pre-deployment testing. These purposes are not interchangeable. A simulation designed to explore possible behavior may not provide sufficient basis for a safety-critical decision. A simulation covering one operating environment cannot automatically support conclusions about another. A simulation examining one configuration cannot silently become evidence for every configuration of the system. SPSS prevents this purpose and scope inflation. Governed Space Simulation Purpose & Scope SPSS governs the transition from: Defined Simulation Object to: Governed Simulation Inquiry It establishes what the simulation is expected to investigate before downstream simulation architecture is constructed around that objective. Governance Flow Simulation Object → Simulation Purpose → Simulation Question → Simulation Scope → Inclusions & Exclusions → Applicability Context → Simulation Depth → Simulation Precision → Governed Simulation Purpose & Scope This governed basis then becomes an input to the next SIMULOS® space: Reality Representation What SPSS Establishes A governed simulation should establish: Purpose — why the simulation is being performed. Simulation Question — what the simulation is expected to investigate or demonstrate. Scope — which parts of the Simulation Object, system, process, environment, behavior, or interaction are included. Exclusions — what the simulation explicitly does not represent or evaluate. Applicability — the environments, configurations, populations, operating conditions, or contexts to which the simulation relates. Simulation Depth — how extensively the simulation must investigate the defined problem. Simulation Precision — what level of representational and analytical precision is appropriate for the intended purpose. Business Value For organizations using simulation, SPSS creates a clear governance basis before significant resources are committed to simulation design and execution. It helps organizations determine whether: the simulation being built actually addresses the business or engineering question, simulation expenditure is aligned with the intended decision, critical operating conditions have been excluded, simulation conclusions are being used beyond their legitimate scope, different simulation projects are addressing comparable questions, and downstream teams understand exactly what the simulation is and is not intended to establish. This becomes increasingly important when simulation results influence investment, engineering, deployment, safety, regulatory, autonomous-system, or high-consequence operational decisions. Governance Boundary SPSS begins when a sufficiently identified Simulation Object requires a defined simulation purpose and governed operational scope. It ends when the simulation purpose, questions, scope, exclusions, applicability context, required depth, and appropriate precision have been sufficiently established to support governed Reality Representation. SPSS does not determine whether the simulation is valid, whether its evidence is sufficient for external validation, or whether operational reliance should ultimately be authorized. Those questions belong to their appropriate downstream SIMULOS® spaces or complementary OOF® architectures. Practical Governance Test Before simulation development proceeds, an organization should be able to answer: What exactly are we trying to learn, test, examine, or demonstrate through this simulation? Which reality does that question concern? What is inside the simulation scope? What is explicitly outside it? Under which conditions will the resulting simulation remain applicable? How much simulation depth and precision does the intended purpose actually require? If these questions cannot be answered, downstream simulation sophistication cannot compensate for the missing governance foundation. Relationship to SIMULOS® SPSS is the second Parent Standard of SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture. It follows: Simulation Object Standard and precedes: Reality Representation governance. Its architectural role is fundamental: The Simulation Object establishes what is being simulated. SPSS establishes why it is being simulated and what the simulation is allowed to cover. Only after both are established should the architecture begin governing how relevant reality will be represented. Foundational Principle A simulation cannot legitimately answer a broader question than the purpose and scope for which it was actually designed. Canonical Closing Statement Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard establishes the governed inquiry boundary of SIMULOS® by defining why a simulation is performed, what questions it is intended to address, what it includes and excludes, where its applicability begins and ends, and what level of depth and precision its purpose requires.
