By establishing these conditions before reality representation, model construction, scenario design, and execution, SPSS prevents simulation results from acquiring broader meaning, authority, or applicability than the simulation was actually designed to support.

title: OOF™ About Simulation Scenario Standard - (SSS)
text: OOF™ About Simulation Scenario Standard - (SSS) About Simulation Scenario Standard - (SSS) Simulation Must Actually Examine A simulation can be technically sophisticated and still miss the conditions that matter most. A model may be correct. The environment may be controlled. The input data may be suitable. Yet the simulation may still provide weak insight if it examines only convenient, expected, or easily modeled conditions. Simulation Scenario Standard (SSS) governs this problem. It determines how materially relevant scenarios are identified, varied, combined, stressed, bounded, prioritized, and assessed for sufficient coverage before simulation execution begins. Canonical Definition Simulation Scenario Standard (SSS) defines the governance conditions under which simulation scenarios are identified, selected, varied, stressed, combined, bounded, and assessed for sufficient coverage so that the simulation examines expected conditions, materially relevant variations, edge cases, failures, uncertainty, stresses, transitions, and plausible alternative conditions capable of affecting simulation outcomes. Why SSS Exists Simulation quality is not determined only by how many simulation runs are performed. A simulation may execute thousands or millions of times while still missing: critical edge cases, combined failures, degraded operating states, rare but severe events, transition failures, uncertainty ranges, environmental extremes, dependency failures, cascading events, or combinations that were never deliberately examined. SSS therefore separates: Simulation Volume from: Scenario Coverage More simulation does not automatically mean better examination. Governed Space Simulation Scenario Design SSS governs the condition space that exists between a prepared simulation basis and actual Simulation Execution. It asks: What must the simulation be asked to examine before its outputs can meaningfully represent the declared simulation inquiry? Governance Flow Governed Simulation Basis ↓ Scenario Requirements ↓ Baseline & Expected Conditions ↓ Scenario Variation ↓ Edge Cases ↓ Stress & Failure Conditions ↓ Scenario Combinations ↓ Scenario Coverage Assessment ↓ Coverage Gaps & Prioritization ↓ Governed Simulation Scenario Set ↓ Simulation Execution From Simulation Capability to Simulation Examination Before SSS, SIMULOS® establishes whether the simulation has a governed foundation. SSS then converts that capability into an intentional examination plan. The distinction is important: The fact that a model can simulate a condition does not mean that condition was actually tested. SSS therefore makes the Scenario Set itself a governed object. Expected Conditions Are Only the Beginning Nominal and expected operating conditions remain necessary. They establish: baseline behavior, routine performance, expected operating states, and controlled comparison points. But they are not sufficient where the Simulation Purpose includes materially relevant non-nominal behavior. SSS therefore expands scenario design beyond the expected state. Scenario Variation Systems operate under variation. Inputs change. Environments change. People behave differently. Resources fluctuate. Dependencies degrade. Autonomous systems encounter situations not present in their nominal operating assumptions. SSS governs deliberate variation across those conditions so that simulation behavior is examined across a meaningful condition space rather than at one convenient point. Edge Cases Some of the most important simulation failures occur outside the center of the operating distribution. An autonomous vehicle may perform well in ordinary traffic but fail when: visibility is partially obstructed, multiple road users interact unexpectedly, lane markings degrade, sensor confidence conflicts, or several individually manageable conditions occur together. A spacecraft may behave correctly during nominal mission phases while a critical issue emerges only during: communication loss, degraded navigation, partial power availability, unusual thermal conditions, or a transition between mission modes. SSS makes these conditions governable as Scenario Requirements rather than optional afterthoughts. Stress Conditions Stress scenarios intentionally push the simulation beyond normal conditions. The objective is not to create arbitrary extreme tests. The objective is to understand: Where does behavior materially change? Where do margins disappear? Where do dependencies become critical? Where does one degradation trigger another? This is especially important for complex autonomous, aerospace, industrial, infrastructure, and mission systems. Combined Conditions Real failures are often not isolated. A system may tolerate: communication delay and separately tolerate: sensor degradation while failing when: communication delay + sensor degradation + reduced power occur together. SSS therefore governs materially relevant combinations rather than assuming that individual-condition testing establishes combined-condition coverage. Transition Scenarios Some systems are most vulnerable not in stable states but during transitions. Examples include: launch, landing, docking, shutdown, restart, handover, human-to-autonomy control transfer, autonomy escalation, failover, recovery, or operational-mode change. SSS explicitly recognizes transition scenarios because: safe State A + safe State B does not automatically mean a safe transition between A and B. Failure and Degraded-State Scenarios A simulation should not examine only complete success and complete failure. Many operational problems occur in degraded states where the system still functions but under reduced capability. Examples include: partial sensing, limited communication, degraded power, reduced computation, incomplete navigation, restricted human support, partial actuator capability, or weakened infrastructure. These conditions are particularly important for autonomous and mission-critical systems because the system may continue operating while its decision environment has materially changed. Rare but High-Consequence Conditions Frequency alone does not determine scenario importance. A condition may be rare but capable of producing catastrophic consequences. SSS therefore supports consequence-aware scenario design. The question is not only: How often might this happen? It is also: What happens if it does? Uncertainty Must Become Scenario Coverage Upstream SIMULOS® standards may identify uncertainty in: assumptions, inputs, environment, parameters, or representation. SSS converts materially relevant uncertainty into scenarios where necessary. For example: uncertain parameter range may require: low / central / high conditions rather than one point estimate. This prevents uncertainty from being documented upstream but ignored during actual simulation. Scenario Coverage Scenario Coverage is one of the central outputs of SSS. It asks whether the Scenario Set sufficiently examines the materially relevant dimensions of the simulation inquiry. Coverage may include: nominal operation, variation, environments, populations, uncertainty, failures, transitions, stress, boundary conditions, rare events, dependencies, combinations, and recovery. Coverage Is Not Scenario Count Ten thousand scenarios may still provide poor coverage. A smaller set may provide much stronger coverage if it deliberately spans the materially relevant condition space. SSS therefore establishes: Scenario Count ≠ Scenario Coverage This is one of the most important practical distinctions in the standard. Scenario Coverage Gaps If a materially relevant condition cannot be simulated, SSS does not allow that absence to disappear. The architecture records a: Scenario Coverage Gap or, where the simulation itself cannot represent the condition: Scenario Capability Gap This is valuable because it turns an unknown weakness into an explicit governance object. Scenario Prioritization For complex systems, exhaustive scenario enumeration may be impossible. The number of possible combinations can become enormous. SSS therefore allows governed prioritization based on: consequence, plausibility, uncertainty, system sensitivity, dependency concentration, boundary proximity, failure history, novelty, and Simulation Purpose. The objective is not brute-force scenario generation. It is governed selection of materially relevant scenario space. Space and Mission Systems Scenario governance has particularly strong application in space systems because many important conditions: cannot be reproduced economically in reality, may occur only once during a mission, are difficult or impossible to reproduce after deployment, involve interacting subsystem failures, depend upon changing environments, or occur during short but high-consequence mission phases. A mission simulation may therefore need to examine not only: nominal trajectory but combinations such as: communication degradation + navigation uncertainty + reduced power + thermal constraint during a mission transition. SSS provides a structure through which such conditions can be identified, separated, combined, prioritized, and traced to actual simulation execution. Autonomous Systems Autonomous systems create a similar challenge. Their behavior can depend upon combinations of: environment, sensor state, incomplete information, other agents, human behavior, communication, timing, uncertainty, and internal decision state. SSS provides the scenario-governance layer through which these combinations can be deliberately examined rather than discovered only after real-world deployment. Scenario Discovery Simulation itself may reveal new scenarios. An unexpected behavior may expose: a previously unknown dependency, a new failure sequence, a new interaction, or a previously unrecognized edge case. SSS therefore treats Scenario Design as capable of evolving. The lifecycle may become: Scenario → Execution → Unexpected Behavior → New Scenario Requirement → Scenario Set Expansion The original Scenario Set remains historically preserved. No Outcome-Seeking Scenario Design Scenario design can become biased if it focuses only on conditions likely to produce favorable outcomes. SSS establishes a simple boundary: Scenario design must remain capable of exposing unfavorable, contradictory, or unexpected system behavior where such behavior is materially relevant to the Simulation Purpose. Relationship to SIDS SIDS — Simulation Input & Data Standard establishes which information may enter the simulation. SSS determines which combinations of those inputs, parameters, environmental states, and other conditions should actually be assembled into scenarios. Therefore: SIDS governs the information basis. SSS governs the condition space examined. Relationship to SMES SMES — Simulation Model & Environment Standard establishes the model, environment, boundaries, parameters, and versioned simulation structure. SSS configures that governed structure into deliberate scenario conditions. Relationship to Simulation Assumptions Scenario design may specifically test: assumption boundaries, uncertain assumptions, high-dependency assumptions, or conditions where assumptions may cease to remain applicable. SSS does not govern assumptions themselves. It determines when those assumptions should become the subject of deliberate simulated conditions. Relationship to VALIDOS® SSS does not determine whether scenario coverage is sufficient for a formal validation claim. VALIDOS® may later consume scenario design, execution, and resulting evidence when evaluating validation requirements. The boundary remains: SSS governs what the simulation examines. VALIDOS® governs what the resulting validation record can legitimately demonstrate. Relationship to ORA™ ORA™ governs actual Operational Reality. SSS may use real operational conditions, incidents, environments, or failure states as inputs to Scenario Requirements. But the scenario remains a simulation object. It is not Operational Reality itself. Relationship to ASGA™ and AIG® ASGA™ and AIG® may identify governance conditions relevant to autonomous-system or AI behavior. Those conditions may become Scenario Requirements when the governed system is simulated. For example: autonomous escalation condition may become: simulation scenario requirement without transferring autonomous-system governance into SSS. Architectural Position SSS is the seventh Parent Standard of SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture. The progression is: Simulation Object ↓ Simulation Purpose & Scope ↓ Reality Representation ↓ Simulation Assumptions ↓ Simulation Model & Environment ↓ Simulation Inputs & Data ↓ Simulation Scenario Design ↓ Simulation Execution SSS therefore marks the transition from: a simulation that is prepared to: a simulation that knows what it must actually examine. Why It Matters A simulation program can invest heavily in: better models, larger computing infrastructure, more data, higher fidelity, faster execution, and more simulation runs while still leaving the most important conditions unexamined. SSS provides a governance structure for identifying that gap. That makes the standard useful not only for designing simulations but also for diagnosing existing simulation programs. An organization may discover that its key bottleneck is not: simulation capability but: scenario selection and scenario coverage. Foundational Principle A simulation cannot claim meaningful coverage merely because it executes successfully; it must deliberately examine the materially relevant conditions, variations, boundaries, uncertainties, failures, stresses, interactions, and alternatives capable of changing the behavior or conclusions of the simulation. Canonical Closing Statement Simulation Scenario Standard (SSS) governs the condition space that a simulation must deliberately examine before execution can meaningfully support broader interpretation. By separating simulation volume from scenario coverage and governing expected conditions, variations, edge cases, boundaries, failures, degraded states, transitions, uncertainty, stress, combinations, prioritization, coverage gaps, scenario discovery, and scenario-to-execution traceability, SSS establishes a technology-neutral methodology for ensuring that simulation capability is converted into deliberate examination of the conditions most capable of changing system behavior or simulation conclusions.

title: OOF™ About Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Standard - (SRCS)
text: OOF™ About Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Standard - (SRCS) About Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Standard - (SRCS) About Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Standard (SRCS) Architecture: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Parent Standard: Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Standard (SRCS) Governed Space: Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Governance Flow Position: 10 of 12 — Simulation Output Governance → Simulation-to-Reality Correlation → Downstream Simulation Governance Canonical Definition Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Standard (SRCS) defines the governance conditions under which simulated behavior, conditions, events, relationships, and outputs are systematically compared with corresponding Operational Reality to determine where meaningful correlation exists, where material deviation occurs, how reality alignment should be characterized, and how uncertainty and limitations constrain any claim that simulation represents reality. SRCS does not assume that a technically sophisticated simulation accurately represents the real world. It establishes a governed relationship between what occurred in simulation and what is observed, measured, or otherwise established in Operational Reality. Why SRCS Matters Organizations increasingly rely on simulation to examine systems before, during, and sometimes instead of direct real-world testing. The critical governance question therefore becomes not merely: Did the simulation run correctly? but: How closely does what happened in simulation correspond to what actually happens in reality? A simulation may be internally consistent, computationally precise, repeatedly executable, and capable of producing enormous volumes of output while still diverging materially from reality. SRCS makes that divergence visible and governable. Core Principle Simulation similarity is not reality equivalence. A simulation may correlate strongly with reality for one: behavior, operating condition, environment, system state, scenario, time period, or output, while correlating poorly in another. Correlation must therefore remain bounded by what was actually compared. Governance Flow Simulation Outputs ↓ Simulation-Reality Comparison ↓ Correlation Criteria ↓ Simulation-Reality Deviation ↓ Reality Alignment Assessment ↓ Correlation Uncertainty ↓ Bounded Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Record What SRCS Governs SRCS governs the relationship between simulated and real-world observations through five distinct questions: SRCM — Simulation-Reality Comparison Module What simulated and real-world phenomena can legitimately be compared? SCCM — Simulation Correlation Criteria Module Against which criteria should correspondence between simulation and reality be assessed? SDMM — Simulation-Reality Deviation Module Where and by how much does simulation materially diverge from reality? SRAM — Reality Alignment Module To what extent does the simulation remain aligned with the relevant Operational Reality? SCUM — Correlation Uncertainty Module How much uncertainty remains in the claimed simulation-to-reality relationship? Bounded Correlation SRCS prevents a narrow correlation result from becoming a universal representation claim. For example: Strong correlation in nominal operating conditions does not establish: Strong correlation under extreme conditions, failures, rare events, different environments, or future configurations. Every material correlation claim should therefore remain connected to its: Object + Reality Reference + Conditions + Criteria + Observations + Deviations + Uncertainty + Scope Relationship to ORA™ ORA™ governs Operational Reality. SIMULOS® does not replace that function. SRCS governs the correlation relationship between the simulation and the relevant Operational Reality supplied, observed, or described through the appropriate reality-governance basis. The architectural distinction is: ORA™ → What is occurring in Operational Reality? SIMULOS® SRCS → How does the simulation correspond to that reality? Relationship to VALIDOS® SRCS does not itself declare a simulation universally valid. It produces governed correlation evidence that may later contribute to validation under VALIDOS®. Therefore: Simulation-to-Reality Correlation ≠ Validation Determination. A high correlation in one governed space may be important validation evidence without establishing universal validity. Relationship to INTEGROS® SRCS does not take ownership of general integrity governance. INTEGROS® may govern integrity properties of evidence, records, measurements, or other artifacts used in the correlation process. SRCS governs what those simulation and reality observations reveal about their relationship. Use Case 1 — Space Mission Simulation A space agency develops a simulation environment for spacecraft navigation, autonomous recovery, communication loss, propulsion behavior, and subsystem failures. After real mission or hardware-test data becomes available, SRCS can compare: Simulated Behavior ↔ Observed Reality The analysis may reveal strong alignment for nominal navigation but significant deviation during combined sensor degradation and communication delay. The important result is therefore not simply: “The simulation correlates with reality.” It is: where it correlates, where it deviates, under which conditions, and with what remaining uncertainty. That information can guide subsequent model improvement, scenario design, simulation reliance, and validation. Use Case 2 — Autonomous System Deployment An autonomous vehicle or industrial robot performs successfully across millions of simulated scenarios before deployment. Operational deployment then produces real-world observations involving: sensor noise, unexpected human behavior, environmental variability, timing differences, physical wear, rare interactions, and conditions insufficiently represented in simulation. SRCS compares the simulated and operational behavior and identifies where the simulation-to-reality gap becomes material. This allows the organization to distinguish: high simulation performance from: demonstrated correspondence with Operational Reality. Enterprise Value SRCS can operate over an organization's existing simulation and operational infrastructure. It does not require replacement of the simulator. It provides a governance framework for answering questions such as: Which simulated behaviors have actually been compared with reality? Against what correlation criteria? Where are the largest deviations? Under which operating conditions does alignment deteriorate? Which parts of the simulation remain uncorrelated? How uncertain is the correlation claim? Can the organization legitimately rely on correlation established in one environment when operating in another? This turns the frequently discussed simulation-to-reality gap into a structured governable space. Foundational Principle Simulation similarity is not reality equivalence. Correlation becomes governable only when correspondence, deviation, alignment, uncertainty, and the boundaries of the comparison remain explicitly visible. Purpose of SRCS Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Standard (SRCS) provides the governance layer through which organizations can determine not whether a simulation merely looks realistic, but where, under what conditions, to what extent, and with what uncertainty its behavior corresponds to Operational Reality. It establishes the bridge between simulated reality and observed reality without confusing correlation with equivalence, validation, or universal truth.

title: OOF™ About SIMULOS®
text: OOF™ About SIMULOS® About SIMULOS® Simulation Governance Architecture Reality is increasingly simulated before it is entered. Systems are tested before they are built. Autonomous systems are exposed to conditions before they encounter them. Missions are evaluated before they are launched. Infrastructure is stressed before it fails. Future conditions are explored before they exist. Simulation is becoming part of how organizations understand, design, test, compare, prepare, validate, and make decisions about reality. SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture was created to provide a stable governance architecture for this expanding simulation domain. SIMULOS® does not define simulation software, numerical solvers, physics engines, digital-twin platforms, modeling languages, computing infrastructure, or implementation technologies. SIMULOS® governs simulation. Why SIMULOS® Exists Simulation can generate enormous amounts of information. But the existence of simulation does not itself answer fundamental governance questions: What exactly is being simulated? Why is it being simulated? Which parts of reality are represented? Which assumptions make that representation possible? Which models, environments, inputs, and scenarios define the simulation? How was the simulation executed? What do its outputs actually mean? How closely do those outputs correspond to reality? What may simulation-derived evidence legitimately support? When does changing reality require resimulation? SIMULOS® addresses these questions by defining the governable spaces that exist throughout the complete simulation lifecycle. Rather than standardizing one simulation technology, SIMULOS® standardizes the governance conditions under which simulation can be identified, scoped, represented, executed, interpreted, correlated with reality, converted into bounded evidence, relied upon, monitored, and resimulated. Simulation Before Reliance The objective of SIMULOS® is not to prescribe how a simulation must be technically built. The objective is to define how simulation must remain governable. Every simulation has an object. Every Simulation Object requires a purpose and scope. Every scope determines what reality must be represented. Every representation depends upon explicit or implicit assumptions. Every simulation requires a model and environment. Every model operates upon inputs and data. Every meaningful simulation requires relevant scenarios. Every scenario must be executed under governed conditions. Every execution produces outputs. Every output requires interpretation before broader meaning can be attributed to it. Claims about reality require a governed simulation-to-reality relationship. Simulation-derived evidence requires qualification before reliance. Continuing reliance requires lifecycle monitoring and, where material change occurs, resimulation. SIMULOS® therefore treats simulation as an independent governance domain. The Simulation Governance Architecture SIMULOS® consists of twelve independent simulation governance spaces. Each space answers one architectural question. Each space governs one distinct part of the simulation lifecycle. Each space has a defined beginning, operational purpose, and governance boundary. Each space begins where the preceding simulation governance requirement has been sufficiently established. Together, these spaces form the complete Simulation Governance Architecture. The architecture progresses through: Simulation Object → Simulation Purpose & Scope → Simulation Reality Representation → Simulation Assumptions → Simulation Model & Environment → Simulation Inputs & Data → Simulation Scenario Design → Simulation Execution → Simulation Output Governance → Simulation-to-Reality Correlation → Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary → Simulation Lifecycle, Drift & Resimulation This progression represents the governance journey from identifying what is being simulated to determining whether simulation-derived evidence remains legitimate enough to support continuing reliance as reality changes . Simulation Spaces Rather Than Technical Components SIMULOS® does not organize simulation governance around software packages, simulation engines, computing architectures, vendors, departments, or technical components. Instead, it organizes governance around distinct simulation governance spaces. Each space represents an independent governance responsibility that exists regardless of the simulation technology used. A digital twin, autonomous-driving simulator, spacecraft mission simulator, engineering model, scientific simulation, physical test simulation, AI training environment, or future simulation technology may be technically very different. Yet each may still require governance of: object → purpose → representation → assumptions → model → inputs → scenarios → execution → outputs → reality correlation → evidence → lifecycle. Because these spaces are technology-neutral, SIMULOS® can remain applicable while simulation technologies continue to evolve. A Methodology Rather Than an Implementation SIMULOS® is a governance methodology. It is not a simulation implementation framework. The architecture defines which simulation governance conditions must exist, how they relate to one another, where their boundaries lie, and what must remain explicit before simulation results acquire broader meaning or reliance. Organizations remain free to select their own: simulation platforms, modeling methods, numerical methods, physics engines, digital-twin technologies, AI models, computing infrastructure, scenario-generation systems, verification tools, data systems, engineering processes. SIMULOS® governs the methodological structure surrounding those implementations rather than replacing them. This separation allows the architecture to remain stable while simulation technology changes. From Simulation Object to Governed Evidence Simulation cannot be governed as a single computational event. Before a simulation can be scoped, the Simulation Object must be identified. Before reality can be represented, the purpose and scope must be known. Before models can legitimately represent reality, assumptions and representation boundaries must be explicit. Before execution, models, environments, inputs, data, and scenarios must be sufficiently governed. Before outputs can become evidence, their meaning must be established. Before simulation-derived evidence can support broader claims, the relationship between simulation and reality must be understood. Before evidence can support reliance, its qualification, weight, applicability, uncertainty, and limitations must be bounded. And before historical simulation evidence can continue to be relied upon, the simulation basis must remain relevant as reality changes. SIMULOS® transforms these dependencies into a structured and navigable simulation governance lifecycle. Simulation Is Not Reality One of the most important distinctions within SIMULOS® is: Simulation ≠ Reality A simulation may reproduce aspects of reality with extraordinary precision. It may execute billions of scenarios. It may demonstrate behavior that appears stable across enormous parameter spaces. It may correlate strongly with observed reality. None of these facts alone makes the simulation equivalent to reality. SIMULOS® therefore preserves the distinction between: Represented Reality and Operational Reality. This distinction enables simulation to be used powerfully without allowing computational representation to acquire greater authority than its governed basis can support. Simulation Output Is Not Automatically Evidence SIMULOS® also establishes another fundamental distinction: Simulation Output ≠ Simulation Evidence A simulation engine may produce millions or billions of outputs. Those outputs do not automatically become evidence merely because they were computationally generated. Simulation-derived information must first acquire a defined evidential purpose, remain traceable to its simulation basis, and retain the assumptions, scenarios, conditions, correlations, uncertainties, and limitations that determine its legitimate meaning. Only then can simulation-derived information enter governed evidential reliance. This creates a methodological boundary between: what a simulation produced and what an organization may legitimately conclude from what the simulation produced. Simulation Evidence Is Not Validation SIMULOS® deliberately separates simulation evidence governance from broader validation governance. SIMULOS® determines what simulation-derived evidence can legitimately mean. VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture determines whether the complete evidence basis is sufficient to support a Validation Determination and intended reliance. This distinction prevents simulation success from automatically becoming a claim of real-world validity. A simulation may provide strong evidence. It may provide decisive evidence for a narrowly defined question. It may substantially reduce uncertainty. But simulation-derived evidence remains one governed evidential source whose broader validation significance must be determined within the appropriate validation architecture. The Simulation-to-Reality Boundary The transition from simulation to reality is one of the most consequential points in the architecture. A simulated autonomous vehicle may perform successfully across millions of scenarios. A simulated spacecraft may survive thousands of modeled failure conditions. A digital twin may reproduce observed industrial behavior with high accuracy. A scientific model may repeatedly predict known outcomes. These results matter. But the governance question is not simply: Did the simulation succeed? The stronger question is: What relationship has actually been established between the simulated result and the reality to which that result is being applied? SIMULOS® therefore treats Simulation-to-Reality Correlation as an independent governable space rather than assuming that simulation performance automatically transfers into operational reality. Lifecycle Governance and Resimulation Simulation does not end when execution stops. Reality changes. Simulation Objects change. Models change. Inputs change. Assumptions become obsolete. Operating environments evolve. New evidence appears. Previously unknown scenarios become relevant. A simulation that legitimately supported a conclusion yesterday may no longer provide the same evidential basis tomorrow. SIMULOS® therefore extends governance beyond execution and evidence into Simulation Lifecycle, Drift & Resimulation. Where material change affects the simulation basis, the architecture supports governed re-entry into the earliest materially affected simulation space. The result is not uncontrolled repetition of the complete lifecycle. It is targeted governed resimulation. Who May Benefit SIMULOS® may support: AI developers and operators, autonomous-system developers, robotics organizations, digital-twin environments, engineering organizations, scientific institutions, research laboratories, aerospace and space organizations, automotive and transportation organizations, healthcare and medical simulation environments, financial and economic modeling environments, industrial operators, infrastructure planners, safety and reliability teams, public institutions, regulators, assurance and validation organizations, critical infrastructure providers, organizations using simulation to support material decisions. Relationship to Other OOF® Architectures SIMULOS® governs simulation. It operates alongside complementary OOF® architectures. GOA™ — Governance Architecture governs governance structure, authority, scope, delegation, accountability, continuity, and interoperability. ORA™ — Operational Reality Architecture governs Operational Reality and provides the methodological distinction between what actually exists or occurs and what is represented through simulation. VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture governs Validation Objects, validation purpose and scope, criteria, methods, evidence fitness, source reliability, execution, determination, Validation States, reliance, and revalidation. INTEGROS® — Integrity Governance Architecture governs integrity across the complete integrity lifecycle. OBIDENITY® — Origin-Bound Identity Governance Architecture governs origin, identity, ownership, authority, permission, provenance, transfer, continuity, and auditability. AGA™ — Accountability Governance Architecture governs accountability, responsibility, attribution, delegation, and accountable relationships. AIG® — AI Governance Architecture governs AI behavior. ASGA™ — Autonomous Systems Governance Architecture governs autonomous systems, autonomous agents, autonomous authority, constraints, execution, and operational autonomy. CLIA® — Cognitive Governance Intelligence Architecture governs cognition, reasoning, interpretation, and cognitive integrity. MGIA™ — Memory Governance Intelligence Architecture governs memory, memory continuity, and memory integrity. ADIT® — Audit in Real Time Architecture governs continuous auditability and evidential observation across operational lifecycles. Together, these architectures allow simulation to interact with operational reality, validation, integrity, accountability, AI, autonomy, cognition, memory, and auditability without collapsing those independent governance domains into one architecture. Use Case 1 — Autonomous System Before Real-World Deployment An organization develops an autonomous robot intended to operate in complex physical environments. Before deployment, the robot is exposed to millions of simulated scenarios involving obstacles, people, environmental variation, sensor degradation, unusual events, system failures, and behavioral edge cases. A conventional analysis may report: 99.97% simulation success. SIMULOS® asks a much larger set of questions. What robot configuration was actually simulated? Which operational reality was represented? Which physical effects were simplified? Which assumptions were required? Were the inputs representative? Which scenarios were absent? Were repeated executions genuinely diverse? What did the outputs actually demonstrate? How strongly did simulated behavior correlate with physical tests? What proposition can the resulting evidence legitimately support? Where does reliance upon that evidence stop? The result may be that simulation provides substantial evidence for performance across the represented scenario space while still requiring physical evidence before unrestricted operational deployment. SIMULOS® does not make simulation less useful. It makes the meaning of simulation success governable. Use Case 2 — Future Space Mission Where Complete Reality Does Not Yet Exist A space organization is preparing a mission to an environment that cannot be completely reproduced on Earth and has never been experienced in the exact intended mission configuration. Simulation becomes essential. Spacecraft behavior, navigation, landing, environmental interaction, equipment failure, mission contingencies, crew behavior, communication delays, and emergency conditions may all be simulated before the mission exists as Operational Reality. SIMULOS® provides the governance structure for establishing: what is being simulated; why; which aspects of the future environment are represented; which assumptions substitute for unavailable knowledge; which models and data create the representation; which scenarios must be explored; how executions are controlled; what the resulting outputs mean; which parts can be correlated with existing reality; what evidential weight those results may legitimately carry; and which assumptions or reality changes would require resimulation. The simulation can therefore provide highly valuable evidence without being represented as proof of conditions that have never yet existed. Where reality cannot yet be fully observed, simulation may extend knowledge—but governance must define where that knowledge ends. The Long-Term Vision Simulation is moving from a specialized engineering technique toward a foundational infrastructure for understanding and acting upon reality. AI systems may learn inside simulated worlds. Autonomous systems may experience millions of synthetic situations before encountering physical ones. Digital twins may continuously mirror infrastructure, factories, cities, biological systems, economies, and operational environments. Scientific simulations may explore conditions humans cannot directly observe. Organizations may increasingly make consequential decisions about real systems based upon events that occurred only inside simulated environments. As this transition accelerates, the central question will no longer be only whether organizations can build more powerful simulations. It will also be: How can society know what those simulations legitimately mean? The long-term objective of SIMULOS® is to provide a common simulation governance language through which organizations can identify, structure, compare, govern, evaluate, rely upon, monitor, and resimulate representations of reality without confusing simulation capability with reality itself. SIMULOS® is intended to make simulation governable before execution, during execution, after execution, at the boundary with reality, at the boundary with evidence, and throughout continuing reliance. Canonical Principle Simulation technologies, models, environments, computational capabilities, and represented realities will continue to change. Simulation governance must remain stable. SIMULOS® therefore governs the methodological conditions that determine what is being simulated, why it is being simulated, how reality is represented, what simulation results legitimately mean, how those results relate to reality, how far simulation-derived evidence may be relied upon, and when material change requires governed resimulation. Canonical Closing Statement SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture provides the governance foundation through which simulation can be formally identified, purpose-bounded, reality-represented, assumption-governed, model-structured, input-controlled, scenario-designed, execution-governed, output-interpreted, reality-correlated, evidentially bounded, and continuously maintained through lifecycle governance and resimulation. By defining the independent governable spaces of the complete simulation lifecycle, SIMULOS® establishes a technology-neutral methodology for ensuring that simulation-derived knowledge remains traceable to the object, purpose, representation, assumptions, models, inputs, scenarios, executions, outputs, correlations, uncertainties, limitations, and changing reality from which its legitimate meaning originates. SIMULOS® therefore enables simulation to become more powerful without allowing computational representation to become indistinguishable from Operational Reality, and provides the methodological infrastructure required for simulation-derived evidence to support engineering, science, AI, autonomy, safety, validation, mission planning, critical infrastructure, and future operational environments with explicitly governed meaning and reliance.

title: OOF™ Reality Abstraction Module (RAM)
text: OOF™ Reality Abstraction Module (RAM) Reality Abstraction Module (RAM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Reality Representation Standard (RRS) Operational Layer: Simulation Reality Representation Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Type: Parent Standard Module Governed Space: Reality Abstraction Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 16 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Governed Space Reality Abstraction Canonical Definition Reality Abstraction Module (RAM) defines the governance conditions under which Reality Elements selected as materially relevant to a simulation are simplified, generalized, aggregated, decomposed, parameterized, discretized, approximated, or otherwise transformed into representations suitable for simulation while preserving the characteristics necessary to answer the governed simulation inquiry. RAM establishes the governance boundary between selected reality and its simulation-level representation, ensuring that reduction of real-world complexity remains explicit, justified, traceable, and bounded by Simulation Purpose & Scope. Operational Role RSM establishes: What parts of reality matter to the simulation? RAM asks the next question: At what level of abstraction may those selected parts of reality be represented without removing characteristics material to the simulation inquiry? The governed progression is: Reality Selection Basis → Reality Element → Material Characteristics → Abstraction Requirement → Abstraction Decision → Abstraction Limitation → Abstracted Reality Representation → Representation Fidelity RAM does not determine the required fidelity or resolution of the completed representation. It governs how real-world complexity may legitimately be reduced before those subsequent representation properties are established. Module Operational Space RAM governs: abstraction objectives, abstraction levels, abstraction boundaries, material characteristic preservation, simplification, generalization, aggregation, decomposition, parameterization, discretization, approximation, behavioral abstraction, structural abstraction, environmental abstraction, temporal abstraction, spatial abstraction, interaction abstraction, dependency abstraction, state abstraction, process abstraction, actor abstraction, abstraction assumptions, abstraction justification, abstraction limitations, abstraction uncertainty, abstraction sensitivity, abstraction consistency, abstraction completeness, abstraction traceability, abstraction change, and Abstraction Basis governance. Module Function Reality contains more complexity than most simulations can or should reproduce. A governed simulation therefore requires abstraction. Abstraction itself is not a defect. Uncontrolled abstraction is. RAM exists to prevent: arbitrary simplification, convenience-driven abstraction, abstraction based solely on computational limitations, removal of materially relevant characteristics, excessive aggregation, hidden assumptions, loss of important dependencies, elimination of relevant failure behavior, unrealistic behavioral simplification, abstraction inconsistent with Simulation Purpose, inconsistent abstraction across related simulation components, and representation of an abstracted model as if it preserved characteristics that were intentionally removed. Reality Abstraction Principle SIMULOS® establishes: Reality may be simplified only to the extent that the simplification does not remove characteristics materially necessary to the governed simulation inquiry. The objective is not: maximum realism. The objective is: sufficient representation of material reality for the intended simulation purpose. Abstraction Is a Governed Transformation Reality Abstraction transforms: Selected Reality into: Abstracted Reality Representation This transformation should remain reconstructable. For every material abstraction, it should be possible to understand: What existed in Relevant Reality? What was selected? What characteristics were retained? What characteristics were simplified or removed? Why was that abstraction considered acceptable? What limitations does the abstraction create? Abstraction Object An Abstraction Object is the Reality Element, relationship, behavior, process, environment, condition, or other selected reality component undergoing abstraction. An Abstraction Object may include: a physical entity, a human actor, an autonomous actor, a process, an environment, a dependency, an interaction, a failure mechanism, a temporal process, a spatial relationship, or another selected Reality Element. Material Characteristic A Material Characteristic is a property of a selected Reality Element whose removal, distortion, aggregation, or simplification could materially affect the simulation inquiry. Material Characteristics may include: physical properties, behavior, state transitions, response characteristics, dependencies, constraints, timing, geometry, variability, uncertainty, interaction patterns, failure behavior, or environmental sensitivity. RAM requires these characteristics to be identified before significant abstraction occurs. Abstraction Requirement An Abstraction Requirement defines what characteristics must remain represented after abstraction. It connects: Reality Selection to: Representation Design and prevents important characteristics from disappearing silently during model simplification. Abstraction Level An Abstraction Level describes the degree to which a Reality Element is represented with reduced complexity. Conceptually, representation may range from: Detailed Representation through: Reduced Representation Aggregated Representation Parameterized Representation to: Highly Abstract Representation These are methodological descriptions rather than universal technical classes. SIMULOS® does not prescribe one abstraction scale for all simulation domains. Abstraction Must Be Purpose-Relative There is no universally correct abstraction level. A representation that is sufficient for one simulation may be inadequate for another. For example, a pedestrian may be represented as: a moving point for one traffic-flow simulation, but may require: orientation, reaction time, visibility, movement variability, decision behavior, and interaction characteristics for an autonomous-vehicle safety simulation. The correct abstraction depends upon what the simulation must legitimately examine. Simplification Simplification removes unnecessary complexity while retaining characteristics required by the simulation inquiry. A simplification should be distinguishable from an omission. RSM determines whether the Reality Element belongs in the representation. RAM determines which characteristics of that selected element may be simplified. Generalization Generalization represents multiple detailed real-world characteristics through a broader representation. Generalization may be appropriate where detailed differences are not material to the simulation inquiry. Where differences could materially affect outcomes, generalization requires stronger justification or should not be used. Aggregation Aggregation combines multiple Reality Elements, states, behaviors, events, or properties into a collective representation. Aggregation may reduce computational and structural complexity. However, it may also hide: local variation, minority behavior, extreme conditions, nonlinear interactions, individual failures, dependency structure, or rare but consequential states. RAM therefore requires material aggregation effects to remain visible. Decomposition Abstraction does not always mean combining reality. A Reality Element may need to be decomposed into smaller representational components where its internal structure materially affects simulation behavior. RAM governs whether such decomposition is necessary to preserve the characteristics relevant to the inquiry. Parameterization Parameterization represents complex real-world behavior or characteristics through governed parameters. Parameterization should preserve: parameter meaning, applicable conditions, source basis, assumptions, ranges, and known limitations where these materially affect representation. Discretization Continuous real-world phenomena may be represented through discrete: time steps, spatial cells, states, categories, events, or value ranges. RAM governs the methodological decision to discretize. The specific granularity required is subsequently governed through Representation Resolution. Approximation Approximation may be necessary where exact representation is impossible, unnecessary, or computationally disproportionate. An approximation should remain bounded by: the simulation inquiry, material characteristics, expected behavior, known error, applicable conditions, and downstream interpretation. Behavioral Abstraction Real-world actors may exhibit highly complex behavior. RAM may govern abstraction of: human behavior, autonomous behavior, organizational behavior, agent behavior, biological behavior, or system response. Behavioral abstraction must not silently eliminate behavior that is material to the simulation inquiry. Human Abstraction Humans may be represented as: deterministic actors, probabilistic actors, behavioral classes, population distributions, decision rules, or more complex cognitive representations. RAM governs whether the selected abstraction is appropriate to the simulation inquiry. It does not govern human cognition itself. Where cognition requires independent governance, CLIA® provides the relevant complementary architecture. Autonomous Actor Abstraction Autonomous actors may require abstraction of: perception, reasoning, decision behavior, permissions, constraints, coordination, escalation, adaptation, or response. RAM governs only how these characteristics are represented inside the simulation. Governance of the autonomous system itself remains within ASGA™ and other applicable architectures. Structural Abstraction Complex systems may be structurally simplified. Structural abstraction may combine or omit internal components while preserving externally relevant behavior. RAM should determine whether internal structures that are removed could materially affect: failure propagation, dependencies, performance, interaction, safety, or simulation outcomes. Environmental Abstraction Simulation environments may abstract: terrain, infrastructure, atmosphere, weather, lighting, electromagnetic conditions, population, traffic, resources, physical obstacles, or other environmental characteristics. Environmental abstraction should remain appropriate to the scenarios the simulation must support. Temporal Abstraction Reality may operate across different timescales. RAM governs whether temporal processes may be: compressed, aggregated, approximated, event-driven, discretized, or otherwise simplified. Temporal abstraction should not remove material: latency, accumulation, sequence, delay, degradation, adaptation, feedback, or timing dependencies. Spatial Abstraction Spatial reality may be simplified through: reduced geometry, zones, cells, coordinates, topological relationships, representative distances, or other spatial models. The abstraction must preserve spatial characteristics material to the simulation inquiry. Interaction Abstraction Two Reality Elements may be represented accurately individually while their interaction is represented inadequately. RAM therefore governs abstraction of: coupling, communication, influence, collision, transfer, feedback, synchronization, coordination, and dependency. Dependency Abstraction Dependencies may be simplified only where their material effect remains sufficiently represented. A hidden dependency removed through abstraction can create a simulation that behaves correctly internally while failing to represent real-world system behavior. Failure Abstraction Failure behavior often differs from nominal behavior. Where failure is material to Simulation Purpose, RAM should determine whether the abstraction preserves: failure initiation, failure propagation, degraded states, recovery behavior, cascading effects, and relevant interaction with other elements. Abstraction Assumption Every material abstraction may create assumptions. An Abstraction Assumption states what is presumed to remain sufficiently true despite reduction of real-world complexity. Example: Individual variation is assumed not to materially affect the aggregate outcome within the defined scenario range. Such assumptions should remain explicit and traceable. Abstraction Justification A material abstraction should have a governed reason. Possible reasons may include: characteristic immateriality, known equivalence, validated simplification, bounded approximation, computational necessity, data limitation, scenario limitation, or established domain methodology. Computational necessity alone does not prove methodological acceptability. Computational Constraint Rule SIMULOS® establishes: A computational limitation may explain an abstraction, but it does not by itself justify that abstraction. Where computational limits force removal of material characteristics, the resulting limitation must remain visible. Abstraction Limitation An Abstraction Limitation identifies where the abstracted representation no longer sufficiently reflects some characteristic of Relevant Reality. Limitations may constrain: scenarios, operating conditions, interpretation, output applicability, comparison, extrapolation, or operational reliance. Abstraction Uncertainty Abstraction may introduce uncertainty because multiple real-world states become represented through one simplified model. Where material, this uncertainty should remain explicit. It should not disappear merely because the abstraction itself is deterministic. Abstraction Sensitivity Where the acceptability of an abstraction is uncertain, its effect may require sensitivity examination. The key governance question is: Would a materially different abstraction plausibly change the simulation outcome or interpretation? Where yes, the abstraction should receive additional scrutiny. Abstraction Consistency Related Reality Elements should not use incompatible abstraction assumptions without explicit justification. For example, one subsystem should not assume: instantaneous communication while another relies upon: material communication latency unless the relationship is governed. Cross-Element Abstraction Abstraction decisions should therefore be evaluated not only independently but also collectively. The combined abstraction structure may create effects not visible when each element is reviewed separately. Abstraction Completeness Abstraction Completeness asks whether every materially selected Reality Element has received sufficient abstraction treatment to proceed into representation governance. This does not mean every element must be simplified. Some may remain detailed. The requirement is that the abstraction status is known. Abstraction Status A selected Reality Element may receive an abstraction status such as: Detailed Representation Required Reduced Representation Approved Aggregated Representation Approved Parameterized Representation Approved Approximation Approved Conditional Abstraction Abstraction Constraint or: Abstraction Undetermined Conditional Abstraction An abstraction may be acceptable only within defined: scenarios, ranges, environments, time periods, operating modes, populations, or system states. These conditions should propagate forward into subsequent representation governance. Abstraction Constraint An Abstraction Constraint exists where required real-world complexity cannot currently be represented at an acceptable abstraction level. This should not be silently converted into an approved simplification. Abstraction Traceability A governed abstraction should support the chain: Simulation Purpose → Reality Selection → Reality Element → Material Characteristic → Abstraction Requirement → Abstraction Decision → Abstracted Representation → Limitation This provides a reconstructable explanation of how reality became simulation representation. Abstraction Change Abstraction may require reassessment where: Simulation Purpose changes, Simulation Scope changes, Reality Selection changes, new interactions are identified, new failure modes emerge, representation capability changes, new evidence becomes available, scenario requirements expand, or simulation outputs demonstrate sensitivity to abstraction. Abstraction Change Propagation Material abstraction changes may affect: Fidelity → Resolution → Representation Limitations → Assumptions → Model & Environment → Inputs & Data → Scenario Design → Execution → Outputs → Reality Correlation Abstraction is therefore an upstream simulation-governance dependency. Abstraction Basis The principal governed output of RAM is the Abstraction Basis. It should establish: Abstraction Objects, material characteristics, abstraction requirements, selected abstraction levels, simplifications, aggregations, decompositions, parameterizations, approximations, abstraction assumptions, abstraction limitations, abstraction uncertainty, abstraction constraints, applicable conditions, and traceability to Reality Selection. Relationship to Reality Selection RSM determines: What reality enters the simulation? RAM determines: How may the complexity of that selected reality be reduced? The distinction protects SIMULOS® from treating omission and abstraction as the same methodological act. Relationship to Representation Fidelity RAM does not establish whether the resulting representation achieves the required fidelity. That is governed by: RFM — Representation Fidelity Module RAM provides the abstraction basis against which fidelity can subsequently be evaluated. Relationship to Representation Resolution RAM may determine that a phenomenon can be discretized or aggregated. It does not determine the exact resolution at which representation must operate. That belongs to: RRM — Representation Resolution Module Relationship to Representation Limitation RAM identifies limitations created specifically by abstraction. RLM — Representation Limitation Module subsequently consolidates and governs the broader limitations of the simulation's Reality Representation. Cross-Architecture Boundary RAM does not determine what Operational Reality is. That remains governed by ORA™. RAM does not validate whether a simulation may support an external validation claim. That remains within VALIDOS®. RAM does not govern general integrity. That remains within INTEGROS®. RAM governs one specific transformation: the controlled reduction of selected reality into simulation-suitable representation. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Establish the Reality Selection Basis Identify the selected Reality Elements and their connection to Simulation Purpose & Scope. 2. Identify Material Characteristics Determine which properties, behaviors, states, interactions, dependencies, temporal effects, spatial effects, and failure characteristics must survive abstraction. 3. Establish Abstraction Requirements Define what must remain represented after complexity reduction. 4. Select the Abstraction Approach Determine whether the element requires detailed, simplified, generalized, aggregated, decomposed, parameterized, discretized, or approximated representation. 5. Evaluate Material Loss Determine what real-world characteristics are removed, compressed, merged, or approximated. 6. Assess Abstraction Acceptability Determine whether the resulting representation remains sufficient for the governed simulation inquiry. 7. Record Assumptions, Conditions, and Limitations Preserve the boundaries under which the abstraction remains legitimate. 8. Assess Cross-Element Consistency Determine whether abstraction decisions remain compatible across interacting Reality Elements. 9. Establish the Abstraction Basis Create the governed representation basis required for fidelity governance. 10. Preserve Traceability and Reassessment Maintain: Reality Selection → Material Characteristics → Abstraction → Limitation → Representation and reassess after material change. Governance Outputs RAM may produce: Abstraction Object Register, Material Characteristic Record, Abstraction Requirement, Abstraction Level Record, Simplification Record, Generalization Record, Aggregation Record, Decomposition Record, Parameterization Record, Discretization Record, Approximation Record, Behavioral Abstraction Record, Structural Abstraction Record, Environmental Abstraction Record, Temporal Abstraction Record, Spatial Abstraction Record, Interaction Abstraction Record, Dependency Abstraction Record, Failure Abstraction Record, Abstraction Assumption Register, Abstraction Justification Record, Abstraction Limitation Record, Abstraction Uncertainty Record, Abstraction Sensitivity Record, Abstraction Consistency Assessment, Conditional Abstraction Record, Abstraction Constraint Record, Abstraction Completeness Assessment, Abstraction Change Record, Abstraction Traceability Map, and Abstraction Basis. Use Case 1 — Autonomous Driving Simulation Scenario An autonomous-driving simulation has already selected pedestrians as materially relevant Reality Elements. Representing every biological and cognitive characteristic of every pedestrian would be unnecessary. Application RAM determines which characteristics must remain represented, such as: position, movement, direction, speed, reaction variability, visibility, road-crossing behavior, and relevant interaction with the vehicle. Other characteristics may legitimately remain abstracted where they cannot materially affect the simulation inquiry. Result The simulation receives a governed pedestrian abstraction that preserves characteristics necessary for the intended safety scenarios without attempting to reproduce the complete human being. Use Case 2 — Spacecraft Thermal Simulation Scenario A spacecraft thermal simulation includes the spacecraft structure, solar exposure, internal heat generation, radiation, and relevant environmental conditions. Application RAM determines whether individual structural components require detailed representation or whether some may be represented through aggregated thermal masses and parameterized heat-transfer relationships. Where local thermal behavior could materially affect critical components, excessive aggregation is prohibited or recorded as a material limitation. Result The abstraction remains aligned with the thermal inquiry rather than with computational convenience alone. Use Case 3 — Industrial Digital Twin Scenario A digital twin represents a complex industrial production system containing thousands of individual operational components. Application RAM allows non-material components to be aggregated while preserving individually significant: bottlenecks, dependencies, failure paths, resource constraints, timing relationships, and critical interactions. Result The digital twin remains computationally manageable without silently eliminating operational relationships material to the simulation objective. Architectural Position Reality Abstraction is the second internal governance space of the Reality Representation Standard (RRS). The complete RRS progression is: Reality Selection → Reality Abstraction → Representation Fidelity → Representation Resolution → Representation Limitation RSM establishes: What parts of reality matter? RAM establishes: How may their complexity be reduced? RFM establishes: How faithfully must the resulting representation reproduce the material characteristics required by the simulation? This sequence prevents three fundamentally different questions from being collapsed into one modeling decision. Foundational Principle Abstraction is legitimate only when reducing the complexity of reality does not silently remove the characteristics that make that reality material to the simulation inquiry. Canonical Closing Statement Reality Abstraction Module establishes the governed transformation through which selected reality becomes simulation-suitable representation without allowing simplification, aggregation, parameterization, discretization, approximation, or computational constraint to silently remove characteristics material to the simulation inquiry. By governing abstraction requirements, material-characteristic preservation, abstraction levels, assumptions, limitations, uncertainty, cross-element consistency, change propagation, and traceability, RAM ensures that simulation complexity may be reduced where justified while preserving a transparent and reconstructable relationship between the reality selected for simulation and the representation subsequently evaluated for fidelity, resolution, and limitation.

title: OOF™ Reality Representation Standard - (RRS)
text: OOF™ Reality Representation Standard - (RRS) Reality Representation Standard - (RRS) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Operational Layer: Simulation Reality Representation Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Type: Parent Standard Governed Space: Simulation Reality Representation Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 16 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Governed Space Simulation Reality Representation Canonical Definition Reality Representation Standard (RRS) defines the governance conditions under which the aspects of reality relevant to a governed Simulation Object, Purpose, Scope, Exclusions, Applicability Context, and required Simulation Depth & Precision are selected, abstracted, represented, resolved, simplified, bounded, and documented within a simulation. RRS establishes the governed relationship between: Operational Reality and: Simulated Representation so that a simulation cannot silently treat an incomplete, simplified, abstracted, or selectively represented model of reality as though it were equivalent to reality itself. Core Question Which aspects of reality must the simulation represent, at what level of abstraction, fidelity, and resolution, and which aspects may legitimately remain simplified, approximated, or unrepresented? Purpose The purpose of RRS is to establish how relevant reality is transformed into a governed simulation representation. The preceding SIMULOS® standards establish: What is being simulated? and: Why, within what scope, and at what depth must it be simulated? RRS addresses the next foundational question: Which parts of reality must now be represented inside the simulation, and how must that representation remain connected to the reality it claims to stand for? A simulation cannot represent all aspects of reality. Selection, abstraction, simplification, approximation, and resolution are unavoidable. RRS makes those transformations governable. Operational Role RRS is the third Parent Standard of SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture. It receives: a governed Simulation Object, a defined Simulation Purpose, a governed Simulation Scope, explicit exclusions, an Applicability Context, and required Simulation Depth & Precision. It transforms those upstream conditions into a governed Reality Representation Basis suitable for subsequent Simulation Assumptions, Model & Environment, Inputs & Data, Scenario Design, and Simulation Execution. RRS prevents: selective representation without disclosure, material reality dimensions disappearing during modeling, abstraction being mistaken for equivalence, simplified representation being presented as complete reality, false fidelity, insufficient resolution, over-resolution without methodological value, hidden representation limitations, and simulation outputs being interpreted as though the simulated representation and operational reality were identical. Governance Flow Governed Simulation Inquiry → Relevant Reality Identification → Reality Selection → Representation Abstraction → Representation Fidelity → Representation Resolution → Simplification & Approximation → Representation Limitations → Reality Representation Basis The resulting Reality Representation Basis becomes an input to: Simulation Assumption Governance and subsequently to governed construction of the: Simulation Model & Environment Reality Representation Reality Representation is the governed transformation through which selected characteristics, structures, behaviors, interactions, conditions, relationships, and dynamics of reality become representable within simulation. Representation may be: physical, mathematical, digital, statistical, behavioral, logical, probabilistic, agent-based, process-based, hybrid, conceptual, or another methodologically appropriate form. RRS does not prescribe one representation technology. It governs whether the representation is suitable for the simulation inquiry. Reality ≠ Representation SIMULOS® establishes a foundational distinction: Reality ≠ Representation A representation may reproduce selected properties of reality. It does not become reality itself. Therefore: Simulation Representation must remain distinguishable from Operational Reality throughout the simulation lifecycle. Representation ≠ Simulation Object The Simulation Object identifies: what is being simulated. Reality Representation determines: which characteristics of that object and its relevant reality are represented inside the simulation. A complete Simulation Object may legitimately have a partial representation where the Simulation Purpose requires only selected characteristics. That partiality must remain explicit. Reality Selection Not every characteristic of reality can or should be represented. Reality Selection determines which reality dimensions are materially relevant to the governed Simulation Purpose and Scope. Selected reality may include: physical characteristics, system structures, behaviors, environmental conditions, operational states, interactions, dependencies, human behavior, autonomous behavior, temporal dynamics, failure conditions, resource conditions, or other simulation-relevant realities. Material Reality Element A Material Reality Element is a characteristic, relationship, behavior, condition, or dynamic whose omission or distortion could materially affect: simulation behavior, simulation outputs, scenario response, reality correlation, interpretation, or downstream reliance. Material Reality Elements require explicit representation treatment. Reality Selection Must Derive From Scope RRS establishes: Reality selection must follow the governed Simulation Purpose, Scope, Exclusions, Applicability Context, and Depth requirements rather than the convenience of the available model. A representation tool must not silently define which parts of reality are considered relevant. Selective Representation Selective representation is legitimate. A simulation may intentionally represent only a subset of reality. However: Selective Representation ≠ Complete Reality Representation The selected subset must remain visible. Representation Relevance A selected reality characteristic should have a clear relationship to the Simulation Purpose. Representation relevance helps prevent simulation complexity from increasing simply because more real-world detail can technically be modeled. Reality Abstraction Reality Abstraction is the governed reduction of real-world complexity into a form suitable for simulation. Abstraction may: aggregate components, simplify behavior, reduce dimensionality, remove irrelevant detail, combine states, approximate relationships, or represent complex phenomena through higher-level constructs. Abstraction is not inherently a weakness. It becomes problematic when its effect on simulation meaning is hidden. Abstraction Level Different elements of the same simulation may legitimately use different abstraction levels. For example: Primary control behavior → detailed representation while: non-material infrastructure → higher abstraction may be appropriate. RRS therefore permits differentiated abstraction. Abstraction Must Preserve Material Behavior SIMULOS® establishes: An abstraction must preserve the characteristics materially necessary for the Simulation Purpose. If abstraction removes the behavior the simulation is intended to examine, the representation becomes methodologically insufficient. No Abstraction Concealment Rule A simulation must not present abstracted behavior as though every underlying real-world mechanism had been represented. Representation Fidelity Representation Fidelity describes the degree to which a simulated representation reproduces the characteristics of reality material to the simulation inquiry. Fidelity may concern: physical behavior, system behavior, interaction behavior, temporal dynamics, environmental behavior, organizational behavior, human behavior, autonomous behavior, or another simulation-relevant dimension. Fidelity Is Purpose-Relative There is no universally correct fidelity level. A representation may be sufficiently faithful for: concept exploration while insufficient for: high-consequence operational assessment. Fidelity must therefore be evaluated relative to: Purpose + Scope + Applicability + Depth Fidelity ≠ Complexity A more complex representation is not automatically more faithful. Additional detail may: introduce unsupported assumptions, increase uncertainty, create unnecessary dependencies, or obscure important behavior. RRS establishes: Representation complexity does not itself demonstrate Representation Fidelity. Fidelity ≠ Precision A representation can be highly precise while poorly representing reality. Likewise, a lower-precision representation may adequately reproduce the behavior material to the inquiry. Therefore: Precision must not be used as a proxy for fidelity. Fidelity Differentiation Different representation elements may require different fidelity levels. For example: Spacecraft Guidance Behavior → High Fidelity Non-Material Visual Appearance → Low Fidelity where visual appearance does not affect the simulation purpose. RRS allows fidelity resources to follow materiality. Representation Resolution Representation Resolution defines the level at which the simulated representation distinguishes relevant characteristics, states, entities, events, spaces, times, and relationships. Resolution may be: spatial, temporal, behavioral, structural, population-based, state-based, event-based, or interaction-based. Resolution Must Be Sufficient Representation resolution must be fine enough to preserve simulation-relevant differences. For example: If a safety event depends upon millisecond timing, a one-second temporal representation may be insufficient. If a regional traffic simulation concerns aggregate traffic flow, centimeter-level road representation may be unnecessary. Resolution ≠ Depth Simulation Depth asks how extensively the inquiry must examine the problem. Representation Resolution asks how finely relevant reality distinctions must be represented. The two must remain aligned but distinct. Resolution Sufficiency Possible representation-resolution outcomes may include: Sufficient Conditionally Sufficient Partially Sufficient Insufficient or: Undetermined Reality Simplification Simulation frequently requires simplification. A Reality Simplification removes or reduces complexity while attempting to preserve the characteristics necessary for the simulation inquiry. Simplification may concern: geometry, interactions, human behavior, environmental variation, component structure, dependencies, system dynamics, or other dimensions. Simplification Must Be Explicit SIMULOS® establishes: A material simplification must remain identifiable wherever it could affect simulation meaning. Simplification ≠ Exclusion A simplified element remains inside the simulation representation. An excluded element remains outside the governed simulation inquiry. Therefore: Simplified ≠ Excluded This distinction is important because an oversimplified representation and a formal exclusion create different governance consequences. Reality Approximation Some real-world characteristics cannot be represented directly and require approximation. An approximation may use: surrogate relationships, estimated values, proxy behavior, statistical distributions, representative profiles, or other substitute mechanisms. Approximation must remain explicit where material. Proxy Representation A representation may use a proxy for a real-world phenomenon. For example: Representative Human Behavior Model may stand in for broader real human behavioral variability. RRS requires the relationship: Reality Target → Proxy Representation to remain visible. No Proxy Equivalence Rule A proxy representation must not automatically be treated as equivalent to the reality it represents. Representation of Dynamic Reality Some reality changes continuously. Examples include: adaptive AI systems, human populations, ecosystems, markets, autonomous systems, weather, organizational structures, and infrastructure networks. RRS must establish whether the representation captures: static state, state range, dynamic transition, adaptation, evolution, or another relevant form of change. Static Representation of Dynamic Reality A dynamic reality may sometimes be represented through a static approximation. This may be legitimate for a narrowly bounded purpose.
