However: Static Representation ≠ Dynamic Equivalence The resulting limitation must remain visible. Representation of Human Behavior Human behavior may be simplified into: behavioral profiles, probabilistic actions, bounded response models, cognitive approximations, scripted behavior, or agent-based representations. RRS governs whether the selected human representation corresponds sufficiently to the simulation purpose. It does not replace human cognition governance under CLIA®. Representation of AI and Autonomous Behavior AI and autonomous systems may require representation of: perception, decision behavior, planning, tool use, autonomy, interaction, constraints, memory effects, adaptation, or other capabilities. RRS governs the simulation representation of those characteristics. AIG®, ASGA™, CLIA®, and MGIA™ govern their respective underlying operational governance spaces. Representation of Operational Environment The Simulation Environment may itself represent selected operational reality. Examples include: road conditions, industrial facilities, orbital environments, weather, infrastructure, networks, human populations, communication systems, or resource environments. RRS establishes what parts of these conditions must be represented. The later Simulation Model & Environment Standard governs how that representation is constructed and configured. Representation Boundary Every Reality Representation should have a defined boundary. The Representation Boundary identifies: which reality dimensions are represented and: which reality dimensions are not represented or are represented only indirectly. Object Boundary ≠ Representation Boundary The Simulation Object may have a broader governed boundary than the portion represented inside one simulation. Therefore: Simulation Object Boundary ≠ Reality Representation Boundary A mismatch is not automatically wrong. It must be explicit and consistent with Simulation Scope. Representation Coverage Representation Coverage asks how much of the reality required by the governed simulation inquiry has actually been represented. Possible statuses may include: Complete for Governed Scope Substantially Complete Partial Materially Incomplete or: Undetermined Coverage refers to required reality within the simulation scope, not all reality. Representation Gap A Representation Gap exists where a reality element required by the governed Simulation Scope is not sufficiently represented. Examples include: missing behavior, missing dependency, missing interaction, missing environmental condition, missing population variation, missing failure dynamics, or missing temporal behavior. Representation gaps must remain visible. Representation Distortion A Representation Distortion exists where the simulation representation materially changes a real-world characteristic in a way capable of affecting the simulation inquiry. Distortion may arise from: oversimplification, poor abstraction, inappropriate proxy behavior, excessive aggregation, inadequate temporal treatment, incorrect scaling, or unsuitable representation relationships. Representation Bias A representation may systematically favor certain states, behaviors, outcomes, or conditions. Where such bias materially affects the simulation inquiry, it should remain governed as a Representation Limitation. Representation Uncertainty A simulation representation may contain uncertainty concerning how well the chosen representation corresponds to reality. RRS does not require artificial certainty. Representation uncertainty should remain explicit where material. Representation Limitation A Representation Limitation is a known condition under which the simulated representation does not fully reproduce a reality element relevant to the governed inquiry. Limitations may result from: abstraction, simplification, unavailable data, incomplete knowledge, model capability, computational constraints, unresolved science, uncertain behavior, proxy use, or representational constraints. Limitation Must Propagate Material Representation Limitations must remain visible to downstream SIMULOS® governance. Conceptually: Representation Limitation → Assumptions → Model & Environment → Scenarios → Execution → Output Governance → Reality Correlation No Reality Equivalence Rule SIMULOS® establishes: A simulation representation must never be presumed equivalent to operational reality merely because the simulation executes successfully. No Completeness-by-Detail Rule High detail in represented elements does not establish that all material reality dimensions were represented. No Fidelity-by-Complexity Rule Greater representation complexity does not automatically establish greater fidelity. No Resolution-by-Compute Rule Greater computational scale does not automatically establish sufficient representation resolution. No Hidden Simplification Rule A material simplification must not remain invisible when it affects interpretation. No Hidden Representation Gap Rule A material reality element required by Simulation Scope must not disappear from the representation without becoming: a governed Representation Gap, an explicit exclusion, an assumption, or a returned scope question. No Retrospective Representation Redefinition Rule Reality Representation must not be materially recharacterized after simulation results are known merely to make results appear more realistic or broadly applicable. Representation Change Reality Representation may change as: new information becomes available, Simulation Scope changes, Applicability Context changes, Simulation Depth increases, object configuration changes, new failure modes emerge, or model capabilities improve. Material Representation Change should remain traceable. Representation Change Propagation A material change to Reality Representation may affect: assumptions, model and environment design, input requirements, scenario design, execution, outputs, reality correlation, and lifecycle resimulation. RRS identifies the changed representation basis and propagates its significance downstream. Representation Versioning Where Reality Representation materially changes, a distinguishable representation version may be required. This preserves the relationship: Simulation Object Version → Reality Representation Version → Simulation Activity Representation Status Possible Reality Representation statuses may include: Established Conditionally Established Partially Established Representation Limited Representation Conflicted Representation Incomplete or: Representation Undetermined Status communicates representation-governance condition. It does not establish validation or operational reliance. Reality Representation Record RRS should support a persistent governed record capable of identifying: selected reality elements, abstraction levels, representation forms, fidelity requirements, achieved fidelity where assessed, resolution requirements, simplifications, approximations, proxies, representation boundaries, gaps, distortions, uncertainties, limitations, material changes, and representation status. Operational Space RRS governs: relevant reality selection, Reality Representation boundaries, abstraction, differentiated abstraction, Representation Fidelity, differentiated fidelity, Representation Resolution, simplification, approximation, proxy representation, dynamic reality representation, representation coverage, representation gaps, representation distortion, representation uncertainty, representation limitations, representation changes, representation versioning, and Reality Representation traceability. Governance Boundary RRS begins when: a governed Simulation Object and Simulation Purpose & Scope basis exist and the relevant reality must be translated into a form suitable for simulation. RRS ends when: the required reality elements have been sufficiently selected, abstracted, bounded, assigned representation fidelity and resolution requirements, simplified or approximated where necessary, and their material limitations documented to support governed Simulation Assumptions and Model & Environment construction. Governance Scope RRS governs only how selected reality is represented for simulation. It does not govern: actual Operational Reality itself, Simulation Object identity, Simulation Purpose & Scope, general assumptions, model implementation, simulation-environment construction, input-data fitness, scenario design, simulation execution, output interpretation, formal validation, validation evidence sufficiency, general integrity, or operational reliance authorization. These responsibilities belong to adjacent SIMULOS® spaces or complementary OOF® architectures. Minimum Governance Requirements A conforming application of RRS should establish: 1. the reality elements material to the governed Simulation Purpose and Scope, 2. an explicit Reality Representation boundary, 3. the selected representation form for material reality elements, 4. appropriate abstraction levels, 5. required Representation Fidelity, 6. required Representation Resolution, 7. material simplifications, 8. material approximations and proxies, 9. treatment of dynamic reality where relevant, 10. identification of Representation Gaps, 11. identification of material distortion or uncertainty, 12. explicit Representation Limitations, 13. prevention of reality-equivalence claims unsupported by the representation, 14. traceability of material Representation Changes, 15. and a persistent Reality Representation Record. Governance Outputs RRS may produce: Reality Selection Record, Material Reality Element Register, Reality Representation Basis, Reality Representation Boundary, Reality Representation Map, Representation Form Record, Abstraction Level Record, Differentiated Abstraction Map, Representation Fidelity Requirement, Representation Fidelity Profile, Representation Resolution Requirement, Spatial Representation Resolution, Temporal Representation Resolution, Behavioral Representation Resolution, Reality Simplification Record, Reality Approximation Record, Proxy Representation Record, Dynamic Reality Representation Record, Representation Coverage Assessment, Representation Gap Record, Representation Distortion Record, Representation Bias Record, Representation Uncertainty Record, Representation Limitation Record, Representation Change Record, Representation Version Record, Reality Representation Status, Reality Representation Traceability Map, and Reality Representation Record. Operational Applications Reality Representation Standard may be applied across: artificial intelligence, autonomous systems, robotics, digital twins, aerospace, aviation, space missions, autonomous vehicles, industrial systems, manufacturing, infrastructure, healthcare simulation, scientific modeling, environmental modeling, financial simulation, population simulation, behavioral simulation, organizational simulation, mission planning, system-of-systems simulation, training environments, critical infrastructure, and future operational ecosystems. Relationship to Other OOF® Architectures Reality Representation Standard interoperates with: GOA™ ORA™ VALIDOS® INTEGROS® ADIT® AGA™ AIG® CLIA® MGIA™ ASGA™ RIS™ while preserving a strict architectural boundary. ORA™ governs Operational Reality itself. RRS governs: how selected Operational Reality is represented within simulation. This distinction is fundamental: ORA™: What is actually occurring? RRS: How is the relevant reality represented for simulation? VALIDOS® may subsequently determine whether a simulation, simulation-derived claim, or simulation evidence is sufficiently validated for a defined purpose. RRS does not make that Validation Determination. INTEGROS® may govern the integrity of representation records, data, models, and related objects. RRS governs their simulation-specific representational role. ADIT® may preserve evidence demonstrating how a representation was constructed, changed, or executed. AIG®, CLIA®, MGIA™, and ASGA™ may define domain-specific characteristics that a simulation representation must reflect when AI, cognition, memory, or autonomous behavior is being simulated. RRS consumes those characteristics without replacing their governance architectures. Architectural Position Reality Representation Standard (RRS) is the third Parent Standard of SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture. The architectural progression is: Simulation Object ↓ Simulation Purpose & Scope ↓ Reality Representation SOS establishes: What exactly is being simulated? SPSS establishes: Why is it being simulated, what must it cover, and within which contextual and depth boundaries? RRS establishes: Which parts of reality must be represented and how must that representation remain bounded by abstraction, fidelity, resolution, simplification, approximation, and known limitations? Once the Reality Representation Basis has been established, SIMULOS® can proceed to the next architectural question: Which assumptions are required to make that representation and the resulting simulation possible, and what limitations do those assumptions introduce? This transition leads directly into: Simulation Assumption Governance Foundational Principle A simulation can legitimately represent reality only to the extent that the reality elements material to its purpose are explicitly selected, appropriately abstracted, sufficiently represented, and bounded by their known representational limitations. Canonical Closing Statement Reality Representation Standard (RRS) establishes the representational bridge between Operational Reality and governed simulation by defining which aspects of reality must be selected, abstracted, simplified, approximated, resolved, and represented for the intended Simulation Purpose and Scope. Through governance of Reality Selection, abstraction, fidelity, resolution, dynamic representation, proxies, coverage, gaps, distortion, uncertainty, limitations, change, and traceability, RRS prevents simulation representations from being mistaken for reality merely because they are technically detailed or successfully executed. By making the transformation from reality to representation explicit and governable, RRS establishes one of the central methodological foundations of SIMULOS® and provides the reality basis upon which assumptions, models, environments, inputs, scenarios, execution, outputs, and later simulation-to-reality correlation can legitimately be constructed. Module Architecture → Reality Selection Module (RSM) → Reality Abstraction Module (RAM) → Representation Fidelity Module (RFM) → Representation Resolution Module (RRM) → Representation Limitation Module (RLM) Related Documents → About Reality Representation Standard (RRS)

title: OOF™ Representation Fidelity Module (RFM)
text: OOF™ Representation Fidelity Module (RFM) Representation Fidelity Module (RFM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Reality Representation Standard (RRS) Operational Layer: Simulation Reality Representation Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Type: Parent Standard Module Governed Space: Representation Fidelity Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 16 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Governed Space Representation Fidelity Canonical Definition Representation Fidelity Module (RFM) defines the governance conditions under which the representation of selected and abstracted reality is required, assessed, bounded, and documented at a level of fidelity sufficient for the governed Simulation Purpose, Scope, scenarios, operating conditions, and intended interpretation. RFM establishes whether the simulation representation preserves the material characteristics, behaviors, relationships, dependencies, states, and dynamics of Relevant Reality with sufficient faithfulness for the simulation inquiry without requiring unnecessary or unjustified replication of reality. Operational Role The preceding modules establish: RSM — What parts of reality must the simulation represent? RAM — How may the complexity of that selected reality legitimately be reduced? RFM asks: How faithfully must the resulting representation reproduce the material characteristics of the reality it claims to represent? The governed progression is: Reality Selection → Reality Abstraction → Fidelity Requirement → Fidelity Assessment → Fidelity Gap → Fidelity Limitation → Representation Fidelity Status → Representation Resolution RFM does not determine whether reality was correctly selected. It does not govern the abstraction decision itself. It does not determine the exact representational granularity. It governs whether the resulting representation is sufficiently faithful to the material reality required by the simulation inquiry. Module Operational Space RFM governs: fidelity objectives, fidelity requirements, fidelity dimensions, fidelity baselines, fidelity thresholds, physical fidelity, behavioral fidelity, structural fidelity, functional fidelity, environmental fidelity, temporal fidelity, spatial fidelity, interaction fidelity, dependency fidelity, state fidelity, process fidelity, failure fidelity, distributional fidelity, variability fidelity, boundary-condition fidelity, cross-component fidelity, scenario-relative fidelity, fidelity assessment, fidelity evidence, fidelity gaps, fidelity trade-offs, fidelity uncertainty, fidelity sensitivity, fidelity limitations, conditional fidelity, fidelity status, fidelity change, and fidelity traceability. Module Function A simulation can contain all relevant Reality Elements and still represent them incorrectly. A simulation may include: the correct actor, the correct environment, the correct process, the correct dependency, and the correct interaction while reproducing their behavior with insufficient fidelity. RFM exists to prevent: presence being mistaken for faithful representation, visual realism being mistaken for operational fidelity, high detail being mistaken for sufficient fidelity, one fidelity dimension compensating invisibly for another, nominal behavior masking poor failure fidelity, environmental fidelity being ignored, interaction fidelity being inferred from component fidelity, fidelity requirements being selected after simulation results are known, fidelity claims exceeding the represented conditions, and simulation outputs being interpreted beyond the fidelity supported by the representation. Fidelity Principle SIMULOS® establishes: Representation fidelity is sufficient only when the characteristics material to the simulation inquiry are represented faithfully enough that their remaining representation error does not invalidate the intended simulation interpretation. Fidelity therefore does not mean: maximum similarity to reality. It means: sufficient similarity in the dimensions that materially matter. Fidelity Is Purpose-Relative There is no universal fidelity level that is correct for every simulation. The required fidelity depends upon: Simulation Object + Simulation Purpose + Simulation Scope + Relevant Reality + Scenarios + Intended Interpretation A representation sufficient for: concept exploration may be insufficient for: safety-critical operational decision support. A representation sufficient for: aggregate traffic analysis may be insufficient for: autonomous collision-avoidance testing. Fidelity Object A Fidelity Object is the represented Reality Element, characteristic, behavior, relationship, process, state, environment, or interaction whose faithfulness to Relevant Reality requires governance. A Fidelity Object may therefore be: an individual simulated entity, a subsystem, a behavioral process, an environmental condition, an interaction, a dependency, a failure mechanism, a population, or the combined simulation representation. Fidelity Requirement A Fidelity Requirement establishes how faithfully a material characteristic must be represented for the simulation inquiry. A Fidelity Requirement should derive from: Simulation Purpose & Scope ↓ Reality Selection ↓ Material Characteristic ↓ Approved Abstraction ↓ Required Fidelity The requirement should not be created merely because a simulator happens to support a particular level of realism. Fidelity Dimensions Fidelity should not automatically be treated as one global property. A representation may have high fidelity in one dimension and low fidelity in another. RFM therefore permits fidelity to be governed across independent dimensions. Physical Fidelity Physical Fidelity concerns the degree to which relevant physical characteristics and physical relationships are represented consistently with Relevant Reality. This may include: mass, force, acceleration, temperature, pressure, material behavior, energy transfer, friction, aerodynamics, structural response, or other physical properties. Behavioral Fidelity Behavioral Fidelity concerns whether simulated actors or systems behave sufficiently like their relevant real-world counterparts. This may include: responses, decisions, transitions, adaptation, reaction patterns, control behavior, human behavior, autonomous behavior, or organizational behavior. RFM governs representation fidelity. It does not replace the governance of cognition, AI behavior, or autonomous authority in their respective OOF® architectures. Structural Fidelity Structural Fidelity concerns whether materially relevant components and relationships are represented with sufficient correspondence to the real structure. A structurally simplified model may remain legitimate where removed internal structure cannot materially affect the simulation inquiry. Functional Fidelity Functional Fidelity concerns whether the simulated object performs the materially relevant functions and produces the materially relevant responses expected from the represented reality. A simulation may therefore possess lower structural fidelity but sufficient functional fidelity for a particular inquiry. This distinction must remain explicit. Environmental Fidelity Environmental Fidelity concerns whether environmental conditions materially affecting simulation behavior are sufficiently represented. This may include: terrain, weather, lighting, temperature, infrastructure, electromagnetic conditions, population density, traffic, resource availability, or other environmental factors. Temporal Fidelity Temporal Fidelity concerns whether materially relevant timing characteristics are sufficiently represented. This may include: latency, duration, sequence, frequency, synchronization, accumulation, degradation, feedback delay, recovery time, or response time. Spatial Fidelity Spatial Fidelity concerns whether materially relevant: positions, distances, geometry, orientation, topology, movement, boundaries, and spatial relationships are represented sufficiently faithfully. Interaction Fidelity Individual components can possess high fidelity while their interaction is represented poorly. RFM therefore treats Interaction Fidelity as an independent governance concern. It may include fidelity of: communication, collision, coordination, coupling, transfer, feedback, influence, negotiation, synchronization, or physical interaction. Dependency Fidelity Dependency Fidelity concerns whether materially relevant dependencies behave sufficiently like their real-world counterparts. A dependency may exist in the model but still be represented incorrectly in: strength, direction, timing, conditionality, failure behavior, or propagation. State Fidelity State Fidelity concerns whether material operational states and transitions between them correspond sufficiently to Relevant Reality. This becomes especially important where a system may operate in: normal, degraded, emergency, recovery, failure, maintenance, or exceptional states. Process Fidelity Process Fidelity concerns whether relevant sequences, workflows, transformations, or causal processes are represented with sufficient faithfulness. Failure Fidelity Nominal fidelity does not establish failure fidelity. A simulation may reproduce normal operation accurately while representing: faults, degradation, cascading failure, abnormal response, emergency behavior, or recovery poorly. Where failure behavior is material to Simulation Purpose, RFM requires it to receive explicit fidelity treatment. Distributional Fidelity Where reality contains populations or stochastic behavior, fidelity may depend upon whether the represented distribution sufficiently corresponds to reality. The average alone may be insufficient. Material characteristics may include: variance, tails, rare events, multimodality, correlations, extreme behavior, and subgroup differences. Variability Fidelity Real systems may vary between: actors, units, environments, time periods, operating conditions, or repeated events. RFM governs whether this variability must be represented and whether its simulated form is sufficiently faithful. Boundary-Condition Fidelity Simulation behavior may depend strongly upon boundary conditions. RFM therefore governs whether relevant boundary conditions sufficiently correspond to those represented by the simulation claim. A model that performs well only within narrow boundary conditions should not receive an unrestricted fidelity representation. Cross-Component Fidelity Fidelity must also be evaluated across interacting simulation components. A high-fidelity vehicle model connected to a highly simplified road, weather, sensor, or human-behavior model may produce a combined fidelity profile materially weaker than the vehicle model alone suggests. Fidelity Baseline A Fidelity Baseline identifies the reference against which fidelity is evaluated. The baseline may derive from: measured reality, observed operational behavior, empirical datasets, accepted physical relationships, controlled experiments, authoritative technical data, domain models, or another sufficiently justified reference. RFM does not govern general evidence validation. Where the baseline itself requires formal validation, VALIDOS® provides the complementary validation governance architecture. Fidelity Evidence A fidelity claim should have a basis. Possible Fidelity Evidence may include: measurement comparison, observed behavior comparison, experimental comparison, known physical relationships, historical operational data, cross-model comparison, controlled test results, or expert technical assessment. The strength of the fidelity claim should remain bounded by the strength of the available basis. Fidelity Threshold A Fidelity Threshold defines the level of representational correspondence required for a particular material characteristic or fidelity dimension. SIMULOS® does not prescribe universal thresholds. Thresholds should derive from the simulation inquiry and consequence of representational error. Fidelity Assessment A Fidelity Assessment compares the represented characteristic against its required Fidelity Requirement and applicable baseline. The assessment asks: Is the representation sufficiently faithful for the intended simulation inquiry? not: Is the representation identical to reality? Fidelity Gap A Fidelity Gap exists where the simulation representation differs materially from the required representation of Relevant Reality. A gap may concern: magnitude, behavior, timing, structure, variability, interaction, dependency, state transition, environmental response, or another material characteristic. Fidelity Gap Classification A Fidelity Gap may be classified conceptually as: Non-Material Material but Acceptable Conditional Material and Unresolved or: Fidelity Undetermined The classification must remain relative to the governed Simulation Purpose and Scope. Fidelity Limitation A Fidelity Limitation identifies where insufficient or uncertain fidelity restricts the legitimate interpretation or application of simulation outputs. A limitation may restrict: scenarios, environments, populations, system states, operating ranges, failure conditions, temporal periods, or output interpretation. Fidelity Trade-Off Simulation design frequently involves trade-offs between fidelity and: computational cost, execution time, data availability, model complexity, interpretability, scenario scale, or repeatability. RFM permits such trade-offs. It does not permit them to become invisible. Computational Constraint Rule SIMULOS® establishes: Computational capability may constrain achievable fidelity, but computational limitation does not redefine the fidelity required by the simulation inquiry. If the required fidelity cannot be achieved, the appropriate result may be: Fidelity Limitation rather than lowering the requirement until the simulation appears sufficient. Visual Fidelity ≠ Operational Fidelity A simulation may appear realistic while reproducing operational behavior poorly. Likewise, a visually simple simulation may reproduce the materially relevant dynamics with high operational fidelity. SIMULOS® therefore establishes: Visual realism is not evidence of sufficient simulation fidelity. Detail ≠ Fidelity Adding detail does not necessarily improve fidelity. Incorrect detail can reduce representational accuracy. RFM therefore separates: Representation Detail from: Representation Fidelity. Representation Resolution is governed separately by RRM. Fidelity Uncertainty A Fidelity Assessment may itself contain uncertainty. This may result from: incomplete baseline data, measurement uncertainty, changing reality, limited observations, stochastic behavior, conflicting reference evidence, or insufficient coverage. Material fidelity uncertainty should remain explicit. Fidelity Sensitivity RFM may assess whether simulation outcomes are sensitive to plausible changes in fidelity. The governing question is: Would a plausible representation error materially alter the simulation outcome or its interpretation? Where yes, stronger fidelity governance may be required. Scenario-Relative Fidelity A representation may possess sufficient fidelity for one scenario and insufficient fidelity for another. Example: A simplified tire model may be sufficient for: normal-speed highway traffic analysis but insufficient for: emergency braking on ice. Fidelity status should therefore remain bound to the scenarios it supports. Conditional Fidelity A representation may be classified as sufficiently faithful only under explicit conditions. Possible conditions include: operating range, environment, scenario class, system configuration, population, temporal period, or simulation mode. Representation Fidelity Status RFM may establish a governed status such as: Fidelity Sufficient Fidelity Conditionally Sufficient Fidelity Partially Sufficient Fidelity Insufficient or: Fidelity Undetermined The status should remain attached to the relevant Fidelity Object, dimension, scope, and conditions. No Global Fidelity Inflation A high-fidelity result for one subsystem must not automatically become a high-fidelity claim for the complete simulation. Likewise: High Physical Fidelity does not automatically establish: High Behavioral Fidelity or: High Environmental Fidelity. Weakest Material Fidelity Principle Where multiple fidelity dimensions materially affect the same simulation claim: The simulation claim cannot assume stronger representation fidelity than its materially limiting fidelity dimension supports. This does not require one global numerical fidelity score. It requires material weaknesses to remain visible. Fidelity Consistency Fidelity assumptions and requirements across interacting simulation elements should remain mutually coherent. A high-fidelity subsystem should not depend upon a low-fidelity representation that invalidates the inquiry without that dependency being visible. Fidelity Change Fidelity should be reassessed where material changes occur in: Simulation Purpose, Simulation Scope, Reality Selection, abstraction, model structure, environment, scenarios, data, operating conditions, simulation capabilities, or Relevant Reality itself. Fidelity Change Propagation Material fidelity changes may affect: Representation Resolution → Representation Limitations → Assumptions → Model & Environment → Inputs & Data → Scenario Design → Execution → Output Governance → Reality Correlation Fidelity therefore forms an upstream simulation-governance dependency. Fidelity Traceability A governed fidelity chain should support: Simulation Purpose → Reality Selection → Material Characteristic → Abstraction Decision → Fidelity Requirement → Fidelity Baseline → Fidelity Assessment → Fidelity Gap → Fidelity Status → Limitation This makes the fidelity basis reconstructable. Relationship to Reality Selection RSM establishes what reality must be represented. RFM cannot compensate for an important Reality Element that was never selected. High fidelity of incomplete reality remains incomplete representation. Relationship to Reality Abstraction RAM establishes how selected reality may be simplified. RFM evaluates whether the resulting abstraction still represents material characteristics with sufficient faithfulness. Thus: RAM governs permitted complexity reduction. RFM governs the faithfulness remaining after that reduction. Relationship to Representation Resolution Fidelity and resolution are related but distinct. Fidelity asks: How faithfully does the representation correspond to Relevant Reality? Resolution asks: At what granularity is that representation expressed? A high-resolution representation can have low fidelity. A lower-resolution representation may have sufficient fidelity for the intended inquiry. RRM governs the next space. Relationship to Representation Limitation RFM identifies limitations specifically arising from fidelity. RLM subsequently governs the broader set of limitations affecting the complete Reality Representation. Relationship to Reality Correlation RFM establishes representation fidelity requirements before and during simulation design. Later SIMULOS® Reality Correlation governance may compare simulation behavior or outputs with observed reality. These are adjacent but distinct spaces. RFM asks: Is the representation designed and demonstrated with sufficient faithfulness? Reality Correlation asks: How does simulation behavior or output correspond with observed reality? Cross-Architecture Boundary RFM does not govern actual Operational Reality. That remains within ORA™. RFM does not perform general validation governance. That remains within VALIDOS®. RFM does not govern general integrity. That remains within INTEGROS®. RFM governs specifically: the sufficiency of correspondence between simulation representation and the material characteristics of reality selected for simulation. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Identify Fidelity Objects Determine which represented Reality Elements, characteristics, behaviors, interactions, dependencies, and processes require fidelity governance. 2. Establish Fidelity Requirements Define the required correspondence for each material fidelity dimension. 3. Establish Fidelity Baselines Identify the governed references against which fidelity can be assessed. 4. Assess Representation Fidelity Compare the simulation representation with the applicable requirements and baselines. 5. Identify Fidelity Gaps Record material differences between required and achieved representation. 6. Evaluate Fidelity Impact Determine whether identified gaps could materially affect simulation behavior, outputs, or interpretation. 7. Establish Fidelity Status Classify fidelity as sufficient, conditional, partial, insufficient, or undetermined within the applicable scope. 8. Establish Fidelity Limitations Bind material limitations to affected scenarios, conditions, outputs, or interpretations. 9. Assess Cross-Component Fidelity Determine whether fidelity remains sufficient across interacting simulation elements. 10. Preserve Fidelity Traceability and Reassessment Maintain the complete fidelity chain and reassess it after material change. Governance Outputs RFM may produce: Fidelity Object Register, Fidelity Requirement, Fidelity Dimension Map, Fidelity Baseline Record, Physical Fidelity Assessment, Behavioral Fidelity Assessment, Structural Fidelity Assessment, Functional Fidelity Assessment, Environmental Fidelity Assessment, Temporal Fidelity Assessment, Spatial Fidelity Assessment, Interaction Fidelity Assessment, Dependency Fidelity Assessment, State Fidelity Assessment, Process Fidelity Assessment, Failure Fidelity Assessment, Distributional Fidelity Assessment, Variability Fidelity Assessment, Boundary-Condition Fidelity Assessment, Cross-Component Fidelity Assessment, Fidelity Evidence Record, Fidelity Threshold Record, Fidelity Gap Record, Fidelity Gap Classification, Fidelity Trade-Off Record, Fidelity Uncertainty Record, Fidelity Sensitivity Assessment, Conditional Fidelity Record, Representation Fidelity Status, Fidelity Limitation Record, Fidelity Change Record, Fidelity Traceability Map, and Representation Fidelity Basis. Use Case 1 — Autonomous Vehicle Simulation Scenario An autonomous-vehicle simulation represents: vehicle dynamics, sensors, pedestrians, road infrastructure, traffic, and weather. Application RFM separately evaluates whether the simulation possesses sufficient: physical fidelity for vehicle dynamics, behavioral fidelity for pedestrians, environmental fidelity for weather, interaction fidelity between vehicle and road users, and failure fidelity for degraded sensor conditions. Result The simulation may be classified: Fidelity Sufficient — Normal Urban Operation while remaining: Fidelity Insufficient — Severe Sensor Degradation The simulation cannot use its normal-operation fidelity to imply sufficient representation of failure scenarios. Use Case 2 — Spacecraft Thermal Simulation Scenario A spacecraft simulation is used to evaluate thermal behavior across orbital conditions. Application RFM compares represented: solar exposure, radiation, material thermal behavior, internal heat generation, heat transfer, and environmental variation against the fidelity required for the thermal inquiry. Result The simulation may demonstrate sufficient thermal fidelity across normal orbital conditions while identifying a fidelity limitation for an extreme orientation not sufficiently represented by the model. The limitation remains attached to subsequent simulation interpretation. Use Case 3 — Industrial Digital Twin Scenario A digital twin represents a production facility. Individual machines are modeled accurately, but interactions between production stages are highly simplified. Application RFM identifies: High Component Fidelity but: Insufficient Interaction Fidelity for analysis of cascading production disruption. Result The digital twin remains suitable for individual-machine analysis but cannot legitimately claim sufficient fidelity for plant-wide cascading-failure simulation until the interaction representation is strengthened. Architectural Position Representation Fidelity is the third internal governance space of the Reality Representation Standard (RRS). The complete RRS progression is: Reality Selection → Reality Abstraction → Representation Fidelity → Representation Resolution → Representation Limitation RSM establishes: What parts of reality must be represented? RAM establishes: How may their complexity be reduced? RFM establishes: How faithfully must the resulting representation correspond to the material characteristics of that reality? RRM next establishes: At what granularity must that representation operate? This separation prevents selection, abstraction, fidelity, and resolution from becoming one undefined concept of simulation “realism.” Foundational Principle A simulation representation is sufficiently faithful only when the characteristics that materially matter to the simulation inquiry remain represented closely enough to reality that the remaining fidelity gap does not invalidate the intended interpretation. Canonical Closing Statement Representation Fidelity Module establishes the governance conditions under which selected and abstracted reality must remain sufficiently faithfully represented for the governed Simulation Purpose and Scope. By separating fidelity from visual realism, detail, resolution, and general validation, and by governing physical, behavioral, structural, functional, environmental, temporal, spatial, interaction, dependency, state, process, failure, distributional, and variability fidelity, RFM ensures that simulation representations cannot claim greater correspondence with reality than their material fidelity dimensions, baselines, evidence, gaps, uncertainty, conditions, and limitations can actually support.

title: OOF™ Representation Limitation Module (RLM)
text: OOF™ Representation Limitation Module (RLM) Representation Limitation Module (RLM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Reality Representation Standard (RRS) Operational Layer: Simulation Reality Representation Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Type: Parent Standard Module Governed Space: Representation Limitation Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 16 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Governed Space Representation Limitation Canonical Definition Representation Limitation Module (RLM) defines the governance conditions under which known, discovered, unavoidable, accepted, conditional, and unresolved limitations in a simulation's representation of reality are identified, classified, assessed, bounded, documented, propagated, monitored, and preserved throughout the simulation lifecycle. RLM establishes the final governance layer of Reality Representation by determining where the internal simulated representation stops being sufficiently representative of the reality it claims to model, what consequences follow from that limitation, and which simulation conclusions, scenarios, conditions, or uses must therefore remain restricted. RLM does not require a simulation to represent reality perfectly. It requires the difference between: Represented Reality and: Relevant Reality to remain governable. Operational Role The preceding Reality Representation modules establish: RSM — What parts of reality must be represented? RAM — How may selected reality legitimately be simplified? RFM — How faithfully must the representation correspond to material reality? RRM — At what resolution must material phenomena remain distinguishable? RLM asks: What material limitations remain after reality selection, abstraction, fidelity, and resolution have been established, and how must those limitations constrain subsequent simulation use and interpretation? The governed progression is: Selected Reality → Approved Abstraction → Required Fidelity → Required Resolution → Limitation Identification → Limitation Classification → Materiality Assessment → Limitation Boundary → Propagation → Representation Limitation Status RLM closes the Reality Representation Standard before the simulation proceeds into subsequent SIMULOS® governance spaces. Module Operational Space RLM governs: representation limitation identification, known limitations, discovered limitations, inherent limitations, technical limitations, methodological limitations, abstraction limitations, fidelity limitations, resolution limitations, data-dependent representation limitations, environmental representation limitations, behavioral representation limitations, interaction limitations, temporal limitations, spatial limitations, boundary limitations, omitted-reality limitations, simplification effects, representational uncertainty, limitation materiality, limitation severity, limitation applicability, limitation dependencies, limitation interaction, limitation accumulation, limitation acceptance, conditional limitation acceptance, unresolved limitations, limitation propagation, limitation disclosure, limitation monitoring, limitation change, limitation reassessment, limitation status, and limitation traceability. Module Function Every simulation represents reality imperfectly. This is not automatically a defect. A simulation necessarily selects, simplifies, discretizes, approximates, aggregates, excludes, and transforms aspects of reality. The governance problem begins when those differences are: unknown, undocumented, misunderstood, materially underestimated, disconnected from simulation outputs, hidden during interpretation, or ignored when simulation results are used. RLM exists to prevent: simplifications becoming invisible, known representation weaknesses disappearing from later simulation stages, omitted reality being mistaken for irrelevant reality, high fidelity in one area masking serious limitations elsewhere, limitations being described generically without identifying affected outcomes, accepted limitations being interpreted as resolved limitations, computational constraints silently redefining represented reality, representation limitations being lost when simulations are reused, and simulation outputs being interpreted beyond what the represented reality can legitimately support. Representation Limitation Principle SIMULOS® establishes: A limitation does not invalidate a simulation merely because it exists. A limitation becomes methodologically dangerous when its existence, materiality, boundary, or consequence is not governed. The objective is therefore not: No Limitations but: Known + Assessed + Bounded + Propagated Limitations Representation Limitation A Representation Limitation is a known or reasonably identifiable condition under which the internal simulation representation does not fully preserve a materially relevant property, behavior, relationship, state, event, variation, or boundary of Relevant Reality. A limitation may arise from: deliberate simplification, unavailable knowledge, unavailable data, computational constraints, measurement constraints, modeling choices, environmental complexity, unknown behavior, resolution limits, abstraction, incomplete representation, or inherent inability to reproduce the relevant phenomenon. Limitation Object A Limitation Object is the specific representation element affected by a limitation. It may include: a represented entity, environment, behavior, interaction, dependency, process, state, event, population, physical phenomenon, temporal condition, spatial condition, or representation boundary. Each material limitation should be linked to the object it affects. Limitation Origin The origin of a limitation should remain identifiable where possible. Possible origins include: Reality Selection Reality Abstraction Representation Fidelity Representation Resolution Source Data Modeling Constraint Computational Constraint Measurement Constraint Environmental Uncertainty Knowledge Gap or: Unknown Origin This distinction matters because different limitation origins may require different downstream treatment. Known Limitation A Known Limitation is identified before or during simulation design. Known limitations should not disappear merely because they were accepted during design. Acceptance does not eliminate their relevance. Discovered Limitation A Discovered Limitation emerges after the representation has been established. It may arise during: scenario design, simulation execution, output examination, reality correlation, external review, incident analysis, or later operational use. A discovered material limitation should be propagated backward and forward through affected simulation governance spaces. Inherent Limitation An Inherent Limitation exists where the phenomenon cannot reasonably be represented with sufficient completeness under the available simulation approach. Examples may include: highly uncertain human behavior, unknown future environmental conditions, unresolved physical processes, incomplete causal knowledge, or phenomena whose relevant characteristics cannot yet be measured. An inherent limitation may still permit simulation. Its consequences must remain bounded. Technical Limitation A Technical Limitation arises from the capabilities of the simulation implementation or infrastructure. Examples may include: computational capacity, memory limits, solver constraints, platform limitations, maximum agent population, sensor emulation limits, or execution-time constraints. Technical limitations must not silently redefine the methodological requirements of the simulation. Methodological Limitation A Methodological Limitation arises from the representational approach itself. It may result from: modeling assumptions, selected abstractions, mathematical formulation, approximation method, behavioral model, aggregation strategy, or representational structure. Abstraction Limitation An Abstraction Limitation exists where an approved simplification removes distinctions that remain relevant under particular conditions. An abstraction may therefore be legitimate generally but limited for a particular scenario. Fidelity Limitation A Fidelity Limitation exists where representation correspondence to reality is weaker than required for a particular phenomenon, state, interaction, or interpretation. RFM identifies fidelity conditions. RLM governs the resulting limitation where the gap remains. Resolution Limitation A Resolution Limitation exists where the representation cannot distinguish material phenomena at the required granularity. RRM identifies and assesses resolution sufficiency. RLM carries unresolved resolution consequences into the complete Representation Limitation profile. Omitted-Reality Limitation Reality excluded from representation may later prove materially relevant. An Omitted-Reality Limitation exists where an excluded element can materially affect the simulation inquiry. This does not automatically mean that the original exclusion was unjustified. It means the exclusion now constrains interpretation. Boundary Limitation A simulation boundary may prevent representation of external effects. A Boundary Limitation may arise where: external systems influence the simulated system, environmental conditions cross the boundary, human actions occur outside the modeled environment, dependencies extend beyond the simulation, or feedback enters from excluded reality. Behavioral Limitation Behavioral models may represent only a bounded set of behaviors. Where real actors or systems may behave outside that set, the difference should remain visible. Interaction Limitation An Interaction Limitation exists where relevant interactions are: simplified, aggregated, delayed, omitted, approximated, or represented conditionally. Interaction limitations can be material even when individual simulation objects are accurately represented. Environmental Limitation An Environmental Limitation exists where environmental complexity exceeds the represented environment. Examples may include incomplete representation of: weather, terrain, infrastructure, traffic, electromagnetic conditions, resource availability, human activity, or operational disturbances. Temporal Limitation A Temporal Limitation exists where the representation cannot sufficiently preserve relevant time-dependent behavior. This may concern: duration, sequence, timing, latency, degradation, seasonality, transition speed, or long-term evolution. Spatial Limitation A Spatial Limitation exists where the representation does not sufficiently preserve materially relevant spatial differences. Data-Dependent Representation Limitation A representation may be structurally capable of representing a phenomenon while available data prevents that capability from being meaningfully populated. RLM distinguishes: Representation Capability from: Representation Support A sophisticated representation built upon weak or incomplete data may remain materially limited. Representational Uncertainty A limitation and uncertainty are related but not identical. Limitation asks: What can the representation not sufficiently preserve? Uncertainty asks: How uncertain are we about the represented condition or its correspondence to reality? A limitation may exist with low uncertainty. For example, a known excluded subsystem. Uncertainty may exist without a known structural limitation. RLM preserves the distinction. Limitation Identification Limitation identification should ask: Where does the simulation representation materially differ from Relevant Reality in a way that could affect the simulation inquiry? Identification should consider: excluded reality, abstractions, fidelity gaps, resolution gaps, model boundaries, environmental simplifications, interaction simplifications, behavioral constraints, data constraints, and known unknowns. Limitation Materiality Not every representation difference is material. A limitation becomes material where it can reasonably affect: simulation behavior, scenario behavior, output interpretation, reality correlation, uncertainty, downstream evidence, intended reliance, or conclusions derived from the simulation. Materiality Is Purpose-Relative A limitation may be immaterial for one simulation purpose and critical for another. For example: A simplified wind model may be acceptable for: Long-Term Energy Production Estimation but materially insufficient for: Emergency Turbine Load Simulation. Therefore: Representation Limitation Materiality = Limitation × Simulation Purpose × Scope × Scenario × Intended Interpretation conceptually, not numerically. Limitation Severity Material limitations may be classified according to their effect. A practical classification may include: Minor The limitation does not materially change the principal simulation interpretation. Moderate The limitation affects defined outputs, scenarios, or conditions. Major The limitation materially restricts important simulation conclusions. Critical The limitation prevents legitimate use of the representation for a material simulation purpose. Undetermined The consequence cannot yet be sufficiently established. Limitation Applicability A limitation should identify where it applies. Applicability may be bounded by: scenario, object, subsystem, environment, population, operational mode, time period, geographic area, failure condition, output, or simulation claim. Global vs Local Limitation A limitation may be: Local affecting only a defined part of the simulation, or: Global affecting the complete representation or principal simulation inquiry. Local limitations should not automatically invalidate unaffected representation. Global limitations should not be hidden by unaffected local strengths. Conditional Limitation A limitation may activate only under defined conditions. For example: Representation sufficient below wind speed X but: Representation limited above wind speed X. Conditional limitations should remain linked to the conditions that activate them. Limitation Interaction Multiple individually acceptable limitations may interact. For example: Moderate Fidelity Limitation Moderate Resolution Limitation Limited Environmental Representation may together create a major limitation for one simulation conclusion. RLM therefore evaluates limitations both individually and collectively. Limitation Accumulation A simulation should not assume that individually accepted limitations remain acceptable when accumulated. RLM asks: Does the combined limitation profile materially weaken the representation beyond the intended simulation boundary? Weakest Material Representation Principle SIMULOS® establishes: A simulation conclusion cannot legitimately assume stronger representation than the materially limiting representation condition upon which that conclusion depends. Strong representation elsewhere does not erase a critical limitation. Limitation Dependency A limitation may affect other representation elements. For example: Environmental Limitation may affect: Sensor Representation → Behavioral Response → Interaction → Simulation Output RLM therefore preserves limitation dependencies where material. Limitation Propagation Material representation limitations must propagate to downstream simulation governance. Conceptually: Representation Limitation ↓ Assumption Governance ↓ Model & Environment ↓ Inputs & Data ↓ Scenario Design ↓ Simulation Execution ↓ Simulation Output ↓ Reality Correlation ↓ Simulation Evidence ↓ Reliance Boundary The limitation need not affect every downstream stage. But affected stages must not remain unaware of it. No Limitation Laundering Rule SIMULOS® establishes: A known material representation limitation may not disappear merely because the simulation proceeds to a later lifecycle stage. Changing terminology does not resolve the limitation. Producing outputs does not resolve the limitation. Successful execution does not resolve the limitation. Limitation Acceptance A material limitation may sometimes be accepted. Acceptance requires a governed basis. The acceptance should establish: the limitation, affected representation, materiality, consequence, applicable scope, conditions, residual uncertainty, and resulting interpretation boundary. Accepted ≠ Resolved SIMULOS® establishes: Accepted Limitation ≠ Resolved Limitation Acceptance means the simulation may proceed while the limitation remains explicitly bounded. Conditional Acceptance A limitation may be accepted only under defined conditions. For example: Accepted for normal operation scenarios but: Not accepted for emergency failure scenarios. Unresolved Limitation An Unresolved Limitation exists where: materiality cannot be established, consequences remain uncertain, mitigation is incomplete, available evidence is insufficient, or the limitation remains incompatible with the intended simulation inquiry. Unresolved limitations must remain visible. Limitation Mitigation Where appropriate, limitations may be reduced through: expanded reality representation, changed abstraction, improved fidelity, increased resolution, better data, improved model structure, broader environment representation, additional scenarios, or narrower simulation claims. RLM governs the limitation status. It does not prescribe one universal mitigation technique. Residual Limitation After mitigation, a limitation may remain. The remaining condition becomes the Residual Representation Limitation. Residual limitations must be assessed independently of the original limitation. Limitation Closure A limitation may be closed only where it is: Resolved or: No Longer Applicable Closure should not be used merely because the limitation was accepted. Representation Limitation Status RLM may establish: Representation Limitations Acceptable Representation Limitations Conditionally Acceptable Representation Partially Limited Representation Materially Limited Representation Critically Limited or: Representation Limitation Status Undetermined The status must remain bounded to the Simulation Purpose, Scope, scenarios, and intended interpretation. Representation Limitation Profile The Representation Limitation Profile consolidates material limitations affecting the simulated representation. It should preserve: Limitation → Origin → Affected Object → Materiality → Severity → Applicability → Dependencies → Acceptance Status → Residual Limitation → Downstream Consequence This profile becomes a primary governance output of RLM. Limitation Disclosure Material limitations should be disclosed wherever simulation results could otherwise be interpreted more broadly than the representation supports. Disclosure should be: specific, understandable, linked to affected results, and proportionate to materiality. Generic statements such as: “The simulation has limitations.” are insufficient where specific material limitations are known. Limitation-to-Output Binding Where a limitation affects only particular outputs, the limitation should remain bound to those outputs. This prevents one global disclaimer from obscuring which conclusions remain strong and which are constrained. Limitation-to-Scenario Binding Where a limitation applies only to certain scenarios, it should remain linked to those scenarios. Limitation-to-Condition Binding Conditional limitations should remain linked to their activation conditions. Limitation Change Representation limitations may change as the simulation evolves. A limitation may: Appear Increase Decrease Change Scope Become Conditional Become Material Become Non-Material Be Resolved or: Become Unknown Material change should trigger reassessment. Limitation Reassessment Reassessment may be required when: Simulation Purpose changes, Scope changes, Relevant Reality changes, abstraction changes, fidelity changes, resolution changes, model structure changes, new data becomes available, new scenarios are introduced, new outputs are used, reality correlation reveals mismatch, or intended reliance expands. Representation Change Rule SIMULOS® establishes: A limitation assessment is valid only for the representation configuration, purpose, scope, conditions, and interpretation against which it was established. Material changes may invalidate the previous assessment. Limitation Versioning Material limitation profiles should remain version-linked to the relevant simulation representation. A limitation profile for: Representation Version 1.2 should not automatically be assumed applicable to: Representation Version 2.0. Historical Limitation Preservation Resolved limitations may remain historically relevant. They may explain: prior outputs, earlier discrepancies, previous simulation decisions, historical reliance, or later model changes. RLM therefore preserves material limitation history. Limitation Traceability A governed limitation chain should support: Relevant Reality → Representation Decision → Limitation Origin → Limitation Object → Materiality → Severity → Applicability → Acceptance / Resolution → Residual Limitation → Downstream Effect This allows an independent reviewer to reconstruct: what was not represented sufficiently, why, and what consequences followed. Representation Limitation Boundary RLM governs limitations of simulation reality representation. It does not own every limitation affecting a simulation. Examples: Representation Limitation → RLM Assumption Limitation → subsequent SIMULOS® assumption governance Input Data Limitation → SIMULOS® Inputs & Data governance Execution Limitation → Simulation Execution governance Validation Limitation → VALIDOS® General Integrity Failure → INTEGROS® This separation prevents RLM from becoming a generic limitation standard for the entire architecture. Relationship to Reality Selection RSM determines what reality belongs inside the representation. RLM governs material consequences where selected or excluded reality creates a representational limitation. Relationship to Reality Abstraction RAM governs whether simplification is legitimate. RLM governs material limitations that remain because of that simplification. Relationship to Representation Fidelity RFM governs required correspondence with reality. RLM governs unresolved consequences where fidelity remains bounded. Relationship to Representation Resolution RRM governs required granularity. RLM governs unresolved consequences where resolution remains limited. Relationship to ORA™ ORA™ governs actual Operational Reality. RLM does not redefine operational reality. It governs where the simulation's representation of that reality remains limited. Relationship to VALIDOS® RLM does not determine whether a simulation or simulation-derived claim is formally valid. VALIDOS® governs validation. RLM provides a governed representation-limitation basis that may become relevant evidence or a validation constraint. Relationship to INTEGROS® RLM does not govern general integrity. INTEGROS® may govern integrity of representation objects, records, limitation records, and related lifecycle artifacts. Relationship to ADIT® Where continuous auditability or evidential reconstruction is required, ADIT® may preserve observation and evidence concerning representation decisions and limitation changes. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Identify Representation Limitations Determine where the simulation representation materially differs from Relevant Reality. 2. Identify Limitation Origin and Object Establish where each limitation originates and which representation object it affects. 3. Assess Materiality Determine whether the limitation can materially affect the Simulation Purpose, Scope, scenario, output, or intended interpretation. 4. Classify Severity and Applicability Establish how significant the limitation is and where it applies. 5. Assess Limitation Interaction Determine whether multiple limitations create a greater combined effect. 6. Establish Acceptance Status Determine whether each material limitation is: Accepted Conditionally Accepted Unresolved or: Unacceptable 7. Establish Residual Limitation Determine what limitation remains after any mitigation or representational change. 8. Propagate Material Limitations Bind limitations to affected downstream simulation stages, scenarios, outputs, and interpretation. 9. Establish Representation Limitation Status Determine the resulting limitation status for the governed representation. 10. Preserve Traceability and Reassessment Maintain limitation history and reassess after material representational or simulation-purpose change. Governance Outputs RLM may produce: Representation Limitation Register, Limitation Object Record, Limitation Origin Record, Known Limitation Record, Discovered Limitation Record, Inherent Limitation Record, Technical Limitation Record, Methodological Limitation Record, Abstraction Limitation Record, Fidelity Limitation Record, Resolution Limitation Record, Omitted-Reality Limitation Record, Boundary Limitation Record, Behavioral Limitation Record, Interaction Limitation Record, Environmental Limitation Record, Temporal Limitation Record, Spatial Limitation Record, Data-Dependent Representation Limitation Record, Representational Uncertainty Record, Limitation Materiality Assessment, Limitation Severity Classification, Limitation Applicability Record, Limitation Interaction Assessment, Limitation Accumulation Assessment, Limitation Dependency Map, Limitation Acceptance Record, Conditional Limitation Acceptance Record, Unresolved Limitation Record, Limitation Mitigation Record, Residual Representation Limitation, Limitation Propagation Map, Limitation Disclosure Record, Limitation-to-Output Map, Limitation-to-Scenario Map, Limitation Change Record, Limitation Reassessment Record, Representation Limitation Status, Representation Limitation Profile, Limitation Traceability Map, and Governed Representation Limitation Basis. Use Case 1 — Autonomous Driving Simulation Scenario An autonomous-driving simulation represents urban traffic with high vehicle and sensor fidelity but models pedestrian behavior using a limited set of deterministic movement patterns. Application RLM identifies a: Behavioral Representation Limitation The limitation is assessed as relatively minor for: Basic Lane-Keeping Simulation but major for: Pedestrian Collision-Risk Simulation. Result The simulation may continue to support the first inquiry. Its use for the second must remain restricted until pedestrian behavioral representation is improved or the limitation is otherwise appropriately bounded. Use Case 2 — Spacecraft Thermal Simulation Scenario A spacecraft thermal simulation accurately represents the spacecraft but uses simplified environmental assumptions for an unusual orbital condition. Application RLM identifies an: Environmental Representation Limitation applicable specifically to the unusual orbital scenario. Result Normal-orbit simulation outputs remain unaffected. Outputs for the unusual orbital condition receive an explicit limitation boundary and cannot inherit the representational confidence of normal-orbit scenarios. Use Case 3 — Financial System Stress Simulation Scenario A systemic financial simulation models institutional relationships but omits several indirect dependency channels because reliable data is unavailable. Application RLM identifies: Omitted-Reality + Data-Dependent + Interaction Limitations Each limitation alone may appear moderate. Their interaction is assessed as potentially major under extreme stress scenarios. Result The limitation profile restricts interpretation of systemic contagion outputs and propagates the limitation into affected scenario and output governance. Architectural Position Representation Limitation is the fifth and final internal governance space of the Reality Representation Standard (RRS). The complete RRS progression is: Reality Selection → Reality Abstraction → Representation Fidelity → Representation Resolution → Representation Limitation Together, the five modules answer: What reality must be represented? ↓ How may it be simplified? ↓ How faithfully must it correspond to reality? ↓ At what granularity must material phenomena remain distinguishable? ↓ What material representational limitations remain and how must they constrain the simulation? RLM therefore closes the Reality Representation governance space by producing a bounded and traceable representation basis for the next SIMULOS® Parent Standard. Foundational Principle A simulation does not become trustworthy by eliminating every representational limitation; it becomes governable when every material limitation remains identifiable, bounded, traceable, and inseparable from the conclusions it can affect. Canonical Closing Statement Representation Limitation Module completes the Reality Representation Standard by governing the material differences that remain between Relevant Reality and its simulation representation after reality selection, abstraction, fidelity, and resolution have been established. Through limitation identification, origin attribution, materiality assessment, severity classification, applicability boundaries, interaction analysis, acceptance governance, residual-limitation assessment, downstream propagation, disclosure, reassessment, versioning, and traceability, RLM prevents known representational weaknesses from disappearing as simulations progress toward scenarios, execution, outputs, evidence, validation, and operational reliance. RLM therefore establishes the governed boundary between what the simulation representation can legitimately support and what remains outside its representational capability.

title: OOF™ Representation Resolution Module (RRM)
text: OOF™ Representation Resolution Module (RRM) Representation Resolution Module (RRM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Reality Representation Standard (RRS) Operational Layer: Simulation Reality Representation Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Type: Parent Standard Module Governed Space: Representation Resolution Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 16 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Governed Space Representation Resolution Canonical Definition Representation Resolution Module (RRM) defines the governance conditions under which the granularity, discretization, segmentation, temporal interval, spatial scale, state detail, interaction detail, and representational precision of a simulation are established, justified, assessed, bounded, and maintained relative to the governed Simulation Purpose, Scope, Relevant Reality, approved abstractions, required fidelity, scenarios, and intended interpretation. RRM ensures that simulation representation operates at a level of resolution capable of exposing the distinctions, transitions, interactions, variations, and events that materially matter to the simulation inquiry without requiring unnecessary representational detail that does not materially improve the simulation outcome. Operational Role The preceding modules establish: RSM — What parts of reality must the simulation represent? RAM — How may the complexity of that selected reality legitimately be reduced? RFM — How faithfully must the resulting representation correspond to material reality? RRM asks: At what level of granularity must that reality be represented so that material simulation phenomena remain observable and distinguishable? The governed progression is: Reality Selection → Reality Abstraction → Representation Fidelity → Resolution Requirement → Resolution Design → Resolution Assessment → Resolution Gap → Resolution Status → Representation Limitation RRM does not determine which reality belongs in the simulation. It does not govern whether abstraction is legitimate. It does not establish general fidelity. It governs specifically whether the simulation representation is sufficiently granular to support the simulation inquiry. Module Operational Space RRM governs: resolution objectives, resolution requirements, resolution dimensions, resolution baselines, resolution thresholds, spatial resolution, temporal resolution, state resolution, behavioral resolution, interaction resolution, environmental resolution, population resolution, event resolution, process resolution, dependency resolution, failure resolution, measurement resolution, input resolution dependencies, output resolution dependencies, multi-resolution representation, adaptive resolution, cross-component resolution, resolution consistency, resolution sufficiency, resolution gaps, resolution trade-offs, resolution uncertainty, resolution sensitivity, resolution limitations, conditional resolution, resolution status, resolution change, and resolution traceability. Module Function A simulation may represent the correct parts of reality with acceptable fidelity and still fail because its representation is too coarse to expose material phenomena. Examples include: a time step too large to capture a rapid failure, a spatial grid too coarse to represent a local hazard, a population represented only through averages when subgroup differences matter, operational states collapsed into one generic state, interactions aggregated so strongly that critical dependencies disappear, rare events removed by coarse event representation, or environmental variation represented at a scale that hides material local conditions. RRM exists to prevent: coarse representation being mistaken for sufficient representation, unnecessary detail being mistaken for methodological strength, resolution being selected only according to available computational capacity, resolution being increased after observing desired results without governance, one high-resolution component masking materially coarse dependencies, material events disappearing between simulation intervals, averages hiding important distributions or subgroups, resolution changes silently altering simulation meaning, and simulation outputs implying greater precision than the underlying representation can support. Resolution Principle SIMULOS® establishes: Representation resolution is sufficient only when the simulation can distinguish the material phenomena, states, transitions, interactions, variations, and events required by the simulation inquiry. Resolution therefore does not mean: maximum detail. It means: sufficient granularity where granularity materially affects the simulation. Resolution Is Purpose-Relative There is no universally correct simulation resolution. Required resolution depends upon: Simulation Purpose + Simulation Scope + Relevant Reality + Material Phenomena + Required Fidelity + Scenario + Intended Interpretation A simulation designed to estimate: annual regional energy demand may legitimately use a substantially different temporal and spatial resolution from a simulation designed to govern: millisecond-level electrical grid instability. The correct resolution is therefore determined by the question being simulated, not by the maximum detail technically available. Resolution Object A Resolution Object is any represented element, process, state, interaction, environment, population, event, dependency, or dimension whose level of granularity may materially affect simulation behavior or interpretation. A Resolution Object may include: physical space, time, individual actors, populations, system states, environmental variables, interactions, dependencies, processes, failure mechanisms, events, or simulation components. Resolution Requirement A Resolution Requirement establishes the minimum granularity necessary for a material Resolution Object. It should derive from: Simulation Purpose & Scope ↓ Relevant Reality ↓ Material Phenomenon ↓ Required Fidelity ↓ Required Resolution The resolution requirement should exist independently of whether the current simulation platform can technically achieve it. Resolution Dimensions Resolution should not automatically be represented as one global characteristic. A simulation may simultaneously possess: High Temporal Resolution and: Low Spatial Resolution or: High Component Resolution and: Low Interaction Resolution. RRM therefore governs resolution dimensionally. Spatial Resolution Spatial Resolution governs the granularity at which spatial reality is represented. It may concern: grid size, geometric segmentation, distance intervals, terrain detail, object dimensions, location precision, infrastructure segmentation, environmental zones, or spatial boundaries. The required spatial resolution depends upon whether smaller spatial differences can materially affect the simulation inquiry. Temporal Resolution Temporal Resolution governs the granularity at which change over time is represented. It may concern: simulation time steps, observation intervals, event intervals, update frequency, response timing, synchronization intervals, degradation periods, or temporal aggregation. A temporal interval that is too large may cause a simulation to miss: rapid transitions, short-duration hazards, feedback effects, transient instability, collisions, cascading failures, or timing-sensitive interactions. State Resolution State Resolution governs how finely operational or representational states are distinguished. For example: Operational may be insufficient where the simulation inquiry requires distinction between: Normal → Degraded → Restricted → Critical → Failed → Recovery. Where different states produce materially different behavior, collapsing them may create a Resolution Gap. Behavioral Resolution Behavioral Resolution governs the level at which differences in actor or system behavior must remain distinguishable. A population represented by one average behavioral profile may be insufficient where material behavioral variation exists. Interaction Resolution Interaction Resolution governs how finely interactions between simulation elements are represented.
