Conceptually: Applicability Context → Required Dependency → Dependency State Where the dependency materially changes, applicability may require reassessment. Applicability Restriction A Simulation Applicability Restriction explicitly prevents interpretation outside a defined contextual boundary. Examples: Not applicable to outdoor operation Not applicable above defined velocity Not applicable to pediatric population Not applicable to fully autonomous operation Restrictions should remain visible in downstream simulation interpretation. Applicability Uncertainty Sometimes it may be unclear whether a simulation remains applicable to a context. Such uncertainty should not be converted automatically into positive applicability. Possible status: Applicability Undetermined until sufficient governance information exists. Applicability Conflict An applicability conflict exists where different parts of the governed simulation record imply incompatible applicability boundaries. For example: Simulation Scope: Global operation. Environmental Applicability: Temperate climates only. The conflict should be resolved or explicitly preserved before broad simulation claims are made. Applicability–Purpose Alignment The applicability context must remain capable of supporting the Simulation Purpose. If the purpose requires: global autonomous navigation safety but applicability is limited to: daytime operation on one mapped campus, the mismatch is material. SACM should expose that mismatch rather than allowing the narrow simulation context to satisfy the broader purpose implicitly. Applicability–Scope Alignment Applicability must remain consistent with the governed Simulation Scope. A scope describing multiple environments cannot be treated as satisfied where the applicability context covers only one environment unless the difference is explicitly governed. Applicability–Exclusion Alignment Material exclusions should be reflected in applicability where appropriate. Conceptually: Material Exclusion → Applicability Consequence For example: Emergency Operation Excluded should prevent the applicability context from silently including emergency operation. No Universal Applicability Rule No simulation should be treated as universally applicable merely because its applicability boundary was not documented. Undefined applicability is not universal applicability. No Context Transfer Rule A simulation designed for Context A must not automatically acquire applicability to Context B merely because the Simulation Object is the same. No Context Generalization Rule Simulation outputs must not be generalized beyond the governed applicability context without an additional basis. No Configuration Transfer Rule Results associated with one materially relevant configuration must not automatically transfer to another materially different configuration. No Population Transfer Rule Results associated with one population must not automatically be generalized to another materially different population. No Environment Transfer Rule Results associated with one environment must not automatically be treated as applicable to another materially different environment. No Autonomy Transfer Rule Simulation under one autonomy condition must not automatically establish applicability under a materially different autonomy condition. No Scenario Inflation Rule Simulation of selected scenarios must not be represented as applicability to all possible scenarios. Applicability Change Applicability may change when the simulation inquiry, Simulation Object, assumptions, model, environment, scenario structure, or operational context changes. SACM therefore treats applicability as a governed contextual state rather than permanent metadata. Applicability Expansion An applicability context may expand when new simulation work sufficiently addresses additional: environments, populations, configurations, scenarios, capabilities, behaviors, or dependencies. Expansion should have a traceable basis. Applicability Narrowing New information may demonstrate that the simulation applies to less than originally expected. Narrowing is a legitimate governance outcome. For example: Originally Intended: Urban Roads may become: Supported Simulation Context: Urban Roads Below 60 km/h after limitations are identified. SACM permits the applicability context to become narrower without treating this as methodological failure. Applicability Change Trigger Material changes that may require applicability reassessment include: Simulation Object version change, configuration change, new capability, new autonomy level, new environment, new population, new scenario class, changed dependency, changed purpose, changed scope, or changed exclusions. Applicability Status Possible statuses may include: Applicable Context Established Conditionally Applicable Partially Applicable Applicability Restricted Applicability Under Review Applicability Conflicted or: Applicability Undetermined Applicability Context Record A governed simulation may maintain a Simulation Applicability Context Record identifying: Simulation Object, Simulation Purpose, Simulation Scope, material exclusions, applicable operational conditions, applicable environments, spatial boundaries, temporal boundaries, applicable populations, configurations, capability states, behavioral modes, autonomy conditions, scenario classes, dependencies, decision context, consequence context, applicability conditions, restrictions, uncertainties, status, and change history. Applicability Traceability Material applicability conditions should remain traceable through the simulation lifecycle. A downstream reviewer should be capable of determining: For which context was this simulation actually designed? and: Does the current interpretation remain inside that context? Failure Conditions SACM governance failure may exist where: applicability context is undefined, a bounded simulation is represented as universally applicable, applicability conflicts with Simulation Purpose, applicability conflicts with Simulation Scope, material exclusions are not reflected in applicability, results are transferred between materially different environments without basis, population differences are ignored, configuration changes are ignored, autonomy changes are ignored, scenario applicability is inflated, dependencies affecting applicability remain undocumented, combined-context effects are ignored, applicability uncertainty is represented as established applicability, applicability expansion occurs without supporting simulation work, applicability restrictions disappear from downstream interpretation, or simulation outputs are represented outside the context for which the simulation was designed. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Identify Applicability Dimensions Determine the operational, environmental, spatial, temporal, population, configuration, capability, behavioral, autonomy, scenario, dependency, and decision dimensions material to the simulation inquiry. 2. Establish Applicability Conditions Define the contextual conditions under which the simulation is intended to apply. 3. Define the Applicability Boundary Distinguish applicable, conditionally applicable, partially applicable, restricted, and undetermined contexts. 4. Align Applicability With Purpose, Scope, and Exclusions Verify that the applicability context does not exceed the governed Simulation Purpose, Scope, or material exclusions. 5. Preserve Applicability Traceability Maintain the Simulation Applicability Context Record and propagate material contextual boundaries into downstream simulation design, outputs, interpretation, and lifecycle reassessment. Governance Outputs SACM may produce: Simulation Applicability Context, Simulation Applicability Context Record, Applicability Dimension Map, Operational Applicability Record, Environmental Applicability Record, Spatial Applicability Record, Temporal Applicability Record, Population Applicability Record, Configuration Applicability Record, Capability Applicability Record, Behavioral Applicability Record, Interaction Applicability Record, Autonomy Applicability Record, Scenario Applicability Record, Dependency Applicability Record, Infrastructure Applicability Record, Decision-Context Applicability Record, Consequence-Context Applicability Record, Applicability Condition Record, Conditional Applicability Record, Partial Applicability Record, Applicability Restriction Record, Applicability Uncertainty Record, Applicability Dependency Map, Combined Context Applicability Record, Simulation Applicability Envelope, Applicability–Purpose Alignment Record, Applicability–Scope Alignment Record, Applicability–Exclusion Alignment Record, Applicability Conflict Record, Applicability Change Record, Applicability Expansion Record, Applicability Narrowing Record, Simulation Applicability Status, and Simulation Applicability Traceability Map. Use Case 1 — Autonomous Vehicle Simulation Scenario An autonomous-driving simulation evaluates collision avoidance. The Simulation Scope covers urban driving. The simulation environment represents: daylight, dry and wet roads, speeds up to 60 km/h, and: defined European road configurations. Snow, severe fog, and speeds above 60 km/h are outside the governed inquiry. Application SACM establishes the Simulation Applicability Context as: Urban European Road Environment Daylight Operation Dry / Wet Surface Conditions ≤ 60 km/h The simulation is not assigned applicability to severe fog, snow, higher speeds, or materially different road environments. Result The simulation outputs retain a clear contextual boundary. The fact that collision avoidance performed successfully within the governed context cannot be used to imply equivalent simulation coverage across all driving environments. Use Case 2 — Spacecraft Autonomous Navigation Simulation Scenario A spacecraft navigation system is simulated for autonomous orbital insertion. The simulation represents: defined spacecraft configuration, specified orbital conditions, nominal communication availability, and: a bounded propulsion-performance range. A later spacecraft configuration introduces a modified propulsion system. Application SACM binds the original Simulation Applicability Context to the original configuration and propulsion conditions. The new propulsion configuration creates an Applicability Change Trigger. The previous simulation is not automatically considered applicable to the modified spacecraft. Result The simulation lifecycle preserves the distinction between: same mission purpose and: different applicability context. Additional simulation work can determine whether applicability may legitimately expand to the new configuration. Architectural Position Simulation Applicability Context Module (SACM) is the fourth internal governance space of the Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard (SPSS). The internal progression is: Simulation Purpose → Simulation Scope → Simulation Exclusions → Simulation Applicability Context → Simulation Depth & Precision SPM establishes why the simulation exists. SSCM establishes what it must cover. SEXM establishes what remains outside the governed inquiry. SACM establishes the contextual envelope within which that inquiry is intended to apply. SDPM subsequently establishes how deeply and precisely the simulation must examine that governed inquiry. SACM does not govern actual Operational Reality under ORA™, general validation applicability under VALIDOS®, integrity under INTEGROS®, or the quality and fidelity with which reality is represented under the subsequent Reality Representation Standard (RRS). It governs specifically: the contextual applicability boundary of the simulation inquiry. Foundational Principle A simulation can legitimately represent only the contextual space for which its inquiry was designed; applicability must therefore remain explicitly bounded wherever changes in environment, time, population, configuration, capability, behavior, scenario, or dependency could materially change the meaning of its results. Canonical Closing Statement Simulation Applicability Context Module (SACM) establishes the contextual boundary of governed simulation by defining the operational, environmental, spatial, temporal, population, configuration, capability, behavioral, autonomy, scenario, dependency, and decision conditions within which a simulation inquiry is intended to apply. Through applicability dimensions, contextual conditions, applicability envelopes, restrictions, dependency mapping, alignment with purpose, scope, and exclusions, anti-generalization rules, change governance, and lifecycle traceability, SACM prevents simulation outputs produced within one bounded context from silently acquiring meaning across materially different contexts. By preserving where, when, for whom, under which configuration, and under which conditions a simulation is intended to apply, SACM ensures that contextual boundaries remain part of the simulation itself rather than becoming invisible after results are produced.

title: OOF™ Simulation Assumption Dependency Module (SADM)
text: OOF™ Simulation Assumption Dependency Module (SADM) Simulation Assumption Dependency Module (SADM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Simulation Assumption Standard (SAS) Operational Layer: Simulation Assumption Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Type: Parent Standard Module Governed Space: Simulation Assumption Dependency Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 17 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Governed Space Simulation Assumption Dependency Canonical Definition Simulation Assumption Dependency Module (SADM) defines the governance framework for identifying, structuring, mapping, classifying, propagating, and maintaining the dependencies through which Simulation Assumptions influence other assumptions, model elements, parameters, scenarios, execution conditions, outputs, and downstream simulation conclusions. It establishes the methodological mechanism through which an identified and sufficiently based Simulation Assumption is connected to everything within the simulation that materially depends upon it. SADM does not determine whether an assumption is universally true, quantify its complete uncertainty, or determine the ultimate validity of simulation outputs. It governs where an assumption matters, what depends upon it, how dependencies interact, and how changes or failures in an assumption must remain traceable through the simulation. Operational Role SADM serves as the third internal governance space of the Simulation Assumption Standard (SAS). The preceding modules establish: SAIM — Which assumptions exist and which are materially relevant? SABM — On what basis is each assumption being used? SADM asks: What depends upon each Simulation Assumption, which assumptions depend upon one another, and how can those dependencies remain visible throughout the simulation lifecycle? The governed progression is: Governed Simulation Assumption → Dependency Discovery → Dependency Classification → Dependency Mapping → Dependency Materiality → Dependency Interaction → Dependency Propagation → Dependency Change → Dependency Record The resulting dependency structure becomes an input to subsequent: Simulation Assumption Uncertainty → Simulation Assumption Limitation Module Operational Space SADM governs: assumption dependency identification, assumption-to-assumption dependency, assumption-to-model dependency, assumption-to-parameter dependency, assumption-to-environment dependency, assumption-to-input dependency, assumption-to-scenario dependency, assumption-to-execution dependency, assumption-to-output dependency, assumption-to-conclusion dependency, direct dependencies, indirect dependencies, upstream dependencies, downstream dependencies, conditional dependencies, shared dependencies, chained dependencies, circular dependencies, hidden dependencies, compound dependencies, dependency concentration, dependency criticality, dependency materiality, dependency interaction, dependency propagation, dependency change, dependency failure propagation, dependency reassessment, and complete assumption-dependency traceability. Module Function A Simulation Assumption may appear to be a single statement while influencing a substantial part of the simulation. For example: Atmospheric density is assumed to remain within Range X. That assumption may influence: Aerodynamic Model → Vehicle Dynamics → Energy Consumption → Trajectory → Mission Outcome If the assumption changes, every materially dependent element may also change. SADM prevents assumptions from being governed as isolated statements when their consequences are structurally distributed throughout the simulation. Its function is therefore to transform: Assumption into: Assumption + Dependency Structure + Affected Simulation Elements + Propagation Path Simulation Assumption Dependency A Simulation Assumption Dependency exists where the state, configuration, behavior, interpretation, execution, or output of one simulation element materially depends upon a Simulation Assumption. Conceptually: Simulation Assumption ↓ Dependent Element ↓ Affected Simulation Behavior A dependency may be explicit or implicit. SADM requires material dependencies to become governable regardless of how they originated. Dependency Object A Simulation Assumption may affect: another assumption, a model component, a simulation environment, a parameter, an input, a transformation, a scenario, an execution condition, an interaction, an output, an interpretation, or a simulation conclusion. Each materially affected element may become a Dependency Object for purposes of assumption governance. Direct Dependency A Direct Dependency exists where an element immediately relies upon an assumption. Example: Assumption A → Parameter P If Parameter P is directly assigned from Assumption A, the dependency is direct. Indirect Dependency An Indirect Dependency exists where the influence of an assumption passes through one or more intermediate elements. Example: Assumption A → Parameter P → Model M → Output O Output O may therefore depend materially upon Assumption A even though the output does not reference the assumption directly. SADM requires material indirect dependencies to remain discoverable. Upstream Dependency An assumption may itself depend upon another assumption or governed simulation condition. Example: Assumption B depends upon Assumption A. Assumption A is therefore upstream of Assumption B. Changes in upstream assumptions may require reassessment of downstream assumptions. Downstream Dependency Every materially affected element following an assumption in the dependency chain is downstream of that assumption. A single assumption may have many downstream dependencies. SADM preserves these relationships so that assumption change can be propagated rather than treated locally. Assumption-to-Assumption Dependency Simulation Assumptions may depend upon one another. For example: Assumption A: Road friction remains above threshold X. Assumption B: Vehicle braking distance remains below threshold Y. If B relies upon A, the relationship should be explicit. The simulation should not represent B as independently established where its operation materially depends upon A. Assumption-to-Model Dependency A model component may depend upon one or several assumptions. Example: Human Response Model may depend upon assumptions concerning: reaction time, attention, movement speed, compliance, environmental visibility, or behavioral variability. SADM maps these relationships. Assumption-to-Parameter Dependency Parameters frequently encode assumptions. A fixed parameter may appear to be a technical value while actually representing an assumption about reality. SADM therefore asks: Does this parameter derive from an assumption, and would the parameter require reassessment if that assumption changed? Where yes, the dependency should remain explicit. Assumption-to-Environment Dependency A simulation environment may rely upon assumptions concerning: temperature, gravity, terrain, traffic, radiation, network conditions, human presence, resource availability, or other environmental states. SADM maps the relationship between those assumptions and the affected environmental representation. Assumption-to-Input Dependency An input may depend upon assumptions used during: selection, transformation, interpolation, extrapolation, normalization, generation, estimation, or preprocessing. The input should not be treated as assumption-independent where such dependence materially exists. Assumption-to-Scenario Dependency Scenarios may exist only because certain assumptions hold. For example: Emergency evacuation completes within five minutes may be a scenario condition dependent upon assumptions about: population mobility, route availability, communication, human response, and environmental conditions. SADM makes those dependencies visible. Assumption-to-Execution Dependency Simulation execution itself may depend upon assumptions. Examples include assumptions about: convergence, timing, resource availability, computational behavior, event ordering, system stability, or execution constraints. Where execution behavior materially depends upon an assumption, the dependency belongs within the governed map. Assumption-to-Output Dependency A simulation output may materially depend upon one or many assumptions. SADM establishes the traceability relationship: Assumption → Simulation Path → Output This relationship is critical because a simulation output may appear precise even when it depends heavily upon assumptions. Assumption-to-Conclusion Dependency A simulation conclusion may depend upon outputs that themselves depend upon assumptions. The complete chain may therefore become: Assumption → Model Element → Execution → Output → Simulation Conclusion SADM preserves this dependency path. It does not determine whether the conclusion may legitimately support external reliance; that remains outside the module boundary. Conditional Dependency A dependency may exist only under specified conditions. Example: Assumption A affects Output O only when Temperature > T. SADM should preserve the triggering condition rather than treating the dependency as universally active. Shared Dependency Multiple simulation elements may depend upon the same assumption. Conceptually: Assumption A ↙ ↓ ↘ Element 1 · Element 2 · Element 3 Shared dependencies can create concentration risk because one assumption may influence many apparently independent outputs. Dependency Concentration Dependency Concentration exists where a large or critical portion of the simulation depends upon one assumption or a small set of assumptions. This condition should remain visible. A simulation containing hundreds of parameters may still depend materially upon only a few foundational assumptions. SADM prevents structural complexity from hiding assumption concentration. Compound Dependency A simulation element may depend simultaneously upon multiple assumptions. For example: Output O = dependent upon A + B + C Where the assumptions interact materially, the dependency should be represented as compound rather than as three unrelated relationships. Dependency Chain A Simulation Assumption Dependency Chain represents the sequence through which assumption influence propagates. Example: Assumption A ↓ Parameter B ↓ Model Component C ↓ Scenario D ↓ Output E ↓ Conclusion F SADM requires material chains to remain reconstructable. Dependency Depth Dependency Depth describes how far an assumption's influence extends through the simulation structure. A shallow dependency may affect one parameter. A deep dependency may propagate through multiple model components, scenarios, outputs, and conclusions. Depth may therefore be relevant when determining assumption materiality. Dependency Breadth Dependency Breadth describes how many materially distinct simulation elements depend upon an assumption. An assumption may have: Low Breadth or: High Breadth depending upon how widely its influence is distributed. Dependency Materiality Not every dependency requires equal governance attention. SADM may evaluate materiality according to factors such as: effect on model behavior, effect on scenario behavior, effect on outputs, effect on conclusions, dependency breadth, dependency depth, sensitivity, reversibility, and consequence of dependency failure. The objective is not to eliminate minor dependencies. The objective is to ensure that material dependencies cannot remain invisible. Critical Assumption Dependency A Critical Assumption Dependency exists where failure, invalidation, or material change of an assumption may substantially alter: simulation behavior, a critical scenario, a key output, a major conclusion, or the intended use of the simulation. Critical dependencies should receive explicit identification. Dependency Interaction Dependencies may interact. For example: Assumption A alone may have limited influence. Assumption B alone may have limited influence. But: A + B may materially change the simulation outcome. SADM therefore recognizes that dependency governance cannot always be reduced to isolated one-to-one relationships. Dependency Amplification A small change in an assumption may produce a disproportionately large downstream effect. This creates Dependency Amplification. Example: Small change in friction assumption ↓ Large change in stopping-distance output Where amplification is material, the dependency should be identifiable for subsequent uncertainty governance. Dependency Dampening The opposite may also occur. A substantial assumption change may produce little downstream effect because other model mechanisms dampen the influence. SADM may preserve this relationship where relevant. Hidden Dependency A Hidden Simulation Assumption Dependency exists where a material relationship influences the simulation but is not represented within the governed dependency structure. Hidden dependencies may arise through: inherited models, reused code, default parameters, embedded constants, external libraries, external datasets, model coupling, undocumented transformations, or inherited assumptions. SADM requires material hidden dependencies, once discovered, to be brought into governance. Inherited Dependency A reused model or simulation component may carry dependency relationships from an earlier simulation. These dependencies should not automatically be assumed applicable. SADM asks whether they remain relevant to the current: Simulation Object, purpose, scope, reality representation, assumptions, model, environment, and scenario context. Circular Dependency A Circular Assumption Dependency exists where assumptions or simulation elements depend recursively upon one another. Example: Assumption A → Model B → Derived Condition C → Assumption A Circularity is not automatically prohibited. Some dynamic systems legitimately contain feedback loops. However, material circular dependencies must be visible so they are not mistaken for independent support. Dependency vs. Basis SADM maintains a strict distinction: SABM asks: Why is this assumption being used? SADM asks: What depends upon this assumption? The basis is upstream justification. The dependency structure is downstream influence. The two should not be conflated. Dependency vs. Uncertainty SADM identifies the pathways through which an assumption matters. SAUM — Simulation Assumption Uncertainty Module subsequently governs uncertainty associated with assumptions and its relevance. SADM therefore identifies: Where uncertainty may propagate without replacing uncertainty governance itself. Dependency vs. Limitation SADM identifies affected simulation elements. SALM — Simulation Assumption Limitation Module governs where assumptions cease to remain applicable and how those limitations must remain visible. This preserves clean module boundaries. Dependency Propagation Where an assumption changes materially, SADM identifies the downstream path requiring reassessment. Conceptually: Assumption Change ↓ Direct Dependencies ↓ Indirect Dependencies ↓ Affected Outputs ↓ Affected Conclusions This is Simulation Assumption Dependency Propagation. Dependency Change Trigger Dependency reassessment may be triggered by: assumption modification, assumption removal, assumption replacement, basis change, model change, environment change, parameter change, scenario change, new dependency discovery, or changed simulation purpose or scope. Assumption Removal Removing an assumption does not necessarily remove its effects. A parameter, model component, or scenario may continue to encode the old assumption. SADM therefore requires the affected dependency path to be examined when an assumption is removed. Assumption Replacement Where: Assumption A is replaced by: Assumption B the simulation should not merely update the assumption register. Material dependencies should be reassessed against the replacement assumption. Dependency Failure Propagation Where an assumption becomes unsupported, materially changed, or otherwise unsuitable for its simulation role, dependent elements may require reassessment. SADM establishes: Assumption Failure ≠ Local Failure Only The impact may propagate throughout the simulation. No Dependency Isolation Principle SIMULOS® establishes: A material assumption must not be treated as isolated when simulation elements, outputs, or conclusions materially depend upon it. No Hidden Propagation Principle A change to an assumption should not be considered fully governed while material downstream consequences remain unidentified. No False Independence Principle SIMULOS® establishes: Two simulation outputs must not be represented as assumption-independent merely because they are produced by different model components when both materially depend upon the same underlying assumption. This is particularly important when multiple outputs appear to provide independent confirmation. No Dependency Laundering Principle An assumption dependency does not disappear merely because the assumption passes through: a parameter, another model, a scenario, an external component, or multiple computational transformations. The dependency remains methodologically relevant while material influence persists. Dependency Traceability SADM should preserve the relationship: Assumption ↓ Direct Dependency ↓ Intermediate Dependency ↓ Affected Simulation Element ↓ Affected Output ↓ Affected Conclusion where applicable. This creates the Simulation Assumption Dependency Traceability Chain. Dependency Map A Simulation Assumption Dependency Map may represent: assumptions, dependency objects, direct relationships, indirect relationships, conditional relationships, shared dependencies, critical dependencies, dependency chains, and affected outputs. The map may be implemented graphically, computationally, or structurally. SIMULOS® governs the required methodological relationships rather than prescribing the implementation technology. Dependency Matrix Where useful, assumptions and affected elements may be represented through a dependency matrix. Conceptually: Assumption Model Parameter Scenario Output Conclusion A1 ✓ ✓ — ✓ ✓ A2 — ✓ ✓ ✓ — A3 ✓ — ✓ ✓ ✓ The matrix does not replace the underlying dependency records. It provides a compact representation of them. Dependency Status A dependency may be classified as: Identified Confirmed Conditional Indirect Critical Under Assessment Changed Inactive Superseded or: Undetermined Dependency Gap A Simulation Assumption Dependency Gap exists where a material dependency: is unknown, cannot be traced, is incompletely mapped, has ambiguous direction, has uncertain affected elements, or cannot be connected to relevant outputs or conclusions. Dependency gaps should remain visible. Dependency Reassessment When a material assumption or dependency changes, affected relationships should be reassessed. The reassessment asks: Does the dependency still exist? Has its strength or materiality changed? Have new dependencies appeared? Have prior dependencies disappeared? Which downstream elements require renewed examination? Dependency Continuity SADM preserves dependency history across simulation changes. Where assumptions or model configurations change, prior dependency maps should remain traceable to the simulation versions in which they applied. This supports reconstruction of historical simulation results. Simulation Version Binding Dependency structures should be bound to the relevant simulation configuration or version. A dependency map from Simulation Version 1 should not automatically be treated as valid for Simulation Version 2 where assumptions, models, parameters, or environments materially changed. Dependency Record For each material dependency, SADM may establish a Simulation Assumption Dependency Record containing: Dependency ID, Assumption ID, Dependency Object ID, Dependency Type, Dependency Direction, Direct / Indirect Status, Applicable Conditions, Dependency Chain, Dependency Breadth, Dependency Depth, Materiality, Criticality, Interaction References, Propagation Path, Change Status, affected outputs, affected conclusions, simulation version, and traceability references. Dependency Set All material assumption dependencies may form a: Governed Simulation Assumption Dependency Set This provides a structured basis for subsequent uncertainty and limitation governance. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Bind the Dependency Inquiry Identify the Simulation Assumption and simulation configuration being examined. 2. Identify Direct Dependencies Determine which assumptions, parameters, models, scenarios, environments, execution conditions, or outputs immediately depend upon the assumption. 3. Trace Indirect Dependencies Follow material dependency chains through intermediate simulation elements. 4. Classify Dependency Relationships Distinguish direct, indirect, conditional, shared, compound, inherited, circular, and other relevant dependency forms. 5. Assess Materiality and Criticality Determine which dependencies can materially influence simulation behavior, outputs, or conclusions. 6. Identify Dependency Interactions Determine whether multiple assumptions or dependency paths interact, amplify, dampen, or concentrate influence. 7. Establish Propagation Paths Map how assumption change or failure may affect downstream simulation elements. 8. Record Dependency Gaps Preserve unknown, incomplete, or unresolved material dependency relationships. 9. Bind Dependencies to Simulation Version Ensure the dependency structure remains associated with the simulation configuration to which it applies. 10. Preserve Dependency Traceability Maintain the reconstructable relationship: Assumption → Dependency → Simulation Element → Output → Conclusion Governance Outputs SADM may produce: Simulation Assumption Dependency Identifier, Simulation Assumption Dependency Record, Direct Dependency Record, Indirect Dependency Record, Conditional Dependency Record, Shared Dependency Record, Compound Dependency Record, Circular Dependency Record, Inherited Dependency Record, Critical Dependency Record, Assumption-to-Assumption Dependency Record, Assumption-to-Model Dependency Record, Assumption-to-Parameter Dependency Record, Assumption-to-Scenario Dependency Record, Assumption-to-Execution Dependency Record, Assumption-to-Output Dependency Record, Assumption-to-Conclusion Dependency Record, Dependency Materiality Assessment, Dependency Criticality Assessment, Dependency Interaction Record, Dependency Concentration Record, Dependency Amplification Record, Dependency Propagation Path, Dependency Change Record, Dependency Reassessment Record, Dependency Gap Record, Simulation Assumption Dependency Map, Simulation Assumption Dependency Matrix, Simulation Assumption Dependency Traceability Chain, and Governed Simulation Assumption Dependency Set. Use Case 1 — Autonomous Vehicle Simulation Scenario A vehicle simulation assumes: Road friction remains above coefficient X. The assumption is explicitly identified and has a documented engineering basis. Application SADM maps the dependency chain: Road-Friction Assumption ↓ Tire-Road Interaction Model ↓ Braking Model ↓ Stopping Distance ↓ Collision-Avoidance Scenario ↓ Safety-Relevant Simulation Output The same assumption also affects steering stability. Result The assumption is classified as having: High Dependency Breadth + Critical Downstream Dependency A change to the friction assumption therefore requires reassessment of more than the braking model alone. Use Case 2 — Space Mission Simulation Scenario A mission simulation assumes: Solar-array degradation remains within the modeled annual range. Application SADM identifies dependencies across: Energy Generation → Battery State → Communications Availability → Thermal Control → Mission Operations The dependency is conditional upon the simulated radiation environment. Result The assumption is recorded as a: Conditional Critical Dependency If the radiation environment changes materially, the dependency chain becomes subject to reassessment before affected mission outputs are treated as unchanged. Architectural Position Simulation Assumption Dependency is the third internal governance space of the Simulation Assumption Standard (SAS). The complete SAS progression is: Simulation Assumption Identification → Simulation Assumption Basis → Simulation Assumption Dependency → Simulation Assumption Uncertainty → Simulation Assumption Limitation SAIM establishes: Which assumptions exist? SABM establishes: Why is each assumption being used? SADM establishes: What depends upon each assumption? SAUM establishes: What uncertainty exists around the assumptions and how must it remain visible? SALM establishes: Where do the assumptions cease to remain applicable and what limitations follow? Together, these modules ensure that Simulation Assumptions remain identifiable, supported, structurally connected to their consequences, uncertainty-aware, and bounded throughout the simulation lifecycle. Foundational Principle A Simulation Assumption cannot be fully governed unless the material simulation elements, outputs, and conclusions that depend upon it can be identified and traced. Canonical Closing Statement Simulation Assumption Dependency Module establishes the dependency-governance layer of the Simulation Assumption Standard by identifying and preserving the pathways through which Simulation Assumptions influence other assumptions, parameters, models, environments, scenarios, execution conditions, outputs, and simulation conclusions. Through direct and indirect dependency mapping, shared and compound dependency governance, materiality and criticality assessment, interaction analysis, dependency propagation, change reassessment, version binding, gap visibility, and complete assumption-to-consequence traceability, SADM prevents material assumptions from functioning as isolated or hidden premises and ensures that changes to an assumption can be systematically propagated to every materially affected part of the simulation. Modul 4

title: OOF™ Simulation Assumption Identification Module (SAIM)
text: OOF™ Simulation Assumption Identification Module (SAIM) Simulation Assumption Identification Module (SAIM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Simulation Assumption Standard (SAS) Operational Layer: Simulation Assumption Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Type: Parent Standard Module Governed Space: Simulation Assumption Identification Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 17 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Governed Space Simulation Assumption Identification Canonical Definition Simulation Assumption Identification Module (SAIM) defines the governance framework for identifying, distinguishing, classifying, documenting, and maintaining the assumptions upon which a simulation materially depends. It establishes the methodological mechanism through which explicit and implicit premises are converted into identifiable Simulation Assumptions before those premises become embedded invisibly within simulation models, environments, parameters, scenarios, execution conditions, or interpretation of simulation outputs. Operational Role SAIM serves as the first internal governance space of the Simulation Assumption Standard (SAS). The preceding Reality Representation Standard (RRS) establishes which aspects of reality are represented within the simulation and at what abstraction, fidelity, resolution, and limitation. SAIM begins where that governed representation requires additional premises in order to become operationally usable within a simulation. SAIM asks: What is being assumed in order for this simulation to operate, and which of those assumptions are material enough to require explicit governance? The governed progression begins: Governed Reality Representation → Assumption Discovery → Assumption Identification → Assumption Classification → Materiality Assessment → Assumption Registration → Governed Simulation Assumption Set The resulting Simulation Assumption Set becomes the basis for subsequent governance of: Assumption Basis → Assumption Dependency → Assumption Uncertainty → Assumption Limitation Module Operational Space SAIM governs: assumption discovery, explicit assumption identification, implicit assumption identification, embedded assumption identification, inherited assumption identification, model assumption identification, environment assumption identification, parameter assumption identification, behavioral assumption identification, temporal assumption identification, scenario assumption identification, operational-condition assumptions, external-dependency assumptions, assumption classification, assumption materiality, assumption ownership reference, assumption-to-simulation binding, assumption identifiers, assumption status, assumption documentation, assumption traceability, assumption duplication, assumption interaction visibility, assumption change detection, and maintenance of the governed Simulation Assumption Set. Module Function SAIM applies after the relevant reality representation has been sufficiently established. Its primary function is to prevent assumptions from becoming invisible components of the simulation. A simulation may contain sophisticated models, extensive data, realistic environments, and technically correct execution while still depending upon premises that were never formally identified. SAIM therefore establishes a controlled distinction between: what is represented, what is known, what is supplied as input, and: what must be assumed. Simulation Assumption A Simulation Assumption is a premise accepted for the purpose of constructing, configuring, executing, or interpreting a simulation where the relevant condition is not established as a complete governed fact within the simulation basis. An assumption may concern: reality, system behavior, human behavior, environmental conditions, physical conditions, relationships, dependencies, timing, availability, future states, operating conditions, boundary behavior, parameter behavior, failure behavior, or another condition required by the simulation. Assumption Identification Principle SIMULOS® establishes: A premise that materially influences simulation behavior should not remain methodologically invisible merely because it is embedded inside a model, configuration, parameter, scenario, or technical implementation. Identification makes the assumption governable. It does not establish that the assumption is correct. Explicit Assumptions An Explicit Simulation Assumption is intentionally declared as an assumption. For example: Average human response time is assumed to remain within the defined operating range. Because the premise is explicit, it can be examined, challenged, changed, tested, or bounded. Implicit Assumptions An Implicit Simulation Assumption exists where the simulation depends upon a premise that has not been formally declared. Implicit assumptions may arise through: default values, model architecture, omitted variables, simplified relationships, expected behavior, inherited engineering practice, software defaults, scenario construction, or interpretation conventions. SAIM seeks to convert materially relevant implicit assumptions into explicit governed assumptions. Embedded Assumptions Some assumptions are embedded directly inside simulation components. For example, a model may mathematically encode that: a relationship remains linear within a particular operating range. Even where no human explicitly labels this as an assumption, the simulation depends upon it. SAIM therefore treats materially consequential embedded premises as governance-relevant assumptions. Inherited Assumptions A simulation may inherit assumptions from: previous simulations, external models, datasets, engineering models, scientific literature, digital twins, third-party components, vendor models, standard operating models, or reused simulation environments. Inherited assumptions should not automatically receive governance acceptance merely because the originating component was previously used. Their role in the current simulation must remain identifiable. Assumption Versus Fact SAIM requires a clear methodological distinction between: Established Condition and: Assumed Condition An assumption must not be silently converted into a fact merely because: it has been used repeatedly, it appears plausible, it originates from an authoritative source, it is embedded in software, it reflects common practice, or previous simulation results were consistent with it. Assumption Versus Input Not every simulation input is an assumption. For example: Measured temperature = 22°C may be a governed simulation input. But: temperature will remain approximately 22°C throughout the simulated period may be an assumption. SAIM preserves this distinction because inputs and assumptions create different governance questions. Assumption Versus Representation Limitation A representation limitation identifies something that the simulation does not fully represent. An assumption identifies a premise accepted so that the simulation can nevertheless proceed. These may be connected but should remain distinguishable. For example: Wind turbulence is represented at reduced resolution may be a Representation Limitation. Reduced-resolution turbulence remains sufficient for the simulated flight condition may be a Simulation Assumption. Assumption Discovery Assumption discovery should examine the simulation from multiple directions. Relevant questions include: What must be true for this simulation model to behave as intended? What conditions are being treated as stable? Which variables have been simplified or held constant? Which relationships are presumed rather than directly established? Which external dependencies are expected to behave in a particular way? Which future conditions are presumed? Which model defaults contain substantive premises? Which omitted elements require compensating assumptions? Assumption Sources Assumptions may originate from: simulation designers, engineers, scientists, domain experts, model developers, operators, datasets, external models, technical specifications, historical experience, organizational practice, prior simulations, automated model-generation systems, AI systems, or inherited technical components. SAIM identifies the assumption and its origin where available. The strength of the supporting basis is governed subsequently by SABM — Simulation Assumption Basis Module. Assumption Classification Identified assumptions may be classified according to their role. Possible classes include: Reality Assumption A premise concerning the represented reality. Model Assumption A premise required by the simulation model. Environment Assumption A premise concerning the simulated environment. Behavioral Assumption A premise concerning expected behavior of humans, systems, agents, or other actors. Parameter Assumption A premise concerning a parameter or parameter range. Temporal Assumption A premise concerning time, sequence, duration, or persistence. Dependency Assumption A premise concerning an external or internal dependency. Scenario Assumption A premise specific to a particular simulation scenario. Boundary Assumption A premise concerning behavior at or beyond a simulation boundary. Other classifications may be established where required by the simulation domain. Assumption Materiality Not every assumption requires the same governance attention. SAIM distinguishes assumptions according to whether they can materially influence: model behavior, scenario behavior, execution, outputs, output interpretation, operational conclusions, downstream validation, or reliance. A Material Simulation Assumption is an assumption whose change or failure could materially alter a relevant simulation behavior, output, conclusion, or subsequent decision basis. Critical Simulation Assumption A Critical Simulation Assumption is a material assumption whose failure could fundamentally alter: a principal simulation outcome, a high-consequence conclusion, safety-relevant behavior, operational feasibility, or the legitimacy of downstream reliance. Critical classification does not itself determine whether the assumption is acceptable. It determines that the assumption requires stronger visibility and downstream governance. Assumption Materiality Test A practical materiality test asks: If this assumption were materially wrong, could the simulation behave differently in a way relevant to its purpose? If yes, the assumption should normally enter the governed Simulation Assumption Set. Assumption-to-Simulation Binding Every material assumption should be connected to the simulation context in which it applies. The binding may identify: Simulation Object Simulation Version Applicable Model Applicable Environment Applicable Scenario Applicable Parameter Applicable Execution Condition or: Applicable Output Domain This prevents an assumption from being interpreted as universally applicable when it belongs only to a bounded simulation context. Assumption Identifier A governed assumption should receive a sufficiently stable identifier where traceability requires one. Conceptually: SA-001 — Network Availability Assumption SA-002 — Human Response-Time Assumption SA-003 — Environmental Stability Assumption The identifier allows downstream simulation artifacts to reference the exact assumption upon which they depend. Assumption Status An identified assumption may carry a current governance status such as: Identified Under Review Accepted for Simulation Use Conditional Challenged Superseded Withdrawn or: Unresolved The status does not substitute for validation. It communicates the assumption's current role within the simulation governance process. Assumption Duplication The same underlying assumption may appear in several parts of a simulation. SAIM should distinguish between: multiple references to one assumption and: multiple materially different assumptions expressed similarly. This prevents artificial multiplication of assumption records while preserving real differences. Assumption Interaction Visibility Identification should also expose where multiple assumptions may jointly influence the same simulation component or outcome. Detailed dependency governance belongs to SADM — Simulation Assumption Dependency Module. SAIM establishes the visibility required for that later analysis. Assumption Change An assumption may change because: new evidence appears, operational reality changes, model design changes, simulation scope changes, parameters change, external dependencies change, or the assumption is challenged. Material changes should preserve continuity between the previous and successor assumption states. No Hidden Assumption Principle SIMULOS® establishes: A material assumption must not remain hidden merely because exposing it would weaken confidence in the simulation. Simulation governance requires methodological visibility, not presentation convenience. No Assumption Inflation Principle An assumption should not gradually become represented as: known, demonstrated, verified, validated, or factual without a separate governed basis supporting that transition. No Assumption Laundering Principle A premise should not escape assumption governance by being embedded into: a parameter, a model constant, a default configuration, a reused component, a scenario, or a third-party simulation asset. Its methodological role determines whether it is an assumption. Assumption Register SAIM may establish a Simulation Assumption Register containing material assumptions associated with the simulation. The register may include: Assumption ID, Assumption Statement, Assumption Class, Simulation Object, applicable model or environment, applicable scenario, origin, materiality, criticality, current status, affected simulation elements, and traceability references. The register provides the structured basis for subsequent SAS modules. Assumption Set Completeness SAIM does not require the impossible claim that every conceivable assumption has been discovered. Instead, it asks whether materially relevant assumptions have been identified with sufficient rigor for the simulation purpose and scope. Possible states may include: Assumption Set Sufficiently Identified Assumption Set Conditionally Identified Material Assumption Gap Detected or: Assumption Identification Undetermined Assumption Gap A Simulation Assumption Gap exists where a materially relevant premise appears necessary to the simulation but has not been sufficiently identified or governed. An assumption gap may require: further model examination, expert review, scenario analysis, technical inspection, documentation review, or simulation redesign. Assumption Identification Traceability SAIM should preserve: Simulation Requirement / Representation ↓ Assumption Need ↓ Identified Assumption ↓ Assumption Classification ↓ Materiality ↓ Affected Simulation Element ↓ Assumption Record This creates a traceable bridge between reality representation and assumption governance. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Establish the Assumption Identification Context Bind assumption discovery to the relevant: Simulation Object, Simulation Purpose, Simulation Scope, Reality Representation, and simulation version. 2. Discover Explicit and Implicit Assumptions Examine: model premises, environmental conditions, parameters, behaviors, scenarios, dependencies, defaults, inherited components, and omitted or simplified reality elements. 3. Convert Material Premises Into Explicit Assumptions Document materially relevant assumptions as governed Simulation Assumptions. 4. Classify and Bind the Assumptions Establish: assumption class, simulation context, affected elements, origin, and applicable boundaries. 5. Assess Materiality Determine which assumptions can materially influence simulation behavior, outputs, interpretation, or downstream reliance. 6. Identify Critical Assumptions Flag assumptions whose failure could fundamentally affect significant or high-consequence simulation outcomes. 7. Establish the Simulation Assumption Register Assign identifiers and preserve the governed assumption set. 8. Assess Assumption Identification Sufficiency Determine whether material assumption gaps remain. 9. Preserve Traceability Maintain the relationship: Representation → Assumption → Simulation Element → Assumption Record 10. Transfer the Governed Assumption Set Provide identified assumptions to subsequent governance of: Basis → Dependency → Uncertainty → Limitation Governance Outputs SAIM may produce: Simulation Assumption Identification Record, Simulation Assumption Register, Explicit Assumption Record, Implicit Assumption Record, Embedded Assumption Record, Inherited Assumption Record, Simulation Assumption Classification, Assumption Materiality Assessment, Critical Simulation Assumption Record, Assumption-to-Simulation Binding Record, Assumption Origin Record, Assumption Status Record, Assumption Interaction Reference, Assumption Change Record, Simulation Assumption Gap Record, Assumption Identification Sufficiency Assessment, Simulation Assumption Traceability Map, and Governed Simulation Assumption Set. Use Case 1 — Autonomous Vehicle Simulation Scenario An autonomous vehicle simulation models urban operation. The simulation explicitly defines road geometry and traffic signals but implicitly assumes that surrounding human drivers generally remain within modeled behavioral ranges. Application SAIM identifies: Human Driver Behavioral Range as a material Behavioral Assumption. The assumption is bound to the relevant traffic scenarios and identified as potentially critical where collision-avoidance behavior depends upon it. Result The premise can no longer remain hidden inside the traffic model. It enters the Simulation Assumption Register and proceeds to basis, dependency, uncertainty, and limitation governance. Use Case 2 — Spacecraft Mission Simulation Scenario A spacecraft mission simulation depends upon expected communication availability during several mission phases. Communication availability is represented through predefined environmental and infrastructure conditions. Application SAIM identifies: Expected Communication Availability as a material Dependency Assumption. The assumption is bound to the relevant mission phases and to simulation outputs that depend upon command availability. Result The simulation can explicitly distinguish outcomes that remain robust from outcomes materially dependent upon the communication assumption. Architectural Position Simulation Assumption Identification is the first internal governance space of the Simulation Assumption Standard (SAS). The complete SAS progression is: Simulation Assumption Identification → Simulation Assumption Basis → Simulation Assumption Dependency → Simulation Assumption Uncertainty → Simulation Assumption Limitation SAIM establishes: Which assumptions exist and which are material? SABM then establishes: What basis supports each assumption? SADM establishes: What depends upon each assumption and how do assumptions depend upon one another? SAUM establishes: How uncertain is the assumption and how must that uncertainty remain represented? SALM establishes: Where does the assumption cease to apply and what limitations follow from it? Together, these modules transform simulation assumptions from hidden premises into explicit, bounded, traceable governance objects. Foundational Principle A simulation assumption becomes governable only when the premise upon which the simulation materially depends is made explicit, distinguishable, bounded, and traceable to the simulation elements it can influence. Canonical Closing Statement Simulation Assumption Identification Module establishes the entry point of assumption governance within SIMULOS® by identifying explicit, implicit, embedded, inherited, and materially consequential premises upon which simulation models, environments, parameters, scenarios, execution conditions, and outputs depend. Through assumption discovery, classification, materiality assessment, criticality identification, simulation binding, registration, gap detection, and traceability, SAIM prevents materially relevant premises from remaining invisible inside simulation design and creates the governed Simulation Assumption Set required for subsequent governance of assumption basis, dependency, uncertainty, and limitation.

title: OOF™ Simulation Assumption Limitation Module (SALM)
text: OOF™ Simulation Assumption Limitation Module (SALM) Simulation Assumption Limitation Module (SALM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Simulation Assumption Standard (SAS) Operational Layer: Simulation Assumption Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Type: Parent Standard Module Governed Space: Simulation Assumption Limitations Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 17 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Governed Space Simulation Assumption Limitations Canonical Definition Simulation Assumption Limitation Module (SALM) defines the governance framework for identifying, defining, bounding, classifying, propagating, disclosing, reassessing, and preserving the limitations created by Simulation Assumptions throughout the simulation lifecycle. It establishes the methodological conditions under which every material Simulation Assumption remains connected to the boundaries within which it may legitimately operate, the conditions under which it may cease to remain applicable, the simulation elements and outputs affected by those limitations, and the consequences those limitations create for interpretation and downstream use. SALM does not determine whether a Simulation Assumption is universally valid. It governs where an assumption stops being safely or legitimately applicable inside the simulation and what consequences follow when that boundary is approached, crossed, changed, or remains unknown. Operational Role SALM serves as the fifth and final internal governance space of the Simulation Assumption Standard (SAS). The preceding modules establish: SAIM — Which assumptions exist and which are materially relevant? SABM — On what basis is each assumption being used? SADM — What depends upon each assumption? SAUM — What remains uncertain about each assumption and where may that uncertainty propagate? SALM asks: Within which conditions may the assumption legitimately operate, where does its applicability end, and what limitations does it impose upon the simulation? The governed progression is: Governed Simulation Assumption → Limitation Identification → Applicability Boundary → Limiting Condition → Dependency Connection → Limitation Propagation → Consequence Assessment → Disclosure → Reassessment → Limitation Record SALM closes the internal governance lifecycle of the Simulation Assumption Standard. Module Operational Space SALM governs: assumption limitation identification, assumption applicability boundaries, limiting conditions, applicability conditions, environmental limitations, temporal limitations, spatial limitations, population limitations, behavioral limitations, operational limitations, parameter limitations, model-context limitations, scenario limitations, evidence-related limitations, uncertainty-derived limitations, dependency-derived limitations, conditional applicability, partial applicability, non-applicability, limitation thresholds, limitation proximity, limitation breach, limitation propagation, limitation interaction, compound limitations, limitation materiality, limitation consequences, output limitations, interpretation limitations, limitation disclosure, limitation reassessment, limitation change, limitation version binding, historical limitation preservation, limitation gaps, and complete assumption-limitation traceability. Module Function Simulation Assumptions allow a simulation to operate where complete representation of reality is impossible, unnecessary, unavailable, or methodologically inappropriate. But every assumption creates a boundary. An assumption may be reasonable: within one environment but not another. It may apply: within one parameter range but fail outside it. It may represent: one population but not another. It may remain useful: during one period but become obsolete after material change. SALM prevents these boundaries from disappearing once an assumption has been incorporated into a model. It transforms: Simulation Assumption into: Simulation Assumption + Applicability Boundary + Limiting Conditions + Affected Dependencies + Consequences Simulation Assumption Limitation A Simulation Assumption Limitation is a governed condition that restricts where, when, how, or to what extent a Simulation Assumption may legitimately represent the condition for which it is used. A limitation may constrain: applicability, parameter range, environment, population, time, scenario, operating state, interpretation, simulation output, or downstream conclusions. Assumption Applicability Boundary Every material assumption should have an identifiable applicability boundary where reasonably possible. The boundary answers: Under which conditions is this assumption intended to apply? and: Under which conditions should it no longer be treated as applicable? Conceptually: Applicable Conditions → Boundary → Non-Applicable Conditions Applicability Context Assumption applicability should be understood relative to: Simulation Object + Purpose + Scope + Reality Representation + Model + Environment + Scenario The same assumption may therefore be legitimate in one simulation context and inappropriate in another. Limiting Condition A Limiting Condition is a condition that narrows or terminates the legitimate applicability of an assumption. Examples may include: temperature above a defined range, velocity outside tested conditions, different population characteristics, changed environmental behavior, altered system configuration, different operating mode, unavailable supporting evidence, changed temporal context, or newly discovered dependency. Conditional Applicability Some assumptions remain legitimate only while specified conditions remain true. Conceptually: Assumption Applicable IF Conditions A + B + C remain satisfied If a material condition changes, the assumption should enter reassessment. Partial Applicability An assumption may remain applicable to only part of the Simulation Object, scenario set, operating envelope, or population. SALM requires that partial applicability remain visible rather than being represented as universal applicability. Non-Applicability A Simulation Assumption becomes non-applicable when the conditions required for its legitimate use are no longer satisfied. Non-applicability should not automatically be interpreted as failure of the entire simulation. It establishes that the affected simulation pathway can no longer legitimately rely upon that assumption without reassessment, replacement, or explicit restriction. Environmental Limitation An assumption may apply only within specified environmental conditions. Examples include: temperature, humidity, radiation, terrain, atmospheric conditions, lighting, network conditions, infrastructure availability, or another environmental state. Temporal Limitation An assumption may be valid only for a defined period or temporal context. Examples include: market behavior derived from a historical period, component degradation assumptions, demographic conditions, seasonal behavior, or technology-performance assumptions. A materially changing temporal context may therefore create a limitation. Spatial Limitation An assumption may apply only within defined geographic, physical, or spatial conditions. An assumption derived from one region should not automatically be treated as applicable globally. Population Limitation An assumption based upon one population may not legitimately represent another. Population limitations may concern: age, behavior, operating experience, physical characteristics, user group, system class, or another materially relevant population property. Behavioral Limitation Human, organizational, AI, autonomous-system, or environmental behavior may be represented through assumptions. Where behavior changes beyond the assumed range, the assumption may cease to provide an adequate representation. Operational Limitation An assumption may apply only within a defined operating envelope. For example: Normal Operation may not legitimately represent: Emergency Operation or: Failure-State Operation. Parameter Limitation An assumption may depend upon parameter ranges. Example: Linear Response Assumption may apply between: Parameter X = 0–100 but not beyond that range. SALM preserves this boundary explicitly. Scenario Limitation Some assumptions apply only to particular scenarios. A scenario-specific assumption should not silently propagate into unrelated scenarios merely because it already exists in the simulation environment. Evidence-Related Limitation SABM may establish that an assumption depends upon limited evidence. SALM governs the resulting applicability restriction where that evidence cannot legitimately support broader use. Conceptually: Limited Basis → Limited Applicability Uncertainty-Derived Limitation SAUM may establish uncertainty that materially constrains assumption use. Where uncertainty becomes sufficiently significant, it may create: narrower applicability, stronger conditions, restricted interpretation, scenario restrictions, or a requirement for reassessment. SAUM governs the uncertainty. SALM governs the limitation that follows from it. Dependency-Derived Limitation SADM identifies what depends upon an assumption. SALM determines where assumption limitations affect those dependencies. Conceptually: Assumption Limitation ↓ Dependency Path ↓ Affected Simulation Element ↓ Affected Scenario ↓ Affected Output / Conclusion Limitation Propagation A limitation attached to an assumption may propagate through the simulation. Example: Battery Temperature Assumption Limited to −10°C to +45°C ↓ Battery Performance Model ↓ Power Availability ↓ Vehicle Range ↓ Mission Feasibility A mission simulated outside the applicable temperature range cannot legitimately inherit the same assumption without reassessment. No Limitation Disappearance Principle SIMULOS® establishes: A limitation attached to a material Simulation Assumption does not disappear when that assumption is embedded inside a model, scenario, computation, or simulation output. The limitation must remain traceable wherever it materially constrains downstream interpretation. Limitation Materiality Not every limitation has equal significance. Materiality may depend upon: affected assumption, dependency depth, dependency breadth, scenario significance, output sensitivity, consequence, intended simulation purpose, and Simulation Depth. The governing question is: Could crossing or ignoring this limitation materially change the simulation behavior, output, or legitimate interpretation? Limitation Threshold Where appropriate, SALM may establish a threshold at which a limitation becomes operationally significant. Conceptually: Within Boundary → Applicable Near Boundary → Conditional / Monitor Beyond Boundary → Reassessment / Non-Applicable The exact states depend upon the simulation context. Boundary Proximity A simulation operating very close to an assumption boundary may require different treatment from one operating comfortably inside it. SALM may therefore distinguish: Inside Boundary Boundary Proximity Boundary Reached Boundary Exceeded This prevents binary treatment of limitations where proximity itself is materially relevant. Limitation Breach A Simulation Assumption Limitation Breach occurs when simulation conditions exceed an established applicability boundary. A breach should trigger evaluation of: affected assumption, affected dependencies, affected scenarios, affected outputs, and required reassessment. SALM does not automatically determine that the entire simulation is invalid. It identifies the affected governance condition. Limitation Interaction Multiple assumption limitations may interact. An individual assumption may remain within its own boundary while the combination of several limiting conditions creates a materially different simulation context. Material interactions should therefore remain visible. Compound Limitation A Compound Limitation exists where multiple assumption limitations jointly constrain a simulation more strongly than each limitation considered independently. This may be particularly important in: coupled systems, multi-agent simulations, environmental simulations, complex engineering simulations, and high-dimensional scenario spaces. Limitation Concentration A simulation may depend heavily upon a small number of assumptions with narrow applicability. SALM may identify such concentration as a governance signal because small changes in context may cause large portions of the simulation to leave their supported assumption boundaries. Output Limitation An assumption limitation may constrain the meaning of simulation outputs. For example: Output applies only under Environment A must not silently become: Output applies universally. SALM therefore preserves the relationship: Assumption Boundary → Output Boundary where materially applicable. Interpretation Limitation Simulation results may be technically produced outside an assumption's legitimate boundary. Computational executability does not establish interpretive legitimacy. SIMULOS® therefore establishes: A simulation can produce an output under conditions where the assumptions supporting that output no longer justify its interpretation. No Computational Legitimacy Principle The ability of a simulation to execute does not prove that its assumptions remain applicable. Execution capability and assumption applicability are separate governance conditions. No Scope Inflation Principle An assumption established for a bounded context must not be silently generalized beyond that context. Conceptually: Assumption Scope ≤ Governed Applicability Basis Broader application requires an additional governed basis. No Hidden Limitation Principle A material assumption limitation must not be omitted merely because disclosure weakens the apparent usefulness, precision, coverage, or confidence of the simulation. Limitation Disclosure Material limitations should remain visible to downstream simulation governance. Disclosure may include: limitation description, applicability boundary, limiting condition, affected assumption, affected dependencies, affected scenarios, affected outputs, materiality, boundary status, and required reassessment conditions. Limitation Gap A Simulation Assumption Limitation Gap exists where: applicability boundaries are unknown, material limiting conditions are unidentified, dependency effects are unclear, downstream consequences cannot be determined, or the assumption is being used outside its documented context without sufficient governance basis. The gap should remain visible. Unknown Boundary Principle SIMULOS® establishes: An unknown applicability boundary must not be represented as unlimited applicability. Where the boundary cannot be established, the correct governance state may be: Applicability Boundary Undetermined rather than: Universally Applicable. Limitation Change Assumption limitations may change when: the Simulation Object changes, the assumption changes, new evidence becomes available, uncertainty changes, dependencies change, model structure changes, simulation environment changes, scenarios change, operational conditions change, or new limiting conditions are discovered. Limitation Reassessment Material changes should trigger reassessment of affected assumption limitations. The reassessment asks: Does the existing applicability boundary still represent the conditions under which this assumption may legitimately operate? Boundary Expansion New evidence may support broader assumption applicability. Conceptually: Previous Boundary → New Basis → Expanded Boundary Expansion should be governed rather than presumed. Boundary Restriction New evidence may demonstrate that an assumption has narrower applicability than previously believed. Conceptually: Previous Boundary → New Evidence → Restricted Boundary Affected simulation outputs produced under the previous broader boundary may require reassessment. Boundary Withdrawal Where an assumption can no longer be supported within its previous context, its applicability boundary may be withdrawn. The assumption may require: replacement, redesign, scenario restriction, or removal. Version Binding Material assumption limitations should remain bound to the relevant: Simulation Object version, assumption version, model version, simulation environment version, scenario version, and simulation configuration where these distinctions affect applicability. Historical Limitation Preservation Later expansion or restriction of an assumption boundary should not erase the limitation state that applied when earlier simulations were executed. Historical preservation supports: reconstruction, comparison, audit, incident analysis, and lifecycle governance. Point-in-Time Limitation Reconstruction SALM should support questions such as: Which assumption boundary applied when this simulation was executed? Was the simulated scenario inside or outside that boundary? Had a limitation already been identified? Was the assumption under reassessment? Which outputs depended upon the affected assumption? Limitation Traceability SALM preserves the chain: Simulation Assumption ↓ Applicability Boundary ↓ Limiting Condition ↓ Dependency ↓ Affected Simulation Element ↓ Scenario / Output ↓ Interpretation Limitation where applicable. Simulation Assumption Limitation Record For each material limitation, SALM may establish: Limitation ID, Simulation Assumption ID, limitation description, limitation type, applicability boundary, applicable conditions, non-applicable conditions, limiting conditions, boundary threshold, boundary proximity, dependency references, affected model elements, affected scenarios, affected outputs, materiality, uncertainty reference, evidence-basis reference, limitation status, reassessment trigger, version binding, change history, and traceability references. Simulation Assumption Limitation Map Material limitations may be represented through a Simulation Assumption Limitation Map: Assumptions → Applicability Boundaries → Dependencies → Scenarios → Outputs → Interpretation Boundaries The map provides a structured view of where the simulation's assumption architecture ceases to support broader representation. Limitation Status A material limitation may receive a governed status such as: Identified Defined Bounded Conditional Approaching Boundary Boundary Reached Boundary Exceeded Under Reassessment Restricted Withdrawn or: Undetermined according to the applicable governance context. Relationship to SAIM SAIM establishes: Which Simulation Assumption exists? SALM establishes: Where does that assumption cease to remain applicable? Relationship to SABM SABM establishes: Why is the assumption being used? SALM establishes: How far does that basis legitimately support its use?
