Possible outcomes may include: Sufficient Conditionally Sufficient Partially Sufficient Insufficient or: Undetermined. Coverage Sufficiency Is Purpose-Bound The same Scenario Set may be: Sufficient for: early design exploration but: Insufficient for: high-consequence deployment reliance. Therefore every sufficiency conclusion must remain tied to the Simulation Purpose. No Universal Sufficiency Transfer SIMULOS® establishes: Scenario Coverage judged sufficient for one Simulation Purpose must not automatically be represented as sufficient for another purpose, consequence level, operational context, or reliance decision. Coverage Saturation A simulation program may eventually reach a point where additional scenarios produce little new information. SCCM may identify Coverage Saturation where repeated scenario expansion no longer materially improves understanding of a defined region. Coverage Saturation ≠ Universal Completeness Saturation within a known region does not establish: complete Scenario Space, complete edge discovery, complete stress discovery, or absence of unknown scenarios. Marginal Coverage Value Additional simulation should ideally improve the governed understanding of Scenario Space. SCCM may therefore assess: Marginal Coverage Value —the additional Scenario Coverage gained from additional simulation effort. Coverage Efficiency Coverage Efficiency concerns how effectively simulation resources expand materially useful Scenario Coverage. This can help distinguish: more simulation from: more useful simulation. No Run-Volume Optimization Principle SIMULOS® establishes: The objective is not to maximize the number of simulated scenarios; it is to maximize materially useful Scenario Coverage relative to the Simulation Purpose and available resources. Coverage Prioritization Where resources are finite, SCCM may prioritize Scenario Space according to: materiality, consequence, uncertainty, operational likelihood, novelty, boundary sensitivity, interaction complexity, failure severity, recovery importance, and existing coverage density. A conceptual relationship may be: Coverage Priority ∝ Materiality × Consequence × Uncertainty × Coverage Deficit This is a governance relationship, not a mandatory mathematical formula. Adaptive Coverage Expansion Simulation results may reveal where additional coverage is needed. The lifecycle can become: Initial Scenario Set ↓ Simulation Execution ↓ Unexpected Behavior / Sensitivity ↓ New Scenario Requirement ↓ Coverage Gap ↓ Scenario Expansion ↓ New Execution ↓ Coverage Reassessment This makes Scenario Coverage adaptive rather than static. Coverage-Driven Simulation Planning SCCM can support simulation planning by identifying where the next simulation resources may create the greatest informational value. Instead of: run more simulations the question becomes: Which currently insufficiently covered region is most material to examine next? Coverage Reduction Scenario Sets may also be reduced. Redundant scenarios may be removed where: equivalent coverage remains, material interactions are preserved, boundaries remain represented, stress requirements remain represented, and traceability is maintained. Coverage Compression Large Scenario Sets may sometimes be represented through smaller strategically selected sets. Methods may include: equivalence classes, representative configurations, boundary selection, combinatorial reduction, sensitivity-guided selection, or other justified methods. SCCM governs the coverage consequence. It does not prescribe one mathematical technique. No Untraceable Compression Scenario reduction must not make it impossible to determine: which material Scenario Space remains represented and which was lost. Coverage Change Scenario Coverage may change when: the Simulation Object changes, Simulation Purpose changes, Simulation Scope changes, assumptions change, model capability changes, inputs change, operating environment changes, new edge cases are discovered, new stress conditions emerge, incidents occur, or new operational evidence becomes available. Coverage Versioning Materially different coverage bases should remain distinguishable. A Coverage Version may identify: Scenario Set version, object version, scope, assumptions, model version, input basis, edge-case basis, stress basis, known gaps, and date. Historical Coverage Preservation New Scenario Coverage must not rewrite previous simulation history. SIMULOS® establishes: A newly discovered scenario cannot be retroactively treated as having been covered by earlier simulation campaigns that did not examine it. Point-in-Time Coverage SCCM supports questions such as: What Scenario Space was considered known at the time? Which scenarios had actually been represented? Which Coverage Gaps were known? Which exclusions were active? Which critical conditions had not yet been discovered? This can become important for: audits, incidents, validation, accountability, certification, and operational decision reconstruction. Coverage Traceability SCCM should support: Simulation Purpose ↓ Scenario Requirement ↓ Scenario ID ↓ Variation Configuration ↓ Edge-Case Requirement ↓ Stress-Condition Requirement ↓ Coverage Requirement ↓ Coverage Status ↓ Simulation Execution ↓ Observed Result This makes Scenario Coverage reconstructable. Coverage Matrix A practical SCCM implementation may use a Scenario Coverage Matrix. For example: Scenario Domain Nominal Variation Edge Stress Recovery Coverage Status Navigation Covered Covered Partial Covered Partial Partially Sufficient Communication Covered Covered Covered Covered Covered Sufficient Autonomous Handover Covered Partial Sparse Partial Uncovered Insufficient Power Management Covered Covered Covered Covered Partial Conditionally Sufficient The matrix is illustrative. SIMULOS® does not require this exact representation. Coverage Heat Map Complex simulation programs may represent Scenario Coverage through a Coverage Heat Map. This can reveal: dense nominal regions, sparse edge regions, uncovered transitions, poorly represented interactions, and critical stress gaps. For organizations operating thousands or millions of simulation runs, this may provide more decision value than raw execution counts. Coverage Bottleneck A Coverage Bottleneck is the materially weakest region limiting the usefulness of the overall Scenario Set for its intended purpose. The bottleneck may be: one missing transition, one unknown dependency interaction, one critical recovery state, one poorly represented environment, or one unsimulated compound stress. Therefore: Overall Scenario Volume may be high while effective Scenario Coverage remains bounded by a small number of critical gaps. Scenario Coverage and Simulation Value Scenario Coverage directly influences the informational value of simulation. A highly accurate model executing poorly selected scenarios may produce precise answers to the wrong questions. SCCM therefore creates a governance bridge between: simulation capability and: simulation usefulness. Relationship to SCIM SCIM establishes the Scenario population that materially belongs in the inquiry. SCCM determines whether that population is sufficiently represented. Relationship to SCVM SCVM defines materially relevant variation. SCCM determines whether that Variation Space has been sufficiently covered. Relationship to SECM SECM identifies difficult edges. SCCM determines whether those Edge Cases remain sufficiently represented or constitute Coverage Gaps. Relationship to SSCM SSCM establishes materially relevant Stress Conditions. SCCM determines whether those conditions are sufficiently represented within the Scenario Set. Relationship to Simulation Purpose & Scope Coverage cannot be judged independently of purpose. A Scenario Set is not simply: well covered or: poorly covered. It is: sufficiently or insufficiently covered for a declared Simulation Purpose and Scope. Relationship to Reality Representation Scenario Coverage cannot compensate for missing reality representation. A simulation may have extensive Scenario Coverage over a Reality Representation that omits a material part of the real system. Therefore: Scenario Coverage ≠ Reality Representation Completeness. Relationship to Simulation Assumptions Scenario Coverage may depend upon assumptions. If an assumption excludes a class of conditions, the Coverage Assessment should remain aware of that boundary. Relationship to Model & Environment Scenario Coverage may exceed the capability of the current model or environment. This should create a visible: Coverage Capability Gap rather than an implicit assumption of coverage. Relationship to SIDS Scenario Coverage depends upon available Simulation Inputs & Data. Insufficient input representativeness may constrain practical coverage even where Scenario Requirements are correctly identified. Relationship to Simulation Execution SCCM establishes the Scenario Coverage basis that execution will instantiate. Execution may subsequently reveal: new gaps, unexpected sensitivity, unknown edge cases, new stress conditions, or redundant scenarios. These findings may return to SCCM for reassessment. Relationship to VALIDOS® SCCM does not determine whether Scenario Coverage is sufficient to validate the Simulation Object or another system. It establishes a governed Scenario Coverage record. VALIDOS® determines what validation conclusion that record may legitimately support. Relationship to ORA™ ORA™ may provide Operational Reality information showing: actual operating conditions, new environments, incidents, unexpected interactions, or emerging conditions that reveal Scenario Coverage Gaps. SCCM governs their effect on Simulation Scenario Coverage. Relationship to ASGA™ ASGA™ may identify autonomy-related operational spaces requiring Scenario Coverage, including: authority transitions, permission boundaries, escalation, override, coordination, fallback, and autonomous continuity. SCCM governs whether these materially relevant spaces have been sufficiently represented in simulation. Relationship to AIG® AIG® may identify AI behavioral conditions that require representation. SCCM does not govern AI behavior itself. It governs whether the relevant behavioral conditions are sufficiently represented within the Scenario Set. Space and Mission Systems Scenario Coverage becomes especially important in space systems because: real-world testing opportunities are limited, mission conditions may be difficult to reproduce, many failures are unrecoverable after deployment, environmental combinations are large, communication can be delayed, autonomy may increase when ground control becomes unavailable, and rare transitions can carry extreme consequence. A space agency may run millions of Monte Carlo simulations. SCCM asks a different question: What materially relevant mission Scenario Space do those millions of runs actually cover? The simulation campaign may be dense around: nominal trajectory, ordinary navigation uncertainty, standard communication conditions, and expected power behavior while remaining sparse around: autonomous recovery during communication loss, compound power and navigation degradation, rare deployment transitions, sensor disagreement during mission-phase change, or recovery after multiple simultaneous subsystem degradations. The bottleneck is therefore not necessarily: insufficient simulation volume. It may be: insufficient governance over what the simulation volume actually represents. Monte Carlo Coverage Governance Monte Carlo simulation can generate enormous numbers of runs. However, random or probabilistic sampling does not automatically guarantee material Scenario Coverage. SCCM may ask: Which dimensions were sampled? Which distributions governed sampling? Which rare but material regions received little probability mass? Which interactions were effectively never sampled? Which boundaries were underrepresented? Which operational states were excluded by the sampling model? Which high-consequence low-frequency conditions require deliberate scenario injection rather than waiting for random occurrence? This creates an important distinction: Statistical Sampling Coverage versus: Governed Material Scenario Coverage. Autonomous Spacecraft Example Scenario An autonomous spacecraft navigation system undergoes: 8 million simulation runs. Management initially interprets the volume as strong evidence of broad coverage. Application SCCM maps the runs against: mission phases, communication states, navigation uncertainty, sensor disagreement, power states, autonomy levels, recovery states, edge conditions, and compound stresses. The mapping reveals: 7.4 million runs are concentrated in nominal or near-nominal conditions. Only a small fraction represent: communication loss during autonomous recovery. Almost none represent: communication loss + low power + sensor disagreement during recovery initiation. Result The problem is not insufficient total simulation. The problem is a Critical Scenario Coverage Gap hidden inside a very large execution volume. SCCM allows simulation resources to be redirected toward the materially weak region. Autonomous Vehicle Example Scenario An autonomous vehicle has extensive simulation coverage across weather, road types, pedestrians, and traffic. Application SCCM identifies strong individual-dimension coverage but weak interaction coverage around: construction zones + low visibility + temporary road markings + emergency vehicle behavior. Result The organization discovers that apparently broad scenario diversity contains a material interaction gap. Additional scenarios can be targeted precisely at the missing region. AI Agent Example Scenario An AI agent has been simulated across thousands of tasks. Application SCCM maps: task type, permission state, tool availability, memory state, information conflict, human oversight, execution latency, and authority transitions. Coverage is strong for task diversity. It is weak for: permission changes during active tool execution and: conflicting instructions during delayed external actions. Result The organization can distinguish: task coverage from: governance-critical behavioral coverage. Industrial Robotics Example Scenario A manufacturer runs extensive robot simulations before deployment. Application SCCM maps coverage across: payload, speed, human proximity, sensor confidence, network availability, environmental conditions, production density, failure states, and recovery behavior. The organization discovers that: high payload and: low sensor confidence have both been extensively simulated individually. Their interaction during: human intervention has almost no coverage. Result A specific Coverage Gap becomes visible before operational deployment. Diagnostic Application SCCM can be applied to an existing simulation program without replacing its simulation technology. An organization can ask: What Scenario Space are we claiming to cover? Which parts are actually covered? Which are merely sampled heavily? Which dimensions have strong individual coverage but weak interaction coverage? Where are the edges? Where are the stress conditions? Which transitions are missing? Which recovery states are missing? Which critical gaps are hidden by high run volume? Which regions are excluded? Which regions cannot currently be simulated? What remains unknown? Which next simulation runs would produce the greatest material coverage improvement? This makes SCCM directly usable as a simulation-program diagnostic layer. Module Boundary SCCM begins when the governed outputs of: Scenario Identification Scenario Variation Scenario Edge Cases and: Scenario Stress Conditions are sufficiently available to define the materially relevant Scenario Space. SCCM ends when: Coverage Requirements are established, Scenario Space is mapped, material Coverage Dimensions are identified, covered and insufficiently covered regions are distinguished, Coverage Gaps are documented, exclusions and infeasible regions remain visible, Coverage Sufficiency is assessed, and a Governed Scenario Coverage Basis is available for Simulation Execution and downstream interpretation. SCCM does not govern: Simulation Execution itself, simulation-output interpretation, Simulation Validity, operational deployment authorization, or final Validation Determination. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Define the Scenario Space Integrate the governed outputs of: SCIM, SCVM, SECM, and SSCM. 2. Establish Coverage Dimensions Identify the dimensions across which coverage materially matters. 3. Establish Coverage Requirements Determine the required breadth, depth, boundary representation, interaction representation, stress representation, and other relevant coverage conditions. 4. Map Existing Scenario Coverage Classify Scenario Space regions as: Covered, Conditionally Covered, Partially Covered, Sparse, Uncovered, Excluded, Infeasible, or Unknown. 5. Identify Scenario Coverage Gaps Record materially insufficient regions and their consequences. 6. Assess Coverage Materiality Prioritize gaps according to: consequence, uncertainty, operational relevance, sensitivity, interaction potential, and downstream reliance. 7. Assess Coverage Sufficiency Determine whether the Scenario Set is: Sufficient, Conditionally Sufficient, Partially Sufficient, Insufficient, or Undetermined for the declared Simulation Purpose. 8. Optimize Coverage Expansion Direct additional simulation effort toward regions offering the greatest material Coverage Value. 9. Preserve Coverage Traceability Maintain the relationship between: Purpose → Requirement → Scenario → Variation → Edge → Stress → Coverage → Execution 10. Establish Governed Scenario Coverage Basis Produce the controlled Scenario Coverage basis for downstream Simulation Execution. Governance Outputs SCCM may produce: Scenario Space Definition, Scenario Coverage Requirement, Coverage Dimension Register, Coverage Domain Map, Scenario Coverage Matrix, Scenario Coverage Heat Map, Nominal Coverage Record, Variation Coverage Record, Edge-Case Coverage Record, Stress-Condition Coverage Record, Boundary Coverage Record, Threshold Coverage Record, Transition Coverage Record, Interaction Coverage Record, Temporal Coverage Record, Sequence Coverage Record, Environmental Coverage Record, Configuration Coverage Record, Dependency Coverage Record, Failure Coverage Record, Recovery Coverage Record, Human-System Interaction Coverage Record, Multi-Agent Coverage Record, Autonomous-Behavior Coverage Record, Coverage Density Assessment, Sparse-Region Record, Coverage Exclusion Record, Coverage Infeasibility Record, Unknown Scenario Space Record, Scenario Coverage Gap, Critical Scenario Coverage Gap, Scenario Coverage Gap Register, Coverage Materiality Assessment, Coverage Priority Record, Coverage Confidence Assessment, Coverage Sufficiency Assessment, Coverage Saturation Assessment, Marginal Coverage Value Assessment, Coverage Efficiency Assessment, Coverage Expansion Plan, Coverage Compression Record, Coverage Change Record, Coverage Version Record, Coverage Traceability Map, and Governed Scenario Coverage Basis. Use Case 1 — Space Agency Monte Carlo Simulation Program Scenario A mission simulation environment executes millions of Monte Carlo runs. The organization possesses enormous execution volume but lacks a structured representation of what those runs collectively cover. Application SCCM maps the execution set across: mission phase, navigation uncertainty, communication state, power availability, environmental state, autonomy mode, failure state, recovery state, and materially relevant interactions. The analysis discovers dense nominal coverage but weak coverage of several high-consequence compound conditions. Result The organization receives: Scenario Coverage Matrix Coverage Heat Map Critical Scenario Coverage Gap Register and: Coverage Expansion Priorities. Instead of purchasing more simulation capacity merely to increase run count, resources can be directed toward the Scenario Space regions with the greatest informational deficit. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Robot Before Deployment Scenario A robot has passed extensive simulation across normal industrial tasks. Application SCCM identifies weak coverage around: human intervention + high payload + reduced perception confidence + network latency. These conditions are individually represented but rarely combined. Result The program discovers a material interaction Coverage Gap before deployment. The gap can be returned to SCVM, SECM, or SSCM for additional scenario design. Use Case 3 — Autonomous AI Agent Scenario An AI agent has completed thousands of simulated workflows successfully. Application SCCM maps the workflows against: authority, permissions, memory availability, tool state, task concurrency, information conflict, external latency, escalation, human oversight, and recovery. Result The analysis reveals strong functional task coverage but insufficient governance-critical coverage of: authority change during active execution and: partial tool failure during delegated multi-step actions. The organization now knows precisely where additional simulation is needed. Architectural Position Scenario Coverage Module (SCCM) is the fifth and final internal governance space of the Simulation Scenario Standard (SSS). The complete progression is: Scenario Identification ↓ Scenario Variation ↓ Scenario Edge Cases ↓ Scenario Stress Conditions ↓ Scenario Coverage Together: SCIM establishes the governed Scenario population. SCVM establishes materially relevant Scenario Variation. SECM identifies difficult edges, thresholds, transitions, sparse regions, and unusual interactions. SSCM establishes deliberate Stress Conditions capable of exposing degradation, limits, failure, cascading effects, and recovery. SCCM determines whether the resulting Scenario Set sufficiently represents the materially relevant Scenario Space and makes remaining gaps visible. The output of the complete Parent Standard becomes: Governed Scenario Space Governed Scenario Set Scenario Coverage Basis ready for downstream Simulation Execution. Foundational Principle Simulation confidence must not be inferred from how many scenarios were executed, but from whether the materially relevant Scenario Space—including variations, boundaries, interactions, edge cases, stress conditions, transitions, failures, and recovery states—was sufficiently and transparently represented. Canonical Closing Statement Scenario Coverage Module completes the internal governance lifecycle of the Simulation Scenario Standard by establishing how materially relevant Scenario Space is mapped against the scenarios actually selected for examination. Through multidimensional Coverage Requirements, nominal and variation coverage, edge and stress coverage, boundary and transition coverage, interaction and temporal coverage, Coverage Gap identification, unknown-space preservation, coverage sufficiency, prioritization, adaptive expansion, compression governance, point-in-time traceability, and coverage-efficiency analysis, SCCM prevents simulation volume from being mistaken for simulation breadth and transforms Scenario Coverage into an explicit governable object. It enables organizations to determine not merely how many simulations they have run, but which parts of the problem space those simulations actually illuminate, which critical regions remain weak or unknown, and where the next unit of simulation effort can produce the greatest material improvement in understanding.

title: OOF™ Scenario Identification Module (SCIM)
text: OOF™ Scenario Identification Module (SCIM) Scenario Identification Module (SCIM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Simulation Scenario Standard (SSS) Operational Layer: Simulation Scenario Governance Layer Category: AI & Simulation Subcategory: Simulation Governance Type: Parent Standard Module Governed Space: Simulation Scenario Identification Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 18 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Governed Space Simulation Scenario Identification Canonical Definition Scenario Identification Module (SCIM) defines the governance framework for identifying, distinguishing, classifying, bounding, documenting, and maintaining the materially relevant scenarios that a simulation may need to examine in order to satisfy its defined Simulation Purpose & Scope. SCIM establishes the first internal governance space of the Simulation Scenario Standard (SSS). Its role is not to generate every mathematically possible situation. Its role is to establish a governed answer to a more important question: Which conditions are sufficiently relevant to become identifiable Simulation Scenarios rather than remaining hidden, assumed, ignored, or informally understood? Operational Role SCIM receives the governed simulation basis established by preceding SIMULOS® Parent Standards: Simulation Object ↓ Simulation Purpose & Scope ↓ Reality Representation ↓ Simulation Assumptions ↓ Simulation Model & Environment ↓ Simulation Inputs & Data SCIM then establishes: Scenario Identification Basis → Candidate Conditions → Materiality Assessment → Scenario Recognition → Scenario Identity → Scenario Classification → Scenario Register The resulting identified scenarios become the governed basis for subsequent: Scenario Variation → Edge Cases → Stress Conditions → Scenario Coverage SCIM therefore governs what enters the Scenario Design space. Module Operational Space SCIM governs: scenario requirements, candidate scenario identification, scenario recognition, scenario relevance, scenario materiality, scenario identity, scenario boundaries, scenario distinction, scenario classification, scenario origin, scenario rationale, scenario dependencies, scenario relationships, scenario applicability, scenario inclusion, scenario exclusion, scenario duplication, scenario families, scenario discovery, emergent scenarios, scenario lifecycle status, scenario version continuity, and Scenario Register formation. Scenario Identification Basis Scenario identification should begin from the governed simulation inquiry rather than from an arbitrary list of situations. Potential scenario requirements may originate from: Simulation Purpose, Simulation Scope, represented reality, system operating states, Simulation Assumptions, Input Sets, parameter ranges, environmental conditions, dependencies, uncertainty, boundaries, known failure mechanisms, operational transitions, interactions, historical events, observed incidents, or simulation-specific exploratory questions. The objective is to establish why a scenario belongs in the simulation inquiry. Scenario Requirement A Scenario Requirement identifies a condition, state, event, interaction, variation, boundary, failure, uncertainty, or other circumstance that may need deliberate simulation examination. It answers: What materially relevant condition must the Scenario Design process consider? A Scenario Requirement does not yet require a fully configured executable scenario. It creates the governed requirement from which one or more Simulation Scenarios may later be designed. Requirement-to-Scenario Separation SCIM distinguishes: What must be examined from: How it will be simulated. For example: Requirement: Examine operation under materially degraded communication. The eventual Scenario Set may contain several distinct communication-degradation scenarios. This separation prevents one convenient technical scenario from being mistaken for complete satisfaction of the underlying scenario requirement. Candidate Scenario A Candidate Scenario is a potential simulation condition identified for governance assessment before formal inclusion in the Scenario Register. Candidate scenarios may arise from: architecture analysis, domain knowledge, operational experience, historical incidents, system design, risk analysis, uncertainty analysis, simulation results, expert input, or automated scenario discovery. Candidate status means: potentially relevant — not yet governed as required. Scenario Materiality Not every conceivable condition deserves scenario status. SCIM evaluates whether a candidate condition is materially relevant to the Simulation Purpose & Scope. Materiality may depend upon whether the condition could materially affect: system behavior, simulation outputs, system-state transitions, performance, safety, failure behavior, decision behavior, resource consumption, interaction behavior, recovery, or downstream interpretation. Materiality Is Not Frequency A condition may be rare and still be material. A condition may be common and still be immaterial to the particular simulation inquiry. SCIM therefore separates: How often might this occur? from: Could this condition materially change what the simulation needs to understand? Scenario Recognition A candidate condition becomes a governed Simulation Scenario when it has sufficient: relevance, identity, boundary, rationale, and connection to the Simulation Purpose & Scope to require deliberate treatment within Scenario Design. Recognition does not mean the scenario has already been executed. It means the scenario has become a governed object that cannot silently disappear from the simulation inquiry. Scenario Identity Every material Simulation Scenario should be distinguishable from materially different scenarios. Scenario Identity may include: Scenario Identifier, scenario name, Scenario Requirement, scenario purpose, applicable Simulation Object, applicable object version, relevant Simulation Scope, scenario condition, scenario state, relevant environment, relevant inputs, relevant parameters, dependencies, applicable assumptions, scenario origin, scenario version, and current scenario status. Scenario Identity Principle SIMULOS® establishes: A scenario that cannot be uniquely identified cannot be reliably executed, compared, reproduced, changed, or traced. Scenario Boundary Every identified scenario should establish what belongs to that scenario and what does not. A Scenario Boundary may distinguish: included conditions, excluded conditions, active system states, applicable environment, applicable actors, applicable dependencies, temporal boundaries, event boundaries, and configuration boundaries. This prevents scenario meaning from changing informally between design and execution. Scenario Distinction Two scenarios should remain separate where a difference between them could materially affect simulation behavior or interpretation. For example: Communication Lost Before Autonomous Handover and: Communication Lost After Autonomous Handover may require separate scenario identities where sequence materially changes system behavior. Scenario Equivalence Two candidate scenarios may be treated as equivalent where their differences are not material to the Simulation Purpose. Equivalence should be justified rather than assumed. Conceptually: Candidate A + Candidate B → Material Difference Assessment → Separate Scenarios / Scenario Equivalence Scenario Classification Identified scenarios may be classified to support systematic Scenario Design. Classification may include: Baseline Nominal Expected Alternative Variation Boundary Edge Rare Stress Extreme Failure Degraded State Transition Recovery Uncertainty-Driven Combined Cascading Emergent or another simulation-specific class. Classification does not determine scenario importance by itself. Multi-Class Scenarios A scenario may belong to more than one class. For example: Rare + Extreme + Transition + Failure may legitimately describe one scenario. SCIM should preserve such relationships rather than forcing every scenario into one exclusive category. Scenario Origin A scenario should remain traceable to why it was identified. Possible origins include: Simulation Purpose Scope Requirement Reality Representation Assumption Input Uncertainty System Boundary Known Failure Historical Incident Operational Observation Dependency Previous Simulation Result New Evidence or: Scenario Discovery Scenario Origin improves later assessment of why the scenario matters. Scenario Rationale A material scenario should have a concise rationale answering: Why does this scenario require simulation consideration? The rationale should connect the scenario to the governed simulation inquiry. This prevents Scenario Registers from becoming unexplained catalogs. Scenario Applicability Not every scenario applies to every: object version, configuration, environment, population, mission phase, operating mode, or Simulation Scope. SCIM therefore establishes applicability boundaries where necessary. Scenario Dependency A scenario may depend upon another condition or event. For example: Backup Navigation Failure may become relevant only after: Primary Navigation Failure. The dependency should remain visible where it affects Scenario Design. Scenario Relationship Scenarios may relate through: prerequisite, sequence, common cause, escalation, dependency, recovery, variation, alternative state, shared boundary, or shared scenario family. These relationships can later become important when Scenario Variation and Scenario Coverage are evaluated. Scenario Family Related scenarios may be grouped into a Scenario Family without losing individual scenario identity. For example: Communication Degradation may include: Latency Increase Intermittent Connection Bandwidth Reduction Partial Data Loss Complete Communication Loss The family provides structural organization. Each materially distinct scenario remains independently governable. Scenario Inclusion A candidate scenario should enter the Scenario Register where its material relevance has been sufficiently established. Inclusion may be: Required Conditionally Required Exploratory or another governed status appropriate to the simulation. Scenario Exclusion A candidate scenario may be excluded where it is: outside Simulation Scope, materially irrelevant, impossible under the governed Simulation Object, equivalent to another governed scenario, duplicative without additional value, or unsupported by the defined simulation inquiry. Material exclusions should remain documented where later users could otherwise assume the scenario was considered or covered. No Convenience Exclusion Principle SIMULOS® establishes: A materially relevant scenario must not disappear from Scenario Design merely because it is difficult, expensive, computationally demanding, inconvenient, or currently impossible to simulate. Where the scenario is material but cannot currently be simulated, the correct result may be: Scenario Required — Simulation Capability Gap rather than exclusion. Scenario Duplication Scenario duplication can create the appearance of broad coverage without expanding the actual condition space examined. SCIM therefore distinguishes: distinct scenario from: duplicate or materially equivalent scenario. This becomes important later when Scenario Coverage is assessed. Scenario Register SCIM produces a governed Scenario Register containing the identified scenario population relevant to the simulation inquiry. A Scenario Register may preserve: Scenario Identifier, Scenario Requirement, scenario name, classification, rationale, origin, materiality, applicability, boundary, dependencies, relationships, scenario family, inclusion status, exclusion status, version, and lifecycle status. The Scenario Register becomes the primary structured input to subsequent SSS modules. Scenario Register ≠ Scenario Set SCIM distinguishes: Scenario Register from: Governed Simulation Scenario Set. The Scenario Register identifies and organizes materially relevant scenarios. The final Scenario Set emerges only after scenarios have been: varied, edge-tested, stress-designed, and coverage-assessed through subsequent SSS governance spaces. Scenario Discovery Scenario identification does not necessarily end before simulation execution. New scenarios may be discovered through: unexpected simulation behavior, newly identified dependencies, operational incidents, changed environments, new evidence, system modifications, or emerging interactions. SCIM therefore supports lifecycle scenario discovery. Emergent Scenario An Emergent Scenario is a materially relevant scenario identified after the original Scenario Register was established. It should receive: identity, rationale, origin, classification, materiality assessment, and lifecycle status like any other governed scenario. Historical Scenario Preservation Adding a newly discovered scenario must not create the false impression that earlier simulation campaigns already covered it. SIMULOS® establishes: New scenario discovery must preserve the historical boundary of prior Scenario Coverage. Scenario Versioning A scenario may change because of: object change, environment change, parameter change, new knowledge, changed assumptions, dependency change, or refined scenario definition. Materially changed scenarios should remain version-distinguishable. Scenario Lifecycle Status A scenario may move through statuses such as: Candidate ↓ Identified ↓ Accepted ↓ Configured ↓ Execution Ready ↓ Executed ↓ Reassessment Required ↓ Retired The exact implementation may differ. The important governance requirement is that current scenario status remains visible. Scenario Identification Gap A Scenario Identification Gap exists where a materially relevant condition appears to exist but cannot yet be sufficiently identified, bounded, or characterized. A gap should not automatically become an invented scenario. The correct governance state may remain: Scenario Identification Incomplete. Unknown Scenario Space Complex systems may contain conditions that cannot be fully enumerated in advance. SCIM does not claim that governance can identify every future scenario. Instead, it requires that: known scenario requirements are governed, material uncertainty remains visible, discovery pathways exist, and later emerging scenarios can enter the lifecycle without rewriting historical records. No Exhaustive-Knowledge Claim SIMULOS® establishes: A governed Scenario Register demonstrates what has been identified; it does not prove that every possible scenario has been discovered. This distinction becomes especially important for autonomous, adaptive, multi-agent, and open-environment systems. Autonomous-System Scenario Identification Autonomous systems can generate scenario requirements from interactions between: perception, decision state, environment, other agents, human behavior, communication, permissions, autonomy level, resource availability, and system objectives. A material scenario may therefore arise from a combination rather than one isolated failure. For example: Reduced Sensor Confidence + Conflicting External Agent Behavior + Communication Delay + Autonomous Decision Requirement may represent a distinct scenario requiring governance even if each individual condition has already been identified separately. Space and Mission Scenario Identification Space and mission systems make Scenario Identification particularly important because operational testing may be: physically impossible, prohibitively expensive, mission-limited, irreversible, or unable to reproduce rare combinations after deployment. A spacecraft simulation may therefore need to identify conditions involving: mission-phase transitions, communication loss, navigation uncertainty, thermal extremes, partial power availability, subsystem degradation, timing deviations, ground-segment limitations, and interacting failures. SCIM does not prescribe these scenarios universally. It provides the governance structure through which mission-specific conditions can become identifiable and traceable Scenario Requirements. Scenario Identification for Existing Simulation Programs SCIM can also be applied retrospectively. An organization may compare an existing simulation program against the module and ask: Which Scenario Requirements are explicit? Which scenarios have unique identities? Why was each scenario selected? Which material conditions were excluded? Which scenarios are duplicates? Which scenarios were discovered later? Can every executed scenario be traced back to a governed reason for its existence? This can expose simulation weaknesses before changing the model itself. Module Boundary SCIM begins when the governed Simulation Object, Purpose & Scope, Reality Representation, Assumptions, Model & Environment, and Input & Data Basis provide sufficient context to identify materially relevant simulation conditions. SCIM ends when candidate conditions have been sufficiently: identified, materiality-assessed, distinguished, bounded, classified, related, included or excluded, and recorded to establish a governed Scenario Register. SCIM does not determine the complete Scenario Set. Subsequent modules govern: SCVM — Scenario Variation SECM — Scenario Edge Cases SSCM — Scenario Stress Conditions SCCM — Scenario Coverage Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Establish Scenario Identification Basis Identify the governed simulation elements from which Scenario Requirements may arise. 2. Identify Candidate Conditions Capture materially plausible: states, events, interactions, boundaries, failures, transitions, uncertainties, and alternatives. 3. Assess Materiality Determine whether each candidate could materially affect the Simulation Purpose, system behavior, simulation outputs, or downstream interpretation. 4. Establish Scenario Identity Assign sufficient identity, boundary, rationale, origin, classification, applicability, and relationship information to each material scenario. 5. Establish the Scenario Register Record included, conditionally included, exploratory, excluded, duplicate, unresolved, and newly discovered scenarios while preserving their lifecycle continuity. Governance Outputs SCIM may produce: Scenario Identification Basis, Scenario Requirement, Candidate Scenario Record, Scenario Materiality Assessment, Scenario Identifier, Scenario Identity Record, Scenario Boundary Record, Scenario Classification, Scenario Origin Record, Scenario Rationale, Scenario Applicability Record, Scenario Dependency Map, Scenario Relationship Map, Scenario Family, Scenario Inclusion Record, Scenario Exclusion Record, Scenario Equivalence Record, Scenario Duplication Record, Scenario Identification Gap, Scenario Capability Gap Reference, Scenario Discovery Record, Emergent Scenario Record, Scenario Version Record, Scenario Lifecycle Status, and Governed Scenario Register. Use Case 1 — Autonomous Vehicle Simulation Scenario An autonomous-driving simulation program contains thousands of road scenarios. Most are variations of normal traffic. SCIM analysis reveals that scenario identification was largely derived from available driving data rather than from a governed Scenario Requirement process. Application The program identifies additional material conditions involving: degraded perception, conflicting road-user behavior, partial map inconsistency, communication limitations, emergency vehicle interaction, unusual transitions, and combinations of these conditions. Each receives an explicit Scenario Requirement and Scenario Identity. Result The primary weakness was not insufficient simulation volume. It was an incomplete Scenario Register. The organization can now determine which missing conditions require variation, edge-case design, stress testing, and coverage analysis. Use Case 2 — Spacecraft Mission Simulation Scenario A mission simulation extensively covers nominal orbital operations and individually modeled subsystem failures. SCIM identifies a missing Scenario Requirement: communication degradation during autonomous recovery while power availability is constrained. Each condition had previously existed elsewhere in the simulation program, but their operational relationship had never been identified as a distinct scenario. Application SCIM establishes the combined condition as a governed Simulation Scenario with: Scenario Identity, mission-phase applicability, dependency relationships, rationale, and explicit origin. Result A previously invisible mission condition becomes part of the Scenario Register before scenario stress and coverage analysis. The architecture has not predicted whether the spacecraft will fail. It has identified a condition that the simulation program should no longer leave structurally invisible. Use Case 3 — Industrial Autonomous Robot Scenario An industrial robot has simulation scenarios for: normal production, sensor failure, human proximity, and reduced actuator performance. An operational incident later reveals that partial sensor degradation combined with unexpected human movement produces behavior not represented in the original scenario population. Application SCIM creates an Emergent Scenario linked to: the incident, the relevant system configuration, the affected operating state, and the original Scenario Register version. Result The new scenario enters future Scenario Design without rewriting historical records. Earlier simulations remain correctly represented as: Scenario Not Previously Identified / Not Previously Covered. Architectural Position Scenario Identification Module (SCIM) is the first internal governance space of the Simulation Scenario Standard (SSS). The complete SSS progression is: Scenario Identification ↓ Scenario Variation ↓ Scenario Edge Cases ↓ Scenario Stress Conditions ↓ Scenario Coverage SCIM establishes the governed scenario population upon which all subsequent Scenario Design governance depends. Without SCIM, scenario variation can vary the wrong scenarios, edge-case analysis can search the wrong boundaries, stress testing can stress irrelevant conditions, and coverage analysis can measure a scenario population whose completeness was never methodologically established. Foundational Principle A simulation cannot deliberately examine a materially relevant condition until that condition has first become an identifiable, bounded, and governable Simulation Scenario. Canonical Closing Statement Scenario Identification Module establishes the entry point into governed Simulation Scenario Design by transforming materially relevant conditions, states, events, interactions, uncertainties, failures, transitions, dependencies, and alternatives into identifiable and traceable Simulation Scenarios. Through Scenario Requirements, materiality assessment, identity, boundaries, classification, origin, rationale, applicability, dependency mapping, inclusion and exclusion governance, scenario families, discovery, versioning, and Scenario Register formation, SCIM ensures that simulation programs do not confuse large numbers of available scenarios with systematic identification of the conditions that actually matter to the simulation inquiry. Modul 2

title: OOF™ Correlation Uncertainty Module (SCUM) defines the governance conditions
text: OOF™ Correlation Uncertainty Module (SCUM) defines the governance conditions Correlation Uncertainty Module (SCUM) defines the governance conditions OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Standard (SRCS) Operational Layer: Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Type: Parent Standard Module Governed Space: Correlation Uncertainty Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 19 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Governed Space Correlation Uncertainty Canonical Definition Correlation Uncertainty Module (SCUM) defines the governance conditions under which uncertainty affecting the relationship between simulation and Operational Reality is identified, attributed where supportable, classified, bounded, propagated, documented, communicated, and preserved throughout Simulation-to-Reality Correlation. SCUM governs uncertainty concerning: how confidently a simulation can be said to correspond to reality within a defined object, condition, scenario, environment, time, comparison basis, and correlation scope. Its purpose is not to eliminate uncertainty. Its purpose is to prevent uncertainty from disappearing when simulation results are compared with reality, aligned against observations, or subsequently used as evidence. Operational Role SCUM is the fifth and final internal governance space of the Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Standard (SRCS). The preceding modules establish: SRCM — What simulation and reality observations may legitimately be compared? SCCM — According to which criteria should correspondence be assessed? SDMM — Where and how materially do simulation and reality differ? SRAM — Which deviations require alignment, and how should that alignment occur? SCUM asks: How certain are we about the resulting Simulation-to-Reality Correlation, what remains unknown, and where does that uncertainty limit interpretation or downstream reliance? The complete internal progression is: Simulation-Reality Comparison ↓ Correlation Criteria ↓ Simulation-Reality Deviation ↓ Reality Alignment ↓ Correlation Uncertainty Module Operational Space SCUM governs: correlation uncertainty identification, uncertainty source identification, uncertainty classification, uncertainty attribution, uncertainty magnitude, uncertainty bounds, measurement uncertainty, observational uncertainty, representation uncertainty, model uncertainty, assumption-related uncertainty, environmental uncertainty, input uncertainty contribution, scenario uncertainty contribution, execution uncertainty contribution, temporal uncertainty, spatial uncertainty, behavioral uncertainty, interaction uncertainty, reality-reference uncertainty, comparison uncertainty, correlation-criteria uncertainty, deviation uncertainty, alignment uncertainty, residual uncertainty, epistemic uncertainty, aleatory uncertainty, unknown uncertainty, uncertainty dependency, uncertainty interaction, uncertainty propagation, uncertainty accumulation, uncertainty reduction, irreducible uncertainty, condition-specific uncertainty, uncertainty thresholds, uncertainty materiality, uncertainty disclosure, uncertainty traceability, uncertainty status, and downstream uncertainty transfer. Module Function SCUM prevents a correlation statement such as: “The simulation matches reality.” from being treated as complete unless the uncertainty surrounding that statement is also visible. A governed correlation statement should instead be capable of expressing: what corresponds, under which conditions, against which reality basis, with what observed deviations, with what remaining uncertainty, and: where that uncertainty becomes material. Correlation Is Not Certainty SIMULOS® establishes: Observed correlation does not eliminate uncertainty about the simulation-reality relationship. Strong correspondence may coexist with uncertainty concerning: unobserved conditions, rare events, measurement limitations, model structure, environmental variability, future conditions, human behavior, autonomous behavior, interaction effects, or incomplete Operational Reality knowledge. Correlation Uncertainty Object Material Correlation Uncertainty should be capable of becoming a governed object. Conceptually: Correlation Uncertainty ID ↓ Affected Correlation Relationship ↓ Uncertainty Source ↓ Uncertainty Type ↓ Affected Condition / Scenario ↓ Magnitude / Bound where supportable ↓ Dependencies ↓ Materiality ↓ Reducibility ↓ Downstream Consequence ↓ Uncertainty Status Uncertainty Source SCUM should identify the origin of uncertainty where evidence permits. Potential sources include: incomplete Operational Reality observations, measurement error, sensor limitations, sparse data, uncertain Reality Representation, uncertain assumptions, model simplification, unknown environmental conditions, input variability, scenario incompleteness, stochastic behavior, execution variability, incomplete comparison, uncertain correlation criteria, deviation measurement limitations, alignment effects, or unknown causes. Unknown Source Must Remain Unknown SIMULOS® establishes: Uncertainty must not be assigned a cause merely because governance requires a classification. Where its source cannot be sufficiently established: Uncertainty Source Undetermined is a legitimate governed state. Epistemic Uncertainty Epistemic Uncertainty arises from incomplete knowledge. Examples include: insufficient observations, incomplete model knowledge, uncertain parameter values, poorly understood interactions, limited environmental knowledge, and incomplete causal understanding. Epistemic uncertainty may potentially be reduced through additional: evidence, measurement, modeling, experimentation, or observation. Aleatory Uncertainty Aleatory Uncertainty arises from inherent variability or stochastic behavior in the represented reality. It may not be eliminable simply by obtaining more information. SCUM distinguishes: uncertainty caused by what we do not know from: uncertainty caused by reality itself being variable. Unknown Uncertainty Some uncertainty cannot yet be meaningfully classified as epistemic or aleatory. SCUM preserves: Unknown / Unclassified Correlation Uncertainty rather than forcing artificial certainty about the nature of uncertainty itself. Reality-Reference Uncertainty Operational Reality is not always perfectly observable. Reality observations may themselves contain: measurement uncertainty, sampling limitations, missing states, incomplete telemetry, human reporting error, sensor limitations, temporal gaps, or inaccessible conditions. Therefore: Reality Observation ≠ Perfect Reality Knowledge. Simulation Uncertainty and Reality Uncertainty Must Remain Distinguishable A simulation-reality difference may arise from: Simulation Uncertainty Reality Observation Uncertainty or: Both. SCUM should preserve this distinction where possible. Comparison Uncertainty Even where both simulation and reality observations are individually strong, uncertainty may exist in whether they are sufficiently comparable. Possible causes include: different environmental conditions, different timing, different configurations, different measurement resolution, different object states, or incomplete contextual equivalence. Criteria Uncertainty Correlation Criteria may themselves contain uncertainty. For example, an organization may not know whether: ±2% or: ±5% represents a materially sufficient correspondence boundary for a particular operational purpose. SCUM preserves uncertainty in the criterion rather than hiding it inside the correlation result. Deviation Uncertainty An observed deviation may have uncertainty around: magnitude, direction, frequency, localization, cause, propagation, or materiality. Therefore: Deviation Record and: Deviation Uncertainty should remain distinguishable. Alignment Uncertainty A Reality Alignment action may improve observed correlation while creating uncertainty about: generalization, unobserved scenarios, model interactions, new parameter regions, or unintended downstream effects. Alignment therefore does not automatically reduce total uncertainty. Residual Correlation Uncertainty After comparison, deviation assessment, and alignment, uncertainty may remain. This becomes: Residual Correlation Uncertainty. Residual uncertainty should be explicitly preserved rather than implicitly converted into confidence. Uncertainty Magnitude Where evidence permits, uncertainty may be expressed quantitatively through: confidence intervals, probability distributions, error ranges, tolerance intervals, sensitivity ranges, variance, credible intervals, or other appropriate methods. Where numerical quantification is not supportable, structured qualitative classification may be used. No False Precision Principle SIMULOS® establishes: Correlation uncertainty must not be expressed more precisely than the available evidence permits. A numerical percentage can create misleading authority where the underlying evidence cannot support that precision. Qualitative Uncertainty Classification Where quantitative measurement is inappropriate, implementation may use classifications such as: Low Moderate High Critical or: Undetermined. These classifications must remain bounded to the applicable correlation context. Uncertainty Bounds Where possible, SCUM should establish the range within which the correlation relationship is reasonably supported. For example: Strong Correlation — Nominal Conditions Moderate Uncertainty — High Temperature High Uncertainty — Extreme Combined Conditions Unknown — Unobserved Failure Configuration This is more informative than a single global confidence score. Condition-Specific Uncertainty Correlation uncertainty may vary significantly across conditions. Therefore: Correlation Confidence is a surface, not necessarily a single number. A simulation may be highly correlated with reality in one operational region and poorly understood in another. Scenario-Specific Uncertainty Each materially relevant scenario may possess a different uncertainty profile. This is particularly important for: edge cases, stress conditions, rare events, novel environments, and combinations never directly observed in Operational Reality. Temporal Uncertainty A simulation may correspond well with current reality while uncertainty increases over time because: the environment changes, system behavior evolves, components degrade, software changes, populations change, or Operational Reality drifts. SCUM therefore allows correlation uncertainty to be time-dependent. Spatial Uncertainty Correlation may be strong in observed geographic or physical regions while remaining uncertain elsewhere. This matters for: autonomous vehicles, robotics, climate simulation, aerospace, infrastructure, and geographically distributed systems. Behavioral Uncertainty Behavioral uncertainty concerns uncertainty about whether simulated actors or systems behave sufficiently like their real counterparts. This can be particularly material for: humans, AI agents, autonomous systems, multi-agent systems, adaptive systems, and adversarial environments. Interaction Uncertainty Even where individual components are well represented, their interactions may remain uncertain. SCUM therefore governs uncertainty arising from: component × component human × system agent × agent system × environment and other interaction relationships. Uncertainty Dependency Uncertainties may depend upon one another. For example: Environmental Uncertainty ↓ Sensor Uncertainty ↓ Perception Uncertainty ↓ Behavioral Uncertainty ↓ Trajectory Correlation Uncertainty SCUM should preserve material dependencies where identifiable. Uncertainty Interaction Multiple individually modest uncertainties may interact to produce a materially larger uncertainty. For example: Sensor Noise Weather Variability Timing Uncertainty may create: High Autonomous Behavior Correlation Uncertainty. Uncertainty Propagation Correlation uncertainty may propagate downstream through the simulation lifecycle and into later governance architectures. Conceptually: Correlation Uncertainty ↓ Simulation Output Interpretation ↓ Validation Evidence ↓ Validation Determination ↓ Operational Reliance SCUM therefore requires material uncertainty to remain transferable rather than disappearing at the SIMULOS® boundary. No Uncertainty Laundering Principle SIMULOS® establishes: Uncertainty identified within Simulation-to-Reality Correlation must not disappear merely because the simulation output enters another governance process. If VALIDOS® uses the simulation as validation evidence, the relevant uncertainty must travel with it. Uncertainty Accumulation Where multiple uncertain relationships contribute to one correlation conclusion, SCUM should determine whether uncertainty accumulates materially. A simulation should not claim high overall certainty merely because each individual uncertainty appears small when assessed separately. Uncertainty Reduction Where uncertainty is reducible, SCUM may identify actions such as: additional Operational Reality observations, additional measurements, broader scenario execution, targeted experiments, higher-fidelity representation, model refinement, parameter reassessment, additional comparison, or repeated execution. Reducible vs Irreducible Uncertainty SCUM distinguishes: Reducible Uncertainty from: Currently Irreducible Uncertainty. This matters because governance responses differ. Reducible uncertainty may create an evidence or simulation improvement requirement. Irreducible uncertainty may instead require: bounded interpretation, explicit conditions, or restricted reliance. Uncertainty Reduction Has a Cost Reducing uncertainty may require: computation, testing, physical experiments, additional missions, new sensors, more data, time, or operational exposure. SIMULOS® does not require uncertainty to be reduced indefinitely. The appropriate reduction depth depends upon the simulation purpose and downstream consequence. Material Uncertainty Uncertainty becomes material when it can materially affect: interpretation, correlation classification, simulation output meaning, validation, safety assessment, operational decision-making, autonomous-system behavior, mission planning, or reliance. Uncertainty Threshold Where appropriate, implementations may establish thresholds beyond which: additional evidence, additional simulation, alignment, validation restriction, or: reliance limitation is required. SIMULOS® does not prescribe one universal uncertainty threshold. Correlation Confidence An implementation may derive a bounded Correlation Confidence representation from the governed uncertainty basis. However: Correlation Confidence must never conceal the conditions, scope, or unresolved uncertainty upon which it depends. Correlation Confidence ≠ Probability of Reality A confidence representation must not imply that the simulation itself has become reality or that all future real-world behavior has been probabilistically captured. Correlation Uncertainty Status Possible implementation states may include: Sufficiently Bounded Conditionally Bounded Material Uncertainty Present High Uncertainty Critical Uncertainty or: Uncertainty Undetermined. Correlation Uncertainty Record A governed record may include: Correlation Uncertainty ID Simulation Object / Version Reality Reference Comparison Basis Affected Scenario / Condition Uncertainty Source Uncertainty Type Magnitude / Range Dependencies Propagation Path Materiality Reducibility Reduction Requirement Residual Uncertainty Downstream Limitation Status Evidence Basis Timestamp / Version Context Uncertainty Across Versions SCUM should support comparison of uncertainty across simulation versions. For example: Simulation v1 → High uncertainty in thermal extremes Simulation v2 → Moderate uncertainty Simulation v3 → Low uncertainty within tested range / Unknown beyond tested range This creates a more meaningful improvement record than simply declaring newer versions “more accurate.” Uncertainty Trend Repeated simulation-reality correlation may reveal: Decreasing Uncertainty Stable Uncertainty Increasing Uncertainty Migrating Uncertainty or: Newly Emergent Uncertainty. These trends may indicate where simulation governance should re-enter upstream spaces. Correlation Coverage and Uncertainty High correlation inside a narrow observed region does not establish low uncertainty outside that region. Therefore: Observed Correlation Coverage must remain distinguishable from Unobserved Correlation Uncertainty. Unknown Regions Where no sufficient Operational Reality basis exists, SCUM should permit explicit classification such as: Correlation Unknown — Insufficient Reality Observation. This is especially important where simulation exists precisely because direct real-world testing is difficult or impossible. Novel Conditions A simulation may be used to explore conditions that have never occurred or cannot safely be reproduced. SCUM does not prohibit this. Instead, it requires the distinction between: Empirically Correlated Region and: Simulation-Only / Uncorrelated Region. Extrapolation Uncertainty Where simulation extends beyond observed reality, SCUM should identify: Extrapolation Uncertainty. The farther the simulation moves beyond the governed correlation basis, the more carefully its correspondence claims should be bounded. No Correlation Transfer by Similarity SIMULOS® establishes: Correlation established for one condition, environment, configuration, or system version must not automatically transfer to another merely because the two appear similar. Transfer requires a governed basis. Cross-Version Reality Correlation A new system or simulation version may inherit some correlation evidence from a previous version only where the relevant relationship remains materially comparable. Otherwise new correlation assessment is required. Correlation Uncertainty and Decision Consequence The same uncertainty level may be acceptable for: early design exploration but unacceptable for: safety-critical deployment authorization. SCUM therefore preserves downstream consequence context without itself making the final reliance decision. Uncertainty Communication Material uncertainty should be communicated in a form usable by: engineers, decision-makers, validators, auditors, regulators, autonomous systems, and downstream AI systems. The communication should preserve both: what is known and: what remains uncertain. Machine-Readable Uncertainty For AI-readable implementations, uncertainty should be capable of being represented structurally. Conceptually: Correlation Scope Correlation Status Uncertainty Type Uncertainty Bound Applicable Conditions Excluded Conditions Known Deviations Unknown Regions Downstream Restrictions This allows downstream systems to consume uncertainty rather than merely consuming a correlation score. Relationship to SRCM SRCM determines whether simulation and reality observations are sufficiently comparable. SCUM preserves uncertainty remaining in that comparison basis. Relationship to SCCM SCCM establishes the criteria for judging correspondence. SCUM governs uncertainty affecting the interpretation and application of those criteria. Relationship to SDMM SDMM governs observed Simulation-Reality Deviations. SCUM governs uncertainty concerning those deviations and the broader correlation relationship. Therefore: Deviation ≠ Uncertainty. A deviation is an observed difference. Uncertainty concerns how confidently that difference and the resulting correlation relationship are understood. Relationship to SRAM SRAM governs Reality Alignment. SCUM determines what uncertainty remains before, during, and after alignment. Therefore: Alignment may reduce deviation without eliminating uncertainty. Relationship to ORA™ ORA™ governs Operational Reality. SCUM does not assign certainty to Operational Reality itself. It governs how uncertainty in the available reality basis affects the simulation-to-reality relationship. Relationship to VALIDOS® VALIDOS® may use simulation and Simulation-to-Reality Correlation as part of a Validation Evidence basis. SCUM ensures that material correlation uncertainty remains attached to that evidence. Therefore: VALIDOS® must not receive simulation correlation as stronger evidence than SIMULOS® has actually established. Relationship to INTEGROS® INTEGROS® may govern integrity properties of: observations, measurements, datasets, records, and uncertainty artifacts. SCUM governs the simulation-specific uncertainty relationship. Relationship to SOGS SOGS governs what simulation outputs are and what may legitimately be inferred from them. SCUM provides a correlation-uncertainty basis that may materially constrain those inferences where outputs are interpreted as representations of reality. Relationship to Operational Reliance SCUM does not itself authorize operational reliance. It provides the uncertainty basis required by downstream governance to determine whether reliance is legitimate. Therefore: Correlation Uncertainty → Reliance Input not: Correlation Uncertainty → Reliance Authorization. Autonomous Systems Application An autonomous system may show excellent simulation-reality correlation across millions of nominal simulation events. However, limited real-world observations may exist for: rare pedestrian behavior, unusual weather combinations, degraded sensors, adversarial interactions, infrastructure failures, multi-agent conflicts, or emergency recovery. SCUM prevents nominal correlation from being generalized automatically into low uncertainty across the entire autonomous operating domain. A machine-readable Correlation Uncertainty Map can identify where the system's simulation evidence is strong and where real-world correspondence remains uncertain. Space and Mission Simulation Application Space agencies frequently rely on simulation precisely where direct reality evidence is sparse. A spacecraft or planetary-landing simulation may possess strong correlation evidence for: subsystem tests, terrestrial hardware testing, known orbital conditions, previous mission telemetry, and observed environmental parameters. But uncertainty may remain high for: never-observed surface interactions, extreme radiation combinations, long-duration degradation, unknown atmospheric behavior, rare subsystem combinations, autonomous recovery, or first-of-kind mission conditions. SCUM allows those regions to remain explicitly: Simulation-Supported but Reality-Correlation Uncertain rather than silently inheriting the confidence of well-tested regions. This can reveal exactly where additional testing, observation, instrumentation, scenario coverage, or conservative mission constraints provide the greatest value. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Establish the Correlation Basis Identify the simulation, Operational Reality reference, comparison basis, criteria, deviations, and alignment state. 2. Identify Material Uncertainty Determine where the correlation relationship remains uncertain. 3. Identify the Uncertainty Source Attribute uncertainty where evidence permits. Otherwise record: Source Undetermined. 4. Classify the Uncertainty Determine whether uncertainty is: epistemic, aleatory, mixed, or unknown. 5. Localize the Uncertainty Identify the affected: condition, scenario, component, environment, behavior, interaction, time, or output. 6. Bound or Quantify Where Supportable Use numerical or qualitative bounds appropriate to the evidence. 7. Map Dependencies and Interaction Determine whether uncertainties depend upon or amplify one another. 8. Assess Propagation Identify where uncertainty can affect downstream interpretation or governance. 9. Determine Materiality Assess whether the uncertainty materially affects the intended simulation purpose or downstream use. 10. Determine Reducibility Identify whether additional evidence or simulation activity can materially reduce the uncertainty. 11. Preserve Residual Uncertainty Record what remains unresolved after available reduction or alignment actions. 12. Establish Correlation Uncertainty Status Assign a bounded status appropriate to the applicable correlation scope. 13. Transfer Material Uncertainty Downstream Ensure that simulation outputs, validation processes, audits, or reliance decisions receive the relevant uncertainty information. 14. Preserve Traceability Maintain the relationship: Reality Basis → Comparison → Criteria → Deviation → Alignment → Uncertainty → Downstream Use. Governance Outputs SCUM may produce: Correlation Uncertainty ID, Correlation Uncertainty Record, Uncertainty Source Record, Uncertainty Classification, Epistemic Uncertainty Record, Aleatory Uncertainty Record, Unknown Uncertainty Record, Reality-Reference Uncertainty Record, Comparison Uncertainty Record, Criteria Uncertainty Record, Deviation Uncertainty Record, Alignment Uncertainty Record, Residual Correlation Uncertainty Record, Quantitative Uncertainty Bound, Qualitative Uncertainty Classification, Condition-Specific Uncertainty Map, Scenario-Specific Uncertainty Map, Temporal Uncertainty Record, Spatial Uncertainty Record, Behavioral Uncertainty Record, Interaction Uncertainty Record, Uncertainty Dependency Map, Uncertainty Propagation Map, Uncertainty Accumulation Assessment, Uncertainty Reduction Requirement, Reducibility Assessment, Extrapolation Uncertainty Record, Unknown Correlation Region Record, Correlation Uncertainty Status, Correlation Confidence Record, Downstream Uncertainty Transfer Record, and Governed Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Uncertainty Basis. Use Case 1 — Autonomous Driving Beyond Tested Conditions An autonomous driving simulation demonstrates strong correlation with Operational Reality across extensive urban driving tests. However, only limited real-world evidence exists for: heavy snow + partially blocked sensors + unusual pedestrian movement + low visibility. SCUM prevents the strong nominal correlation from automatically extending into this region. The system records: Nominal Urban Conditions → Correlation Uncertainty Low Heavy Snow → Correlation Uncertainty Moderate Heavy Snow + Sensor Degradation + Rare Pedestrian Interaction → Correlation Uncertainty High This uncertainty can then travel with the simulation evidence into validation and operational decision-making. Use Case 2 — First-of-Kind Space Mission A space agency uses simulation to assess an autonomous landing sequence for a destination where direct Operational Reality observations are necessarily limited. The simulation correlates strongly with: terrestrial hardware testing, propulsion tests, sensor testing, and comparable prior mission data. However, the exact combination of: surface properties + environmental conditions + autonomous response + landing dynamics has never been directly observed. SCUM prevents correlation from known regions from being silently transferred into the unknown mission region. The resulting correlation basis may state: Subsystem Correlation — Strong Known Environmental Range — Sufficiently Bounded Exact Landing Environment — Material Epistemic Uncertainty Combined First-of-Kind Landing Interaction — Correlation Unknown / Simulation-Supported This gives engineers and decision-makers a governed map of where additional evidence can reduce uncertainty and where uncertainty must instead remain an explicit mission constraint. Architectural Position SCUM is the fifth and final module of the Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Standard (SRCS). The complete SRCS progression is: SRCM — Simulation-Reality Comparison ↓ SCCM — Simulation Correlation Criteria ↓ SDMM — Simulation-Reality Deviation ↓ SRAM — Reality Alignment ↓ SCUM — Correlation Uncertainty Together, these five modules answer: What can be compared? ↓ According to what criteria? ↓ Where does simulation differ from reality? ↓ What should be aligned? ↓ How certain are we about the resulting relationship? This closes the governed Simulation-to-Reality Correlation space without converting correlation into validation or simulation into reality. Foundational Principle Simulation similarity is not reality equivalence, and correlation confidence must never exceed the reality evidence, comparison basis, observed conditions, and unresolved uncertainty that actually support it. Canonical Closing Statement Correlation Uncertainty Module (SCUM) completes the Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Standard by governing what remains uncertain after simulation and Operational Reality have been compared, deviations identified, and justified alignment performed. By distinguishing simulation uncertainty from reality-reference uncertainty, epistemic uncertainty from aleatory variability, observed correlation from unobserved regions, deviation from uncertainty, alignment from certainty, and empirical correspondence from extrapolation, SCUM prevents strong correlation in known conditions from becoming an unsupported claim about reality as a whole. Through uncertainty identification, classification, bounding, dependency mapping, propagation, reduction, residual-uncertainty preservation, machine-readable disclosure, and downstream transfer, SCUM ensures that every Simulation-to-Reality Correlation remains only as certain, broad, and operationally meaningful as the evidence actually permits.

title: OOF™ Scenario Variation Module (SCVM)
text: OOF™ Scenario Variation Module (SCVM) Scenario Variation Module (SCVM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Simulation Scenario Standard (SSS) Operational Layer: Simulation Scenario Governance Layer Category: AI & Simulation Subcategory: Simulation Governance Type: Parent Standard Module Governed Space: Simulation Scenario Variation Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 18 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Governed Space Simulation Scenario Variation Canonical Definition Scenario Variation Module (SCVM) defines the governance framework for deliberately varying materially relevant conditions within and across identified Simulation Scenarios so that simulation behavior can be examined beyond a single nominal, expected, convenient, or fixed configuration. SCVM governs how variation dimensions, ranges, levels, combinations, dependencies, sequences, distributions, and controlled differences are established, bounded, documented, executed as scenario configurations, and preserved for comparison. Its purpose is to ensure that a Simulation Scenario is not treated as one static point where the governed simulation inquiry requires examination across a materially relevant range of possible conditions. Operational Role SCVM serves as the second internal governance space of the Simulation Scenario Standard (SSS). The preceding module: SCIM — Scenario Identification Module establishes: Which materially relevant conditions should become identifiable Simulation Scenarios? SCVM asks: Across which materially relevant variations of those scenarios must the simulation operate to understand how changing conditions affect behavior and outcomes? The progression is: Governed Scenario Register ↓ Variation Requirement Identification ↓ Variation Dimension ↓ Variation Range ↓ Variation Level / Distribution ↓ Controlled Scenario Variation ↓ Multi-Dimensional Variation ↓ Variation Dependency & Interaction ↓ Variation Configuration Set ↓ Edge-Case Governance SCVM therefore converts identified scenarios into a structured variation space.
