Module Function SDRM exists to prevent: available data being assumed representative by default, large datasets being confused with representative datasets, one population being silently generalized to another, normal-operation data being generalized to failure conditions, one geographic environment being generalized globally, one system version being treated as representative of materially different versions, averages concealing relevant distributions, majority populations hiding minority or rare cases, proxy data being treated as direct representation, historical operating conditions being generalized to structurally different environments, missing representation being interpreted as absence of the represented phenomenon, and simulation outputs appearing broadly applicable when the input basis supports only a narrower context. Representativeness Simulation Data Representativeness is the degree to which an identified Simulation Input or Input Set sufficiently reflects the materially relevant characteristics of the reality segment it is intended to represent within a defined simulation. Representativeness is not an intrinsic universal property of data. It is relational. Conceptually: Data + Representation Target + Simulation Context → Representativeness Assessment Representation Target A Representation Target defines what the input is expected to represent. The target may be: population, environment, geographic region, operating state, system configuration, behavior, physical condition, temporal condition, distribution, event class, failure state, or another materially relevant reality segment. Without a defined Representation Target, the statement: “The data is representative.” is incomplete. Representativeness Is Purpose-Relative SIMULOS® establishes: No dataset is representative in the abstract; it is representative only relative to a defined simulation inquiry and representation target. The same dataset may therefore be: Representative for one simulation, and: Non-Representative for another. Representativeness ≠ Accuracy Data may be highly accurate and still be unrepresentative. For example: a perfectly measured dataset from dry-road driving may accurately describe dry-road conditions while being unsuitable as the sole representative basis for snow-road simulation. Therefore: Accuracy asks whether the recorded information is correct. Representativeness asks whether the information sufficiently reflects what the simulation needs to represent. Representativeness ≠ Volume A billion observations from one narrow operating condition may provide less representative coverage than a much smaller dataset covering materially different relevant conditions. SIMULOS® establishes: Data volume cannot compensate for missing representation of materially relevant reality. Population Representativeness Where a simulation represents a population, SDRM determines whether materially relevant population characteristics are sufficiently represented. Population may include: humans, vehicles, machines, organizations, infrastructure assets, biological entities, software systems, autonomous agents, devices, or other classes of objects. Relevant dimensions may include: subgroup, capability, age, configuration, size, performance class, technical generation, behavioral profile, or another simulation-relevant distinction. Subgroup Representation A population-level dataset may conceal weak coverage of materially relevant subgroups. SDRM therefore asks: Which subgroups materially affect simulation behavior, and are they sufficiently represented? Overall population coverage does not automatically establish subgroup coverage. Environmental Representativeness Environmental data should represent the environments within which simulated behavior is expected to be examined. Relevant environmental dimensions may include: weather, terrain, temperature, lighting, infrastructure, electromagnetic conditions, network conditions, traffic density, physical obstacles, or other environmental factors. Geographic Representativeness Data obtained in one geographic region may not sufficiently represent another where material differences exist. Possible differences include: infrastructure, climate, terrain, regulation, traffic behavior, architecture, population characteristics, or environmental conditions. Geographic transfer should therefore remain explicit where material. Operational-State Representativeness Data from one operational state should not automatically represent another. Relevant states may include: Normal Degraded Failure Emergency Recovery Maintenance Startup Shutdown or another defined operating state. A simulation intended to explore failures may require data that represents more than normal operation. System-Version Representativeness Simulation data may originate from a different version or configuration of the represented system. SDRM asks whether differences between: Data-Origin System and: Simulation-Represented System are material to simulation behavior. Behavioral Representativeness Where behavior affects simulation outcomes, input data should sufficiently represent materially relevant behavioral variation. This may include: human behavior, autonomous behavior, organizational behavior, market behavior, system response, interaction behavior, or adversarial behavior. Distributional Representativeness Representativeness includes more than averages. Relevant characteristics may include: mean, variance, distribution shape, tails, correlations, clusters, multimodality, extremes, and conditional distributions. Average ≠ Representative Distribution SIMULOS® establishes: A representative average does not establish a representative distribution. Two populations may have the same average while producing materially different simulation behavior. Range Representativeness The observed range of an input should be compared with the range relevant to the simulation. For example: Training / observed temperature range: 0°C–30°C Simulation scope: −30°C–50°C The input basis does not fully represent the simulation range. Variation Representativeness Simulation behavior may depend upon variation rather than absolute values alone. SDRM therefore evaluates whether material variation patterns are sufficiently represented. This may include: rapid changes, cyclic changes, random variation, seasonal variation, load variation, behavioral variation, or environmental variation. Rare-Condition Representation Rare events may have low frequency but high simulation importance. Examples include: catastrophic failures, extreme weather, unusual human behavior, collision conditions, cascading infrastructure failures, unusual system interactions, or low-frequency safety events. SIMULOS® establishes: Low frequency does not imply low representational importance. Consequence-Weighted Representativeness The required representation of a condition may increase where failure to represent it could materially affect a high-consequence simulation conclusion. This does not mean every rare condition must always be included. It means representativeness decisions should reflect the purpose and consequence of the simulation. Boundary-Condition Representativeness Simulation behavior may change near operational boundaries. Data concentrated in the center of an operating range may therefore fail to represent behavior near: maximum load, minimum load, speed limits, thermal limits, stability limits, communication limits, control limits, or other material boundaries. Representation Coverage Representation Coverage describes how much of the materially relevant Representation Target is sufficiently represented by the available input basis. Coverage may be assessed across multiple dimensions rather than reduced to one percentage. Multidimensional Representativeness A dataset may be representative along one dimension and weak along another. For example: Population Coverage — Strong Geographic Coverage — Strong Failure-State Coverage — Weak Extreme-Weather Coverage — Missing SDRM preserves these distinctions. No Single-Score Requirement SDRM does not require representativeness to be compressed into one numerical score. A single score may hide material gaps. Representativeness may instead be represented through: dimensional assessments, coverage maps, statuses, conditions, restrictions, and gap records. Representation Gap A Simulation Data Representativeness Gap exists where available information does not sufficiently represent a materially relevant part of the Representation Target. Examples include: missing population, missing environment, missing state, missing behavior, missing distribution tail, missing failure condition, missing configuration, or insufficient range. Representation Gap Classification A gap may be classified as: Non-Material The gap is not expected to materially affect the defined simulation inquiry. Material but Bounded The gap matters but its effect can be sufficiently restricted or isolated. Conditional Simulation use remains possible only under explicit conditions. Material and Unresolved The gap materially weakens the simulation basis and has not been sufficiently addressed. Representativeness Undetermined Available information is insufficient to determine materiality or coverage. Underrepresentation Underrepresentation occurs where a relevant condition exists in the target reality but appears insufficiently in the simulation input basis. Underrepresentation can produce artificially weak exposure to that condition. Overrepresentation Overrepresentation occurs where a condition appears disproportionately in the input basis relative to the Representation Target. This may distort simulation behavior if the simulation interprets the data as naturally distributed. Representation Imbalance A dataset may contain all required classes while still representing them in proportions inconsistent with the intended simulation context. SDRM therefore distinguishes: Presence from: Representative Proportion. Intentional Oversampling Overrepresentation is not always a defect. Rare or high-consequence conditions may intentionally be oversampled for testing. Where intentional, the difference between: Natural Representation and: Test Amplification should remain explicit. Proxy Representation A Proxy Input represents a target indirectly because direct data is unavailable or impractical. For example: data from one machine type may be used as a proxy for another similar machine. Proxy use may be legitimate. SDRM requires the representational relationship to remain explicit. Proxy ≠ Target SIMULOS® establishes: Similarity between a proxy and a target does not establish representational equivalence. Material differences must remain visible. Cross-Context Transfer Data may be transferred from one context to another. Conceptually: Source Context → Transfer Basis → Target Simulation Context SDRM governs whether the transfer preserves sufficient representativeness. Cross-Context Representativeness Conditions Transfer may depend upon similarities in: population, environment, system configuration, behavior, operating range, physical properties, or causal structure. Where differences matter, restrictions should follow the transferred data. Synthetic Representation Synthetic data may intentionally fill representativeness gaps. For example: real-world datasets may contain too few critical failure events. Synthetic data may increase coverage. SDRM asks: Does the synthetic information sufficiently represent the intended condition? Its synthetic origin remains governed under SIIM. Synthetic Coverage ≠ Real-World Frequency Synthetic datasets may deliberately alter frequencies. Therefore: Synthetic Scenario Coverage should not automatically be interpreted as: Observed Real-World Distribution. Representativeness and Simulation Assumptions Simulation Assumptions may influence representativeness requirements. For example: if the simulation assumes operation only within a narrow environmental range, data outside that range may not be required. If the scope expands, the representativeness requirement may change. Representativeness and Reality Representation RRS — Reality Representation Standard determines which aspects of reality the simulation must represent. SDRM determines whether the input basis sufficiently represents those selected aspects. The relationship is: Selected Reality → Representation Requirement → Input Representation Target → Representativeness Assessment Representativeness and Scenario Design SDRM does not determine which scenarios must be executed. However, representativeness gaps may become important inputs to SSS — Simulation Scenario Standard. For example: a weakly represented rare failure may justify deliberate scenario coverage. Representativeness Materiality Not every representational difference matters. Materiality depends upon whether the difference could reasonably affect: simulation behavior, simulation outputs, scenario conclusions, downstream validation, or operational reliance. Materiality Assessment A representativeness gap should be evaluated relative to: Simulation Object Simulation Purpose Simulation Scope Reality Representation Simulation Assumptions Model & Environment and where relevant: intended downstream reliance. Representativeness Restriction An input may remain usable despite limited representativeness if its use is explicitly restricted. For example: Representative only for dry-road daytime operation. The restriction should propagate to downstream simulation interpretation. Representativeness Condition A Simulation Input may receive a condition such as: Suitable only when ambient temperature remains between 0°C and 30°C. Conditional representativeness should not become unconditional merely because simulation execution succeeds. Representativeness Status A material Simulation Input or Input Set may receive a status such as: Representative Conditionally Representative Partially Representative Non-Representative or: Representativeness Undetermined The status is always relative to a defined Representation Target and simulation context. No Universal Representative Status SIMULOS® establishes: Representative for one simulation does not mean representative for all simulations. Representativeness status must therefore remain context-bound. Input-Level vs Input-Set Representativeness Individual inputs may be representative while the complete Input Set is not. Conversely, several individually incomplete datasets may together provide sufficient representation. SDRM therefore supports assessment at: Individual Input Level and: Simulation Input Set Level. Complementary Representation Multiple datasets may complement one another. For example: Dataset A — Normal Operation Dataset B — Failure Operation Dataset C — Extreme Weather may collectively provide stronger representation than any dataset alone. Representativeness Conflict Different datasets may imply materially different representations of the same target. For example: Dataset A: failure frequency 0.1% Dataset B: failure frequency 2.5% The conflict should remain visible rather than being silently averaged away. Representation Basis A Simulation Representation Basis records why an input or Input Set is considered sufficiently representative for a defined simulation context. It may reference: target definition, coverage, gaps, materiality, restrictions, conditions, proxies, synthetic supplementation, and unresolved uncertainty. Representativeness Traceability SDRM establishes: Simulation Input ↓ Representation Target ↓ Relevant Representation Dimensions ↓ Coverage ↓ Gap ↓ Materiality ↓ Representativeness Status ↓ Conditions / Restrictions ↓ Simulation Use This enables downstream users to determine what the data actually supports. Representativeness Change Representativeness may change even when the dataset itself does not. For example: the Simulation Scope may expand. A new environment may be introduced. A new population may be added. The represented system may change configuration. The same data may therefore become less representative because the target changed. Representativeness Reassessment Trigger Reassessment may be required when there is material change in: Simulation Object, Purpose, Scope, Reality Representation, Assumptions, Model, Environment, target population, operational conditions, system configuration, or available input basis. No Representativeness Inheritance Principle SIMULOS® establishes: Representativeness must not be inherited automatically from a previous simulation when the Representation Target or simulation context has materially changed. No Availability-to-Representativeness Principle Available data is not representative data by default. No Size-to-Representativeness Principle More data does not resolve a missing reality dimension if the additional data comes from the same unrepresentative condition. No Majority-to-Whole Principle Strong representation of the majority does not establish representation of every materially relevant subgroup or condition. No Normal-to-Extreme Principle Data representative of normal operation does not automatically represent degraded, failure, emergency, boundary, or extreme conditions. No Proxy Equivalence Principle Proxy data must not silently acquire the identity or representativeness status of the target it approximates. No Successful-Execution Principle A simulation running successfully with an input does not establish that the input was representative of the reality being simulated. Representativeness Limitation Propagation Material representativeness limitations should propagate downstream. Conceptually: Representativeness Gap → Scenario / Execution Limitation → Output Interpretation Limitation → Downstream Reliance Limitation The relevant downstream Parent Standards govern those later stages. SDRM ensures the original limitation remains visible. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Identify the Representation Target Define what each material Simulation Input or Input Set is expected to represent. 2. Identify Material Representation Dimensions Determine which dimensions matter, such as: population, environment, geography, operating state, behavior, configuration, distribution, range, variation, or rare conditions. 3. Assess Representation Coverage Determine which materially relevant portions of the target are sufficiently represented. 4. Identify Representation Gaps Record missing, weak, imbalanced, proxy-based, or uncertain representation. 5. Assess Gap Materiality Determine whether each gap could materially affect the defined simulation inquiry. 6. Assess Distribution and Range Determine whether averages, ranges, tails, variation, and dependencies are sufficiently represented where material. 7. Assess Rare and Boundary Conditions Determine whether low-frequency or boundary conditions require representation because of their simulation relevance or consequence. 8. Govern Proxy and Cross-Context Use Document the basis and limitations where information is transferred from another population, environment, configuration, or context. 9. Assess Synthetic Supplementation Where synthetic information fills representation gaps, preserve its role and the limits of what it represents. 10. Establish Conditions and Restrictions Bound simulation use where representativeness is incomplete but sufficiently manageable. 11. Assign Representativeness Status Determine whether the input basis is: Representative, Conditionally Representative, Partially Representative, Non-Representative, or Representativeness Undetermined. 12. Preserve Representativeness Traceability Maintain the relationship between target, coverage, gaps, materiality, status, restrictions, and simulation use. Governance Outputs SDRM may produce: Representation Target Record, Representation Dimension Map, Population Representativeness Assessment, Subgroup Representation Record, Environmental Representativeness Assessment, Geographic Representativeness Assessment, Operational-State Representativeness Assessment, System-Version Representativeness Assessment, Behavioral Representativeness Assessment, Distributional Representativeness Assessment, Range Representativeness Record, Variation Representativeness Record, Rare-Condition Representation Record, Boundary-Condition Representation Record, Representation Coverage Map, Representation Imbalance Record, Underrepresentation Record, Overrepresentation Record, Representation Gap Record, Representation Gap Materiality Assessment, Proxy Representation Record, Cross-Context Transfer Record, Synthetic Representation Record, Complementary Representation Record, Representativeness Conflict Record, Representativeness Condition Record, Representativeness Restriction Record, Representativeness Status, Simulation Representation Basis, Representativeness Reassessment Trigger, Representativeness Change Record, and Simulation Data Representativeness Traceability Map. Use Case 1 — Autonomous Vehicle Simulation Scenario An autonomous vehicle simulation is intended to assess operation across: daytime and nighttime, dry and wet roads, urban and rural environments, normal traffic, emergency braking, and pedestrian interactions. The available driving dataset contains millions of kilometers of data. However, almost all observations come from: daytime + dry roads + urban operation. Application SDRM does not treat dataset size as proof of representativeness. It identifies material gaps in: nighttime conditions, wet-road behavior, rural environments, emergency braking, and uncommon pedestrian interactions. Result The dataset receives: Partially Representative status for the declared simulation scope. Its use may remain legitimate for defined urban dry-road scenarios while additional real or synthetic information is required for broader scenario coverage. Use Case 2 — Spacecraft Landing Simulation Scenario A spacecraft landing simulation relies upon atmospheric and terrain information derived primarily from previously observed regions. The planned landing zone contains terrain and atmospheric conditions that are only partially represented by those observations. Application SDRM establishes: Observed Region ≠ Landing Target Region and evaluates: terrain coverage, atmospheric ranges, geographic transfer, boundary conditions, and proxy assumptions. Result The available input basis may be classified: Conditionally Representative with explicit limitations requiring additional synthetic or model-derived coverage for materially underrepresented landing conditions. Architectural Position Simulation Data Representativeness is the second internal governance space of the Simulation Input & Data Standard (SIDS). The complete SIDS progression is: Simulation Input Identification ↓ Simulation Data Representativeness ↓ Simulation Data Transformation ↓ Simulation Temporal Data ↓ Simulation Input Uncertainty SIIM determines: What information is entering the simulation? SDRM determines: What reality can that information legitimately represent? The next module, SDTM — Simulation Data Transformation Module, governs what happens when that identified and representationally understood information must be transformed before simulation use. Foundational Principle Simulation data becomes representative only relative to a defined representation target, and no simulation may legitimately generalize its input basis beyond the populations, environments, states, behaviors, distributions, conditions, and boundaries that the available information can sufficiently represent. Canonical Closing Statement Simulation Data Representativeness Module establishes the representational governance layer of the Simulation Input & Data Standard by determining whether identified Simulation Inputs and Input Sets sufficiently represent the populations, environments, geographic contexts, operating states, behaviors, configurations, distributions, ranges, variations, rare events, and boundary conditions required by a defined simulation inquiry. Through explicit Representation Targets, multidimensional coverage assessment, gap and materiality analysis, proxy governance, synthetic supplementation, conditional applicability, restrictions, reassessment triggers, and representativeness traceability, SDRM prevents data availability, volume, accuracy, technical compatibility, or successful execution from being mistaken for sufficient representation of the reality a simulation is intended to examine.

title: OOF™ Simulation Data Transformation Module (SDTM)
text: OOF™ Simulation Data Transformation Module (SDTM) Simulation Data Transformation Module (SDTM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Simulation Input & Data Standard (SIDS) Operational Layer: Simulation Input & Data Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Type: Parent Standard Module Governed Space: Simulation Data Transformation Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 18 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Governed Space Simulation Data Transformation Canonical Definition Simulation Data Transformation Module (SDTM) defines the governance framework through which identified Simulation Inputs may be cleaned, filtered, normalized, converted, aggregated, disaggregated, interpolated, extrapolated, encoded, imputed, derived, synthesized, resampled, aligned, or otherwise transformed before or during simulation use while preserving the traceability, meaning, limitations, uncertainty, provenance, and material consequences of those transformations. SDTM establishes the transformation layer of SIDS by governing the transition: Source Information → Transformation → Simulation-Usable Input so that transformed information cannot silently acquire properties, precision, representativeness, certainty, or observational status that the transformation process did not legitimately establish. Operational Role SDTM serves as the third internal governance space of the Simulation Input & Data Standard (SIDS). The preceding modules establish: SIIM — What information is entering the simulation? SDRM — What reality can that information legitimately represent? SDTM asks: What has been done to that information before the simulation consumes it, why was the transformation necessary, and what did the transformation materially change? The governed progression is: Identified Input → Transformation Need → Transformation Method → Transformation Execution → Transformed Input → Transformation Effect Assessment → Transformation Status → Simulation-Usable Input Module Operational Space SDTM governs: transformation identification, transformation purpose, transformation necessity, transformation methods, transformation rules, transformation parameters, data cleaning, filtering, normalization, standardization, unit conversion, format conversion, aggregation, disaggregation, interpolation, extrapolation, resampling, encoding, decoding, feature derivation, imputation, synthetic supplementation, dimensional transformation, temporal alignment transformation, spatial transformation, coordinate transformation, data fusion, data reduction, outlier treatment, missing-value treatment, transformation sequencing, transformation dependencies, transformation reproducibility, transformation reversibility where relevant, information loss, transformation-induced bias, transformation-induced uncertainty, transformation limitations, transformation validation references, transformation versioning, transformation change, transformed-input identity, and transformation traceability. Module Function SDTM exists to prevent: transformed information being treated as raw information, cleaning decisions disappearing from the simulation record, filtering silently removing material observations, normalization changing meaning without disclosure, unit conversion errors, aggregation hiding material variation, interpolation being represented as observation, extrapolation being represented as measured reality, imputed values appearing as recorded values, synthetic supplementation appearing as empirical data, transformations introducing hidden bias, precision being artificially increased, information loss becoming invisible, multiple transformation stages becoming unreconstructable, changed transformation logic being applied under an unchanged identity, and simulation outputs becoming impossible to trace back to the information basis from which they were produced. Simulation Data Transformation A Simulation Data Transformation is any governed operation that materially changes the: representation, structure, scale, format, resolution, composition, value, distribution, temporal organization, spatial organization, completeness, or interpretation of information before or during simulation use. Conceptually: Input A → Transformation T → Input B Input B may remain related to Input A, but it is not necessarily methodologically identical to it. Transformation Need Every material transformation should have an identifiable reason. A Transformation Need may arise because: the simulation requires another unit, sources use incompatible formats, sampling frequencies differ, missing information must be treated, data contains technical noise, model interfaces require normalization, multiple sources must be aligned, resolution must change, derived variables are required, or information must be adapted to the simulation representation. Transformation Purpose The transformation purpose should explain: Why must this information be changed before simulation use? Examples include: Compatibility Alignment Noise Reduction Feature Construction Missing-Value Treatment Resolution Adjustment Unit Harmonization Data Fusion or: Simulation Interface Preparation Transformation Necessity SDTM distinguishes: Necessary Transformation from: Convenience Transformation. A transformation may be technically convenient without being methodologically justified. Where a transformation materially affects simulation behavior, convenience alone should not establish its legitimacy. Transformation Method A Transformation Method defines how the original information is converted into the transformed Simulation Input. It may specify: operation, algorithm, formula, rule, threshold, parameter, model, software process, sequence, or another transformation mechanism. Transformation Rule A transformation should be sufficiently explicit that the relationship between: Input Before Transformation and: Input After Transformation can be understood and, where required, reconstructed. Transformation Parameters Material parameters should remain traceable. For example: a smoothing filter may require: window size, threshold, frequency, kernel, or another parameter. Changing these parameters may materially change the resulting Simulation Input. Data Cleaning Cleaning may include: invalid-record removal, duplicate removal, formatting correction, impossible-value treatment, corrupted-record treatment, or consistency correction. Cleaning should not become an invisible mechanism for removing inconvenient data. Cleaning ≠ Evidence Removal SIMULOS® establishes: Data should not be removed merely because it produces undesirable simulation behavior. Where materially relevant records are excluded, the basis for exclusion should remain identifiable. Filtering Filtering may remove: noise, frequencies, observations, events, values, or records. SDTM requires material filtering logic to remain visible. Filter Effect A filter may improve usability while reducing information. Therefore: Cleaner Data ≠ More Complete Data The effect of filtering should be assessed where material. Normalization Normalization may transform values into a common range or representation. For example: 0–100 → 0–1 The normalized value should remain connected to: original scale, transformation rule, and semantic meaning. Standardization Standardization may express values relative to a distribution. The underlying basis should remain identifiable where the transformed values affect simulation interpretation. Unit Conversion Unit transformations must preserve the relationship: Original Value + Original Unit → Conversion Rule → Converted Value + Target Unit SDTM prevents converted values from becoming detached from their original measurement basis. Format Conversion Data may move between: structured formats, numerical representations, image formats, coordinate systems, encoding systems, categorical structures, or simulation-specific schemas. Technical conversion should preserve materially relevant meaning. Semantic Preservation Principle SIMULOS® establishes: A transformation that preserves technical readability but changes material meaning is not semantically neutral. Aggregation Aggregation combines multiple observations into a reduced representation. Examples include: second → minute individual → group sensor points → regional average Aggregation may simplify simulation input while hiding: variation, extremes, sequences, correlations, or rare events. Aggregation Loss Where aggregation removes materially relevant information, the loss should remain visible. For example: an average temperature may hide short thermal spikes capable of affecting system failure. Disaggregation Disaggregation converts aggregated information into a more granular representation. Where the original information does not contain that granularity, disaggregated values may depend upon assumptions or models. SIMULOS® establishes: Disaggregation must not be represented as direct observation where the additional granularity was inferred. Interpolation Interpolation estimates values between known observations. Conceptually: Observed A → Estimated Intermediate Value → Observed B Interpolated values should remain distinguishable from direct observations where material. Extrapolation Extrapolation estimates information beyond the observed range. Because extrapolation extends beyond available observation, its methodological basis and limitations should remain visible. No Extrapolation-as-Observation Principle A value generated beyond the observed data range does not become observed reality merely because it is numerically precise. Resampling Resampling changes the frequency, density, or structure of observations. Examples include: 100 Hz → 10 Hz or: hourly → minute-level representation Resampling may: remove information, introduce estimated information, alter signal behavior, or change temporal relationships. Encoding Information may be encoded into representations required by simulation systems. For example: Category → Numerical Vector The encoded representation should remain traceable to the original semantic category. Derived Input A Derived Simulation Input is produced from one or more existing inputs. Conceptually: Input A + Input B + Rule → Derived Input C The derivation relationship should remain preserved. Derived ≠ Observed SIMULOS® establishes: A calculated value must not silently acquire the status of a directly observed value. Feature Derivation Simulation models may require derived features. Examples include: velocity from position changes, acceleration from velocity, risk indicator from multiple variables, density from count and area, or another constructed feature. The derivation method should remain traceable where material. Missing-Value Treatment Missing information may be treated through: exclusion, substitution, interpolation, imputation, default value, synthetic replacement, or another governed method. SDTM requires the treatment to remain explicit. Missing ≠ Zero SIMULOS® establishes: Absence of information must not automatically become a zero-valued observation. Imputation Imputation replaces missing information with an estimated value. An imputed value should remain identifiable as: Imputed rather than: Observed or: Measured. Imputation Basis The basis may include: statistical estimate, neighboring observations, historical values, model output, population average, or another method. The selected basis may materially influence simulation behavior. Default Values A simulation may technically require a value where none is available. A default value may be used where methodologically justified. The default should remain identifiable as a default rather than being silently treated as source data. Synthetic Supplementation Synthetic information may be introduced during transformation to supplement missing or weak data. SDTM governs the transformation process that introduces it. SIIM preserves its synthetic identity. SDRM governs what reality it can legitimately represent. Outlier Treatment Outliers may be: retained, excluded, capped, transformed, separately modeled, or investigated. Outlier treatment should depend upon the simulation purpose and data basis. Outlier ≠ Error SIMULOS® establishes: An unusual observation is not automatically an invalid observation. Rare values may represent precisely the conditions a simulation needs to examine. Data Fusion Multiple information sources may be combined into one Simulation Input. Conceptually: Source A + Source B + Fusion Method → Fused Input The fusion process should preserve materially relevant source relationships and transformation logic. Fusion ≠ Independent Confirmation Two sources combined into one input do not necessarily constitute independent evidence. Their dependencies may remain relevant. Spatial Transformation Spatial information may require: coordinate conversion, map projection, spatial aggregation, interpolation, alignment, or resolution change. Material spatial transformation should remain traceable where it can influence simulated relationships. Coordinate Transformation Coordinate-system changes must preserve the applicable reference system and transformation basis. Errors in coordinate conversion can produce apparently valid but physically incorrect simulation inputs. Dimensional Transformation Information may be reduced or expanded across dimensions. For example: 3D Reality → 2D Representation or: Multiple Variables → Composite Index Such transformations may intentionally simplify reality. The simplification should remain connected to the simulation's Reality Representation under RRS. Transformation Sequence Simulation data may undergo multiple transformations. For example: Raw Sensor Data ↓ Cleaning ↓ Filtering ↓ Unit Conversion ↓ Resampling ↓ Normalization ↓ Simulation Input SDTM requires material sequence to remain reconstructable. Transformation Order Matters Transformations may not be commutative. Conceptually: Filter → Aggregate may produce a different result from: Aggregate → Filter Where order materially affects the resulting input, transformation sequence becomes a governed property. Transformation Dependency One transformation may depend upon the output of another. These dependencies should remain visible where they affect reproducibility or interpretation. Transformation Chain A Simulation Transformation Chain records the material progression: Original Input → T1 → Intermediate Input → T2 → Intermediate Input → T3 → Simulation-Usable Input Transformation Identity Each material transformation may receive an identifiable reference. For example: SDT-0042 This allows simulation records to reference the exact transformation logic used. Transformation Version Transformation logic may change. For example: Filter v1 may become: Filter v2 A simulation executed under v1 should remain distinguishable from one executed under v2. No Silent Transformation Update Principle SIMULOS® establishes: Materially changing transformation logic must not silently rewrite the transformation basis of previous simulation executions. Transformation Reproducibility Where required by the simulation purpose, a transformation should be sufficiently documented to allow an authorized independent implementation to reproduce the transformed input from the same original basis. Reproducibility may require: method, parameters, software version, transformation sequence, source input version, and relevant execution conditions. Transformation Reversibility Not every transformation is reversible. For example: aggregation may permanently discard detail. SDTM therefore distinguishes: Reproducibility from: Reversibility. A transformation may be reproducible while information loss makes reversal impossible. Information Loss Transformation may remove information. Loss may be: Intentional Incidental Necessary or: Unrecognized SDTM requires material information loss to remain visible. Transformation Gain Some transformations create additional information representations. For example: interpolation may create additional values. But: More values ≠ More observations. Generated resolution should not be confused with additional empirical evidence. Precision Inflation Transformation may produce numerically precise outputs from imprecise inputs. For example: an estimated value may mathematically produce: 17.384729 This numerical precision does not establish equivalent informational certainty. No Precision Inflation Principle SIMULOS® establishes: Transformation must not create an appearance of certainty or observational precision unsupported by the underlying information basis. Transformation-Induced Bias Transformation logic may systematically alter the information basis. Examples include: selective filtering, biased imputation, asymmetric clipping, population-dependent normalization, or model-based reconstruction. Material transformation-induced bias should be identified and carried forward. Transformation-Induced Uncertainty A transformation may introduce additional uncertainty. For example: interpolation uncertainty, extrapolation uncertainty, imputation uncertainty, fusion uncertainty, conversion uncertainty, or model-derived uncertainty. The subsequent SIUM — Simulation Input Uncertainty Module governs the consolidated input uncertainty. SDTM identifies transformation-induced contributions to that uncertainty. Transformation Effect Assessment After transformation, the resulting input should be assessed for material changes in: meaning, range, distribution, resolution, completeness, representativeness, uncertainty, and simulation influence. Representativeness Reassessment Transformation may change representativeness. For example: aggressive filtering may remove rare conditions that SDRM previously considered represented. Where transformation materially affects representation: SDRM reassessment may be required. Transformation Cannot Launder Weak Input SIMULOS® establishes: Transformation does not automatically cure an unrepresentative, uncertain, ambiguous, or otherwise limited input basis. A weak source input may remain weak after sophisticated processing. Transformation Limitation A Transformation Limitation identifies a material restriction introduced or preserved by transformation. Examples include: lost high-frequency behavior, inferred missing values, reduced spatial resolution, extrapolation beyond observed range, or uncertain source alignment. Transformation Condition A transformed input may be suitable only under explicit conditions. For example: Interpolated values suitable only where gaps do not exceed 5 seconds. The condition should remain attached to downstream simulation use. Transformation Status A material transformation may receive a status such as: Transformation Accepted Conditionally Accepted Transformation Restricted Transformation Rejected or: Transformation Undetermined The status applies to the transformation's suitability for the defined simulation use. Transformed Input Status The resulting Simulation Input may be classified as: Simulation-Usable Conditionally Simulation-Usable Restricted Not Simulation-Usable or: Suitability Undetermined This status does not replace subsequent temporal or uncertainty governance. Transformation Change A material change may occur in: transformation method, parameters, software, source mapping, sequence, threshold, imputation rule, fusion logic, or another transformation property. Material changes should trigger reassessment of affected transformed inputs. Transformation Impact Propagation Where transformation materially affects downstream simulation use, the effect should propagate. Conceptually: Transformation Change → Transformed Input Change → Scenario / Execution Effect → Output Effect → Reliance Effect The later SIMULOS® Parent Standards govern those downstream consequences. Point-in-Time Transformation Reconstruction SDTM supports questions such as: Which transformation was used for this execution? Which parameters were active? Which source input version entered it? Which values were imputed? Which observations were removed? Which transformations introduced additional uncertainty? Transformation Traceability SDTM establishes: Source Input ↓ Transformation Need ↓ Transformation Method ↓ Transformation Parameters ↓ Transformation Execution ↓ Intermediate States ↓ Transformed Input ↓ Transformation Effects ↓ Conditions / Limitations ↓ Simulation Use Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Identify Material Transformations Determine which input changes can materially affect simulation behavior or interpretation. 2. Establish Transformation Purpose Record why each material transformation is required. 3. Define Transformation Method Specify the applicable: operation, rule, algorithm, formula, parameters, or processing method. 4. Preserve Source Input Identity Bind every material transformation to the exact input version from which it originates. 5. Execute and Record the Transformation Preserve the material transformation sequence and resulting input state. 6. Identify Generated, Removed, or Modified Information Determine whether the transformation: removes information, generates inferred information, changes resolution, changes distribution, changes meaning, or changes simulation influence. 7. Assess Transformation Effects Evaluate material effects upon: representativeness, uncertainty, completeness, precision, semantics, and simulation applicability. 8. Govern Missing Values, Outliers, and Synthetic Supplementation Ensure treatment remains explicit and traceable. 9. Assess Transformation Limitations Identify information loss, extrapolation, imputation, bias, uncertainty, or other material restrictions. 10. Assign Transformation Status Determine whether the transformation is: Accepted, Conditionally Accepted, Restricted, Rejected, or Undetermined. 11. Establish Transformed Input Status Determine whether the resulting input may proceed to subsequent SIDS governance. 12. Preserve Transformation Traceability Maintain the complete relationship: Source Input → Transformation → Transformed Input → Transformation Effect → Simulation Use Governance Outputs SDTM may produce: Simulation Transformation Requirement, Transformation Purpose Record, Transformation Identifier, Transformation Method Record, Transformation Rule, Transformation Parameter Record, Data Cleaning Record, Filtering Record, Normalization Record, Standardization Record, Unit Conversion Record, Format Conversion Record, Aggregation Record, Disaggregation Record, Interpolation Record, Extrapolation Record, Resampling Record, Encoding Record, Derived Input Record, Feature Derivation Record, Missing-Value Treatment Record, Imputation Record, Default-Value Record, Synthetic Supplementation Record, Outlier Treatment Record, Data Fusion Record, Spatial Transformation Record, Coordinate Transformation Record, Dimensional Transformation Record, Transformation Sequence Record, Simulation Transformation Chain, Transformation Dependency Map, Transformation Version Record, Transformation Reproducibility Record, Information Loss Record, Transformation-Induced Bias Record, Transformation-Induced Uncertainty Record, Transformation Effect Assessment, Representativeness Reassessment Signal, Transformation Limitation Record, Transformation Condition Record, Transformation Status, Transformed Input Status, Transformation Change Record, and Simulation Data Transformation Traceability Map. Use Case 1 — Autonomous Vehicle Sensor Simulation Scenario A simulation consumes vehicle sensor data sampled at different frequencies: camera — 30 Hz, radar — 20 Hz, lidar — 10 Hz, vehicle telemetry — 100 Hz. The simulation requires a synchronized input stream. Application SDTM governs: Source Inputs ↓ Timestamp Alignment ↓ Resampling ↓ Interpolation Where Required ↓ Synchronized Simulation Inputs Interpolated values remain distinguishable from direct measurements, and the transformation parameters remain traceable. Result The simulation can determine exactly how the synchronized input stream was produced and which portions contain transformed rather than directly observed information. Use Case 2 — Industrial Failure Simulation Scenario Historical sensor records contain missing values and extreme temperature spikes. A preprocessing process proposes to: replace missing values with averages, remove extreme values as outliers, smooth the resulting signal. Application SDTM prevents automatic treatment. The temperature spikes are assessed before removal because they may represent precisely the failure conditions the simulation intends to examine. Missing values remain distinguishable from observed measurements after imputation. Result The transformation produces a governed Simulation Input without silently removing potentially material failure behavior or representing imputed values as direct observations. Architectural Position Simulation Data Transformation is the third internal governance space of the Simulation Input & Data Standard (SIDS). The complete SIDS progression is: Simulation Input Identification ↓ Simulation Data Representativeness ↓ Simulation Data Transformation ↓ Simulation Temporal Data ↓ Simulation Input Uncertainty SIIM establishes: What is the input? SDRM establishes: What can it legitimately represent? SDTM establishes: What happened to it before simulation use? The next module, STDM — Simulation Temporal Data Module, establishes whether the information and its transformed state are temporally appropriate for the simulation context in which they will be used. Foundational Principle A transformed Simulation Input remains legitimate only when the path from its original information basis to its simulation-usable form remains sufficiently identifiable, justified, reproducible, limitation-aware, and traceable, without allowing transformation to manufacture unsupported meaning, representativeness, observational status, precision, or certainty. Canonical Closing Statement Simulation Data Transformation Module establishes the transformation governance layer of the Simulation Input & Data Standard by governing how identified Simulation Inputs are cleaned, filtered, normalized, converted, aggregated, interpolated, extrapolated, resampled, encoded, derived, imputed, fused, supplemented, aligned, or otherwise transformed for simulation use. Through explicit transformation purpose, method, parameters, sequencing, source binding, versioning, information-loss assessment, generated-information distinction, bias and uncertainty identification, representativeness reassessment, conditions, limitations, status, and complete transformation traceability, SDTM ensures that simulation-ready information remains methodologically connected to the information from which it originated and that preprocessing cannot silently manufacture properties the underlying data never possessed.

title: OOF™ Simulation Execution Control Module (SECM)
text: OOF™ Simulation Execution Control Module (SECM) Simulation Execution Control Module (SECM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Simulation Execution Standard (SES) Operational Layer: Simulation Execution Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Type: Parent Standard Module Governed Space: Simulation Execution Control Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 19 August 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Governed Space Simulation Execution Control Canonical Definition Simulation Execution Control Module (SECM) defines the governance framework through which an instantiated Simulation Execution is initiated, progressed, constrained, synchronized, monitored, intervened in where permitted, paused, resumed, terminated, and completed while preserving the execution conditions necessary to determine what actually occurred during the run. SECM establishes the active-control layer of Simulation Execution. Its purpose is to ensure that a simulation does not become an uncontrolled computational process once execution begins and that material runtime changes cannot occur without remaining visible within the execution record. Operational Role SECM is the second internal governance space of the Simulation Execution Standard (SES). The preceding module: SIM — Simulation Instantiation Module establishes: What exact simulation configuration has been instantiated for execution? SECM asks: How must that instantiated simulation remain governed while it is actually running? The governed progression is: Instantiated Simulation → Execution Authorization → Execution Initiation → Runtime Control → State Monitoring → Intervention / Deviation Handling → Pause / Resume / Termination → Execution Completion Status Module Operational Space SECM governs: execution authorization, execution initiation, execution start conditions, runtime control, execution sequencing, control-state management, runtime constraints, temporal control, synchronization control, resource control, execution-state transitions, intervention permissions, intervention execution, runtime modification, runtime deviation, anomaly response, pause, resume, restart, cancellation, termination, emergency termination, timeout, dependency failure response, execution boundary enforcement, control loss, control recovery, execution completion, and execution-control traceability. Execution Authorization A Simulation Execution may require an explicit authorization before it begins. Authorization may define: who or what may initiate execution, which Scenario may run, which configuration may be used, which resources may be consumed, which interventions are permitted, which external connections may be active, which control limits apply, and who or what may terminate the run. Execution Authorization ≠ Simulation Validity Authorization means the simulation is permitted to run under defined conditions. It does not establish that: the model is correct, the scenario is sufficient, the output will be valid, or the simulated system is safe. Execution Initiation Execution Initiation marks the transition: Instantiated ↓ Running A governed initiation may require that: the intended Simulation Instance exists, required dependencies are available, applicable inputs are loaded, runtime conditions are satisfied, control mechanisms are active, and authorization is confirmed. Start Condition A Simulation Start Condition establishes the requirements that must exist before execution may begin. Possible start conditions may include: environment ready, input set available, scenario loaded, parameter configuration applied, required services active, simulation clock synchronized, required hardware connected, required participant ready, or execution authority confirmed. No Unverified Start Principle SIMULOS® establishes: A simulation should not be assumed to have started under its intended configuration merely because the execution engine reports that a run began. Material start conditions should be verifiable where necessary. Execution State A Simulation Execution should maintain an identifiable current state. Possible states may include: Prepared Initialized Running Paused Waiting Degraded Interrupted Restarting Terminating Completed Failed or: Execution State Unknown depending upon implementation. Execution State Transition Material changes between execution states should remain identifiable. Conceptually: Initialized → Running → Paused → Running → Completed or: Running → Degraded → Failed The execution history should preserve the actual path. Runtime Control Runtime Control governs how the active Simulation Execution remains aligned with the conditions under which it was instantiated. This may include: state progression, event sequencing, clock progression, resource allocation, scenario progression, environmental updates, external inputs, actor activation, dependency use, and termination criteria. Execution Control ≠ Outcome Control SIMULOS® establishes: Execution Control must govern how the simulation runs, not manipulate the simulation merely to force a preferred output. Unexpected results should remain observable. Unfavorable system behavior must not become a reason to silently alter the run. Runtime Constraint A Runtime Constraint defines a condition that must remain satisfied during execution. Examples may include: allowed resource consumption, allowed scenario bounds, permitted external interfaces, maximum execution duration, parameter locks, environmental limits, intervention permissions, or synchronization requirements. Constraint Violation A Constraint Violation occurs when actual execution moves outside a materially relevant runtime condition. The response may include: Continue with Record Pause Restrict Reconfigure Restart Terminate or: Escalate depending upon the Simulation Purpose. Execution Boundary The Execution Boundary defines what the active simulation is permitted to do. It may govern: accessible resources, connected systems, external actions, scenario range, execution duration, control authority, or other material runtime limits. Boundary Enforcement A simulation should not silently operate outside the execution boundary merely because the underlying technology permits it. Execution Sequence Some simulations require governed sequencing. For example: Initialize ↓ Activate Environment ↓ Activate Agents ↓ Introduce Scenario Event ↓ Observe Response ↓ Terminate Changing sequence may materially change the simulation. SECM therefore governs sequence where order matters. No Sequence Substitution Principle SIMULOS® establishes: A materially different execution sequence should not be represented as the same controlled execution merely because the same components were eventually activated. Temporal Control Simulation execution may rely upon: simulation time, wall-clock time, event time, mission time, synchronized system time, or accelerated / slowed simulation time. SECM governs the execution-control side of these timing conditions. Clock Control Where the simulation clock materially affects behavior, relevant clock state should remain controlled. This may include: clock start, clock rate, time acceleration, time pause, synchronization, reset, and clock discontinuities. Synchronization Control Distributed simulations may require multiple: agents, models, services, hardware systems, sensors, or environments to remain synchronized. Synchronization failure may create behavior that reflects infrastructure error rather than the intended scenario. Synchronization Deviation A material synchronization deviation should remain identifiable. Possible treatment may include: tolerance-based continuation, pause, resynchronization, partial restart, run invalidation, or termination. Resource Control Execution may require controlled access to: compute, memory, storage, network bandwidth, energy, hardware, external services, or human participants. Resource constraints may materially alter simulation behavior. Resource Exhaustion A simulation may terminate or degrade because computational or infrastructural resources are exhausted. This should remain distinguishable from: failure of the simulated system itself. No Infrastructure-Failure-as-System-Failure Principle SIMULOS® establishes: Failure of the simulation infrastructure must not automatically be interpreted as failure of the Simulation Object. Dependency Control Simulation execution may depend upon: APIs, external models, databases, hardware, external services, or distributed infrastructure. Dependency state should remain visible where changes can materially affect execution. Dependency Failure Possible responses to dependency failure may include: Fallback Pause Substitute Continue Degraded Restart or: Terminate. The selected response should remain traceable. Runtime Intervention A Runtime Intervention is a deliberate action that materially changes an active Simulation Execution. Examples include: parameter modification, scenario injection, human command, failure injection, environment modification, control transfer, agent override, pause, or forced state transition. Intervention Authority Where interventions are allowed, SECM should identify who or what may perform them. Possible intervention authorities include: Human Operator Simulation Controller Automated Control Logic AI Controller Autonomous Simulation Agent or another governed execution actor. No Invisible Intervention Principle A material runtime intervention must remain visible in the execution history. Planned Intervention Some interventions are part of Scenario Design. Examples include: injecting a failure at time T, reducing communication availability, triggering handover, or introducing an environmental event. Such interventions remain governed actions even where planned. Unplanned Intervention An intervention may occur unexpectedly because: simulation instability develops, infrastructure fails, safety boundaries are crossed, an operator acts, or an execution anomaly requires control. Unplanned interventions should be distinguished from planned scenario events. Runtime Modification A simulation may permit certain configuration changes during execution. Material modifications may include: parameter adjustment, model switching, environment changes, agent activation, dependency replacement, or runtime configuration change. Where permitted, the modification should remain identifiable. No Silent Configuration Mutation Principle SIMULOS® establishes: A materially changed runtime configuration must not continue to be represented as if the original execution configuration remained unchanged. Execution Deviation An Execution Deviation is a material difference between: intended controlled execution and: actual runtime behavior or condition. Possible deviations include: wrong sequence, unexpected delay, missing dependency, incorrect configuration, intervention, resource exhaustion, synchronization failure, runtime exception, timing deviation, or control-state mismatch. Deviation Classification A deviation may be classified as: Minor Material Critical Execution-Limiting Execution-Invalidating or: Undetermined depending upon the simulation context. Deviation ≠ Automatic Failure A deviation does not necessarily invalidate a simulation. The module requires the deviation to remain explicit so its consequence can later be assessed. Execution Anomaly An Execution Anomaly is an unexpected runtime event or state that differs materially from expected execution behavior. An anomaly may originate from: the Simulation Object, the Simulation Model, the environment, infrastructure, external dependencies, configuration, or control logic. SECM does not determine the cause automatically. It ensures the event remains governable. Control Response A material anomaly may trigger a controlled response such as: Observe Continue Restrict Pause Escalate Recover Restart or: Terminate. Pause A Simulation Execution may enter a controlled Paused State. Pause should preserve sufficient execution state to determine: when the pause occurred, why it occurred, what state existed, what changed while paused, and whether resume remains comparable to uninterrupted execution. Pause ≠ No Change The simulation may be paused while: external services continue changing, hardware state changes, humans act, external clocks advance, or dependencies change. Therefore the assumption that a paused simulation preserves identical execution conditions may require verification. Resume Resume returns a paused Simulation Execution to active execution. Material changes occurring during the pause should remain visible. Restart A Restart begins execution again after: interruption, failure, modification, or control decision. Restart may occur: from initial state or: from checkpoint. These are materially different execution paths. Checkpoint A simulation may preserve a checkpoint from which execution can later resume. A checkpoint should remain connected to: Execution ID, execution state, simulation clock, configuration, relevant memory/state, environment, and applicable dependencies. Checkpoint ≠ Original Execution Restart from checkpoint may preserve continuity, but it should not automatically be represented as identical to uninterrupted execution. Execution Interruption An interruption occurs when active execution stops before intended completion. Possible causes include: infrastructure failure, external dependency failure, operator intervention, resource exhaustion, software failure, or emergency control. Interruption Status An interrupted run may become: Resumable Restart Required Terminated Failed or: Status Undetermined. Execution Termination Termination deliberately ends an execution. Termination may be: Normal Conditional Early Failure-Based Safety-Based Resource-Based Operator-Initiated Automatically Triggered or: Emergency where relevant. Termination Criteria Termination criteria should be established where materially relevant. Examples include: scenario complete, target state reached, maximum duration reached, failure state reached, invalid simulation region entered, resource limit exceeded, safety boundary crossed, or information objective achieved. Early Termination An execution may terminate before planned completion because the simulation has already reached a state that satisfies or invalidates the execution purpose. Early termination should remain explicit. Emergency Termination Emergency Termination may be required when continuing execution could: damage hardware, affect external systems, violate resource constraints, create unsafe human interaction, or move beyond authorized simulation boundaries. Timeout A Timeout occurs when execution exceeds a predefined temporal or processing condition. Timeout should remain distinguishable from: simulated-system failure, execution infrastructure failure, or intentional termination. Execution Completion Execution Completion occurs when the Simulation Execution reaches an accepted terminal state. Completion may be: Complete Conditionally Complete Partially Complete Incomplete Failed or: Completion Undetermined. Completion ≠ Positive Result SIMULOS® establishes: A fully completed simulation may show complete system failure, while an incomplete simulation may appear to show a positive result. Execution completion and simulation outcome must remain distinct. Control Loss A Simulation Execution Control Loss occurs where the execution can no longer be governed according to its required runtime controls. Examples include: inability to pause, inability to terminate, lost synchronization, uncontrolled parameter change, uncontrolled external interaction, controller failure, or execution-state uncertainty. Control Loss Response Where control loss is material, the execution may require: Containment Emergency Termination Isolation Restart or: Execution Invalidity Assessment. Control Recovery Where control is restored, the execution should preserve: when control was lost, how long control was absent, what occurred during the gap, how control was recovered, and whether execution continuity remains acceptable. Autonomous Execution Control Simulation campaigns may increasingly be controlled by autonomous orchestration systems. An autonomous controller may: launch runs, select scenarios, modify configurations, detect anomalies, stop executions, allocate resources, or generate follow-up runs. SECM remains applicable. The controller's execution authority and actions should remain governable. No Autonomous Control Opacity Principle SIMULOS® establishes: Autonomous execution control must not remove visibility into why materially relevant runtime actions occurred. Adaptive Execution Control Some simulations adapt during execution. The simulation may: Observe Behavior ↓ Change Runtime Condition ↓ Continue Execution ↓ Observe New Behavior This may be legitimate. However, the adaptive path should remain explicit. Execution-Control Traceability SECM should support reconstruction of: Who / What Controlled the Run ↓ Which Controls Applied ↓ What Execution State Existed ↓ What Interventions Occurred ↓ What Deviations Occurred ↓ How the Run Ended Simulation Campaign Control For large simulation campaigns, execution control may occur at two levels: Campaign-Level Control and: Run-Level Control. Campaign-level rules may establish: permitted scenarios, run counts, resource allocations, stopping criteria, failure handling, retry logic, and exception treatment. Individual runs may still require their own execution-state history. Retry Governance Automated campaigns may retry failed runs. A retry should remain distinguishable from the original execution. Conceptually: Run 001 — Failed ↓ Retry 001A Rather than: Run 001 — Successful where the first failure disappears. No Failure Erasure by Retry Principle SIMULOS® establishes: A successful retry must not erase the existence of the execution failure that triggered it. Execution Selection Bias Large campaigns may automatically discard runs classified as: failed, anomalous, incomplete, or outlying. SECM requires material execution-control exclusions to remain visible. No Success-Only Preservation Principle Execution governance must not preserve only completed or desirable runs where failed, interrupted, anomalous, or deviating executions are materially relevant to understanding the simulation. Space and Mission Execution Control Mission simulations may include: spacecraft dynamics, communication delay, autonomous response, hardware-in-the-loop systems, ground-control simulation, navigation systems, power simulation, and environmental models. A runtime deviation may originate from: the simulated spacecraft or: the simulation infrastructure. SECM preserves this distinction. A mission run showing loss of navigation cannot automatically be interpreted as spacecraft navigation failure if synchronization loss inside the simulator caused the event. Autonomous Systems For autonomous systems, execution control may need to preserve: autonomy mode, human override, permission state, fallback state, communication state, external-agent interaction, and runtime authority transitions. This becomes particularly important where the simulation itself allows dynamic changes in authority. Industrial Systems A digital-twin or industrial simulation may interact with: real hardware, production data, live sensor feeds, or control systems. SECM provides the control layer needed to prevent simulation execution from becoming an unbounded interaction with operational infrastructure. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Establish Execution Authorization Identify who or what may initiate, control, intervene in, and terminate the Simulation Execution. 2. Verify Start Conditions Confirm the materially required configuration, dependencies, controls, and runtime conditions before execution begins. 3. Initiate the Execution Create the active execution state and preserve the execution start record. 4. Maintain Runtime Control Govern: sequence, timing, synchronization, resources, dependencies, state transitions, and applicable runtime boundaries. 5. Govern Interventions Record and classify planned and unplanned runtime interventions. 6. Govern Deviations and Anomalies Identify material differences between intended and actual execution. 7. Govern Pause, Resume, Restart, and Retry Preserve execution continuity and distinguish interrupted or repeated execution paths. 8. Govern Termination Apply explicit termination criteria and preserve the reason and state at termination. 9. Determine Completion Status Classify execution as: Complete, Conditionally Complete, Partially Complete, Incomplete, Failed, or Undetermined. 10. Preserve Execution-Control Traceability Maintain the runtime control history required for subsequent observation, repetition, and execution documentation. Governance Outputs SECM may produce: Simulation Execution Authorization Record, Simulation Start Condition Record, Execution Initiation Record, Execution State Record, Execution State Transition Record, Runtime Control Record, Runtime Constraint Record, Execution Boundary Record, Execution Sequence Record, Simulation Clock Control Record, Synchronization Control Record, Synchronization Deviation Record, Resource Control Record, Resource Exhaustion Record, Dependency Control Record, Dependency Failure Record, Runtime Intervention Record, Intervention Authority Record, Planned Intervention Record, Unplanned Intervention Record, Runtime Modification Record, Execution Deviation Record, Execution Deviation Classification, Execution Anomaly Record, Control Response Record, Pause Record, Resume Record, Restart Record, Checkpoint Record, Execution Interruption Record, Execution Termination Record, Emergency Termination Record, Timeout Record, Control Loss Record, Control Recovery Record, Retry Record, Execution Completion Record, Execution Completion Status, Campaign Control Record, Run-Level Exception Record, and Simulation Execution Control Traceability Record. Use Case 1 — Autonomous Vehicle Simulation Campaign Scenario A large autonomous-driving simulation campaign runs thousands of scenarios. One execution shows unexpected failure of collision avoidance. The run was automatically retried and the second execution completed successfully. Application SECM preserves: Original Run — Failure Runtime Conditions Execution Deviation Retry Trigger Retry Execution Differences Between Runs rather than replacing the failed run with the successful retry. Result Engineers can determine whether the original behavior came from: the autonomous system, simulation infrastructure, timing, synchronization, runtime configuration, or another execution condition. The failed execution remains part of the governed simulation history. Use Case 2 — Spacecraft Hardware-in-the-Loop Simulation Scenario A spacecraft autonomy simulation is connected to flight-like hardware and communication subsystems. During an autonomous recovery scenario, synchronization between the simulation environment and hardware begins to drift. Application SECM identifies a material Synchronization Deviation. Execution enters: Paused rather than silently continuing. The synchronization state is restored and the execution is resumed from an identified checkpoint. Result The mission team can distinguish: behavior of the spacecraft autonomy logic from: behavior produced by simulation-infrastructure timing error. The resumed execution remains traceable to the synchronization deviation and checkpoint rather than being represented as an uninterrupted nominal run. Architectural Position Simulation Execution Control Module (SECM) is the second internal governance space of the Simulation Execution Standard (SES). The complete SES progression is: Simulation Instantiation ↓ Simulation Execution Control ↓ Simulation Observation ↓ Simulation Repetition ↓ Simulation Execution Documentation SIM establishes: What exactly has been instantiated? SECM establishes: How does that instantiated simulation remain controlled while running? The next module, SOM — Simulation Observation Module, governs what materially relevant states, events, transitions, anomalies, and runtime behavior must be observed and preserved during execution. Foundational Principle A simulation execution remains governable only while the conditions controlling how it starts, progresses, changes, pauses, resumes, deviates, and terminates remain explicit and traceable. Canonical Closing Statement Simulation Execution Control Module establishes the runtime governance layer of the Simulation Execution Standard by governing authorization, start conditions, execution states, sequencing, timing, synchronization, resource and dependency control, interventions, deviations, anomalies, pause and resume, restart, retry, termination, control loss, recovery, and completion. SECM ensures that active simulation execution cannot silently diverge from its instantiated basis, that infrastructure failures remain distinguishable from simulated-system failures, that retries do not erase failed runs, and that every materially relevant runtime control event remains reconstructable as part of the governed Simulation Execution history.

title: OOF™ Simulation Execution Documentation Module (SEDM)
text: OOF™ Simulation Execution Documentation Module (SEDM) Simulation Execution Documentation Module (SEDM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Simulation Execution Standard (SES) Operational Layer: Simulation Execution Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Type: Parent Standard Module Governed Space: Simulation Execution Documentation Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 19 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Governed Space Simulation Execution Documentation Canonical Definition Simulation Execution Documentation Module (SEDM) defines the governance framework through which materially relevant information about Simulation Execution is captured, structured, linked, preserved, version-bounded, and made sufficiently reconstructable to establish what was actually executed, under which configuration and conditions, what occurred during execution, which interventions and deviations arose, how repetitions were related, whether execution was completed, and which Simulation Outputs originated from that execution. SEDM converts distributed execution information into a governed: Simulation Execution Record. Its purpose is not to require documentation for documentation's sake. Its purpose is to ensure that material Simulation Outputs and downstream claims do not become detached from the execution history required to understand how they were produced. Operational Role SEDM serves as the fifth and final internal governance space of the Simulation Execution Standard (SES). The preceding modules establish: SIM — What exact simulation instance was instantiated? SECM — How was active execution controlled? SOM — What materially relevant events and behaviors occurred during execution? SRPM — How were executions repeated, related, varied, and compared?
