SEDM asks: Can the complete materially relevant execution history now be reconstructed sufficiently to determine what actually ran, what occurred, how the execution changed, and which outputs it produced? The governed progression is: Simulation Instantiation Record ↓ Execution Control Record ↓ Simulation Observation Record ↓ Simulation Repetition Record ↓ Execution Documentation Assembly ↓ Execution Traceability ↓ Execution Provenance ↓ Execution Lineage ↓ Execution Completeness Documentation ↓ Execution-to-Output Linkage ↓ Governed Simulation Execution Record Module Operational Space SEDM governs: execution documentation requirements, Execution Record identity, documentation scope, documentation granularity, documentation timing, execution metadata, configuration documentation, model-version documentation, environment-version documentation, scenario documentation, input documentation, parameter documentation, initialization documentation, authorization documentation, execution-state documentation, runtime-condition documentation, control-action documentation, intervention documentation, deviation documentation, observation documentation, anomaly documentation, interruption documentation, restart documentation, termination documentation, failure documentation, completion documentation, repetition documentation, randomization documentation, seed documentation where applicable, execution provenance, execution lineage, campaign documentation, run-to-campaign relationships, documentation completeness, documentation gaps, documentation uncertainty, execution reconstruction, point-in-time reconstruction, execution-to-output traceability, record retention, record continuity, and formation of the Governed Simulation Execution Record. Module Function SEDM exists to prevent: simulation outputs with no identifiable originating execution, intended configurations being substituted for actual executed configurations, model versions becoming detached from execution records, undocumented runtime interventions, execution deviations disappearing after completion, failed and interrupted runs being removed from history, observations losing their execution context, repetitions becoming indistinguishable, seeds or stochastic conditions becoming untraceable, simulation campaigns becoming collections of anonymous output files, later reconstruction depending upon individual memory, partial documentation being represented as complete documentation, and downstream validation or audit being forced to infer what happened during execution. Simulation Execution Record A Simulation Execution Record is the governed documentation structure representing a specific Simulation Execution and its materially relevant execution history. Conceptually: Execution Identity Instantiated Configuration Execution Conditions Execution Controls Observed Events Interventions Deviations Execution State History Repetition Context Completion Status Output Linkage = Governed Simulation Execution Record Execution Record Identity Every materially relevant Execution Record should be bound to an identifiable Simulation Execution. Conceptually: Simulation Execution ID → Simulation Execution Record The record should not exist merely as an anonymous log file or output directory. Documentation Scope Documentation requirements should correspond to the Simulation Purpose, consequence, complexity, execution environment, and downstream reliance. SEDM does not require every technical event to be permanently recorded. It requires: materially relevant execution information to remain sufficiently available for the intended governance purpose. Documentation Granularity Documentation may operate at different levels: Run Level Episode Level Batch Level Scenario Level Campaign Level or another defined execution unit. Large-scale simulation may combine these levels. Run-Level Documentation Run-level documentation may preserve: Execution ID, configuration, inputs, parameters, seed, execution state, interventions, deviations, observations, completion status, and outputs. Campaign-Level Documentation Campaign-level documentation may preserve shared conditions across large populations of executions. For example: Campaign C-001 may define: model version, environment version, common scenario family, infrastructure, orchestration configuration, repetition rules, and shared execution controls. Individual runs then document material differences from that common basis. No Duplicate Documentation Requirement SEDM does not require identical information to be copied into every run record where a governed shared Campaign Record already establishes that information. The requirement is: traceable inheritance. Documentation Inheritance A run may inherit documented conditions from a Campaign Record where: the inherited condition is explicitly linked, the relevant version is stable, exceptions remain visible, and the run can be reconstructed without ambiguity. No Assumed Inheritance Principle SIMULOS® establishes: A run must not be assumed to inherit campaign conditions where material evidence shows that its actual execution differed. Actual execution takes precedence over intended campaign configuration. Actual Configuration Documentation SEDM should preserve the materially relevant configuration that actually entered execution. This may include: Simulation Object version, model version, environment version, scenario version, Input Set, parameter set, software build, hardware configuration, dependencies, randomization basis, and initialization state. Intended vs Executed Configuration SEDM distinguishes: Intended Configuration from: Executed Configuration. Where these differ, the difference becomes part of the Execution Record. Configuration Delta Record A Configuration Delta Record may identify: Expected Configuration → Actual Configuration → Material Difference This supports later interpretation of unexpected behavior. Execution State History SEDM may preserve state transitions such as: Prepared ↓ Initialized ↓ Running ↓ Paused ↓ Restarted ↓ Running ↓ Completed This is materially different from a record that merely states: Completed. Execution Timeline Where timing is material, SEDM may preserve an Execution Timeline connecting: Initialization Start Control Events Observations Interventions Anomalies Interruptions Restarts Termination and: Completion. Event Ordering The order of execution events may itself be material. SEDM should therefore preserve event ordering where causal interpretation depends upon sequence. Timestamp Governance Where timestamps are used, the record should preserve sufficient context to determine what they represent. This may include: simulation time, wall-clock time, mission time, relative execution time, or another defined temporal reference. Simulation Time ≠ Wall-Clock Time A simulation may represent: 24 hours of operational behavior while executing in: 12 minutes of wall-clock time. SEDM preserves which temporal frame an event belongs to. Execution Control Documentation Material execution-control actions should remain linked to the execution. Examples include: pause, resume, termination, resource restriction, synchronization, scenario progression, injected event, controlled failure, recovery command, or another runtime control. Intervention Documentation A material intervention should document where applicable: Who or what intervened When Under which authority What changed Why and: Which part of execution may have been affected. Human Intervention Where humans intervene during execution, SEDM may preserve: role, intervention type, decision point, timing, authority, and resulting execution effect. AI or Autonomous Intervention Where an AI or autonomous system modifies simulation execution, SEDM may preserve: initiating system, decision basis where available, authorized capability, action performed, affected parameters or scenario state, and resulting execution path. No Invisible Intervention Principle A material intervention capable of changing Simulation Execution must not disappear from the execution history. Deviation Documentation A material Execution Deviation should remain connected to: the expected condition, actual condition, time or execution stage, affected execution component, response, and resulting execution status. Deviation Resolution A deviation may be: Resolved During Execution Accepted Conditionally Accepted Unresolved Execution-Limiting or: Execution-Terminating. SEDM documents the status. It does not independently determine downstream validity. Observation Documentation Material observations produced under SOM should remain linked to the execution context in which they occurred. An observation should not become: Behavior X occurred without sufficient ability to determine: during which execution, scenario, state, configuration, and conditions Behavior X occurred. Observation Context Preservation Where material: Observation → Execution ID → Execution State → Scenario → Configuration → Time Context should remain traceable. Observation Limitation Documentation If portions of execution were not observable, that limitation should remain part of the Execution Record. Examples include: telemetry loss, missing internal state, insufficient sampling, sensor dropout, logging failure, or inaccessible agent state. No Full-Observation Assumption SIMULOS® establishes: Absence of a recorded event does not establish absence of the event where the relevant execution region was not sufficiently observable. Anomaly Documentation Material anomalies should remain visible even where the execution ultimately completes successfully. Anomaly records may include: anomaly identity, observation time, affected component, execution context, response, persistence, and relationship to resulting outputs. Failure Documentation Failed Simulation Executions remain part of the governed execution history where material. A failure record may preserve: failure state, failure point, observed cause where known, affected scenario, affected configuration, recovery attempt, and output status. Failure Cause ≠ Failure Observation SEDM distinguishes: Observed Failure from: Determined Cause of Failure. The execution record should not present an unverified causal explanation as established fact. Interrupted Execution An interrupted execution should remain distinguishable from: Completed Execution and: Failed Execution. An interruption may later be restarted or abandoned. Restart Documentation Where execution restarts, SEDM should preserve whether the restart: resumed from prior state, restored from checkpoint, restarted from initialization, changed configuration, changed input, changed seed, or created a new Execution ID. Execution Continuity A restarted execution should not automatically be treated as continuous with the original run. The continuity relationship should be explicitly governed. Termination Documentation Termination may be: Normal Rule-Based Human-Initiated AI-Initiated Safety-Initiated Failure-Induced or another defined condition. Where material, the termination basis should remain visible. Execution Completion Documentation SEDM preserves the Execution Completeness status established under SES. Possible statuses may include: Complete Conditionally Complete Partially Complete Incomplete Failed or: Undetermined. Completion ≠ Success SIMULOS® establishes: A Simulation Execution may be completely executed while the simulated system fails catastrophically. Execution completion describes execution status. It does not describe desirability of the simulated outcome. Repetition Documentation SEDM preserves the repetition structure established by SRPM. This may include: Repetition Set ID, Reference Execution, controlled constants, permitted variation, seed relationship, execution order, run dependency, repetition drift, comparability status, and repetition sufficiency. Repetition Lineage A repetition history may be represented: Run R001 ↓ Unexpected Divergence ↓ Focused Repeat R002 ↓ Focused Repeat R003 ↓ Rare Behavior Reproduced ↓ New Scenario Requirement SEDM preserves this lineage so that the discovery pathway remains reconstructable. Randomization Documentation Where randomness materially affects execution, SEDM may preserve: randomization method, random seed, sampling configuration, stochastic parameter state, and relationship between randomization and execution. No Seed-Only Reconstruction Principle A seed should not be treated as a complete execution record. Reconstruction may also depend upon: model version, environment version, dependencies, initialization, inputs, hardware, software, timing, and execution controls. Execution Provenance Execution Provenance establishes the origin of the Simulation Execution Record and its material components. It may connect: Execution Record to: simulation system, execution engine, orchestration platform, infrastructure, configuration source, input source, scenario source, observation source, and responsible execution authority where applicable. Provenance ≠ Integrity SEDM governs execution-specific provenance relationships. General integrity properties remain governed under INTEGROS®. Execution Lineage Execution Lineage establishes relationships between Simulation Executions over time. Examples include: Baseline → Repeat Baseline → Modified Parameter Run Failure → Recovery Run Scenario → Stress Escalation Model v1 Run → Model v2 Comparative Run Initial Campaign → Follow-Up Campaign Why Lineage Matters Without lineage, a simulation repository may contain millions of outputs while losing the reasoning path that explains: why later executions were performed. SEDM preserves that relationship. Execution Reconstruction Execution Reconstruction is the ability to recover the materially relevant execution basis after the original execution has ended. A reconstruction should answer, where applicable: What was executed? Which versions were used? Which scenario ran? Which inputs entered? Which parameters were active? Which randomization conditions applied? What occurred during execution? Which interventions occurred? Which deviations occurred? Was the execution interrupted or restarted? Was it part of a Repetition Set? Was execution complete? Which outputs came from it? Reconstruction ≠ Reproduction A simulation may be sufficiently documented for reconstruction even where exact technical reproduction is impossible. For example, external dependencies may no longer exist. SEDM distinguishes: Can we determine what happened? from: Can we execute exactly the same run again? Point-in-Time Reconstruction SEDM should support reconstruction of the execution state at a materially relevant point in time. For example: What was the active parameter configuration when the anomaly occurred? or: Had the human intervention already occurred when the autonomous recovery behavior began? Causal Sequence Preservation SEDM does not determine causality. However, it should preserve sufficient temporal and execution relationships to allow downstream analysis to investigate causality. Documentation Completeness Documentation Completeness asks: Does the Execution Record contain the materially required information necessary for its intended governance and downstream use? Possible statuses may include: Complete Conditionally Complete Partially Complete Incomplete or: Completeness Undetermined. Documentation Completeness ≠ Execution Completeness These are separate conditions. A simulation may be: Execution Complete + Documentation Incomplete or: Execution Failed + Documentation Complete. This distinction is critical. Documentation Gap A Documentation Gap exists where materially relevant execution information is missing, inaccessible, ambiguous, or insufficiently linked. Examples include: unknown model version, missing seed, unknown intervention, missing runtime log, unidentified scenario revision, missing input version, unknown restart state, or orphan output. Documentation Gap Classification A gap may be: Minor Material Critical or: Undetermined relative to the intended downstream use. No Documentation Inflation Principle SIMULOS® establishes: A partially documented execution must not be represented as fully reconstructable merely because large volumes of technical logs exist. Volume of logging is not equivalent to documentation sufficiency. Machine Logs ≠ Governed Documentation Raw logs may be important evidence. But a collection of logs does not automatically establish: execution identity, configuration binding, lineage, material event classification, completion status, or output linkage. SEDM provides the governance structure around technical records. Documentation Uncertainty Where documentation cannot establish a material fact with sufficient confidence, the uncertainty should remain visible. Possible representation: Known Conditionally Known Inferred Unknown or another governed classification. No Retrospective Certainty Principle SIMULOS® establishes: Missing execution information must not later be converted into certainty merely because a downstream conclusion requires it. Execution-to-Output Traceability Every material Simulation Output should remain traceable to the Simulation Execution or governed execution population that produced it. Conceptually: Simulation Execution ID ↓ Output ID or: Simulation Campaign / Repetition Set ↓ Aggregated Output ID Output Origin SEDM establishes the execution-side provenance of an output. SOGS then governs: what the output is, how it is classified, how it is bounded, and what may legitimately be inferred from it. No Orphan Output Principle A material Simulation Output should not become detached from the execution basis that produced it. Aggregated Output Traceability An aggregated result may represent: multiple runs, a Repetition Set, a Scenario Set, or a complete Simulation Campaign. SEDM should preserve the population of executions contributing to the aggregate where material. No Anonymous Aggregation Principle SIMULOS® establishes: An aggregate Simulation Output should not conceal which materially relevant executions were included, excluded, failed, or unavailable. Excluded Execution Documentation Where runs are excluded from aggregation or analysis, the exclusion may itself require documentation. This can prevent: cherry-picking, survivor bias, silent removal of failed runs, and post hoc population manipulation. Campaign Documentation Large Simulation Campaigns may require hierarchical documentation: Campaign Record ↓ Scenario Families ↓ Repetition Sets ↓ Individual Executions ↓ Outputs This structure allows governance at scale without losing material run-level traceability. Large-Scale Execution Documentation A campaign containing millions or billions of runs cannot always preserve every technical artifact indefinitely. SEDM therefore supports risk- and purpose-appropriate documentation strategies while protecting material reconstructability. Possible approaches include: structured metadata, hierarchical records, exception-focused retention, representative execution preservation, aggregate lineage, checkpoint preservation, reproducibility packages, and selective high-resolution logging. Selective Retention Selective retention may be legitimate where the selection logic itself is governed. For example, an organization may preserve: all failed runs, all anomalous runs, all rare-event runs, representative successful runs, complete metadata for every run, and aggregated technical logs. No Selective Success Preservation Principle Retention policy must not systematically preserve favorable executions while eliminating materially relevant unfavorable executions. Record Retention Retention periods may depend upon: simulation purpose, consequence, regulatory context, contractual requirements, validation use, audit requirements, operational reliance, incident exposure, and reproducibility needs. SEDM does not prescribe one universal retention period. Documentation Continuity Documentation should remain sufficiently interpretable across: software changes, model changes, environment changes, personnel changes, organizational changes, storage migrations, and simulation-platform replacement. Format Obsolescence Long-lived simulation programs may lose access to historical records because: proprietary formats disappear, software versions become unavailable, dependencies expire, or storage systems change. SEDM treats continued interpretability as part of documentation continuity where materially required. Documentation Versioning Execution documentation structures may evolve. Where schema changes affect interpretation, the applicable documentation version should remain identifiable. AI-Readable Execution Records Where technically appropriate, SEDM supports machine-readable records capable of connecting: Object → Model → Environment → Scenario → Input → Execution → Observation → Repetition → Output This can support automated: simulation governance, anomaly investigation, validation, audit, comparison, and future simulation planning. Automated Documentation Simulation platforms may automatically generate substantial portions of the Execution Record. Automation is encouraged where appropriate. However: Automated capture ≠ automatically sufficient governance. The record still needs to capture the materially relevant relationships required by SEDM. AI-Generated Documentation AI systems may summarize execution histories, classify anomalies, or construct documentation records. Where AI-generated documentation introduces interpretation rather than direct observation, that distinction should remain visible. Observed Fact vs Generated Summary SEDM should preserve the difference between: Machine-Captured Execution Event and: AI-Generated Description of the Event. This prevents generated summaries from silently replacing source execution evidence. Autonomous Simulation Campaigns Future autonomous systems may: generate scenarios, launch simulations, analyze observations, select follow-up runs, terminate low-value branches, and generate new campaigns without continuous human direction. SEDM becomes particularly important because the execution pathway itself may be machine-generated. Autonomous Execution Lineage For autonomous campaigns, documentation should preserve where material: Trigger ↓ Simulation Selection ↓ Execution ↓ Observation ↓ Machine Decision ↓ Follow-Up Execution ↓ Result This allows later reconstruction of why the simulation system chose to execute what it did. No Hidden Autonomous Path Principle When an autonomous system materially determines the simulation path, that path should remain reconstructable rather than appearing as an unexplained collection of simulation outputs. Space and Mission Simulation Space agencies and aerospace organizations may run enormous simulation campaigns before: launch, docking, landing, autonomous navigation, recovery, fault response, or mission-critical maneuvers. The challenge may not be generating simulation data. The challenge may be answering months later: Which exact spacecraft configuration produced this anomaly? Which environmental assumptions applied? Which run first revealed the failure mode? Was the anomaly reproduced? Which software version was running? Was that run included in the final aggregate? Which follow-up simulations were triggered by it? SEDM provides the documentation structure required to preserve these relationships. Autonomous Vehicle Simulation An autonomous-vehicle organization may execute hundreds of millions of simulated driving episodes. A later incident may require comparison with historical simulation. SEDM allows the organization to determine: whether the relevant condition had been simulated, which execution population contained it, what system version was tested, what behavior occurred, whether anomalous runs existed, and whether those runs were included in downstream analysis. Simulation Documentation Bottleneck At simulation scale, the bottleneck may shift from: Can we run enough simulations? to: Can we reconstruct why the simulations produced what they produced? Organizations may possess enormous computational capacity while lacking governed relationships between: execution, configuration, observation, repetition, anomaly, and output. SEDM defines that relationship as a governable space. Relationship to SIM SIM — Simulation Instantiation Module establishes the exact executable simulation instance. SEDM preserves the resulting instantiation record as part of the permanent Execution Record. Relationship to SECM SECM — Simulation Execution Control Module governs runtime execution control. SEDM preserves materially relevant control events, interventions, deviations, and execution-state transitions. Relationship to SOM SOM — Simulation Observation Module governs observation of materially relevant execution behavior. SEDM preserves those observations with their execution context. Relationship to SRPM SRPM — Simulation Repetition Module governs repeated executions. SEDM preserves Repetition Sets, run relationships, variation, drift, comparability, and repetition lineage. Relationship to SOGS SEDM provides the formal handoff from execution to output governance. The relationship is: Governed Simulation Execution Record ↓ Simulation Output ↓ SOGS — Simulation Output Governance Standard SEDM establishes: Where did this output come from? SOGS establishes: What exactly does this output represent, and what may legitimately be inferred from it? Relationship to ADIT® ADIT® may audit evidence derived from Simulation Execution. SEDM ensures that the execution-side record exists and remains sufficiently structured for audit examination. The boundary remains: SIMULOS® governs Simulation Execution Documentation. ADIT® governs audit activity over relevant evidence and records. Relationship to INTEGROS® INTEGROS® governs general integrity properties. SEDM does not duplicate general integrity governance. It governs the simulation-specific structure, context, lineage, and reconstructability of execution documentation. Relationship to VALIDOS® VALIDOS® may use Simulation Execution Records and Simulation Outputs as part of a validation basis. SEDM does not determine whether those records are sufficient validation evidence. It ensures that the simulation execution from which such evidence originates remains governable. Relationship to ORA™ ORA™ governs Operational Reality. SEDM documents what occurred inside the Simulation Execution. A complete Simulation Execution Record does not establish that simulated behavior corresponds to Operational Reality. Governance Boundary SEDM begins when materially relevant records from Simulation Instantiation, Execution Control, Observation, and Repetition require consolidation into a persistent and reconstructable execution history. SEDM ends when the Simulation Execution has been sufficiently: identified, configuration-bound, temporally documented, state-documented, intervention-documented, deviation-documented, observation-linked, repetition-linked, provenance-linked, lineage-linked, completeness-assessed, and connected to its resulting Simulation Outputs to form a Governed Simulation Execution Record. SEDM does not determine: output meaning, output classification, legitimate inference, simulation validity, correspondence with Operational Reality, validation outcome, or operational reliance. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Establish Execution Record Identity Bind documentation to the relevant Simulation Execution ID or Campaign ID. 2. Capture the Executed Configuration Preserve the materially relevant actual: object version, model version, environment version, scenario, inputs, parameters, dependencies, initialization, and randomization basis. 3. Preserve Execution State History Document material transitions from initialization through completion, interruption, failure, or termination. 4. Document Material Controls and Interventions Preserve actions capable of materially affecting execution. 5. Document Deviations and Anomalies Keep materially relevant departures from intended execution visible. 6. Link Observations to Execution Context Preserve where and under which conditions material observations occurred. 7. Preserve Repetition Relationships Connect repeated runs to their Reference Execution and Repetition Set. 8. Establish Execution Provenance and Lineage Record where the execution originated and how it relates to prior and subsequent executions. 9. Assess Documentation Completeness Identify material Documentation Gaps and uncertainty. 10. Establish Execution-to-Output Traceability Bind material Simulation Outputs to their originating execution or execution population. 11. Preserve Documentation Continuity Ensure records remain interpretable for the required lifecycle period. 12. Establish the Governed Simulation Execution Record Consolidate the material execution history into the formal downstream handoff to SOGS. Governance Outputs SEDM may produce: Simulation Execution Record, Simulation Campaign Record, Execution Documentation Requirement, Execution Metadata Record, Executed Configuration Record, Configuration Delta Record, Model-Version Execution Record, Environment-Version Execution Record, Scenario Execution Record, Input Execution Record, Parameter Execution Record, Initialization Record, Execution Authorization Record, Execution State History, Execution Timeline, Temporal Reference Record, Execution Control Documentation, Intervention Record, Human Intervention Record, Autonomous Intervention Record, Execution Deviation Record, Deviation Resolution Record, Observation Context Record, Observation Limitation Record, Anomaly Record, Failure Record, Interruption Record, Restart Record, Termination Record, Execution Completion Record, Repetition Documentation Record, Repetition Lineage Record, Randomization Record, Seed Record, Execution Provenance Record, Execution Lineage Map, Execution Reconstruction Record, Point-in-Time Reconstruction Record, Documentation Completeness Assessment, Documentation Gap Record, Documentation Uncertainty Record, Execution-to-Output Traceability Record, Aggregated Output Lineage Record, Excluded Execution Record, Documentation Retention Record, Documentation Continuity Record, and Governed Simulation Execution Record. Use Case 1 — Autonomous Spacecraft Mission Simulation Scenario A space organization runs a large pre-mission simulation campaign for autonomous spacecraft recovery. Several months later, engineers discover an unusual recovery behavior and need to determine whether it had appeared during simulation. Application SEDM connects the relevant historical execution to: spacecraft software version, simulation model version, environment version, scenario, navigation inputs, power state, random seed, execution observations, runtime interventions, and follow-up repetitions. The original anomaly can be reconstructed and its lineage traced into later simulation runs. Result Instead of searching through disconnected logs and output files, the organization can establish: which exact execution first produced the behavior, under which conditions, whether it was repeated, and which downstream outputs incorporated it. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Vehicle Simulation Campaign Scenario An autonomous-driving developer executes millions of simulated driving episodes across changing software versions. A rare operational incident later raises the question of whether a similar condition had previously appeared in simulation. Application SEDM allows historical Simulation Execution Records to be queried by: scenario conditions, vehicle software version, environment version, observed behavior, anomaly classification, execution completion, and output lineage. The organization discovers that similar behavior occurred in several historical runs, but some of those executions had been excluded from an aggregate because they were classified as incomplete. Result SEDM makes the exclusion and its execution context visible. The organization can determine what actually occurred without retroactively treating the aggregate output as a complete representation of all historical executions. Architectural Position Simulation Execution Documentation Module (SEDM) is the fifth and final internal governance space of the Simulation Execution Standard (SES). The complete SES progression is: SIM — Simulation Instantiation ↓ SECM — Simulation Execution Control ↓ SOM — Simulation Observation ↓ SRPM — Simulation Repetition ↓ SEDM — Simulation Execution Documentation ↓ Governed Simulation Execution Record This closes the Simulation Execution governance space. The resulting record becomes the governed handoff into: 9. Simulation Output Governance Standard (SOGS). Foundational Principle Simulation Execution becomes governable beyond the moment of execution only when the material configuration, conditions, events, interventions, deviations, repetitions, provenance, lineage, and resulting outputs remain connected through a reconstructable execution record. Canonical Closing Statement Simulation Execution Documentation Module completes the Simulation Execution Standard by transforming materially relevant execution information into a persistent, structured, and reconstructable Governed Simulation Execution Record. Through execution identity, actual-configuration documentation, state and timeline preservation, intervention and deviation records, observation context, failure and restart documentation, repetition lineage, provenance, documentation-completeness assessment, campaign-scale traceability, and execution-to-output linkage, SEDM prevents Simulation Outputs from becoming detached from the computational events that produced them. It establishes the formal execution record through which individual runs, repeated executions, large-scale campaigns, autonomous simulation pathways, anomalies, failures, exclusions, and resulting outputs can remain traceable across the simulation lifecycle and provides the governed handoff from Simulation Execution into Simulation Output Governance.

title: OOF™ Simulation Environment Versioning Module (SEVM)
text: OOF™ Simulation Environment Versioning Module (SEVM) Simulation Environment Versioning Module (SEVM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Simulation Model & Environment Standard (SMES) Operational Layer: Simulation Model & Environment Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Type: Parent Standard Module Governed Space: Simulation Environment Versioning Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 17 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Governed Space Simulation Environment Versioning Canonical Definition Simulation Environment Versioning Module (SEVM) defines the governance framework for identifying, establishing, distinguishing, freezing, changing, comparing, preserving, restoring, and reconstructing the versions and materially relevant configuration states of a governed Simulation Environment. SEVM establishes the version-control layer through which simulation executions remain bound to the exact environmental configuration under which they occurred, preventing materially different Simulation Environments from being treated as if they were the same simulation context. Operational Role SEVM is the fifth and final internal governance space of the Simulation Model & Environment Standard (SMES). The preceding modules establish: SMMM — What is the Simulation Model structurally composed of? SECM — Within what configured Simulation Environment does that model operate? SBIM — How do the model, environment, and connected domains interact across their boundaries? SPHM — Which controlled parameters configure the model and environment for simulation activity? SEVM asks: Which exact version of the Simulation Environment existed for a particular simulation execution, what changed between environment versions, and can the environment state relevant to that execution later be reconstructed? The governed progression is: Model Structure → Environment Configuration → Boundary Interaction → Parameterization → Environment Version Identification → Version Baseline → Change Control → Execution Binding → Version Reconstruction → Governed Simulation Environment Version Module Operational Space SEVM governs: Simulation Environment version identity, environment version identifiers, environment configuration states, environment baselines, environment snapshots, version composition, version lineage, version ancestry, version succession, version differentiation, version equivalence, version compatibility, version activation, version deactivation, version supersession, version freezing, version restoration, version rollback, environment forks, environment branches, environment merges, environment change, material change classification, environment configuration drift, dependency version change, boundary configuration change, parameter configuration change references, environment release states, execution-to-version binding, output-to-version traceability, version comparability, historical environment preservation, point-in-time environment reconstruction, and environment-version lifecycle continuity. Module Operational Scope SEVM applies wherever a change in the Simulation Environment may materially alter simulation behavior, execution conditions, comparability, repeatability, interpretation, or resulting Simulation Outputs. It may apply across: engineering simulations, robotics simulations, autonomous-system simulations, AI simulations, digital twins, scientific simulations, industrial simulations, infrastructure simulations, transportation simulations, aerospace simulations, mission simulations, financial simulations, environmental simulations, cyber-physical simulations, multi-agent simulations, distributed simulations, federated simulations, software-in-the-loop environments, hardware-in-the-loop environments, cloud-based simulation platforms, live-system-connected simulations, and future simulation environments. Governance depth should remain proportional to the material effect environment change may have upon the simulation inquiry. Module Function A simulation environment is rarely static. Software changes. Libraries change. Dependencies change. External services change. Hardware changes. Boundary configurations change. Environmental assets change. Parameter baselines change. Models connected to the environment change. If these changes are not version-governed, two executions may appear to use the same simulation while actually operating under materially different conditions. SEVM exists to prevent: unidentified environment versions, silent environment updates, loss of historical configurations, execution against unknown environment states, uncontrolled dependency changes, environment drift, inappropriate comparison across materially different versions, loss of reproducibility, ambiguous rollback, and inability to reconstruct the environment that produced a simulation result. Simulation Environment Version A Simulation Environment Version is an identifiable governed state of the Simulation Environment representing a materially distinguishable configuration applicable during a defined simulation context. Conceptually: Simulation Environment + Governed Configuration State + Version Identity = Simulation Environment Version Version Identity Each materially relevant Simulation Environment Version should be distinguishable. A Version Identity may include: Environment Identifier, Version Identifier, configuration reference, release identifier, activation date, dependency state, parameter baseline reference, boundary configuration reference, and applicable model compatibility. Version Identifier A Version Identifier provides a persistent reference to a specific governed environment state. For example: SEV-1.0 SEV-1.1 SEV-2.0 The numbering mechanism may differ by implementation. The governance requirement is not a particular numbering convention. The requirement is: materially distinguishable environment states must remain distinguishable. Environment Version Composition A Simulation Environment Version may be composed of multiple governed components. Conceptually: Environment Version = Environment Configuration + Dependencies + Boundary Configuration + Parameter Baseline + Relevant Runtime State Where these components have independent versions, their relationships should remain traceable. Composite Version Identity Complex Simulation Environments may require a Composite Version Identity. For example: Environment Version 4.2 may consist of: Simulation Engine 7.1 Physics Library 3.4 Sensor Package 2.8 Weather Model 5.0 Boundary Configuration B12 Parameter Baseline P17 The composite relationship should remain reconstructable where material. Environment Baseline An Environment Baseline establishes an approved reference state of the Simulation Environment. The baseline provides a controlled point against which subsequent change may be evaluated. Conceptually: Baseline Environment → Change → Successor Environment Version Baseline Content A material Environment Baseline may identify: environment structure, software components, dependency versions, relevant hardware, environmental assets, interfaces, boundary configurations, parameter references, runtime configuration, external service dependencies, and other materially relevant environment properties. Baseline ≠ Permanent Environment A baseline is a governed reference state. It does not prohibit change. It makes change visible. Environment Snapshot An Environment Snapshot captures the materially relevant environment state at a defined point in time or execution context. Snapshots may support: forensic reconstruction, repeatability, rollback, comparison, incident analysis, and execution traceability. Snapshot ≠ Version A snapshot records a state. A version represents a governed environment identity. Multiple snapshots may exist within one version where transient runtime state differs without constituting a new governed version. Version Lineage SEVM should preserve the lineage between environment versions. Conceptually: Version 1.0 → Version 1.1 → Version 1.2 → Version 2.0 Lineage allows later determination of: predecessor, successor, change path, branching, rollback, and historical dependency. Version Ancestry Where environments are derived from earlier configurations, ancestry should remain visible. For example: Environment B v1.0 derived from Environment A v3.2 This may be important where assumptions, dependencies, or configuration defects propagate between versions. Environment Version Change An Environment Version Change occurs when a materially relevant property of the governed Simulation Environment changes. Possible changes include: simulation engine update, dependency update, library update, hardware replacement, environment asset change, boundary configuration change, external service change, parameter baseline change, timing-system change, synchronization change, network configuration change, or runtime architecture change. Material Version Change Not every technical modification requires a new governed environment version. The governing question is: Could the change materially affect simulation behavior, execution conditions, repeatability, comparability, interpretation, or reconstruction? If yes, the change should be visible to environment-version governance. Version Change Classification Environment changes may be classified as: Non-Material Minor Material Major Critical or another implementation-specific classification. Classification should reflect simulation consequence rather than software-release terminology alone. No Silent Version Change Principle A materially changed Simulation Environment must not continue to be represented as the same governed environment version merely because the technical system retained the same name or deployment location. Version Differentiation Two environment states should be considered materially different where their differences can materially alter simulation behavior or interpretation. Version differentiation may depend upon: changed dependencies, changed interaction behavior, changed parameterization, changed timing, changed physical components, changed external services, changed environmental assets, or changed runtime conditions. Version Equivalence Two technical environment instances may be treated as version-equivalent only where their materially relevant configuration states are sufficiently equivalent for the simulation inquiry. Technical duplication does not automatically establish governance equivalence. Environment Compatibility A Simulation Environment Version may be compatible only with certain: Simulation Model versions, parameter configurations, boundary configurations, scenario structures, execution engines, hardware, or dependencies. Compatibility should remain identifiable where incompatibility could materially alter execution. Model–Environment Version Compatibility A Simulation Model Version should not be assumed compatible with every Simulation Environment Version. Conceptually: Model Version + Environment Version → Compatibility Status Possible statuses may include: Compatible Conditionally Compatible Incompatible Compatibility Undetermined Dependency Versioning A Simulation Environment may rely upon external or internal dependencies. Examples include: software libraries, physics engines, databases, AI models, APIs, external services, hardware firmware, operating systems, middleware, or communication infrastructure. Material dependency versions should remain identifiable. Dependency Change A dependency change may create a new environment state even where the primary Simulation Environment software remains unchanged. For example: Same Simulation Platform + New Physics Engine = Potentially Different Simulation Environment External Service Version Change External services may change outside direct simulation control. Where such change materially affects simulation behavior, the affected environment state should not remain invisible. SEVM may preserve: External Service Identity → Previous State → Changed State → Affected Environment Version Boundary Configuration Version Relationship SBIM governs Simulation Boundary Interaction. SEVM preserves which governed boundary configuration applied to a particular Simulation Environment Version. Conceptually: Environment Version → Boundary Configuration Reference A material boundary change may therefore require environment-version reassessment. Parameter Configuration Version Relationship SPHM governs Simulation Parameterization. SEVM preserves the applicable Parameter Baseline or configuration relationship where it forms part of the environment version. Conceptually: Environment Version → Parameter Baseline Reference Not every parameter change requires a new Environment Version. But a material baseline-level configuration change may. Version Activation A Simulation Environment Version should have an identifiable activation point where necessary. This allows determination of which version was operational for a specific simulation execution. Version Deactivation When an environment version is no longer approved for new execution, its deactivation should remain distinguishable from deletion. Historical versions may still be required for reconstruction. Version Supersession A new environment version may supersede a prior version. Conceptually: SEV-1.0 → Superseded by → SEV-1.1 Supersession does not erase the historical environment state. Version Freeze A Version Freeze prevents material changes to an environment configuration during a defined simulation campaign, controlled comparison, benchmark, investigation, or validation activity. The purpose is to maintain stable execution conditions. Frozen Environment Principle A frozen Simulation Environment Version must not materially change during the governed freeze period without creating an explicit exception or successor version. Environment Release State An environment version may hold a governed release state such as: Draft Test Approved Active Frozen Deprecated Superseded Archived or another implementation-specific state. Release state should not be confused with validation status. Environment Version ≠ Validation State SEVM identifies and governs Simulation Environment Versions. VALIDOS® governs validation conclusions and Validation States. Therefore: Environment Version 3.0 does not mean: Validated Environment Version 3.0 unless a separate validation process establishes that state. Environment Version Fork A Version Fork occurs when one governed environment state develops into multiple successor configurations. For example: Environment 2.0 ↓ Environment 2.1-A and Environment 2.1-B Forks should preserve common ancestry. Environment Branch Branches may support: experimental environments, alternative configurations, hardware variants, regional configurations, different scenario families, or research variants. A branch should not silently replace the primary environment baseline. Environment Merge Where branches are recombined, the resulting environment should identify the material configuration inherited from each branch. Merge complexity should not destroy version traceability. Environment Rollback A Rollback restores a previous governed environment configuration. Rollback should identify: current version, target version, reason, affected executions, activation point, and any retained changes. Rollback ≠ Erasure A rollback does not erase the intervening version history. Conceptually: V1 → V2 → Rollback to V1-derived state should preserve the existence and use of V2. Environment Restoration Restoration may reconstruct a historical environment for: repeat execution, forensic analysis, validation, comparison, or incident investigation. The restored environment should remain distinguishable from the historical original where differences remain. Restoration Fidelity A restored environment may be: Exact Functionally Equivalent Partially Reconstructed or: Reconstruction Uncertain depending upon what can actually be restored. This distinction should remain explicit. Environment Configuration Drift Environment Configuration Drift occurs where the actual Simulation Environment progressively departs from its governed version or baseline without corresponding version governance. Examples include: silent dependency updates, changed runtime settings, modified hardware, external service changes, unrecorded configuration changes, parameter baseline changes, or altered boundary behavior. Drift Detection SEVM should support detection of material divergence between: Declared Environment Version and: Actual Environment State Declared–Actual Version Consistency A simulation execution should not claim: Environment Version X when the actual materially relevant environment state no longer corresponds to Version X. Version Integrity Interface SEVM does not own general integrity governance. Where preservation, tamper resistance, authenticity, or record integrity requires dedicated controls, INTEGROS® may apply. SEVM governs: which version existed and what it contained. INTEGROS® may govern: whether the relevant version records and artifacts preserved their required integrity. Execution-to-Version Binding Every material Simulation Execution should be bindable to the Simulation Environment Version under which it occurred. Conceptually: Simulation Execution ID → Simulation Environment Version ID This relationship is fundamental to repeatability and interpretation. Execution Environment Record An execution record may preserve: Execution Identifier, Environment Version Identifier, Model Version reference, Parameter Configuration reference, Boundary Configuration reference, dependency state, execution time, and relevant environment snapshot. No Unbound Execution Principle A material Simulation Execution should not produce governable Simulation Output without an identifiable relationship to the Simulation Environment Version under which that execution occurred. Output-to-Version Traceability Downstream Simulation Output should remain traceable to the environment version that contributed to its production. Conceptually: Environment Version → Simulation Execution → Simulation Output SEVM establishes the environment-version side of this chain. Version Comparability Two simulation executions should not be assumed comparable merely because they used the same Simulation Model. Their environment versions may differ. SEVM therefore asks: Are the materially relevant environment conditions sufficiently equivalent for the intended comparison? Version Comparison A Version Comparison may identify: common components, changed components, changed dependencies, changed boundaries, changed parameter baselines, changed runtime conditions, and expected behavioral consequences. Comparability Status Possible statuses may include: Environment-Comparable Conditionally Environment-Comparable Partially Environment-Comparable Not Environment-Comparable or: Environment Comparability Undetermined Version Delta A Version Delta represents the material differences between two Simulation Environment Versions. Conceptually: Version B − Version A = Environment Version Delta The delta may identify: added components, removed components, updated components, dependency changes, boundary changes, parameter baseline changes, runtime changes, and configuration changes. Version Delta Propagation A material Environment Version Delta may affect later SIMULOS® governance spaces. Conceptually: Environment Version Change ↓ Input / Scenario Conditions ↓ Simulation Execution ↓ Simulation Output ↓ Reality Correlation ↓ Simulation Evidence SEVM preserves the version change. Downstream Parent Standards govern their respective consequences. Environment Version Continuity SEVM should preserve the lifecycle: Environment Creation → Baseline → Active Version → Change → Successor Version → Supersession / Branch / Rollback → Archive This allows the environment to remain governable across repeated simulation activity. Historical Environment Preservation Historical environment versions may be necessary to answer: Which environment produced this result? What changed afterward? Could the execution be repeated? Did a later environment update alter behavior? Was the relevant defect present at the time of execution? Point-in-Time Environment State SEVM should support determination of the environment state applicable at a specific point in time. This is particularly important for: incident reconstruction, scientific reproducibility, regulatory review, certification support, validation, dispute resolution, and audit. Point-in-Time Reconstruction A Point-in-Time Reconstruction should establish, where possible: Environment Identity Environment Version Configuration State Dependencies Boundary Configuration Parameter Baseline Runtime State and: Execution Relationship for the relevant time. Environment Version Reconstruction SEVM should enable reconstruction sufficient to answer: Which environment version was active? What did that version contain? Which dependencies were present? Which boundary configuration applied? Which parameter baseline applied? What changed from the previous version? Was the version frozen, active, deprecated, or superseded? Which executions used it? Can the relevant state be restored? Version Traceability A complete version traceability path may be represented as: Simulation Environment ↓ Environment Baseline ↓ Environment Version ↓ Environment Configuration ↓ Dependency State ↓ Boundary Configuration ↓ Parameter Baseline ↓ Simulation Execution ↓ Simulation Output Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Identify the Simulation Environment Establish the governed environment whose versions require control. 2. Establish Environment Version Identity Assign distinguishable version references to materially different environment states. 3. Establish the Environment Baseline Define the controlled reference configuration. 4. Capture Material Version Composition Preserve materially relevant components, dependencies, boundaries, and parameter references. 5. Govern Environment Change Determine whether changes require a successor version or other governed treatment. 6. Preserve Version Lineage Maintain predecessor, successor, branch, merge, rollback, and ancestry relationships. 7. Control Activation, Freeze, Supersession, and Restoration Ensure environment lifecycle states remain explicit. 8. Detect Material Configuration Drift Identify divergence between the declared version and actual environment state. 9. Bind Simulation Execution to Environment Version Preserve the exact environment-version relationship for material executions. 10. Preserve Historical Reconstruction Maintain sufficient information to compare, restore, and reconstruct materially relevant environment states. Governance Outputs SEVM may produce: Simulation Environment Version Identifier, Environment Version Record, Environment Baseline, Environment Snapshot, Environment Version Composition Record, Composite Version Identity, Version Lineage Record, Version Ancestry Record, Environment Version Change Record, Material Change Classification, Environment Version Delta, Environment Version Comparison, Environment Comparability Status, Model–Environment Compatibility Record, Dependency Version Record, External Service Version Record, Boundary Configuration Version Reference, Parameter Baseline Version Reference, Environment Activation Record, Environment Deactivation Record, Version Supersession Record, Version Freeze Record, Environment Release State, Environment Fork Record, Environment Branch Record, Environment Merge Record, Environment Rollback Record, Environment Restoration Record, Restoration Fidelity Record, Environment Configuration Drift Record, Declared–Actual Version Consistency Record, Execution Environment Record, Execution-to-Version Binding, Output-to-Version Traceability Reference, Point-in-Time Environment State, Environment Version Reconstruction Record, Historical Environment Record, and Simulation Environment Version Traceability Map. Use Case 1 — Autonomous Vehicle Simulation Platform Scenario An autonomous vehicle simulation is executed using: Environment Version 4.2 containing a defined physics engine, road environment, sensor emulation system, weather model, dependency set, boundary configuration, and parameter baseline. The physics engine is later updated. Application SEVM evaluates the change as material because vehicle behavior may change. A successor environment becomes: Environment Version 4.3 rather than silently retaining Version 4.2. Result Results generated under 4.2 and 4.3 remain distinguishable, and any comparison can account for the environment change. Use Case 2 — Space Mission Simulation Scenario A mission simulation produces a critical navigation result. Months later, a defect is discovered in a communication-model dependency. Application SEVM traces the affected dependency across environment-version lineage and identifies which executions used the defective version. The historical environment is reconstructed. Result Investigators can determine whether the critical simulation result was produced under the affected environment rather than rerunning the mission unknowingly under a corrected configuration. Use Case 3 — Scientific Climate Simulation Scenario A long-running scientific simulation program produces results across several years. During that period: libraries change, computational infrastructure changes, parameter baselines evolve, and external datasets are updated. Application SEVM preserves distinct governed Simulation Environment Versions and binds each execution to its corresponding environment state. Result Researchers can distinguish scientific differences caused by changed simulation assumptions or scenarios from differences potentially introduced by changes in the Simulation Environment itself. Architectural Position Simulation Environment Versioning is the fifth and final internal governance space of the Simulation Model & Environment Standard (SMES). The complete SMES progression is: Simulation Model Structure → Simulation Environment Configuration → Simulation Boundary Interaction → Simulation Parameterization → Simulation Environment Versioning Together, the five modules establish: what the Simulation Model contains, where it operates, how it interacts across its boundaries, how its configurable properties are instantiated, and: which exact governed environment version exists for simulation execution. Within the broader SIMULOS® lifecycle: Simulation Object → Simulation Purpose & Scope → Reality Representation → Simulation Assumptions → Simulation Model & Environment → Inputs & Data → Scenario Design → Simulation Execution → Simulation Output Governance → Reality Correlation → Simulation Evidence → Validation Interface → Operational Reliance → Drift / Resimulation / Retirement SEVM closes the Simulation Model & Environment governance space and establishes the controlled versioned configuration required before the architecture proceeds into simulation inputs, data, scenarios, and execution. Foundational Principle A simulation result cannot be fully reconstructed or meaningfully compared unless the materially relevant Simulation Environment Version that produced it remains identifiable. Canonical Closing Statement Simulation Environment Versioning Module completes the Simulation Model & Environment Standard by establishing the governed version-control layer through which materially distinct Simulation Environment states remain identifiable across simulation activity. Through environment baselines, version identity, composition, dependency tracking, lineage, change classification, compatibility, activation, freezing, branching, rollback, drift detection, execution binding, comparability, historical preservation, and point-in-time reconstruction, SEVM ensures that changes to the environment cannot silently alter simulation behavior while historical and current executions continue to be represented as if they occurred under the same governed simulation conditions.

title: OOF™ Simulation Exclusion Module (SEXM)
text: OOF™ Simulation Exclusion Module (SEXM) Simulation Exclusion Module (SEXM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard (SPSS) Operational Layer: Simulation Purpose & Scope Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Type: Parent Standard Module Governed Space: Simulation Exclusions Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 16 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Governed Space Simulation Exclusions Canonical Definition Simulation Exclusion Module (SEXM) defines the governance conditions under which simulation-relevant objects, functions, behaviors, interactions, conditions, environments, populations, scenarios, temporal periods, failure modes, capabilities, variables, dependencies, and other material elements are explicitly identified as outside the governed Simulation Scope and preserved as visible limitations of the simulation inquiry. SEXM establishes the formal negative boundary of a simulation: not merely what the simulation covers, but what it does not cover and therefore cannot legitimately be assumed to have simulated. Operational Role SEXM serves as the third internal governance space of the Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard (SPSS). The preceding modules establish: SPM — Why is the simulation being performed? SSCM — What exactly must the simulation cover? SEXM asks: What remains outside that scope, why is it excluded, and what consequences does the exclusion create for simulation interpretation? The governed progression is: Simulation Purpose → Simulation Scope → Candidate Exclusions → Exclusion Classification → Exclusion Justification → Materiality Assessment → Exclusion Consequence → Governed Simulation Exclusions SEXM prevents absence from becoming invisible. Module Operational Space SEXM governs: Simulation Exclusion identification, explicit exclusions, implicit-exclusion detection, object exclusions, component exclusions, functional exclusions, behavioral exclusions, interaction exclusions, environmental exclusions, operational-condition exclusions, spatial exclusions, temporal exclusions, population exclusions, capability exclusions, autonomy exclusions, scenario exclusions, event exclusions, failure-mode exclusions, variable exclusions, dependency exclusions, boundary-condition exclusions, data-related scope exclusions, excluded uncertainty domains, exclusion rationale, exclusion classification, exclusion materiality, exclusion dependencies, exclusion consequences, exclusion conflicts, exclusion change, exclusion traceability, and Simulation Exclusion status. Module Function A simulation can appear broader than it actually is when omitted elements remain undocumented. SEXM exists to prevent: Not Simulated → Not Mentioned → Assumed Covered from becoming an acceptable simulation-governance pathway. Its function is to transform material absence into governed information. The required relationship becomes: Excluded Element → Reason for Exclusion → Materiality → Affected Scope → Interpretive Consequence An exclusion does not automatically make a simulation inadequate. An undisclosed material exclusion may. Simulation Exclusion A Simulation Exclusion is an identifiable simulation-relevant element intentionally or necessarily maintained outside the governed Simulation Scope. An exclusion may concern: part of the Simulation Object, a system function, a behavior, an interaction, an environment, an operating condition, a population, a time period, a scenario, a failure mode, a dependency, or another materially relevant dimension. Positive and Negative Simulation Boundaries SSCM establishes the positive boundary: What is inside the simulation inquiry? SEXM establishes the negative boundary: What is outside the simulation inquiry? Together they create a more complete scope structure: Included Space | Governed Boundary | Excluded Space A simulation boundary is methodologically stronger when both sides are visible. Explicit Exclusion Principle SIMULOS® establishes: A material element outside Simulation Scope should remain explicitly identifiable where its absence could affect interpretation of the simulation or its outputs. Silence is not a sufficient exclusion mechanism. Exclusion Does Not Mean Irrelevance An excluded element may remain operationally important. For example: Snow conditions may be excluded from an autonomous-vehicle simulation because the current simulation campaign addresses dry and rainy environments. This does not establish: Snow is irrelevant. It establishes: Snow is outside the current governed Simulation Scope. Exclusion Classification Simulation Exclusions may be classified according to why they exist. Possible classes include: Purpose-Based Exclusion The element is not required for the governed Simulation Purpose. Scope-Based Exclusion The element falls outside the explicitly approved Simulation Scope. Capability-Based Exclusion The available simulation environment cannot adequately represent the element. Evidence-Based Exclusion Required inputs or supporting information are insufficient. Methodological Exclusion The simulation methodology is not suitable for representing the element. Resource-Based Exclusion The element is omitted because of time, computational, financial, infrastructure, or other resource constraints. Dependency-Based Exclusion The element cannot be simulated because a required dependency is unavailable or unresolved. Uncertainty-Based Exclusion The element cannot be represented with sufficient confidence for the intended inquiry. Regulatory or Governance Exclusion Applicable governance conditions prevent or constrain its inclusion. Deferred Exclusion The element is intentionally reserved for a later simulation cycle. The classification should make clear why the exclusion exists. Intentional Exclusion An Intentional Exclusion is deliberately established before or during simulation planning. Intentional exclusions should remain traceable to their rationale. A deliberate exclusion may be completely legitimate where it is compatible with the Simulation Purpose. Necessary Exclusion A Necessary Exclusion exists where an element cannot reasonably be included under the current simulation conditions. For example: unavailable data, unavailable model capability, unresolved physics, unavailable environmental representation, inaccessible dependencies, or insufficient computational capability. Necessary exclusions remain limitations even when unavoidable. Deferred Exclusion A material element may be excluded from one simulation cycle because it will be addressed separately. For example: Nominal Operation Simulation may precede: Failure & Recovery Simulation The first simulation must not be represented as having covered the deferred failure conditions. Object Exclusion Parts of the Simulation Object may remain outside scope. For example: A spacecraft simulation may include: Guidance + Navigation + Propulsion while excluding: Crew Life-Support Dynamics SEXM preserves that distinction. Functional Exclusion A system may possess functions not examined by the simulation. These functions should remain identifiable where their omission affects interpretation. Behavioral Exclusion Behavioral modes may be excluded. Examples include: degraded behavior, emergency behavior, adversarial behavior, adaptive behavior, rare behavior, or human intervention. Simulation of nominal behavior does not imply simulation of excluded behaviors. Interaction Exclusion A simulation may represent multiple actors while excluding certain interactions among them. This distinction matters because: Objects Represented ≠ All Interactions Represented For example, two autonomous agents may both exist in a simulation while agent-to-agent negotiation remains excluded. Environmental Exclusion Environmental conditions may materially affect simulation outcomes. Possible exclusions include: extreme temperature, rain, snow, radiation, low visibility, high wind, electromagnetic interference, network degradation, terrain classes, or other operational environments. Environmental exclusions should remain connected to output applicability. Operational Condition Exclusion A simulation may cover: Normal Operation while excluding: Emergency Operation or: Maximum Load Conditions Such exclusions must remain visible wherever simulation outputs could otherwise be interpreted more broadly. Spatial Exclusion Simulation applicability may exclude specific geographic, physical, or logical regions. A simulation performed for one operating region must not silently imply coverage of excluded regions. Temporal Exclusion A simulation may exclude: startup periods, long-term degradation, seasonal variation, future system states, specific mission phases, or extended operating durations. A simulation covering short-term behavior cannot establish long-term behavior where long-term dynamics remain excluded. Population Exclusion Where humans, users, agents, organizations, or other populations are relevant, specific groups may remain outside scope. For example: Adult Population Included Pediatric Population Excluded The exclusion must remain visible wherever outputs could otherwise be generalized. Capability Exclusion A simulation of an AI or autonomous system may intentionally exclude capabilities. For example: Navigation Included Autonomous Tool Execution Excluded Simulation results must remain bounded accordingly. Autonomy Exclusion A simulation may examine a system under: Human Supervision while excluding: Fully Autonomous Operation The system's broader technical capability does not remove this exclusion. Scenario Exclusion Not every possible scenario must be simulated. SEXM governs which materially relevant scenario classes remain outside the simulation campaign. Examples may include: rare events, edge cases, adversarial scenarios, extreme-load scenarios, cascading failures, or multi-system emergencies. Failure-Mode Exclusion Failure modes may be excluded from a simulation. Where safety, resilience, recovery, or reliability conclusions are intended, such exclusions may become highly material. SEXM does not determine whether a failure mode must be simulated. It ensures that exclusion remains visible and interpretable. Dependency Exclusion A simulation may exclude a dependency or simplify its role. Examples include: external infrastructure, third-party systems, communications networks, human operators, supply dependencies, external AI services, or environmental dependencies. The excluded dependency may still materially influence real-world behavior. Variable Exclusion Some variables may be held constant, omitted, or intentionally removed from the simulation inquiry. Where the excluded variable could materially affect outcomes, the exclusion should remain explicit. Excluded Uncertainty A simulation may deliberately avoid or defer uncertainty domains that cannot yet be sufficiently represented. SEXM requires such uncertainty exclusions to remain visible rather than being converted into artificial certainty. Implicit Exclusion An Implicit Exclusion exists where an element is outside actual simulation coverage but has not been formally declared outside scope. Implicit exclusions are methodologically dangerous because they can create false assumptions of coverage. Implicit-Exclusion Detection SEXM should support comparison between: Simulation Purpose Governed Simulation Scope Planned Representation Scenario Coverage and: Actual Simulation Coverage to identify material elements that have disappeared without explicit exclusion. Unknown Exclusion Some relevant conditions may not be known when Simulation Scope is established. Where later analysis identifies a previously unknown omitted condition, it should become a governed exclusion, scope gap, or scope-change question rather than remaining invisible. Exclusion Justification Material exclusions should have a documented basis. Possible justifications include: not relevant to current purpose, outside approved scope, separately simulated, technically unavailable, insufficient evidence, insufficient model capability, unacceptable uncertainty, deferred to future simulation, or resource limitation. A justification explains the exclusion. It does not automatically make the exclusion acceptable for every intended interpretation. Exclusion Materiality Not all exclusions have equal significance. An exclusion is material where its absence could reasonably affect: simulation design, output interpretation, comparison, applicability, decision relevance, safety relevance, reliance, or downstream validation. Materiality should be assessed relative to the governed Simulation Purpose and Scope. Material Exclusion A Material Simulation Exclusion is an exclusion capable of changing the meaning, applicability, or interpretation of simulation outputs. Material exclusions should propagate downstream. Non-Material Exclusion An exclusion may be non-material where its absence cannot reasonably affect the governed inquiry. Non-materiality should not be inferred merely because an excluded element produced no observed problem. Exclusion Consequence Each material exclusion should identify the consequence it creates. Possible consequences include: No Material Consequence Interpretation Limitation Applicability Limitation Scenario Limitation Coverage Limitation Representation Limitation Output Qualification Required Additional Simulation Required or: Consequence Undetermined Exclusion Propagation Material exclusions should remain available to downstream SIMULOS® governance. Conceptually: Exclusion → Reality Representation → Assumptions → Model & Environment → Scenario Design → Execution → Output Governance → Reality Correlation This prevents an exclusion declared early in the lifecycle from disappearing before outputs are interpreted. Exclusion Dependency One exclusion may create additional exclusions. For example: External Communication Network Excluded may also require exclusion of: Network-Failure Recovery Behavior where that behavior depends upon representation of the network. SEXM should preserve such dependency chains. Compound Exclusions Several individually limited exclusions may collectively become material. For example: Night Excluded Rain Excluded High-Speed Operation Excluded Emergency Braking Excluded may collectively make a broad claim of: Urban Autonomous Driving Simulation methodologically misleading. SEXM therefore permits cumulative exclusion assessment. Exclusion–Purpose Conflict An Exclusion–Purpose Conflict exists where an excluded element is materially required to answer the governed Simulation Purpose. Example: Simulation Purpose: Evaluate emergency landing safety. Exclusion: Hydraulic failure conditions. If hydraulic failure is materially relevant to emergency landing safety, the exclusion creates a direct purpose conflict. Exclusion–Scope Conflict An exclusion conflicts with Simulation Scope where an element is simultaneously represented as: inside governed scope and: excluded from actual simulation coverage. Such a conflict must be resolved or preserved explicitly as a scope gap. Exclusion Cannot Be Hidden by Abstraction Simplifying a material element through abstraction is not necessarily equivalent to excluding it. However, where abstraction removes the material behavior the inquiry depends upon, the architecture should prevent the simplification from being used to disguise functional exclusion. Reality Representation governance addresses the quality of representation. SEXM governs whether the relevant element is actually inside or outside the simulation inquiry. Exclusion Cannot Become Assumption by Default An excluded element and an assumed condition are not the same governance concept. For example: Wind Excluded is different from: Wind Assumed Constant at 5 m/s The first removes wind dynamics from scope. The second represents wind through an assumption. SEXM preserves this distinction while later Assumption governance governs the assumption itself. Exclusion Cannot Become Validation The fact that an excluded condition was not simulated cannot support a positive conclusion about that condition. SIMULOS® establishes: Not Simulated ≠ Successfully Simulated and: Excluded ≠ Validated No Silent Exclusion Rule A material simulation element must not disappear from the governed inquiry without becoming either explicitly excluded, represented as a scope gap, or returned for scope reassessment. No Exclusion Concealment Rule An exclusion must not be hidden because disclosure would weaken the perceived completeness of a simulation.
