No Convenience Relevance Rule An element must not be declared irrelevant solely because: it is difficult to model, data are unavailable, computation is expensive, the current tool cannot represent it, or its inclusion produces unfavorable outcomes. These conditions may justify exclusion. They do not establish irrelevance. No Exclusion-to-Coverage Conversion Rule A collection of successfully simulated conditions cannot convert excluded conditions into covered conditions. Covered Scope + Excluded Scope ≠ Complete Scope unless the exclusions are genuinely outside the required inquiry. No Retrospective Exclusion Rule A condition must not be retrospectively declared excluded merely because its simulation produced undesirable results. Where a condition was within the governed Simulation Scope during execution, removing it after results are known constitutes a material scope change and must be governed accordingly. No Exclusion Generalization Rule Results obtained inside included conditions must not automatically be generalized to excluded conditions. Exclusion Change Simulation Exclusions may change. An element may move: Excluded → Included or: Included → Excluded Such changes can alter downstream simulation requirements. Exclusion Removal When an excluded element becomes included, its removal from the exclusion set should trigger assessment of whether new: representation, assumptions, model capability, inputs, scenarios, execution, or output interpretation are required. New Exclusion A new exclusion introduced after simulation planning may materially narrow the inquiry. The resulting scope and downstream applicability should be reassessed. Exclusion Status Possible statuses may include: Established Exclusion Conditionally Excluded Deferred Temporarily Excluded Exclusion Under Review Exclusion Conflicted or: Exclusion Undetermined Exclusion Register A governed simulation may maintain a Simulation Exclusion Register. The register may identify: Exclusion ID, excluded element, exclusion class, rationale, affected scope, materiality, dependencies, downstream consequences, status, effective point, and change history. Exclusion Traceability Material exclusions should remain traceable through simulation outputs. A reviewer examining an output should be capable of determining whether a relevant condition was: Included Excluded Not Represented or: Undetermined where that distinction materially affects interpretation. Failure Conditions SEXM governance failure may exist where: material exclusions are undocumented, excluded conditions are represented as simulated, absence is treated as successful coverage, an exclusion conflicts with the Simulation Purpose without disclosure, exclusions conflict with declared Simulation Scope, technical inability is presented as irrelevance, resource constraints are hidden, material excluded dependencies remain invisible, cumulative exclusions materially narrow the simulation without disclosure, excluded populations are generalized into represented populations, excluded operating conditions are treated as covered, retrospective exclusions remove unfavorable results, excluded uncertainty is converted into apparent certainty, exclusions fail to propagate to downstream interpretation, or simulation claims extend into explicitly excluded space. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Identify Excluded Simulation Elements Determine which materially relevant objects, functions, behaviors, conditions, interactions, environments, populations, scenarios, dependencies, and other elements remain outside the governed Simulation Scope. 2. Classify and Justify Exclusions Establish why each material exclusion exists and distinguish purpose-based, capability-based, methodological, resource-based, deferred, dependency-based, and other applicable exclusion classes. 3. Assess Materiality and Consequence Determine whether each exclusion affects simulation coverage, representation, interpretation, applicability, downstream validation, or required additional simulation. 4. Govern Exclusion Dependencies and Change Preserve cumulative exclusions, dependency effects, inclusion/exclusion transitions, conflicts, and material changes. 5. Preserve Exclusion Traceability Maintain a Simulation Exclusion Register and propagate material exclusions into downstream simulation design, execution, outputs, and interpretation. Governance Outputs SEXM may produce: Simulation Exclusion Definition, Simulation Exclusion Register, Simulation Exclusion Record, Exclusion Classification Record, Exclusion Rationale Record, Exclusion Materiality Assessment, Exclusion Consequence Record, Purpose-Based Exclusion Record, Scope-Based Exclusion Record, Capability-Based Exclusion Record, Methodological Exclusion Record, Resource-Based Exclusion Record, Evidence-Based Exclusion Record, Dependency-Based Exclusion Record, Uncertainty-Based Exclusion Record, Deferred Exclusion Record, Object Exclusion Record, Functional Exclusion Record, Behavioral Exclusion Record, Interaction Exclusion Record, Environmental Exclusion Record, Operational Condition Exclusion Record, Spatial Exclusion Record, Temporal Exclusion Record, Population Exclusion Record, Capability Exclusion Record, Autonomy Exclusion Record, Scenario Exclusion Record, Failure-Mode Exclusion Record, Dependency Exclusion Record, Variable Exclusion Record, Implicit Exclusion Record, Unknown Exclusion Record, Compound Exclusion Assessment, Exclusion–Purpose Conflict Record, Exclusion–Scope Conflict Record, Exclusion Change Record, Exclusion Removal Record, New Exclusion Record, Simulation Exclusion Status, and Simulation Exclusion Traceability Map. Use Case 1 — Autonomous Robot Safety Simulation Scenario A mobile industrial robot is simulated to examine collision avoidance within a warehouse. The simulation covers: normal warehouse traffic, human workers, standard lighting, and: defined operating speeds. It does not represent emergency power loss, smoke-obscured sensors, or operation outside the warehouse. Application SEXM formally establishes these as Simulation Exclusions. Emergency power loss is classified as a Deferred Exclusion scheduled for a separate safety simulation. Smoke-obscured perception is classified as a Capability-Based Exclusion because the current environment cannot adequately represent the sensor degradation. Outdoor operation is a Purpose-Based Exclusion because it falls outside the governed Simulation Purpose. Result The simulation may support interpretation within its governed warehouse conditions. It cannot legitimately be presented as comprehensive simulation of the robot across emergency, degraded-visibility, and outdoor environments. Use Case 2 — Spacecraft Mission Simulation Scenario A spacecraft simulation examines orbital insertion and autonomous navigation. Solar radiation effects are simplified, crew behavior is excluded, and one rare propulsion-failure mode is not represented because the required physical model is unavailable. Application SEXM distinguishes the three conditions. Simplified solar radiation remains inside the simulation and is governed through Reality Representation and Assumption governance. Crew behavior is an explicit Scope Exclusion. The propulsion failure becomes a Capability-Based Material Exclusion because the simulation environment cannot currently represent it. Result The architecture prevents all three conditions from being treated identically. The simulation record can distinguish: represented through simplification, explicitly excluded, and: materially excluded because simulation capability is insufficient. This distinction remains available when simulation outputs are later interpreted. Architectural Position Simulation Exclusion Module (SEXM) is the third internal governance space of the Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard (SPSS). The internal progression is: Simulation Purpose → Simulation Scope → Simulation Exclusions → Simulation Applicability Context → Simulation Depth & Precision SPM establishes why the simulation exists. SSCM establishes what the simulation must cover. SEXM establishes what remains outside that governed inquiry and what consequences follow from that absence. The subsequent modules determine where the resulting simulation is contextually applicable and how deeply and precisely the simulation must represent the intended inquiry. SEXM does not govern general integrity under INTEGROS®, Validation Scope under VALIDOS®, actual Operational Reality under ORA™, or the fidelity of Reality Representation under RRS. It governs specifically: the explicit negative boundary of the simulation inquiry. Foundational Principle A simulation is governed not only by what it includes, but by whether everything materially excluded from the inquiry remains visible wherever that absence can affect the meaning of its results. Canonical Closing Statement Simulation Exclusion Module (SEXM) establishes the negative boundary of governed simulation by identifying, classifying, justifying, assessing, and preserving the objects, functions, behaviors, interactions, environments, populations, scenarios, failure modes, dependencies, uncertainties, and other material elements that remain outside Simulation Scope. Through explicit exclusion governance, materiality assessment, dependency mapping, anti-concealment rules, change control, exclusion propagation, and complete traceability, SEXM prevents unmodeled conditions from becoming invisible assumptions of coverage and prevents simulation results from expanding into conditions that were never simulated. By making absence itself governable, SEXM ensures that the limitations of a simulation remain as structurally visible as the conditions it successfully represents.

title: OOF™ Simulation Input Identification Module (SIIM)
text: OOF™ Simulation Input Identification Module (SIIM) Simulation Input Identification Module (SIIM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Simulation Input & Data Standard (SIDS) Operational Layer: Simulation Input & Data Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Type: Parent Standard Module Governed Space: Simulation Input Identification Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 18 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Governed Space Simulation Input Identification Canonical Definition Simulation Input Identification Module (SIIM) defines the governance framework through which every materially relevant data object, value, signal, measurement, state, distribution, event, record, synthetic input, derived input, human-supplied input, model-generated input, or other information capable of influencing a simulation is identified, classified, distinguished, source-referenced, bound to its simulation role, and maintained as a traceable Simulation Input. SIIM establishes the first internal governance space of SIDS by determining what is entering the simulation before questions of representativeness, transformation, temporal applicability, and uncertainty are evaluated. Operational Role SIIM serves as the first internal governance space of the Simulation Input & Data Standard (SIDS). The preceding Parent Standard, Simulation Model & Environment Standard (SMES), establishes the controlled model and environment through which simulation occurs. SIIM asks: What information is proposed to enter that governed simulation structure, what exactly is each input, where does it originate, and what role can it influence? The governed progression is: Governed Simulation Model & Environment → Input Requirement → Proposed Input → Input Identification → Input Classification → Origin Reference → Simulation Role Binding → Simulation Input Register The resulting identified input basis becomes available to the subsequent SIDS modules for representativeness, transformation, temporal, and uncertainty governance. Module Operational Space SIIM governs: simulation input discovery, input identification, input naming, input distinction, input classification, input origin reference, source association, input type, input format, input unit, input semantics, input state, input role, input ownership reference where relevant, observed inputs, measured inputs, historical inputs, live inputs, derived inputs, estimated inputs, synthetic inputs, human-supplied inputs, externally supplied inputs, model-generated inputs, scenario-specified inputs, input-to-object binding, input-to-model binding, input-to-environment binding, input-to-configuration binding, input-to-scenario reference, input dependencies, composite inputs, duplicate inputs, ambiguous inputs, unidentified inputs, input substitution visibility, input-set membership, input identifiers, and input traceability. Module Function SIIM exists to prevent a simulation from consuming materially influential information whose identity or role is unclear. It prevents: unidentified inputs entering simulation execution, ambiguous variables being treated as equivalent, different data objects sharing an indistinguishable identity, source origin disappearing after ingestion, synthetic information appearing as observed information, derived information appearing as directly measured information, historical information appearing as live information, units or semantics becoming detached from values, input roles becoming unclear, substitutions occurring invisibly, input dependencies being hidden, and simulation outputs becoming impossible to reconstruct because the actual consumed inputs cannot be determined. Simulation Input A Simulation Input is any identifiable information object capable of materially influencing: simulation initialization, model behavior, environmental state, actor behavior, state transitions, simulation progression, scenario conditions, or simulation outputs. A Simulation Input may be: Data Value Signal Measurement State Event Distribution Record Sequence Instruction External Observation Synthetic Information or another governed information object consumed by the simulation. Material Input SIIM focuses on material Simulation Inputs. An input is material where changing, removing, substituting, or misidentifying it could materially affect: simulation configuration, simulation behavior, scenario conditions, execution, output, interpretation, or downstream reliance. Not every technical field requires equal governance depth. Input Requirement Before an input is identified, the simulation may establish an Input Requirement. An Input Requirement defines what information the simulation needs without presupposing which specific data object will satisfy that need. For example: Requirement: Current external temperature may later be satisfied by: Sensor TEMP-04 measurement This distinction prevents the required information from being confused with the particular source selected to provide it. Input Identification Every material Simulation Input should be sufficiently identifiable before governed simulation use. Identification may establish: Simulation Input Identifier, input name, input description, input type, input origin, source reference, unit, format, semantic meaning, temporal reference where known, transformation state, applicable Simulation Object, applicable model or environment element, and intended simulation role. Simulation Input Identifier A Simulation Input Identifier provides a persistent reference through which a material input can remain distinguishable throughout the simulation lifecycle. Conceptually: SI-0001 may identify one governed input object. The identifier should remain connected to the actual input rather than merely to a display label. Identity ≠ Variable Name SIMULOS® establishes: A variable name is not sufficient input identity where materially different information can exist under that same name. For example: Temperature could refer to: external temperature, engine temperature, battery temperature, historical average temperature, predicted temperature, or synthetic scenario temperature. SIIM requires sufficient distinction. Input Naming Input names should communicate the represented information with enough specificity to prevent material ambiguity. Where necessary: Temperature should become: External Ambient Temperature or another sufficiently precise representation. Naming alone does not establish full identity, but poor naming can weaken traceability. Input Semantics SIIM governs what the input means, not only how it is technically encoded. For example: 0.75 may represent: 75% probability, normalized sensor output, friction coefficient, model confidence, actuator position, or another quantity. The numerical value alone is insufficient. Input Units Where units materially affect interpretation, they must remain associated with the input. For example: 50 is not a sufficiently defined physical input if it could mean: 50 km/h 50 mph 50 °C or: 50 milliseconds. Input Format Input format may include: scalar, vector, matrix, categorical value, time series, event stream, image, audio, text, geospatial data, structured record, distribution, or another machine- or human-readable form. Format should remain identifiable where it affects simulation interpretation. Input Classification SIIM classifies Simulation Inputs according to their material origin and role. Possible classes include: Observed Input Information obtained through observation of represented reality. Measured Input Information produced through a measurement process. Historical Input Information originating from a previous period. Live Input Information supplied from an active operational environment during or near simulation execution. Estimated Input Information established through estimation where direct measurement or observation is unavailable. Derived Input Information calculated from other information objects. Synthetic Input Information generated rather than directly observed from the represented reality. Human-Supplied Input Information introduced by a human participant or operator. Externally Supplied Input Information supplied by an external organization, system, service, or data provider. Model-Generated Input Information produced by another model and consumed by the simulation. Scenario-Specified Input Information deliberately introduced to establish a scenario condition. One input may require multiple classifications where its provenance or role is composite. Classification Must Follow Reality SIMULOS® establishes: Input classification must describe how the information was actually produced, not how the simulation wishes to interpret it. A model-generated estimate does not become a measured input merely because it is formatted like sensor data. Input Origin Input Origin identifies the point from which the information entered the governed simulation chain. Origin may refer to: sensor, database, organization, person, operational system, AI system, external model, simulator, scientific instrument, historical dataset, synthetic generator, or another identifiable origin. Origin ≠ Reliability SIIM identifies origin. It does not establish that the origin is reliable. Source reliability may require governance under VALIDOS® or another applicable architecture. The distinction is important: Known Origin ≠ Trusted Origin Origin Preservation Where materially relevant, origin should remain attached throughout: Origin → Input → Transformation → Simulation Use Subsequent transformation should not silently erase the origin of the information. Source Reference An input may maintain a reference to the source object or system from which it originates. The source reference may include: source identifier, system identifier, dataset identifier, sensor identifier, provider identifier, model identifier, or another persistent reference. Input State An input may exist in different states. For example: Raw Cleaned Normalized Aggregated Derived Imputed Synthetic or: Transformed SIIM identifies the state. SDTM — Simulation Data Transformation Module governs the transformation itself. Raw Input A Raw Simulation Input is information before simulation-specific transformation. Raw does not mean: correct, reliable, representative, complete, or suitable. It only describes its position relative to subsequent processing. Derived Input A Derived Input should preserve the relationship: Source Input(s) → Derivation → Derived Input SIIM identifies the resulting object as derived. SDTM governs the methodological transformation. Synthetic Input Identification Synthetic inputs must remain distinguishable from directly observed or measured information. SIMULOS® establishes: Synthetic information must never acquire an observed-data identity merely because it is technically indistinguishable in format. Estimated Input Identification Estimated values should remain identifiable as estimates. For example: Estimated Vehicle Mass = 1,850 kg should not silently become: Measured Vehicle Mass = 1,850 kg after ingestion. Live vs Historical Input SIIM distinguishes whether information originates from: current or near-current operational conditions or: historical records. Detailed temporal suitability is governed by STDM — Simulation Temporal Data Module. SIIM preserves the initial classification required for that assessment. Input Role An input should remain connected to the role it performs in the simulation. Possible roles include: initialization, state update, environmental condition, actor condition, control signal, disturbance, behavioral input, scenario condition, external event, calibration reference, or another defined simulation function. Input-to-Simulation Object Binding Where relevant: Simulation Input → Simulation Object should remain identifiable. This prevents inputs associated with one Simulation Object from being silently applied to another. Input-to-Model Binding Where an input affects a specific model component: Simulation Input → Model Component should remain traceable. This supports later analysis of which information could have influenced which simulated behavior. Input-to-Environment Binding Inputs affecting environmental conditions should preserve: Simulation Input → Environment Element / State For example: Rainfall Input → Road Surface Environment State Input-to-Configuration Binding Where an input is valid only under a particular simulation configuration, that relationship should remain visible. Input-to-Scenario Reference An input may be associated with one or more scenarios. SIIM records the association where known. SSS — Simulation Scenario Standard governs scenario design and coverage. Input Dependency One input may depend upon another. For example: Vehicle Speed may contribute to: Calculated Braking Distance Input The dependency should remain visible where it materially affects traceability. Composite Input A Composite Input combines multiple information objects into one simulation-consumed input. Conceptually: Input A + Input B + Input C → Composite Input D The composite should not erase the identities of its materially relevant components. Duplicate Input Two technically separate inputs may represent the same underlying information. Duplicate inputs can create: double counting, unintended weighting, correlated influence, or false independence. SIIM identifies material duplication for subsequent treatment. Ambiguous Input An Ambiguous Simulation Input exists where the available information is insufficient to determine exactly: what the input represents, where it originated, which unit applies, which object it describes, or which role it performs. Material ambiguity should be resolved or explicitly preserved before simulation use. Unidentified Input An Unidentified Simulation Input is a materially influential input whose identity cannot be sufficiently established. Possible treatment may include: Resolve Restrict Exclude or: Escalate for further assessment depending upon the simulation context. No Anonymous Material Input Principle SIMULOS® establishes: A materially influential input should not enter governed simulation execution anonymously. Input Equivalence Two inputs should not be considered equivalent merely because: their values match, their names match, their formats match, or they occupy the same software field. Input equivalence may depend upon: semantics, origin, unit, population, environment, time, transformation, and simulation role. Input Substitution An identified input may later be substituted. For example: Live Sensor Input may be replaced with: Historical Replay Input The replacement should receive its own identity and classification. The simulation record should preserve: Original Intended Input → Substitution → Actual Consumed Input Actual Consumed Input SIIM distinguishes: Planned Input from: Actual Consumed Input. This distinction becomes critical when execution does not consume exactly what was originally configured. Input Set Membership Each material Simulation Input may belong to one or more governed Simulation Input Sets. Conceptually: Simulation Input Set SIS-001 may contain: SI-001 + SI-002 + SI-003 + SI-004 Input-set governance enables reconstruction of the complete information basis of an execution. Input Set Identifier A Simulation Input Set may receive a persistent identifier. This allows: Execution → Input Set → Individual Inputs to remain traceable. Input Set Composition The composition of an Input Set should identify materially relevant: inputs, input versions, classifications, states, source references, and applicable simulation configuration. Input Version Distinction Where materially changed information exists under the same logical input identity, versions should remain distinguishable. For example: Weather Dataset v3 should not silently overwrite: Weather Dataset v2 where previous executions relied upon v2. Input Change A material input may change because: source data changes, values change, origin changes, classification changes, format changes, unit changes, derivation changes, or its simulation role changes. The changed input should remain distinguishable from the previous state where required for reconstruction. Input Identity Continuity Input Identity Continuity preserves the relationship between successive states or versions of the same logical input. Conceptually: SI-001 v1 → SI-001 v2 → SI-001 v3 while preventing materially different objects from being falsely treated as one unchanged input. Point-in-Time Input Identity SIIM supports reconstruction of: Which exact input existed at the time of a particular simulation execution? This is essential where input data changes after execution. No Retrospective Input Replacement Principle SIMULOS® establishes: Updating an input must not silently rewrite the historical input identity of completed simulation executions. Input Traceability SIIM establishes the traceability foundation: Input Requirement ↓ Simulation Input ↓ Origin / Source Reference ↓ Classification ↓ Simulation Role ↓ Model / Environment / Scenario Binding ↓ Input Set ↓ Simulation Execution Reference This chain enables later governance of simulation behavior and outputs. Input Identification Status A material Simulation Input may receive an identification status such as: Identified Conditionally Identified Ambiguous Unidentified Superseded or: Excluded The status concerns input identity. It does not establish representativeness, temporal suitability, uncertainty, or general validity. Identification Sufficiency Input identification is sufficient when the information necessary to distinguish and trace the material input is adequate for its intended simulation role. The required identification depth may vary with: simulation consequence, input influence, system complexity, simulation purpose, and downstream reliance. Identification Failure An Input Identification Failure occurs where a material input cannot be sufficiently distinguished or traced for governed use. Possible causes include: missing origin, ambiguous semantics, unknown units, indistinguishable versions, undocumented substitution, unknown derivation, or inability to determine the actual consumed input. Identification Failure ≠ Data Invalidity Failure to identify an input sufficiently does not prove the underlying information is false. It establishes that the information cannot currently support the required level of governed simulation traceability. Simulation Input Register SIIM may maintain a Simulation Input Register containing material Simulation Inputs and their governance attributes. A register entry may contain: Simulation Input Identifier, input name, description, classification, origin, source reference, unit, format, semantic definition, input state, simulation role, applicable object, model binding, environment binding, scenario reference, input-set membership, version, and identification status. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Identify Input Requirements Determine which information the governed simulation requires. 2. Discover Material Proposed Inputs Identify all materially influential information proposed for simulation use. 3. Assign Simulation Input Identity Create a persistent identifier for each material input where appropriate. 4. Define Input Meaning Record sufficient: name, semantics, unit, format, and represented quantity or state. 5. Classify Input Origin and Type Determine whether the input is: observed, measured, historical, live, estimated, derived, synthetic, human-supplied, externally supplied, model-generated, scenario-specified, or another defined class. 6. Preserve Origin and Source Reference Bind the input to its identifiable origin and source where available. 7. Bind the Input to Simulation Role Establish which: Simulation Object, model component, environment element, configuration, or scenario context the input may influence. 8. Identify Dependencies and Composite Inputs Preserve material relationships between inputs. 9. Detect Ambiguity, Duplication, and Substitution Identify materially unclear, duplicated, replaced, or unexpectedly consumed inputs. 10. Establish Input Set Membership Bind the identified inputs to the applicable Simulation Input Set. 11. Assign Identification Status Determine whether each material input is sufficiently identified for further SIDS governance. 12. Preserve Input Traceability Maintain the chain from input requirement and origin through simulation role and eventual execution use. Governance Outputs SIIM may produce: Simulation Input Requirement Record, Simulation Input Identifier, Simulation Input Record, Simulation Input Classification, Simulation Input Origin Record, Simulation Input Source Reference, Simulation Input Semantic Definition, Simulation Input Unit Record, Simulation Input Format Record, Simulation Input State Record, Simulation Input Role Record, Input-to-Simulation Object Binding, Input-to-Model Binding, Input-to-Environment Binding, Input-to-Configuration Binding, Input-to-Scenario Reference, Simulation Input Dependency Map, Composite Input Record, Duplicate Input Record, Ambiguous Input Record, Unidentified Input Record, Synthetic Input Identification Record, Derived Input Identification Record, Estimated Input Identification Record, Input Substitution Record, Actual Consumed Input Record, Simulation Input Set, Simulation Input Set Identifier, Input Set Composition Record, Input Version Record, Input Identity Continuity Record, Point-in-Time Input Identity Record, Input Identification Status, Input Identification Failure Record, Simulation Input Register, and Simulation Input Traceability Map. Use Case 1 — Autonomous Vehicle Simulation Scenario An autonomous vehicle simulation consumes: camera data, radar measurements, weather information, road geometry, vehicle state, synthetic pedestrian behavior, and traffic signals. Application SIIM identifies each material input and distinguishes: Measured Radar Input from: Synthetic Pedestrian Input and: Historical Weather Dataset from: Current Vehicle-State Input. Each input is bound to the relevant model or environment component. Result The simulation possesses an identifiable input basis before representativeness, transformation, temporal applicability, and uncertainty are assessed. Use Case 2 — Spacecraft Landing Simulation Scenario A spacecraft landing simulation uses: terrain elevation data, gravitational model outputs, estimated atmospheric density, vehicle telemetry, engine-performance measurements, and synthetic failure conditions. Application SIIM identifies the origin, classification, meaning, units, and simulation role of each material input. The module prevents: Estimated Atmospheric Density from becoming indistinguishable from: Direct Atmospheric Measurement and preserves synthetic failure conditions as synthetic inputs. Result Every materially influential input can be traced to its origin and simulation role, providing a controlled basis for subsequent SIMULOS® input governance. Architectural Position Simulation Input Identification is the first internal governance space of the Simulation Input & Data Standard (SIDS). The complete SIDS progression is: Simulation Input Identification ↓ Simulation Data Representativeness ↓ Simulation Data Transformation ↓ Simulation Temporal Data ↓ Simulation Input Uncertainty SIIM therefore establishes the identity layer upon which all subsequent SIDS governance depends. Representativeness cannot be meaningfully assessed until the input being assessed is known. Transformation cannot be governed unless the source and resulting input can be distinguished. Temporal applicability cannot be evaluated without an identifiable information object. Input uncertainty cannot remain attached to an input whose identity is unstable. Foundational Principle A simulation cannot govern the suitability of information it cannot first identify, distinguish, classify, and trace to the role through which that information can influence simulated behavior. Canonical Closing Statement Simulation Input Identification Module establishes the identity and traceability foundation of the Simulation Input & Data Standard by governing how materially influential data, values, signals, measurements, states, distributions, events, synthetic information, derived information, and other simulation inputs are discovered, identified, classified, source-referenced, distinguished, versioned, bound to their simulation roles, assembled into controlled Input Sets, and preserved across execution history. Through explicit separation of observed, measured, estimated, derived, synthetic, historical, live, human-supplied, externally supplied, model-generated, and scenario-specified information, SIIM prevents anonymous, ambiguous, substituted, or semantically unclear inputs from silently entering governed simulation activity and establishes the traceability basis required for representativeness, transformation, temporal, uncertainty, execution, and downstream simulation governance.

title: OOF™ Simulation Instantiation Module (SIM)
text: OOF™ Simulation Instantiation Module (SIM) Simulation Instantiation Module (SIM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Simulation Execution Standard (SES) Operational Layer: Simulation Execution Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Type: Parent Standard Module Governed Space: Simulation Instantiation Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 19 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Governed Space Simulation Instantiation Canonical Definition Simulation Instantiation Module (SIM) defines the governance framework through which a governed simulation specification is transformed into a specific executable Simulation Instance by binding the applicable Simulation Object, object version, model, environment, scenario, inputs, parameters, dependencies, randomization state, execution infrastructure, and other materially relevant conditions into an identifiable execution configuration before simulation activity begins. SIM establishes the first internal governance space of the Simulation Execution Standard (SES). Its purpose is to ensure that: what was designed to be simulated can be distinguished from: what was actually assembled for execution. SIM therefore establishes the exact governed starting configuration from which subsequent Simulation Execution Control, Observation, Repetition, and Documentation proceed. Operational Role The preceding Simulation Scenario Standard (SSS) establishes: which materially relevant conditions should be simulated. SIM receives that governed scenario basis and asks: What exact executable simulation instance has now been assembled from the approved simulation components and conditions? The governed progression is: Governed Simulation Basis ↓ Execution Requirement ↓ Simulation Instance Creation ↓ Object Binding ↓ Model & Environment Binding ↓ Scenario Binding ↓ Input & Parameter Binding ↓ Dependency & Infrastructure Binding ↓ Randomization / Initial-State Binding ↓ Instantiation Verification ↓ Executable Simulation Instance ↓ Simulation Execution Control Module Operational Space SIM governs: Simulation Instance identity, Simulation Execution identity initialization, instantiation requirements, Simulation Object binding, object-version binding, model binding, model-version binding, environment binding, environment-version binding, scenario binding, scenario-version binding, input-set binding, input-version binding, parameter binding, parameter-baseline binding, assumption reference binding where material, dependency binding, software dependency binding, external-service binding, hardware binding, runtime binding, infrastructure binding, configuration binding, randomization binding, seed binding, initial-state binding, initial-condition binding, actor-population binding, agent-state binding, temporal starting-state binding, execution-resource binding, execution authorization reference, instantiation consistency, intended-versus-instantiated configuration comparison, configuration conflict identification, missing-component identification, unexpected-component identification, instantiation completeness, instantiation status, instantiation versioning, and Simulation Instance traceability. Module Function SIM exists because a simulation may be perfectly designed at the architectural level while the actual executable instance differs materially from that design. Possible causes include: wrong model version, wrong environment version, outdated Scenario Set, wrong Input Set, missing dependency, incorrect parameter baseline, unexpected default values, changed software library, changed hardware, unavailable external service, wrong randomization configuration, incorrect initial state, different agent population, unrecorded infrastructure change, or manual configuration error. SIM prevents those differences from remaining invisible. Simulation Specification ≠ Simulation Instance SIMULOS® establishes a fundamental distinction: Simulation Specification describes the governed simulation that is intended to be executable. Simulation Instance represents the exact materially relevant configuration actually assembled for a particular execution. Therefore: Intended Configuration ≠ Instantiated Configuration by default. The relationship must be established. Simulation Instance A Simulation Instance is the identifiable and execution-ready realization of a governed simulation configuration assembled for one Simulation Execution or defined group of executions. Conceptually: Simulation Object Model Environment Scenario Inputs Parameters Dependencies Initial State Execution Infrastructure = Simulation Instance Simulation Instance Identity Every materially relevant Simulation Instance should be sufficiently identifiable. The identity may include: Simulation Instance ID, planned Execution ID, Simulation Object ID, object version, model version, environment version, Scenario ID, Scenario Set version, Input Set ID, parameter baseline, randomization configuration, dependency state, execution infrastructure, instantiation timestamp, and instantiation status. Instance Identity ≠ Scenario Identity A Scenario identifies the condition intended for examination. A Simulation Instance identifies the complete executable realization of that Scenario under a particular technical and governed configuration. One Scenario may therefore produce many Simulation Instances. For example: Scenario S-021 may be instantiated as: Instance I-021-A Instance I-021-B Instance I-021-C under different: model versions, random seeds, Input Sets, environments, or execution infrastructures. Execution Requirement Instantiation should begin from an identifiable Execution Requirement. The requirement may originate from: Scenario Set, simulation campaign plan, validation requirement, engineering inquiry, autonomous follow-up simulation, incident analysis, stress escalation, scenario discovery, or another governed simulation need. The requirement should make clear: Why is this simulation instance being created? Instantiation Requirement An Instantiation Requirement defines which governed components must be assembled before execution can begin. This may include mandatory: object version, model version, environment version, scenario, Input Set, parameters, dependencies, initial conditions, and runtime conditions. Object Binding Every Simulation Instance should remain bound to the exact Simulation Object it represents. Conceptually: Simulation Instance → Simulation Object ID → Object Version This prevents an execution associated with one object version from later being interpreted as if it represented another. Object-Version Binding Where the Simulation Object changes materially, the applicable instance should identify which object version was instantiated. For example: Spacecraft Configuration v4.2 must remain distinguishable from: Spacecraft Configuration v4.3. No Object Substitution Principle SIMULOS® establishes: A simulation execution must not silently substitute a materially different Simulation Object version while preserving the identity of the original execution basis. Model Binding A Simulation Instance should identify the exact Simulation Model configuration used. This may include: model identifier, model version, component versions, active model modules, enabled capabilities, model configuration, and relevant model dependencies. Model-Version Binding Where multiple model versions exist, a Simulation Instance should not rely solely upon the statement: “Latest model used.” It should preserve the exact version instantiated. No Latest-Version Ambiguity Principle SIMULOS® establishes: A dynamically changing reference such as “latest” is insufficient where exact model identity materially affects execution reconstruction. Environment Binding The Simulation Instance should identify the exact governed Simulation Environment in which the execution is instantiated. This includes the environment version established under SMES. Conceptually: Simulation Instance → Simulation Environment Version Environment Configuration Binding Materially relevant environment attributes may include: environment version, simulation engine, runtime configuration, physics engine, network model, terrain state, environmental model, agent environment, external interfaces, and dependency state. Scenario Binding Every Simulation Instance should bind to the Scenario or Scenario Configuration it is intended to execute. Conceptually: Simulation Instance → Scenario ID → Scenario Version Scenario Configuration Binding Where the Scenario contains variation, edge-case, or stress configurations, the instance should preserve the exact applicable configuration. For example: Scenario: Autonomous Recovery Variation: Communication Delay = 8 s Edge: Power near autonomy-transition threshold Stress: Navigation uncertainty elevated These are materially different from the generic Scenario identity alone. No Generic-Scenario Binding Principle SIMULOS® establishes: Binding an execution only to a broad Scenario name is insufficient where materially relevant Scenario Variation, Edge, or Stress conditions determine execution behavior. Input Set Binding Every materially relevant Simulation Instance should identify the Input Set it will consume. Conceptually: Simulation Instance → Input Set ID → Input Versions This preserves the SIDS governance basis established before execution. Input Version Binding Where inputs change over time, the instance should preserve the exact versions selected. A new dataset must not silently replace the dataset originally intended for a historical execution. Input Availability Check Instantiation may identify whether required inputs are: Available Conditionally Available Substituted Missing or: Unavailable. Material input absence should be resolved before execution or preserved as an explicit Instantiation Deviation. Input Substitution at Instantiation Where an intended input is unavailable and another is substituted, the relationship should remain visible. Conceptually: Required Input A ↓ Unavailable ↓ Substituted Input B ↓ Instantiation Deviation / Approved Substitution The substitute does not become the originally required input merely because execution proceeds successfully. Parameter Binding A Simulation Instance should preserve the applicable parameter configuration established under SMES and the relevant Scenario Variation. Parameter binding may include: baseline parameters, Scenario parameters, control parameters, runtime limits, threshold values, physical constants, behavioral parameters, and configuration switches. Default Parameter Governance Simulation software may contain default values. SIM establishes: A default value is still part of the instantiated configuration where it can materially influence execution. Material defaults should not disappear merely because they were not manually entered. No Invisible Default Principle SIMULOS® establishes: A simulation must not treat materially influential default configuration as if no configuration decision existed. Assumption Reference Binding SAS governs Simulation Assumptions. SIM does not re-govern those assumptions. Where an assumption materially conditions execution, however, the Simulation Instance may preserve a reference to the applicable assumption basis. Dependency Binding Simulation execution may depend upon external or internal systems including: libraries, APIs, databases, AI models, services, operating systems, middleware, simulation engines, communication services, external models, or hardware. SIM should bind material dependencies to the Simulation Instance. Dependency State A dependency may be: Available Degraded Restricted Emulated Substituted Unavailable or: Dependency State Undetermined. The instantiated state may materially affect execution. External Service Binding Where execution depends upon an external service, SIM may preserve: service identity, version where available, configuration, API state, endpoint behavior, availability, and relevant execution conditions. No External-Service Assumption Principle SIMULOS® establishes: An external dependency must not be assumed materially unchanged merely because the simulation configuration itself was not modified. Software Binding A Simulation Instance may preserve materially relevant: software build, simulator version, compiler, libraries, runtime, container image, orchestration layer, operating system, or another technical state. SIM does not prescribe how deeply every software component must be recorded. Governance depth should reflect materiality. Hardware Binding Where hardware may materially influence execution, SIM may bind: processor type, accelerator, embedded hardware, sensor emulator, actuator hardware, hardware-in-the-loop component, firmware version, or other physical components. Execution Infrastructure Binding Simulation behavior may depend upon execution infrastructure. Relevant infrastructure may include: workstation, cloud environment, HPC cluster, distributed simulation environment, hardware-in-the-loop bench, robotic test platform, mission simulator, or another execution environment. Infrastructure Identity SIM may preserve: Simulation Instance → Execution Infrastructure ID where infrastructure materially affects timing, performance, determinism, or execution behavior. Randomization Binding Where execution uses randomness, the Simulation Instance should identify the applicable randomization basis where material. This may include: randomization method, seed, sampling distribution, agent initialization, stochastic environment, random event schedule, or other stochastic configuration. Seed Binding Where applicable: Simulation Instance → Random Seed may support later repeatability or diagnostic analysis. Seed governance does not imply that execution will necessarily be perfectly reproducible. Initial-State Binding Simulation behavior frequently depends strongly upon the initial state. SIM therefore governs the explicit binding of materially relevant initial conditions. These may include: system state, environment state, agent state, position, velocity, resource levels, memory state, mission phase, authority state, sensor state, or active dependencies. No Initial-State Neutrality Principle SIMULOS® establishes: Two executions using the same Scenario and Model are not necessarily comparable if their materially relevant initial states differ. Agent-Population Binding Multi-agent simulations may require identification of: number of agents, agent types, agent versions, roles, goals, behavioral configurations, authority relationships, and initial positions or states. Autonomous-Agent State Binding Where autonomous agents contain persistent or adaptive state, the Simulation Instance may need to preserve: memory state, policy version, permission state, tool availability, authority level, active goals, or previous interaction history. This becomes particularly important where nominally identical runs can diverge because agent state differs. Temporal Starting State SIM may establish the temporal position from which the simulation begins. Examples include: mission time, operational time, historical timestamp, relative simulation time, system lifecycle state, or event position. Instantiation Time The time at which the Simulation Instance was created may itself be relevant where: dependencies change, external services change, data update, model versions change, or execution infrastructure is dynamic. Planned vs Actual Instantiation SIM distinguishes: Planned Configuration from: Instantiated Configuration. The two should be compared before execution where material. Instantiation Delta An Instantiation Delta represents the material difference between the intended simulation configuration and the configuration actually assembled. Conceptually: Actual Instantiated Configuration − Intended Configuration = Instantiation Delta Instantiation Delta Examples A delta may include: different model version, changed environment, substituted Input Set, parameter difference, missing dependency, different seed, infrastructure change, altered agent population, different initial state, or unexpected software version. Instantiation Delta Status A material Instantiation Delta may be: Accepted Conditionally Accepted Requires Correction Requires Reauthorization Execution-Blocking or: Undetermined. No Silent Delta Principle SIMULOS® establishes: A material difference between intended and instantiated configuration must not disappear merely because the simulation is technically capable of running. Configuration Conflict A Configuration Conflict exists where two required simulation components impose incompatible conditions. Examples include: Scenario requires Model v4 but environment supports only Model v3, Input Set uses units incompatible with the selected model, parameter configuration violates environment limits, hardware version does not support the required execution state, or scenario assumes a dependency that is unavailable. Conflict Resolution A Configuration Conflict may be: Resolved Conditionally Resolved Accepted as Limitation Execution-Blocking or: Unresolved. The resolution should remain traceable where material. Missing Instantiation Component A required component may be absent. Examples include: missing input, missing parameter, unavailable dependency, absent model module, missing environment element, or unresolved initial state. No Missing-to-Default Principle SIMULOS® establishes: A required but missing instantiation component must not silently become a default configuration unless that substitution is itself governed. Unexpected Instantiation Component A component may appear in the assembled Simulation Instance despite not being part of the intended basis. Examples include: automatically loaded library, inherited configuration, persistent agent memory, cached state, environment plugin, external tool, or additional subsystem. Where materially influential, it should remain visible. Configuration Inheritance Simulation systems may inherit configuration from: templates, previous runs, campaign defaults, environment defaults, user profiles, persistent state, or parent configurations. SIM requires material inherited configuration to remain traceable. No Hidden Inheritance Principle SIMULOS® establishes: Inherited configuration is part of the Simulation Instance where it materially influences execution, even if it was not explicitly selected for the current run. Simulation Instance Completeness Instantiation Completeness asks: Have all materially required components of the intended simulation been sufficiently assembled and identified for execution? Possible statuses may include: Instantiation Complete Conditionally Complete Partially Complete Incomplete or: Instantiation Completeness Undetermined. Instantiation Completeness ≠ Execution Readiness An instance may contain every required component while unresolved: conflicts, authorization, compatibility problems, or blocking deviations still prevent execution. Simulation Instance Readiness A Simulation Instance may receive a readiness status such as: Execution Ready Conditionally Execution Ready Execution Restricted Not Execution Ready or: Execution Readiness Undetermined. Instantiation Verification Before transfer to Simulation Execution Control, SIM should verify that the instantiated configuration sufficiently corresponds to the governed Execution Requirement. Verification may examine: identity, version, compatibility, completeness, dependencies, inputs, parameters, initial state, infrastructure, randomization, and material deltas. Instantiation Verification ≠ Validation Instantiation Verification confirms the consistency of the executable configuration with the governed simulation basis. It does not establish that: the model is valid, the simulation is accurate, the output will be correct, or the system is safe. Instance Freeze Where required, an instantiated configuration may be frozen before execution. An Instance Freeze prevents material configuration change between: Instantiation Verification and: Execution Initiation unless the change is explicitly governed. No Pre-Execution Drift Principle SIMULOS® establishes: A verified Simulation Instance should not materially change before execution without creating an identifiable configuration change or successor instance. Successor Instance Where a material change occurs before execution, the system may create a successor instance. Conceptually: Instance I-001 ↓ Material Configuration Change ↓ Instance I-002 rather than silently modifying I-001. Simulation Instance Versioning A logical Simulation Instance may require version distinction where configuration changes before execution or across campaign preparation. Campaign Instantiation Large-scale Simulation Campaigns may instantiate thousands or millions of related executions. SIM may govern these through: Campaign Configuration Run-Specific Configuration The campaign basis can define common configuration while individual runs preserve material differences. Campaign Template A Simulation Campaign may establish a common template including: model version, environment version, infrastructure, common Input Set, scenario family, parameter ranges, randomization strategy, and logging requirements. Run-Specific Instantiation Each run may then instantiate its own: Scenario configuration, random seed, parameter values, actor population, initial state, or other run-specific attributes. No Campaign-Level Identity Substitution SIMULOS® establishes: A Campaign ID must not replace run-level identity where materially different execution configurations exist inside the campaign. Autonomous Instantiation Simulation Instances may increasingly be created automatically by AI or autonomous systems. For example: Observed Simulation Anomaly ↓ AI identifies unexplored condition ↓ New Scenario Configuration ↓ Autonomous Simulation Instantiation SIM remains applicable. Where material, the instantiation record should preserve: initiating actor/system, selection basis, generated configuration, authorization state, and parent execution relationship. Instantiation Authority A Simulation Instance may be created by: Human Operator Automated Workflow AI System Autonomous Agent Simulation Orchestrator or another authorized actor. The initiating actor does not necessarily own the authority to execute the simulation. Instantiation and execution authorization remain separable. No Autonomous-Origin Opacity Principle SIMULOS® establishes: Automatically generated Simulation Instances must remain traceable to the process or system that generated their material configuration. Instance Parentage A new Simulation Instance may derive from: baseline run, previous execution, failed run, edge-case discovery, stress escalation, scenario expansion, or incident investigation. SIM may preserve: Parent Instance → Derived Instance where this relationship materially explains why the new simulation exists. Instantiation Lineage A lineage may appear as: Baseline Instance ↓ Variation Instance ↓ Edge-Case Instance ↓ Stress Instance ↓ Recovery Instance This provides a structured relationship between related executions. Point-in-Time Reconstruction SIM should allow later questions such as: What exactly was instantiated? Which Simulation Object version was represented? Which model version was loaded? Which environment version was active? Which Scenario configuration applied? Which Input Set was selected? Which parameters and defaults applied? Which dependencies were active? Which seed or randomization state applied? What was the initial state? Which execution infrastructure was selected? Did the actual instance differ from the intended configuration? Instantiation Traceability The complete traceability chain may be represented as: Execution Requirement ↓ Simulation Object ↓ Model ↓ Environment ↓ Scenario ↓ Input Set ↓ Parameters ↓ Dependencies ↓ Initial State ↓ Infrastructure ↓ Randomization State ↓ Simulation Instance ↓ Execution ID Relationship to SOS Simulation Object Standard (SOS) governs the identity and boundary of the Simulation Object. SIM binds the applicable governed Simulation Object to an executable instance. Relationship to SMES Simulation Model & Environment Standard (SMES) governs the model and simulation environment. SIM selects and binds their exact governed versions for execution. Relationship to SIDS Simulation Input & Data Standard (SIDS) governs which inputs may enter the simulation. SIM records which exact governed Input Set is instantiated. Relationship to SSS Simulation Scenario Standard (SSS) governs Scenario Design and Scenario Coverage. SIM transforms a selected governed Scenario configuration into an executable instance. Relationship to SECM SIM ends when a sufficiently governed Simulation Instance is ready for execution. SECM — Simulation Execution Control Module then governs what happens once that instance begins running. The handoff is: Governed Simulation Instance ↓ Simulation Execution Initiation Relationship to INTEGROS® INTEGROS® may govern integrity of: configuration records, instance records, software artifacts, dependencies, or other relevant objects. SIM does not duplicate general integrity governance. Relationship to ADIT® ADIT® may later audit whether the instantiated simulation basis is sufficiently evidenced and traceable. SIMULOS® owns the simulation-specific instantiation process itself. Relationship to VALIDOS® VALIDOS® may later evaluate whether simulation execution and its resulting record can support a Validation Purpose. SIM does not determine validation status. Module Boundary SIM begins when a governed Scenario or Simulation Campaign requires transformation into an actual executable simulation configuration. SIM ends when: the Simulation Instance has an identity, materially relevant components are bound, intended and instantiated configurations are compared, material conflicts and deltas are visible, required dependencies are established, initial state is defined, Instantiation Completeness is assessed, Execution Readiness is established, and the resulting instance can enter Simulation Execution Control. SIM does not govern: active runtime control, observation during execution, repeated execution, final execution documentation, simulation-output interpretation, or validation. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Establish the Execution Requirement Identify the Scenario, campaign, investigation, or other governed basis requiring execution. 2. Create Simulation Instance Identity Assign a persistent Simulation Instance identifier and planned Execution identity. 3. Bind the Simulation Object Identify the exact Simulation Object and version represented by the instance. 4. Bind Model, Environment, Scenario, Inputs, and Parameters Establish the materially relevant governed configuration. 5. Bind Dependencies, Infrastructure, Randomization, and Initial State Record the supporting conditions capable of materially affecting execution. 6. Compare Intended and Instantiated Configuration Identify material Instantiation Deltas, missing components, unexpected components, inherited configuration, and conflicts. 7. Assess Instantiation Completeness Determine whether the materially required configuration has been assembled. 8. Establish Execution Readiness Classify the Simulation Instance as: Execution Ready, Conditionally Execution Ready, Execution Restricted, Not Execution Ready, or Execution Readiness Undetermined. 9. Freeze or Version the Instance Where Required Prevent silent configuration change before execution. 10. Preserve Instantiation Traceability Maintain: Execution Requirement → Simulation Instance → Bound Configuration → Execution ID Governance Outputs SIM may produce: Simulation Instantiation Requirement, Simulation Instance Identifier, Simulation Instance Record, Execution Requirement Record, Object Binding Record, Object-Version Binding, Model Binding Record, Model-Version Binding, Environment Binding Record, Environment-Version Binding, Scenario Binding Record, Scenario-Version Binding, Scenario Configuration Binding, Input Set Binding, Input Version Binding, Parameter Binding Record, Parameter Baseline Binding, Default Parameter Record, Assumption Reference Binding, Dependency Binding Record, External Service Binding, Software Configuration Binding, Hardware Configuration Binding, Execution Infrastructure Binding, Randomization Configuration Record, Seed Binding Record, Initial-State Record, Agent-Population Record, Autonomous-Agent State Record, Temporal Starting-State Record, Instantiation Authority Record, Configuration Inheritance Record, Instantiation Delta, Configuration Conflict Record, Missing Instantiation Component Record, Unexpected Instantiation Component Record, Instantiation Completeness Assessment, Simulation Instance Readiness Status, Instantiation Verification Record, Instance Freeze Record, Successor Instance Record, Simulation Instance Version Record, Campaign Instantiation Record, Run-Specific Instantiation Record, Simulation Instance Parentage Record, Instantiation Lineage Map, and Governed Simulation Instance. Use Case 1 — Autonomous Vehicle Simulation Campaign Scenario An autonomous vehicle company runs a large simulation campaign involving a pedestrian-interaction edge case. The intended configuration specifies: Perception Model v12.4, Environment v7.2, Scenario S-441, defined sensor-noise distribution, mapped pedestrian behavior, and a controlled Input Set. One cluster of executions produces unusually strong collision-avoidance performance. Application SIM reconstructs the instantiated configuration and identifies that the affected runs used: Perception Model v12.5 because the simulation orchestrator automatically loaded the latest available model. All other Scenario identifiers remained unchanged. Result The organization does not mistakenly attribute the behavioral improvement to the Scenario or new control logic. A material Instantiation Delta is identified: Intended Model v12.4 → Instantiated Model v12.5 and affected executions remain separately traceable. Use Case 2 — Spacecraft Mission Simulation Scenario A space organization prepares autonomous recovery simulations for a spacecraft under: communication delay, navigation uncertainty, constrained power, and partial sensor degradation. The mission model and Scenario are correctly defined. However, a critical run uses an updated thermal-environment dependency that differs from the version used in the rest of the campaign. Application SIM binds each execution to: Spacecraft Configuration → Mission Model → Environment → Scenario → Inputs → Dependency State → Initial State → Infrastructure and detects the materially different thermal-model dependency before execution results are aggregated with the broader campaign. Result The organization can distinguish: same mission Scenario from: same executable simulation basis. The run may still be useful, but its configuration difference cannot disappear inside a large Monte Carlo campaign. Use Case 3 — Autonomous AI Agent Simulation Scenario An AI agent is simulated under a scenario involving: restricted tool permissions, delayed external responses, conflicting information, and autonomous task continuation. Two apparently identical executions produce materially different behavior. Application SIM identifies that one Simulation Instance began with: empty agent memory while the second inherited: persistent state from a previous simulation episode. The scenario, model, tools, and explicit parameters were otherwise identical. Result The difference becomes an explicit Initial-State / Configuration Inheritance difference rather than being misclassified as unexplained model nondeterminism. The organization can now determine whether persistent state should be deliberately included, excluded, or separately governed in future executions. Architectural Position Simulation Instantiation Module (SIM) is the first internal governance space of the Simulation Execution Standard (SES). The complete SES progression is: Simulation Instantiation ↓ Simulation Execution Control ↓ Simulation Observation ↓ Simulation Repetition ↓ Simulation Execution Documentation SIM answers: What exactly has been assembled for execution? SECM then asks: How must that Simulation Instance remain controlled while it runs? SOM asks: What materially relevant events occurred during execution? SRPM asks: How should repeated executions remain distinguishable and comparable? SEDM asks: Can the complete execution later be reconstructed? SIM therefore establishes the execution starting-state governance layer upon which the rest of SES depends. Foundational Principle A simulation cannot be governed as executed merely because its intended configuration is known; the exact Simulation Object, model, environment, scenario, inputs, parameters, dependencies, initial state, and execution conditions actually assembled for the run must remain identifiable. Canonical Closing Statement Simulation Instantiation Module establishes the entry point into governed Simulation Execution by transforming a governed simulation specification into a specific, identifiable, and execution-ready Simulation Instance. Through object, model, environment, scenario, input, parameter, dependency, infrastructure, randomization, and initial-state binding; intended-versus-instantiated configuration comparison; configuration conflict and inheritance visibility; Instantiation Delta governance; completeness assessment; readiness determination; versioning; and complete instantiation traceability, SIM prevents intended simulation configuration from being mistaken for the configuration that actually entered execution and creates the controlled starting basis required for Simulation Execution Control, Observation, Repetition, Documentation, and downstream Simulation Output Governance.

title: OOF™ Simulation Assumption Standard - (SAS)
text: OOF™ Simulation Assumption Standard - (SAS) Simulation Assumption Standard - (SAS) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Operational Layer: Simulation Assumption Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Type: Parent Standard Governed Space: Simulation Assumptions Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 17 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Governed Space Simulation Assumptions Canonical Definition Simulation Assumption Standard (SAS) defines the governance conditions under which assumptions necessary to construct, configure, execute, interpret, or maintain a simulation are explicitly identified, justified, bounded, related to their supporting basis, connected to their dependencies, assessed for uncertainty, constrained by their limitations, and preserved as traceable components of the simulation lifecycle. SAS ensures that simulation behavior, outputs, and downstream conclusions cannot silently depend upon assumptions whose existence, basis, uncertainty, dependency, or consequence remains unknown. Core Question Which assumptions enable the simulation, and how must their basis, dependencies, uncertainty, limitations, and consequences remain governed? Purpose Simulation cannot operate without assumptions. Some assumptions are explicit. Others emerge from: incomplete knowledge, simplified reality, missing data, uncertain environments, unresolved behavior, unavailable measurements, model boundaries, computational constraints, or necessary approximations. Assumptions may concern: physical conditions, system behavior, human behavior, autonomous behavior, environmental conditions, dependencies, parameters, distributions, operating conditions, boundary behavior, failure conditions, or future states. The purpose of SAS is not to eliminate assumptions. The purpose is to make them governable. Operational Role SAS is the fourth Parent Standard of SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture. The preceding standards establish: SOS — What exactly is being simulated? SPSS — Why is it being simulated, what must it cover, and within which boundaries? RRS — Which aspects of reality must be represented, at what abstraction, fidelity, resolution, and limitation? SAS asks: Which conditions must now be assumed so that this governed representation can become an executable simulation, and what risks or interpretive limits do those assumptions introduce? SAS creates the methodological bridge between: Governed Reality Representation and: Simulation Model & Environment construction. Governance Flow Reality Representation Basis → Assumption Need → Assumption Identification → Assumption Basis → Assumption Dependency → Assumption Uncertainty → Assumption Limitation → Assumption Consequence → Governed Simulation Assumption Basis The resulting Simulation Assumption Basis becomes an input to: Simulation Model & Environment Governance Simulation Assumption A Simulation Assumption is an explicitly or implicitly adopted condition treated as sufficiently true, stable, representative, bounded, or usable for purposes of the simulation despite incomplete direct knowledge or complete representation. An assumption may define: what is held constant, what is presumed, what is simplified, what is treated as representative, what relationship is expected to hold, what behavior is presumed, what dependency is expected to remain available, what uncertainty is bounded, or what condition is accepted for simulation purposes. Assumption ≠ Fact SIMULOS® establishes: Simulation Assumption ≠ Established Fact An assumption may be reasonable, evidence-supported, conventional, conservative, provisional, or necessary. It must not silently become represented as independently established reality merely because the simulation depends upon it. Assumption ≠ Reality Representation Reality Representation establishes how selected reality is represented. Simulation Assumptions establish what must be presumed in order for that representation and subsequent simulation to function. For example: Represented Weather System belongs to Reality Representation. Weather remains within defined range X during the scenario may be a Simulation Assumption. The distinction must remain explicit. Assumption ≠ Input An assumption and an input may appear technically similar. However: Input provides a value, dataset, signal, or condition to simulation execution. Assumption establishes the governing premise under which that value or condition is treated as usable or meaningful. For example: Input: Temperature = 25°C Assumption: Ambient temperature remains approximately stable during the simulated event. The two concepts should not be collapsed. Assumption ≠ Parameter A parameter controls or characterizes the simulation model or environment. An assumption may determine why that parameter has a particular value, range, distribution, or behavior. Parameterization belongs to the subsequent Model & Environment governance space. SAS governs the assumption behind or around that parameter where relevant. Explicit Assumption An Explicit Simulation Assumption is formally identified and documented. Explicit assumptions provide a stronger governance basis because they can be: reviewed, challenged, traced, tested, changed, or bounded. Implicit Assumption An Implicit Simulation Assumption exists where the simulation depends upon a premise that has not been formally declared. Implicit assumptions may arise through: default settings, inherited models, software conventions, engineering habits, undocumented parameter choices, assumed independence, assumed stationarity, assumed user behavior, or unchallenged historical practices. SAS seeks to convert materially relevant implicit assumptions into explicit governed assumptions. Hidden Assumption A Hidden Assumption is a materially relevant premise upon which simulation behavior depends but whose existence is not visible to downstream users or reviewers. Hidden assumptions are methodologically dangerous because simulation outputs may appear to arise from the model alone when they actually depend upon undisclosed premises. Assumption Identification Assumption governance begins by asking: What must be presumed for this simulation to operate as designed? Potential assumptions should be sought across: Simulation Object, Scope, Reality Representation, model behavior, environment, parameters, inputs, scenarios, dependencies, actors, interactions, timing, failure behavior, and output interpretation. Assumption Necessity Not every uncertain condition must become an assumption. A condition becomes assumption-relevant where the simulation must treat it in some defined way despite incomplete certainty or direct representation. Assumption Basis Every material Simulation Assumption should have an identifiable Assumption Basis where possible. The basis may derive from: observed operational data, historical behavior, empirical evidence, engineering knowledge, physical principles, scientific literature, expert judgment, design specifications, prior simulation, validated domain models, contractual conditions, regulatory requirements, conservative convention, or another documented source. No Basis ≠ Invalid by Default A simulation may sometimes require an assumption despite weak or unavailable supporting basis. SAS does not prohibit this. Instead, the assumption should be classified accordingly and its uncertainty and limitation strengthened. Assumption Strength Assumptions may vary in methodological strength. Conceptually, an assumption may be: Strongly Supported Supported Conditionally Supported Weakly Supported Unsupported but Necessary or: Basis Undetermined The classification should remain tied to the simulation inquiry. Assumption Justification Assumption Justification explains why the simulation adopts a particular assumption. Justification should answer: Why is this assumption necessary? Why is this assumption considered reasonable for this simulation? What supports it? Where does it stop being reasonable? Assumption Materiality A Simulation Assumption is material where changing, violating, or removing the assumption could materially affect: simulation behavior, scenario progression, simulation outputs, interpretation, comparison, reality correlation, downstream evidence, or reliance. Material assumptions require stronger governance than assumptions with negligible effect. Materiality Is Purpose-Relative The same assumption may be material in one simulation and immaterial in another. Example: Stable network latency may be immaterial for: high-level strategic simulation but critical for: real-time autonomous coordination simulation. Critical Simulation Assumption A Critical Simulation Assumption is an assumption whose failure could materially alter or invalidate a major simulation conclusion. Critical assumptions should remain highly visible. They may require: stronger basis, stronger uncertainty treatment, explicit scenario testing, sensitivity analysis, tighter monitoring, or narrower interpretation. Assumption Hierarchy Assumptions may exist at different levels: Foundational Assumptions support the overall simulation framework. Structural Assumptions support model architecture or relationships. Environmental Assumptions define simulated surrounding conditions. Behavioral Assumptions define actor or system behavior. Parameter Assumptions support selected parameter values or ranges. Scenario Assumptions support specific simulated conditions. Interpretive Assumptions affect how outputs are understood. SAS allows such classification without requiring one universal taxonomy. Physical Assumption A Physical Assumption concerns a physical relationship, condition, or constraint. Examples include: constant gravity, material stability, friction behavior, heat transfer behavior, or known physical boundary conditions.
