title: OOF™ Simulation Object Standard - (SOS)
text: OOF™ Simulation Object Standard - (SOS) Simulation Object Standard - (SOS) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Simulation Object Standard (SOS) Operational Layer: Simulation Object Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Type: Parent Standard Governed Space: Simulation Object Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 15 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Governed Space Simulation Object Canonical Definition Simulation Object Standard (SOS) defines the governance conditions under which the exact object, system, process, behavior, environment, event, interaction, infrastructure, population, mission, organization, or other reality target intended to be represented through simulation is formally identified, bounded, distinguished, versioned, configured, and documented as a governed Simulation Object. SOS establishes the foundational object layer of SIMULOS® by ensuring that simulation governance begins with an explicitly defined and traceable simulation target rather than an ambiguous, unstable, retrospectively reconstructed, or silently changing object. Core Question What exactly is being simulated, and how must the Simulation Object be identified, bounded, versioned, configured, and documented so that every downstream simulation activity remains connected to the same governed object? Purpose The purpose of SOS is to establish the object foundation upon which the complete SIMULOS® lifecycle depends. Simulation cannot be meaningfully governed if the object it claims to represent is unclear. Before SIMULOS® can govern: Simulation Purpose & Scope, Reality Representation, Simulation Assumptions, Simulation Model & Environment, Simulation Inputs & Data, Scenario Design, Simulation Execution, Simulation Output Governance, Simulation-to-Reality Correlation, simulation-derived evidence, or lifecycle resimulation, the architecture must first establish: What exactly is being simulated? Operational Role SOS is the first Parent Standard of SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture. It transforms an intended simulation target into a formally governable Simulation Object. Its role is to ensure that downstream simulation activities remain traceably connected to: the same object, the correct version, the relevant configuration, the correct boundaries, and the applicable object state. Governance Flow Candidate Simulation Target → Simulation Object Identification → Object Boundary → Object Structure → Object Version → Object Configuration → Object State → Object Documentation → Governed Simulation Object The governed Simulation Object becomes the input to: Simulation Purpose & Scope Governance Simulation Object A Simulation Object is the formally governed reality target whose selected characteristics, states, behaviors, relationships, interactions, processes, or conditions are intended to be represented through simulation. A Simulation Object may be: physical, digital, biological, behavioral, organizational, environmental, infrastructural, economic, cognitive, autonomous, hybrid, process-based, event-based, population-based, mission-based, system-based, system-of-systems based, conceptual, or future-state based. The Simulation Object defines what the simulation claims to represent. Simulation Object ≠ Simulation Representation SIMULOS® distinguishes between: Simulation Object and: Simulation Representation The Simulation Object is the governed subject being simulated. The Simulation Representation is the constructed representation through which selected characteristics of that object are later reproduced or examined. Therefore: Object ≠ Representation Simulation Object ≠ Simulation Model The Simulation Object must also remain distinct from the simulation model. For example: Operational Robot may be the Simulation Object. A mathematical, digital, behavioral, or hybrid model of the robot is not the object itself. Therefore: Simulation Object ≠ Simulation Model Simulation Object ≠ Simulation Environment The environment surrounding an object may materially affect simulation, but it does not automatically become part of the Simulation Object. A governed distinction must exist between: Object Environment and: Object–Environment Interaction unless the simulation intentionally defines them as one composite object. Simulation Object Identification Every Simulation Object must be sufficiently identifiable to distinguish it from materially different objects. Relevant identity characteristics may include: object name, object identifier, object class, system identity, product identity, mission identity, process identity, population identity, object version, configuration, state, component structure, relevant dependencies, and applicable temporal condition. The required identification depth depends upon what differences could materially affect downstream simulation. Object Distinction A generic category is insufficient where materially different members of the category may behave differently in simulation. For example: Autonomous Vehicle may be insufficient where the simulation outcome materially depends upon: Vehicle Platform + Hardware Version + Software Version + Sensor Configuration + Autonomy Configuration SIMULOS® therefore requires Simulation Object identification at the level necessary to preserve simulation meaning. Simulation Object Boundary Every Simulation Object must have a defined boundary. The boundary establishes: what belongs to the Simulation Object and: what remains outside it. The boundary may be: physical, digital, logical, functional, organizational, behavioral, temporal, spatial, systemic, or hybrid. Object Inclusion Material components, actors, processes, functions, relationships, and dependencies included in the Simulation Object must remain identifiable. Inclusion should be deliberate rather than inferred after simulation. Object Exclusion Material exclusions must remain visible. A simulation of part of a system must not silently become represented as simulation of the whole system. SIMULOS® therefore establishes: Object exclusion must remain visible wherever it materially limits simulation meaning. Simulation Object Structure Complex Simulation Objects may contain multiple governed levels. These may include: Composite Object System Object Subsystem Object Component Object Dependent Object and: External Object Where multiple levels exist, findings from one level must not automatically be generalized to another. Composite and System-of-Systems Objects Multiple interacting systems may collectively form a Simulation Object. In such cases SOS preserves: Composite Object Identity while maintaining visibility of the identities and boundaries of materially relevant subordinate objects. This allows SIMULOS® to govern: vehicles and infrastructure, spacecraft and ground systems, robot fleets, AI agents and tools, industrial production systems, energy networks, or other system-of-systems simulations without collapsing all components into one indistinguishable object. Object Dependencies A Simulation Object may depend upon systems or conditions outside its boundary. Dependencies may include: external infrastructure, software services, communications, human operators, data services, energy, environmental conditions, external control systems, organizational dependencies, or other external objects. Dependency does not automatically establish object inclusion. The relationship must remain explicit. Simulation Object Version Where the Simulation Object can materially change over time, the applicable version must be identifiable. Version change may arise from: hardware modification, software update, component replacement, architecture revision, process revision, capability change, mission revision, organizational change, or another material modification. Version Binding A governed simulation must remain traceable to the object version it claims to represent. Conceptually: Simulation → Simulation Object → Object Version A simulation performed against one materially distinct version may not automatically be represented as applying to another. Simulation Object Configuration Version alone may not sufficiently define the Simulation Object. The same version may operate under multiple configurations. Configuration may include: enabled capabilities, disabled capabilities, software settings, sensor configuration, actuator configuration, payload, autonomy level, permissions, operating mode, control configuration, safety configuration, network configuration, dependency configuration, or mission configuration. Where these materially affect simulated behavior, they form part of governed Simulation Object definition. Configuration Binding Simulation results must remain connected to the configuration actually represented. Therefore: Simulation of Configuration A ≠ Simulation of Configuration B unless a governed basis demonstrates sufficient applicability between them. Simulation Object State A Simulation Object may change materially without receiving a formal new version. Relevant object state may include: operational state, degradation state, maintenance state, failure state, learning state, load state, damage state, resource state, or another material condition. Where object state affects simulation meaning, the state must remain identifiable. Temporal Object Condition Some Simulation Objects must be bound to a point in time or period. Therefore: Object at T1 may not be equivalent to: Object at T2 where material change occurred between those states. SOS governs the temporal identity necessary to preserve this distinction. Dynamic Simulation Objects Dynamic objects may continuously evolve. Examples include: adaptive AI systems, autonomous agents, organizations, populations, biological systems, economic systems, infrastructure networks, and ecosystems. For dynamic objects, SOS requires a sufficiently bounded: Object State or: Object-State Range so that downstream simulation does not rely on an undefined moving target. Object Change Material Simulation Object change may affect downstream simulation governance. Relevant changes include: identity change, boundary change, version change, configuration change, component change, dependency change, capability change, state change, or structural change. Object Change Propagation SIMULOS® establishes: Material change to the Simulation Object must propagate to every downstream simulation space materially dependent upon that object definition. SOS identifies the object-level change. Subsequent SIMULOS® Parent Standards determine its effect on: purpose, representation, assumptions, models, inputs, scenarios, execution, outputs, correlation, evidence, and lifecycle relevance. Object Equivalence Two objects must not be treated as simulation-equivalent solely because they share: a name, product family, general function, manufacturer, architecture, or superficial similarity. Object equivalence must be sufficient relative to the simulation question. Object Substitution Where one object is used as a proxy or substitute for another, the substitution must remain explicit. The record must distinguish: Target Simulation Object from: Proxy or Substitute Object A proxy must not silently become the object the simulation claims to represent. No Object Inflation Rule A simulation of: one component must not silently become: simulation of the complete system. A simulation of: one configuration must not silently become: simulation of all configurations. A simulation of: one version must not silently become: simulation of the full product family. No Silent Object Change Rule A materially changed Simulation Object must not continue through the simulation lifecycle under an unchanged object definition where doing so would conceal a material difference. No Retrospective Object Redefinition Rule The Simulation Object must not be materially redefined after simulation results become known merely to increase apparent applicability of those results. Material redefinition requires explicit governance and downstream reassessment. Simulation Object Documentation The Simulation Object must remain sufficiently documented so that a qualified reviewer can determine: what was actually intended to be simulated. Documentation should preserve, where materially relevant: identity, boundary, inclusions, exclusions, version, configuration, state, component structure, dependencies, temporal applicability, and object changes. Simulation Object Traceability The architecture should support reconstruction of: Simulation → Simulation Object → Version → Configuration → State to the level required by the simulation purpose. Operational Space SOS governs: Simulation Object identification, object distinction, object boundaries, inclusions and exclusions, composite and nested object structures, dependencies and interfaces, object versions, object configurations, object states, temporal applicability, proxy and substitute objects, object change, object equivalence, object documentation, and object traceability. SOS does not govern how the object is later represented inside the simulation. Governance Boundary SOS begins when: a candidate target is proposed for simulation. SOS ends when: the Simulation Object has been sufficiently identified, bounded, distinguished, versioned, configured, state-defined, and documented to support governed Simulation Purpose & Scope. Governance Scope SOS governs only Simulation Object governance. It does not govern: why the simulation is performed, complete simulation scope, representation fidelity, simulation assumptions, model construction, simulation environment construction, input-data suitability, scenario design, execution controls, output interpretation, simulation-to-reality correlation, general validation, general integrity, audit governance, accountability governance, or operational deployment authorization. These responsibilities belong to subsequent SIMULOS® Parent Standards or adjacent OOF® architectures. Minimum Governance Requirements A conforming application of SOS should establish: 1. an identifiable Simulation Object, 2. sufficient object distinction, 3. an explicit Simulation Object boundary, 4. material inclusions and exclusions, 5. material component and object relationships, 6. material external dependencies, 7. applicable object version, 8. applicable object configuration, 9. relevant object state, 10. relevant temporal applicability, 11. visibility of proxy or substitution relationships, 12. material object-change traceability, 13. prevention of silent object inflation, 14. prevention of retrospective object redefinition, 15. and a persistent Simulation Object Record. Governance Outputs SOS may produce: Simulation Object Identifier, Simulation Object Definition, Simulation Object Boundary Record, Object Inclusion Record, Object Exclusion Record, Simulation Object Structure Map, Composite Object Record, Object Dependency Record, Object Interface Record, Simulation Object Version Record, Simulation Object Configuration Record, Simulation Object State Record, Temporal Object Record, Proxy Object Declaration, Object Equivalence Record, Object Change Record, Simulation Object Traceability Record, Simulation Object Status, and Simulation Object Governance Record. Operational Applications Simulation Object Standard may be applied across: artificial intelligence, autonomous systems, robotics, aerospace, space missions, aviation, autonomous vehicles, industrial systems, manufacturing, digital twins, critical infrastructure, healthcare, financial systems, scientific simulation, environmental modeling, infrastructure planning, mission simulation, organizational simulation, population simulation, policy simulation, system-of-systems environments, and future operational ecosystems. Relationship to Other OOF® Architectures Simulation Object Standard interoperates with: GOA™ ORA™ OBIDENITY® VALIDOS® INTEGROS® ADIT® AGA™ AIG® CLIA® MGIA™ ASGA™ RIS™ by establishing the simulation-specific object foundation consumed by downstream simulation governance. ORA™ may define or observe the operational reality from which a Simulation Object is derived. OBIDENITY® may govern broader identity, origin, ownership, provenance, and authority relationships. VALIDOS® may later treat the simulation, simulation output, or simulation-derived claim as a Validation Object. INTEGROS® governs general integrity conditions affecting objects and records. ADIT® may preserve evidential and audit traceability surrounding simulation activity. AGA™ governs accountability for decisions involving the Simulation Object. Specialized AI, cognition, memory, and autonomous-system architectures may govern characteristics of the actual system being simulated. SOS does not replace those architectures. It governs specifically: what the simulation claims to represent. Architectural Position Simulation Object Standard is the first Parent Standard of SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture. It establishes the first transition in the simulation governance lifecycle: Candidate Simulation Target → Governed Simulation Object The next architectural question is: Why is this object being simulated, what must the simulation cover, and what remains outside its intended scope? This transition leads directly into: Simulation Purpose & Scope Governance Foundational Principle A simulation cannot legitimately claim to represent an object more precisely than that object has been identified, bounded, versioned, configured, and documented. Canonical Closing Statement Simulation Object Standard establishes the foundational object layer of SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture by transforming an intended simulation target into an explicitly identified, bounded, versioned, configured, state-aware, and traceable Simulation Object. Through governance of object identity, distinction, boundaries, component structure, dependencies, versions, configurations, states, temporal applicability, proxy relationships, material change, documentation, and traceability, SOS prevents simulation activity from becoming detached from the object it claims to represent. By establishing a stable Simulation Object before simulation purpose, reality representation, assumptions, modeling, scenarios, execution, outputs, correlation, evidence use, or lifecycle governance begins, SOS creates the first methodological anchor of the complete SIMULOS® simulation governance lifecycle. Module Architecture → Simulation Object Identification Module (SOIM) → Simulation Object Boundary Module (SOBM) → Simulation Object Versioning Module (SOVM) → Simulation Object Configuration Module (SOCM) → Simulation Object Documentation Module (SODM) Related Documents → About Simulation Object Standard (SOS)

title: OOF™ Simulation Output Governance Standard - (SOGS)
text: OOF™ Simulation Output Governance Standard - (SOGS) Simulation Output Governance Standard - (SOGS) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Simulation Output Governance Standard (SOGS) defines the governance conditions under which outputs produced by Simulation Execution are formally identified, classified, bounded, interpreted, documented, and connected to the execution basis that produced them so that the distinction between what the simulation directly produced, what is subsequently derived or inferred from that output, what limitations constrain its interpretation, and what the output does not establish remains explicit throughout downstream use. SOGS governs the transition from: Simulation Execution to: Governed Simulation Output without allowing computational results to acquire meaning, certainty, applicability, or evidential strength that the Simulation Execution itself did not establish. Core Question What exactly did the simulation produce, how must Simulation Outputs be bounded and interpreted, and what may legitimately be inferred from them? Operational Role SOGS serves as the ninth Parent Standard of SIMULOS® and establishes the first governance layer after Simulation Execution. The preceding standard: SES — Simulation Execution Standard establishes how the simulation was instantiated, controlled, observed, repeated, and documented. SOGS asks the next architectural question: What exactly emerged from that execution, what kind of output is it, what does it directly represent, and where must interpretation stop? The governed progression is: Governed Simulation Execution Record ↓ Raw Simulation Output ↓ Output Identification ↓ Output Classification ↓ Output Context Binding ↓ Inference Governance ↓ Output Limitation ↓ Output Documentation ↓ Governed Simulation Output ↓ Reality Correlation Governed Modules 1. SOIM — Simulation Output Identification Module Governs the identification, differentiation, origin binding, execution linkage, version relationship, and traceability of individual and aggregated Simulation Outputs. 2. SOCM — Simulation Output Classification Module Governs how Simulation Outputs are classified according to their form, origin, processing state, aggregation, uncertainty context, and intended interpretive role. 3. SIM — Simulation Inference Module Governs what may legitimately be inferred from Simulation Outputs and preserves the distinction between: Observed Simulation Result and: Interpretive Inference. 4. SOLM — Simulation Output Limitation Module Governs material limitations, applicability boundaries, unresolved conditions, uncertainty constraints, exclusions, and interpretive restrictions attached to Simulation Outputs. 5. SODM — Simulation Output Documentation Module Governs the structured documentation, lineage, contextual binding, inference record, limitation record, and downstream traceability of governed Simulation Outputs. Governance Flow Simulation Execution ↓ SOIM — Output Identification ↓ SOCM — Output Classification ↓ SIM — Simulation Inference ↓ SOLM — Output Limitation ↓ SODM — Output Documentation ↓ Governed Simulation Output ↓ Reality Correlation Governance Governed Output Object SOGS introduces the governed concept: Simulation Output Object A Simulation Output Object is an identifiable output or governed output collection produced from one or more Simulation Executions and preserved with sufficient execution context, classification, inference boundaries, limitations, and documentation to support legitimate downstream examination. A Simulation Output Object may include: numerical result, state trajectory, event sequence, simulated failure, behavioral trace, probability distribution, performance measure, optimization result, agent action, decision path, generated scenario outcome, Monte Carlo distribution, visualization, aggregated execution result, statistical summary, or another identifiable product of Simulation Execution. Direct Output A Direct Simulation Output is produced directly by the Simulation Execution. Examples include: collision occurred trajectory reached state X temperature exceeded threshold Y agent selected action Z 18 of 250,000 executions entered recovery failure These are execution-derived outputs. Derived Output A Derived Simulation Output results from processing one or more Direct Simulation Outputs. Examples include: averages, distributions, percentiles, rankings, aggregate failure rates, confidence estimates, transformed metrics, comparative measures, and post-processed visualizations. Derived Outputs should remain traceable to their contributing Simulation Outputs and executions where material. Inference An Inference is a conclusion drawn from one or more Simulation Outputs. For example: Output: 18 of 250,000 simulated executions entered recovery failure. Inference: Recovery failure appears concentrated under a particular combination of simulated conditions. These are not the same object. Output ≠ Inference Principle SIMULOS® establishes: A Simulation Output is what the simulation produced. An inference is what an actor concludes from that output. The two must remain distinguishable. Inference ≠ Reality Principle SIMULOS® further establishes: An inference supported inside a simulation does not by itself establish that the same relationship exists in Operational Reality. That transition belongs to downstream governance. Output Context Binding A Simulation Output should remain sufficiently connected to the execution basis that produced it. Where material, this includes: Simulation Object ↓ Purpose & Scope ↓ Reality Representation ↓ Assumptions ↓ Model & Environment ↓ Inputs & Data ↓ Scenario ↓ Execution ↓ Output Without this context, an output may remain computationally correct while becoming methodologically misleading. No Context-Free Output Principle Simulation Outputs must not acquire broader meaning merely because their originating simulation context has been removed. Output Classification Outputs may require classification according to characteristics such as: Direct / Derived Individual / Aggregated Deterministic / Stochastic Expected / Unexpected Nominal / Edge-Case / Stress Complete / Partial Final / Intermediate Observed / Calculated Comparative / Standalone Execution-Specific / Campaign-Level Classification enables downstream users to understand what type of Simulation Output they are examining. Aggregated Simulation Output An aggregated output may combine many executions. For example: 2,000,000 Monte Carlo runs → Failure Probability Estimate SOGS requires the aggregate to remain sufficiently connected to: contributing execution population, relevant exclusions, failed runs, scenario population, repetition structure, and aggregation method. No Aggregation Concealment Principle Aggregation must not erase materially relevant execution behavior that changes interpretation of the aggregated result. Output Population A Simulation Output may represent: one execution one Repetition Set one Scenario multiple scenarios one campaign or: multiple simulation populations. The population basis should remain identifiable. Output Exclusion Where executions or results are excluded from an output population, material exclusions should remain visible. This prevents: silent failed-run removal, cherry-picking, survivor-only reporting, post hoc filtering, and misleading aggregate construction. Output Limitation Every materially relevant Simulation Output may carry limitations arising from: assumptions, abstraction, fidelity, model boundaries, environment boundaries, input uncertainty, data representativeness, scenario coverage, execution conditions, repetition sufficiency, observation limitations, output processing, or unresolved simulation behavior. SOGS does not require all limitations to invalidate the output. It requires them to remain visible where they materially constrain interpretation. Inherited Limitation Principle A Simulation Output inherits materially relevant limitations from the simulation conditions upon which it depends. Post-processing does not erase those limitations. No Precision Inflation Principle A highly precise numerical output does not establish equivalent certainty about reality. For example: Failure Probability = 0.003742% may be computationally precise while remaining highly sensitive to: assumptions, scenario selection, model fidelity, data quality, and representation boundaries. Computational Precision ≠ Epistemic Certainty SIMULOS® establishes: The numerical precision of a Simulation Output must not be confused with the strength of what that output legitimately establishes. Unexpected Output A Simulation Output may reveal behavior not anticipated by the Simulation Purpose or Scenario Design. Unexpected output should not automatically be: deleted, classified as error, excluded, or normalized away. It may reveal: hidden interaction, model instability, unmodeled dependency, scenario insufficiency, rare behavior, or a new simulation question. Output-to-Scenario Feedback A materially unexpected output may therefore create: New Scenario Requirement or: Scenario Expansion Requirement under SSS. SIMULOS® is therefore capable of recursive simulation learning. Output-to-Assumption Feedback An output may expose sensitivity to an assumption. This may create: Assumption Reassessment under SAS. Output-to-Model Feedback Unexpected or unstable outputs may create a need to reassess: Simulation Model & Environment under SMES. Output-to-Input Feedback Output behavior may expose input sensitivity, missing data regions, or representativeness problems requiring reassessment under SIDS. Output-to-Execution Feedback An output anomaly may originate from: execution deviation, hidden state, incomplete run, control intervention, or repetition drift. SOGS therefore preserves backward traceability into SES. No Automatic Failure Attribution An unexpected Simulation Output does not establish that the simulated system failed, the simulation failed, or Operational Reality would fail. Those remain separate questions requiring appropriate governance. Inference Boundary An inference should remain bounded by: Simulation Purpose, Simulation Scope, represented reality, assumptions, model and environment, inputs, scenario population, execution population, output population, uncertainty, and known limitations. Inference Escalation SOGS distinguishes between increasingly strong claims. For example: Level 1 — Execution Observation “Failure occurred in Run 184.” Level 2 — Repetition Observation “Failure occurred in 18 of 250,000 repetitions.” Level 3 — Simulation Pattern Inference “Failure is associated with simulated low-power recovery conditions.” Level 4 — Reality-Oriented Claim “The real spacecraft will fail under low-power recovery conditions.” The first three may potentially be governed within simulation output analysis. The fourth crosses toward: Reality Correlation and cannot be established by SOGS alone. No Reality Leap Principle SIMULOS® establishes: A Simulation Output must not move directly from simulated behavior to a claim about Operational Reality without passing through the appropriate reality-correlation and validation governance. Output Documentation A governed Simulation Output should preserve, where material: Output ID, Output Type, originating Execution ID, Repetition Set, Scenario ID, model version, environment version, Input Set, relevant parameters, output population, aggregation method, processing history, inference status, limitations, uncertainty context, exclusions, and downstream use. Output Lineage Output lineage may follow: Execution ↓ Direct Output ↓ Derived Output ↓ Aggregated Output ↓ Inference ↓ Downstream Assessment This allows later reconstruction of how a conclusion emerged from Simulation Execution. No Output Laundering Principle SIMULOS® establishes: A Derived Output or inference must not acquire stronger methodological status merely because its relationship to the original Simulation Execution has become less visible. Output Transformation Outputs may undergo: filtering, normalization, aggregation, smoothing, dimensional reduction, statistical transformation, visualization, AI summarization, or other processing. Material transformations should remain traceable where they affect interpretation. AI Interpretation of Simulation Outputs AI systems may analyze enormous Simulation Output populations. They may: identify patterns, detect anomalies, cluster failures, generate summaries, propose causal hypotheses, or identify new scenarios. SOGS distinguishes: Simulation Output from: AI-Generated Interpretation of Simulation Output. AI-Generated Inference Principle An AI-generated interpretation does not become a Simulation Output merely because it was generated automatically from Simulation Outputs. Its interpretive status should remain visible. Output Conflict Different executions or Simulation Output populations may support conflicting interpretations. SOGS preserves conflict rather than forcing artificial agreement. Possible status: Output Consistent Output Conditionally Consistent Output Mixed Output Conflicted Output Relationship Undetermined Output Uncertainty Output uncertainty may arise from multiple sources. SOGS may preserve: Input Uncertainty Parameter Uncertainty Stochastic Uncertainty Model Uncertainty Scenario Uncertainty Execution Uncertainty Observation Uncertainty and: Inference Uncertainty. These should not automatically be collapsed into one generic uncertainty number. Output Sufficiency A Simulation Output may be technically valid as an output while still insufficient for a particular downstream inference. Therefore: Output Existence ≠ Inference Sufficiency. Simulation Campaign Bottleneck Modern simulation systems can produce more outputs than organizations can meaningfully interpret. The governance bottleneck may therefore shift from: Can we generate simulation results? to: Can we determine what those results actually mean, what they do not mean, and which decisions they may legitimately support? SOGS governs this transition. Space & Mission Simulation Application A space organization may run millions of mission simulations producing: trajectory distributions, navigation errors, failure modes, communication losses, recovery outcomes, fuel margins, and mission-success estimates. The critical governance question is not merely: What percentage succeeded? It is also: Which execution population produced that percentage? Which scenarios were included? Which failed executions were excluded? Which assumptions materially shaped the result? What does the output directly establish? Which conclusions are interpretations? Which conclusions require correlation with Operational Reality? SOGS provides the structure required to answer these questions. Autonomous Systems Application An autonomous robot may complete: 99.97% of simulated tasks successfully. SOGS prevents this result from automatically becoming: The robot is 99.97% safe in reality. The simulation output may legitimately establish a performance property within the governed simulation conditions. Moving from that result toward real-world safety requires downstream governance. Relationship to SES SES governs: how Simulation Execution occurs. SOGS governs: what emerges from that execution and how that output may be interpreted. The formal handoff is: Governed Simulation Execution Record ↓ Simulation Output Object Relationship to RRS RRS governs how reality is represented inside the simulation. SOGS preserves relevant representation limitations when interpreting outputs. Relationship to SAS SAS governs Simulation Assumptions. SOGS ensures materially relevant assumption limitations propagate into output interpretation. Relationship to SSS SSS governs Scenario Design and Coverage. SOGS ensures outputs are not interpreted beyond the scenario population that produced them. Relationship to ORA™ ORA™ governs actual Operational Reality. SOGS does not determine whether a Simulation Output corresponds to reality. That question belongs to the downstream reality-correlation governance space. Relationship to VALIDOS® VALIDOS® determines whether a Simulation Output, inference, correlation claim, simulation methodology, or other Validation Object can legitimately support a formal validation claim. SOGS governs the Simulation Output before that validation determination. Relationship to INTEGROS® SOGS deliberately does not govern general Output Integrity. General integrity remains under INTEGROS®. SOGS governs: identification, classification, inference, limitation, and documentation of Simulation Outputs. Relationship to ADIT® ADIT® may audit Simulation Output records, inference pathways, exclusions, and traceability. SOGS governs the output space itself. Governance Boundary SOGS begins when one or more identifiable outputs emerge from a governed Simulation Execution. SOGS ends when those outputs have been sufficiently: identified, execution-bound, classified, population-bounded, inference-bounded, limitation-bound, transformation-traced, and documented to form a Governed Simulation Output suitable for downstream Reality Correlation. SOGS does not determine: whether the simulation accurately represents Operational Reality, whether a Simulation Output is externally valid, whether the simulated behavior will occur in reality, whether a system is operationally safe, whether a Simulation Output constitutes sufficient Validation Evidence, or whether operational reliance is justified. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Identify the Simulation Output Assign a stable Output ID and establish what exactly was produced. 2. Bind the Output to Execution Connect the output to its originating Simulation Execution, Repetition Set, or Campaign. 3. Classify the Output Determine whether the output is: direct, derived, aggregated, deterministic, stochastic, intermediate, final, or another governed class. 4. Establish the Output Population Identify which executions and scenarios contribute to the output. 5. Preserve Material Exclusions Document excluded executions, failed runs, filtered results, and other material population changes. 6. Trace Material Transformations Preserve transformations affecting output interpretation. 7. Separate Output From Inference Distinguish what the simulation produced from conclusions subsequently drawn from it. 8. Bound the Inference Ensure inference does not exceed the simulation conditions supporting it. 9. Propagate Material Limitations Carry forward relevant limitations from upstream simulation governance. 10. Assess Output Uncertainty Context Identify material uncertainty affecting interpretation. 11. Establish Output Documentation Preserve the context, lineage, inference, limitations, and downstream relationships. 12. Establish the Governed Simulation Output Create the formal output object suitable for Reality Correlation and downstream validation. Governance Outputs SOGS may produce: Simulation Output ID, Simulation Output Object, Direct Simulation Output Record, Derived Simulation Output Record, Aggregated Simulation Output Record, Output Classification, Output Population Record, Output Exclusion Record, Output Transformation Record, Output-to-Execution Traceability Record, Output Lineage Record, Simulation Inference Record, Inference Classification, Inference Boundary, Inference Limitation Record, Output Limitation Record, Inherited Limitation Record, Output Uncertainty Record, Output Conflict Record, Output Sufficiency Assessment, AI-Generated Interpretation Record, Output Documentation Record, Reality-Correlation Handoff Record, and Governed Simulation Output. Architectural Position Simulation Output Governance Standard (SOGS) is the ninth Parent Standard of SIMULOS®. Its position is: 8. Simulation Execution Standard (SES) ↓ 9. Simulation Output Governance Standard (SOGS) ↓ 10. Reality Correlation Governance SOGS therefore forms the critical boundary between: what happened inside the simulation and: what that simulated result may legitimately tell us about something beyond the simulation. Foundational Principle A Simulation Output becomes governable only when what the simulation directly produced remains distinguishable from how that output was processed, interpreted, limited, aggregated, and ultimately used to support claims beyond the execution that produced it. Canonical Closing Statement Simulation Output Governance Standard establishes the governed transition from Simulation Execution to interpretable Simulation Output by defining how outputs are identified, classified, execution-bound, population-bounded, transformed, inferred from, limitation-bound, uncertainty-contextualized, and documented. Through explicit separation of direct output, derived output, aggregation, and inference, SOGS prevents computational precision from becoming false certainty, simulation behavior from becoming an unsupported claim about Operational Reality, and large-scale simulation results from losing the execution context and limitations necessary for legitimate interpretation. SOGS therefore creates the governed Simulation Output Object that can move forward into Reality Correlation and downstream validation without exceeding what the simulation itself actually established. title: OOF™ Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard - (SPSS)
text: OOF™ Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard - (SPSS) Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard - (SPSS) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Operational Layer: Simulation Purpose & Scope Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Type: Parent Standard Governed Space: Simulation Purpose & Scope Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 16 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Governed Space Simulation Purpose & Scope Canonical Definition Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard (SPSS) defines the governance conditions under which the reason for performing a simulation, the questions the simulation is intended to address, the portions of the governed Simulation Object to which it applies, the conditions and contexts included within the simulation inquiry, the material exclusions and limitations surrounding that inquiry, and the required simulation depth and precision are formally established before downstream simulation representation begins. SPSS ensures that a technically successful simulation cannot silently acquire a broader purpose, scope, applicability, or interpretive meaning than was actually established before simulation design and execution. Core Question Why is the simulation being performed, what exactly must it examine, what remains outside its governed scope, and at what depth and precision must the simulation operate for its intended purpose? Purpose The purpose of SPSS is to transform a governed Simulation Object into a governed simulation inquiry. SOS establishes: What exactly is being simulated? SPSS establishes: Why is it being simulated and what must the simulation actually cover? The distinction is fundamental. The same Simulation Object may be simulated for radically different purposes. A spacecraft may be simulated for: thermal behavior, navigation, structural stress, docking, autonomous control, communication loss, mission failure, or complete mission performance. The Simulation Object may remain the same while the required simulation scope, depth, precision, conditions, and exclusions change substantially. SPSS governs those differences. Operational Role SPSS is the second Parent Standard of SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture. It receives the governed Simulation Object produced by SOS and establishes the simulation-specific purpose and scope required before the object can be represented inside a simulation. Its role is to prevent: undefined simulation purpose, purpose substitution, scope ambiguity, hidden scope expansion, hidden scope contraction, partial simulation represented as whole-object simulation, excluded conditions being treated as simulated, inappropriate generalization of simulation outputs, insufficient simulation depth, unjustified precision, and downstream simulation design becoming detached from the question the simulation was originally intended to answer. Governance Flow Governed Simulation Object → Simulation Purpose → Simulation Questions → Simulation Scope → Scope Inclusions → Scope Exclusions → Applicability Context → Simulation Depth → Simulation Precision → Purpose & Scope Record → Governed Simulation Inquiry The governed Simulation Purpose & Scope becomes the input to: Reality Representation Governance Simulation Purpose Simulation Purpose defines why simulation is being performed and what decision, inquiry, exploration, comparison, investigation, design activity, operational question, or knowledge requirement it is intended to support. A Simulation Purpose may include: design exploration, performance assessment, behavior analysis, mission planning, safety investigation, failure exploration, scenario examination, stress assessment, training, operational preparation, comparative analysis, system optimization, autonomous-system testing, policy exploration, scientific inquiry, forecasting support, or another explicitly governed simulation objective. The purpose must be sufficiently explicit to guide downstream simulation governance. Purpose Must Be Object-Bound The Simulation Purpose must remain connected to the governed Simulation Object. A simulation purpose should therefore answer: What are we trying to learn, examine, reproduce, compare, explore, or understand about this Simulation Object? A purpose that cannot be connected to the governed object is not sufficiently established. Primary and Secondary Purpose A simulation may have more than one legitimate purpose. SPSS may distinguish: Primary Simulation Purpose from: Secondary Simulation Purposes where necessary. Secondary purposes must not silently become equivalent to the primary purpose if they require different representation, scenarios, depth, or precision. Purpose Substitution Purpose Substitution occurs when a simulation performed for one purpose is later treated as though it had been performed for another materially different purpose. For example: Design Exploration must not automatically become: Operational Safety Demonstration and: Training Simulation must not automatically become: Real-World Performance Evidence without a governed basis. SPSS prohibits silent purpose substitution. Simulation Question A Simulation Purpose should be translated into one or more sufficiently clear Simulation Questions. Examples may include: How does the system behave under condition X? What happens if component Y fails? How does the object respond across operating range Z? Which scenario produces the greatest system stress? How does autonomous behavior change when communication is lost? The Simulation Question provides a bridge between broad purpose and concrete simulation scope. Simulation Scope Simulation Scope defines the governed extent of the simulation inquiry. It determines which portions, characteristics, behaviors, conditions, interactions, operating modes, temporal periods, environments, populations, scenarios, and relationships are intended to be examined. Simulation Scope establishes: what the simulation covers and: what it does not cover. Object Boundary ≠ Simulation Scope SIMULOS® establishes an important distinction: Simulation Object Boundary ≠ Simulation Scope SOS may define an entire aircraft as the Simulation Object. SPSS may define the simulation scope as: Landing Behavior Under Crosswind Conditions The object remains the aircraft. The simulation does not automatically cover every possible aircraft behavior. Scope Inclusion Material inclusions should be sufficiently explicit. Depending upon the simulation, scope may include: specific components, functions, behaviors, operating modes, mission phases, environmental conditions, failure conditions, populations, interactions, geographic regions, temporal periods, or consequence pathways. Scope Exclusion Material exclusions must remain visible. An exclusion identifies a condition, characteristic, behavior, environment, population, operating mode, component, or interaction intentionally outside the governed simulation inquiry. SPSS establishes: Excluded from Simulation Scope ≠ Demonstrated by Simulation This distinction must remain preserved throughout downstream interpretation. No Hidden Scope Expansion Rule A simulation must not acquire broader scope after execution merely because the resulting outputs appear useful beyond the original inquiry. For example: Simulated urban daytime driving must not silently become: simulated autonomous driving under all operational conditions. Any material expansion requires explicit reassessment of Simulation Purpose & Scope and affected downstream SIMULOS® spaces. No Hidden Scope Contraction Rule Likewise, difficult, adverse, or inconvenient conditions must not be silently removed from the Simulation Scope after they were established as materially relevant. Scope contraction must remain explicit and its effect on downstream simulation claims must be preserved. Scope Inflation Scope Inflation occurs when a narrow simulation inquiry becomes represented as supporting a substantially broader conclusion. Examples include: Single Scenario → Complete Scenario Coverage One Environment → All Environments One Operating Mode → Complete Operational Envelope One Population → General Population One Mission Phase → Entire Mission SPSS prohibits scope inflation without a governed basis. Scope Fragmentation A complex Simulation Scope may be divided into smaller governed simulation scopes. This may be appropriate where different: environments, operating modes, components, scenarios, populations, or mission stages require different simulation methods or representations. Fragmentation must preserve the relationship between each partial scope and the complete intended inquiry. Partial Simulation Scope A partial scope is legitimate. SIMULOS® does not require every simulation to cover the complete Simulation Object or complete operational reality. It requires partial scope to remain explicit. Therefore: Partial Simulation ≠ Incomplete Governance provided the boundary of the partial inquiry is clearly established. Simulation Applicability Context Simulation Applicability Context defines the conditions within which the simulation is intended to have meaning. It may include: operational environment, geographic context, user population, mission phase, deployment condition, system state, autonomy level, interaction pattern, resource condition, consequence context, or another relevant domain. Applicability Context is not equivalent to later validation or operational authorization. It defines the context the simulation itself is intended to examine. Simulation Purpose vs Operational Reliance SPSS does not determine whether simulation outputs may be relied upon operationally. It may record an intended downstream use where that use influences the required simulation design. However: Intended Use ≠ Authorized Reliance Formal validation and reliance questions belong to VALIDOS® and other applicable governance layers. Simulation Purpose vs Validation Purpose SIMULOS® and VALIDOS® must remain separate. SPSS asks: Why are we performing this simulation and what must it cover? VALIDOS® VPSS asks: Why are we validating this Validation Object and what must that validation establish? A simulation may later become: validation evidence, a Validation Object, part of a Validation Method, or one input into a broader validation determination. The purposes may interact, but they are not the same governance question. Simulation Depth Simulation Depth defines how deeply the governed simulation inquiry must examine the selected Simulation Object characteristics and conditions. Depth may increase where the simulation purpose involves: high consequence, high complexity, high uncertainty, autonomous behavior, significant interaction effects, rare failure conditions, safety-critical operations, irreversible decisions, or broad downstream dependence. Simulation Depth should remain proportional to the purpose. Simulation Depth ≠ Validation Depth SIMULOS® establishes: Simulation Depth ≠ Validation Depth Simulation Depth governs the required depth of the simulation inquiry. Validation Depth under VALIDOS® governs the strength and assurance level required to establish a validation conclusion. One may influence the other without becoming the same concept. Simulation Precision Simulation Precision defines the level of detail, granularity, resolution, or quantitative specificity required to satisfy the Simulation Purpose. Precision may concern: temporal resolution, spatial resolution, behavioral granularity, component detail, parameter resolution, scenario resolution, measurement granularity, or output specificity. Greater precision is not automatically better. No False Precision Rule SIMULOS® establishes: Simulation precision must not exceed what the simulation purpose, object definition, representation basis, assumptions, inputs, and model structure can meaningfully support. A highly precise numerical output does not automatically imply highly precise representation of reality. Purpose-Depth Alignment Simulation Depth should be sufficient for the Simulation Purpose. A mismatch may occur where: High-Consequence Purpose → Low Simulation Depth or: Exploratory Purpose → Excessive Simulation Burden SPSS governs alignment rather than maximum complexity. Purpose-Precision Alignment Simulation Precision should also be appropriate to purpose. A simulation intended only to identify broad directional behavior may not require the same precision as one intended to examine a narrow engineering tolerance. Scope-Depth Alignment Depth must apply to the actual Simulation Scope. A simulation cannot compensate for missing scope merely by examining the included portion in extreme detail. Therefore: Deep Simulation of Narrow Scope ≠ Broad Simulation Coverage Scope-Precision Alignment High precision within one narrow scope does not justify claims concerning excluded conditions. This prevents precise outputs from creating artificial scope credibility. Consequence Context The consequence attached to the intended simulation use may influence required: depth, precision, scenario breadth, representation fidelity, documentation, or later validation. SPSS may therefore record a Simulation Consequence Context where materially relevant. It does not replace general risk governance. Exploratory Simulation An exploratory simulation may intentionally operate with: broader uncertainty, lower precision, incomplete knowledge, wider hypothesis space, or provisional assumptions. This is legitimate if the Simulation Purpose clearly identifies the exploratory nature of the inquiry. Exploratory results must not silently become high-assurance conclusions. Decision-Support Simulation Where simulation is intended to support a decision, the decision context should be sufficiently described to establish the required scope, depth, and precision. SPSS does not govern the decision itself. It governs the simulation inquiry supporting that decision. High-Consequence Simulation Where simulation may materially influence: safety, critical infrastructure, autonomous operation, medical decisions, aerospace operations, mission-critical systems, financial stability, or other high-consequence environments, SPSS should require correspondingly explicit purpose, scope, exclusions, depth, and applicability. Simulation Purpose Change The Simulation Purpose may change during the lifecycle. A Material Purpose Change occurs where the new purpose would require materially different: representation, assumptions, model structure, inputs, scenarios, execution, outputs, or correlation requirements. Material purpose change requires downstream reassessment. Simulation Scope Change Simulation Scope may also change. Relevant changes include: Scope Expansion Scope Contraction Scope Recomposition Scope Extension Scope Restriction or: Applicability Change Material scope change must remain traceable. Purpose & Scope Change Propagation SIMULOS® establishes: A material change to Simulation Purpose or Scope must propagate to every downstream simulation governance space materially dependent upon that purpose or scope. Potentially affected spaces include: Reality Representation, Simulation Assumptions, Model & Environment, Inputs & Data, Scenario Design, Simulation Execution, Simulation Output Governance, Simulation-to-Reality Correlation, Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary, and Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation. No Retrospective Purpose Redefinition Rule A Simulation Purpose must not be materially redefined after results become known merely to make those results appear more successful or relevant. Material change must be explicitly documented and affected simulation governance reconsidered. No Retrospective Scope Redefinition Rule Likewise, the scope must not be silently changed after execution so that failed or unmodeled conditions disappear from the represented inquiry. Purpose & Scope Traceability The simulation lifecycle should remain traceable to: Simulation Object → Simulation Purpose → Simulation Questions → Simulation Scope → Inclusions → Exclusions → Applicability → Depth → Precision This relationship allows later reviewers to determine what the simulation was actually designed to establish. Simulation Purpose & Scope Record SPSS should produce a persistent Simulation Purpose & Scope Record sufficient to reconstruct: why the simulation was performed, which questions it addressed, what was included, what was excluded, where the simulation applied, how deeply it was intended to examine the object, and what level of precision was required. Operational Space SPSS governs: Simulation Purpose, primary and secondary purposes, Simulation Questions, Simulation Scope, scope inclusions, scope exclusions, applicability context, partial scope, scope fragmentation, Simulation Depth, Simulation Precision, consequence context, intended simulation use, purpose changes, scope changes, scope limitations, purpose and scope traceability, and the persistent Simulation Purpose & Scope Record. Governance Boundary SPSS begins when: a governed Simulation Object exists and requires a defined reason, inquiry boundary, and simulation extent. SPSS ends when: Simulation Purpose, Simulation Questions, Scope, material inclusions and exclusions, Applicability Context, Simulation Depth, and required Simulation Precision are sufficiently established to support governed Reality Representation. Governance Scope SPSS governs only the purpose and scope of simulation. It does not govern: Simulation Object identity, Simulation Object boundary itself, reality-representation fidelity, simulation assumptions, model construction, simulation environment construction, input-data suitability, scenario design, execution, outputs, simulation-to-reality correlation, formal validation, Validation State, operational reliance authorization, general integrity, risk governance, accountability, or audit execution. These responsibilities belong to other SIMULOS® Parent Standards or adjacent OOF® architectures. Minimum Governance Requirements A conforming application of SPSS should establish: 1. an explicit Simulation Purpose, 2. a clear relationship between purpose and the governed Simulation Object, 3. one or more identifiable Simulation Questions, 4. a bounded Simulation Scope, 5. explicit material scope inclusions, 6. explicit material scope exclusions, 7. a defined Simulation Applicability Context, 8. sufficient Simulation Depth relative to purpose, 9. appropriate Simulation Precision, 10. visibility of intended downstream use where materially relevant, 11. prevention of purpose substitution, 12. prevention of scope inflation, 13. prevention of retrospective purpose or scope redefinition, 14. traceability of material purpose and scope changes, 15. and a persistent Simulation Purpose & Scope Record. Governance Outputs SPSS may produce: Simulation Purpose Statement, Primary Simulation Purpose, Secondary Simulation Purpose Record, Simulation Question Set, Simulation Scope Definition, Simulation Scope Map, Scope Inclusion Record, Scope Exclusion Record, Partial Scope Record, Scope Fragmentation Map, Simulation Applicability Context, Simulation Depth Requirement, Simulation Precision Requirement, Simulation Consequence Context, Intended Simulation Use Record, Purpose Limitation Record, Scope Limitation Record, Purpose Change Record, Scope Expansion Record, Scope Contraction Record, Scope Recomposition Record, Purpose & Scope Change Assessment, Purpose & Scope Traceability Map, and Simulation Purpose & Scope Record. Operational Applications Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard may be applied across: artificial intelligence, autonomous systems, robotics, aerospace, space missions, aviation, autonomous vehicles, manufacturing, digital twins, scientific simulation, engineering simulation, healthcare, financial systems, critical infrastructure, environmental systems, mission planning, system-of-systems simulation, policy simulation, organizational simulation, population simulation, training environments, safety analysis, failure analysis, and future operational ecosystems. Relationship to Other OOF® Architectures Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard interoperates with: GOA™ ORA™ OBIDENITY® VALIDOS® INTEGROS® ADIT® AGA™ AIG® CLIA® MGIA™ ASGA™ RIS™ by establishing the simulation-specific inquiry boundary that downstream simulation governance consumes. GOA™ may govern broader governance authority and institutional scope. ORA™ may provide the operational-reality context that the simulation intends to examine or represent. VALIDOS® may establish a separate Validation Purpose & Scope where simulation outputs, models, or simulation-derived claims enter formal validation. RIS™ may influence required Simulation Depth, consequence context, and later scenario intensity. AGA™ may establish responsibility for simulation-purpose decisions and scope authorization. ADIT® may preserve evidence showing which Simulation Purpose & Scope governed a simulation at a particular point in time. INTEGROS® may govern integrity of the underlying scope and purpose records. Specialized AI, cognition, memory, and autonomous-system architectures may contribute domain conditions that influence what the simulation must examine without replacing SPSS. SPSS governs specifically: why the simulation exists and what the simulation inquiry is permitted to claim it covers. Architectural Position Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard (SPSS) is the second Parent Standard of SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture. The architecture begins: Simulation Object ↓ Simulation Purpose & Scope SOS establishes: What exactly is being simulated? SPSS establishes: Why is it being simulated, what must the simulation cover, what is excluded, and how deeply must the inquiry operate? Once those conditions are sufficiently established, the next architectural question becomes: Which aspects of reality must now be represented inside the simulation, and at what level of abstraction and fidelity? This transition leads directly into: Reality Representation Governance Foundational Principle A simulation cannot legitimately answer a broader question than the purpose and scope for which it was actually designed. Canonical Closing Statement Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard (SPSS) establishes the inquiry boundary of SIMULOS® by governing why a simulation is performed, which questions it is intended to answer, what portions of the Simulation Object and surrounding conditions it covers, what remains explicitly excluded, where its applicability begins and ends, and what depth and precision are required for the intended simulation purpose. Through purpose definition, scope governance, inclusion and exclusion control, applicability bounding, depth and precision alignment, anti-inflation rules, change propagation, and persistent traceability, SPSS prevents technically successful simulations from acquiring purposes, meanings, or coverage that they were never designed to support. By transforming a governed Simulation Object into a bounded simulation inquiry, SPSS establishes the second methodological foundation of the SIMULOS® lifecycle and prepares that inquiry for governed representation of reality. Module Architecture → Simulation Purpose Definition Module (SPDM) → Simulation Scope Module (SSCM) → Simulation Exclusion Module (SEXM) → Simulation Applicability Context Module (SACM) → Simulation Depth & Precision Module (SDPM) Related Documents → About Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard (SPSS)

title: OOF™ Simulation Scenario Standard - (SSS)
text: OOF™ Simulation Scenario Standard - (SSS) Simulation Scenario Standard - (SSS) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Simulation Scenario Standard (SSS) defines the governance conditions under which simulation scenarios are identified, selected, structured, varied, bounded, stressed, combined, prioritized, documented, and assessed for sufficient coverage so that a governed simulation examines not only expected operating conditions but also materially relevant variations, edge cases, stress conditions, uncertainty ranges, alternative states, transitions, failures, interactions, and plausible combinations capable of affecting simulation outcomes. SSS establishes the scenario-governance layer through which the governed Simulation Object, Purpose & Scope, Reality Representation, Assumptions, Model & Environment, and Input & Data Basis are transformed into an explicit set of conditions that the simulation will actually examine. It ensures that a technically capable simulation cannot create an appearance of adequate examination merely because it executes many runs while materially relevant scenarios remain absent. Core Governance Question Which scenarios must be simulated to represent expected conditions, variations, edge cases, stresses, uncertainty, and materially relevant alternatives? Purpose A simulation can possess: a correctly identified Simulation Object, a clear purpose and scope, a strong representation of reality, governed assumptions, a well-constructed model and environment, and suitable input data, and still fail to provide useful simulation insight because the wrong scenarios were selected. A simulation may test only: normal conditions while the real risk exists in: degraded conditions. It may test: individual failures while the critical problem arises from: combined failures. It may test: average behavior while material consequences occur at: distribution tails. It may test: steady-state operation while the dangerous condition appears only during: transition. SSS exists to govern this problem. Operational Role SSS is the seventh Parent Standard of SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture. The preceding Parent Standards establish: 1. Simulation Object — What exactly is being simulated? 2. Simulation Purpose & Scope — Why is the simulation being performed and what must it cover? 3. Reality Representation — Which aspects of reality must be represented and at what abstraction and fidelity? 4. Simulation Assumptions — Which premises enable the simulation and under what limitations? 5. Simulation Model & Environment — Through which controlled model and environment will the simulation operate? 6. Simulation Inputs & Data — Which information may enter and influence the simulation? SSS asks: Which governed combinations of conditions must that simulation actually examine? It therefore establishes the scenario basis required before governed Simulation Execution begins. Governance Flow Governed Simulation Object ↓ Simulation Purpose & Scope ↓ Reality Representation ↓ Governed Assumptions ↓ Governed Model & Environment ↓ Governed Input & Data Basis ↓ Scenario Requirement Identification ↓ Baseline & Expected Conditions ↓ Scenario Variation ↓ Edge-Case Identification ↓ Stress-Condition Design ↓ Scenario Combination & Interaction ↓ Scenario Coverage Assessment ↓ Scenario Acceptance / Expansion / Restriction ↓ Governed Simulation Scenario Set ↓ Simulation Execution Operational Space SSS governs simulation-specific conditions relating to: scenario identification, scenario purpose, scenario identity, scenario classification, baseline scenarios, nominal scenarios, expected-condition scenarios, alternative scenarios, scenario variation, parameter variation, input variation, environmental variation, behavioral variation, uncertainty-driven scenarios, boundary scenarios, edge cases, rare conditions, failure scenarios, degraded-state scenarios, transition scenarios, recovery scenarios, stress conditions, extreme conditions, combined conditions, correlated conditions, multi-factor scenarios, cascading scenarios, sequential scenarios, scenario interaction, scenario dependency, scenario prioritization, scenario exclusion, scenario sufficiency, scenario coverage, scenario gaps, scenario redundancy, scenario comparability, scenario change, scenario versioning, and scenario-to-execution traceability. Operational Scope SSS applies wherever a simulation must intentionally determine which conditions are to be examined. It may govern scenario design for: AI systems, autonomous systems, autonomous agents, robotics, aerospace systems, spacecraft, mission systems, industrial systems, manufacturing, critical infrastructure, transportation, digital twins, financial systems, energy systems, healthcare systems, scientific models, climate and environmental systems, cyber systems, defense systems, emergency systems, organizational processes, human-machine systems, multi-agent environments, and future operational ecosystems. SSS does not prescribe which domain-specific scenarios are universally correct. It governs how a simulation establishes that the scenarios selected for its specific purpose are sufficiently structured and sufficiently complete. Simulation Scenario A Simulation Scenario is a governed configuration of materially relevant conditions, states, inputs, parameters, events, behaviors, interactions, constraints, or transitions under which a Simulation Object is examined through simulation. Conceptually: Scenario = Defined Simulation Conditions + Applicable Configuration + Relevant Variation + Execution Intent A scenario may describe: one operating condition, one failure, one environmental state, one behavior pattern, one combination of conditions, one transition, one stress state, or a complete event sequence. Scenario Identity Every material scenario should be sufficiently identifiable. A Scenario Identity may establish: Scenario Identifier, scenario name, scenario purpose, relevant Simulation Object, applicable Simulation Scope, model and environment configuration, relevant Input Set, parameter configuration, environmental conditions, assumptions, scenario state, intended variation, and scenario version. Scenario Requirement Before scenarios are selected, SSS establishes Scenario Requirements. A Scenario Requirement answers: What condition, variation, boundary, uncertainty, interaction, or potential failure must the simulation be capable of examining? The requirement exists independently of the exact technical scenario used to satisfy it. This distinction supports traceability: Scenario Requirement → Designed Scenario → Simulation Execution Baseline Scenario A Baseline Scenario represents the governed reference condition against which materially different scenarios may be compared. Baseline does not mean: correct reality or: most likely future. It establishes a controlled reference. Nominal Scenario A Nominal Scenario represents expected or intended operating conditions. Nominal conditions may be important for: normal behavior, expected performance, baseline comparison, and operational-state understanding. But nominal scenarios alone rarely establish sufficient scenario coverage for complex or high-consequence systems. No Nominal-Only Principle SIMULOS® establishes: Successful simulation under nominal conditions does not demonstrate adequate simulation coverage when materially relevant non-nominal conditions exist. Expected-Condition Scenario Expected-condition scenarios represent conditions reasonably anticipated within the intended Simulation Scope. They may include variation within: normal operating ranges, known environments, expected populations, expected loads, routine disturbances, or normal operational transitions. Scenario Variation Scenario Variation governs deliberate changes to one or more materially relevant simulation conditions. Variation may involve: parameters, inputs, environmental conditions, system states, actor behavior, timing, resource availability, communication conditions, failures, or dependencies. Controlled Scenario Variation Where comparative interpretation matters, the simulation should identify which conditions are intentionally changed and which remain controlled. Conceptually: Baseline Scenario ↓ Change X ↓ Variation Scenario This supports determination of whether differences in behavior are associated with the intended variation rather than hidden scenario changes. Single-Factor Variation A scenario may vary one material factor while maintaining other conditions. This may help isolate sensitivity or causal contribution within the simulation. Multi-Factor Variation Some behavior emerges only when several factors change simultaneously. SSS therefore allows scenarios involving: Factor A + Factor B + Factor C where combined conditions are materially relevant. No Single-Failure Sufficiency Principle SIMULOS® establishes: Testing individual failures does not establish coverage of combinations of failures where combined failures can produce materially different system behavior. Edge Case An Edge Case is a scenario representing conditions near or beyond the normal operating distribution, common expectation, typical configuration, or frequently observed state where simulation behavior may materially differ from nominal behavior. An edge case may arise from: unusual inputs, rare environmental conditions, uncommon interactions, boundary values, atypical behavior, unusual sequencing, unexpected combinations, or low-frequency events. Edge ≠ Impossible A condition should not be excluded merely because it is rare. The relevant governance question is: Is the condition materially plausible and consequential within the Simulation Purpose & Scope? Rare Scenario A Rare Scenario may have low occurrence probability while retaining high consequence. SSS therefore distinguishes: Frequency from: Scenario Importance. Consequence-Weighted Scenario Selection Scenario selection should consider not only: How likely is this condition? but also: What happens if it occurs? A low-frequency catastrophic condition may warrant stronger scenario coverage than a high-frequency trivial variation. Boundary Scenario A Boundary Scenario examines behavior close to an applicable operating, environmental, physical, behavioral, or governance boundary. Examples may involve: maximum load, minimum power, communication limits, environmental tolerance, control limits, resource exhaustion, operational envelopes, or response thresholds. Boundary Crossing Scenario Where materially relevant, scenarios should examine not only operation near a boundary but also what occurs when the boundary is crossed. Conceptually: Inside Boundary → Boundary Reached → Boundary Exceeded The system may behave differently at each state. Stress Scenario A Stress Scenario intentionally subjects the simulated system to conditions beyond ordinary operating variation to determine how behavior changes under increased pressure or constraint. Stress may involve: load, resource scarcity, environmental extremes, communication degradation, timing pressure, component degradation, information loss, actor density, adversarial behavior, or other system-specific stressors. Stress Does Not Mean Arbitrary Extremity Stress scenarios should remain relevant to the Simulation Purpose. SSS does not require testing arbitrary impossible conditions merely to maximize scenario count. Extreme Scenario An Extreme Scenario represents a materially severe condition at or beyond ordinary expectations where system behavior or consequences may change significantly. Extreme scenarios may be appropriate where: consequence is high, operational resilience matters, safety margins matter, rare-event behavior matters, or failure containment is being examined. Failure Scenario A Failure Scenario represents the failure of a component, dependency, capability, resource, interface, actor, process, or environmental condition relevant to the Simulation Object. Failures may be: Single Multiple Sequential Simultaneous Dependent Cascading or: Common-Cause where those distinctions matter. Common-Cause Scenario Multiple failures may arise from one common underlying cause. For example: Power Loss may simultaneously affect: Communications + Sensors + Cooling + Control Treating the failures as statistically independent may miss the actual scenario structure. Cascading Scenario A Cascading Scenario examines a sequence in which one material event causes or enables another. Conceptually: Failure A → Degradation B → Resource Loss C → Failure D Complex systems may fail through chains rather than isolated events. Sequential Scenario The order of conditions may materially change the outcome. Therefore: A → B → C may require separate examination from: C → B → A. Transition Scenario A system may behave safely in State A and safely in State B while becoming vulnerable during the transition between them. A Transition Scenario therefore examines changes such as: startup, shutdown, mode change, handover, control transfer, autonomy escalation, environment transition, recovery, docking, landing, or state switching. No Stable-State-Only Principle SIMULOS® establishes: Testing stable states alone does not establish coverage of transitions between those states where transition behavior may materially affect outcomes. Degraded-State Scenario A Degraded-State Scenario examines operation where the system remains functional but one or more capabilities, resources, dependencies, or operating conditions are reduced. Examples may involve: reduced sensing, reduced communication, degraded power, limited computation, partial actuator availability, incomplete information, reduced human support, or degraded infrastructure. Recovery Scenario A Recovery Scenario examines behavior after disruption or failure. It may address: restoration, restart, failover, fallback, state reconstruction, resource recovery, human intervention, or return to nominal operation. SSS governs selection of the scenario. ORA™ may govern actual Operational Recovery in real-world operation. Uncertainty-Driven Scenario Uncertainty identified in upstream SIMULOS® spaces may require deliberate scenario representation. For example: Input Uncertainty Range may generate: Low → Central → High scenario conditions. Uncertainty should not remain documented while scenario design tests only one convenient point estimate. Unresolved-Uncertainty Scenario Where uncertainty cannot be sufficiently quantified, scenario design may require alternative plausible states rather than one probabilistic representation. Scenario Interaction Scenarios may interact with: Simulation Assumptions, Input Sets, Environment Configurations, Parameters, actor behavior, dependencies, and execution conditions. These relationships should remain explicit. Scenario Dependency A scenario may depend upon another condition being active. For example: Emergency Power Failure Scenario may become relevant only after: Primary Power Failure. Scenario dependencies should remain traceable where material. Scenario Combination Individual scenario elements may need to be combined. Conceptually: Extreme Weather + Sensor Degradation + Communication Delay may produce behavior not observable when each condition is simulated separately.
