Combination Explosion Complex systems can generate an enormous number of possible scenario combinations. SSS does not require brute-force simulation of every mathematically possible combination. It requires governed determination of which combinations are materially relevant. Scenario Prioritization Where exhaustive simulation is impractical, scenarios may be prioritized according to factors such as: materiality, consequence, probability, uncertainty, boundary proximity, dependency concentration, scenario novelty, known failure history, operational importance, and unresolved governance gaps. Prioritization must not silently erase excluded material scenarios. Scenario Selection Basis Each material scenario or scenario family should have an identifiable selection basis. This may include: Simulation Purpose, Reality Representation, Assumptions, uncertainty, input limitations, model sensitivities, operational states, known failure modes, boundary conditions, historical events, or defined exploratory objectives. Scenario Exclusion A potential scenario may be excluded where it is: outside Simulation Scope, materially impossible, non-relevant, duplicative, already sufficiently covered, or otherwise methodologically unnecessary. Material exclusions should remain visible where omission could later be misunderstood as coverage. No Convenience Exclusion Principle SIMULOS® establishes: A materially relevant scenario must not be excluded solely because it is difficult, computationally expensive, inconvenient, or likely to produce an undesirable result. Scenario Feasibility Scenario feasibility may involve: computational constraints, model capability, data availability, environment capability, time, physical interface limitations, or other constraints. Where a materially required scenario cannot be simulated, the resulting Scenario Coverage Gap should remain visible. Scenario Coverage Scenario Coverage describes the extent to which the governed Scenario Set examines the materially relevant conditions required by the Simulation Purpose & Scope. Coverage may include: normal conditions, variation, populations, environments, boundaries, uncertainty ranges, failure states, transitions, stresses, rare events, combinations, and recovery conditions. Scenario Coverage ≠ Scenario Count SIMULOS® establishes: A large number of simulation scenarios does not establish adequate scenario coverage. Ten thousand scenarios concentrated in one narrow region may provide weaker coverage than a smaller scenario set deliberately spanning all materially relevant condition classes. Scenario Coverage Dimension Coverage may be evaluated across multiple dimensions, such as: Operating State Environment Population Input Range Uncertainty Failure Mode Transition Stress Interaction Dependency Recovery or another simulation-specific dimension. Coverage Matrix Where useful, scenario coverage may be represented through a multidimensional matrix connecting: Scenario Requirement × Condition Class × Scenario × Coverage Status This allows gaps to become visible without reducing scenario completeness to one numerical count. Scenario Coverage Status A scenario requirement may receive a status such as: Covered Conditionally Covered Partially Covered Not Covered or: Coverage Undetermined Scenario Coverage Gap A Scenario Coverage Gap exists where a materially relevant condition required by the Simulation Purpose & Scope is not sufficiently examined by the governed Scenario Set. A gap may arise from: missing data, model limitation, environment limitation, computational constraints, unrecognized scenario need, excluded edge cases, missing combinations, or incomplete uncertainty coverage. Coverage Gap Materiality Scenario gaps should be assessed according to whether the omitted condition could materially affect: system behavior, outputs, risk understanding, failure understanding, operational decisions, or downstream validation and reliance. Coverage Sufficiency Scenario Coverage Sufficiency asks: Does the Scenario Set provide enough governed variation and condition coverage to support the Simulation Purpose without claiming broader examination than was actually performed? No Full-Coverage Claim Without Basis SIMULOS® establishes: Scenario coverage must not be represented as comprehensive where materially relevant scenario classes remain unexamined. Scenario Redundancy Multiple scenarios may examine substantially the same condition. Redundancy may be useful for: repeatability, uncertainty exploration, random variation, or sensitivity testing. But scenario count should not be inflated through redundant scenarios while important gaps remain. Scenario Independence Two scenarios should not be assumed independent where they depend upon the same: Input Set, Assumption, environment, failure source, behavioral model, or dependency. This may matter when scenario results appear to provide independent confirmation. Scenario Equivalence Two scenarios may be scenario-equivalent where material differences do not alter the simulation inquiry. Equivalence should be established rather than presumed. Scenario Family Related scenarios may be grouped into a Scenario Family. Examples may include: Communication Degradation Family Power Failure Family Extreme Environment Family Autonomous Interaction Family Scenario families may support systematic coverage without eliminating scenario-level identity. Scenario Set A Governed Simulation Scenario Set is the complete collection of scenarios approved for a defined simulation campaign or inquiry. It may identify: scenario identities, scenario families, requirements, configurations, applicable inputs, variation dimensions, edge conditions, stress conditions, coverage relationships, exclusions, gaps, priorities, and execution status. Scenario Set Version Scenario design may evolve. A new Scenario Set Version should be distinguishable where materially relevant scenarios are: added, removed, modified, combined, reprioritized, or reclassified. Scenario Change Scenario change may be triggered by: new evidence, new input uncertainty, model change, environment change, discovered failure mode, changed Simulation Scope, new operational condition, changed assumptions, incident, or new system capability. Scenario Reassessment Material upstream change should trigger reassessment of whether existing scenario coverage remains sufficient. No Static Scenario Set Principle SIMULOS® establishes: A Scenario Set that was sufficient for one simulation configuration or lifecycle state must not automatically be treated as sufficient after material change. Scenario-to-Input Traceability Scenarios should remain traceable to the input conditions they consume where material. Conceptually: Scenario → Simulation Input Set Scenario-to-Parameter Traceability Where scenarios differ through parameter configuration: Scenario → Parameter Configuration should remain traceable. Scenario-to-Assumption Traceability A scenario may exist specifically to test an assumption boundary or uncertainty. Conceptually: Simulation Assumption → Relevant Scenario Requirement → Scenario Scenario-to-Environment Traceability Environment-specific scenarios should remain connected to the Simulation Environment Configuration they require. Scenario-to-Execution Binding Every Simulation Execution should be bindable to the scenario under which it occurred. Conceptually: Simulation Execution ID → Scenario ID This allows outputs to remain traceable to the exact conditions examined. Scenario Reproducibility Where required, a scenario should be defined sufficiently to permit reconstruction of the materially relevant conditions under which it was executed. Not every stochastic simulation will reproduce the identical output. But the governed scenario configuration should remain reconstructable. Scenario Comparability Two scenario executions may be compared only where materially relevant differences are understood. Scenario comparison should distinguish: Intended Variation from: Unintended Configuration Difference. Scenario Escalation Scenario execution may reveal a condition that requires stronger or broader scenario coverage. For example: a nominal stress scenario may unexpectedly expose a cascading dependency. Scenario governance should allow: Observed Simulation Behavior → New Scenario Requirement → Scenario Set Expansion without altering completed historical records. Scenario Discovery Not every relevant scenario is known before simulation begins. SIMULOS® therefore permits scenario discovery during the lifecycle. Discovered scenarios should enter governance rather than remain informal observations. Emergent Scenario An Emergent Scenario is a materially relevant condition discovered through simulation interaction, execution behavior, external events, incident analysis, or new knowledge that was not part of the original Scenario Set. Scenario Discovery Does Not Erase Earlier Gap When an important scenario is discovered later, the architecture should preserve that earlier simulations did not examine it. This distinction matters for historical reliance and reconstruction. Scenario Selection Bias Scenario design may become biased toward: expected successful behavior, easy-to-model conditions, familiar failure modes, available data, or scenarios supporting a desired conclusion. SSS requires material selection logic to remain visible. No Outcome-Seeking Scenario Principle SIMULOS® establishes: Scenario design must not be structured solely to produce the desired simulation outcome. The Scenario Set should remain capable of exposing unfavorable, unexpected, or contradictory behavior relevant to the Simulation Purpose. No Data-Convenience Scenario Principle Scenario selection should not be limited exclusively to conditions for which convenient datasets already exist where material conditions outside those datasets remain within Simulation Scope. No Model-Convenience Scenario Principle A scenario does not cease to matter merely because the current Simulation Model cannot represent it sufficiently. The result may instead be: Scenario Required — Current Simulation Capability Insufficient Scenario Capability Gap A Scenario Capability Gap exists where the simulation architecture identifies a materially required scenario that cannot currently be represented or executed with sufficient governance. The gap should remain explicit. Scenario Readiness A Scenario Set may receive a readiness status such as: Scenario Ready Conditionally Scenario Ready Partially Scenario Ready Scenario Not Ready or: Scenario Readiness Undetermined Readiness applies to progression into governed Simulation Execution. Scenario Readiness ≠ Simulation Validity A Scenario Ready status means the scenario basis is sufficiently governed for execution. It does not establish: correct execution, valid outputs, reality correlation, or legitimate operational reliance. Those questions belong to downstream SIMULOS® spaces and VALIDOS® where applicable. Governance Boundary SSS begins when the governed Simulation Object, Purpose & Scope, Reality Representation, Assumptions, Model & Environment, and Input & Data Basis are sufficiently established to determine which conditions the simulation should examine. SSS ends when materially relevant scenarios have been sufficiently identified, varied, bounded, stressed, combined, prioritized, coverage-assessed, gap-documented, versioned, and assembled into a governed Simulation Scenario Set suitable for controlled Simulation Execution. Architectural Boundary SSS does not govern: general operational scenario planning, enterprise risk management, actual Operational Reality, general validation methodology, general integrity governance, Simulation Execution, Simulation Output governance, Reality Correlation, final simulation validation, or operational reliance. SSS governs specifically: the design and coverage of the conditions that SIMULOS® will ask the simulation to examine. Minimum Governance Requirements A conforming application of SSS should establish: 1. identifiable Scenario Requirements, 2. identifiable Simulation Scenarios, 3. baseline or reference scenarios where relevant, 4. expected-condition coverage, 5. material scenario variation, 6. edge-case identification, 7. boundary-condition coverage, 8. materially relevant stress conditions, 9. failure and degraded-state scenarios where applicable, 10. transition and recovery scenarios where applicable, 11. uncertainty-driven scenario treatment, 12. materially relevant scenario combinations, 13. scenario prioritization where exhaustive coverage is impractical, 14. explicit material scenario exclusions, 15. multidimensional Scenario Coverage assessment, 16. Scenario Coverage Gaps, 17. scenario-to-input/configuration traceability, 18. scenario versioning and change visibility, 19. Scenario Readiness, 20. and sufficient scenario-to-execution traceability for reconstruction. Governance Outputs SSS may produce: Scenario Requirement Register, Simulation Scenario Identifier, Simulation Scenario Record, Scenario Classification, Baseline Scenario, Nominal Scenario, Expected-Condition Scenario, Scenario Variation Record, Single-Factor Variation Record, Multi-Factor Variation Record, Edge-Case Scenario Record, Rare Scenario Record, Boundary Scenario Record, Boundary-Crossing Scenario Record, Stress Scenario Record, Extreme Scenario Record, Failure Scenario Record, Common-Cause Scenario Record, Cascading Scenario Record, Sequential Scenario Record, Transition Scenario Record, Degraded-State Scenario Record, Recovery Scenario Record, Uncertainty-Driven Scenario Record, Scenario Interaction Map, Scenario Dependency Map, Scenario Combination Record, Scenario Priority Record, Scenario Selection Basis, Scenario Exclusion Record, Scenario Capability Gap, Scenario Family, Scenario Coverage Matrix, Scenario Coverage Assessment, Scenario Coverage Status, Scenario Coverage Gap, Scenario Coverage Gap Materiality Assessment, Scenario Coverage Sufficiency Assessment, Scenario Set, Scenario Set Identifier, Scenario Set Version, Scenario Change Record, Scenario Reassessment Trigger, Scenario Discovery Record, Emergent Scenario Record, Scenario-to-Assumption Traceability Reference, Scenario-to-Input Traceability Map, Scenario-to-Parameter Traceability Map, Scenario-to-Environment Traceability Map, Scenario-to-Execution Binding Requirement, Scenario Readiness Status, and Governed Simulation Scenario Set. Relationship to Other OOF® Architectures SSS remains bounded to simulation-specific Scenario Design. ORA™ governs actual Operational Reality. SSS may use operational conditions as scenario references but does not govern real-world operational states themselves. VALIDOS® governs validation. Scenario coverage produced under SSS may later become evidence relevant to validation, but SSS does not itself determine whether the simulation or its results satisfy a formal Validation Determination. INTEGROS® may govern integrity of scenario definitions, records, configurations, and preserved scenario history. ADIT® may preserve evidence of scenario design, selection, change, execution, and coverage. AGA™ may govern accountability for material scenario selection, exclusion, prioritization, or approval decisions. ASGA™ may define autonomous-system governance conditions that become scenario requirements when autonomous systems are simulated. AIG® may contribute AI behavioral conditions that require scenario representation. SSS does not replace those architectures. It governs specifically which simulation conditions must be deliberately constructed and examined before simulation execution can claim meaningful scenario coverage. Architectural Position Simulation Scenario Standard (SSS) is the seventh Parent Standard of SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture. Its position in the 12-Parent-Standard architecture is: 1. Simulation Object ↓ 2. Simulation Purpose & Scope ↓ 3. Reality Representation ↓ 4. Simulation Assumptions ↓ 5. Simulation Model & Environment ↓ 6. Simulation Inputs & Data ↓ 7. Simulation Scenario Design ↓ 8. Simulation Execution ↓ 9–12. Downstream SIMULOS® lifecycle governance SSS occupies the point where the previously governed simulation foundation becomes an explicit testable condition space. Before SSS, SIMULOS® establishes: what is being simulated, why, how reality is represented, what is assumed, through which model and environment the simulation operates, and which information may enter it. SSS then determines: which materially relevant conditions that governed simulation must actually examine. Only after that scenario basis exists should the architecture proceed into controlled Simulation Execution. Foundational Principle A simulation cannot claim meaningful coverage merely because it executes successfully; it must deliberately examine the materially relevant conditions, variations, boundaries, uncertainties, failures, stresses, interactions, and alternatives capable of changing the behavior or conclusions of the simulation. Canonical Closing Statement Simulation Scenario Standard establishes the scenario-design governance layer of SIMULOS® by defining how materially relevant simulation conditions are identified, structured, varied, combined, stressed, bounded, prioritized, coverage-assessed, and preserved before execution. By governing nominal conditions, expected variation, edge cases, boundary conditions, rare events, degraded and failure states, transitions, cascading interactions, uncertainty-driven scenarios, stress conditions, scenario exclusions, coverage gaps, scenario readiness, versioning, and complete scenario-to-execution traceability, SSS prevents simulation volume from being mistaken for simulation coverage and ensures that a simulation cannot appear comprehensively examined while the conditions most capable of changing its behavior remain outside the governed Scenario Set. Module Architecture → Scenario Identification Module (SCIM) → Scenario Variation Module (SCVM) → Scenario Edge-Case Module (SECM) → Scenario Stress-Condition Module (SSCM) → Scenario Coverage Module (SCCM) Related Documents → About Simulation Scenario Standard (SSS)

title: OOF™ Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Standard - (SRCS)
text: OOF™ Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Standard - (SRCS) Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Standard - (SRCS) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Standard (SRCS) defines the governance conditions under which materially relevant simulated conditions, behaviors, states, relationships, events, transitions, and outputs are systematically compared with corresponding Operational Reality in order to establish where meaningful correlation exists, where material deviation occurs, how alignment varies across conditions and dimensions, and what uncertainty and limitations bound any resulting Simulation-to-Reality Correlation claim. SRCS establishes the governed relationship between: what the simulation produces and: what corresponding reality demonstrates. It does not assume that similarity establishes equivalence. It does not assume that one successful comparison establishes general correspondence. It does not convert observed agreement into Validation State. Instead, SRCS provides the methodological correlation layer through which similarities and differences between Simulation and Operational Reality remain explicit, bounded, condition-specific, traceable, and available for subsequent validation, reliance, recalibration, or simulation lifecycle governance. Foundational Distinction SIMULOS® establishes: Simulation Similarity ≠ Reality Equivalence A simulation may resemble Operational Reality closely in one dimension while diverging materially in another. It may correlate strongly: under nominal conditions, and weakly: near boundaries, during transitions, under stress, in rare events, or when multiple conditions interact. Therefore Simulation-to-Reality Correlation must remain multidimensional, contextual, and bounded. Purpose The purpose of SRCS is to prevent simulation programs from moving directly from: “The simulation produced this.” to: “Reality behaves this way.” without a governed correlation process between those statements. SRCS exists because: a realistic-looking output may still be materially wrong, aggregate agreement may conceal local deviation, one accurate subsystem may coexist with another poorly represented subsystem, correct nominal behavior may coexist with incorrect failure behavior, apparent statistical similarity may conceal different causal or dynamic structures, correlation may deteriorate over time, reality itself may change, and simulation agreement may depend upon conditions narrower than the resulting claim implies. Architectural Position SRCS is the tenth Parent Standard of SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture. Its architectural position follows: Simulation Execution ↓ Simulation Output Governance ↓ Simulation-to-Reality Correlation and precedes downstream SIMULOS® lifecycle governance concerning the legitimacy, continued applicability, reliance, change, and future use of simulation results. SRCS is therefore the point at which SIMULOS® asks: How does the governed simulated result relate to the actual reality it claims to represent? Governance Flow Position Governed Simulation Outputs ↓ Corresponding Operational Reality Basis ↓ Simulation–Reality Comparison ↓ Correlation Criteria ↓ Correlation Assessment ↓ Deviation Identification ↓ Reality Alignment Assessment ↓ Correlation Uncertainty ↓ Bounded Simulation-to-Reality Correlation ↓ Downstream Validation / Reliance / Recalibration / Lifecycle Governance Operational Space SRCS governs: Simulation-to-Reality comparison, comparison-object identity, reality reference identity, correlation target definition, comparison dimension selection, correlation criteria, correspondence thresholds, behavioral correspondence, state correspondence, event correspondence, transition correspondence, output correspondence, distributional correspondence, temporal correspondence, spatial correspondence, sequence correspondence, interaction correspondence, boundary correspondence, stress-condition correspondence, recovery correspondence, comparative context, correlation strength, conditional correlation, partial correlation, local correlation, global correlation, correlation asymmetry, deviation identification, deviation magnitude, deviation direction, deviation localization, deviation persistence, deviation pattern, systematic deviation, random deviation, reality alignment, alignment boundaries, alignment deterioration, alignment improvement, correlation uncertainty, correlation limitations, correlation scope, correlation conditions, correlation change, correlation traceability, and Simulation-to-Reality Correlation records. Operational Scope SRCS applies wherever a simulation explicitly or implicitly claims to represent aspects of reality sufficiently for comparison. It may apply across: aerospace, spacecraft and mission simulation, autonomous systems, robotics, AI systems, digital twins, industrial processes, manufacturing systems, transportation, infrastructure, energy systems, environmental simulation, scientific models, financial systems, healthcare systems, human-system interaction, multi-agent systems, cyber-physical systems, operational planning, and future simulation environments. SRCS is technology-neutral. It does not prescribe one mathematical correlation coefficient, statistical method, physical measurement system, calibration method, or validation technique. The governed question remains: Does the simulation correspond to reality sufficiently for the specific relationship being claimed? Correlation Object A Correlation Object is the specific simulation behavior, state, output, event, relationship, transition, or other simulation result being compared with a corresponding reality reference. Examples may conceptually include: Simulated trajectory ↔ observed trajectory Simulated thermal behavior ↔ measured thermal behavior Simulated agent response ↔ observed agent response Simulated failure progression ↔ operational failure progression Simulated demand pattern ↔ actual demand pattern Simulated system transition ↔ observed system transition SRCS requires clarity about what exactly is being correlated. Reality Reference A Simulation-to-Reality Correlation requires a corresponding Reality Reference. A Reality Reference may consist of: operational measurements, sensor records, physical observations, mission telemetry, field behavior, experimental observations, operational incidents, verified historical records, or another sufficiently identified representation of Operational Reality. SRCS does not govern Operational Reality itself. ORA™ may provide or govern the relevant Operational Reality basis. SRCS governs the relationship between that basis and the simulation. Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Basis A governed correlation should preserve the relationship: Simulation Object ↓ Simulation Configuration ↓ Scenario ↓ Simulation Execution ↓ Simulation Output / Behavior ↔ Corresponding Reality Condition ↓ Operational Observation ↓ Comparison ↓ Correlation Assessment This creates a traceable bridge rather than an unsupported statement of realism. Comparable Conditions Principle Simulation and reality should not be compared as if they were equivalent where materially relevant conditions differ. Possible comparison dimensions may include: object version, environment, input conditions, initial state, operating state, system configuration, population, timing, scenario, boundary conditions, stress level, and dependencies. SIMULOS® establishes: Correlation requires sufficient comparability of the conditions being compared. Correlation Target A Correlation Target defines what correspondence is being examined. For example: Trajectory correspondence is different from: energy-consumption correspondence which is different from: failure-sequence correspondence. Strong correlation in one target must not be generalized automatically to another. No Correlation Transfer Principle SIMULOS® establishes: Correlation demonstrated for one behavior, condition, subsystem, environment, population, or scenario does not automatically transfer to materially different ones. Correlation Criteria Every material Simulation-to-Reality Correlation assessment should operate against sufficiently defined criteria. Correlation Criteria may concern: allowable deviation, behavioral pattern, directionality, ordering, timing, distribution, state transition, physical tolerance, response shape, event occurrence, frequency, magnitude, or another simulation-specific relationship. Criteria should be defined sufficiently to distinguish: acceptable correspondence from: material deviation. Correlation Criteria ≠ Validation Criteria Correlation Criteria answer: How similar or aligned are the Simulation and Reality with respect to this defined relationship? VALIDOS® Validation Criteria may later answer: Is the resulting correlation evidence sufficient to support a particular Validation Determination? These are related but distinct governance questions. Direct Correlation Direct Correlation occurs where a simulated quantity or behavior can be compared directly with a corresponding observed quantity or behavior. Conceptually: Simulated X ↔ Observed X Direct correspondence may be strong, weak, conditional, or absent. Indirect Correlation Some simulated properties cannot be observed directly. Correlation may therefore depend upon: proxies, derived observations, intermediate measurements, aggregate behavior, or indirect operational signals. Where correlation is indirect, the intermediate relationship should remain explicit. Proxy Correlation Principle SIMULOS® establishes: Agreement with a proxy does not automatically establish equivalence with the underlying reality the proxy represents. Behavioral Correlation Behavioral Correlation assesses whether simulated behavior sufficiently corresponds to observed behavior. This may include: response to inputs, adaptation, recovery, escalation, coordination, failure, control behavior, or agent interaction. State Correlation State Correlation assesses whether the simulated system reaches or occupies states corresponding sufficiently to observed states. Transition Correlation Transition Correlation assesses whether the simulation reproduces materially relevant movement between states. This is important because: Correct State A + Correct State B ≠ Correct A→B Transition Temporal Correlation Temporal Correlation concerns whether simulation events occur: at comparable times, with comparable delays, in comparable sequences, or across comparable durations. A simulation may reproduce an event but still materially misrepresent when it occurs. Spatial Correlation Spatial Correlation concerns whether simulated positions, distributions, paths, fields, or spatial relationships correspond sufficiently to reality. Distributional Correlation Aggregate values may agree while distributions differ. For example: same mean may coexist with: different variance, tails, clustering, or multimodality. SRCS therefore does not allow aggregate similarity automatically to establish distributional correlation. Sequence Correlation Systems may generate the correct events in the wrong order. Where order matters, SRCS evaluates: Event Identity + Event Sequence rather than event presence alone. Interaction Correlation Interaction Correlation concerns whether simulated relationships between: agents, subsystems, humans, environments, dependencies, or other actors correspond sufficiently to observed relationships. Boundary Correlation A simulation may correlate well in the center of the operating envelope but poorly near limits. SRCS therefore supports correlation assessment across: Nominal Region Boundary Region Threshold Region and where relevant: Beyond-Nominal Region. Stress Correlation Where Operational Reality provides evidence from degraded or stressed conditions, SRCS may compare: Simulated Stress Behavior with: Observed Stress Behavior. Strong nominal correlation must not substitute for absent stress correlation where stress behavior materially matters. Recovery Correlation Recovery behavior may require separate correlation. A model may accurately reproduce failure onset while poorly reproducing: fallback, restoration, adaptation, restart, or recovery duration. Local Correlation Local Correlation exists where Simulation and Reality correspond sufficiently within a bounded region of: state, environment, population, configuration, parameter space, or scenario conditions. Global Correlation Global Correlation represents broader correspondence across the declared Simulation Scope. Global correlation should not be claimed by extrapolating from narrow local correlation without an adequate basis. No Local-to-Global Inflation Principle SIMULOS® establishes: Strong local Simulation-to-Reality Correlation does not establish global correlation across unexamined Scenario Space. Conditional Correlation Correlation may hold only under explicit conditions. For example: Strong correlation under nominal thermal conditions but: weak correlation under rapid thermal transition. The resulting correlation record should preserve those conditions. Partial Correlation Different aspects of the same simulation may correlate differently. For example: Position — Strong Velocity — Strong Energy Consumption — Moderate Recovery Timing — Weak The simulation should not be given one undifferentiated correlation label if material dimensions differ. Correlation Profile A Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Profile may represent multidimensional correspondence across relevant dimensions. This is often methodologically stronger than one global score. No Single-Score Requirement SIMULOS® does not require correlation to be represented through one numerical metric. A single score may conceal: strong and weak dimensions, local deviation, conditional relationships, failure-region divergence, or uncertainty. Where a numerical score is used, its meaning and limitations should remain explicit. Correlation Strength Where useful, correlation may be classified as: Strong Moderate Weak Conditional Partial No Material Correlation or: Correlation Undetermined provided the classification is tied to explicit criteria. Correlation Strength ≠ Validity SIMULOS® establishes: Strong Simulation-to-Reality Correlation does not itself establish that the simulation is Validated for every intended use. Correlation may become one component of a broader VALIDOS® validation record. Deviation A Simulation-to-Reality Deviation is a materially relevant difference between simulated behavior and corresponding Operational Reality. Deviation may concern: value, timing, direction, sequence, magnitude, distribution, state, transition, interaction, failure, recovery, or another governed property. Deviation Is Not Automatically Failure A deviation may be: expected, acceptable, immaterial, explainable, model-induced, data-induced, environment-induced, reality-induced, or materially problematic. SRCS governs identification and characterization before drawing stronger conclusions. Deviation Magnitude Deviation Magnitude describes how large the difference is relative to the applicable comparison basis. Magnitude should be interpreted together with materiality. A numerically small deviation may be critical near a threshold. A numerically larger deviation may be inconsequential elsewhere. Deviation Direction Deviation may systematically: overestimate, underestimate, anticipate, delay, amplify, suppress, accelerate, or otherwise bias simulated behavior relative to reality. Direction can reveal patterns that aggregate absolute error may hide. Systematic Deviation A Systematic Deviation persists predictably across comparable conditions. This may signal: model bias, incorrect parameterization, representation weakness, input mismatch, missing interaction, or another simulation limitation. SRCS identifies the pattern. The appropriate upstream SIMULOS® governance space determines what requires correction. Random Deviation Some deviations may vary without stable direction. Random deviation may still be material where its magnitude affects the intended Simulation Purpose. Localized Deviation A simulation may correlate strongly overall while diverging materially in one bounded region. This creates a Localized Correlation Gap rather than necessarily a global simulation failure. Deviation Map Where appropriate, SRCS may represent: Scenario Space → Correlation Strength / Deviation This may reveal regions where the simulation remains strongly reality-aligned and regions where it does not. Deviation Attribution Where possible, deviations should be connected to potential contributing factors such as: Reality Representation, Simulation Assumptions, model structure, environment configuration, parameters, inputs, transformation, Scenario Coverage, execution conditions, output interpretation, or changed Operational Reality. Attribution should remain evidence-bounded. No Automatic Cause Principle SIMULOS® establishes: Observed Simulation-to-Reality deviation identifies a difference; it does not automatically establish why that difference exists. Reality Alignment Reality Alignment describes the degree to which the simulation continues to correspond sufficiently to relevant Operational Reality across the declared conditions. Alignment may be: Strong Conditional Partial Weak Misaligned or: Undetermined. Reality Alignment Boundary A simulation may have a clearly bounded region where alignment is sufficient. Conceptually: Aligned Region ↓ Transition Region ↓ Misaligned Region Identifying this boundary may be more informative than assigning one global realism label. No Reality-Equivalence Claim SIMULOS® establishes: No degree of observed Simulation-to-Reality similarity should be represented as complete Reality Equivalence unless such equivalence has been independently and legitimately established for the exact governed claim. For complex systems, such universal equivalence may often be impossible to establish. Correlation Uncertainty A Simulation-to-Reality Correlation claim itself contains uncertainty. Possible sources include: measurement uncertainty, operational observation limitations, limited reality data, sparse comparison conditions, input uncertainty, scenario mismatch, temporal mismatch, stochastic behavior, environment differences, system change, and uncertainty in correlation methods. Correlation Uncertainty Must Remain Attached A correlation statement should not imply greater certainty than its comparison basis supports. Conceptually: Correlation Result + Correlation Uncertainty + Conditions + Scope should remain connected. No Correlation Precision Inflation A precisely calculated correlation metric does not imply equivalent certainty in the reality relationship where the observational basis is limited. Reality Observation Limitation Operational Reality may itself be incompletely observable. For example: internal system states may not be measurable, field observations may be sparse, critical failures may be rare, measurements may be noisy, mission data may be incomplete, or historical records may lack relevant context. SRCS preserves this limitation rather than treating reality observations as perfect ground truth by default. Operational Reality ≠ Perfect Knowledge of Reality This distinction is important. ORA™ may govern the best available Operational Reality representation. SRCS then correlates the simulation against that governed reality basis. The limitations of that basis should remain visible. Correlation Coverage Simulation-to-Reality Correlation should be assessed relative to the Scenario Space actually represented by Operational Reality observations. If correlation has been established only under: Conditions A, B, and C then the simulation should not claim established correlation under: D, E, and F without further basis. Correlation Coverage Gap A Correlation Coverage Gap exists where materially relevant Simulation Scenario Space lacks sufficient corresponding Operational Reality evidence for meaningful correlation assessment. This may occur because: the event has never occurred operationally, the condition cannot safely be reproduced, mission opportunities are limited, observations are incomplete, or future systems do not yet exist operationally. Uncorrelatable Scenario Space Some Scenario Space may currently be impossible to correlate directly with reality. For example: catastrophic spacecraft combinations never observed, future autonomy modes, novel environmental conditions, future infrastructure configurations, or hypothetical emergency states. The correct governance state may be: Correlation Not Yet Establishable rather than: Correlation Assumed. No Absence-of-Reality-Data Inference SIMULOS® establishes: Where corresponding Operational Reality evidence does not exist, correlation must not be manufactured from simulation evidence alone. Correlation Change Simulation-to-Reality Correlation may change even if the simulation itself does not. Reality may evolve through: system modifications, environmental change, population change, infrastructure change, operational behavior change, software updates, mission changes, or new dependencies. Correlation Drift Correlation Drift occurs when previously established correspondence between Simulation and Reality weakens or changes over time. This may be caused by: Simulation Change Reality Change or: Both. No Permanent Correlation Principle SIMULOS® establishes: A previously established Simulation-to-Reality Correlation must not be assumed permanent when the simulation or corresponding Operational Reality materially changes. Correlation Reassessment Trigger Reassessment may be required when there is material change in: Simulation Object, Reality Representation, Simulation Assumptions, model, environment, parameters, inputs, scenarios, execution, output interpretation, operational environment, object version, population, mission phase, dependency, or available reality evidence. Correlation Improvement Correlation may improve after: model refinement, better Reality Representation, improved parameters, better input data, new operational observations, additional scenario coverage, or correction of systematic deviation. Improvement should be demonstrated, not presumed. Correlation Deterioration New Operational Reality evidence may reveal that previous correspondence was overstated or limited. SRCS must remain capable of producing a weaker correlation conclusion. No Positive-Bias Principle SIMULOS® establishes: Simulation-to-Reality Correlation governance must remain capable of demonstrating weak correlation, partial correlation, material deviation, or unresolved correspondence. Simulation Calibration Boundary Correlation findings may inform simulation calibration. However: SRCS does not own general model calibration. Its role is to identify: where and how Simulation and Reality correspond or diverge. The appropriate model, parameter, input, representation, or environment governance space may then address the cause. No Calibration-to-Correlation Circularity A simulation tuned using one reality dataset should not automatically be represented as independently correlated against that same dataset without disclosure. SIMULOS® establishes: Data used to calibrate the simulation and data used to demonstrate Simulation-to-Reality Correlation should remain distinguishable where independence materially affects the claim. Correlation Independence Where a stronger correlation claim requires independent reality evidence, that independence should remain explicit. This prevents: fit from being confused with: independent correspondence. Overfitting to Reality Samples A simulation may reproduce observed cases closely while generalizing poorly to new operational conditions. SRCS therefore distinguishes: Correlation with Known Observations from: Correlation across materially broader Operational Reality. Reality Holdout Principle Where appropriate, previously unused Operational Reality observations may provide stronger evidence of generalizable correlation than observations used to construct or calibrate the simulation. SRCS does not prescribe a specific holdout method. It preserves the methodological distinction. Cross-Environment Correlation Correlation in one environment must not automatically transfer to another. Examples: Earth Laboratory ≠ Orbital Environment Dry Road ≠ Snow Factory A ≠ Factory B Population A ≠ Population B Low-Traffic Environment ≠ Dense Multi-Agent Environment Cross-Version Correlation A correlation conclusion for one Simulation Object or real-system version should not automatically apply to materially changed versions. Correlation Across Mission Phases For mission systems, correlation may differ across: launch, cruise, orbital operations, docking, landing, autonomous recovery, safe mode, or other phases. A global mission-level correlation statement may conceal weak phase-specific correspondence. Autonomous-System Correlation Autonomous systems present a particularly important correlation problem. Their simulated behavior may depend upon: perception, internal state, external agents, communication, timing, memory, changing permissions, human intervention, uncertainty, and adaptive decision paths. SRCS therefore supports correlation not only of final outputs but of: state transitions, decisions, timing, fallback, escalation, recovery, and interaction patterns. Space and Mission Correlation Space systems create a particularly difficult Simulation-to-Reality Correlation environment because: real mission observations are expensive, some events occur only once, catastrophic states may never be directly observed before deployment, space environments can be difficult to reproduce physically, mission phases differ materially, telemetry can be incomplete, and operational configurations evolve. SRCS therefore does not require impossible reality equivalence. Instead it provides a governed structure for distinguishing: what has been correlated from: what remains extrapolated, simulated-only, uncertain, or operationally unobserved. This distinction can be critical where mission decisions depend heavily upon simulation. Autonomous Vehicle Correlation An autonomous vehicle simulation may correlate strongly with reality for: ordinary road following, standard braking, common pedestrian behavior, and normal weather. That does not establish equivalent correlation for: rare interactions, construction zones, degraded sensors, unusual road markings, emergency vehicle behavior, or compound edge conditions. SRCS keeps the correlation boundary visible. Digital Twin Correlation A digital twin may continuously compare: Simulated State with: Operational State. SRCS may govern: alignment, deviation, temporal lag, drift, systematic mismatch, and correlation deterioration. A digital twin that ceases to correlate sufficiently with the physical system should not continue to be represented as an equivalent operational representation merely because the software remains active. Correlation Status A governed Simulation-to-Reality Correlation assessment may result in statuses such as: Strongly Correlated Conditionally Correlated Partially Correlated Weakly Correlated Materially Deviated Not Correlated or: Correlation Undetermined depending upon the governed criteria and scope. The status must remain tied to: Correlation Target, Scope, Conditions, Reality Reference, Comparison Basis, and Correlation Uncertainty. Correlation Status ≠ Simulation State SRCS does not create a general Validation State. A correlation status is a governed statement about the Simulation-to-Reality relationship. VALIDOS® may later determine how that relationship contributes to a formal Validation Determination and Validation State. Correlation Claim Boundary Any resulting correlation claim must remain no broader than: Compared Simulation Conditions Corresponding Operational Reality Conditions Correlation Criteria Observed Relationship Known Deviation Correlation Uncertainty Applicable Scope No Upward Correlation Claim Principle SIMULOS® establishes: A Simulation-to-Reality Correlation claim must not exceed the strongest correspondence demonstrated by the materially relevant comparison record. Correlation Traceability A complete correlation path should remain reconstructable: Simulation Object ↓ Scenario ↓ Simulation Execution ↓ Simulation Output / Behavior ↓ Correlation Target ↔ Operational Reality Reference ↓ Comparison Criteria ↓ Observed Correspondence ↓ Deviation ↓ Reality Alignment ↓ Correlation Uncertainty ↓ Correlation Status Point-in-Time Correlation Reconstruction SRCS should support questions such as: Which Simulation version was compared? Against which Operational Reality basis? Under which conditions? Which criteria were used? Which dimensions correlated strongly? Where did material deviation occur? Which Scenario Space lacked reality evidence? How uncertain was the correlation claim? Has the correlation changed since then? Governance Boundary SRCS begins when governed Simulation Outputs or Simulation Behaviors exist and corresponding Operational Reality evidence is sufficiently identifiable for comparison. SRCS ends when: the comparison target is identified, the corresponding reality basis is established, relevant correlation criteria are applied, material deviations are identified, Reality Alignment is assessed, correlation uncertainty and limitations are preserved, and the Simulation-to-Reality relationship is expressed as a bounded, traceable correlation record. SRCS does not determine: Operational Reality itself, universal simulation validity, general model integrity, final Validation Determination, deployment authorization, operational safety, or unrestricted reliance. Relationship to ORA™ ORA™ governs Operational Reality. It may establish: operational states, observed conditions, actual events, system configurations, real-world dependencies, or other reality references. SRCS consumes the relevant governed reality basis and asks: How does the simulation correspond to it? Therefore: ORA™ → Reality SIMULOS® SRCS → Simulation ↔ Reality Relationship Relationship to VALIDOS® SRCS does not replace validation. Its output may become important validation evidence. VALIDOS® may subsequently assess: evidence fitness, source reliability, method, execution, determination, state, and reliance. The architectural boundary is: SRCS determines the governed correlation relationship. VALIDOS® determines what validation conclusion that relationship can legitimately support. Relationship to INTEGROS® INTEGROS® may govern integrity of: Simulation Outputs, operational observations, comparison records, correlation artifacts, or preserved correlation history. SRCS governs the meaning and boundaries of the correlation relationship itself. Relationship to ADIT® ADIT® may audit the evidence trail supporting Simulation-to-Reality Correlation. SRCS remains the simulation-specific governance owner of the correlation relationship. Relationship to SOGS Simulation Output Governance Standard (SOGS) establishes: what the simulation produced and what may legitimately be inferred directly from those outputs. SRCS asks the next distinct question: How does what the simulation produced correspond to Operational Reality? Therefore: Simulation Output ≠ Simulation-to-Reality Correlation. Relationship to Reality Representation Standard RRS governs how selected reality is represented inside the simulation. SRCS provides an important downstream feedback mechanism: Does that representation actually produce behavior corresponding sufficiently to Operational Reality? Material deviation may indicate that Reality Representation requires reassessment. Relationship to Simulation Assumptions Simulation-to-Reality deviation may expose assumptions that: were inaccurate, became obsolete, apply only conditionally, or fail in particular Scenario Space. SRCS identifies the correlation consequence. SAS governs the assumption itself. Relationship to Model & Environment Governance Correlation deviation may arise from: model structure, environment configuration, parameters, versions, or boundary interactions. SRCS identifies the mismatch. SMES governs the relevant model and environment changes. Relationship to Input & Data Governance Input mismatch may affect correlation. SRCS identifies the resulting Simulation-to-Reality difference. SIDS governs the Simulation Input basis itself. Relationship to Scenario Governance Scenario Coverage limits Correlation Coverage. A simulation cannot demonstrate Simulation-to-Reality Correlation in Scenario Space that has neither been adequately simulated nor observed in Operational Reality. Relationship to Simulation Execution Correlation relies upon traceable Simulation Execution. If the execution that produced a Simulation Output cannot be reconstructed sufficiently, the correlation basis may itself become weakened or indeterminate. Governance Outputs SRCS may produce: Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Basis, Correlation Object Record, Reality Reference Record, Correlation Target, Comparison Context Record, Simulation–Reality Comparison Record, Correlation Criteria Record, Behavioral Correlation Record, State Correlation Record, Transition Correlation Record, Temporal Correlation Record, Spatial Correlation Record, Distributional Correlation Record, Sequence Correlation Record, Interaction Correlation Record, Boundary Correlation Record, Stress Correlation Record, Recovery Correlation Record, Local Correlation Record, Conditional Correlation Record, Partial Correlation Record, Correlation Profile, Correlation Strength Record, Simulation-to-Reality Deviation Record, Deviation Magnitude Record, Deviation Direction Record, Systematic Deviation Record, Localized Correlation Gap, Deviation Map, Reality Alignment Record, Reality Alignment Boundary, Correlation Coverage Record, Correlation Coverage Gap, Uncorrelatable Scenario Space Record, Correlation Uncertainty Record, Correlation Limitation Record, Correlation Change Record, Correlation Drift Record, Correlation Reassessment Trigger, Correlation Status, Simulation-to-Reality Traceability Map, and Governed Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Record. Architectural Separation SRCS must remain separated from four neighboring governance questions: Reality Representation → How is reality represented inside the simulation? Simulation Output Governance → What exactly did the simulation produce and what may be inferred from it? Simulation-to-Reality Correlation → How does that simulated result correspond to actual Operational Reality? Validation Governance → What formal validation conclusion may legitimately be established from the complete validation record? This separation is fundamental to SIMULOS®. Canonical Principle Simulation similarity is not reality equivalence. Supporting Principle A simulation should be trusted as representative of reality only to the extent that the relevant relationship between simulated and observed reality has actually been examined, bounded, and kept traceable to the conditions under which that correspondence was established. Foundational Principle Simulation-to-Reality Correlation becomes methodologically legitimate only when similarity and deviation are evaluated against an identifiable Operational Reality basis, within explicit comparison conditions, using governed criteria, while preserving the uncertainty and boundaries of the resulting correlation claim. Canonical Closing Statement Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Standard establishes the governed bridge between Simulation and Operational Reality within SIMULOS®. By governing the identification of correlation targets, comparison conditions, correlation criteria, behavioral and state correspondence, transitions, distributions, timing, interactions, boundaries, deviations, Reality Alignment, Correlation Coverage, uncertainty, drift, reassessment, and complete Simulation-to-Reality traceability, SRCS prevents realistic appearance, numerical similarity, nominal agreement, or isolated successful comparison from being mistaken for Reality Equivalence. It enables simulations to state not merely that they resemble reality, but precisely where, under which conditions, to what extent, and with what uncertainty that correspondence has actually been demonstrated—while preserving the architectural boundary through which ORA™ governs Operational Reality and VALIDOS® governs the validation conclusions that may ultimately be drawn from the correlation record. Module Architecture → Simulation-Reality Comparison Module (SRCM) → Simulation Correlation Criteria Module (SCCM) → Simulation-Reality Deviation Module (SDMM) → Reality Alignment Module (SRAM) → Correlation Uncertainty Module (SCUM) Related Documents → About Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Standard (SRCS)

title: OOF™ SIMULOS® Architecture Map
text: OOF™ SIMULOS® Architecture Map SIMULOS® Architecture Map Simulation Governance Architecture — Simulation Governance Layer SIMULOS® serves as the official OOF® simulation governance reference map used to identify, define, classify, navigate, govern, evaluate, and understand governable simulation spaces across AI systems, autonomous systems, robotics, digital twins, engineering systems, scientific models, critical infrastructure, space systems, and future simulation environments. The purpose of SIMULOS® is not to define the technical implementation of a simulation system. The purpose of SIMULOS® is to identify, define, separate, and map the governable spaces through which a Simulation Object is identified, scoped, represented, assumption-bounded, modeled, supplied with inputs, exposed to scenarios, executed, interpreted through outputs, correlated with reality, converted into bounded evidence, and governed throughout its continuing lifecycle. SIMULOS® serves as the official simulation governance reference map for: AI Systems Autonomous Systems Autonomous Agents Robotics Digital Twins Engineering Systems Scientific Models Physical Simulations Hybrid Simulations Mission Simulations Space Systems Safety-Critical Systems Industrial Systems Transportation Systems Healthcare Simulations Financial and Economic Simulations Critical Infrastructure Multi-System Environments Future Simulation Ecosystems Core Architectural Principle Every simulation governance space answers one primary governance question. No simulation governance space duplicates the purpose of another simulation governance space. Every simulation governance space has a defined beginning, a defined operational purpose, and a defined governance boundary. Every simulation governance space begins where the preceding simulation governance requirement has been sufficiently established. Together, these simulation governance spaces form the official simulation governance reference map of SIMULOS®. Official Simulation Governance Flow Simulation Object → Simulation Purpose & Scope → Simulation Reality Representation → Simulation Assumptions → Simulation Model & Environment → Simulation Inputs & Data → Simulation Scenario Design → Simulation Execution → Simulation Output Governance → Simulation-to-Reality Correlation → Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary → Simulation Lifecycle, Drift & Resimulation 1. Simulation Object Standard (SOS) Governed Space: Simulation Object Core Question What exactly is being simulated, and how must the Simulation Object be identified, bounded, versioned, and distinguished? Canonical Definition Simulation Object Standard (SOS) defines the governance conditions under which the object, system, process, environment, phenomenon, configuration, relationship, or other subject being represented through simulation is formally identified, bounded, versioned, configured, distinguished, and documented as a governable Simulation Object. Governance Boundary Begins when an intended simulation requires explicit identification of what is actually being simulated. Ends when the Simulation Object has been sufficiently identified, bounded, versioned, configured, and documented to support definition of the simulation purpose and scope. 2. Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard (SPSS) Governed Space: Simulation Purpose & Scope Core Question Why is the simulation being performed, what must it cover, and what remains outside its simulation boundary? Canonical Definition Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard (SPSS) defines the governance conditions under which the purpose, intended inquiry, scope, exclusions, applicability context, required depth, and required precision of a simulation are formally established and documented. Governance Boundary Begins when the Simulation Object has been sufficiently established and the reason for simulating it must be formally defined. Ends when the simulation purpose, scope, exclusions, applicability context, depth, and precision have been sufficiently established to determine which aspects of reality must be represented. 3. Reality Representation Standard (RRS) Governed Space: Simulation Reality Representation Core Question Which aspects of reality must the simulation represent, at what abstraction and fidelity, and which aspects may legitimately remain simplified or excluded? Canonical Definition Reality Representation Standard (RRS) defines the governance conditions under which relevant aspects of reality are selected, abstracted, represented, resolved, simplified, limited, or excluded within a simulation according to the simulation's governed purpose and scope. Governance Boundary Begins when the simulation purpose and scope are sufficiently established to determine which aspects of reality materially require representation. Ends when the required reality representation, abstraction, fidelity, resolution, exclusions, and known representational limitations have been sufficiently defined to support explicit governance of simulation assumptions. 4. Simulation Assumption Standard (SAS) Governed Space: Simulation Assumptions Core Question Which assumptions enable the simulation, and how must their basis, dependencies, uncertainty, limitations, and consequences remain governed? Canonical Definition Simulation Assumption Standard (SAS) defines the governance conditions under which assumptions enabling or materially influencing a simulation are identified, justified, linked to their basis and dependencies, characterized for uncertainty, bounded by limitations, and maintained as explicit elements of the simulation basis. Governance Boundary Begins when the selected representation of reality requires assumptions, approximations, inferred conditions, or other propositions that cannot simply be treated as established simulation facts. Ends when material assumptions, their bases, dependencies, uncertainties, and limitations have been sufficiently established to support construction and configuration of the simulation model and environment. 5. Simulation Model & Environment Standard (SMES) Governed Space: Simulation Model & Environment Core Question How must the simulation model and simulation environment be constructed, configured, bounded, and controlled? Canonical Definition Simulation Model & Environment Standard (SMES) defines the governance conditions under which simulation models and simulation environments are structurally constituted, configured, parameterized, bounded, versioned, and controlled to represent the governed Simulation Object under the established simulation basis. Governance Boundary Begins when the Simulation Object, purpose, reality representation, and material assumptions provide a sufficient basis for model and environment construction. Ends when the simulation model, environment, parameters, boundary interactions, configuration, and version have been sufficiently established to govern the inputs and data entering the simulation. 6. Simulation Input & Data Standard (SIDS) Governed Space: Simulation Inputs & Data Core Question Which inputs and data may enter the simulation, and under what representativeness, transformation, temporal, and uncertainty conditions? Canonical Definition Simulation Input & Data Standard (SIDS) defines the governance conditions under which simulation inputs and data are identified, selected, assessed for representativeness, transformed, temporally situated, uncertainty-characterized, and admitted into a governed simulation. Governance Boundary Begins when the configured simulation model and environment require governed inputs, parameters, datasets, signals, initial conditions, or other simulation-driving information. Ends when the simulation input basis has been sufficiently identified, represented, transformed, temporally bounded, and uncertainty-characterized to support governed scenario design. 7. Simulation Scenario Standard (SSS) Governed Space: Simulation Scenario Design Core Question Which scenarios must be simulated to represent expected conditions, variations, edge cases, stresses, uncertainty, and materially relevant alternatives? Canonical Definition Simulation Scenario Standard (SSS) defines the governance conditions under which simulation scenarios are identified, varied, structured, stress-tested, extended toward relevant edge cases, and evaluated for coverage against the governed simulation purpose and represented reality. Governance Boundary Begins when the Simulation Object, represented reality, assumptions, model, environment, and input basis are sufficiently established to determine which conditions and variations require simulation. Ends when the required scenario space, variations, edge cases, stress conditions, and coverage have been sufficiently established to support governed simulation execution. 8. Simulation Execution Standard (SES) Governed Space: Simulation Execution Core Question How must a simulation be instantiated, executed, observed, repeated, controlled, and documented? Canonical Definition Simulation Execution Standard (SES) defines the governance conditions under which a simulation is instantiated, controlled, executed, observed, repeated, and documented so that the execution process remains connected to its approved Simulation Object, configuration, inputs, scenarios, and simulation basis. Governance Boundary Begins when the simulation object, model, environment, inputs, and required scenario conditions are sufficiently established for execution. Ends when governed simulation executions have been completed, observed, repeated where required, and sufficiently documented to establish identifiable simulation outputs. 9. Simulation Output Governance Standard (SOGS) Governed Space: Simulation Output Governance Core Question What exactly did the simulation produce, how must simulation outputs be bounded and interpreted, and what may legitimately be inferred from them? Canonical Definition Simulation Output Governance Standard (SOGS) defines the governance conditions under which simulation outputs are identified, classified, interpreted, bounded, documented, and distinguished from derived inferences so that the meaning and limitations of what the simulation produced remain explicit. Governance Boundary Begins when governed simulation execution produces observable, measurable, derived, aggregated, or otherwise identifiable outputs. Ends when simulation outputs and governed inferences have been sufficiently identified, classified, bounded, limited, and documented to support comparison with the reality they claim to represent. 10. Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Standard (SRCS) Governed Space: Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Core Question To what extent do simulated behavior, conditions, and outputs correspond to the reality they claim to represent? Canonical Definition Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Standard (SRCS) defines the governance conditions under which simulated behavior, states, conditions, relationships, and outputs are systematically compared with available reality to determine correspondence, deviation, alignment, uncertainty, and the limits of simulation-to-reality correlation. Governance Boundary Begins when governed simulation outputs exist and a relevant reality basis is available or can legitimately be established for comparison. Ends when the simulation-to-reality relationship has been sufficiently characterized through comparison, correlation criteria, deviation analysis, alignment assessment, and correlation uncertainty to support evaluation of simulation-derived evidence. Simulation similarity is not reality equivalence. 11. Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard (SERBS) Governed Space: Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Core Question What evidential meaning may simulation results legitimately carry, and where does simulation-specific reliance end before broader validation governance becomes necessary? Canonical Definition Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard (SERBS) defines the governance conditions under which simulation-derived information may legitimately qualify as evidence, acquire simulation-specific evidential weight, support explicitly bounded reliance, remain subject to defined use limitations, and enter broader validation governance without losing the conditions that establish its legitimate meaning. Governance Boundary Begins when governed simulation outputs and, where relevant, simulation-to-reality correlation provide a basis from which simulation-derived evidence may be considered. Ends when the simulation-derived evidence has been sufficiently qualified, weighted, bounded for reliance, constrained by applicable use limitations, and prepared for transfer into broader validation governance where required. Simulation-derived evidence must not travel farther than its governed meaning can legitimately support. 12. Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Standard (SLRS) Governed Space: Simulation Lifecycle, Drift & Resimulation Core Question How must simulation relevance be monitored over time, and when must changed reality trigger update, resimulation, replacement, or retirement? Canonical Definition Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Standard (SLRS) defines the governance conditions under which the continuing relevance of a simulation is monitored, material simulation drift is recognized, resimulation triggers are established, resimulation scope is determined, and simulations are updated, repeated, replaced, transitioned, or retired as the Simulation Object, represented reality, assumptions, models, inputs, scenarios, operational conditions, evidence basis, or intended reliance materially change. Governance Boundary Begins when a governed simulation and its outputs, correlations, or evidence enter continuing use, reference, reliance, monitoring, or preservation beyond the initial simulation process. Continues throughout the remaining simulation lifecycle while the simulation, its outputs, or simulation-derived evidence retain operational, evidential, scientific, engineering, analytical, or decision relevance. Where material change invalidates or weakens the existing simulation basis, Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Standard may trigger governed re-entry into the appropriate earlier SIMULOS® governance space rather than requiring the entire lifecycle to restart automatically. Core Governed Simulation Spaces Simulation Object Simulation Purpose & Scope Simulation Reality Representation Simulation Assumptions Simulation Model & Environment Simulation Inputs & Data Simulation Scenario Design Simulation Execution Simulation Output Governance Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Simulation Lifecycle, Drift & Resimulation Recursive Simulation Lifecycle SIMULOS® does not end when a simulation execution is completed. Once simulation results, simulation-derived evidence, or simulation-supported decisions remain in use, the architecture becomes recursive: Governed Simulation → Simulation Output → Simulation-Derived Evidence → Permitted Reliance → Lifecycle Monitoring → Material Change → Simulation Drift Recognition → Resimulation Trigger → Resimulation Scope → Lifecycle Re-Entry → Updated Simulation / Resimulation / Replacement / Retirement Lifecycle re-entry occurs at the earliest materially affected governance space. A changed Simulation Object may require re-entry into Simulation Object Standard. A changed purpose may require re-entry into Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard. A changed understanding of reality may require re-entry into Reality Representation Standard. A failed assumption may require re-entry into Simulation Assumption Standard. A changed model or environment may require re-entry into Simulation Model & Environment Standard. Changed data may require re-entry into Simulation Input & Data Standard. A newly relevant operating condition may require re-entry into Simulation Scenario Standard. The architecture therefore supports targeted governed resimulation rather than uncontrolled repetition. Architectural Position SIMULOS® governs the complete simulation governance lifecycle. The architecture progresses through: Simulation Object → Simulation Purpose & Scope → Simulation Reality Representation → Simulation Assumptions → Simulation Model & Environment → Simulation Inputs & Data → Simulation Scenario Design → Simulation Execution → Simulation Output Governance → Simulation-to-Reality Correlation → Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary → Simulation Lifecycle, Drift & Resimulation Together, these simulation governance spaces govern how the object of simulation is formally established, why simulation is performed, how reality is represented, which assumptions enable that representation, how models and environments are constituted, which inputs enter the simulation, which scenarios are examined, how simulations are executed, what their outputs legitimately mean, how those outputs correspond to reality, what evidential significance and reliance they may support, and when changing conditions require governed resimulation, replacement, transition, or retirement. SIMULOS® therefore provides a complete governance path from the first identification of what is being simulated to the continuing determination of whether that simulation remains relevant enough to be relied upon. What SIMULOS® Defines SIMULOS® defines: - where simulation governance begins, - how a Simulation Object is formally identified and bounded, - why a simulation is being performed, - what the simulation must and must not cover, - which aspects of reality must be represented, - what abstraction, fidelity, and resolution are appropriate, - which assumptions enable or materially affect the simulation, - how the simulation model and environment are governed, - which inputs and data may enter the simulation, - which scenarios, variations, edge cases, and stress conditions require simulation, - how simulation execution is governed, - how simulation outputs are identified and interpreted, - where output interpretation ends and inference begins, - how simulated behavior is compared with reality, - how simulation-to-reality deviation and uncertainty are represented, - what simulation-derived information may legitimately become evidence, - how much simulation-specific evidential weight that evidence may carry, - where legitimate simulation-specific reliance ends, - which uses and interpretations must remain limited, - how simulation-derived evidence interfaces with VALIDOS® validation governance, - how simulation relevance is monitored over time, - what constitutes material simulation drift, - when resimulation must be triggered, - where lifecycle re-entry must occur, - when a simulation should be updated, replaced, transitioned, or retired. SIMULOS® provides the official simulation governance language used for simulation-space identification, simulation lifecycle navigation, governance classification, structural diagnosis, evidence-boundary determination, resimulation governance, and simulation architecture design across complex operational environments. Critical Architectural Distinctions Simulation Object ≠ Validation Object Represented Reality ≠ Operational Reality Simulation Assumption ≠ Established Fact Representation Fidelity ≠ Reality Equivalence Model Sophistication ≠ Model Applicability Input Volume ≠ Input Representativeness Scenario Count ≠ Scenario Coverage Simulation Execution ≠ Audit of Simulation Execution Simulation Output ≠ Simulation Evidence Simulation Inference ≠ Direct Simulation Observation Simulation-to-Reality Correlation ≠ Reality Equivalence Evidence Volume ≠ Evidential Strength Repeated Simulation ≠ Independent Evidence High Evidential Weight ≠ Broad Reliance Simulation Evidence ≠ Validation Determination Past Simulation Relevance ≠ Continuing Simulation Relevance Resimulation ≠ Failure of the Original Simulation Cross-Architecture Governance Boundaries SIMULOS® ↔ ORA™ — Operational Reality Architecture Operational Reality Architecture governs what exists and occurs in actual Operational Reality. SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture governs how selected aspects of that reality are represented, modeled, simulated, compared, and governed inside the simulation lifecycle. Operational Reality ≠ Simulated Reality. SIMULOS® ↔ VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture determines what simulation-derived evidence can legitimately represent, mean, and support within its simulation-specific reliance boundary. VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture determines whether the complete validation basis is sufficient to support a Validation Determination and intended reliance. Simulation Evidence ≠ Validation Determination. SIMULOS® ↔ INTEGROS® — Integrity Governance Architecture SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture governs simulation-specific structure, conditions, execution, outputs, correlation, evidence boundaries, and lifecycle. INTEGROS® — Integrity Governance Architecture governs integrity across governed objects, structures, conditions, states, evidence, and processes. Simulation Governance ≠ Integrity Governance. SIMULOS® ↔ ADIT® — Audit in Real Time Architecture SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture governs simulation execution and the simulation lifecycle itself. ADIT® — Audit in Real Time Architecture governs evidential observation, preservation, verification, traceability, and auditability of what occurred where applicable. Execution Governance ≠ Audit Governance. SIMULOS® ↔ AGA™ — Accountability Governance Architecture SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture governs the methodological conditions under which simulation activities and simulation-derived evidence acquire legitimate meaning. AGA™ — Accountability Governance Architecture governs who holds authority, responsibility, accountability, attribution, and decision ownership surrounding those activities. Methodological Governance ≠ Accountability Governance. SIMULOS® ↔ AIG® — AI Governance Architecture SIMULOS® may simulate AI systems and their behavior. AIG® — AI Governance Architecture continues to govern the behavioral governance lifecycle of actual AI systems. Simulated AI Behavior ≠ Governance of Actual AI Behavior. SIMULOS® ↔ ASGA™ — Autonomous Systems Governance Architecture SIMULOS® may simulate autonomous agents, robots, vehicles, machines, and multi-agent systems. ASGA™ — Autonomous Systems Governance Architecture continues to govern the authority, autonomy, constraints, execution, coordination, escalation, and operational behavior of actual autonomous systems. Simulated Autonomy ≠ Governed Operational Autonomy. Compatible OOF® Architectures GOA™ — Governance Architecture ORA™ — Operational Reality Architecture VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture INTEGROS® — Integrity Governance Architecture OBIDENITY® — Origin-Bound Identity Governance Architecture AGA™ — Accountability Governance Architecture AIG® — AI Governance Architecture ASGA™ — Autonomous Systems Governance Architecture CLIA® — Cognitive Governance Intelligence Architecture MGIA™ — Memory Governance Intelligence Architecture ADIT® — Audit in Real Time Architecture Canonical Principle SIMULOS® does not define Operational Reality, general validation sufficiency, general integrity, accountability, auditability, or the operational authority and behavior of actual AI and autonomous systems. SIMULOS® governs the conditions under which a Simulation Object is identified, simulation purpose is bounded, reality is represented, assumptions are made explicit, models and environments are constituted, inputs are admitted, scenarios are designed, simulations are executed, outputs are interpreted, simulation-to-reality relationships are established, simulation-derived evidence acquires bounded meaning and reliance, and material change triggers governed lifecycle re-entry, resimulation, replacement, transition, or retirement. Canonical Closing Statement SIMULOS® serves as the official simulation governance reference map for AI systems, autonomous systems, robotics, digital twins, engineering systems, scientific models, critical infrastructure, space systems, and future simulation environments.
