By defining the primary governable spaces of the complete simulation lifecycle, SIMULOS® provides the architecture used to identify what is being simulated, establish why it is being simulated, determine how reality is represented, govern assumptions, models, environments, inputs, scenarios and execution, establish what simulation outputs legitimately mean, determine how simulated results correspond to reality, bound the evidential meaning and reliance of simulation-derived evidence, and continuously determine whether material change requires lifecycle re-entry, resimulation, replacement, transition, or retirement. SIMULOS® therefore establishes simulation not as an isolated computational event, but as a continuously governable relationship between a Simulation Object, a representation of reality, a governed simulation process, simulation-derived evidence, and the changing reality within which that evidence may ultimately be relied upon.

title: OOF™ SIMULOS® Complete Standards & Modules Index
text: OOF™ SIMULOS® Complete Standards & Modules Index SIMULOS® Complete Standards & Modules Index Simulation Governance Architecture — Simulation Governance Layer This document serves as the official OOF® simulation governance architecture map and structural index used for simulation governance design, simulation governance navigation, simulation governance classification, simulation diagnostics, simulation architecture development, simulation governance assessment, simulation lifecycle governance, and simulation interoperability across AI systems, autonomous systems, robotics, digital twins, engineering systems, scientific models, critical infrastructure, space systems, and future simulation environments. SIMULOS® consists of 12 Parent Standards and 60 Core Modules. Additional standards and modules may be added when new governable simulation spaces are identified. However, the standards and modules listed below form the core structural backbone of SIMULOS®. 1. Simulation Object Standard (SOS) Governed Space: Simulation Object Core Question: What exactly is being simulated, and how must the Simulation Object be identified, bounded, versioned, and distinguished? Modules: SOIM — Simulation Object Identification Module SOBM — Simulation Object Boundary Module SOVM — Simulation Object Versioning Module SOCM — Simulation Object Configuration Module SODM — Simulation Object Documentation Module 2. Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard (SPSS) Governed Space: Simulation Purpose & Scope Core Question: Why is the simulation being performed, what must it cover, and what remains outside its simulation boundary? Modules: SPM — Simulation Purpose Module SSCM — Simulation Scope Module SEXM — Simulation Exclusion Module SACM — Simulation Applicability Context Module SDPM — Simulation Depth & Precision Module 3. Reality Representation Standard (RRS) Governed Space: Simulation Reality Representation Core Question: Which aspects of reality must the simulation represent, at what abstraction and fidelity, and which aspects may legitimately remain simplified or excluded? Modules: RSM — Reality Selection Module RAM — Reality Abstraction Module RFM — Representation Fidelity Module RRM — Representation Resolution Module RLM — Representation Limitation Module 4. Simulation Assumption Standard (SAS) Governed Space: Simulation Assumptions Core Question: Which assumptions enable the simulation, and how must their basis, dependencies, uncertainty, limitations, and consequences remain governed? Modules: SAIM — Simulation Assumption Identification Module SABM — Simulation Assumption Basis Module SADM — Simulation Assumption Dependency Module SAUM — Simulation Assumption Uncertainty Module SALM — Simulation Assumption Limitation Module 5. Simulation Model & Environment Standard (SMES) Governed Space: Simulation Model & Environment Core Question: How must the simulation model and simulation environment be constructed, configured, bounded, and controlled? Modules: SMMM — Simulation Model Structure Module SECM — Simulation Environment Configuration Module SBIM — Simulation Boundary Interaction Module SPHM — Simulation Parameterization Module SEVM — Simulation Environment Versioning Module 6. Simulation Input & Data Standard (SIDS) Governed Space: Simulation Inputs & Data Core Question: Which inputs and data may enter the simulation, and under what representativeness, transformation, temporal, and uncertainty conditions? Modules: SIIM — Simulation Input Identification Module SDRM — Simulation Data Representativeness Module SDTM — Simulation Data Transformation Module STDM — Simulation Temporal Data Module SIUM — Simulation Input Uncertainty Module 7. Simulation Scenario Standard (SSS) Governed Space: Simulation Scenario Design Core Question: Which scenarios must be simulated to represent expected conditions, variations, edge cases, stresses, uncertainty, and materially relevant alternatives? Modules: SCIM — Scenario Identification Module SCVM — Scenario Variation Module SECM — Scenario Edge-Case Module SSCM — Scenario Stress-Condition Module SCCM — Scenario Coverage Module 8. Simulation Execution Standard (SES) Governed Space: Simulation Execution Core Question: How must a simulation be instantiated, executed, observed, repeated, controlled, and documented? Modules: SIM — Simulation Instantiation Module SECM — Simulation Execution Control Module SOM — Simulation Observation Module SRPM — Simulation Repetition Module SEDM — Simulation Execution Documentation Module 9. Simulation Output Governance Standard (SOGS) Governed Space: Simulation Output Governance Core Question: What exactly did the simulation produce, how must simulation outputs be bounded and interpreted, and what may legitimately be inferred from them? Modules: SOIM — Simulation Output Identification Module SOCM — Simulation Output Classification Module SIM — Simulation Inference Module SOLM — Simulation Output Limitation Module SODM — Simulation Output Documentation Module 10. Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Standard (SRCS) Governed Space: Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Core Question: To what extent do simulated behavior, conditions, and outputs correspond to the reality they claim to represent? Modules: SRCM — Simulation-Reality Comparison Module SCCM — Simulation Correlation Criteria Module SDMM — Simulation-Reality Deviation Module SRAM — Reality Alignment Module SCUM — Correlation Uncertainty Module 11. Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard (SERBS) Governed Space: Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Core Question: What evidential meaning may simulation results legitimately carry, and where does simulation-specific reliance end before broader validation governance becomes necessary? Modules: SEQM — Simulation Evidence Qualification Module SEWM — Simulation Evidence Weight Module SRBM — Simulation Reliance Boundary Module SUM — Simulation Use Limitation Module SVIM — Simulation Validation Interface Module 12. Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Standard (SLRS) Governed Space: Simulation Lifecycle, Drift & Resimulation Core Question: How must simulation relevance be monitored over time, and when must changed reality trigger update, resimulation, replacement, or retirement? Modules: SLMM — Simulation Lifecycle Monitoring Module SDRM — Simulation Drift Recognition Module SRGM — Resimulation Trigger Module SRSM — Resimulation Scope Module SRTM — Simulation Retirement & Transition Module SIMULOS® Architecture Summary Parent Standards: 12 Core Modules: 60 Core Governed Simulation Spaces Simulation Object Simulation Purpose & Scope Simulation Reality Representation Simulation Assumptions Simulation Model & Environment Simulation Inputs & Data Simulation Scenario Design Simulation Execution Simulation Output Governance Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Simulation Lifecycle, Drift & Resimulation SIMULOS® Navigation Layer Core Questions Map SOS → What exactly is being simulated, and how must the Simulation Object be identified, bounded, versioned, and distinguished? SPSS → Why is the simulation being performed, what must it cover, and what remains outside its simulation boundary? RRS → Which aspects of reality must the simulation represent, at what abstraction and fidelity, and which aspects may legitimately remain simplified or excluded? SAS → Which assumptions enable the simulation, and how must their basis, dependencies, uncertainty, limitations, and consequences remain governed? SMES → How must the simulation model and simulation environment be constructed, configured, bounded, and controlled? SIDS → Which inputs and data may enter the simulation, and under what representativeness, transformation, temporal, and uncertainty conditions? SSS → Which scenarios must be simulated to represent expected conditions, variations, edge cases, stresses, uncertainty, and materially relevant alternatives? SES → How must a simulation be instantiated, executed, observed, repeated, controlled, and documented? SOGS → What exactly did the simulation produce, how must simulation outputs be bounded and interpreted, and what may legitimately be inferred from them? SRCS → To what extent do simulated behavior, conditions, and outputs correspond to the reality they claim to represent? SERBS → What evidential meaning may simulation results legitimately carry, and where does simulation-specific reliance end before broader validation governance becomes necessary? SLRS → How must simulation relevance be monitored over time, and when must changed reality trigger update, resimulation, replacement, or retirement? Architectural Position SIMULOS® governs the complete simulation governance lifecycle. The architecture progresses: Simulation Object → Simulation Purpose & Scope → Reality Representation → Simulation Assumptions → Simulation Model & Environment → Simulation Inputs & Data → Simulation Scenario Design → Simulation Execution → Simulation Output Governance → Simulation-to-Reality Correlation → Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary → Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Together these standards govern what is being simulated, why it is being simulated, how reality is represented, which assumptions enable that representation, how the model and simulation environment are constituted, what inputs enter the simulation, which scenarios are tested, how simulation execution occurs, what outputs are produced and interpreted, how those outputs correspond to reality, what evidential meaning and reliance they may legitimately support, and when changed reality requires resimulation, replacement, transition, or retirement. SIMULOS® therefore does not terminate when a simulation execution ends. Its lifecycle becomes recursive when simulation-derived results enter operational use: Simulation → Operational Use → Reality Change → Simulation Drift → Resimulation Trigger → Resimulation Scope → Lifecycle Re-Entry → Resimulation / Replacement / Retirement This recursive structure allows simulation governance to remain responsive to changes in the Simulation Object, represented reality, assumptions, models, inputs, scenarios, operational conditions, correlation basis, evidence applicability, and intended reliance. Cross-Architecture Boundary SIMULOS® ↔ ORA™ ORA™ governs what is actually happening in Operational Reality. SIMULOS® governs how selected reality is represented and simulated. SIMULOS® ↔ VALIDOS® SIMULOS® governs what simulation and simulation-derived evidence can legitimately represent and support. VALIDOS® governs whether the total validation basis sufficiently supports a Validation Determination and intended reliance. SIMULOS® ↔ INTEGROS® SIMULOS® governs simulation-specific structure and lifecycle. INTEGROS® governs integrity across objects, states, evidence, and processes. SIMULOS® ↔ ADIT® SIMULOS® governs simulation execution. ADIT® governs evidential observation, preservation, verification, and auditability of what occurred. SIMULOS® ↔ AGA™ SIMULOS® governs simulation methodology and governed simulation conditions. AGA™ governs authority, responsibility, accountability, attribution, and decision relationships surrounding simulation activities. SIMULOS® ↔ AIG® / ASGA™ SIMULOS® may simulate AI and autonomous systems. AIG® and ASGA™ continue to govern the behavior, authority, autonomy, constraints, and operation of the actual systems. Foundational Architecture Distinctions Simulation Object ≠ Validation Object Represented Reality ≠ Operational Reality Simulation Assumption ≠ Established Fact Model Sophistication ≠ Reality Representation Sufficiency Input Volume ≠ Input Representativeness Scenario Count ≠ Scenario Coverage Simulation Execution ≠ Audit of Simulation Execution Simulation Output ≠ Simulation Evidence Simulation Similarity ≠ Reality Equivalence Simulation Evidence ≠ Validation Determination Evidence Volume ≠ Evidential Strength High Evidential Weight ≠ Unlimited Reliance Past Simulation Relevance ≠ Continuing Simulation Relevance Resimulation ≠ Failure of the Original Simulation Canonical Principle SIMULOS® does not govern Operational Reality itself, general validation sufficiency, general integrity, auditability, accountability, or the behavior and authority of actual AI and autonomous systems. SIMULOS® governs the methodological conditions under which a Simulation Object is identified, reality is represented through simulation, assumptions and simulation conditions remain explicit, simulation activity is structured and executed, outputs acquire bounded meaning, simulation-derived evidence acquires legitimate reliance boundaries, and material changes in reality trigger governed resimulation, replacement, transition, or retirement throughout the complete simulation lifecycle.

title: OOF™ SIMULOS®
url: SIMULOS® Simulation Governance Architecture - Simulation Governance Layer.html
text: OOF™ SIMULOS® SIMULOS® Simulation Governance Architecture — Simulation Governance Layer SIMULOS® serves as the official OOF® simulation governance architecture used for simulation governance design, simulation space identification, simulation methodology structuring, reality representation governance, assumption governance, simulation execution governance, simulation output governance, simulation-to-reality correlation, simulation evidence governance, reliance boundary definition, lifecycle monitoring, and resimulation governance across AI systems, autonomous systems, robotics, digital twins, engineering systems, scientific models, critical infrastructure, space systems, organizations, and future simulation environments. Simulation Governance Architecture (SIMULOS®) does not define simulation itself. SIMULOS® defines the governance architecture required to ensure that simulations remain explicitly identified, purpose-bounded, reality-aware, assumption-governed, structurally controlled, input-aware, scenario-governed, execution-traceable, output-bounded, reality-correlated, evidentially constrained, and lifecycle-governed throughout the complete simulation lifecycle. SIMULOS® consists of 12 Core Parent Standards and 60 Core Modules forming the primary simulation governance backbone within the OOF® ecosystem. Additional compatible standards, bridge standards, and specialized simulation governance standards may extend the architecture when new simulation governance spaces are identified. However, the standards listed below form the official core simulation governance structure of SIMULOS®. Canonical Definition Simulation Governance Architecture (SIMULOS®) is the simulation governance architecture that defines the structural and methodological conditions under which a simulation is explicitly identified, purpose-bounded, connected to represented reality, assumption-governed, modelled within controlled environments, supplied with governed inputs, tested through relevant scenarios, executed under defined conditions, interpreted through bounded outputs, correlated with reality, converted into legitimately bounded evidence, and continuously reconsidered as reality and simulation conditions change throughout the complete simulation lifecycle. Core Question How can simulations remain methodologically governed from the identification of what is being simulated through representation, assumptions, modeling, execution, outputs, reality correlation, evidential reliance, and eventual resimulation, replacement, or retirement? Governance Flow Simulation Object → Simulation Purpose & Scope → Reality Representation → Simulation Assumptions → Simulation Model & Environment → Simulation Inputs & Data → Simulation Scenario Design → Simulation Execution → Simulation Output Governance → Simulation-to-Reality Correlation → Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary → Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Core Parent Standards 1. Simulation Object Standard (SOS) Governed Space: Simulation Object Core Question: What exactly is being simulated, and how must the Simulation Object be identified, bounded, versioned, and distinguished? 2. Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard (SPSS) Governed Space: Simulation Purpose & Scope Core Question: Why is the simulation being performed, what must it cover, and what remains outside its simulation boundary? 3. Reality Representation Standard (RRS) Governed Space: Simulation Reality Representation Core Question: Which aspects of reality must the simulation represent, at what abstraction and fidelity, and which aspects may legitimately remain simplified or excluded? 4. Simulation Assumption Standard (SAS) Governed Space: Simulation Assumptions Core Question: Which assumptions enable the simulation, and how must their basis, dependencies, uncertainty, limitations, and consequences remain governed? 5. Simulation Model & Environment Standard (SMES) Governed Space: Simulation Model & Environment Core Question: How must the simulation model and simulation environment be constructed, configured, bounded, and controlled? 6. Simulation Input & Data Standard (SIDS) Governed Space: Simulation Inputs & Data Core Question: Which inputs and data may enter the simulation, and under what representativeness, transformation, temporal, and uncertainty conditions? 7. Simulation Scenario Standard (SSS) Governed Space: Simulation Scenario Design Core Question: Which scenarios must be simulated to represent expected conditions, variations, edge cases, stresses, uncertainty, and materially relevant alternatives? 8. Simulation Execution Standard (SES) Governed Space: Simulation Execution Core Question: How must a simulation be instantiated, executed, observed, repeated, controlled, and documented? 9. Simulation Output Governance Standard (SOGS) Governed Space: Simulation Output Governance Core Question: What exactly did the simulation produce, how must simulation outputs be bounded and interpreted, and what may legitimately be inferred from them? 10. Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Standard (SRCS) Governed Space: Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Core Question: To what extent do simulated behavior, conditions, and outputs correspond to the reality they claim to represent? 11. Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard (SERBS) Governed Space: Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Core Question: What evidential meaning may simulation results legitimately carry, and where does simulation-specific reliance end before broader validation governance becomes necessary? 12. Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Standard (SLRS) Governed Space: Simulation Lifecycle, Drift & Resimulation Core Question: How must simulation relevance be monitored over time, and when must changed reality trigger update, resimulation, replacement, or retirement? Compatible OOF® Architectures SIMULOS® interoperates with multiple OOF® architectures governing complementary governance spaces. GOA™ — Governance Architecture provides the constitutional governance layer defining how governance itself is structured, bounded, delegated, and maintained. ORA™ — Operational Reality Architecture governs what is actually occurring in Operational Reality, while SIMULOS® governs how selected aspects of that reality are represented and simulated. VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture governs whether the total validation basis sufficiently supports a Validation Determination and intended reliance, while SIMULOS® determines what simulation and simulation-derived evidence can legitimately represent and support. INTEGROS® — Integrity Governance Architecture governs integrity across objects, states, evidence, and processes, while SIMULOS® governs simulation-specific structure, methodology, execution, representation, correlation, evidence boundaries, and lifecycle. ADIT® governs evidential observation, preservation, verification, and auditability of what occurred, while SIMULOS® governs simulation execution itself and the simulation-specific meaning of its resulting outputs and evidence. AGA™ — Accountability Governance Architecture governs authority, responsibility, accountability, attribution, and decision relationships surrounding simulation activities and reliance. AIG® — AI Governance Architecture governs the behavioral governance lifecycle of actual AI systems that may be represented, tested, or evaluated through simulation. ASGA™ — Autonomous Systems Governance Architecture governs actual autonomous systems, agents, authority, constraints, and autonomous operational behavior that may be represented or evaluated through simulation. SIMULOS® serves as the common simulation governance architecture supporting the broader OOF® ecosystem by ensuring that simulations remain methodologically connected to the objects, realities, assumptions, conditions, executions, outputs, evidence, and lifecycle states they claim to represent. Architectural Position SIMULOS® governs the complete simulation governance lifecycle. The architecture progresses through: Simulation Object → Simulation Purpose & Scope → Reality Representation → Simulation Assumptions → Simulation Model & Environment → Simulation Inputs & Data → Simulation Scenario Design → Simulation Execution → Simulation Output Governance → Simulation-to-Reality Correlation → Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary → Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Together these standards govern how a simulation target is identified, why simulation is undertaken, how reality is represented, which assumptions make the simulation possible, how models and environments are constituted, which inputs enter the simulation, which scenarios are tested, how execution occurs, what outputs are produced, how those outputs correspond to reality, what evidential meaning may legitimately be derived from them, and when changed reality requires resimulation, replacement, transition, or retirement. Unlike a linear simulation methodology, SIMULOS® becomes recursive after operational use begins. The extended lifecycle becomes: Simulation → Operational Use → Reality Change → Simulation Drift → Resimulation Trigger → Resimulation Scope → Lifecycle Re-Entry → Resimulation / Replacement / Retirement This enables a governed simulation to remain connected not merely to the reality represented when it was created, but also to the reality that continues to change after simulation results begin influencing operational decisions. Core Governed Simulation Spaces SIMULOS® establishes twelve distinct governable simulation spaces: Simulation Object → what exactly is being simulated. Simulation Purpose & Scope → why the simulation exists and what it must and must not cover. Simulation Reality Representation → which parts of reality are represented, simplified, abstracted, or excluded. Simulation Assumptions → which assumptions enable the simulation and how their consequences remain visible. Simulation Model & Environment → how the model and simulation environment are structured, configured, and controlled. Simulation Inputs & Data → what enters the simulation and under which representativeness, transformation, temporal, and uncertainty conditions. Simulation Scenario Design → what conditions, variations, edge cases, stresses, and alternatives are actually tested. Simulation Execution → how simulations are instantiated, controlled, observed, repeated, and documented. Simulation Output Governance → what the simulation produced and what may legitimately be inferred from those outputs. Simulation-to-Reality Correlation → how simulated behavior, conditions, and outputs correspond to observed or governed reality. Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary → what simulation-derived evidence may legitimately mean and where simulation-specific reliance must stop. Simulation Lifecycle, Drift & Resimulation → how continuing relevance is monitored and when change requires resimulation, replacement, transition, or retirement. Each space answers a different methodological question. Each can fail independently. Their separation is therefore foundational to the SIMULOS® architecture. Cross-Architecture Boundary Lock SIMULOS® is intentionally bounded to prevent duplication with adjacent OOF® architectures. SIMULOS® ↔ ORA™ ORA™: What is actually happening in Operational Reality? SIMULOS®: How is selected reality represented and simulated? Operational Reality ≠ Simulated Representation of Reality. SIMULOS® ↔ VALIDOS® SIMULOS®: What does the simulation and simulation-derived evidence legitimately represent and support? VALIDOS®: Does the total validation basis sufficiently support the Validation Determination and intended reliance? Simulation Evidence ≠ Validation Determination. SIMULOS® ↔ INTEGROS® SIMULOS®: governs simulation-specific structure, representation, assumptions, execution, outputs, correlation, evidence boundaries, and lifecycle. INTEGROS®: governs integrity across objects, states, evidence, and processes. Simulation Governance ≠ General Integrity Governance. SIMULOS® ↔ ADIT® SIMULOS®: governs simulation execution and the simulation-specific structures through which simulation activity occurs. ADIT®: governs evidential observation, preservation, verification, examination, and auditability of what occurred. Simulation Execution ≠ Audit of Simulation Execution. SIMULOS® ↔ AGA™ SIMULOS®: governs simulation methodology and simulation-specific conditions. AGA™: governs who holds authority, responsibility, accountability, and attribution for simulation-related decisions and failures. Simulation Methodology ≠ Accountability Allocation. SIMULOS® ↔ AIG® / ASGA™ SIMULOS® may simulate AI systems, autonomous agents, robots, and autonomous operational environments. SIMULOS®: governs their simulated representation and simulation lifecycle. AIG® / ASGA™: govern the behavior, autonomy, authority, constraints, and operation of the actual systems. Simulating an autonomous system ≠ governing the autonomy of the actual system. Architectural Origin SIMULOS® evolved from the foundational: SIMULOS® — Simulation Integrity Standard which established the original methodological concern that simulation must remain structurally connected to the reality, assumptions, conditions, execution basis, and outputs it claims to represent. As the governed space expanded, simulation integrity was identified as only one part of a substantially larger governance problem. The architecture therefore evolved from a single integrity-oriented standard into a complete simulation governance architecture. Its foundational principles are distributed primarily across: Reality Representation → Simulation Assumptions → Simulation Model & Environment → Simulation Execution → Simulation Output Governance → Simulation-to-Reality Correlation → Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary The original standard remains part of the architectural history of SIMULOS® as its Foundational Reference Standard, while the twelve Parent Standards constitute the current canonical architecture. Architectural Structure Architecture: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Core Parent Standards: 12 Core Modules: 60 Architecture Model: Lifecycle-Based · Modular · Recursive Primary Governance Domain: Simulation Governance The architecture deliberately separates governable spaces that can independently fail. A simulation may: - represent the wrong object; - pursue an unclear purpose; - represent reality inadequately; - depend upon unsupported assumptions; - use an inappropriate model; - consume unrepresentative inputs; - omit decisive scenarios; - execute incorrectly; - produce misinterpreted outputs; - correlate poorly with reality; - generate evidence used beyond its legitimate meaning; - remain operational after reality has materially changed. SIMULOS® treats these not as one generic simulation quality problem, but as distinct governance spaces requiring distinct methodological controls. Recursive Lifecycle Principle SIMULOS® does not end when a simulation run ends. A simulation may remain operationally influential for months, years, or decades after execution. During that period: Reality may change. The Simulation Object may change. Assumptions may become obsolete. Inputs may shift. New scenarios may emerge. Models may become outdated. Correlation may deteriorate. Evidence may lose applicability. SIMULOS® therefore closes recursively through SLRS: Operational Use → Reality Change → Simulation Drift → Resimulation Trigger → Resimulation Scope → Lifecycle Re-Entry → Resimulation / Replacement / Retirement This makes lifecycle change part of simulation governance rather than an external maintenance concern. Foundational Architecture Principles A simulation cannot legitimately represent an object more precisely than that object has been identified and bounded. Simulation purpose determines what the simulation must represent, not what the technology happens to be capable of simulating. Represented reality is not Operational Reality. Simulation similarity is not reality equivalence. An assumption that remains hidden cannot remain governed. Model sophistication does not compensate for an incorrectly represented problem. More data does not correct an incorrectly bounded simulation. Scenario volume is not scenario coverage. Execution precision does not guarantee interpretive legitimacy. Simulation output is not automatically simulation evidence. Evidence volume is not evidential strength. Simulation-derived evidence must not travel farther than its governed meaning can legitimately support. A simulation that was once relevant does not remain relevant merely because it continues to execute. Changed reality may require changed simulation. Resimulation is part of simulation governance, not an admission that the original simulation failed. Canonical Principle SIMULOS® does not govern Operational Reality itself, general validation sufficiency, general integrity, auditability, accountability, or the behavior and authority of actual AI and autonomous systems. SIMULOS® governs the methodological conditions under which reality is represented through simulation, simulation activity is structured and executed, simulation outputs acquire bounded meaning, simulation-derived evidence acquires legitimate reliance boundaries, and continuing changes in reality trigger governed resimulation, replacement, transition, or retirement throughout the complete simulation lifecycle.

title: OOF™ Simulation Input Uncertainty Module (SIUM)
text: OOF™ Simulation Input Uncertainty Module (SIUM) Simulation Input Uncertainty Module (SIUM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Simulation Input & Data Standard (SIDS) Operational Layer: Simulation Input & Data Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Type: Parent Standard Module Governed Space: Simulation Input Uncertainty Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 18 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Governed Space Simulation Input Uncertainty Canonical Definition Simulation Input Uncertainty Module (SIUM) defines the governance framework through which uncertainty associated with Simulation Inputs is identified, classified, bounded, quantified or qualitatively characterized where appropriate, propagated into simulation execution, and preserved through downstream interpretation so that uncertainty in the input basis cannot disappear merely because the simulation produces precise outputs. SIUM establishes the final internal governance layer of SIDS by governing the transition: Identified + Representative + Transformed + Temporally Governed Inputs → Input Uncertainty Identification → Uncertainty Characterization → Dependency Assessment → Uncertainty Propagation Requirements → Simulation Input Uncertainty Status Its purpose is not to eliminate uncertainty. Its purpose is to ensure that uncertainty remains visible, attributable, bounded, and operationally consequential wherever it can materially affect simulation behavior or conclusions. Operational Role SIUM serves as the fifth and final internal governance space of the Simulation Input & Data Standard (SIDS). The preceding modules establish: SIIM — What information is entering the simulation? SDRM — What reality can that information legitimately represent? SDTM — What happened to that information before simulation use? STDM — Is that information temporally appropriate for the reality and dynamics being simulated? SIUM asks: What uncertainty remains in the complete Simulation Input basis, where does that uncertainty originate, how may uncertainties interact, and what must remain visible when the simulation uses those inputs? The governed progression is: Simulation Input Basis → Uncertainty Sources → Uncertainty Classification → Uncertainty Magnitude / Character → Dependency → Materiality → Propagation Requirement → Input Uncertainty Status → Simulation Use Module Operational Space SIUM governs: input uncertainty identification, uncertainty source attribution, measurement uncertainty, observational uncertainty, sampling uncertainty, representativeness uncertainty, transformation-induced uncertainty, temporal uncertainty, estimation uncertainty, interpolation uncertainty, extrapolation uncertainty, imputation uncertainty, synthetic-input uncertainty, parameter uncertainty, classification uncertainty, source-dependent uncertainty, missing-information uncertainty, uncertainty range, uncertainty distribution, uncertainty bounds, qualitative uncertainty, quantitative uncertainty, known uncertainty, partially characterized uncertainty, unknown or unresolved uncertainty, uncertainty dependency, correlated uncertainty, compounded uncertainty, uncertainty materiality, uncertainty sensitivity, uncertainty propagation requirements, uncertainty aggregation, uncertainty conditions, uncertainty limitations, uncertainty status, uncertainty reassessment, and uncertainty traceability. Module Function SIUM exists to prevent: uncertain inputs being represented as certain, estimated values being treated as observations, measurement uncertainty disappearing during ingestion, transformation-induced uncertainty being ignored, temporal uncertainty being lost, multiple uncertainties being assumed independent without basis, uncertainty being hidden by numerical precision, uncertainty ranges being collapsed into single values without justification, incomplete information being interpreted as certainty, uncertainty being averaged away, model inputs being presented as exact merely because the simulation requires exact numerical values, simulation outputs appearing more certain than their input basis legitimately supports, and downstream users losing visibility into material uncertainty inherited from Simulation Inputs. Simulation Input Uncertainty Simulation Input Uncertainty is the material uncertainty associated with the identity, value, state, origin, representation, transformation, timing, completeness, or applicability of information entering a simulation. It may concern: What the value is Whether the value is correct Whether the value represents the intended reality When the value applies How the value was produced How complete the information is or: How confidently the input may be relied upon within the simulation context. Uncertainty Is Not Error SIMULOS® establishes: Uncertainty does not necessarily mean that an input is wrong. An input may be the best available representation while still containing material uncertainty. For example: Temperature = 20°C ± 1°C does not mean the measurement is invalid. It means the information basis contains a bounded uncertainty. Error vs Uncertainty SIUM distinguishes: Known Error from: Uncertainty. A known incorrect value may require correction. An uncertain value may remain legitimate if the uncertainty is sufficiently understood and governed. Uncertainty Source Every material uncertainty should be attributable, where possible, to an identifiable source. Possible sources include: measurement process, sensor precision, sampling, source reliability, missing information, estimation, transformation, interpolation, extrapolation, temporal misalignment, synthetic generation, model-derived inputs, classification, environmental variability, or unresolved knowledge limitations. Measurement Uncertainty Measurement systems have finite accuracy and precision. A measured value may therefore represent: Observed Value ± Measurement Uncertainty rather than an exact physical state. Where material, the uncertainty should remain connected to the input. Observational Uncertainty Some phenomena cannot be observed perfectly. Observational uncertainty may arise from: incomplete visibility, ambiguous detection, limited sensor coverage, human observation, environmental interference, or indirect observation. Sampling Uncertainty A sample represents only part of a broader population, period, environment, or state space. Sampling uncertainty asks: How uncertain is the inference from the observed sample to the reality the simulation intends to represent? SDRM governs representativeness. SIUM governs the uncertainty remaining within that representation. Representativeness Uncertainty A dataset may be accepted as sufficiently representative while still containing uncertainty about how completely it captures: rare conditions, subpopulations, environmental variation, extreme behavior, or future conditions. Acceptance under SDRM does not eliminate that uncertainty. Transformation-Induced Uncertainty SDTM may introduce uncertainty through: filtering, aggregation, interpolation, extrapolation, imputation, normalization, data fusion, synthetic supplementation, or derived-variable construction. SIUM consolidates these uncertainty contributions into the governed Simulation Input basis. Temporal Uncertainty STDM may identify uncertainty involving: timestamps, synchronization, latency, event timing, temporal alignment, applicability periods, drift, or regime transition. SIUM ensures material temporal uncertainty remains part of the complete uncertainty basis. Estimation Uncertainty Estimated inputs should preserve uncertainty associated with the estimation method. Conceptually: Observed Basis + Estimation Method → Estimated Input + Estimation Uncertainty Interpolation Uncertainty Values generated between observations may contain uncertainty dependent upon: distance between observations, variability, interpolation method, system dynamics, and missing-data structure. Extrapolation Uncertainty Extrapolation extends beyond observed information. Uncertainty may increase as extrapolation moves further from the observed basis. SIMULOS® establishes: Numerical continuation beyond observed data does not establish equivalent informational confidence. Imputation Uncertainty An imputed value may be necessary for simulation execution. But the simulation should preserve that: Imputed Value ≠ Observed Value and that the imputation carries uncertainty derived from its method and basis. Synthetic Input Uncertainty Synthetic information may represent plausible conditions without being direct observation. Where synthetic inputs are used, SIUM governs uncertainty associated with: generation assumptions, generator limitations, distribution fit, scenario coverage, and divergence from observed reality. Parameter Uncertainty Simulation Inputs may include parameters whose exact values are unknown. A parameter may therefore be represented as: Fixed Estimate Range Distribution Scenario Set or: Unknown within defined bounds. The representation should reflect the available basis rather than artificial precision. Classification Uncertainty Some inputs depend upon classification. For example: an object may be classified as: Pedestrian with: 92% confidence. Where classification uncertainty can materially affect simulation behavior, it should remain visible. Missing-Information Uncertainty Missing information creates uncertainty even where no substitute value is inserted. SIMULOS® establishes: Unknown does not become known merely because the simulation can execute without the missing information. Known Uncertainty A Known Uncertainty has an identifiable source and sufficiently characterized effect or range. Example: Sensor accuracy ±0.5°C Partially Characterized Uncertainty A Partially Characterized Uncertainty is known to exist but cannot be fully quantified or bounded. It should remain explicitly represented. Unresolved Uncertainty An Unresolved Uncertainty exists where material uncertainty is known but its magnitude, distribution, or consequences cannot yet be sufficiently established. Unresolved uncertainty may require: restriction, sensitivity analysis, scenario expansion, additional evidence, or downstream limitation. Unknown Uncertainty Not every uncertainty can be anticipated. SIUM does not claim to identify unknowable conditions. It requires that known limitations in the ability to characterize uncertainty remain visible. Quantitative Uncertainty Where appropriate, uncertainty may be expressed through: range, interval, probability distribution, confidence interval, variance, standard deviation, tolerance, error bound, or another justified quantitative representation. Qualitative Uncertainty Not all uncertainty should be forced into numerical form. Qualitative states may include: Low Moderate High Material but Unquantified Unresolved or another governed classification. No False Quantification Principle SIMULOS® establishes: Uncertainty should not be assigned artificial numerical precision where the available information cannot legitimately support it. Uncertainty Bounds Where uncertainty can be bounded, the relevant range should be identified. For example: Input X ∈ [8.5, 10.2] A bounded range should reflect the available evidence rather than an arbitrary convenience range. Unbounded or Open Uncertainty Some uncertainty may not have a defensible upper or lower bound. Such uncertainty should not be converted into a narrow interval merely to satisfy a simulation interface. Point Estimate Governance A simulation may technically require a single value. Where a point estimate represents an uncertain quantity, the record should preserve: Point Estimate + Uncertainty Basis rather than allowing the estimate to become indistinguishable from exact observation. No Point-Estimate Certainty Principle A single numerical input does not become certain merely because the simulation engine accepts only one number. Uncertainty Dependency Uncertainties may be dependent. For example: multiple inputs derived from the same sensor may share the same measurement uncertainty. Treating them as independent may underestimate total uncertainty. Correlated Uncertainty Where uncertainty in one input is materially correlated with another, the relationship should be preserved where feasible. Conceptually: Uncertainty A ↔ Uncertainty B rather than: Uncertainty A + Independent Uncertainty B Shared-Source Uncertainty Multiple inputs may inherit uncertainty from a common source. For example: Input A Input B and: Input C may all depend upon: Sensor S A failure or bias in Sensor S may therefore affect all three inputs simultaneously. No Independence-by-Default Principle SIMULOS® establishes: Input uncertainties must not be assumed independent merely because they are represented as separate variables. Compounded Uncertainty Multiple uncertainties may interact. Conceptually: Measurement Uncertainty + Transformation Uncertainty + Temporal Uncertainty + Parameter Uncertainty may create a broader uncertainty condition than any individual contribution alone. Uncertainty Aggregation Where multiple uncertainty contributions are aggregated, the aggregation method should be: identifiable, appropriate, reproducible where required, and bounded by known dependencies. No Simple Addition Rule Uncertainty components should not automatically be added, averaged, or multiplied without a justified methodological basis. Uncertainty Materiality Not every uncertainty requires the same governance intensity. An uncertainty is material where it could reasonably affect: simulation behavior, scenario outcome, output interpretation, validation, operational decision, or reliance. Materiality Is Context-Dependent An uncertainty of: ±1 mm may be irrelevant in one simulation and critical in another. Therefore: Uncertainty Magnitude ≠ Uncertainty Materiality Materiality depends upon the Simulation Purpose and the sensitivity of the simulated system. Uncertainty Sensitivity A simulation may respond differently to uncertainty across inputs. Some inputs may have little effect. Others may produce major output changes. SIUM therefore supports identification of: Uncertainty-Sensitive Inputs where uncertainty requires stronger downstream attention. Sensitivity Requirement Where material uncertainty exists, downstream simulation design may require sensitivity analysis. The relevant later SIMULOS® governance spaces determine how that analysis is executed. SIUM establishes that the uncertainty requiring examination must not disappear before reaching them. Uncertainty Propagation Input uncertainty may propagate through: Simulation Inputs ↓ Simulation Model ↓ Simulation Execution ↓ Simulation Outputs ↓ Simulation Interpretation ↓ Operational Reliance SIUM governs the input-side uncertainty basis and establishes propagation requirements for later SIMULOS® stages. Uncertainty Does Not End at Input Boundary SIMULOS® establishes: Material uncertainty attached to an input remains relevant until a governed downstream process demonstrates why it no longer materially affects the simulation result. No Uncertainty Erasure Principle A transformation, model, or simulation execution must not silently erase material uncertainty merely because the downstream output is deterministic. Deterministic Model ≠ Certain Result A deterministic simulation may produce exactly the same output from exactly the same input. That does not mean the simulated result is certain where the input itself is uncertain. Precision vs Certainty A simulation may produce: 0.87346192 from uncertain input data. The number of decimal places does not determine the certainty of the result. No Precision-to-Certainty Principle SIMULOS® establishes: Computational precision must not be represented as evidentiary certainty. Uncertainty Scenario Representation Where uncertainty cannot be adequately represented through a single input, the simulation may require multiple input conditions. For example: Low Estimate Central Estimate High Estimate or: Multiple Probability-Based Samples SIUM establishes the uncertainty basis requiring such treatment. Boundary Conditions Uncertain inputs may require simulation at boundary values. This can reveal whether conclusions remain stable across plausible input ranges. Worst-Credible Input Condition Where consequence is high, the simulation may need to examine credible adverse input combinations. SIUM identifies the uncertainty basis. Scenario governance determines how those conditions are represented. Uncertainty Interaction With Scenario Design SIUM connects directly to the subsequent Simulation Scenario Standard (SSS). Uncertainty may require scenarios that explore: plausible ranges, adverse combinations, edge conditions, uncertainty distributions, alternative input states, and unresolved input assumptions. SIUM does not design those scenarios. It establishes what uncertainty the scenario design must be capable of addressing. Uncertainty Register Material input uncertainties should be capable of being preserved within a Simulation Input Uncertainty Register. The register may identify: uncertainty identifier, affected input, uncertainty source, uncertainty type, magnitude or characterization, dependency, materiality, downstream relevance, condition, and current status. Uncertainty Identifier A material uncertainty may receive a persistent identifier. For example: SIU-0047 This allows later simulation records to reference the same uncertainty across: scenario design, execution, output interpretation, validation, and reliance. Uncertainty Status Possible uncertainty statuses may include: Characterized Partially Characterized Bounded Conditionally Bounded Unresolved Material Unquantified or: Not Material for Defined Simulation Use Uncertainty Acceptance An uncertainty may be accepted for simulation use where: it is sufficiently understood, its effect is bounded, required downstream treatment exists, and the Simulation Purpose permits reliance upon that uncertainty level. Acceptance does not mean the uncertainty disappears. Conditional Uncertainty Acceptance A Simulation Input may remain usable subject to conditions. For example: Input accepted only if sensitivity testing covers ±10% variation. Uncertainty Restriction An input may be restricted where uncertainty prevents broader use. For example: Suitable for exploratory simulation only. but: Not suitable for safety-critical operational reliance. Uncertainty Rejection Where uncertainty is too great or too poorly understood for the intended simulation purpose, the input may be rejected. Uncertainty Undetermined Where the available information is insufficient to assess uncertainty, the correct state may be: Uncertainty Undetermined rather than an assumed acceptable level. Uncertainty Threshold A simulation may define thresholds beyond which input uncertainty requires: additional evidence, broader scenarios, stronger sensitivity testing, restriction, or rejection. Thresholds should derive from the Simulation Purpose and consequence rather than convenience. Uncertainty Budget Where appropriate, a simulation may establish an Input Uncertainty Budget defining how much uncertainty can be tolerated across material input categories. The budget should not permit one uncertainty to disappear merely because another input is highly precise. No Precision Compensation Principle SIMULOS® establishes: High certainty in one Simulation Input cannot automatically compensate for material uncertainty in another input upon which the simulated outcome critically depends. Uncertainty Concentration A simulation may contain many high-quality inputs but depend critically upon one highly uncertain variable. SIUM therefore assesses uncertainty according to influence, not merely average input quality. Weakest Critical Input Principle Where an outcome materially depends upon a highly uncertain critical input, the simulation conclusion should remain bounded by that uncertainty. Uncertainty Change Input uncertainty may change when: new evidence becomes available, sensors are recalibrated, source reliability changes, transformation logic changes, temporal distance increases, missing values increase, new environments are introduced, or Simulation Scope changes. Uncertainty Reassessment Trigger Material changes should trigger reassessment of the affected uncertainty basis. Scope Expansion and Uncertainty Expanding Simulation Scope may expose uncertainty that was immaterial under the original scope. For example: an input sufficiently certain for: normal operating conditions may be insufficiently characterized for: extreme operating conditions. Version Change and Uncertainty A new input version should not automatically inherit the uncertainty characterization of its predecessor. The new version may require reassessment where: source, measurement, transformation, temporal basis, or distribution has materially changed. Uncertainty Traceability SIUM establishes: Simulation Input ↓ Uncertainty Source ↓ Uncertainty Type ↓ Magnitude / Characterization ↓ Dependency ↓ Materiality ↓ Propagation Requirement ↓ Condition / Restriction ↓ Uncertainty Status ↓ Simulation Use Input Uncertainty Basis The final SIUM result should establish a coherent Simulation Input Uncertainty Basis for the complete Simulation Input Set. This basis should identify: material uncertainties, their origins, their relationships, their characterization, unresolved uncertainty, downstream treatment requirements, and limitations upon simulation use. Input-Set Uncertainty Individual inputs may each have acceptable uncertainty while their combination creates material uncertainty. SIUM therefore distinguishes: Input-Level Uncertainty from: Input-Set Uncertainty. Input-Set Uncertainty Coherence The complete uncertainty basis should account for: shared sources, dependencies, correlations, transformation chains, temporal relationships, and interacting uncertainty. Simulation Input Readiness After SIUM, the complete SIDS input basis may receive an overall readiness status such as: Simulation Input Ready Conditionally Simulation Input Ready Partially Simulation Input Ready Simulation Input Not Ready or: Simulation Input Readiness Undetermined This status represents completion of the SIDS input-governance sequence. Input Readiness Does Not Mean Simulation Validity SIMULOS® establishes: Simulation Input Readiness confirms only that the input basis is sufficiently governed for its defined simulation use. It does not establish that the model, scenarios, execution, outputs, or simulation itself are valid. Those questions belong to subsequent SIMULOS® Parent Standards. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Identify Material Input Uncertainties Determine which Simulation Inputs contain uncertainty capable of materially affecting simulation behavior or interpretation. 2. Identify Uncertainty Sources Bind each material uncertainty to its known or suspected origin. 3. Classify Uncertainty Determine whether uncertainty is associated with: measurement, observation, sampling, representativeness, transformation, time, estimation, interpolation, extrapolation, imputation, synthetic generation, parameterization, classification, or another relevant source. 4. Characterize Uncertainty Use justified: quantitative bounds, distributions, qualitative classifications, or explicit unresolved status. 5. Assess Dependencies Determine whether material uncertainties are: independent, correlated, shared-source, sequentially dependent, or otherwise linked. 6. Assess Materiality Determine whether each uncertainty can materially affect the Simulation Purpose, behavior, outputs, or downstream reliance. 7. Establish Propagation Requirements Identify which uncertainties must remain visible through subsequent simulation stages. 8. Establish Conditions and Restrictions Define limitations upon simulation use where uncertainty remains material. 9. Assign Uncertainty Status Classify material uncertainties as: Characterized, Partially Characterized, Bounded, Conditionally Bounded, Unresolved, Material Unquantified, or Not Material for Defined Simulation Use. 10. Assess Input-Set Uncertainty Evaluate interactions across the complete Simulation Input basis. 11. Determine Simulation Input Readiness Establish whether the governed input basis is: Ready, Conditionally Ready, Partially Ready, Not Ready, or Readiness Undetermined. 12. Preserve Uncertainty Traceability Maintain: Input → Uncertainty → Source → Characterization → Dependency → Materiality → Propagation → Condition → Status → Simulation Use Governance Outputs SIUM may produce: Simulation Input Uncertainty Register, Input Uncertainty Identifier, Uncertainty Source Record, Measurement Uncertainty Record, Observational Uncertainty Record, Sampling Uncertainty Record, Representativeness Uncertainty Record, Transformation-Induced Uncertainty Record, Temporal Uncertainty Record, Estimation Uncertainty Record, Interpolation Uncertainty Record, Extrapolation Uncertainty Record, Imputation Uncertainty Record, Synthetic Input Uncertainty Record, Parameter Uncertainty Record, Classification Uncertainty Record, Missing-Information Uncertainty Record, Quantitative Uncertainty Assessment, Qualitative Uncertainty Assessment, Uncertainty Bound, Uncertainty Distribution Record, Unresolved Uncertainty Record, Uncertainty Dependency Map, Correlated Uncertainty Record, Shared-Source Uncertainty Record, Compounded Uncertainty Assessment, Uncertainty Materiality Assessment, Uncertainty Sensitivity Signal, Uncertainty Propagation Requirement, Input Uncertainty Budget, Uncertainty Condition Record, Uncertainty Restriction Record, Uncertainty Status, Input-Set Uncertainty Assessment, Simulation Input Uncertainty Basis, Simulation Input Readiness Status, Uncertainty Reassessment Trigger, and Simulation Input Uncertainty Traceability Map. Use Case 1 — Autonomous Robot Simulation Scenario A robot-navigation simulation receives: object-position measurements with sensor error, estimated surface-friction values, partially observed pedestrian movement, and interpolated localization data. Each input is technically usable. However, each contains a different uncertainty basis. Application SIUM identifies: measurement uncertainty in object position, estimation uncertainty in surface friction, observational uncertainty in pedestrian movement, and interpolation uncertainty in localization. Dependencies between localization and object-position measurements are also identified because both depend partly upon the same sensor system. Result The input basis becomes: Conditionally Simulation Input Ready with a requirement that material uncertainty be propagated into subsequent scenario and execution governance rather than treating the nominal input values as exact reality. Use Case 2 — Energy Infrastructure Simulation Scenario A long-term energy simulation uses: historical demand, future population projections, weather forecasts, estimated technology adoption, and assumed future industrial demand. The simulation produces precise annual energy-demand figures. Application SIUM distinguishes: Observed Historical Inputs from: Projected Inputs Estimated Inputs and: Assumed Inputs. The largest material uncertainty is found in future industrial demand. Sensitivity to this input is high. Result The simulation may continue, but the uncertainty basis requires downstream scenarios covering materially different industrial-demand conditions. The final simulation cannot legitimately present the central numerical trajectory as a certain future state. Architectural Position Simulation Input Uncertainty is the fifth and final internal governance space of the Simulation Input & Data Standard (SIDS). The complete SIDS progression is: Simulation Input Identification ↓ Simulation Data Representativeness ↓ Simulation Data Transformation ↓ Simulation Temporal Data ↓ Simulation Input Uncertainty Together, the five modules answer: What information is entering the simulation? ↓ What reality can it legitimately represent? ↓ What happened to it before simulation use? ↓ Is it temporally appropriate? ↓ What uncertainty remains in the complete input basis? The resulting: Simulation Input Uncertainty Basis and: Simulation Input Readiness Status provide the governed input foundation required by subsequent SIMULOS® lifecycle spaces. The next Parent Standard, Simulation Scenario Standard (SSS), governs which scenarios must be designed to examine expected conditions, variations, edge cases, stresses, uncertainty, and materially relevant alternatives. Foundational Principle Simulation Inputs become uncertainty-governed only when material uncertainty remains identifiable from its source through its characterization, dependencies, conditions, and downstream propagation requirements, so that computational precision cannot transform uncertain information into an appearance of certain reality. Canonical Closing Statement Simulation Input Uncertainty Module completes the Simulation Input & Data Standard by governing the uncertainty that remains after Simulation Inputs have been identified, assessed for representativeness, transformed, and temporally governed. Through uncertainty-source attribution, classification, quantitative and qualitative characterization, dependency and correlation assessment, materiality, sensitivity, propagation requirements, conditions, restrictions, reassessment, Input-Set Uncertainty, readiness determination, and complete uncertainty traceability, SIUM ensures that uncertainty entering a simulation cannot disappear merely because the simulation can process the data or produce precise numerical outputs. The module establishes the final governed Simulation Input Uncertainty Basis from which subsequent SIMULOS® scenario design and simulation execution can legitimately proceed.

title: OOF™ Simulation Lifecycle Monitoring Module (SLMM)
text: OOF™ Simulation Lifecycle Monitoring Module (SLMM) Simulation Lifecycle Monitoring Module (SLMM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Standard (SLRS) Module: SLMM — Simulation Lifecycle Monitoring Module Operational Layer: Simulation Lifecycle Monitoring Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Simulation Lifecycle Monitoring Origin ID: SIMULOS-SLRS-SLMM-012.1 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 20 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Simulation Lifecycle Monitoring Module (SLMM) is the first Core Module of the Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Standard (SLRS) within SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture. SLMM governs the continuing observation of conditions capable of materially affecting the relevance, applicability, representativeness, evidential meaning, or continued use of an existing simulation and its governed results. The Module establishes a structured relationship between the simulation basis that existed when simulation evidence was produced and the conditions that exist as the simulation continues through its lifecycle. SLMM does not determine whether observed change constitutes Simulation Drift, nor whether resimulation is required. Its task is foundational: to ensure that material changes capable of affecting simulation relevance can become visible rather than allowing a simulation to remain operationally influential after its governing basis has silently changed. Core Question Which conditions must remain monitored so that material changes affecting simulation relevance can be detected throughout the simulation lifecycle? Architectural Position SLMM is the first module within SLRS. It follows the completed active simulation lifecycle: Simulation Object → Purpose & Scope → Reality Representation → Assumptions → Model & Environment → Inputs & Data → Scenario Design → Execution → Output Governance → Simulation-to-Reality Correlation → Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary and begins lifecycle governance. SLMM precedes: SDRM — Simulation Drift Recognition Module. The relationship is: Lifecycle Monitoring → Drift Recognition. SLMM observes and structures relevant change. SDRM determines whether that change creates a material divergence between the existing simulation basis and the conditions to which that simulation remains applied. Internal Flow Position Governed Simulation Lifecycle Basis → Monitoring Context Definition → Change-Sensitive Condition Identification → Lifecycle Observation → Change Signal Detection → Material Change Candidate Registration → Simulation Relevance Review Input → SDRM — Simulation Drift Recognition Module Operational Space SLMM governs the space between: an established governed simulation basis and subsequent changes capable of affecting that basis. This includes monitoring relevant change affecting: Simulation Object identity; object version; object configuration; object state; simulation purpose; simulation scope; represented reality; abstraction; fidelity requirements; assumptions; model applicability; model version; simulation environment; parameterization; inputs; data distributions; temporal data relevance; input uncertainty; scenario relevance; scenario coverage; observed operational conditions; simulation-to-reality correlation; evidence applicability; evidence weight; reliance conditions; known limitations; previously unknown conditions. Operational Scope SLMM applies wherever simulation results, evidence, models, scenarios, or simulation-derived conclusions continue to be retained, reused, referenced, compared, relied upon, or maintained after their initial production. It may govern lifecycle monitoring for: individual simulations; simulation models; repeated simulation programs; scenario portfolios; Monte Carlo studies; digital twins; engineering simulations; scientific simulations; safety simulations; infrastructure simulations; mission simulations; economic simulations; AI simulations; autonomous-system simulations; large-scale simulation campaigns; long-duration simulation programs; future simulation technologies. The Module remains technology-neutral. Its concern is not how frequently a simulator executes. Its concern is whether the conditions supporting simulation relevance remain sufficiently observable over time. Simulation Completion ≠ Lifecycle Completion SLMM establishes the distinction: Simulation Execution Completion ≠ Simulation Lifecycle Completion A simulation run may end. A simulation campaign may end. The simulator may be switched off. But the simulation results may continue influencing: engineering; design; planning; scientific reasoning; safety assessment; mission preparation; system development; validation; operational decisions; deployment; future simulation campaigns. Lifecycle governance therefore continues for as long as simulation-derived information remains materially relevant or relied upon. Lifecycle Monitoring Basis SLMM requires a Simulation Lifecycle Monitoring Basis to identify which parts of the governed simulation lifecycle are capable of materially affecting continuing relevance. The monitoring basis may reference: Simulation Object → what was simulated. Purpose & Scope → why and within what boundaries it was simulated. Reality Representation → which reality was represented and how. Assumptions → what conditions were presumed. Model & Environment → which model and simulation environment generated the behavior. Inputs & Data → which information basis entered the simulation. Scenarios → which conditions were tested. Execution → how the simulation was actually executed. Outputs → what was produced. Simulation-to-Reality Correlation → what relationship with reality was established. Evidence & Reliance Boundary → what the simulation-derived evidence was permitted to support. Lifecycle monitoring does not require every element to be monitored equally. It requires monitoring to remain proportionate to the conditions capable of materially changing simulation relevance. Change-Sensitive Condition Principle Not every characteristic of a simulation requires continuous monitoring. SLMM identifies Change-Sensitive Conditions: conditions whose material change could alter the relevance, applicability, representativeness, evidential meaning, or legitimate reliance of an existing simulation. Examples may include: object redesign; software update; hardware replacement; environmental change; changed operational profile; new observed behavior; changed data distribution; new failure mode; revised assumption; model discovery; changed mission condition; new regulatory operating constraint; new physical observation; changed scenario prevalence; newly discovered edge case; degraded simulation-to-reality correlation. The monitoring burden should therefore follow material relevance, not indiscriminate observation. Reality Change Monitoring A simulation may remain unchanged while reality changes around it. SLMM therefore requires relevant changes in represented or relied-upon reality to remain observable where those changes can affect simulation relevance. Examples may include: environmental change; infrastructure change; human behavioral change; operational practice change; traffic pattern change; climate condition change; market structure change; mission environment update; newly observed physical behavior; new operational interactions. ORA™ continues to govern Operational Reality itself. SLMM governs whether changes in relevant reality are being observed for their potential effect on simulation relevance. Simulation Object Change Monitoring A simulation may become stale because the Simulation Object itself changes. SLMM may monitor: new object versions; configuration changes; component replacement; software changes; hardware changes; changed interfaces; changed capabilities; changed constraints; changed operational modes; changed dependencies. A simulation of Object Version V3 does not automatically remain representative of Object Version V7. Object evolution must therefore remain connected to lifecycle monitoring. Assumption Change Monitoring Assumptions that were reasonable when a simulation was constructed may later become questionable, obsolete, contradicted, or unnecessary. SLMM may therefore monitor: newly available evidence affecting assumptions; observed contradiction; changed uncertainty; revised scientific understanding; changed operational conditions; dependence on assumptions no longer applicable. SLMM does not govern the assumptions themselves. That remains under SAS — Simulation Assumption Standard. It monitors changes capable of affecting their continued applicability. Model and Environment Change Monitoring Simulation models and environments may evolve independently of the simulation evidence already produced. SLMM may monitor: model replacement; model revision; environment updates; parameterization changes; discovered model defects; corrected physical relationships; changed solver behavior; updated simulation infrastructure; changed environmental representations. A newer model does not automatically invalidate earlier simulations. But material differences must become visible for lifecycle assessment. Input and Data Change Monitoring Simulation relevance may degrade when the distributions or conditions represented by simulation inputs materially change. SLMM may monitor: new operational data; changed distributions; changed populations; changed environmental data; temporal shifts; new sensor characteristics; newly available empirical data; changed uncertainty; changed input-generation methods. SIDS continues to govern simulation inputs and data at the simulation-input boundary. SLMM monitors subsequent changes that may affect the relevance of previously generated simulation results. Scenario Relevance Monitoring Scenario sets may become incomplete over time. SLMM may identify changes such as: new operational scenarios; newly observed edge cases; changed scenario frequency; emerging stress conditions; newly relevant interactions; previously unknown failure combinations; changed environmental combinations. The discovery of a new scenario does not automatically invalidate existing simulations. It may, however, reveal that existing scenario coverage no longer represents the relevant problem space sufficiently. Correlation Change Monitoring Simulation-to-reality correlation is not necessarily permanent. New real-world observations may show: stronger correlation; weaker correlation; systematic deviation; condition-specific divergence; temporal degradation; newly discovered mismatch. SLMM therefore monitors information capable of changing the existing correlation basis established through SRCS. It does not recalculate correlation. That remains within Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Standard (SRCS). Evidence Relevance Monitoring Simulation-derived evidence may remain technically unchanged while its relevance changes. SLMM may monitor conditions capable of affecting: evidence qualification; evidential weight; applicability; reliance boundaries; use limitations; temporal relevance. Where a material lifecycle change affects simulation evidence, the relevant SERBS governance may require reassessment. SLMM does not independently redefine evidential weight or reliance. Change Signal SLMM introduces the Simulation Lifecycle Change Signal. A Change Signal is: an observed or reported change that may materially affect the continuing relevance of a governed simulation basis. A Change Signal is not yet Simulation Drift. It is an input for further assessment. Possible sources include: operational observations; engineering change records; new measurements; updated datasets; new scientific findings; system version changes; mission updates; incident findings; model corrections; new scenario discoveries; changed environmental conditions; changed correlation results. Material Change Candidate Where a Change Signal has a plausible relationship to simulation relevance, SLMM may register it as a Material Change Candidate. The distinction is: Change Signal → something changed. Material Change Candidate → the change may matter to the simulation. Simulation Drift → the change has produced a material divergence affecting the governed simulation basis. The final determination of Simulation Drift belongs to SDRM. Monitoring by Dependency Simulation relevance may be affected indirectly. For example: Component Change → changes system behavior → changes object configuration → affects scenario behavior → changes simulation applicability. SLMM therefore permits lifecycle monitoring across material dependency chains rather than monitoring only direct changes to the simulator. This is especially important for complex systems where a seemingly small change may propagate into a simulation-relevant difference. Event-Driven Monitoring Lifecycle monitoring may be event-driven. Relevant events may include: object update; software release; hardware change; new operational dataset; incident; newly observed failure; mission redesign; environmental change; assumption challenge; model correction; correlation deterioration; regulatory operating change. An event may initiate a simulation relevance review without waiting for a scheduled lifecycle review. Periodic Monitoring Where simulation relevance may degrade gradually or where material change is not tied to a discrete event, organizations may use periodic monitoring. The appropriate interval may depend upon: rate of object change; rate of environmental change; consequence of stale simulation reliance; simulation purpose; operational volatility; evidence importance; availability of new reality information. SLMM does not impose one universal review interval. Continuous Monitoring Certain simulation contexts may justify continuous or near-continuous lifecycle monitoring. Examples include: digital twins; rapidly changing autonomous systems; high-frequency operational environments; continuously updated models; adaptive systems; dynamic infrastructure environments. Continuous monitoring does not imply continuous resimulation. It provides a higher-frequency basis for detecting potentially material change. Monitoring Proportionality Principle SLMM rejects the assumption that all simulations require identical monitoring intensity. Monitoring should be proportionate to: rate of relevant change; consequence of outdated reliance; simulation reuse; operational importance; uncertainty; dependence on volatile assumptions; dependence on changing reality; expected lifecycle duration. A one-time exploratory simulation may require minimal lifecycle monitoring. A simulation supporting years of safety-critical operational reliance may require substantially stronger monitoring. Dormant Simulation Principle A simulation may remain unused for a period and later return to active use. Dormancy must not create an assumption of continuing relevance. Before material reuse, the simulation may require review against accumulated lifecycle changes. Therefore: Stored Simulation ≠ Current Simulation Basis. Monitoring at Scale Large organizations may maintain thousands or millions of simulation artifacts and evidence objects. SLMM must therefore support lifecycle monitoring at scale. Monitoring may operate through: simulation families; object families; model versions; scenario families; evidence classes; dependency relationships; change-event propagation; lifecycle status registers. A material change affecting one shared model may therefore identify many dependent simulation results requiring review. Lifecycle Monitoring State SLMM may assign a lifecycle monitoring state such as: 1. Active Monitoring Relevant lifecycle conditions are currently monitored. 2. Reduced Monitoring Monitoring continues at a reduced level because active reliance or change exposure is limited. 3. Dormant The simulation is retained but not currently subject to active reliance. 4. Review Required A material Change Signal or accumulated lifecycle change requires assessment. 5. Monitoring Suspended Required monitoring cannot currently be performed sufficiently. 6. Lifecycle Exit Candidate The simulation may no longer justify continued monitoring and may require retirement assessment. These are governance states rather than universal technical classifications. Lifecycle Traceability SLMM requires material lifecycle changes to remain traceable to the simulation assets potentially affected by them. A lifecycle trace may connect: Change Event → Affected Reality Condition → Affected Simulation Basis Element → Affected Simulation → Affected Outputs → Affected Evidence → Potential Reliance Impact This relationship enables downstream drift recognition and proportionate resimulation decisions. SLMM Boundary with SDRM SLMM identifies and structures potentially relevant lifecycle change. SDRM determines whether the change constitutes material Simulation Drift. Therefore: Monitoring Signal ≠ Drift Determination. SLMM Boundary with SRGM SLMM does not determine whether resimulation must occur. That decision belongs to: SRGM — Resimulation Trigger Module. The lifecycle sequence is: Monitoring → Drift Recognition → Trigger Determination. SLMM Boundary with ORA™ ORA™ governs actual Operational Reality. SLMM may consume relevant reality-change information to determine whether simulation relevance requires review. It does not redefine, reconstruct, or govern Operational Reality itself. SLMM Boundary with SERBS SERBS governs simulation-derived evidence, evidential weight, reliance boundaries, and use limitations.
