SLMM monitors changes capable of affecting those governed evidence conditions. It does not independently redefine evidence qualification, weight, or permitted reliance. SLMM Boundary with VALIDOS® VALIDOS® governs validation and revalidation. SLMM governs simulation lifecycle monitoring. A lifecycle change detected by SLMM may eventually contribute to revalidation processes, but: Simulation Lifecycle Review ≠ Validation Reassessment. SLMM Boundary with INTEGROS® SLMM does not govern general lifecycle integrity. INTEGROS® continues to govern integrity properties of objects, states, evidence, and processes. SLMM governs only lifecycle monitoring specifically required to preserve the continuing relevance of simulation. SLMM Boundary with ADIT® ADIT® may audit whether lifecycle records, change evidence, and monitoring activities are observable, preserved, and verifiable. SLMM owns the simulation-specific monitoring logic. Lifecycle Monitoring ≠ Lifecycle Audit. Governance Outputs SLMM may produce: Simulation Lifecycle Monitoring Basis Change-Sensitive Condition Register Simulation Lifecycle Monitoring Profile Simulation Lifecycle Change Signal Material Change Candidate Record Simulation Object Change Link Reality Change Link Assumption Change Link Model & Environment Change Link Input & Data Change Link Scenario Relevance Change Link Correlation Change Link Evidence Relevance Change Link Simulation Dependency Change Record Lifecycle Monitoring State Simulation Relevance Review Input Simulation Lifecycle Monitoring Record These outputs provide the governed input basis for: SDRM — Simulation Drift Recognition Module. Enterprise Application SLMM enables organizations to answer a lifecycle question that conventional simulation programs frequently leave implicit: How will we know when the simulation we trusted yesterday no longer represents the problem we face today? An organization may use SLMM to detect when: a simulated product has changed configuration; new operational behavior has emerged; a mission environment has been revised; new physical measurements challenge earlier assumptions; an autonomous system receives a significant software update; operational data distributions change; new edge cases appear; a model defect is discovered; simulation-to-reality correlation deteriorates; simulation evidence remains in organizational use long after its original basis has changed. SLMM does not force the organization to rerun every simulation whenever something changes. Instead, it creates the governed observation layer necessary to determine whether the change matters at all. This allows later modules to distinguish between: irrelevant change, material drift, targeted resimulation, broad resimulation, replacement, and retirement. Foundational Principles Simulation completion is not simulation lifecycle completion. A simulation may remain computationally unchanged while becoming operationally stale. Lifecycle monitoring must follow the conditions that give simulation results their meaning. Not every change is material to simulation relevance. A detected change is not automatically Simulation Drift. Monitoring intensity should be proportional to the consequence and likelihood of simulation obsolescence. Stored simulation results do not automatically remain current simulation evidence. Reality change, object change, assumption change, model change, data change, scenario change, and correlation change may all affect continuing simulation relevance. Continuous monitoring does not require continuous resimulation. A simulation cannot remain governably relevant over time if material changes to the basis supporting its relevance are allowed to remain invisible. Canonical Closing Statement Simulation Lifecycle Monitoring Module establishes the lifecycle observation layer of the Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Standard by maintaining structured visibility over changes capable of affecting the continuing relevance, applicability, representativeness, evidential meaning, and legitimate use of governed simulations. Through governance of monitoring bases, change-sensitive conditions, object change, reality change, assumption change, model and environment change, input and data change, scenario relevance, correlation change, evidence relevance, dependency propagation, change signals, material change candidates, monitoring states, and lifecycle traceability, SLMM prevents simulation results from remaining operationally influential merely because the conditions that once supported them are no longer being examined. By separating lifecycle observation from Simulation Drift recognition and resimulation decisions, SLMM creates the first governed control point of the recursive SIMULOS® lifecycle and provides the structured change basis required by SDRM. A simulation can remain governably relevant over time only when material changes capable of altering its meaning can first become visible.

title: OOF™ Simulation Model Structure Module (SMMM)
text: OOF™ Simulation Model Structure Module (SMMM) Simulation Model Structure Module (SMMM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Simulation Model & Environment Standard (SMES) Operational Layer: Simulation Model & Environment Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Type: Parent Standard Module Governed Space: Simulation Model Structure Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 17 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Governed Space Simulation Model Structure Canonical Definition Simulation Model Structure Module (SMMM) defines the governance framework for identifying, constructing, decomposing, organizing, documenting, and controlling the structural composition of a Simulation Model so that its components, relationships, dependencies, interfaces, internal states, interaction pathways, and structural boundaries remain explicit, traceable, and consistent with the governed Simulation Object, Purpose & Scope, Reality Representation, and Simulation Assumptions. SMMM establishes the structural foundation through which a simulation representation becomes an identifiable executable model rather than an opaque technical implementation. Operational Role SMMM is the first internal governance space of the Simulation Model & Environment Standard (SMES). It answers: What is the Simulation Model structurally composed of, how are its components related, and what structural arrangement actually produces the behavior being simulated? The governed progression is: Governed Reality Representation → Governed Simulation Assumptions → Model Structure Definition → Component Identification → Relationship & Dependency Mapping → Interface Definition → Structural Boundary Establishment → Governed Simulation Model Structure SMMM establishes the model structure upon which the remaining SMES governance spaces can operate. Module Operational Space SMMM governs: Simulation Model identification, model structural definition, model decomposition, model composition, component identification, component classification, component roles, component relationships, structural dependencies, model hierarchy, model topology, interaction pathways, internal interfaces, external model interfaces, state relationships, structural constraints, model coupling, model composition rules, structural abstraction, structural completeness, structural consistency, structural change visibility, model-structure version binding, representation-to-model traceability, assumption-to-model traceability, and structural reconstruction. Module Operational Scope SMMM applies to any Simulation Model whose internal structure materially affects simulation behavior, interpretation, reproducibility, comparability, or downstream reliance. The module may govern: mathematical models, computational models, physics-based models, statistical models, behavioral models, agent-based models, AI-based simulation models, autonomous-system models, digital twins, system-of-systems models, discrete-event models, continuous models, hybrid models, multi-model simulations, coupled models, scientific models, industrial models, infrastructure models, economic models, biological models, and future simulation-model structures. The required governance depth should remain proportional to the Simulation Purpose, Scope, complexity, and consequence. Module Function SMMM exists to prevent the Simulation Model from becoming a technical black box whose structural composition cannot be connected back to the simulation inquiry it is intended to represent. Its function is to ensure that material model structure remains sufficiently explicit to determine: what components exist, what each component represents, how components interact, which components depend upon others, where structural boundaries exist, which interfaces connect the structure, and: how the complete model structure relates to the governed representation of reality. Simulation Model Structure A Simulation Model Structure is the governed arrangement of model components and the relationships through which those components collectively represent and execute the modeled behavior of the Simulation Object or relevant represented reality. The structure may be: Monolithic Modular Hierarchical Distributed Networked Layered Coupled Composite Agent-Based or: Hybrid provided that its material structural properties remain governable. Model Structure Identification Every governed Simulation Model should have a sufficiently identifiable structural representation. At minimum, where materially relevant, the structure should establish: model identity, model version, structural architecture, primary components, component relationships, material dependencies, interfaces, state relationships, structural boundaries, and relevant external dependencies. A model name alone does not establish model structure. Model Decomposition Complex Simulation Models may require decomposition into governable components. Conceptually: Simulation Model ↓ Subsystem ↓ Component ↓ Subcomponent ↓ Relevant Structural Element Decomposition should continue only to the level necessary for the intended simulation governance purpose. SMMM does not require unnecessary decomposition where additional structural detail would not materially improve governance. Model Component A Model Component is an identifiable structural element performing a distinguishable function within the Simulation Model. A component may represent: an object, actor, subsystem, process, rule system, behavior, physical mechanism, computational mechanism, AI model, controller, population, resource, network, or another modeled element. Component Identity Material components should remain distinguishable from one another. Where two components perform materially different simulation functions, their identities should not be collapsed merely because they share the same technical implementation. Component Role Each material component should have an identifiable role within the model. A Component Role may establish: what the component represents, what behavior it produces, which inputs it receives, which outputs it generates, which states it maintains, and which other components depend upon it. Component Relationship SMMM governs material relationships between model components. Relationships may include: Input → Processing Cause → Effect Parent → Child Controller → Controlled Component Producer → Consumer Agent → Agent System → Subsystem State → Transition or other simulation-specific relationships. Structural Dependency A Structural Dependency exists where the function, state, behavior, or interpretation of one model component materially depends upon another model component or structural element. Dependencies should remain visible where their failure or modification could materially affect simulation behavior. Dependency Direction Where relevant, dependency direction should be identifiable. For example: Component B depends upon Component A does not necessarily mean: Component A depends upon Component B. Bidirectional dependencies should be represented explicitly where they exist. Model Hierarchy Where a model contains hierarchical relationships, SMMM should preserve the hierarchy sufficiently to understand how lower-level behavior contributes to higher-level simulation behavior. Conceptually: System Model ↓ Subsystem Model ↓ Component Model ↓ Behavioral Element Hierarchy should support governance, not merely documentation. Model Topology Where interaction structure materially affects simulation behavior, the topology of the model should remain identifiable. This may include: networks, graphs, communication pathways, resource pathways, causal pathways, control pathways, or spatial relationships. Interaction Pathways A Simulation Model may produce behavior through sequences of interactions. Material pathways should be traceable where necessary. For example: Input → Sensor Model → Interpretation Model → Decision Model → Action Model → Environment Interaction If a material pathway cannot be reconstructed, simulation behavior may become difficult to explain or compare. Internal Interfaces An Internal Model Interface connects two or more components within the Simulation Model. Where materially relevant, an interface should establish: connected components, exchanged information or state, direction, format or representation, timing conditions, interaction rules, and applicable constraints. External Model Interfaces A model may also interact with elements outside its structural boundary. External interfaces may connect the model to: Simulation Environment, input sources, external models, live systems, humans, AI systems, hardware, external services, or other simulation environments. SMMM identifies the structural interface. Governance of the broader simulation boundary interaction remains within the appropriate SMES governance space. State Structure Where a model contains states, the structural relationship between those states should remain sufficiently defined. Examples: Operational → Degraded → Failed Idle → Active → Terminated Untrained → Trained → Adapted State transitions may materially alter model behavior. Structural Constraints Some model relationships are subject to structural constraints. Examples may include: prohibited interactions, maximum connectivity, required component presence, dependency ordering, synchronization conditions, or topology restrictions. Material structural constraints should remain explicit. Model Coupling Where multiple models or components influence one another, their coupling should be identifiable. Coupling may be: Loose Tight Unidirectional Bidirectional Synchronous Asynchronous Static or: Dynamic where such distinctions materially affect simulation behavior. Composite Simulation Models A simulation may combine several models into a composite structure. Conceptually: Model A + Model B + Model C → Composite Simulation Model SMMM requires the composition to preserve sufficient visibility into: constituent models, their identities, versions, roles, interfaces, dependencies, and interaction logic. Composition must not erase material differences between constituent models. Model-of-Models Structure Some simulations contain models that themselves govern or invoke other models. Where this occurs, SMMM should preserve: Model → Submodel → Invoked Model → External Model relationships sufficiently for structural reconstruction. Structural Abstraction Not every real-world element requires a separate model component. SMMM permits structural abstraction where consistent with the governed Reality Representation. However: Structural simplification must not silently remove a material element that the governed Reality Representation requires the simulation to represent. Representation-to-Structure Binding The model structure should remain connected to the Reality Representation from which it was constructed. Conceptually: Reality Element → Represented Element → Model Component This enables later determination of where a relevant aspect of reality appears within the executable model. Assumption-to-Structure Binding Material Simulation Assumptions may affect: component existence, component behavior, component relationships, dependencies, interfaces, state transitions, or structural constraints. Where material, the relationship should remain traceable: Simulation Assumption → Structural Element An assumption should not become invisible merely because it has been encoded into model architecture. Structural Completeness Structural Completeness asks: Does the governed model structure contain the material elements required by the approved Reality Representation and Simulation Purpose & Scope? Completeness is relative to the governed simulation inquiry. It does not require complete representation of reality. Structural Consistency Structural Consistency asks whether the components and relationships of the model remain mutually compatible with the intended structural design. Examples of structural inconsistency may include: incompatible interfaces, contradictory dependencies, missing required components, invalid component relationships, incompatible state transitions, or broken composition rules. Structural Coherence A structurally complete model may still be incoherent if its elements cannot operate together as intended. SMMM therefore distinguishes: Structural Presence from: Structural Coherence. No Hidden Component Principle A material model component must not influence simulation behavior while remaining outside the governed model structure merely because it is technically embedded, externally invoked, or automatically generated. No Hidden Dependency Principle A material dependency must not be treated as irrelevant merely because it exists below the visible simulation interface. No Structural Substitution Principle A materially different structural implementation should not be treated as the same governed Simulation Model without assessing whether the change affects: representation, assumptions, dependencies, interfaces, states, execution behavior, or downstream interpretation. Model Structure Change A Model Structure Change may include: component addition, component removal, component replacement, hierarchy change, topology change, dependency change, interface change, state-model change, coupling change, or structural constraint change. Material changes should remain identifiable. Structural Change Classification A change may be classified as: Non-Material Material Critical or: Undetermined relative to the Simulation Purpose & Scope. Structural Change Propagation A structural change may affect other SIMULOS® governance spaces. For example: Component Replacement may affect: Assumptions → Parameters → Inputs → Scenarios → Execution → Outputs SMMM identifies the structural change. Affected downstream spaces govern their respective consequences. Model Structure Version Binding The governed structure should remain connected to the applicable Simulation Model Version. A simulation execution should therefore be capable of identifying which governed structural version was active. Structural Reconstruction SMMM should enable reconstruction sufficient to answer: What was the model structurally composed of at the relevant time? Which components existed? How were they connected? Which dependencies were active? Which interfaces existed? Which structural assumptions applied? Which model version contained this structure? Structural Traceability The complete structural traceability path may be represented as: Simulation Object ↓ Simulation Purpose & Scope ↓ Reality Representation ↓ Simulation Assumptions ↓ Simulation Model ↓ Model Components ↓ Relationships & Dependencies ↓ Interfaces ↓ Structural Boundaries ↓ Model Structure Version Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Identify the Simulation Model Establish the model identity and applicable model version. 2. Define the Structural Architecture Determine the material organization of the model. 3. Identify Material Components Establish the components required for the governed simulation inquiry. 4. Map Relationships and Dependencies Identify how material components interact and depend upon one another. 5. Establish Interfaces Document material internal and external structural interfaces. 6. Bind Structure to Representation and Assumptions Preserve traceability from governed representation and assumptions into the model structure. 7. Establish Structural Boundaries Determine which elements belong to the model structure and which remain external. 8. Assess Structural Completeness and Consistency Determine whether required structural elements are present and mutually coherent. 9. Bind Structure to Model Version Ensure the governed structure can be associated with the correct model version. 10. Preserve Structural Reconstruction Maintain sufficient records to reconstruct the relevant model structure later. Governance Outputs SMMM may produce: Simulation Model Structure Record, Model Component Register, Model Component Identity Record, Component Role Map, Model Hierarchy Map, Model Topology Record, Component Relationship Map, Structural Dependency Map, Interaction Pathway Map, Internal Interface Record, External Model Interface Reference, State Structure Record, Structural Constraint Record, Model Coupling Record, Composite Model Structure Record, Reality Representation-to-Model Map, Assumption-to-Structure Map, Structural Completeness Assessment, Structural Consistency Assessment, Structural Coherence Assessment, Model Structure Change Record, Structural Change Classification, Structural Change Propagation Record, Model Structure Version Binding, Structural Reconstruction Record, and Simulation Model Structure Traceability Map. Use Case 1 — Autonomous Vehicle Simulation A vehicle simulation contains separate models for: Perception → Planning → Control → Vehicle Dynamics SMMM identifies each as a material model component and governs their interfaces and dependencies. If the planning component is replaced by a new AI model, the change cannot remain hidden merely because the rest of the simulation remains unchanged. The new structural relationship and affected dependencies become visible for downstream governance. Use Case 2 — Multi-Agent Financial Market Simulation A financial simulation contains thousands of autonomous trading agents interacting through a simulated market. SMMM governs the structural classes of agents, market mechanism, interaction topology, information pathways, and dependencies required to understand how collective market behavior emerges. The module does not determine whether the simulated market accurately predicts the real market. It establishes whether the model structure producing the simulated behavior is identifiable and governable. Use Case 3 — Spacecraft Mission Simulation A spacecraft simulation combines: Flight Dynamics Model + Guidance Model + Propulsion Model + Thermal Model + Communication Model SMMM preserves the identity, role, dependencies, interfaces, and version relationships of the constituent models. If the propulsion model changes, the simulation can identify which structural pathways and dependent components may be affected before subsequent simulation execution. Architectural Position Simulation Model Structure is the first internal governance space of the Simulation Model & Environment Standard (SMES). The complete SMES progression is: Simulation Model Structure → Simulation Environment Configuration → Simulation Boundary Interaction → Simulation Parameterization → Simulation Environment Versioning SMMM establishes the structural model basis required by the remaining SMES modules. Within the broader SIMULOS® lifecycle: Simulation Object → Simulation Purpose & Scope → Reality Representation → Simulation Assumptions → Simulation Model & Environment → downstream simulation governance SMMM therefore governs the first internal transition from the conceptual representation of the simulation into the controlled executable structure through which simulation behavior will later be produced. Foundational Principle A simulation model cannot be structurally governed when the components, relationships, dependencies, interfaces, and assumptions producing its behavior cannot be identified and reconstructed. Canonical Closing Statement Simulation Model Structure Module establishes the structural governance foundation of the Simulation Model & Environment Standard by making the internal composition of a Simulation Model explicit, bounded, traceable, and reconstructable. Through component identification, decomposition, relationship and dependency mapping, hierarchy, topology, interface governance, state structure, coupling, structural abstraction, representation and assumption binding, change visibility, version binding, completeness, consistency, and reconstruction, SMMM ensures that simulation behavior cannot emerge from an invisible model structure whose relationship to the governed Simulation Object, Reality Representation, and Simulation Assumptions cannot be demonstrated.

title: OOF™ Simulation Object Boundary Module (SOBM)
text: OOF™ Simulation Object Boundary Module (SOBM) Simulation Object Boundary Module (SOBM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Simulation Object Standard (SOS) Operational Layer: Simulation Object Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Type: Parent Standard Module Governed Space: Simulation Object Boundary Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 15 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Governed Space Simulation Object Boundary Canonical Definition Simulation Object Boundary Module (SOBM) defines the governance conditions under which the limits of an identified Simulation Object are formally established, distinguished from surrounding systems, environments, dependencies, actors, processes, interfaces, and external conditions, and maintained as a traceable Simulation Object Boundary throughout downstream simulation governance. SOBM ensures that a simulation cannot silently expand, contract, or redefine what belongs to the Simulation Object after its identity has been established. Operational Role SOBM serves as the second internal governance space of the Simulation Object Standard (SOS). SOIM establishes: What exactly is the Simulation Object? SOBM asks: Where does that Simulation Object begin and end, and what lies outside it? The governed progression is: Identified Simulation Object → Boundary Context → Included Elements → Excluded Elements → Interfaces & Dependencies → Boundary Conditions → Boundary Status → Governed Simulation Object Boundary SOBM establishes the structural perimeter within which subsequent object version, configuration, representation, assumptions, modeling, scenario, execution, and output governance can operate. Module Operational Space SOBM governs: Simulation Object boundary establishment, object inclusion, object exclusion, internal elements, external elements, system boundaries, subsystem boundaries, component boundaries, process boundaries, behavioral boundaries, organizational boundaries, spatial boundaries, temporal boundaries, functional boundaries, operational boundaries, environmental interfaces, external actors, external systems, dependencies, boundary-crossing interactions, boundary conditions, boundary assumptions, boundary ambiguity, boundary conflicts, boundary change, boundary expansion, boundary contraction, boundary inheritance, boundary traceability, and Simulation Object Boundary status. Module Function SOBM exists to prevent an identified Simulation Object from becoming structurally ambiguous once simulation design begins. Its function is to establish which elements are: Inside the Simulation Object Outside the Simulation Object and: Connected Across the Simulation Object Boundary This distinction matters because simulation conclusions may change materially depending upon what the simulation treats as part of the object itself versus part of its external environment. SOBM therefore prevents: hidden boundary expansion, hidden boundary contraction, omitted material components, uncontrolled inclusion of external systems, environmental conditions being mistaken for object properties, dependencies being absorbed into the object without disclosure, object behavior being confused with external interaction, and simulation findings being generalized beyond the established object boundary. Simulation Object Boundary A Simulation Object Boundary is the governed perimeter separating the Simulation Object from the external conditions, entities, systems, processes, actors, and environments with which it may interact. The boundary may be: physical, digital, logical, functional, organizational, behavioral, spatial, temporal, operational, or composite. A single Simulation Object may therefore require several mutually consistent boundary dimensions. Boundary Establishment Once the Simulation Object has been identified through SOIM, its relevant boundaries must be established before downstream simulation structures depend upon them. Boundary establishment should answer: What belongs to the object? What does not belong to the object? Which external elements materially interact with it? Through which interfaces do those interactions occur? Which boundary conditions materially affect simulation behavior? The required precision depends upon the intended simulation. Included Elements An Included Element is an element treated as part of the Simulation Object for the governed simulation. Included elements may consist of: components, subsystems, software, hardware, internal processes, internal actors, internal control mechanisms, internal data structures, internal resources, or other constituent elements. Inclusion must be sufficiently explicit where the element could materially affect simulation interpretation. Excluded Elements An Excluded Element is an element intentionally outside the Simulation Object Boundary. Exclusion does not mean irrelevance. An excluded element may still influence the object through an external interaction or dependency. SOBM therefore distinguishes: Outside the Object from: Irrelevant to the Simulation These are not equivalent. Boundary Interfaces A Boundary Interface is a governed point through which the Simulation Object interacts with something outside its boundary. Interfaces may include: data interfaces, physical connections, control interfaces, communication channels, human interactions, resource inputs, energy flows, sensor inputs, actuator outputs, organizational interactions, or environmental interactions. Boundary interfaces should remain identifiable where their behavior materially affects simulation. External Dependencies A Simulation Object may depend upon entities that remain outside its boundary. Examples may include: cloud infrastructure, navigation systems, external databases, communication networks, human operators, power systems, supply chains, regulatory inputs, external AI services, or supporting infrastructure. SOBM requires these dependencies to remain distinguishable from the Simulation Object itself. The existence of dependency does not automatically justify boundary inclusion. Object Boundary vs Simulation Environment SIMULOS® establishes a critical distinction: Simulation Object Boundary ≠ Simulation Environment Boundary The Simulation Object defines what is being simulated as the target. The Simulation Environment defines the conditions within which simulation activity occurs. For example: Autonomous Drone may be the Simulation Object. Urban Airspace + Weather + Navigation Infrastructure + Other Aircraft may form part of the simulated environment. Those concepts must not be collapsed merely because they interact during simulation. Object Boundary vs Reality Representation SOBM establishes the boundary of the target object. It does not determine whether that boundary has been represented accurately inside the simulation. That later question belongs to the appropriate SIMULOS® Reality Representation governance space. Therefore: Object Boundary = What belongs to the target while: Representation Boundary = What the simulation representation actually models A difference between the two may become a material simulation-governance issue. Functional Boundary A Simulation Object may require a functional boundary specifying which functions belong to the object being simulated. For example, an autonomous vehicle simulation may include: Perception Planning Decision Vehicle Control while an external navigation service remains outside the object. The boundary should preserve this distinction even where the systems operate as one practical service. Spatial Boundary Where location or physical extent matters, the object may require a spatial boundary. This may define: physical dimensions, geographic area, infrastructure extent, operational zone, or another spatial perimeter. Spatial boundaries should not be confused with the wider simulation environment. Temporal Boundary A Simulation Object may also require a temporal boundary. The object represented at: Time T1 may not be materially equivalent to the same nominal object at: Time T2 where its relevant characteristics have changed. Detailed version governance belongs to the appropriate SOS module, but SOBM preserves the temporal perimeter relevant to the object definition. Operational Boundary An operational boundary identifies which operational functions, modes, states, or interactions belong to the Simulation Object for the particular simulation. An object may have broader real-world capability than the operational portion included within a simulation. SOBM requires this difference to remain explicit. Composite Object Boundary Composite Simulation Objects require governance over the relationship between: Composite Boundary and: Constituent Boundaries For example: Autonomous Warehouse System may contain: Robots + Control System + Internal Network + Charging Infrastructure while: External Electrical Grid remains outside the object boundary. SOBM preserves both the composite perimeter and relevant internal constituent boundaries. Nested Boundaries Simulation Objects may contain nested boundaries. Conceptually: System Boundary ↓ Subsystem Boundary ↓ Component Boundary ↓ Functional Boundary SOBM allows these boundaries to coexist where needed. A lower-level simulation claim must not automatically be represented as applying to every higher-level boundary. Boundary-Crossing Interaction A Boundary-Crossing Interaction occurs whenever information, resources, commands, forces, signals, behaviors, or effects pass between the Simulation Object and an external element. Such interactions may materially influence simulation behavior even though the external element remains outside the Simulation Object. SOBM therefore requires material boundary-crossing interactions to remain visible. Boundary Conditions A Simulation Object Boundary Condition defines a governed condition applying at the interface between the object and its surroundings. Examples may include: incoming data characteristics, resource availability, communication latency, physical forces, environmental exposure, human commands, external control signals, or other interface conditions. Boundary conditions must not silently become assumed constants where variability is material. Boundary Assumptions Where a boundary cannot be fully established from known information, a boundary assumption may be necessary. SOBM requires such assumptions to remain explicit. Detailed governance of the assumption itself belongs to the SIMULOS® assumption-governance space. SOBM preserves the fact that the object boundary depends upon that assumption. Boundary Ambiguity Simulation Object Boundary Ambiguity exists where it is unclear whether a materially relevant element belongs inside or outside the Simulation Object. Ambiguity may arise from: incomplete architecture records, unclear ownership, dynamic system composition, external services, shared infrastructure, distributed control, unclear subsystem relationships, or evolving operational configurations. Material ambiguity should not be silently resolved. Boundary Conflict A Boundary Conflict exists where credible sources define materially different boundaries for the same Simulation Object. For example: one system architecture may include an external decision service within the system boundary, while another treats it as an external dependency. Where the difference can affect simulation design or interpretation, the conflict must remain visible until governed. No Silent Boundary Expansion Rule SIMULOS® establishes: A Simulation Object Boundary must not be expanded after simulation activity begins without explicit governance of the change. Adding new components, functions, populations, dependencies, or operational modes may materially change the Simulation Object. No Silent Boundary Contraction Rule Likewise: Material elements may not be removed from the Simulation Object Boundary without explicit governance of the exclusion. A simulation must not obtain more favorable results by quietly removing difficult or high-risk portions of the object. No Environment Absorption Rule An environmental element does not become part of the Simulation Object merely because it materially affects object behavior. This rule protects the distinction between: Object and: Environment throughout the simulation lifecycle. No Dependency Absorption Rule A dependency does not automatically become part of the Simulation Object merely because the object cannot operate without it. Dependency relationships must be visible. Boundary inclusion requires an explicit basis. No Boundary Inflation Rule A simulation result established within one object boundary must not automatically be represented as applying to a broader boundary. Therefore: Subsystem Simulation ≠ Whole-System Simulation Component Simulation ≠ Product Simulation Single Operational Mode ≠ Complete Operational Capability unless a governed basis supports the broader claim. Boundary Change A Simulation Object Boundary Change occurs when the governed perimeter of the object changes materially. Possible changes include: Expansion Contraction Recomposition Interface Change Dependency Change or: Boundary Reclassification A boundary change may require downstream simulation governance to be reassessed. Boundary Change Propagation A material boundary change may affect: object version, configuration, reality representation, assumptions, model structure, input requirements, scenarios, execution, outputs, reality correlation, or simulation reliance. SOBM therefore preserves boundary-change information for downstream governance rather than determining all downstream consequences itself. Boundary Continuity Where the Simulation Object remains in use across multiple simulations, its boundary should remain traceable between simulation cycles. This enables comparison between: Previous Simulation Object Boundary and: Current Simulation Object Boundary and prevents materially different simulation scopes from being treated as equivalent. Boundary Equivalence Two simulations may use different technical representations while still concern the same Simulation Object Boundary. Conversely, two simulations using the same model may concern materially different object boundaries. SOBM therefore does not infer boundary equivalence from model similarity alone. Simulation Object Boundary Status Possible boundary statuses may include: Established Conditionally Established Partially Established Boundary Conflicted Boundary Ambiguous or: Boundary Undetermined Boundary status describes the strength of the object-boundary basis. It does not establish simulation validity or operational reliance. Simulation Object Boundary Record SOBM should establish a persistent Simulation Object Boundary Record sufficient to reconstruct what was considered inside, outside, and connected to the Simulation Object when downstream simulation governance occurred. The record may preserve: Simulation Object Identifier, boundary definition, boundary dimensions, included elements, excluded elements, constituent boundaries, external dependencies, boundary interfaces, boundary-crossing interactions, boundary conditions, boundary assumptions, ambiguity, conflicts, boundary status, boundary changes, and boundary traceability. Failure Conditions SOBM governance failure may exist where: the Simulation Object has no sufficiently defined boundary, material included elements are unidentified, material exclusions remain hidden, object and environment are improperly collapsed, dependencies are silently absorbed, material interfaces remain unidentified, boundary-crossing interactions are omitted, boundary assumptions remain hidden, conflicting boundaries are ignored, the object boundary is silently expanded or contracted, subsystem results are represented as whole-system results without sufficient basis, or downstream simulation activity cannot be traced to the boundary under which it was performed. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Establish the Candidate Object Boundary Determine the physical, digital, logical, functional, spatial, temporal, operational, organizational, or composite perimeter required for the identified Simulation Object. 2. Classify Included, Excluded, and External Elements Establish which material elements belong inside the object, which are explicitly excluded, and which remain external but relevant. 3. Identify Interfaces, Dependencies, and Boundary Conditions Map material relationships crossing the Simulation Object Boundary and preserve conditions capable of affecting simulation behavior. 4. Resolve or Record Boundary Ambiguity Identify conflicts, assumptions, uncertain inclusions, exclusions, and boundary limitations and assign the appropriate Simulation Object Boundary Status. 5. Establish the Simulation Object Boundary Record Preserve the governed boundary, material elements, interfaces, dependencies, conditions, limitations, status, changes, and traceability required for downstream simulation governance. Governance Outputs SOBM may produce: Simulation Object Boundary Record, Object Boundary Definition, Boundary Dimension Record, Included Element Register, Excluded Element Register, External Element Register, Composite Object Boundary Record, Constituent Boundary Map, Boundary Interface Register, External Dependency Register, Boundary-Crossing Interaction Map, Boundary Condition Record, Boundary Assumption Reference, Boundary Ambiguity Record, Boundary Conflict Record, Simulation Object Boundary Status, Boundary Change Record, Boundary Expansion Record, Boundary Contraction Record, Boundary Continuity Record, Boundary Equivalence Assessment, and Simulation Object Boundary Traceability Map. Use Case 1 — Spacecraft Mission Simulation Scenario A space institution simulates a spacecraft operating during a lunar mission. The spacecraft depends upon: ground-control infrastructure, navigation data, communication networks, and mission-support systems. Application SOBM establishes the spacecraft and its defined onboard systems as the Simulation Object. Ground control, external communication infrastructure, lunar environment, and navigation services remain outside the Simulation Object Boundary while their material interfaces and dependencies remain explicitly represented. Result Simulation findings cannot silently treat the entire mission ecosystem as if it were part of the spacecraft itself. The distinction between: Spacecraft External Infrastructure and: Simulation Environment remains traceable throughout downstream SIMULOS® governance. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Industrial Facility Scenario An organization simulates an autonomous warehouse containing robots, control software, internal communications, charging systems, human workers, and external cloud services. Application SOBM establishes which elements form the governed Simulation Object. The autonomous warehouse control system and designated robotic fleet may fall inside the object boundary. Human workers and external cloud services may remain outside the boundary while their interactions with the system remain material simulation inputs and interfaces. Result The simulation cannot later be represented as covering the complete warehouse ecosystem if only the autonomous control system and robotic fleet were actually within the governed Simulation Object Boundary. Architectural Position Simulation Object Boundary Module (SOBM) is the second internal governance space of the Simulation Object Standard (SOS). The internal progression begins: Simulation Object Identification → Simulation Object Boundary SOIM establishes: Which object is being simulated? SOBM establishes: What belongs to that object, what remains outside it, and where does the object end? Subsequent SOS modules may then govern the object's version, configuration, and documentation against a sufficiently identified and bounded Simulation Object. SOBM does not replace governance of general governance boundaries under GOA™, operational boundaries under ORA™, validation scope under VALIDOS®, integrity under INTEGROS®, or autonomous-system constraints under ASGA™. It governs specifically: the boundary of the object that a simulation claims to represent. Foundational Principle A simulation claim cannot legitimately extend beyond the Simulation Object Boundary under which the simulation was governed and executed. Canonical Closing Statement Simulation Object Boundary Module (SOBM) establishes the structural perimeter of the Simulation Object by governing what belongs to the object, what remains outside it, and how material interfaces, dependencies, interactions, conditions, ambiguities, and boundary changes remain visible throughout the simulation lifecycle. Through explicit inclusion and exclusion, object-environment separation, interface and dependency mapping, anti-expansion and anti-contraction rules, boundary-status governance, change propagation, continuity, and traceability, SOBM prevents simulation results from acquiring broader object coverage than the boundary actually represented. By establishing a persistent Simulation Object Boundary before downstream version, configuration, representation, modeling, scenario, execution, and output governance proceeds, SOBM provides the second foundational object-governance mechanism of SIMULOS®.

title: OOF™ Simulation Object Configuration Module (SOCM)
text: OOF™ Simulation Object Configuration Module (SOCM) Simulation Object Configuration Module (SOCM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Simulation Object Standard (SOS) Operational Layer: Simulation Object Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Type: Parent Standard Module Governed Space: Simulation Object Configuration Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 15 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Governed Space Simulation Object Configuration Canonical Definition Simulation Object Configuration Module (SOCM) defines the governance conditions under which the specific configuration of a Simulation Object is identified, bounded, recorded, differentiated, changed, and maintained as a traceable simulation-governance state. SOCM ensures that simulation activity remains bound not merely to the correct Simulation Object and version, but to the specific arrangement of components, settings, parameters, options, dependencies, interfaces, capabilities, and operational features that materially define the object state represented by the simulation. Operational Role SOCM serves as the fourth internal governance space of the Simulation Object Standard (SOS). The preceding modules establish: SOIM — What exactly is the Simulation Object? SOBM — Where does the Simulation Object begin and end? SOVM — Which materially distinguishable version of that object is being simulated? SOCM asks: What exact configuration of that Simulation Object Version is represented by the simulation? The governed progression is: Identified Object → Bounded Object → Object Version → Configuration Basis → Configuration Identification → Material Configuration State → Configuration Change → Simulation Binding → Governed Simulation Object Configuration Module Operational Space SOCM governs: Simulation Object configuration identity, configuration basis, configuration parameters, configuration components, configuration settings, configuration options, configuration dependencies, configuration interfaces, enabled capabilities, disabled capabilities, operational modes, feature states, component combinations, configuration baselines, configuration variants, configuration relationships, configuration changes, configuration materiality, temporary configurations, experimental configurations, configuration ambiguity, configuration conflict, configuration equivalence, configuration divergence, configuration applicability, configuration status, configuration history, configuration-to-simulation binding, configuration-to-output binding, cross-configuration applicability, and configuration traceability. Module Function A Simulation Object Version may exist in multiple configurations. Those configurations may behave differently even though they belong to the same version. An autonomous vehicle may operate with different sensor packages. A robot may operate with different payloads. An AI system may have different tools enabled. A spacecraft may use different subsystem arrangements. An industrial system may operate under different control settings. A digital system may expose different capabilities depending upon deployment configuration. Therefore: Object Identity + Version Identity alone may be insufficient to establish what was actually simulated. SOCM prevents: undefined configurations, silent configuration substitution, materially different configurations being treated as equivalent, configuration-dependent results being represented as version-wide results, configuration changes being hidden, outputs being detached from the configuration that produced them, temporary settings being mistaken for baseline configuration, and simulation conclusions being transferred between configurations without a governed basis. Simulation Object Configuration A Simulation Object Configuration is the defined arrangement of simulation-relevant characteristics within a Simulation Object Version at a particular governed state. A configuration may include: installed components, activated components, disabled components, software settings, control parameters, operational modes, feature flags, interfaces, connected subsystems, dependency states, tool permissions, sensor arrangements, actuator arrangements, hardware options, safety mechanisms, or other simulation-relevant object characteristics. Configuration Basis The Configuration Basis establishes which object characteristics must be known to distinguish one simulation-relevant configuration from another. The Configuration Basis should focus on characteristics capable of materially affecting: object behavior, available capabilities, interactions, assumptions, scenario response, simulation execution, outputs, reality correlation, or interpretation of simulation results. Configuration Identity Where configuration differences can materially affect simulation outcomes, the represented configuration should possess sufficient identity to distinguish it from other configurations. Conceptually: Simulation Object → Version → Configuration For example: Robot R1 → Version 4.2 → Configuration C7 The configuration identifier may be internally assigned or derived from another controlled configuration system. SIMULOS® does not require a particular naming convention. Configuration Baseline A Simulation Object Configuration Baseline establishes the reference configuration represented by the simulation. The baseline may identify: Simulation Object, object version, configuration identifier, material components, material settings, enabled capabilities, disabled capabilities, operational mode, material dependencies, relevant interfaces, effective state, and known configuration limitations. Material Configuration Element A Material Configuration Element is any configurable characteristic capable of materially affecting the simulation or interpretation of its results. Materiality is simulation-relative. A setting irrelevant to one simulation may be critical to another. Therefore: Configuration Materiality must be evaluated relative to the Simulation Purpose and the behavior being represented. Configuration Completeness Configuration Completeness asks: Are all materially relevant configurable characteristics sufficiently identified to know which object state was actually represented? Configuration completeness does not require documentation of every technically possible parameter. It requires sufficient representation of the configuration characteristics material to the governed simulation. Configuration Variants One Simulation Object Version may contain multiple valid configurations. For example: Version 5.0 may exist as: Configuration A — Standard Configuration B — Extended Capability Configuration C — Restricted Safety Mode Configuration D — Experimental These remain configurations of the same version unless the underlying change satisfies the governed conditions for a new version. Parallel Configurations Multiple configurations may exist simultaneously. SOCM preserves their distinction where simulation results could differ materially between them. Parallel configurations must not be collapsed into one generic object state merely because they share the same version. Temporary Configuration A Simulation Object may temporarily enter a configuration used only for: testing, maintenance, emergency operation, degraded operation, experimentation, calibration, or another temporary purpose. Where that configuration is simulated, its temporary nature should remain explicit. Experimental Configuration An experimental configuration should remain distinguishable from the approved or operational baseline configuration. Simulation findings from an experimental configuration must not silently become findings about the operational configuration. Configuration Change A Configuration Change occurs when one or more configuration characteristics change while the underlying Simulation Object identity remains continuous. Conceptually: Version V1 / Configuration A → Configuration Change → Version V1 / Configuration B A configuration change may or may not create a new Simulation Object Version. Configuration Change Materiality A configuration change is material where it can materially affect: simulated behavior, available capabilities, scenario response, system interaction, expected outputs, reality representation, or interpretation of simulation results. Material configuration changes should remain explicitly traceable. Configuration Change vs Version Change SIMULOS® distinguishes: Configuration Change ≠ Version Change A configuration change modifies the arrangement or state of configurable characteristics. A version change establishes a materially distinguishable object generation or state requiring separate version identity. For example: Version 3.0 / Sensor Package A and: Version 3.0 / Sensor Package B may represent two configurations of the same version. A fundamental redesign of the sensing architecture may instead require: Version 4.0 SOVM governs version identity. SOCM governs configuration identity. Configuration Change Escalation A configuration change may become sufficiently significant that the existing version classification should be reconsidered. SOCM should therefore be capable of generating a: Version Reassessment Signal where configuration change appears to exceed the current version boundary. SOVM determines the resulting version consequence. Configuration-to-Simulation Binding Every governed simulation should be capable of answering: Which configuration of the Simulation Object Version was represented? The relationship becomes: Simulation Object → Version → Configuration → Simulation Activity This binding prevents simulation results from becoming detached from the actual configured state represented during simulation. Configuration-to-Output Binding Where outputs depend materially upon configuration, the relationship should remain reconstructable: Object Configuration → Simulation Execution → Simulation Output SOCM governs the configuration relationship. It does not govern the substantive Simulation Output. No Silent Configuration Substitution Rule SIMULOS® establishes: A materially different Simulation Object Configuration must not replace the configuration represented by a simulation without explicit governance of the change. If a simulation begins against Configuration A and execution materially shifts to Configuration B, the change must remain visible. No Configuration-Wide Assumption Rule SIMULOS® establishes: Results established for one configuration must not automatically be represented as applicable to every configuration of the same Simulation Object Version. Shared version identity does not establish configuration equivalence. Cross-Configuration Applicability A result established for Configuration A may remain applicable to Configuration B where the changed configuration characteristics do not materially affect the simulation question. Possible applicability states may include: Fully Applicable Conditionally Applicable Partially Applicable Not Applicable or: Applicability Undetermined The basis should remain explicit. Configuration Equivalence Two configurations may be treated as simulation-equivalent for a specific simulation purpose where their differences do not materially affect the characteristics being simulated. Therefore: Technical Configuration Difference ≠ Automatic Simulation Difference but equally: Shared Version ≠ Automatic Simulation Equivalence Configuration Divergence Configuration Divergence exists where configurations differ sufficiently that simulation findings cannot legitimately be transferred between them without additional governance. Divergence may result from differences in: components, capabilities, permissions, control settings, operational modes, dependencies, interfaces, safety mechanisms, or other material configuration elements. Configuration Ambiguity Configuration Ambiguity exists where the exact configuration represented by the simulation cannot be established with sufficient confidence. Material ambiguity should remain visible. It must not be silently converted into an assumed configuration. Configuration Conflict A Configuration Conflict exists where credible records indicate materially different configurations for the same Simulation Object during the same relevant simulation state. The conflict should be resolved or explicitly preserved before configuration-dependent conclusions are relied upon. Configuration Status A configuration may have a governed status such as: Baseline Operational Alternative Temporary Experimental Degraded Emergency Superseded Retired Ambiguous or: Undetermined Configuration Status describes the relationship of the configuration to the Simulation Object. It does not determine simulation validity. Configuration History SOCM should preserve material configuration history where configuration changes affect interpretation of simulation activity. Conceptually: Configuration A → Change → Configuration B → Change → Configuration C This allows later reconstruction of which configuration existed at each relevant simulation point. Configuration Freeze For some simulations, the represented configuration may need to remain fixed during execution. A Configuration Freeze identifies the configuration state that must remain stable for the governed simulation activity. Where a material change occurs during a freeze, the change should produce a governance signal rather than being silently incorporated. Dynamic Configuration Some Simulation Objects legitimately change configuration during operation. Examples include: adaptive robots, reconfigurable spacecraft, autonomous systems, modular industrial systems, dynamically provisioned computing systems, and AI systems with changing tool availability. In such cases, SOCM should not artificially freeze the object. Instead, it governs the allowed configuration state space and the transitions occurring within it. Configuration State Transition For dynamically configurable objects, a simulation may intentionally represent: Configuration A → Configuration B → Configuration C The transition itself may be part of the simulated behavior. SOCM preserves which configuration states existed and when transitions occurred. Allowed Configuration State Space Where dynamic configuration is expected, an Allowed Configuration State Space may define which configurations or configuration transitions belong to the intended simulation representation. A transition outside that space may generate a configuration deviation signal. Configuration Deviation A Configuration Deviation exists where the represented or executed configuration differs materially from the approved Simulation Object Configuration Basis. Possible outcomes include: Accepted Deviation Conditional Deviation Material Deviation Configuration Conflict or: Deviation Undetermined SOCM records the deviation. Downstream simulation governance determines its consequences. Configuration Dependency Some configuration characteristics depend upon external or internal components. SOCM records the configuration relationship where necessary to know the actual object state. It does not assume governance ownership over the external dependency itself. Configuration vs Environment SOCM governs characteristics belonging to the Simulation Object. It does not govern the simulated environment surrounding the object. For example: Robot Sensor Package belongs to: Simulation Object Configuration while: Warehouse Lighting Conditions belong to the relevant simulation environment governance space. The distinction preserves the object/environment boundary established by SOBM. Configuration vs Simulation Inputs Configuration characteristics define the state of the object. Simulation inputs are values, data, stimuli, or conditions supplied to simulation execution. Therefore: Object Configuration ≠ Simulation Input A parameter may appear technically similar in both contexts, but its governance role determines its architectural location. Configuration vs Scenario A configuration describes: what state the Simulation Object is in. A scenario describes: what governed situation the simulation subjects that object to. SOCM does not govern scenario design. Configuration vs Reality Representation SOCM identifies the actual object configuration claimed to be represented. It does not determine whether the simulation model accurately represents that configuration. That question belongs to the later Reality Representation governance space of SIMULOS®. Configuration vs Integrity SOCM does not govern the general integrity of configuration records, components, or configuration processes. That belongs to INTEGROS® where applicable. SOCM governs specifically: which configuration is relevant to the Simulation Object and how that configuration remains identifiable and traceable throughout simulation governance. Configuration vs Validation SOCM does not determine whether a configuration has been validated for operational reliance. That belongs to VALIDOS® where formal validation is required. SOCM supplies the configuration identity and change information that validation may consume. Configuration Change Propagation A material configuration change may affect downstream SIMULOS® governance, including: reality representation, assumptions, model and environment, inputs and data, scenario design, execution, outputs, reality correlation, simulation evidence, and operational reliance. SOCM identifies the change and preserves its traceability. It does not replace those downstream governance spaces. Simulation Object Configuration Record SOCM should establish a persistent Simulation Object Configuration Record sufficient to reconstruct the configuration represented by the simulation. The record may preserve: Simulation Object Identifier, Simulation Object Version Identifier, Simulation Object Configuration Identifier, Configuration Basis, Configuration Baseline, material components, material settings, material parameters, enabled capabilities, disabled capabilities, operational modes, dependencies, interfaces, configuration status, configuration variants, temporary states, experimental states, configuration changes, configuration deviations, configuration ambiguity, configuration conflicts, configuration equivalence, cross-configuration applicability, configuration history, simulation bindings, output references, and configuration traceability. Failure Conditions SOCM governance failure may exist where: the Simulation Object Configuration cannot be identified, material configuration elements remain unknown, simulation activity cannot be bound to the configuration represented, materially different configurations are treated as equivalent without basis, configuration changes occur silently, configuration-dependent findings are represented as version-wide findings, temporary or experimental configurations are confused with operational configurations, configuration ambiguity is hidden, conflicting configuration records remain undisclosed, configuration transitions cannot be reconstructed, configuration changes are confused with version changes, object configuration is confused with environmental conditions, or downstream simulation conclusions cannot be traced to the configuration from which they originated. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Establish the Configuration Basis Identify which configurable characteristics are material to the governed simulation. 2. Establish the Configuration Baseline Record the material components, settings, capabilities, modes, interfaces, dependencies, and other configuration characteristics represented. 3. Bind Configuration to Object Version Establish: Simulation Object → Version → Configuration and preserve sufficient identity to distinguish materially different configurations. 4. Govern Configuration Change Detect material configuration changes, preserve transitions and deviations, and trigger version reassessment where configuration change may exceed the current version boundary. 5. Preserve Simulation Traceability Bind the relevant configuration to simulation activity and preserve sufficient history to determine which configuration produced or influenced downstream simulation outputs. Governance Outputs SOCM may produce: Simulation Object Configuration Identifier, Simulation Object Configuration Record, Configuration Basis Record, Configuration Baseline, Material Configuration Element Record, Configuration Completeness Assessment, Configuration Variant Record, Parallel Configuration Record, Temporary Configuration Record, Experimental Configuration Record, Configuration Change Record, Configuration Materiality Assessment, Configuration Transition Record, Configuration Freeze Record, Allowed Configuration State Space, Configuration Deviation Record, Configuration Equivalence Assessment, Cross-Configuration Applicability Assessment, Configuration Divergence Record, Configuration Ambiguity Record, Configuration Conflict Record, Configuration Status, Configuration History Record, Version Reassessment Signal, Configuration-to-Simulation Binding, Configuration-to-Output Reference, and Simulation Object Configuration Traceability Map. Use Case 1 — Autonomous Robot Tool Configuration Scenario An autonomous industrial robot operates under the same software and hardware version but may use different tools: Configuration A — Welding Tool Configuration B — Cutting Tool The control system version remains unchanged. Application SOCM preserves the two configurations as distinct object states. A simulation executed against the welding configuration remains bound to: Robot R1 → Version 5.2 → Welding Configuration Simulation findings dependent upon tool geometry, payload, motion, or operational capability are not automatically transferred to the cutting configuration. Result Shared version identity does not erase material configuration differences. Use Case 2 — Spacecraft Operational Configuration Scenario A spacecraft operates in multiple governed configurations: Launch Configuration Orbital Configuration Docking Configuration The spacecraft remains the same object and version. Application SOCM identifies each configuration and the permitted transitions between them. A simulation evaluating docking behavior remains bound to the Docking Configuration rather than being represented generically as a simulation of the spacecraft in every operational state. Result Simulation conclusions remain attached to the configuration actually represented. Architectural Position Simulation Object Configuration Module (SOCM) is the fourth internal governance space of the Simulation Object Standard (SOS). The internal progression is: Simulation Object Identification → Simulation Object Boundary → Simulation Object Versioning → Simulation Object Configuration SOIM establishes: What is being simulated? SOBM establishes: Where does the object begin and end? SOVM establishes: Which version of the object is being simulated? SOCM establishes: What exact configuration of that version is being simulated? The next internal governance space, SODM — Simulation Object Documentation Module, governs the persistent documentation necessary to preserve the complete governed Simulation Object definition. Foundational Principle A simulation of the correct object and correct version may still represent the wrong operational reality if the configuration actually simulated is not the configuration to which its conclusions are applied. Canonical Closing Statement Simulation Object Configuration Module (SOCM) establishes the configuration-governance layer of the Simulation Object by ensuring that the specific arrangement of components, settings, parameters, capabilities, interfaces, dependencies, and operational modes represented by simulation remains explicitly identifiable and traceable. Through configuration baselines, materiality assessment, configuration variants, controlled change, dynamic configuration transitions, equivalence, divergence, deviation governance, cross-configuration applicability, and explicit simulation binding, SOCM prevents shared object or version identity from concealing materially different configured states. By preserving the relationship between Simulation Object identity, version, configuration, simulation activity, and downstream outputs, SOCM provides the fourth foundational object-governance mechanism of SIMULOS®.

title: OOF™ Simulation Object Documentation Module (SODM)
text: OOF™ Simulation Object Documentation Module (SODM) Simulation Object Documentation Module (SODM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Simulation Object Standard (SOS) Operational Layer: Simulation Object Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Type: Parent Standard Module Governed Space: Simulation Object Documentation Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 15 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Governed Space Simulation Object Documentation Canonical Definition Simulation Object Documentation Module (SODM) defines the governance conditions under which the identity, boundary, version, configuration, material characteristics, changes, limitations, and simulation-relevant state of a Simulation Object are consolidated into a persistent, traceable, reconstructable, and operationally usable governed record. SODM ensures that the Simulation Object established through the preceding SOS modules does not remain distributed across disconnected definitions, assumptions, records, systems, or undocumented knowledge. It creates the persistent documentary representation through which the exact object intended for simulation can be reconstructed and referenced throughout the SIMULOS® lifecycle. Operational Role SODM serves as the fifth and final internal governance space of the Simulation Object Standard (SOS). The preceding modules establish: SOIM — What exactly is the Simulation Object? SOBM — Where does the Simulation Object begin and end? SOVM — Which materially distinguishable version of the Simulation Object is being simulated? SOCM — What exact configuration of that version is being simulated? SODM asks: How must the complete governed definition of that Simulation Object be documented and preserved so that every downstream simulation activity refers to the same reconstructable object basis? The governed progression is: Object Identity → Object Boundary → Object Version → Object Configuration → Documentation Basis → Object Record Formation → Documentation Qualification → Simulation Object Reference → Documentation Change → Persistent Simulation Object Record Module Operational Space SODM governs: Simulation Object documentation basis, object record formation, object definition consolidation, object identity documentation, object boundary documentation, version documentation, configuration documentation, material characteristic documentation, inclusion documentation, exclusion documentation, object-state documentation, object limitation documentation, object dependency references, object relationship references, object documentation completeness, object documentation consistency, object documentation currency, object documentation ambiguity, object documentation conflict, object documentation gaps, object documentation change, object documentation supersession, object record status, simulation-object reference, downstream object referencing, point-in-time reconstruction, historical object documentation, documentation continuity, and Simulation Object record traceability. Module Function A Simulation Object may be correctly identified, bounded, versioned, and configured while still remaining operationally unusable for governed simulation if those characteristics cannot be reconstructed from a coherent record. Material information may otherwise exist across: engineering documents, software repositories, configuration systems, model inventories, technical specifications, databases, operational records, human knowledge, external documentation, or temporary simulation records. SODM prevents: undocumented Simulation Objects, fragmented object definitions, downstream use of inconsistent object descriptions, loss of object boundaries, undocumented version or configuration state, obsolete object records being treated as current, silent modification of the documented object, historical object states being overwritten, object limitations disappearing from downstream simulation activity, and simulation findings becoming detached from the object definition on which they were based. Simulation Object Documentation Basis The Simulation Object Documentation Basis is the governed set of information required to establish a sufficiently complete documentary representation of the Simulation Object. It may draw from: SOS governance records, technical documentation, controlled object records, configuration records, authoritative specifications, system descriptions, engineering records, object inventories, operational records, or other identifiable sources. SODM does not require all information to exist in one technical system. It requires the governed Simulation Object definition to remain reconstructable. Simulation Object Record A Simulation Object Record is the persistent governed representation of the Simulation Object used throughout the SIMULOS® lifecycle. At minimum, where applicable, it should establish: Simulation Object Identifier, object name or designation, object type, object description, object boundary, material inclusions, material exclusions, object version, object configuration, material characteristics, relevant operational state, known limitations, material dependencies, relevant relationships, documentation status, effective point, historical references, and sufficient traceability to the underlying SOS governance basis. Documentation Consolidation SODM does not require duplication of every underlying document. Instead, it establishes a governed documentary layer capable of connecting distributed object information into one coherent Simulation Object definition. Conceptually: Identity Record + Boundary Record + Version Record + Configuration Record + Material Object Information ↓ Simulation Object Record The record may therefore operate as a controlled reference layer rather than a duplicate technical repository. Authoritative Object Reference A governed simulation should have an identifiable Authoritative Simulation Object Reference. This reference establishes which Simulation Object Record governs the simulation. Where multiple object descriptions exist, the authoritative reference prevents downstream simulation activities from selecting incompatible object definitions without visibility. Documentation Completeness Documentation Completeness asks: Is sufficient information available to reconstruct the Simulation Object relevant to the intended simulation? Completeness is relative to the Simulation Object and the material information required to distinguish it. It does not require documentation of every technically knowable characteristic. Material Documentation Requirement A characteristic should be documented where its omission could materially affect: object identification, object distinction, object boundary, version identification, configuration identification, downstream simulation design, interpretation of simulation results, or later reconstruction of what was simulated. Documentation Consistency Documentation Consistency asks whether material Simulation Object records describe a mutually compatible object state.
