For example: Version Record: V4.2 and: Configuration Record: only valid for V5.0 would create a documentation inconsistency requiring resolution. Documentation Currency A Simulation Object Record should indicate the object state and effective period it represents. A record may remain historically valid while no longer being current. Therefore: Historically Accurate ≠ Currently Applicable Current Documentation State Where the Simulation Object changes, SODM should make it possible to distinguish: Current Object Record from: Historical Object Record and: Superseded Object Record This prevents documentation history from being mistaken for present object reality. Documentation Ambiguity Documentation Ambiguity exists where the available records permit multiple materially different interpretations of the Simulation Object. Examples include uncertainty regarding: object identity, boundary, version, configuration, included components, excluded components, or relevant operational state. Material ambiguity should remain explicit until resolved. Documentation Conflict A Documentation Conflict exists where credible object records materially contradict one another. For example: Record A → Configuration C4 Record B → Configuration C7 for the same relevant object state. SODM requires the conflict to remain visible. It must not be silently resolved through undocumented preference. Documentation Gap A Documentation Gap exists where information necessary to reconstruct a material characteristic of the Simulation Object is absent. Possible statuses may include: Non-Material Gap Conditionally Acceptable Gap Material Gap or: Gap Materiality Undetermined The gap itself does not determine simulation validity. It becomes an explicit input to downstream simulation governance. Documentation Qualification Before the Simulation Object Record becomes the governing object reference, its documentation basis should be sufficiently qualified for: completeness, consistency, currency, applicability, ambiguity, conflict, and material gaps. SODM does not perform general evidence validation. It determines whether the Simulation Object has a sufficiently usable governed documentary representation. No Undocumented Object Substitution Rule SIMULOS® establishes: A Simulation Object materially different from the documented governing object must not be substituted without explicit change to the Simulation Object Record. The simulation cannot silently move from: Object A to: Object A′ while preserving the original object reference. No Documentation Override Rule An informal description, label, filename, or operational shorthand must not silently override a materially different governed Simulation Object Record. Where disagreement exists, the difference should be resolved or preserved as a conflict. Documentation Change A Documentation Change occurs when information within the Simulation Object Record is modified. A documentation change may represent: correction, clarification, additional information, object change, version change, configuration change, boundary change, status change, or removal of obsolete information. The reason for material changes should remain traceable. Documentation Change ≠ Object Change SIMULOS® distinguishes: Documentation Change from: Simulation Object Change Correcting an incorrectly recorded serial number may change documentation without changing the object. Changing the physical subsystem represented may change the object itself. SODM records the documentary consequence. The appropriate preceding SOS module determines the underlying object-governance consequence. Material Documentation Change A documentation change is material where it changes how the Simulation Object would be: identified, bounded, versioned, configured, interpreted, distinguished, or represented in downstream simulation activity. Material documentation changes should generate downstream reassessment where necessary. Documentation Supersession Where a new Simulation Object Record replaces a previous record, the previous record should not disappear. The relationship should remain reconstructable: Previous Record → Supersession Event → Successor Record Historical Preservation Historical Simulation Object Records should remain available where required to reconstruct previous simulations. This enables questions such as: What object definition governed Simulation Run SR-104? Which version and configuration were documented at that time? Which boundaries were applicable? Which limitations were known? Point-in-Time Reconstruction SODM should support reconstruction of the Simulation Object as it was documented at a specific relevant point. This is particularly important where: the object evolves, configuration changes, multiple simulations occur over time, simulation outputs are later reused, incidents occur, or historical simulation conclusions are reviewed. Object Documentation Continuity Documentation Continuity preserves the relationship: Object Identity ↓ Boundary ↓ Version ↓ Configuration ↓ Simulation Object Record ↓ Simulation Activity ↓ Subsequent Object Change ↓ Successor Object Record This ensures that object evolution does not erase the basis of earlier simulation activity. Simulation Object Reference Once sufficiently established, the Simulation Object Record becomes the controlled reference consumed by subsequent SIMULOS® Parent Standards. Downstream simulation governance should reference the governed object rather than independently redefining it. Downstream Reference Principle SIMULOS® establishes: A downstream simulation activity should not silently redefine the Simulation Object established by SOS. Where a downstream requirement demonstrates that the object definition is insufficient or incorrect, the issue should return to the appropriate SOS governance space. Documentation and Purpose & Scope SODM establishes the object documentation basis. It does not determine: why the simulation is being performed, what the simulation must evaluate, what reliance is intended, or how broad the simulation inquiry should be. Those questions belong to the subsequent Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard. Documentation and Reality Representation SODM documents the real or conceptual object claimed to be represented. It does not determine whether a simulation model accurately represents that object. That belongs to the later Reality Representation governance space. Documentation and Simulation Model A Simulation Object Record is not the Simulation Model. The distinction is: Simulation Object Record → What is intended to be represented Simulation Model → How that object is represented for simulation Confusing these two layers can cause a model description to replace the actual object definition. Documentation and Environment SODM governs documentation of the Simulation Object. It does not govern the complete simulated environment surrounding that object. Environmental characteristics belong to the relevant SIMULOS® environment governance space. Documentation and Evidence A Simulation Object Record may later become part of a validation or audit evidence basis. SODM does not determine its general evidential fitness. Where formal validation is required, VALIDOS® governs validation evidence fitness. Where audit evidence is required, ADIT® governs the relevant audit-evidence lifecycle. Documentation and Integrity SODM does not replace INTEGROS®. INTEGROS® may govern the integrity of: records, data, documentation structures, storage, change history, or other integrity-relevant elements. SODM governs specifically whether the Simulation Object possesses a sufficiently persistent and reconstructable documentary representation for simulation governance. Documentation and Identity SODM does not replace broader identity governance. Where identity, origin, ownership, provenance, or transfer require independent governance, complementary OOF® identity architectures may apply. SODM consumes the identity necessary to maintain the Simulation Object as a stable simulation reference. Documentation and Auditability SODM creates traceability necessary for later reconstruction. It does not govern the complete audit lifecycle. ADIT® may consume SODM records where continuous or retrospective audit is required. Documentation Change Propagation A material change to the Simulation Object Record may affect downstream governance. Potentially affected spaces may include: Simulation Purpose & Scope, Reality Representation, Assumptions, Model & Environment, Inputs & Data, Scenario Design, Simulation Execution, Simulation Output, Reality Correlation, Simulation Evidence, Operational Reliance, and Resimulation. SODM identifies the documentary change. The affected downstream governance spaces determine its consequence. Documentation Reassessment Signal Where a material documentation change may invalidate the current object basis, SODM should generate a Simulation Object Reassessment Signal. Possible causes include: corrected object identity, changed boundary, new version information, configuration discovery, previously unknown material component, corrected exclusion, newly identified limitation, or resolved documentation conflict. Documentation Status A Simulation Object Record may carry a status such as: Draft Qualified Current Conditionally Current Superseded Historical Conflicted Incomplete or: Undetermined Status indicates documentary condition. It does not establish simulation validity. Persistent Simulation Object Record The complete SOS lifecycle should result in a persistent record capable of preserving: object identity, object boundary, object version, object configuration, material characteristics, relevant limitations, dependencies, documentation basis, documentation qualification, conflicts, gaps, changes, status, effective period, supersession, historical continuity, and downstream references. SOS Completion Gate SODM establishes the final internal completion gate of SOS. The key question is: Is the Simulation Object sufficiently identified, bounded, versioned, configured, documented, and reconstructable to enter governed Simulation Purpose & Scope? Possible outcomes may include: SOS Complete SOS Conditionally Complete SOS Incomplete or: SOS Completion Undetermined A conditional or incomplete status should remain visible downstream. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Establish the Documentation Basis Identify the records necessary to reconstruct the Simulation Object. 2. Consolidate the Governed Object Definition Connect identity, boundary, version, configuration, material characteristics, limitations, and relevant references into the Simulation Object Record. 3. Qualify the Documentation Assess completeness, consistency, currency, applicability, ambiguity, conflict, and material gaps. 4. Establish the Authoritative Object Reference Identify the Simulation Object Record that governs downstream simulation activity. 5. Preserve Change and Historical Continuity Record material documentation changes, supersession, prior object states, and point-in-time applicability. 6. Bind the Record to Downstream Simulation Governance Ensure subsequent SIMULOS® spaces reference the established Simulation Object rather than silently redefining it. 7. Generate Reassessment Signals Where new information materially changes the object basis, return the issue to the relevant SOS governance space and propagate the resulting change downstream. 8. Determine SOS Completion Establish whether the Simulation Object is sufficiently governed to proceed into Simulation Purpose & Scope. Governance Outputs SODM may produce: Simulation Object Documentation Basis, Simulation Object Record, Authoritative Simulation Object Reference, Object Definition Consolidation Record, Object Documentation Completeness Assessment, Object Documentation Consistency Assessment, Object Documentation Currency Assessment, Object Documentation Applicability Record, Object Documentation Ambiguity Record, Object Documentation Conflict Record, Object Documentation Gap Record, Material Documentation Change Record, Object Documentation Supersession Record, Historical Simulation Object Record, Point-in-Time Object Reconstruction Record, Object Documentation Status, Simulation Object Reassessment Signal, Downstream Object Reference, Simulation Object Documentation Traceability Map, SOS Completion Record, and Persistent Simulation Object Record. Use Case 1 — Autonomous Vehicle Simulation Scenario An autonomous vehicle platform is represented across: engineering specifications, sensor configuration records, software version records, and operational configuration databases. No single record identifies the complete object state used by the simulation. Application SODM consolidates the relevant governed references into: Vehicle AV-17 → Version 6.3 → Configuration C12 The Simulation Object Record identifies the applicable sensor package, control software, material boundaries, exclusions, and known object limitations. Result The simulation no longer depends upon an informal assumption about which vehicle configuration is being represented. Every downstream SIMULOS® space can reference the same governed Simulation Object. Use Case 2 — Spacecraft Simulation History Scenario A spacecraft undergoes configuration changes during its operational lifecycle. A simulation performed two years earlier becomes relevant after an operational anomaly. Application SODM reconstructs the historical Simulation Object Record applicable to the earlier simulation. The record establishes: Object Identity → Historical Version → Historical Configuration → Applicable Boundary → Known Limitations → Simulation Reference Result Investigators can determine exactly which spacecraft state the historical simulation represented rather than applying current spacecraft documentation retrospectively. Architectural Position Simulation Object Documentation Module (SODM) is the fifth and final internal governance space of the Simulation Object Standard (SOS). The complete SOS progression is: Simulation Object Identification → Simulation Object Boundary → Simulation Object Versioning → Simulation Object Configuration → Simulation Object Documentation Together, these five modules establish the governed Simulation Object before simulation purpose, representation, assumptions, models, data, scenarios, execution, outputs, correlation, evidence, reliance, or lifecycle governance begins. SOS therefore answers one foundational architectural question: What exactly is being simulated? Once SODM establishes a sufficiently persistent and reconstructable Simulation Object Record, the object may proceed to the next SIMULOS® Parent Standard: Simulation Purpose & Scope Standard. Foundational Principle A Simulation Object is not sufficiently governed merely because its identity is known; the complete object basis must remain reconstructable so that every simulation activity can demonstrate exactly what object it represented. Canonical Closing Statement Simulation Object Documentation Module (SODM) completes the Simulation Object Standard by consolidating object identity, boundary, version, configuration, material characteristics, limitations, changes, and historical continuity into a persistent and reconstructable Simulation Object Record. Through documentation qualification, authoritative referencing, ambiguity and conflict preservation, change governance, supersession, point-in-time reconstruction, downstream binding, and SOS completion control, SODM prevents simulation activity from becoming detached from the exact object it claims to represent. By establishing a stable documentary bridge between Simulation Object governance and every subsequent SIMULOS® lifecycle space, SODM completes the foundational answer to the first question of Simulation Governance Architecture: exactly what is being simulated.

title: OOF™ Simulation Object Identification Module (SOIM)
text: OOF™ Simulation Object Identification Module (SOIM) Simulation Object Identification Module (SOIM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Simulation Object Standard (SOS) Operational Layer: Simulation Object Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Type: Parent Standard Module Governed Space: Simulation Object Identification Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 15 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Governed Space Simulation Object Identification Canonical Definition Simulation Object Identification Module (SOIM) defines the governance conditions under which the exact object, system, process, environment, behavior, event, interaction, mission, population, infrastructure, organization, or other target intended to be represented through simulation is formally identified, distinguished from materially different targets, connected to sufficient identity attributes, and established as a traceable Simulation Object before downstream simulation governance proceeds. SOIM ensures that simulation does not begin from an assumed, ambiguous, substituted, overly broad, or insufficiently identifiable target. Operational Role SOIM establishes the first internal governance condition of the Simulation Object Standard (SOS). Its primary question is: What exactly is the object that this simulation claims to represent? SOIM transforms an intended simulation target into an identifiable Simulation Object capable of being governed by subsequent SOS mechanisms. The governed progression is: Candidate Simulation Target → Object Identification → Object Distinction → Identity Attribute Establishment → Object Reference → Identification Status → Governed Simulation Object Identity SOIM does not determine the Simulation Object boundary, version, configuration, or complete documentation lifecycle. It establishes the identity anchor upon which those subsequent object-governance functions depend. Module Operational Space SOIM governs: candidate Simulation Object identification, Simulation Object naming, object identifiers, object type, object class, object-instance distinction, object-family distinction, physical and digital identity references, actual and hypothetical object identification, proxy-object identification, composite-object identification, constituent-object identification, object hierarchy, material identity attributes, object-reference sources, object ambiguity, duplicate identification, conflicting identity claims, object substitution detection, identity continuity, and Simulation Object identification traceability. Module Function SOIM exists to prevent simulation from being performed against an object whose identity is: undefined, assumed, overly generic, inconsistent, duplicated, confused with a related object, silently substituted, represented through an undisclosed proxy, or materially broader than the object actually being simulated. Its function is not merely to assign a name. It establishes a sufficiently precise identity relationship between: the simulation activity and: the object that activity claims to represent. Simulation Object Identification Every governed simulation requires an identifiable target. A Simulation Object may be: a physical asset, digital system, AI system, autonomous system, process, behavior, organization, mission, infrastructure, environment, population, event, hypothetical system, future system, or composite system. The object need not physically exist. It must, however, be sufficiently identifiable to preserve the meaning of subsequent simulation activity. Identification Sufficiency Simulation Object identification is sufficient when the available identity attributes distinguish the intended target from materially different targets that could alter: simulation representation, assumptions, model selection, input requirements, scenario design, execution, output interpretation, reality correlation, or downstream simulation relevance. Identification sufficiency therefore depends upon the simulation context. A broad conceptual study may tolerate broader object identity. A high-consequence operational simulation may require significantly greater identity precision. Object Class and Object Instance SOIM distinguishes: Object Class from: Object Instance For example: Autonomous Vehicle may describe an object class. Vehicle Platform X may describe a narrower class. Vehicle X · Hardware Revision 4 · Sensor Package C may identify the materially relevant target. SOIM requires the identification level necessary for the simulation claim being made. Material Identity Attributes A Material Identity Attribute is an attribute whose difference could materially alter the meaning or applicability of the simulation. Such attributes may include: product identity, system designation, component structure, architecture, hardware generation, software generation, mission identity, operating role, physical asset identity, population definition, geographic identity, temporal identity, or other distinguishing information. SOIM does not require every possible attribute. It requires the attributes necessary to prevent materially different targets from being treated as the same Simulation Object. Object Distinction Two Simulation Objects must remain distinguishable where their differences could materially affect simulation. Similarity alone does not establish equivalence. Objects are not necessarily identical merely because they share: a manufacturer, product family, system architecture, name, general purpose, physical appearance, or functional role. The governing question is: Would treating these objects as identical materially affect the simulation? If yes, the distinction must remain visible. Object Identity vs Simulation Representation SOIM establishes a critical distinction: Simulation Object Identity ≠ Simulation Representation Identity The object being simulated and the artifact representing that object in simulation may each have their own identity. For example: Spacecraft Design Revision D may be the Simulation Object. Digital Simulation Model v8.4 may be the representation used later. These identities must not be collapsed. Object Identity vs Simulation Instance SOIM also distinguishes: Simulation Object from: Simulation Instance A single Simulation Object may be used across thousands of executions. Each execution does not become a new Simulation Object merely because the simulation is run again. This distinction preserves continuity across repeated simulation activity. Actual, Proposed, and Hypothetical Objects A Simulation Object may be: Existing Proposed Hypothetical Future-State or: Counterfactual Where the object does not yet exist, identity may be established through: approved design records, architecture definitions, controlled specifications, planning documents, configuration definitions, or another governed reference. The absence of a physical object does not eliminate the need for object identification. Proxy Simulation Objects A proxy may be used where the target object cannot be directly represented. SOIM allows proxy use but requires explicit distinction between: Target Simulation Object and: Proxy Simulation Object Examples may include: prototype systems, predecessor systems, scaled models, representative populations, synthetic systems, surrogate components, or reference architectures. SOIM establishes: Proxy Object ≠ Target Object The proxy relationship must remain visible. Object Substitution Object Substitution occurs when one object is simulated while the resulting simulation is presented as representing another object without a governed basis for that transfer. SOIM prohibits silent substitution. Where substitution occurs, the record should identify: Object Intended Object Actually Used and: Nature of the Relationship Subsequent SIMULOS® governance may determine what that relationship means for simulation relevance. Composite Simulation Object Identification Several interacting objects may collectively form a single Simulation Object. For a composite target, SOIM preserves: Composite Object Identity and: Constituent Object Identities where component-level differences may affect the simulation. This allows system-of-systems simulations to remain understandable without reducing the target to one undifferentiated label. Object Hierarchy Simulation Object identification may operate across multiple levels: System ↓ Subsystem ↓ Component ↓ Subcomponent or another appropriate hierarchy. SOIM should preserve which level is actually being simulated. A simulation concerning one component must not automatically acquire the identity of the complete system. Multi-Object Simulation A single simulation may include several independently relevant Simulation Objects. For example: Vehicle A Vehicle B Traffic Control System Pedestrian Group may all participate in the same simulation. Where their identities materially affect the simulation, SOIM should preserve each separately rather than collapsing them into one generic target. Identity Ambiguity Simulation Object Identity Ambiguity exists when the available information does not sufficiently determine which object the simulation concerns. This may arise from: inconsistent naming, missing identifiers, incomplete records, conflicting technical documentation, multiple candidate objects, undocumented substitutions, or insufficient distinction among configurations or systems. Ambiguity must remain visible until sufficiently resolved. Identification Conflict An Identification Conflict exists where credible identity records point to materially different Simulation Objects. For example: one source may identify the simulated system as: Revision A while another identifies: Revision B. The conflict must not be silently resolved in favor of whichever identity produces the preferred simulation result. No Assumed Identity Rule SIMULOS® establishes: Missing identity information must not be silently converted into known identity. Where an assumption is necessary, the assumption must be explicit and transferred into the appropriate assumption-governance space. No Silent Object Substitution Rule A simulation performed against Object A must not be represented as simulation of Object B unless the relationship between A and B is explicitly identified and governed. No Object Inflation Rule The claimed Simulation Object must not be broader than the object identity actually established. Therefore: Component ≠ Entire System One Variant ≠ Product Family One Population ≠ All Populations One Mission Configuration ≠ All Mission Configurations unless a governed basis supports broader applicability. No Automatic Identity Inheritance Rule A new or related object does not automatically inherit the Simulation Object identity of another object merely because it: derives from the same design, shares the same architecture, belongs to the same product family, performs the same function, or replaces an earlier system. Material identity continuity must be established rather than presumed. Object Identity Continuity Once established, Simulation Object identity should remain traceable through downstream simulation governance. The relationship: Simulation Object → Representation → Assumptions → Model → Inputs → Scenarios → Execution → Outputs should not lose the original object reference. SOIM therefore provides an identity anchor consumed throughout the broader SIMULOS® lifecycle. Object Identity Change Where the underlying target materially changes, SOIM must allow determination of whether the simulation still concerns: the same identifiable object or: a materially different Simulation Object. Detailed version and configuration governance occurs elsewhere within SOS. SOIM governs whether fundamental identity continuity still exists. Simulation Object Identification Status Possible identification statuses may include: Identified Conditionally Identified Partially Identified Identification Conflicted Identification Ambiguous or: Identification Undetermined These statuses describe object-identification strength. They do not determine simulation quality, simulation validity, or operational reliance. Simulation Object Identification Record SOIM should establish a persistent Simulation Object Identification Record sufficient to reconstruct the identity basis used when downstream simulation governance began. The record may preserve: Simulation Object Identifier, object name, object type, object class, object-instance reference, material identity attributes, actual/proposed/hypothetical status, proxy status, composite-object status, constituent-object references, identity source references, unresolved ambiguity, identification conflict, identification status, and identity traceability. Failure Conditions SOIM governance failure may exist where: no Simulation Object can be sufficiently identified, object identity remains materially ambiguous, materially different objects are treated as identical, an object class is represented as a specific object without sufficient basis, a proxy remains undisclosed, object substitution is concealed, multiple objects are incorrectly collapsed, composite-object components lose necessary identity, the claimed object becomes broader than the identified object, identity conflicts are ignored, or downstream simulation artifacts cannot be traced back to the object they claim to represent. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Identify the Candidate Simulation Target Establish the entity, system, process, behavior, environment, event, population, mission, or other target proposed for simulation. 2. Establish Material Identity Attributes Determine which identity attributes are necessary to distinguish the target from materially different objects. 3. Resolve or Record Identity Ambiguity Identify conflicting, missing, proxy, substitute, composite, or uncertain identity conditions and prevent them from becoming hidden assumptions. 4. Assign Simulation Object Identification Status Classify the strength of the object identity basis as identified, conditional, partial, conflicted, ambiguous, or undetermined. 5. Create the Simulation Object Identification Record Preserve the object identifier, material identity attributes, references, limitations, ambiguity, status, and traceability required for downstream SOS governance. Governance Outputs SOIM may produce: Simulation Object Identifier, Simulation Object Identification Record, Object Type Record, Object Class Record, Object Instance Record, Material Identity Attribute Record, Object Distinction Record, Composite Simulation Object Record, Constituent Object Register, Object Hierarchy Record, Proxy Simulation Object Declaration, Object Substitution Record, Identification Conflict Record, Identity Ambiguity Record, Simulation Object Identification Status, Object Identity Continuity Record, Object Identity Change Record, and Simulation Object Identity Traceability Map. Use Case 1 — Future Spacecraft Simulation Scenario A space organization intends to simulate a spacecraft before the final physical spacecraft exists. Several design revisions are under development. Application SOIM identifies the Simulation Object through the applicable controlled spacecraft design and establishes the material identity attributes that distinguish it from previous and alternative revisions. The simulation remains bound to: Spacecraft Design Revision D rather than a generic: Future Spacecraft A later revision materially changes propulsion architecture. That revision does not silently inherit the identity of the previously simulated object. Result Simulation outputs remain attributable to the exact spacecraft design they were generated to represent, enabling later SIMULOS® governance to determine whether additional simulation is necessary after design change. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Vehicle Product Family Scenario An autonomous vehicle manufacturer operates several vehicles under the same commercial model name. Different vehicles use materially different sensor packages and autonomy software generations. Application SOIM prevents the commercial product name from functioning as the only Simulation Object identity. The simulated vehicle is identified at the level required to distinguish the relevant system from materially different vehicles in the same family. A simulation conducted using one sensor and autonomy configuration therefore remains anchored to that specific Simulation Object. Result Simulation findings cannot automatically be represented as applying to every vehicle sold under the same model name. The object identity remains sufficiently precise for subsequent boundary, version, configuration, scenario, execution, and output governance. Architectural Position Simulation Object Identification Module (SOIM) is the first internal governance space of the Simulation Object Standard (SOS). It answers: Which object? The remaining SOS governance then establishes: Where does that object begin and end? Which version applies? Which configuration applies? and: How must the object remain documented and traceable? SOIM therefore provides the initial identity anchor upon which the complete Simulation Object governance layer depends. It does not replace general identity governance under OBIDENITY®, validation governance under VALIDOS®, integrity governance under INTEGROS®, operational reality governance under ORA™, or audit and evidence governance under ADIT®. It governs specifically: the identity of the object that a simulation claims to represent. Foundational Principle A simulation cannot be more precisely attributed than the Simulation Object to which it is explicitly identified and traceably anchored. Canonical Closing Statement Simulation Object Identification Module (SOIM) establishes the first internal governance mechanism of SIMULOS® by ensuring that every simulation begins with a sufficiently identifiable and distinguishable Simulation Object. Through material identity attributes, object distinction, proxy disclosure, composite-object identification, hierarchy preservation, ambiguity and conflict governance, substitution prevention, object-inflation control, identification status, and lifecycle traceability, SOIM prevents simulation outputs from being attributed to assumed, substituted, materially different, or unjustifiably broader targets. By creating a persistent Simulation Object identity anchor before boundary, version, configuration, representation, assumptions, modeling, scenario design, execution, or output interpretation proceeds, SOIM establishes the first operational foundation of governed simulation.

title: OOF™ Simulation Output Limitation Module (SOLM)
text: OOF™ Simulation Output Limitation Module (SOLM) Simulation Output Limitation Module (SOLM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Simulation Output Governance Standard (SOGS) Operational Layer: Simulation Output Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Type: Parent Standard Module Governed Space: Simulation Output Limitation Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 19 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · CLIA® · MGIA™ · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Governed Space Simulation Output Limitation Canonical Definition Simulation Output Limitation Module (SOLM) defines the governance framework through which material limitations attached to Simulation Outputs are identified, classified, bounded, documented, propagated, and preserved so that outputs cannot be interpreted, generalized, transferred, compared, or relied upon beyond the conditions actually supported by the simulation that produced them. SOLM governs the boundary between: what a Simulation Output shows and: what that output does not legitimately establish. Its purpose is to prevent computational precision, high simulation volume, visually convincing outputs, successful scenario execution, or apparently stable results from expanding the legitimate meaning of a Simulation Output beyond its governed simulation basis. Operational Role SOLM serves as the fourth internal governance space of the Simulation Output Governance Standard (SOGS). The preceding modules establish: SOIM — What exactly did the simulation produce? SOCM — What type of Simulation Output is it? SIM — What inference, if any, may legitimately be drawn from that output? SOLM asks: Where does the legitimate meaning of that output stop, what conditions constrain its interpretation, and which limitations must remain attached whenever the output is communicated, compared, reused, or relied upon? The governed progression is: Identified Simulation Output ↓ Output Classification ↓ Governed Inference ↓ Limitation Identification ↓ Limitation Materiality ↓ Interpretation Boundary ↓ Applicability Restriction ↓ Transfer / Generalization Restriction ↓ Limitation Propagation ↓ Bounded Simulation Output ↓ Output Documentation Module Operational Space SOLM governs: Simulation Output limitation identification, limitation source, limitation classification, limitation materiality, output applicability boundaries, scenario-bound limitations, model-bound limitations, environment-bound limitations, input-bound limitations, assumption-bound limitations, parameter-bound limitations, execution-bound limitations, observation-bound limitations, statistical limitations, uncertainty limitations, resolution limitations, temporal limitations, spatial limitations, population limitations, configuration limitations, version limitations, edge-case limitations, stress-condition limitations, scenario-coverage limitations, inference limitations, generalization limitations, transfer limitations, comparison limitations, reuse limitations, extrapolation limitations, aggregation limitations, communication limitations, decision-use limitations, unresolved limitation, limitation propagation, limitation reassessment, limitation versioning, and Output Limitation Traceability. Module Function SOLM exists to prevent: scenario-specific results being presented as universal results, model-specific behavior being presented as real-world certainty, nominal-condition outputs being generalized to edge or stress conditions, outputs produced under one environment being applied to another without qualification, outputs based on one population being generalized to another, simulated time horizons being extended beyond what was modeled, stochastic results being represented as deterministic truth, point estimates being presented without material uncertainty, averages hiding adverse distributions, incomplete Scenario Coverage being forgotten, unknown Scenario Space disappearing from downstream interpretation, simulation capability limits being mistaken for system limits, inferred results being presented as direct observations, correlation being presented as causation, output precision being confused with output certainty, and output reuse occurring after the governing simulation conditions have materially changed. Simulation Output Limitation A Simulation Output Limitation is any material condition restricting what a Simulation Output may legitimately: describe, imply, represent, compare, generalize, predict, support, transfer, or be relied upon to establish. A limitation may arise from any upstream SIMULOS® governance space. Limitation Origin A material output limitation should remain traceable to its origin where possible. Possible origins include: Simulation Object Simulation Purpose & Scope Reality Representation Simulation Assumptions Model & Environment Simulation Inputs & Data Scenario Design Simulation Execution Output Classification or: Inference Process Conceptually: Upstream Limitation → Simulation Output Limitation Upstream Limitation Propagation SIMULOS® establishes: A material limitation does not disappear merely because the simulation successfully produced an output. If a limitation exists upstream and materially affects what the result can mean, it should propagate into Output Governance. Output Applicability Boundary An Output Applicability Boundary defines where a Simulation Output may legitimately apply. Applicability may depend upon: Simulation Object version, system configuration, population, environment, geography, time period, operating state, scenario family, parameter range, input conditions, autonomy state, or another relevant boundary. Scope-Bound Output A Simulation Output should remain bounded by the Simulation Purpose & Scope under which it was produced. For example: simulation of braking behavior at 0–80 km/h does not automatically support conclusions about: 120 km/h behavior. No Scope Expansion Principle SIMULOS® establishes: A Simulation Output must not acquire a broader scope than the simulation inquiry that produced it unless that broader applicability is independently established. Reality Representation Limitation Outputs are constrained by what the simulation represented. If Reality Representation excluded a material real-world feature, the resulting Output cannot legitimately establish behavior involving that omitted feature. Therefore: Unrepresented Reality → Unsupported Output Claim Abstraction Limitation A simulation may deliberately simplify reality. An output derived from that abstraction should not be presented as if the omitted detail had been simulated. Fidelity Limitation Simulation fidelity may be sufficient for one purpose but insufficient for another. For example: a low-fidelity simulation may support early design exploration while remaining unsuitable for detailed safety reliance. SOLM preserves that boundary. Assumption-Bound Limitation Simulation Outputs may depend upon assumptions established under SAS. Where an output materially depends upon an assumption, its interpretation should remain conditional upon that assumption or upon the range within which it remains applicable. Conceptually: Output Validity of Interpretation ≤ Applicability of Material Assumption No Assumption Erasure Principle A simulation assumption must not disappear from output interpretation when the output materially depends upon that assumption. Model-Bound Limitation A Simulation Output reflects behavior of the governed simulation model. It does not automatically establish equivalent behavior of the real system. This distinction is fundamental: Model Behavior ≠ Operational Reality by Default Environment-Bound Limitation The simulation environment may constrain the legitimate meaning of the output. A result produced under: Environment Version A may not automatically transfer to: Environment Version B where material conditions differ. Configuration Limitation Outputs may apply only to a specific: hardware configuration, software version, model version, sensor package, mission configuration, autonomy level, or operational configuration. Input-Bound Limitation Simulation Outputs cannot legitimately exceed the representativeness, temporal applicability, transformation basis, and uncertainty of the Simulation Inputs on which they materially depend. For example: Input Population A does not automatically support: Output Claim for Population B. Representativeness Limitation Where SIDS identifies incomplete representativeness, that limitation should remain attached to the output. A simulation using input data representative only of: urban daytime driving cannot silently produce an output interpreted as representative of: all driving environments. Temporal Input Limitation Historical or temporally restricted inputs may bound Output applicability. For example: an economic simulation using pre-regime-change data may not automatically support post-regime conclusions. Input Uncertainty Limitation Material uncertainty in the Simulation Input basis should constrain downstream interpretation. A precise output derived from uncertain inputs may remain materially uncertain. No Precision Laundering Principle SIMULOS® establishes: A simulation may transform uncertain inputs into computationally precise outputs, but it may not transform uncertainty into certainty merely through computation. Scenario-Bound Limitation Outputs may apply only to the Scenario or Scenario Family under which they were generated. A nominal-scenario Output does not automatically establish behavior under: edge cases, stress conditions, degraded states, failure conditions, transitions, or recovery scenarios. Scenario Coverage Limitation A Simulation Output may be locally strong while the overall Scenario Set remains incomplete. SCCM may identify: Scenario Coverage Gap or: Critical Scenario Coverage Gap. SOLM ensures that such gaps constrain any broader Output claim. No Coverage Inflation Principle SIMULOS® establishes: Strong results inside covered Scenario Space do not establish behavior inside uncovered Scenario Space. Unknown Scenario Space Limitation Where unknown Scenario Space remains material, Output interpretation should avoid implying exhaustive behavioral knowledge. Edge-Case Limitation Outputs produced under nominal or ordinary variation should not be interpreted as demonstrating behavior at difficult edges unless those edges were explicitly examined. Stress-Condition Limitation Successful performance under ordinary conditions does not establish robustness under stress. Likewise, one stress condition does not establish robustness across all stress combinations. Execution-Bound Limitation A Simulation Output inherits relevant limitations from the execution that produced it. Examples include: execution deviation, interrupted run, incomplete run, unexpected intervention, configuration mismatch, resource limitation, execution drift, or incomplete observation. Execution Completeness Limitation An output from a partially completed execution should not be represented as if it came from a complete execution where completion materially affects interpretation. Observation Limitation SES may identify Observation Blind Spots. Where material internal events or states were not observable, Output interpretation should not imply knowledge about those hidden regions. Randomness Limitation Where simulation behavior is stochastic, one run may not characterize the distribution of possible outcomes. SOLM may therefore preserve a limitation such as: Single stochastic realization — not sufficient to characterize outcome distribution. Repetition Limitation Repeated runs may remain insufficient where: repetitions are too few, configuration drift exists, seed coverage is narrow, relevant variation is missing, or runs are not comparable. Statistical Limitation Simulation Outputs may have statistical limitations involving: sample size, variance, confidence, distribution tails, sampling strategy, rare-event representation, convergence, or estimator uncertainty. Mean Limitation Average behavior may conceal: extremes, variance, multimodality, adverse tails, or subgroup differences. SIMULOS® establishes: An average Simulation Output does not represent every simulated condition or every possible outcome. Distribution Limitation A distribution estimated from simulation is bounded by: scenario generation, sampling method, assumptions, model behavior, input distributions, and number of executions. It is not automatically equivalent to the real-world distribution. Rare-Event Limitation Low observed frequency in simulation may result from: genuine rarity, inadequate sampling, scenario-selection bias, insufficient run count, or missing Scenario Space. A rare simulated event rate should therefore not automatically be interpreted as a reliable real-world probability. Resolution Limitation Output resolution may constrain interpretation. Examples include: temporal resolution, spatial resolution, state resolution, population granularity, behavioral granularity, or aggregated outputs. No Resolution Inflation Principle A Simulation Output cannot legitimately reveal distinctions that the simulation did not represent or observe at sufficient resolution. Temporal Output Limitation A Simulation Output may apply only within a defined simulated time horizon. For example: 0–24 hours does not automatically support: 30-day behavior. Long-Horizon Limitation Uncertainty, model drift, state accumulation, or changing environments may increase with simulated horizon. Outputs should remain bounded accordingly. Spatial Limitation A simulation covering one: location, terrain, orbital region, climate, infrastructure topology, or geographic region does not automatically support spatial generalization elsewhere. Population Limitation Outputs may be bounded to the population represented by: data, actor models, simulation scenarios, or relevant configuration. Version Limitation Simulation Outputs are attached to the versions that produced them. Conceptually: Output O1 → Model v3.1 + Environment v5.0 + Input Set 22 + Scenario Set 7 A later model or environment version should not automatically inherit the Output. No Version Inheritance Principle SIMULOS® establishes: Simulation Outputs do not automatically remain applicable after a material change in the Simulation Object, Model, Environment, Inputs, Parameters, or Scenario Basis. Inference Limitation SIM — Simulation Inference Module establishes what may legitimately be inferred from a Simulation Output. SOLM establishes the boundary beyond which that inference must not expand. Direct Output vs Inferred Meaning For example: Direct Output: simulated component temperature reached 112°C. Possible inference: Under the simulated conditions, the component model crossed the defined thermal threshold. Unsupported inference without further basis: The real component will fail at exactly 112°C in all operational environments. SOLM governs that distinction. No Observation-to-Causation Principle A simulated association does not automatically establish causal truth. If: Condition A and: Output B occur together in simulation, causality requires a sufficient simulation and inference basis. No Simulation-to-Reality Equivalence Principle SIMULOS® establishes: What occurred in simulation is evidence of simulated behavior under governed simulated conditions; it is not automatically proof of identical behavior in Operational Reality. ORA™ and VALIDOS® may participate in downstream correlation and validation. Generalization Limitation A Generalization Limitation restricts extension of an output beyond the represented conditions. Generalization may concern: population, environment, geography, time, configuration, system type, behavior, or operating condition. Transfer Limitation A Simulation Output generated for one Simulation Object should not automatically be transferred to another object merely because the objects are similar. Cross-System Transfer For example: Robot Model A may share architecture with: Robot Model B but differences in: mass, software, sensors, actuators, control logic, or environment may materially limit transfer. Comparison Limitation Two Simulation Outputs should not be compared as equivalent where material differences exist in: Simulation Purpose, Scenario, Model, Environment, Inputs, Parameters, execution conditions, output type, or inference basis. No Apples-to-Oranges Principle SIMULOS® establishes: Numerically similar Simulation Outputs are not necessarily methodologically comparable. Reuse Limitation A Simulation Output may be reused in: another analysis, another scenario, another model, another validation process, another decision, or another simulation. Reuse should remain bounded by the Output's original applicability and limitations. No Context-Free Reuse Principle A Simulation Output must not be detached from the conditions necessary to understand what it legitimately means. Extrapolation Limitation Outputs should not be extrapolated outside: modeled ranges, simulated horizons, Scenario Space, input distributions, or represented boundaries without explicit governance. Aggregation Limitation Aggregated Simulation Outputs may hide important: scenario differences, subgroup differences, tail behavior, failures, or contradictory outcomes. Output Selection Limitation If only selected outputs or successful runs are presented, interpretation may become biased. Material negative, anomalous, or contradictory outputs should remain visible where they affect the legitimate conclusion. No Cherry-Picked Output Principle SIMULOS® establishes: A Simulation Output claim must not be strengthened by selectively excluding materially relevant outputs that contradict or weaken that claim. Output Contradiction Simulation Outputs may conflict across: scenarios, repetitions, versions, parameter configurations, or model states. A contradiction may itself create an Output Limitation. Unresolved Contradiction Limitation Where conflicting outputs cannot yet be reconciled, the legitimate inference may need to remain: Conditional Partial Conflicted or: Undetermined. SOLM preserves the limitation. Decision-Use Limitation A Simulation Output may support: exploration without supporting: deployment authorization. It may support: design comparison without supporting: safety certification. It may support: hypothesis generation without supporting: operational reliance. The intended decision context matters. Exploratory Output An exploratory Simulation Output may legitimately support: investigation, hypothesis generation, design direction, anomaly discovery, or scenario refinement. It should not automatically be represented as validated evidence for high-consequence reliance. Operational Reliance Limitation SOGS does not authorize operational reliance. VALIDOS®, ORA™, ASGA™, GOA™, or other relevant architectures may determine what downstream reliance is legitimate. SOLM preserves limitations that those downstream processes need to know. Communication Limitation Limitations should remain visible when Simulation Outputs are: reported, visualized, summarized, presented to management, published, transferred between teams, used by AI systems, or integrated into decision-support tools. No Limitation Loss Through Summarization Principle SIMULOS® establishes: A material Output Limitation must not disappear merely because the underlying simulation record is summarized into a dashboard, chart, score, executive summary, or AI-generated explanation. Machine-Readable Limitation Where Simulation Outputs are consumed automatically, limitations may require machine-readable representation. Examples may include: applicability tags, scenario constraints, object-version references, uncertainty flags, scope boundaries, comparison restrictions, or reliance warnings. Limitation Classification A material Output Limitation may be classified as: Scope Limitation Representation Limitation Assumption Limitation Model Limitation Environment Limitation Input Limitation Scenario Limitation Coverage Limitation Execution Limitation Observation Limitation Statistical Limitation Uncertainty Limitation Temporal Limitation Spatial Limitation Population Limitation Configuration Limitation Version Limitation Inference Limitation Generalization Limitation Transfer Limitation Comparison Limitation Reuse Limitation or another simulation-specific class. Limitation Materiality Not every known limitation requires equal prominence. A limitation is material where ignoring it could reasonably change: interpretation, inference, comparison, decision, validation, operational reliance, or assessment of the Simulation Object. Critical Output Limitation A Critical Output Limitation exists where ignoring the limitation could produce materially misleading or high-consequence interpretation. Limitation Severity A simulation implementation may classify limitations as: Informational Material Major Critical or another justified structure. SIMULOS® does not mandate one universal severity scale. Limitation Status Possible statuses may include: Active Conditionally Resolved Resolved Superseded Unresolved or: Applicability Undetermined. Resolved Limitation A limitation may be resolved only when an appropriate governed process establishes that the restriction no longer materially applies. For example: an earlier population limitation may be resolved after additional simulations extend the represented population sufficiently. No Silent Resolution Principle SIMULOS® establishes: A Simulation Output Limitation must not be treated as resolved merely because later results are favorable. Limitation Propagation A material limitation should follow the Output into downstream use. Conceptually: Simulation Output ↓ Output Limitation ↓ Inference ↓ Documentation ↓ Validation / Analysis / Decision / Reliance The limitation should remain visible wherever its absence could materially distort meaning. Limitation Propagation Failure A Limitation Propagation Failure occurs where the original simulation record contains a material limitation but downstream reporting or use no longer communicates it. Examples include: dashboard removes uncertainty, executive summary removes scope restriction, reused data loses Scenario reference, AI-generated answer omits model limitation, or published graph removes excluded conditions. Output Limitation Register SOLM may maintain a Simulation Output Limitation Register. A limitation record may identify: Limitation ID, affected Output, limitation class, origin, description, materiality, applicability, affected inference, affected comparison, downstream propagation requirement, status, version, and reassessment trigger. Limitation-to-Output Binding Every material limitation should be bound to the relevant: individual Output, Output Set, Scenario Output, Campaign Output, derived result, or inference. Limitation-to-Inference Binding Where a specific limitation constrains a particular inference: Output → Inference → Limitation should remain traceable. Limitation-to-Decision Binding Where an Output is used for decision support, material limitations should remain available to that decision process. Limitation Reassessment Trigger Reassessment may be required when: additional scenarios are executed, coverage expands, new data becomes available, model fidelity improves, environment changes, assumptions change, input uncertainty decreases, new validation evidence appears, the Output is reused for another purpose, or a new reliance context is proposed. Output Limitation Change A limitation may: narrow, expand, become more severe, become less severe, resolve, or become newly discovered as the simulation lifecycle evolves. Historical Limitation Preservation Later resolution of a limitation must not rewrite the limitation state of earlier Output use. Point-in-time reconstruction should remain possible. No Retrospective Strengthening Principle SIMULOS® establishes: A later improvement in simulation capability must not retroactively strengthen what an earlier Simulation Output legitimately established at the time it was produced. Point-in-Time Output Interpretation SOLM should support questions such as: What limitations were known when this Output was produced? Which assumptions constrained it? Which Scenario Space was uncovered? Which model version produced it? Which inference was allowed? Which generalizations were prohibited? Was the limitation later resolved? Was the Output reused outside its original context? Simulation Output Boundary Statement A governed Output may carry a concise boundary statement such as: This Simulation Output applies only to the identified Simulation Object version, Simulation Scope, Scenario Set, Model & Environment configuration, Input & Data Basis, execution conditions, and Output limitations recorded for the producing simulation activity. Space and Mission Systems Space and mission simulation creates particularly important Output Limitation questions because operational reality may be difficult or impossible to reproduce before deployment. A mission simulation may produce: 95.8% successful autonomous recovery across a large Monte Carlo campaign. That number alone does not establish: 95.8% real-mission recovery probability. SOLM asks: Which mission conditions were represented? Which communication states were absent? Which hardware failures were modeled? Which dependency combinations remained uncovered? Which environmental uncertainties were simplified? Was the recovery model validated against comparable operational behavior? The Output may remain extremely useful. But its legitimate meaning must remain bounded by the simulated conditions. Autonomous Systems An autonomous system may achieve: 99.9% simulated task success. SOLM prevents that number from silently becoming: 99.9% operational safety or: 99.9% real-world reliability unless the required governance basis independently supports those claims. The Output might legitimately establish: 99.9% success within the defined governed Scenario Set and simulation conditions. That is a stronger methodological statement because its boundary is explicit. AI Agent Systems An AI agent may complete: 98% of simulated workflows within a test environment. SOLM may reveal that: tool permissions were fixed, external systems were stable, memory was always available, human instructions were unambiguous, and authority transitions were not simulated. The legitimate Output claim therefore remains bounded to that condition space. Industrial Simulation A manufacturer may simulate equipment under: normal + elevated load and observe no failures. SOLM prevents that result from being generalized automatically to: extreme temperature, degraded maintenance, sensor failure, long-duration operation, or combined load and environmental stress if those conditions were not represented. Existing Simulation Program Diagnostic SOLM can be applied to existing simulation programs by asking: What claims are being made from our Simulation Outputs? Which output limitations are explicit? Which limitations exist upstream but disappear from reporting? Do dashboards show precision without uncertainty? Are nominal outputs being generalized to uncovered Scenario Space? Are outputs from old Model Versions still being reused? Are Monte Carlo frequencies being presented as real-world probabilities without qualification? Are outputs being used for decisions beyond the purpose for which the simulation was designed? Can each output claim be traced to its limiting conditions? This can reveal that the key weakness is not the quality of the simulation itself but the way its outputs are interpreted and communicated. Module Boundary SOLM begins when a Simulation Output has been sufficiently: identified under SOIM, classified under SOCM, and associated with a governed inference basis under SIM. SOLM ends when the materially relevant limitations affecting: interpretation, inference, applicability, generalization, comparison, transfer, reuse, and downstream reliance have been sufficiently identified, classified, bounded, documented, and attached to the affected Simulation Output. SOLM does not govern: general integrity, data integrity, output tamper resistance, validation determination, operational deployment authorization, general risk management, or final reliance authorization. Integrity remains under INTEGROS®. Architectural Boundary SOLM specifically avoids the concept: Output Integrity because that governance space belongs to INTEGROS®. The architectural distinction is: SOLM → What limitations constrain the meaning and use of this Simulation Output? INTEGROS® → Has the relevant Output or record preserved the integrity properties required of it? This separation prevents SIMULOS® from duplicating integrity governance. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Identify Material Output Limitations Determine which upstream or output-specific conditions materially constrain interpretation. 2. Classify Limitation Origin Identify whether the limitation arises from: scope, representation, assumption, model, environment, inputs, scenarios, execution, observation, statistics, uncertainty, or inference. 3. Assess Limitation Materiality Determine whether ignoring the limitation could materially alter interpretation, comparison, validation, or reliance. 4. Establish Output Applicability Boundary Define where the Output may and may not legitimately apply. 5. Establish Inference Boundary Determine what the Output may support and which broader conclusions remain unsupported. 6. Establish Generalization and Transfer Restrictions Identify restrictions upon use across: populations, environments, versions, systems, scenarios, time periods, and configurations. 7. Bind Limitations to Outputs Ensure each material limitation remains attached to the affected Output or Output Set. 8. Establish Propagation Requirements Determine where limitations must remain visible in downstream: documentation, reporting, validation, analysis, decision support, and reuse. 9. Define Reassessment Triggers Identify which new simulations, evidence, model changes, Scenario expansions, or reuse contexts require limitation reassessment. 10. Preserve Historical Limitation State Maintain the limitation record applicable at the time the Output was produced and used. Governance Outputs SOLM may produce: Simulation Output Limitation Identifier, Simulation Output Limitation Record, Output Applicability Boundary, Scope Limitation Record, Reality Representation Limitation Record, Abstraction Limitation Record, Fidelity Limitation Record, Assumption-Bound Limitation Record, Model-Bound Limitation Record, Environment-Bound Limitation Record, Configuration Limitation Record, Input-Bound Limitation Record, Representativeness Limitation Record, Temporal Input Limitation Record, Input Uncertainty Limitation Record, Scenario-Bound Limitation Record, Scenario Coverage Limitation Record, Unknown Scenario Space Limitation Record, Edge-Case Limitation Record, Stress-Condition Limitation Record, Execution-Bound Limitation Record, Execution Completeness Limitation Record, Observation Limitation Record, Randomness Limitation Record, Repetition Limitation Record, Statistical Limitation Record, Distribution Limitation Record, Rare-Event Limitation Record, Resolution Limitation Record, Temporal Output Limitation Record, Spatial Limitation Record, Population Limitation Record, Version Limitation Record, Inference Limitation Record, Generalization Limitation Record, Transfer Limitation Record, Comparison Limitation Record, Reuse Limitation Record, Extrapolation Limitation Record, Aggregation Limitation Record, Output Contradiction Limitation Record, Decision-Use Limitation Record, Critical Output Limitation, Output Limitation Register, Limitation Propagation Requirement, Limitation Propagation Failure Record, Limitation Reassessment Trigger, Limitation Change Record, Point-in-Time Limitation Record, Output Boundary Statement, and Simulation Output Limitation Traceability Map. Use Case 1 — Spacecraft Autonomous Landing Simulation Scenario A spacecraft landing simulation produces a result showing: 99.4% successful autonomous landing across a large governed Simulation Campaign. The number appears highly convincing. Application SOLM identifies material limitations: only the modeled terrain classes were represented, communication-loss conditions were limited, certain sensor-failure combinations remained outside Scenario Coverage, atmospheric uncertainty was bounded to a defined range, the Output applies to one vehicle configuration, and the result is a simulated campaign frequency, not a direct empirical mission-success probability. Result The legitimate Output statement becomes: 99.4% simulated landing success across the governed Scenario Set, Model & Environment configuration, Input basis, and uncertainty conditions represented by the identified Simulation Campaign. The limitation does not weaken the simulation. It prevents a strong simulation result from being converted into a stronger real-world claim than the simulation can legitimately support. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Vehicle Safety Simulation Scenario An autonomous-driving platform reports: 99.99% collision-free simulation performance. Application SOLM identifies that most Simulation Executions occur within: mapped urban environments, defined weather ranges, supported sensor configurations, known road-user classes, and a bounded Scenario Set. Some compound edge conditions remain uncovered. Result The organization cannot legitimately communicate the Output as: 99.99% real-world safety. The governed Output remains: 99.99% collision-free performance within the identified simulated conditions and Scenario Coverage basis. The remaining limitations become explicit inputs to further Scenario expansion, validation, and operational reliance assessment. Architectural Position Simulation Output Limitation Module (SOLM) is the fourth internal governance space of the Simulation Output Governance Standard (SOGS). The complete SOGS progression is: Simulation Output Identification ↓ Simulation Output Classification ↓ Simulation Inference ↓ Simulation Output Limitation ↓ Simulation Output Documentation SOIM establishes: What exactly was produced? SOCM establishes: What kind of Simulation Output is it? SIM establishes: What may legitimately be inferred from it? SOLM establishes: Where does that legitimate interpretation stop? SODM then preserves: the Output, its classification, inference, limitations, provenance, and documentation basis. Foundational Principle A Simulation Output is only as broadly meaningful as the governed conditions under which it was produced, and no output may legitimately escape the assumptions, representation, data, scenarios, execution conditions, uncertainty, and coverage boundaries that materially constrain what it can demonstrate. Canonical Closing Statement Simulation Output Limitation Module establishes the boundary-governance layer of the Simulation Output Governance Standard by ensuring that the meaning of Simulation Outputs cannot silently expand beyond the conditions the simulation actually represented and executed. Through explicit limitation origin, materiality, applicability boundaries, assumption, model, environment, input, Scenario Coverage, execution, observation, statistical, temporal, spatial, population, version, inference, generalization, transfer, comparison, reuse, and decision-use limitations, SOLM preserves the distinction between computational output and legitimate conclusion. By propagating material limitations into downstream documentation, validation, analysis, communication, and reliance while explicitly leaving Output Integrity to INTEGROS®, SOLM ensures that strong simulation results remain useful precisely because their boundaries remain visible, traceable, and governable.

title: OOF™ Simulation Observation Module (SOM)
text: OOF™ Simulation Observation Module (SOM) Simulation Observation Module (SOM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Simulation Execution Standard (SES) Operational Layer: Simulation Execution Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Type: Parent Standard Module Governed Space: Simulation Observation Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 19 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Governed Space Simulation Observation Canonical Definition Simulation Observation Module (SOM) defines the governance framework through which materially relevant states, events, transitions, interactions, anomalies, interventions, failures, recoveries, resource conditions, and runtime behaviors occurring during Simulation Execution are identified, observed, captured, contextualized, and preserved so that the execution record reflects not merely that a simulation ran, but what materially occurred while it was running. SOM establishes the observation layer of the Simulation Execution Standard (SES). Its purpose is to ensure that materially relevant simulation behavior cannot disappear merely because the simulation technically completed or produced an output. Operational Role SOM serves as the third internal governance space of the Simulation Execution Standard (SES). The preceding modules establish: SIM — What exact Simulation Instance has been instantiated? SECM — How is that execution controlled while it runs? SOM asks: What materially relevant events, states, transitions, behaviors, anomalies, and interventions occurred during the execution, and under what execution context did they occur? The progression is: Instantiated Simulation ↓ Controlled Execution ↓ Observation Requirements ↓ Runtime Observation ↓ Event & State Capture ↓ Anomaly / Intervention Capture ↓ Observation Context ↓ Observation Limitation Assessment ↓ Governed Simulation Observation Record The observation record then supports: Simulation Repetition → Execution Documentation → Simulation Output Governance Module Operational Space SOM governs: observation requirements, observation targets, observable states, observable events, runtime behaviors, system transitions, state transitions, scenario transitions, environment transitions, agent behavior, human-system interaction, subsystem interaction, multi-agent interaction, control events, execution interventions, anomalies, unexpected behavior, failure events, degradation events, recovery events, threshold crossings, timing events, synchronization events, resource conditions, computational conditions, communication conditions, sensor conditions, execution-state changes, observation timing, observation frequency, observation resolution, event-triggered observation, threshold-triggered observation, continuous observation, sampled observation, selective observation, observation blind spots, missing observations, observation loss, observation uncertainty, observation provenance, observation traceability, and Governed Simulation Observation Record formation. Observation Requirement An Observation Requirement defines what materially relevant behavior or state must be observable during Simulation Execution. It answers: What must we be able to see, detect, capture, or reconstruct during this execution in order to understand what materially occurred? Observation Requirements may arise from: Simulation Purpose, Scenario Requirements, Edge Cases, Stress Conditions, system boundaries, expected transitions, known failure modes, recovery behavior, autonomous decision states, human interventions, dependencies, timing conditions, resource limits, or previous simulation findings. Observation Target An Observation Target is the specific state, event, object, interaction, process, or condition that the simulation must observe. Targets may include: Simulation Object state, model state, environment state, subsystem state, agent state, sensor state, communication state, energy state, computational state, control state, autonomy state, authority state, human intervention, failure event, recovery event, or another materially relevant execution condition. Observation ≠ Logging Everything SOM does not require every internal variable to be logged continuously. Observation depth should reflect the Simulation Purpose and material execution questions. A simulation may generate enormous amounts of technical telemetry that provide little governance value. SOM therefore asks: Which observations are materially necessary to understand execution behavior? Observation Materiality An observation is material where failure to capture it could materially weaken understanding of: why the simulation behaved as it did, whether a scenario condition actually occurred, whether a threshold was crossed, whether a system degraded, whether an intervention changed behavior, whether failure or recovery occurred, whether outputs can be interpreted, or whether execution can later be reconstructed. Observation Context A materially relevant observation should preserve enough context to determine: What happened When it happened Where in the execution it happened Under which Scenario Under which Simulation Configuration Under which input and parameter conditions and where relevant: What happened immediately before and after it. Observation Identity A material observation may receive an identifiable reference. For example: OBS-00421 An Observation Identity can connect: Execution ID → Observation ID → Event / State → Output or Downstream Analysis Observation Timestamp Where timing matters, each observation should preserve a relevant temporal reference. Possible references include: simulation time, wall-clock time, mission time, event time, system-relative time, or another defined temporal basis. Event Observation An Event Observation captures the occurrence of a materially relevant event. Examples include: collision, threshold crossing, communication loss, sensor failure, mode transition, authority transfer, resource depletion, recovery initiation, emergency response, or scenario termination. State Observation A State Observation captures the condition of a simulated object or system at a defined moment or interval. Examples include: Nominal Degraded Fallback Critical Failed Recovering or another simulation-specific state. State Transition Observation SOM gives particular importance to transitions. A system may behave correctly in two stable states while exhibiting unexpected behavior during the change between them. Therefore: State A → State B may require explicit observation rather than only observing: State A and: State B. Transition Context A transition record may preserve: originating state, destination state, trigger, transition time, authority involved, relevant inputs, relevant resource state, intermediate behavior, and resulting state. Threshold Observation Simulation behavior may change when a threshold is crossed. SOM may observe: Threshold − Δ ↓ Threshold Reached ↓ Threshold + Δ where behavior around the threshold matters. Threshold Crossing Event A Threshold Crossing Observation may record: threshold identifier, relevant variable, crossing direction, crossing rate, time, resulting state, and downstream behavior. Anomaly Observation An Anomaly Observation captures simulation behavior that differs materially from expected, baseline, or previously characterized behavior. An anomaly may include: unexpected state, unexpected sequence, unexpected delay, contradictory behavior, output discontinuity, unstable oscillation, resource spike, control conflict, unexpected fallback, or another materially unusual execution condition. Anomaly ≠ Failure SIMULOS® establishes: An anomaly is an observed deviation from expected or characterized behavior; it does not automatically establish system failure. The consequence requires downstream analysis. Unexpected Behavior Unexpected behavior should remain part of the execution record even where: it was not part of the original Scenario Requirement, it does not immediately affect the final output, or the simulation later recovers.
