Controlled Comparison For controlled comparative simulation: Compared Executions should differ only in the variables intentionally changed or otherwise explicitly disclosed. This enables parameter-level causal interpretation without assuming broader methodological validation. Parameter Change Propagation A material parameter change may propagate through later SIMULOS® spaces. Conceptually: Parameter Change ↓ Scenario Configuration ↓ Simulation Execution ↓ Simulation Output ↓ Reality Correlation ↓ Simulation Evidence SPHM preserves the parameter change. The downstream spaces govern their respective consequences. Parameter-to-Execution Binding Every material simulation execution should be bindable to the Parameter Configuration under which it occurred. Conceptually: Simulation Execution ID → Parameter Configuration ID Without this relationship, repeatability and reconstruction may become impossible. Parameter-to-Output Traceability Where material, simulation outputs should remain traceable to the parameter configuration that contributed to their production. Conceptually: Parameter Configuration → Execution → Simulation Output SPHM establishes the parameter side of that traceability chain. Parameter Reconstruction SPHM should enable reconstruction sufficient to answer: Which parameters were active? Which values were assigned? Which units applied? Which ranges and constraints applied? Which values were inherited or overridden? Which parameters were dynamic or stochastic? Which dependencies existed? Which parameter configuration produced the execution? Did any material parameter change during execution? Parameterization Traceability A complete parameterization traceability path may be represented as: Simulation Purpose & Scope ↓ Reality Representation ↓ Simulation Assumptions ↓ Simulation Model & Environment ↓ Simulation Parameter ↓ Parameter Basis ↓ Parameter Value / Distribution ↓ Parameter Configuration ↓ Simulation Execution Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Identify Material Simulation Parameters Determine which configurable properties may materially influence simulation behavior. 2. Define and Classify Parameters Establish meaning, type, unit, role, and governed component. 3. Establish Parameter Basis Identify the basis supporting material parameter values or distributions. 4. Establish Values, Ranges, and Distributions Define applicable values and permissible variation. 5. Govern Constraints and Dependencies Identify relationships that limit or modify parameter configuration. 6. Control Defaults, Inheritance, and Overrides Prevent invisible parameterization through technical defaults or inherited configurations. 7. Establish Parameter Sets and Baselines Create controlled parameter configurations for simulation activity. 8. Govern Material Parameter Change Preserve changes, substitutions, drift, and dynamic behavior. 9. Bind Parameter Configuration to Execution Ensure each material execution can identify its applicable parameter configuration. 10. Preserve Parameter Reconstruction Maintain sufficient traceability to reconstruct the parameterization that produced simulation behavior. Governance Outputs SPHM may produce: Simulation Parameter Register, Simulation Parameter Identifier, Parameter Definition Record, Parameter Classification Record, Parameter Basis Record, Parameter Source Record, Parameter Unit Record, Parameter Value Record, Parameter Range Record, Parameter Distribution Record, Parameter Constraint Record, Cross-Parameter Constraint Record, Parameter Dependency Map, Parameter Correlation Record, Default Parameter Record, Parameter Inheritance Record, Parameter Override Record, Parameter Set, Parameter Configuration, Parameter Configuration Identifier, Parameter Baseline, Parameter Variation Record, Parameter Sweep Record, Parameter Sensitivity Record, High-Sensitivity Parameter Record, Parameter Substitution Record, Parameter Change Record, Parameter Drift Record, Parameter Lock Record, Parameter Freeze Record, Assumption-to-Parameter Traceability Map, Reality-Representation-to-Parameter Traceability Map, Parameter Configuration Completeness Assessment, Parameter Configuration Consistency Assessment, Parameter Configuration Coherence Assessment, Parameter-to-Execution Binding, Parameter Reconstruction Record, and Simulation Parameterization Traceability Map. Use Case 1 — Autonomous Vehicle Simulation Scenario An autonomous vehicle simulation uses configurable values for: Vehicle Mass + Sensor Range + Reaction Delay + Road Friction + Visibility + Traffic Density Application SPHM identifies each material parameter, establishes units and ranges, preserves the source or assumption supporting each value, and binds the resulting Parameter Configuration to the simulation execution. A change from: Road Friction = 0.8 to: Road Friction = 0.3 creates a materially different parameter configuration. Result The resulting vehicle behavior can be traced to the exact parameter configuration under which it was produced. Use Case 2 — Spacecraft Mission Simulation Scenario A spacecraft simulation includes: Vehicle Mass + Fuel Load + Engine Performance + Communication Delay + Thermal Conditions + Orbital Parameters Application SPHM governs the values, units, permissible ranges, dependencies, and parameter sets. If spacecraft mass changes, dependent fuel and propulsion parameters can be identified rather than remaining silently inconsistent. Result Mission simulation executions remain reconstructable and parameter-comparable. Use Case 3 — Financial Stress Simulation Scenario A financial simulation varies: Interest Rate + Default Probability + Liquidity + Asset Correlation + Market Volatility Application SPHM governs parameter ranges, distributions, correlations, parameter sweeps, and the specific configuration applied to each execution. Result A stress result can be distinguished from a baseline result through its governed Parameter Configuration rather than only through its final output. Architectural Position Simulation Parameterization is the fourth internal governance space of the Simulation Model & Environment Standard (SMES). The complete SMES progression is: Simulation Model Structure → Simulation Environment Configuration → Simulation Boundary Interaction → Simulation Parameterization → Simulation Environment Versioning SPHM receives: the governed Simulation Model Structure from SMMM, the governed Simulation Environment Configuration from SECM, and the governed Simulation Boundary Interaction structure from SBIM. It then establishes the controlled parameter configuration required to determine which specific configuration of the model and environment is actually prepared for simulation activity. The resulting governed configuration becomes an input to Simulation Environment Versioning and later SIMULOS® lifecycle spaces. Foundational Principle A simulation cannot be meaningfully reconstructed, compared, or governed when the material parameters shaping its behavior are unknown, uncontrolled, or detached from the execution they produced. Canonical Closing Statement Simulation Parameterization Module establishes the parameter governance layer of the Simulation Model & Environment Standard by transforming configurable model, environment, and boundary properties into explicit, bounded, traceable, and reconstructable Simulation Parameter Configurations. Through parameter identification, definition, classification, basis, units, values, ranges, distributions, constraints, dependencies, defaults, inheritance, overrides, sensitivity, controlled variation, change governance, configuration baselines, and execution binding, SPHM ensures that materially different simulation behavior cannot be produced by invisible parameter choices while being represented as if it arose from the same governed simulation configuration.

title: OOF™ Reality Alignment Module (SRAM) defines the governance conditions under
text: OOF™ Reality Alignment Module (SRAM) defines the governance conditions under Reality Alignment Module (SRAM) defines the governance conditions under OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Standard (SRCS) Operational Layer: Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Type: Parent Standard Module Governed Space: Reality Alignment Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 19 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Governed Space Reality Alignment Canonical Definition Reality Alignment Module (SRAM) defines the governance conditions under which material Simulation-Reality Deviations are translated into controlled alignment requirements, priorities, actions, boundaries, and reassessment pathways so that a simulation may be brought into closer correspondence with the Operational Reality it is intended to represent without erasing legitimate abstraction, uncertainty, simplification, or known differences. SRAM governs the transition from: Known Simulation-Reality Deviation to: Governed Reality Alignment. Its purpose is not to force simulation and reality into artificial equivalence. Its purpose is to determine: which deviations require alignment, what should be aligned, how alignment should occur, what should legitimately remain different, and whether the resulting simulation-reality relationship has materially improved. Operational Role SRAM is the fourth internal governance space of the Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Standard (SRCS). The internal progression is: SRCM — Simulation-Reality Comparison Module → establishes what may legitimately be compared. SCCM — Simulation Correlation Criteria Module → establishes the criteria governing correspondence. SDMM — Simulation-Reality Deviation Module → identifies and structures material differences. SRAM — Reality Alignment Module → determines how identified deviations should affect the simulation-reality relationship. SCUM — Correlation Uncertainty Module → governs uncertainty remaining after correlation and alignment. SRAM therefore asks: Given what we now know about the difference between simulation and reality, what should change, what should remain unchanged, and how should the new alignment state be established? Module Operational Space SRAM governs: alignment requirement identification, alignment necessity, alignment eligibility, alignment prioritization, alignment scope, alignment target definition, alignment depth, alignment pathway selection, model alignment, environment alignment, parameter alignment, assumption alignment, input alignment, scenario alignment, behavioral alignment, temporal alignment, spatial alignment, interaction alignment, boundary alignment, condition-specific alignment, subsystem alignment, alignment dependencies, alignment sequencing, alignment authority, alignment controls, alignment implementation, alignment traceability, alignment verification, post-alignment comparison, residual deviation, alignment effectiveness, alignment limitations, alignment conflict, over-alignment prevention, alignment rollback, alignment status, and alignment documentation. Module Function SDMM establishes that a difference exists. SRAM determines what should happen because of that difference. It prevents organizations from assuming that every deviation should automatically result in modification of the simulation. A deviation may instead require: Correction Calibration Refinement Boundary Restriction Scenario Expansion Parameter Adjustment Representation Change Assumption Revision Environmental Adjustment Additional Reality Observation or: No Alignment Action where the difference is intentional, immaterial, unavoidable, or legitimately outside the simulation purpose. Deviation Does Not Automatically Require Alignment SIMULOS® establishes: Observed deviation creates an alignment question, not an automatic alignment instruction. A simulation is necessarily a representation. Some differences from reality may be: intentional, methodologically necessary, computationally justified, immaterial, outside scope, purpose-specific, or inherent to abstraction. SRAM therefore distinguishes: Deviation from: Alignment Requirement. Alignment Requirement An Alignment Requirement exists where an identified Simulation-Reality Deviation materially weakens the simulation's intended correspondence with reality and sufficient basis exists to require a governed response. Conceptually: Governed Deviation ↓ Materiality Assessment ↓ Simulation Purpose & Scope ↓ Correlation Criteria ↓ Alignment Necessity ↓ Alignment Requirement Alignment Necessity For every material deviation, SRAM should ask: Does this difference actually require the simulation to change? Possible outcomes may include: Alignment Required Alignment Conditionally Required Alignment Recommended Alignment Not Required Alignment Not Currently Feasible or: Alignment Necessity Undetermined. Alignment Eligibility Not every observed deviation is sufficiently understood to justify modification. Alignment Eligibility considers whether: the deviation is sufficiently established, the comparison basis is reliable, Operational Reality is sufficiently understood, the probable alignment target is identifiable, relevant dependencies are known, and modification would not introduce greater uncertainty. Do Not Calibrate to Uncertain Reality A critical SRAM principle is: A simulation should not be modified merely to fit a reality observation whose own reliability is materially uncertain. Where the reality basis is insufficient, additional Operational Reality evidence may be required before alignment. Alignment Target An Alignment Target identifies the specific simulation element or relationship requiring modification. Targets may include: Reality Representation, assumption, model component, environment, parameter, input transformation, temporal behavior, scenario condition, interaction rule, subsystem relationship, response function, boundary condition, or another simulation element. Alignment Target ≠ Deviation Location The place where a deviation becomes visible may not be the place where alignment should occur. For example: Trajectory Deviation may originate from: Sensor Representation Error rather than the trajectory model itself. Therefore: Observed Deviation Location ≠ Proven Alignment Target. Alignment Attribution Before modifying a simulation, SRAM should determine whether sufficient evidence connects the deviation to the proposed alignment target. Where attribution remains uncertain: Alignment Target Undetermined should remain legitimate. Alignment Priority Not all deviations require equal attention. Alignment priority may depend upon: Materiality Consequence Frequency Operational Relevance Scenario Importance Deviation Propagation Reliance Correctability and: Uncertainty. Critical Alignment A deviation may receive Critical Alignment priority where simulation-reality divergence materially affects: safety, mission success, autonomous behavior, critical infrastructure, high-consequence decisions, system boundaries, or downstream reliance. Alignment Scope Alignment should be bounded. Possible scopes include: Local Alignment Subsystem Alignment Scenario-Specific Alignment Environment-Specific Alignment Parameter-Range Alignment Behavioral Alignment Whole-Model Alignment or: Multi-Layer Alignment. Minimum Necessary Alignment Principle SIMULOS® establishes: Alignment should modify no more of the simulation than is justified by the governed deviation basis. This reduces the risk that correction of one region unintentionally damages correlation elsewhere. Local Alignment A localized deviation may require only a localized change. For example: incorrect low-temperature battery behavior should not automatically require redesign of unrelated simulation components. Condition-Specific Alignment A simulation may require alignment only under defined conditions. For example: Nominal Conditions → Existing Representation Retained High Radiation → Updated Representation Low Power + High Radiation → Additional Conditional Model This allows the simulation to preserve valid existing behavior while improving deficient regions. Model Alignment Model Alignment modifies the simulation model where evidence demonstrates that model structure or behavior contributes materially to Simulation-Reality Deviation. Environment Alignment Environment Alignment modifies the simulated environment where reality observations demonstrate that the environment does not sufficiently represent relevant Operational Reality. Parameter Alignment Parameter Alignment adjusts parameter values or parameter relationships where the governing basis supports such adjustment. Parameter Fitting ≠ Reality Alignment A simulation can be tuned until historical observations match closely while still representing reality poorly outside the fitted region. SIMULOS® therefore establishes: Parameter fit alone does not establish Reality Alignment. Assumption Alignment Where an assumption materially contributes to deviation, SRAM may require reassessment of that assumption. The assumption itself remains governed under SAS — Simulation Assumption Standard. SRAM governs the correlation-driven requirement to revisit it. Input Alignment Where deviation results from input representation or transformation, SRAM may route the alignment requirement toward the relevant SIDS governance space. Scenario Alignment Reality observations may reveal operational conditions missing from the Scenario Space. In such cases, alignment may require: new scenario identification, new variations, new edge cases, new stress conditions, or: expanded scenario coverage. The relevant scenario design remains governed by SSS — Simulation Scenario Standard. Behavioral Alignment Behavioral Alignment concerns simulation behavior that differs materially from observed Operational Reality. This may involve: autonomous decisions, agent responses, human-system interaction, recovery behavior, coordination, escalation, adaptation, or other dynamic behavior. Temporal Alignment Temporal Alignment addresses material differences in: response latency, event timing, sequencing, duration, recovery time, synchronization, and transition speed. Spatial Alignment Spatial Alignment may address differences in: trajectory, position, geometry, movement, distribution, coverage, or spatial interaction. Interaction Alignment Complex simulations may accurately represent individual components while poorly representing interactions among them. SRAM therefore permits alignment of: relationships rather than merely individual objects. Alignment Dependencies A proposed alignment may affect multiple simulation elements. For example: Environment Alignment ↓ Sensor Response Changes ↓ Autonomous Decision Changes ↓ Trajectory Changes ↓ Output Distribution Changes Alignment dependencies should therefore be mapped before material modification where practical. Alignment Sequencing Where multiple deviations share dependencies, alignment actions should be sequenced so that upstream corrections can be evaluated before unnecessary downstream modifications are made. Conceptually: Probable Root Alignment ↓ Re-Execution ↓ Recomparison ↓ Residual Deviation ↓ Additional Alignment if Required No Cascading Correction Without Reassessment SIMULOS® establishes: A correction should not automatically trigger an uncontrolled chain of additional corrections without renewed simulation-reality assessment. Alignment Authority Material alignment actions should have identifiable authority where changes can affect: safety conclusions, mission models, autonomous behavior, regulatory evidence, operational reliance, validation, or high-consequence decisions. Alignment Implementation Implementation may include: model modification, environment modification, parameter update, assumption revision, scenario expansion, input change, boundary change, resolution increase, interaction-model change, or another controlled simulation modification. Alignment Traceability Every material alignment should remain traceable through: Deviation ID ↓ Alignment Requirement ↓ Alignment Target ↓ Alignment Action ↓ Simulation Version Change ↓ Re-Execution ↓ Post-Alignment Comparison ↓ Alignment Outcome Alignment Does Not End With Modification A simulation is not considered aligned merely because someone changed it. The change must be reassessed against Operational Reality. Therefore: Modification ≠ Alignment. Post-Alignment Comparison After material alignment, the affected simulation region should be compared again against the relevant Operational Reality basis. This creates: Pre-Alignment Deviation ↓ Alignment Action ↓ Post-Alignment Comparison ↓ Residual Deviation Alignment Effectiveness Alignment Effectiveness asks: Did the governed modification materially improve the intended Simulation-Reality Correlation? Possible outcomes may include: Alignment Effective Alignment Partially Effective Alignment Conditionally Effective Alignment Ineffective Alignment Degraded Other Regions or: Alignment Effectiveness Undetermined. Residual Deviation Alignment does not require elimination of all difference. A Residual Deviation is the difference remaining after alignment. Residual deviations may be: acceptable, conditional, material, unresolved, or uncertain. They must remain visible. No Zero-Deviation Requirement SIMULOS® does not establish: Simulation = Reality as the goal. The appropriate goal is: sufficiently governed correspondence for the defined simulation purpose. Over-Alignment Over-Alignment occurs when a simulation is modified beyond what the evidence and intended purpose justify. This can result in: overfitting, loss of generalizability, hidden assumptions, reduced scenario performance, artificial historical fit, or degraded representation elsewhere. No Reality Overfitting Principle SIMULOS® establishes: A simulation should not become so fitted to observed historical reality that it loses legitimate capability to represent unobserved but materially plausible conditions. This is especially important for: rare-event simulation, safety analysis, mission simulation, autonomous systems, climate and environmental simulation, and stress testing. Alignment Conflict An Alignment Conflict exists where improving correlation in one region materially worsens correlation in another. For example: Alignment improves nominal behavior but: degrades edge-case behavior. Such conflict must remain explicit. Multi-Objective Alignment Where multiple correlation objectives exist, alignment may require balancing: nominal accuracy, edge-case representation, temporal behavior, physical behavior, system interaction, safety-critical behavior, and computational feasibility. Alignment Rollback Where an alignment action materially worsens the simulation-reality relationship, the implementation should support rollback or equivalent restoration where technically feasible. Alignment Versioning Material alignment should create or identify a new simulation version where the change affects correlation behavior. Conceptually: Simulation v2.4 ↓ Alignment A-017 ↓ Simulation v2.5 This preserves the relationship between simulation versions and reality-correlation history. Reality Alignment Status A simulation or defined simulation region may receive a status such as: Aligned Conditionally Aligned Partially Aligned Alignment Required Alignment In Progress Alignment Unresolved or: Alignment Status Undetermined. These states should always remain bounded to the applicable correlation scope. Aligned ≠ Reality Equivalent A critical SIMULOS® rule is: Aligned does not mean equivalent to reality. It means that within the defined comparison basis, criteria, conditions, and known uncertainty, the simulation-reality relationship satisfies the applicable alignment requirements. Alignment Across Simulation Versions SRAM may preserve: Version → Deviation Profile → Alignment Actions → Post-Alignment Correlation This creates a historical record of whether simulation evolution actually improves correspondence with reality. Alignment Regression A new simulation version may solve one deviation while reintroducing an older one. SRAM should therefore support detection of: Reality Alignment Regression. Alignment Learning Repeated alignment cycles may reveal persistent structural weaknesses. For example: Repeated environment-related deviations may indicate that the underlying Reality Representation requires deeper revision rather than continued parameter adjustment. Escalation to Upstream SIMULOS® Standards SRAM does not silently take ownership of every simulation component it affects. Instead, it can route required changes back to the appropriate Parent Standard. For example: Representation problem → RRS Assumption problem → SAS Model / Environment problem → SMES Input problem → SIDS Scenario problem → SSS Execution problem → SES This preserves architectural separation. Alignment Re-Entry After an upstream simulation element changes, affected downstream SIMULOS® governance spaces may need reassessment. Conceptually: Reality Deviation ↓ Alignment Requirement ↓ Upstream Simulation Change ↓ Affected Lifecycle Re-Entry ↓ Re-Execution ↓ New Output ↓ New Simulation-Reality Comparison This makes SIMULOS® capable of iterative simulation improvement without collapsing governance spaces into one correction process. Relationship to SRCM SRCM supplies the governed comparison basis. SRAM depends upon that basis when determining whether alignment materially improves correspondence. Relationship to SCCM SCCM provides the criteria defining relevant correspondence. SRAM should not optimize alignment against an undeclared or changing correlation criterion. Relationship to SDMM SDMM produces the governed deviation basis. SRAM consumes that basis and determines the appropriate alignment response. Therefore: Deviation Identification precedes Alignment Action. Relationship to SCUM Even after successful alignment, uncertainty remains. SCUM governs uncertainty in the resulting simulation-to-reality correlation relationship. Therefore: Alignment does not eliminate Correlation Uncertainty. Relationship to ORA™ ORA™ governs Operational Reality itself. SRAM does not redefine reality to make the simulation appear accurate. SIMULOS® uses sufficiently governed reality information to govern the alignment relationship. Relationship to VALIDOS® Successful Reality Alignment does not automatically establish validation. VALIDOS® may use simulation-reality correlation and alignment evidence as part of a broader Validation Determination. Therefore: Reality Alignment ≠ Validation. Relationship to INTEGROS® INTEGROS® may govern integrity properties of alignment evidence, configuration records, measurements, and resulting artifacts. SRAM owns the simulation-specific Reality Alignment relationship. Autonomous Systems Application Autonomous systems may behave differently in simulation and Operational Reality because of: sensor imperfections, timing, physical interactions, human behavior, communication conditions, environment complexity, agent interactions, hardware limitations, or adaptive behavior. SRAM can identify which deviations require actual simulation changes rather than indiscriminate tuning. For example: Simulated autonomous recovery: 1.8 seconds Observed operational recovery: 3.1 seconds The difference alone does not tell engineers what to modify. SRAM requires the deviation to be traced sufficiently before an Alignment Target is established. Space and Mission Simulation Application Space simulation creates an especially important Reality Alignment problem because the most consequential mission conditions may have limited direct real-world observations. A spacecraft simulation may be calibrated against: ground testing, hardware-in-the-loop testing, historical missions, telemetry, subsystem experiments, environmental observations, and limited operational flight data. SRAM prevents the available observations from being treated as complete reality. Alignment may improve correspondence for known conditions while preserving uncertainty for: unobserved radiation combinations, rare subsystem interactions, unknown surface conditions, extreme thermal states, long-duration degradation, communication anomalies, and autonomous recovery behavior. The goal is therefore not: make the simulation look like available historical data. The goal is: improve justified correspondence without destroying the simulation's ability to explore materially plausible reality beyond the observed dataset. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Receive the Governed Deviation Use the SDMM deviation record as the alignment basis. 2. Determine Alignment Necessity Establish whether the deviation requires action. 3. Assess Alignment Eligibility Determine whether the available evidence is sufficient to justify modification. 4. Identify the Alignment Target Determine which simulation element should change. 5. Define Alignment Scope Bound the required modification. 6. Prioritize Alignment Determine urgency and materiality. 7. Map Dependencies Identify potentially affected simulation elements and downstream relationships. 8. Select the Alignment Pathway Determine whether the response requires: calibration, correction, refinement, upstream lifecycle re-entry, scenario expansion, boundary restriction, or another controlled action. 9. Authorize and Implement Alignment Apply the change under controlled configuration governance. 10. Re-Execute the Simulation Produce a new governed execution basis. 11. Perform Post-Alignment Comparison Compare the affected simulation behavior with the relevant Operational Reality basis. 12. Assess Alignment Effectiveness Determine whether correspondence improved and whether new deviations emerged. 13. Preserve Residual Deviation and Uncertainty Do not hide remaining differences. 14. Establish Alignment Status Record the resulting bounded alignment state. Governance Outputs SRAM may produce: Alignment Requirement Record, Alignment Necessity Assessment, Alignment Eligibility Assessment, Alignment Priority, Alignment Target Record, Alignment Scope, Alignment Depth, Alignment Pathway, Alignment Dependency Map, Alignment Sequence, Alignment Authorization Record, Model Alignment Requirement, Environment Alignment Requirement, Parameter Alignment Requirement, Assumption Alignment Requirement, Input Alignment Requirement, Scenario Alignment Requirement, Behavioral Alignment Requirement, Temporal Alignment Requirement, Spatial Alignment Requirement, Interaction Alignment Requirement, Alignment Implementation Record, Alignment Version Record, Post-Alignment Comparison Record, Residual Deviation Record, Alignment Effectiveness Assessment, Alignment Conflict Record, Alignment Regression Record, Alignment Rollback Record, Reality Alignment Status, and Governed Reality Alignment Record. Use Case 1 — Autonomous Robot Reality Gap A warehouse robot performs reliably in simulation but shows materially longer stopping distances on real warehouse floors when: payload is high + surface friction is reduced + rapid turning occurs. SDMM identifies a conditional physical-behavior deviation. SRAM determines that the appropriate Alignment Target is not the autonomous decision logic itself but the simulated physical interaction between: payload + tire behavior + floor friction. The environment and physical model are updated, the affected scenarios are re-executed, and post-alignment comparison determines whether the Reality Gap has materially decreased. Use Case 2 — Spacecraft Thermal Simulation A spacecraft thermal simulation correlates strongly with ground tests and nominal mission telemetry but consistently underestimates temperature accumulation during a particular combination of: high solar exposure + constrained orientation + reduced thermal dissipation. SRAM classifies the deviation as requiring targeted alignment. Instead of globally recalibrating the entire thermal model, the affected environmental and subsystem relationship is modified and the relevant mission scenarios are re-executed. The updated simulation improves correspondence in the affected region while preserving separate uncertainty for extreme mission conditions that have never been directly observed. Architectural Position SRAM is the fourth module of the Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Standard (SRCS). The progression is: SRCM — Simulation-Reality Comparison ↓ SCCM — Simulation Correlation Criteria ↓ SDMM — Simulation-Reality Deviation ↓ SRAM — Reality Alignment ↓ SCUM — Correlation Uncertainty SRAM occupies the point where: knowledge of simulation-reality difference becomes governed action toward improved correspondence. Foundational Principle Reality Alignment must reduce unjustified simulation-reality difference without converting simulation into an overfitted imitation of observed reality or implying that simulation and reality have become equivalent. Canonical Closing Statement Reality Alignment Module (SRAM) governs how identified Simulation-Reality Deviations are translated into justified, bounded, traceable, and reassessable alignment actions. By separating deviation from alignment necessity, observed deviation location from alignment target, modification from demonstrated alignment, parameter fitting from reality correspondence, and alignment from reality equivalence, SRAM enables simulations to improve against Operational Reality without erasing legitimate abstraction, uncertainty, or unobserved but materially plausible conditions. Through controlled alignment scope, dependency mapping, lifecycle re-entry, re-execution, post-alignment comparison, residual-deviation preservation, regression detection, and bounded alignment status, SRAM establishes the governed pathway through which simulation models may learn from reality while remaining simulations rather than becoming artificial reproductions of historical observations.

title: OOF™ Simulation-Reality Comparison Module (SRCM) defines the governance
text: OOF™ Simulation-Reality Comparison Module (SRCM) defines the governance Simulation-Reality Comparison Module (SRCM) defines the governance OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Standard (SRCS) Operational Layer: Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Type: Parent Standard Module Governed Space: Simulation-Reality Comparison Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 19 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Governed Space Simulation-Reality Comparison Canonical Definition Simulation-Reality Comparison Module (SRCM) defines the governance conditions under which simulated conditions, states, behaviors, events, relationships, trajectories, and outputs are systematically compared with corresponding observations from Operational Reality so that similarities, differences, missing correspondence, and unavailable comparison evidence remain explicitly identifiable and traceable. SRCM establishes the first governed comparison layer between: what occurred in simulation and: what occurred in reality. It does not assume that similarity establishes equivalence, nor does it determine whether the observed level of correlation is sufficient for a particular reliance or validation purpose. Operational Role SRCM serves as the first internal governance space of the Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Standard (SRCS). The module asks: What exactly can be compared between the simulation and Operational Reality, and what does that comparison actually show? The governed progression begins: Simulation Evidence + Operational Reality Evidence → Comparison Basis → Correspondence Mapping → Difference Identification → Comparison Record The resulting comparison basis becomes an input to: SCCM — Simulation Correlation Criteria Module. Module Operational Space SRCM governs: simulation-reality comparison objects, comparison purpose, comparison scope, simulation-side evidence, reality-side evidence, comparable variables, comparable states, comparable behaviors, comparable events, comparable trajectories, comparable conditions, comparable outputs, temporal alignment, spatial alignment, state alignment, unit alignment, resolution alignment, abstraction alignment, correspondence mapping, comparison windows, baseline comparison, event comparison, behavioral comparison, trajectory comparison, distributional comparison, sequence comparison, comparison gaps, unavailable reality evidence, unavailable simulation evidence, incomparable elements, observed similarity, observed difference, and complete comparison traceability. Module Function SRCM prevents organizations from moving directly from: “the simulation looks realistic” to: “the simulation represents reality.” Its function is to create an explicit comparison basis before correlation strength, deviations, alignment, or uncertainty are evaluated. The module separates: Simulation Evidence from: Operational Reality Evidence and then establishes which elements can legitimately be compared. Simulation-Reality Comparison Object Every governed comparison should identify the exact phenomenon being compared. A Comparison Object may include: system behavior, autonomous decision, physical trajectory, sensor response, thermal behavior, structural response, failure sequence, communication behavior, resource consumption, human-system interaction, environmental response, recovery behavior, or another materially relevant phenomenon. Comparison Pair SRCM establishes a basic relationship: Simulation Observation ↕ Corresponding Reality Observation A comparison is meaningful only where the relationship between the two sides is sufficiently defined. Comparison Identity A materially relevant comparison should be distinguishable through a stable Comparison ID or equivalent mechanism. Conceptually: Comparison ID ↓ Simulation Execution ↓ Simulation Observation / Output ↓ Reality Observation ↓ Comparison Object ↓ Comparison Conditions ↓ Comparison Result This preserves the provenance of the comparison. Comparison Purpose Before comparison, the organization should establish why the comparison is being performed. Examples include: behavioral correspondence, model calibration support, mission reconstruction, failure investigation, autonomous-system assessment, performance comparison, environmental correspondence, or post-deployment simulation review. Different purposes may require different comparison depth. Comparison Scope SRCM requires the comparison boundary to remain explicit. The comparison may concern: Entire System Subsystem Specific Behavior Specific Scenario Specific Operating Region Specific Failure Mode Specific Time Window or another bounded domain. No Whole-Simulation Inference from Partial Comparison SIMULOS® establishes: Correlation observed within one bounded comparison region must not automatically be represented as correlation across the entire simulation. A simulation may correspond strongly to reality in one region and poorly in another. Simulation-Side Basis The simulation side of the comparison should remain connected to the governed execution that produced it. Where material, this may include: Simulation Execution ID, model version, environment version, scenario, inputs, parameters, assumptions, runtime conditions, observations, and Simulation Outputs. Reality-Side Basis The reality side should identify the Operational Reality evidence against which simulation is compared. This may include: physical measurements, sensor records, operational telemetry, observed system behavior, incident records, mission data, environmental observations, human observations, field-test results, production-system records, or another sufficiently identifiable reality source. ORA™ Relationship ORA™ governs Operational Reality itself. SRCM does not redefine Operational Reality. SRCM consumes or references sufficiently governed reality observations and governs the comparison relationship between those observations and the simulation. Therefore: ORA™ → Operational Reality SIMULOS® SRCM → Simulation ↔ Reality Comparison Comparison Correspondence Mapping Before numerical or qualitative comparison occurs, SRCM should establish which simulation element corresponds to which reality element. Conceptually: Simulation Variable A ↔ Reality Variable A Simulation Event B ↔ Reality Event B Simulation State C ↔ Reality State C Simulation Trajectory D ↔ Reality Trajectory D This prevents comparison between superficially similar but materially different phenomena. Semantic Correspondence Two variables carrying similar names may not represent the same underlying phenomenon. SRCM therefore distinguishes: Label Similarity from: Semantic Correspondence. Unit Alignment Where quantitative comparison is performed, units must be sufficiently aligned. For example: meters ↔ meters seconds ↔ seconds degrees Celsius ↔ degrees Celsius or converted through an explicit transformation. Temporal Alignment Simulation time and Operational Reality time may not correspond directly. SRCM may require alignment of: timestamps, event sequence, elapsed time, phase, cycle, mission stage, or relative temporal position. Temporal Distortion A simulation may reproduce the correct event sequence but at materially different timing. That difference should remain visible. For example: Simulation failure occurs after 120 seconds while: Operational failure occurs after 37 seconds. The presence of the same failure does not establish temporal correspondence. Spatial Alignment Physical and spatial simulations may require alignment of: position, coordinate system, orientation, altitude, distance, geometry, or reference frame. Resolution Alignment Reality observations and simulation observations may exist at different resolutions. For example: Simulation sampling: 1 millisecond Reality telemetry: 1 second A direct point-by-point comparison may therefore be misleading. SRCM requires resolution differences to remain explicit. Abstraction Alignment Simulation may represent reality at a higher abstraction level. For example: Operational Reality may contain: hundreds of interacting physical components while simulation represents them as: one aggregated subsystem. SRCM does not prohibit this abstraction. It requires the comparison to recognize it. Condition Alignment Simulation and reality should not be treated as directly comparable merely because they concern the same system. Relevant conditions may include: environment, load, temperature, velocity, system configuration, software version, hardware version, autonomy state, population, external actors, weather, communication state, or mission phase. Comparable Condition Set SRCM may establish a: Comparable Condition Set representing the conditions sufficiently aligned for comparison. Condition Mismatch Where material conditions differ, the comparison should preserve the mismatch. A condition mismatch does not necessarily make comparison useless. It limits what may legitimately be inferred from it. Behavioral Comparison SRCM may compare how a simulated system behaves relative to the real system. Examples include: decision sequence, control response, navigation behavior, obstacle avoidance, recovery behavior, failure response, resource allocation, or human interaction. Event Comparison Events may be compared according to: Occurrence Non-Occurrence Timing Order Frequency Duration Magnitude and: Context. Trajectory Comparison Trajectory comparison may apply to: spacecraft, aircraft, robots, vehicles, physical processes, economic states, system states, or other evolving phenomena. A trajectory should not be reduced to final-state similarity where the path itself is materially relevant. Sequence Comparison Some simulations must reproduce not merely events but their ordering. For example: Sensor degradation → Navigation error → Recovery attempt → Safe-state transition may differ materially from: Navigation error → Sensor degradation → System shutdown. Even if both end in a safe state, the underlying behavior is different. Distributional Comparison For stochastic systems, individual-run comparison may be insufficient. SRCM may compare: Simulation Distribution with: Observed Reality Distribution. This can include: frequency, variance, tails, rare events, failure rates, response ranges, or other statistical characteristics. Population Comparison Where simulation represents populations, SRCM may govern comparison across: demographic groups, system fleets, agent populations, operating environments, geographic regions, or other relevant populations. Baseline Comparison A baseline may be established to determine whether later simulation versions move: closer to or: further from observed reality. Observed Similarity SRCM may record areas where simulation and reality correspond. However: Observed Similarity is an observation, not a declaration of reality equivalence. Observed Difference Differences should be preserved even where overall correspondence appears strong. Differences may concern: magnitude, timing, sequence, frequency, direction, state, behavior, distribution, or occurrence. No Selective Similarity Principle SIMULOS® establishes: A Simulation-Reality Comparison must not preserve only the dimensions in which simulation performs well while silently excluding materially relevant dimensions in which correspondence is weak. Comparison Gap A Comparison Gap exists where a materially relevant simulation phenomenon cannot currently be compared with Operational Reality. Reasons may include: reality has not yet occurred, measurement is unavailable, telemetry is missing, the phenomenon cannot be safely tested, reality evidence is inaccessible, the simulation contains an abstract construct with no direct physical equivalent, or the comparison method is insufficient. No Reality Evidence ≠ Simulation Confirmation A foundational SRCM rule is: The absence of contradictory reality evidence does not establish that the simulation corresponds to reality. Where Operational Reality evidence does not exist, the comparison status should remain appropriately bounded. Comparison Availability States SRCM may classify comparison availability as: Directly Comparable Conditionally Comparable Partially Comparable Indirectly Comparable Not Currently Comparable or: Comparability Undetermined. Incomparable Elements Some simulation elements may legitimately have no direct reality counterpart. These should remain identifiable rather than being forced into artificial comparison. Comparison Evidence Quality SRCM does not own general validation of evidence quality. However, it should preserve whether the comparison basis depends upon: incomplete measurements, sparse observations, uncertain telemetry, transformed data, indirect observations, or another material limitation. These limitations propagate downstream. Point-in-Time Comparison SRCM may support reconstruction of questions such as: Which simulation version was compared? Which real system version was observed? Which scenario was used? Which operational conditions existed? Which variables were compared? Which variables were unavailable? Which transformations were applied? Which differences were observed? Comparison Matrix A practical SRCM implementation may establish a Simulation-Reality Comparison Matrix. Example structure: Phenomenon → Simulation Representation → Reality Observation → Alignment Conditions → Comparison Availability → Observed Relationship → Limitation This creates a structured basis for downstream correlation assessment. Space and Mission Simulation For space missions, direct Operational Reality evidence may be expensive, sparse, delayed, or available only after deployment. SRCM can compare: simulated trajectories with mission trajectories, predicted thermal states with flight telemetry, simulated communication loss with actual communication behavior, simulated navigation uncertainty with observed navigation error, simulated subsystem failures with mission anomalies, and simulated autonomous recovery with actual recovery behavior. This allows every mission to become a potential source of evidence for improving the simulation-reality relationship. Autonomous Systems For autonomous systems, comparison may extend beyond final performance. SRCM can compare: decisions, action sequences, recovery paths, timing, interaction patterns, environmental responses, failure behavior, and emergent system behavior. This matters because two systems may achieve the same final outcome through materially different behavioral paths. Digital Twins A digital twin may appear visually or numerically close to its physical counterpart while diverging in specific operational regions. SRCM provides a structured basis for comparing: Digital Representation against: Physical Operational Reality without presuming that the existence of the digital twin establishes correspondence. Comparison at Scale Organizations may possess millions of simulation runs but only limited Operational Reality observations. SRCM allows reality evidence to be mapped against relevant subsets of the simulation population rather than treating the complete simulation corpus as equally correlated. Reality Evidence Accumulation Simulation-to-Reality Comparison may improve over time as Operational Reality produces additional evidence. The comparison relationship is therefore potentially dynamic. A previously: Not Currently Comparable simulation phenomenon may later become: Directly Comparable when operational evidence becomes available. Historical Comparison Preservation New Operational Reality evidence should not erase earlier comparison states. Historical comparison records may reveal whether simulation correspondence is: improving, degrading, stable, condition-dependent, or previously misunderstood. Comparison Does Not Equal Correlation Determination SRCM establishes the comparison basis. It does not determine: how much similarity is sufficient. That question moves to: SCCM — Simulation Correlation Criteria Module. Comparison Does Not Equal Deviation Governance SRCM identifies observed differences. Detailed governance of material simulation-reality deviations belongs to: SDMM — Simulation-Reality Deviation Module. Comparison Does Not Equal Reality Alignment SRCM identifies correspondence and difference. Governance of how the simulation may be brought into better alignment with reality belongs to: SRAM — Reality Alignment Module. Comparison Does Not Resolve Correlation Uncertainty Uncertainty surrounding the simulation-reality relationship belongs to: SCUM — Correlation Uncertainty Module. Internal SRCS Flow SRCM — Simulation-Reality Comparison ↓ SCCM — Simulation Correlation Criteria ↓ SDMM — Simulation-Reality Deviation ↓ SRAM — Reality Alignment ↓ SCUM — Correlation Uncertainty SRCM therefore creates the empirical comparison foundation upon which the remainder of SRCS operates. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Define the Comparison Object Identify exactly which simulated and real phenomenon is being compared. 2. Establish Comparison Purpose Define why the comparison is required. 3. Establish Comparison Scope Identify included and excluded regions, conditions, variables, behaviors, and time periods. 4. Bind Simulation Evidence Connect the comparison to the applicable Simulation Execution and outputs. 5. Bind Operational Reality Evidence Identify the corresponding real-world observations. 6. Establish Correspondence Mapping Map simulation variables, states, events, behaviors, and outputs to their reality counterparts. 7. Align Comparison Conditions Assess temporal, spatial, unit, resolution, abstraction, state, and environmental alignment. 8. Perform the Comparison Compare the materially relevant phenomena. 9. Preserve Similarities and Differences Do not selectively retain favorable correspondence. 10. Identify Comparison Gaps Record unavailable, incomplete, indirect, or incomparable elements. 11. Establish Comparison Availability Status Classify the degree to which meaningful comparison is currently possible. 12. Produce the Simulation-Reality Comparison Record Create the governed comparison basis for downstream correlation criteria and deviation governance. Governance Outputs SRCM may produce: Simulation-Reality Comparison ID, Comparison Object Record, Comparison Purpose Record, Comparison Scope Record, Simulation Evidence Binding, Operational Reality Evidence Binding, Correspondence Map, Comparable Variable Set, Comparable State Set, Comparable Event Set, Comparable Behavior Set, Comparable Condition Set, Temporal Alignment Record, Spatial Alignment Record, Unit Alignment Record, Resolution Alignment Record, Abstraction Alignment Record, Condition Mismatch Record, Behavioral Comparison Record, Event Comparison Record, Trajectory Comparison Record, Sequence Comparison Record, Distributional Comparison Record, Population Comparison Record, Observed Similarity Record, Observed Difference Record, Comparison Gap Record, Incomparable Element Record, Comparison Availability Status, Simulation-Reality Comparison Matrix, and Governed Simulation-Reality Comparison Record. Use Case 1 — Spacecraft Mission Simulation vs Flight Reality A space agency executes extensive pre-mission simulations covering trajectory, thermal behavior, navigation, communication, subsystem failure, and autonomous recovery. After launch, SRCM maps actual mission telemetry against the corresponding simulation conditions. The comparison reveals that trajectory and thermal behavior correspond closely within tested regions, while communication degradation begins materially earlier in Operational Reality than in simulation. SRCM does not declare the simulation valid or invalid. It establishes exactly: where correspondence exists, where difference exists, under which conditions, and where reality evidence remains insufficient. The resulting comparison record provides the basis for correlation criteria, deviation analysis, and future reality alignment. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Robot Simulation vs Deployment Behavior An autonomous mobile robot performs reliably across millions of simulated warehouse scenarios. After deployment, operational records show that its obstacle-avoidance behavior differs when reflective surfaces, human movement, and temporary sensor degradation occur simultaneously. SRCM compares the relevant simulated behaviors with the corresponding Operational Reality observations across: decision sequence, sensor state, response timing, trajectory, recovery behavior, and environmental conditions. The organization can then distinguish between simulation regions that correspond strongly to deployment reality and regions where the simulation-reality relationship remains weak or insufficiently observed. Architectural Position SRCM is the first module of the Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Standard (SRCS). It transforms: Simulation Evidence + Operational Reality Evidence into: Governed Simulation-Reality Comparison Record. That record becomes the foundation for determining correlation criteria, identifying deviations, governing reality alignment, and expressing correlation uncertainty. Foundational Principle Simulation similarity is not reality equivalence. Canonical Closing Statement Simulation-Reality Comparison Module establishes the governed empirical bridge between simulation and Operational Reality by identifying what can legitimately be compared, binding simulation evidence to corresponding reality observations, aligning materially relevant conditions, preserving both similarities and differences, exposing comparison gaps, and maintaining complete comparison traceability. SRCM prevents visual similarity, isolated matching outcomes, or the absence of contradictory evidence from being transformed into unsupported claims of reality correspondence. By establishing a structured Simulation-Reality Comparison Record before correlation is judged, deviation is interpreted, alignment is attempted, or uncertainty is bounded, SRCM provides the foundational comparison layer through which SIMULOS® can determine what simulation actually demonstrates about the reality it claims to represent.

title: OOF™ Resimulation Trigger Module (SRGM)
text: OOF™ Resimulation Trigger Module (SRGM) Resimulation Trigger Module (SRGM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Standard (SLRS) Module: SRGM — Resimulation Trigger Module Operational Layer: Resimulation Trigger Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Resimulation Trigger Governance Origin ID: SIMULOS-SLRS-SRGM-012.3 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 20 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Resimulation Trigger Module (SRGM) is the third Core Module of the Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Standard (SLRS) within SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture. SRGM governs the determination of when recognized Simulation Drift, material change, new evidence, changed simulation conditions, changed reality relationships, or other simulation-relevant lifecycle developments require a simulation to be executed again, updated before execution, partially repeated, comprehensively repeated, reconsidered, or escalated toward replacement or retirement assessment. The Module transforms recognized lifecycle divergence into an explicit Resimulation Trigger State. SRGM does not determine the detailed scope of the required resimulation. That responsibility belongs to SRSM — Resimulation Scope Module. Its task is narrower and foundational: to determine whether the existing governed simulation basis remains sufficient for continued simulation-specific use or whether a new simulation cycle must be initiated. Architectural Position SRGM is the third module within SLRS. It follows: SDRM — Simulation Drift Recognition Module and precedes: SRSM — Resimulation Scope Module. The sequence is: Lifecycle Monitoring → Drift Recognition → Resimulation Trigger → Resimulation Scope. SLMM identifies materially relevant lifecycle changes. SDRM determines whether those changes constitute Simulation Drift. SRGM determines whether the resulting condition requires a new simulation cycle. SRSM then determines what must actually be resimulated. Internal Flow Position Governed Simulation Drift Record Material Change Evidence Current Simulation Use Context → Trigger Candidate Identification → Trigger Relevance Assessment → Materiality Assessment → Existing Simulation Sufficiency Assessment → Continued-Use Consequence Assessment → Trigger Threshold Evaluation → Resimulation Trigger State → Governed Resimulation Trigger Record → SRSM — Resimulation Scope Module Operational Space SRGM governs the space between: recognized simulation-relevant change or drift and the formal initiation of a new simulation cycle. This operational space includes: trigger candidate identification; trigger source classification; drift-trigger relationships; material-change triggers; threshold-based triggers; event-based triggers; cumulative triggers; temporal triggers; evidence-based triggers; uncertainty-driven triggers; scenario emergence triggers; object-change triggers; model-change triggers; input-change triggers; correlation-change triggers; reliance-change triggers; trigger materiality; trigger urgency; trigger state; trigger escalation; trigger deferral conditions; trigger documentation. Operational Scope SRGM applies wherever previously governed simulations continue to be referenced, reused, compared, interpreted, relied upon, or incorporated into subsequent simulation, evidential, validation, engineering, scientific, mission, safety, or operational processes. It may govern resimulation triggers for: individual simulation runs; repeated simulation programs; scenario portfolios; simulation campaigns; digital twins; engineering simulations; scientific simulations; mission simulations; safety simulations; infrastructure simulations; economic simulations; AI simulations; autonomous-system simulations; continuously updated simulations; long-lived simulation programs; future simulation technologies. The Module remains technology-neutral. Its concern is not how expensive or computationally difficult resimulation may be. Its concern is whether continued use of the existing simulation basis remains methodologically supportable without a new simulation cycle. Drift Recognition ≠ Automatic Resimulation SRGM establishes the fundamental distinction: Recognized Simulation Drift ≠ Automatic Resimulation Not every recognized divergence requires another simulation. A drift condition may be: immaterial to the current use; outside the applicable scope; confined to an unused configuration; limited to an irrelevant scenario family; already bounded by an existing limitation; insufficiently developed to justify immediate resimulation; appropriate for continued monitoring. Conversely, relatively small drift may require immediate resimulation where it affects a highly sensitive or consequential simulation condition. The trigger must therefore be determined from the relationship between the change and the continuing use of the simulation. Trigger Candidate Principle Any lifecycle development capable of materially affecting the legitimate continuing use of a simulation may become a Resimulation Trigger Candidate . Trigger Candidates may originate from: Simulation Object change; configuration change; reality change; representation change; assumption change; model change; simulation environment change; input or data change; scenario change; execution anomaly; output anomaly; correlation change; evidence degradation; changed reliance context; temporal expiration; newly discovered uncertainty; newly discovered failure mode; new operational observations; cumulative minor changes; compound Simulation Drift. A Trigger Candidate is not yet a Resimulation Trigger. It must first be assessed. Trigger Source Classification SRGM requires the source of a potential trigger to remain explicit. A trigger may be classified as: Object Trigger A material change to the Simulation Object. Reality Trigger A material change in the reality represented by the simulation. Representation Trigger A material deficiency or change in how reality is represented. Assumption Trigger A material assumption has changed, weakened, failed, or become uncertain. Model Trigger The simulation model has materially changed or become insufficient for continued use. Environment Trigger The simulation environment or relevant simulation dependencies have materially changed. Input Trigger The input basis or relevant data distribution has materially changed. Scenario Trigger A new materially relevant scenario, edge case, stress condition, or scenario class has emerged. Execution Trigger Execution behavior reveals anomalies, instability, drift, or conditions requiring renewed simulation. Output Trigger Outputs reveal unexpected or materially unresolved behavior. Correlation Trigger Simulation-to-reality correlation materially changes or deteriorates. Evidence Trigger Simulation-derived evidence loses qualification, weight, applicability, or relevance. Temporal Trigger A defined review period or simulation applicability period has expired. Multiple trigger sources may coexist. Material Change Trigger A material change may require resimulation where it alters one or more conditions upon which the existing simulation results materially depend. Examples include: new hardware configuration; software revision; changed physical component; changed environmental range; altered operating conditions; changed mission profile; changed behavioral logic; changed sensor characteristics; changed parameter range; changed infrastructure dependency. The relevant question is not: Did the object change? It is: Does the change materially affect the simulation basis upon which continued use depends? Scenario Emergence Trigger A new real-world or anticipated scenario may create a Resimulation Trigger even where the Simulation Object itself has not changed. Examples include: newly observed failure combinations; new environmental extremes; new interaction patterns; new adversarial conditions; newly relevant edge cases; expanded operational domains; new mission phases; new human-system interactions. Where the new scenario lies outside previously governed scenario coverage and materially affects the intended use of the simulation evidence, resimulation may be required. Correlation Trigger A previously acceptable simulation may require resimulation where new reality observations materially alter the established simulation-to-reality relationship. Examples include: systematic real-world deviation; unexpected operational behavior; repeated prediction mismatch; degraded physical correspondence; changed environmental relationship; new empirical measurements. SRCS governs the correlation relationship. SRGM determines whether a material change in that relationship activates a new simulation cycle. Evidence Degradation Trigger Simulation evidence may become weaker even where the original simulation remains technically reproducible. SERBS or lifecycle monitoring may identify: degraded evidential weight; reduced applicability; expired temporal relevance; new contradictory evidence; changed reliance conditions; weakened correlation; invalidated assumptions. SRGM may treat such developments as Trigger Candidates. Reproducible Simulation ≠ Permanently Sufficient Evidence. Cumulative Trigger Principle A series of individually non-triggering changes may collectively require resimulation. Therefore: No Single Trigger ≠ No Resimulation Requirement SRGM must permit cumulative trigger assessment. For example: Minor Object Revision Small Input Distribution Shift New Edge Cases Moderate Correlation Deterioration may collectively cross a resimulation threshold even though none independently would do so. Compound Trigger Principle Trigger conditions may interact non-linearly. A changed assumption may become material only after a model update. A new scenario may become critical only after an operational-domain expansion. A modest correlation decline may become significant after reliance expands. SRGM therefore evaluates both: individual Trigger Candidates and combined Trigger Conditions. Trigger Threshold Organizations may define explicit Resimulation Trigger Thresholds. Thresholds may be: qualitative; quantitative; probabilistic; event-based; consequence-based; sensitivity-based; time-based; configuration-based; evidence-based; hybrid. SIMULOS® does not prescribe one universal numerical threshold. The threshold must instead remain: explicit; relevant to the simulation purpose; connected to materiality; sensitive to the consequence of continued use; reviewable; traceable to its governance basis. Trigger Sensitivity Different simulation contexts may legitimately require different trigger sensitivity. A minor change may justify resimulation where: simulation evidence supports safety-critical decisions; the model is highly sensitive to the changed variable; the simulation governs narrow tolerance conditions; correlation is already uncertain; consequences of unsupported reliance are severe. The same change may not justify immediate resimulation for: exploratory analysis; historical comparison; broad conceptual modeling; an unaffected scenario family. Therefore: Trigger Sensitivity Must Follow Simulation Relevance, Not Change Magnitude Alone. Trigger Urgency SRGM distinguishes whether resimulation is: Non-Urgent Resimulation is required but continued bounded use remains temporarily acceptable. Scheduled Resimulation must occur within a defined lifecycle or review window. Priority Resimulation should occur before specified further reliance or decision activity. Immediate Existing simulation reliance should not continue for the affected use until resimulation or another governed response occurs. Urgency does not determine scope. SRSM determines the required resimulation scope. Resimulation Trigger States SRGM may assign a governed Resimulation Trigger State. 1. No Trigger Available change or drift does not require a new simulation cycle for the defined use. 2. Monitor A Trigger Candidate exists, but current evidence does not justify resimulation. The condition remains under lifecycle monitoring. 3. Conditional Trigger Resimulation becomes required if a defined condition, threshold, event, use expansion, or additional change occurs. 4. Triggered A governed basis exists for initiating resimulation. 5. Priority Trigger Resimulation is required before specified further reliance, use, or lifecycle progression. 6. Immediate Trigger The affected simulation basis should not continue to support the relevant use without immediate resimulation or another governed lifecycle response. 7. Indeterminate Available information is insufficient to determine whether resimulation is required. An Indeterminate state must not silently become No Trigger. Trigger Deferral A valid trigger may sometimes be deferred. Deferral may occur where: required data are temporarily unavailable; a replacement model is being prepared; the affected simulation use has been suspended; the relevant operational condition will not occur before resimulation; another controlled mitigation temporarily bounds reliance. Deferral must identify: reason; affected simulation; affected use; temporary limitations; expiration condition; review point. Deferred Trigger ≠ Cancelled Trigger. Trigger Closure A Trigger Candidate or Trigger State must eventually reach a governed disposition. Possible dispositions include: no resimulation required; continue monitoring; conditional trigger retained; resimulation initiated; trigger superseded; simulation replaced; simulation retired. Unresolved Trigger Candidates must not disappear merely because time passes. Resimulation Trigger ≠ Resimulation Scope SRGM determines whether a new simulation cycle is required. It does not determine whether the response requires: one repeated run; one scenario; one parameter region; one subsystem; one configuration; a partial campaign; a complete campaign; model reconstruction; simulation replacement. That determination belongs to: SRSM — Resimulation Scope Module. Therefore: Trigger ≠ Scope. Resimulation Trigger ≠ Validation Trigger A Simulation Resimulation Trigger concerns the need to re-enter the simulation lifecycle. A Validation Trigger concerns broader validation governance. A change may trigger: resimulation only; revalidation only; both; neither. VALIDOS® remains responsible for broader validation lifecycle governance. Negative Results as Trigger Inputs Failed or anomalous simulations may themselves generate Trigger Candidates. Examples include: unexpected instability; unexplained divergence; inconsistent repetitions; previously unseen failure; unexplained sensitivity; execution-specific anomalies; output patterns inconsistent with prior campaigns. A failed execution does not automatically require resimulation. But failure must remain available to trigger governance rather than being discarded as computational noise without assessment. Traceability of Trigger Decisions Every material trigger determination should remain traceable through: Change Signal → Simulation Drift Record → Trigger Candidate → Affected Simulation Basis → Current Use Context → Materiality → Threshold → Trigger State → Urgency → Disposition → Resimulation Scope Assessment This enables organizations to reconstruct not merely that resimulation occurred, but why it became necessary. SRGM Boundary with SLMM SLMM identifies lifecycle change. SRGM does not independently replace lifecycle monitoring. It receives relevant lifecycle information as trigger inputs. Monitoring Signal ≠ Resimulation Trigger. SRGM Boundary with SDRM SDRM determines whether lifecycle change constitutes Simulation Drift. SRGM determines whether that recognized drift requires a new simulation cycle. Therefore: Simulation Drift ≠ Automatic Resimulation. SRGM Boundary with SRSM SRGM determines whether resimulation is required. SRSM determines what portion of the simulation lifecycle, scenario space, configuration space, or simulation campaign must be repeated or reconstructed. Therefore: Trigger Decision ≠ Scope Decision. SRGM Boundary with SERBS SERBS may identify degraded evidence, changed applicability, reduced evidential weight, or changed reliance boundaries. SRGM may consume these conditions as Trigger Candidates. It does not independently redefine simulation evidence qualification, weight, or reliance. SRGM Boundary with SRCS SRCS governs simulation-to-reality correlation. SRGM may consume material correlation change as a trigger input. It does not determine correlation itself. SRGM Boundary with VALIDOS® SRGM does not determine whether broader revalidation is required. Its decision is simulation-specific: Must a new simulation cycle be initiated? VALIDOS® governs whether a Validation Object requires revalidation and what validation lifecycle response is necessary. SRGM Boundary with ORA™ ORA™ governs Operational Reality. Changes in Operational Reality may create Trigger Candidates where they affect the simulation basis. SRGM does not determine or govern Operational Reality itself. SRGM Boundary with INTEGROS® INTEGROS® governs integrity properties. An integrity issue may become a Trigger Candidate where it materially affects simulation relevance, but SRGM does not replace integrity governance. SRGM Boundary with ADIT® ADIT® may audit whether trigger evidence, decisions, thresholds, records, and lifecycle actions are preserved and verifiable. SRGM governs the simulation-specific trigger determination itself. Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum SRGM implementation should establish: 1. Trigger Candidate Intake Receive recognized Simulation Drift, material changes, new evidence, anomalies, correlation changes, and other simulation-relevant lifecycle signals. 2. Affected Simulation Identification Identify the simulation, campaign, configuration, scenario family, evidence basis, or other simulation asset potentially affected. 3. Current Use Context Determine how the existing simulation is currently being used, interpreted, or relied upon. 4. Trigger Relevance Assessment Determine whether the Trigger Candidate can materially affect that continuing use. 5. Materiality Assessment Assess the significance of the change relative to the simulation basis and intended reliance. 6. Cumulative and Compound Assessment Evaluate whether multiple changes collectively create a trigger condition. 7. Trigger Threshold Evaluation Compare the condition against the applicable qualitative, quantitative, event-based, temporal, or hybrid trigger criteria. 8. Trigger State Assignment Assign an explicit Resimulation Trigger State. 9. Urgency and Deferral Control Determine urgency and document any controlled trigger deferral. 10. Trigger Record Creation Create a traceable record linking the trigger determination to its originating lifecycle conditions and downstream scope assessment. Use Case 1 — Space Mission Simulation: Mission Configuration Changes After Qualification Campaign A spacecraft mission completes an extensive simulation campaign covering guidance, navigation, propulsion, thermal behavior, landing sequences, communication loss, contingency procedures, and mission-critical failure conditions. The simulation evidence supports a defined mission configuration. Months later, before launch, several changes occur: a flight-software update modifies guidance behavior; spacecraft mass distribution changes; a component is replaced; new environmental observations alter part of the landing-condition model; mission planners modify one phase of the descent profile. None of these changes automatically proves that the previous simulation campaign is unusable. Equally, the organization cannot safely assume that millions of previously successful simulation executions still represent the modified mission configuration. SRGM receives the recognized drift conditions and determines whether they cross a governed Resimulation Trigger. The Module asks: Which changes materially affect the basis upon which the existing mission simulations continue to be relied upon? A guidance-software modification affecting descent control may create a Priority Trigger. A component change outside the simulated behavioral pathway may create No Trigger. Updated environmental observations may create a Conditional Trigger pending assessment of whether the new conditions fall outside previous scenario coverage. The result is not automatic repetition of the entire mission campaign. It is a governed determination that establishes whether resimulation is required before deciding what must be resimulated. This prevents two costly failures: continuing to rely on stale mission simulations and repeating enormous simulation campaigns after changes that do not materially affect their basis. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Vehicle or Robot: New Real-World Failure Pattern After Deployment An autonomous vehicle or mobile robot has completed millions of simulated scenarios before deployment. After limited real-world operation, a previously rare interaction pattern begins appearing: a combination of unusual lighting, partial sensor obstruction, human movement, and environmental geometry causes behavior that was not adequately represented in the original scenario portfolio. The individual real-world events are uncommon. However, they reveal: a new scenario class; changed understanding of sensor behavior; possible representation limitations; weakened simulation-to-reality correlation in the affected conditions; reduced evidential applicability of the original simulation campaign. SRGM does not automatically order a complete rerun of millions of simulations. Instead, it evaluates whether the new evidence creates a Resimulation Trigger. If the condition affects a safety-relevant operational domain and lies outside previously governed scenario coverage, SRGM may assign an Immediate Trigger or Priority Trigger for the affected simulation basis. The decision then passes to SRSM, which may determine that only: the affected sensor conditions + scenario family + environmental range + related autonomous behaviors require targeted resimulation. The governance advantage is substantial.
