Without a trigger framework, an organization may either dismiss rare real-world failures because the system passed millions of simulations or repeatedly rerun huge campaigns without knowing which part actually requires renewed testing. SRGM creates the decision layer between those extremes: new real-world evidence does not automatically invalidate all previous simulation, but material evidence must be capable of forcing simulation back into the lifecycle when the existing basis is no longer sufficient. Governance Outputs SRGM may produce: Resimulation Trigger Candidate Record Trigger Source Classification Affected Simulation Basis Record Current Simulation Use Context Record Trigger Relevance Assessment Trigger Materiality Assessment Cumulative Trigger Assessment Compound Trigger Assessment Trigger Threshold Record Resimulation Trigger State Trigger Urgency Classification Trigger Deferral Record Trigger Disposition Record Governed Resimulation Trigger Record Resimulation Scope Assessment Input These outputs provide the governed basis for: SRSM — Resimulation Scope Module. Enterprise Application SRGM gives organizations a systematic method for deciding when simulation must be performed again. This becomes increasingly important as simulation programs grow larger, more expensive, more continuous, and more deeply connected to operational decisions. Without explicit trigger governance, organizations risk two opposite failures: under-resimulation — continuing to rely upon simulation after material conditions have changed; and over-resimulation — repeatedly executing expensive simulation campaigns after changes that do not materially affect the relevant simulation basis. SRGM enables organizations to establish trigger logic around: product revisions; software updates; hardware changes; environmental changes; newly discovered edge cases; changed data distributions; model updates; new operational observations; degraded simulation-to-reality correlation; evidence degradation; changed reliance contexts; accumulated lifecycle drift. For very large simulation campaigns, this can materially reduce unnecessary computational effort while ensuring that genuinely consequential change forces the simulation lifecycle to reopen. SRGM therefore transforms resimulation from an ad hoc organizational judgment into a traceable governance decision. Foundational Principles Simulation Drift does not automatically require resimulation. Absence of one decisive change does not mean absence of a cumulative trigger. A Resimulation Trigger must be connected to the continuing use of the simulation. Trigger sensitivity should reflect simulation relevance and consequence, not change magnitude alone. New scenarios can trigger resimulation even when the Simulation Object has not changed. New reality evidence can trigger resimulation even when the simulation remains technically reproducible. Deferred resimulation is not cancelled resimulation. An indeterminate trigger must not silently become No Trigger. Trigger determination and resimulation scope are separate governance decisions. The purpose of trigger governance is neither to maximize nor minimize resimulation, but to ensure that resimulation occurs when the existing simulation basis can no longer legitimately support continued use. Canonical Closing Statement Resimulation Trigger Module establishes the lifecycle decision layer of the Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Standard by transforming recognized Simulation Drift, material change, emerging scenarios, new evidence, correlation change, uncertainty, anomalies, temporal conditions, and cumulative or compound lifecycle developments into explicit and traceable Resimulation Trigger States. Through governance of Trigger Candidates, trigger sources, materiality, thresholds, sensitivity, cumulative and compound conditions, urgency, deferral, disposition, and traceability, SRGM prevents simulations from being repeated merely because change occurred while also preventing materially stale simulation bases from remaining in use because no single change appeared sufficient to force reconsideration. By separating lifecycle monitoring from drift recognition, drift recognition from trigger determination, trigger determination from resimulation scope, and resimulation from broader validation governance, SRGM creates the controlled decision point through which a governed simulation lifecycle may legitimately reopen. A simulation should be performed again not simply because reality changed, but because the change materially affects the basis upon which continued simulation use depends.

title: OOF™ Simulation Repetition Module (SRPM)
text: OOF™ Simulation Repetition Module (SRPM) Simulation Repetition Module (SRPM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Simulation Execution Standard (SES) Operational Layer: Simulation Execution Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Type: Parent Standard Module Governed Space: Simulation Repetition Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 19 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Governed Space Simulation Repetition Canonical Definition Simulation Repetition Module (SRPM) defines the governance framework through which Simulation Executions are deliberately repeated under controlled, traceable, and sufficiently comparable conditions so that repeated runs can reveal stochastic variation, consistency, instability, sensitivity, rare behavior, execution divergence, and other materially relevant differences without allowing repetition volume to be mistaken for independent evidence or methodological strength. SRPM governs: what must remain constant, what may deliberately vary, why repetition is required, how repeated executions are related, and under which conditions their results may legitimately be compared or aggregated. Its purpose is to transform repeated simulation from: “run it again” into: a governed repetition process. Operational Role SRPM serves as the fourth internal governance space of the Simulation Execution Standard (SES). The preceding modules establish: SIM — What exact simulation instance was instantiated? SECM — How was active execution controlled? SOM — What materially relevant behavior and events were observed during execution? SRPM asks: When the simulation is repeated, which execution conditions must remain fixed, which may change, and how can the resulting runs remain meaningfully distinguishable and comparable? The governed progression is: Completed / Repeatable Simulation Execution ↓ Repetition Requirement ↓ Reference Execution ↓ Controlled Constant Conditions ↓ Permitted Variation ↓ Repetition Identity ↓ Repeated Simulation Executions ↓ Repetition Comparability ↓ Repetition Variance & Divergence ↓ Repetition Sufficiency ↓ Governed Simulation Repetition Set ↓ Execution Documentation Module Operational Space SRPM governs: repetition requirements, repetition purpose, repetition identity, reference executions, repetition sets, repeat-run configuration, controlled constants, permitted variation, intentional variation, accidental variation, repeated execution binding, repeatability, reproducibility conditions, stochastic repetition, deterministic repetition, randomization, random seed governance, seed variation, initialization variation, execution-order variation, repetition sequencing, repetition independence, repetition dependence, repeated-run comparability, repeated-run equivalence, repetition divergence, repetition variance, rare-event emergence, convergence signals, repetition saturation, repetition sufficiency, repetition gaps, repetition failure, repetition drift, repetition versioning, repetition lineage, and repetition traceability. Module Function SRPM exists to prevent: repeated runs being treated as independent when they are not, identical runs being counted as broad simulation evidence, hidden parameter changes across repetitions, changed model or environment versions being treated as repetition of the same simulation, random seed changes disappearing, uncontrolled execution drift being mistaken for stochastic behavior, deterministic divergence being ignored, stochastic consistency being overstated, rare events being dismissed as anomalies without governance, successful repetitions being retained while failed repetitions disappear, arbitrary repetition counts being represented as methodological sufficiency, and large Monte Carlo campaigns being treated as meaningful merely because the run count is large. Simulation Repetition A Simulation Repetition is a subsequent governed Simulation Execution intentionally related to one or more prior executions for the purpose of examining behavior under materially equivalent or deliberately modified execution conditions. Conceptually: Reference Execution → Governed Repetition Conditions → Repeated Execution Repetition Requirement A Repetition Requirement establishes why simulation repetition is necessary. Possible purposes include: examining stochastic variability, assessing consistency, determining execution stability, exploring uncertainty, evaluating sensitivity, identifying rare behavior, comparing alternative seeds, confirming unexpected observations, examining nondeterminism, evaluating distributional behavior, or supporting a broader simulation campaign. No Repetition-for-Volume Principle SIMULOS® establishes: A simulation should not be repeated merely to inflate execution count where additional repetitions do not materially improve the governed simulation inquiry. Reference Execution A Reference Execution provides a defined execution basis against which subsequent repetitions may be compared. It should remain traceable to: Execution ID, Simulation Object, model version, environment version, scenario, Input Set, parameter configuration, randomization state, execution controls, and relevant runtime conditions. Reference Execution ≠ Correct Execution A Reference Execution establishes comparison context. It does not establish that the reference behavior was valid, expected, correct, or desirable. Controlled Constants A repetition process should identify which materially relevant execution conditions are intended to remain constant. These may include: Simulation Object version, model version, environment version, Scenario ID, Input Set, parameter configuration, hardware state, software state, execution-control rules, initialization conditions, external dependencies, or other materially relevant conditions. Controlled Constant Principle A condition cannot support repetition comparability if the repetition process does not know whether that condition remained unchanged. Permitted Variation Some repetition dimensions may deliberately change. Possible examples include: random seed, stochastic sampling, initial state, timing, actor behavior, uncertain parameter values, external-event ordering, or another explicitly governed variable. Permitted variation should remain distinguishable from uncontrolled deviation. Intentional vs Accidental Variation SRPM establishes: Intentional Variation → deliberately introduced to examine a defined simulation question. Accidental Variation → arises without governed design or adequate control. These two conditions must not be conflated. Repetition Identity Every repeated execution should retain its own execution identity while remaining connected to its repetition family. Conceptually: Repetition Set RS-001 may include: Execution E-001 Execution E-002 Execution E-003 and: Execution E-004 Each run remains independently traceable. Repetition Set A Simulation Repetition Set is a governed collection of related Simulation Executions performed under explicitly defined repetition conditions. The set may identify: Reference Execution, repetition purpose, controlled constants, permitted variation, number of executions, randomization basis, comparability conditions, and resulting execution statuses. Repetition Set ≠ Scenario Set A Scenario Set defines which conditions should be simulated. A Repetition Set defines how one or more scenario executions are repeated. Therefore: Scenario diversity ≠ Repetition and: Repetition volume ≠ Scenario Coverage. Deterministic Repetition A deterministic simulation is expected to produce materially equivalent behavior when materially equivalent execution conditions are reproduced. Where materially different behavior emerges, SRPM may identify: Unexpected Execution Divergence. No Determinism Assumption A simulation should not be classified as deterministic merely because its design intends determinism. Actual execution behavior must remain governable. Stochastic Repetition A stochastic simulation intentionally permits variability. SRPM governs: randomization mechanism, random seed, distribution sampling, number of repetitions, relation between repetitions, and whether observed variation is consistent with the intended stochastic structure. Random Seed A random seed may determine a stochastic execution path. Where material, SRPM preserves: Seed Identity → Execution ID This supports reconstruction and comparison. Seed Reuse Seed reuse may be deliberate. For example, the same stochastic path may be replayed while one parameter changes. This can strengthen controlled comparison. The reuse should remain explicit. Seed Variation Different seeds may be used to explore distributional behavior. The simulation record should preserve which execution used which seed where technically applicable. Seed ≠ Reproducibility SIMULOS® establishes: Preserving the random seed does not establish reproducibility when other materially relevant execution conditions differ. Initialization Variation Repeated simulations may vary initial states. Examples include: actor placement, resource state, environmental state, memory state, system state, mission phase, or another initialization condition. Where initialization varies intentionally, it should remain part of the repetition design. Execution-Order Effects Some simulation systems may behave differently depending upon execution order because of: shared state, cache behavior, external dependencies, persistent environment state, adaptive models, memory, or resource contention. SRPM should identify materially relevant execution-order effects. No Independent-Run Assumption SIMULOS® establishes: Separate execution IDs do not prove statistical or operational independence. Runs may remain dependent through: shared initialization, shared randomization, shared data, shared adaptive state, shared infrastructure, previous-run state, or common external services. Repetition Independence Where independence matters, the repetition process should identify whether executions are: Independent Conditionally Independent Dependent or: Independence Undetermined. Shared-State Repetition Repeated simulations may unintentionally inherit state from earlier runs. Examples include: memory, cache, learned model state, environment state, persistent agent state, database state, or external service state. This can make apparently repeated executions materially non-equivalent. No Hidden State Carryover Principle A repetition must not be represented as a fresh execution where material state from earlier executions persists invisibly. Repeatability Repeatability concerns whether materially equivalent executions performed under sufficiently equivalent conditions produce behavior consistent with the simulation's expected execution characteristics. Repeatability does not necessarily require identical outputs. The required equivalence depends upon whether the simulation is deterministic, stochastic, adaptive, distributed, or human-in-the-loop. Repeatability Conditions Repeatability may depend upon: identical model version, identical environment, identical inputs, identical parameters, identical seed, equivalent hardware, equivalent software dependencies, equivalent timing, and absence of hidden state. Repeatability Failure A Repeatability Failure occurs where executions expected to be materially equivalent produce unexplained materially different behavior. The result should not immediately be treated as simulation invalidity. It creates a governed question requiring explanation. Reproducibility Reproducibility concerns whether materially comparable simulation behavior can be recreated under another suitably controlled execution context. This may involve: another machine, another environment, another organization, another implementation, or a later point in time. Repeatability ≠ Reproducibility A simulation may be repeatable on one platform while not reproducible elsewhere. These remain distinct properties. Repetition Comparability Two repeated executions should be treated as comparable only where their materially relevant similarities and differences are known. Comparability may be: Fully Comparable Conditionally Comparable Partially Comparable Not Comparable or: Comparability Undetermined. No Same-Scenario Comparability Principle SIMULOS® establishes: Sharing the same Scenario ID does not establish that two Simulation Executions are sufficiently comparable. Material differences may exist in: inputs, parameters, environment version, model version, timing, infrastructure, randomization, or runtime intervention. Repetition Equivalence A repeated execution may be considered materially equivalent to another where relevant differences do not materially affect the repetition purpose. Equivalence should remain tied to the specific comparison question. Repetition Variance Repetition Variance describes materially relevant differences across repeated executions. Variance may be expected. For example, stochastic simulations may deliberately generate different outcomes. SRPM asks: Is the variance expected, explainable, bounded, and traceable to governed repetition conditions? Execution Divergence Execution Divergence occurs where repeated executions move into materially different behavior. Divergence may arise from: stochasticity, chaotic system behavior, timing, hidden state, model instability, adaptive behavior, environment differences, or uncontrolled execution drift. Expected vs Unexpected Divergence SRPM distinguishes: Expected Divergence from: Unexpected Divergence. Expected divergence follows from the simulation design. Unexpected divergence requires investigation because materially equivalent execution conditions were expected to behave differently only within known bounds. Divergence Trigger A material divergence may create: additional observation requirements, new repetition requirements, new scenario requirements, edge-case discovery, stress-condition requirements, or execution-control review. Rare-Event Emergence Repeated simulation may reveal low-frequency behavior absent from earlier runs. A rare event should not automatically be discarded as: simulation noise. SRPM preserves: Rare Observed Behavior → Execution Identity → Repetition Context so the condition can be evaluated by downstream governance. Rare Event ≠ Error SIMULOS® establishes: Low-frequency behavior must not be classified as execution error solely because it occurred rarely. Rare-Event Confirmation A newly observed rare condition may justify additional repetition to determine whether it: recurs, depends upon specific conditions, represents stochastic variation, reflects hidden instability, or reveals a new scenario requirement. Repetition Convergence Some simulation campaigns seek evidence that repeated results have stabilized sufficiently for the Simulation Purpose. A Convergence Signal may indicate that additional repetitions produce diminishing material changes in the relevant result distribution or observed behavior. Convergence ≠ Truth SIMULOS® establishes: Stable repeated output does not establish that the simulation correctly represents reality. It establishes only a property of repeated simulation behavior. Reality correlation and validation remain separate governance questions. Repetition Saturation A Repetition Set may reach Repetition Saturation where additional repeated runs provide little additional information for the defined repetition purpose. This can prevent wasteful run-volume growth. No Fixed Run-Count Principle SIMULOS® does not establish that: 10 runs 1,000 runs or: 1,000,000 runs are universally sufficient. Repetition sufficiency depends upon: purpose, stochasticity, uncertainty, variability, rarity, sensitivity, consequence, and the simulation question being examined. Repetition Sufficiency Repetition Sufficiency asks: Have enough controlled repetitions been performed to support the repetition purpose without claiming more than the resulting execution set can demonstrate? Possible statuses may include: Sufficient Conditionally Sufficient Partially Sufficient Insufficient or: Undetermined. Repetition Gap A Repetition Gap exists where additional governed repetition is materially required but has not been completed. A gap may arise because of: insufficient run count, rare-event uncertainty, unexplained divergence, inadequate stochastic sampling, resource limitations, interrupted campaign, or missing repeatability analysis. Repetition Failure A repeated execution may itself fail. Failed repetitions should remain visible. A simulation campaign should not preserve: successful runs only while removing failures from the repetition basis. No Survivor-Only Repetition Principle SIMULOS® establishes: Repetition governance must preserve materially relevant failed, interrupted, anomalous, and divergent executions rather than allowing only successful repetitions to define the observed simulation behavior. Repetition Drift Repetition Drift occurs where repeated executions gradually cease to share the material conditions required for the intended comparison. Possible causes include: model updates, environment updates, configuration changes, dependency updates, hardware changes, data refresh, adaptive state, or altered execution controls. Repetition Drift vs Intended Evolution Not every change is drift. A repetition campaign may deliberately evolve. The distinction is: Governed Change versus: Uncontrolled Change affecting repetition comparability. Version-Bounded Repetition Repetition Sets should remain bounded to relevant: model versions, environment versions, scenario versions, input versions, and execution-control versions where changes materially affect comparability. Cross-Version Repetition Cross-version comparison may be legitimate where the purpose is explicitly to evaluate change. For example: Model Version 1 vs Model Version 2 However, this is not repetition under equivalent conditions. It is a governed comparative repetition structure. Baseline Replay A prior execution may be replayed as a baseline against a changed system version. This can help isolate the effect of a change where other materially relevant conditions remain controlled. Repetition Lineage SRPM preserves lineage such as: Reference Execution ↓ Repeat 1 ↓ Repeat 2 ↓ Rare Behavior Detected ↓ Focused Repeat Set ↓ Controlled Reproduction ↓ New Scenario Requirement This allows repeated simulation to become a source of structured discovery. Adaptive Repetition An execution campaign may adapt repetition based on observed results. For example: Initial 100 Runs ↓ Rare Divergence Detected ↓ Additional 1,000 Targeted Runs ↓ Behavior Region Identified The adaptive decision should remain traceable. No Hidden Adaptive Sampling Principle Where observed simulation results materially determine which additional repetitions occur, the selection logic should remain visible. Otherwise the final repetition population may appear unbiased when it was adaptively selected. Monte Carlo Repetition Monte Carlo simulation is a major application of SRPM. SRPM may govern: run identity, seed generation, sampling distributions, sample dependence, repeated configuration, randomization logic, execution failures, coverage of relevant probability regions, and relation between run volume and actual repetition purpose. Monte Carlo Volume ≠ Evidence Sufficiency SIMULOS® establishes: Millions of Monte Carlo runs do not establish methodological sufficiency if the sampling model, scenario basis, execution conditions, or materially relevant low-probability regions remain poorly governed. Stochastic Tail Repetition High-consequence behavior may occur in distribution tails. Random sampling may generate too few such executions for meaningful examination. SRPM may therefore identify a need for: targeted tail repetition, stratified repetition, controlled seed selection, scenario injection, or another deliberate method. Scenario design remains governed under SSS. SRPM governs the repetition structure. Repeated Edge Cases An Edge Case identified under SSS may require repetition to determine whether observed behavior is: deterministic, stochastic, unstable, timing-dependent, or conditional upon another execution variable. Repeated Stress Conditions Stress scenarios may require repeated execution because system behavior near a failure or degradation boundary may vary. SRPM can support examination of whether: Failure always occurs Failure sometimes occurs or: Failure depends upon specific stochastic conditions. Autonomous-System Repetition Autonomous systems may produce different behaviors under apparently similar conditions because of: nondeterministic decision processes, adaptive state, memory, multi-agent interaction, environment timing, or stochastic components. SRPM preserves the distinction between: same scenario and: same execution path. AI Agent Repetition An AI agent may be executed repeatedly on the same task while producing materially different: plans, tool calls, escalation behavior, recovery behavior, or final actions. SRPM can govern: prompt or task identity, model version, tool state, permissions, memory state, environment state, temperature or sampling configuration, and repetition results. This helps reveal behavioral dispersion that a single successful run cannot expose. Space and Mission Simulation Space simulation programs frequently rely upon large repeated campaigns to examine uncertainty in: trajectory, navigation, component behavior, environment, communication, timing, power, sensor error, and mission recovery. SRPM asks: Are these repetitions actually controlled enough to interpret their differences? For example, if a spacecraft recovery simulation fails in: 7 of 100,000 runs the relevant questions include: Which seven? Which seeds? Which input combinations? Did those runs share a dependency state? Can the behavior be reproduced? Was the same environment version used? Did any run contain an execution deviation? The value lies not in the number: 100,000 but in the governed ability to understand what the repetitions collectively demonstrate. Industrial Autonomous Systems A manufacturing robot may pass: 999 of 1,000 repetitions of one scenario. The remaining execution may reveal a rare coordination failure. SRPM prevents that execution from being discarded merely because: 99.9% succeeded. Instead the rare behavior can be: reconstructed, repeated, isolated, and transferred to Scenario Design if a new material condition is discovered. Repetition Campaign Diagnostic SRPM can be used on an existing simulation program to ask: Why are these runs repeated? Which variables remain constant? Which variables intentionally change? Which variables changed unintentionally? Are the runs independent? Are seeds traceable? Are failed runs preserved? Are repeated executions actually comparable? What variance is expected? What divergence is unexplained? Has repetition reached saturation? Are millions of executions producing materially new information? This can expose substantial inefficiency and weak execution governance without changing the simulation engine itself. Relationship to SIM SIM — Simulation Instantiation Module establishes the exact simulation instance. SRPM depends upon that execution identity to determine whether a later run is sufficiently comparable to a prior one. Relationship to SECM SECM — Simulation Execution Control Module governs the active control conditions applied during each run. SRPM determines whether those execution controls remained sufficiently equivalent across repetitions. Relationship to SOM SOM — Simulation Observation Module captures materially relevant behavior during each execution. SRPM compares the resulting observations across a Repetition Set. Relationship to SEDM SEDM — Simulation Execution Documentation Module preserves the repetition records, lineage, differences, and resulting execution history. SRPM establishes the repetition governance logic. SEDM ensures that logic and its execution record remain reconstructable. Relationship to SSS SSS governs: which scenarios and condition spaces should be examined. SRPM governs: how an execution of those scenarios is repeated. Therefore: Scenario Coverage ≠ Repetition Sufficiency. Both may be required, but they govern different methodological questions. Relationship to SIDS SIDS governs the suitability of Simulation Inputs. SRPM preserves which exact Input Set or input variations applied across repeated executions. Relationship to SMES SMES governs the Simulation Model & Environment. SRPM relies upon model and environment version binding to determine whether repeated runs remain comparable. Relationship to SOGS SOGS governs the outputs produced by repeated executions. SRPM establishes the repetition basis needed to determine whether outputs represent: one run, one Repetition Set, a distribution, a rare execution, an aggregated result, or another repetition-derived output structure. Relationship to VALIDOS® Repeated simulation may later become part of a Validation Evidence Basis. VALIDOS® determines what that repetition evidence can legitimately support. SRPM does not establish formal validation. Relationship to ADIT® ADIT® may audit whether repetition records, run populations, seed usage, execution failures, and comparability claims are sufficiently supported. SRPM governs repetition itself. Governance Boundary SRPM begins when one or more governed Simulation Executions require deliberate repetition for a defined simulation purpose. SRPM ends when repeated executions have been sufficiently: identified, related, controlled, differentiated, compared, variance-assessed, divergence-assessed, sufficiency-assessed, and preserved as a governed Repetition Set for downstream Execution Documentation and Output Governance. SRPM does not determine: general Scenario Coverage, model validity, output interpretation, formal validation, or operational reliance. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Establish the Repetition Requirement Define why repeated execution is required. 2. Identify the Reference Execution Bind the repetition process to a sufficiently defined execution basis. 3. Define Controlled Constants Identify the materially relevant conditions intended to remain unchanged. 4. Define Permitted Variation Identify which conditions may intentionally change across repetitions. 5. Establish Repetition Identity Assign distinct Execution IDs and a common Repetition Set relationship. 6. Govern Randomization Where applicable, preserve: randomization method, seed, distribution, and relevant stochastic configuration. 7. Execute Controlled Repetitions Perform repeated runs while preserving intended constants and permitted variation. 8. Detect Repetition Drift Identify material unintended changes affecting comparability. 9. Assess Variance and Divergence Distinguish expected stochastic variation from unexplained execution divergence. 10. Preserve Failed and Rare Executions Ensure materially relevant anomalous, failed, interrupted, and low-frequency runs remain part of the repetition record. 11. Assess Repetition Sufficiency Determine whether additional repetition would materially improve the defined simulation inquiry. 12. Establish the Governed Repetition Set Preserve the complete repetition basis for Execution Documentation and downstream Output Governance. Governance Outputs SRPM may produce: Repetition Requirement, Reference Execution Record, Repetition Set Identifier, Simulation Repetition Set, Controlled Constant Record, Permitted Variation Record, Repetition Execution Record, Repetition Identity Map, Randomization Record, Random Seed Record, Seed-Reuse Record, Seed-Variation Record, Initialization Variation Record, Execution-Order Effect Record, Repetition Independence Assessment, Shared-State Record, Repeatability Assessment, Repeatability Failure Record, Reproducibility Condition Record, Repetition Comparability Assessment, Repetition Equivalence Record, Repetition Variance Record, Execution Divergence Record, Rare-Event Observation Record, Rare-Event Confirmation Requirement, Convergence Signal, Repetition Saturation Assessment, Repetition Sufficiency Assessment, Repetition Gap, Repetition Failure Record, Repetition Drift Record, Cross-Version Repetition Record, Adaptive Repetition Record, Repetition Lineage Map, and Governed Simulation Repetition Set. Use Case 1 — Spacecraft Autonomous Recovery Monte Carlo Campaign Scenario A spacecraft autonomous-recovery simulation executes 250,000 repeated runs under uncertainty in: navigation error, communication delay, power state, sensor noise, and recovery timing. A small number of executions fail to recover correctly. Application SRPM preserves: Repetition Set identity, individual Execution IDs, seeds, input and parameter combinations, environment version, controlled constants, permitted stochastic variation, and failed-run lineage. The failed executions are compared with successful repetitions. A common pattern is discovered: high navigation uncertainty + delayed communication + low remaining power at recovery initiation. Result The organization can move beyond: 249,982 successful / 18 unsuccessful runs to determine: which governed conditions are associated with the rare failure behavior and whether that behavior can be deliberately reproduced. The 18 executions may then create new Scenario or Stress-Condition requirements rather than disappearing inside aggregate statistics. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Robot Repetition Divergence Scenario An industrial autonomous robot is simulated repeatedly under what is intended to be the same degraded-sensor scenario. Most runs behave consistently. A small subset produces different fallback behavior. Application SRPM compares: model version, environment version, input basis, parameterization, randomization, memory state, and prior execution state. The analysis discovers that persistent agent state was not reset between some repetitions. Result The behavior is not incorrectly classified as inherent stochastic variation. It is identified as: Hidden State Carryover → Repetition Comparability Failure. The simulation program can correct the repetition process and rerun the affected executions under controlled conditions. Architectural Position Simulation Repetition Module (SRPM) is the fourth internal governance space of the Simulation Execution Standard (SES). The complete SES progression is: Simulation Instantiation ↓ Simulation Execution Control ↓ Simulation Observation ↓ Simulation Repetition ↓ Simulation Execution Documentation SIM establishes what exact simulation instance enters execution. SECM governs how that instance is controlled while running. SOM governs what materially relevant behavior occurs during execution. SRPM governs how executions are deliberately repeated and meaningfully compared. SEDM then preserves the complete execution and repetition history as a reconstructable governed record. Foundational Principle Repeated simulation creates methodological value only when the conditions that remained constant, the conditions that changed, the dependencies between runs, and the reasons for observed variance remain sufficiently governed to distinguish meaningful repetition from mere execution volume. Canonical Closing Statement Simulation Repetition Module establishes the repetition governance layer of the Simulation Execution Standard by defining how governed Simulation Executions are repeated, related, randomized, compared, and assessed for repeatability, reproducibility conditions, variance, divergence, rare behavior, convergence, saturation, and sufficiency. Through controlled constants, permitted variation, run identity, seed governance, independence assessment, hidden-state detection, repetition drift control, preservation of failed and anomalous runs, adaptive repetition, and complete repetition lineage, SRPM prevents high execution counts from being mistaken for methodological strength and ensures that repeated simulations remain interpretable as a governed body of execution evidence rather than an undifferentiated collection of runs.

title: OOF™ Resimulation Scope Module (SRSM)
text: OOF™ Resimulation Scope Module (SRSM) Resimulation Scope Module (SRSM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Standard (SLRS) Module: SRSM — Resimulation Scope Module Operational Layer: Resimulation Scope Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Resimulation Scope Origin ID: SIMULOS-SLRS-SRSM-012.4 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 20 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Resimulation Scope Module (SRSM) is the fourth Core Module of the Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Standard (SLRS) within SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture. SRSM governs the determination of what must be resimulated after a governed Resimulation Trigger has been established. The Module determines the minimum sufficient and methodologically justified resimulation boundary across affected Simulation Objects, configurations, representations, assumptions, models, environments, inputs, scenarios, executions, outputs, correlations, and simulation-derived evidence. SRSM prevents two opposite governance failures: insufficient resimulation, where the renewed simulation scope fails to cover materially affected dependencies; and unnecessary resimulation, where unaffected simulation spaces are repeated without a methodological reason. Its task is therefore: to translate a Resimulation Trigger into an explicit, dependency-aware, traceable, and proportionate Resimulation Scope. Architectural Position SRSM is the fourth module within SLRS. It follows: SRGM — Resimulation Trigger Module and precedes: SRTM — Simulation Retirement & Transition Module. The sequence is: Lifecycle Monitoring → Drift Recognition → Resimulation Trigger → Resimulation Scope → Retirement & Transition. SRGM establishes: whether resimulation is required. SRSM establishes: what must be resimulated. SRTM subsequently governs whether a simulation should continue through its lifecycle, transition toward a replacement, or be retired. Internal Flow Position Governed Resimulation Trigger Record → Affected Simulation Basis Identification → Dependency Propagation Analysis → Affected Object / Configuration Identification → Affected Scenario Space Identification → Affected Model / Environment Identification → Affected Input Basis Identification → Affected Execution Requirements → Affected Output / Correlation / Evidence Identification → Scope Sufficiency Assessment → Resimulation Scope Determination → Governed Resimulation Scope Record → Resimulation Lifecycle Re-Entry / SRTM Operational Space SRSM governs the space between: a confirmed need to resimulate and the definition of the simulation lifecycle elements that must be reopened, updated, repeated, reconstructed, or reassessed. This operational space includes: resimulation scope identification; affected simulation component identification; dependency propagation; impact boundaries; scenario re-entry; configuration re-entry; model re-entry; input re-entry; assumption re-entry; representation re-entry; execution re-entry; output reassessment; correlation reassessment; evidence consequence identification; partial resimulation; targeted resimulation; campaign resimulation; comprehensive resimulation; scope expansion; scope reduction; unaffected-space preservation; scope sufficiency; scope documentation. Operational Scope SRSM applies whenever a Resimulation Trigger requires some portion of an existing simulation basis to be reconsidered or executed again. It may govern: one simulation run; one parameter range; one scenario; one scenario family; one Simulation Object configuration; one subsystem; one model component; one environmental condition; one input distribution; one failure mode; one mission phase; one behavioral domain; one simulation campaign; multiple interconnected campaigns; the complete simulation lifecycle. It applies across engineering, scientific, physical, digital, hybrid, mission, safety, infrastructure, economic, AI, autonomous-system, digital-twin, and future simulation environments. SRSM remains technology-neutral. Trigger ≠ Scope SRSM establishes the fundamental distinction: Resimulation Trigger ≠ Resimulation Scope A trigger establishes that the existing simulation basis requires renewed simulation activity. It does not establish how much must be repeated. A material change in one subsystem may require: targeted resimulation rather than: complete campaign repetition. Conversely, a seemingly localized change may propagate through dependencies and require much broader resimulation than its initial location suggests. Therefore: The size of the originating change does not determine the size of the required resimulation scope. Minimum Sufficient Scope Principle SRSM seeks the Minimum Sufficient Resimulation Scope. This means: the smallest resimulation boundary that fully captures all materially affected simulation dependencies necessary to restore the governed simulation basis for the intended use. “Minimum” prevents unnecessary repetition. “Sufficient” prevents under-scoping. The objective is not computational minimization at any cost. The objective is methodologically justified proportionality. Affected Simulation Basis Every Resimulation Trigger must be mapped to the simulation basis it potentially affects. The affected basis may include: Simulation Object; object version; object configuration; simulation purpose; scope; exclusions; reality representation; abstraction; fidelity; assumptions; model structure; environment; parameters; inputs; data; temporal conditions; scenarios; scenario coverage; execution configuration; outputs; correlation relationships; evidence objects. The scope cannot be determined reliably until these dependencies are visible. Dependency Propagation Principle A change may propagate beyond the simulation element where it originated. For example: Input Change → affects Model Behavior → affects Scenario Outcomes → affects Outputs → affects Simulation-to-Reality Correlation → affects Simulation Evidence. Or: Object Configuration Change → affects Reality Representation → affects Assumptions → affects Model Parameterization → affects Scenario Relevance → affects Execution → affects Outputs. SRSM therefore requires dependency-aware scope determination. Local Change ≠ Local Scope A localized technical change does not guarantee a localized resimulation requirement. A single changed parameter may influence: multiple model components; multiple scenario families; downstream control behavior; interaction effects; failure thresholds; evidence already derived from previous executions. Conversely, a large physical modification may have no material effect on a narrowly defined simulation question. Scope must follow material simulation dependency, not superficial change size. Resimulation Scope Levels SRSM may classify scope into governed levels. 1. Execution-Level Resimulation Repeat one or more executions without materially changing the upstream simulation basis. Appropriate where the issue concerns: execution anomaly; stochastic repetition; failed run; incomplete execution; runtime instability. 2. Scenario-Level Resimulation Repeat or expand specific scenarios or scenario families. Appropriate where: new edge cases emerge; scenario conditions change; coverage gaps are discovered; one scenario class becomes materially relevant. 3. Input-Level Resimulation Renew simulation where input or data conditions materially change. This may require: new datasets; updated distributions; changed temporal inputs; changed uncertainty ranges. 4. Configuration-Level Resimulation Repeat simulations for affected Simulation Object, model, or environment configurations. 5. Model-Level Resimulation Reopen the simulation model or environment basis before execution. Appropriate where: model structure changes; model limitations are discovered; environment behavior changes; parameterization must be reconstructed. 6. Representation-Level Resimulation Reopen the representation of reality itself. Appropriate where previously simplified, excluded, or inaccurately represented reality becomes materially relevant. 7. Comprehensive Resimulation Re-enter multiple or all materially relevant simulation lifecycle stages. This may be necessary where change is systemic, dependencies are extensive, or the previous simulation basis can no longer support meaningful partial reuse. These levels may overlap. They are governance classifications, not rigid technical implementation categories. Partial Resimulation SRSM permits partial resimulation where the unaffected simulation basis remains legitimate. A partial scope should establish: what remains unchanged; why it remains reusable; what must be updated; what must be repeated; what downstream results become affected; what previous evidence remains applicable; what evidence requires reassessment. Partial resimulation must not become an assumption of convenience. Its sufficiency must be demonstrable. Targeted Resimulation Targeted resimulation may focus computational and analytical resources upon the specific conditions affected by the Trigger. Examples include: one failure mode; one sensor condition; one mission phase; one environmental range; one scenario family; one subsystem interaction; one parameter region. Targeted resimulation can dramatically reduce unnecessary simulation effort while preserving methodological sufficiency. Comprehensive Resimulation Comprehensive resimulation may be required where: Simulation Object identity materially changes; reality representation becomes structurally insufficient; foundational assumptions fail; model architecture changes substantially; multiple scenario families become affected; dependencies cannot be reliably isolated; correlation deteriorates broadly; accumulated drift becomes systemic; previous evidence can no longer be cleanly separated from the affected basis. Comprehensive resimulation should result from governed scope analysis rather than default organizational habit. Scope Expansion Principle An initially narrow Resimulation Scope may need to expand. During renewed simulation activity, organizations may discover: additional affected dependencies; new failure modes; broader scenario impact; unexpected sensitivity; new model interactions; wider correlation deterioration; additional evidence consequences. SRSM therefore allows: Initial Scope → New Information → Scope Reassessment → Expanded Scope. A scope determination must not become immutable when new material information emerges. Scope Reduction Principle A provisional scope may also be reduced where evidence establishes that suspected dependencies are not materially affected. Reduction must be justified. It should identify: the excluded simulation space; the evidence supporting exclusion; the dependency analysis; remaining uncertainty. Scope Reduction ≠ Convenience-Based Exclusion. Unchanged Basis Preservation SRSM should preserve simulation components that remain legitimately reusable. This may include: unaffected scenarios; unchanged input sets; unaffected model components; stable environmental configurations; previous execution records; unaffected outputs; still-applicable correlation evidence. This prevents simulation governance from creating unnecessary computational waste. However, reuse requires a governed basis. Previously Simulated ≠ Automatically Reusable. Scenario Scope Where the Trigger affects scenario coverage, SRSM determines which scenario space must be reopened. This may include: expected conditions; variations; edge cases; stress conditions; uncertainty conditions; interaction scenarios; newly observed scenarios; previously excluded scenarios. SSS continues to govern scenario design. SRSM determines which scenario governance must be re-entered because of the Trigger. Model & Environment Scope Where the Trigger affects the simulation model or environment, SRSM determines which model or environmental elements require renewed governance. Possible consequences include: model component revision; parameterization revision; environment reconfiguration; boundary interaction reassessment; version change; dependency reconstruction. SMES governs these elements when re-entered. SRSM governs the requirement to reopen them. Input & Data Scope Where simulation inputs are affected, SRSM determines which input basis must be reconsidered. Possible scope may include: one variable; one dataset; one distribution; one time period; one environmental source; one uncertainty range; the complete input basis. SIDS governs the renewed input and data conditions. SRSM defines the affected boundary. Assumption Scope A changed assumption may propagate through many simulation layers. SRSM must determine: which assumption changed; which model components depend upon it; which scenarios rely upon it; which executions used it; which outputs were affected; which correlation conclusions depend upon it; which evidence objects inherit the dependency. SAS governs the assumption itself. SRSM governs the lifecycle scope affected by its change. Output and Evidence Consequence Scope Resimulation scope does not stop at new execution. Where prior outputs or simulation-derived evidence depend upon the affected simulation basis, SRSM should identify them for downstream reconsideration. This may require renewed governance through: SOGS → SRCS → SERBS. A new simulation execution may therefore invalidate, supersede, narrow, strengthen, or leave unchanged different portions of the previous evidence basis. Scope Sufficiency Assessment Before a Resimulation Scope is accepted, SRSM should determine whether the proposed scope is sufficient to address the Trigger. The assessment may ask: Have all material dependencies been identified? Are affected scenarios included? Are changed assumptions covered? Are model consequences captured? Are affected inputs reconsidered? Are downstream outputs identified? Is correlation reassessment required? Is existing evidence affected? Are excluded simulation spaces demonstrably unaffected? Could residual uncertainty materially undermine the intended use? The purpose is to prevent a technically completed resimulation from remaining methodologically incomplete. Scope Uncertainty Sometimes the required scope cannot initially be determined with confidence. SRSM may therefore establish: Provisional Resimulation Scope where uncertainty remains. The provisional scope may be expanded or reduced as evidence emerges. Uncertainty about scope should be documented rather than hidden through arbitrary boundary selection. Resimulation Re-Entry Principle SRSM does not require every Resimulation Trigger to restart SIMULOS® from Standard 1. Instead, it determines the earliest materially affected governance point. Examples: Execution anomaly → re-enter at SES. New scenario → re-enter at SSS. Input distribution shift → re-enter at SIDS. Model revision → re-enter at SMES. Assumption failure → re-enter at SAS. Reality representation deficiency → re-enter at RRS. Simulation Object material change → potentially re-enter at SOS. This enables SIMULOS® to operate recursively without forcing unnecessary full-lifecycle repetition. Lifecycle Propagation Once the re-entry point is established, downstream governance should be reconsidered wherever materially affected. For example: SAS Re-Entry → SMES → SIDS where affected → SSS → SES → SOGS → SRCS → SERBS. Not every downstream element must necessarily change. But every materially dependent downstream element must be considered. SRSM Boundary with SRGM SRGM determines: whether resimulation is required. SRSM determines: what must be resimulated. Therefore: Trigger ≠ Scope. SRSM must not redefine the original Trigger merely to reduce or expand workload. SRSM Boundary with SSS SRSM may determine that a scenario space must be reopened. SSS governs the actual identification, variation, edge-case design, stress conditions, and coverage of those scenarios. SRSM Boundary with SMES SRSM may determine that the model or environment must be reopened. SMES governs model structure, environmental configuration, boundary interactions, parameterization, and environment versioning. SRSM Boundary with SIDS SRSM may identify affected input and data spaces. SIDS governs those inputs once simulation governance re-enters that layer. SRSM Boundary with SES SRSM determines which executions must occur again. SES governs how those simulations are instantiated, controlled, observed, repeated, and documented. SRSM Boundary with SOGS SRSM may determine which prior or newly produced outputs require renewed governance. SOGS governs output identification, classification, inference, limitations, and documentation. SRSM Boundary with SRCS SRSM may determine that simulation-to-reality correlation must be reassessed because the simulation basis has materially changed. SRCS governs the actual correlation process. SRSM Boundary with SERBS SRSM identifies simulation-derived evidence potentially affected by resimulation. SERBS determines the qualification, weight, reliance boundary, limitations, and validation interface of that evidence. SRSM Boundary with VALIDOS® SRSM determines the simulation-specific scope of resimulation. It does not determine the broader scope of revalidation. A VALIDOS® revalidation process may require additional evidence or activities outside simulation. SRSM Boundary with ORA™ Operational Reality may provide changes that influence scope determination. ORA™ continues to govern Operational Reality itself. SRSM governs only the resulting simulation lifecycle re-entry boundary. SRSM Boundary with INTEGROS® SRSM does not govern general integrity. Integrity issues may create dependencies affecting resimulation scope, but integrity governance remains under INTEGROS®. SRSM Boundary with ADIT® ADIT® may audit whether the basis, exclusions, dependency analysis, scope determination, and resulting resimulation records are preserved and verifiable. SRSM governs the scope determination itself. Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum SRSM implementation should establish: 1. Trigger Intake Receive the governed Resimulation Trigger and its supporting basis. 2. Affected Basis Identification Identify the simulation lifecycle elements directly affected by the Trigger. 3. Dependency Mapping Determine material upstream, downstream, and cross-component dependencies. 4. Re-Entry Point Determination Identify the earliest materially affected SIMULOS® governance layer. 5. Scope Classification Determine whether execution-level, scenario-level, input-level, configuration-level, model-level, representation-level, or comprehensive resimulation is required. 6. Unaffected Basis Assessment Identify previous simulation elements that remain legitimately reusable. 7. Downstream Consequence Assessment Identify outputs, correlation relationships, evidence objects, and reliance boundaries requiring reconsideration. 8. Scope Sufficiency Assessment Determine whether the proposed boundary captures all material consequences of the Trigger. 9. Scope Adjustment Control Permit governed expansion or reduction where new information materially changes the required boundary. 10. Resimulation Scope Record Document the final or provisional Resimulation Scope, exclusions, dependencies, re-entry point, and downstream consequences. Use Case 1 — Space Mission Simulation: Flight Software Change Before Launch A spacecraft has completed a very large pre-launch simulation campaign covering: ascent; navigation; orbital operations; descent; landing; communication failures; propulsion anomalies; contingency scenarios. A late flight-software update modifies the guidance algorithm used during descent. SRGM has already established a Priority Resimulation Trigger. The organization now faces a major practical question: Must the complete mission simulation campaign be repeated? SRSM maps the change through the simulation dependency structure. The updated guidance algorithm affects: Descent Control → Navigation Interaction → Propulsion Commands → Landing Trajectory → Fuel Consumption → Landing-Site Dispersion → Failure and Contingency Scenarios → Mission Outputs → Relevant Simulation Evidence. But the change may have no material relationship to unrelated orbital communication scenarios or other unaffected mission phases. SRSM therefore establishes a targeted but dependency-complete Resimulation Scope. The organization re-enters the simulation lifecycle at the affected model/configuration layer, reconstructs the relevant scenario space, repeats the affected execution campaign, regenerates governed outputs, and reassesses relevant simulation-to-reality correlation and evidence. This avoids both extremes: repeating the entire mission campaign unnecessarily and testing only the modified algorithm while missing its downstream mission interactions. The governing principle is: Resimulate the dependency chain affected by the change, not merely the component where the change originated. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Robot: Rare Failure Reveals a Missing Scenario Domain A mobile autonomous robot has successfully completed millions of simulations before deployment. Operational observation later reveals failures occurring when three conditions combine: low-angle sunlight + partially contaminated sensor surface + unusual pedestrian movement. SRGM determines that the new failure pattern creates a Resimulation Trigger. SRSM must now determine the required scope. Repeating the complete historical campaign may consume enormous computational resources while adding little information. Repeating only the exact failed event may be too narrow because the failure could belong to a broader interaction domain. SRSM therefore traces the affected dependencies: New Reality Condition → Reality Representation → Sensor Model → Environmental Inputs → Scenario Family → Autonomous Behavior → Execution → Outputs → Sim-to-Real Correlation → Existing Evidence. The resulting scope may require: updating the representation of contaminated sensors; expanding relevant lighting ranges; creating variations of human movement; testing combinations rather than isolated conditions; rerunning the affected behavioral scenario family; reassessing outputs; recalculating relevant correlation; reconsidering simulation evidence previously used for that operational domain. Unaffected simulation domains remain reusable where their independence is established. The organization therefore avoids the misleading choice between: rerun everything and rerun only the failure. SRSM establishes the third option: rerun everything materially connected to the failure, and preserve everything demonstrably unaffected. Governance Outputs SRSM may produce: Resimulation Scope Assessment Affected Simulation Basis Map Simulation Dependency Map Resimulation Re-Entry Point Resimulation Scope Classification Affected Scenario Scope Affected Input Scope Affected Model & Environment Scope Affected Configuration Scope Required Execution Scope Downstream Output Reassessment Scope Correlation Reassessment Requirement Affected Simulation Evidence Register Unaffected Simulation Basis Statement Scope Exclusion Record Scope Sufficiency Assessment Provisional Resimulation Scope Final Resimulation Scope Governed Resimulation Scope Record Enterprise Application SRSM gives organizations a method for answering one of the most expensive questions in simulation lifecycle management: When something changes, how much simulation must actually be repeated? Without governed scope determination, organizations may either repeat massive simulation campaigns unnecessarily or perform narrow retesting that fails to capture downstream dependencies. SRSM enables simulation-intensive organizations to determine: the earliest lifecycle point requiring re-entry; which scenarios must be repeated; which model components require revision; which inputs must be updated; which configurations are affected; which executions must be repeated; which previous outputs remain usable; which correlation relationships require reassessment; which simulation-derived evidence has become affected; which unaffected simulation assets may legitimately be preserved. This becomes especially important where simulation campaigns contain millions or billions of executions. The objective is not simply to reduce simulation cost. It is to ensure that computational effort follows methodological necessity . Foundational Principles Resimulation Trigger does not determine Resimulation Scope. The size of a change does not determine the size of its simulation consequence. Local change does not necessarily imply local resimulation. Resimulation scope must follow material dependency. The minimum scope must still be sufficient. Unaffected simulation assets should not be discarded merely because another part of the simulation changed. Previously simulated does not mean automatically reusable. A resimulation may re-enter SIMULOS® at any materially affected lifecycle layer. Downstream outputs and evidence must be reconsidered where their simulation basis has changed. Scope may expand or contract when new information changes the known dependency boundary. Resimulation should repeat neither less nor more than the materially affected simulation basis requires. Canonical Closing Statement Resimulation Scope Module establishes the scope-determination layer of the Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Standard by transforming a governed Resimulation Trigger into an explicit, dependency-aware, proportionate, sufficient, and traceable Resimulation Scope. Through governance of affected simulation bases, dependency propagation, lifecycle re-entry points, scenario scope, input scope, model and environment scope, configuration scope, execution requirements, downstream output consequences, correlation reassessment, evidence consequences, unaffected-basis preservation, scope sufficiency, and scope adjustment, SRSM prevents both insufficient resimulation and unnecessary repetition of unaffected simulation spaces. By separating the decision that resimulation is required from the decision concerning what must be resimulated, SRSM enables SIMULOS® to operate recursively across individual executions, targeted scenario families, model revisions, configuration changes, large simulation campaigns, and complete lifecycle reconstruction. Resimulation should not restart more of the simulation lifecycle than necessary, but it must reopen every materially affected dependency required to restore a legitimate governed simulation basis.

title: OOF™ Simulation Retirement & Transition Module (SRTM)
text: OOF™ Simulation Retirement & Transition Module (SRTM) Simulation Retirement & Transition Module (SRTM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Standard (SLRS) Module: SRTM — Simulation Retirement & Transition Module Operational Layer: Simulation Retirement & Transition Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Simulation Retirement & Transition Origin ID: SIMULOS-SLRS-SRTM-012.5 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 20 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Simulation Retirement & Transition Module (SRTM) is the fifth and final Core Module of the Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Standard (SLRS) within SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture. SRTM governs the controlled retirement, supersession, replacement, transition, archival disposition, and residual-use status of simulations that can no longer legitimately continue under their existing lifecycle state. The Module establishes when a simulation should cease active use, when its governed role should transfer to a successor simulation, how dependencies and simulation-derived evidence must be treated during transition, and what historical simulation assets may remain available for explicitly bounded purposes. SRTM prevents obsolete, superseded, materially drifted, unsupported, or retired simulations from continuing to influence decisions merely because they remain technically accessible. Its task is: to ensure that the end of active simulation use becomes a governed lifecycle state rather than an informal disappearance, silent replacement, or uncontrolled continuation. Architectural Position SRTM is the fifth and final module within SLRS. It follows: SRSM — Resimulation Scope Module. The complete SLRS module sequence is: SLMM — Lifecycle Monitoring → SDRM — Drift Recognition → SRGM — Resimulation Trigger → SRSM — Resimulation Scope → SRTM — Retirement & Transition SRTM closes the active lifecycle where continued resimulation is no longer the appropriate response. It may produce three principal lifecycle directions: Continue → existing governed simulation remains active. Transition / Replace → simulation responsibility moves toward a successor simulation basis. Retire → simulation ceases active governed use. Internal Flow Position Lifecycle Monitoring Record Recognized Simulation Drift Resimulation Trigger Resimulation Scope Determination → Continuation Feasibility Assessment → Retirement / Transition Condition Assessment → Dependency Identification → Successor Simulation Identification where applicable → Transition Boundary Definition → Residual Use Determination → Evidence Consequence Identification → Lifecycle State Assignment → Retirement / Transition Record → Archived / Superseded / Retired Simulation State Where a successor simulation is established: Retired or Superseded Simulation → Successor Simulation Basis → Applicable SIMULOS® Lifecycle Re-Entry Operational Space SRTM governs the lifecycle space where a simulation can no longer simply be assumed to remain current. This includes: simulation retirement; simulation supersession; simulation replacement; simulation transition; successor simulation identification; transition boundaries; residual simulation use; historical simulation use; retirement conditions; retirement state; supersession state; transition state; dependency transfer; simulation lineage; evidence consequences; unresolved limitation preservation; archive status; lifecycle closure; controlled reactivation where justified. Operational Scope SRTM applies where continued use of an existing simulation requires explicit reconsideration because of: material reality change; Simulation Object change; accumulated simulation drift; model obsolescence; environment obsolescence; unsupported assumptions; unavailable dependencies; obsolete input basis; inadequate scenario coverage; technological replacement; architecture change; unresolved correlation deterioration; inability to resimulate sufficiently; excessive reconstruction requirement; successor simulation introduction; termination of the original simulation purpose; loss of support or reproducibility; end of relevant operational lifecycle. SRTM applies to individual simulation models, simulation environments, digital twins, scenario systems, simulation platforms, integrated simulation systems, mission simulations, engineering simulations, scientific simulations, safety simulations, AI simulations, autonomous-system simulations, large simulation campaigns, and future simulation technologies. Resimulation ≠ Indefinite Continuation SLRS must not assume that every lifecycle problem can or should be solved through another simulation run. Repeated resimulation may become inappropriate where the underlying simulation basis itself has become obsolete. Therefore: Resimulation Capability ≠ Continued Simulation Legitimacy A simulation may remain technically executable while no longer being methodologically appropriate for its original purpose. Retirement Principle Simulation retirement occurs when a simulation ceases to hold an active governed role for its defined purpose. Retirement may occur because: its Simulation Object no longer exists in the represented form; the object has materially changed; the original purpose has ended; its representation has become materially obsolete; assumptions can no longer be supported; the model can no longer represent relevant behavior; the environment has become obsolete; required inputs are unavailable; scenario space has changed beyond practical adaptation; correlation with reality has materially deteriorated; a successor simulation has replaced it; the simulation cannot be reconstructed sufficiently; continued use would exceed legitimate reliance boundaries. Retirement should be explicit. Non-use ≠ Governed Retirement. Retirement State SRTM establishes a formal Retired Simulation State. A retired simulation should be distinguishable from: active simulation; temporarily suspended simulation; simulation under review; simulation undergoing resimulation; superseded simulation; archived simulation; successor simulation. The state should indicate: retirement date; retirement basis; affected purpose; affected Simulation Object; final applicable configuration; successor where applicable; residual permitted uses; prohibited uses; evidence consequences; archival disposition. Transition Principle Not every simulation lifecycle ends through simple retirement. Many simulations transition into: updated simulation versions; successor models; replacement environments; new digital twins; new mission simulators; new system configurations; redesigned simulation architectures. SRTM governs the transition relationship between: Outgoing Simulation Basis and Incoming Simulation Basis. Transition must not create an unexamined assumption that the successor inherits the legitimacy of the predecessor. Successor Simulation Principle A successor simulation must be identifiable as a distinct governed simulation basis where material changes justify that distinction. The relationship may be: Version Successor Configuration Successor Model Successor Environment Successor Representation Successor Purpose Successor Complete Simulation Replacement SRTM preserves lineage between predecessor and successor without treating them as methodologically identical. Simulation Lineage ≠ Simulation Equivalence. Transition Boundary A transition must identify what crosses from the predecessor into the successor. Potentially transferable elements include: Simulation Object definitions; purpose definitions; scope structures; reality representations; assumptions; model components; environmental configurations; parameter structures; input datasets; scenario libraries; execution procedures; historical outputs; correlation records; simulation evidence; known limitations; unresolved anomalies; lifecycle records. Transferability must be assessed rather than assumed. Inherited Basis Principle A successor simulation may inherit parts of an earlier simulation basis. But inherited elements must remain identifiable as: Inherited and Reconfirmed Inherited with Modification Inherited Conditionally Not Transferable Replaced This prevents simulation modernization from silently carrying obsolete assumptions, limitations, scenarios, or evidence into a new simulation generation. Retirement ≠ Deletion SRTM establishes a critical distinction: Simulation Retirement ≠ Simulation Deletion A retired simulation may remain valuable for: historical comparison; research; incident reconstruction; longitudinal analysis; methodological analysis; regression comparison; training; audit support; understanding previous decisions; comparison with successor simulations. Retirement governs active legitimacy, not necessarily physical existence. Residual Use A retired simulation may retain explicitly bounded residual uses. Examples include: historical reconstruction; comparison with past system versions; educational use; research; regression analysis; archival reference; legacy incident analysis. Residual use must not recreate active reliance implicitly. A simulation retired from operational decision support should not regain that role merely because someone can still execute it. Residual Use Limitation Where residual use is permitted, SRTM should define: permitted purpose; prohibited purpose; applicable object version; applicable temporal period; known limitations; successor status; warning that the simulation is retired; whether new execution is permitted; whether outputs may enter current evidence processes. This creates a governed distinction between: historically useful and currently authoritative. Supersession Principle A simulation becomes Superseded where another governed simulation basis has formally replaced its active role. Supersession should identify: Predecessor Simulation → Successor Simulation together with: transition date; transferred elements; non-transferred elements; changed assumptions; changed representation; changed models; changed scenarios; changed inputs; evidence consequences; residual predecessor use. Supersession must not erase methodological history. Transition Completeness A transition is not complete merely because the successor simulation can execute. Transition completeness may require confirmation that: successor identity is established; purpose and scope are established; transferred elements are known; non-transferable elements are identified; relevant assumptions are reconsidered; model and environment changes are governed; inputs remain appropriate; scenario space is sufficient; execution basis is established; outputs are distinguishable from predecessor outputs; correlation relationships are reconsidered where necessary; simulation evidence is not improperly inherited; predecessor status is updated. Evidence Transition Principle Simulation-derived evidence from a predecessor simulation must not automatically become evidence of the successor simulation. A successor may materially change: representation; assumptions; model; environment; input basis; scenario structure; execution behavior; output meaning; reality correlation. SRTM therefore requires inherited evidence to be identified for reassessment where the successor basis materially differs. SERBS continues to govern the evidential meaning and reliance boundary. SRTM governs the lifecycle consequence of the transition. Historical Evidence Preservation Retirement does not erase the historical evidential meaning that a simulation legitimately possessed at the time it was active. Historical evidence may remain relevant to: historical decisions; previous system configurations; prior mission states; earlier operational periods; longitudinal comparison. However: Historically Legitimate Evidence ≠ Currently Applicable Evidence. Retirement Due to Reality Change A simulation may require retirement where Operational Reality has moved beyond the representational space the simulation can reasonably maintain. Examples may include: fundamentally changed operating environments; new physical conditions; redesigned infrastructure; new system architecture; changed human behavior; changed regulatory or operational constraints; newly discovered phenomena; previously unknown interactions. ORA™ governs Operational Reality. SRTM governs whether the resulting change makes continued simulation use inappropriate. Retirement Due to Model Obsolescence A simulation may become obsolete because its underlying model no longer represents the relevant system sufficiently. Model obsolescence may result from: new scientific knowledge; better physical models; discovered model deficiencies; unsupported software; changed system architecture; unavailable dependencies; inability to reproduce historical execution conditions. SRTM does not determine general model quality. It governs the lifecycle consequence where model obsolescence makes continued simulation use inappropriate. Retirement Due to Accumulated Drift Individual drift events may initially remain tolerable. Over time, however: Small Reality Changes Object Changes Input Changes Scenario Changes Model Limitations Correlation Degradation → Accumulated Simulation Drift Accumulated drift may eventually make incremental resimulation insufficient. SRTM provides the governance point at which the organization may determine: stop adapting the old simulation and establish a new simulation basis. Replacement Threshold Organizations may define a Replacement Threshold representing the point at which continued modification of an existing simulation becomes methodologically inappropriate relative to replacement. The threshold may consider: extent of structural change; number of affected lifecycle layers; accumulated assumptions; representation divergence; model modification burden; dependency obsolescence; scenario reconstruction requirements; correlation deterioration; inability to preserve traceability; evidence discontinuity. The threshold should not be based solely upon economic convenience. It is a simulation lifecycle governance decision. Retirement with Unresolved Issues A simulation may be retired while unresolved anomalies, limitations, discrepancies, or evidence questions remain. These should not disappear with retirement. SRTM requires material unresolved issues to remain attached to the retired simulation record where relevant. This prevents retirement from functioning as a mechanism for eliminating inconvenient simulation history. Reactivation Principle A retired simulation may sometimes need to be reactivated. Examples include: historical incident reconstruction; comparison against a successor; renewed research; legacy-system analysis. Reactivation does not automatically restore the simulation's former active status. SRTM requires the intended reactivation purpose to be explicit. Where the simulation is intended to return to active current use, the relevant SIMULOS® lifecycle layers must be reconsidered. Technical Reactivation ≠ Governance Reinstatement.
