text: OOF™ About Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard - (SERBS) About Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard - (SERBS) About Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard (SERBS) Architecture: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Parent Standard: Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard (SERBS) Governed Space: Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Canonical Definition Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard (SERBS) governs what simulation-derived information may legitimately become evidence, what evidential meaning and weight that evidence may carry, how far reliance upon it may extend, which uses must remain limited, and how simulation evidence must interface with broader validation governance. SERBS addresses a fundamental simulation problem: A simulation can produce technically precise, repeatable, and convincing results without those results necessarily providing equally strong evidence about reality. The Standard creates the governance layer between simulation results and reliance upon simulation results. Why SERBS Matters Organizations increasingly use simulation to support decisions that cannot be tested easily, safely, economically, or repeatedly in the real world. This creates a methodological risk. A simulation may contain millions of executions, high-fidelity models, sophisticated physics, realistic environments, and highly precise outputs while still depending upon assumptions, abstractions, scenario limitations, incomplete reality representation, uncertain correlations, or conditions that do not fully transfer to the real world. SERBS prevents simulation sophistication from being mistaken for evidential certainty. It requires organizations to establish: What is evidence? What does that evidence actually support? How much evidential weight may it carry? Under which conditions does that meaning remain valid? Where does legitimate reliance stop? What additional validation is required before broader conclusions are made? Governance Flow Governed Simulation Outputs + Simulation-to-Reality Correlation → Simulation Evidence Qualification → Simulation Evidence Weight → Simulation Reliance Boundary → Simulation Use Limitation → Simulation Validation Interface → Governed Simulation Evidence & Reliance Record Where broader validation is required: Governed Simulation Evidence & Reliance Record → VALIDOS® Validation Governance What SERBS Helps Organizations Govern SERBS provides a structured method for determining whether simulation-derived information can legitimately support a particular engineering, scientific, safety, mission, operational, or deployment proposition. It helps organizations distinguish between: Simulation Output ≠ Simulation Evidence Simulation Evidence ≠ Validation Determination Evidence Volume ≠ Evidential Strength Correlation ≠ Reality Equivalence Repeated Runs ≠ Independent Evidence Technical Precision ≠ Evidential Certainty The result is not less reliance on simulation. It is better-governed reliance on simulation. Reliance Boundary SERBS requires simulation evidence to remain bounded by the conditions that created its meaning. Those boundaries may include: Simulation Object and configuration; simulation purpose and scope; represented reality; assumptions; model applicability; input basis; scenario coverage; execution conditions; output classification; simulation-to-reality correlation; uncertainty; temporal relevance; known limitations. Evidence may therefore be highly useful while still being legitimately narrow. SERBS prevents narrow evidence from silently becoming a broad claim. Boundary with VALIDOS® SERBS does not determine whether an entire system, object, claim, or operational proposition has been validated. The architectural boundary is explicit: SIMULOS® determines what simulation-derived evidence can legitimately mean. VALIDOS® determines whether that evidence, alone or together with other evidence, is sufficient to support a Validation Determination or intended reliance. This allows simulation evidence to enter broader validation without losing the conditions, uncertainty, provenance, and limitations that define its legitimate meaning. Use Case 1 — Space Mission Simulation: Evidence Before Reality Exists A space organization is preparing a future lunar landing mission. Large simulation programs reproduce spacecraft dynamics, navigation, landing trajectories, crew interaction, surface operations, failure conditions, environmental effects, and mission contingencies. Thousands or millions of simulation executions may demonstrate apparently stable mission performance. But a fundamental problem remains: the operational reality being predicted may not yet have been experienced in the exact mission configuration being simulated. Some environmental effects can only be approximated. Real mission data may be sparse. Crew behavior under actual lunar conditions may not yet exist. A highly sophisticated simulator may therefore provide powerful evidence without providing complete real-world proof. Without SERBS, an organization could gradually transform: “The mission architecture performed successfully across these governed simulations.” into: “The mission architecture is proven to perform successfully in lunar operations.” Those statements are not methodologically equivalent. SERBS requires the simulation evidence to carry its actual basis: tested mission configuration → represented lunar conditions → assumptions → scenario coverage → executions → observed outputs → available reality correlation → remaining uncertainty → permitted reliance. The resulting evidence may legitimately support mission design, contingency planning, crew preparation, engineering decisions, or a broader validation program while still carrying an explicit boundary against claims that the simulation alone cannot establish. The value of SERBS is not to weaken the simulation evidence. It is to prevent that evidence from being asked to prove more than the simulation actually tested. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Vehicle or Robot: Simulation Success Before Real-World Transfer An organization develops an autonomous vehicle, mobile robot, delivery robot, industrial robot, or other autonomous system primarily through large-scale simulation. The system completes millions of simulated scenarios involving traffic, pedestrians, obstacles, sensor conditions, failures, environmental variation, unusual events, and behavioral edge cases. The simulation campaign reports extremely high success rates. The organization now considers the system ready for broader real-world deployment. But another fundamental problem appears: success inside a simulated environment does not automatically establish equivalent behavior after transfer into physical reality. Real sensors may respond differently. Friction and dynamics may vary. Lighting, weather, surfaces, object appearance, human behavior, sensor noise, actuator behavior, latency, hardware faults, and combinations of rare conditions may differ from the simulated representation. Even millions of successful executions can share the same underlying model assumptions or representation gaps. SERBS therefore asks a different question from: “How many simulated scenarios did the system pass?” It asks: “What real-world proposition may those passed simulations legitimately support?” SERBS qualifies the evidence, evaluates its simulation-specific weight, identifies common dependencies across the simulation campaign, establishes the permitted reliance boundary, and preserves use limitations before the results enter broader validation or deployment decisions. The organization may conclude that the evidence strongly supports: performance across the represented scenario space while not yet supporting: equivalent performance across unrestricted operational reality. Additional real-world testing, observation, correlation, or other validation evidence can then be added through VALIDOS®. A million successful simulations can increase confidence. They cannot eliminate an ungoverned reality gap. Enterprise Value SERBS gives organizations a repeatable governance structure for turning simulation results into decision-usable evidence without overstating what that evidence proves. It is particularly valuable where: real-world testing is expensive; failure is dangerous; physical testing cannot cover enough scenarios; the operational environment does not yet exist; simulations operate at enormous scale; simulation is used to support safety or deployment decisions; simulation outputs feed regulatory or validation processes; sim-to-real transfer remains uncertain. SERBS therefore provides the missing boundary between what simulation can show and what an organization may legitimately conclude from what simulation has shown. Foundational Principle Simulation-derived evidence must not travel farther than its governed meaning can legitimately support.

title: OOF™ Simulation Evidence Qualification Module (SEQM)
text: OOF™ Simulation Evidence Qualification Module (SEQM) Simulation Evidence Qualification Module (SEQM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard (SERBS) Module: SEQM — Simulation Evidence Qualification Module Operational Layer: Simulation Evidence Qualification Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Simulation Evidence Qualification Origin ID: SIMULOS-SERBS-SEQM-011.1 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 20 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Simulation Evidence Qualification Module (SEQM) is the first Core Module of the Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard (SERBS) within SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture. SEQM governs the transformation of simulation-derived outputs, observations, correlations, comparisons, and governed inferences into explicitly qualified Simulation Evidence for a defined evidential purpose. The Module establishes whether a simulation-derived information object is sufficiently identified, traceable, context-bound, purpose-linked, condition-aware, and methodologically interpretable to be treated as governed evidence within the SIMULOS® lifecycle. SEQM does not determine the ultimate strength, sufficiency, or validation consequence of that evidence. Its task is narrower and foundational: to determine whether simulation-derived information legitimately qualifies as evidence at all, and to define the evidential basis under which that qualification is valid. Core Question What simulation-derived information legitimately qualifies as evidence, and for what evidential purpose? Architectural Position SEQM is the first module within SERBS. It receives governed information from: Simulation Output Governance Standard (SOGS) and Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Standard (SRCS). It precedes: SEWM — Simulation Evidence Weight Module. Its architectural role is therefore to establish the evidence object before any attempt is made to assign evidential weight, define reliance boundaries, impose use limitations, or transfer the evidence into broader validation governance. Internal Flow Position Governed Simulation Output Governed Inference Basis Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Basis → Evidence Candidate Identification → Evidential Purpose Definition → Simulation Basis Traceability → Qualification Condition Assessment → Applicability Definition → Uncertainty Preservation → Evidence Qualification State → Qualified Simulation Evidence → SEWM — Simulation Evidence Weight Module Operational Space SEQM governs the point at which simulation-derived information crosses from: simulation result into: qualified simulation evidence. This operational space includes: evidence candidate identification; evidential purpose definition; proposition linkage; simulation basis traceability; output provenance; inference provenance; correlation basis linkage; contextual qualification; applicability definition; qualification conditions; uncertainty preservation; temporal applicability; version applicability; scenario applicability; configuration applicability; evidence qualification state; evidence disqualification where the required basis is absent. Operational Scope SEQM applies to any simulation-derived information that an organization intends to use as evidence. Such information may include: numerical outputs; state transitions; observed simulated behavior; event frequencies; failure patterns; scenario outcomes; threshold crossings; sensitivity results; comparative results; stochastic distributions; trajectory results; predicted behaviors; simulated interactions; failure modes; anomaly patterns; scenario coverage observations; simulation-to-reality comparisons; governed simulation inferences. The Module applies equally to: a single simulation execution; repeated runs; scenario portfolios; Monte Carlo campaigns; high-performance simulation campaigns; digital twins; physical simulations; hybrid simulations; mission simulations; engineering simulations; scientific simulations; safety simulations; AI simulations; autonomous-system simulations; future simulation technologies. Evidence Candidate Principle A simulation-derived result must first be identified as an Evidence Candidate before it can be qualified. An Evidence Candidate is: a defined simulation-derived information object proposed for use in supporting, challenging, comparing, informing, or constraining a specific proposition, question, assessment, or decision context. An Evidence Candidate may originate from: one execution; multiple executions; one scenario; a scenario set; a simulation campaign; a correlation result; a pattern across outputs; a governed inference. But existence alone does not establish evidential status. Simulation Output ≠ Simulation Evidence SEQM enforces the distinction: Simulation Output ≠ Simulation Evidence A result becomes governed evidence only when the relationship between that result and an explicit evidential purpose is established. For example: “The simulator produced a maximum temperature of 912°C.” is an output statement. “Under Scenario S-47, Configuration C-3, and the governed assumptions of Simulation Model M-12, the simulation produced a maximum temperature of 912°C, supporting evidence concerning thermal behavior under those represented conditions.” is an evidentially qualified statement. The difference is governance context. Evidential Purpose Principle Every qualified Simulation Evidence object must have a defined Evidential Purpose. The Evidential Purpose specifies what the evidence is intended to inform. It may relate to: a hypothesis; a design question; a performance question; a safety proposition; a comparative assessment; a mission condition; a failure hypothesis; a scenario question; a behavioral proposition; a threshold condition; an engineering claim; a validation input; an operational question. Evidence without a defined evidential purpose remains analytically informative but methodologically underqualified. Evidence-to-Proposition Relationship SEQM requires a defined relationship between: Simulation Evidence and the proposition or question the evidence is intended to inform. The relationship may be: supporting; challenging; contradicting; comparative; conditional; exclusionary; sensitivity-based; exploratory. This distinction matters because the same simulation result may legitimately serve different evidential functions in different contexts. A failure result may weaken one proposition while strongly supporting another. Simulation Basis Traceability Qualified Simulation Evidence must remain traceable, where materially relevant, to the governed simulation basis from which it originated. The traceability chain may include: Simulation Evidence → Simulation Output → Execution Record → Scenario → Input Basis → Model & Environment → Assumptions → Reality Representation → Purpose & Scope → Simulation Object Where SRCS applies: Simulation Evidence → Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Basis This chain ensures that evidential meaning cannot become detached from the conditions that created it. Evidence Context Principle Simulation evidence is inherently context-dependent. SEQM therefore requires relevant evidential context to remain visible. Context may include: Simulation Object identity; object version; configuration; purpose; scope; excluded conditions; reality representation; abstraction level; fidelity level; assumptions; model version; environment version; input set; temporal basis; scenario; parameter range; execution conditions; output type; correlation basis; uncertainty. Context is not metadata decoration. It is part of the evidential meaning. Qualification Conditions An Evidence Candidate may be qualified only where the minimum material conditions necessary to interpret it are established. Qualification conditions may require: identifiable evidence object; identifiable originating output; defined evidential purpose; traceable simulation basis; known Simulation Object; known object version or configuration; known scenario basis; known execution source; known material assumptions; known output meaning; known correlation basis where reality claims are involved; known uncertainty affecting interpretation; known applicability conditions; known material exclusions. The precise combination depends on the evidential purpose. SEQM therefore does not impose unnecessary uniformity. It requires sufficient contextual definition for legitimate evidential interpretation. Evidence Qualification State SEQM establishes explicit qualification states. A Simulation Evidence Candidate may be classified as: 1. Unqualified The simulation-derived information exists but lacks sufficient evidential context or purpose definition. 2. Conditionally Qualified The information may function as evidence only under explicitly defined conditions or limitations. 3. Qualified The information has sufficient simulation-specific basis, traceability, purpose alignment, and contextual definition to function as governed Simulation Evidence. 4. Qualification Suspended A previously qualified evidence object has encountered a material change, unresolved discrepancy, missing provenance, or other condition requiring reassessment. 5. Disqualified The information cannot legitimately function as Simulation Evidence for the stated evidential purpose. Qualification state must remain distinguishable from evidential weight. Qualified ≠ strong evidence. Qualification determines whether the object may enter evidence governance. SEWM determines how much simulation-specific evidential weight it may carry. Conditional Qualification Many simulation results can be evidentially valid only under specified conditions. SEQM therefore permits conditional qualification. Example: Qualified only for Object Version V4, environmental range E2–E5, Scenario Family S3, and model configuration M7. Such evidence remains legitimate. Its qualification is simply bounded. Conditional qualification must not be silently transformed into universal qualification downstream. Negative Evidence Qualification SEQM explicitly allows negative, failed, anomalous, unstable, or contradictory results to qualify as evidence. Evidence qualification must not depend upon whether the result supports the preferred hypothesis. Examples include: failure to achieve mission objectives; model divergence; repeated instability; scenario-specific failure; unexpected collision; thermal exceedance; non-convergence; behavioral anomaly; disagreement with operational data; unexpected sensitivity. If the result is relevant, traceable, and contextually interpretable, it may qualify as evidence. Inference Qualification Some simulation evidence is directly observed in simulation outputs. Other evidence is derived through inference. SEQM requires this distinction to remain visible. Direct Simulation Observation ≠ Derived Simulation Inference Where evidence depends upon an inference, the qualification basis must identify: originating outputs; inference method; inferential assumptions; transformation or aggregation; inference scope; uncertainty introduced by inference. The existence of a governed inference does not automatically increase or decrease evidence weight. It simply changes the evidential pathway that must remain traceable. Aggregated Evidence Qualification Simulation campaigns frequently aggregate outputs across large numbers of runs. SEQM requires aggregated evidence to identify: aggregation basis; included executions; excluded executions; scenario composition; common assumptions; common model dependencies; statistical method; aggregation transformation; treatment of failed runs; treatment of anomalous runs; dependence structure where known. An aggregate metric must not obscure the evidence objects from which it was created. Evidence Independence Awareness SEQM does not determine final evidential weight, but it must preserve information relevant to later assessment of evidence dependence. Examples include: repeated use of the same model; shared assumptions; identical input generation; common scenario design; shared execution infrastructure; common data transformations; common correlation basis. This enables SEWM to distinguish between: many evidence objects and many independently informative evidence objects. Applicability Definition Every qualified evidence object should identify the context within which its evidential meaning applies. Applicability may be defined by: object; configuration; scenario; environment; parameter range; temporal interval; operational condition; mission phase; behavior class; model state; input family; uncertainty range. Applicability defines where the evidence may meaningfully enter subsequent governance. It does not yet define the maximum reliance boundary; that is owned by SRBM. Temporal Qualification Evidence qualification may depend upon time. Evidence can become underqualified where: the Simulation Object changes; a model is replaced; assumptions become obsolete; new operational data appears; reality correlation changes; input distributions materially shift; scenario relevance changes. SEQM must therefore support: Qualification Review and Qualification Reassessment. This creates the interface to SLRS lifecycle governance. Evidence Provenance SEQM requires simulation evidence to preserve sufficient provenance to identify how the evidence came into existence. Provenance may include: originating simulation; originating execution ID; simulation campaign ID; scenario ID; model version; environment version; object version; input package; output reference; transformation history; inference history; aggregation history; qualification record. SEQM governs the simulation-specific evidential provenance relationship. General provenance integrity and audit assurance remain outside its boundary where governed by INTEGROS® or ADIT®. Qualification Failure Conditions An Evidence Candidate should not qualify where material information necessary to understand its evidential meaning is absent. Examples include: unknown originating execution; unknown Simulation Object version; missing scenario basis; unclear evidential purpose; untraceable transformed output; unidentified material assumption; unknown model configuration; missing relationship to the proposition being supported; output used outside its represented context; correlation claim without a governed correlation basis; aggregation that conceals materially relevant failures; evidence whose meaning cannot be reconstructed. Qualification failure does not necessarily mean the underlying simulation is invalid. It means the information cannot currently function as governed Simulation Evidence for the intended purpose. SEQM Boundary with SOGS SOGS governs: what the simulation produced; output identity; output classification; inference; output limitation; output documentation. SEQM governs: whether that governed output or inference may legitimately function as evidence; for what evidential purpose; under what qualification conditions; with what simulation basis. Therefore: Governed Output ≠ Qualified Evidence. SEQM Boundary with SRCS SRCS governs the correlation relationship between simulation and reality. SEQM may use that governed correlation relationship as part of an evidence qualification basis. It does not recalculate or redefine correlation. Therefore: Correlation Result → Evidence Qualification Input not Evidence Qualification → Correlation Determination. SEQM Boundary with SEWM SEQM determines whether simulation-derived information qualifies as evidence. SEWM determines the simulation-specific evidential weight of that qualified evidence. Therefore: Qualification ≠ Weight. A result may be fully qualified yet carry weak evidential weight. A result may also be conditionally qualified yet carry strong evidential weight within a narrow context. SEQM Boundary with VALIDOS® SEQM does not determine whether evidence is sufficient for a broader Validation Determination. It governs only the qualification of simulation-derived information as Simulation Evidence. The boundary is: SEQM: Does this simulation-derived information legitimately qualify as evidence for this defined evidential purpose? VALIDOS®: Does the total validation evidence basis sufficiently support the Validation Determination and intended reliance? SEQM Boundary with INTEGROS® SEQM does not own general evidence integrity. It may require evidence provenance, traceability, and contextual completeness as conditions of qualification. INTEGROS® governs broader integrity properties of the evidence and its supporting structures. SEQM Boundary with ADIT® SEQM may require a reconstructable evidential basis. ADIT® may audit whether records, evidence, observations, and execution traces are sufficiently preserved and verifiable. SEQM does not own auditability governance. Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum SEQM implementation should establish: 1. Evidence Candidate Identification Identify the exact simulation-derived information proposed as evidence. 2. Evidential Purpose Definition Define the proposition, question, comparison, or decision context the evidence is intended to inform. 3. Evidence Source Identification Identify the originating outputs, observations, correlations, comparisons, or inferences. 4. Simulation Basis Traceability Link the Evidence Candidate to the relevant governed simulation lifecycle elements. 5. Context Definition Identify object, version, configuration, scenario, model, environment, assumptions, inputs, and other materially relevant conditions. 6. Applicability Definition Define where the evidential meaning applies. 7. Uncertainty Preservation Preserve material uncertainty affecting interpretation. 8. Qualification Condition Assessment Determine whether the minimum required conditions for legitimate evidential interpretation are satisfied. 9. Qualification State Assignment Assign the Evidence Candidate a governed qualification state. 10. Qualification Record Creation Document the basis supporting the qualification decision. Governance Outputs SEQM may produce: Simulation Evidence Candidate Record Simulation Evidential Purpose Statement Simulation Evidence Source Record Simulation Evidence Traceability Chain Simulation Evidence Context Record Simulation Evidence Applicability Statement Simulation Evidence Qualification Condition Record Simulation Evidence Uncertainty Link Simulation Evidence Qualification State Simulation Evidence Disqualification Record Simulation Evidence Qualification Record Qualified Simulation Evidence Object These outputs provide the input basis for SEWM — Simulation Evidence Weight Module. Enterprise Application SEQM enables organizations to prevent a common simulation governance failure: treating every technically generated result as evidence. An organization may use SEQM to determine: whether a particular simulation result legitimately supports a stated proposition; whether the result remains connected to the correct Simulation Object version; whether scenario and execution context are preserved; whether a derived inference is traceable to its source outputs; whether failed and anomalous outcomes remain evidentially visible; whether aggregated campaign results conceal material dependencies; whether evidence is still applicable after material change; whether an output should remain unqualified, become conditionally qualified, become fully qualified, or be disqualified; whether simulation-derived information is ready to proceed into evidential weight assessment. This becomes especially important in very large simulation programs where millions or billions of outputs may exist but only a subset may legitimately function as evidence for a particular claim. SEQM therefore creates an explicit methodological gate between simulation production and simulation evidence governance. Foundational Principles Simulation output is not automatically simulation evidence. Evidence qualification requires an explicit evidential purpose. Evidence must remain connected to the simulation basis that gives it meaning. Qualification is contextual, not universal. Qualified evidence may still carry weak evidential weight. Conditional evidence must remain conditional. Negative simulation results may qualify as evidence. Aggregated evidence must not erase its originating simulation basis. Evidence provenance is part of evidential qualification. A simulation result that cannot be meaningfully traced, contextualized, and interpreted should not be treated as governed Simulation Evidence. Canonical Closing Statement Simulation Evidence Qualification Module establishes the first evidential control point within the Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard by transforming simulation-derived outputs, observations, correlations, comparisons, and governed inferences into explicitly identified, purpose-linked, traceable, context-bound, applicability-defined, uncertainty-aware, and qualification-state-controlled Simulation Evidence. Through governance of Evidence Candidates, evidential purpose, proposition relationships, simulation basis traceability, contextual conditions, provenance, inference pathways, aggregation, applicability, qualification states, temporal relevance, and qualification failure, SEQM prevents simulation results from acquiring evidential status merely because they were computationally produced or analytically persuasive. By separating evidence qualification from evidential weight, reliance, validation sufficiency, integrity, and auditability, SEQM preserves the architectural boundaries of SIMULOS®, VALIDOS®, INTEGROS®, and ADIT® while creating the governed evidence object required for downstream evidence assessment. No simulation-derived result should legitimately enter broader evidential reliance until the conditions under which it becomes evidence have first been made explicit.

title: OOF™ Simulation Evidence Weight Module (SEWM)
text: OOF™ Simulation Evidence Weight Module (SEWM) Simulation Evidence Weight Module (SEWM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard (SERBS) Module: SEWM — Simulation Evidence Weight Module Operational Layer: Simulation Evidence Weight Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Simulation Evidence Weight Origin ID: SIMULOS-SERBS-SEWM-011.2 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 20 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Simulation Evidence Weight Module (SEWM) is the second Core Module of the Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard (SERBS) within SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture. SEWM governs the simulation-specific evidential weight assigned to qualified Simulation Evidence by determining how strongly that evidence may legitimately support, challenge, constrain, compare, or inform a defined evidential proposition within its governed simulation context. The Module evaluates the material factors that strengthen, weaken, condition, narrow, or qualify evidential significance, including reality representation, assumption dependence, model applicability, input representativeness, scenario relevance, execution basis, repetition structure, output meaning, inference distance, simulation-to-reality correlation, uncertainty, evidence dependence, and temporal relevance. SEWM does not determine whether the complete evidence basis is sufficient for a Validation Determination. Its task is narrower: to determine how much simulation-specific evidential significance qualified Simulation Evidence may legitimately carry before reliance boundaries and broader validation sufficiency are considered. Core Question How much evidential significance may qualified simulation evidence legitimately carry within its defined context? Architectural Position SEWM is the second module within SERBS. It follows: SEQM — Simulation Evidence Qualification Module and precedes: SRBM — Simulation Reliance Boundary Module. SEQM establishes: what legitimately qualifies as Simulation Evidence. SEWM then establishes: how much simulation-specific evidential weight that qualified evidence may carry. SRBM subsequently determines: how far reliance upon that evidence may legitimately extend. The sequence is therefore: Qualification → Weight → Reliance Boundary. Internal Flow Position Qualified Simulation Evidence → Evidential Proposition Alignment → Evidence Strength Factor Identification → Evidence Weakness Factor Identification → Dependence Assessment → Uncertainty Effect Assessment → Correlation Contribution Assessment → Contextual Weight Determination → Simulation Evidence Weight State → Weighted Simulation Evidence → SRBM — Simulation Reliance Boundary Module Operational Space SEWM governs the space between: qualified evidence and the evidential significance attributed to that evidence. This operational space includes: evidence-to-proposition strength; representational contribution; assumption dependence; model applicability; environmental applicability; input representativeness; scenario relevance; scenario coverage relevance; execution consistency; repetition value; evidence independence; common-mode weakness; output directness; inference distance; correlation contribution; uncertainty effects; contradictory evidence; evidence convergence; evidence divergence; temporal relevance; evidence degradation; contextual weight assignment. Operational Scope SEWM applies whenever qualified simulation evidence is expected to carry evidential significance beyond mere existence. It may govern evidence derived from: individual simulation runs; repeated simulations; Monte Carlo studies; scenario portfolios; large simulation campaigns; comparative simulations; sensitivity studies; failure simulations; mission simulations; engineering simulations; safety simulations; scientific simulations; digital twins; infrastructure simulations; economic simulations; AI simulations; autonomous-system simulations; physical simulations; hybrid simulations; future simulation technologies. The Module remains technology-neutral. Its concern is not computational sophistication. Its concern is: how much evidential meaning the governed simulation basis can legitimately support. Evidence Qualification ≠ Evidence Weight SEWM enforces the distinction: Qualified Evidence ≠ Strong Evidence SEQM may determine that an evidence object is: Qualified because it is sufficiently identified, traceable, contextualized, and interpretable. SEWM may nevertheless determine that the evidence carries: low evidential weight because it depends heavily upon uncertain assumptions, weak reality representation, narrow scenarios, limited correlation, or other material constraints. Conversely, conditionally qualified evidence may carry substantial evidential weight within a narrow context. Qualification answers: May this information function as evidence? Weight answers: How strongly may this evidence support the defined proposition? Evidence Weight Is Proposition-Specific Evidential weight does not exist in isolation. The same simulation evidence may carry different weight for different propositions. For example, a simulation may provide: high evidential weight for the proposition: “Configuration A performs more efficiently than Configuration B under Scenario Set S.” while providing: low evidential weight for the proposition: “Configuration A will outperform Configuration B across unrestricted operational reality.” SEWM therefore requires evidence weight to remain linked to the specific proposition being considered. Representational Strength SEWM evaluates how the governed reality representation affects evidential weight. Relevant factors may include: whether materially relevant aspects of reality were represented; abstraction level; fidelity; resolution; excluded phenomena; proxy use; simplified interactions; representation limitations. High representational sophistication does not automatically produce high evidential weight. The relevant question is: Was the reality necessary for this evidential proposition represented sufficiently? Assumption Dependence Simulation evidence may depend materially upon assumptions. SEWM therefore evaluates: number of material assumptions; consequence of assumption failure; sensitivity to assumption variation; dependencies between assumptions; uncertainty surrounding assumptions; whether assumptions are empirically supported; whether results remain stable when assumptions change. Evidence whose conclusion disappears under plausible assumption variation may legitimately carry less weight. Model Applicability A simulation model may be technically valid within one range while poorly suited to another. SEWM therefore considers whether: the model was used within its intended applicability; extrapolation occurred; relevant behaviors are represented; model simplifications affect the proposition; parameter ranges remain supported; model structure creates known systematic limitations. Model sophistication ≠ model applicability. Input Representativeness Qualified evidence may still carry limited weight where its input basis poorly represents the evidential context. SEWM may consider: source relevance; distribution representativeness; temporal representativeness; environmental representativeness; population representativeness; transformation effects; synthetic-data dependence; input uncertainty; missing input conditions. The relevant question is: Do the inputs support the evidential proposition being made? Scenario Relevance Evidence weight depends partly upon whether the simulated scenarios materially address the proposition. SEWM evaluates: relevance of scenarios to the evidential question; coverage of expected conditions; representation of material variations; edge-case inclusion; stress-condition inclusion; uncertainty coverage; scenario omission; scenario overconcentration. A very large simulation campaign may carry little weight for a specific proposition if the decisive scenario was never simulated. Execution Basis SEWM may consider whether evidential weight is strengthened or weakened by the execution basis. Relevant factors may include: controlled execution; configuration consistency; execution reproducibility; runtime intervention; failed executions; execution anomalies; incomplete runs; execution drift; campaign consistency; reconstructability. SEWM does not govern execution itself. That remains under SES. It uses governed execution information as an input into evidential weight assessment. Repetition Value Principle Repeated simulation may increase evidential weight. But repetition does not automatically do so. SEWM distinguishes: Repeated Evidence from Independent Evidential Support. Repeated runs may increase weight where they legitimately test: stochastic variation; uncertainty; parameter variation; scenario diversity; sensitivity; reproducibility; robustness. Repeated runs may add little weight where every execution reproduces the same material weakness. Evidence Independence SEWM requires evidence dependence to remain visible. Evidence objects may share: the same model; the same assumptions; the same input source; the same scenario design; the same reality representation; the same execution infrastructure; the same correlation basis; the same transformation methodology. Ten thousand evidence objects sharing one material weakness may not provide ten thousand independent confirmations. Therefore: Evidence Count ≠ Evidence Independence. Common-Mode Weakness A common-mode weakness is a material limitation shared across multiple evidence objects. Examples include: one incorrect assumption; one omitted physical phenomenon; one unrepresentative dataset; one systematic sensor model error; one missing scenario class; one correlation deficiency; one shared transformation error. SEWM requires common-mode weaknesses to reduce the apparent independence of aggregated evidence where materially relevant. Output Directness Evidence may carry different weight depending on how directly it arises from governed outputs. SEWM distinguishes between: Directly Observed Simulation Evidence and Derived or Inferred Simulation Evidence. Direct evidence may include: observed state; threshold crossing; collision event; simulated failure; measured simulated parameter. Derived evidence may require: aggregation; transformation; inference; statistical interpretation; causal interpretation; model-based extrapolation. Derived evidence is not automatically weaker. But the inferential pathway must be included when assessing weight. Inference Distance SEWM introduces Inference Distance as the methodological distance between: what the simulation directly produced and what the evidence is being used to claim. Short inference distance may occur where: output → directly corresponding proposition. Long inference distance may occur where: output → transformation → aggregation → statistical inference → causal interpretation → real-world claim. Greater inference distance may introduce additional dependence, assumptions, and uncertainty. It must therefore remain visible in evidence-weight determination. Correlation Contribution Simulation-to-reality correlation established through SRCS may materially influence evidential weight. SEWM may consider: strength of observed correlation; number of reality comparison points; diversity of comparison conditions; correlation uncertainty; known deviations; systematic discrepancies; temporal stability; correlation applicability to the evidential proposition. However: Correlation Strength ≠ Reality Equivalence. Strong correlation may strengthen evidence. It does not remove all remaining limitations. Uncertainty Effect SEWM requires material uncertainty to influence evidence weight. Relevant uncertainty may arise from: inputs; assumptions; parameters; model structure; scenario selection; execution variability; outputs; inference; correlation; represented reality. Uncertainty need not make evidence unusable. It must make evidential weight more realistic. Sensitivity Principle Evidence weight should reflect the sensitivity of the evidential conclusion to material changes in the simulation basis. Where small changes in: assumptions; inputs; parameters; scenarios; environmental conditions; model structure produce major changes in the conclusion, evidence may require lower or more conditional weight. Where the conclusion remains stable across materially relevant variation, evidence weight may be strengthened. Evidence Convergence Multiple evidence objects may increase evidential weight where they converge upon the same proposition through meaningfully different evidential pathways. Convergence may be stronger where evidence differs across: models; assumptions; input sources; scenarios; methods; environmental configurations; execution structures; correlation sources. SEWM therefore distinguishes: Repeated Agreement from Independent Convergence. Contradictory Evidence SEWM must preserve material contradictory simulation evidence. Evidence weight cannot legitimately be determined only from evidence supporting the preferred proposition. Contradictory evidence may include: different model results; scenario-specific failures; alternative parameter outcomes; inconsistent repeated runs; operational disagreement; correlation failures; unexpected sensitivities. Contradiction may: reduce evidential weight; narrow applicability; require conditional weighting; trigger further simulation; require separate evidence classes. Evidence Weight States SEWM may assign a governed evidence-weight state. A minimum state model may include: 1. Indeterminate Weight Evidence is qualified, but the simulation basis is insufficiently characterized to assign meaningful evidential weight. 2. Limited Weight Evidence legitimately informs the proposition but is materially constrained by uncertainty, representation, assumptions, scenarios, correlation, dependence, or other weaknesses. 3. Moderate Weight Evidence provides meaningful support within a defined context, while material limitations remain. 4. Substantial Weight Evidence provides strong simulation-specific support for the defined proposition under the governed conditions. 5. Conditional Weight Evidence may carry substantial or moderate weight only within explicitly defined conditions. 6. Degraded Weight Previously assigned weight has materially weakened because of new information, reality change, model change, evidence contradiction, correlation deterioration, or another material change. The states are not universal scientific truth categories. They are governance states requiring defined organizational criteria. Weight State ≠ Validation Status An evidence object with Substantial Weight is not automatically sufficient for validation. Likewise, multiple substantial-weight evidence objects do not automatically establish validation sufficiency. SEWM governs: simulation-specific evidential significance. VALIDOS® governs: the sufficiency of the total validation basis. Quantitative and Qualitative Weighting SEWM may support: qualitative weighting; ordinal weighting; numerical weighting; probabilistic weighting; multi-factor weighting; evidence matrices; structured expert assessment; hybrid approaches. SIMULOS® does not require one universal scoring method. The weighting method must remain: explicit; interpretable; proposition-linked; context-aware; reproducible where appropriate; transparent about uncertainty; bounded by its intended use. A numerical score must not create false precision. Weight Calibration Organizations may establish evidence-weight criteria appropriate to their context. Calibration should consider: consequence of reliance; simulation type; evidential purpose; available reality data; expected uncertainty; model maturity; scenario criticality; safety relevance; operational significance. SEWM governs the simulation-specific structure of weighting. It does not establish organization-wide risk appetite or accountability. Temporal Weight Evidence weight may change over time. Weight may increase where: new real-world correlation becomes available; additional independent evidence converges; model limitations are reduced; relevant scenario coverage expands. Weight may decrease where: reality changes; the Simulation Object changes; assumptions become obsolete; contradictory evidence emerges; correlation deteriorates; new failure modes are discovered. Evidence weight must therefore be reviewable rather than permanently fixed. SEWM Boundary with SEQM SEQM determines whether simulation-derived information legitimately qualifies as evidence. SEWM determines how much evidential weight the qualified evidence may carry. Therefore: Qualification ≠ Weight. SEWM must not retroactively redefine evidence qualification except where weight assessment reveals missing information that requires SEQM reassessment. SEWM Boundary with SRBM SEWM determines: how strong the evidence is within its governed context. SRBM determines: how far reliance upon that evidence may extend. A strong evidence object may still have a narrow reliance boundary. Therefore: High Weight ≠ Broad Reliance. SEWM Boundary with VALIDOS® SEWM does not determine: total evidence sufficiency; validation criteria satisfaction; Validation Determination; operational reliance authorization. VALIDOS® remains responsible for broader validation governance. The boundary is: SEWM: How much simulation-specific evidential significance may this evidence carry? VALIDOS®: Is the total evidence basis sufficient for the relevant validation claim and intended reliance? SEWM Boundary with SRCS SRCS determines the governed correlation relationship between simulation and reality. SEWM may use correlation as one evidential-strength factor. SEWM does not establish correlation independently. SEWM Boundary with SSS SSS governs scenario design and scenario coverage. SEWM may assess how scenario relevance and coverage affect evidential weight. It does not redesign or retroactively redefine the scenario space. SEWM Boundary with SAS SAS governs simulation assumptions. SEWM evaluates how dependence upon those governed assumptions affects evidential weight. It does not determine the universal validity of the assumptions. SEWM Boundary with SIDS SIDS governs simulation inputs and data at the simulation-input boundary. SEWM evaluates how input representativeness and uncertainty affect evidential significance. It does not become a general data-quality framework. SEWM Boundary with INTEGROS® SEWM does not determine general evidence integrity. It assumes governed integrity information may be relevant to evidence-weight assessment where supplied by INTEGROS®. Integrity and evidential weight remain distinct governance questions. SEWM Boundary with ADIT® ADIT® may determine whether evidential records and execution evidence are sufficiently observable, preserved, verifiable, or auditable. SEWM determines the simulation-specific evidential weight those governed records may support. Auditability ≠ Evidential Weight. Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum SEWM implementation should establish: 1. Qualified Evidence Input Receive a qualified Simulation Evidence object from SEQM. 2. Evidential Proposition Confirm the specific proposition or question against which weight is being assessed. 3. Strength Factor Identification Identify material factors strengthening evidential meaning. 4. Weakness Factor Identification Identify material factors weakening or constraining evidential meaning. 5. Dependence Assessment Identify dependencies across evidence objects and common-mode weaknesses. 6. Uncertainty Assessment Determine how material uncertainty affects evidential significance. 7. Correlation Contribution Determine how governed simulation-to-reality correlation affects evidence weight where relevant. 8. Contradictory Evidence Review Identify materially conflicting or divergent evidence. 9. Weight Determination Assign a governed simulation-specific evidence-weight state or value. 10. Weight Basis Record Document the basis, conditions, uncertainty, dependencies, and factors supporting the determination. Governance Outputs SEWM may produce: Simulation Evidence Weight Assessment Evidence Strength Factor Record Evidence Weakness Factor Record Assumption Dependence Record Scenario Relevance Assessment Evidence Independence Assessment Common-Mode Weakness Record Inference Distance Record Correlation Contribution Record Evidence Uncertainty Effect Record Contradictory Evidence Record Evidence Convergence Record Simulation Evidence Weight State Simulation Evidence Weight Basis Weighted Simulation Evidence Object These outputs provide the governed basis for: SRBM — Simulation Reliance Boundary Module. Enterprise Application SEWM enables organizations to solve a problem that appears repeatedly in large-scale simulation programs: a simulation may generate enormous quantities of qualified evidence without all of that evidence carrying equal significance. An organization may use SEWM to determine: whether repeated simulations provide genuinely new evidence; whether millions of runs share one common model weakness; whether evidence depends critically upon one assumption; whether scenario coverage actually addresses the proposition being supported; whether correlation with reality meaningfully strengthens evidence; whether an aggregate success rate conceals important failures; whether multiple models independently converge; whether inference from output to real-world claim is short or extensive; whether uncertainty materially weakens the evidential conclusion; whether previously strong evidence has degraded after reality change; whether evidence should carry limited, moderate, substantial, conditional, indeterminate, or degraded weight. SEWM therefore prevents organizations from equating: more simulations with more proof. A billion simulations using the same incomplete representation may provide less evidential strength than a smaller body of independently convergent simulations supported by strong reality correlation and materially different evidential pathways. The Module gives organizations a method for distinguishing evidence volume from evidence strength. Foundational Principles Qualified evidence is not automatically strong evidence. Evidence weight is proposition-specific. Evidence volume is not evidential strength. Repeated evidence is not automatically independent evidence. Common assumptions create common evidential dependencies. Simulation sophistication does not determine evidence weight. Numerical precision does not create evidential certainty. Scenario relevance matters more than scenario count. Correlation may strengthen evidence without creating reality equivalence. Independent convergence may carry greater evidential significance than repeated agreement generated through one common pathway. High evidential weight does not automatically create broad reliance. Simulation evidence should carry only the weight that its governed representation, assumptions, model, inputs, scenarios, execution basis, outputs, correlation, dependencies, and uncertainty can legitimately support. Canonical Closing Statement Simulation Evidence Weight Module establishes the evidential significance layer within the Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard by determining how strongly qualified Simulation Evidence may legitimately support, challenge, constrain, compare, or inform a defined proposition within its governed simulation context. Through governance of representational strength, assumption dependence, model applicability, input representativeness, scenario relevance, execution basis, repetition value, evidence independence, common-mode weakness, output directness, inference distance, correlation contribution, uncertainty, sensitivity, convergence, contradiction, temporal relevance, and evidence-weight states, SEWM prevents simulation evidence from acquiring strength merely through scale, repetition, complexity, numerical precision, or apparent sophistication. By separating evidence qualification from evidential weight, and evidential weight from reliance boundaries and validation sufficiency, SEWM preserves the methodological boundaries of SERBS and VALIDOS® while creating the governed basis required for downstream reliance control. Simulation evidence should carry neither more nor less evidential significance than the governed simulation conditions can legitimately support.

title: OOF™ Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard - (SERBS)
text: OOF™ Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard - (SERBS) Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard - (SERBS) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard (SERBS) is the Parent Standard within SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture that governs what simulation-derived information may legitimately become evidence, what evidential meaning and weight that evidence may carry, how far reliance upon it may extend, which uses must remain limited or prohibited, and how simulation-derived evidence must interface with broader validation governance. SERBS establishes the methodological boundary between simulation output, simulation-derived evidence, and validation reliance. It requires simulation evidence to remain connected to the Simulation Object, simulation purpose and scope, represented reality, assumptions, model and environment, input basis, scenario conditions, execution record, governed outputs, and simulation-to-reality correlation from which its evidential meaning originates. SERBS does not determine whether an object, system, claim, process, or operational proposition is validated. It governs the simulation-specific evidential basis that may legitimately be transferred into broader validation processes. Core Question What evidential meaning may simulation results legitimately carry, and where does simulation-specific reliance end before broader validation governance becomes necessary? Architectural Position SERBS occupies the eleventh governed space of the SIMULOS® simulation governance lifecycle. It follows: Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Standard (SRCS) and precedes: Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Standard (SLRS). The preceding standards establish: what is simulated → why it is simulated → how reality is represented → what assumptions are used → how the model and environment are constituted → what inputs enter → what scenarios are tested → how execution occurs → what outputs are produced → how those outputs correlate with reality. SERBS then asks the next methodological question: What may those governed simulation results legitimately support as evidence? The purpose of SERBS is therefore not to produce additional simulation results, but to establish the legitimate evidential meaning and reliance boundary of results already produced and governed through the preceding SIMULOS® lifecycle. Governance Flow Position Governed Simulation Outputs + Governed Simulation-to-Reality Correlation → Simulation Evidence Qualification → Simulation Evidence Weight → Simulation Reliance Boundary → Simulation Use Limitation → Simulation Validation Interface → Governed Simulation Evidence & Reliance Record → Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Where broader validation is required: Governed Simulation Evidence & Reliance Record → VALIDOS® Validation Governance Operational Space SERBS governs the operational space between simulation-derived information and legitimate reliance upon that information. Its governed space includes: simulation evidence identification; simulation evidence qualification; evidence-purpose alignment; evidence provenance; simulation-specific evidential weight; conditional evidential meaning; evidence applicability; uncertainty affecting evidential meaning; aggregation of evidence across runs or campaigns; reliance boundaries; unsupported reliance; use limitations; prohibited interpretations; temporal applicability of simulation evidence; evidence transfer into broader validation processes; preservation of simulation-specific qualifications during downstream use. SERBS transforms simulation-derived information from an unbounded analytical product into an explicitly governed evidential basis. Operational Scope SERBS applies whenever simulation results are expected to support or influence a material claim, assessment, comparison, engineering judgment, scientific conclusion, design decision, safety argument, mission decision, operational decision, validation process, deployment decision, or other form of reliance. It applies across: individual simulation runs; repeated simulations; scenario portfolios; large-scale simulation campaigns; engineering simulations; scientific simulations; physical simulations; digital simulations; hybrid simulations; digital twins; infrastructure simulations; safety simulations; mission simulations; economic simulations; AI simulations; autonomous-system simulations; future simulation technologies. SERBS remains technology-neutral. Its concern is not how sophisticated the simulation technology is, but what evidential meaning its results can legitimately support. Core Governance Distinctions Simulation Output ≠ Simulation Evidence A simulation output is information produced by simulation execution. Simulation evidence is simulation-derived information that has been explicitly qualified for a defined evidential purpose. The existence of an output does not automatically create an evidential basis. Simulation Evidence ≠ Validation Determination Simulation evidence may contribute materially to validation. It does not automatically establish validation. A Validation Determination may require simulation evidence together with empirical, operational, observational, experimental, documentary, or other evidence governed through VALIDOS®. Evidence Availability ≠ Evidence Sufficiency Large quantities of simulation evidence do not necessarily create sufficient evidence. A million executions based upon the same inaccurate representation, assumption, model limitation, or missing scenario may reproduce the same weakness one million times. Evidence Weight ≠ Evidence Volume The amount of simulation data is not equivalent to the strength of its evidential meaning. Evidence weight depends on the governed relationship between the evidence and the proposition it is intended to support. Correlation ≠ Equivalence Even strong simulation-to-reality correlation does not establish that the simulation and reality are equivalent. The evidential meaning of a simulation result remains bounded by the conditions under which the correlation was established. Reliance ≠ Unlimited Generalization Evidence legitimately applicable to one scenario, configuration, operational condition, time period, or purpose must not automatically be generalized to another. Simulation Evidence Qualification Simulation-derived information may be treated as governed simulation evidence only where its evidential basis is sufficiently identifiable. Qualification should establish, where materially relevant: the simulation-derived information being relied upon; the evidential question or proposition; originating Simulation Object; relevant Simulation Object version and configuration; simulation purpose and scope; applicable exclusions; reality representation; material assumptions; model and environment; input and data basis; relevant scenario or scenario set; execution basis; output identity and classification; inference basis; simulation-to-reality correlation; material uncertainty; temporal applicability; known limitations. Evidence qualification therefore creates an explicit relationship between: Evidence → Simulation Basis → Evidential Meaning. Simulation Evidence Weight SERBS requires the evidential weight of simulation-derived evidence to remain distinct from the mere existence of the evidence. Evidence weight may be influenced by: strength of reality representation; representational fidelity; model applicability; assumption dependence; input representativeness; scenario relevance; scenario coverage; execution consistency; repetition results; output classification; inference distance; simulation-to-reality correlation; uncertainty; known limitations; temporal relevance; dependence between evidence sources. Evidence weight must not be inferred merely from: computational scale; simulation sophistication; graphical realism; institutional prestige; number of runs; number of generated outputs; apparent precision. Precision of simulation output does not itself establish strength of simulation evidence. Simulation Evidence Aggregation SERBS recognizes that simulation campaigns may create evidence across thousands, millions, or more individual executions. Evidence aggregation must therefore distinguish between: More executions and More independent evidential support. Repeated executions may strengthen evidence where repetition legitimately tests variability, uncertainty, stochastic behavior, scenario diversity, or reproducibility. They may add little evidential strength where all executions share the same material: assumption; model weakness; representation error; input deficiency; scenario omission; correlation limitation. Common-mode weaknesses must therefore remain visible when simulation evidence is aggregated. Simulation Reliance Boundary The Simulation Reliance Boundary establishes the maximum simulation-specific reliance that may legitimately be placed upon qualified evidence. A reliance boundary may be constrained by: Simulation Object; object version; object configuration; purpose; scope; exclusion; represented reality; abstraction; fidelity; assumption; parameter range; model applicability; environmental configuration; input basis; scenario; execution condition; output class; inference; correlation; uncertainty; temporal validity. Reliance outside these boundaries requires a new governed basis. SERBS therefore prevents the transformation: Evidence valid under Condition A → claim assumed valid everywhere. Simulation Use Limitation Every material limitation affecting legitimate use of simulation-derived evidence must remain attached to that evidence. Use limitations may establish that evidence: supports only a defined proposition; applies only to specified scenarios; applies only to a defined Simulation Object configuration; applies only within a defined parameter range; depends upon identified assumptions; excludes particular conditions; does not represent specified real-world phenomena; cannot support specified decisions; cannot independently establish operational performance; requires additional evidence; cannot be generalized beyond a stated environment; expires or requires review after material change; may support comparison but not absolute prediction; may support exploration but not validation; may support validation only together with additional evidence. A limitation that is separated from the evidence it constrains is no longer an effective governance control. Unsupported Reliance SERBS requires unsupported reliance to be identifiable. Unsupported reliance may arise where simulation evidence is used: outside its simulation purpose; beyond its scope; for an excluded condition; for a different Simulation Object version; beyond tested parameter ranges; outside represented reality; outside scenario coverage; beyond established correlation; beyond temporal applicability; after material change; contrary to a documented limitation; as sole validation evidence where broader evidence is required. Unsupported reliance must not become legitimate merely because it becomes organizational practice. Negative Evidence Principle SERBS recognizes that failed, anomalous, contradictory, unstable, divergent, or unexpected simulation results may carry significant evidential meaning. Simulation campaigns must therefore not treat only favorable or successful outcomes as evidence. Governable simulation evidence may include: failure; non-convergence; instability; unexpected behavior; threshold violation; scenario failure; sensitivity; disagreement between models; divergence from observed reality; unexpected variance; evidence against an intended claim. An unwanted simulation result does not cease to be evidentially relevant because it is inconvenient. Temporal Evidence Principle Simulation evidence has a temporal dimension. Evidence qualified at one point in time may become less relevant where: the Simulation Object changes; operating conditions change; reality changes; new observations become available; assumptions become obsolete; models are replaced; inputs change materially; new scenarios become relevant; correlation deteriorates. SERBS therefore connects directly to Simulation Lifecycle & Resimulation Standard (SLRS). Evidence whose simulation basis has materially changed must not retain an unchanged reliance status automatically. Validation Interface Principle SERBS establishes the methodological interface between SIMULOS® and VALIDOS®. The boundary is explicit: SIMULOS® determines what simulation-derived evidence can legitimately mean. VALIDOS® determines whether that evidence is sufficient, alone or together with other evidence, to support a Validation Determination or intended reliance. SERBS may therefore qualify: what evidence exists; what proposition it supports; what weight it may carry; under what conditions it applies; what uncertainties affect it; what limitations govern its use. SERBS does not decide: whether the complete Validation Object is valid; whether the complete evidence basis is sufficient; whether validation criteria have been satisfied; whether a Validation Determination may be issued; whether operational reliance is justified by the total validation basis. Cross-Architecture Boundaries SERBS ↔ VALIDOS® SIMULOS® / SERBS governs simulation-derived evidence and the legitimate boundary of simulation-specific reliance. VALIDOS® governs the sufficiency of the complete validation basis and formal Validation Determination. Simulation evidence qualification ≠ validation sufficiency. SERBS ↔ INTEGROS® SERBS governs the simulation-specific meaning and use of simulation-derived evidence. INTEGROS® governs broader integrity properties affecting objects, processes, states, information, and evidence. SERBS must therefore not redefine general evidence integrity. SERBS ↔ ORA™ ORA™ governs actual Operational Reality. SIMULOS® may use governed Operational Reality and SRCS correlation relationships when establishing simulation evidential meaning. SERBS does not determine what operational reality is. SERBS ↔ ADIT® ADIT® may govern auditability, preservation, evidential observation, verification, and examination of what occurred. SERBS governs the simulation-specific meaning and reliance boundary of simulation-derived evidence. Auditability of evidence ≠ evidential meaning of simulation evidence. SERBS ↔ AGA™ AGA™ governs who holds authority, responsibility, accountability, and attribution for decisions involving simulation evidence. SERBS governs what the evidence can legitimately support. SERBS ↔ AIG® / ASGA™ SIMULOS® may generate evidence concerning AI or autonomous systems. SERBS governs that simulation-derived evidence. AIG® and ASGA™ continue to govern the actual behavior, authority, autonomy, constraints, and operation of the systems themselves. Parent Standard Modules 1. SEQM — Simulation Evidence Qualification Module Governs the transformation of simulation-derived outputs, observations, correlations, and inferences into explicitly qualified simulation evidence. SEQM establishes: evidence identity; evidential purpose; simulation basis; provenance; qualification conditions; applicability; uncertainty; evidential qualification state. Its core question is: What simulation-derived information legitimately qualifies as evidence, and for what evidential purpose? 2. SEWM — Simulation Evidence Weight Module Governs the simulation-specific evidential weight assigned to qualified simulation evidence. SEWM evaluates factors that materially strengthen, weaken, condition, or constrain evidential meaning. Its core question is: How much evidential significance may qualified simulation evidence legitimately carry within its defined context? 3. SRBM — Simulation Reliance Boundary Module Governs the maximum legitimate reliance that may be placed upon simulation-derived evidence within the simulation governance context. Its core question is: How far may reliance upon this simulation evidence legitimately extend before the evidence is being used beyond its governed basis? 4. SUM — Simulation Use Limitation Module Governs conditions, exclusions, restrictions, caveats, unsupported interpretations, and prohibited uses attached to simulation evidence. Its core question is: What must simulation-derived evidence not be used to claim, infer, justify, or support? 5. SVIM — Simulation Validation Interface Module Governs the transfer boundary between SIMULOS® simulation evidence governance and VALIDOS® validation governance. SVIM ensures that evidence entering validation retains its: identity; provenance; qualification; evidential weight; applicability; uncertainty; reliance boundary; limitations. Its core question is: How must simulation-derived evidence enter broader validation governance without losing the conditions that define its legitimate meaning? Internal Module Flow Governed Simulation Outputs + Governed Simulation-to-Reality Correlation → SEQM — Simulation Evidence Qualification Module → SEWM — Simulation Evidence Weight Module → SRBM — Simulation Reliance Boundary Module → SUM — Simulation Use Limitation Module → SVIM — Simulation Validation Interface Module → Governed Simulation Evidence & Reliance Record The internal logic is: What qualifies as evidence → what weight it carries → how far reliance may extend → what uses remain prohibited or constrained → how evidence may enter broader validation governance. Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum SERBS implementation should establish: 1. Evidence Object Identify the precise simulation-derived information proposed for evidential use. 2. Evidential Purpose Define the proposition, question, decision, or claim the evidence is intended to inform. 3. Simulation Basis Trace the evidence to its originating Simulation Object, purpose, scope, representation, assumptions, model, inputs, scenarios, executions, outputs, and correlation basis where relevant. 4. Evidence Qualification Determine whether the simulation-derived information legitimately qualifies as evidence for the stated purpose. 5. Evidence Weight Determine the simulation-specific weight that the evidence may legitimately carry. 6. Reliance Boundary Establish the maximum context in which reliance remains supported. 7. Use Limitations Record material exclusions, restrictions, unsupported interpretations, and prohibited uses. 8. Uncertainty Preserve uncertainty affecting evidential meaning. 9. Validation Interface Preserve all relevant evidence conditions when evidence enters VALIDOS® or another downstream validation process. 10. Lifecycle Sensitivity Identify changes capable of invalidating or weakening the current evidential basis and triggering review or resimulation. Governance Outputs SERBS may generate: Simulation Evidence Qualification Record Simulation Evidence Basis Record Simulation Evidence Weight Assessment Simulation Evidence Provenance Record Simulation Evidence Applicability Statement Simulation Reliance Boundary Statement Simulation Use Limitation Record Unsupported Reliance Register Simulation Evidence Uncertainty Record Simulation Evidence Aggregation Record Simulation Validation Interface Package Governed Simulation Evidence & Reliance Record Together, these outputs make the evidential meaning of simulation results explicit, transferable, reviewable, and bounded. Enterprise Application SERBS enables an organization to determine not merely whether a simulation has produced results, but what those results can legitimately support. It can be used to govern simulation evidence used for: engineering decisions; design decisions; safety cases; scientific claims; infrastructure planning; mission preparation; product development; system qualification; operational planning; AI evaluation; autonomous-system evaluation; validation programs; regulatory submissions; investment decisions; risk analysis; scenario comparison. SERBS is particularly relevant where simulation produces highly convincing, precise, or large-scale outputs that may create an appearance of certainty greater than their actual evidential basis. A simulation may produce billions of data points without adequately supporting the real-world proposition for which those data are being used. Equally, a narrowly designed simulation may provide strong evidence for a precisely bounded question even though it cannot support broader claims. SERBS gives organizations the governance structure needed to distinguish between these situations. Foundational Principles Simulation output is not automatically simulation evidence. Simulation evidence is not automatically validation evidence sufficient for a Validation Determination. Evidence availability is not evidence sufficiency. Evidence volume is not evidential strength. Repeated simulation is not automatically independent evidence. Simulation complexity is not evidential authority. Numerical precision is not evidential certainty. Correlation with reality does not establish equivalence with reality. Evidence must remain bounded by the conditions that give it meaning. Use limitations are part of the evidence itself. Negative and anomalous simulation results may carry material evidential meaning. Simulation-derived evidence must not be relied upon beyond the object, conditions, scenarios, assumptions, executions, outputs, correlations, and temporal context from which its evidential meaning was established. SIMULOS® determines what simulation-derived evidence can legitimately mean. VALIDOS® determines whether the total evidence basis is sufficient to support a Validation Determination or intended reliance. Canonical Closing Statement Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard establishes the evidential boundary layer of SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture by transforming simulation-derived outputs, observations, correlations, and inferences into explicitly qualified, weighted, bounded, limitation-aware, and validation-interface-ready simulation evidence. Through governance of evidential purpose, qualification, provenance, weight, applicability, uncertainty, aggregation, reliance boundaries, use limitations, unsupported interpretations, temporal relevance, and validation transfer, SERBS prevents simulation results from acquiring greater authority, certainty, generality, or operational meaning than their governed simulation basis can legitimately support. By separating simulation evidence qualification from broader validation sufficiency, SERBS preserves the methodological boundary between SIMULOS® and VALIDOS® while enabling simulation-derived evidence to enter validation, engineering, scientific, safety, mission, operational, and decision processes without losing the conditions that define its legitimate meaning. SERBS therefore establishes the final evidential gateway of the active simulation process before lifecycle governance begins, ensuring that no simulation-derived evidence can legitimately be relied upon more broadly than the Simulation Object, purpose, reality representation, assumptions, model, inputs, scenarios, executions, outputs, correlations, uncertainties, limitations, and temporal conditions from which that evidence was derived. title: OOF™ Simulation Reliance Boundary Module (SRBM)
