text: OOF™ Simulation Reliance Boundary Module (SRBM) Simulation Reliance Boundary Module (SRBM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard (SERBS) Module: SRBM — Simulation Reliance Boundary Module Operational Layer: Simulation Reliance Boundary Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Simulation Reliance Boundary Origin ID: SIMULOS-SERBS-SRBM-011.3 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 20 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Simulation Reliance Boundary Module (SRBM) is the third Core Module of the Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard (SERBS) within SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture. SRBM governs the maximum legitimate simulation-specific reliance that may be placed upon qualified and weighted Simulation Evidence by defining the objects, purposes, configurations, conditions, scenarios, parameter ranges, environments, temporal contexts, propositions, decisions, and forms of use within which reliance remains supported by the governed simulation basis. The Module establishes the methodological boundary between: what simulation evidence legitimately supports and what would constitute reliance beyond that support. SRBM does not determine whether the total evidence basis is sufficient for a broader Validation Determination, nor does it authorize deployment, operational use, or organizational decisions. Its task is narrower: to determine how far reliance upon simulation-derived evidence may legitimately extend before that evidence is being used beyond the governed basis that gives it meaning. Core Question How far may reliance upon simulation-derived evidence legitimately extend before the evidence is being used beyond its governed basis? Architectural Position SRBM is the third module within SERBS. It follows: SEQM — Simulation Evidence Qualification Module → determines what legitimately qualifies as Simulation Evidence and: SEWM — Simulation Evidence Weight Module → determines how much simulation-specific evidential significance that evidence may carry. SRBM then establishes: where legitimate reliance upon that evidence stops. It precedes: SUM — Simulation Use Limitation Module which governs explicit restrictions, exclusions, caveats, unsupported uses, and prohibited interpretations associated with that reliance boundary. The sequence is therefore: Qualification → Weight → Reliance Boundary → Use Limitation. Internal Flow Position Qualified Simulation Evidence Simulation Evidence Weight → Intended Reliance Identification → Reliance Purpose Definition → Evidence-to-Reliance Alignment → Reliance Condition Identification → Boundary Constraint Assessment → Reliance Expansion Assessment → Unsupported Reliance Detection → Reliance Boundary Determination → Simulation Reliance Boundary State → Governed Simulation Reliance Boundary → SUM — Simulation Use Limitation Module Operational Space SRBM governs the space between: evidential significance and permitted simulation-specific reliance. This operational space includes: intended reliance; reliance purpose; reliance object; reliance proposition; reliance context; reliance conditions; object-specific reliance; configuration-specific reliance; scenario-specific reliance; parameter-specific reliance; environment-specific reliance; temporal reliance; conditional reliance; comparative reliance; predictive reliance; extrapolative reliance; reliance expansion; unsupported reliance; reliance boundary crossing; reliance degradation; reliance suspension; reliance reassessment. Operational Scope SRBM applies whenever simulation-derived evidence is expected to influence or support: engineering judgment; design decisions; scientific conclusions; safety arguments; mission planning; mission decisions; system qualification; comparative evaluation; performance assessment; scenario selection; infrastructure planning; operational preparation; risk analysis; AI evaluation; autonomous-system evaluation; deployment preparation; validation processes; regulatory evidence packages; investment or resource decisions; other material forms of reliance. The Module applies regardless of whether the evidence originates from: one simulation; repeated simulations; Monte Carlo studies; scenario portfolios; large simulation campaigns; digital twins; engineering simulations; mission simulations; safety simulations; scientific simulations; physical simulations; hybrid simulations; AI simulations; autonomous-system simulations; future simulation technologies. SRBM remains technology-neutral. Its concern is not: How advanced is the simulation? Its concern is: How far may the evidence produced through that simulation legitimately be relied upon? Evidence Weight ≠ Reliance Boundary SRBM enforces the distinction: High Evidence Weight ≠ Broad Reliance Evidence may carry substantial evidential weight for a narrowly defined proposition while providing little or no legitimate basis for broader generalization. For example: A simulation campaign may provide substantial evidence that: Configuration A remains stable under Scenario Family S within Parameter Range P. That does not automatically support: Configuration A will remain stable under all operational conditions. SEWM determines evidential strength. SRBM determines the extent of legitimate reliance. Reliance Must Be Explicit Reliance must not remain implicit. SRBM requires the intended form of reliance to be identified before its legitimacy can be assessed. The intended reliance should establish: what decision, proposition, comparison, judgment, or action is being informed; which Simulation Evidence objects are being relied upon; what evidence weight those objects carry; which Simulation Object is concerned; which object version and configuration apply; which represented conditions apply; which scenario space applies; which uncertainty remains; what temporal context applies; what extension beyond directly simulated conditions is proposed. Without an explicit intended reliance, a reliance boundary cannot be meaningfully governed. Reliance Object Principle Simulation evidence may be relied upon only in relation to a sufficiently defined Reliance Object. The Reliance Object may be: a system; a component; a configuration; a design; a process; a mission phase; an operational concept; a simulated behavior; a comparative alternative; a parameter range; another explicitly bounded subject. The Reliance Object must remain aligned with the Simulation Object and evidential basis. Evidence concerning one object must not silently migrate to another. Reliance Purpose Principle The legitimacy of reliance depends upon why the evidence is being used. The same evidence may legitimately support: exploratory engineering while not supporting: safety-critical deployment. It may support: comparison between two simulated configurations while not supporting: absolute prediction of real-world performance. It may support: mission contingency analysis while not independently supporting: mission readiness determination. SRBM therefore requires reliance to remain purpose-specific. Reliance Context Every governed reliance boundary should identify the context within which reliance remains supported. Context may include: Simulation Object; object version; object configuration; simulation purpose; simulation scope; represented reality; abstraction level; fidelity; assumptions; model version; environment configuration; input basis; scenario family; parameter range; execution basis; output class; inference basis; correlation basis; uncertainty; temporal applicability; evidence weight. The boundary is therefore multidimensional. It is not merely a statement that evidence is: usable or not usable. Object Boundary Simulation evidence must remain bounded to the object for which its evidential meaning was established. Evidence derived from: Object Version V3 must not automatically be relied upon for: Object Version V4 where the change may materially affect the evidence. Similarly: Component Evidence ≠ System Evidence unless a governed basis supports that extension. Configuration Boundary Evidence may apply only to a specific configuration. Configuration differences may include: hardware; software; model parameters; architecture; sensor configuration; actuator configuration; material properties; mission configuration; operating mode; system integration state. A materially changed configuration may require reliance reassessment. Scenario Boundary Evidence produced within a defined scenario space must not automatically be generalized outside that scenario space. SRBM requires distinction between: Tested Scenario Space and Untested Scenario Space. Scenario coverage may be broad without being universal. Therefore: Scenario Coverage ≠ Universal Coverage. Parameter Boundary Simulation evidence may be valid only within defined parameter ranges. Examples include: velocity; temperature; pressure; load; mass; latency; sensor range; environmental condition; resource availability; probability distribution; behavioral parameter. Reliance beyond tested or governed parameter ranges constitutes extrapolation and requires explicit justification. Environment Boundary Evidence may be dependent upon the environment represented by the simulation. Environmental boundaries may include: terrain; weather; atmospheric conditions; lighting; traffic; infrastructure; physical interaction; human behavior; electromagnetic conditions; gravity; thermal conditions; communication availability. Evidence derived from one represented environment must not automatically be generalized to materially different environments. Temporal Boundary Simulation evidence may have a legitimate reliance period. Reliance may degrade where: the Simulation Object changes; operational reality changes; input distributions change; assumptions become obsolete; models are updated; new failures emerge; new evidence contradicts earlier results; simulation-to-reality correlation changes; relevant scenarios evolve. SRBM therefore recognizes: Evidence can remain historically correct while becoming operationally stale. Correlation Boundary Where reliance concerns real-world behavior, SRBM must consider the governed simulation-to-reality correlation basis established through SRCS. Strong correlation under: Conditions A, B, and C does not automatically establish equivalent correlation under: Conditions D, E, and F. Therefore: Correlation within a tested domain ≠ correlation outside that domain. Uncertainty Boundary Reliance must reflect material uncertainty. Uncertainty may constrain: the confidence of a conclusion; the parameter range; the scenario range; the temporal applicability; the permitted decision class; the degree of extrapolation; the strength of predictive claims. SRBM does not require uncertainty to eliminate reliance. It requires uncertainty to constrain reliance where materially relevant. Direct Reliance and Extended Reliance SRBM distinguishes between: Direct Reliance Reliance that remains within the object, conditions, scenarios, parameters, purposes, and propositions directly supported by the governed evidence. Extended Reliance Reliance that moves beyond one or more dimensions directly supported by the evidence. Extended reliance is not automatically prohibited. But it requires an explicit governed justification. Reliance Expansion Reliance Expansion occurs when evidence is used beyond its established boundary. Expansion may involve: another object; another configuration; another scenario; another environment; another parameter range; another time period; another decision purpose; another operational condition; another population; another mission phase; a broader proposition. SRBM requires expansion to be visible. Reliance must not expand silently. Reliance Expansion Test Before reliance is expanded, SRBM should determine: 1. What boundary dimension is being crossed? 2. How materially different is the new context? 3. Which simulation assumptions remain applicable? 4. Which representation conditions remain applicable? 5. Does the model remain applicable? 6. Do the inputs remain representative? 7. Does scenario coverage support the extension? 8. Does the correlation basis transfer? 9. What new uncertainty is introduced? 10. Is additional simulation, evidence, correlation, or validation required? Extrapolation Principle Extrapolation is a particularly important form of reliance expansion. Simulation evidence may be extrapolated beyond directly tested conditions only where the extrapolation basis is explicitly governed. The extrapolation should identify: originating evidence; originating range; target range; methodological basis; assumptions; expected uncertainty; model applicability; correlation relevance; known limitations. Extrapolation must be treated as extrapolation, not silently presented as direct evidence. Comparative Reliance Simulation evidence may provide strong support for comparative propositions even where it cannot support absolute real-world claims. For example: Configuration A performs better than Configuration B under governed Scenario Set S may be strongly supported. That does not necessarily establish: Configuration A will achieve Performance Level X in operational reality. SRBM therefore distinguishes: Comparative Reliance from Absolute Reliance. Predictive Reliance Where simulation evidence is used predictively, SRBM requires the predictive reliance boundary to remain explicit. Predictive reliance should consider: future condition uncertainty; representation limits; assumption stability; model applicability; input distribution shift; scenario completeness; correlation basis; temporal horizon. A simulation may legitimately inform a prediction without guaranteeing the predicted outcome. Reliance Boundary States SRBM may assign a governed reliance-boundary state. A minimum state model may include: 1. Undefined Reliance Evidence exists, but no explicit legitimate reliance boundary has been established. 2. Narrow Reliance Evidence supports reliance only within tightly defined conditions. 3. Conditional Reliance Reliance is legitimate only while explicitly defined conditions remain satisfied. 4. Bounded Reliance Evidence supports a clearly established and documented reliance domain. 5. Extended Reliance — Justified Reliance extends beyond directly simulated conditions, but the extension has an explicit governed basis. 6. Reliance Suspended Previously supported reliance requires reassessment because of material change, contradiction, uncertainty, or loss of applicability. 7. Unsupported Reliance The intended use exceeds the legitimate simulation-specific evidence basis. These states are governance classifications rather than universal measures of scientific certainty. Unsupported Reliance Unsupported Reliance exists where simulation evidence is used beyond the boundary its governed basis can legitimately support. Examples include reliance: outside simulation scope; for an excluded condition; on a materially changed object; on a materially changed configuration; outside tested parameter ranges; outside represented environments; beyond scenario coverage; beyond established correlation; after evidence becomes stale; contrary to material uncertainty; for a materially different purpose; beyond the proposition actually supported; as proof of operational performance where only simulated performance was established. Unsupported reliance must remain identifiable even where the organization has historically relied upon the evidence in that manner. Repeated unsupported reliance does not create legitimate reliance. Boundary Crossing Detection SRBM should enable organizations to detect when downstream use crosses a governed reliance boundary. Boundary crossing may be triggered by: object change; configuration change; scenario change; environmental change; parameter expansion; purpose change; temporal change; decision-class change; new evidence; new uncertainty; correlation deterioration; contradiction; material reality change. A detected boundary crossing should trigger: Reliance Review and where necessary: Use Limitation → Additional Simulation → Additional Correlation → Validation Review → Resimulation. Reliance Degradation A reliance boundary may degrade over time. Degradation may occur when: the evidence weight decreases; reality changes; the model becomes obsolete; assumptions become less defensible; scenario relevance declines; new operational observations appear; correlation weakens; contradictory evidence emerges. SRBM therefore requires reliance boundaries to remain reviewable. Reliance Boundary ≠ Decision Authority SRBM determines whether simulation-derived evidence supports a particular reliance domain. It does not determine: who may make the decision; who accepts the risk; who authorizes deployment; who owns accountability; whether the organization should act. Those questions belong to the relevant authority, accountability, operational, risk, or validation governance structures. Therefore: Supported Reliance ≠ Authorized Decision. SRBM Boundary with SEWM SEWM determines: how much evidential weight qualified Simulation Evidence carries. SRBM determines: how far reliance upon that evidence may extend. Evidence weight is an input into reliance governance. It is not the reliance boundary itself. SRBM Boundary with SUM SRBM establishes the legitimate reliance domain. SUM translates that boundary into explicit: restrictions; exclusions; caveats; prohibited uses; unsupported interpretations; required conditions. Therefore: SRBM defines where reliance stops. SUM defines what must not happen beyond or within that boundary. SRBM Boundary with VALIDOS® SRBM does not determine overall validation sufficiency or authorize operational reliance based on the total evidence basis. Its question is: How far may this simulation-derived evidence legitimately be relied upon as simulation evidence? VALIDOS® asks: Does the total validation basis sufficiently support the Validation Determination and intended reliance? Therefore: Simulation Reliance Boundary ≠ Validation Reliance Determination. SRBM Boundary with SRCS SRCS governs the simulation-to-reality correlation relationship. SRBM uses that governed relationship when determining how far reality-directed reliance may extend. It does not establish or recalculate correlation. SRBM Boundary with ORA™ ORA™ governs actual Operational Reality. SRBM may determine whether simulation-derived evidence legitimately supports propositions concerning a bounded part of that reality. It does not determine operational reality itself. SRBM Boundary with AGA™ AGA™ governs authority, responsibility, accountability, and attribution. SRBM governs the methodological boundary of reliance upon simulation-derived evidence. It does not assign accountability for reliance decisions. SRBM Boundary with AIG® / ASGA™ Where simulation evidence concerns AI or autonomous systems, SRBM may govern how far that simulation evidence can legitimately support propositions about the simulated system. It does not govern the actual behavior, authority, autonomy, permissions, constraints, or operation of the deployed system. SRBM Boundary with INTEGROS® SRBM does not determine general integrity. Evidence or records may possess high integrity while still having a narrow reliance boundary. Therefore: Integrity ≠ Breadth of Reliance. SRBM Boundary with ADIT® ADIT® may audit whether the evidence basis and reliance records are observable, preserved, traceable, or verifiable. SRBM establishes the simulation-specific methodological boundary itself. Auditability ≠ Legitimate Reliance. Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum SRBM implementation should establish: 1. Evidence Input Receive qualified and weighted Simulation Evidence from SEQM and SEWM. 2. Intended Reliance Identify the precise proposition, decision, judgment, comparison, or use for which reliance is proposed. 3. Reliance Object Identify the object, version, configuration, or subject to which reliance applies. 4. Reliance Context Define the relevant scenario, environment, parameter, purpose, temporal, correlation, and uncertainty conditions. 5. Evidence-to-Reliance Alignment Determine whether the evidence directly supports the intended reliance. 6. Boundary Constraint Identification Identify all material conditions constraining legitimate reliance. 7. Reliance Expansion Assessment Identify whether the proposed use extends beyond directly supported conditions. 8. Unsupported Reliance Detection Determine whether any proposed use exceeds the legitimate evidence basis. 9. Reliance Boundary State Assign an explicit governed reliance-boundary state. 10. Reliance Boundary Record Document the supported domain, boundary conditions, expansion basis, uncertainty, and conditions requiring reassessment. Governance Outputs SRBM may produce: Simulation Intended Reliance Statement Simulation Reliance Object Record Simulation Reliance Purpose Record Simulation Reliance Context Record Evidence-to-Reliance Alignment Assessment Simulation Reliance Constraint Record Simulation Reliance Expansion Assessment Simulation Extrapolation Record Simulation Reliance Boundary State Unsupported Reliance Record Reliance Boundary Crossing Record Simulation Reliance Degradation Record Simulation Reliance Boundary Statement Governed Simulation Reliance Boundary These outputs provide the governed basis for: SUM — Simulation Use Limitation Module. Enterprise Application SRBM enables organizations to answer one of the most consequential questions in simulation governance: Where exactly does legitimate reliance on the simulation stop? An organization may possess: millions of successful simulation runs; high-fidelity models; substantial evidence weight; strong correlation within tested conditions; extensive scenario coverage. Yet none of those facts independently establish unlimited reliance. For a spacecraft, evidence concerning a governed landing envelope may not support an untested environmental regime. For an autonomous vehicle, millions of simulated kilometers may strongly support performance within represented traffic, sensor, weather, and behavioral conditions while leaving materially different conditions outside the legitimate reliance boundary. For a robot, evidence generated for one hardware configuration may not transfer automatically after sensors, actuators, software, payload, or operating environment change. For an engineering system, evidence within a tested load or temperature range may not justify performance claims outside that range. SRBM makes those boundaries explicit before narrow simulation evidence becomes broad organizational belief. It allows organizations to distinguish: what was simulated from what was evidenced from what may legitimately be relied upon. Foundational Principles Evidence weight is not breadth of reliance. High evidence weight does not create unlimited reliance. Reliance must remain purpose-specific. Reliance must remain object-specific where object differences are material. Scenario coverage does not create universal coverage. Correlation within one domain does not establish correlation outside that domain. Extrapolation must remain identifiable as extrapolation. Comparative evidence does not automatically establish absolute performance. Evidence can remain historically correct while becoming operationally stale. Reliance expansion requires a governed basis. Repeated unsupported reliance does not create legitimate reliance. Supported simulation reliance does not itself constitute deployment authorization or Validation Determination. Simulation-derived evidence must not be relied upon beyond the object, purpose, configuration, represented conditions, assumptions, parameters, scenarios, environments, correlations, uncertainties, and temporal context that establish its legitimate meaning. Canonical Closing Statement Simulation Reliance Boundary Module establishes the reliance-control layer within the Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard by determining how far qualified and weighted Simulation Evidence may legitimately support a proposition, judgment, comparison, decision context, or other defined form of simulation-specific reliance. Through governance of reliance objects, purposes, contexts, configurations, scenarios, parameters, environments, temporal applicability, correlation domains, uncertainty, direct and extended reliance, extrapolation, reliance expansion, unsupported reliance, boundary crossing, degradation, suspension, and reliance-boundary states, SRBM prevents simulation evidence from silently acquiring broader applicability than the governed conditions from which its evidential meaning originates. By separating evidential weight from breadth of reliance, simulation-specific reliance from validation sufficiency, and supported reliance from decision authority, SRBM preserves the methodological boundaries of SIMULOS®, VALIDOS®, ORA™, INTEGROS®, ADIT®, AGA™, AIG®, and ASGA™ while creating the governed reliance domain required for explicit downstream use limitations. Simulation evidence may legitimately inform consequential decisions, but it must never travel beyond its governed evidential basis without an explicit and justified expansion of reliance.

title: OOF™ Simulation Use Limitation Module (SUM)
text: OOF™ Simulation Use Limitation Module (SUM) Simulation Use Limitation Module (SUM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard (SERBS) Module: SUM — Simulation Use Limitation Module Operational Layer: Simulation Use Limitation Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Simulation Evidence Use Limitation Origin ID: SIMULOS-SERBS-SUM-011.4 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 20 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Simulation Use Limitation Module (SUM) is the fourth Core Module of the Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard (SERBS) within SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture. SUM governs the explicit restrictions, exclusions, conditions, caveats, unsupported interpretations, prohibited uses, and dependency conditions that must remain attached to simulation-derived evidence when that evidence is interpreted, communicated, transferred, or used. The Module translates the governed reliance boundary established by SRBM — Simulation Reliance Boundary Module into explicit controls over what simulation evidence may not legitimately be used to claim, infer, justify, demonstrate, predict, authorize, or support. SUM does not determine whether simulation evidence qualifies as evidence, how much evidential weight it carries, or whether the complete validation basis is sufficient. Its task is narrower: to ensure that the limitations governing simulation-derived evidence remain explicit, persistent, interpretable, transferable, and inseparable from downstream use of that evidence. Core Question What must simulation-derived evidence not be used to claim, infer, justify, or support? Architectural Position SUM is the fourth module within SERBS. It follows: SEQM — Simulation Evidence Qualification Module → establishes what qualifies as Simulation Evidence; SEWM — Simulation Evidence Weight Module → establishes how much simulation-specific evidential significance the evidence may carry; SRBM — Simulation Reliance Boundary Module → establishes how far legitimate reliance may extend. SUM then converts those boundaries into explicit use controls. It precedes: SVIM — Simulation Validation Interface Module which governs transfer of simulation-derived evidence into broader validation governance under VALIDOS®. The sequence is therefore: Qualification → Weight → Reliance Boundary → Use Limitation → Validation Interface. Internal Flow Position Weighted Simulation Evidence Governed Simulation Reliance Boundary → Intended Use Identification → Limitation Source Identification → Use Condition Definition → Restriction Definition → Exclusion Definition → Unsupported Interpretation Identification → Prohibited Use Definition → Limitation Persistence Requirements → Use Limitation State → Governed Simulation Use Limitation Record → SVIM — Simulation Validation Interface Module Operational Space SUM governs the space between: where legitimate simulation reliance ends and how that boundary must constrain actual evidence use. This operational space includes: intended evidence use; permitted-use conditions; conditional use; restricted use; excluded use; unsupported interpretation; prohibited inference; prohibited generalization; prohibited extrapolation; decision-class limitation; configuration limitation; scenario limitation; parameter limitation; environmental limitation; temporal limitation; uncertainty limitation; correlation limitation; dependency limitation; communication limitation; transfer limitation; limitation persistence; limitation review; limitation withdrawal following material change. Operational Scope SUM applies whenever simulation-derived evidence is: interpreted; summarized; aggregated; communicated; transferred; presented; cited; compared; used in engineering; used in scientific analysis; used in safety arguments; used in mission planning; used in design decisions; used in system qualification; used in regulatory submissions; used in validation processes; used in operational preparation; used in deployment decisions; used in AI or autonomous-system evaluation; used in consequential organizational decisions. It applies to evidence derived from: individual simulation runs; repeated executions; Monte Carlo studies; scenario portfolios; simulation campaigns; engineering simulations; scientific simulations; safety simulations; mission simulations; digital twins; physical simulations; hybrid simulations; AI simulations; autonomous-system simulations; future simulation technologies. SUM remains technology-neutral. Reliance Boundary ≠ Use Limitation SUM enforces the distinction: Reliance Boundary ≠ Use Limitation SRBM determines: where legitimate reliance stops. SUM determines: what restrictions must govern use because that boundary exists. For example, SRBM may establish that evidence applies only to: Object Version V4 + Scenario Family S3 + Parameter Range P2 + Environment E1. SUM may translate this into explicit controls: Do not apply this evidence to Object Version V5. Do not generalize this evidence beyond Scenario Family S3. Do not use this evidence to support performance outside Parameter Range P2. Do not represent this evidence as demonstrating performance in environments materially different from E1. SRBM defines the boundary. SUM operationalizes it. Use Limitation Principle A Simulation Use Limitation is: an explicit governance condition constraining how simulation-derived evidence may be interpreted, communicated, transferred, generalized, or relied upon. A limitation may arise from: simulation purpose; simulation scope; exclusions; reality representation; abstraction; fidelity; assumptions; model applicability; environmental configuration; input basis; scenario coverage; execution conditions; output classification; inference basis; simulation-to-reality correlation; uncertainty; evidence weight; reliance boundary; temporal relevance. Use limitations must remain linked to their source. Limitations Are Part of the Evidence SUM establishes a central principle: A material limitation is part of the governed evidential meaning, not optional commentary attached to it. Removing a material limitation while preserving the evidence can materially change the meaning of the evidence. Therefore: Evidence − Material Limitation ≠ Same Evidence Meaning. Where a limitation materially determines legitimate interpretation, the limitation must travel with the evidence. Intended Use Identification SUM requires the intended use of simulation evidence to be explicit. An Intended Use may include: exploration; comparison; screening; engineering design; optimization; hypothesis support; safety analysis; scenario planning; mission planning; training; system qualification; validation input; operational preparation; deployment support; regulatory evidence; predictive analysis. The same evidence may have different limitations for different intended uses. Permitted Use Conditions SUM may establish conditions under which evidence remains legitimately usable. Examples include: Permitted only for comparative analysis. Permitted only for the governed Simulation Object configuration. Permitted only within represented environmental conditions. Permitted only within Parameter Range P. Permitted only while Assumption Set A remains applicable. Permitted only as one input to a broader validation process. Conditional use must remain distinguishable from unrestricted use. Restriction A restriction narrows how evidence may be used without completely prohibiting its use. Restrictions may concern: purpose; object; configuration; scenario; environment; parameter range; decision type; temporal period; inference class; communication context. For example: Evidence may support comparative design selection but must not be used as independent evidence of operational safety. Exclusion An exclusion identifies a condition or domain that the evidence does not cover. Examples include: weather conditions not represented; hardware versions not simulated; excluded failure modes; populations not modeled; untested terrain; unrepresented physical phenomena; mission phases outside simulation scope; operating conditions outside parameter limits. An exclusion must not disappear merely because downstream users are unaware of it. Unsupported Interpretation An Unsupported Interpretation occurs where the evidence is described as meaning more than its governed basis supports. Examples include: Simulation demonstrated safe behavior when the evidence only establishes: no unsafe behavior was observed within the simulated scenario set. Or: The system performs reliably in reality when the evidence establishes only: high simulated performance within represented conditions. SUM requires unsupported interpretations to be identifiable and preventable. Observed Absence ≠ Demonstrated Impossibility Simulation campaigns frequently produce no instance of a particular failure. SUM establishes: Failure Not Observed ≠ Failure Impossible The absence of an event within a simulated scenario space may provide evidence concerning that tested space. It does not automatically establish impossibility outside that space. This distinction is especially important in: rare-event simulation; safety analysis; autonomous systems; mission simulation; infrastructure failure analysis; high-consequence engineering. Simulation Success ≠ Operational Safety A simulation campaign may demonstrate extensive successful simulated behavior. That does not independently establish operational safety. Therefore: Simulation Success ≠ Operational Safety Determination. SUM must prevent simulation success metrics from being communicated as broader safety determinations where the evidence basis does not support that interpretation. Scenario Success ≠ Universal Performance Successful performance across all executed scenarios means: successful performance across those governed executed scenarios. It does not mean: successful performance across every possible condition. SUM therefore preserves: Tested Scenario Space ≠ Total Possible Reality Space. Comparative Evidence ≠ Absolute Evidence Evidence demonstrating that: Configuration A outperformed Configuration B does not necessarily establish: Configuration A meets an absolute operational performance requirement. SUM requires comparative claims and absolute claims to remain distinct. Simulation Prediction ≠ Guaranteed Outcome Where simulation evidence supports prediction, SUM requires the distinction: Predicted Outcome ≠ Guaranteed Outcome. Predictive simulation evidence may legitimately inform planning and decision-making. It must not acquire deterministic meaning merely because the simulation produces precise numerical outputs. Precision Limitation Highly precise simulation outputs may create false confidence. SUM therefore establishes: Numerical Precision ≠ Evidential Certainty. An output of: 0.003721 failure probability does not necessarily mean the real-world probability is known to six significant digits. The precision communicated must remain compatible with: model uncertainty; input uncertainty; scenario uncertainty; representation limits; correlation uncertainty; inference uncertainty. Extrapolation Limitation Where evidence is extrapolated beyond directly simulated conditions, the extrapolation must remain explicitly identified. SUM may require statements such as: This conclusion includes extrapolation beyond the directly simulated parameter range. or: This evidence does not independently support performance beyond the simulated environmental domain. Unidentified extrapolation is a use-governance failure. Decision-Class Limitation Simulation evidence may legitimately inform one decision class while remaining insufficient for another. For example: Exploratory Design Decision may require less evidential support than: Safety-Critical Deployment Decision. SUM may therefore assign different use limitations based upon the intended decision class. It does not define organizational decision authority. Configuration Limitation Evidence associated with one Simulation Object configuration must retain limitations concerning materially different configurations. Changes may include: hardware; software; architecture; sensor suite; actuator system; material; payload; model configuration; operating mode. Evidence transfer across configurations requires a governed basis. Scenario Limitation SUM requires scenario limitations to remain visible. Evidence may be limited to: expected scenarios; edge cases; stress conditions; specified scenario families; defined uncertainty ranges; specific failure combinations. A scenario limitation should identify both: what was represented and, where material: what was not represented. Environmental Limitation Evidence may be valid only under specified represented environments. Limitations may concern: weather; terrain; lighting; atmosphere; gravity; thermal conditions; traffic; infrastructure; communication availability; human interaction; electromagnetic conditions. Environmental limitations are especially important where simulation-to-reality transfer is material. Temporal Limitation Simulation evidence may have a temporal use boundary. A limitation may require review when: the Simulation Object changes; the operational environment changes; new reality data becomes available; model versions change; assumptions become obsolete; new failure modes emerge; input distributions shift; correlation deteriorates. Evidence should not retain permanent unrestricted use merely because it was once appropriately qualified. Uncertainty Limitation Material uncertainty must constrain interpretation where relevant. SUM may require: confidence qualification; uncertainty ranges; conditional language; restricted extrapolation; additional evidence; prohibition of deterministic claims. Uncertainty is not a reason to discard useful evidence. It is a reason to govern how strongly that evidence is expressed and used. Dependency Limitation Where evidence objects share material dependencies, downstream users must not interpret their quantity as equivalent independent confirmation. SUM may therefore require disclosure that: runs share the same model; evidence shares the same assumptions; outputs share the same input source; models share a common representation; scenario sets share common omissions; evidence shares one correlation basis. Multiple dependent evidence objects must not be presented as independent confirmation. Aggregation Limitation Aggregated simulation metrics must not erase material information. An aggregate success rate may conceal: rare failures; scenario-specific failures; environmental clusters; configuration-specific weaknesses; anomalous executions; distribution tails; common-mode failures. SUM may therefore require that material underlying limitations remain attached to aggregate evidence. Communication Limitation Simulation evidence can be methodologically distorted through communication even when the underlying evidence remains unchanged. SUM therefore applies to: reports; dashboards; executive summaries; regulatory submissions; presentations; scientific communication; engineering documentation; automated AI-generated summaries; machine-readable evidence transfers. A summary must not remove limitations necessary to interpret the evidence correctly. Human-Readable and Machine-Readable Limitations Because simulation evidence may move through automated systems, limitations should be capable of being represented in both: human-readable form and machine-readable form. Machine-readable limitation fields may include: permitted use; restricted use; prohibited use; applicable object; applicable version; applicable configuration; scenario domain; parameter domain; environmental domain; temporal validity; uncertainty condition; correlation condition; review trigger. This allows limitations to survive automated evidence pipelines. Limitation Persistence Principle SUM establishes: A limitation must travel at least as far as the evidence it limits. If evidence is: copied; exported; aggregated; summarized; transferred; transformed; entered into another system; entered into validation; reused in another analysis, material limitations must remain discoverable and linked. Limitation Detachment Limitation Detachment occurs when evidence continues downstream while its governing limitations are lost, hidden, omitted, weakened, or separated. Examples include: copying a simulation metric without its scenario boundary; presenting a success percentage without excluded failures; transferring evidence without uncertainty; using a graph without its parameter range; citing a simulation conclusion after the Simulation Object configuration changed; removing caveats from an executive summary. SUM treats material limitation detachment as a simulation governance failure. Limitation Conflict Different evidence objects may carry conflicting use limitations. One evidence object may support a proposition under one condition while another constrains it under another. SUM requires such conflicts to remain visible rather than collapsing them into one apparently unrestricted conclusion. Use Limitation States SUM may assign a governed Use Limitation State. A minimum state model may include: 1. Undefined Limitation Evidence exists, but material use limitations have not yet been explicitly established. 2. Conditional Use Evidence may be used only while defined conditions remain satisfied. 3. Restricted Use Evidence may be used only for specified purposes, contexts, objects, scenarios, or decision classes. 4. Prohibited Use A specified use, interpretation, inference, or decision application is not supported by the governed simulation evidence. 5. Review Required Material change or new information requires reassessment before continued use. 6. Limitation Superseded A previous limitation has been replaced by a newly governed limitation basis. These states govern evidence use rather than overall validation status. Prohibited Use A Prohibited Use is a use that exceeds the legitimate simulation-specific evidential basis sufficiently that it should not proceed without a new governed basis. Examples may include: claiming universal behavior from bounded scenarios; claiming real-world equivalence from simulation alone; claiming operational safety solely from simulated success; applying evidence to a materially different object configuration; concealing known scenario exclusions; treating correlated simulations as independent evidence; presenting inferred results as directly observed results; using stale evidence after material reality change; treating extrapolation as direct simulation evidence; representing simulation evidence as a formal Validation Determination. Prohibited Use ≠ Organizational Prohibition SUM defines methodological prohibited use within simulation evidence governance. It does not itself impose legal, regulatory, corporate, or disciplinary sanctions. Other governance structures may use SUM outputs to establish such controls. Limitation Review Trigger Use limitations should be reassessed when materially relevant changes occur. Triggers may include: Simulation Object change; configuration change; new simulation results; new scenarios; new model; new input basis; new correlation evidence; operational observations; newly discovered failure; changed intended use; changed decision class; changed environment; expired temporal applicability. Review may result in: limitation retained → limitation narrowed → limitation expanded → limitation replaced → additional simulation required. SUM Boundary with SRBM SRBM determines the maximum legitimate reliance boundary. SUM operationalizes that boundary through explicit restrictions and prohibited uses. Therefore: SRBM = Where reliance stops. SUM = What use must be constrained because it stops there. SUM Boundary with SVIM SUM establishes the limitations. SVIM ensures that those limitations remain attached when evidence crosses into broader validation governance. SUM therefore provides a critical input to SVIM. SUM Boundary with VALIDOS® SUM does not determine validation sufficiency. It may establish that simulation evidence: must not independently be used to support a Validation Determination. VALIDOS® then determines whether the total evidence basis is sufficient. Therefore: Simulation Use Limitation ≠ Validation Determination. SUM Boundary with SOGS SOGS governs limitations associated with what simulation outputs themselves mean. SUM governs limitations on evidential use after those outputs have become qualified Simulation Evidence. Therefore: Output Limitation ≠ Evidence Use Limitation. An output limitation may become an input into SUM, but the governed spaces remain distinct. SUM Boundary with SRCS SRCS governs simulation-to-reality correlation. SUM may impose use limitations based upon the correlation conditions established by SRCS. It does not determine correlation itself. SUM Boundary with ORA™ ORA™ governs Operational Reality. SUM may prohibit or restrict claims about Operational Reality where simulation evidence does not support them. It does not define Operational Reality. SUM Boundary with INTEGROS® SUM does not govern general evidence integrity. INTEGROS® may govern whether evidence and limitations retain integrity through processing or transfer. SUM governs what limitations must exist and remain associated with simulation evidence. SUM Boundary with ADIT® ADIT® may audit whether limitations were preserved, communicated, or followed. SUM defines the simulation-specific limitations that should govern evidence use. SUM Boundary with AGA™ AGA™ governs who holds responsibility and accountability for decisions involving evidence. SUM governs what simulation evidence may legitimately be used to support. It does not assign accountability for violating a limitation. SUM Boundary with AIG® / ASGA™ SUM may constrain claims derived from simulations of AI or autonomous systems. It does not govern the actual deployed system's behavior, autonomy, authority, permissions, or operational constraints. Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum SUM implementation should establish: 1. Evidence Input Receive qualified, weighted, reliance-bounded Simulation Evidence. 2. Intended Use Identification Define how the evidence is intended to be interpreted or used. 3. Limitation Source Identification Identify the simulation conditions creating material use limitations. 4. Permitted Use Conditions Define conditions under which use remains legitimate. 5. Restriction Definition Identify materially restricted uses. 6. Exclusion Definition Identify contexts, conditions, objects, scenarios, or claims outside the evidence basis. 7. Unsupported Interpretation Assessment Identify interpretations that exceed the governed meaning. 8. Prohibited Use Definition Define uses that cannot legitimately proceed on the existing simulation evidence basis. 9. Persistence Control Ensure material limitations remain linked to evidence through communication, aggregation, transformation, and transfer. 10. Limitation State and Review Assign a governed limitation state and identify conditions requiring reassessment. Governance Outputs SUM may produce: Simulation Intended Use Record Simulation Permitted Use Condition Simulation Evidence Restriction Record Simulation Evidence Exclusion Record Unsupported Interpretation Record Prohibited Simulation Evidence Use Record Simulation Extrapolation Limitation Simulation Decision-Class Limitation Simulation Configuration Limitation Simulation Scenario Limitation Simulation Environmental Limitation Simulation Temporal Limitation Simulation Uncertainty Limitation Simulation Evidence Dependency Limitation Simulation Limitation Persistence Record Simulation Use Limitation State Governed Simulation Use Limitation Record These outputs provide the limitation basis required by: SVIM — Simulation Validation Interface Module. Enterprise Application SUM enables organizations to solve a critical problem that occurs after simulation evidence has already been produced correctly: the evidence may be governed correctly at its source but used incorrectly downstream. A simulation team may clearly understand that a result applies only to: one configuration; one scenario family; one environment; one parameter range; one model version; one uncertainty range. But after the result enters a dashboard, management report, validation package, regulatory submission, engineering decision, or automated evidence pipeline, those qualifications may disappear. The result may remain numerically identical while its organizational meaning becomes distorted. SUM prevents that separation. For a spacecraft simulation, evidence concerning a defined landing envelope must not silently become evidence for all landing conditions. For an autonomous vehicle, millions of successful simulated scenarios must not be represented as proving unrestricted real-world safety where the simulation did not represent all materially relevant conditions. For a robot, evidence produced for one sensor, actuator, payload, software, and environmental configuration must not automatically transfer to another configuration. For engineering simulation, results generated within defined physical assumptions and parameter ranges must not be presented as universal physical behavior. SUM therefore ensures that organizations preserve not only: the simulation result but also: the rules governing what that result may legitimately be used to mean. Foundational Principles A material use limitation is part of the evidential meaning. Reliance boundaries must become operational use controls. Evidence must not travel without the limitations that govern it. Failure not observed does not mean failure impossible. Simulation success does not independently establish operational safety. Scenario success does not establish universal performance. Comparative evidence does not automatically establish absolute performance. Simulation prediction does not guarantee outcome. Numerical precision does not create evidential certainty. Extrapolation must remain identifiable as extrapolation. Multiple dependent evidence objects must not be represented as independent confirmation. Summarization must not remove limitations necessary for legitimate interpretation. A limitation must travel at least as far as the evidence it limits. Simulation-derived evidence must never become more general, certain, transferable, or authoritative merely because the limitations that originally constrained it have been forgotten. Canonical Closing Statement Simulation Use Limitation Module establishes the explicit evidence-use control layer within the Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard by transforming governed reliance boundaries into persistent conditions, restrictions, exclusions, caveats, unsupported interpretations, prohibited uses, and review requirements attached to simulation-derived evidence. Through governance of intended use, permitted-use conditions, configuration, scenario, environmental, parameter, temporal, uncertainty, dependency, extrapolation, decision-class, communication, aggregation, and transfer limitations, SUM prevents simulation evidence from acquiring broader meaning merely through reuse, summarization, organizational transfer, automation, or loss of context. By distinguishing reliance boundaries from use limitations, output limitations from evidential limitations, and simulation-specific restrictions from broader validation determinations, SUM preserves the architectural boundaries of SIMULOS®, VALIDOS®, ORA™, INTEGROS®, ADIT®, AGA™, AIG®, and ASGA™. A simulation limitation is therefore not peripheral commentary: where it materially constrains evidential meaning, it is part of the governed evidence itself and must remain attached for as long and as far as that evidence is used.

title: OOF™ Simulation Validation Interface Module (SVIM)
text: OOF™ Simulation Validation Interface Module (SVIM) Simulation Validation Interface Module (SVIM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture Parent Standard: Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard (SERBS) Module: SVIM — Simulation Validation Interface Module Operational Layer: Simulation Validation Interface Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Simulation Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Simulation-to-Validation Interface Origin ID: SIMULOS-SERBS-SVIM-011.5 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 20 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · AIG® · ASGA™ · RIS™ AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Simulation Validation Interface Module (SVIM) is the fifth Core Module of the Simulation Evidence & Reliance Boundary Standard (SERBS) within SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture. SVIM governs the methodological transfer boundary through which qualified simulation-derived evidence leaves simulation-specific evidence governance and enters broader validation governance. The Module ensures that Simulation Evidence transferred beyond SIMULOS® retains the identity, provenance, evidential purpose, qualification state, evidential weight, applicability, reliance boundary, uncertainty, dependencies, use limitations, and simulation basis necessary to preserve its legitimate meaning. SVIM does not determine whether the transferred evidence is sufficient for validation, whether validation criteria have been satisfied, whether a Validation Determination may be issued, or whether operational reliance is justified. Those questions belong to VALIDOS®. Its task is narrower and architecturally critical: to ensure that simulation-derived evidence crosses into broader validation governance without becoming detached from the conditions that define what that evidence legitimately means. Core Question How must simulation-derived evidence enter broader validation governance without losing the conditions that define its legitimate meaning? Architectural Position SVIM is the fifth and final module within SERBS. It follows: SEQM — Simulation Evidence Qualification Module → determines what simulation-derived information qualifies as evidence. SEWM — Simulation Evidence Weight Module → determines how much simulation-specific evidential significance it may carry. SRBM — Simulation Reliance Boundary Module → determines how far reliance may legitimately extend. SUM — Simulation Use Limitation Module → determines what uses, claims, interpretations, or generalizations must remain constrained or prohibited. SVIM then governs the controlled transfer of this complete simulation-specific evidential meaning into broader validation governance. The sequence is: Qualification → Weight → Reliance Boundary → Use Limitation → Validation Interface. SVIM therefore represents the final simulation-evidence gateway before validation governance begins. Internal Flow Position Qualified Simulation Evidence Simulation Evidence Weight Simulation Reliance Boundary Simulation Use Limitations Simulation Evidence Provenance Material Uncertainty → Validation Transfer Purpose Identification → Evidence Package Assembly → Simulation Basis Preservation → Qualification Preservation → Weight Preservation → Boundary Preservation → Limitation Preservation → Uncertainty Preservation → Transfer Completeness Assessment → Validation Interface State → Simulation Validation Interface Package → VALIDOS® Validation Governance Operational Space SVIM governs the space between: completed simulation-specific evidence governance and entry into broader validation governance. This operational space includes: validation transfer purpose; evidence package identity; transferred evidence identity; simulation evidence provenance; originating Simulation Object linkage; simulation lifecycle traceability; evidential purpose preservation; qualification-state preservation; evidence-weight preservation; applicability preservation; reliance-boundary preservation; use-limitation preservation; uncertainty preservation; dependency disclosure; inference disclosure; correlation-basis preservation; negative-evidence preservation; contradictory-evidence preservation; transfer completeness; transfer versioning; evidence-package status; receiving validation context; validation-interface state; re-entry following evidence change. Operational Scope SVIM applies whenever simulation-derived evidence is transferred into a broader process intended to determine, support, challenge, reconsider, or inform: validation; system qualification; engineering acceptance; scientific validation; safety validation; mission validation; performance validation; deployment validation; operational readiness; regulatory validation; design validation; infrastructure validation; AI validation; autonomous-system validation; other governed validation processes. It applies regardless of whether the transferred evidence originates from: one simulation; repeated simulations; Monte Carlo studies; scenario portfolios; large simulation campaigns; engineering simulations; scientific simulations; mission simulations; safety simulations; digital twins; physical simulations; hybrid simulations; AI simulations; autonomous-system simulations; future simulation technologies. SVIM remains technology-neutral. Simulation Evidence Governance ≠ Validation Governance SVIM enforces the architectural distinction: Simulation Evidence Governance ≠ Validation Governance SIMULOS® may establish: what evidence exists; what proposition it addresses; how it was produced; what it legitimately means; what simulation-specific weight it carries; where reliance upon it stops; what limitations constrain its use. SIMULOS® must not then make the separate determination: Is the complete validation basis sufficient? That question belongs to VALIDOS®. The interface exists precisely because these are different governance spaces. Interface Principle SVIM establishes: A validation interface must transfer evidential meaning, not merely evidence content. A simulation result copied into a validation package without its governing conditions is not methodologically equivalent to the governed evidence object from which it originated. Therefore: Transferred Result ≠ Transferred Evidential Meaning unless the material simulation-specific evidence conditions are preserved. Validation Transfer Purpose Every SVIM transfer should identify why simulation evidence is entering validation governance. The transfer purpose may include: supporting a validation criterion; challenging a validation proposition; supplementing empirical evidence; supporting comparative validation; identifying unresolved uncertainty; demonstrating bounded simulated behavior; documenting failure conditions; contributing to a safety argument; supporting mission readiness evaluation; informing operational readiness; supporting a broader validation determination. The transfer purpose must not silently expand the evidential purpose originally established under SEQM. Simulation Validation Interface Package SVIM establishes the Simulation Validation Interface Package as the governed transfer object between SIMULOS® and broader validation governance. A package may contain one or multiple Simulation Evidence objects. At minimum, where materially relevant, the package should preserve: Evidence Identity → What simulation-derived evidence is being transferred? Evidential Purpose → What proposition was the evidence qualified to address? Simulation Basis → From which governed simulation conditions did the evidence originate? Provenance → Which outputs, executions, scenarios, models, inputs, assumptions, and object configurations produced it? Qualification State → Is the evidence Qualified, Conditionally Qualified, Suspended, or otherwise governed? Evidence Weight → What simulation-specific evidential significance was assigned? Applicability → Where does the evidence apply? Reliance Boundary → How far may simulation-specific reliance legitimately extend? Use Limitations → What uses, interpretations, claims, or generalizations remain constrained? Uncertainty → What uncertainty materially affects evidential meaning? Correlation Basis → What simulation-to-reality relationship supports or constrains the evidence? Dependencies → Which common models, assumptions, inputs, scenarios, or other dependencies affect independence? Temporal Applicability → When does the evidence remain applicable? Evidence Content ≠ Evidence Context SVIM establishes: Evidence Content ≠ Evidence Context A numerical value, chart, probability, trajectory, success rate, failure rate, confidence interval, comparison, or simulation conclusion may be correctly copied while its evidential meaning is incorrectly transferred. For example: 99.97% simulated success without: scenario domain; model basis; environmental representation; excluded conditions; failure treatment; uncertainty; object configuration; correlation basis; does not preserve the original governed evidential meaning. SVIM therefore treats contextual preservation as part of transfer governance. Provenance Preservation Simulation evidence entering validation must remain traceable to its originating simulation basis. Where materially relevant, SVIM preserves: Simulation Evidence → Simulation Output → Execution Record → Scenario → Input Basis → Model & Environment → Assumptions → Reality Representation → Purpose & Scope → Simulation Object and, where applicable: Simulation Evidence → Simulation-to-Reality Correlation Basis SVIM does not replace general provenance or integrity governance. It ensures that the simulation-specific provenance required to understand the evidence remains available at the interface. Qualification Preservation An evidence object must not acquire a stronger qualification state merely because it enters validation. Therefore: Conditionally Qualified Simulation Evidence must not become Unconditionally Qualified Validation Evidence through transfer alone. Likewise: Qualification Suspended must remain visible to the receiving validation process. Transfer does not repair qualification deficiencies. Evidence Weight Preservation SVIM requires simulation-specific evidential weight to remain visible during transfer. A validation process may subsequently evaluate the evidence differently within the complete validation basis. But it must be able to identify the simulation-specific weight established under SEWM and the basis supporting that determination. Therefore: Validation Entry ≠ Automatic Evidence Weight Increase. Reliance Boundary Preservation The reliance boundary established under SRBM must remain attached to the evidence entering validation. If evidence applies only to: Object Version V3 + Scenario Family S7 + Environment E4 + Parameter Range P2 the validation process must receive that boundary. The transfer must not silently convert it into evidence applicable to: all object versions + all scenarios + all environments + unrestricted parameter ranges. Use Limitation Preservation All material SUM limitations must remain available at the validation interface. These may include: prohibited generalization; prohibited extrapolation; configuration restriction; scenario restriction; environmental restriction; temporal restriction; uncertainty limitation; decision-class limitation; comparative-only use; prohibition against independent safety claims; requirement for additional empirical evidence. SVIM establishes: A limitation omitted at transfer is a limitation no longer capable of governing downstream interpretation. Uncertainty Preservation Simulation evidence must not become artificially more certain when transferred. SVIM therefore requires material uncertainty to remain visible. This may include uncertainty originating from: reality representation; assumptions; model structure; parameters; inputs; scenarios; execution; outputs; inference; simulation-to-reality correlation. Validation transfer must not convert bounded uncertainty into apparent certainty. Dependency Preservation Large simulation campaigns may generate many evidence objects sharing common dependencies. SVIM requires relevant dependencies to accompany evidence where they affect interpretation. Examples include: common model; common assumption set; common input source; common scenario generator; common environment model; common transformation; common inference methodology; common correlation basis. This allows validation governance to distinguish: multiple evidence objects from multiple independent evidence sources. Negative Evidence Preservation SVIM must preserve materially relevant negative evidence. A validation interface must not transfer only: successful runs; favorable outputs; confirming evidence; preferred scenarios. Material: failures; anomalies; contradictions; divergence; instability; non-convergence; threshold violations; correlation failures; must remain visible where relevant to the validation proposition. Validation transfer must not become evidence selection. Contradictory Evidence Preservation Where simulation evidence objects materially disagree, the disagreement must cross the interface. SVIM must not resolve contradiction by simply transferring the preferred evidence object. The validation process may need to determine the significance of the contradiction. SVIM's responsibility is to preserve it. Inference Preservation Where evidence is derived through inference rather than direct simulation observation, the validation interface must identify that inferential pathway. The receiving validation process should be able to distinguish: Direct Simulation Observation from Simulation-Derived Inference. Where materially relevant, the transfer should preserve: originating outputs; inference methodology; transformations; assumptions; aggregation; inference uncertainty; inference limitations. Correlation Basis Preservation Where evidence makes or supports claims concerning reality, the relevant SRCS correlation basis should remain available. This may include: reality reference; comparison conditions; correlation criteria; observed deviations; alignment basis; correlation uncertainty; applicability boundary. SVIM does not determine whether correlation is sufficient. It preserves the governed correlation information necessary for the receiving validation process. Transfer Completeness SVIM requires assessment of whether the evidence package is sufficiently complete for transfer. Completeness is purpose-specific. A package may be incomplete where it lacks materially necessary: evidence identity; evidential purpose; simulation provenance; qualification state; evidence-weight basis; applicability; reliance boundary; limitation; uncertainty; correlation basis; dependency disclosure; negative evidence; temporal applicability. An incomplete package should not be represented as a complete simulation evidence transfer. Transfer Completeness ≠ Validation Sufficiency SVIM establishes an important distinction: Complete Transfer ≠ Sufficient Validation Basis A perfectly constructed Simulation Validation Interface Package may still provide only a small part of the evidence needed for validation. Conversely, a validation process may ultimately have sufficient evidence from multiple sources even where simulation evidence contributes only limited weight. SVIM governs transfer quality. VALIDOS® governs validation sufficiency. Validation Interface States SVIM may assign a governed interface state. A minimum state model may include: 1. Interface Not Ready Material evidence conditions required for transfer remain unresolved. 2. Conditionally Transferable Evidence may enter validation only with explicit unresolved conditions or restrictions. 3. Transfer Ready The simulation evidence package contains the material simulation-specific information required for governed transfer. 4. Transferred The governed evidence package has entered the designated validation process. 5. Transfer Review Required A material change has occurred that may affect evidence meaning after transfer. 6. Transfer Superseded A newer governed evidence package replaces the previous transfer basis. These states describe the simulation-validation interface. They are not validation states. Validation Interface State ≠ Validation State SVIM must not create a parallel validation determination. Therefore: Transfer Ready ≠ Validated Transferred ≠ Validated Conditionally Transferable ≠ Conditionally Validated The interface state answers only: Is the simulation evidence appropriately constituted for transfer into validation governance? Versioned Evidence Transfer Simulation evidence may evolve after: additional executions; model updates; new scenarios; revised assumptions; new reality data; new correlation analysis; evidence requalification; changed evidence weight; revised reliance boundaries; new use limitations. SVIM should therefore support versioned Simulation Validation Interface Packages. A new package should not silently overwrite the evidential basis of an earlier validation process. Evidence Change After Transfer Where evidence changes materially after transfer, SVIM should support notification or re-entry into the validation interface. Possible triggers include: qualification suspension; evidence disqualification; degraded weight; changed reliance boundary; newly discovered limitation; contradictory evidence; new simulation failure; new correlation deviation; object change; reality change; resimulation. The downstream validation basis may need reassessment. SVIM identifies the interface condition. VALIDOS® determines the validation consequence. Interface Re-Entry Evidence may cross the interface more than once. The lifecycle may therefore become: Simulation Evidence → Validation Interface → Validation Governance → New Simulation Evidence / Material Change → Interface Re-Entry → Validation Reassessment This supports recursive governance rather than one-time evidence transfer. Machine-Readable Validation Interface SVIM should support machine-readable evidence transfer where simulation and validation pipelines are automated. Machine-readable interface fields may include: evidence ID; simulation object ID; object version; evidence version; evidential purpose; qualification state; evidence-weight state; applicability; reliance boundary; use limitations; uncertainty; dependency references; scenario references; execution references; output references; correlation references; temporal applicability; transfer state; supersession relationship. This allows automated validation systems to ingest simulation evidence without stripping away governance context. Human-Readable Validation Interface Machine-readable transfer does not eliminate the need for understandable human interpretation. SVIM therefore supports human-readable statements such as: What the evidence shows. What it does not show. Under which conditions it applies. What uncertainty remains. How strongly the simulation evidence supports the proposition. Where reliance must stop. What additional validation may be necessary. SVIM Boundary with SEQM SEQM qualifies simulation-derived information as evidence. SVIM transfers that qualified evidence into validation governance. SVIM must not independently requalify evidence except where transfer review identifies a condition requiring return to SEQM. SVIM Boundary with SEWM SEWM determines simulation-specific evidential weight. SVIM preserves that weight and its basis during transfer. It does not determine validation-level evidence weight within the total validation basis. SVIM Boundary with SRBM SRBM establishes the simulation reliance boundary. SVIM preserves that boundary when evidence enters validation. It does not broaden the boundary. SVIM Boundary with SUM SUM establishes evidence-use limitations. SVIM ensures those limitations survive transfer. Therefore: SUM defines the limitation. SVIM preserves the limitation across the validation boundary. SVIM Boundary with VALIDOS® This is the primary architectural boundary governed by SVIM. SVIM / SIMULOS®: packages simulation-derived evidence; preserves simulation-specific meaning; preserves qualification; preserves evidence weight; preserves applicability; preserves uncertainty; preserves reliance boundaries; preserves limitations; preserves provenance; transfers the evidence. VALIDOS®: identifies the Validation Object; establishes Validation Purpose & Scope; applies validation criteria; governs validation methodology; evaluates validation evidence fitness; evaluates source reliability; executes validation; issues Validation Determinations; governs Validation States; governs reliance and revalidation. The boundary is: SIMULOS® prepares and transfers simulation-derived evidence. VALIDOS® determines what that evidence means within the complete validation basis. SVIM Boundary with INTEGROS® SVIM does not establish general evidence integrity. INTEGROS® may govern integrity properties of the evidence package, records, transformations, and transfer mechanisms. SVIM governs which simulation-specific evidential conditions must survive the transfer. SVIM Boundary with ADIT® ADIT® may audit: whether the transfer occurred; what package was transferred; whether records were preserved; whether evidence conditions were omitted or altered; whether transfer history is reconstructable. SVIM defines the simulation-specific transfer structure. It does not own audit governance. SVIM Boundary with ORA™ Operational Reality information may become relevant to validation. SVIM does not determine Operational Reality. It preserves the simulation-specific relationship to reality established through SRCS where that relationship is material to transferred evidence. SVIM Boundary with AGA™ AGA™ governs responsibility, authority, accountability, and attribution for validation-related decisions. SVIM does not determine who may approve validation, accept evidence, authorize deployment, or assume operational risk. SVIM Boundary with AIG® / ASGA™ Where simulation evidence concerns AI or autonomous systems, SVIM may transfer that evidence into validation governance. It does not govern the behavior, authority, autonomy, permissions, constraints, or deployment of the actual AI or autonomous system. Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum SVIM implementation should establish: 1. Transfer Purpose Identification Define why the Simulation Evidence is entering broader validation governance. 2. Evidence Package Identification Identify the precise evidence object or evidence set being transferred. 3. Simulation Basis Preservation Preserve traceability to the governed simulation lifecycle that produced the evidence. 4. Qualification Preservation Transfer the current evidence qualification state and qualification basis. 5. Evidence Weight Preservation Transfer the simulation-specific evidence weight and material factors supporting or constraining it. 6. Reliance Boundary Preservation Transfer the maximum simulation-specific reliance boundary. 7. Use Limitation Preservation Transfer material restrictions, exclusions, caveats, unsupported interpretations, and prohibited uses. 8. Uncertainty and Dependency Preservation Transfer material uncertainty and evidence dependencies relevant to interpretation. 9. Transfer Completeness Assessment Determine whether the package contains the simulation-specific information necessary for governed validation entry. 10. Interface State Assignment Assign and document the current Validation Interface State. 11. Transfer Record Record the evidence package version, receiving validation context, transfer state, and material interface conditions. 12. Change and Re-Entry Control Define conditions requiring updated transfer, supersession, or validation-interface re-entry. Governance Outputs SVIM may produce: Simulation Validation Transfer Purpose Statement Simulation Validation Evidence Package Simulation Evidence Transfer Manifest Simulation Basis Transfer Record Simulation Evidence Qualification Transfer Record Simulation Evidence Weight Transfer Record Simulation Reliance Boundary Transfer Statement Simulation Use Limitation Transfer Record Simulation Evidence Uncertainty Transfer Record Simulation Evidence Dependency Disclosure Simulation Negative Evidence Disclosure Simulation Correlation Basis Transfer Record Simulation Validation Interface State Simulation Validation Interface Package Simulation Evidence Transfer Record Simulation Validation Interface Re-Entry Record Together these outputs form the governed interface between: SIMULOS® Simulation Evidence Governance and VALIDOS® Validation Governance. Enterprise Application SVIM solves a major organizational problem: simulation teams and validation teams frequently work with the same results but not necessarily with the same evidential meaning. A simulation team may know that a result: applies only to one configuration; depends upon specific assumptions; covers a defined scenario family; excludes particular environmental conditions; contains significant uncertainty; derives from dependent simulations; has limited reality correlation; supports comparison rather than absolute prediction.
