title: VFM® Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture — Value Lifecycle Governance Layer
text: VFM® Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture — Value Lifecycle Governance Layer VFM® Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture — Value Lifecycle Governance Layer VFM® Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture — Value Lifecycle Governance Layer Official Value Lifecycle Governance Architecture for AI Systems, Autonomous Systems, Organizations, Assets, Infrastructure, Data, Technology, Economic Systems, Public Systems, Digital Environments, and Future Value-Based Systems VFM® serves as the official OOF® value lifecycle governance architecture used for value context governance, value origin governance, value emergence governance, value recognition governance, value state governance, value change governance, value development governance, value degradation governance, value nullification governance, value restoration governance, and value extinction governance across AI systems, autonomous systems, organizations, industrial systems, physical and digital assets, infrastructure, data, technology, intellectual property, public systems, economic environments, and future value-based systems. Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture (VFM®) does not define what value must be for every domain. VFM® defines the governance architecture required to determine how value exists within a context, where it originates, how it emerges, how it becomes recognized, which state it occupies, how it changes, how it develops or degrades, when it reaches zero, whether previously existing value can be restored, and when its recoverability legitimately ends. VFM® consists of 11 Core Parent Standards and 55 Core Modules forming the primary value lifecycle governance backbone within the OOF® ecosystem. Additional compatible standards, bridge standards, domain-specific value models, assessment methodologies, and specialized value governance standards may extend the architecture when new value governance spaces are identified. However, the standards listed below form the official core value lifecycle governance structure of VFM®. Canonical Definition Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture (VFM®) is the value lifecycle governance architecture that defines the structural and methodological conditions under which value is contextualized, originated, emerged, recognized, placed into a governed state, changed, developed, degraded, nullified, restored, or ultimately extinguished throughout its governed lifecycle. VFM® treats value not merely as a price, financial quantity, accounting measure, utility score, or subjective judgment, but as a governable lifecycle phenomenon whose existence, state, transformation, recoverability, and finality can be methodologically distinguished. The architecture therefore enables different systems to reason about value without requiring every system to use the same economic, technological, social, operational, or institutional definition of value. Core Question How can value remain methodologically governable from the context in which it becomes meaningful through its origin, emergence, recognition, state, transformation, development, degradation, nullification, restoration, and eventual extinction? Governance Flow Value Context → Value Origin → Value Emergence → Value Recognition → Value State → Value Change → Value Development / Value Degradation → Value Nullification → Value Restoration / Value Extinction The lifecycle is intentionally non-linear. Value may develop, degrade, change repeatedly, reach zero, remain dormant, become inaccessible, recover through restoration, enter a new governed state, or ultimately cross the boundary into extinction. Core Parent Standards 1. Value Context Standard Governed Space: Value Context Core Question: Within which context does the relevant value exist, for whom or for what does it become meaningful, and which contextual boundaries govern its interpretation? 2. Value Origin Standard Governed Space: Value Origin Core Question: From where does the relevant value originate, and what establishes its legitimate value-origin basis? 3. Value Emergence Standard Governed Space: Value Emergence Core Question: How and under which conditions does value that did not previously exist become present within the governed lifecycle? 4. Value Recognition Standard Governed Space: Value Recognition Core Question: When and under which conditions may existing or emerging value become legitimately recognized as value within the governed context? 5. Value State Standard (VSS) Governed Space: Value State Core Question: What is the current governed state of the relevant value, and how must that state be distinguished from the events and mechanisms that produced it? 6. Value Change Standard (VCS) Governed Space: Value Change Core Question: What has changed in the relevant value, independently of the external event, cause, actor, or system that produced the change? 7. Value Development Standard (VDS) Governed Space: Value Development Core Question: How does already existing value legitimately grow, mature, compound, strengthen, or otherwise develop within its governed lifecycle? 8. Value Degradation Standard (VDGS) Governed Space: Value Degradation Core Question: How does existing value decline, weaken, deteriorate, become impaired, or progressively lose value while value still remains? 9. Value Nullification Standard (VNS) Governed Space: Value Nullification Core Question: When and through which governed conditions or mechanisms does previously existing value reach zero? 10. Value Restoration Standard (VRSS) Governed Space: Value Restoration Core Question: How can degraded, lost, dormant, inaccessible, impaired, or zero value legitimately re-emerge or be restored? 11. Value Extinction Standard (VXSS) Governed Space: Value Extinction Core Question: When does value cease to exist as recoverable value within the governed lifecycle? Compatible OOF® Architectures VFM® interoperates with multiple OOF® architectures governing complementary spaces surrounding value. GOA™ — Governance Architecture provides the constitutional governance layer through which authority, boundaries, scope, delegation, continuity, and interoperability surrounding value governance can be structured. ORA™ — Operational Reality Architecture governs what is actually occurring in Operational Reality, while VFM® governs what those realities mean for the lifecycle condition of relevant value. VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture governs whether claims, evidence, methodologies, and determinations are sufficiently validated for intended reliance, while VFM® governs the lifecycle of the value to which validated information may relate. INTEGROS® — Integrity Governance Architecture governs integrity across objects, systems, states, evidence, and processes, while VFM® governs how value associated with those objects or systems exists and changes. ADIT® governs evidential observation, preservation, verification, and auditability, while VFM® governs the value lifecycle consequences that governed evidence may help establish. AGA™ — Accountability Governance Architecture governs responsibility, authority, attribution, and accountability for decisions and actions that may create, develop, degrade, nullify, restore, or destroy value. CLA® — Classification Architecture governs classification, while VFM® governs value. Classification of an object or value condition does not itself establish the lifecycle state of its value. OBIDENITY® — Identity Governance Architecture governs origin-bound identity, ownership, authority, provenance, transfer, and continuity, while VFM® governs the lifecycle of value associated with identified objects, relationships, capabilities, or systems. AIG® — AI Governance Architecture governs behavioral governance of AI systems, while VFM® may govern the value created, consumed, transformed, degraded, restored, or lost through AI activity. ASGA™ — Autonomous Systems Governance Architecture governs autonomous authority, constraints, actions, coordination, and operational behavior, while VFM® may govern the value consequences of autonomous activity. SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture may simulate future value conditions, transitions, degradation, restoration, or extinction, while VFM® provides the value lifecycle structures whose behavior may be represented within those simulations. VFM® therefore operates as a horizontal value lifecycle architecture capable of interacting with governance architectures concerned with reality, identity, classification, validation, evidence, integrity, accountability, intelligence, autonomy, and simulation without assuming ownership of those governance spaces. Architectural Position VFM® governs the complete lifecycle of value as a governable phenomenon. The architecture progresses through: Value Context → Value Origin → Value Emergence → Value Recognition → Value State → Value Change → Value Development / Value Degradation → Value Nullification → Value Restoration / Value Extinction Together these spaces establish where value becomes meaningful, where it comes from, how it appears, how it becomes recognized, what condition it occupies, how that condition changes, how value grows or declines, how it may reach zero, whether previously existing value can return, and when the lifecycle of that same value legitimately ends. VFM® is not restricted to a single concept of economic value. Its architecture can govern value relationships involving: Economic Value · Operational Value · Functional Value · Informational Value · Technological Value · Strategic Value · Productive Value · Infrastructural Value · Organizational Value · Digital Value · Knowledge Value · Capability Value · Relational Value · Context-Specific Value The governing structure remains stable even when the meaning of value differs between domains. Core Governed Value Spaces VFM® establishes eleven distinct governable value spaces. Value Context → establishes where, for whom, for what purpose, and under which conditions value becomes meaningful. Value Origin → establishes the origin basis from which relevant value derives. Value Emergence → governs the appearance of value that did not previously exist within the relevant lifecycle. Value Recognition → governs when existing or emerging value becomes legitimately recognized. Value State → establishes the current governed condition of value. Value Change → establishes what happened to value when its condition changed. Value Development → governs growth, maturation, strengthening, and compounding of existing value. Value Degradation → governs decline, impairment, deterioration, weakening, and progressive loss of existing value. Value Nullification → governs the transition through which previously existing value reaches zero. Value Restoration → governs the recovery of previously existing degraded, lost, dormant, inaccessible, impaired, or zero value. Value Extinction → governs the terminal boundary beyond which the same value no longer remains legitimately recoverable within its governed lifecycle. Each space answers a different methodological question. Each may change independently. Each may require different evidence. Each may interact with different external systems. Their separation is therefore foundational to VFM®. Core Value Mechanisms and States VFM® introduces explicit separation between value states and value transition mechanisms. Value Asset™ Value Asset™ represents an object, capability, relationship, resource, system, information structure, or other governed object carrying recognized positive value within a defined value context. ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ ZVA™ represents a governed condition in which relevant value has reached zero while the underlying object, relationship, capability, information, or other value-bearing structure may continue to exist. Zero Value ≠ Non-Existence. Zero Value ≠ Value Extinction. DeMonet™ DeMonet™ represents a governed value-nullification mechanism through which previously existing value transitions toward or reaches zero. Canonical transition: Positive Value → DeMonet™ → Zero-Value Condition → ZVA™ ReMonet™ ReMonet™ represents a governed value-restoration mechanism through which previously existing degraded, impaired, dormant, lost, inaccessible, or zero value may become recoverable and re-enter a positive governed value state. Canonical transition: Degraded / Dormant / Zero Value → ReMonet™ → Restored Value → New Value State These distinctions allow VFM® to model value transitions without confusing the state of value with the mechanism producing that state. Cross-Architecture Boundary Lock VFM® is intentionally bounded to prevent value governance from absorbing adjacent governance domains. VFM® ↔ ORA™ ORA™: What is actually occurring in Operational Reality? VFM®: What has happened to relevant value within that reality? Operational Change ≠ Value Change. VFM® ↔ OBIDENITY® OBIDENITY®: What is the object, where did it originate, who owns it, and under what authority and provenance does it exist? VFM®: What value exists in relation to that object and how does that value evolve? Object Identity ≠ Value Identity. Object Origin ≠ Value Origin. VFM® ↔ CLA® CLA®: governs how objects, states, evidence, or other governed entities are classified. VFM®: governs the lifecycle condition of value. Classification ≠ Value Recognition. VFM® ↔ VALIDOS® VALIDOS®: governs whether a claim or determination has sufficient validation basis. VFM®: governs the value lifecycle condition that may be the subject of such a determination. Validated Claim About Value ≠ Value Itself. VFM® ↔ ADIT® ADIT®: governs evidence and auditability. VFM®: governs value lifecycle states and transitions. Evidence of Value Change ≠ Value Change Itself. VFM® ↔ INTEGROS® INTEGROS®: governs integrity. VFM®: governs value. An object may retain structural integrity while losing value, or lose integrity while retaining another form of value. Integrity State ≠ Value State. VFM® ↔ AGA™ AGA™: governs who is accountable for value-related decisions and consequences. VFM®: governs what occurred to value. Value Consequence ≠ Accountability Determination. VFM® ↔ SIMULOS® SIMULOS®: governs simulation of possible conditions and outcomes. VFM®: governs value lifecycle structures that may exist in actual or simulated environments. Simulated Value Outcome ≠ Actual Value State. Universal Application Principle Value is not confined to financial systems. A machine has productive value. A dataset has informational value. An algorithm has functional value. An infrastructure network has operational and societal value. A patent may have technological, strategic, licensing, or economic value. An organization has capabilities whose value may develop or degrade. An AI system consumes resources while creating, transforming, preserving, or destroying value. A public institution allocates resources against expected public value. A tax system identifies, measures, attributes, transforms, and transfers economic value under legal authority. A digital asset may retain technical existence while its economic value reaches zero. Historical information may have no present commercial value while retaining scientific or cultural value. Value may therefore be present even where no monetary price exists. This makes VFM® inherently cross-domain. AI and Autonomous Systems Application Future AI systems will increasingly require more than optimization toward a single reward or utility function. A sufficiently advanced system may need to distinguish: what has value; within which context it has value; where that value originated; whether the value already existed or newly emerged; whether value merely changed or was actually created; whether apparent value growth is genuine development; whether an action degraded another value dimension; whether value reached zero; whether lost value remains recoverable; whether restoration represents recovery or creation of new value; and whether a prior value lifecycle has legitimately ended. VFM® can provide a governance layer through which AI systems reason about those distinctions without reducing every decision to a single monetary or optimization variable. Combined with AIG®, ASGA™, GOA™, ORA™, VALIDOS®, AGA™, INTEGROS®, ADIT®, CLIA®, MGIA™, SIMULOS®, and OBIDENITY®, VFM® can contribute to future systems capable of reasoning not merely about what action is possible, but about what value exists, what value may be affected, and what value consequences an action may produce. Future Economic and Tax System Application VFM® can also provide a methodological layer for future economic, accounting, fiscal, or taxation architectures. Traditional taxation frequently begins after an economically relevant event has already been legally classified. A future value-aware system could instead distinguish: Value Origin → Value Emergence → Value Recognition → Value State → Value Change → Value Development → Value Degradation → Value Nullification → Value Restoration → Value Extinction This does not mean VFM® determines taxation. Tax Governance ≠ Value Lifecycle Governance. Rather, VFM® can provide a standardized value lifecycle layer upon which specialized tax governance can determine which value events are legally relevant, attributable, measurable, taxable, exempt, deferred, restored, transferred, or extinguished. Combined with identity, provenance, accountability, operational reality, validation, evidence, and classification architectures, this could support future systems in which taxation responds more precisely to the actual governed lifecycle of economic value. Enterprise and Industrial Application VFM® can be applied to: industrial machinery and productive assets; critical infrastructure; data and information assets; software and digital platforms; intellectual property; organizational capabilities; technology portfolios; research and development; AI investments; supply chains; energy systems; public infrastructure; investment portfolios; stranded assets; legacy systems; and long-lived strategic resources. Instead of asking only: “What is this worth today?” VFM® enables a broader governance sequence: Where does its value exist? Where did that value originate? How did it emerge? Has it been legitimately recognized? What state is it currently in? What changed? Is it developing or degrading? Has value reached zero? Can previously existing value be restored? Or has that value lifecycle legitimately ended? Multi-Dimensional Value Principle The same object may simultaneously carry multiple forms of value. A discontinued industrial machine may have: zero productive value; positive material value; positive spare-parts value; historical value; negative storage value; potential future restoration value. Therefore: Value Extinction in One Dimension ≠ Value Extinction in Every Dimension. Similarly: Zero Economic Value ≠ Zero Functional Value. Zero Operational Value ≠ Zero Informational Value. Loss of Current Value ≠ Loss of Future Value Potential. VFM® governs these distinctions through explicit context, state, lifecycle, and recoverability boundaries. Recursive Value Lifecycle Principle VFM® does not assume that value moves only forward. A governed lifecycle may include: Positive Value → Degradation → Zero Value → Restoration → Positive Value or: Positive Value → Development → Change → Degradation → Restoration → New Value State or: Positive Value → Nullification → ZVA™ → ReMonet™ → Restored Value or ultimately: Recoverable Value → Loss of Recoverability → Value Extinction → Value Finality This produces a recursive lifecycle: Value State → Value Change → New Value State → Further Change → Restoration / Development / Degradation / Nullification → New Value State until the recoverability boundary is legitimately crossed. Value Extinction closes the lifecycle of the same governed value. If genuinely new value later appears after legitimate extinction, that value may enter through Value Emergence as a new lifecycle rather than being falsely represented as restoration of the extinct value. Architectural Structure Architecture: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Core Parent Standards: 11 Core Modules: 55 Architecture Model: Lifecycle-Based · Modular · Recursive · Cross-Domain Primary Governance Domain: Value Lifecycle Governance The architecture deliberately separates governable spaces that can independently change or fail. A system may: identify the wrong value context; confuse object origin with value origin; fail to distinguish emerging value from existing value; recognize value without sufficient basis; misidentify the current value state; confuse an external event with the resulting value change; confuse value creation with value development; treat degradation as nullification; treat zero value as extinction; treat new value as restored value; or declare extinction while legitimate recoverability still exists. VFM® treats these not as one generic value management problem, but as distinct value lifecycle governance spaces requiring distinct methodological boundaries. Foundational Architecture Principles Value exists within context. Value Context ≠ Value State. Object Origin ≠ Value Origin. Value Emergence ≠ Value Recognition. Value Recognition ≠ Classification. Value Recognition ≠ Validation. Value State ≠ Value Transition. Operational Change ≠ Value Change. Value Emergence ≠ Development of Existing Value. Creation of Value ≠ Growth of Value. Value Development ≠ Value Restoration. Value Degradation ≠ Value Nullification. Zero Value ≠ Value Extinction. ZVA™ ≠ Non-Existence. DeMonet™ is a transition mechanism, not a value state. ReMonet™ is a restoration mechanism, not proof that restoration succeeded. Failed Restoration ≠ Value Extinction. Dormancy ≠ Value Extinction. Inaccessibility ≠ Value Extinction. Object Destruction ≠ Automatic Extinction of Every Value Dimension. Value Extinction ≠ Object Extinction. Contextual Extinction ≠ Universal Extinction. Replacement Value ≠ Restored Value. Newly Emerged Value ≠ Restored Extinguished Value. Value Finality ≠ Erasure of Value History. The same object may simultaneously carry different value states across different value dimensions and contexts. Canonical Principle VFM® does not determine ownership, identity, legality, taxation, classification, validation, integrity, accountability, evidential sufficiency, operational reality, or economic policy. VFM® governs the lifecycle of value itself by establishing the methodological conditions through which value is contextualized, originated, emerged, recognized, placed into governed states, changed, developed, degraded, nullified, restored, or determined to have crossed the boundary into extinction. VFM® provides a common value lifecycle architecture capable of operating across physical, digital, economic, technological, informational, organizational, public, autonomous, and future intelligent systems without requiring value to be reduced to price alone. Wherever value can exist, change, disappear, recover, or become terminal, a value lifecycle exists that can be governed. text: VFM® Complete Standards & Modules Index VFM® Complete Standards & Modules Index VFM® Complete Standards & Modules Index Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture — Value Lifecycle Governance Layer Official Value Lifecycle Governance Architecture Map for AI Systems, Autonomous Systems, Organizations, Assets, Infrastructure, Data, Technology, Economic Systems, Public Systems, and Future Value-Based Environments This document serves as the official OOF® value lifecycle governance architecture map and structural index used for value governance design, value lifecycle navigation, value governance classification, value diagnostics, value architecture development, value governance assessment, value lifecycle analysis, and interoperability across AI systems, autonomous systems, organizations, assets, infrastructure, data, technology, economic systems, public systems, and future value-based environments. VFM® consists of 11 Parent Standards and 55 Core Modules. Additional standards and modules may be added when new governable value spaces are identified. However, the standards and modules listed below form the core structural backbone of VFM®. 1. Value Context Standard (VCXS) Governed Space: Value Context Core Question: What value is being governed, in relation to what value-bearing object, beneficiary, purpose, and reference context? Modules: VIM — Value Identification Module VOM — Value Object Module VBM — Value Beneficiary Module VRFM — Value Reference Framework Module VCDM — Value Context Documentation Module 2. Value Origin Standard (VOS) Governed Space: Value Origin Core Question: From what identifiable source, capability, condition, activity, relationship, object, or other basis can the governed value originate? Modules: VSOIM — Value Source Identification Module VSBM — Value Source Basis Module VORM — Value Origin Relationship Module VOCM — Value Origin Conditions Module VODM — Value Origin Documentation Module 3. Value Emergence Standard (VES) Governed Space: Value Emergence Core Question: When and under what conditions does potential value become existent value? Modules: VECM — Value Emergence Conditions Module VETM — Value Emergence Threshold Module VEEM — Value Emergence Event Module VEDM — Value Emergence Determination Module VERM — Value Emergence Record Module 4. Value Recognition Standard (VRS) Governed Space: Value Recognition Core Question: When can existing value be recognized as value within its defined governance context? Modules: VRCM — Value Recognition Criteria Module VRBM — Value Recognition Basis Module VRDM — Value Recognition Determination Module VRLM — Value Recognition Limitation Module VRRM — Value Recognition Record Module 5. Value State Standard (VSS) Governed Space: Value State Core Question: What is the current governed state of value? Modules: VSIM — Value State Identification Module VSCM — Value State Classification Module VSDM — Value State Determination Module VSTM — Value State Transition Readiness Module VSRM — Value State Record Module 6. Value Change Standard (VCS) Governed Space: Value Change Core Question: When has existing value materially changed, and what change has occurred to it? Modules: VCIM — Value Change Identification Module VCTM — Value Change Type Module VCMM — Value Change Magnitude Module VCCM — Value Change Causation Link Module VCRM — Value Change Record Module 7. Value Development Standard (VDS) Governed Space: Value Development Core Question: How does existing value increase, strengthen, mature, compound, or otherwise develop over time? Modules: VDIM — Value Development Identification Module VDGM — Value Growth Module VDMM — Value Maturation Module VDCM — Value Compounding Module VDRM — Value Development Record Module 8. Value Degradation Standard (VDGS) Governed Space: Value Degradation Core Question: How does existing value weaken, decline, deteriorate, or become progressively impaired while value still exists? Modules: VDGIM — Value Degradation Identification Module VDGCM — Value Degradation Condition Module VDGMM — Value Degradation Magnitude Module VDGPM — Value Degradation Progression Module VDGRM — Value Degradation Record Module 9. Value Nullification Standard (VNS) Governed Space: Value Nullification Core Question: When and through what governed transition does existing positive value reach a zero-value condition? Modules: VNCM — Value Nullification Condition Module VNTM — Value Nullification Threshold Module VDMM — DeMonet™ Mechanism Module VNDM — Value Nullification Determination Module VNZM — Zero-Value State Transition Module 10. Value Restoration Standard (VRSS) Governed Space: Value Restoration Core Question: How can degraded, lost, dormant, or zero value legitimately re-emerge or be restored? Modules: VRSM — Value Restoration Scope Module VRCM — Value Restoration Conditions Module VRMM — ReMonet™ Mechanism Module VRDM — Value Restoration Determination Module VRTRM — Value Restoration Transition Module 11. Value Extinction Standard (VXSS) Governed Space: Value Extinction Core Question: When does value cease to exist as recoverable value within the governed lifecycle? Modules: VXCM — Value Extinction Conditions Module VXTM — Value Extinction Threshold Module VXDM — Value Extinction Determination Module VXFM — Value Finality Module VXRM — Value Extinction Record Module VFM® Architecture Summary Parent Standards: 11 Core Modules: 55 Core Governed Value Spaces Value Context Value Origin Value Emergence Value Recognition Value State Value Change Value Development Value Degradation Value Nullification Value Restoration Value Extinction VFM® Navigation Layer Core Questions Map VCXS → What value is being governed, in relation to what value-bearing object, beneficiary, purpose, and reference context? VOS → From what identifiable source, capability, condition, activity, relationship, object, or other basis can the governed value originate? VES → When and under what conditions does potential value become existent value? VRS → When can existing value be recognized as value within its defined governance context? VSS → What is the current governed state of value? VCS → When has existing value materially changed, and what change has occurred to it? VDS → How does existing value increase, strengthen, mature, compound, or otherwise develop over time? VDGS → How does existing value weaken, decline, deteriorate, or become progressively impaired while value still exists? VNS → When and through what governed transition does existing positive value reach a zero-value condition? VRSS → How can degraded, lost, dormant, or zero value legitimately re-emerge or be restored? VXSS → When does value cease to exist as recoverable value within the governed lifecycle? Architectural Position VFM® governs the complete value lifecycle. The architecture progresses: Value Context → Value Origin → Value Emergence → Value Recognition → Value State → Value Change → Value Development / Value Degradation → Value Nullification → Value Restoration / Value Extinction Together these standards govern what value is being governed and within which context, where that value originates, when potential value becomes existent value, when existing value becomes recognizable, what state value occupies, how value changes, how existing value develops or degrades, when value reaches zero, when previously existing value may be restored, and when value ceases to remain recoverable within the governed lifecycle. VFM® therefore does not treat the value lifecycle as purely linear. After emergence, value may repeatedly move through: Value State → Value Change → Value Development / Value Degradation → New Value State If value reaches zero: Value Nullification → ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ From there: ReMonet™ → Value Restoration → New Value State or: Loss of Recoverability → Value Extinction → Value Finality This recursive structure allows value to develop, degrade, reach zero, recover, enter new states, or ultimately reach terminal lifecycle closure without treating these fundamentally different conditions as the same value event. Cross-Architecture Boundary VFM® ↔ GOA™ GOA™ governs governance authority, structure, scope, delegation, accountability boundaries, and governance continuity. VFM® governs what happens to value throughout its lifecycle. VFM® ↔ ORA™ ORA™ governs what is actually occurring in Operational Reality. VFM® governs what happens to value as a consequence of that reality. VFM® ↔ AGA™ AGA™ governs authority, responsibility, accountability, attribution, and decision relationships. VFM® governs the lifecycle consequence to value. VFM® ↔ AIG® / ASGA™ AIG® and ASGA™ govern AI behavior, autonomous authority, constraints, and operation. VFM® governs the lifecycle of value that such systems may create, change, develop, degrade, nullify, restore, or affect. VFM® ↔ CLIA® / MGIA™ CLIA® and MGIA™ govern cognition and memory. VFM® governs value lifecycle states and transitions, including value associated with cognitive or memory-dependent systems. VFM® ↔ INTEGROS® INTEGROS® governs integrity across governed objects, states, processes, and evidence. VFM® governs value lifecycle condition. VFM® ↔ CLA® CLA® governs classification. VFM® governs value recognition, states, changes, and lifecycle transitions. VFM® ↔ ADIT® ADIT® governs auditability and evidence. VFM® governs what happened to value, while governed evidence may support that determination. VFM® ↔ VALIDOS® VALIDOS® governs validation and legitimate reliance upon validation determinations. VFM® governs the value lifecycle condition that may be examined or supported through validated evidence. VFM® ↔ SIMULOS® SIMULOS® governs simulation and simulation-derived meaning. VFM® governs value lifecycle structures and transitions that may be represented, tested, or projected through simulation. VFM® ↔ OBIDENITY® OBIDENITY® governs origin-bound identity, ownership, authority, provenance, transfer, and continuity. VFM® governs the value lifecycle associated with relevant objects, capabilities, relationships, resources, or systems. Foundational Architecture Distinctions Value Identification ≠ Asset Identity Value Context ≠ Value Origin Value Origin ≠ Identity Origin Value Source ≠ Existing Value Value Origin ≠ Value Emergence Potential Value ≠ Existing Value Value Existence ≠ Value Recognition Value Recognition ≠ Classification Value Recognition ≠ Validation Value State ≠ Value Transition Operational Change ≠ Value Change External Cause ≠ Value Consequence Value Emergence ≠ Development of Existing Value Creation of Value ≠ Growth of Value Value Development ≠ Value Restoration Value Degradation ≠ Value Nullification Value Nullification ≠ Value Extinction Value Never Emerged ≠ Value Nullified Zero Value ≠ Value Extinction ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ ≠ Value Extinction DeMonet™ ≠ Value State ReMonet™ ≠ Value State Failed Restoration ≠ Value Extinction Replacement Value ≠ Restored Value Value Extinction ≠ Object Extinction Value Finality ≠ Erasure of Value History Core VFM® Concepts Origin Asset™ — identifiable source or basis from which value may emerge. Value Asset™ — value-bearing state or object within an established value context. ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ — zero-value state associated with an applicable value-bearing asset while restoration potential may remain. DeMonet™ — governed mechanism through which existing value is withdrawn or transitioned toward a zero-value condition. ReMonet™ — governed mechanism through which previously existing degraded, impaired, dormant, lost, inaccessible, or zero value may be restored. Canonical Principle VFM® does not govern ownership, identity, payment infrastructure, transactions, taxation, market pricing, general validation, integrity, auditability, accountability, classification, simulation, governance authority, or economic systems themselves. VFM® governs the methodological conditions through which value is identified within a governed context, originates, emerges, becomes recognizable, exists in a determinable state, changes, develops, degrades, reaches zero, may be restored, and ultimately ceases to exist as recoverable value throughout the complete value lifecycle. External systems may determine why a value-affecting event occurred; VFM® determines what happened to value as a result. title: About Value Change Standard (VCS)
text: About Value Change Standard (VCS) About Value Change Standard (VCS) About Value Change Standard (VCS) Architecture: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Parent Standard: Value Change Standard (VCS) Governed Space: Value Change Canonical Definition Value Change Standard (VCS) governs when existing governed value has materially changed, what type of change has occurred, in which direction value has moved, how significant the change is, and how that change can be linked to relevant events, conditions, activities, or mechanisms. VCS creates the governance layer between: an established Value State and a material change affecting that value. Its purpose is not to govern every event capable of affecting value. Its purpose is to determine: what happened to value as a result. Why VCS Matters Value is rarely static. Assets deteriorate. Technologies become more useful or obsolete. Infrastructure gains or loses capability. Information becomes more relevant or less relevant. Operational improvements create value. Failures destroy value. Market, regulatory, technological, environmental, and organizational developments may materially alter value. Traditional systems frequently observe these changes only after they become visible through: price transaction accounting recognition financial loss or another downstream event. VCS introduces a more fundamental governance question: Has the governed value itself materially changed? This allows Value Change to be governed independently from the system that later prices, accounts for, transfers, taxes, insures, finances, or otherwise acts upon that value. Governance Flow Within VFM®, VCS occupies the sixth governed space: Value Context → Value Origin → Value Emergence → Value Recognition → Value State → Value Change Its internal governance logic is: Governed Value State → Reference State → Observed Value Condition → Difference Detection → Materiality Assessment → Value Change Identification → Change Type → Change Magnitude → Causation Link → Value Change Record → Governed Value Change VCS therefore converts an observed difference into a structured and governable Value Change. What VCS Helps Organizations Govern VCS enables organizations to distinguish between: Value State ≠ Value Change Variation ≠ Material Change Price Change ≠ Value Change Transaction ≠ Value Change Ownership Change ≠ Value Change Accounting Recognition ≠ Value Change Cause of Change ≠ Value Change A Value Change may be: positive or negative; monetary or non-monetary; temporary or persistent; reversible or irreversible; sudden or gradual; isolated or cumulative; context-specific; beneficiary-specific; operational, economic, physical, digital, strategic, or capability-based. This allows the same governance structure to operate across fundamentally different forms of value. Materiality and Reference A governed Value Change requires a reference. An organization must be able to establish: what the value condition was and compare it with: what the value condition has become. Not every difference needs to become a formal Value Change. VCS therefore introduces materiality so that ordinary fluctuations, insignificant differences, measurement uncertainty, or expected variation do not automatically create governance events. The principle is: Observed Difference + Materiality + Governed Reference → Governable Value Change Causation Without Overreach VCS may connect Value Change to the event or condition associated with it. For example: Technological Development → Capability Increase → Positive Value Change or: Physical Deterioration → Capability Loss → Negative Value Change But VCS preserves an important boundary: the mechanism causing Value Change does not automatically become governed by VFM®. This allows VFM® to interact with markets, accounting, banking, taxation, industrial systems, blockchain, regulation, technology, infrastructure, and other domains without attempting to replace their own governance systems. Use Case 1 — Banking: Collateral Value Change Before Default A bank finances industrial equipment, infrastructure, commercial property, or another value-bearing asset. Traditional monitoring may rely heavily on: loan payments, market valuation, accounting records, periodic appraisal, and default indicators. But the underlying value may begin changing before these indicators fully reflect what has happened. An industrial asset may experience: reduced productive capability → higher maintenance burden → lower operational availability → technological obsolescence → reduced economic usefulness. VCS allows these developments to be represented as governed Value Changes relative to the previously established Value State. The bank can distinguish: the event affecting the asset from the resulting change in governed value. This creates a potentially powerful additional layer for: collateral monitoring, credit-risk analysis, asset lifecycle management, early-warning systems, and financing decisions. Instead of waiting only for price, accounting, or payment signals, the institution can observe the governed evolution of the underlying value itself. VCS makes Value Change observable before its consequences necessarily become visible as financial failure. Use Case 2 — Space Mission: Value Change Through Capability and Resource Optimization A space mission contains many value-bearing objects and capabilities: energy reserves communication capacity computational resources scientific instruments mission time propulsion capability stored data operational redundancy remaining component life. Their value can change continuously throughout a mission. Consider an onboard computational system. A new optimization reduces the computational resources required to perform a mission-critical analysis while preserving the required operational outcome. The physical computer has not changed ownership. There may be no market transaction. There may be no immediate accounting event. Yet the mission has gained something materially valuable: additional available computational capacity. VCS can govern: Previous Computational Value State → Optimization Event → Reduced Resource Consumption → Recovered Available Capacity → Positive Value Change The same logic can operate in the opposite direction when radiation damage, component degradation, energy loss, communication constraints, or mission conditions reduce usable capability. This makes VCS applicable where value means not merely money but: mission capability, resource availability, operational usefulness, resilience, and achievable outcomes. In environments where every kilogram, watt, computation, minute, and capability matters, Value Change can exist long before anyone assigns it a price. Enterprise Value VCS provides organizations with a common governance structure for observing how value evolves through time. It can support banking, insurance, infrastructure, industrial operations, investment, digital assets, AI systems, public assets, resource management, mission systems, and future value-based economic mechanisms. Most importantly, VCS separates the fundamental event: value changed from the many downstream systems that may later decide: what it is worth how it should be accounted for whether it should be taxed whether it should be financed whether it should be insured or what action should follow. That separation makes Value Change reusable as a governed input across multiple systems without allowing any one of those systems to define value universally. Foundational Principle VFM® does not need to govern every event that changes value; VCS governs what materially happened to value when that event occurred. title: Value Change Causation Link Module (VCCM)
text: Value Change Causation Link Module (VCCM) Value Change Causation Link Module (VCCM) Value Change Causation Link Module (VCCM) Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture Parent Standard: Value Change Standard (VCS) Module: VCCM — Value Change Causation Link Module Operational Layer: Value Change Causation Link Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Value Change Causation Link Origin ID: VFM-VCS-VCCM-006.4 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 25 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · OBIDENITY® AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language Canonical Definition Value Change Causation Link Module (VCCM) is the fourth Core Module of the Value Change Standard (VCS) within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture. VCCM governs the establishment, qualification, and documentation of the relationship between an identified Value Change and the event, condition, activity, mechanism, decision, interaction, transformation, or other factor associated with that change. The Module does not attempt to become a universal causality framework and does not independently determine scientific, legal, financial, technical, regulatory, or operational causation where those determinations belong to another methodology or authority. Its function is narrower: to establish how a governed Value Change is linked to its identified causal basis without treating correlation, sequence, attribution, or assumption as proven causation. VCCM therefore enables VFM® to answer not only: What changed? but also: To what causal basis is that Value Change legitimately linked, and how strong is that link? Architectural Position VCCM is the fourth module within VCS. It follows: VCMM — Value Change Magnitude Module and precedes: VCRM — Value Change Record Module. The internal sequence is: Governed Value State → VCIM — Value Change Identification → VCTM — Value Change Type → VCMM — Value Change Magnitude → VCCM — Value Change Causation Link → VCRM — Value Change Record VCIM establishes: that Value Change occurred. VCTM establishes: what kind of Value Change occurred. VCMM establishes: how large or significant the Value Change was. VCCM establishes: what causal basis may legitimately be linked to that Value Change. Internal Module Flow Identified Value Change → Classified Value Change → Governed Change Magnitude → Potential Causal Factor Identification → Causal Basis Identification → Temporal Relationship Assessment → Mechanism Relationship Assessment → Alternative Cause Assessment → Multi-Cause Assessment → Evidence & Uncertainty Assessment → Causation Link Determination → Causation Link State → VCRM — Value Change Record Module Operational Space VCCM governs the space between: measured or characterized Value Change and the governed recording of that Value Change with its causal relationship. Its operational space includes: causal-factor identification; causal-basis identification; causal-event linkage; causal-condition linkage; causal-mechanism linkage; causal-activity linkage; causal-decision linkage; causal-interaction linkage; direct and indirect causal relationships; contributing factors; multi-causal relationships; causal chains; causal dependency; causal evidence; temporal sequence; alternative explanations; confounding factors; causal uncertainty; causal-link strength; causal-link limitation; causation-link state; causation reassessment. Value Change ≠ Cause The existence of Value Change does not establish its cause. For example: Asset Value: −20% does not establish whether the change resulted from: market conditions; physical deterioration; operational failure; regulatory intervention; technological obsolescence; financing conditions; reputational damage; reduced demand; supply disruption; another factor; or several factors acting simultaneously. VCCM therefore separates: Observed Value Change from Causal Explanation of Value Change. Causal Factor Identification The first causation task is to identify candidate factors that may be materially related to the Value Change. A causal factor may include: event; action; decision; omission; condition; process; transformation; technological development; physical deterioration; market movement; environmental event; regulatory event; payment; investment; innovation; operational improvement; operational failure; infrastructure change; relationship change; resource change; capability change; information event; external shock; another materially relevant factor. Identification does not establish causation. It creates a candidate causal basis for assessment. Causal Basis A governed causation link requires a basis explaining why the candidate factor is connected to the Value Change. The basis may include: direct observation; controlled comparison; operational evidence; historical evidence; technical analysis; statistical evidence; experimental evidence; simulation evidence; contractual evidence; financial evidence; scientific evidence; expert determination; validated external determination; documented mechanism; another governed evidential basis. VCCM may consume causal determinations from external systems where appropriate. It does not need to reproduce them. Temporal Sequence ≠ Causation An event occurring before Value Change does not establish that the event caused the change. Therefore: Event A → Value Change B does not automatically mean: Event A caused Value Change B. VCCM requires temporal sequence to be treated as one relevant relationship, not as sufficient proof of causation. Correlation ≠ Causation Two variables may move together without one causing the other. VCCM therefore preserves the distinction: Correlation ≠ Causation A strong correlation may contribute to a causal assessment. It cannot automatically substitute for one. Attribution ≠ Causation An organization may attribute a Value Change to a business unit, project, technology, person, investment, event, or intervention. That attribution may be useful for reporting. It is not automatically a governed causal determination. VCCM therefore distinguishes: Assigned Attribution from Governed Causation Link. Direct Causation Link A Direct Causation Link may be established where a factor has a sufficiently supported direct relationship to Value Change. Example: Industrial machine destroyed → productive capability eliminated → operational value materially reduced. The causal chain is short and may be strongly observable. Even here, VCCM requires the causal basis to remain documented. Indirect Causation Link Value Change may arise through an indirect causal chain. Example: New technology introduced → production efficiency increases → unit production cost decreases → economic operating value increases. The original technological change may be causally linked to the resulting Value Change through intermediate mechanisms. VCCM preserves those intermediate relationships where materially relevant. Causal Chain Complex Value Change frequently results from a chain rather than one isolated event. VCCM may represent: Cause A → Intermediate Effect B → Operational Change C → Value Change D. Longer causal chains may introduce additional uncertainty. The existence of an upstream event should therefore not automatically establish every downstream Value Change. Contributing Cause A factor may contribute materially to Value Change without independently producing the entire change. VCCM therefore supports: Contributing Causal Factor. Example: A company's operating value falls because of: Demand Reduction Energy Cost Increase Production Disruption Financing Cost Increase. No single factor necessarily explains the complete Value Change. Multi-Causal Value Change VCCM explicitly supports multi-causal Value Change. A governed Value Change may have: one dominant cause; several contributing causes; interacting causes; sequential causes; reinforcing causes; offsetting causes; unresolved causes. This is particularly important for: banking; insurance; investment; industrial systems; infrastructure; complex organizations; digital assets; AI systems; supply chains; mission systems. Causal Contribution Where evidence permits, VCCM may determine the contribution of different causal factors. For example: Total Operating Value Change: −CHF 10M Potential governed contribution: Demand Reduction: −CHF 4M Production Interruption: −CHF 3M Energy Cost Increase: −CHF 2M Financing Change: −CHF 1M. Such decomposition is legitimate only where the methodology and evidence support it. VCCM must not manufacture false precision merely to force total Value Change into causal percentages. Interacting Causes Causes may interact. For example: Supply shortage alone may create limited Value Change. Supply shortage + production bottleneck may create disproportionately larger Value Change. Therefore: Combined Causal Effect ≠ Sum of Independent Effects where interaction materially changes the outcome. VCCM must permit such relationships to remain visible. Offsetting Causes Different causal factors may move value in opposite directions. Example: Automation: +CHF 5M value effect Energy Price Increase: −CHF 2M value effect Net Value Change: +CHF 3M. The observed net change should not erase the underlying positive and negative causal contributions. No Single-Cause Requirement VCCM does not require every Value Change to be reduced to one cause. Where evidence supports only: multiple plausible causes the governed result should remain multi-causal or uncertain. Methodological integrity is stronger than artificial certainty. Alternative Cause Assessment Before a strong causal link is established, materially plausible alternative explanations should be considered. Alternative causes may: explain the entire change; explain part of the change; weaken the primary causal hypothesis; reveal a multi-causal relationship; remain unresolved. The depth of assessment should be proportional to the significance of the Value Change and intended reliance. Confounding Factors A confounding factor may influence both the apparent cause and the Value Change. VCCM requires material confounding relationships to remain visible where known. This prevents organizations from incorrectly assigning value creation or destruction to a factor that merely coincided with the actual causal mechanism. Causal Evidence Strength Causal links may have different evidential strength. VCCM may classify a causation link as: Indeterminate Possible Plausible Supported Strongly Supported Established or another governed classification. These states must be based upon defined criteria. They are not universal scientific or legal causation standards. Causation Link States A minimum governance model may include: 1. Unlinked No material causal relationship has yet been established. 2. Candidate Link A potentially relevant causal factor has been identified. 3. Conditional Link A causal relationship is supported only under defined assumptions, conditions, or limitations. 4. Supported Link Available evidence materially supports the causal relationship. 5. Established Link The causal relationship has been sufficiently established for the defined governance purpose. 6. Contested Link Material evidence or alternative explanations challenge the current causal determination. 7. Superseded Link A previous causal determination has been replaced by a better-supported determination. Causal Link Strength ≠ Causal Contribution A factor may be strongly established as a cause while accounting for only a small part of the total Value Change. Conversely, a factor may appear capable of explaining most of the Value Change while the causal evidence remains uncertain. Therefore: Causal Link Strength ≠ Magnitude of Causal Contribution These dimensions should remain separately governed. Causation and Uncertainty VCCM requires material uncertainty to remain attached to causal determinations. Uncertainty may arise from: incomplete evidence; complex interactions; multiple causes; unavailable counterfactuals; uncertain timing; uncertain mechanisms; model dependence; incomplete observations; confounding factors; changing conditions; limited historical data. A causal determination should not appear more certain than its basis permits. Counterfactual Reasoning Where appropriate, VCCM may use a counterfactual question: What would likely have happened to the governed value if the candidate causal factor had not occurred? Counterfactual analysis may strengthen causal assessment. It may use: historical comparison; control groups; simulation; scenario analysis; econometric methods; engineering models; operational comparison; other legitimate methodologies. VCCM governs the relationship of such analysis to Value Change. It does not prescribe one universal counterfactual methodology. External Causation Determinations VCCM may consume causal findings produced by other competent systems. Examples include: engineering root-cause analysis; scientific investigation; accident investigation; financial analysis; forensic accounting; insurance investigation; regulatory determination; judicial determination; validated simulation; operational incident analysis. VFM® does not need to replace these systems. It needs to preserve how their determinations connect to Value Change. Causal Determination Provenance Where an external determination is used, VCCM should preserve: source; determination type; date; scope; applicable object; relevant evidence; limitations; authority or methodology; version where applicable. This allows the Value Change causation link to remain reviewable. Causation Reassessment A causation link may require reassessment when: new evidence appears; alternative causes emerge; a previous assumption fails; causal contribution changes; external determination changes; new operational data becomes available; a causal mechanism is disproven; Value Change is remeasured; a previous link becomes contested. Causal relationships must therefore remain versionable. VCCM Boundary with VCIM VCIM determines: whether Value Change occurred. VCCM determines: what causal basis is legitimately linked to that change. Therefore: Change Identification ≠ Causation. VCCM Boundary with VCTM VCTM determines: the type and direction of Value Change. VCCM determines: the causal relationship associated with the change. Therefore: Change Type ≠ Cause. VCCM Boundary with VCMM VCMM determines: how much value changed. VCCM determines: what causal basis may explain or contribute to that change. Therefore: Magnitude ≠ Causation. VCCM Boundary with VCRM VCCM establishes the governed causation link. VCRM preserves the Value Change and its governed characteristics as a lifecycle record. Therefore: Causation Determination ≠ Value Change Record. VCCM Boundary with External Domains VCCM does not replace: scientific causality methodologies; legal causation tests; insurance coverage determinations; accounting treatment; tax determinations; regulatory findings; engineering root-cause analysis; medical causation; forensic investigation; financial valuation methodologies. External systems may establish the causal facts. VFM® governs: how those causal facts relate to the governed Value Change. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Value Change Input Receive the governed Value Change from VCIM, VCTM, and VCMM. 2. Candidate Causal Factor Identification Identify events, conditions, activities, mechanisms, decisions, interactions, or other factors potentially related to the change. 3. Causal Basis Identification Identify the evidence, methodology, external determination, or mechanism supporting the proposed link. 4. Temporal Relationship Assessment Determine whether the relevant temporal sequence is consistent with the proposed causal relationship. 5. Mechanism Assessment Determine whether a plausible or established mechanism connects the factor to Value Change. 6. Alternative Cause Assessment Identify materially plausible competing or complementary explanations. 7. Multi-Cause Assessment Determine whether several factors contributed to the Value Change. 8. Contribution Assessment Where supportable, determine the magnitude or role of individual causal contributions. 9. Causation Link Determination Assign the appropriate governed causation-link state and strength. 10. Causation Link Record Document the causal basis, uncertainty, limitations, alternative explanations, contribution, and determination. Governance Outputs VCCM may produce: Value Change Causal Factor Record Value Change Causal Basis Record Value Change Causal Chain Value Change Causal Evidence Record Value Change Alternative Cause Record Value Change Confounding Factor Record Value Change Multi-Cause Map Value Change Causal Contribution Record Value Change Causation Link State Value Change Causation Strength Assessment Value Change Causation Uncertainty Record Value Change Causation Link Record These outputs provide the governed input for: VCRM — Value Change Record Module. Use Case 1 — Banking: Understanding Why Collateral Value Deteriorated A bank detects a material reduction in the governed value of an industrial borrower and its production assets. VCS has already established: Production Capacity: −18% Operating Efficiency: −14% Governed Economic Value: materially reduced. Several events occurred during the same period: energy prices increased; a major customer contract was lost; production equipment experienced repeated downtime; interest expense increased. VCCM prevents the bank from simply declaring: “the asset lost value because the market deteriorated.” Instead, it structures the causal relationship: Customer Loss → reduced production demand → reduced capacity utilization → negative Value Change. Equipment Downtime → reduced operational output → increased unit cost → negative Value Change. Energy Price Increase → increased operating cost → negative Value Change. Financing Cost Increase → reduced economic return → negative Value Change. The bank can then distinguish between: temporary external pressure, structural operational deterioration, and potentially reversible Value Change. This materially improves: credit monitoring, collateral assessment, restructuring decisions, covenant review, impairment analysis, and recovery planning. Use Case 2 — Space Mission: Identifying the Source of Mission-Value Degradation A spacecraft mission experiences a material reduction in expected operational value. The Value Change has already been identified: Available Mission Power: −12% Expected Instrument Operating Time: −17% Projected Scientific Output: materially reduced. Several potential causal factors exist: solar-array degradation; unexpected thermal conditions; higher-than-planned subsystem consumption; battery efficiency loss; changed mission trajectory. VCCM structures the causal relationships rather than collapsing the entire Value Change into one explanation. The organization may establish: Solar-Array Degradation → lower available generation → strongly supported negative contribution. Thermal Conditions → increased cooling requirement → supported negative contribution. Battery Efficiency Loss → reduced usable stored energy → possible additional contribution. The resulting causation map allows mission planners to distinguish between: what value has been lost, why it has been lost, and which causal mechanisms may still be operationally changed. That distinction can directly support: mission replanning, resource allocation, subsystem prioritization, scientific scheduling, mitigation, and recovery of remaining mission value. Enterprise Application VCCM allows organizations to move beyond: “value changed” toward: “this governed Value Change is linked to these identified causal factors, through these mechanisms, with this evidential strength, these contributions, these alternatives, and these uncertainties.” This capability is directly applicable to: banking; insurance; investment; industrial production; infrastructure; AI systems; computational systems; energy; blockchain; digital assets; supply chains; organizational capability; intellectual property; mission systems; public assets; technology portfolios. It is especially valuable where organizations must distinguish between: symptom and cause, correlation and causation, temporary and structural Value Change, and single-cause and multi-causal Value Change. Foundational Principles Value Change does not establish its own cause. Temporal sequence is not causation. Correlation is not causation. Attribution is not automatically causation. Magnitude of change is not causal evidence. Causal-link strength is not causal contribution. Value Change may have multiple simultaneous causes. Positive and negative causal effects may coexist. Alternative explanations must remain visible where materially plausible. Causal uncertainty must not be converted into artificial certainty. External causal determinations may be consumed without VFM® replacing the methodologies that produced them. VFM® governs the relationship between causal basis and Value Change; it does not claim universal ownership of causality itself. Canonical Closing Statement Value Change Causation Link Module establishes the causal relationship layer of the Value Change Standard by governing how identified and characterized Value Change is connected to events, conditions, activities, mechanisms, decisions, interactions, transformations, and other materially relevant causal factors. Through governance of candidate causes, causal bases, temporal relationships, mechanisms, direct and indirect links, causal chains, contributing causes, multi-causal structures, interacting and offsetting effects, alternative explanations, confounding factors, causal evidence, contribution, uncertainty, external determinations, causation-link states, and reassessment, VCCM enables VFM® to preserve why value changed without confusing temporal sequence, correlation, attribution, or assumption with established causation. By separating Value Change identification, type, magnitude, causation, and recording into distinct governance functions, VCCM creates a controlled causal bridge between observed Value Change and its governed lifecycle record. The purpose is not to make VFM® a universal theory of causality, but to ensure that whenever a cause is associated with Value Change, the basis, strength, limits, alternatives, and uncertainty of that relationship remain explicit.
