title: Value Emergence Record Module (VERM)
text: Value Emergence Record Module (VERM) Value Emergence Record Module (VERM) Value Emergence Record Module (VERM) Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture Parent Standard: Value Emergence Standard (VES) Module: VERM — Value Emergence Record Module Operational Layer: Value Emergence Record Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Value Emergence Record Origin ID: VFM-VES-VERM-003.5 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 24 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · INTEGROS® · CLA™ · ADIT® · VALIDOS® · SIMULOS® · OBIDENITY® AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language Canonical Definition Value Emergence Record Module (VERM) is the fifth Core Module of the Value Emergence Standard (VES) within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture. VERM governs the formal recording, preservation, traceability, contextualization, versioning, and lifecycle transfer of a Value Emergence Determination after the emergence process has been assessed through the preceding modules. Its purpose is to ensure that a determination that value has emerged, has not emerged, has emerged conditionally, remains indeterminate, or has been superseded does not survive merely as an isolated statement. VERM preserves the governed relationship: What Value → From What Origin → Under What Context → Under What Conditions → At What Threshold → Through What Event → On What Determination Basis → At What Time → With What Scope and Limitations → With What Emergence State VERM therefore converts the result of Value Emergence governance into a persistent and reconstructable Value Emergence Record capable of entering the next stage of the VFM® lifecycle. Architectural Position VERM is the fifth and final module within the Value Emergence Standard. It follows: VEDM — Value Emergence Determination Module and completes the internal Value Emergence sequence: Emergence Conditions → Emergence Threshold → Emergence Event → Emergence Determination → Emergence Record The internal module roles are: VECM establishes the conditions under which value may emerge. VETM establishes the threshold separating potential value from existent value. VEEM identifies the event or event structure associated with crossing that boundary. VEDM determines whether the governed value has actually emerged. VERM preserves that determination and its governing basis for subsequent lifecycle use. VERM is therefore the persistence and transfer layer of Value Emergence. Governance Flow Position Within the complete VFM® governance flow: Value Context → Value Origin → Value Emergence → Value Recognition → Value State → Value Change → Value Development / Value Degradation → Value Nullification → Value Restoration / Value Extinction VERM operates at the final boundary of: Value Emergence immediately before: Value Recognition. Its architectural role is critical because the next standard must not receive merely an assertion that: “value exists.” It should receive a governed record explaining which value exists, why its emergence was determined, under what conditions that determination applies, and what limitations remain attached to it. Internal Value Flow Potential Value → Emergence Conditions → Emergence Threshold → Emergence Event → Emergence Determination → Determination State → Record Assembly → Context Linkage → Origin Linkage → Conditions / Threshold / Event Linkage → Determination Basis Preservation → Scope & Limitation Preservation → Temporal Anchoring → Record Versioning → Value Emergence Record → Value Recognition Governance This establishes a controlled lifecycle transition: Emergence Determination → Governed Emergence Record → Recognition Candidate Operational Purpose Value claims frequently become detached from the conditions that originally supported them. An organization may initially determine: “This capability created value under these conditions.” Months or years later, the surviving organizational statement may become simply: “This capability has value.” The original: beneficiary; context; threshold; evidence; assumptions; timing; limitations; uncertainty; configuration; determination basis may disappear. VERM exists to prevent this loss of methodological meaning. The record preserves enough information to reconstruct: what was determined and why that determination was legitimate at the time it was made. Value Emergence Record A Value Emergence Record is the governed representation of a Value Emergence Determination together with the material lifecycle information required to interpret that determination correctly. At minimum, a record should be capable of identifying: 1. the governed value; 2. the relevant Value Context; 3. the Value Origin; 4. applicable emergence conditions; 5. applicable emergence threshold; 6. qualifying emergence event; 7. emergence determination; 8. determination state; 9. determination basis; 10. effective emergence time; 11. determination time; 12. applicable scope; 13. beneficiary where relevant; 14. material limitations; 15. material uncertainty; 16. record version; 17. subsequent changes or supersession. The exact implementation may vary according to the value domain. The governance requirement does not. Record ≠ Determination VERM maintains a strict distinction: Value Emergence Determination ≠ Value Emergence Record VEDM determines whether value emerged. VERM records that determination and preserves the conditions that give it meaning. A record must not silently change the underlying determination. If a determination requires reassessment, that reassessment belongs in the governed determination process. VERM then records the resulting new state. Record ≠ Evidence A Value Emergence Record may contain references to evidence. It is not itself equivalent to all underlying evidence. The record may preserve: evidence identifiers; evidence references; evidence summaries; evidence relationships; evidence states; determination basis. Underlying evidence may remain governed by the relevant evidence, integrity, audit, validation, operational, or external systems. Therefore: Record of Evidence ≠ Evidence Itself and Value Emergence Record ≠ Universal Evidence Repository. Record Identity Every material Value Emergence Record should be independently identifiable. Record identity may include: Record ID; governed value identifier; Value Context reference; Value Origin reference; Value Emergence Determination reference; version; status; creation time; effective time. This enables multiple emergence records to coexist without being silently merged. Context Preservation VERM must preserve the Value Context under which emergence was determined. This is necessary because the same underlying object may create different forms of value for different: beneficiaries; purposes; environments; periods; systems; relationships; reference frameworks. A record stating only: “Value emerged” is insufficient where the value cannot be understood without its context. VERM therefore preserves: Value Emerged → For Whom → In Relation to What → For What Purpose → Under What Reference Context where materially applicable. Origin Preservation The record should preserve the relationship between the emerged value and its governed Value Origin. This allows later lifecycle analysis to distinguish: the value from the source from which that value emerged. The distinction is essential because one Value Origin may generate multiple values, and one governed value may depend upon multiple contributing origins. Therefore: Origin Asset™ ≠ Emerged Value. VERM preserves the relationship without collapsing the two. Condition Preservation The emergence conditions established through VECM should remain linked to the record where materially relevant. This allows later users to determine whether the value emerged: only under specific conditions; under a defined configuration; for a particular beneficiary; during a specific operational state; after a defined capability became available; only when multiple conditions converged. Without this information, downstream systems may incorrectly generalize the value. Threshold Preservation VERM should preserve the emergence threshold that separated: Potential Value from: Existing Value. The record should make it possible to understand what threshold was crossed and why that crossing was considered sufficient. This is particularly important where later review asks: Why was value considered to exist at this point rather than earlier or later? Emergence Event Preservation Where an identifiable emergence event or composite event exists, VERM should preserve its relationship to the record. Relevant information may include: event identity; event type; event time; event sequence; event conditions; event relationship to threshold crossing; event relationship to the governed value. The record does not need to reproduce the complete operational event history. It preserves the event relationship necessary to reconstruct value emergence. Determination Basis Preservation VERM must preserve the basis supporting the emergence determination. The basis may include references to: observed outcomes; measurements; operational evidence; simulation evidence; financial evidence; scientific evidence; capability evidence; beneficiary effects; performance results; threshold evidence; contextual evidence; contradictory evidence; uncertainty. VERM does not independently validate every source. It preserves the basis upon which the determination was made. Temporal Anchoring Value emergence has more than one relevant time. VERM should distinguish where applicable: Value Origin Time Emergence Condition Satisfaction Time Threshold Crossing Time Emergence Event Time Value Emergence Effective Time Emergence Determination Time Record Creation Time These timestamps may be identical. They may also differ substantially. Preserving them allows later systems to reconstruct the lifecycle without forcing one artificial timestamp onto multiple distinct events. Retroactive Emergence Record Where VEDM establishes retroactively that value emerged at an earlier time, VERM should preserve both: Emergence Effective Time: T1 and Determination / Record Time: T2. This distinction can be important for: investment evaluation; project assessment; public expenditure analysis; accounting interfaces; economic measurement; infrastructure governance; intellectual property; future tax-governance interfaces; historical value reconstruction. VERM records the temporal relationship without itself determining legal or accounting consequences. Record Scope Every Value Emergence Record must remain bounded by the scope of the determination it represents. Scope may include: value type; beneficiary; object; capability; jurisdictional context; operational context; purpose; configuration; period; environment; value dimension. A narrow determination must produce a narrow record. VERM must not convert: Value Emerged for Beneficiary A under Condition B into: Value Exists Universally. Conditional Emergence Record Where VEDM establishes: Conditionally Emerged VERM must preserve those conditions as part of the record. The conditions are not optional annotations. They are part of the meaning of the emergence state. A conditional record that loses its conditions becomes methodologically misleading. Partial Emergence Record Where only part of a governed value structure has emerged, VERM may preserve: emerged component; non-emerged component; component relationship; partial emergence state; remaining emergence requirements. This enables downstream governance to distinguish: partially emerged value from fully emerged value. Composite Emergence Record Complex value may depend upon several constituent components or emergence pathways. VERM may therefore preserve composite structures such as: Component A → Emerged Component B → Emerged Component C → Conditionally Emerged Composite Value → Emergence Not Yet Fully Established This is useful for infrastructure, banking, industrial systems, AI, research programs, mission systems, supply chains, public investment, and other complex value structures. Uncertainty Preservation Material uncertainty associated with the Value Emergence Determination must remain attached to the record. The record should distinguish where possible between uncertainty concerning: whether value exists; how much value exists; scope of value; beneficiary effect; duration; future persistence; causal contribution; supporting evidence. A record should not create greater certainty than the underlying determination possessed. Contradiction Preservation Material contradictory information considered during the determination should not disappear from the record merely because a positive emergence determination was issued. Where relevant, VERM may preserve: contradiction identifier; contradiction type; effect on determination; unresolved issue; reason the determination remained supportable; reassessment trigger. This prevents downstream users from seeing only the favorable basis. Record Versioning A Value Emergence Record may evolve. VERM therefore requires controlled versioning where material changes occur. A later version should not silently overwrite the historical record. Possible states may include: Active Under Review Amended Superseded Withdrawn Archived The applicable implementation may vary, but the lifecycle history should remain reconstructable. Supersession A new Value Emergence Determination may supersede an earlier determination. VERM should preserve: Previous Record → Superseding Record rather than deleting the previous state. This makes it possible to reconstruct: what was believed; on what basis; when it changed; why it changed; which determination became authoritative afterward. Record Correction A factual or administrative error in a record may require correction without changing the underlying emergence determination. VERM should distinguish: Record Correction from: Determination Change. For example, correcting an incorrect timestamp transcription does not necessarily require a new emergence determination. Changing the conclusion from: Emerged to: Emergence Not Established does. Record Integrity VERM requires the record to remain sufficiently protected against uncontrolled alteration, loss of context, or ambiguous versioning. However, VERM does not replace INTEGROS®. The boundary is: VERM: defines what emergence information must remain preserved and connected. INTEGROS®: may govern the broader integrity properties of the record and supporting systems. Record Auditability VERM requires sufficient traceability for the emergence record to be reconstructed. It does not own general audit governance. ADIT® may govern: audit observation; evidence preservation; verification; audit execution; findings; assurance. Therefore: Emergence Record Traceability ≠ Audit Governance. Record ≠ Accounting Entry A Value Emergence Record does not automatically create an accounting entry. VFM® may determine: Value Emerged while accounting standards determine: No Recognizable Accounting Asset Exists. These outcomes are not inherently contradictory because they govern different questions. VERM can provide a structured upstream value record that accounting systems may reference where appropriate. Record ≠ Tax Record A Value Emergence Record does not establish: taxable income; taxable event; tax base; taxpayer; tax liability; jurisdiction; tax timing. A future tax-governance architecture may consume VFM® records as inputs. But: Value Emergence Record ≠ Tax Assessment. Record ≠ Ownership Record VERM does not determine who owns the value or underlying object. Where ownership, identity, authority, provenance, or transfer matters, the relevant governance may be supplied by OBIDENITY® or other applicable systems. Therefore: Emergence Record ≠ Ownership Register. Record ≠ Validation Certificate A Value Emergence Record records the VFM® emergence determination. It does not automatically establish a VALIDOS® Validation State. A Value Emergence Record or the underlying emergence claim may itself become a Validation Object. Therefore: Recorded Value Emergence ≠ Validated Value Claim. Recognition Interface VERM creates the formal interface from: Value Emergence to: Value Recognition. The next lifecycle question is no longer: Does the value exist? That question has already been governed through VES. The next question becomes: Can this existing value be recognized as value within the defined governance context? The transfer should therefore preserve: Governed Value Identity Value Context Value Origin Relationship Emergence State Emergence Effective Time Determination Basis Scope Conditions Limitations Uncertainty This becomes the governed input to the Value Recognition Standard (VRS). Recognition Candidate Where emergence has been positively or conditionally established, VERM may produce a: Value Recognition Candidate A Value Recognition Candidate is not yet formally recognized value. It is: an existing value whose governed emergence basis is sufficiently recorded to enter Value Recognition governance. This creates the lifecycle distinction: Existing Value ≠ Recognized Value. Machine-Readable Value History VERM enables the value lifecycle to be represented as structured state history. For example: Value ID: V-2048 Origin State: Established Potential Value State: Active Emergence Threshold: Reached Emergence Event: Recorded Emergence Determination: Emerged Effective Time: T1 Determination Time: T2 Emergence Record Version: 1.0 Next Lifecycle State: Recognition Candidate This structure enables VFM® to become usable by: enterprise systems; AI governance systems; banking systems; investment platforms; public-sector systems; accounting interfaces; economic measurement systems; industrial systems; digital asset infrastructures; future value-governance platforms. Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum VERM implementation should establish: 1. Record Identity Create an independently identifiable Value Emergence Record. 2. Value Linkage Link the record to the governed value established under the Value Context. 3. Origin Linkage Preserve the relevant Value Origin relationship. 4. Emergence Basis Preserve the applicable conditions, threshold, event, and determination basis. 5. Determination State Record the formal emergence determination state. 6. Temporal Structure Record relevant emergence, determination, and record times. 7. Scope and Conditions Preserve the boundaries within which the determination applies. 8. Limitations and Uncertainty Preserve material limitations, contradictions, and uncertainty. 9. Version Control Maintain controlled amendment, correction, supersession, and historical continuity. 10. Lifecycle Transfer Create the governed interface into Value Recognition where appropriate. Governance Outputs VERM may produce: Value Emergence Record Value Emergence Record ID Value Emergence Traceability Chain Value Emergence Context Link Value Origin Link Value Emergence Condition Record Value Emergence Threshold Record Value Emergence Event Link Value Emergence Determination Link Value Emergence Effective-Time Record Value Emergence Scope Record Value Emergence Limitation Record Value Emergence Uncertainty Record Value Emergence Contradiction Link Value Emergence Version History Value Emergence Supersession Record Value Recognition Candidate Together, these outputs close the governed Value Emergence lifecycle and create the structured input for Value Recognition. Use Case 1 — Banking & Investment: Persistent Proof of Where Value Actually Emerged A bank finances a large industrial modernization program. The borrower installs: new production lines; automation; robotics; AI systems; energy infrastructure; digital control systems. The program costs CHF 800 million. Two years later, management states that the investment “created substantial value.” Without a governed value record, analysts may need to reconstruct the claim from fragmented: financial reports; project documentation; operational metrics; management statements; production records; technical reports. VFM® instead preserves the lifecycle: Value Context → Value Origin → Potential Value → Emergence Conditions → Emergence Threshold → Emergence Event → Emergence Determination → Value Emergence Record Suppose the governed value is: additional sustainable production capability of 400,000 units annually at a defined cost and quality threshold. VERM records: what capability emerged, when it emerged, under which operational configuration, what threshold was crossed, what evidence supported the determination, which limitations remained, and which version of the production system generated the value. Years later, the bank can distinguish: Capital Invested from Assets Installed from Value Emerged from Value Later Recognized from Value Subsequently Developed or Degraded. This gives banking and investment systems something conventional project reporting often lacks: a reconstructable lifecycle history of value itself. Use Case 2 — Space Mission / AI: Preserving Value Beyond Technical Success A space agency deploys an AI navigation capability intended to increase scientific access during a planetary mission. The mission generates thousands of technical and scientific records. The AI operates successfully. But the governed value is not merely: AI System Activated. The governed value is: additional scientifically relevant mission access produced by autonomous navigation capability. The emergence pathway establishes that the capability enabled the spacecraft to reach scientifically valuable locations that could not otherwise have been accessed within the mission constraints. VEDM determines: Value Emerged. VERM then preserves: which mission value emerged from which capability for which mission purpose under which conditions at which mission phase through which emergence event on what evidence basis with what remaining uncertainty and within what scope the determination remains legitimate. Years later, the organization can compare this record against subsequent missions. It can determine whether the original value: persisted; developed; degraded; was reproduced; became obsolete; was restored; disappeared. The technical mission archive tells the organization: what happened. The VFM® Value Emergence Record tells it: what value emerged from what happened. Foundational Principles A Value Emergence Determination without a persistent governed record is vulnerable to loss of meaning. A record must preserve the context that gives the emergence determination meaning. Value Emergence Record ≠ Value Emergence Determination. Value Emergence Record ≠ Evidence Repository. Value Emergence Record ≠ Accounting Entry. Value Emergence Record ≠ Tax Assessment. Value Emergence Record ≠ Ownership Register. Value Emergence Record ≠ Validation Certificate. Emergence Effective Time ≠ Determination Time ≠ Record Creation Time. A narrow emergence determination must remain narrow when recorded. Conditional emergence must remain conditional. Uncertainty must not disappear when value is recorded. Historical records must not be silently overwritten by later determinations. Existing Value ≠ Recognized Value. The record closes Value Emergence and opens the governed path into Value Recognition. Canonical Closing Statement Value Emergence Record Module establishes the persistence, traceability, temporal continuity, and lifecycle- transfer layer of the Value Emergence Standard by transforming a Value Emergence Determination into a governed and reconstructable Value Emergence Record. Through preservation of the governed value, Value Context, Value Origin, emergence conditions, threshold, event, determination basis, determination state, effective time, scope, limitations, contradictions, uncertainty, version history, and supersession relationships, VERM prevents value-existence claims from becoming detached from the conditions that originally gave them meaning. By distinguishing the emergence record from evidence, accounting recognition, taxation, ownership, validation, and downstream Value Recognition, VERM preserves the architectural boundary of VFM® while enabling existing value to move through subsequent lifecycle stages without losing its origin or emergence history. VERM therefore completes the Value Emergence governance sequence and creates the persistent methodological bridge from Potential Value through established Existing Value to the next governed question: whether that existing value may legitimately become Recognized Value. Governed Links → Value Emergence Standard (VES) → VFM® Architecture Map → Previous: Value Emergence Determination Module (VEDM)

title: Value Emergence Threshold Module (VETM)
text: Value Emergence Threshold Module (VETM) Value Emergence Threshold Module (VETM) Value Emergence Threshold Module (VETM) Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture Parent Standard: Value Emergence Standard (VES) Module: VETM — Value Emergence Threshold Module Operational Layer: Value Emergence Threshold Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Value Emergence Threshold Origin ID: VFM-VES-VETM-003.2 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 24 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · INTEGROS® · CLA™ · ADIT® · VALIDOS® · SIMULOS® · OBIDENITY® AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language Canonical Definition Value Emergence Threshold Module (VETM) is the second Core Module of the Value Emergence Standard (VES) within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture. VETM governs the identification, definition, structuring, assessment, and documentation of the threshold at which sufficiently established Value Emergence Conditions become capable of supporting the transition from Potential Value to Existing Value. The Module establishes the governed boundary separating: conditions that may enable value from conditions sufficient for value to cross toward existence. VETM does not determine that value has actually emerged. That determination remains downstream. Its task is: to establish when the conditions necessary for value emergence become sufficiently satisfied for the emergence boundary to be crossed. Architectural Position VETM is the second module within the Value Emergence Standard. It follows: VECM — Value Emergence Conditions Module and precedes: VEEM — Value Emergence Event Module The sequence is: Emergence Conditions → Emergence Threshold → Emergence Event → Emergence Determination → Emergence Record VECM establishes what must become true. VETM establishes how much, how completely, or under what combination those conditions must become true. VEEM then governs the identifiable event or transition through which emergence occurs. Internal Value Flow Defined Potential Value → Governed Emergence Conditions → Condition Satisfaction Assessment → Threshold Structure → Threshold Requirement → Threshold Comparison → Threshold State → Threshold Crossing → Emergence-Ready Value State → Value Emergence Event The internal value flow establishes a controlled transition between: Potential Value and Value capable of entering existence. Governance Flow Position Value Context → Value Origin → Value Emergence Within Value Emergence: VECM — Value Emergence Conditions → VETM — Value Emergence Threshold → VEEM — Value Emergence Event → VEDM — Value Emergence Determination → VERM — Value Emergence Record Then: Value Recognition → Value State → Value Change → Value Development / Value Degradation → Value Nullification → Value Restoration / Value Extinction VETM therefore governs the threshold layer inside the Value Emergence space. Operational Purpose Value may have: an identifiable source; clear potential; defined beneficiaries; a legitimate purpose; favorable conditions; available capabilities; allocated resources; operational readiness; without yet having emerged. The missing question is: When are the relevant conditions sufficient? VETM prevents organizations from treating partial readiness, investment, technical completion, resource availability, market expectation, or anticipated benefit as proof that value already exists. It creates a governed threshold between: Possibility and Emergence Readiness. Value Emergence Threshold A Value Emergence Threshold is the defined level, combination, state, boundary, condition set, event requirement, or other governed criterion at which the established Value Emergence Conditions become sufficient to support transition toward existent value. The threshold may be: Quantitative Qualitative Binary Composite Conditional Sequential Temporal Contextual or a governed combination of these. VFM® does not require one universal threshold model. The threshold must fit the value being governed. Threshold ≠ Condition A condition identifies something necessary or materially relevant to value emergence. A threshold establishes the point at which the relevant condition or combination of conditions becomes sufficient. For example: Condition: A capability must be operationally available. Threshold: The capability must be available at a defined level, quality, duration, capacity, accessibility, or performance sufficient to produce the governed value. Therefore: Emergence Condition ≠ Emergence Threshold and: Condition Presence ≠ Threshold Satisfaction Threshold ≠ Value Crossing a threshold does not automatically mean that value exists. The threshold establishes that the governed conditions have reached the point necessary for emergence. The actual emergence pathway remains governed through: Threshold Crossing → Emergence Event → Emergence Determination Therefore: Threshold Crossing ≠ Value Emergence Determination This distinction protects the architecture from declaring value too early. Threshold Structure A Value Emergence Threshold may depend upon one requirement or several interacting requirements. Single Threshold One defined requirement is sufficient. Condition A ≥ Required Level Compound Threshold Multiple requirements must be satisfied. Condition A + Condition B + Condition C ≥ Emergence Requirement Alternative Threshold Different legitimate pathways may permit emergence. Path A OR Path B Sequential Threshold Requirements must be satisfied in a defined order. A → B → C Contextual Threshold The required threshold changes according to the governed context. Temporal Threshold A condition must remain satisfied for a defined period before emergence readiness is established. This allows VETM to govern value emergence across very different systems without forcing them into one artificial measurement structure. Threshold Sufficiency VETM requires the architecture to distinguish between: Condition Satisfaction and Threshold Sufficiency. A condition may be partially or fully satisfied while the complete threshold remains unmet. For example: Technical Capability: Satisfied Beneficiary Access: Satisfied Operational Applicability: Partial Required Combined Threshold: Not Met The system therefore remains within: Potential Value rather than progressing prematurely into value emergence. Threshold States VETM may assign states including: Undefined Threshold No sufficient emergence threshold has been established. Defined Threshold The threshold has been formally established. Below Threshold Current conditions remain insufficient. Approaching Threshold Conditions are materially progressing toward the defined threshold. Threshold Satisfied The defined threshold requirements are currently satisfied. Threshold Crossed The governed boundary has been crossed. Threshold Uncertain Available information does not support a reliable threshold assessment. Threshold Lost A previously satisfied threshold is no longer satisfied before emergence has been established. These states allow emergence readiness to be governed dynamically. Threshold Crossing A Threshold Crossing occurs when the governed emergence conditions reach or exceed the defined emergence threshold. The crossing must remain distinguishable from the subsequent determination that value has emerged. The transition is: Potential Value → Conditions Established → Threshold Satisfied → Threshold Crossed → Emergence Event / Transition → Emergence Determination → Existing Value This creates an explicit methodological bridge between value potential and value existence. Threshold Persistence Some value may require only an instantaneous threshold crossing. Other value may require persistence. For example: Threshold satisfied for one second may not establish the same emergence basis as: Threshold continuously satisfied for six months. Where duration materially affects emergence, VETM requires that duration to become part of the threshold definition. Therefore: Threshold Magnitude + Threshold Duration may jointly determine threshold sufficiency. Threshold Reversibility A threshold may be crossed and subsequently lost before value emergence is determined. VETM therefore supports: Threshold Crossing → Threshold Loss where appropriate. This prevents temporary conditions from being incorrectly converted into permanent value-existence claims. Threshold Dependency Thresholds may depend upon multiple Value Emergence Conditions established through VECM. VETM should preserve those dependencies. For example: Technical Readiness Operational Accessibility Beneficiary Usability Required Performance → Emergence Threshold If one materially necessary dependency fails, the threshold may remain unsatisfied even where all other conditions are strong. Threshold Calibration Thresholds must be sufficiently demanding to distinguish genuine emergence readiness from mere potential. But they must not be arbitrarily demanding. Threshold calibration may therefore consider: value type; value purpose; beneficiary; reference context; materiality; expected value mechanism; relevant conditions; duration; operational environment; uncertainty; consequence of premature emergence determination. VETM governs the threshold structure. It does not prescribe one universal numerical threshold for all value. Threshold Evidence A threshold assessment should have an identifiable basis. Depending on context, this may include: measured performance; observed capability; operational data; beneficiary access; resource availability; utilization; realized output; verified condition state; documented activation; time-based persistence; comparative evidence; governed calculation. The evidence required should be proportional to the significance of the emergence determination. VETM does not replace ADIT®, VALIDOS®, or INTEGROS® where their broader evidence, validation, or integrity governance is required. Uncertainty at the Threshold Threshold assessment may contain uncertainty. VETM must therefore permit: Threshold Uncertain rather than forcing a binary conclusion. Uncertainty may concern: measurement; condition status; threshold definition; data; timing; beneficiary effect; causal relationship; contextual applicability. Where uncertainty is material, it must remain visible when the threshold basis moves downstream. Dynamic Thresholds Some thresholds may legitimately change as the governed context changes. For example, the emergence threshold for operational value from an energy technology may differ between: normal demand; peak demand; emergency conditions; isolated infrastructure; highly interconnected infrastructure. Dynamic thresholds must therefore remain tied to their applicable context. A threshold established in one context must not silently become universal. Threshold Change Governance Where the threshold itself changes, VETM should preserve: Previous Threshold → Reason for Change → New Threshold → Effective Context / Time → Effect on Current Emergence Assessment This prevents retrospective manipulation of the threshold merely to make a preferred value claim appear to have emerged. Emergence-Ready Value VETM may establish an intermediate governance condition: Emergence-Ready Value This does not mean that value already exists. It means: the governed potential value has satisfied the defined threshold conditions required to proceed into the emergence event and determination stages. This is particularly useful in complex value systems where the architecture needs to distinguish: Potential Value from Threshold-Satisfied Potential Value from Existing Value. Internal Value Flow Control VETM acts as a value-flow gate. The Module should permit progression only where the relevant threshold has been sufficiently established. The internal logic is: Below Threshold → Remain Potential Threshold Uncertain → Hold / Assess Threshold Satisfied → Eligible for Emergence Transition Threshold Crossed → Transfer to Emergence Event Threshold Lost → Return to Pre-Threshold State where applicable This makes the module operational rather than merely descriptive. Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum VETM implementation should establish: 1. Value Reference Identify the governed potential value. 2. Emergence Condition Input Receive the relevant emergence conditions from VECM. 3. Threshold Definition Define the threshold separating insufficient conditions from emergence readiness. 4. Threshold Structure Determine whether the threshold is single, compound, alternative, sequential, contextual, temporal, or hybrid. 5. Threshold Measurement Basis Establish how threshold satisfaction can be assessed. 6. Threshold Sufficiency Assessment Compare current condition states against the threshold. 7. Uncertainty Assessment Identify uncertainty affecting the threshold conclusion. 8. Threshold State Assignment Assign the appropriate governed threshold state. 9. Threshold Crossing Record Record a crossing where the governed threshold has been reached. 10. Downstream Transfer Transfer the threshold basis to VEEM — Value Emergence Event Module. Governance Outputs VETM may produce: Value Emergence Threshold Definition Value Emergence Threshold Structure Threshold Requirement Record Threshold Condition Map Threshold Dependency Map Threshold Measurement Basis Threshold Sufficiency Assessment Threshold Uncertainty Record Value Emergence Threshold State Threshold Crossing Record Threshold Loss Record Emergence-Ready Value Record These outputs provide the governed basis for: VEEM — Value Emergence Event Module. Use Case 1 — Banking: Financing Capacity vs. Actual Economic Value A bank finances a new industrial facility. The facility exists. Capital has been deployed. Equipment has been installed. Production capability is technically available. None of these facts alone establishes that the financed project is already producing the economic value expected when the financing decision was made. VECM may identify the emergence conditions: Operational Capability + Production Readiness + Customer Demand + Deliverable Output + Beneficiary Relationship VETM then establishes the threshold at which these conditions become sufficient for the defined value to move beyond potential. For example, the governed threshold might require: operational production + defined utilization + deliverable output + sustained ability to serve the intended economic purpose. The bank can therefore distinguish: Capital Deployed → Asset Constructed → Potential Value → Emergence Conditions Established → Threshold Crossed → Value Emergence This creates a much stronger basis for portfolio monitoring, project finance, restructuring, investment assessment, and value-based risk analysis than simply assuming: Asset Exists = Value Exists. Use Case 2 — Space Mission: Capability vs. Mission Value A space agency develops an expensive observation system for a planetary mission. The spacecraft exists. The instruments work. The launch succeeds. The spacecraft reaches its target. Yet the intended scientific or operational value may still not have emerged. For the defined mission value, VECM may establish conditions including: Instrument Availability + Correct Positioning + Data Acquisition + Data Integrity + Transmission Capability + Ground Reception + Scientific Usability VETM determines when those conditions collectively become sufficient. The threshold might require that the system not merely collect data, but produce data of sufficient quality, coverage, continuity, and usability to satisfy the defined mission-value context. The value flow becomes: Mission Investment → Technical Capability → Potential Mission Value → Emergence Conditions → Mission-Specific Threshold → Threshold Crossing → Emergence Event → Existing Mission Value This allows a space organization to separate: mission cost from mission capability from mission value. That distinction becomes particularly powerful when comparing alternative mission architectures, evaluating cost overruns, determining whether capabilities are actually producing intended value, or deciding whether additional investment is justified. Foundational Principles Value potential does not become existing value merely because favorable conditions exist. Emergence conditions define what must be true; emergence thresholds define when those conditions become sufficient. Condition presence is not threshold satisfaction. Threshold satisfaction is not Value Emergence Determination. Investment completion is not a value-emergence threshold. Technical readiness is not automatically value readiness. A threshold must remain connected to the specific value, beneficiary, purpose, and context it governs. A dynamic threshold must not be treated as universally fixed. Threshold uncertainty must remain visible. A crossed threshold may be lost before value emergence is established. The Value Emergence Threshold is the governed boundary between potential value and value that is ready to enter the emergence transition. Canonical Closing Statement Value Emergence Threshold Module establishes the governed boundary at which defined Value Emergence Conditions become sufficiently satisfied for potential value to proceed toward existence. Through governance of threshold structure, condition sufficiency, dependencies, measurement basis, persistence, reversibility, uncertainty, contextual variation, threshold states, threshold crossing, and threshold loss, VETM prevents investments, assets, capabilities, activities, or partially satisfied conditions from being prematurely treated as existing value. By separating Value Emergence Conditions from Value Emergence Threshold, Threshold Crossing from Value Emergence Event, and emergence readiness from Value Emergence Determination, VETM creates the controlled value-flow gate required to move from potential value toward legitimate value existence within VFM®. title: Value Emergence Standard (VES)
text: Value Emergence Standard (VES) Value Emergence Standard (VES) Value Emergence Standard (VES) Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture Parent Standard: Value Emergence Standard (VES) Operational Layer: Value Emergence Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Type: Parent Standard Governed Space: Value Emergence Origin ID: VFM-VES-003 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 24 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · AGA™ · INTEGROS® · CLA™ · ADIT® · VALIDOS® · SIMULOS® · OBIDENITY® AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Value Emergence Standard (VES) is the third Parent Standard within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture and governs the conditions under which potential value arising from an identified value origin becomes existent value within a defined Value Context. VES establishes the methodological transition between the existence of a potential basis capable of producing value and the point at which value can legitimately be treated as having emerged. The Standard governs the conditions, thresholds, events, determinations, and records necessary to establish that transition. Its fundamental distinction is: Potential Value ≠ Existing Value A source may possess the capability, condition, resource, relationship, knowledge, technology, asset, activity, or other basis from which value could arise without value having yet emerged. VES therefore prevents value potential from being automatically treated as value existence. Core Question When and under what conditions does potential value become existent value? Architectural Position Value Emergence Standard occupies the third governed space of the VFM® value lifecycle. It follows: Value Origin Standard and precedes: Value Recognition Standard. The first three architectural stages establish three fundamentally different questions: Value Context Standard → What value is being governed? Value Origin Standard → From what basis can that value originate? Value Emergence Standard → Has that potential value actually come into existence? The next standard then asks: Value Recognition Standard → Can that existing value be recognized within its defined governance context? These stages must remain methodologically separate. VFM® Governance Flow Value Context → Value Origin → Value Emergence → Value Recognition → Value State → Value Change → Value Development → Value Degradation → Value Nullification → Value Restoration → Value Extinction Governance Flow Position Value Context → Value Origin → Value Emergence → Value Recognition VES specifically governs: Identified Value Origin → Potential Value → Emergence Conditions → Emergence Threshold → Emergence Event → Emergence Determination → Existing Value This is the point in the VFM® lifecycle where value crosses the methodological boundary from: could exist to: does exist. Operational Space VES governs the emergence of value itself. Its operational space includes: potential value; emergence conditions; emergence prerequisites; emergence dependencies; emergence thresholds; threshold satisfaction; emergence events; emergence timing; emergence determination; conditional emergence; partial emergence; progressive emergence; simultaneous emergence; delayed emergence; failed emergence; emergence uncertainty; emergence evidence; emergence recording; relationship between value origin and emerged value. VES does not assume that every identified value source necessarily produces value. Value Origin ≠ Value Emergence The existence of a Value Origin establishes that there is an identifiable basis from which value can originate. It does not establish that value has emerged. For example: A patent may contain technological potential. A dataset may contain analytical potential. A mineral deposit may contain extractive potential. Unused manufacturing capacity may contain productive potential. A scientific discovery may contain commercial or societal potential. A new capability may contain operational potential. An unused building may contain economic potential. A relationship may contain strategic potential. But the existence of these sources does not automatically establish that the relevant governed value has emerged. VES governs the missing transition. Value Origin → potential for value is not equivalent to: Value Emergence → existence of value. Potential Value Within VES, Potential Value represents value that may emerge from an identified Value Origin but whose existence has not yet been sufficiently established. Potential Value may depend upon: activation; use; transformation; combination; access; capability realization; demand; application; performance; relationship formation; technological readiness; operational deployment; knowledge application; resource conversion; fulfillment of another defined emergence condition. Potential Value is therefore not treated as zero value. It is also not treated as existing positive value. This distinction is essential to the later VFM® lifecycle. Potential Value ≠ Zero Value A ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ concerns a governed zero-value state where applicable. Potential Value concerns a condition before value has been established as existent. Emergence Conditions Value may emerge only where the conditions necessary for that particular form of value are sufficiently present. VES therefore requires explicit Value Emergence Conditions. Depending upon context, these may include: existence of a usable capability; realization of a functional outcome; accessibility; utility; applicability; demand; operational readiness; productive use; successful transformation; scarcity; relevance; beneficiary relationship; resource availability; knowledge application; technological capability; combination with another value source; satisfaction of a defined performance condition. VFM® does not prescribe one universal set of emergence conditions. The emergence conditions must correspond to the specific value identified under the Value Context Standard. Emergence Threshold Some forms of value emerge gradually. Others become existent only after a definable threshold has been crossed. VES therefore establishes the concept of a Value Emergence Threshold. The threshold represents: the minimum governed condition at which potential value may be determined to have become existent value. A threshold may be: quantitative; qualitative; functional; operational; relational; temporal; capability-based; outcome-based; use-based; condition-based; composite. For example, a technology may exist for years while remaining incapable of producing the value for which it was created. Once a required capability, cost, reliability, performance, accessibility, or operational threshold is reached, value may emerge. The underlying asset did not necessarily emerge at that moment. The value did. Emergence Event VES distinguishes the Emergence Threshold from the Emergence Event. The threshold defines the condition that must be satisfied. The Emergence Event identifies the occurrence through which that condition becomes satisfied or materially observable. An Emergence Event may include: first successful operation; first productive use; first realized benefit; first capability activation; first successful application; completion of a transformation; establishment of a necessary relationship; crossing of a performance threshold; achievement of required accessibility; activation of a previously dormant resource; combination of previously separate value sources. Therefore: Emergence Condition ≠ Emergence Threshold ≠ Emergence Event. Emergence Determination Value existence must not depend solely upon assertion. VES therefore requires an Emergence Determination where formal governance of value emergence is necessary. The determination establishes whether the defined emergence conditions and applicable threshold have been sufficiently satisfied. A determination may conclude: Not Emerged The identified source exists, but the governed value has not yet emerged. Emergence Pending Relevant conditions are developing, but the emergence threshold has not yet been established as satisfied. Conditionally Emerged Value exists only under explicitly defined conditions. Partially Emerged A divisible or multidimensional value has emerged only in part. Emerged The governed value has crossed its applicable emergence threshold and exists within the defined Value Context. Emergence Indeterminate Available information is insufficient to determine whether emergence has occurred. These are governance states, not universal accounting classifications. Emergence ≠ Recognition A fundamental VFM® distinction is: Value may exist before it is formally recognized. VES therefore ends when value existence has been sufficiently established. It does not require: market recognition; accounting recognition; regulatory recognition; legal recognition; institutional recognition; taxation; ownership attribution; pricing; classification; validation status. Those external systems may later interact with the value. But they do not define the VFM® emergence boundary. The next architectural stage — Value Recognition Standard — governs recognition within the defined value lifecycle context. Emergence ≠ Price Value does not need to possess a market price in order to emerge. A new manufacturing capability may generate operational value before it is separately priced. A scientific discovery may create knowledge value before commercial valuation exists. A dataset may create analytical value before being monetized. An efficiency improvement may generate cost-reduction value without being sold. A risk-reduction capability may create value through avoided loss. VES therefore prevents: Price = Value Existence from becoming an architectural assumption. Emergence ≠ Transaction A transaction may reveal, transfer, exchange, or influence value. It does not necessarily create the value. Value may emerge: before a transaction; without a transaction; through productive activity; through knowledge; through capability; through utility; through reduced cost; through avoided loss; through improved efficiency; through a relationship; through transformation; through technological development. Payment and transaction governance remain outside the VES boundary. Emergence ≠ Accounting Recognition An accounting system may recognize an asset or economic event according to its own rules. VES governs a different question: Has the governed value emerged? Accounting treatment may subsequently use information produced by VFM®, but VFM® does not replace accounting standards. This distinction enables VFM® to identify forms of value that may exist operationally before they are formally represented in conventional accounting systems. Emergence ≠ Validation VES does not determine that a value claim has been universally validated. Where formal validation of evidence, claims, sources, methods, or determinations is required, VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture may govern that process. VFM® governs the value lifecycle question: Has value emerged? VALIDOS® may govern: Is the basis used to support that determination sufficiently validated for its intended reliance? Emergence ≠ Integrity VES does not govern the general integrity of the system, asset, evidence, or process from which value emerges. Those questions may fall under INTEGROS® — Integrity Governance Architecture. The architectures therefore remain distinct: VFM® → emergence of value INTEGROS® → integrity Emergence Evidence Where emergence must be formally demonstrated, the determination should be supported by sufficient information concerning: the governed value context; the identified Value Origin; applicable emergence conditions; applicable emergence threshold; observed Emergence Event where relevant; timing; dependencies; limitations; uncertainty; basis of determination. VES governs the relationship of this information to the value-emergence determination. General evidence governance, auditability, validation, and integrity remain governed by their respective architectures. Temporal Emergence Value emergence has a temporal dimension. VES therefore permits the emergence point to be associated with: a specific event; a defined date; a period; a progressive interval; a condition becoming continuously satisfied; an uncertain but bounded emergence window. This matters because different systems may subsequently rely upon the emergence point. For example: management systems; investment analysis; value reporting; economic analysis; taxation architectures; accounting systems; asset governance; lifecycle analysis. VFM® establishes the value lifecycle event. External architectures determine their own consequences. Progressive Emergence Not all value appears instantaneously. Some value may emerge progressively. Examples include: a developing technology; a growing network; accumulating knowledge; infrastructure becoming operational in stages; a dataset increasing in usefulness; organizational capability maturing over time. VES therefore allows value emergence to be represented as a governed progression where binary treatment would distort reality. Multiple Value Emergence One Value Origin may produce multiple forms of value. For example, a technological capability may generate: operational value; economic value; knowledge value; strategic value; risk-reduction value; productivity value. These forms of value must not automatically be collapsed into one undifferentiated value. Each must remain connected to the Value Context established under the Value Context Standard. Therefore: One Origin ≠ One Value and: One Emergence Event may produce multiple distinct Value Emergence Determinations. Failed Emergence An identified Value Origin may never produce the anticipated value. VES explicitly governs this possibility. Failed emergence may occur where: required conditions never materialize; a threshold is never reached; capability remains unusable; expected utility does not materialize; the relevant beneficiary never receives value; technological development fails; required relationships do not form; a resource cannot be activated; the anticipated outcome does not occur. This distinction prevents expected value from being retrospectively treated as value that necessarily existed. Emergence Reversal Before Recognition In some contexts, value may emerge briefly and disappear before it becomes formally recognized. VFM® must preserve this lifecycle reality. Such a case may produce: Value Emergence → Existing Value → Value Change / Degradation / Nullification even where formal Value Recognition never occurred. Recognition therefore does not create the underlying existence of value. It governs recognition of that existence. Governance Outputs VES may produce: Potential Value Record Value Emergence Conditions Record Value Emergence Threshold Value Emergence Event Record Value Emergence Determination Value Emergence State Conditional Emergence Statement Partial Emergence Record Failed Emergence Record Value Emergence Timeline Value Emergence Dependency Record Value Emergence Limitation Record Value Emergence Record These outputs provide the governed input basis for the Value Recognition Standard. Enterprise Application Value Emergence Standard can be applied wherever organizations need to distinguish between: something capable of creating value and: value that has actually come into existence. This distinction can support: banking; investment analysis; enterprise valuation; innovation portfolios; intellectual property; technology development; infrastructure; manufacturing; energy; digital assets; AI systems; data assets; public investment; government programs; research; cost reduction; productivity improvement; supply chains; resource development; strategic capability. For example, a bank may identify a portfolio of technological assets with substantial theoretical value potential. VES provides a method for determining which of those assets have actually crossed the conditions necessary for value emergence rather than treating projected potential as existing value. Similarly, an industrial organization may deploy an AI system intended to reduce production costs. The software's existence does not itself establish the anticipated value. VES can distinguish: AI capability exists from: measurable cost-reduction value has emerged. That distinction creates a stronger basis for later value recognition, state determination, development, degradation, restoration, accounting interfaces, investment analysis, and future value-based economic governance. Cross-Architecture Boundaries VFM® / VES governs whether potential value has become existent value. GOA™ — Governance Architecture governs governance authority and governance structure. ORA™ — Operational Reality Architecture governs actual Operational Reality. OBIDENITY® — Origin-Bound Identity Governance Architecture governs origin-bound identity, ownership, authority, provenance, transfer, and continuity. CLA™ — Classification Architecture governs classification. INTEGROS® — Integrity Governance Architecture governs integrity. ADIT® — Continuous Audit & Evidence Governance Architecture governs audit and evidence. VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture governs validation. SIMULOS® — Simulation Governance Architecture governs simulation and simulation-derived meaning. An external architecture may establish information relevant to a Value Emergence Determination. It does not thereby acquire governance ownership of Value Emergence itself. Foundational Principles Potential value is not existing value. Value origin is not value emergence. Value emergence is not value recognition. Value emergence is not market pricing. Value emergence is not accounting recognition. Value emergence is not a transaction. Potential value is not a zero-value state. An asset, capability, resource, relationship, or activity may exist before the relevant value emerges. One Value Origin may produce multiple distinct forms of value. Expected value must not be treated as existing value merely because its source exists. Value becomes existent within VFM® only when the conditions separating potential value from existent value have been sufficiently established. Canonical Closing Statement Value Emergence Standard establishes the third governed space of VFM® by defining the methodological transition through which potential value arising from an identified Value Origin becomes existent value within a defined Value Context. Through governance of emergence conditions, emergence thresholds, emergence events, emergence determinations, temporal emergence, progressive emergence, conditional and partial emergence, failed emergence, dependencies, limitations, and emergence records, the Standard prevents potential, expectation, capability, asset existence, market anticipation, accounting treatment, or projected benefit from being automatically treated as value that already exists. By separating Value Origin from Value Emergence and Value Emergence from Value Recognition, the Standard creates a distinct and governable lifecycle boundary between the source capable of producing value and the existence of value itself. This boundary provides VFM® with the methodological foundation required to determine when value truly enters its lifecycle before recognition, state governance, change, development, degradation, nullification, restoration, and eventual extinction can legitimately follow. Nahlad Value Emergence Standard (VES) Architecture: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture · Category: Governance & Enforcement · Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Canonical Definition: Value Emergence Standard governs the transition through which potential value arising from an identified Value Origin becomes existent value within a defined Value Context by establishing the conditions, thresholds, events, and determinations necessary to distinguish value potential from actual value existence. Governed Space: Value Emergence Potential value must not be treated as existing value until the conditions separating potential from actual value existence have been sufficiently established. → View Standard About standard Module Architecture → Value Emergence Conditions Module (VECM) → Value Emergence Threshold Module (VETM) → Value Emergence Event Module (VEEM) → Value Emergence Determination Module (VEDM) → Value Emergence Record Module (VERM) Related Documents → About Value Emergence Standard (VES) → VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture

title: About Value Identification Standard (VIS)
text: About Value Identification Standard (VIS) About Value Identification Standard (VIS) About Value Identification Standard (VIS) Architecture: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Parent Standard: Value Identification Standard (VIS) Governed Space: Value Identification Canonical Definition Value Identification Standard (VIS) governs how potential or existing manifestations of value are identified, distinguished, bounded, contextualized, and established as governable Value Objects before their origin, existence, state, change, development, degradation, nullification, restoration, or extinction can be determined. VIS establishes the first methodological control point of the VFM® value lifecycle. Its foundational question is simple: What exactly is the value being governed? Why VIS Matters Value is frequently discussed without first identifying the precise subject to which the value claim relates. Organizations may refer to the value of an asset, capability, service, technology, relationship, right, resource, information object, infrastructure, process, opportunity, or future benefit without clearly separating: the object or source associated with value from the value itself. This creates ambiguity throughout every later stage of the value lifecycle. Before asking where value originated, whether value exists, how much it has changed, whether it has degraded, whether it has reached zero, or whether it can be restored, the relevant value must first be identifiable as a governable object. VIS creates that foundation. Identification Before Valuation VIS does not determine how much something is worth. It does not assign a price. It does not determine market value, accounting value, taxable value, legal value, economic value, or social value. Its function comes earlier. VIS establishes: what value is being referred to, what it is associated with, where its boundaries lie, and which value manifestation is entering governance. This distinction is fundamental: Value Identification ≠ Value Measurement A value cannot be meaningfully measured, classified, tracked, or governed if the subject of the value claim remains ambiguous. The Value Object VIS introduces the Value Object as the governable subject through which a particular manifestation of value can be identified and followed across the VFM® lifecycle. A Value Object may relate to value associated with: a physical asset; a digital asset; a capability; a service; a process; knowledge or information; intellectual property; infrastructure; a resource; a contractual or economic relationship; access or availability; productive capacity; technological capability; an opportunity; an operational function; another identifiable source or manifestation capable of carrying value. The Value Object does not itself prove that value exists. Identification establishes the object of inquiry. Subsequent VFM® standards determine what happens to value. Value Object ≠ Asset Not every Value Object must be an asset. An asset may contain, support, generate, preserve, lose, or recover multiple forms of value. Likewise, value may arise from relationships, capabilities, conditions, access, knowledge, coordination, timing, or other phenomena that cannot be adequately described as conventional assets. VIS therefore prevents VFM® from becoming merely an asset-governance architecture. VFM® governs value itself. Value Identification Before Value Origin Value Identification precedes Value Origin for a methodological reason. Before asking: Where did this value originate? the architecture must know: Which value are we investigating? VIS therefore creates the entry point: Value Identification → Value Origin → Value Emergence → Value Recognition → Value State → Value Change → Value Development / Value Degradation → Value Nullification → Value Restoration / Value Extinction Identification does not establish origin. It establishes the governable subject for which origin can subsequently be investigated. Multiple Values Within One Object A single object may contain or support multiple distinct Value Objects. For example, industrial equipment may simultaneously have: productive value, operational value, resale value, material recovery value, technological value, strategic value, and informational value. These values may follow different lifecycles. One may degrade while another increases. One may reach zero while another remains substantial. VIS therefore requires value manifestations to be sufficiently distinguished rather than assuming that an object possesses one universal value state. This capability becomes particularly important when VFM® is applied across complex organizations, public infrastructure, technology, finance, industrial systems, or national economic environments. Context Matters Value identification may depend upon context. The same underlying object may represent different value within different: purposes; environments; users; systems; time periods; operational conditions; economic contexts; institutional contexts; technological contexts. VIS therefore does not treat value as automatically universal merely because the underlying object is identifiable. It requires the relevant value context to be made explicit. What VIS Does Not Determine VIS does not determine: whether the identified value actually exists; where that value originated; whether value has emerged; whether value should be recognized; the amount of value; the current Value State; whether value increased or decreased; whether value has reached zero; whether value can be restored; who owns the underlying object; whether the object is legally recognized; whether a value claim is validated; whether a transaction is taxable; whether the value is ethically desirable. These questions belong to subsequent VFM® standards or other governance architectures. This boundary protects VIS from becoming a general valuation, identity, ownership, accounting, taxation, or validation framework. Use Case 1 — Industrial Asset A factory owns a machine that is no longer used for its original production function. A conventional assessment may simply ask: What is the machine worth? VIS first separates the possible Value Objects. The machine may have lost most of its productive value while retaining: resale value, component value, material value, replacement-part value, technological value, or strategic reserve value. VFM® can then govern each relevant value lifecycle separately. The machine therefore does not have to be simplistically classified as either: valuable or worthless. VIS identifies which value is actually being discussed before its lifecycle is assessed. Use Case 2 — Digital or Technological Capability An organization develops a software model that is no longer commercially successful. Its immediate commercial value may have significantly degraded. However, the same development may retain: technical knowledge, training data relationships, reusable components, intellectual capability, research value, integration capability, or future redevelopment potential. VIS enables these value manifestations to be distinguished before VFM® determines their respective origins, states, changes, degradation, zero-value conditions, restoration possibilities, or extinction. This prevents the disappearance of one form of value from being incorrectly interpreted as the disappearance of all value associated with the underlying object. Relationship to Other VFM® Standards VIS establishes the Value Object. The Value Origin Standard determines where the identified value originates. The Value Emergence Standard determines whether and when value actually comes into existence. The Value Recognition Standard governs when existing value becomes recognized within the value lifecycle. The Value State Standard determines the current governed state of value. Subsequent VFM® standards govern change, development, degradation, nullification, restoration, and extinction. VIS therefore provides the identification layer upon which the complete VFM® lifecycle depends. Relationship to Other OOF® Architectures VIS identifies the value being governed but does not absorb responsibilities belonging to other architectures. OBIDENITY® may govern identity, origin-bound identity, ownership, authority, provenance, transfer, and continuity of the underlying entity. CLA™ may govern formal classification. VALIDOS® may govern whether relevant claims or determinations have been sufficiently validated. INTEGROS® may govern integrity. ADIT® may govern audit and evidence. GOA™ may govern governance authority and structure. VFM® remains concerned with the independent question: What is happening to value? Enterprise Value VIS provides organizations with a repeatable method for identifying value before attempting to measure, manage, account for, preserve, develop, recover, tax, exchange, or govern it. This can expose value that conventional object-level assessments may overlook. It can also prevent fundamentally different forms of value from being combined into one ambiguous valuation. The result is a clearer foundation for downstream value governance and for interfaces with accounting, economic, investment, taxation, asset-management, public-policy, and decision systems. Foundational Principle Before value can be governed, the value being governed must be identifiable. An object may contain many forms of value. A value may exist in many contexts. A change in one value does not necessarily represent a change in another. VIS therefore establishes identification before origin, emergence, state, change, or valuation. Canonical Closing Statement Value Identification Standard establishes the entry point of VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture by defining how potential or existing manifestations of value become identifiable, distinguishable, bounded, contextualized, and governable Value Objects. By separating the identification of value from the identification of the underlying asset, from value measurement, ownership, classification, validation, accounting, taxation, and market pricing, VIS creates the methodological foundation required to follow value independently throughout its complete lifecycle. VFM® can govern where value originates, when it emerges, how it changes, how it develops or degrades, when it reaches zero, whether it can be restored, and when it becomes extinct only after the value being governed has first been made explicit.
