title: Value Context Documentation Module (VCDM)
text: Value Context Documentation Module (VCDM) Value Context Documentation Module (VCDM) Value Context Documentation Module (VCDM) Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanism Parent Standard: Value Context Standard (VCXS) Module: VCDM — Value Context Documentation Module Operational Layer: Value Context Documentation Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Value Context Documentation Origin ID: VFM-VCXS-VCDM-001.5 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 23 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · AGA™ · INTEGROS® · CLA™ · ADIT® · VALIDOS® · OBIDENITY® AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Value Context Documentation Module (VCDM) is the fifth Core Module of the Value Context Standard (VCXS). VCDM governs the structured documentation of the value context established through the preceding modules of the Value Context Standard. The Module creates a persistent, interpretable, and reconstructable record of: what value is being governed → what value-bearing object it relates to → who or what may benefit from that value → within which reference framework the value is understood → under which contextual conditions that meaning applies. VCDM does not determine whether value exists, where value originated, how much value exists, whether value is legally recognized, or whether a valuation is economically correct. Its purpose is to ensure that the meaning of the governed value context does not become detached from the conditions under which that value was identified. Architectural Position VCDM is the fifth and final module within the Value Context Standard. It follows: VIM — Value Identification Module → VOM — Value Object Module → VBM — Value Beneficiary Module → VRFM — Value Reference Framework Module and consolidates their governed outputs into: Value Context Record The internal sequence is therefore: Value Identification → Value Object → Value Beneficiary → Value Reference Framework → Value Context Documentation Once the Value Context Record has been established, the governed value may proceed to: Value Origin Standard (VOS). Operational Space VCDM governs the documentation layer between: established Value Context and subsequent value lifecycle governance. It preserves the contextual foundation necessary for later VFM® processes to determine whether they are still governing the same value under the same relevant context. The governed documentation may include: governed value identification; value description; value type or form where defined; value-bearing object relationship; object context; beneficiary relationship; beneficiary context; reference framework; purpose of the value context; applicable conditions; relevant boundaries; contextual assumptions; contextual dependencies; temporal context; jurisdictional context where relevant; environmental or operational context; contextual exclusions; contextual changes; documentation provenance; version state; documentation status. Value Context Record The principal governance object produced by VCDM is the: Value Context Record (VCR). The Value Context Record provides the minimum structured reference through which the governed value can be recognized consistently throughout its subsequent lifecycle. A Value Context Record should establish, where materially relevant: Value → What value is being governed? Value-Bearing Object → In relation to what object, capability, activity, relationship, resource, system, right, condition, or other value-bearing basis is the value being considered? Beneficiary → For whom or for what may the value exist? Reference Framework → Relative to which purpose, environment, condition, comparison, objective, or reference basis is the value understood? Context Conditions → Under which conditions does this interpretation remain applicable? The resulting record creates a governed answer to: What exactly do we mean when we refer to this value? Documentation Principle Value cannot be governed consistently if its context changes silently. A statement such as: “This asset has value.” is methodologically incomplete unless the relevant value context is understood. The same object may possess: financial value to an investor; operational value to an organization; strategic value to a government; scientific value to a research institution; utility value to a user; recovery value to a creditor; replacement value to an insurer; informational value to an AI system; mission value to a space organization; no relevant value to another beneficiary. VCDM therefore preserves the context that gives the value statement its meaning. Value Record ≠ Asset Record VCDM does not create a universal record of the underlying asset, object, person, organization, system, or resource. It creates a record of the governed value context associated with it. Therefore: Object Documentation ≠ Value Context Documentation and: Asset Identity ≠ Value Identity Where identity governance is required, OBIDENITY® — Origin-Bound Identity Governance Architecture may provide the appropriate identity governance layer. VFM® remains concerned with the value. Context Persistence Once value enters the wider lifecycle, its original context must remain reconstructable. VCDM therefore preserves the relationship: Value Lifecycle State → Value Context Record A later observer should be able to determine: which value was originally identified; which object it concerned; which beneficiary was relevant; which reference framework was applied; which contextual conditions existed; whether those conditions subsequently changed. This prevents later lifecycle events from being interpreted against a context that never existed when the value was originally governed. Context Versioning Value context may change. A beneficiary may change. The relevant purpose may change. The underlying object may change. Operational conditions may change. The reference framework may change. The same physical or digital object may therefore participate in multiple legitimate value contexts. VCDM should support explicit contextual versioning such as: Value Context V1 → Material Context Change → Value Context V2 The previous context should not be silently overwritten where historical reconstruction remains materially important. Context Change Record Where a material contextual element changes, VCDM may create a: Value Context Change Record Material changes may include: change of beneficiary; change of value-bearing object configuration; change of purpose; change of reference framework; change of relevant operational environment; change of material contextual assumptions; change of time horizon; change of applicable value relationship. The existence of a contextual change does not automatically mean that the value itself has changed. That distinction is fundamental: Context Change ≠ Value Change The Value Change Standard governs change in value itself. VCDM records changes in the context through which that value is understood. Multiple Value Contexts One object may legitimately support multiple Value Context Records. For example, a manufacturing robot may simultaneously possess: Production Value for the manufacturing organization. Resale Value for the asset owner. Collateral Value for a financial institution. Data Generation Value for an analytics operation. Strategic Capability Value for the enterprise. These should not automatically be collapsed into one undifferentiated concept of “value.” VCDM allows each materially distinct value context to remain separately documented. Temporal Context Value context may be time-dependent. A Value Context Record may therefore specify: effective date; observation period; expected duration; relevant lifecycle phase; reference period; review condition; expiration condition where applicable. A context established for one period must not automatically be assumed to remain unchanged indefinitely. Context Documentation Status VCDM may assign a documentation status such as: Draft — context documentation is incomplete. Established — the required contextual elements have been sufficiently documented. Conditionally Established — the context is usable subject to explicit conditions. Under Review — a material contextual change requires reassessment. Superseded — a newer Value Context Record governs the current context. Archived — the record is retained for historical reconstruction but is no longer operationally active. These states concern the documentation record. They do not determine whether value exists. Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum VCDM implementation should establish: 1. Value Reference Record the governed value identified through the Value Identification Module. 2. Value-Bearing Object Reference Record the relationship between the governed value and its relevant value-bearing object. 3. Beneficiary Reference Record the beneficiary or beneficiary class relevant to the value context. 4. Reference Framework Record the framework, purpose, objective, environment, comparison basis, or other reference condition through which the value is understood. 5. Context Conditions Record materially relevant conditions, dependencies, assumptions, boundaries, and exclusions. 6. Temporal Context Establish the time or lifecycle conditions relevant to the context where necessary. 7. Context Version Assign an identifiable version or equivalent state where contextual evolution must be traceable. 8. Documentation Status Establish whether the Value Context Record is draft, established, conditional, under review, superseded, or archived. 9. Change Traceability Preserve material changes to the governed context. 10. Value Context Record Consolidate the governed information into a reusable Value Context Record capable of accompanying the value into subsequent VFM® lifecycle governance. Governance Outputs VCDM may produce: Value Context Record Value Context Identifier Value Context Summary Value-Bearing Object Reference Value Beneficiary Reference Value Reference Framework Record Value Context Condition Record Value Context Assumption Record Value Context Exclusion Record Value Context Version Record Value Context Change Record Value Context Documentation Status Historical Value Context Record These outputs provide the contextual foundation for subsequent governance under the Value Origin Standard and the wider VFM® lifecycle. Enterprise Application VCDM enables organizations to solve a deceptively important problem: the word “value” is frequently used without preserving what that value actually means in context. Without a governed Value Context Record, different departments, systems, institutions, algorithms, auditors, financial models, or decision-makers may use the same word while referring to fundamentally different value relationships. VCDM creates a common contextual reference. This can support: banking and financial systems; asset management; insurance; enterprise accounting environments; public finance; infrastructure; manufacturing; supply chains; digital assets; AI systems; autonomous systems; energy systems; scientific programs; space missions; intellectual property; resource allocation; cost-reduction programs; future value-governance environments. Use Case 1 — Banking: One Asset, Different Value Contexts A bank evaluates an industrial property connected to several financial relationships. The property may simultaneously have: market value for a potential sale, collateral value for secured lending, recovery value under a default scenario, and operational value for the company using the property. If these contexts are not explicitly separated, systems may appear to discuss the same “asset value” while actually using different beneficiaries, purposes, conditions, time horizons, and reference frameworks. VCDM establishes separate Value Context Records. For example: Property X → Collateral Value → Bank → Lending Reference Framework and: Property X → Operational Value → Manufacturing Company → Production Continuity Reference Framework The underlying object may be identical. The governed value context is not. This gives later VFM® processes a stable basis for determining what happens to each form of value independently as conditions change. Use Case 2 — Space Mission: Value as Avoided Mission Cost A space organization evaluates a simulation capability that can reduce the need for expensive physical testing. The relevant value is not necessarily the purchase price of the simulation infrastructure. A materially important value context may be: avoided physical-test cost and avoided mission-development expenditure. VCDM may establish: Simulation Capability → Cost-Avoidance Value → Mission Program → Mission Development Cost Reference Framework → Defined Mission Phase and Test Conditions Suppose the simulation capability allows the organization to identify a design failure before construction of a physical prototype. The prevented expenditure may represent substantial value to the mission program. VCDM does not calculate whether the claimed savings are correct. It establishes which value is being governed and under which context the claimed value has meaning. That governed context can then enter subsequent VFM® stages to determine: where that value originated → whether it actually emerged → what state it entered → how it subsequently developed, changed, degraded, disappeared, or was restored. Foundational Principles Value without context is methodologically ambiguous. The same object may carry multiple distinct forms of value simultaneously. The same value-bearing object does not imply the same value. Value for one beneficiary does not automatically constitute equivalent value for another beneficiary. Context change is not automatically value change. Historical value context should remain reconstructable when materially relevant. A Value Context Record must preserve the relationship between the governed value, its value-bearing object, its beneficiary, its reference framework, and the conditions under which that value is understood. Canonical Closing Statement Value Context Documentation Module establishes the persistent contextual record through which governed value remains identifiable, interpretable, distinguishable, and reconstructable throughout the VFM® value lifecycle. By documenting the governed value, value-bearing object, beneficiary, reference framework, contextual conditions, assumptions, exclusions, temporal context, versions, and material contextual changes, VCDM prevents value from becoming detached from the conditions that give it meaning. The Module enables multiple forms of value associated with the same object to remain methodologically distinct, preserves historical context as value moves through subsequent lifecycle states and transitions, and provides the structured Value Context Record required for downstream Value Origin governance. Before VFM® can determine where value originates, emerges, changes, develops, degrades, reaches zero, is restored, or becomes extinct, the architecture must preserve exactly which value it is governing. title: Value Context Module (VCM)
text: Value Context Module (VCM) Value Context Module (VCM) Value Context Module (VCM) Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture Parent Standard: Value Identification Standard (VIS) Module: VCM — Value Context Module Operational Layer: Value Context Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Value Context Origin ID: VFM-VIS-VCM-001.4 Version: 1.0 Status: Draft · Open Standard Effective Date: 23 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · AGA™ · INTEGROS® · CLA™ · ADIT® · VALIDOS® · SIMULOS® · OBIDENITY® AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Value Context Module (VCM) is the fourth Core Module of the Value Identification Standard (VIS) within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture. VCM governs the explicit identification and structuring of the context within which a bounded and differentiated Value Object is being examined for value. The Module establishes the relevant purpose, perspective, environment, time, conditions, relationships, dependencies, use context, and other materially relevant contextual dimensions required before statements concerning the Value Object can be interpreted consistently within the value lifecycle. VCM addresses a foundational problem: the same Value Object may legitimately exhibit different value relevance, value states, value changes, or value trajectories under different contexts without becoming a different Value Object. VCM does not determine whether value exists, how much value exists, whether value has emerged, what price should be assigned, whether the object is legally owned, or whether a valuation is correct. Its task is narrower: to establish the governed context within which subsequent statements about the Value Object and its value lifecycle are intended to apply. Core Question Within what context is this Value Object being examined for value, and which contextual conditions materially affect the meaning of its value lifecycle? Architectural Position VCM is the fourth Core Module of the Value Identification Standard. It follows: VOIM — Value Object Identification Module → VOBM — Value Object Boundary Module → VODM — Value Object Differentiation Module and precedes the final identification function of VIS. The methodological sequence is: Value Object Identification → Value Object Boundary → Value Object Differentiation → Value Context → Governed Value Identification VOIM establishes: What is the Value Object? VOBM establishes: Where does the Value Object begin and end? VODM establishes: What must remain distinct? VCM establishes: Under what context is this Value Object being examined for value? Internal Flow Position Identified + Bounded + Differentiated Value Object → Context Purpose Identification → Perspective Identification → Use Context Identification → Environmental Context Identification → Temporal Context Identification → Relational Context Identification → Dependency Context Identification → Condition Identification → Context Boundary Definition → Context Assumption Identification → Context Variation Assessment → Context Record → Contextualized Value Object Operational Space VCM governs the space between: a structurally defined Value Object and a Value Object situated within an explicit value-relevant context. This operational space includes: value context identification; contextual purpose; contextual perspective; use context; operational context; environmental context; temporal context; relational context; dependency context; technological context; economic context where relevant; geographic context where relevant; institutional context where relevant; condition definition; context boundaries; contextual assumptions; contextual variability; context change; multi-context relationships; context traceability; context uncertainty. Context Principle Value must not be interpreted as though every Value Object exists in one universal context. A Value Object may possess materially different value relevance depending upon: who or what uses it; where it exists; when it exists; what purpose it serves; which system it belongs to; which capabilities depend upon it; which alternatives exist; which environmental conditions apply; which relationships enable its function; which dependencies constrain it; which technological conditions exist. Therefore: Value Object ≠ Value Context and: Same Value Object + Different Context ≠ Automatically Same Value Outcome Context Does Not Create the Value Object VCM must preserve the distinction between: what the Value Object is and the context in which it is examined. For example, one industrial machine may be the same Value Object in: an operating factory; an idle warehouse; a region without compatible infrastructure; a production line where it is mission-critical; a market where replacement equipment is abundant. The machine does not necessarily become a different Value Object merely because the context changes. Its value lifecycle, however, may be affected materially. Context Purpose Every governed Value Context should identify why the Value Object is being examined. Possible purposes may include: operational use; investment analysis; asset management; public-sector analysis; infrastructure planning; economic analysis; lifecycle management; resource allocation; strategic planning; restructuring; restoration analysis; technology transition; value-loss analysis; value-development analysis. Purpose does not determine value. It defines the contextual question under which value is being examined. Perspective Identification VCM recognizes that value may be examined from different perspectives. These may include: individual; organization; network; ecosystem; public institution; infrastructure system; community; economy; operational system; technological system. A Value Object may create value for one perspective while providing little or no value for another. VCM therefore requires perspective to remain explicit where it materially affects interpretation. Perspective ≠ Ownership The perspective from which value is examined does not determine ownership. For example: a bridge may be owned by one public authority while its value is examined from the perspective of: commuters; logistics networks; emergency services; regional economy; infrastructure resilience. VCM governs the perspective relevant to value analysis. Ownership remains outside its boundary. Use Context VCM identifies the use context within which the Value Object is relevant. A machine may be examined as: active production equipment; reserve capacity; spare equipment; resale equipment; component source; training equipment; obsolete equipment; restoration candidate. The physical object may remain identical. Its use context may materially change the value lifecycle. Operational Context Operational context describes the relevant operating conditions surrounding the Value Object. Examples include: active operation; standby; maintenance; emergency operation; degraded operation; high-load operation; isolated operation; integrated operation. VCM identifies the context. It does not govern Operational Reality itself. That remains within ORA™. Environmental Context Environmental conditions may materially influence value. These may include: physical environment; climate; infrastructure availability; energy availability; network access; resource availability; logistics conditions; surrounding system conditions. An asset capable of producing substantial value in one environment may be unable to do so in another. VCM makes the environmental basis explicit before downstream value governance interprets the difference. Temporal Context Value context must include time where time materially affects interpretation. Relevant temporal dimensions may include: assessment date; lifecycle period; operational phase; technology generation; market period; seasonal condition; pre-event state; post-event state; future planning horizon. Therefore: Value at Time T1 ≠ necessarily Value at Time T2 even where the Value Object remains unchanged. VCM does not determine the resulting Value State. It establishes the temporal context under which that state will later be governed. Relational Context Value may depend materially upon relationships. Examples include: supplier access; customer relationships; interoperability; contractual access; platform participation; distribution networks; collaboration; service relationships; ecosystem membership. VCM identifies which relationships form part of the context. Where a relationship itself constitutes a Value Object, VODM must preserve it separately. Dependency Context A Value Object may depend upon external capabilities for value to emerge or remain usable. Dependencies may include: electricity; transport; software; data; infrastructure; personnel; networks; complementary assets; regulatory access; technical compatibility. VCM records the dependency context where relevant. It does not govern the external dependency itself. Dependency ≠ Value A Value Object's dependence upon another object does not determine its value. Likewise, the existence of a dependency does not establish value. VCM therefore separates: dependency condition from value consequence. The dependency may later cause value to emerge, change, degrade, reach zero, or recover. Those consequences belong to subsequent VFM® governed spaces. Technological Context Technology may materially change the context in which a Value Object exists. For example, a manufacturing machine may remain physically functional while a new production technology changes: compatibility; usefulness; integration potential; replacement availability; productive relevance. VCM identifies the technological context. VFM® later governs what happens to value as a result. Economic Context Where materially relevant, VCM may identify economic conditions affecting the Value Object's value context. These may include: scarcity; abundance; availability of substitutes; demand conditions; resource constraints; access conditions; economic disruption. VCM does not govern the economy itself. It records economic context only where that context is necessary to understand the Value Object's value lifecycle. Geographic Context Location may materially influence value. The same Value Object may have different relevance in different locations because of: infrastructure; access; demand; scarcity; environmental conditions; logistics; compatibility; surrounding capabilities. Therefore: Physical Object Identity ≠ Universal Geographic Value Context Institutional Context Institutions may form part of the environment in which value is examined. Examples may include: public infrastructure systems; healthcare systems; education systems; industrial ecosystems; research environments; organizational structures. VCM identifies the institutional context where it materially affects the Value Object. It does not govern institutional authority or legality. Context Boundary Every governed Value Context should establish a Context Boundary. The Context Boundary identifies which contextual factors are: included and which are: excluded from the current value analysis. This prevents a Value Statement produced under one context from silently being interpreted as universal. Context Assumptions Some contextual conditions may be assumed rather than directly established. Examples: infrastructure remains available; a production line continues operating; software support continues; demand remains within a defined range; complementary assets remain accessible. VCM requires material contextual assumptions to remain explicit. It does not validate those assumptions. Context Assumption ≠ Value Assumption A contextual assumption describes the environment within which value is examined. A value assumption directly assumes something about value itself. The two must remain separate. For example: “Grid access remains available.” is a contextual assumption. “The facility will therefore retain high value.” is a value conclusion or assumption. VCM governs the first. It does not pre-establish the second. Multi-Context Governance A single Value Object may be examined simultaneously across several contexts. For example: Electric Vehicle Battery may be examined within: Context A — vehicle propulsion Context B — stationary energy storage Context C — materials recovery The battery may remain the same underlying Value Object while its value lifecycle differs across these contexts. VCM therefore permits parallel contextualization. Context Comparison VCM enables controlled comparison between contexts. The methodological structure may be: Value Object X + Context A versus Value Object X + Context B This makes it possible to distinguish: change in the Value Object from change in the context surrounding the Value Object. That distinction becomes critical when identifying why value changed. Context Change A material Context Change occurs when one or more contextual conditions change sufficiently to affect downstream value governance. Examples include: loss of infrastructure; new technology; disappearance of demand; new use capability; loss of compatibility; geographic relocation; dependency failure; restoration of access; new relationship; changed operational environment. Context Change does not automatically mean Value Change. It creates a trigger to assess whether Value Change occurred. Context Change ≠ Value Change This distinction is fundamental. A context may change without materially changing value. Likewise, value may change without a major context change. Therefore: Context Change → Value Reassessment Trigger not: Context Change = Value Change Context and Value Emergence Context may create conditions under which value can emerge. For example: an unused technology may acquire practical value when complementary infrastructure becomes available. VCM identifies the changed context. The Value Emergence Standard governs whether value actually emerges. Context and Value Development A favorable context may enable existing value to grow. Examples include: network expansion; complementary infrastructure; increased interoperability; improved access; new capabilities. VCM identifies the contextual development. The Value Development Standard governs the resulting development of value. Context and Value Degradation A Value Object may remain unchanged while its context deteriorates. Examples include: loss of compatible infrastructure; declining usefulness; disappearing ecosystem support; loss of complementary capability. VCM governs the changed context. The Value Degradation Standard governs the resulting value degradation where it occurs. Context and Value Nullification A context change may contribute to value reaching zero. But VCM does not issue a zero-value determination. For example: a specialized machine may remain physically operational but become unusable because the only compatible production system disappears. VCM identifies: loss of compatibility context. The Value Nullification Standard determines whether the resulting value reaches a zero-value condition. Context and ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ A Value Object may be a ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ in a defined context while retaining potential value under another context. This distinction is essential. For example: a machine may have zero productive value in Facility A because supporting infrastructure no longer exists. The same machine may regain productive relevance if relocated to Facility B. Therefore, where appropriate: Zero Value must remain context-bound. VCM supplies the contextual basis necessary for later Value State governance. Context and ReMonet™ A change of context may enable value restoration. Examples include: relocation; technological adaptation; new infrastructure; new use; restored network access; new relationships; changed demand; repurposing. VCM identifies the contextual change. ReMonet™ governs the value-restoration mechanism where value actually returns. Context and Value Extinction Value Extinction must not be inferred merely because value is absent in one context. If a Value Object may possess recoverable value under another legitimate context, its broader value lifecycle may not yet have reached extinction. Therefore: Context-Specific Zero Value ≠ Automatic Value Extinction This distinction protects VFM® from collapsing temporary contextual uselessness into terminal value loss. Value Context ≠ Valuation Context VCM does not establish a valuation methodology. It may identify the context in which a valuation is being conducted, but it does not determine: valuation method; discount rate; fair value; market value; accounting value; price; monetary amount. Therefore: Value Context Governance ≠ Valuation Methodology Value ≠ Price VCM explicitly preserves the distinction between: value context and price context. A market price may be one contextual signal relevant to a Value Object. It does not define the complete value lifecycle governed by VFM®. VCM Boundary with VOIM VOIM identifies the Value Object. VCM identifies the context in which that object is examined. Therefore: Object Identity ≠ Object Context VCM Boundary with VOBM VOBM establishes the Value Object Boundary. VCM establishes the Value Context Boundary. These boundaries must remain distinct. Value Object Boundary answers: What belongs to the object? Value Context Boundary answers: Which surrounding conditions belong to the present value analysis? VCM Boundary with VODM VODM determines whether objects, components, capabilities, relationships, or configurations must remain differentiated. VCM then contextualizes those differentiated Value Objects. Therefore: Differentiation precedes contextualization. VCM Boundary with ORA™ ORA™ governs actual Operational Reality. VCM may identify operational conditions as part of Value Context. It does not govern those operational conditions themselves. Therefore: Operational Reality ≠ Value Context VCM Boundary with GOA™ GOA™ governs governance itself, including authority, scope, delegation, accountability, and governance boundaries. VCM governs only the contextual conditions necessary for value lifecycle interpretation. VCM Boundary with CLA™ CLA™ may classify contextual factors. VCM determines which contextual factors are materially relevant to the Value Object's value lifecycle. Therefore: Context Identification ≠ Classification Governance VCM Boundary with VALIDOS® VCM does not determine whether contextual claims are valid. Where formal validation is required, VALIDOS® may govern validation of those claims. Therefore: Context Definition ≠ Context Validation VCM Boundary with INTEGROS® VCM does not determine contextual integrity. INTEGROS® may govern whether contextual information maintains required integrity properties. VCM Boundary with ADIT® ADIT® may provide evidence concerning contextual conditions and contextual changes. VCM governs how those conditions are structured as Value Context. Therefore: Evidence of Context ≠ Context Governance VCM Boundary with SIMULOS® SIMULOS® may simulate future, hypothetical, or alternative contexts. VCM may use a clearly identified simulated context as a value-analysis context. It does not govern the simulation itself. Therefore: Simulated Context ≠ Value Context Governance VCM Boundary with OBIDENITY® VCM does not determine: identity; ownership; authority; permission; provenance; transfer. Those may be relevant contextual inputs, but their governance remains outside VCM. Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum VCM implementation should establish: 1. Value Object Input Receive the identified, bounded, and differentiated Value Object. 2. Context Purpose Define why the Value Object is being examined. 3. Perspective Identify the relevant perspective where material. 4. Use Context Identify the relevant use or capability context. 5. Environmental & Operational Context Identify materially relevant surrounding conditions. 6. Temporal Context Define the relevant time, period, or lifecycle moment. 7. Relational & Dependency Context Identify material relationships and dependencies. 8. Context Boundary Define which contextual factors are included and excluded. 9. Context Assumptions Record material contextual assumptions. 10. Context Variation Identify alternative contexts where materially relevant. 11. Context State Establish the current contextual basis. 12. Context Record Create a traceable governed Value Context record. Governance Outputs VCM may produce: Value Context Record Value Context Statement Value Context Boundary Value Context Purpose Record Value Perspective Record Value Use Context Record Value Environmental Context Record Value Operational Context Record Value Temporal Context Record Value Relational Context Record Value Dependency Context Record Value Context Assumption Record Value Context Variation Record Value Context Change Record Multi-Context Comparison Record Contextualized Value Object These outputs provide the contextual basis required for the final Value Identification function and subsequent VFM® lifecycle governance. Enterprise Application VCM addresses one of the most important problems in real-world value analysis: organizations frequently speak about “the value” of something without specifying the context in which that value exists. Consider an industrial robot. The same robot may be: highly useful in a factory with compatible software, tooling, trained operators, energy, maintenance, and production demand; weakly useful in a facility where only part of that supporting environment exists; or operationally useless in a location where the required infrastructure is absent. The robot may not have changed. The context has. A conventional system may record only a financial amount. VCM records the context necessary to understand why the value lifecycle may differ. This becomes especially important for: accounting; asset management; investment; taxation analysis; infrastructure; public finance; technology; AI systems; industrial equipment; intellectual property; digital assets; energy systems; supply chains; strategic capabilities. VCM enables later VFM® standards to distinguish: Value Object Change from Value Context Change and therefore prevents downstream value governance from attributing a value transition to the wrong cause. Foundational Principles Value cannot be governed consistently without governing the context in which value is being examined. The same Value Object may exist across multiple legitimate Value Contexts. A change in context does not automatically create a new Value Object. A change in context does not automatically create a change in value. Context Change is a trigger for value reassessment, not a Value Change determination. Value Object Boundary and Value Context Boundary are different methodological controls. Perspective does not determine ownership. Dependency does not itself establish value. Context does not determine price. Context-specific zero value does not automatically establish Value Extinction. A ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ state may be context-dependent where recoverable value remains possible under another legitimate context. The conditions surrounding value must remain distinguishable from value itself. Canonical Closing Statement Value Context Module establishes the fourth methodological control point of the Value Identification Standard by situating an identified, bounded, and differentiated Value Object within the explicit purpose, perspective, use, environment, operational conditions, time, relationships, dependencies, assumptions, and contextual boundaries necessary for consistent value lifecycle governance. Through governance of Value Context, VCM prevents value statements generated under one set of conditions from being silently generalized across other contexts and enables VFM® to distinguish changes in the Value Object from changes in the environment surrounding it. By separating context from object identity, object boundary, differentiation, valuation, price, validation, integrity, audit, operational reality, and value state, VCM provides the contextual foundation required to determine whether value originates, emerges, develops, degrades, reaches zero, is restored, or becomes extinct. A Value Object must therefore never be treated as though its value exists independently of context when the conditions surrounding that object materially affect the lifecycle of value. title: Value Object Boundary Module (VOBM)
text: Value Object Boundary Module (VOBM) Value Object Boundary Module (VOBM) Value Object Boundary Module (VOBM) Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture Parent Standard: Value Identification Standard (VIS) Module: VOBM — Value Object Boundary Module Operational Layer: Value Object Boundary Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Value Object Boundary Origin ID: VFM-VIS-VOBM-001.2 Version: 1.0 Status: Draft · Open Standard Effective Date: 23 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · AGA™ · INTEGROS® · CLA™ · ADIT® · VALIDOS® · SIMULOS® · OBIDENITY® AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Value Object Boundary Module (VOBM) is the second Core Module of the Value Identification Standard (VIS) within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture. VOBM governs the methodological boundary of an identified Value Object by determining what belongs inside the Value Object for the relevant value lifecycle, what remains outside it, which components, relationships, capabilities, conditions, dependencies, or interfaces materially constitute the object, and where the object must be separated from its surrounding environment. The Module transforms an identified Value Object into a bounded Value Object capable of supporting consistent downstream value governance. VOBM does not determine whether value exists, where value originates, whether value has emerged, how much value exists, or how value changes. Its foundational task is narrower: to establish where the Value Object begins and ends before the value associated with that object enters the wider value lifecycle. Core Question Where does the identified Value Object begin and end for the value lifecycle being governed? Architectural Position VOBM is the second Core Module of the Value Identification Standard. It follows: VOIM — Value Object Identification Module and precedes the subsequent VIS modules governing differentiation, context, and the remaining conditions necessary to establish the Value Object as a governed entry point into the value lifecycle. VOIM establishes: What is the Value Object? VOBM establishes: What belongs to that Value Object, and where does it end? The sequence is therefore: Value Object Identification → Value Object Boundary → Value Differentiation → Value Context → Governed Value Identification Internal Flow Position Identified Value Object → Boundary Purpose Definition → Constituent Identification → Inclusion Assessment → Exclusion Assessment → Dependency Assessment → Interface Identification → Composite / Component Boundary Assessment → Temporal Boundary Assessment → Boundary Determination → Boundary State Assignment → Bounded Value Object Operational Space VOBM governs the space between: an identified Value Object and a sufficiently bounded Value Object capable of entering further value governance. This operational space includes: Value Object boundary purpose; object inclusion; object exclusion; constituent identification; component boundaries; composite-object boundaries; relational boundaries; capability boundaries; process boundaries; service boundaries; digital boundaries; physical boundaries; functional boundaries; dependency boundaries; interface boundaries; contextual boundaries where necessary for object separation; temporal boundaries; configuration boundaries; boundary uncertainty; boundary change; boundary state; boundary traceability. Why Value Boundaries Matter Value cannot be governed consistently where the object carrying, enabling, producing, receiving, or relating to that value changes silently during analysis. Consider an industrial facility. One analysis may treat the Value Object as: the land. Another may treat it as: land + buildings. Another: land + buildings + machinery. Another: the complete operational production capability. Another: the business operating from that facility. All may appear to discuss the same asset. They are not necessarily discussing the same Value Object. Their boundaries differ. VOBM exists to make that difference explicit. Value Object Boundary A Value Object Boundary is: the governed methodological separation defining which elements, components, relationships, capabilities, conditions, and interfaces constitute the Value Object for the relevant value lifecycle and which remain outside it. The boundary does not need to correspond to: a physical perimeter; legal ownership; accounting consolidation; organizational structure; technical architecture; contractual structure; regulatory jurisdiction. Those boundaries may provide relevant inputs. They do not automatically determine the VFM® Value Object Boundary. Physical Boundary ≠ Value Object Boundary A physical asset may have a clear physical perimeter while the relevant Value Object extends beyond it. For example, a factory building has a physical boundary. But the Value Object: Operational Production Capability may depend upon: machinery; energy access; workforce capability; software; process knowledge; supply access; logistics; licenses; external infrastructure. The physical factory perimeter therefore does not automatically define the boundary of the relevant Value Object. Conversely, the relevant Value Object may concern only one machine located inside the factory. Therefore: Physical Boundary ≠ Value Object Boundary Legal Boundary ≠ Value Object Boundary Legal ownership may identify who owns an object or right. It does not automatically determine what constitutes the Value Object for a specific value lifecycle. A company may legally own: land; machinery; patents; software; inventory; contractual rights. But a particular Value Object may consist of only one of those elements or a governed combination of several. Therefore: Ownership Boundary ≠ Value Object Boundary Ownership remains governed outside VOBM where relevant. Accounting Boundary ≠ Value Object Boundary Accounting systems may group objects according to accounting rules. VOBM does not assume that an accounting asset corresponds exactly to a Value Object. One accounting asset may contain multiple value-relevant objects. Multiple accounting assets may together form one Value Object. Some Value Objects may not be represented as conventional balance-sheet assets at all. Examples may include: dormant capability; network position; operational access; organizational knowledge; technological potential; unused capacity; relational capability; data-derived capability. Therefore: Accounting Asset Boundary ≠ Value Object Boundary Boundary Purpose Every boundary determination should identify why the Value Object is being bounded. The purpose may relate to: value lifecycle analysis; value origin examination; value emergence; value state determination; value change analysis; value degradation; value nullification; value restoration; value extinction; comparison between Value Objects; organizational decision support; policy analysis; economic analysis; asset restructuring; other governed value purposes. Boundary purpose prevents the same object from being bounded differently without explanation. Constituent Identification VOBM identifies the constituents potentially forming part of the Value Object. Constituents may include: physical components; digital components; information objects; capabilities; rights; processes; activities; relationships; resources; access conditions; infrastructure dependencies; contractual elements; operational elements; environmental elements; other materially relevant constituents. Constituent identification does not automatically mean inclusion. Each constituent must be assessed against the boundary purpose. Inclusion Principle An element should be included within the Value Object Boundary where its presence is materially constitutive of the object being governed. The relevant question is: Would removing this element materially change what the identified Value Object is? Where the answer is yes, inclusion may be justified. Where the element merely affects the Value Object externally, it may instead remain an external dependency or contextual condition. This distinction is essential. Exclusion Principle VOBM requires explicit exclusion of elements that are adjacent, influential, related, or economically relevant but do not constitute the Value Object itself. Examples may include: market conditions; taxation; financing conditions; regulation; external demand; external infrastructure; customer behavior; supplier conditions; macroeconomic conditions. These factors may strongly affect value. That does not automatically make them part of the Value Object. Therefore: Influence on Value ≠ Membership in Value Object Constituent ≠ Dependency VOBM distinguishes: Constituent from Dependency. A constituent forms part of the Value Object. A dependency exists outside the object but materially affects its ability to function, exist, or produce relevant value. For example: A data center may include servers as constituents. Electric-grid access may remain an external dependency. But where the Value Object is defined as: Integrated Data-Center Operational Capability the relevant energy infrastructure relationship may need to be represented differently. Boundary determination therefore depends upon the precise Value Object identified by VOIM. Dependency Boundary External dependencies must remain identifiable even when they are excluded from the Value Object itself. A bounded Value Object may therefore be represented as: Internal Constituents → Object Boundary → External Dependencies This enables later VFM® analysis to distinguish: change to the Value Object from change in an external condition affecting the value of the Value Object. Interface Boundary Where the Value Object interacts with external systems, VOBM identifies the relevant interfaces. Interfaces may include: physical interfaces; digital interfaces; contractual interfaces; resource interfaces; information interfaces; service interfaces; infrastructure interfaces; operational interfaces; market interfaces. The interface defines where interaction occurs. It does not automatically move the external system inside the Value Object Boundary. Composite Value Object Boundary A composite Value Object may contain multiple independently identifiable components. For example: Integrated Manufacturing Capability may include: Facility + Machinery + Control Software + Process Capability + Defined Operational Integration VOBM must determine whether the governed lifecycle concerns: each component separately or the integrated composite object. This distinction is necessary because: Value of Composite Object ≠ Sum of Isolated Component Values A composite object may possess value that emerges only through integration. Likewise, loss of one critical constituent may disproportionately degrade the value of the complete object. Component Value Object Boundary A component inside a composite Value Object may itself have an independent value lifecycle. VOBM therefore supports nested boundaries: Composite Value Object A → Component Value Object A.1 → Component Value Object A.2 → Component Value Object A.3 Each boundary must remain distinguishable. This enables VFM® to govern: component value and composite value without collapsing them into one undifferentiated value object. Relational Value Object Boundary Some Value Objects exist primarily through relationships. Examples may include: distribution relationships; network participation; access arrangements; partnerships; contractual opportunities; platform relationships; supply relationships. In such cases, VOBM must determine what constitutes the relationship-based Value Object without treating the complete identities, organizations, or assets of all participating parties as part of that Value Object. Therefore: Relationship Participation ≠ Full Object Inclusion Capability Boundary Capabilities often create difficult boundary questions. A production capability may depend on: equipment; people; knowledge; software; infrastructure; procedures; permissions; supply availability. VOBM determines which of these constitute the identified capability Value Object and which remain enabling dependencies or contextual conditions. This prevents capability value from being confused with the value of every object contributing to that capability. Process Boundary Where a process is the Value Object, the boundary may be defined through: process entry; process activities; transformation stages; required resources; process exit; interfaces; dependencies. VOBM does not govern operational execution of the process. It establishes what process is included within the Value Object being examined. Temporal Boundary A Value Object Boundary may change over time. For example: Factory Capability — 2024 may include one production line. After expansion: Factory Capability — 2026 may include three lines, automation infrastructure, and a new digital control system. VOBM therefore requires material boundary changes to remain visible. A historical value determination must not silently inherit a later object boundary. Configuration Boundary Where configuration materially determines the Value Object, VOBM records the configuration associated with the boundary. Examples include: industrial system configuration; software stack; AI system configuration; infrastructure topology; portfolio composition; organizational composition; service bundle; production configuration. A material configuration change may require a new or revised Value Object Boundary. Dynamic Boundaries Some Value Objects have boundaries that change during their lifecycle. Examples may include: evolving digital platforms; portfolios; supply networks; project ecosystems; integrated capabilities; data environments. VOBM therefore permits: Dynamic Value Object Boundaries provided that the basis, time, conditions, and material changes remain traceable. Dynamic does not mean undefined. Boundary Uncertainty Not every Value Object can initially be bounded with complete certainty. VOBM therefore permits boundary uncertainty to be explicitly represented. Uncertainty may concern: component inclusion; dependency classification; relationship extent; temporal applicability; configuration; interface definition; composite structure. Uncertainty must not be hidden through arbitrary precision. Where material uncertainty remains, the boundary may receive a conditional state. Boundary States VOBM may assign a governed boundary state. 1. Unbounded The Value Object has been identified but its relevant boundary has not yet been established. 2. Candidate Boundary A proposed boundary exists but requires further assessment. 3. Conditionally Bounded The boundary is sufficiently established only under defined assumptions, contexts, configurations, or temporal conditions. 4. Bounded The Value Object Boundary is sufficiently established for downstream value governance. 5. Boundary Under Review A material change or unresolved issue requires reassessment. 6. Boundary Superseded A previously governed boundary has been replaced by a newer boundary while remaining preserved for historical traceability. Boundary states must not be confused with Value States. Boundary State ≠ Value State A Value Object may be: Bounded while its value is: unknown, emerging, positive, developing, degrading, zero, restored, or extinct. VOBM governs the object boundary. Later VFM® standards govern value states and transitions. Boundary Change A boundary change occurs when the governed constitution of the Value Object materially changes. Examples include: component addition; component removal; merger; separation; integration; configuration change; relationship termination; capability expansion; capability contraction; structural reorganization. A boundary change may affect value. But: Boundary Change ≠ Value Change The boundary change is an event concerning the Value Object. Later VFM® governance determines what happened to value as a result. Boundary with VOIM VOIM answers: What is the Value Object? VOBM answers: Where does that Value Object begin and end? Therefore: Identification ≠ Boundary Determination VOIM must provide a sufficiently identified Value Object before VOBM can establish its boundary. Boundary with Value Differentiation & Separation VOBM determines what is inside and outside the Value Object. The subsequent differentiation function determines whether multiple objects, value relationships, value types, components, or value phenomena must remain analytically separate. Therefore: Boundary ≠ Differentiation An object can be correctly bounded while still containing several distinct value relationships requiring separation. Boundary with Value Context & Condition VOBM may use context where necessary to establish the object boundary. The Value Context & Condition function governs the broader circumstances under which the object enters value analysis. Therefore: Boundary Context ≠ Value Context Governance Boundary with Value Origin Standard VOBM does not determine where value comes from. It establishes the bounded object in relation to which Value Origin can subsequently be examined. Therefore: Object Boundary ≠ Value Origin Boundary with Value Emergence Standard VOBM does not determine whether value has emerged. A perfectly bounded Value Object may still possess: no emerged value. Therefore: Bounded Object ≠ Existing Value Boundary with Value Recognition Standard VOBM does not determine whether value is recognized. It establishes only the object boundary required for consistent value governance. Boundary with GOA™ GOA™ governs governance boundaries. VOBM governs the boundary of the Value Object for the value lifecycle. Therefore: Governance Boundary ≠ Value Object Boundary Boundary with ORA™ ORA™ governs actual Operational Reality and operational boundaries. VOBM may use operational information when defining a Value Object but does not govern Operational Reality itself. Therefore: Operational Boundary ≠ Value Object Boundary Boundary with OBIDENITY® OBIDENITY® governs origin-bound identity, ownership, authority, permission, responsibility, provenance, transfer, and continuity. VOBM does not determine ownership boundaries or identity boundaries. A Value Object may cross multiple ownership boundaries. Likewise, one owner may hold multiple distinct Value Objects. Boundary with CLA™ VOBM may identify constituents and boundary forms necessary for object separation. Formal classification remains governed by CLA™ where required. Boundary with VALIDOS® VOBM does not validate the correctness of a boundary claim. It defines the methodological boundary required by VFM®. Where formal validation of the boundary or supporting claims is required, VALIDOS® governs that validation process. Boundary with INTEGROS® VOBM does not determine boundary integrity. INTEGROS® may govern whether a defined boundary remains structurally or operationally intact where integrity governance is required. Boundary with ADIT® VOBM establishes the Value Object Boundary. ADIT® may provide governed audit evidence concerning whether the recorded constituents, exclusions, dependencies, interfaces, or boundary changes are supported by evidence. Boundary Governance ≠ Audit Governance Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum VOBM implementation should establish: 1. Identified Value Object Receive the identified Value Object from VOIM. 2. Boundary Purpose Define why the object boundary is required. 3. Constituent Candidates Identify components, relationships, capabilities, processes, resources, or other elements potentially belonging inside the object. 4. Inclusion Assessment Determine which constituent candidates form part of the Value Object. 5. Exclusion Assessment Determine which adjacent or influential elements remain outside the object. 6. Dependency Assessment Identify external dependencies without automatically incorporating them into the object. 7. Interface Identification Define relevant interfaces between the Value Object and external systems or environments. 8. Composite / Component Assessment Determine whether nested Value Object boundaries are required. 9. Temporal & Configuration Reference Establish the time and configuration to which the boundary applies. 10. Boundary State Assign the governed Value Object Boundary State. 11. Boundary Record Document the basis, inclusions, exclusions, dependencies, interfaces, uncertainty, and applicable conditions. Governance Outputs VOBM may produce: Value Object Boundary Record Value Object Boundary Statement Value Object Constituent Register Value Object Inclusion Record Value Object Exclusion Record Value Object Dependency Record Value Object Interface Record Composite Value Object Boundary Record Component Value Object Boundary Record Relational Value Object Boundary Record Value Object Temporal Boundary Value Object Configuration Boundary Value Object Boundary Uncertainty Record Value Object Boundary State Value Object Boundary Change Record Bounded Value Object These outputs provide the governed basis for the next VIS module. Enterprise Application VOBM enables organizations to resolve one of the most important hidden problems in value analysis: different assessments often assign value to differently bounded objects while treating them as though they were the same object. This can affect: enterprise valuation; infrastructure; industrial assets; digital assets; intellectual property; data; production capacity; environmental resources; public assets; projects; services; technology platforms; dormant assets; composite systems; capabilities. For example, two analysts may disagree about the value of a production facility. One values: land + building + machinery. The other values: the complete operational production capability, including integrated software, process capability, and operational access. Their numerical disagreement may be secondary. Their first disagreement is architectural: they have not bounded the same Value Object. VOBM makes that difference visible before downstream valuation, accounting, taxation, investment, policy, or economic analysis attempts to use the resulting value information. Foundational Principles A Value Object cannot be governed consistently if its boundary is undefined. Identification establishes what the Value Object is; boundary governance establishes where it ends. Physical boundary is not automatically Value Object Boundary. Legal ownership boundary is not automatically Value Object Boundary. Accounting asset boundary is not automatically Value Object Boundary. Influence on value does not automatically create membership in the Value Object. A constituent is not the same as a dependency. A composite Value Object may possess a value lifecycle distinct from the value lifecycles of its components. A component may simultaneously be part of a composite Value Object and possess its own independently governed value lifecycle. Dynamic boundaries must remain governed boundaries. Boundary change is not automatically value change. Boundary State is not Value State. Canonical Closing Statement Value Object Boundary Module establishes the second methodological control point of the Value Identification Standard by determining where an identified Value Object begins and ends for the relevant value lifecycle. Through governance of constituents, inclusions, exclusions, dependencies, interfaces, composite and component structures, relational and capability boundaries, temporal applicability, configuration, uncertainty, boundary states, and boundary change, VOBM prevents value analysis from silently expanding, contracting, combining, or substituting the object whose value is being governed. By separating Value Object Boundary from physical perimeter, legal ownership, accounting treatment, governance boundary, operational boundary, classification, validation, integrity, and audit, VOBM creates a stable methodological object upon which subsequent value governance can operate. Before value origin, emergence, recognition, state, development, degradation, nullification, restoration, or extinction can be governed consistently, the boundaries of the object to which that value relates must first be explicit.
