title: Value Object Differentiation Module (VODM)
text: Value Object Differentiation Module (VODM) Value Object Differentiation Module (VODM) Value Object Differentiation Module (VODM) Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture Parent Standard: Value Identification Standard (VIS) Module: VODM — Value Object Differentiation Module Operational Layer: Value Object Differentiation Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Value Object Differentiation Origin ID: VFM-VIS-VODM-001.3 Version: 1.0 Status: Draft · Open Standard Effective Date: 23 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · AGA™ · INTEGROS® · CLA™ · ADIT® · VALIDOS® · SIMULOS® · OBIDENITY® AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Value Object Differentiation Module (VODM) is the third Core Module of the Value Identification Standard (VIS) within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture. VODM governs the methodological differentiation of a bounded Value Object by determining whether the object must remain governed as one Value Object or be distinguished from other objects, components, capabilities, relationships, functions, value-bearing configurations, or analytically separate value phenomena before the value lifecycle can be governed consistently. The Module prevents materially different Value Objects from being collapsed into one object and prevents one Value Object from being unnecessarily fragmented into multiple objects without a governed basis. VODM does not determine whether value exists, what value is worth, where value originates, whether value has emerged, or how value subsequently changes. Its task is foundational: to determine what must remain the same Value Object and what must be treated as a distinct Value Object before downstream value governance begins. Core Question Which Value Objects, components, relationships, capabilities, or configurations must remain distinct for their value lifecycles to be governed correctly? Architectural Position VODM is the third Core Module of the Value Identification Standard. It follows: VOIM — Value Object Identification Module → VOBM — Value Object Boundary Module and precedes the subsequent VIS functions governing the context and conditions under which the identified Value Object enters the wider value lifecycle. The methodological sequence is: Value Object Identification → Value Object Boundary → Value Object Differentiation → Value Context → Governed Value Identification VOIM establishes: What is the Value Object? VOBM establishes: Where does the Value Object begin and end? VODM establishes: What must remain distinct within, between, or around those bounded Value Objects? Internal Flow Position Bounded Value Object → Differentiation Purpose Definition → Differentiation Candidate Identification → Similarity Assessment → Material Difference Assessment → Component / Composite Assessment → Functional Differentiation → Relational Differentiation → Configuration Differentiation → Temporal Differentiation → Value-Lifecycle Independence Assessment → Differentiation Determination → Differentiation State Assignment → Differentiated Value Object Structure Operational Space VODM governs the space between: a bounded Value Object and a differentiated Value Object structure suitable for downstream value governance. This operational space includes: object differentiation; object equivalence assessment; component differentiation; composite differentiation; capability differentiation; functional differentiation; relational differentiation; configuration differentiation; temporal differentiation; lifecycle differentiation; duplicate-object detection; object aggregation risk; object fragmentation risk; value-lifecycle independence; differentiation uncertainty; differentiation state; differentiation traceability; differentiation reassessment after material change. Why Differentiation Matters Two things may appear to be the same asset while possessing different value lifecycles. Likewise, several things may appear separate while together constituting one meaningful Value Object. Consider a manufacturing facility containing three production lines. The facility may be governed as: one integrated production capability or the three lines may be governed as: Value Object A — Production Line 1 Value Object B — Production Line 2 Value Object C — Production Line 3 Both approaches may be legitimate. The correct differentiation depends upon what Value Object has been identified, how its boundary has been established, and whether the components possess materially independent value lifecycles. Without explicit differentiation, later value analysis may silently mix: component value; composite value; capability value; replacement value; operational value; relational value; value created through integration. VODM makes these distinctions governable before value itself is analyzed. Differentiation Principle A Value Object should be differentiated where a material distinction exists that would cause its value lifecycle to be governed differently from another object or component. A material distinction may arise through: different constitution; different function; different capability; different relationship; different configuration; different lifecycle; different dependency structure; different temporal existence; different value-origin relationship; different value-emergence conditions; different degradation pathway; different restoration possibility; different extinction condition. The governing question is not: Do these objects look different? It is: Would treating them as the same Value Object materially distort governance of their value lifecycles? Similarity ≠ Identity Two Value Objects may be highly similar without being the same governed object. Examples include: two identical machines; two identical software licenses; two apartments in the same building; two units of inventory; two identical datasets; two equivalent production lines; two contractual rights with identical terms. Similarity may support comparison. It does not erase object distinction. Therefore: Similarity ≠ Value Object Identity Difference ≠ Separate Value Object Conversely, the existence of differences does not automatically require separate Value Objects. An integrated industrial system may contain: different machines; different software components; different operational processes; different infrastructure elements. Those differences may remain internal to one composite Value Object where the governed object is the integrated operational capability. Therefore: Internal Difference ≠ Automatic Object Separation Differentiation Candidate A Differentiation Candidate is: an object, component, capability, relationship, configuration, or other materially distinguishable element whose value lifecycle may require governance separately from another Value Object or from the composite object within which it exists. Identification of a Differentiation Candidate does not automatically create a new Value Object. It creates a requirement for differentiation assessment. Material Difference Assessment VODM assesses whether differences are material to the value lifecycle. A difference may be material where it changes: what value may originate from the object; when value may emerge; whether value may be independently recognized; the state of value; how value may change; how value may develop; how value may degrade; whether value may reach zero independently; whether value may be restored independently; whether value may become extinct independently. This creates a powerful architectural test: Can the relevant value lifecycle materially diverge? If yes, separate Value Object governance may be required. Value-Lifecycle Independence Test VODM introduces the Value-Lifecycle Independence Test. The test asks whether a candidate can possess a materially independent lifecycle across one or more VFM® stages. For example: Can it have its own: Value Origin? Can value emerge from it independently? Can its value state differ from the surrounding object? Can it develop while the surrounding object degrades? Can it reach zero while the composite retains value? Can it be restored independently? Can its value become extinct while another related object continues to possess value? The greater the lifecycle independence, the stronger the basis for differentiation. Object Differentiation Object differentiation separates distinct Value Objects that may otherwise be treated as one. Example: A company owns two physically identical warehouses. They may share: design; purpose; ownership; accounting category. But they occupy different locations, have different dependencies, different operational conditions, and potentially different value lifecycles. VODM preserves them as distinct Value Objects where required. Component Differentiation A component within a composite Value Object may require independent differentiation. For example: Aircraft may constitute one composite Value Object. But: Engine A and Engine B may each possess independently relevant value lifecycles. VODM can therefore establish: Aircraft — Composite Value Object with nested: Engine A — Component Value Object Engine B — Component Value Object without dissolving the aircraft as the composite Value Object. Composite Differentiation Multiple components may together produce a value phenomenon that does not exist at the component level. Consider: Land + Building + Machinery + Software + Workforce Capability + Process Integration Each element may possess independent value. But their integration may create: Operational Manufacturing Capability with a separate value lifecycle. VODM therefore recognizes that: Component Value Objects and Composite Value Objects may legitimately coexist. Composite Value ≠ Component Value Sum A composite object may possess value arising from integration. This means: Composite Value ≠ necessarily Σ Component Values Integration may create: operational capability; network effects; interoperability; coordination capability; scale effects; access; strategic capability; productive capacity. Conversely, dysfunctional integration may reduce the value of the composite even where individual components retain substantial value. VODM does not measure this value. It ensures the composite and its components can be governed separately where their value lifecycles differ. Functional Differentiation One physical or digital object may support several functions. Those functions may create distinct value relationships. For example, a building may function as: production space; storage; office space; rental property; collateral; redevelopment opportunity. VODM determines whether these functions merely affect one Value Object or whether one or more functions constitute independently governable Value Objects or capabilities. The distinction must be explicit. Capability Differentiation Capabilities may require differentiation from the physical objects that enable them. For example: Machine and Production Capability are not automatically the same Value Object. A machine may retain resale value even where the production capability has collapsed. Likewise, a production capability may remain valuable after individual machines are replaced. Therefore: Enabling Asset ≠ Capability Value Object where their value lifecycles are materially independent. Relational Differentiation Value may relate to a relationship rather than exclusively to either participating object. Examples include: supplier relationship; distribution relationship; customer network; platform access; partnership; licensing relationship; contractual access; interoperability relationship. VODM may differentiate: Party A from Party B from Relationship AB where each represents a materially distinct Value Object or value-bearing phenomenon. This prevents relational value from being incorrectly assigned entirely to one participant. Configuration Differentiation The same underlying object may possess materially different value characteristics under different configurations. Examples include: machine configuration; software configuration; AI model configuration; infrastructure topology; production configuration; service bundle; portfolio composition. VODM determines whether configuration change merely modifies the same Value Object or creates a sufficiently distinct Value Object configuration requiring separate governance. Version Differentiation Versions may need to remain distinguishable where value-relevant characteristics materially differ. For example: Software Version 4.1 and Software Version 7.0 may share identity continuity while possessing different: capabilities; dependencies; compatibility; market relevance; operational utility; lifecycle position. VODM may therefore preserve version-specific Value Object differentiation without redefining identity governance. Temporal Differentiation A Value Object may materially change across time. The same physical object may represent different governed Value Object states or configurations at different moments. For example: Industrial Facility — 2024 Configuration and Industrial Facility — 2026 Configuration may require differentiation where expansion, automation, restructuring, or capability changes materially alter the value lifecycle. VODM therefore supports temporally differentiated Value Objects where required. Value Object ≠ Legal Entity A legal entity may contain many Value Objects. A Value Object may also span multiple legal entities. Therefore: Legal Entity Boundary ≠ Value Object Differentiation Rule VODM does not determine corporate identity, legal ownership, or legal consolidation. Value Object ≠ Accounting Unit Accounting systems may aggregate or separate assets according to accounting requirements. VODM differentiates Value Objects according to the methodological requirements of value lifecycle governance. Therefore: Accounting Unit ≠ Value Object and: Accounting Separation ≠ Automatic Value Object Differentiation Value Object ≠ Market Product A product sold as one commercial unit may contain multiple Value Objects. Likewise, several products may depend upon one common Value Object. Commercial packaging therefore does not determine methodological differentiation. Differentiation and Dependencies Objects may share dependencies without becoming one Value Object. For example: two factories may depend upon the same: energy grid; transport network; software platform; supplier; workforce pool. Shared dependency does not erase object differentiation. Therefore: Shared Dependency ≠ Shared Value Object Differentiation and Ownership Common ownership does not merge Value Objects. Different ownership does not automatically separate a composite Value Object. Ownership may be relevant contextual information, but ownership governance belongs outside VODM. Therefore: Ownership Structure ≠ Value Object Differentiation Differentiation and Value Origin VODM does not determine Value Origin. However, different value-origin relationships may indicate that differentiation is necessary. If two components derive value through materially different origins, their value lifecycles may need to remain separately governable. The actual governance of Value Origin belongs to the Value Origin Standard. Differentiation and Value State Two components of one composite object may simultaneously occupy different Value States. For example: Component A — positive value Component B — degraded value Component C — zero-value condition while: Composite Object — positive value This is possible only if object differentiation is explicit. VODM therefore creates the structural basis necessary for later Value State governance. Differentiation and DeMonet™ A DeMonet™ transition may affect one differentiated Value Object without nullifying another. For example: a technology component may lose all admissible value while the broader system retains value through replacement, adaptation, or alternative capability. VODM ensures that value nullification is applied to the correct Value Object. Differentiation and ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ A ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ state belongs to a defined Value Object. Without differentiation, a zero-value condition affecting one component could be incorrectly generalized to: the entire composite object; related objects; the owner; the surrounding system. VODM prevents this category error. Differentiation and ReMonet™ ReMonet™ may restore value to: one component; one capability; one relationship; one configuration; the complete composite object. VODM provides the object structure necessary to identify exactly what is being restored. Differentiation State VODM may assign a governed differentiation state. 1. Undifferentiated Potential distinctions exist but have not yet been assessed. 2. Differentiation Candidate One or more potential independent Value Objects have been identified. 3. Conditionally Differentiated Separate governance is required only under defined conditions, purposes, configurations, or temporal contexts. 4. Differentiated The relevant Value Objects or components are sufficiently distinguished for downstream value governance. 5. Integrated The assessed elements remain governed as one composite Value Object despite internal differences. 6. Differentiation Under Review Material change or unresolved uncertainty requires reassessment. 7. Superseded Differentiation A previous differentiation structure has been replaced while remaining preserved for historical traceability. Differentiation State ≠ Value State A Value Object may be: Differentiated while its value state remains unknown. Likewise: Integrated does not mean valuable. Differentiation states govern methodological object structure. Value States govern the condition of value. Over-Differentiation Risk Excessive differentiation may fragment one meaningful Value Object into artificial pieces. This can obscure: integration value; network effects; system capability; relational value; composite performance; coordinated value creation. VODM therefore requires differentiation to have a material value-lifecycle basis. Under-Differentiation Risk Insufficient differentiation may combine materially different Value Objects. This can conceal: independent value states; degradation; zero-value conditions; restoration potential; lifecycle differences; component-level extinction; independent value origins. VODM therefore governs both: over-differentiation and under-differentiation. VODM Boundary with VOIM VOIM identifies the Value Object. VODM determines whether identified or bounded objects must remain methodologically distinct from other objects or components. Therefore: Identification ≠ Differentiation VODM Boundary with VOBM VOBM establishes what belongs inside or outside a Value Object Boundary. VODM establishes whether elements inside, between, or adjacent to those boundaries require separate Value Object governance. Therefore: Boundary ≠ Differentiation A component may be inside a composite boundary and simultaneously be a differentiated Value Object. VODM Boundary with Value Context VODM determines object separation. The subsequent context function determines the conditions under which the differentiated object enters value analysis. Therefore: Object Differentiation ≠ Value Context VODM Boundary with CLA™ VODM does not establish a universal classification system. It distinguishes Value Objects only to the extent necessary for value lifecycle governance. CLA™ governs formal classification structures, criteria, decisions, lifecycle, registry, and assurance. Therefore: Differentiation ≠ Classification VODM Boundary with OBIDENITY® VODM does not determine: identity ownership; legal ownership; authority; permission; provenance; transfer rights. OBIDENITY® governs those spaces. A single identity may contain multiple Value Objects. Multiple identities may participate in one relational or composite Value Object. VODM Boundary with GOA™ GOA™ governs governance structure and governance boundaries. VODM governs differentiation of Value Objects for value lifecycle purposes. Therefore: Governance Separation ≠ Value Object Differentiation VODM Boundary with ORA™ ORA™ governs Operational Reality. VODM may use operational distinctions as evidence that Value Objects differ, but it does not govern operational execution or operational-state separation. VODM Boundary with INTEGROS® INTEGROS® governs integrity. VODM does not determine whether a differentiated object possesses integrity. It determines only whether the object should remain separately governable within the value lifecycle. VODM Boundary with VALIDOS® VODM establishes methodological differentiation. VALIDOS® may validate claims concerning whether a differentiation basis is sufficiently supported where formal validation is required. Therefore: Differentiation Determination ≠ Validation Determination VODM Boundary with ADIT® ADIT® may provide evidence concerning components, configurations, relationships, historical changes, or other facts relevant to differentiation. VODM governs what those distinctions mean for Value Object separation. Evidence of Difference ≠ Differentiation Governance Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum VODM implementation should establish: 1. Bounded Value Object Input Receive the bounded Value Object from VOBM. 2. Differentiation Purpose Define why differentiation is required. 3. Differentiation Candidates Identify objects, components, capabilities, relationships, functions, or configurations potentially requiring separate governance. 4. Material Difference Assessment Determine whether differences are material to the value lifecycle. 5. Value-Lifecycle Independence Test Assess whether candidate objects may possess materially independent value origins, states, transitions, degradation, restoration, or extinction. 6. Composite / Component Assessment Determine whether component and composite Value Objects must coexist. 7. Relational & Capability Assessment Determine whether relationships or capabilities constitute independently governable Value Objects. 8. Configuration & Temporal Assessment Determine whether configuration or time creates materially distinct Value Objects. 9. Differentiation Determination Establish which objects remain integrated and which must remain distinct. 10. Differentiation State Assign a governed differentiation state. 11. Differentiation Record Document the basis, conditions, uncertainty, relationships, and resulting Value Object structure. Governance Outputs VODM may produce: Value Object Differentiation Record Value Object Differentiation Statement Differentiation Candidate Register Material Difference Assessment Value-Lifecycle Independence Assessment Component Differentiation Record Composite Value Object Structure Capability Differentiation Record Relational Differentiation Record Configuration Differentiation Record Temporal Differentiation Record Integrated Value Object Determination Differentiation Uncertainty Record Value Object Differentiation State Differentiated Value Object Structure These outputs provide the governed object structure required for the remaining Value Identification functions and subsequent VFM® standards. Enterprise Application VODM addresses a fundamental problem in valuation, accounting, taxation, investment, asset management, public finance, infrastructure, digital systems, and economic analysis: before value can be governed, it must be clear whether analysts are talking about one Value Object or several different Value Objects. Consider an industrial site containing: Land + Building + Machinery + Software + Intellectual Property + Production Capability + Energy Access + Customer Relationships A conventional analysis may treat all of these as one asset. Another may treat each separately. A third may recognize both individual component value and an additional integrated production capability. VODM provides a methodology for deciding which distinctions must remain explicit. This becomes particularly important when: one component degrades while others remain valuable; one capability reaches zero value; one relationship disappears; a component can be sold independently; integration creates additional value; a configuration change creates a new capability; value is restored only to part of the system; one Value Object becomes extinct while another survives. Without differentiation, later value governance may assign a value event to the wrong object. VODM therefore establishes the methodological separation necessary before VFM® begins governing the origin, emergence, recognition, state, change, development, degradation, nullification, restoration, and extinction of value. Foundational Principles Value governance requires knowing not only what the Value Object is, but what must remain distinct from it. Similarity does not establish identity. Difference does not automatically require separation. Shared ownership does not create one Value Object. Shared dependency does not create one Value Object. A component may belong to a composite Value Object while simultaneously possessing its own value lifecycle. A composite Value Object may possess value that does not exist independently in its components. Value-lifecycle independence is a primary basis for Value Object differentiation. Over-differentiation can destroy the visibility of composite value. Under-differentiation can conceal independent value states and transitions. Differentiation is not classification. Differentiation State is not Value State. A zero-value condition must attach to the correct Value Object. Value restoration must identify exactly which Value Object is being restored. Canonical Closing Statement Value Object Differentiation Module establishes the third methodological control point of the Value Identification Standard by determining which bounded objects, components, capabilities, relationships, functions, configurations, and temporally distinct forms must remain separate for their value lifecycles to be governed consistently. Through governance of material difference, Value-Lifecycle Independence, component and composite structures, functional and capability distinctions, relational objects, configuration and temporal differentiation, integration, uncertainty, and differentiation states, VODM prevents materially different Value Objects from being collapsed into one analytical object while preventing one meaningful Value Object from being fragmented without methodological justification. By separating differentiation from identity, ownership, classification, validation, integrity, audit, operational reality, and value state, VODM establishes the object structure upon which subsequent VFM® governance can operate. Before value origin, emergence, recognition, state, change, development, degradation, nullification, restoration, or extinction can be attributed correctly, it must first be clear whether the value lifecycle belongs to one Value Object, one of its components, a relationship, a capability, a configuration, or the composite object created through their integration. title: Value Object Identification Module (VOIM)
text: Value Object Identification Module (VOIM) Value Object Identification Module (VOIM) Value Object Identification Module (VOIM) Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture Parent Standard: Value Identification Standard (VIS) Module: VOIM — Value Object Identification Module Operational Layer: Value Object Identification Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Value Object Identification Origin ID: VFM-VIS-VOIM-001.1 Version: 1.0 Status: Draft · Open Standard Effective Date: 23 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · AGA™ · INTEGROS® · CLA™ · ADIT® · VALIDOS® · SIMULOS® · OBIDENITY® AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Value Object Identification Module (VOIM) is the first Core Module of the Value Identification Standard (VIS) within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture. VOIM governs the methodological identification of the precise Value Object whose value is to be governed through the value lifecycle. The Module establishes whether a sufficiently identifiable object, capability, resource, activity, relationship, right, condition, information object, physical object, digital object, service, process, outcome, opportunity, or other governable subject exists to serve as the reference object to which value may relate. VOIM separates three concepts that must not be treated as equivalent: Underlying Object ≠ Value Object ≠ Value An underlying object may exist without becoming relevant to a particular value lifecycle. A Value Object is the explicitly identified subject in relation to which value is being examined. Value itself is the governed phenomenon whose lifecycle VFM® subsequently governs. VOIM does not determine whether the identified Value Object actually possesses value, how much value exists, where that value originated, or whether value has yet emerged. Its foundational task is narrower: to establish exactly what the value lifecycle is about before any determination concerning value origin, emergence, recognition, state, change, development, degradation, nullification, restoration, or extinction is made. Core Question What exactly is the Value Object whose value lifecycle is to be governed? Architectural Position VOIM is the first Core Module of the first Parent Standard of VFM®. It therefore establishes the initial methodological entry point into the complete value lifecycle. Before VFM® asks: Where does value originate? it must first know: What is the object in relation to which value is being examined? The sequence begins: Potential Value-Relevant Subject → Value Object Candidate → Identification Basis → Value Object Determination → Governable Value Object The identified Value Object can then proceed through the remaining modules of the Value Identification Standard before entering Value Origin Standard. Internal Flow Position Potential Value-Relevant Subject → Value Object Candidate Identification → Object Reference Definition → Object Type Determination → Object Distinguishability Assessment → Object Context Identification → Object Version / State Reference → Value Object Determination → Value Object Identifier → Governable Value Object → Value Object Boundary Module Operational Space VOIM governs the space between: something that may be relevant to value and a sufficiently identified Value Object capable of entering governed value analysis. This operational space includes: Value Object Candidate identification; object reference; object distinguishability; object type; object form; object configuration; object version; object temporal reference; object contextual reference; composite-object identification; component-object identification; relationship-object identification; capability identification; activity identification; process identification; outcome identification; opportunity identification; Value Object determination; Value Object identifier; Value Object traceability. Value Object Concept For VFM®, a Value Object is: a sufficiently identifiable and distinguishable subject in relation to which a specific value lifecycle may be governed. A Value Object may be tangible or intangible. It may be persistent or temporary. It may already exist physically or digitally, or represent a sufficiently defined capability, relationship, opportunity, activity, process, or outcome. Examples may include: land; buildings; machinery; raw materials; infrastructure; energy capacity; software; algorithms; datasets; intellectual property; patents; licenses; contractual rights; services; skills; capabilities; processes; production capacity; organizations; projects; relationships; access rights; information; knowledge; opportunities; environmental resources; digital assets; operational capabilities; future sufficiently defined value-bearing subjects. The list is intentionally non-exhaustive. VFM® must remain capable of governing value associated with forms of objects that do not yet exist today. Underlying Object ≠ Value Object An object does not automatically become a Value Object merely because it exists. Consider a building. The underlying object may be: Building A But different value inquiries may concern: Building A as operational production capacity Building A as rentable space Building A as redevelopment potential Building A as material recovery potential Building A as strategic location The physical object may be the same. The Value Object reference may differ according to what exactly is entering the governed value lifecycle. VOIM therefore prevents the existence of an underlying object from being mistaken for sufficient identification of the Value Object. Value Object ≠ Value This distinction is foundational to VFM®. Value Object answers: What is the subject whose value lifecycle is being examined? Value answers a different question: What value exists, originates, emerges, changes, develops, degrades, disappears, returns, or becomes extinct in relation to that subject? A machine may be identifiable even where its economic use has disappeared. A patent may remain identifiable even where its commercial value reaches zero. A dataset may remain identifiable while its value changes across different contexts. Therefore: Object existence does not establish value existence. And: Value Object identification does not constitute Value Recognition. Value Object Candidate Before formal identification, a potential subject enters VOIM as a Value Object Candidate. A Value Object Candidate is: a subject proposed for entry into VFM® because a value lifecycle may exist in relation to it. Candidate status does not establish: value existence; value origin; value emergence; positive value; market value; financial value; legal value; ownership; validity; integrity; classification; price; monetary amount. It establishes only that the subject requires examination as a possible Value Object. Identification Basis Every Value Object should have a sufficient Identification Basis. Depending on the object, this may include: name; reference number; physical description; digital identifier; location reference; technical configuration; version; temporal state; component structure; process definition; capability definition; relationship definition; contractual reference; project reference; dataset reference; asset reference; other sufficiently distinguishing characteristics. The identification basis must be sufficient to answer: Which exact object are we talking about? Object Type VOIM may classify the basic identification form of the Value Object for methodological navigation. Examples may include: Physical Object Digital Object Information Object Capability Resource Activity Process Service Right Relationship Opportunity Outcome Composite Object Other Governable Value Object These are identification forms rather than universal economic classifications. Formal classification governance remains within CLA™ — Classification Architecture where required. Object Distinguishability Principle A Value Object must be sufficiently distinguishable from other objects to permit its value lifecycle to be governed. The object need not always be physically separable. It must be methodologically distinguishable. For example: a production line may be identifiable as one Value Object even though it contains hundreds of physical components. Likewise: production capacity may constitute a Value Object even though the capability arises from a combination of machinery, people, processes, energy, knowledge, and infrastructure. The requirement is not physical isolation. The requirement is: sufficient distinction for value governance. Composite Value Objects A Value Object may consist of multiple components. Examples include: an industrial facility; an infrastructure network; a business unit; a technology platform; a production system; a portfolio; an integrated capability. VOIM must identify when the value inquiry concerns: the composite object rather than merely the sum of its individual components. This distinction matters because: Value of Composite Object ≠ Automatic Sum of Component Values Interactions, dependencies, complementarities, constraints, network effects, configuration, and context may produce a different value lifecycle at the composite level. Component Value Objects A component of a larger object may itself become a separate Value Object where its value lifecycle requires independent governance. Therefore: Object A may contain: Value Object A.1 Value Object A.2 Value Object A.3 while the complete system may simultaneously constitute: Value Object A Each lifecycle must remain distinguishable. Multiple Values Associated with One Object A single underlying object may support multiple distinct value lifecycles. For example, a forest may carry: timber value; carbon-related value; ecological value; recreational value; water-regulation value; strategic land value. VOIM must therefore avoid assuming: One Object = One Value Instead: One Object → Potentially Multiple Distinct Value Relationships The subsequent modules and Parent Standards determine how those value relationships are bounded and governed. Same Value Across Multiple Objects Conversely, one value phenomenon may depend upon multiple underlying objects. For example: network value may arise from the interaction of many participants. production capability may depend upon machinery, workforce, infrastructure, knowledge, and supply access. VOIM must therefore support identification of: Composite Value Objects and Relational Value Objects where the relevant subject cannot legitimately be reduced to one isolated physical asset. Value Object Context Identification may require contextual information where the same object can function differently across environments. Context may include: intended use; operational environment; economic environment; temporal period; technological environment; organizational context; geographic context; dependency context; relationship context. VOIM identifies relevant context necessary to distinguish the object. It does not yet determine the value produced by that context. Temporal Identification A Value Object may change over time. Therefore, identification should establish the relevant temporal reference where material. For example: Factory X — Configuration 2024 may not represent the same Value Object state as: Factory X — Configuration 2026 after automation upgrade. VOIM must preserve enough temporal distinction to prevent value analysis performed on materially different object states from being silently combined. Version and Configuration Awareness For digital, technological, industrial, organizational, or composite Value Objects, version and configuration may materially affect identification. Relevant distinctions may include: software version; model version; machinery configuration; infrastructure configuration; organizational structure; production configuration; contractual configuration; dataset version; capability state. VOIM does not govern configuration integrity. It ensures only that the object being subjected to value governance is sufficiently identifiable. Potential Value ≠ Existing Value VOIM may identify a Value Object even where value has not yet emerged. This is essential for the VFM® lifecycle. A newly discovered technology may be identifiable. A development site may be identifiable. An unused patent may be identifiable. An unexploited resource may be identifiable. A future production capability may be identifiable. None of this automatically means that value already exists. Therefore: Value Object Identification → does not imply → Value Emergence This preserves the boundary with later VFM® Parent Standards. Zero Value Does Not Eliminate the Value Object A Value Object may remain identifiable after its relevant value reaches zero. This is critical for the later VFM® concept: ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ A zero-value condition does not necessarily mean that the underlying Value Object has ceased to exist. The object may remain identifiable while: Value State = Zero and may later enter: Value Restoration where a legitimate restoration pathway exists. Therefore: Object Extinction ≠ Value Nullification and Zero Value ≠ Value Extinction Value Object Identification State VOIM may assign a governed identification state. A minimum model may include: 1. Unidentified A potentially value-relevant subject exists, but it has not been sufficiently identified. 2. Candidate A subject has been proposed as a Value Object but requires additional identification. 3. Conditionally Identified The subject is sufficiently identifiable only under specified contextual, temporal, configuration, or relational conditions. 4. Identified The Value Object is sufficiently identified and distinguishable to proceed through VFM® governance. 5. Identification Suspended A previously identified Value Object has materially changed or contains unresolved ambiguity requiring reassessment. 6. Identification Retired The identification reference is no longer active for the governed value lifecycle but is preserved for traceability. These states govern identification only. They do not describe value state. Identification State ≠ Value State VOIM enforces: Value Object Identification State ≠ Value State An object may be: Identified while its value is: unknown, emerging, positive, degraded, zero, restored, or extinct. The two governance dimensions must remain separate. VOIM Boundary with Value Object Boundary Module VOIM answers: What is the Value Object? The Value Object Boundary Module answers: Where does that Value Object begin and end for the relevant value lifecycle? Identification precedes boundary determination. A subject cannot be meaningfully bounded before it is sufficiently identified. VOIM Boundary with Value Differentiation & Separation Module VOIM identifies the subject. The Value Differentiation & Separation Module determines whether multiple value phenomena, objects, components, or value relationships must remain analytically separate. Therefore: Identification ≠ Differentiation. VOIM Boundary with Value Context & Condition Module VOIM may record context necessary to identify the object. The Value Context & Condition Module governs the broader conditions under which the identified Value Object is being examined for value purposes. Therefore: Identification Context ≠ Value Context Governance. VOIM Boundary with Value Origin Standard VOIM identifies: what the value lifecycle concerns. The Value Origin Standard determines: where the relevant value originates. Therefore: Value Object ≠ Value Origin and: Identification ≠ Origin Determination. VOIM Boundary with Value Emergence Standard VOIM does not determine whether value has actually come into existence. That belongs to the Value Emergence Standard. A Value Object may be fully identified while no value has yet emerged. VOIM Boundary with Value Recognition Standard VOIM does not recognize value. It identifies the object to which a possible value lifecycle relates. Therefore: Object Identification ≠ Value Recognition. VOIM Boundary with CLA™ VOIM may establish an identification type necessary to distinguish a Value Object. It does not replace formal classification governance. Where formal classification is required: CLA™ — Classification Architecture governs classification. VOIM Boundary with OBIDENITY® VOIM does not determine: legal identity; ownership; authority; permission; responsibility; provenance rights; transfer rights. Where origin-bound identity governance is required, those questions remain within OBIDENITY® — Origin-Bound Identity Governance Architecture. A Value Object may be identified for value governance without VFM® determining who owns it. VOIM Boundary with VALIDOS® VOIM does not determine whether the Value Object or any claim concerning it is valid. VALIDOS® — Validation Governance Architecture governs validation. Identification is a prerequisite for many validation activities but does not constitute validation. VOIM Boundary with INTEGROS® VOIM does not determine whether the Value Object possesses integrity. INTEGROS® — Integrity Governance Architecture governs integrity. An object can be sufficiently identified even while its integrity remains unknown or impaired. VOIM Boundary with ADIT® VOIM establishes the methodological identity of the Value Object for value governance. ADIT® — Continuous Audit & Evidence Governance Architecture may govern evidence and auditability concerning that identification and subsequent events. Identification ≠ Audit Evidence. Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum VOIM implementation should establish: 1. Value Object Candidate Identify the subject proposed for value governance. 2. Object Reference Establish the primary reference through which the subject can be distinguished. 3. Object Form Determine whether the subject is physical, digital, informational, relational, capability-based, process-based, composite, or another governable form. 4. Distinguishability Determine whether the subject can be sufficiently distinguished from adjacent objects or subjects. 5. Context Reference Record contextual information necessary for identification. 6. Temporal Reference Establish the relevant time or lifecycle reference where material. 7. Version / Configuration Identify the relevant version or configuration where material. 8. Composite / Component Relationship Record whether the Value Object forms part of, contains, or depends upon other Value Objects. 9. Identification State Assign the governed Value Object Identification State. 10. Value Object Identifier Create or associate a stable reference enabling the Value Object to remain traceable through the VFM® lifecycle. Governance Outputs VOIM may produce: Value Object Candidate Record Value Object Identification Record Value Object Reference Value Object Type Record Value Object Context Reference Value Object Temporal Reference Value Object Version Record Value Object Configuration Reference Composite Value Object Relationship Record Component Value Object Relationship Record Value Object Identification State Value Object Identifier Governable Value Object These outputs provide the governed input for the next module: Value Object Boundary Module. Enterprise Application VOIM gives organizations a foundational capability that is often missing from conventional valuation and economic systems: the ability to establish exactly what is being treated as the subject of value before value is measured, priced, recognized, changed, taxed, impaired, restored, or transferred. This becomes especially important where value does not map cleanly onto a conventional asset. An organization may use VOIM to identify value objects such as: unused production capacity; data; algorithms; intellectual property; infrastructure capability; technological potential; resource access; contractual opportunities; network relationships; dormant assets; recovered materials; digital capabilities; environmental resources; composite operational systems. VOIM can therefore expose a fundamental error before it propagates through later analysis: different parties may appear to disagree about value when they are actually assigning value to different Value Objects. By making the Value Object explicit first, VFM® creates a stable reference for the entire downstream value lifecycle. Foundational Principles Value cannot be governed coherently until the subject of that value is identified. Underlying Object ≠ Value Object ≠ Value. Object existence does not establish value existence. Value Object identification does not establish value recognition. One underlying object may support multiple distinct value lifecycles. One Value Object may consist of multiple underlying objects. A Value Object may remain identifiable when its value reaches zero. Potential value is not existing value. Identification state is not value state. Ownership is not required to identify a Value Object. Price is not required to identify a Value Object. A governable value lifecycle requires a sufficiently identifiable subject to which that lifecycle can remain anchored. Canonical Closing Statement Value Object Identification Module establishes the first methodological control point of VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture by determining exactly what subject enters the governed value lifecycle as a Value Object. Through governance of Value Object Candidates, identification basis, object reference, distinguishability, object form, contextual reference, temporal reference, version and configuration awareness, composite and component relationships, identification states, and stable Value Object identifiers, VOIM prevents value governance from beginning with an ambiguous or undefined subject. By explicitly separating the underlying object from the Value Object and the Value Object from value itself, VOIM preserves the methodological boundaries between identification, value origin, value emergence, value recognition, value state, ownership, classification, validation, integrity, and audit. VFM® can therefore begin the lifecycle of value from a precise foundational question: before asking where value comes from, how it changes, whether it reaches zero, whether it can be restored, or when it becomes extinct, first establish exactly what the value is about. title: Value Identification Standard (VIS)
text: Value Identification Standard (VIS) Value Identification Standard (VIS) Value Identification Standard (VIS) Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture Parent Standard: Value Identification Standard (VIS) Operational Layer: Value Identification Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Type: Parent Standard Governed Space: Value Identification Origin ID: VFM-VIS-001 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 23 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · AGA™ · INTEGROS® · CLA™ · ADIT® · VALIDOS® · SIMULOS® · OBIDENITY® AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Value Identification Standard (VIS) is the first Parent Standard within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture and governs the methodological conditions under which a potential or existing manifestation of value can be identified, distinguished, bounded, described, and established as a governable Value Object within the value lifecycle. VIS establishes the first governance point of VFM®. Before value can be traced to an origin, recognized as having emerged, assigned a state, observed for change, developed, degraded, nullified, restored, or determined to have reached extinction, the subject whose value is being governed must first be identifiable. VIS therefore establishes the governed relationship between: Potential Value Phenomenon → Value Candidate → Value Identification → Value Object The Standard does not determine how much something is worth. It does not determine whether a market recognizes it, whether it is legally owned, whether it is taxable, whether it has been validated, or whether its integrity has been established. Its task is more fundamental: to determine what value is being referred to and whether that value can be sufficiently identified to enter a governed value lifecycle. Core Question What value is being governed, and how can it be sufficiently identified and bounded before its origin, existence, state, and lifecycle are determined? Architectural Position Value Identification is the first governed space of VFM®. It precedes: Value Origin Standard and therefore establishes the object required for all subsequent value governance. The architectural sequence begins: Value Identification → Value Origin → Value Emergence → Value Recognition → Value State → Value Change → Value Development → Value Degradation → Value Nullification → Value Restoration → Value Extinction VIS asks: What value are we talking about? Only after that question has been sufficiently answered can the architecture ask: Where does that value originate? This distinction is foundational. Identification ≠ Origin. Something may be identified as a candidate for value governance before its actual value origin has been established. Governance Flow Position Potential Value Phenomenon → Value Candidate Identification → Value Object Definition → Value Boundary Determination → Value Context Identification → Value Distinction → Value Identification State → Governed Value Object → Value Origin Governance Operational Space VIS governs the methodological space between: an observed, proposed, inferred, expected, claimed, or potentially relevant manifestation of value and: an explicitly identified Value Object capable of entering the VFM® lifecycle. This space includes: Value Candidate identification; Value Object identification; value-reference definition; value boundary determination; value context; value distinction; value manifestation; value subject; value relationship; value dependency awareness; value aggregation awareness; value decomposition; value identification state; identification uncertainty; identification documentation; identification reassessment. Value Candidate A Value Candidate is an object, capability, condition, relationship, activity, outcome, resource, right, information object, process, state, opportunity, or other phenomenon proposed for examination within the VFM® value lifecycle. Identification as a Value Candidate does not establish that value exists. Therefore: Value Candidate ≠ Existing Value The purpose of the concept is to permit governance to begin before value existence has been determined. This prevents a circular methodological problem in which something must already be accepted as valuable before its value can be investigated. Value Object A Value Object is the explicitly identified and bounded subject whose value lifecycle is governed through VFM®. A Value Object may relate to: a physical asset; a digital asset; intellectual property; information; data; a capability; infrastructure; technology; a service; a process; an activity; an opportunity; access; capacity; a relationship; a contractual position; a productive resource; a natural resource; an economic resource; an organizational capability; a computational capability; an energy resource; a future capability; another sufficiently identifiable value-bearing or potentially value-bearing phenomenon. VFM® does not require the Value Object to be a legally recognized asset. It requires the object of value governance to be methodologically identifiable. Value Object ≠ Asset Identity VIS must not be confused with identity governance. A Value Object may reference an asset, entity, resource, or capability whose identity is governed elsewhere. VIS asks: What is the subject of value governance? OBIDENITY® may ask: What is the governed identity and origin-bound identity relationship of the relevant entity or asset? These questions may interact. They are not the same governance space. Value Identification ≠ Value Recognition This distinction is critical to VFM®. Value Identification establishes: what value or potential value is being examined. Value Recognition establishes: whether existing value may be recognized within the governed value lifecycle. Something can therefore be: identified without yet being: recognized as existing value. This allows VFM® to examine dormant, uncertain, emerging, disputed, unrealized, inaccessible, latent, degraded, or potentially recoverable value without assuming the conclusion in advance. Value Identification ≠ Valuation VIS does not determine monetary worth. It does not assign: price; market value; fair value; accounting value; taxable value; liquidation value; replacement value; investment value; economic value. Those determinations may be performed by external methodologies. VIS establishes the object to which such determinations may later relate. Therefore: Identification of Value ≠ Measurement of Value. Value Identification ≠ Value Existence Identification does not prove that value exists. A Value Candidate may enter VFM® and subsequently be determined not to have reached Value Emergence. This distinction enables VFM® to govern: potential value without automatically declaring: existent value. Value Boundary Every Value Object requires a sufficiently explicit Value Boundary. The Value Boundary determines what is included in the Value Object being governed and what remains outside it. A boundary may be: physical; functional; temporal; relational; informational; operational; economic; contextual; capability-based; resource-based; outcome-based; composite. Without a boundary, changes in value cannot be reliably attributed to the same governed Value Object. Boundary Stability A Value Boundary need not remain permanently unchanged. However, material boundary change must remain visible. Examples include: assets being combined; assets being divided; capabilities being added; rights being removed; operational scope changing; data being incorporated; infrastructure being separated; relationships being terminated; previously separate value objects becoming interdependent. A materially changed Value Object may require re-identification. Value Context Value does not necessarily exist independently of context. VIS therefore permits the identification of a relevant Value Context. Context may include: intended use; user; beneficiary; operational environment; time; location; availability; scarcity; dependency; technological environment; economic environment; organizational environment; physical conditions. VIS does not determine whether those contextual factors create value. It preserves them so that subsequent VFM® standards can determine their relevance. Value Distinction VIS requires distinguishable Value Objects where different value lifecycles exist. For example, one physical object may contain: material value; functional value; information value; intellectual-property value; productive value; strategic value; recovery value. These must not automatically be treated as one indivisible value phenomenon. Where materially different value lifecycles exist, they may require separate Value Objects or explicitly defined value dimensions. Composite Value Objects VFM® may govern composite Value Objects. A composite Value Object consists of multiple components whose combined configuration produces a relevant value relationship. VIS requires the composite basis to remain identifiable. This allows VFM® to distinguish: component value from: value arising from combination. Latent Value A Value Candidate may contain conditions capable of producing future value even where value has not yet emerged. VIS allows this to be identified without prematurely declaring value existence. This creates an important pathway: Value Candidate → Identified Potential → Value Origin → Value Emergence Latent value is therefore not automatically an existing Value Asset. Value Identification State VIS establishes governed identification states. A minimum state model may include: 1. Unidentified A potential value phenomenon is observable or suspected but has not been sufficiently defined for governance. 2. Candidate Identified A Value Candidate has been identified but its Value Object boundary or context remains insufficiently established. 3. Conditionally Identified The Value Object can be identified only under explicit conditions, assumptions, boundaries, or unresolved dependencies. 4. Identified The Value Object is sufficiently defined, bounded, distinguished, and contextualized to enter Value Origin governance. 5. Identification Suspended A material change or unresolved inconsistency prevents continued reliance upon the current identification. 6. Re-identification Required The Value Object has changed sufficiently that the existing identification can no longer support the subsequent lifecycle without reassessment. These states govern identification only. They do not establish value existence or worth. Identification Uncertainty VIS requires material uncertainty concerning Value Object identity or boundary to remain visible. Uncertainty may concern: what is included; what is excluded; whether multiple value objects exist; whether value is separable; whether a relationship is material; whether a capability exists independently; whether the relevant object has changed; whether context fundamentally changes the object being governed. Uncertainty does not always prevent identification. It may require conditional identification. No Presumed Value Principle VFM® must not assume value merely because something has been presented as valuable. VIS therefore establishes: Identification for Value Governance ≠ Confirmation of Value A claimed valuable asset may be admitted as a Value Candidate. Subsequent VFM® governance may determine that value: has not emerged; existed previously but has degraded; has reached zero; remains recoverable; has become extinct. This preserves methodological neutrality. Value Granularity Identification must occur at a granularity appropriate to the governance question. An organization may be examined as: one Value Object for one purpose, while its: intellectual property; machinery; datasets; production capability; contracts; customer relationships; technological capabilities may each become separate Value Objects for another purpose. VFM® therefore does not impose one universal level of value granularity. Temporal Identity of Value The identity of a Value Object may persist while its value state changes. For example: Positive Value → Degradation → Zero Value → Restoration may occur without the underlying Value Object ceasing to be identifiable. This distinction is essential for ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™. A Value Object can remain identifiable even when its admissible value reaches zero. Therefore: Loss of Value ≠ Loss of Value Object Identity. Relationship to Origin Asset™ Origin Asset™ belongs primarily to the subsequent Value Origin governed space. VIS identifies the Value Object. Value Origin governance then determines the source, basis, capability, condition, relationship, or other origin from which its value may emerge. Therefore: Value Object Identification → Value Origin Determination → Origin Asset™ relationship where applicable. VIS must not presume an Origin Asset™ before the origin relationship has been established. Relationship to Value Asset™ A Value Object does not automatically become a Value Asset™. Value Asset™ represents a value-bearing state where the relevant conditions have been established through subsequent VFM® governance. Therefore: Value Object ≠ Value Asset™ A Value Object is the governed subject. Value Asset™ describes an applicable value-bearing state. Relationship to ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ VIS also preserves the identity required for zero-value governance. A ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ cannot be meaningfully governed unless the underlying Value Object remains identifiable. Therefore, when value reaches zero: Value State may change while Value Object identity persists. This enables the later sequence: Value Asset™ → DeMonet™ → ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ → ReMonet™ → restored Value State without losing continuity of the governed Value Object. Cross-Architecture Boundaries VIS ↔ OBIDENITY® OBIDENITY® governs origin-bound identity, ownership, authority, permission, responsibility, provenance, transfer, continuity, and auditability. VIS governs identification of the subject of value governance. Identity Governance ≠ Value Identification. VIS ↔ CLA™ CLA™ governs how classifications are formally established and maintained. VIS may later consume a governed classification where useful. It does not become a general classification architecture. VIS ↔ VALIDOS® VALIDOS® governs whether validation claims can legitimately be established and relied upon. VIS does not validate value. It identifies the Value Object to which subsequent value governance applies. Value Identification ≠ Value Validation. VIS ↔ INTEGROS® INTEGROS® governs integrity. VIS may require sufficient structural coherence to identify a Value Object but does not determine its general integrity. VIS ↔ ADIT® ADIT® governs audit and evidence. VIS may generate identification records that become auditable evidence. It does not govern auditability itself. VIS ↔ GOA™ GOA™ governs governance authority, boundaries, scope, delegation, accountability, validation, integrity, transparency, continuity, and interoperability. VIS governs the Value Object. It does not establish governance authority over that object. VIS ↔ ORA™ ORA™ governs actual Operational Reality. Operational conditions may help establish the context in which a Value Object exists. VIS does not govern Operational Reality itself. Parent Standard Modules 1. VCIM — Value Candidate Identification Module Governs identification of a potential value phenomenon as a Value Candidate without presuming that value already exists. Core Question: What phenomenon should enter the value lifecycle for governed examination? 2. VOIM — Value Object Identification Module Governs establishment of the specific Value Object whose value lifecycle will be governed. Core Question: What precisely is the subject of value governance? 3. VOBM — Value Object Boundary Module Governs the inclusion, exclusion, extent, granularity, and boundary of the Value Object. Core Question: Where does the governed Value Object begin and end? 4. VCXM — Value Context Module Governs identification of the material context within which the Value Object is being examined. Core Question: Within what context is the identified Value Object entering value governance? 5. VISM — Value Identification State Module Governs assignment, maintenance, suspension, and reassessment of the Value Identification State. Core Question: Has the Value Object been sufficiently identified to proceed into Value Origin governance? Internal Module Flow Potential Value Phenomenon → VCIM — Value Candidate Identification Module → VOIM — Value Object Identification Module → VOBM — Value Object Boundary Module → VCXM — Value Context Module → VISM — Value Identification State Module → Governed Value Object → Value Origin Standard The internal logic is: What may contain or represent value → what precisely is being governed → where its boundary lies → within what context it is examined → whether identification is sufficient to continue. Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum VIS implementation should establish: 1. Value Candidate Identify the phenomenon proposed for value governance. 2. Value Object Define the precise subject whose value lifecycle will be governed. 3. Value Boundary Determine what is included and excluded. 4. Value Granularity Determine the appropriate level at which the Value Object is governed. 5. Value Context Identify materially relevant contextual conditions. 6. Value Distinction Separate materially different Value Objects or value dimensions where required. 7. Dependency Awareness Identify dependencies capable of affecting the interpretation of the Value Object. 8. Identification Uncertainty Record unresolved uncertainty affecting identification or boundaries. 9. Identification State Assign a governed Value Identification State. 10. Identification Record Create a reconstructable record of the basis on which the Value Object was identified. Governance Outputs VIS may produce: Value Candidate Record Value Object Record Value Object Definition Value Boundary Statement Value Inclusion Record Value Exclusion Record Value Granularity Record Value Context Record Value Distinction Record Value Dependency Record Value Identification Uncertainty Record Value Identification State Value Re-identification Trigger Governed Value Object These outputs provide the governed input for the Value Origin Standard. Enterprise Application VIS enables organizations to answer a deceptively difficult question: What exactly are we calling value? This matters because organizations frequently aggregate fundamentally different phenomena under one financial or operational label. A company may say: “This asset is worth CHF 10 million.” But that apparent single value may depend upon: physical property; productive capacity; intellectual property; access rights; customer relationships; contractual rights; data; technology; scarcity; expected future capability. VIS allows those value phenomena to be identified and bounded before their origins, emergence, states, changes, degradation, nullification, or restoration are governed. The same method can be applied to: public assets; infrastructure; corporate assets; intellectual property; digital assets; technology; data; energy resources; natural resources; productive capability; government programs; investment projects; abandoned assets; dormant assets; impaired assets; future technologies; AI-created capabilities. This makes VIS relevant not only to conventional accounting contexts but also to value phenomena that conventional accounting systems may not yet represent effectively. Why This Matters for Future Value Systems A value-based accounting, economic, public-finance, or taxation methodology cannot begin reliably with: How much is it worth? It must first establish: What exactly is the Value Object? Then: Where does its value originate? Then: Has value actually emerged? Then: What state is that value in? Only afterward can external accounting, measurement, economic, or taxation systems determine how that governed value should be treated. VFM® therefore creates a methodological value layer that can potentially operate beneath multiple downstream systems without becoming those systems itself. Foundational Principles Value cannot be governed until the subject of value governance is identifiable. Value identification does not presume value existence. Value identification is not valuation. Value identification is not value recognition. Value Object identity is distinct from asset identity. A Value Candidate may exist before value emerges. A Value Object may remain identifiable after its value reaches zero. Loss of value does not necessarily mean loss of the Value Object. Different value phenomena within one asset may require different governed Value Objects. The boundary of the Value Object determines the boundary of the value lifecycle being governed. Before asking how value changes, VFM® must first establish what value is being governed. Canonical Closing Statement Value Identification Standard establishes the first governed space of VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture by creating the methodological conditions under which potential or existing manifestations of value can be identified, distinguished, bounded, contextualized, and established as governed Value Objects without presuming value existence, recognition, validity, price, ownership, legality, or economic treatment. Through governance of Value Candidates, Value Objects, boundaries, granularity, context, distinctions, dependencies, uncertainty, identification states, and re-identification, VIS creates the stable reference object required for the complete downstream value lifecycle. By separating value identification from asset identity, classification, validation, valuation, recognition, and value state, VIS preserves the architectural boundaries of VFM® and complementary OOF® architectures while establishing the foundation required for Value Origin governance. Before value can emerge, change, develop, degrade, reach zero, be restored, or become extinct, the value being governed must first be identifiable. Nahlad Value Identification Standard (VIS) Architecture: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture · Category: Governance & Enforcement · Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Canonical Definition: Value Identification Standard governs how potential or existing manifestations of value are identified, distinguished, bounded, contextualized, and established as governable Value Objects before their origin, existence, state, change, or lifecycle can be determined.
