title: Value Nullification Standard (VNS)
text: Value Nullification Standard (VNS) Value Nullification Standard (VNS) Value Nullification Standard (VNS) Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture Parent Standard: Value Nullification Standard (VNS) Operational Layer: Value Nullification Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Type: Parent Standard Governed Space: Value Nullification Origin ID: VFM-VNS-009 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 27 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · OBIDENITY® AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language Canonical Definition Value Nullification Standard (VNS) is the Parent Standard within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture that governs the conditions, thresholds, mechanisms, determinations, and governed transitions through which previously existing positive value reaches a legitimate zero-value condition. VNS establishes the methodological boundary between declining value and nullified value. The Standard governs the point at which value no longer merely weakens, deteriorates, loses utility, becomes impaired, or approaches zero, but crosses a defined value boundary through which the relevant positive value ceases to exist within its governed Value Context. VNS is the architectural home of DeMonet™, the governed value-nullification mechanism through which existing positive value may transition toward a zero-value condition where the applicable nullification conditions and thresholds are satisfied. The Standard also establishes the governed relationship between a determined zero-value condition and ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™, while preserving the critical distinction between value that previously existed and was subsequently nullified, value that temporarily reaches zero, value that permanently reaches zero, and potential value that never emerged. Its foundational principle is: Value Never Emerged ≠ Value Nullified. Core Question When and through what governed transition does existing positive value reach a zero-value condition? Architectural Position VNS occupies the ninth governed space within the VFM® value lifecycle. It follows: Value Degradation Standard (VDGS) and precedes: Value Restoration Standard (VRSS). The preceding VFM® lifecycle has already governed: Value Context → Value Origin → Value Emergence → Value Recognition → Value State → Value Change → Value Development → Value Degradation VNS governs the next critical boundary: when existing positive value ceases to remain positive. The architectural transition is: Positive Value → Nullification Conditions → Nullification Threshold → DeMonet™ → Value Nullification Determination → Zero-Value Condition → ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ where applicable VNS therefore governs a boundary transition, not merely another degree of degradation. VFM® Governance Flow Position Value Context → Value Origin → Value Emergence → Value Recognition → Value State → Value Change → Value Development → Value Degradation → Value Nullification → Value Restoration → subsequent VFM® lifecycle spaces Within the Value Nullification governed space: Existing Positive Value → Nullification Condition → Nullification Threshold → DeMonet™ Mechanism → Nullification Determination → Zero-Value State Transition The output of VNS may subsequently enter: Value State Governance or, where restoration becomes possible: Value Restoration Governance. Operational Space VNS governs the transition between: positive existing value and a governed zero-value condition. Its operational space includes: nullification-condition identification; zero-value boundary definition; nullification-threshold establishment; threshold crossing; deliberate value withdrawal; degradation-to-zero; functional exhaustion; contextual nullification; temporal nullification; permanent nullification; partial or dimension-specific nullification; DeMonet™ mechanism governance; nullification determination; zero-value transition; ZVA™ state relationship; nullification provenance; distinction between nullification and non-emergence; distinction between zero value and negative consequences; restoration eligibility interface. Value Nullification Principle Value Nullification occurs only where: positive value previously existed and that value subsequently reaches a governed zero-value condition. This creates the minimum logical sequence: Positive Value existed at T₁ → material value change occurred → the applicable zero-value boundary was reached at T₂ → Value Nullification may be determined. Without previously existing value, there is nothing to nullify. Therefore: Potential Value that never emerged cannot be nullified. Value Never Emerged ≠ Value Nullified This distinction is foundational to VNS. Consider two assets. Asset A has potential commercial utility but never becomes operational, usable, recognized, or otherwise value-producing within the relevant Value Context. Its potential value never emerges. Asset B has established operational value for ten years and subsequently becomes completely unusable within the same governed Value Context. Asset B may undergo Value Nullification. Asset A does not. Therefore: Non-Emergence and Nullification represent fundamentally different value histories. VFM® must preserve that distinction. Degradation ≠ Nullification Value Degradation governs declining value while positive value remains. Value Nullification begins only where the relevant governed positive value reaches zero. Therefore: 100 → 70 → 40 → 10 remains within Value Degradation. The transition: 10 → 0 may enter Value Nullification. The architectural boundary is: Positive Value > 0 versus Zero Value = 0 where the applicable value methodology permits quantitative expression. Where value is qualitative rather than numerical, an equivalent governed threshold must establish when positive value ceases to exist. Approaching Zero ≠ Zero Severe degradation does not automatically establish nullification. An asset may retain: residual utility; residual knowledge; residual strategic significance; salvage value; recovery potential; operational capability; contextual usefulness; option value; informational value; another legitimate positive value dimension. Therefore: Near-Zero Value ≠ Zero Value. VNS requires the zero-value condition to be determined, not presumed from severity. Nullification Condition A Value Nullification Condition is a governed condition under which existing positive value may legitimately become eligible for nullification determination. Possible conditions may include: complete loss of relevant utility; total functional failure; complete contextual irrelevance; expiry of time-dependent value; exhaustion of usable value; irreversible obsolescence within the defined context; deliberate withdrawal of a value-conferring capability; destruction of the relevant value-bearing property; complete loss of accessibility where accessibility constitutes the governed value; termination of a value-conferring relationship; another defined condition capable of eliminating the relevant positive value. The presence of a condition does not automatically establish nullification. The applicable threshold must also be satisfied. Nullification Threshold The Value Nullification Threshold establishes the boundary at which the governed value dimension ceases to remain positive. The threshold may be: quantitative; qualitative; functional; temporal; contextual; contractual; operational; technological; structural; capability-based. The threshold must correspond to the defined Value Context. A universal zero-value threshold cannot be assumed across all forms of value. Threshold Crossing Principle A nullification threshold must be distinguished from proximity to that threshold. For example: Minimum Operational Capability = 5 units An asset operating at: 6 units may be critically degraded. But if the governed value remains positive above 5 units, nullification has not yet occurred. Only when the applicable threshold is crossed or satisfied may a Value Nullification Determination become possible. DeMonet™ DeMonet™ is the canonical VFM® mechanism governing the transition through which previously existing positive value is nullified into a governed zero-value condition. The canonical transition is: Positive Value → DeMonet™ → Zero-Value Condition → ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ where applicable DeMonet™ is not merely another word for: depreciation; deterioration; financial loss; market decline; destruction; impairment; write-down; devaluation; obsolescence. Those events or mechanisms may contribute to nullification. DeMonet™ governs the value transition itself. DeMonet™ ≠ Cause of Nullification The external cause of nullification may originate outside VFM®. Examples include: technological change; physical destruction; market collapse; regulatory prohibition; contract expiry; loss of access; infrastructure failure; organizational decision; scientific discovery; replacement technology; environmental change; deliberate withdrawal; another external event. VFM® does not need to own those causal systems. Its question is: What happened to the governed value as a result? DeMonet™ therefore governs the value-nullification mechanism, not necessarily the external causal mechanism. DeMonet™ ≠ Value Degradation DeMonet™ must not be applied to every reduction in value. If value changes: 100 → 80 or 80 → 20 positive value remains. That remains a Value Change and potentially Value Degradation. DeMonet™ becomes relevant when the governed transition concerns: Positive Value → Zero Value. This preserves the architectural separation between: VDGS — Value Degradation and VNS — Value Nullification. Deliberate Value Withdrawal Value Nullification may occur intentionally. An organization may deliberately withdraw or eliminate an existing value-conferring property. Examples may include: disabling a capability; terminating access; retiring a service; revoking a functional entitlement; withdrawing interoperability; destroying a value-bearing asset; intentionally eliminating commercial availability; permanently decommissioning an operational function. Where such action legitimately produces a zero-value condition within the governed Value Context, VNS may govern the resulting nullification. Therefore: Value Nullification does not require accidental loss. Degradation-to-Zero One pathway into VNS is progressive degradation. Example: 100 → 75 → 43 → 18 → 4 → 0 The stages above zero remain governed as degradation. The final boundary transition into zero is governed through VNS. This creates the interface: VDGS → VNS without collapsing the two standards into one another. Immediate Nullification Value does not always decline progressively. A single event may cause: Positive Value → Zero Value without an extended degradation phase. Examples may include: total destruction; immediate loss of essential functionality; instantaneous expiry; irreversible access termination; sudden contextual invalidation. VNS therefore does not require prior progressive degradation. It requires only that: positive value previously existed and a governed zero-value condition subsequently occurred. Temporary Zero Value A zero-value condition may be temporary. Example: A production asset loses all operational value because a critical component fails. At that moment: Operational Value = Zero. The asset may nevertheless remain repairable. After restoration: Zero Operational Value → Restored Positive Operational Value. VNS therefore distinguishes: Temporary Zero Value from Permanent Zero Value. Temporary zero remains genuine zero within the applicable context and period. Its potential reversibility does not mean the zero-value state never existed. Permanent Zero Value A zero-value condition may also be effectively permanent within the defined governance context. Examples may include: irreversible destruction; complete expiration of time-bound value; permanent loss of required capability; permanent contextual displacement; irrecoverable elimination of the relevant value-bearing property. Permanent zero must nevertheless remain context-specific. An object may have zero operational value while retaining: historical value; informational value; material recovery value; legal relevance; evidence value; research value. Therefore: Permanent Zero in one Value Context ≠ Universal Absence of All Value. Contextual Nullification Value may be nullified in one context while remaining positive in another. Example: A machine may have: Operational Production Value = 0 while retaining: Salvage Value > 0 and Historical Evidence Value > 0. VNS therefore does not permit the statement: “This object has zero value.” unless the relevant Value Context and value dimension justify that statement. The governed formulation is: “The relevant value has reached zero within the defined Value Context.” Dimension-Specific Nullification A Value Object may contain multiple simultaneous value dimensions. For example: Economic Value Operational Value Strategic Value Knowledge Value Utility Value Cultural Value Recovery Value One dimension may reach zero while others remain positive. Therefore: Nullification of Value Dimension A ≠ Nullification of the entire Value Object. VNS must preserve dimension-specific nullification where materially relevant. Zero-Value Condition A Zero-Value Condition is the governed condition in which the relevant previously existing positive value no longer remains positive within its defined Value Context. A Zero-Value Condition does not automatically establish: destruction of the object; absence of every possible value dimension; illegality; lack of ownership; lack of market price; accounting write-off; tax treatment; invalidity; permanent irrecoverability. It establishes one specific proposition: the governed value represented by the determination has reached zero. ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ represents a governed zero-value state where applicable within VFM®. A Value Object may enter a ZVA™ state when the applicable value dimension or governed value basis has legitimately reached zero through a recognized VFM® lifecycle pathway. VNS provides one principal pathway: Existing Positive Value → Value Nullification → Zero-Value Condition → ZVA™. But the existence of a ZVA™ designation must remain attached to its Value Context. ZVA™ must not become an uncontrolled statement that the object possesses no conceivable value whatsoever. Zero Value ≠ Nonexistence An object may continue to exist after its governed value reaches zero. Therefore: Object Existence ≠ Value Existence. A physical asset can remain physically present while its relevant operational value is zero. A digital asset can continue to exist in storage while its governed utility value is zero. A contractual right can remain documented while its time-dependent economic value has expired. VNS governs value nullification, not object annihilation. Zero Value ≠ Negative Value Zero value and negative value are distinct states. A zero-value asset may create: disposal costs; liabilities; maintenance costs; environmental burdens; legal exposure; operational risk. These negative consequences do not mean that zero value was incorrectly determined. They may represent another governed value or liability dimension. Therefore: Zero Value ≠ Negative Value. VNS must not collapse positive value, zero value, cost, liability, and negative externality into one concept. Nullification Determination A Value Nullification Determination establishes that the applicable governed value has legitimately reached the defined zero-value condition. A defensible determination should establish, where materially relevant: the Value Object; the Value Context; the value dimension; evidence that positive value previously existed; the relevant prior Value State; the nullification condition; the applicable nullification threshold; whether the threshold was reached; the DeMonet™ mechanism basis; temporal point or interval of nullification; uncertainty; reversibility status where known; whether zero is temporary, persistent, or permanent; the resulting zero-value state. The determination must remain distinguishable from the event that caused the value loss. Nullification Time VNS recognizes that the time of nullification may be materially important. Relevant temporal states may include: T₀ — Positive Value → T₁ — Degradation or Nullification Event → T₂ — Threshold Reached → T₃ — Nullification Determined → T₄ — Zero-Value State Recorded These moments may be identical. They may also differ. For example, an asset may have actually lost all relevant value before an organization formally identifies or determines that the zero-value threshold was crossed. Therefore: Time of Nullification ≠ Time of Discovery ≠ Time of Determination. Nullification Reversibility VNS must preserve whether the zero-value state is potentially reversible. A nullified value may be: Restorable Conditionally Restorable Restoration Unknown Non-Restorable within the defined context. This classification does not itself restore value. It establishes the interface to: Value Restoration Standard (VRSS). VNS → VRSS Interface VNS establishes: the legitimate arrival at zero. VRSS governs: the legitimate recovery from impaired, dormant, lost, or zero value. The interface may therefore be: Positive Value → DeMonet™ → Zero-Value Condition → ZVA™ → ReMonet™ → Restored Positive Value → New Value State. This creates a governed reversible lifecycle where restoration remains possible. However: DeMonet™ does not guarantee ReMonet™. A value may be nullified without ever being restored. Restoration Potential ≠ Existing Value An object at zero value may possess restoration potential. That potential must not be confused with currently existing positive value. For example: A damaged machine may have: Current Operational Value = 0 while possessing: high restoration potential. Therefore: Restoration Potential ≠ Restored Value. This distinction prevents anticipated future recovery from erasing the legitimacy of a current ZVA™ state. Nullification Provenance A governed Value Nullification Determination should remain traceable to the lifecycle from which it arose. The chain may include: Value Context → Value Origin → Value Emergence → Value Recognition → Prior Value State → Value Change → Value Degradation where applicable → Nullification Condition → Threshold → DeMonet™ → Nullification Determination → Zero-Value State. This allows systems to distinguish a genuinely nullified value from a value that never existed. Nullification Record Continuity The transition to zero must not erase the preceding positive-value history. If an asset moves: 100 → 70 → 30 → 0 its record must not simply become: Current Value = 0. The lifecycle must remain capable of showing: positive value existed → value changed → value degraded → the zero boundary was crossed → nullification occurred. This historical continuity becomes especially important if restoration later occurs. Cross-Architecture Boundaries VNS ↔ VES VES governs the emergence of value. VNS governs the nullification of previously existing value. Therefore: Value Never Emerged ≠ Value Nullified. VNS ↔ VRS Recognition does not create nullification. A value may cease to be recognized while still existing. Likewise, a recognized value may subsequently be nullified. Therefore: Loss of Recognition ≠ Value Nullification. VNS ↔ VSS VSS governs the current Value State. VNS governs the transition through which positive value reaches zero. After nullification, VSS may identify the resulting state as: ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ where applicable. Therefore: Transition ≠ State. VNS ↔ VCS VCS governs material change to existing value. VNS governs the specific boundary transition in which existing positive value reaches zero. Every nullification involves a value transition. Not every Value Change is a nullification. VNS ↔ VDS VDS governs development of existing positive value. VNS governs its nullification. The two may occur at different points within the same lifecycle but must remain methodologically distinct. VNS ↔ VDGS VDGS governs deterioration while positive value remains. VNS governs crossing into zero. Therefore: Declining Positive Value ≠ Nullified Value. VNS ↔ VRSS VNS governs: Positive Value → Zero Value. VRSS governs legitimate restoration from degraded, dormant, lost, or zero value toward restored positive value. Therefore: Nullification ≠ Restoration and Restoration Potential ≠ Existing Positive Value. VNS ↔ ORA™ ORA™ may govern the operational reality in which events affecting value occur. VNS governs what those events mean for the relevant value transition. Operational Event ≠ Value Nullification Determination. VNS ↔ VALIDOS® VALIDOS® may validate evidence, claims, determinations, methods, or other Validation Objects associated with a nullification determination. VNS owns the value-nullification governance logic. Validation of a determination ≠ ownership of the value-nullification space. VNS ↔ INTEGROS® INTEGROS® may govern integrity properties associated with value records, evidence, states, and transitions. VNS governs whether the value has crossed the nullification boundary. VNS ↔ ADIT® ADIT® may audit evidence concerning the value history, threshold crossing, determination, and resulting state. VNS governs the meaning of the value-nullification transition itself. Governance Outputs Implementation of VNS may produce: Value Nullification Condition Record Value Nullification Threshold Value Nullification Threshold Status DeMonet™ Transition Record Value Nullification Determination Zero-Value Condition Record Value Nullification Time Record Value Nullification Context Record Value Dimension Nullification Record Temporary Zero-Value Determination Permanent Zero-Value Determination Nullification Reversibility Status ZVA™ State Transition Record Value Nullification Provenance Chain Value Restoration Eligibility Interface These outputs provide the governed basis for subsequent Value State, Value Restoration, audit, validation, and broader lifecycle processes. Enterprise Application VNS enables organizations to answer a deceptively difficult question: When has something actually lost its value rather than merely lost some of its value? This distinction matters across: physical assets; infrastructure; technology; software; intellectual property; knowledge assets; digital assets; organizational capabilities; contractual rights; licenses; data assets; operational systems; financial structures; AI systems; industrial equipment; inventory; platforms; services. Without an explicit nullification architecture, organizations may incorrectly treat: severe degradation as zero value, temporary inactivity as permanent loss, loss of recognition as loss of value, never-realized potential as destroyed value, or zero value in one dimension as zero value everywhere. VNS creates the governance structure necessary to separate these states. Foundational Principles Value Never Emerged ≠ Value Nullified. Value Degradation ≠ Value Nullification. Approaching zero is not zero. Positive Value → Zero Value is a governed boundary transition. DeMonet™ governs value nullification, not every decline in value. DeMonet™ ≠ the external cause of value loss. Nullification may be progressive or immediate. Nullification may be deliberate or externally caused. Temporary Zero Value ≠ Permanent Zero Value. Zero value in one Value Context ≠ absence of all possible value. Nullification of one value dimension ≠ nullification of the entire Value Object. Zero Value ≠ Object Nonexistence. Zero Value ≠ Negative Value. Restoration potential is not currently existing positive value. A ZVA™ state may be reversible without ceasing to be a legitimate zero-value state while it exists. A governed zero-value state must preserve the history of the positive value from which it originated. Canonical Closing Statement Value Nullification Standard establishes the zero-boundary governance layer of VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture by governing the conditions, thresholds, mechanisms, determinations, and transitions through which previously existing positive value legitimately reaches a zero-value condition. Through explicit separation of degradation from nullification, non-emergence from value loss, threshold proximity from threshold crossing, temporary zero from permanent zero, contextual nullification from universal absence of value, zero value from negative value, and object existence from value existence, VNS prevents materially different value states from being collapsed into a single concept of “lost value.” By establishing DeMonet™ as the governed mechanism of value nullification and defining the transition from Positive Value through a legitimate Zero-Value Condition toward ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ where applicable, VNS creates the architectural boundary at which existing positive value ceases while preserving its lifecycle provenance, Value Context, temporal history, dimensional meaning, reversibility, and potential interface with subsequent Value Restoration governance. Value may decline without disappearing, an object may remain while its relevant value reaches zero, and potential value may fail to emerge without ever being nullified; only where previously existing positive value legitimately crosses its governed zero-value boundary does Value Nullification occur. Nahlad Value Nullification Standard (VNS) Architecture: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Canonical Definition: Value Nullification Standard governs the conditions, thresholds, mechanisms, determinations, and transitions through which previously existing positive value legitimately reaches a zero- value condition, while distinguishing nullification from degradation, non-emergence, temporary inactivity, and the absence of value in other contexts. Governed Space: Value Nullification Governance Flow: Positive Value → Nullification Condition → Nullification Threshold → DeMonet™ → Value Nullification Determination → Zero-Value Condition → ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ Governance Flow Position: Value Context → Value Origin → Value Emergence → Value Recognition → Value State → Value Change → Value Development → Value Degradation → Value Nullification → Value Restoration Previously existing positive value becomes nullified only when it legitimately crosses its governed zero-value boundary; value that never emerged cannot be nullified. → View Standard About standard Module Architecture → Value Nullification Condition Module (VNCM) → Value Nullification Threshold Module (VNTM) → DeMonet® Mechanism Module (VDMM) → Value Nullification Determination Module (VNDM) → Zero-Value State Transition Module (VNZM) Related Documents → About Value Nullification Standard (VNS) → VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture

title: About Value Origin Standard (VOS)
text: About Value Origin Standard (VOS) About Value Origin Standard (VOS) About Value Origin Standard (VOS) Architecture: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanism Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Parent Standard: Value Origin Standard (VOS) Governed Space: Value Origin Canonical Definition Value Origin Standard (VOS) governs how the identifiable source, basis, capability, condition, activity, relationship, object, or other foundation from which value may emerge is identified, structured, related to the governed value context, and documented. The Standard establishes the methodological starting point for understanding where value comes from before determining whether value has actually emerged. Its central distinction is: Value Source ≠ Existing Value A resource, capability, asset, technology, relationship, right, activity, infrastructure, dataset, invention, natural resource, human capability, or other source may possess the potential to generate value while the corresponding value has not yet come into existence. VOS makes that origin governable. Why Value Origin Matters Value is frequently measured, priced, exchanged, taxed, invested, depreciated, impaired, restored, or reported without a structured methodology for identifying its underlying origin. This can create a fundamental analytical problem: the observable value may be known while the mechanism from which that value originates remains poorly understood. VOS establishes the value-origin layer before later VFM® standards govern emergence, recognition, state, change, development, degradation, nullification, restoration, or extinction. It allows an organization to ask: What is capable of producing this value? What is the underlying basis of that capability? Under which conditions can that source generate value? What relationship exists between the source and the governed value? Has value already emerged, or does only value potential currently exist? Value Source Before Value Emergence VOS separates three concepts that should not be treated as equivalent: Source of Value Potential for Value Existing Value A source may exist without producing value. A source may possess value-generating potential without that potential being realized. Value may emerge only when the relevant conditions, relationships, capabilities, activities, or other mechanisms become effective. This distinction creates a clear architectural boundary between: Value Origin Standard and the subsequent: Value Emergence Standard. VOS identifies where value can come from. Value Emergence Standard determines when value actually comes into existence. Origin Asset™ Origin Asset™ operates as a foundational value-origin concept within this governed space. An Origin Asset™ may represent an identifiable asset, capability, resource, condition, relationship, knowledge base, technology, infrastructure, right, process, or other foundation capable of contributing to the emergence of value. However: Origin Asset™ ≠ Existing Value The existence of an Origin Asset™ does not itself prove that value has emerged. This distinction allows dormant, unused, undeveloped, inaccessible, unactivated, or unrealized value sources to remain identifiable without artificially treating their potential value as already realized value. What VOS Governs VOS provides the methodological structure for identifying: the source from which governed value may originate; the basis upon which that source possesses value-generating potential; the relationship between the source and the governed value; the conditions necessary for value to originate from that source; multiple sources contributing to one form of value; one source contributing to multiple forms of value; direct and indirect value origins; dormant or unrealized value sources; changes affecting the ability of a source to generate value; documentation of the value-origin relationship. The Standard does not determine the price of the source or the value that may eventually emerge from it. It establishes the origin structure from which subsequent value governance can proceed. Why This Is Different From Asset Identification VOS does not attempt to become an identity, ownership, accounting, property, or asset-classification standard. An underlying object may be identified through another governance architecture. VFM® asks a different question: What role does this object, capability, activity, relationship, or condition play in the origin of the governed value? Therefore: Object Identity ≠ Value Origin Asset Ownership ≠ Value Origin Asset Price ≠ Value Origin Value Source ≠ Existing Value This separation allows VFM® to examine value across physical, digital, financial, organizational, technological, environmental, intellectual, social, and future value environments without depending upon one particular asset model. Practical Value Value Origin Standard can help organizations move beyond observing value only after it has already become economically visible. By identifying value sources earlier, organizations may better understand: where value-generating capacity exists; which capabilities remain underutilized; which dependencies support existing value; which sources contribute disproportionately to value creation; where dormant value potential exists; which source conditions must be preserved; where loss of a source could later cause value degradation; where investment may activate previously unrealized value potential. This makes Value Origin governance relevant not only to economic analysis but also to strategic planning, infrastructure, technology, public administration, banking, investment, industry, digital assets, and emerging economic systems. Use Case 1 — Banking and Financial Infrastructure A financial institution possesses extensive infrastructure including transaction networks, customer relationships, data, risk models, distribution channels, specialized expertise, technology, licenses, operational capabilities, and institutional relationships. Traditional financial reporting may assign values to some of these elements while others remain difficult to represent as direct economic value. VOS begins with a different question: Which identifiable sources actually generate or enable the value being governed? The institution can map a particular form of value back to its underlying sources and distinguish between: an asset that exists and a source that is actively capable of generating value. This can expose dormant capabilities, critical value dependencies, underutilized infrastructure, and sources whose deterioration could threaten future value. VOS therefore creates a methodological basis for understanding where economic value originates before that value is priced, exchanged, impaired, restored, or otherwise transformed. Use Case 2 — Space Mission and Advanced Infrastructure A space organization develops a reusable launch system. The program contains enormous potential sources of value: engineering knowledge, propulsion technology, launch infrastructure, simulation capability, manufacturing processes, reusable components, mission data, intellectual capability, operational experience, and future launch capacity. Not every source has yet produced realized economic or operational value. VOS allows these sources to be identified without prematurely declaring their potential value to be existing value. For example, a new reusable propulsion capability may represent a significant Value Source because it could reduce future launch costs, increase launch frequency, extend mission capability, or enable entirely new missions. But until the relevant conditions exist and the capability produces a governed value outcome: Value Potential ≠ Emerged Value This distinction allows organizations to map future value-generating capacity while preserving methodological discipline between what could create value and what value actually exists. Relationship to the VFM® Lifecycle Value Origin Standard occupies the second governed space of VFM®, following Value Context Standard. The sequence begins: Value Context → Value Origin → Value Emergence Value Context Standard establishes: what value is being governed. Value Origin Standard establishes: where that value can originate. Value Emergence Standard subsequently establishes: when that value actually comes into existence. This sequence prevents value potential, value source, and existing value from being collapsed into a single concept. Foundational Principles Value must be identified before its origin can be meaningfully governed. A value source may exist before value emerges. Value-generating potential is not the same as existing value. An Origin Asset™ may exist without having produced value. One value may originate from multiple sources. One source may contribute to multiple forms of value. The source of value must remain distinguishable from the systems that price, exchange, own, classify, validate, tax, or account for it. Canonical Closing Statement Value Origin Standard establishes the origin layer of the governed value lifecycle by identifying the sources, bases, capabilities, conditions, activities, relationships, objects, and other foundations from which value may emerge. By separating Value Source, Value Potential, and Existing Value, the Standard enables value-generating capacity to be identified before value becomes economically, operationally, or institutionally visible. Value Origin Standard therefore provides the methodological foundation required to trace governed value back to its origin while preserving the fundamental principle that the existence of a value source does not itself establish the existence of value.
