title: Value Origin Conditions Module (VOCM)
text: Value Origin Conditions Module (VOCM) Value Origin Conditions Module (VOCM) Value Origin Conditions Module (VOCM) Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanism Parent Standard: Value Origin Standard (VOS) Module: VOCM — Value Origin Conditions Module Operational Layer: Value Origin Conditions Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Value Origin Conditions Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 23 August 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Value Origin Conditions Module (VOCM) is the fourth Core Module of the Value Origin Standard (VOS). VOCM governs the conditions that must exist, remain satisfied, become activated, or interact for an established Value Source, Value Source Basis, and Value Origin Relationship to provide a legitimate pathway toward the emergence of the governed value. The Module establishes the conditions under which a potential value-origin relationship becomes capable of producing or enabling value. VOCM does not determine that value has already emerged. It establishes whether the necessary origin conditions exist for the value-origin pathway to operate. The distinction is fundamental: Value Source ≠ Value Source Basis ≠ Value Origin Relationship ≠ Value Origin Conditions ≠ Existing Value Architectural Position VOCM is the fourth module within the Value Origin Standard. It follows: VORM — Value Origin Relationship Module and precedes: VODM — Value Origin Documentation Module. The internal sequence is: Identified Value Source → Established Value Source Basis → Established Value Origin Relationship → Origin Condition Identification → Condition Classification → Condition Dependency Assessment → Condition State Assessment → Origin Readiness → Value Origin Conditions Record → VODM — Value Origin Documentation Module The first three modules establish: Where can value originate? What about that source can contribute to value? How is that basis related to the governed value? VOCM asks: What must be true for that relationship to become capable of producing or enabling value? Operational Space VOCM governs conditions affecting the activation and operation of a Value Origin Relationship. These conditions may include: availability; accessibility; capability readiness; resource availability; demand; timing; environmental conditions; operational readiness; technological compatibility; infrastructure availability; complementary capability; economic feasibility; utilization; coordination; scale; knowledge; human capability; network participation; system compatibility; temporal alignment; dependency satisfaction; threshold achievement. The relevant conditions depend upon the governed value. VOCM does not prescribe one universal set of conditions. Origin Relationship ≠ Origin Condition VORM establishes: how a source may contribute to value. VOCM establishes: what must be true for that relationship to become operationally capable of contributing to value. Example: Solar Installation Value Source: solar generation system Value Source Basis: electricity-generation capability Value Origin Relationship: generation capability → production of usable electricity → potential energy value Value Origin Conditions may include: sufficient solar irradiation operational equipment grid or storage connection ability to use or transfer generated electricity. The relationship can exist while one or more required conditions are absent. Therefore: Existing Value Origin Relationship ≠ Satisfied Value Origin Conditions Necessary Conditions A Necessary Origin Condition is a condition without which the relevant Value Origin Relationship cannot operate for the governed value. Example: A manufacturing machine may possess productive capability. But if production requires electrical power: electricity availability may be a necessary condition. If the condition is absent: the source remains and the capability remains but the pathway toward value emergence may be inactive. VOCM therefore prevents the existence of productive capability from being mistaken for realized value. Enabling Conditions An Enabling Origin Condition allows or facilitates the Value Origin Relationship without necessarily being the fundamental source of the value. Examples may include: infrastructure access; network connectivity; compatible software; transportation; regulatory access where relevant to operation; distribution capability; specialized equipment; trained personnel. VOCM governs the condition's role in the value-origin pathway. It does not govern the external system responsible for establishing that condition. Conditional Thresholds Some Value Origin Relationships become materially capable of producing value only after a threshold is reached. Examples include: minimum production volume minimum network participation minimum utilization minimum performance minimum data availability minimum demand minimum energy availability minimum reliability VOCM may therefore establish: Condition Variable → Required Threshold → Condition Satisfaction State A source may be technically capable of creating value while remaining below the threshold required for meaningful value emergence. Combined Conditions Value origin frequently depends upon several conditions being satisfied together. For example: Technology Capability Required Infrastructure Qualified Personnel Operational Demand Resource Availability may collectively create the conditions under which a Value Origin Relationship can operate. VOCM therefore supports: Condition Set → Combined Origin Readiness rather than assuming that each condition independently produces value. Alternative Condition Paths The same Value Origin Relationship may operate through different sets of conditions. For example, a digital service may reach customers through: Direct Digital Distribution or Partner Distribution or Integrated Platform Distribution. Different condition sets may therefore activate alternative pathways toward the same governed value. VOCM may represent: Condition Set A → Origin Pathway or Condition Set B → Alternative Origin Pathway This allows value-origin governance to remain adaptable without redefining the underlying value each time implementation changes. Dependency Conditions Some conditions depend upon other conditions. Example: A production facility may require: raw materials but raw-material availability may depend upon: supplier capability → logistics availability → transport infrastructure → delivery timing. VOCM may therefore map: Primary Condition → Supporting Condition → Dependent Condition → Origin Readiness This is particularly important in complex supply chains, financial systems, infrastructure, digital platforms, and multi-actor ecosystems. Temporal Conditions Value Origin Conditions may exist only during particular periods. They may be: Continuous Temporary Periodic Seasonal Event-Triggered Time-Limited Delayed Recurring For example: A hydroelectric asset may possess the same physical generation capability throughout the year while water availability changes materially. The Value Source remains. The Value Source Basis remains. The Value Origin Relationship remains. But the conditions supporting actual value emergence may change over time. External Conditions Value origin may depend upon conditions outside the Value Source itself. Examples include: customer demand; network availability; weather; energy supply; access to infrastructure; complementary services; resource availability; market access; interoperability; physical environment. VOCM may recognize these conditions without claiming governance authority over the external domain. The principle is: VFM® governs the condition insofar as it affects the value-origin pathway — not the external system that produces the condition. Internal Conditions Some conditions arise within the Value Source or Value Object. Examples include: operational readiness; functional capability; sufficient capacity; configuration state; resource level; availability; performance threshold. VOCM may therefore distinguish: Internal Origin Conditions from External Origin Conditions. Both may be required for the same value-origin pathway. Demand as a Value Origin Condition Certain forms of value may depend materially upon demand or beneficiary need. A capability can exist without producing the relevant value if no beneficiary needs, uses, or can access it within the defined Value Context. For example: A transportation service may possess: vehicles + drivers + routes + operational capability but passenger-service value may remain unrealized if there is no relevant demand. VOCM therefore permits demand to function as an Origin Condition where appropriate. It does not establish market price or economic valuation. Access as a Value Origin Condition Value may exist potentially while access prevents its emergence for a specific beneficiary. Examples: Medical capability without patient access Digital capability without network access Energy capability without transmission access Knowledge without usable access Financial infrastructure without participant access VOCM may therefore govern: Access Condition Satisfied / Unsatisfied where access materially determines whether the Value Origin Relationship can operate. Utilization Condition Some Value Sources create value only when their capability is used. For example: A factory may possess unused production capacity. The productive capability exists. Its relationship to production value exists. The required infrastructure may exist. But without utilization, the corresponding production value may not emerge. VOCM can therefore distinguish: Available Capability from Activated Capability. Complementary Capability Condition Value may require another capability. For example: AI model may possess analytical capability. But operational value may require: usable data + computing infrastructure + integration + decision process. The AI model alone does not establish the complete value-origin condition set. VOCM therefore makes complementary capability requirements explicit. Origin Readiness VOCM may establish a governed Value Origin Readiness State. A minimum state model may include: 1. Undefined The relevant Origin Conditions have not been sufficiently identified. 2. Unsatisfied One or more necessary Origin Conditions are absent. 3. Partially Satisfied Some required conditions exist, but the complete condition set is not established. 4. Conditionally Ready The value-origin pathway can operate only under explicitly defined conditions. 5. Ready The identified material Origin Conditions necessary for the governed pathway are currently satisfied. 6. Interrupted Conditions previously supporting the pathway have materially ceased or become unavailable. These are governance states. They do not themselves establish Value Emergence. Origin Readiness ≠ Value Emergence This distinction is essential to VFM®. A value-origin pathway may be fully ready without value having emerged yet. For example: A manufacturing line may be: installed powered staffed supplied tested ready for operation while no product has yet been produced. Therefore: Origin Readiness = conditions for value emergence are present. It does not mean: Value has emerged. That distinction preserves the boundary between: Value Origin and the subsequent: Value Emergence governance space. Condition Failure An Origin Condition may fail after previously being satisfied. Examples: electricity interruption; supply disruption; loss of access; infrastructure failure; disappearance of demand; unavailable personnel; incompatible system update; resource depletion. VOCM requires material condition failure to remain identifiable. A condition failure may: prevent value emergence or interrupt the origin pathway without necessarily destroying the Value Source itself. Condition Restoration A failed Origin Condition may later be restored. Example: Network outage → access condition fails → value-origin pathway interrupted → network restored → access condition satisfied again. This does not necessarily constitute ReMonet™. ReMonet™ belongs to later value-restoration governance where value itself has been lost, degraded, dormant, or reduced to a zero-value state as defined by the architecture. VOCM governs restoration of the origin condition, not restoration of the value state itself. Condition Change Origin Conditions may change even when the source and relationship remain stable. A condition may become: Satisfied → Partially Satisfied Satisfied → Unsatisfied Unsatisfied → Satisfied Ready → Interrupted Conditional → Ready VOCM therefore supports ongoing condition-state updates where Value Origin is monitored over time. Condition Criticality Not every Origin Condition has equal importance. Organizations may classify conditions as: Critical Necessary Enabling Supporting Optional Alternative The classification should reflect the specific governed value pathway. A condition classified as critical should have a documented reason for that status. Condition Dependency Map For complex systems, VOCM may produce a Value Origin Condition Dependency Map. Example: Governed Value ↑ Value Origin Relationship ↑ Condition Set ↙ Energy Availability ↙ Material Availability ↙ Operational Capability ↙ Demand ↙ Distribution Access Each condition may itself contain dependencies. This enables organizations to see not only where value can originate, but also what the origin of that value depends upon. Condition Evidence Where materially relevant, a claimed Origin Condition should be supportable. Support may include: operational data; contractual availability; technical status; resource records; utilization data; demand indicators; system measurements; capacity information; infrastructure status; observed conditions; documented readiness. VOCM does not own general validation or audit. Where required: VALIDOS® may govern validation. ADIT® may govern audit and evidence. INTEGROS® may govern integrity. VOCM governs the value-origin condition being asserted. Minimum Implementation Framework A practical VOCM implementation should establish: 1. Value Origin Relationship Input Receive the governed Value Origin Relationship from VORM. 2. Condition Identification Identify the conditions materially affecting operation of the value-origin pathway. 3. Condition Classification Determine whether each condition is necessary, enabling, supporting, critical, optional, or alternative. 4. Condition Dependency Identify material dependencies between conditions. 5. Condition Threshold Define relevant thresholds where the condition is not purely binary. 6. Condition State Determine whether each condition is satisfied, partially satisfied, unsatisfied, conditional, or interrupted. 7. Temporal Applicability Identify whether the condition is continuous, temporary, periodic, event-triggered, or time-bounded. 8. Origin Readiness Determine the current readiness of the Value Origin pathway. 9. Condition Support Identify the basis supporting material condition assertions where required. 10. Value Origin Conditions Record Create the governed conditions record for downstream documentation and later Value Emergence governance. Governance Outputs VOCM may produce: Value Origin Condition Record Value Origin Condition Set Necessary Origin Condition Record Enabling Origin Condition Record Critical Origin Condition Record Alternative Origin Condition Path Value Origin Condition Dependency Map Value Origin Condition Threshold Value Origin Condition State Value Origin Readiness State Value Origin Condition Failure Record Value Origin Condition Change Record Value Origin Condition Restoration Record Value Origin Conditions Assessment These outputs provide the governed basis for: VODM — Value Origin Documentation Module and subsequently for the transition from: Value Origin → Value Emergence. Use Case 1 — Banking: AI Fraud Prevention Value A bank has an AI fraud-detection system. The preceding modules establish: Value Source: fraud-detection system Value Source Basis: analytical and transaction-pattern detection capability Value Origin Relationship: earlier detection of suspicious transactions may prevent or reduce financial loss. VOCM then identifies the conditions required for that pathway to operate: relevant transaction data available system operational fraud patterns detectable within the available information analysis completed before irreversible settlement or loss alerts reach the appropriate decision process intervention capability exists. This exposes an important distinction. A bank may own an advanced AI system worth millions of francs. The technology may function correctly. But if alerts arrive after transactions become irreversible, one critical Origin Condition fails. The technical asset still exists. The analytical capability still exists. The Value Origin Relationship still exists. But the expected avoided-loss value may fail to emerge. VOCM therefore allows the bank to identify exactly which conditions separate: expensive capability from capability capable of originating economic value. Use Case 2 — Space Mission: Reusable Launch System A space organization develops a reusable launch system to reduce lifecycle mission costs. The preceding modules identify: Value Sources: reusable vehicle, propulsion system, inspection capability, refurbishment capability, operational learning. Value Source Bases: reuse, inspection, recovery, refurbishment, repeated operational capability. Value Origin Relationships: reduced replacement requirements, shorter turnaround, repeated component utilization, and accumulated operational learning may contribute to lower lifecycle mission resource requirements. VOCM then establishes the conditions necessary for those relationships to operate: successful recovery acceptable post-flight component condition inspection capability refurbishment within economically meaningful limits sufficient reliability across repeated use available launch demand turnaround compatible with mission schedules reuse cost below relevant replacement alternatives. The reusable vehicle itself therefore does not automatically create cost value. If recovery succeeds but refurbishment becomes more expensive than replacement, an important condition fails. If refurbishment is efficient but launch frequency is too low, another condition may remain unsatisfied. If both become favorable, the value-origin pathway may become ready. VOCM therefore transforms: “Reusable systems create value.” into the governable question: “Under which conditions does reusability actually become capable of originating value?” Foundational Principles A Value Origin Relationship does not automatically create value. Value Origin Conditions determine whether the relationship is capable of operating. Value Source existence does not establish Origin Readiness. Capability availability does not establish capability utilization. Necessary conditions must be distinguished from enabling and supporting conditions. Multiple conditions may jointly determine one value-origin pathway. External conditions may affect value origin without becoming governed external domains of VFM®. Origin Conditions may change while the Value Source remains unchanged. Restoration of an Origin Condition is not automatically restoration of value. Origin Readiness is not Value Emergence. Value should not be treated as having emerged merely because the conditions for its emergence exist. Canonical Closing Statement Value Origin Conditions Module establishes the conditional layer of Value Origin governance by identifying, classifying, relating, and assessing the conditions required for an established Value Origin Relationship to become capable of producing or enabling the governed value. Through governance of necessary, enabling, supporting, critical, alternative, dependent, temporal, internal, external, threshold-based, and combined conditions, VOCM separates the existence of a Value Source and its capability from the operational conditions required for that capability to contribute to value. By establishing explicit Value Origin Readiness states while preserving the distinction between readiness and actual Value Emergence, VOCM prevents potential value, available capability, operational readiness, and realized value from being treated as equivalent. The Module therefore creates the final conditional structure required before Value Origin can be documented and the architecture can proceed toward governance of the moment at which value actually comes into existence. Modul5 Governed Links → Value Origin Standard (VOS) → VFM® Architecture Map → Previous: Value Origin Relationship Module (VORM) → Next: Value Origin Documentation Module (VODM)

title: Value Origin Documentation Module (VODM)
text: Value Origin Documentation Module (VODM) Value Origin Documentation Module (VODM) Value Origin Documentation Module (VODM) Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanism Parent Standard: Value Origin Standard (VOS) Module: VODM — Value Origin Documentation Module Operational Layer: Value Origin Documentation Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Value Origin Documentation Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 23 August 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Value Origin Documentation Module (VODM) is the fifth Core Module of the Value Origin Standard (VOS). VODM governs the structured documentation of the complete governed basis through which the origin of a defined value can be identified, understood, reconstructed, compared, reviewed, and transferred into subsequent value lifecycle governance. The Module consolidates the outputs of: VSOIM — Value Source Identification Module VSBM — Value Source Basis Module VORM — Value Origin Relationship Module VOCM — Value Origin Conditions Module into a coherent Value Origin Record. VODM does not determine that value has emerged. It establishes the documented origin basis required to understand: where the governed value can originate, what within the source can contribute to it, how that contribution occurs, and under which conditions the value-origin pathway can operate. The distinction is fundamental: Documented Value Origin ≠ Existing Value Architectural Position VODM is the fifth and final Core Module of the Value Origin Standard. It follows: VOCM — Value Origin Conditions Module and completes the internal Value Origin governance sequence: Value Source Identification → Value Source Basis → Value Origin Relationship → Value Origin Conditions → Value Origin Documentation VODM therefore creates the final governed record before the architecture proceeds from: Value Origin to: Value Emergence. Operational Purpose The existence of a Value Source, Value Source Basis, Value Origin Relationship, and Value Origin Conditions is insufficient if those elements cannot be connected and reconstructed as one governed origin pathway. VODM prevents Value Origin governance from becoming fragmented across: isolated records; organizational departments; technical systems; financial models; contracts; operational databases; undocumented assumptions; institutional knowledge; individual expert knowledge; disconnected analytical outputs. Its purpose is to create one reconstructable methodological chain: Governed Value → Value Source → Value Source Basis → Value Origin Relationship → Value Origin Conditions → Origin Readiness → Value Origin Record Operational Space VODM governs documentation relating specifically to the origin of value. This may include: governed value reference; Value Source identity; Value Source description; Value Source Basis; source-to-value relationship; origin pathway; necessary Origin Conditions; enabling Origin Conditions; critical Origin Conditions; alternative Origin Conditions; condition dependencies; condition thresholds; Origin Readiness; material limitations; temporal applicability; unresolved origin questions; changes affecting the origin basis; supporting references; Value Origin Record status. VODM governs how these elements are assembled into a coherent value-origin record. The Value Origin Record The principal governance object produced by VODM is the: Value Origin Record (VOR). A Value Origin Record is the structured representation of the governed basis through which a defined value may originate. At minimum, the record should answer: What value is being governed? What is the Value Source? What within that source provides the basis for value? How is that basis related to the governed value? What conditions must exist for the relationship to operate? What is the current Origin Readiness state? What material dependencies or limitations affect the origin pathway? This transforms Value Origin from a general statement into a reconstructable governance object. Documentation Principle VODM follows a simple rule: A value-origin claim should be reconstructable from its documented basis. A statement such as: “This technology creates value.” is insufficient as a governed Value Origin record. VODM requires the statement to be decomposed. For example: Governed Value: reduced operational energy cost Value Source: intelligent energy-management system Value Source Basis: capability to optimize energy consumption Value Origin Relationship: optimization of consumption can reduce unnecessary energy use, creating potential cost reduction Origin Conditions: measurable consumption, controllable loads, usable optimization decisions, operational implementation, relevant energy-cost structure Origin Readiness: Ready The resulting record explains the origin pathway rather than merely asserting value. Documentation ≠ Evidence Validation VODM requires the basis of Value Origin to be documented. It does not automatically determine that every statement contained within the record has been independently validated. Where formal validation is required: VALIDOS® may govern validation. Where integrity must be governed: INTEGROS® may govern integrity. Where evidence and auditability are required: ADIT® may govern audit and evidence. VODM owns the Value Origin documentation structure. This boundary prevents documentation from being mistaken for proof. Source Documentation The Value Origin Record should identify the relevant Value Source sufficiently for the governed value to remain connected to its origin. Source documentation may include: source name; source type; source reference; source configuration; source location where relevant; source version; source state; relevant capability; temporal applicability. VODM does not replace identity governance. Where formal identity, ownership, authority, provenance, or continuity is required, the relevant external architecture may govern those questions. Value Source Basis Documentation The record should identify what within the Value Source provides the basis from which value may originate. Examples include: Capability Resource Knowledge Function Relationship Access Capacity Position Process Property Opportunity Infrastructure The basis should be specific enough that the origin relationship can be understood independently of the general existence of the source. Origin Relationship Documentation VODM requires the relationship between: Value Source Basis and Governed Value to remain explicit. The relationship should explain the pathway through which the source basis may contribute to the governed value. For example: Predictive Maintenance Capability → identifies developing equipment failure earlier → enables intervention before catastrophic failure → may reduce downtime and repair requirements → creates a pathway toward avoided-loss and continuity value. The documentation should preserve the pathway rather than reducing it to: “Predictive maintenance has value.” Origin Conditions Documentation Material conditions established through VOCM should remain connected to the relevant origin relationship. The record may distinguish: Necessary Conditions Enabling Conditions Supporting Conditions Critical Conditions Alternative Conditions Threshold Conditions Temporal Conditions External Conditions Internal Conditions This makes it possible to determine why an origin pathway is: Ready or Not Ready. Dependency Documentation Where Value Origin depends upon several interacting conditions, VODM should preserve the material dependency structure. Example: Manufacturing Value depends upon: Production Capability Material Availability Energy Availability Qualified Personnel Operational Demand Material Availability may itself depend upon: Supplier Capability → Logistics → Delivery Access. The Value Origin Record should make material dependencies visible where their failure can interrupt the origin pathway. Alternative Origin Pathways The same governed value may originate through multiple pathways. VODM therefore supports documentation such as: Governed Value ↙ Origin Pathway A ↘ Origin Pathway B ↘ Origin Pathway C For example, operational cost reduction may originate through: energy efficiency or automation or waste reduction or maintenance optimization. These pathways should not be silently combined. Each may have different: Value Sources; Value Source Bases; relationships; conditions; dependencies; readiness states. Multiple Sources of One Value One governed value may depend upon multiple Value Sources. Example: Reduced Hospital Treatment Delay may depend upon: diagnostic capability staff availability information availability coordination capability treatment capacity. VODM may therefore represent a multi-source Value Origin Record. This allows organizations to identify situations where no single asset or actor can legitimately be described as the sole origin of the governed value. One Source, Multiple Values A single Value Source may also support several different values. For example, an industrial robot may contribute to: production value safety value quality value time value cost value capacity value. VODM requires those values to remain separately identifiable where their origin relationships differ. This prevents one broad statement such as: “The robot creates value” from obscuring multiple distinct value pathways. Origin Record Status A Value Origin Record may carry a governance status. A practical minimum model may include: 1. Draft The Value Origin basis is being documented. 2. Incomplete Material elements required to reconstruct the origin pathway are missing. 3. Documented The material Value Origin structure has been sufficiently recorded. 4. Conditionally Documented The record is usable subject to explicitly identified unresolved conditions or limitations. 5. Superseded A newer Value Origin Record has replaced the current record. 6. Archived The record is retained for historical, comparative, or reconstruction purposes. These statuses concern documentation. They do not establish whether value exists. Temporal Documentation Value Origin is not necessarily static. Sources may change. Capabilities may change. Relationships may change. Conditions may change. Dependencies may change. The Value Origin Record should therefore identify its relevant temporal basis. Where materially required, VODM may support: Effective From Effective Until Review Date Last Material Change Superseding Record This allows the architecture to distinguish historical Value Origin from current Value Origin. Change Documentation A material change to the origin basis should remain visible. Examples include: Value Source replacement; capability change; source degradation; new dependency; removed dependency; changed relationship; changed threshold; condition failure; condition restoration; new alternative pathway; change in beneficiary or context affecting the origin pathway. The purpose is not to create unnecessary administrative history. It is to preserve the ability to understand why the Value Origin pathway changed. Unresolved Origin Questions VODM should allow unresolved questions to remain explicit. Examples: Source basis not fully established Dependency uncertain Condition threshold unknown Alternative source under assessment Relationship partly understood Origin Readiness indeterminate An unresolved issue should not be hidden merely to create a complete-looking record. A documented uncertainty is methodologically stronger than an undocumented assumption. Documentation Granularity VODM does not require every Value Origin Record to contain the same level of detail. Documentation should be proportionate to: complexity of the value; materiality; number of sources; number of beneficiaries; number of dependencies; operational significance; decision significance; lifecycle significance; expected downstream reliance. A simple value pathway may require a compact record. A national infrastructure project may require a complex multi-source Value Origin model. Machine-Readable Value Origin VODM should support machine-readable representation of Value Origin. A machine-readable Value Origin Record may contain structured fields for: Value Context ID Value Source ID Value Source Basis Value Origin Relationship Origin Condition IDs Condition States Origin Readiness State Dependency Links Temporal State Record Version Supporting References This enables Value Origin governance to become usable by: AI systems; financial systems; enterprise platforms; accounting systems; public administration; asset-management systems; digital twins; economic models; automated decision systems. Value Origin Graph For complex environments, VODM may represent Value Origin as a graph: Value Source ↓ Value Source Basis ↓ Value Origin Relationship ↓ Origin Conditions ↓ Governed Value Multiple sources and pathways can then be connected. This enables organizations to analyze: Where does this value originate? Which sources contribute to it? Which conditions are critical? Which dependencies threaten it? Which alternative origin pathways exist? What happens if one source disappears? The Value Origin Record therefore becomes more than documentation. It becomes a navigable representation of value origin. Transition to Value Emergence VODM completes the governance of potential Value Origin. The next architectural question is fundamentally different. Value Origin asks: Where can the governed value come from? Value Emergence asks: Has the governed value actually come into existence? The transition is: Documented Value Origin → Origin Readiness → Value-Producing Event / Condition / Interaction → Value Emergence Assessment The existence of a complete Value Origin Record does not permit the architecture to skip this transition. Therefore: Documented Origin ≠ Emerged Value Minimum Implementation Framework A practical VODM implementation should establish: 1. Governed Value Reference Connect the record to the Value Context established under VCXS. 2. Value Source Record Document the identified Value Source or Sources. 3. Value Source Basis Record Document the relevant capability, resource, relationship, condition, or other basis. 4. Value Origin Relationship Record Document how the source basis may contribute to the governed value. 5. Value Origin Conditions Record Document material conditions required for the origin pathway. 6. Dependency Record Document material dependencies and alternative pathways. 7. Origin Readiness Record Preserve the current readiness state established through VOCM. 8. Limitation and Uncertainty Record Identify material limitations, unresolved questions, and uncertainty. 9. Temporal and Version Record Identify the applicable time, version, and material changes. 10. Value Origin Record Consolidate the complete governed origin basis into one reconstructable record. Governance Outputs VODM may produce: Value Origin Record Value Origin Source Record Value Source Basis Record Value Origin Relationship Record Value Origin Conditions Record Value Origin Dependency Record Value Origin Pathway Map Alternative Value Origin Pathway Record Multi-Source Value Origin Record Origin Readiness Record Value Origin Limitation Record Value Origin Uncertainty Record Value Origin Change Record Value Origin Version Record Machine-Readable Value Origin Record Value Origin Graph These outputs complete the Value Origin Standard and provide the governed input for the next Parent Standard in the VFM® lifecycle. Use Case 1 — Banking: Origin of Fraud- Prevention Value A bank deploys several capabilities intended to reduce fraud losses: transaction monitoring AI fraud detection customer authentication behavioral analytics human investigation payment intervention. Without structured Value Origin documentation, the organization may record a general conclusion: “The fraud platform creates CHF X in value.” VODM decomposes that claim. For avoided fraud-loss value, the Value Origin Record may establish: Value Sources: detection models, transaction data, investigation capability, intervention mechanisms Value Source Bases: anomaly detection, pattern recognition, human judgment, transaction blocking Value Origin Relationships: earlier detection and intervention may prevent otherwise realizable fraud losses Origin Conditions: relevant data, sufficiently early detection, operational alerts, investigation availability, intervention authority, actionable transaction state Dependencies: payment infrastructure, data availability, model operation, staff response Origin Readiness: Ready / Partially Ready / Interrupted depending upon the current condition state. This allows the bank to distinguish between: money spent on fraud capability and the actual governed pathway through which fraud-prevention value can originate. The record can subsequently be compared with Value Emergence and later Value State information to determine whether the expected value actually came into existence. Use Case 2 — Space Mission: Documenting the Origin of Cost-Reduction Value A space organization develops a reusable launch architecture intended to reduce mission costs. The organization may have multiple potential Value Sources: reusable launch vehicle recoverable propulsion components automated inspection predictive maintenance rapid refurbishment operational learning from repeated missions. VODM creates a structured origin model for the governed: lifecycle cost-reduction value. The record may show: Reusable Vehicle → repeated component utilization → reduced replacement requirement Automated Inspection → faster condition assessment → reduced inspection resource requirement Predictive Maintenance → earlier intervention → reduced failure and repair exposure Operational Learning → improved turnaround processes → reduced resource consumption per mission. Each pathway receives its own conditions and dependencies. The organization can therefore determine that the same cost-reduction value may originate from several interacting mechanisms rather than one asset. If one pathway fails—for example, refurbishment becomes excessively expensive—the Value Origin Record still shows whether alternative pathways continue to support the governed value. This gives mission planners a structured answer to a question that ordinary asset accounting does not fully answer: Where does the expected lifecycle value actually come from? Foundational Principles Value Origin should be documented as a reconstructable pathway, not merely asserted. A Value Source is not sufficient documentation of Value Origin. The basis, relationship, conditions, and dependencies of value origin must remain distinguishable. One source may originate multiple forms of value. One value may originate from multiple sources. Alternative Value Origin pathways should remain separately identifiable. Documentation does not establish validation. A complete Value Origin Record does not establish that value has emerged. Material uncertainty should remain documented rather than hidden. Value Origin documentation should remain proportionate to the complexity and significance of the governed value. Machine-readable Value Origin can transform value from an assumed economic concept into a governable lifecycle object. Canonical Closing Statement Value Origin Documentation Module completes the Value Origin Standard by transforming the identified Value Source, Value Source Basis, Value Origin Relationship, Value Origin Conditions, dependencies, readiness state, limitations, uncertainty, temporal applicability, and material changes into a coherent and reconstructable Value Origin Record. By preserving the complete pathway through which a defined value may originate, VODM prevents value-origin claims from being reduced to unsupported assertions that an asset, technology, organization, activity, or capability simply “creates value.” The Module enables Value Origin to be represented as a documented, reviewable, comparable, and machine-readable governance object while preserving the critical distinction between potential origin and actual Value Emergence. VODM therefore closes the governance of where value can come from and creates the documented foundation required for VFM® to proceed to the next question in the value lifecycle: whether that value has actually come into existence. Governed Links → Value Origin Standard (VOS) → VFM® Architecture Map → Previous: Value Origin Conditions Module (VOCM)

title: Value Origin Relationship Module (VORM)
text: Value Origin Relationship Module (VORM) Value Origin Relationship Module (VORM) Value Origin Relationship Module (VORM) Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanism Parent Standard: Value Origin Standard (VOS) Module: VORM — Value Origin Relationship Module Operational Layer: Value Origin Relationship Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Value Origin Relationship Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 23 August 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Value Origin Relationship Module (VORM) is the third Core Module of the Value Origin Standard (VOS). VORM governs the explicit relationship between an identified Value Source, its established Value Source Basis, and the governed value to which that source may contribute. The Module determines how the source and its value-relevant basis are connected to the potential origin of the governed value. VORM operates after: VSOIM — Value Source Identification Module and VSBM — Value Source Basis Module. The distinction is fundamental: VSOIM identifies the source. VSBM identifies what about the source can contribute to value. VORM establishes how that basis is related to the origin of the specific governed value. VORM does not establish that value has already emerged. It establishes the origin relationship capable of supporting subsequent Value Emergence. Architectural Position VORM is the third module within the Value Origin Standard. It follows: VSBM — Value Source Basis Module and precedes: VOCM — Value Origin Conditions Module. The internal sequence is: Identified Value Source → Established Value Source Basis → Value Origin Relationship Identification → Relationship Type → Relationship Structure → Contribution Pathway → Dependency Identification → Value Origin Relationship Record → VOCM — Value Origin Conditions Module VORM therefore moves Value Origin governance from: Why can this source matter? to: How can this source contribute to the origin of this specific value? Operational Space VORM governs relationships connecting: Value Source to: Governed Value through an established: Value Source Basis. These relationships may be: direct; indirect; enabling; dependent; conditional; complementary; cumulative; sequential; substitutive; synergistic; network-based; multi-source; multi-stage; temporal; latent. The Module does not assume that one source produces one value through one simple causal pathway. Complex value may originate through networks of relationships. Source Basis ≠ Origin Relationship VORM establishes the distinction: Value Source Basis ≠ Value Origin Relationship A basis describes what the source possesses, enables, provides, or can do. An origin relationship describes how that basis connects to the origin of the governed value. Example: Industrial Robot Value Source Basis: automation capability Value Origin Relationship: automation capability → reduction of repetitive manual production effort → potential production-cost value The capability exists independently. The relationship explains why that capability matters to the particular governed value. Relationship to the Governed Value Context Every Value Origin Relationship must remain connected to the Value Context established under the Value Context Standard (VCXS). The same source and the same capability may create different Value Origin Relationships depending upon: value being governed; Value Object; beneficiary; purpose; reference framework; operational context. For example: Battery Storage System may have the basis: energy-storage capability but different Value Origin Relationships: energy storage → peak-demand reduction → cost value energy storage → backup availability → resilience value energy storage → renewable balancing → system-efficiency value energy storage → reduced grid dependency → strategic value The source is the same. The basis may be the same. The relationship to value is different. Direct Value Origin Relationship A Direct Value Origin Relationship exists where the established source basis contributes directly to the governed value pathway without requiring another independent value-producing mechanism between the source and the value. Example: Solar installation → electricity-generation capability → usable electricity generation → energy-production value. Direct does not mean unconditional. Conditions may still determine whether value actually emerges. Indirect Value Origin Relationship An Indirect Value Origin Relationship exists where the source contributes through one or more intermediate capabilities, processes, states, or outcomes. Example: Predictive maintenance system → failure-prediction capability → earlier maintenance intervention → reduced unplanned downtime → increased productive availability → operational value. The source does not directly produce the final value. It contributes through a governed value-origin pathway. Enabling Value Origin Relationship Some sources do not independently originate the governed value but enable another source to do so. Example: Charging infrastructure → access to energy replenishment → enables electric vehicle operation → supports transportation value. The charging infrastructure may therefore hold an enabling relationship to transportation value even though it does not itself perform transportation. Complementary Relationship Value may require two or more sources whose bases complement one another. Example: AI Model Operational Data Computational Infrastructure may collectively support: decision-support capability which may contribute to: faster or more accurate operational decisions. None of the three sources may independently establish the complete value-origin pathway. VORM therefore supports: Multiple Sources → Complementary Origin Relationship → Governed Value Dependent Relationship A Value Origin Relationship may depend upon another source, capability, infrastructure, condition, or relationship. Example: High-speed manufacturing equipment may possess substantial productive capability. But its relationship to production value may depend upon: electricity; trained operators; raw materials; software; maintenance; logistics; downstream demand. VORM identifies material dependencies affecting the origin relationship. VOCM subsequently governs the conditions under which that relationship can become operationally effective. Sequential Relationship Value may originate through a sequence. For example: Scientific Knowledge → engineering method → manufacturing capability → product performance → customer utility. VORM allows the value-origin pathway to preserve intermediate stages rather than incorrectly attributing all value directly to the final visible source. This is particularly important where organizations need to understand where value actually originates across complex systems. Cumulative Relationship Multiple small contributions may collectively support value even when no individual contribution is sufficient. Example: 1% energy reduction 2% material reduction shorter production cycle lower maintenance requirement may collectively produce substantial lifecycle cost value. VORM can represent: Multiple Value-Origin Contributions → Cumulative Value-Origin Relationship without requiring each contribution to be treated as a separate final value. Synergistic Relationship Some combinations produce a value-origin capability greater than the contribution available from the sources independently. For example: high-quality data + AI model + domain expertise may produce an analytical capability unavailable from any one component alone. VORM may therefore identify a: Synergistic Value Origin Relationship where the relevant origin pathway depends upon the interaction between multiple sources. VORM identifies the relationship. It does not automatically quantify the resulting value. Substitutive Relationship Different Value Sources may provide alternative pathways toward the same governed value. For example: human inspection and machine-vision inspection may both contribute to defect-detection value. VORM may therefore represent: Source A → Value Origin Pathway and Source B → Alternative Value Origin Pathway This enables later comparison without assuming that the sources, costs, risks, or resulting value are identical. Network Value Origin Relationship In complex ecosystems, value may originate through a network rather than a linear chain. Examples include: payment networks; supply chains; telecommunications networks; digital platforms; logistics ecosystems; healthcare networks; financial markets; distributed energy systems; blockchain ecosystems; AI agent ecosystems. VORM may map: Source Network → Interdependent Bases → Relationship Network → Governed Value This makes distributed value origin governable without forcing artificial attribution to one source. Multi-Beneficiary Relationship The same Value Source may contribute to different values for different beneficiaries. Example: A digital payment infrastructure may create: for the customer: transaction convenience for the merchant: payment acceptance capability for the bank: transaction-service capability for the wider network: interoperability and settlement efficiency. VORM therefore preserves the beneficiary established in the Value Context. Same Source ≠ Same Value Relationship for Every Beneficiary. Positive and Protective Value-Origin Relationships A Value Origin Relationship does not need to produce additional output. It may originate value by preserving an existing desirable state or preventing an undesirable state. Examples include: Cybersecurity capability → reduced probability of disruption → preservation of operational value. Backup infrastructure → recovery capability → reduction of expected continuity loss. Preventive maintenance → reduced failure exposure → preservation of productive capability. This allows VFM® to recognize value originating through: creation and through: preservation / avoided loss without treating them as identical mechanisms. Cost-Reduction Relationship Cost reduction represents an important value-origin pathway. VORM may establish relationships such as: Reusable component → repeated-use capability → reduced replacement requirement → potential lifecycle cost value. Automation system → automated execution capability → reduced manual processing requirement → potential process-cost value. Energy optimization system → consumption optimization capability → reduced energy requirement → potential operating-cost value. The Module identifies the relationship. It does not yet declare that the savings have actually occurred. Temporal Relationship A source may contribute to value at different times. A relationship may therefore be: Immediate Delayed Recurring Periodic Long-Term Dormant Time-Bounded Event-Triggered For example, emergency infrastructure may remain unused for years while retaining a legitimate relationship to resilience value. VORM must therefore avoid equating: lack of current utilization with absence of Value Origin Relationship. Latent Origin Relationship A Value Origin Relationship may exist before the conditions necessary for value emergence are satisfied. Example: A patented technology possesses a technological basis and a defined relationship to potential manufacturing efficiency. However: production infrastructure may not yet exist; implementation cost may remain too high; complementary technology may be missing. The relationship can therefore be classified as: Latent Value Origin Relationship. This preserves the distinction: Origin Relationship Exists ≠ Value Has Emerged. Relationship Strength Where useful, organizations may characterize how strongly the identified source basis is connected to the governed value. Possible governance states may include: Primary Material Supporting Enabling Conditional Marginal Unresolved These states do not represent universal monetary valuation. They describe the role of the source within the value-origin structure. Relationship Dependency VORM requires material dependencies to remain visible where they affect the origin relationship. A relationship may depend upon: another Value Source; complementary capability; infrastructure; access; timing; knowledge; demand; resource availability; interoperability; external event; operational process. Dependency must not be mistaken for Value Origin Condition. VORM identifies what the relationship depends upon structurally. VOCM determines which conditions must be satisfied for the origin pathway to operate. Relationship Evidence A claimed Value Origin Relationship should be supportable where materially relevant. Support may include: operational observation; technical evidence; historical performance; comparative analysis; financial records; scientific evidence; simulation; controlled testing; production data; empirical relationships; documented capability pathways. VORM does not own general validation or evidence integrity. Where required: VALIDOS® may govern validation. ADIT® may govern audit and evidence. INTEGROS® may govern integrity. VORM governs the value-origin relationship being asserted. Relationship Change A Value Origin Relationship may change even when the Value Source itself remains unchanged. For example: A technology may remain technically identical while: a complementary infrastructure appears; market conditions change; another technology replaces part of its role; a new use is discovered; regulation changes access; operating costs change; interoperability improves. The underlying source remains. Its relationship to governed value may strengthen, weaken, disappear, or transform. VORM therefore requires material relationship changes to remain identifiable. Relationship Map For complex value systems, VORM may produce a Value Origin Relationship Map. A simplified structure may be: Value Source A → Basis A → Contribution A Value Source B → Basis B → Contribution B Value Source C → Basis C → Enabling Contribution ↓ Combined Value Origin Relationship ↓ Governed Value This allows VFM® to map where value may originate before later lifecycle stages determine whether that value actually emerges, changes, develops, degrades, reaches zero, is restored, or becomes extinct. Minimum Implementation Framework A practical VORM implementation should establish: 1. Value Source Input Receive the identified Value Source from VSOIM. 2. Value Source Basis Input Receive the established Value Source Basis from VSBM. 3. Governed Value Context Identify the specific governed value, Value Object, beneficiary, purpose, and reference context. 4. Relationship Identification Determine how the source basis connects to the potential origin of the governed value. 5. Relationship Type Identify whether the relationship is direct, indirect, enabling, complementary, dependent, cumulative, sequential, synergistic, substitutive, network-based, or another relevant type. 6. Contribution Pathway Document the pathway through which the source may contribute to the governed value. 7. Dependency Identification Identify material structural dependencies affecting the relationship. 8. Relationship State Determine whether the relationship is active, latent, conditional, weakened, interrupted, or unresolved. 9. Relationship Support Identify the basis supporting the asserted relationship where required. 10. Value Origin Relationship Record Create the governed relationship record for downstream Value Origin governance. Governance Outputs VORM may produce: Value Origin Relationship Record Value Origin Relationship Type Value Contribution Pathway Direct Value Origin Relationship Record Indirect Value Origin Relationship Record Enabling Value Origin Relationship Record Complementary Value Origin Relationship Record Dependent Value Origin Relationship Record Sequential Value Origin Relationship Record Cumulative Value Origin Relationship Record Synergistic Value Origin Relationship Record Substitutive Value Origin Relationship Record Network Value Origin Relationship Map Value Origin Dependency Record Value Origin Relationship State Value Origin Relationship Change Record These outputs provide the governed input for: VOCM — Value Origin Conditions Module. Use Case 1 — Banking: From Data Capability to Fraud-Loss Reduction A bank identifies its transaction-data environment as a Value Source. VSBM establishes: transaction information and analytical capability as relevant Value Source Bases. VORM then establishes the relationship: transaction data → pattern-analysis capability → earlier identification of suspicious activity → potential prevention or reduction of fraudulent transactions → potential avoided-loss value for the bank and affected customers. This matters because the dataset itself is not the value. Nor is analytical capability automatically value. The value-origin relationship explains how those capabilities may contribute to an economically meaningful outcome. If fraud detection does not actually prevent loss, the relationship may still exist while the expected value fails to emerge. That distinction becomes critical when organizations assess investments in AI, analytics, cybersecurity, or financial infrastructure. Use Case 2 — Space Mission: Mapping the Origin of Reusability Value A launch organization identifies a reusable launch system as a Value Source. VSBM identifies multiple bases: reusable propulsion reusable structures rapid inspection capability operational learning refurbishment capability. VORM maps how those bases relate to the governed value: reusable hardware → reduced replacement requirement rapid inspection → shorter turnaround operational learning → improved repeat-mission execution refurbishment capability → extended component utilization Together: multiple Value Source Bases → combined Value Origin Relationship → potential reduction in lifecycle mission resource requirements and cost. The architecture therefore avoids the simplistic conclusion: “Reusability = value.” Instead, it identifies the actual pathways through which reusability may originate value. VOCM can then determine whether the conditions necessary for those pathways to function are actually present. Foundational Principles A Value Source Basis must be connected to the governed value through an identifiable Value Origin Relationship. Value Source Basis is not Value Origin Relationship. Value Origin Relationship is not Value Emergence. The same source may have multiple relationships to different forms of value. The same source may create different value relationships for different beneficiaries. Multiple sources may jointly support one Value Origin Relationship. A Value Origin Relationship may be direct, indirect, enabling, dependent, cumulative, sequential, synergistic, substitutive, or network-based. Avoided cost and avoided loss may form legitimate value-origin pathways. A latent relationship may exist before value emerges. Complex value should remain traceable to the sources, bases, relationships, and dependencies from which it can originate. Canonical Closing Statement Value Origin Relationship Module establishes the relational layer of Value Origin governance by defining how an identified Value Source and its established Value Source Basis connect to the potential origin of a specific governed value. Through governance of direct, indirect, enabling, complementary, dependent, cumulative, sequential, synergistic, substitutive, network-based, temporal, and latent relationships, VORM makes complex value-origin pathways explicit without prematurely declaring that value has emerged. By separating the existence of a source, the capability contained within that source, the relationship of that capability to value, and the later conditions under which value can actually emerge, VORM creates the governed relational structure necessary for determining where value comes from across financial, industrial, digital, scientific, infrastructure, and other complex systems. title: Value Source Basis Module (VSBM)
text: Value Source Basis Module (VSBM) Value Source Basis Module (VSBM) Value Source Basis Module (VSBM) Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanism Parent Standard: Value Origin Standard (VOS) Module: VSBM — Value Source Basis Module Operational Layer: Value Source Basis Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Value Source Basis Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 23 August 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Value Source Basis Module (VSBM) is the second Core Module of the Value Origin Standard (VOS). VSBM governs the determination and documentation of the basis through which an identified Value Source is capable of contributing to the origin of the governed value. The Module operates after a Value Source has been identified through VSOIM — Value Source Identification Module. VSOIM establishes: What is the Value Source? VSBM establishes: What about that source makes it capable of contributing to this value? This distinction prevents the mere existence, ownership, recognition, or possession of a source from being confused with an actual value-origin basis. Architectural Position VSBM is the second module within the Value Origin Standard. It follows: VSOIM — Value Source Identification Module and precedes: VORM — Value Origin Relationship Module The internal sequence is: Identified Value Source → Source Capability Examination → Value-Relevant Basis Identification → Basis Characterization → Basis Condition Assessment → Value Source Basis Record → VORM — Value Origin Relationship Module The Module therefore moves Value Origin governance from: identifying the source to: understanding why that source can matter for value. Operational Space VSBM governs the value-relevant basis contained in or enabled by an identified Value Source. A Value Source Basis may arise from: productive capability; functional capability; economic utility; physical properties; technological capability; intellectual capability; knowledge; information; scarcity; availability; accessibility; location; timing; interoperability; network position; relationships; rights; permissions; productive capacity; computational capacity; energy availability; transformation capability; reuse capability; substitution capability; risk reduction; cost reduction; time reduction; resource reduction; performance improvement; resilience; optionality; combinations of multiple bases. The list is not exhaustive. VFM® remains neutral as to which type of basis must create value. Its purpose is to make that basis governable. Source Existence ≠ Value Source Basis VSBM establishes a foundational distinction: Source Existence ≠ Value Source Basis Something may exist without possessing a relevant basis for the governed value. A building exists. A dataset exists. A patent exists. A machine exists. A relationship exists. A mineral deposit exists. But existence alone does not explain why any of these can contribute to a particular form of value. VSBM therefore requires the relevant basis to be made explicit. For example: Machine → manufacturing capability Dataset → information capable of improving a decision Patent → protected technological capability Warehouse → storage and distribution capability Reusable spacecraft component → repeated-use capability reducing replacement requirements The source and its value-relevant basis are related but methodologically distinct. Value Basis Is Context-Specific A source does not possess one universal value basis for every context. The same source may have different bases for different governed values. For example, a logistics network may provide: delivery capability for customer-service value, distribution reach for market-access value, redundancy for resilience value, and consolidation capability for cost-reduction value. VSBM therefore requires the basis to remain connected to the specific governed Value Context. Capability Basis Many Value Sources originate value through capability. A capability basis describes what the source is capable of doing that is relevant to the governed value. Examples include: Factory → production capability AI system → analytical or automation capability Battery → energy-storage capability Hospital → diagnostic and treatment capability Satellite → observation or communication capability Financial infrastructure → capital allocation capability Capability itself does not prove that value has emerged. It establishes a potential basis from which value may originate. Utility Basis Some sources contribute to value because they provide utility. Utility may include the ability to: solve a problem; satisfy a requirement; perform a function; enable access; reduce effort; improve availability; increase convenience; provide information; enable coordination; support another capability. VSBM identifies the utility basis without assigning universal economic worth to it. Cost-Reduction Basis Value may originate not from producing more output but from requiring fewer resources to achieve the same or better outcome. A Value Source may therefore have a basis in: reduced energy consumption; reduced material consumption; reduced labor requirement; reduced computation; reduced infrastructure use; reduced downtime; reduced maintenance; reduced failure; reduced waste; reduced transaction cost; reduced process complexity; reduced time. This is particularly important because value systems focused only on revenue or asset appreciation may fail to identify avoided consumption and avoided loss as sources of value. VSBM makes such bases explicit. Performance-Improvement Basis A source may contribute to value by improving an existing outcome. Relevant improvements may include: speed; precision; reliability; availability; throughput; durability; efficiency; quality; scalability; recoverability; interoperability. The relevant value basis is the improvement capability, not merely the existence of the underlying technology or asset. Risk-Reduction Basis Value may originate through reduced exposure to undesirable outcomes. A source may therefore possess a basis capable of: preventing failure; reducing loss probability; reducing operational disruption; increasing resilience; enabling earlier detection; improving recovery; reducing uncertainty; preserving continuity. VSBM identifies the value-origin basis. It does not replace risk governance or determine the actual risk state. Access Basis Some sources become value-relevant because they provide access. Examples include access to: markets; infrastructure; information; capital; technology; distribution; networks; customers; expertise; locations; resources; platforms. Access itself may therefore constitute a Value Source Basis even where the accessed object belongs to another entity. Scarcity Basis Scarcity may contribute to value where limited availability is materially relevant to the governed Value Context. However: Scarcity ≠ Value Something can be scarce and have no relevant value. VSBM therefore treats scarcity as a possible basis, not as proof that value exists. Knowledge and Information Basis Knowledge may become a Value Source Basis where it enables an outcome that could not otherwise be achieved as effectively. Examples include: manufacturing know-how; scientific knowledge; operational experience; proprietary methodologies; process knowledge; historical datasets; diagnostic knowledge; engineering knowledge. The underlying information does not need to be monetized before its value-origin basis can be identified. Relationship Basis A relationship itself may create a basis from which value can originate. Examples include: trusted supplier relationships; distribution relationships; strategic partnerships; customer networks; research collaborations; institutional relationships; ecosystem participation. VSBM does not govern the relationship itself. It identifies what capability or advantage arising from that relationship is relevant to the governed value. Combination Basis A Value Source may possess several relevant bases simultaneously. For example: Reusable launch system may contain: reusability capability + rapid inspection capability + manufacturing knowledge + operational experience + infrastructure compatibility which together create a basis for lower mission cost. VSBM therefore permits: One Value Source → Multiple Value Source Bases It also permits multiple sources to contribute complementary bases toward one governed value. Direct and Enabling Basis VSBM may distinguish between: Direct Basis A basis capable of contributing directly to the governed value. Enabling Basis A basis that enables another source or capability to contribute to the governed value. Example: Manufacturing robot → productive capability → Direct Basis Predictive maintenance capability → increased availability of manufacturing robot → Enabling Basis Both can matter to the value origin without being methodologically identical. Latent Basis A source may possess a legitimate value basis even when that basis is not currently being used. This may occur where capability is: dormant; inaccessible; underutilized; technologically constrained; economically impractical; awaiting complementary infrastructure; awaiting demand; awaiting knowledge; awaiting activation. VSBM therefore recognizes: Latent Value Source Basis A latent basis does not mean that value has emerged. It means the source contains or enables a basis from which value may emerge under appropriate conditions. Basis Strength A Value Source Basis may exist with different levels of relevance or capability. Organizations may therefore assess whether the identified basis is: Weak Moderate Strong Conditional Latent Unresolved These are not universal value measurements. They are governance states describing how clearly and materially the identified basis is connected to the governed Value Context. The criteria should be defined for the relevant implementation. Basis Evidence The assertion that a source possesses a particular value-relevant basis should be supportable. Relevant evidence may include: operational records; technical specifications; observed capability; performance data; financial information; production data; scientific evidence; contractual rights; documented access; historical results; comparative analysis; simulation evidence; empirical observation. VSBM does not own general evidence validation. Where necessary, VALIDOS®, ADIT®, INTEGROS®, or other relevant architectures may govern the reliability, validation, auditability, or integrity of the supporting basis. Potential Basis ≠ Emerged Value VSBM preserves another critical distinction: Value Source Basis ≠ Value Emergence A source may possess an extraordinary capability and still produce no current value. Examples: Unused patent → technological basis exists → value may not yet have emerged Unused factory capacity → production basis exists → production value may not currently emerge Unexploited dataset → informational basis exists → decision value may not yet emerge Reusable technology → reuse basis exists → cost-saving value does not emerge until reuse actually changes the relevant resource requirement. This distinction protects the later VFM® lifecycle from treating potential as realized value. Basis Change A Value Source Basis may strengthen, weaken, disappear, or transform over time. Examples include: technology becoming obsolete; expertise increasing; infrastructure becoming available; access being lost; production capacity expanding; a patent expiring; energy becoming cheaper; interoperability improving; a relationship ending; knowledge becoming widely available. VSBM therefore requires material basis changes to remain identifiable where they affect the origin of governed value. Minimum Implementation Framework A practical VSBM implementation should establish: 1. Identified Value Source Receive the Value Source identified through VSOIM. 2. Governed Value Context Preserve the specific value context against which the source basis is being examined. 3. Basis Identification Identify the capability, utility, condition, property, relationship, access, knowledge, resource advantage, reduction capability, or other basis relevant to value. 4. Basis Type Classify the basis sufficiently for practical governance. 5. Basis Relevance Determine why the basis is relevant to the governed value. 6. Basis Structure Determine whether the basis is direct, enabling, composite, dependent, latent, or another materially relevant form. 7. Basis Condition Identify material conditions affecting whether the basis can operate. 8. Basis State Determine whether the basis is active, latent, conditional, constrained, degraded, or unresolved. 9. Basis Support Identify the information or evidence supporting the asserted basis where necessary. 10. Value Source Basis Record Document the basis for downstream Value Origin governance. Governance Outputs VSBM may produce: Value Source Basis Record Value Source Capability Record Value Source Basis Type Value Source Basis State Direct Value Basis Record Enabling Value Basis Record Latent Value Basis Record Composite Value Basis Record Value Basis Condition Record Value Basis Support Record Value Basis Change Record Value Source Basis Map These outputs provide the governed input for: VORM — Value Origin Relationship Module. Use Case 1 — Banking: Value Beyond the Balance Sheet A bank identifies its customer transaction infrastructure as a Value Source. VSBM does not stop at the existence of the infrastructure. It identifies the bases through which that source may contribute to different forms of value: transaction capability → payment-service value transaction information → analytical value customer connectivity → distribution value operational scale → unit-cost reduction potential historical transaction patterns → risk-analysis capability. The same source may therefore contain several different value-origin bases. VSBM enables the bank to identify those bases without prematurely assigning a monetary value or declaring that the potential has already been realized. Use Case 2 — Space Mission: Reusability as a Value Basis A space organization identifies a reusable launch vehicle as a Value Source. The physical vehicle itself does not explain the origin of cost-reduction value. VSBM identifies the relevant bases: reusable propulsion reusable structures rapid inspection reduced refurbishment requirements operational learning repeat-use infrastructure compatibility These capabilities collectively create a basis from which lower cost per mission may emerge. If the vehicle can technically be reused but refurbishment costs remain higher than replacement, the reuse capability still exists—but the expected cost-reduction value may not emerge. VSBM therefore separates: the capability capable of producing value from the later emergence of value itself. Foundational Principles A Value Source must have an identifiable basis through which it can contribute to governed value. Source existence is not a Value Source Basis. A Value Source Basis is context-specific. Capability is not automatically value. Scarcity is not automatically value. Potential value is not Emerged Value. Cost reduction, avoided loss, reduced resource consumption, and improved performance may constitute legitimate value-origin bases. A source may contain multiple Value Source Bases. Multiple sources may provide complementary bases for one governed value. A latent basis may exist before value emerges. Value Source Basis must remain distinguishable from the later Value Origin Relationship and Value Emergence. Canonical Closing Statement Value Source Basis Module establishes the second operational layer of Value Origin governance by determining what capability, utility, property, condition, knowledge, access, relationship, resource advantage, productive capacity, reduction capability, performance improvement, or other identifiable basis enables a Value Source to contribute to the origin of governed value. By separating source existence from value-relevant basis, and value- relevant basis from Value Emergence, VSBM prevents assets, capabilities, resources, rights, technologies, relationships, and potential advantages from being treated as value merely because they exist. The Module creates the governed basis required to determine how an identified source is actually related to the origin of value in the subsequent Value Origin Relationship Module.
