title: Value Source Identification Module (VSOIM)
text: Value Source Identification Module (VSOIM) Value Source Identification Module (VSOIM) Value Source Identification Module (VSOIM) Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanism Parent Standard: Value Origin Standard (VOS) Module: VSOIM — Value Source Identification Module Operational Layer: Value Source Identification Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Value Source Identification Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 23 August 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Value Source Identification Module (VSOIM) is the first Core Module of the Value Origin Standard (VOS). VSOIM governs the systematic identification of the specific source, capability, condition, activity, relationship, object, resource, knowledge, right, infrastructure, process, or other identifiable basis from which the governed value may originate. The Module establishes a fundamental starting point: Before the origin of value can be understood, the source capable of producing, enabling, supporting, or contributing to that value must first be identifiable. VSOIM does not determine whether value has already emerged. It identifies where the potential origin of that value resides. Architectural Position VSOIM is the first module within the Value Origin Standard. It receives the governed value context established by the preceding Value Context Standard (VCXS) and identifies the source or combination of sources potentially responsible for the origin of that value. The internal sequence begins: Governed Value Context → Value Source Discovery → Value Source Identification → Source Differentiation → Source-to-Value Linkage → Identified Value Source The identified source then proceeds to: VSBM — Value Source Basis Module where the basis upon which that source can generate value is examined. Operational Space VSOIM governs the identification of value sources. A Value Source may include: physical assets; natural resources; infrastructure; technologies; intellectual property; knowledge; data; human capability; organizational capability; productive capacity; manufacturing capability; services; processes; relationships; networks; access; rights; permissions; locations; time advantages; operational capabilities; computational capability; energy resources; financial resources; biological resources; scientific discoveries; inventions; unused capacity; combinations of multiple sources. The architecture does not require value to originate from a conventional economic asset. Anything capable of contributing to the emergence of the governed value may become a Value Source candidate. Value Source Identification VSOIM requires the source to be identified with sufficient specificity to distinguish it from other possible sources. A Value Source identification should establish, where relevant: Source Type What kind of source is involved? Source Object What specific object, capability, activity, relationship, condition, or resource represents the source? Source Location Where does the source exist operationally, physically, digitally, institutionally, or logically? Source Context Within what context can the source contribute to value? Source Function How is the source capable of contributing to the governed value? Source Relationship What relationship exists between the source and the value under examination? The objective is not merely to create a list of assets. The objective is to identify the actual origin candidates of the governed value. Value Source ≠ Asset VSOIM establishes an important distinction: Value Source ≠ Asset An asset may be a Value Source. But value may also originate from something that is not conventionally recognized as an asset. Examples include: collaboration between organizations; geographic position; access to infrastructure; accumulated operational knowledge; unused production capacity; network effects; timing; interoperability; reputation; human expertise; scientific insight; process improvement; reduced complexity; avoided failure; reduced resource consumption. VFM® therefore does not limit value-origin analysis to accounting or legal asset categories. Value Source ≠ Existing Value Identification of a Value Source does not establish that value currently exists. This distinction is foundational: Value Source → may enable Value Emergence but: Value Source ≠ Value Emergence A patent may exist without commercial value being realized. A factory may contain unused productive capacity. A dataset may exist without being operationally exploited. A scientific discovery may exist decades before a valuable application emerges. A natural resource may exist without economically usable extraction capability. A computational optimization may exist before it produces measurable cost reduction. VSOIM identifies the source. Later VFM® governance determines what happens to value. Single-Source Value Some value may originate predominantly from one identifiable source. For example: Patent → licensing capability → economic value or: Energy-efficiency improvement → reduced energy consumption → operational cost value VSOIM identifies the source without prematurely determining the amount or state of resulting value. Multi-Source Value Many forms of value do not originate from one source. They emerge from combinations. For example: Technology + Data + Human Expertise + Infrastructure + Market Access may together enable a valuable service that none of the sources could independently produce. VSOIM therefore permits: One Value ← Multiple Value Sources The contribution of each source may later be examined without forcing the entire value origin into one artificial source. One Source, Multiple Values The reverse relationship is equally important. One source may contribute to several forms of value. For example, a satellite constellation may produce: navigation value communication value scientific value security value commercial value infrastructure value Therefore: One Value Source → Multiple Governed Values Each value remains connected to its own governed Value Context. Direct and Indirect Value Sources VSOIM distinguishes between direct and indirect sources where useful. A Direct Value Source contributes directly to the emergence of the governed value. An Indirect Value Source enables another source to generate that value. For example: Manufacturing Machine → direct production capability while: Predictive Maintenance System → increased machine availability → increased production capability. Both may contribute to value, but through different pathways. The distinction prevents enabling conditions from being confused with immediate value-producing sources. Dormant Value Sources A Value Source may exist without currently producing value. Such a source may be: unused; inaccessible; undeveloped; underutilized; disconnected; technologically unavailable; economically impractical; awaiting another capability; awaiting infrastructure; awaiting demand; awaiting activation conditions. VSOIM allows these sources to remain identifiable without declaring that their potential has already become value. This creates an important analytical category: Identified Value Source + No Current Value Emergence Such a condition can be strategically significant. Hidden Value Sources Organizations may possess sources of value that are not recognized by conventional accounting, asset-management, or operational structures. Examples may include: accumulated internal knowledge; unused datasets; manufacturing know-how; cross-system compatibility; spare infrastructure capacity; operational relationships; process knowledge; reusable engineering components; historical information; internal methodologies; underused intellectual property. VSOIM provides a method for making these potential value sources visible. It does not automatically declare them valuable. It identifies them as candidate origins requiring further governance. Source Dependency A source may depend upon another source before it can contribute to value. For example: AI Model depends upon Data + Computing Infrastructure + Energy + Operational Access before a particular value outcome can emerge. VSOIM should therefore preserve materially relevant source dependencies. This allows VFM® to distinguish between: Independent Value Source and Dependent Value Source without converting the Module into general dependency governance. Source Combination Some value emerges only when multiple sources interact. A source combination may therefore itself become analytically relevant. Example: Battery Technology + Charging Infrastructure + Energy Availability + Vehicle Platform may together create a value-generating capability that cannot be meaningfully attributed to one component alone. VSOIM may therefore identify: Composite Value Source where the governed value originates from a defined combination of sources. Source-to-Value Linkage Every identified Value Source should be linked to the governed value established under the Value Context Standard. The linkage should answer: Why is this source relevant to this specific governed value? A source should not be included merely because it exists. There must be a plausible value-origin relationship. This relationship is then examined more deeply by the subsequent Value Origin modules. Source Identification State For practical implementation, VSOIM may classify source identification as: 1. Candidate Source A possible source has been identified but the relationship to governed value remains insufficiently established. 2. Identified Source The source and its plausible relationship to the governed value are sufficiently distinguishable. 3. Composite Source The governed value depends upon an identifiable combination of sources. 4. Dependent Source The source requires another source or enabling condition before it can contribute to value. 5. Unresolved Source The governed value is observable or suspected, but its source cannot yet be sufficiently identified. These states allow organizations to work with uncertainty without inventing a source that evidence does not support. Minimum Implementation Framework A practical VSOIM implementation should establish: 1. Governed Value Context Identify the value context received from the Value Context Standard. 2. Candidate Source Discovery Identify potential sources capable of contributing to that value. 3. Source Identification Define the specific source sufficiently to distinguish it from alternatives. 4. Source Type Determine whether the source is an object, capability, resource, activity, relationship, condition, right, knowledge base, infrastructure, process, or another source type. 5. Source Relationship Establish the plausible relationship between the source and governed value. 6. Source Structure Determine whether the source is single, composite, direct, indirect, independent, or dependent. 7. Source State Determine whether the source is active, dormant, underutilized, inaccessible, undeveloped, or otherwise materially constrained. 8. Source Identification Record Preserve the identified source and its relationship to the governed value for downstream Value Origin governance. Governance Outputs VSOIM may produce: Value Source Candidate Record Value Source Identification Record Value Source Type Value Source-to-Value Link Direct Value Source Record Indirect Value Source Record Composite Value Source Record Dependent Value Source Record Dormant Value Source Record Unresolved Value Source Record Value Source Map These outputs provide the input basis for VSBM — Value Source Basis Module. Use Case 1 — Banking: Identifying Underused Sources of Value A bank may traditionally evaluate value through revenue, assets, deposits, loans, investments, and other recognized financial measures. VSOIM can expand the analysis to identify the underlying sources from which future value may originate. These could include: transaction data + customer relationships + payment infrastructure + risk expertise + distribution network + regulatory capability + technological infrastructure. The Module does not assign monetary value to those sources. Instead, it identifies which capabilities may actually be responsible for producing particular forms of value. This allows the institution to distinguish between: what it owns and what actually possesses value-generating capability. Use Case 2 — Space Mission: Finding Value in Cost Reduction A space organization develops a reusable launch architecture. The obvious Value Source may appear to be the launch vehicle itself. VSOIM may reveal that the governed value—such as lower cost per mission—actually originates from several interacting sources: reusable propulsion + rapid inspection capability + reusable structures + automated diagnostics + launch infrastructure + operational knowledge. The launch vehicle alone does not explain the value origin. The value may originate from the combined capability to reuse the system repeatedly at lower marginal cost. VSOIM identifies that source structure before VFM® determines whether the expected cost-reduction value has actually emerged. Foundational Principles Value cannot be traced to its origin until its source is identifiable. A Value Source is not automatically an asset. An asset is not automatically a Value Source. A Value Source is not Existing Value. Potential value is not Emerged Value. One value may originate from multiple sources. One source may contribute to multiple forms of value. A dormant source may remain strategically important even while producing no current value. Source identification must remain connected to the governed Value Context. Canonical Closing Statement Value Source Identification Module establishes the first operational layer of Value Origin governance by identifying the specific sources, capabilities, resources, activities, relationships, conditions, objects, knowledge, rights, infrastructure, processes, and source combinations from which governed value may originate. By distinguishing Value Sources from assets, Existing Value, Value Emergence, and external identity or ownership structures, VSOIM enables organizations to identify direct, indirect, composite, dependent, dormant, underutilized, and unresolved sources of value without prematurely asserting that value already exists. The Module therefore creates the traceable starting point required to determine not merely that value may exist, but where its potential origin can actually be found. title: Value Origin Standard (VOS)
text: Value Origin Standard (VOS) Value Origin Standard (VOS) 2. Value Origin Standard (VOS) Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanism Parent Standard: Value Origin Standard (VOS) Operational Layer: Value Origin Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Type: Parent Standard Governed Space: Value Origin Origin ID: VFM-VOS-002 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 23 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · AGA™ · INTEGROS® · CLA™ · ADIT® · VALIDOS® · OBIDENITY® AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Value Origin Standard (VOS) is the second Parent Standard within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanism and governs the identification, definition, relationship, conditions, and documentation of the origin from which governed value can emerge. VOS establishes the methodological distinction between the source capable of producing value and value that has actually come into existence. The Standard recognizes that value does not appear without a basis. It may originate from an object, capability, resource, activity, relationship, information, knowledge, right, condition, process, infrastructure, system, opportunity, natural resource, human capability, technological capability, or another identifiable source. VOS does not determine whether value has already emerged, how much value exists, what its current state is, how it changes, or whether it will ultimately be realized. Its purpose is foundational: to establish where the governed value can originate and the basis connecting that potential value to its source. Core Question From what identifiable source, capability, condition, activity, relationship, object, or other basis can the governed value originate? Architectural Position VOS occupies the second governed space of the VFM® value lifecycle. It follows: Value Context Standard (VCXS) and precedes: Value Emergence Standard (VES). The preceding standard establishes: What value is being governed? VOS then establishes: Where can that value come from? The next standard determines: Has value actually emerged? The sequence is therefore: Value Context → Value Origin → Value Emergence This distinction prevents a potential source of value from being treated automatically as existing value. Governance Flow Position Governed Value Context → Value Source Identification → Value Source Basis → Value Origin Relationship → Value Origin Conditions → Value Origin Documentation → Governed Value Origin → Value Emergence Operational Space VOS governs the space between: identified value context and actual emergence of value. Its governed space includes: value source identification; value-source differentiation; source basis; source capability; origin relationships; origin dependencies; origin conditions; latent value potential; multiple-source value origin; composite value origin; conditional value origin; temporal origin; origin continuity; origin change; origin documentation. The Standard asks whether a sufficiently identifiable basis exists from which the governed value can arise. It does not presume that value already exists. Value Source Principle A Value Source is an identifiable basis from which a defined form of value may potentially emerge. A Value Source may include: physical assets; natural resources; intellectual property; knowledge; data; infrastructure; technology; human capability; organizational capability; production capability; relationships; networks; contractual rights; access rights; operational capacity; energy resources; financial resources; land; biological resources; algorithms; software; inventions; scientific discoveries; market access; time; location; information; combinations of multiple sources. A source becomes relevant to VOS only in relation to the governed value context established by VCXS. Value Source ≠ Value The central distinction of VOS is: Value Source ≠ Existing Value An object, capability, resource, or relationship may possess the capacity to generate value without that value having yet emerged. For example: A mineral deposit may exist without economically recoverable value having emerged. A patent may exist without generating licensing value. A manufacturing machine may exist without producing operational value. A dataset may exist without creating informational or economic value. A technology may exist without creating cost-saving value. A scientific discovery may exist before commercial or operational value emerges. VOS therefore prevents potential from being silently treated as realized value. Origin Asset™ Origin Asset™ has its natural architectural home within Value Origin governance. An Origin Asset™ represents an identifiable asset, capability, resource, relationship, condition, or other governed basis capable of functioning as an origin from which value may emerge. The concept does not itself establish: existing value; monetary value; ownership; legality; validation; market recognition; accounting recognition; taxable value; asset identity; value realization. Its function within VFM® is narrower: Origin Asset™ identifies a potential value-origin basis. Therefore: Origin Asset™ ≠ Value Asset™ An Origin Asset™ may become associated with a Value Asset™ only after the relevant value has legitimately emerged and entered an applicable value state. Source Basis Identifying a source is insufficient unless the basis through which that source may produce value is understood. VOS therefore distinguishes: Value Source from Value Source Basis. For example: Factory → source. Capability to manufacture a required product → source basis. Dataset → source. Capability to reduce decision uncertainty → source basis. Satellite → source. Capability to generate Earth-observation information → source basis. Patent → source. Exclusive technological capability capable of enabling commercial exploitation → source basis. The source identifies where value may originate. The basis explains why that source is capable of producing the governed value. Value Origin Relationship Value may originate through a relationship rather than through an isolated object. VOS therefore governs the relationship between: Value Source → Governed Value The relationship may be: direct; indirect; enabling; dependent; conditional; composite; sequential; network-based; temporal; reciprocal. A source should not be attributed as the origin of value merely because it is associated with the value-bearing object. There must be a methodologically intelligible relationship between the source and the value capable of emerging from it. Multiple Value Sources One form of value may originate from multiple sources. For example: AI service value may originate from a combination of: model capability + data + computing infrastructure + software + human expertise + distribution network. No single source may independently explain the value. VOS therefore supports: Composite Value Origin where multiple sources jointly establish the basis from which value may emerge. One Source, Multiple Values The reverse is also possible. One source may generate several distinct forms of value. A satellite may generate: scientific value commercial data value strategic value navigation value security value environmental monitoring value These values must remain distinguishable according to the Value Context established under VCXS. Therefore: One Value Source ≠ One Value Latent Value Origin Some sources contain a value-generating capability that has not yet produced actual value. VOS recognizes this as: Latent Value Origin Examples may include: unused intellectual property; undeveloped land; unexploited mineral resources; dormant datasets; unused production capacity; uncommercialized scientific discoveries; unused spectrum; inactive infrastructure; unused technological capabilities. Latent origin is not equivalent to zero value. Nor is it equivalent to positive value. It identifies a potential value-origin condition prior to value emergence. Value Origin Conditions A Value Source may require particular conditions before value can emerge. These conditions may include: access; demand; technological capability; infrastructure; complementary resources; operational readiness; environmental conditions; human capability; network participation; timing; scarcity; usability; interoperability; availability; deployment; combination with another source. The existence of a source therefore does not imply that the conditions necessary for value emergence are present. Conditional Value Origin Where value can originate only under specified conditions, VOS recognizes: Conditional Value Origin For example: A renewable-energy installation may become a source of grid value only where grid connection exists. A dataset may become a source of analytical value only where sufficient processing capability exists. A manufacturing capability may become a source of commercial value only where demand exists. A technology may become a source of cost-saving value only when integrated into an operational process. The source exists. Its ability to produce the governed value remains conditional. Origin Dependency Some value origins depend upon other origins. For example: Software Service Value may depend upon: Software → Compute Infrastructure → Energy → Network Access VOS may therefore document Origin Dependencies where the ability of one source to produce value depends materially upon another source. This enables later lifecycle governance to distinguish between: loss of value and loss of a condition enabling the source to produce value. Value Origin Change A Value Source may change over time. Its capability may: increase; decrease; become inaccessible; become obsolete; combine with another source; split into multiple sources; become substituted; disappear. VOS therefore permits a governed Value Origin to be versioned or reassessed where material source conditions change. However: Value Origin Change ≠ Value Change A change in the source may eventually cause a change in value, but VFM® must preserve these as distinct lifecycle events. Origin Extinction ≠ Value Extinction A source may disappear while previously generated value continues to exist. Likewise, a source may continue to exist after the value associated with it has disappeared. Therefore: Value Source Extinction ≠ Value Extinction This distinction becomes important later in the VFM® lifecycle. Parent Standard Modules 1. VSOIM — Value Source Identification Module Governs identification and differentiation of the source, capability, resource, activity, relationship, condition, object, or other basis from which the governed value may originate. It establishes the identifiable Value Source. 2. VSBM — Value Source Basis Module Governs the basis explaining how and why the identified Value Source is capable of producing the governed value. It distinguishes simple association from an intelligible value-origin basis. 3. VORM — Value Origin Relationship Module Governs the relationship connecting the Value Source to the governed value. It supports direct, indirect, composite, enabling, conditional, sequential, and multi-source origin relationships. 4. VOCM — Value Origin Conditions Module Governs the conditions, dependencies, circumstances, thresholds, capabilities, or environmental states required for the identified source to function as an origin of the governed value. 5. VODM — Value Origin Documentation Module Governs the structured documentation, traceability, versioning, dependencies, conditions, and reconstruction of the governed Value Origin. Internal Module Flow Governed Value Context → VSOIM — Value Source Identification → VSBM — Value Source Basis → VORM — Value Origin Relationship → VOCM — Value Origin Conditions → VODM — Value Origin Documentation → Governed Value Origin → Value Emergence Standard The logic is: Where could the value originate? → Why can this source produce it? → How is the source connected to the value? → Under what conditions can that relationship operate? → How is the complete origin basis preserved? Cross-Architecture Boundaries VOS governs value origin, not general identity, validation, integrity, audit, authority, classification, or operational execution. OBIDENITY® may establish the identity, origin-bound identity, ownership, authority, provenance, or continuity of an underlying entity. VALIDOS® may determine whether a claim concerning a Value Source or origin relationship is sufficiently validated. INTEGROS® may govern integrity of the source, records, conditions, or supporting information. ADIT® may govern audit and evidence concerning how the origin determination was established. GOA™ may govern authority and responsibility for the process. VFM® retains the narrower question: From where can this governed value originate? Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum VOS implementation should establish: 1. Governed Value Context Identify the value context inherited from VCXS. 2. Value Source Identify the source or sources from which the value may originate. 3. Source Basis Define why the source is capable of producing the governed value. 4. Origin Relationship Define how the source relates to the value. 5. Origin Conditions Identify conditions required for the value-origin relationship to operate. 6. Dependencies Identify material dependencies affecting the source's ability to produce value. 7. Multi-Source Structure Where necessary, identify composite or interacting sources. 8. Temporal Basis Identify material timing or lifecycle conditions affecting origin. 9. Origin Status Establish whether the origin is active, latent, conditional, changed, unavailable, or otherwise appropriately governed. 10. Value Origin Record Document the complete governed origin basis for transfer into Value Emergence governance. Governance Outputs VOS may produce: Value Source Record Value Source Identifier Value Source Basis Record Value Origin Relationship Record Composite Value Origin Map Value Origin Dependency Record Value Origin Condition Record Latent Value Origin Record Conditional Value Origin Record Value Origin Change Record Value Origin Status Value Origin Record These outputs establish the basis required by the next lifecycle stage: Value Emergence Standard (VES). Enterprise Application VOS allows an organization to distinguish between: what exists and what actually creates the possibility of value. This is particularly useful in banking, investment, public finance, industrial systems, intellectual property, digital assets, AI, infrastructure, energy, natural resources, scientific research, and technology portfolios. Instead of beginning with an assumed monetary value, an organization can trace the governed value backward to the source or combination of sources capable of producing it. This creates a stronger methodological basis for later determining whether value has actually emerged, what state it occupies, and how it subsequently changes. Use Case 1 — Banking: Identifying the Real Source of Credit Value A financial institution evaluates a manufacturing company seeking financing. Traditional analysis may begin with assets, financial statements, collateral, and expected cash flows. VOS permits a different question: From what sources does the company's ability to generate the relevant value actually originate? The analysis may identify: manufacturing equipment + skilled workforce + production knowledge + customer relationships + intellectual property + supply-chain access as a composite Value Origin. This distinction matters because the physical equipment alone may not explain the value-generating capability. If critical customer relationships disappear or specialized production knowledge is lost, the underlying Value Origin may weaken even though the accounting assets remain physically present. VOS therefore provides a structured method for understanding the origin architecture behind value-generating capability before later VFM® stages govern actual value emergence and change. Use Case 2 — Space Mission: Locating the Source of Cost-Avoidance Value A space organization introduces a high-fidelity simulation capability intended to reduce expensive physical testing. The governed value context established under VCXS is: Cost-Avoidance Value → Mission Program → Mission Development Reference Framework. VOS then identifies where that value can originate. The source may not simply be: simulation software. The actual Value Origin may be composite: simulation model + computing infrastructure + validated engineering knowledge + scenario capability + mission data + engineering expertise. The source basis is the capability to detect design problems before expensive physical construction or testing occurs. The value has not necessarily emerged yet. VOS establishes only the governed origin from which that cost-avoidance value can emerge. When the simulation subsequently identifies a design defect and prevents a CHF 20 million physical-test failure, the architectural question moves from: Value Origin to: Value Emergence. This clean separation allows VFM® to trace the value lifecycle from its source rather than recognizing value only after financial consequences appear. Foundational Principles Value must not be assumed merely because a potential source of value exists. Value Source ≠ Existing Value. Origin Asset™ ≠ Value Asset™. One source may originate multiple forms of value. One form of value may originate from multiple sources. Value origin may be latent, active, conditional, composite, dependent, or changing. The source of value and the conditions enabling value emergence must remain distinguishable. A change in Value Origin does not automatically constitute a change in value. The disappearance of a Value Source does not automatically constitute Value Extinction. Canonical Closing Statement Value Origin Standard establishes the governed origin layer of the VFM® value lifecycle by identifying the sources, capabilities, resources, activities, relationships, objects, conditions, and composite structures from which a defined form of value may emerge. Through governance of Value Sources, source bases, origin relationships, enabling conditions, dependencies, latent origins, conditional origins, multi-source structures, temporal changes, and origin documentation, VOS prevents potential value from being confused with existing value and establishes the methodological distinction between the capability to produce value and the actual emergence of value. By positioning Origin Asset™ as a value-origin concept rather than an automatic declaration of value, VOS provides the traceable foundation required for the next lifecycle question: not merely where value could come from, but whether value has actually come into existence. Nahlad Value Origin Standard (VOS) Architecture: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanism Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Canonical Definition: Value Origin Standard governs the identification, basis, relationships, conditions, and documentation of the sources from which a defined form of value may emerge, while preserving the fundamental distinction between a potential source of value and value that has actually come into existence. Governed Space: Value Origin A source may possess the capability to generate value without that value having yet emerged. Value Source ≠ Existing Value. → View Standard About standard Module Architecture → Value Source Identification Module (VSOIM) → Value Source Basis Module (VSBM) → Value Origin Relationship Module (VORM) → Value Origin Conditions Module (VOCM) → Value Origin Documentation Module (VODM) Related Documents → About Value Origin Standard (VOS) → VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture

title: About Value Recognition Standard (VRS)
text: About Value Recognition Standard (VRS) About Value Recognition Standard (VRS) About Value Recognition Standard (VRS) Architecture: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Parent Standard: Value Recognition Standard (VRS) Governed Space: Value Recognition Canonical Definition Value Recognition Standard (VRS) governs when existing value may be formally recognized as value within a defined governance context and establishes the criteria, basis, determination, limitations, and traceability required for that recognition. VRS creates a governed separation between two fundamentally different conditions: Value exists. and Value is recognized. Recognition does not create value merely by declaration, and failure to recognize value does not prove that value does not exist. Why VRS Matters Many systems recognize only the forms of value they are designed to see. An accounting system may recognize one form of value. A bank may recognize another. A company may recognize operational or strategic value that does not appear on its balance sheet. A government may recognize public or infrastructural value that has no direct market price. A technological system may reveal previously unrecognized value in data, capacity, energy, knowledge, or resources. Without an explicit recognition layer, these different recognition systems can easily be confused with the existence of value itself. VRS prevents that confusion. It asks: What existing value is being recognized? Within what context? According to what criteria? On what basis? With what limitations? For how long does that recognition remain applicable? Governance Flow Within the complete VFM® lifecycle: Value Context → Value Origin → Value Emergence → Value Recognition → Value State → Value Change → Value Development / Value Degradation → Value Nullification → Value Restoration / Value Extinction VRS governs the fourth governed space: Existing Value → Recognition Criteria → Recognition Basis → Recognition Determination → Recognition Limitations → Recognition Record → Recognized Value → Value State Governance This position is important because recognition can occur only after the architecture has established what value is being governed, where it originates, and whether that value has actually emerged. What VRS Helps Organizations Govern VRS provides a structured method for distinguishing: Value Existence ≠ Value Recognition Recognition ≠ Value Creation Non-Recognition ≠ Zero Value Recognition Status ≠ Value State Recognition Change ≠ Value Change Market Price ≠ Value Recognition Accounting Recognition ≠ VFM® Value Recognition Recognized Value ≠ Taxable Value The result is a recognition layer that can coexist with financial, accounting, market, regulatory, operational, technological, or institutional systems without allowing any one of those systems to become the universal definition of whether value exists. Contextual Recognition Recognition under VRS is explicitly contextual. The same value may simultaneously be: recognized operationally, unrecognized financially, recognized strategically, conditionally recognized institutionally, or recognized for one beneficiary but not another. These outcomes are not necessarily contradictory. They may reflect different recognition contexts, purposes, criteria, and beneficiaries. VRS therefore preserves the relationship: Value + Context + Recognition Basis + Recognition Determination + Limitations rather than reducing value recognition to a universal yes/no declaration. Recognition Does Not Control Value Existence One of the strongest protections created by VRS is that the recognizing system does not automatically gain authority over the existence of value. A bank failing to recognize a particular form of value does not prove that the value does not exist. An accounting framework not representing a form of operational value does not automatically eliminate that value. A market assigning no price does not automatically establish a zero-value state. An institution withdrawing recognition does not automatically extinguish the underlying value. These questions belong to different stages of the VFM® lifecycle. Recognition governs the relationship to existing value — not the existence of value itself. Use Case 1 — Banking: Recognizing Value Beyond Conventional Asset Representation A bank evaluates a company whose conventional financial statements show physical assets, cash flows, liabilities, and recognized intangible assets. However, the company also possesses substantial capabilities that may materially affect its future performance: proprietary datasets, specialized operational knowledge, AI capability, infrastructure access, technological capacity, established networks, or other resources that may not be represented in the same way within conventional financial reporting. VRS does not tell the bank what those resources are worth. Nor does it replace accounting standards, valuation methodology, credit methodology, or financial regulation. Instead, VRS provides a governance layer for asking: Does value associated with this resource already exist? If so: Does the bank recognize that value for this specific analytical purpose? What criteria support recognition? What evidence or basis supports it? What limitations apply? The bank might therefore establish: Existing Value → Recognized for Strategic Assessment while simultaneously maintaining: Not Recognized as Accounting Asset and: Not Yet Recognized for Collateral Purposes. Instead of forcing one recognition system to represent every form of value, VRS allows several recognition relationships to coexist transparently. This creates a potentially powerful foundation for more sophisticated banking, investment, credit, enterprise-value, and risk-analysis systems. Use Case 2 — Space Mission: Recognizing Value Created by Avoided Cost and Preserved Capability A space organization develops a new mission-planning system that reduces unnecessary fuel consumption, simulation workload, mission preparation time, hardware testing, or operational risk. Traditional project accounting can record many of the costs involved. But the organization may also need to understand another question: What value has been created by resources that no longer need to be consumed? Suppose improved mission planning avoids: 500 hours of engineering work, thousands of simulation executions, unnecessary hardware testing, or additional mission fuel requirements. The underlying benefit may already exist because the organization has materially avoided resource consumption. VRS provides the recognition layer for determining whether that existing benefit is recognized as value within the relevant mission, operational, strategic, or resource-efficiency context. The recognition can remain explicitly bounded: Recognized Operational Value without automatically becoming: Accounting Asset Market Value or Taxable Value. Subsequent VFM® standards can then govern the state, development, degradation, nullification, or restoration of that value. This allows organizations to govern value that conventional systems may not have been designed to represent directly. Enterprise Value VRS gives organizations a common methodological layer for recognizing different forms of existing value without collapsing them into price, accounting treatment, taxation, ownership, or market acceptance. This can be particularly useful across banking, investment, public finance, industrial systems, infrastructure, technology, AI, energy, science, digital assets, intellectual property, resource optimization, and government decision-making. The deeper advantage is interoperability. Different systems may disagree about whether they recognize a value while still referring to the same governed value object and lifecycle. That makes recognition differences visible, comparable, traceable, and eventually machine-readable. Foundational Principle Value does not begin to exist because a system recognizes it, and it does not cease to exist merely because a system fails to recognize it. title: Value Recognition Basis Module (VRBM)
text: Value Recognition Basis Module (VRBM) Value Recognition Basis Module (VRBM) VRBM — Value Recognition Basis Module Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture Parent Standard: Value Recognition Standard (VRS) Module: VRBM — Value Recognition Basis Module Operational Layer: Value Recognition Basis Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Value Recognition Basis Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 24 August 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language Canonical Definition Value Recognition Basis Module (VRBM) is the second Core Module of the Value Recognition Standard (VRS) within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture. VRBM governs the identifiable basis upon which an existing value may be considered for formal recognition against the recognition criteria established by VRCM — Value Recognition Criteria Module. The Module establishes what information, observation, relationship, condition, capability, effect, measurement, evidence, or other support forms the basis for determining whether applicable recognition criteria are satisfied. Its purpose is not to create value, establish value existence, define recognition criteria, or issue the final recognition determination. Its function is narrower: to establish the governed basis upon which recognition can be assessed. This creates the methodological relationship: Recognition Criteria → Recognition Basis → Recognition Determination Architectural Position VRBM operates within the fourth governed space of the VFM® lifecycle: Value Context → Value Origin → Value Emergence → Value Recognition → Value State → Value Change → Value Development / Value Degradation → Value Nullification → Value Restoration / Value Extinction Within the Value Recognition Standard, VRBM follows the establishment of recognition criteria and precedes the actual recognition determination. Internal Module Flow Existing Value → VRCM — Value Recognition Criteria → VRBM — Value Recognition Basis → VRDM — Value Recognition Determination → VRLM — Value Recognition Limitation → VRRM — Value Recognition Record → Recognized Value The internal logic is: What must be satisfied → What supports that assessment → What recognition determination follows → What limitations apply → How recognition is recorded VRBM therefore provides the methodological bridge between recognition rules and recognition decisions. Operational Space VRBM governs the basis used to support, challenge, condition, or prevent recognition of existing value within a defined context. A recognition basis may derive from: observable effects; measurable outcomes; demonstrated capability; operational contribution; beneficiary benefit; resource availability; resource preservation; cost avoidance; efficiency improvement; productive capacity; strategic capability; technological capability; economic contribution; functional utility; realized benefit; documented relationships; comparative performance; temporal persistence; accessibility; usability; reproducible outcomes; governed evidence; other contextually relevant support. The relevant basis depends upon the recognition context and the criteria established by VRCM. VRBM does not prescribe one universal form of proof for all value. Recognition Basis Principle A recognition determination should not rest solely upon an unsupported assertion that something is valuable. The basis for recognition must be identifiable. The governing relationship is: Existing Value + Recognition Criteria + Recognition Basis → Recognition Determination The recognition basis answers: What supports the conclusion that this existing value satisfies, fails to satisfy, or conditionally satisfies the applicable recognition criteria? Basis Must Relate to Criteria VRBM requires a traceable relationship between: Recognition Criterion and Recognition Basis. A large amount of information is not necessarily a relevant recognition basis. The basis must address the criterion actually being assessed. For example, if the criterion concerns: measurable reduction in resource consumption, relevant basis may include: before-and-after resource consumption; controlled operational measurements; comparative execution results; documented avoided consumption; attributable efficiency effects. Information concerning unrelated market popularity would not automatically satisfy that criterion. Therefore: Available Information ≠ Applicable Recognition Basis Recognition Basis ≠ Recognition Criteria VRCM determines what must be demonstrated. VRBM determines what supports the assessment of whether it has been demonstrated. For example: Criterion: The capability must materially reduce operating cost. Basis: Operational records demonstrate a recurring 18% reduction in the governed cost category after deployment. These are methodologically distinct. If criteria and basis are collapsed into one layer, organizations can silently change the recognition rule according to whatever information happens to be available. VRBM prevents this. Recognition Basis ≠ Recognition Determination A strong recognition basis does not itself issue recognition. The basis is evaluated by the subsequent VRDM — Value Recognition Determination Module. Therefore: Recognition Basis → Input to Determination not: Recognition Basis = Recognition This distinction enables the same underlying basis to be examined consistently by different authorized systems, processes, or decision mechanisms. Recognition Basis ≠ Value Existence Value existence precedes recognition governance. VRBM therefore does not determine whether the underlying value exists. That architectural question belongs to the Value Emergence Standard (VES). VRBM asks only what basis supports recognition of that existing value within the specified context. Therefore: Insufficient Recognition Basis ≠ No Value An existing value may remain unrecognized because the basis required by a particular recognition system is unavailable, incomplete, inaccessible, or insufficiently established. Recognition Basis ≠ Value Measurement Recognition basis may include quantitative measurements. But the existence of measurement does not mean VRBM governs value magnitude. For example: 500 engineering hours avoided may form part of a recognition basis. Determining the full magnitude, economic significance, financial valuation, or market price associated with that effect may require another methodology or governance system. Therefore: Measured Effect ≠ Complete Value Measurement Recognition Basis Types A governed recognition system may distinguish several forms of basis. 1. Observational Basis Recognition is supported by directly observable conditions, effects, states, or outcomes. 2. Measurement Basis Recognition is supported by measurable changes, quantities, performance, resource effects, or other quantified relationships. 3. Operational Basis Recognition is supported by demonstrated contribution to actual operations. 4. Capability Basis Recognition is supported by an existing capability capable of producing a defined benefit. 5. Beneficiary Basis Recognition is supported by an identifiable benefit to the relevant beneficiary. 6. Comparative Basis Recognition is supported by comparison between alternatives, states, periods, systems, or configurations. 7. Evidential Basis Recognition is supported by governed evidence produced through another applicable governance or evidential process. 8. Composite Basis Recognition depends upon multiple basis types considered together. These categories are not required to be exhaustive. They provide a structured vocabulary for distinguishing how recognition is supported. Direct and Indirect Recognition Basis VRBM distinguishes: Direct Recognition Basis from Indirect Recognition Basis. A direct basis has a relatively immediate relationship to the recognition criterion. Example: Criterion: reduction of electricity consumption. Direct Basis: verified electricity consumption decreased by 20% under comparable operating conditions. An indirect basis supports recognition through an intermediate relationship. Example: new control capability → reduced machine idle time → reduced electricity consumption → operational benefit. Indirect basis is not automatically weaker. However, the relationship between the basis and the recognition criterion must remain explicit. Internal and External Recognition Basis Recognition basis may originate internally or externally. Internal Basis may include: operational records; internal measurements; production data; capability records; cost records; resource records; performance data; internal simulations; internal assessments. External Basis may include: market information; external measurements; independent assessments; public data; customer outcomes; external evidence; scientific observations; regulatory information; third-party analysis. VRBM does not assume that external information is inherently superior to internal information. The relevant question is whether the basis legitimately supports the recognition criterion within the defined context. Actual and Prospective Basis Recognition may concern value whose effects are already observable or value associated with a capability whose future benefit remains contextually relevant. VRBM therefore distinguishes: Actual Basis from Prospective Basis. Actual basis derives from effects that have already occurred or are currently observable. Prospective basis derives from a governed relationship between an existing capability and a future value-relevant effect. Prospective basis must not be silently represented as realized benefit. Therefore: Expected Benefit ≠ Realized Benefit Both may support recognition in appropriate contexts, but they must remain distinguishable. Attribution Principle Where recognition is based upon an observed benefit or effect, VRBM should establish whether the effect can reasonably be related to the governed value. For example: operating cost decreased does not automatically establish: the governed capability created the reduction. Other factors may have contributed. VRBM therefore requires the recognition basis to preserve material attribution conditions where relevant. This may include: causal relationship; contributory relationship; comparative relationship; temporal relationship; dependency relationship; beneficiary relationship. VRBM does not need to establish universal causality. It requires the claimed relationship supporting recognition to be explicit. Counterfactual Basis Some forms of value are most visible through what did not occur. Examples include: cost avoided; downtime prevented; energy not consumed; failure prevented; material waste avoided; capacity preserved; risk exposure reduced; engineering work eliminated; infrastructure expansion avoided. These forms of benefit may require a counterfactual basis: Observed or Expected State compared with Relevant Alternative State VRBM permits counterfactual recognition basis where the comparison is sufficiently defined for the relevant recognition context. This is particularly important because value does not always appear as a new asset, payment, or revenue stream. Sometimes value appears as: resources that no longer need to be consumed. Basis Quality VRBM does not reduce basis quality to a single universal score. However, the recognition basis should be sufficiently characterized to determine whether it is suitable for the recognition context. Relevant characteristics may include: relevance; completeness; traceability; specificity; temporal relevance; representativeness; reproducibility; attribution strength; uncertainty; consistency; independence; accessibility; comparability. The required quality depends upon the significance and purpose of recognition. Basis Sufficiency VRBM may determine whether the available basis is sufficiently established to proceed to recognition determination. Possible basis states may include: Established Basis The basis required for assessment is sufficiently available and applicable. Conditional Basis The basis supports assessment only under explicitly defined conditions. Partial Basis Some required support exists, but material elements remain incomplete. Conflicting Basis Material supporting and opposing information coexist and require explicit treatment. Insufficient Basis The available basis does not sufficiently support a recognition assessment. Unavailable Basis The required basis cannot presently be established or accessed. These states describe the recognition basis. They do not determine the final recognition outcome. Conflicting Recognition Basis Recognition governance must preserve materially conflicting information. For example: operational records may indicate that a capability reduces cost, while another dataset indicates that maintenance requirements eliminate much of the benefit. VRBM should not discard one basis merely because it produces an inconvenient result. Instead, the conflict should remain visible for VRDM — Value Recognition Determination Module. Therefore: Recognition Basis Governance includes supporting, limiting, and contradictory basis. Temporal Basis A recognition basis may weaken or become obsolete over time. Examples include: technology changes; operational conditions change; beneficiary needs change; market structure changes; resource scarcity changes; capability deteriorates; new information becomes available; the underlying value changes; recognition criteria change. VRBM therefore requires material temporal applicability to remain identifiable. A basis valid in one period should not automatically be treated as permanently applicable. Multiple Recognition Contexts The same existing value may have different recognition bases in different contexts. For example, an AI optimization capability may have: Operational Recognition Basis: measured reduction in process time. Energy Recognition Basis: measured reduction in electricity consumption. Strategic Recognition Basis: demonstrated capability unavailable to competitors. Financial Recognition Basis: documented recurring cost reduction. Collateral Recognition Basis: insufficient basis. These different outcomes do not alter the existence of the underlying value. They describe different relationships between the value and different recognition systems. Basis Traceability A governed recognition basis should remain traceable to its source. Where relevant, the record should identify: Value Reference → Recognition Context → Recognition Criterion → Basis Object → Basis Source → Basis Relationship → Basis Conditions → Basis Limitations → Basis State This makes recognition reconstructable rather than dependent upon undocumented judgment. Machine-Readable Recognition Basis VRBM provides a structure suitable for machine-readable value recognition. A machine-readable implementation may represent: Value ID → Recognition Context ID → Criterion ID → Basis ID → Basis Type → Source → Observed / Prospective Status → Attribution Relationship → Temporal Applicability → Uncertainty → Basis State → VRDM Determination This can allow AI, banking, enterprise, public-sector, infrastructure, and other systems to distinguish between: a value claim and the basis supporting recognition of that value claim. Boundary with VRCM VRCM — Value Recognition Criteria Module establishes the criteria that must be satisfied. VRBM — Value Recognition Basis Module establishes the basis used to assess those criteria. Therefore: Criteria = What must be demonstrated Basis = What supports whether it has been demonstrated Boundary with VRDM VRBM does not issue the recognition determination. VRDM — Value Recognition Determination Module evaluates the applicable criteria against the governed recognition basis and determines the recognition outcome. Therefore: Criteria + Basis → Determination Boundary with VALIDOS® VRBM does not replace general validation governance. Where a recognition process requires formally validated evidence, VALIDOS® may govern whether that evidence is sufficiently validated for its intended reliance. VRBM governs a different question: What basis is being used for value recognition? VALIDOS® governs: Can a validation claim legitimately be established and relied upon? The same evidence may participate in both systems while the governance questions remain distinct. Boundary with ADIT® VRBM may use audit evidence or auditable records as recognition basis. It does not govern audit execution or general evidence governance. ADIT® may establish what occurred and preserve evidence concerning it. VRBM determines how that information functions as a basis for value recognition. Boundary with INTEGROS® VRBM does not govern general integrity. Where the integrity of a recognition-basis object is material, INTEGROS® may govern its integrity properties. VRBM governs the role of that object within value recognition. Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum VRBM implementation should establish: 1. Value Reference Identify the existing value being considered for recognition. 2. Recognition Context Identify the context within which recognition is being assessed. 3. Applicable Recognition Criteria Receive the applicable criteria established through VRCM. 4. Basis Identification Identify the information, observation, capability, relationship, effect, measurement, evidence, or other support relevant to those criteria. 5. Basis Source Identify where the recognition basis originates. 6. Criterion-to-Basis Relationship Establish which basis supports, challenges, limits, or conditions each criterion. 7. Attribution Relationship Identify material relationships between the governed value and observed or expected benefit where relevant. 8. Basis Conditions and Limitations Preserve material assumptions, conditions, uncertainty, temporal limits, and exclusions. 9. Basis State Determine whether the recognition basis is established, conditional, partial, conflicting, insufficient, or unavailable. 10. Recognition Basis Record Preserve the governed basis for downstream recognition determination. Governance Outputs VRBM may produce: Value Recognition Basis Record Recognition Basis Object Recognition Basis Source Record Criterion-to-Basis Mapping Recognition Basis Type Classification Direct / Indirect Basis Record Actual / Prospective Basis Record Attribution Relationship Record Counterfactual Basis Record Recognition Basis Condition Record Recognition Basis Limitation Record Recognition Basis Conflict Record Recognition Basis State Recognition Basis Traceability Chain These outputs provide the governed input for VRDM — Value Recognition Determination Module. Use Case 1 — Banking: Recognition of Operational and Strategic Value A bank assesses a company that has developed a proprietary automation platform. The company claims that the platform represents substantial value. The claim itself is not a sufficient recognition basis. VRCM may already have established criteria such as: material operational contribution; recurring economic benefit; demonstrated capability; continued usability; beneficiary relevance. VRBM then establishes the basis against those criteria. The governed basis might include: production time reduced by 27% → operational measurement basis external software expenditure reduced by CHF 1.8 million annually → cost-avoidance basis system deployed across 14 production locations → capability and operational basis three years of recurring performance improvement → temporal persistence basis continued dependence of critical workflows upon the platform → operational relevance basis The bank can now distinguish: “Management claims this technology is valuable.” from: “A defined recognition basis exists showing how this capability produces material value within the specified enterprise context.” VRBM does not determine collateral eligibility, accounting recognition, market valuation, or credit treatment. It provides a governed basis that those downstream systems may use according to their own rules. Use Case 2 — Space Mission: Value Through Avoided Resource Consumption A space organization introduces a new mission-planning and simulation capability. The organization believes the capability creates value because it reduces mission preparation cost and resource consumption. VRCM establishes recognition criteria such as: measurable resource reduction; preserved mission capability; avoided engineering workload; reduced simulation consumption; reduced physical testing; reduced fuel requirement. VRBM establishes the recognition basis. For example: 8,000 engineering hours avoided → labor-resource basis 35% fewer high-performance simulation executions required → computational-resource basis two physical prototype test campaigns eliminated → avoided-testing basis projected mission fuel requirement reduced within the governed mission configuration → mission-resource basis The recognition basis can also preserve the relevant counterfactual: mission preparation with the capability versus mission preparation without the capability. The organization can therefore establish a governed basis for recognizing value created through non-consumption of resources. This is important because no new physical asset necessarily appears. The value may exist precisely because something costly no longer has to happen. Enterprise Application VRBM gives organizations a governed answer to a fundamental question: What is the basis for saying that this existing value should be recognized? This is applicable across banking, investment, enterprise management, public finance, infrastructure, AI, energy, manufacturing, science, digital systems, intellectual assets, resource optimization, government programs, and mission- critical operations. It allows recognition systems to move from: asserted value toward: basis-supported recognition. More importantly, it allows different recognition systems to use different legitimate bases without redefining value itself. The same value may have a strong operational basis, a partial financial basis, an insufficient collateral basis, and a strong strategic basis simultaneously. VFM® can preserve all of those relationships without forcing them into one universal recognition outcome. Foundational Principles Recognition requires an identifiable basis. Recognition basis does not create value. Recognition basis is not recognition criteria. Recognition basis is not recognition determination. Insufficient recognition basis does not prove absence of value. Available information is not automatically applicable recognition basis. Recognition basis must remain connected to the criterion it is intended to support. Expected benefit must remain distinguishable from realized benefit. Supporting and contradictory recognition basis must both remain visible. Value may be recognized through what is created, preserved, enabled, improved, or no longer needs to be consumed. A value claim becomes governable when the basis supporting its recognition can be identified, related to explicit criteria, and reconstructed. Canonical Closing Statement Value Recognition Basis Module establishes the governed support layer of the Value Recognition Standard by defining the identifiable basis upon which existing value may be assessed against explicit recognition criteria. Through governance of basis identity, source, type, criterion relationship, attribution, direct and indirect support, actual and prospective effects, counterfactual comparison, conflicting information, temporal applicability, limitations, basis states, and traceability, VRBM prevents value recognition from resting solely upon unsupported assertion, institutional convention, or undocumented judgment. By separating recognition criteria from recognition basis and recognition basis from final recognition determination, VRBM creates a reconstructable methodological chain from existing value to recognition decision while preserving the foundational VFM® principle that insufficient recognition basis within one context does not establish that the underlying value does not exist.
