title: Value Restoration Determination Module (VRDM)
text: Value Restoration Determination Module (VRDM) Value Restoration Determination Module (VRDM) Value Restoration Determination Module (VRDM) Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture Parent Standard: Value Restoration Standard (VRSS) Module: VRDM — Value Restoration Determination Module Operational Layer: Value Restoration Determination Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Value Restoration Determination Origin ID: VFM-VRSS-VRDM-010.4 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 27 August 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Value Restoration Determination Module (VRDM) is the fourth Core Module of the Value Restoration Standard (VRSS). VRDM governs the formal determination of whether previously degraded, impaired, dormant, lost, inaccessible, or zero value has actually been restored following a governed restoration process. The Module receives the Restoration Candidate produced through the preceding ReMonet™ mechanism and determines whether restoration has occurred, what value has been recovered, to what extent recovery has occurred, whether the recovered value corresponds to previously existing value, and what evidential basis supports the determination. VRDM establishes the critical distinction between: attempted restoration and determined restoration. Its foundational function is: to prevent restoration activity, expenditure, intervention, technical recovery, reactivation, or apparent improvement from being treated as restored value until the resulting value has been explicitly determined. Architectural Position VRDM is the fourth module within VRSS. It follows: VRMM — ReMonet™ Mechanism Module and precedes: VRTRM — Value Restoration Transition Module. The preceding modules establish: what previously existing value is being considered for restoration → whether restoration conditions exist → how ReMonet™ acts upon the affected value. VRDM then establishes: whether value was actually restored and what restoration legitimately occurred. VRTRM subsequently governs the formal transition of the determined restored value into its resulting Value State. Internal Flow Restoration Candidate → Prior Value Reference → Recovery Evidence Identification → Restored Value Comparison → Restoration Extent Assessment → Restoration Attribution Assessment → Restoration Boundary Test → Restoration Determination → Determination Record → VRTRM — Value Restoration Transition Module Operational Space VRDM governs the space between: a completed or materially progressed restoration mechanism and formal recognition that value has been restored. Its operational space includes: Restoration Candidate identification; prior-value reference; recovery evidence; restoration comparison; restoration extent; restoration magnitude; partial restoration; full restoration; over-restoration classification; restoration attribution; restoration uncertainty; failed restoration determination; indeterminate restoration; conditional restoration; restoration boundary testing; separation of restored value from newly emerged value; separation of restored value from subsequent Value Development; determination documentation; downstream transition readiness. Restoration Candidate Principle VRDM does not begin with the assumption that restoration succeeded. It begins with a: Restoration Candidate. A Restoration Candidate represents value that may have been recovered through a governed restoration mechanism. The purpose of VRDM is to determine whether that candidate legitimately constitutes restored value. Therefore: Restoration Candidate ≠ Restored Value. Prior Value Reference Restoration requires a relationship to value that existed previously. VRDM must therefore establish an appropriate Prior Value Reference. The reference may identify: prior value existence; prior Value State; prior value magnitude; prior value capability; prior productive function; prior economic utility; prior operational utility; prior access; prior rights; prior informational utility; prior strategic utility; another relevant value condition. The reference does not always need to be numerical. What matters is that restoration can be distinguished from the emergence of value that never previously existed. Prior Value ≠ Historical Maximum The appropriate restoration reference is not automatically the highest value ever associated with an asset. An asset may historically have passed through several Value States. VRDM must determine the relevant reference according to: restoration scope; governed value relationship; temporal basis; previous legitimate state; restoration objective; available evidence. Therefore: Prior Value Reference ≠ Automatic Historical Maximum. Recovery Evidence A restoration determination requires evidence that value has actually recovered. Evidence may include: restored functionality; recovered productive capability; resumed economic utility; restored access; renewed usability; recovered rights; restored information; operational performance; restored market relevance; recovered capacity; verified technical capability; restored serviceability; another value-relevant outcome. VRDM determines the value consequence. It does not automatically treat the completion of a technical activity as evidence that equivalent value has returned. Activity ≠ Restoration This distinction is fundamental. An asset may be: repaired without recovering meaningful value. A system may be: restarted without becoming operationally useful. Data may be: recovered without recovering their former informational value. A patent may be: reactivated without regaining economic relevance. Therefore: Restoration Activity ≠ Restored Value. VRDM exists specifically to govern this distinction. Restoration Extent Restoration may occur to different extents. VRDM may determine: No Restoration Partial Restoration Substantial Restoration Full Restoration or another explicitly defined organizational state. The state must be supported by the governed value basis rather than by the amount of effort invested in restoration. Partial Restoration Previously existing value does not need to be recovered completely for restoration to be legitimate. Example: Prior Value = 100 Degraded Value = 30 Post-ReMonet™ Value = 70 The recovered value: 30 → 70 may represent legitimate restoration. The remaining gap: 70 → 100 represents value not yet recovered. Therefore: Incomplete Recovery ≠ Failed Restoration. Full Restoration Full restoration occurs where the relevant previously existing value has been recovered to the governed reference condition. This does not necessarily mean the Value Object is identical to its historical form. A modernized machine may restore the productive value of an older machine through different technology. A migrated digital system may restore access and functionality through a new technical architecture. VRDM therefore determines restoration of value, not restoration of historical physical or technical identity. Restoration Beyond Prior Value A restoration process may produce a resulting value greater than the relevant prior-value reference. Example: Prior Value = 100 Degraded Value = 40 Post-Restoration Value = 130 VRDM must not automatically classify all: 40 → 130 as restored value. The architecture must distinguish: 40 → 100 = potentially restored value from: 100 → 130 = value requiring separate classification. Depending upon the governed basis, the additional value may represent: Value Development or new Value Emergence. Therefore: Value Produced During Restoration ≠ Automatically Restored Value. Restoration Attribution VRDM determines whether the observed recovery can legitimately be associated with the governed restoration process. This does not require universal causal proof. It requires a sufficient governed basis to distinguish restoration from unrelated value movement. For example, value may increase during a restoration project because: market prices increased; regulation changed; external demand returned; another asset became scarce; a new subsidy appeared; broader technological change occurred. VRDM must preserve material external contributions where they affect the restoration determination. Restoration Mechanism ≠ Restoration Cause ReMonet™ governs the restoration mechanism. The complete cause of value recovery may involve multiple internal and external factors. VRDM therefore does not require every restored unit of value to be attributed exclusively to ReMonet™. It requires the determination to remain honest about the basis upon which restoration is being recognized. Restoration Magnitude Where meaningful and methodologically supportable, VRDM may determine the magnitude of restored value. Magnitude may be expressed through: monetary value; productive capacity; functional capability; utility; availability; usable information; access; performance; rights; strategic capability; another governed value measure. VRDM does not require all forms of value to be reduced to money. The measure must correspond to the value relationship under determination. Quantitative Determination Where value is quantifiable, VRDM may compare: Pre-Restoration Value State with Post-Restoration Value Candidate. For example: 20 → 65 may indicate: 45 units of recovered value where the measurement basis legitimately supports that interpretation. The numerical difference alone does not establish restoration. The value identity, basis, scope, and attribution must remain governed. Qualitative Determination Some restoration cannot legitimately be expressed through one numerical value. Examples may include: restored access to critical information; restored institutional capability; restored interoperability; restored legal rights; restored operational capability; restored strategic usefulness. VRDM therefore supports qualitative and hybrid determinations where numerical measurement would create false precision. Conditional Restoration Restored value may exist only under defined conditions. For example: A repaired industrial system may recover productive value only: within a restricted operating range. A recovered dataset may regain informational value only: for a defined analytical purpose. A restored infrastructure asset may operate only: under temporary load restrictions. VRDM may therefore determine: Conditionally Restored Value. The conditions must travel with the determination. Temporary Restoration Value may be restored temporarily. A temporary restoration remains a legitimate restoration where the temporal boundary is explicit. Therefore: Temporary Restoration ≠ Permanent Restoration. VRDM must not allow short-term recovery to be recorded as indefinite restoration. Restoration Uncertainty A restoration determination may contain uncertainty. Uncertainty may concern: magnitude; durability; attribution; measurement; future usability; external dependencies; market conditions; technical stability; accessibility; operational performance. Uncertainty does not automatically prevent a restoration determination. It must remain visible where materially relevant. Restoration Determination States VRDM may establish the following minimum determination states: 1. Not Restored The available evidence does not establish recovery of the relevant previously existing value. 2. Indeterminate Available information is insufficient to determine whether restoration has occurred. 3. Partially Restored A defined portion or dimension of previously existing value has been recovered. 4. Conditionally Restored Value has been recovered, but the restoration remains dependent upon explicit conditions. 5. Temporarily Restored Value has been recovered for a defined or currently limited temporal period. 6. Restored The relevant previously existing value has been recovered to the governed restoration basis. These states may be extended where an implementation requires greater resolution. Failed ReMonet™ Determination A ReMonet™ mechanism may be successfully executed as a process while failing to restore value. For example: A company may complete: repair modernization reconfiguration and operational restart yet discover that the resulting asset has no meaningful productive or economic value. VRDM may therefore determine: ReMonet™ Executed — Value Not Restored. This is not a contradiction. It is one of the most important governance outcomes the Module must support. Indeterminate Restoration VRDM must permit an indeterminate result. Where evidence is insufficient, conflicting, immature, inaccessible, or incapable of establishing the value consequence, the correct determination may be: Indeterminate. The architecture must never force: Restored or Not Restored where the evidence does not legitimately support either conclusion. Restoration Boundary Test Before recognizing restored value, VRDM should test whether the observed value represents: recovery of previously existing value rather than: newly emerged value or development of value that already survived. The test may consider: Did this value exist previously? Was that value materially degraded, lost, dormant, inaccessible, or zero? Does the current value correspond to the previously existing value relationship? Is the observed increase recovery, new creation, or subsequent development? This prevents restoration from becoming an unlimited category for every positive value movement following intervention. VRDM Boundary with VRMM VRMM governs: how restoration is attempted. VRDM governs: whether restoration actually occurred. Therefore: Mechanism ≠ Determination. VRDM Boundary with VRTRM VRDM establishes the restoration determination. VRTRM governs the resulting transition into the appropriate Value State. Therefore: Determination ≠ State Transition. A restoration determination must exist before the corresponding lifecycle transition is formally recorded. VRDM Boundary with Value State Standard VRDM determines the restoration outcome. VSS determines the resulting current governed Value State. Therefore: Restoration Determination ≠ Value State. VRDM may establish that value was restored. VSS establishes what the current state of that value is. VRDM Boundary with Value Development Value Development governs strengthening, growth, maturation, or compounding of value that already exists. VRDM governs recovery of previously impaired value. Therefore: Recovery ≠ Growth. Where both occur within the same intervention, the architecture should separate the restored portion from subsequent development where materially possible. VRDM Boundary with Value Emergence Value that never previously existed cannot be restored. Therefore: New Value ≠ Restored Value. If a restoration intervention generates an entirely new value relationship, that value must be governed through the appropriate Value Emergence pathway. VRDM Boundary with Value Change A restoration determination may establish that material Value Change occurred. But Value Change and Value Restoration answer different questions. Value Change asks: What happened to existing value? VRDM asks: Did previously impaired value legitimately recover? VRDM Boundary with Value Nullification A ZVA™ may undergo ReMonet™ and subsequently receive a positive restoration determination. Value Nullification therefore does not prohibit later restoration where restoration potential remains. VRDM Boundary with Value Extinction Value Extinction establishes that the relevant value no longer exists as recoverable value within the governed lifecycle. Therefore: Extinguished Value cannot subsequently be determined as restored within the same governed value lifecycle. If value later appears, the architecture must determine whether a new value has emerged rather than retroactively treating extinction as temporary zero value. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Receive Restoration Candidate Receive the governed Restoration Candidate produced through VRMM. 2. Establish Prior Value Reference Identify the relevant previously existing value against which restoration is evaluated. 3. Identify Recovery Evidence Determine what evidence demonstrates actual recovery of the governed value. 4. Compare Value Conditions Compare the relevant pre-restoration and post-restoration conditions. 5. Determine Restoration Extent Establish whether recovery is absent, partial, conditional, temporary, substantial, full, or otherwise appropriately classified. 6. Assess Attribution Determine whether the observed recovery can legitimately be associated with the restoration process and identify material external contributions. 7. Test Restoration Boundary Separate recovered prior value from new Value Emergence or subsequent Value Development. 8. Preserve Uncertainty Record material uncertainty affecting the determination. 9. Issue Restoration Determination Assign the appropriate governed restoration determination state. 10. Create Determination Record Preserve the basis, evidence, reference condition, extent, attribution, limitations, uncertainty, and determination. 11. Transfer to Transition Governance Transfer the determined restoration outcome to VRTRM. Governance Outputs VRDM may produce: Restoration Candidate Assessment Prior Value Reference Record Recovery Evidence Record Restoration Comparison Record Restoration Magnitude Assessment Restoration Extent Determination Restoration Attribution Record Restoration Boundary Assessment Restoration Uncertainty Record Partial Restoration Determination Conditional Restoration Determination Temporary Restoration Determination Failed Restoration Determination Indeterminate Restoration Record Value Restoration Determination Value Restoration Determination Record These outputs provide the governed basis for: VRTRM — Value Restoration Transition Module. Use Case 1 — Restoration of Degraded Production Capacity An industrial production line previously operated at a governed productive capacity of: 100 units. Through deterioration and technological obsolescence, its productive value declines to: 35 units. A ReMonet™ program replaces critical components, modernizes control systems, restores process stability, and reactivates production. After the intervention, measured productive capability reaches: 80 units. VRDM does not ask merely whether the modernization project was completed. It determines whether productive value actually recovered. The governed comparison establishes: Prior Reference = 100 Pre-Restoration Condition = 35 Post-ReMonet™ Condition = 80 The line therefore demonstrates a substantial but incomplete recovery of previously existing productive value. VRDM may issue: Partially Restored with the restored portion and remaining value gap explicitly recorded. If subsequent optimization increases productive capability from: 80 → 115 VRDM prevents the entire increase from being classified as restoration. The architecture can distinguish the recovery of previously impaired productive value from later Value Development. Use Case 2 — Restoration of Dormant Data Value An organization possesses a historical technical dataset that once supported engineering analysis. Over time, the dataset becomes inaccessible because the original storage environment, software, formats, metadata structures, and interfaces become obsolete. The data continue to physically exist, but their usable informational value becomes dormant or effectively zero for the intended analytical purpose. A ReMonet™ process recovers the files, reconstructs metadata, migrates formats, validates accessibility, and integrates the dataset into a modern analytical environment. VRDM then determines whether the original informational value has actually been restored. File recovery alone is insufficient. The determination examines whether: the information is accessible the relevant content remains interpretable the dataset can again support the intended analytical purpose material information was preserved the recovered dataset corresponds to the previously existing value relationship. If only 70% of the historically useful information can be reliably reconstructed, VRDM may determine: Partially Restored Informational Value. If new analytics later derive insights that never previously existed, those new insights are not automatically classified as restored value. They represent a separate value event. Enterprise Application VRDM gives organizations a formal decision layer for answering a deceptively difficult question: Did we actually restore value, or did we merely perform restoration activity? It can be applied to: distressed assets; industrial rehabilitation; infrastructure recovery; digital recovery; legacy-system modernization; dormant intellectual property; impaired investments; data recovery; rights restoration; organizational capability recovery; operational restart; technological rehabilitation; productive-capacity recovery; asset reactivation; value recovery programs. The Module prevents organizations from equating: money spent work completed systems repaired assets reactivated or projects delivered with: value actually restored. Foundational Principles Restoration Candidate is not Restored Value. Restoration activity is not proof of restoration. ReMonet™ execution is not Restoration Determination. Restoration requires a relationship to previously existing value. Prior Value Reference is not automatically historical maximum value. Incomplete recovery may constitute legitimate partial restoration. Restoration beyond prior value must be separated from Value Development or new Value Emergence. Restoration cost does not determine restoration magnitude. Technical recovery does not automatically establish value recovery. Conditional restoration must remain conditional. Temporary restoration must not be represented as permanent restoration. Indeterminate is a legitimate determination where the evidence is insufficient. Value that never previously existed cannot be restored. Value Extinction must remain distinct from temporary or recoverable zero value. Canonical Closing Statement Value Restoration Determination Module establishes the formal determination layer of Value Restoration by governing whether a Restoration Candidate produced through ReMonet™ legitimately represents recovery of previously degraded, impaired, dormant, lost, inaccessible, or zero value. Through prior-value reference, recovery evidence, value comparison, restoration extent, magnitude, attribution, uncertainty, partial and conditional restoration, failure and indeterminate states, and explicit boundary testing against Value Emergence and Value Development, VRDM prevents restoration activity from being mistaken for restoration outcome. The Module ensures that repaired assets, recovered systems, reactivated capabilities, restored access, renewed rights, or completed interventions acquire restored-value status only where the relevant value consequence can actually be established. VRDM therefore creates the governed determination required before restored value may transition into a new Value State: restoration is not established because recovery was attempted, but because previously existing value can legitimately be shown to have returned. title: ReMonet® Mechanism Module (VRMM)
text: ReMonet® Mechanism Module (VRMM) ReMonet® Mechanism Module (VRMM) ReMonet™ Mechanism Module (VRMM) Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture Parent Standard: Value Restoration Standard (VRSS) Module: VRMM — ReMonet™ Mechanism Module Operational Layer: Value Restoration Mechanism Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Value Restoration Mechanism Origin ID: VFM-VRSS-VRMM-010.3 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 27 August 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition ReMonet™ Mechanism Module (VRMM) is the third Core Module of the Value Restoration Standard (VRSS). VRMM governs ReMonet™, the mechanism through which previously degraded, impaired, dormant, lost, inaccessible, or zero value is acted upon in order to recover previously existing value. The Module establishes how restoration is initiated, what restoration mechanism acts upon the affected value, how that mechanism operates, what value relationship it is intended to recover, what resources and interventions participate in the mechanism, and how the restoration process remains traceable from its governed starting condition to its resulting restoration candidate. VRMM does not determine merely whether favorable conditions for restoration exist. It governs the actual mechanism of restoration. Its foundational function is: to govern the mechanism through which previously existing but impaired value is intentionally or operationally moved toward recoverable value again. ReMonet™ ReMonet™ is the canonical VFM® mechanism for restoration of previously existing value. ReMonet™ may operate upon value that is: Degraded Impaired Dormant Lost Inaccessible or: Zero. ReMonet™ is therefore deliberately broader than recovery from absolute zero. Its canonical meaning is: a governed value-restoration mechanism through which previously existing value that has become degraded, impaired, dormant, lost, inaccessible, or zero is acted upon so that recoverable value may re-emerge. This establishes the critical distinction: Value Development = existing value grows. ReMonet™ = previously impaired value is recovered. Architectural Position VRMM is the third module within VRSS. It follows: VRSM — Value Restoration Scope Module VRCM — Value Restoration Conditions Module and precedes: VRDM — Value Restoration Determination Module VRTRM — Value Restoration Transition Module VRSM establishes: what previously existing value is proposed for restoration. VRCM establishes: whether the conditions necessary for restoration exist. VRMM establishes: how the restoration mechanism acts upon that value. VRDM subsequently determines: whether restoration actually occurred and what value was restored. Internal Flow Governed Restoration Scope → Satisfied Restoration Conditions → Restoration Mechanism Identification → ReMonet™ Initiation → Restoration Intervention → Mechanism Execution → Value Recovery Observation → Restoration Candidate → Mechanism Record → VRDM — Value Restoration Determination Module Operational Space VRMM governs the space between: restoration readiness and a value condition capable of being evaluated as potentially restored. Its operational space includes: restoration mechanism identification; ReMonet™ initiation; mechanism purpose; restoration intervention; mechanism inputs; mechanism resources; mechanism dependencies; restoration actions; mechanism sequence; mechanism execution; mechanism modification; mechanism interruption; mechanism failure; mechanism completion; restoration observation; restoration candidate generation; mechanism traceability; restoration mechanism record. Mechanism Principle ReMonet™ is not the favorable condition that makes restoration possible. It is the mechanism acting upon the affected value under those conditions. Therefore: Restoration Condition ≠ ReMonet™ Mechanism. A market may reopen. A regulation may change. New technology may become available. Financing may become available. Demand may return. These events can create restoration conditions. They do not automatically constitute ReMonet™. ReMonet™ begins when a mechanism actually acts upon the affected value in a manner directed toward recovery. Mechanism Identification Every governed ReMonet™ process should identify the mechanism through which restoration is expected to occur. A restoration mechanism may involve: repair; rehabilitation; reactivation; reconfiguration; reconstruction; recovery; reprocessing; modernization; reaccess; reintegration; repurposing; remediation; rights restoration; capability recovery; market re-entry; operational restart; technological adaptation; data recovery; another defined restoration mechanism. The mechanism must remain linked to the restoration scope established through VRSM. Mechanism ≠ Outcome The existence or execution of a ReMonet™ mechanism does not prove that value has been restored. Therefore: ReMonet™ Executed ≠ Value Restored. A repair may fail to recover functional value. A software modernization may fail to recover operational value. A data recovery process may retrieve information that no longer carries useful value. A market re-entry strategy may fail commercially. The mechanism creates a Restoration Candidate. VRDM determines whether restored value actually exists. Restoration Intervention A Restoration Intervention is an action or structured set of actions performed through the ReMonet™ mechanism to recover the scoped value. An intervention may be: Physical Digital Technical Operational Economic Organizational Legal Informational Market-based or: Hybrid. The intervention type does not define whether restoration has succeeded. It identifies how the recovery mechanism operates. Single-Mechanism Restoration Some value may be restored through one dominant mechanism. Example: Damaged Equipment → Repair → Recovered Function The repair may constitute the primary ReMonet™ mechanism. However, the resulting recovered function still requires determination through VRDM. Multi-Mechanism Restoration Complex value may require several mechanisms. For example: Dormant Industrial Facility may require: Equipment Rehabilitation → Software Modernization → Workforce Reconstitution → Operational Restart → Market Reintegration These mechanisms may collectively constitute a governed ReMonet™ process. VRMM must preserve their relationships rather than treating restoration as one undefined action. Sequential ReMonet™ Restoration mechanisms may depend upon a sequence. For example: Data Access Recovery → Data Reconstruction → Format Migration → System Reintegration → Operational Reuse If sequence materially affects restoration, VRMM should preserve that order. Parallel ReMonet™ Some mechanisms may operate simultaneously. For example: Physical Rehabilitation and Digital System Modernization may occur in parallel before an industrial asset can return to productive use. VRMM therefore supports both sequential and parallel restoration structures. Partial ReMonet™ ReMonet™ does not require complete recovery. A mechanism may restore only part of previously existing value. Therefore: Partial Recovery May Constitute Legitimate ReMonet™. For example: A degraded production system once provided productive value of 100. Its value declines to 20. A restoration mechanism recovers the system to 65. The movement: 20 → 65 may represent restored value. The fact that historical value of 100 has not been fully recovered does not invalidate the restoration mechanism. ReMonet™ from ZVA™ A ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ may enter ReMonet™ where: the relevant value is currently zero but: recoverable value remains within the governed lifecycle. The mechanism may then act upon the Value Object to recover previously existing value. Therefore: ZVA™ → ReMonet™ → Potentially Restored Value does not imply: ZVA™ = Value Extinction. This distinction is fundamental. ReMonet™ from Degraded Value ReMonet™ may begin before value reaches zero. For example: 100 → 40 through degradation. A restoration mechanism may subsequently move the value: 40 → 75. The recovered portion may constitute restored value. Therefore: ReMonet™ does not require prior Value Nullification. ReMonet™ from Dormant Value Value may remain latent or dormant rather than destroyed. Examples include: unused intellectual property; inaccessible historical data; idle production capacity; inactive infrastructure; dormant licenses; abandoned technologies; unused organizational capability. Reactivation may constitute ReMonet™ where the mechanism restores previously existing value. ReMonet™ from Inaccessible Value Value may continue to exist conceptually while becoming inaccessible. Examples include: inaccessible data; locked digital assets; unavailable rights; inaccessible infrastructure; isolated systems; unavailable knowledge repositories. A mechanism restoring access may produce restored value where access is materially required for the value to become usable again. Restoration by Repurposing A Value Object may recover previously existing value through a different use. This requires careful classification. If the new use recovers a relevant value relationship that previously existed, the process may contain ReMonet™. If the new use creates an entirely new value relationship that never previously existed, the process may represent Value Emergence. Therefore: Repurposing ≠ Automatically ReMonet™. The classification depends upon what value is actually being recovered. Restoration Through External Change Sometimes relatively little changes within the Value Object itself. External conditions may change so that previously dormant or zero value becomes recoverable. For example: A mineral asset may have zero economic value because extraction is uneconomic. A new processing technology may change the economics. The technology itself is an external condition. The mechanism through which the asset is brought back into economically productive use may constitute ReMonet™. VRMM governs the value-restoration mechanism. It does not govern the external technological system as a whole. Restoration Inputs A ReMonet™ mechanism may require inputs such as: capital; technology; labor; information; energy; materials; infrastructure; permissions; rights; access; data; expertise; organizational capacity; time. VRMM identifies materially relevant mechanism inputs where necessary for understanding how restoration occurred. Restoration Resource Principle The amount of resources consumed by restoration does not determine the amount of value restored. Therefore: Restoration Cost ≠ Restored Value. An organization may spend CHF 10 million attempting to restore an asset and recover only CHF 2 million of value. Another asset may require a minor intervention and recover substantial value. The mechanism record must not confuse resource expenditure with value outcome. Mechanism Causation Link VRMM should establish a traceable relationship between: Restoration Intervention and Observed Value Recovery Candidate. This does not require VRMM to determine universal causality. It requires enough mechanism linkage to show why the observed change is being considered a restoration candidate rather than an unrelated value event. Mechanism Attribution Where multiple mechanisms contribute to recovery, VRMM should preserve their contributions where materially distinguishable. For example: Repair Market Recovery Software Upgrade New Access Rights may jointly contribute to the resulting value condition. The Module should avoid assigning all restored value to one intervention where the recovery basis is materially multi- mechanistic. ReMonet™ ≠ Value Development This boundary is critical. Suppose value historically existed at 100. It degrades to 40. After intervention, value reaches 130. The process may contain: 40 → 100 = restoration of previously existing value and: 100 → 130 = development or newly emerging value depending upon the governed value basis. Therefore: Recovery Beyond Prior Value Requires Classification. ReMonet™ must not automatically absorb all positive value created after restoration begins. ReMonet™ ≠ Value Emergence Where value never previously existed, its appearance is not restoration. Therefore: No Prior Value → No ReMonet™ of That Value. A restoration project may simultaneously produce new value. That new value must remain distinguishable from restored value. ReMonet™ ≠ Value Change Value Change governs the fact and character of material change to value. VRMM governs a specific restoration mechanism acting upon previously impaired value. Therefore: Every ReMonet™ may produce Value Change. But: Every Value Change is not ReMonet™. ReMonet™ ≠ Value State A Value State describes the governed condition of value. ReMonet™ describes the mechanism through which restoration is attempted. Therefore: State ≠ Mechanism. A ZVA™ is a Value State. ReMonet™ is a restoration mechanism. Restored Value is a resulting value condition subject to determination and state assignment. ReMonet™ ≠ DeMonet™ The two mechanisms operate in opposite lifecycle directions but must not be treated as simple mathematical inverses. DeMonet™ governs the mechanism through which existing positive value reaches a zero-value condition. ReMonet™ governs the mechanism through which previously impaired value is acted upon toward recovery. Therefore: DeMonet™ ≠ Reverse ReMonet™ and: ReMonet™ ≠ Reverse DeMonet™. The mechanisms may involve completely different causes, interventions, conditions, and value relationships. Mechanism Initiation A ReMonet™ mechanism should have an identifiable initiation point. The initiation point establishes when the governed restoration process begins. This may be: repair commencement; reactivation authorization; data recovery initiation; system migration start; rights reinstatement; rehabilitation commencement; market re-entry; operational restart process; another defined event. The initiation point helps distinguish the restoration mechanism from preceding restoration conditions. Mechanism Modification A ReMonet™ mechanism may change during execution. Changes may include: intervention method; technology; resources; sequence; scope; dependencies; restoration target; execution strategy. Material modifications should remain traceable because they may affect downstream restoration determination. Mechanism Interruption A restoration mechanism may be interrupted. Interruption may result from: missing resources; failed conditions; technical failure; regulatory change; market change; safety issue; loss of access; strategic decision; another material event. Interruption does not automatically establish mechanism failure. The mechanism may remain suspended and later resume. Mechanism Failure A ReMonet™ mechanism may fail. Failure means the restoration intervention did not produce a restoration candidate capable of supporting the intended restoration determination. Failure should remain recorded. A failed ReMonet™ attempt is still a governed lifecycle event. Repeated ReMonet™ A Value Object may undergo multiple restoration attempts. For example: Attempt 1 → Failed Attempt 2 → Partial Recovery Attempt 3 → Additional Recovery Each material restoration attempt should remain distinguishable. This prevents later value analysis from collapsing multiple interventions into one artificial restoration event. Mechanism Completion Completion of the restoration mechanism means the defined intervention has reached its governed endpoint. It does not mean restored value has been established. Therefore: Mechanism Completion ≠ Restoration Determination. The resulting condition proceeds to VRDM. Restoration Candidate The principal output of VRMM is a: Restoration Candidate. A Restoration Candidate is: a value condition produced or materially affected through a governed ReMonet™ mechanism and presented for determination as potentially restored value. This preserves the methodological sequence: Mechanism first. Determination second. Boundary with VRSM VRSM determines: what value is being restored. VRMM determines: how restoration acts upon that value. Therefore: Restoration Scope ≠ ReMonet™ Mechanism. Boundary with VRCM VRCM determines: whether the conditions necessary for restoration exist. VRMM determines: what mechanism acts under those conditions to recover value. Therefore: Restoration Readiness ≠ Restoration Mechanism. Boundary with VRDM VRMM produces the Restoration Candidate. VRDM determines: whether value was actually restored and to what governed extent. Therefore: ReMonet™ ≠ Restoration Determination. Boundary with VRTRM VRMM governs the restoration mechanism. VRTRM governs the formal movement of determined restored value into its resulting Value State. Therefore: Mechanism ≠ Transition. Boundary with Value Degradation Value Degradation governs progressive decline while value remains. ReMonet™ may act upon degraded value to recover previously existing value. Therefore: Degradation → ReMonet™ may occur before zero value is reached. Boundary with Value Nullification Value Nullification governs the transition through which positive value reaches zero. ReMonet™ may subsequently act upon the resulting ZVA™ where restoration potential remains. Therefore: Value Nullification does not automatically prevent future ReMonet™. Boundary with Value Extinction ReMonet™ requires recoverable prior value. Once the relevant value has reached legitimate Value Extinction, restoration of that same value within the governed lifecycle is no longer available. Therefore: ZVA™ may enter ReMonet™. Extinguished Value may not. If value later appears after extinction, it requires classification as a new value event rather than automatic restoration. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Receive Governed Restoration Scope Identify the previously existing value governed through VRSM. 2. Confirm Restoration Conditions Confirm the relevant readiness basis established through VRCM. 3. Identify ReMonet™ Mechanism Define the mechanism through which restoration will be attempted. 4. Identify Restoration Inputs Record materially relevant resources, capabilities, technologies, rights, or other inputs. 5. Initiate Mechanism Establish the governed starting point of the restoration intervention. 6. Execute Restoration Intervention Apply the defined mechanism to the scoped value. 7. Record Material Mechanism Events Preserve material modifications, interruptions, failures, dependencies, and interventions. 8. Observe Recovery Candidate Identify the resulting value condition potentially attributable to the restoration mechanism. 9. Establish Mechanism Traceability Connect the resulting candidate to the governed restoration mechanism and relevant intervention basis. 10. Transfer Restoration Candidate Transfer the candidate to VRDM for formal restoration determination. Governance Outputs VRMM may produce: ReMonet™ Mechanism Record Restoration Mechanism Identification Restoration Intervention Record Restoration Input Record Restoration Resource Record Restoration Mechanism Dependency Record ReMonet™ Initiation Record Mechanism Modification Record Mechanism Interruption Record Mechanism Failure Record Mechanism Completion Record Restoration Mechanism Traceability Record Restoration Candidate ReMonet™ Record These outputs provide the governed input for: VRDM — Value Restoration Determination Module. Use Case 1 — ReMonet™ of a ZVA™ Industrial Asset A production facility previously generated substantial productive value. Technological obsolescence and loss of market demand eventually reduce its relevant productive value to zero. The facility becomes a: ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ within the defined productive-value context. Years later, new market demand and new manufacturing technology create the conditions under which the facility may again become useful. Those changes establish restoration conditions under VRCM. They do not themselves restore the facility's value. A ReMonet™ mechanism is then initiated. The mechanism includes: equipment rehabilitation → control-system modernization → production-line reconfiguration → operational restart The facility begins producing again. VRMM records the intervention, resources, mechanism sequence, modifications, and resulting recovery candidate. The facility is not yet automatically classified as restored. The resulting productive-value condition proceeds to VRDM, where the amount and legitimacy of restored value are determined. This distinction prevents: investment in restoration from being confused with: successful restoration of value. Use Case 2 — ReMonet™ of Dormant Intellectual Property A company owns an industrial technology patent portfolio that previously generated licensing and strategic value. Market conditions change and the technology becomes commercially dormant. The intellectual property continues to exist, but its active economic value falls dramatically. Years later, a new technological application makes part of the original patent portfolio relevant again. The new market opportunity is a restoration condition. It is not itself ReMonet™. The company initiates a ReMonet™ mechanism through: technical reassessment → portfolio reconfiguration → new application mapping → licensing redevelopment → commercial reactivation Some patents regain licensing value. Others remain commercially inactive. Still others support entirely new applications that did not exist previously. VRMM preserves these distinctions. The recovered licensing capability may become a Restoration Candidate. Value generated by entirely new uses may require separate classification as Value Emergence or Value Development rather than being automatically absorbed into ReMonet™. This allows the organization to distinguish: value recovered from value newly created. Enterprise Application VRMM gives organizations a governed method for identifying how previously impaired value is actually being recovered. It can be applied to: distressed assets; industrial rehabilitation; infrastructure recovery; dormant intellectual property; legacy software; historical data; abandoned projects; impaired investments; unused productive capacity; digital assets; inactive rights; organizational capabilities; obsolete technologies; system reactivation; asset repurposing. The Module makes it possible to distinguish: favorable restoration conditions from the mechanism that actually acts upon value and from: the eventual determination that value has been restored. This creates a traceable methodological bridge between restoration readiness and restored value. Foundational Principles ReMonet™ governs restoration of previously existing value. ReMonet™ may operate upon degraded, impaired, dormant, lost, inaccessible, or zero value. ReMonet™ does not require prior Value Nullification. A ZVA™ may retain restoration potential and therefore may enter ReMonet™. Value Extinction terminates restoration of the same value within the governed lifecycle. Restoration conditions are not the restoration mechanism. Execution of a restoration mechanism does not prove restoration success. Restoration cost is not restored value. Partial restoration may constitute legitimate ReMonet™. ReMonet™ must remain distinguishable from Value Development and Value Emergence. DeMonet™ and ReMonet™ are not simple inverse mechanisms. A completed ReMonet™ mechanism produces a Restoration Candidate, not an automatic declaration of restored value. Canonical Closing Statement ReMonet™ Mechanism Module establishes the mechanism layer of Value Restoration by governing how previously degraded, impaired, dormant, lost, inaccessible, or zero value is acted upon toward recovery. Through identification of restoration mechanisms, interventions, inputs, resources, dependencies, initiation, execution, modification, interruption, failure, completion, partial recovery, multi-mechanism restoration, mechanism traceability, and Restoration Candidates, VRMM separates the conditions that make restoration possible from the mechanism that actually attempts to recover value and from the later determination that restoration has succeeded. By defining ReMonet™ broadly enough to operate before or after Value Nullification while preserving the boundaries between restored value, Value Development, Value Emergence, ZVA™, and Value Extinction, VRMM establishes a reusable mechanism for governing value recovery across physical, digital, economic, operational, technological, informational, organizational, and future value systems. ReMonet™ does not declare that value has returned; it governs the mechanism through which previously existing value is given a legitimate pathway to return. title: Value Restoration Scope Module (VRSM)
text: Value Restoration Scope Module (VRSM) Value Restoration Scope Module (VRSM) Value Restoration Scope Module (VRSM) Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture Parent Standard: Value Restoration Standard (VRSS) Module: VRSM — Value Restoration Scope Module Operational Layer: Value Restoration Scope Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Value Restoration Scope Origin ID: VFM-VRSS-VRSM-010.1 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 27 August 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Value Restoration Scope Module (VRSM) is the first Core Module of the Value Restoration Standard (VRSS). VRSM governs the identification and bounding of the exact previously existing value proposed for restoration. The Module establishes what value existed, what part of that value became degraded, impaired, dormant, lost, inaccessible, or zero, what portion remains relevant for recovery, and what exact value dimension, object, context, and boundary the restoration process is permitted to address. VRSM prevents restoration from being treated as an undefined claim that an object has simply “become valuable again.” Its foundational function is: to establish exactly what previously existing value is being proposed for restoration before restoration conditions or mechanisms are considered. Architectural Position VRSM is the first module within VRSS. It precedes: VRCM — Value Restoration Conditions Module VRMM — ReMonet™ Mechanism Module VRDM — Value Restoration Determination Module VRTRM — Value Restoration Transition Module VRSM establishes the governed restoration scope. The subsequent modules determine whether restoration conditions exist, how restoration occurs, whether value was actually restored, and how the resulting value enters a new governed Value State. Internal Flow Previously Existing Value → Prior Value State Identification → Impaired / Lost Value Identification → Value Object Boundary → Value Dimension Boundary → Value Context Boundary → Restoration Target Definition → Restoration Exclusions → Governed Restoration Scope → VRCM — Value Restoration Conditions Module Operational Space VRSM governs the space between: recognition that previously existing value has been impaired or lost and a formally bounded value-restoration scope. Its operational space includes: prior value identification; prior Value State; Value Object identification; affected value component; affected value dimension; degradation or loss boundary; dormant-value scope; zero-value scope; restoration context; temporal boundary; restoration target; restoration exclusions; partial restoration scope; dimensional restoration scope; contextual restoration scope; restoration dependencies; restoration-scope record. Prior Value Requirement Restoration requires a relationship to previously existing value. VRSM therefore begins by establishing: What value existed before the impairment, degradation, dormancy, loss, inaccessibility, or zero-value condition occurred? Without an identifiable prior value basis, the process may represent: Value Emergence rather than: Value Restoration. Therefore: No Identifiable Prior Value → No Established Restoration Scope. This does not mean new value cannot emerge. It means that newly emerging value must not be mislabeled as restored value. Prior Value State Identification Where available, VRSM should establish the prior governed Value State against which restoration is being considered. The prior state may identify: Value Object; value type; value dimension; value magnitude; value context; temporal state; operational condition; dependencies; limitations; supporting basis. The historical value state does not automatically become the restoration target. It provides the reference point from which the restoration relationship can be understood. Value Object Boundary VRSM must identify the Value Object to which the restoration claim applies. The object may be: a physical asset; infrastructure; technology; software; data; intellectual property; capability; process; organizational resource; digital asset; right; license; product; service; system; operational capability; another governable Value Object. Restoration of one object must not automatically be attributed to a larger system containing that object. Restored Component ≠ Restored System. Affected Value Identification VRSM identifies the value that became impaired. The affected value may have become: Degraded Impaired Dormant Lost Inaccessible or: Zero. More than one condition may coexist. For example, an industrial facility may retain physical value while its productive economic value becomes zero. VRSM therefore scopes the affected value, not merely the physical or digital object carrying that value. Value Dimension Boundary Value is frequently multidimensional. A Value Object may simultaneously possess: economic value; operational value; strategic value; functional value; informational value; technological value; market value; productive value; utility value; option value; another governed value dimension. VRSM requires the restoration scope to specify which dimension is being restored. Therefore: Restoration of One Value Dimension ≠ Restoration of the Entire Value Object. Partial Restoration Scope The restoration target does not need to represent complete recovery. VRSM may establish a scope for: Partial Restoration. Example: A production asset previously operated at full productive capability. After deterioration, only 30% of that capability remains. The restoration project may legitimately target recovery to 70%. VRSM therefore records: Prior Capability: 100% Current Capability: 30% Restoration Scope: recovery toward 70% The remaining 30% difference is outside the current restoration scope. Context Boundary Value may exist only within a particular context. VRSM therefore identifies the context within which restoration is being proposed. Context may include: jurisdiction; market; organization; operational environment; technological environment; regulatory environment; geographic region; customer segment; infrastructure configuration; temporal period; use condition. An asset may regain value in one context while remaining valueless in another. Therefore: Contextual Restoration ≠ Universal Restoration. Temporal Boundary Restoration scope may also be time-bound. VRSM may distinguish between: temporary restoration and: persistent restoration. For example, a dormant energy asset may regain economic value during a temporary supply shortage. Its value may subsequently decline again when market conditions normalize. The restoration scope must therefore preserve the relevant temporal context. Restoration Target VRSM establishes the value condition toward which restoration is directed. A Restoration Target may represent: previous value magnitude; partial previous value; previous functionality; previous utility; previous productive capability; previous accessibility; previous economic condition; previous operational state; an explicitly defined equivalent value condition. The target must be measurable or otherwise determinable through an appropriate governed basis. Restoration Target ≠ Guaranteed Restoration Outcome. It defines what recovery is being attempted. Historical State ≠ Mandatory Restoration Target VRSM does not require restoration to reproduce the exact historical state. A Value Object may be restored through: new technology; new operating conditions; different infrastructure; changed market conditions; modified configuration; new access mechanisms. The restored value may therefore be equivalent in relevant function or value without recreating the original historical configuration. Restoration Exclusions A strong restoration scope must identify not only what is included but also what is excluded. Exclusions may include: value dimensions not being restored; unrelated Value Objects; newly emerging value; future speculative value; unsupported historical value claims; value belonging to another context; value outside the restoration period; improvements beyond the restoration target. Explicit exclusions prevent scope expansion after the restoration process begins. Restoration Scope ≠ Restoration Potential VRSM may identify a value as potentially recoverable. This does not establish that restoration is possible or justified. Therefore: Restoration Scope ≠ Restoration Eligibility. Restoration Scope ≠ Restoration Conditions. Restoration Scope ≠ Restored Value. VRCM subsequently determines the conditions under which the scoped value may legitimately be restored. Restoration Scope ≠ Value Development Scope VRSM must prevent ordinary growth from being classified as restoration. Suppose an asset currently possesses positive value of 70 and historically possessed value of 100. An intervention increases its value to 120. The movement may contain two different value processes: 70 → 100 = potentially restored value 100 → 120 = potentially developed or newly emerged value The exact classification depends upon the governed value basis. VRSM provides the scope boundary needed to separate them. Restoration Scope and ZVA™ A ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ may enter VRSM where previously existing value has reached a governed zero-value state while restoration potential remains. VRSM must identify: which previous value reached zero and: which value is now proposed for restoration. The existence of the underlying object alone does not establish restoration scope. The relevant value relationship must remain identifiable. Scope Revision Restoration scope may require revision where new information establishes that: prior value was incorrectly identified; the affected value dimension differs; additional impairment exists; restoration dependencies changed; the object boundary changed; the restoration target changed; contextual conditions changed; previously assumed value never existed; part of the expected restored value is actually new Value Emergence. Scope revision must remain documented rather than silently changing the restoration basis. Boundary with VRCM VRSM determines: what value is proposed for restoration. VRCM determines: under what conditions that value may legitimately be restored. Therefore: Scope ≠ Conditions. Boundary with VRMM VRSM establishes the restoration target and boundary. VRMM governs the ReMonet™ mechanism through which restoration occurs. Therefore: Restoration Scope ≠ Restoration Mechanism. Boundary with VRDM VRSM defines what restoration is attempting to recover. VRDM determines whether the scoped value was actually restored. Therefore: Restoration Target ≠ Restoration Determination. Boundary with VRTRM VRSM establishes the initial restoration boundary. VRTRM governs the formal transition of legitimately restored value into its resulting Value State. Therefore: Restoration Scope ≠ Restoration Transition. Boundary with Value Development Value Development governs strengthening, maturation, growth, or compounding of existing positive value. VRSM governs the scope of recovery of previously impaired value. Therefore: Existing Value Growth ≠ Previously Lost Value Recovery. Boundary with Value Emergence Where no relevant prior value existed, restoration cannot be established merely because new value later appears. Therefore: New Value ≠ Restored Value. VRSM protects this distinction by requiring a traceable prior-value basis. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Identify the Value Object Define the object carrying the value proposed for restoration. 2. Establish Prior Value Identify the relevant previously existing value. 3. Establish Prior Value State Determine the historical state or reference basis where available. 4. Identify Impaired Value Determine what value became degraded, dormant, lost, inaccessible, impaired, or zero. 5. Define Value Dimension Specify the exact value dimension or dimensions within scope. 6. Define Context Establish the market, jurisdiction, operational environment, technology environment, or other relevant context. 7. Define Restoration Target Specify the value condition restoration is intended to recover. 8. Establish Exclusions Identify what value, dimensions, objects, contexts, or improvements remain outside scope. 9. Establish Temporal Boundary Define the relevant restoration period where materially applicable. 10. Record Governed Restoration Scope Create a persistent record of the approved restoration boundary before downstream restoration governance proceeds. Governance Outputs VRSM may produce: Value Restoration Scope Record Prior Value Identification Record Prior Value State Reference Affected Value Record Value Dimension Scope Value Object Boundary Record Restoration Context Record Restoration Target Statement Restoration Exclusion Record Temporal Restoration Boundary Partial Restoration Scope ZVA™ Restoration Scope Record Governed Restoration Scope These outputs provide the governed input for: VRCM — Value Restoration Conditions Module. Use Case 1 — Restoring a Zero-Value Industrial Asset A specialized production line previously generated substantial productive and economic value. A technological shift makes its original production function commercially obsolete. The machinery remains physically intact, but its relevant productive value reaches zero and the asset enters a ZVA™ state. Several years later, a new manufacturing process can reuse approximately 70% of the existing equipment. Before deciding whether ReMonet™ can occur, VRSM establishes exactly what is being proposed for restoration. It separates: physical asset existence from: previous productive value and defines: Value Object: existing production line Prior Value: productive manufacturing capability Current Condition: zero productive value in the original context Restoration Dimension: productive and operational value Restoration Target: recovery of reusable productive capability Excluded: entirely new capabilities created by newly installed technology This prevents the organization from treating every future improvement to the facility as restored value. VRSM establishes which portion represents recovery of previously existing value and which portion must be governed separately as new value. Use Case 2 — Recovering Dormant Value from Historical Data An organization holds twenty years of industrial operating data. The dataset previously supported engineering and operational decisions, but changes in systems and analytical methods gradually make much of it inaccessible and practically unusable. Its informational potential remains, but its active operational value becomes dormant. A new AI-based analytical capability later makes the historical dataset usable again. VRSM does not immediately classify the resulting opportunity as restored value. It first defines the restoration scope: Value Object: historical industrial dataset Prior Value: operational and informational utility Impaired Condition: practical inaccessibility and analytical dormancy Restoration Dimension: recoverable informational utility Restoration Context: defined industrial analytics environment Restoration Target: recovery of usable historical information Excluded: new predictive capabilities created solely by the AI system This separation is critical. The historical information that becomes usable again may constitute: Restored Value. Predictive capabilities that never previously existed may constitute: New Value Emergence. VRSM establishes the boundary before the two forms of value become mixed. Enterprise Application VRSM enables organizations to define exactly what they are attempting to recover before investing resources into restoration. This can be applied to: distressed industrial assets; infrastructure rehabilitation; legacy software; historical data; dormant intellectual property; abandoned projects; impaired investments; unused licenses; obsolete technologies; organizational capabilities; digital assets; inactive production capacity. The Module prevents organizations from combining restoration, development, new value creation, and speculative future value into one undefined recovery claim. It creates a precise starting point for determining: what value existed, what was lost, what remains recoverable, and what exactly is being proposed for restoration. Foundational Principles Restoration requires an identifiable relationship to previously existing value. No identifiable prior value means no established restoration scope. Restoration of one value dimension does not establish restoration of the entire Value Object. Restoration of one component does not establish restoration of the whole system. Contextual restoration is not universal restoration. A Restoration Target is not a Restoration Determination. Restoration Scope is not Restoration Potential. Restoration Scope is not ReMonet™. New Value Emergence must remain distinguishable from recovery of previously existing value. The value proposed for restoration must be bounded before the mechanism intended to restore it is governed. Canonical Closing Statement Value Restoration Scope Module establishes the first control point of Value Restoration by identifying and bounding the precise previously existing value proposed for recovery. Through governance of prior value, prior Value State, Value Object boundaries, affected value, value dimensions, restoration context, temporal scope, restoration targets, exclusions, partial restoration, and the distinction between restored and newly emerging value, VRSM prevents restoration from becoming an undefined claim that value has simply returned. By establishing exactly what value is being recovered before restoration conditions, ReMonet™, restoration determination, or transition are considered, VRSM creates the governed foundation upon which the entire Value Restoration process depends.
