title: Value Restoration Transition Module (VRTRM)
text: Value Restoration Transition Module (VRTRM) Value Restoration Transition Module (VRTRM) Value Restoration Transition Module (VRTRM) Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture Parent Standard: Value Restoration Standard (VRSS) Module: VRTRM — Value Restoration Transition Module Operational Layer: Value Restoration Transition Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Value Restoration Transition Origin ID: VFM-VRSS-VRTRM-010.5 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 27 August 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Value Restoration Transition Module (VRTRM) is the fifth Core Module of the Value Restoration Standard (VRSS). VRTRM governs the formal transition through which value that has been determined as legitimately restored is transferred from its prior degraded, impaired, dormant, lost, inaccessible, or zero-value condition into a new governed Value State. The Module establishes the transition boundary between: Restoration Determination and Resulting Value State. VRTRM does not determine whether restoration occurred. That determination belongs to VRDM — Value Restoration Determination Module. Its function is: to ensure that determined restored value enters the value lifecycle through an explicit, traceable, bounded, and governable transition rather than appearing as an unexplained new Value State. Architectural Position VRTRM is the fifth and final module within VRSS. It follows: VRDM — Value Restoration Determination Module. The preceding modules establish: restoration scope → restoration conditions → ReMonet™ mechanism → restoration determination. VRTRM then governs: the formal transition of determined restored value into its resulting Value State. Internal Flow Value Restoration Determination → Pre-Transition Value State Identification → Restored Value Identification → Transition Basis Confirmation → Transition Boundary Definition → Resulting Value Condition Identification → Transition Execution → Resulting Value State Entry → Transition Record Operational Space VRTRM governs the space between: value determined as restored and value formally recognized in its resulting governed state. Its operational space includes: restoration determination receipt; pre-transition Value State; restored-value identity; transition eligibility; transition basis; transition conditions; transition boundaries; partial restoration transitions; conditional restoration transitions; temporary restoration transitions; zero-to-positive transitions; degraded-to-improved transitions; dormant-to-active transitions; inaccessible-to-accessible transitions; restored-value separation; resulting Value State entry; transition timestamp; transition provenance; transition record; downstream Value State governance. Restoration Determination ≠ Restoration Transition VRTRM establishes a fundamental distinction: Determination ≠ Transition. VRDM may determine that value has been restored. That determination does not itself update the governed lifecycle state. VRTRM controls the formal movement from the previous condition into the resulting Value State. This prevents a restoration assessment from silently rewriting the lifecycle record. Transition Eligibility Principle A restoration transition should occur only where a valid restoration determination exists. The transition basis should establish, where materially relevant: what value was restored; what prior value condition existed; what restoration determination was issued; what extent of value was restored; whether restoration is partial; whether restoration is conditional; whether restoration is temporary; what limitations remain; what resulting Value State is appropriate. Therefore: Restoration Attempt ≠ Transition Eligibility. Pre-Transition Value State VRTRM requires the value condition immediately preceding transition to remain identifiable. The pre-transition state may represent: Degraded Value Dormant Value Impaired Value Inaccessible Value Lost Value or ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ where applicable. This creates continuity between the historical value condition and the restored state. Resulting Value State Every completed restoration transition must produce or enter a defined resulting Value State. The resulting state may represent: partially restored value; conditionally restored value; temporarily restored value; substantially restored value; fully restored value; another governed positive-value condition. The resulting Value State itself is governed under: Value State Standard (VSS). VRTRM governs the transition into that state. It does not replace VSS. Zero-to-Positive Transition One of the most important transitions governed by VRTRM is: ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ → Positive Value State where legitimate restoration has occurred. This transition demonstrates why: Zero Value ≠ Value Extinction. A zero-value condition may preserve restoration potential. Where ReMonet™ successfully restores recoverable value and VRDM determines that restoration occurred, VRTRM formally governs the return from zero to positive value. Degraded-to-Restored Transition Value does not need to reach zero before restoration occurs. Example: Prior Value = 100 Degraded Value = 35 Restored Value = 75 VRTRM governs: 35 → 75 as the formal restoration transition. The remaining difference: 75 → 100 does not invalidate the transition. The resulting Value State simply reflects partial restoration. Dormant-to-Active Transition Value may continue to exist while becoming dormant. Examples may include: unused intellectual property; inaccessible data; inactive productive capacity; temporarily unusable infrastructure; dormant rights; inactive organizational capability. Where the value becomes usable again through a governed restoration process, VRTRM may govern: Dormant Value → Active Restored Value. Partial Restoration Transition Where VRDM determines only partial restoration, VRTRM must preserve that limitation. A partially restored value must not transition into a state implying complete recovery. Therefore: Partial Restoration Determination → Partial Restored Value State. The transition must carry forward the unresolved value deficit where materially relevant. Conditional Restoration Transition Where restored value depends upon defined conditions, those conditions must survive the transition. For example: Conditionally Restored Value may depend upon: restricted operating conditions; continued maintenance; external infrastructure; temporary authorization; specific environmental conditions; continuing data access; limited technical configurations. VRTRM must prevent: Conditional Restoration from becoming: Unconditional Value State merely through transition. Temporary Restoration Transition Restoration may be explicitly temporary. VRTRM must therefore preserve: temporal limitation; review date; expiry condition; triggering event; expected degradation; required reassessment; where applicable. A temporary restoration transition may establish: Zero / Degraded Value → Temporarily Restored Value. If the temporary basis later expires, a new governed value event must be recognized. Transition Boundary The restoration transition must have a defined boundary. The boundary identifies where: the prior value condition ends and the restored Value State begins. Depending upon the value context, this boundary may be established through: timestamp; threshold achievement; operational activation; restoration acceptance; verified capability recovery; access restoration; legal effectiveness; technical commissioning; functional recovery; another governed transition event. Transition Threshold Where a threshold is required, VRTRM may use a defined transition threshold. The threshold should represent the minimum condition necessary for the restoration determination to become operationally reflected in the Value State. A transition threshold must not be invented merely for administrative convenience. It must correspond to the governed restoration basis. Transition Execution Transition execution is the formal act through which the value lifecycle record recognizes the restoration outcome. Execution may include: state update; asset record update; lifecycle record update; value classification update; operational status update; registry update; system-of-record update; activation of restored-value status; another governed state-recognition mechanism. VRTRM does not prescribe one technical implementation. It governs the methodological requirements of the transition. Transition Continuity A restoration transition must preserve lifecycle continuity. The lifecycle should remain capable of showing: Previous Value State → Restoration Process → Restoration Determination → Restoration Transition → Resulting Value State. The restored state must therefore not erase the fact that degradation, dormancy, nullification, or another impairment previously occurred. Historical State Preservation Restoration does not rewrite history. Where value was previously: degraded dormant impaired or zero that historical condition remains part of the governed lifecycle. VRTRM therefore requires: New State ≠ Erasure of Prior State. Restored Value Identity VRTRM must preserve the relationship between restored value and the value that previously existed. This is essential because restoration is fundamentally different from new Value Emergence. The transition record should therefore preserve sufficient identity continuity to establish: what value returned. Where identity continuity cannot be established, the resulting value may require treatment as newly emerged value rather than restored value. Restoration Transition ≠ Value Emergence VRTRM governs return of previously existing value. It does not govern the first legitimate appearance of new value. Therefore: Previously Existing Value → Recovery → Restoration Transition is distinct from: No Prior Value → Value Emergence. Restoration Transition ≠ Value Development A restoration transition may place an asset into a positive Value State from which further development occurs. Example: Degraded Value = 30 → Restored Value = 80 → Developed Value = 120 VRTRM governs: 30 → 80. Value Development governs: 80 → 120. This boundary prevents growth following restoration from being retroactively classified as restoration. Restoration Transition ≠ Value Change Governance Every restoration transition represents a change in value. But VRTRM governs a specific lifecycle transition: recovery of previously impaired value into a resulting Value State. The broader fact and character of value change remain governed through the Value Change Standard (VCS). Restoration Transition ≠ Nullification Reversal A restoration transition from zero value does not invalidate the previous nullification. If value legitimately reached zero, that historical state remains valid. The lifecycle may therefore contain: Positive Value → DeMonet™ → ZVA™ → ReMonet™ → Restored Positive Value. The restoration does not mean the nullification never occurred. Restoration Transition ≠ Extinction Reversal VRTRM cannot reverse a legitimate Value Extinction determination within the same governed value lifecycle. Where value has reached: Value Extinction the relevant value is no longer considered recoverable within that lifecycle. Therefore: Value Extinction → ReMonet™ → Restoration is not a legitimate restoration pathway within the same governed lifecycle. If value later appears, it requires assessment as a new value event. Transition Failure A valid restoration determination does not guarantee that the corresponding transition will be successfully executed. Transition failure may occur because of: missing state authority; unresolved identity; conflicting lifecycle records; incomplete transition conditions; technical record failure; contradictory determination; unavailable system-of-record; unresolved boundary conditions. VRTRM must therefore distinguish: Restoration Determined from Restoration Transition Completed. Pending Transition Where restoration has been determined but the state transition has not yet legitimately occurred, the Module may establish: Pending Restoration Transition. This prevents premature state recognition while preserving the valid restoration determination. Transition Rejection A proposed transition may be rejected where: no valid restoration determination exists; the determination applies to another Value Object; transition conditions are unmet; the proposed resulting state exceeds the restoration determination; the restoration basis has materially changed; required lifecycle continuity cannot be established; extinction has already been legitimately determined. A rejected transition does not automatically invalidate the restoration process. It means the proposed lifecycle transition cannot currently be governed as legitimate. Transition Record Every material restoration transition should create a reconstructable record. The record may contain: Value Object identity; prior Value State; restoration determination reference; restored-value identity; restoration extent; transition conditions; transition boundary; transition threshold where applicable; transition time; resulting Value State; remaining limitations; uncertainty; transition authority where externally governed; transition status; relevant provenance. Transition States VRTRM may recognize minimum transition states such as: 1. Not Eligible No sufficient governed basis exists for restoration transition. 2. Pending A restoration determination exists, but transition requirements remain incomplete. 3. Conditional Transition Transition is legitimate only under explicitly defined conditions. 4. Temporary Transition Transition establishes a temporally bounded restored Value State. 5. Completed The determined restored value has formally entered its resulting Value State. 6. Rejected The proposed transition does not satisfy the governed transition requirements. These are transition states, not Value States. VRTRM Boundary with VRDM VRDM determines: whether value has been restored. VRTRM determines: whether and how that determined restoration enters the governed value lifecycle as a state transition. Therefore: Restoration Determination ≠ Restoration Transition. VRTRM Boundary with VSS VRTRM governs: movement into the resulting Value State. VSS governs: what the resulting current Value State is. Therefore: Transition Governance ≠ State Governance. VRTRM Boundary with VDS VRTRM governs restoration. VDS governs subsequent development of existing value. A restored asset may immediately become subject to Value Development after its restoration transition, but the two lifecycle events must remain distinguishable. VRTRM Boundary with VNS VNS governs transition of existing positive value into a zero-value condition. VRTRM may govern a later legitimate restoration from ZVA™ where recoverability remains. Therefore: Nullification and Restoration are distinct lifecycle transitions, not cancellation operations. VRTRM Boundary with VXSS VXSS governs terminal Value Extinction. VRTRM cannot be used to bypass a legitimate extinction determination. This maintains the architectural distinction: Zero Value may remain recoverable. Extinguished Value does not remain recoverable within the governed lifecycle. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Receive Restoration Determination Receive the governed restoration determination from VRDM. 2. Identify Pre-Transition State Establish the Value State or value condition immediately preceding restoration transition. 3. Confirm Restored Value Identify the value determined as restored and its relationship to previously existing value. 4. Confirm Transition Eligibility Verify that the restoration determination and transition conditions support formal state movement. 5. Define Transition Boundary Establish when or under what governed condition the restoration transition occurs. 6. Preserve Conditions Carry forward partial, conditional, temporary, uncertain, or otherwise material limitations. 7. Execute Transition Formally recognize the movement from the previous condition into the resulting Value State. 8. Establish Resulting State Entry Transfer the restored value into Value State governance under VSS. 9. Preserve Lifecycle Continuity Maintain the relationship between prior state, restoration process, determination, transition, and resulting state. 10. Create Transition Record Create a reconstructable record of the completed, pending, conditional, temporary, rejected, or otherwise governed transition. Governance Outputs VRTRM may produce: Restoration Transition Eligibility Record Pre-Transition Value State Record Restored Value Identity Record Restoration Transition Basis Restoration Transition Boundary Restoration Transition Condition Record Partial Restoration Transition Record Conditional Restoration Transition Record Temporary Restoration Transition Record Pending Restoration Transition Record Restoration Transition Rejection Record Restoration Transition Completion Record Resulting Value State Entry Value Restoration Transition Record Use Case 1 — Industrial Asset Returned from Zero Value A production asset has lost all economically usable productive value and has legitimately entered: ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™. The physical asset still exists and retains recoverability. A ReMonet™ program replaces obsolete controls, repairs critical components, restores certification requirements, and returns the equipment to productive operation. VRDM determines that meaningful productive value has legitimately returned. VRTRM then governs the formal lifecycle transition: ZVA™ → Restoration Determination → Restoration Transition → Positive Value State. The transition record preserves the previous zero-value condition rather than deleting it. The lifecycle can therefore show that the asset: possessed value → lost value → reached zero → retained restoration potential → was restored → returned to positive value. This creates a governable value history rather than a sequence of disconnected valuations. Use Case 2 — Dormant Intellectual Property Reactivated A company owns intellectual property that historically generated substantial value but has remained commercially dormant for years. The underlying rights continue to exist, but the asset no longer generates meaningful operational or commercial value. A new technological environment creates an opportunity to reactivate the intellectual property. Following a governed ReMonet™ process, the organization establishes new licensing capability and VRDM determines that part of the previously dormant economic value has legitimately been restored. VRTRM does not classify the asset simply as: valuable again. It governs the transition: Dormant Value → Partially Restored Value and preserves: the previous dormant condition the restoration determination the transition basis the remaining limitations the resulting Value State. If the intellectual property subsequently generates additional value beyond the restored historical value relationship, that additional increase can enter Value Development rather than being indefinitely attributed to restoration. Enterprise Application VRTRM provides organizations with the lifecycle control required to convert a restoration determination into a formally recognized Value State. It can be applied across: industrial asset recovery; infrastructure rehabilitation; distressed assets; dormant intellectual property; digital asset recovery; legacy-system restoration; data recovery; productive-capacity restoration; operational restart; impaired investments; rights restoration; capability recovery; asset reactivation; technological rehabilitation. The Module prevents restored value from appearing in organizational records without a governed relationship to: where the value came from what happened to it how restoration was determined and when the restored state legitimately began. Foundational Principles Restoration Determination is not Restoration Transition. Restoration Transition is not Value State governance. A restoration attempt does not create transition eligibility. A restored Value State must remain connected to the value condition from which it emerged. Partial restoration must not transition into a state implying full restoration. Conditional restoration must remain conditional after transition. Temporary restoration must remain temporally bounded. Restoration does not erase prior degradation or nullification. Zero Value may transition back to positive value where restoration potential remains. Value Extinction cannot be reversed through restoration within the same governed lifecycle. Restored value must remain distinguishable from newly emerged value. Value created beyond restoration must remain distinguishable from Value Development. Every material restoration transition should preserve lifecycle continuity. Canonical Closing Statement Value Restoration Transition Module establishes the final transition layer of the Value Restoration Standard by governing how value formally moves from a degraded, impaired, dormant, lost, inaccessible, or zero-value condition into a resulting governed Value State after restoration has been legitimately determined. Through transition eligibility, pre-transition state identification, restored-value identity, transition boundaries, partial, conditional and temporary transitions, zero-to-positive recovery, lifecycle continuity, historical-state preservation, transition execution, resulting-state entry, failure, rejection, and transition records, VRTRM ensures that restored value does not simply reappear within the lifecycle without a governed explanation of how and when that change occurred. By separating Restoration Determination from Restoration Transition and Restoration Transition from Value State governance, the Module preserves the architectural boundaries between VRSS, VSS, VDS, VNS, and VXSS. VRTRM therefore completes the restoration pathway by ensuring that recovered value enters its new governed state without erasing the history, conditions, limitations, or value relationships that make that restoration legitimate. title: Value Restoration Standard (VRSS)
text: Value Restoration Standard (VRSS) Value Restoration Standard (VRSS) Value Restoration Standard (VRSS) Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture Parent Standard: Value Restoration Standard (VRSS) Operational Layer: Value Restoration Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Type: Parent Standard Governed Space: Value Restoration Origin ID: VFM-VRSS-010 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 27 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · OBIDENITY® AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Value Restoration Standard (VRSS) is the tenth Parent Standard within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture governing how previously existing value that has become degraded, impaired, lost, dormant, inaccessible, or zero may legitimately re-emerge as governed value. VRSS establishes the methodological structure through which a prior Value State is identified, the recoverable value scope is bounded, restoration conditions are established, the ReMonet™ mechanism is governed, restoration is determined, and the resulting transition into a restored Value State is formally recorded. The Standard distinguishes restoration of previously existing value from creation of new value and development of value that already remains positively present. Its foundational rule is: Value Restoration requires a governed relationship between previously existing value, its impairment or loss, the mechanism enabling recovery, and the value that subsequently re-emerges. Core Question How can degraded, lost, dormant, or zero value legitimately re-emerge or be restored? Architectural Position VRSS occupies the tenth governed space within VFM®. It follows: Value Nullification Standard (VNS) and precedes: Value Extinction Standard (VXSS). However, restoration is not restricted to value that has passed through complete nullification. VRSS may receive value from multiple lifecycle conditions: Degraded Value Impaired Value Dormant Value Lost Value Inaccessible Value Zero Value ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ where a legitimate restoration pathway remains available. This creates an essential architectural distinction: Value Development = existing positive value develops. Value Restoration = previously impaired, lost, dormant, degraded, or zero value is recovered. Governance Flow Position Prior Value State → Value Impairment / Degradation / Dormancy / Loss / Zero State → Restoration Scope → Restoration Conditions → ReMonet™ Mechanism → Restoration Determination → Restoration Transition → Restored Value → New Value State For a zero-value pathway: Positive Value → DeMonet™ → Zero-Value Condition → ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ → ReMonet™ → Restored Value → New Value State VRSS therefore creates a governed recovery pathway inside the value lifecycle. Operational Space VRSS governs the space between: a previously existing value that has become materially impaired, dormant, lost, inaccessible, degraded, or zero and the legitimate re-establishment of that value as a governed positive Value State. Its operational space includes: identification of previously existing value; restoration scope; restoration eligibility; recoverability; restoration conditions; restoration dependencies; restoration mechanisms; ReMonet™; partial restoration; dimensional restoration; contextual restoration; temporary restoration; restoration magnitude; restoration determination; restoration transition; restored-state identification; restoration provenance; restoration records; lifecycle continuity. Restoration Requires Prior Value VRSS governs restoration only where a legitimate relationship to previously existing value can be established. Therefore: Value That Never Existed ≠ Restored Value. Where value emerges for the first time, the applicable governance belongs to Value Emergence. Where positive existing value increases, the applicable governance belongs to Value Development. Where impaired or lost previous value is recovered, VRSS applies. The distinction is: No Prior Value → Value Emergence Existing Positive Value → Value Development Previously Existing but Impaired/Lost/Zero Value → Value Restoration Restoration Scope Before restoration is governed, the exact Restoration Scope must be established. The scope should identify, where materially applicable: Value Object; previous Value State; affected value dimension; Value Context; value component; impairment or loss condition; restoration target; temporal scope; restoration boundary; dependencies; exclusions. This prevents an improvement in one dimension from being represented as restoration of the entire value object. Restoration Eligibility Not every impaired or zero-value object is necessarily restorable. VRSS therefore requires a governed distinction between: Restoration Possible Restoration Conditional Restoration Currently Unsupported and, where VXSS independently establishes it: Value Extinct. Restoration eligibility may depend upon: continued object existence; retained identity; retained rights; technical recoverability; economic feasibility; legal permissibility; operational accessibility; restoration capability; availability of dependencies; recoverable information; recoverable functionality; recoverable demand; recoverable utility. Eligibility does not establish successful restoration. It establishes whether a legitimate restoration pathway remains available. Restoration Conditions VRSS requires the conditions necessary for restoration to be explicitly identified. These may include: repair; reactivation; reconfiguration; reconstruction; technological improvement; infrastructure recovery; dependency restoration; rights restoration; market recovery; regulatory change; data recovery; capability recovery; demand recovery; access recovery; ownership clarification; environmental change; operational reintegration. Restoration conditions establish what must become true before previously impaired value can legitimately re-emerge. ReMonet™ VRSS is the architectural home of: ReMonet™ ReMonet™ is the governed mechanism through which previously existing value that became degraded, impaired, dormant, lost, inaccessible, or zero is restored into a positive governed Value State. The canonical mechanism is: Previously Existing Value → Value Impairment / Loss / Dormancy / Zero → Restoration Conditions → ReMonet™ → Restored Value → New Value State ReMonet™ must remain broad enough to govern restoration before and after complete nullification. Therefore: ReMonet™ ≠ Restoration from Zero Only. ReMonet™ from Degraded Value Value does not need to reach zero before restoration becomes possible. Example: An industrial asset loses 60% of its operational value because of deterioration. Repair restores most of the lost capability. The transition may be: 100 Value → Degradation → 40 Value → ReMonet™ → 85 Value. This is restoration because previously existing impaired value has been recovered. It is not ordinary Value Development. ReMonet™ from Zero Value Where value has been nullified, VRSS creates the governed recovery pathway from the zero-value condition. Canonical transition: Positive Value → DeMonet™ → Zero-Value Condition → ZVA™ → ReMonet™ → Restored Positive Value → New Value State This establishes one of VFM®'s central lifecycle relationships: DeMonet™ and ReMonet™ are directionally opposite value-transition mechanisms, but they are not automatic reversals of one another. A prior DeMonet™ event does not guarantee future ReMonet™ eligibility. Restoration ≠ Reversal Restoration does not require the Value Object to return to its exact historical state. A restored object may: regain only part of its former value; regain value through a different mechanism; operate in a new context; serve a different function; acquire a different value composition; regain one value dimension but not another. Therefore: Restoration ≠ Exact Historical Reversal. The legitimate question is whether previously impaired or lost value has been recovered—not whether history has been perfectly reconstructed. Partial Restoration VRSS supports restoration of only part of previously lost value. Example: Prior Value = 100 → Degraded Value = 20 → Restored Value = 65. The object has experienced legitimate restoration even though its former value has not been fully recovered. VRSS must therefore distinguish: Partial Restoration from: Full Restoration. Full Restoration Full restoration occurs where the relevant previously existing value has been restored to the defined restoration target. The restoration target may correspond to: previous value level; previous capability; previous utility; previous economic condition; previous operational condition; another explicitly governed equivalent state. Full restoration must not automatically imply that every historical property of the object has been restored. Dimensional Restoration Value may be restored in one dimension without being restored in another. For example: Operational Value: restored while: Market Value: remains zero. Or: Economic Value: restored while: Strategic Value: remains impaired. VRSS therefore requires restoration determinations to identify the exact value dimension affected. Restoration in Dimension A ≠ Restoration in All Dimensions. Contextual Restoration Value may be restored only within a particular context. For example: A technology that became commercially unusable in one jurisdiction may become valuable again after regulatory change. The restoration may therefore be: Jurisdiction-Specific rather than universal. Similarly: Market A → Restored Value while: Market B → Zero Value. Context must remain attached to the restoration determination. Restoration Magnitude VRSS must preserve the magnitude of restoration where materially relevant. Restoration magnitude may be expressed through: absolute restored value; relative restored value; percentage recovery; restored capability; restored utility; restored economic value; restored operational value; restored strategic value; another governed measure. The architecture does not require one universal valuation method. It requires the restoration claim to remain tied to a defined basis. Restoration Determination Restoration activity alone does not establish restored value. VRSS distinguishes: Restoration Attempt from: Restoration Determination. A repair may fail. A reactivation may not restore utility. A regulatory change may not restore demand. A technological upgrade may not restore the affected value dimension. Therefore: Restoration Action ≠ Restored Value. A governed determination must establish whether value actually re-emerged. Restoration Determination States A restoration determination may result in: 1. Restoration Not Established Restoration activity occurred, but recovery of the relevant value has not been established. 2. Partial Restoration A defined portion of previously impaired or lost value has returned. 3. Conditional Restoration Value has returned only while specified conditions remain satisfied. 4. Contextual Restoration Value has returned within a defined context. 5. Full Restoration The governed restoration target has been satisfied. 6. Restoration Indeterminate Available information is insufficient to determine whether restoration occurred. These states prevent binary treatment of complex restoration processes. Restoration Transition Once restoration is legitimately determined, VRSS governs the transition into the resulting positive Value State. The transition is: Impaired / Dormant / Lost / Zero Value → ReMonet™ → Restoration Determination → Restored Positive Value → New Value State. The resulting state then becomes governable under: Value State Standard (VSS). New Value State Restored value must enter a new governed Value State. The new state should identify, where materially relevant: Value Object; restored value dimension; restoration magnitude; Value Context; restoration conditions; effective time; dependencies; remaining impairment; restoration limitations; previous state; ReMonet™ basis. The new Value State must not erase the restoration history. Restoration Provenance Every material restoration should remain traceable to: Previous Positive Value → Impairment / Loss / Dormancy / Nullification → Restoration Scope → Restoration Conditions → ReMonet™ Mechanism → Restoration Determination → Restoration Transition → New Value State. This enables later analysis of how value was lost and how it returned. Restored Value May Differ from Historical Value VRSS recognizes that recovered value may not have the same composition as the original value. An obsolete industrial building may lose manufacturing value but later recover substantial value after conversion into a data center. An old dataset may lose immediate commercial value but regain value after new AI capabilities make previously inaccessible information usable. A dormant patent may regain value after technological change. In each case, VRSS must distinguish between: restoration of previously impaired value and: emergence of genuinely new value. Both may occur simultaneously. Mixed Restoration and Emergence A single event may produce both restored value and newly emerged value. Example: A legacy factory is modernized. The modernization restores: previous production capability while simultaneously creating: new automation capability that never existed before. The resulting value should therefore be decomposed: Restored Value → VRSS Newly Emerged Value → Value Emergence governance. This prevents all post-recovery improvement from being mislabeled as restoration. Restoration and Development May Coexist After restoration, the recovered value may continue to grow. Example: Zero Value → ReMonet™ → Restored Value = 30 → Value Development → Value = 60. The first transition belongs to VRSS. The subsequent growth belongs to VDS. Therefore: Restoration Ends Where Development of the Restored Positive Value Begins. Restoration Potential ≠ Restored Value A ZVA™ may possess substantial restoration potential. That potential does not mean value has already been restored. Therefore: Restoration Potential ≠ Restoration Determination. This distinction is essential for dormant technologies, distressed assets, abandoned infrastructure, intellectual property, data, rights, and recoverable capabilities. Restoration Cost ≠ Restored Value The resources spent on restoration do not determine the amount of value restored. An organization may spend: CHF 10 million and restore: CHF 2 million of value. Or spend: CHF 1 million and restore: CHF 20 million of value. VRSS therefore distinguishes: Restoration Input from: Restored Value Outcome. Restoration Activity ≠ Value Creation Repair, investment, modernization, restructuring, data recovery, technological intervention, or regulatory action may enable restoration. These activities are not themselves proof that value has returned. The value consequence must be independently determined. Restoration Failure VRSS explicitly recognizes failed restoration. A restoration process may: fail completely; restore less value than expected; restore value temporarily; restore one dimension while damaging another; restore functionality without restoring economic value; create new value without restoring the old value; reveal that the value is no longer recoverable. Failed restoration must remain visible in the lifecycle record. Repeated Restoration A Value Object may undergo multiple restoration cycles. For example: Positive Value → Degradation → ReMonet™ → Restoration → New Degradation → ReMonet™ → Restoration. VRSS therefore supports recursive restoration across the lifecycle. Each restoration event must retain its own basis and record. Restoration and Value Extinction VRSS creates the strongest boundary with VXSS. A zero-value state may still possess restoration potential. Therefore: Zero Value ≠ Value Extinction. VRSS remains available while recoverable value continues to exist within the governed lifecycle. Once VXSS legitimately determines that the relevant value has become extinct: ReMonet™ cannot simply be assumed to remain available for that same extinct value. If value later appears after genuine extinction, governance must determine whether this represents: new Value Emergence rather than restoration of the extinct value. Boundary with VDS VDS governs: development of existing positive value. VRSS governs: recovery of previously impaired, lost, dormant, inaccessible, degraded, or zero value. Therefore: Growth ≠ Restoration. Boundary with VDGS VDGS governs: decline while positive value remains. VRSS may begin where intervention reverses or recovers the value lost through degradation. Therefore: Degradation → Value Loss may subsequently become: ReMonet™ → Value Restoration. Boundary with VNS VNS governs the transition of positive value into zero value. VRSS may govern a subsequent recovery from that zero-value condition. Therefore: DeMonet™ → Zero and ReMonet™ → Restored Value are distinct lifecycle mechanisms. Boundary with VSS VSS determines the current governed state of value. VRSS governs the restoration transition. After restoration: VRSS → New Value State → VSS. Boundary with VCS VCS governs the fact and character of material change to value. VRSS governs the specific class of change in which previously impaired or lost value is restored. Therefore: Every restoration is a Value Change. But: Not every Value Change is a Value Restoration. Boundary with VXSS VXSS governs the terminal condition in which the relevant value no longer exists as recoverable value within the governed lifecycle. VRSS governs value while restoration remains legitimately possible. Therefore: Restoration Potential → VRSS remains relevant. Value Extinction Determined → VRSS no longer governs restoration of that same extinct value. Boundary with ORA™ ORA™ may govern changes in Operational Reality that enable or prevent restoration. VRSS governs the value consequence: whether previously impaired value actually returned. Boundary with VALIDOS® VALIDOS® may validate evidence, methods, claims, or determinations supporting restoration. VRSS owns the governed meaning of Value Restoration within VFM®. Boundary with INTEGROS® INTEGROS® may govern integrity properties of restoration records, evidence, objects, and supporting information. VRSS governs the restoration lifecycle itself. Boundary with ADIT® ADIT® may audit restoration actions, records, determinations, evidence, and transitions. VRSS defines what constitutes governed Value Restoration. Parent Standard Modules 1. VRSM — Value Restoration Scope Module Governs identification and bounding of the exact previously existing value proposed for restoration. It establishes: what value is being restored, from what prior condition, in which value dimension, and within what context. 2. VRCM — Value Restoration Conditions Module Governs the conditions that must exist before legitimate restoration can occur. It establishes restoration eligibility, dependencies, constraints, prerequisites, and recoverability conditions. 3. VRMM — ReMonet™ Mechanism Module Governs the mechanism through which previously degraded, impaired, dormant, lost, inaccessible, or zero value is recovered. It is the canonical module-level home of: ReMonet™. 4. VRDM — Value Restoration Determination Module Governs the determination of whether restoration actually occurred and, where applicable, its scope, magnitude, conditions, and completeness. It separates: Restoration Activity from: Restored Value. 5. VRTRM — Value Restoration Transition Module Governs the formal transition from the impaired, dormant, lost, degraded, or zero-value condition into the resulting restored positive Value State. It preserves lifecycle continuity between: Previous Value → Loss/Impairment → ReMonet™ → Restored Value → New Value State. Internal Module Flow Previously Existing Value Basis → VRSM — Value Restoration Scope Module → VRCM — Value Restoration Conditions Module → VRMM — ReMonet™ Mechanism Module → VRDM — Value Restoration Determination Module → VRTRM — Value Restoration Transition Module → Restored Value → New Value State The internal logic is: What value can be restored → under what conditions → through what restoration mechanism → whether restoration actually occurred → how restored value enters its new governed state. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Prior Value Identification Establish that the relevant value previously existed. 2. Restoration Scope Identify the exact object, dimension, component, context, and prior Value State proposed for restoration. 3. Current Condition Identify the current degraded, impaired, dormant, lost, inaccessible, or zero-value condition. 4. Restoration Eligibility Determine whether a legitimate restoration pathway remains available. 5. Restoration Conditions Establish the conditions and dependencies necessary for recovery. 6. ReMonet™ Mechanism Identify and govern the mechanism through which recovery is attempted. 7. Restoration Evidence Establish the evidence required to determine whether value actually returned. 8. Restoration Determination Determine whether restoration is absent, partial, conditional, contextual, full, or indeterminate. 9. Restoration Transition Govern the transition into the resulting positive Value State. 10. Lifecycle Record Preserve the complete restoration pathway and resulting state for future governance. Governance Outputs VRSS may produce: Value Restoration Scope Record Prior Value State Record Restoration Eligibility Determination Value Restoration Conditions Record Restoration Dependency Record ReMonet™ Mechanism Record Restoration Attempt Record Restoration Evidence Record Value Restoration Determination Restoration Magnitude Record Restoration Limitation Record Restoration Transition Record Restored Value Record New Value State Record Restoration Provenance Chain Enterprise Application VRSS enables organizations to govern something conventional asset systems often treat inconsistently: the return of value after material impairment or complete loss. Organizations may use VRSS across: distressed assets; industrial equipment; infrastructure; intellectual property; data; digital assets; software; AI capabilities; organizational capabilities; technologies; licenses; rights; brands; products; supply-chain capabilities; dormant projects; abandoned assets; recovered resources. The Standard enables organizations to distinguish whether an intervention: restored old value developed existing value created new value or merely: spent resources without restoring value. This distinction becomes especially important in restructuring, technological recovery, asset reuse, digital transformation, distressed investment, infrastructure rehabilitation, data recovery, IP reactivation, and AI-enabled rediscovery of previously unusable assets. Foundational Principles Value restoration requires previously existing value. Value restoration does not require value to have reached zero first. ReMonet™ governs restoration from degraded, impaired, dormant, lost, inaccessible, or zero-value conditions. Restoration potential is not restored value. Restoration activity is not restoration determination. Restoration cost is not restored value. Partial restoration is legitimate restoration. Restoration in one dimension does not establish restoration in every dimension. Restoration in one context does not establish universal restoration. Restoration does not require exact historical reversal. Restored value may coexist with newly emerged value. Restored value may subsequently enter Value Development. DeMonet™ and ReMonet™ are distinct governed value-transition mechanisms. Zero Value does not prevent restoration. Value Extinction does. Canonical Closing Statement Value Restoration Standard establishes the governed recovery layer of VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture by defining how previously existing value that has become degraded, impaired, dormant, lost, inaccessible, or zero may legitimately re-emerge as governed positive value. Through governance of restoration scope, eligibility, conditions, dependencies, ReMonet™, restoration evidence, determination, magnitude, partial and dimensional recovery, contextual restoration, transition, provenance, and the resulting new Value State, VRSS distinguishes genuine recovery from ordinary growth, new Value Emergence, restoration attempts, expenditure, and unsupported claims that value has returned. By allowing restoration both before and after complete Value Nullification, VRSS establishes ReMonet™ as the general governed mechanism of value recovery while preserving the critical boundary that Zero Value remains potentially recoverable whereas Value Extinction represents the terminal loss of recoverability. VRSS therefore ensures that value which disappears from active use, deteriorates, becomes dormant, loses accessibility, or reaches zero does not simply vanish from governance, but remains methodologically traceable through any legitimate pathway by which it may return. Nahlad Value Restoration Standard (VRSS) Architecture: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Canonical Definition: Value Restoration Standard governs how previously existing value that has become degraded, impaired, dormant, lost, inaccessible, or zero may legitimately be recovered and re-established as governed positive value through defined restoration conditions and the ReMonet™ mechanism. Governed Space: Value Restoration Previously existing value becomes legitimately restored only when its recovery can be traced from the prior Value State through the impairment or loss condition, restoration conditions, ReMonet™ mechanism, restoration determination, and transition into a new governed Value State. → View Standard About standard Module Architecture → Value Restoration Scope Module (VRSM) → Value Restoration Conditions Module (VRCM) → ReMonet® Mechanism Module (VRMM) → Value Restoration Determination Module (VRDM) → Value Restoration Transition Module (VRTRM) Related Documents → About Value Restoration Standard (VRSS) → VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture

title: About Value State Standard (VSS)
text: About Value State Standard (VSS) About Value State Standard (VSS) About Value State Standard (VSS) Architecture: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Parent Standard: Value State Standard (VSS) Governed Space: Value State Canonical Definition Value State Standard (VSS) governs the identification, classification, determination, transition readiness, and persistent representation of the current governed state of value. VSS establishes the methodological layer through which an organization can determine not merely whether value exists, but what condition that value currently occupies within a defined context and reference point. The Standard creates a critical distinction: Value ≠ Value State and: Value State ≠ Value Change A value can continue to exist while moving through materially different states over time. Why VSS Matters Organizations frequently know that an asset, capability, resource, technology, relationship, or other value-bearing object exists, but lack a structured method for determining what state its value is actually in now. Traditional systems may show that an object: exists on an asset register; has an accounting value; remains legally owned; has a market price; remains physically available. None of these facts necessarily establishes its current governed value state. A machine may still exist but provide zero operational value. A technology may currently have little commercial value while carrying substantial strategic value. A capability may temporarily have zero value in one context while remaining highly valuable in another. VSS makes these distinctions explicit and governable. Governance Flow Value Context → Value Origin → Value Emergence → Value Recognition → Value State → Value Change Within VSS: Governed Value Recognition Record → Value State Identification → Value State Classification → Value State Determination → Value State Transition Readiness → Value State Record → Governed Current Value State The resulting state becomes the baseline for downstream Value Change Governance. What VSS Helps Organizations Govern VSS provides a structured method for answering: What value is currently present? What state does that value occupy? Under what context is that state valid? At what reference point was the state determined? What conditions or limitations apply? Is the state stable or approaching a possible transition? What evidence supports the current state? When must the state be reviewed? This creates a persistent value-state layer rather than treating value as a static number. Value Asset™ VSS provides the natural governance location for the canonical concept: Value Asset™ A Value Asset™ represents a governed value-bearing condition in which an identified object, capability, relationship, resource, right, process, system, or other governed basis carries recognized value within a defined VFM® context. Importantly: Value Asset™ ≠ Accounting Asset Value Asset™ ≠ Legal Property Value Asset™ ≠ Marketable Asset An organization may therefore identify forms of operational, technological, strategic, informational, infrastructural, or other value that conventional asset classifications do not adequately represent. ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ VSS also provides the governance location for: ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ ZVA™ represents a governed state in which an identifiable value-bearing object or basis continues to exist while its value within the defined context has reached zero. This creates several important distinctions: Zero Value ≠ Non-Existence Zero Value ≠ Negative Value Zero Value ≠ Permanent Extinction Zero Value in Context A ≠ Zero Value in Context B A ZVA™ may therefore remain identifiable, monitorable, transferable, recoverable, or capable of future value restoration. Current State Before Change VSS establishes an essential requirement for the wider VFM® lifecycle: You cannot govern what changed in value unless you first know what state the value was in. A value-state record creates that reference baseline. For example: State at T₁: Value Asset™ — Active → material event → State at T₂: Value Asset™ — Degraded VFM® can then govern the difference between the two states through the subsequent Value Change Standard (VCS). Without VSS, value change can become an assertion without a governed baseline. Use Case 1 — Banking: Dynamic Collateral and Enterprise Value State A bank evaluates a corporate borrower whose balance sheet contains industrial equipment, intellectual property, production capabilities, software, contracts, inventories, and other value-bearing objects. Conventional financial records may establish accounting values and legal ownership. But the bank may need a different question answered: What state is the underlying value actually in today? A production machine may remain on the balance sheet while being technologically obsolete. A patent may carry little current revenue but substantial strategic value. A manufacturing capability may be temporarily inactive but readily recoverable. Another asset may still physically exist while providing zero value within the operating model for which it was acquired. VSS allows these conditions to be represented as governed value states rather than forcing every object into a single static valuation view. The bank can therefore preserve: Object → Value Context → Recognized Value → Current Value State → State Conditions → Transition Readiness This does not replace accounting, credit analysis, collateral valuation, or banking regulation. It provides an additional value-state governance layer through which changing economic and operational conditions can be represented more explicitly. The bank no longer sees only what the borrower owns. It can govern what state the underlying value is actually in. Use Case 2 — Space Mission: Capability Value Across Mission Phases A space mission contains thousands of systems, capabilities, resources, technologies, data assets, components, and operational options. Their value is not constant throughout the mission. A propulsion capability may carry extremely high value during one mission phase and little operational value after the relevant maneuver is complete. A backup system may remain dormant for months while carrying substantial contingency value. A component that has exhausted its original function may enter a ZVA™ state for that mission purpose while remaining valuable for another scientific, technical, recovery, or diagnostic purpose. VSS allows mission planners to represent: Mission Phase → Capability → Value Context → Current Value State → Dependencies → Transition Readiness This creates a dynamic map of mission value. The organization can identify capabilities whose value is: active conditional dormant constrained degraded zero or otherwise classified according to the mission's governed value-state taxonomy. This can support better resource allocation, redundancy decisions, mission planning, capability preservation, and cost reduction. Instead of asking only: “Does this capability still exist?” mission governance can ask: “Does this capability still create value for the mission, in what state, and under what conditions?” Enterprise Value VSS enables organizations to build a dynamic value-state layer across assets, capabilities, technologies, infrastructure, resources, relationships, digital systems, projects, and other value-bearing objects. It can reveal situations where: physical existence ≠ operational value accounting recognition ≠ current value state market price ≠ strategic value state zero current value ≠ permanent value extinction one object ≠ one universal value state This makes VSS particularly relevant to banking, investment, industry, public finance, infrastructure, technology portfolios, AI systems, resource management, mission systems, and other environments where value continuously changes. Foundational Principle A governed value lifecycle must know the current state of value before it can legitimately determine how that value has changed. title: Value State Classification Module (VSCM)
text: Value State Classification Module (VSCM) Value State Classification Module (VSCM) Value State Classification Module (VSCM) Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture Parent Standard: Value State Standard (VSS) Module: VSCM — Value State Classification Module Operational Layer: Value State Classification Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Value State Classification Origin ID: VFM-VSS-VSCM-005.2 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 25 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · OBIDENITY® AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language Canonical Definition Value State Classification Module (VSCM) is the second Core Module of the Value State Standard (VSS) within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture. VSCM governs the systematic classification of an identified Value State Candidate into a defined value-state class according to the governed value context, reference point, observed condition, applicable classification criteria, and material limitations. The Module establishes a common methodological structure through which materially different value conditions can be distinguished without prematurely issuing the final Value State Determination. Its purpose is to transform: Identified Value Condition → Governed Value-State Class while preserving the distinction: Classification ≠ Determination VSCM does not determine whether the classified state is formally established. That function belongs to: VSDM — Value State Determination Module. Architectural Position VSCM is the second module within VSS. It follows: VSIM — Value State Identification Module and precedes: VSDM — Value State Determination Module. VSIM establishes: what current value condition is being examined. VSCM establishes: what kind of value state that condition represents. VSDM subsequently establishes: whether that state can be formally determined as the governed current Value State. The sequence is: Identification → Classification → Determination Internal Module Flow Value State Candidate → Value Context Confirmation → Classification Basis Selection → Classification Criteria Application → State Characteristic Assessment → Contextual State Separation → State Class Assignment → Classification Limitation Identification → Classification Record → VSDM — Value State Determination Module Operational Space VSCM governs the space between: an identified current value condition and a formally determined current Value State. Its operational space includes: value-state taxonomy; classification basis; classification criteria; value-state characteristics; state differentiation; context-specific classification; active value; conditional value; dormant value; constrained value; degraded value; zero value; negative-value conditions where applicable; recoverable value; state ambiguity; multi-context classification; classification uncertainty; classification limitations; classification traceability. The classification structure may be adapted to the governed environment while preserving the canonical distinctions established by VFM®. Classification Basis Every classification must remain linked to the value context established upstream. A classification should therefore identify, where applicable: Governed Value Value-Bearing Object Beneficiary Value Context Reference Framework Reference Point Observed Condition Classification Criteria Classification Result Without these relationships, a value-state label can become detached from the conditions that give it meaning. Value-State Taxonomy VSCM permits organizations to establish a governed taxonomy appropriate to their value environment. A minimum taxonomy may distinguish states such as: Active Value Value currently contributes materially within the governed context. Conditional Value Value exists, but its realization or usefulness depends upon defined conditions. Dormant Value Value exists but is not currently being exercised, utilized, or realized. Constrained Value Value exists but material restrictions limit its present realization or use. Degraded Value Value remains present but has materially declined relative to the applicable reference condition. Recoverable Value Value is not presently realized at its expected level but may be restored through identifiable conditions or actions. Zero Value The governed value within the defined context is classified as having reached a zero-value condition. Where the applicable requirements are subsequently satisfied through VSDM, this classification may support determination of: ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ Other Governed State Organizations may define additional value-state classes where materially necessary. The taxonomy must remain explicit and interpretable. Value Asset™ Classification VSCM provides the classification layer through which a governed value condition may be classified as belonging to a value-bearing state capable of supporting downstream determination as a: Value Asset™ This classification does not depend solely upon: accounting recognition; legal ownership; marketability; physical existence; purchase price; book value. Instead, classification remains connected to the governed VFM® value context. A capability with no conventional accounting asset entry may therefore still qualify for a value-bearing classification where recognized value exists within the governed context. ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ Classification VSCM provides the classification pathway for a potential: ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ A zero-value classification means that the governed value has reached zero within the specific defined context and reference point. It does not automatically mean that: the underlying object has ceased to exist. It does not automatically mean that: the object has zero value in every context. It does not automatically mean that: the state is permanent. It does not automatically mean that: the object should be disposed of. Therefore: Zero Value ≠ Non-Existence Zero Value ≠ Universal Worthlessness Zero Value ≠ Disposal Requirement Zero Value ≠ Permanent State This distinction is fundamental to VFM®. Zero Value ≠ Negative Value VSCM must preserve a further distinction: Zero Value and Negative Value are not necessarily the same state. An object may create no positive value within a context while imposing: maintenance cost; storage cost; energy consumption; regulatory burden; operational burden; risk; disposal cost; capital lock-up; infrastructure burden. Where an organization chooses to govern negative-value conditions, they must remain distinguishable from the canonical zero-value condition. This prevents: no value from being confused with: value destruction or burden. Dormant Value ≠ Zero Value A dormant capability may not currently generate observable operational output. That does not establish zero value. For example: Emergency Backup System may remain unused for years while carrying substantial contingency value. Likewise: Unused Patent may carry strategic or defensive value despite generating no current licensing income. Therefore: Non-Use ≠ Zero Value and: No Current Revenue ≠ Zero Value VSCM requires the relevant value context to decide which classification is appropriate. Constrained Value ≠ Degraded Value A value may remain fundamentally intact while its realization is externally constrained. For example: a production capability may remain technically functional but unavailable because of: regulatory restriction; missing input; temporary infrastructure failure; contractual limitation; market access restriction. This may support: Constrained Value rather than: Degraded Value. By contrast, degradation concerns deterioration in the value condition itself relative to the governed reference. This distinction can be operationally significant because the restoration pathway may be completely different. Conditional Value Conditional value exists where the value-bearing condition depends materially upon identifiable circumstances. Examples may include: Technology valuable only if regulatory approval occurs Mineral resource valuable only if extraction becomes economically viable Digital capability valuable only within a compatible ecosystem Contractual right valuable only upon occurrence of a defined event VSCM preserves those conditions as part of the classification. A conditional state must not be represented downstream as unconditional value. Recoverable Value Recoverable value is particularly important where current underperformance does not imply permanent value loss. A machine may currently be unusable but repairable. A customer relationship may be inactive but recoverable. A technological capability may become relevant after system reconfiguration. A data asset may be unusable until missing metadata or permissions are restored. Classification as recoverable value enables organizations to distinguish: value that has disappeared from value whose realization is temporarily interrupted. Multi-Context Classification The same value-bearing object may occupy multiple value-state classes simultaneously across different governed contexts. For example: Legacy Industrial Machine may be: Zero Value — Current Production Context while simultaneously: Active Value — Spare Parts Context and: Conditional Value — Resale Context and: Strategic Value — Emergency Capacity Context VSCM therefore prohibits universalizing a context-specific classification without a governed basis. The canonical rule is: One Object ≠ One Universal Value State Multi-Beneficiary Classification Value state may also differ according to beneficiary. An asset may have: low value to Organization A while having: high value to Organization B. A technology abandoned by one enterprise may be strategically valuable to another. A dataset may have limited internal value but substantial research value to a different beneficiary. Where beneficiary materially affects value state, VSCM preserves that distinction. Classification Granularity Classification must occur at a level appropriate to the governed value. For example: Factory may remain a Value Asset™ overall. Yet: Production Line 4 may contain degraded value. Within that line: Machine 12 may be a potential ZVA™. Within that machine: Control Unit may remain independently recoverable or transferable. VSCM prevents higher-level value from automatically masking lower-level zero or degraded value. It equally prevents one lower-level failure from automatically determining the value state of the entire system. Classification Criteria Organizations implementing VSCM should establish explicit criteria for each state class. Criteria may consider: current value contribution; operational usability; beneficiary relevance; realization conditions; utilization; functional capability; recoverability; strategic relevance; economic relevance; technological relevance; constraints; dependency availability; deterioration; substitution; temporal relevance; cost burden; value realization potential. Classification criteria must be appropriate to the governed value context. VFM® does not impose one universal economic formula across every form of value. Classification Evidence Classification should be supported by a sufficient basis appropriate to the governed context. This may include: operational information; financial information; market information; utilization records; technical assessments; system telemetry; production records; contractual information; strategic assessments; capability records; resource data; external valuation information; governed observations. VSCM does not own these evidence systems. It governs their use in supporting value-state classification. Classification Uncertainty Where available information supports more than one plausible classification, uncertainty must remain visible. For example: Dormant Value? or: Zero Value? may remain unresolved where future usability, strategic relevance, or recoverability is unclear. VSCM must not force artificial certainty merely because a classification system requires a field to be populated. Possible treatment may include: Provisional Classification Conditional Classification Multiple Candidate Classes Unresolved Classification until sufficient basis exists for downstream determination. Classification Conflict Different organizational functions may classify the same value differently. For example: Finance: low-value asset Operations: critical backup capability Engineering: technologically obsolete Strategy: essential transition asset VSCM does not automatically select one organizational view. It separates the underlying value contexts and determines whether the apparent conflict represents: different classifications of the same governed value or different governed values attached to the same object. This distinction can eliminate false organizational disagreement. Classification ≠ Valuation VSCM does not require every state to have a monetary amount. Classification may exist independently from monetary valuation. Therefore: Value State Class ≠ Price Value State Class ≠ Market Value Value State Class ≠ Book Value Value State Class ≠ Tax Value A monetary valuation may become relevant through another methodology or system. VSCM governs the state class of value, not the universal financial amount assigned to it. Classification ≠ Accounting Treatment An accounting system may classify an item according to applicable accounting standards. VSCM does not replace those classifications. An accounting asset may occupy a zero-value operational state. A non-capitalized capability may occupy an active strategic-value state. VFM® therefore creates a value-governance layer capable of operating alongside accounting rather than attempting to become accounting itself. Classification ≠ Legal Status VSCM does not determine: ownership; legal title; regulatory status; tax treatment; contractual enforceability; intellectual-property rights. Those characteristics may affect value classification where relevant. They do not become governed by VSCM merely because they influence value. Classification Stability A classification should remain valid only while the conditions supporting it remain materially unchanged. Potential review triggers may include: operational change; technological change; market change; regulatory change; beneficiary change; context change; restoration; deterioration; new dependency; lost dependency; new evidence; material cost change. VSCM identifies the classification. Later modules govern determination, transition readiness, and state recording. Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum VSCM implementation should establish: 1. Value State Candidate Receive the identified Value State Candidate from VSIM. 2. Context Confirmation Confirm the governed value, object, beneficiary, context, and reference point. 3. Classification Taxonomy Define the state classes available within the governed environment. 4. Classification Criteria Define the conditions required for each applicable state class. 5. Candidate Assessment Compare the identified condition against applicable classification criteria. 6. Context Separation Separate materially different value contexts or beneficiaries where necessary. 7. Classification Assignment Assign the most appropriate state class or provisional classification. 8. Uncertainty and Limitation Preserve material uncertainty, competing classifications, and classification limitations. 9. Classification Basis Record the information and reasoning supporting the classification. 10. Downstream Transfer Transfer the classified Value State Candidate to VSDM for formal Value State Determination. Governance Outputs VSCM may produce: Value State Classification Value State Classification Basis Value State Taxonomy Reference Value State Criteria Record Value Asset™ Classification Candidate ZVA™ Classification Candidate Dormant Value Classification Conditional Value Classification Constrained Value Classification Degraded Value Classification Recoverable Value Classification Multi-Context Classification Record Classification Uncertainty Record Classification Limitation Record Classified Value State Candidate These outputs provide the governed input for: VSDM — Value State Determination Module. Use Case 1 — Banking: Separating Real Collateral Value States Before Risk Decisions A bank finances an industrial enterprise whose collateral pool contains hundreds of machines, technologies, production systems, licenses, inventories, and other value-bearing objects. A conventional register may show: Asset exists → Ownership confirmed → Recorded amount available But these objects may occupy fundamentally different value states. VSCM can classify them individually: Machine A → Active Value → currently essential to profitable production. Machine B → Dormant Value → currently unused but immediately deployable as backup capacity. Machine C → Constrained Value → functional but unavailable because a critical input is temporarily unavailable. Machine D → Degraded Value → operational but technologically deteriorated relative to current production requirements. Machine E → Potential ZVA™ → physically present but carrying zero identified value within the governed production context. Patent F → Conditional Value → no current revenue but potentially valuable if a planned product receives market authorization. Instead of treating the collateral base as one homogeneous stock of assets, the bank gains a classified map of the actual states through which underlying value exists. This can support more precise: collateral review; credit monitoring; restructuring analysis; recovery planning; portfolio surveillance; early-warning systems. Most importantly, VSCM can expose a hidden risk: the legal and accounting asset base may remain relatively stable while the operational value-state composition underneath it is deteriorating. That divergence may become visible before conventional asset disappearance occurs. Use Case 2 — Blockchain and Digital Assets: Separating Token Existence From Actual Value State A blockchain ecosystem may contain millions of tokens, digital rights, protocol assets, liquidity positions, smart-contract relationships, digital credentials, or tokenized claims. The technical existence of these objects is easy to establish. Their current value state is much harder. A token may still exist on-chain while: its underlying service has disappeared. Another token may have no active market but retain redemption rights. A digital asset may be temporarily unusable because a bridge, oracle, protocol dependency, or access mechanism is unavailable. Another may have no present utility but retain strategic governance rights. A tokenized real-world claim may remain technically transferable while the underlying economic relationship has materially deteriorated. VSCM can classify these states separately: Active Value Conditional Value Dormant Value Constrained Value Degraded Value Recoverable Value Potential ZVA™ rather than allowing: Token Exists to become equivalent to: Token Has Current Value. The classification can remain attached to: Digital Object → Value Context → Beneficiary → Reference Point → Current Condition → Value-State Class This creates a powerful governance distinction for digital economies: technical persistence is not value persistence. A blockchain may preserve an object's existence indefinitely. VFM® can separately govern whether the value associated with that object remains active, dormant, constrained, degraded, recoverable, conditional, or zero within the defined context. Foundational Principles Identified condition must be classified before the governed state can be formally determined. Classification is not determination. Value-state classification is context-specific, not universally transferable. One object may carry multiple value states across different contexts. One object may carry different value states for different beneficiaries. Non-use is not automatically zero value. Dormant value is not zero value. Constrained value is not necessarily degraded value. Zero value is not negative value. Zero value is not non-existence. Zero value in one context does not establish zero value in every context. A Value State is not a price. A Value State is not an accounting classification. Technical existence does not establish current value. Canonical Closing Statement Value State Classification Module establishes the classification layer of the Value State Standard by transforming an identified Value State Candidate into an explicit, context-bound, criteria-based Value-State Class before formal determination occurs. Through governance of classification taxonomy, state criteria, active, conditional, dormant, constrained, degraded, recoverable and zero-value conditions, multi-context and multi-beneficiary distinctions, granularity, uncertainty, classification conflicts, and the separation of value state from price, accounting treatment, legal status, physical existence, and technical persistence, VSCM creates a common methodological language for distinguishing materially different conditions of value. By preserving the distinctions between dormant and zero value, constrained and degraded value, zero and negative value, and contextual and universal value claims, VSCM provides the classified basis required for VSDM to determine what governed state value actually occupies.
