title: Value State Transition Readiness Module (VSTM)
text: Value State Transition Readiness Module (VSTM) Value State Transition Readiness Module (VSTM) Value State Transition Readiness Module (VSTM) Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture Parent Standard: Value State Standard (VSS) Module: VSTM — Value State Transition Readiness Module Operational Layer: Value State Transition Readiness Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Value State Transition Readiness Origin ID: VFM-VSS-VSTM-005.4 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 25 August 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · GOA™ · ORA™ · VALIDOS® · INTEGROS® · ADIT® · AGA™ · OBIDENITY® AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language Canonical Definition Value State Transition Readiness Module (VSTM) is the fourth Core Module of the Value State Standard (VSS) within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture. VSTM governs whether a determined current Value State has reached the conditions under which a potential transition away from that state must become governable, observable, or ready for downstream value-change governance. The Module establishes the methodological bridge between: Current Governed Value State and Potential Value State Transition without determining that a value change has already occurred. Its foundational distinction is: Transition Readiness ≠ Value Change VSTM answers: Is the current Value State sufficiently exposed to, approaching, or meeting defined transition conditions that downstream change governance should become active? The actual identification and governance of material value change belongs to: Value Change Standard (VCS). Architectural Position VSTM is the fourth module within VSS. It follows: VSIM — Value State Identification Module → VSCM — Value State Classification Module → VSDM — Value State Determination Module and precedes: VSRM — Value State Record Module. The internal logic is: Identify State → Classify State → Determine State → Assess Transition Readiness → Record State VSTM therefore prevents a determined Value State from being treated as static when material conditions indicate that the value may be approaching another state. VFM® Governance Flow Position VSTM occupies an important transition point in the broader VFM® governance flow: Value Context → Value Origin → Value Emergence → Value Recognition → Value State → Value Change VSTM operates at the end of the active Value State assessment and creates the readiness interface toward Value Change. The architectural relationship is: Current Value State → Transition Readiness → Potential Material Change → Value Change Governance VSTM does not move value between states. It determines whether the conditions for monitoring or examining such movement have become materially relevant. Internal Module Flow Determined Value State → Transition Sensitivity Identification → Transition Condition Definition → Relevant Signal Identification → Threshold Proximity Assessment → Dependency Assessment → Transition Constraint Assessment → Transition Readiness Assessment → Readiness State Assignment → Transition Readiness Record → VSRM — Value State Record Module Where a material change is subsequently observed: Transition Signal → VCS — Value Change Standard Operational Space VSTM governs the space between: a determined current Value State and a potentially emerging change to that state. Its operational space includes: transition sensitivity; transition conditions; transition indicators; transition signals; transition thresholds; threshold proximity; value-state instability; state persistence; transition dependencies; transition constraints; transition blockers; transition enablers; recovery conditions; degradation conditions; zero-value approach; reactivation conditions; readiness classification; transition uncertainty; transition monitoring requirements; downstream change-governance triggers. Transition Readiness Principle A Value State may remain formally unchanged while conditions around it materially evolve. For example: Active Value may remain the determined state while operational performance is deteriorating. Dormant Value may remain the determined state while reactivation conditions are approaching. Degraded Value may remain the determined state while recovery becomes increasingly feasible. Conditional Value may remain the determined state while its defining condition approaches satisfaction. Zero Value may remain the determined state while a new use case creates a credible pathway toward renewed value. VSTM governs this intermediate space. It allows VFM® to distinguish: Current State from Readiness to Leave Current State. Transition Condition A Transition Condition is a defined condition whose satisfaction, deterioration, restoration, appearance, disappearance, or material alteration may make movement from the current Value State possible or relevant. Transition conditions may concern: utilization; capability; demand; technological relevance; operational performance; cost; resource availability; dependency availability; regulatory conditions; market access; beneficiary needs; infrastructure availability; system compatibility; recoverability; deterioration; restoration; strategic relevance; environmental conditions; contractual conditions. VSTM does not govern these external systems themselves. It governs their relevance to Value State transition readiness. Transition Signal A Transition Signal is an observable indication that one or more relevant transition conditions may be changing. Signals may include: declining utilization; increasing failure frequency; rising maintenance burden; disappearing demand; increasing operational cost; technological displacement; restored infrastructure; renewed customer demand; new compatibility; regulatory approval; dependency restoration; new beneficiary; new use case; resource scarcity; capability recovery; measurable deterioration. A signal does not prove that value has changed. Therefore: Transition Signal ≠ Value Change Transition Threshold Organizations may establish thresholds indicating when a Value State requires closer transition governance. Examples may include: Utilization below defined level Operating cost above defined level Capability below defined requirement Recovery probability above defined level Dependency restored Critical technology support withdrawn Strategic demand activated A threshold may be: quantitative; qualitative; event-based; condition-based; composite. Crossing a transition-readiness threshold does not automatically establish a new Value State. It establishes that transition governance has become materially relevant. Threshold Proximity VSTM should not operate only after a threshold has already been crossed. Where useful, it may govern proximity to a transition threshold. A state may therefore be: Stable while far from any relevant transition threshold. It may become: Transition-Sensitive as conditions begin moving materially toward a threshold. It may become: Transition-Ready when defined readiness conditions are satisfied. This gives VFM® the ability to identify value movement before a formal state change is determined. Transition Readiness States A minimum VSTM implementation may use the following states: 1. Stable No material transition condition currently indicates credible movement from the determined Value State. 2. Transition-Sensitive Material indicators exist that could affect the persistence of the current Value State. 3. Approaching Transition One or more relevant transition conditions are materially approaching a defined threshold. 4. Transition-Ready Defined conditions exist under which transition from the current Value State has become materially actionable or governable. 5. Transition-Constrained A potential transition exists but one or more material constraints currently prevent or materially limit it. 6. Transition-Indeterminate Available information is insufficient to establish transition readiness. These are governance states. They do not themselves establish that value has changed. Transition Readiness ≠ Prediction VSTM does not predict with certainty what the next Value State will be. It may identify: credible transition pathways without asserting: future transition outcome. For example: Degraded Value may have potential pathways toward: Recoverable Value or Zero Value. VSTM may establish that both pathways are materially possible. It does not need to predict which will occur. Therefore: Transition Readiness ≠ Transition Prediction Where formal prediction governance is required, that belongs to the appropriate prediction architecture. Transition Readiness ≠ Transition Execution A system may be ready for value transition without anyone deciding to execute an intervention. For example: a dormant production line may be ready for reactivation. VSTM can establish: Reactivation-Ready without deciding: Reactivate Production Line. Likewise, an obsolete system may be ready for retirement without VSTM authorizing disposal. Therefore: Readiness ≠ Decision and: Readiness ≠ Execution Value Degradation Pathway VSTM can identify when a currently positive Value State approaches degradation. Example: Active Value → declining capability → increasing maintenance → decreasing utilization → reduced beneficiary relevance → Transition-Sensitive → Approaching Transition If a material value change subsequently occurs, the matter proceeds into VCS. This enables organizations to observe value deterioration before it becomes invisible inside static asset records. Zero-Value Approach One of the strongest applications of VSTM is governance of the pathway toward: ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ A Value Asset™ may remain in a positive Value State while moving progressively toward zero value. VSTM can identify: Active Value → Degradation Signals → Transition-Sensitive → Approaching Zero-Value Threshold → Transition-Ready without prematurely determining: ZVA™ The zero-value state itself must still be established through the applicable state and change governance. This prevents both: premature zero-value classification and late recognition of value collapse. Recovery Pathway Transition governance is equally important in the opposite direction. A zero-value, dormant, constrained, or degraded object may develop new value potential. Examples include: new technology; new beneficiary; restored dependency; new market; regulatory change; infrastructure restoration; new use case; component reuse; new strategic requirement. VSTM can identify: Current Low/Zero Value State → Recovery Signal → Recovery Conditions → Transition Readiness without automatically determining that value has already re-emerged. This provides an important foundation for future VFM® concepts concerning ReMonet™ and value restoration. State Persistence Not every changing external condition requires a Value State transition. VSTM therefore considers whether the current state remains sufficiently persistent despite changing conditions. For example: a temporary market decline may not materially alter the strategic value of a capability. A short operational outage may not change an Active Value state. A temporary cost increase may not establish degradation. The Module therefore protects VFM® from excessive state volatility. Transition Dependencies Some transitions depend upon external conditions. A dormant asset may become active only if: energy supply returns or: regulatory approval is granted or: a critical component becomes available. VSTM records those dependencies as part of transition readiness. The transition may therefore be classified as: Transition-Constrained until the dependency is satisfied. Transition Constraints Material constraints may prevent an otherwise credible value transition. These may include: technical constraints; resource constraints; legal constraints; contractual constraints; infrastructure constraints; capability constraints; market constraints; timing constraints; dependency constraints. VSTM does not resolve those constraints. It makes their effect on transition readiness explicit. Multiple Transition Pathways A current Value State may have several potential next states. For example: Dormant Value may transition toward: Active Value if demand returns, toward: Degraded Value if deterioration continues, or toward: Zero Value if the capability loses all relevant value within the governed context. VSTM may preserve multiple credible transition pathways simultaneously. Therefore: One Current State ≠ One Inevitable Next State Context-Specific Transition Readiness The same value-bearing object may have different transition readiness across different contexts. For example: Industrial Robot may be: Stable — Current Production Context while: Transition-Ready — Resale Context and: Transition-Sensitive — Technology Relevance Context. VSTM therefore preserves the context established upstream. Transition readiness must not be universalized across unrelated value contexts. Beneficiary-Specific Transition Readiness A transition may also be beneficiary-specific. A technology may be approaching zero value for one organization while simultaneously becoming increasingly valuable to another. VSTM can preserve both relationships. This is particularly important for: secondary markets; asset transfer; technology reuse; industrial restructuring; intellectual property; data; infrastructure; circular economy models. Transition Uncertainty Where readiness cannot be established confidently, uncertainty must remain visible. Sources may include: incomplete data; uncertain demand; unknown recoverability; unclear dependency status; unstable technology conditions; ambiguous beneficiary relevance; uncertain regulatory outcome; incomplete cost information. VSTM should not convert uncertainty into artificial readiness. The appropriate state may remain: Transition-Indeterminate until sufficient information becomes available. Transition Monitoring A determined Value State may require monitoring where transition sensitivity is material. Monitoring may focus on: threshold variables; critical dependencies; deterioration indicators; recovery indicators; utilization; operational output; cost burden; beneficiary demand; market relevance; technology relevance; regulatory conditions. VSTM governs what transition-relevant signals should remain observable. It does not become a general monitoring architecture. Interface with Value Change Standard VSTM provides an explicit methodological bridge to: 6. Value Change Standard (VCS) VSTM determines: whether conditions indicate readiness or sensitivity for potential movement from the current Value State. VCS determines: whether existing value has materially changed and what change has occurred. Therefore: VSTM: Potential movement becomes governable. VCS: Material value change becomes identifiable. The architectural boundary is: Readiness ≠ Change Interface with Value Emergence A transition from zero or non-realized value toward positive value may eventually interact with Value Emergence Standard (VES) where genuinely new value emerges. VSTM does not determine value emergence. It may identify conditions indicating that a current state is approaching a transition requiring reassessment through the appropriate VFM® governed space. This preserves the distinction: State Transition Readiness ≠ Value Emergence Interface with Value Recognition A changed or newly emerged value may require recognition under: Value Recognition Standard (VRS). VSTM does not recognize value. It identifies transition readiness within an already governed Value State. Interface with External Events External events may influence transition readiness. Examples include: market shocks; innovation; regulation; physical damage; infrastructure failure; technological substitution; contractual change; payment; environmental event. VFM® does not need to govern the external event itself. VSTM governs: what that event means for readiness of the governed value to leave its current state. Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum VSTM implementation should establish: 1. Current Value State Receive the determined current Value State from VSDM. 2. Transition Sensitivity Identify conditions capable of materially affecting persistence of that state. 3. Transition Conditions Define conditions relevant to movement from the current state. 4. Transition Signals Identify observable signals associated with those conditions. 5. Transition Thresholds Establish thresholds where appropriate. 6. Dependency Assessment Identify dependencies enabling or constraining transition. 7. Readiness Assessment Determine whether the current state is stable, sensitive, approaching transition, transition-ready, constrained, or indeterminate. 8. Potential Pathways Identify materially credible next-state pathways without treating them as predictions. 9. Monitoring Requirement Identify transition-relevant conditions requiring continued observation. 10. Downstream Trigger Where material change is subsequently identified, transfer the matter into Value Change governance. Governance Outputs VSTM may produce: Value State Transition Readiness Assessment Transition Condition Record Transition Signal Record Transition Threshold Record Threshold Proximity Assessment Transition Dependency Record Transition Constraint Record Transition Readiness State Potential Transition Pathway Record Zero-Value Approach Signal Recovery Readiness Signal Transition Monitoring Requirement Value Change Governance Trigger These outputs preserve the bridge between current Value State governance and downstream Value Change governance. Use Case 1 — Banking: Detecting Collateral Value Deterioration Before the Asset Reaches Zero A bank finances an industrial company whose loan is secured by production equipment. The equipment remains: operational and therefore retains a determined: Active Value State. Traditional collateral monitoring may continue to treat the machinery as performing collateral until a major impairment, default, valuation event, or operational failure becomes visible. VSTM introduces an earlier governance layer. The bank may observe: utilization decline → maintenance cost increase → technology obsolescence → loss of spare-part support → declining secondary-market demand → reduced productive relevance. None of these signals alone necessarily establishes a new Value State. Together, however, they may move the asset from: Stable to: Transition-Sensitive and eventually: Approaching Transition. The bank can therefore identify that the governed value supporting its collateral is approaching a materially different state before the underlying machine disappears, defaults, or becomes formally worthless. This creates a potential early-warning layer between: asset existence and value deterioration. For banking, credit, insurance, restructuring, and collateral governance, that distinction can be materially significant. Use Case 2 — Space Mission: Determining When Mission Assets Become Ready for a Different Value State A space mission contains satellites, scientific instruments, computing systems, communication infrastructure, energy systems, spare capacity, data resources, and mission capabilities. A scientific instrument may currently occupy: Active Value because it is producing mission-relevant data. Over time: sensor degradation increases → energy consumption rises → measurement precision declines → mission priorities change → new instruments become available. The instrument may still carry active value. VSTM therefore does not prematurely classify it as degraded or zero. Instead, it determines whether the current state has become: Transition-Sensitive or: Approaching Transition. At the same time, an apparently obsolete instrument may gain a new use: secondary observation backup capability calibration support experimental reuse or new scientific purpose. VSTM can therefore identify both: declining value pathways and renewed value pathways. This is important in environments such as space missions where physical replacement may be impossible and extracting additional value from existing resources can materially reduce mission cost and extend mission capability. The result is a governed answer not merely to: What is this asset worth now? but to: Is its current Value State stable, deteriorating, recoverable, or approaching a materially different state? Foundational Principles Current Value State does not imply permanent Value State. Transition readiness is not Value Change. Transition signal is not Value Change. Threshold proximity is not threshold crossing. Transition readiness is not prediction. Transition readiness is not authorization. Transition readiness is not execution. One current Value State may have multiple credible transition pathways. Value deterioration may become governable before zero value occurs. Value recovery may become governable before positive value re-emerges. A Value Asset™ may approach ZVA™ without yet becoming ZVA™. A ZVA™ may develop transition readiness toward renewed value without yet possessing renewed value. VFM® must govern not only what state value occupies, but when that state is becoming materially unstable. Canonical Closing Statement Value State Transition Readiness Module establishes the transition-readiness layer of the Value State Standard by determining whether a governed current Value State remains stable or has become sensitive, constrained, indeterminate, approaching transition, or ready for potential movement into another value condition. Through governance of transition conditions, signals, thresholds, threshold proximity, dependencies, constraints, uncertainty, state persistence, degradation pathways, zero-value approach, recovery pathways, monitoring requirements, and potential next-state pathways, VSTM makes value-state instability governable before a material value change is formally established. By separating transition readiness from prediction, authorization, execution, value emergence, value recognition, and actual Value Change, VSTM preserves the boundary between the current governed state and downstream change governance while creating the early-warning and recovery interface required for dynamic value governance. title: Value State Standard (VSS)
text: Value State Standard (VSS) Value State Standard (VSS) Value State Standard (VSS) Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture Parent Standard: Value State Standard (VSS) Operational Layer: Value State Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Type: Parent Standard Governed Space: Value State Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 25 August 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language Canonical Definition Value State Standard (VSS) is the fifth Parent Standard within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture governing the identification, classification, determination, transition readiness, and persistent representation of the current governed state of value. VSS establishes a structured governance layer through which value that has emerged and entered the governed value lifecycle can be represented according to its current condition without confusing that condition with its origin, recognition, previous condition, future condition, or the mechanism through which change occurred. The Standard establishes the methodological distinction between: the existence of value and the current state in which that value exists. Its governing principle is: Value State ≠ Value Transition. VSS determines where value currently stands. It does not determine the mechanism through which value arrived there or the mechanism through which it may subsequently move to another state. Core Question What is the current governed state of value? Architectural Position VSS occupies the fifth governed space within the VFM® value lifecycle. It follows: Value Recognition Standard (VRS) and precedes: Value Change Standard (VCS). The VFM® governance flow at this point is: Value Context → Value Origin → Value Emergence → Value Recognition → Value State → Value Change → Value Development / Value Degradation → Value Nullification → Value Restoration / Value Extinction The architectural transition is therefore: What value is being governed? → Where can that value originate? → Has value actually emerged? → Can that existing value be recognized within the defined context? → What is its current governed state? VSS establishes the baseline state against which subsequent value change can be governed. Governance Flow Position Governed Value Recognition Record → Value State Identification → Value State Classification → Value State Determination → Value State Transition Readiness → Value State Record → Governed Current Value State → Value Change Governance This creates a critical lifecycle control: Recognized Value → Governed Current Value State Once that state exists, subsequent VFM® standards can determine whether the value has materially changed. Operational Space VSS governs the operational space in which existing value is assigned an explicit and current governed state. This includes: value-state identification; value-state classification; state criteria; state determination; state applicability; state conditions; state boundaries; state uncertainty; state temporal applicability; zero-value state; positive-value state; conditional value state; state review; state transition readiness; state versioning; state history; current-state representation; machine-readable value-state records. The purpose is to prevent value from being treated merely as: present or absent when its actual governed condition may be materially more complex. Value State Principle A value can exist while occupying different states. For example, a capability may have: Potential Value before emergence. After emergence and recognition it may become: Recognized Existing Value and later occupy states representing materially different conditions within the value lifecycle. The state is therefore not the value itself. It is a governed representation of the value's current condition. Thus: Value ≠ Value State and: Value Identity ≠ Value State The same governed value may persist while its state changes repeatedly. State Independence Principle VSS requires the current value state to be determinable independently from the historical pathway that produced it. Two values may arrive at the same current state through completely different mechanisms. For example: Value A: innovation → development → current state X Value B: degradation → restoration → current state X Their histories differ. Their current governed state may nevertheless be equivalent. VSS therefore governs: Current Condition rather than: Historical Mechanism. The historical pathway remains relevant to other VFM® lifecycle spaces but must not prevent consistent state representation. Value State ≠ Value Recognition Recognition and state answer different governance questions. Value Recognition asks: Can existing value be recognized as value within this defined governance context? Value State asks: What is the current governed condition of that value? A recognition determination may therefore remain valid while the underlying value subsequently changes state. Recognition must not be repeatedly mistaken for the current value condition. Value State ≠ Value Change VSS establishes the state. VCS establishes whether that state or its underlying value condition has materially changed. Therefore: State(t₁) ≠ Change(t₁→t₂) A state is a condition at a governed reference point. A change is a relationship between conditions across reference points. This distinction enables VFM® to represent value dynamically without collapsing state and movement into the same concept. Value State ≠ Value Transition A value may be in a particular state without currently transitioning. Likewise, evidence may indicate that a transition is becoming possible or imminent without establishing that the transition has occurred. VSS therefore preserves: Current State separately from: Transition Readiness and: Completed Transition. Transition readiness is a state-governance signal. Actual value change belongs downstream. State Reference Point Every meaningful value-state determination requires a reference point. The reference point may be: a date; a reporting period; an operational configuration; a transaction stage; a technological stage; a project phase; an accounting period; a mission phase; a contractual condition; a system version; another governed temporal or operational reference. Without a reference point, the statement: “The value is in State X.” may become detached from the conditions under which it was true. VSS therefore treats state as reference-bound. State Classification VSS permits value states to be classified according to the governance context in which value is being represented. VFM® does not require every sector, asset type, organization, or value system to use one rigid universal state taxonomy. Instead, state classifications must be: explicitly defined; mutually interpretable where required; connected to the governed value; contextually appropriate; sufficiently distinguishable; consistently applied; machine-readable where implementation requires. This allows VFM® to govern value across financial, industrial, technological, public, digital, environmental, scientific, infrastructure, and other contexts without forcing unlike value systems into an artificial common scale. Canonical Value-State Concepts VFM® may establish canonical value-state concepts where they represent recurring value conditions across multiple domains. Two foundational concepts are: Value Asset™ and ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™. These concepts must remain governed states or value-state constructs within the VFM® lifecycle and must not silently acquire meanings belonging to accounting, property, taxation, securities law, valuation, or another external system. Value Asset™ Value Asset™ represents a governed value-bearing condition in which an identified object, capability, relationship, resource, right, process, system, or other governed basis carries recognized value within a defined VFM® context. The concept is broader than conventional accounting recognition. Therefore: Value Asset™ ≠ Accounting Asset Value Asset™ ≠ Legal Property Value Asset™ ≠ Marketable Asset Value Asset™ ≠ Taxable Asset A Value Asset™ may have significant operational, strategic, technological, social, informational, infrastructure, or other value even where an external accounting or legal framework does not classify it as an asset. External systems remain responsible for their own classifications. ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ represents a governed zero-value state where an identified value-bearing object or basis remains governable but its value within the defined VFM® context is determined to be zero. The concept establishes an important distinction: Zero Value ≠ Non-Existence An object can continue to exist while the governed value associated with it is zero. Likewise: Zero Value ≠ Extinction A zero-value state does not automatically establish that value can never return. And: Zero Value ≠ Worthless in Every Context An object may occupy a zero-value state under one value context while carrying value under another. ZVA™ therefore creates a governed representation of zero value without forcing the lifecycle immediately into extinction. Zero as a Governed State Zero is not merely the absence of a number. Within VFM®, zero may represent a materially meaningful lifecycle condition. For example, an industrial capability may temporarily have no operational value because the production system it serves has been suspended. A technological asset may have zero value within a current architecture but regain value after compatibility is restored. A digital resource may have zero current utility while retaining recoverable future value. A mission capability may have zero value for one mission configuration while remaining valuable for another. VSS makes those distinctions governable. Zero Value ≠ Negative Value Where a governance context supports negative-value conditions, VSS must distinguish them from zero. Zero Value means the governed value state is zero within the defined context. Negative Value may indicate that the governed object, condition, activity, or relationship creates a net adverse value effect under the applicable value model. These states are not interchangeable. A zero-value object may create neither value nor material value loss. A negative-value condition may actively destroy, consume, offset, or impose value. The applicable methodology must define the distinction. State Granularity A value-state system may operate at different levels of granularity. For example: High-Level State may indicate whether value is: Positive / Zero / Negative / Indeterminate while a more detailed state model may distinguish: Active / Conditional / Constrained / Dormant / Degraded / Zero / Recoverable / Other Defined State. VSS does not require unnecessary complexity. The state taxonomy should be sufficiently granular to support the decisions and downstream governance for which it is intended. Conditional Value State A value state may depend upon defined conditions. For example: Value Asset™ — Conditional may indicate that the governed value remains present only while: a capability remains available; a contract remains active; a technology remains compatible; an infrastructure dependency remains available; a regulatory condition remains satisfied; a resource remains accessible; a particular operational configuration remains active. The condition must remain attached to the state determination. Indeterminate Value State VSS must permit an indeterminate state where available information does not support a legitimate current-state determination. This prevents governance systems from forcing false certainty. Unknown ≠ Zero and: Indeterminate ≠ No Value An inability to determine the current value state must not automatically convert into a zero-value determination. State Determination Principle A Value State Determination should identify: Value Reference → Governance Context → State Reference Point → Applicable State Criteria → Available State Basis → Current State Determination → Conditions → Limitations → Uncertainty → Review Conditions The determination must be sufficiently explicit to distinguish: what state was determined from: why that determination was made. State Evidence VSS may use information produced elsewhere to support state determination. Such information may include: operational results; market information; technical condition; capability availability; utilization; performance; demand; contractual status; financial information; resource availability; technological compatibility; external valuations; governed recognition records; other relevant evidence. VSS governs how that information supports a Value State Determination. It does not take ownership of the external systems that generated the information. Temporal State Principle Value state is inherently temporal. A value may be: State A at T₁ and: State B at T₂. The current state must therefore be distinguishable from: previous state; projected state; target state; possible state; historical state. This is especially important for AI and automated systems, which may otherwise confuse an old value record with the current value condition. Current State ≠ Future State VSS does not predict what value will become. A state determination may identify transition readiness, but it does not establish the future state. Therefore: Transition Readiness ≠ Predicted Transition and: Predicted State ≠ Current State. Prediction governance remains outside VSS. Transition Readiness VSS includes transition readiness because a current state may contain conditions indicating that state reassessment or downstream change governance is required. Transition-readiness indicators may include: threshold proximity; material dependency change; deterioration signal; capability activation; value recovery condition; market threshold; contractual trigger; technological transition; resource exhaustion; restoration condition; material uncertainty change. Transition readiness does not itself establish a value change. It establishes that the current state may no longer remain stable or sufficient as the sole representation of value. State Review Trigger A state review may be triggered when: material new evidence appears; a value-change signal is detected; recognition conditions change; the value object changes materially; a dependency changes; a state condition fails; a defined threshold is crossed; the reference period expires; the governance context changes; uncertainty becomes material; an external event potentially affects value. The trigger initiates review. It does not predetermine the new state. State Persistence A value state remains the governed current state until: a new state is legitimately determined; the existing determination expires; the state is suspended; the applicable governance context ceases; or another defined lifecycle condition invalidates its applicability. This prevents uncontrolled state changes based merely on unverified signals. State History VSS requires historical states to remain distinguishable where lifecycle traceability is required. A value lifecycle may therefore show: State A — Active → State B — Constrained → State C — ZVA™ → State D — Restored Value Asset™ The state history provides a governed record of where value has been. The mechanisms responsible for those movements remain governed through the relevant downstream standards. Multi-Context State The same underlying object may legitimately occupy different value states in different contexts. For example: Industrial Machine may be: ZVA™ within Production Line A while remaining: Value Asset™ within Spare-Part Recovery Context B. Likewise, intellectual property may have: high strategic value and simultaneously: zero current licensing value. VSS therefore prohibits silent collapse of multiple value contexts into one universal state. Aggregation Principle Value states may be aggregated for portfolio, enterprise, infrastructure, governmental, or analytical purposes. However: State Aggregation ≠ State Homogenization An enterprise containing: high-value assets; conditional-value assets; zero-value assets; degraded-value assets; indeterminate-value objects must not be represented as though every underlying value object occupies the same state merely because a portfolio- level metric exists. Granular states should remain traceable where material. State Transfer Principle A value-state record may move between systems. For example: Operational System → Enterprise System → Banking Analysis → Investment Analysis → Government Analysis The technical transfer of a state record does not force the receiving institution to adopt the same value-state determination. Therefore: State Record Transfer ≠ Institutional State Adoption The receiving system may apply its own governance context and criteria. Boundary with Value Recognition Standard VRS establishes whether existing value may be recognized within the defined context. VSS establishes its current governed state. Therefore: Recognition → State but: Recognition ≠ State. A recognition record may serve as an input to state governance without dictating every future state determination. Boundary with Value Change Standard VSS establishes the current value state. VCS governs whether existing value has materially changed and what change occurred. The boundary is: VSS: What is the current governed state? VCS: Has that value materially changed, and what changed? Therefore: State ≠ Change. Boundary with Value Development and Value Degradation VSS may identify that value currently occupies a developed, constrained, degraded, zero, or other defined state where the applicable state taxonomy supports such classifications. It does not govern the mechanism or lifecycle pathway of development or degradation. Those processes belong to their respective downstream governed spaces. Boundary with Value Nullification A ZVA™ determination identifies a governed zero-value state. It does not automatically determine that a formal Value Nullification event or process has occurred. This distinction is essential: Zero-Value State ≠ Nullification Mechanism VSS answers: What is the value state now? Value Nullification governance answers: Through what governed lifecycle condition did value become nullified? Boundary with Value Restoration A ZVA™ may later regain value. VSS may record the resulting new state once legitimately determined. The restoration mechanism itself belongs to Value Restoration Governance. Therefore: Restored State ≠ Restoration Process. Boundary with External Valuation Systems VSS does not determine: market price; fair value; accounting value; tax value; collateral value; insurance value; legal ownership; regulatory classification. Those systems may provide inputs into a Value State Determination where appropriate. VFM® preserves the methodological distinction between: governed value state and: external institutional valuation or classification. Machine-Readable Value State A machine-readable VSS implementation may represent: Value ID → Context ID → Value Object Reference → Recognition Record Reference → State Taxonomy ID → Current State → State Reference Point → State Conditions → State Limitations → State Uncertainty → Transition Readiness → Review Triggers → State Version → Previous State Reference → Current State Record Status This enables AI and digital systems to distinguish between: what value exists and: what state that value currently occupies. Governance Outputs Implementation of VSS may produce: Value State Identification Record Value State Classification Value State Determination Value State Basis Record Value State Condition Record Value State Limitation Record Value State Uncertainty Record Value State Reference Point Value State Transition Readiness Record Value State Review Trigger Value State History ZVA™ State Record Value Asset™ State Record Governed Current Value State Machine-Readable Value State Record These outputs create the baseline required for downstream Value Change Governance. Enterprise Application VSS enables organizations to maintain an explicit map of what state their governed value currently occupies rather than relying only upon static asset lists, accounting classifications, market valuations, or isolated management judgments. The Standard can be applied to: enterprises; banking; investment; public finance; industrial assets; technology portfolios; intellectual property; infrastructure; energy systems; supply chains; digital assets; AI capabilities; organizational capabilities; scientific programs; space missions; resource systems; public-sector assets. This makes it possible to identify value that conventional systems may fail to represent clearly. An organization may discover, for example, that an object still exists on its asset register while occupying a ZVA™ state operationally, or that a capability not recognized as a conventional accounting asset nevertheless constitutes a material Value Asset™ within the organization's operational context. VSS therefore creates a structured bridge between value existence and dynamic value lifecycle governance. Foundational Principles Value is not the same thing as its current state. Value recognition is not value state. Value state is reference-bound and context-bound. Current state is not historical state. Current state is not predicted state. Value State ≠ Value Change. Value State ≠ Value Transition. Transition readiness does not establish that transition occurred. Unknown value state is not zero value. Zero value is not non-existence. Zero value is not automatically extinction. Zero value is not automatically negative value. ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ may remain capable of future restoration. Value Asset™ does not automatically mean accounting, legal, taxable, collateral, or market-recognized asset. The same object may legitimately occupy different value states under different value contexts. A governed value lifecycle requires an explicit current state before material change can be meaningfully determined. Canonical Closing Statement Value State Standard establishes the current-condition governance layer of VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture by providing a structured method for identifying, classifying, determining, recording, reviewing, and representing the current governed state of value. Through explicit separation of value identity, recognition, state, change, transition, nullification, restoration, external valuation, and institutional classification, VSS enables value to remain governable as its condition evolves across time and context. By introducing persistent state representation, contextual and temporal reference points, state conditions, uncertainty, transition readiness, historical traceability, multi-context state governance, machine-readable state records, and canonical concepts including Value Asset™ and ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™, the Standard establishes the baseline from which subsequent changes in value can be detected and governed without confusing the state of value with the mechanisms that produced it. A governed value lifecycle can determine what changed only when it can first determine what state the value was in. Nahlad Value State Standard (VSS) Architecture: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Canonical Definition: Value State Standard governs the identification, classification, determination, transition readiness, and persistent representation of the current governed state of value, establishing an explicit baseline from which subsequent value change can be detected and governed. Governed Space: Value State Governance Flow: Value Context → Value Origin → Value Emergence → Value Recognition → Value State → Value Change Value must have an explicitly governed current state before a subsequent material change in that value can be meaningfully identified and governed. → View Standard About standard Module Architecture → Value State Identification Module (VSIM) → Value State Classification Module (VSCM) → Value State Determination Module (VSDM) → Value State Transition Readiness Module (VSTM) → Value State Record Module (VSRM) Related Documents → About Value State Standard (VSS) → VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture

title: About Value Extinction Standard (VXSS)
text: About Value Extinction Standard (VXSS) About Value Extinction Standard (VXSS) About Value Extinction Standard (VXSS) Architecture: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Parent Standard: Value Extinction Standard (VXSS) Governed Space: Value Extinction Canonical Definition Value Extinction Standard (VXSS) governs the terminal lifecycle condition in which previously existing value ceases to remain recoverable as the same governed value within its defined lifecycle. VXSS establishes one of the most important boundaries in VFM®: Zero Value ≠ Value Extinction. Value may fall to zero, become dormant, inaccessible, obsolete, impaired, economically unattractive, or temporarily impossible to restore while still retaining restoration potential. Value Extinction begins only when the governed basis for recovering that same value has legitimately ended. Why VXSS Matters Organizations frequently treat zero value and permanent value loss as if they were the same condition. They are not. An industrial asset may currently produce no economic value but remain technically recoverable. A dormant dataset may currently provide no usable value but become valuable again when access, technology, or analytical capability changes. Intellectual property may temporarily lose commercial relevance and later regain it. Infrastructure may remain inactive for years and subsequently return to productive use. VXSS prevents these situations from being prematurely classified as terminal. At the same time, organizations also need a legitimate point at which value that can no longer be recovered stops remaining indefinitely inside restoration governance. VXSS establishes that boundary. The Central Distinction VFM® separates: Zero Value from Value Extinction. A ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ represents a governed zero-value condition in which restoration potential may still exist. The value lifecycle may therefore legitimately follow: Positive Value → DeMonet™ → ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ → ReMonet™ → Restored Value Value Extinction represents a fundamentally different condition: the same governed value no longer remains legitimately recoverable within that lifecycle. Once that boundary is legitimately established, the value moves toward Value Finality rather than Value Restoration. Recoverability Is the Boundary VXSS does not ask only: Does this value exist today? It asks: Can the previously existing value still legitimately return as the same governed value? That distinction matters. A value may not be immediately restorable because of: unavailable technology; insufficient capital; missing infrastructure; temporary market conditions; regulatory restrictions; inaccessible information; missing capabilities; operational limitations. None of these conditions automatically proves extinction. Not Currently Restorable ≠ Extinct. The relevant issue is whether meaningful restoration potential remains within the governed lifecycle. Failed Restoration ≠ Value Extinction A failed attempt to recover value does not automatically prove that the value is extinct. The restoration attempt may have failed because of: an unsuitable mechanism; insufficient resources; incomplete intervention; temporary external conditions; incorrect assumptions; missing technology; execution failure. VXSS therefore prevents: Failed ReMonet™ from automatically becoming: Value Extinction. Extinction requires a governed basis for concluding that recoverability itself has ended. Value Object ≠ Value VXSS also separates the existence of an object from the existence of a particular value associated with that object. Object Existence ≠ Value Existence. A machine can physically exist after its productive value has become extinct. A dataset can physically remain stored after its original informational value becomes irrecoverable. A technology can continue functioning after a particular commercial value has disappeared. Conversely, destruction of an object does not necessarily mean that every value associated with it disappears. The object may still generate: scrap value historical value informational value component value or another value relationship. VXSS therefore governs specific value relationships, not simplistic declarations that an entire object either “has value” or “has no value.” Extinction of One Value ≠ Extinction of All Value A single Value Object may support multiple values simultaneously. An industrial machine may lose its original productive manufacturing value while retaining component, recycling, historical, training, or technological value. VXSS may therefore determine that one value has become extinct while other values continue to exist. This protects VFM® from collapsing multiple value relationships into one universal valuation. Value Finality When Value Extinction has been legitimately established, the relevant value reaches the terminal boundary of its governed lifecycle. It should no longer remain classified indefinitely as: degraded value dormant value zero value awaiting restoration or a ReMonet™ candidate. Instead, the lifecycle reaches: Value Finality. But finality does not erase history. The previous emergence, states, changes, development, degradation, nullification, restoration attempts, and extinction of the value remain part of its governed lifecycle record. Value Finality ends the lifecycle. It does not erase the lifecycle. Extinction Does Not Prevent Future Value Value Extinction does not mean that the underlying object can never generate value again. New circumstances may later create: a new use; a new market; a new technology; a new capability; a new context; a new information relationship; a new economic function. But if the original governed value genuinely became extinct, this later value should not automatically be called restoration. It may represent: New Value Emergence. This preserves another critical VFM® boundary: Restoration of Existing Historical Value ≠ Emergence of New Value. Use Case 1 — Industrial Asset at Zero Value A specialized production machine once generated substantial manufacturing value. After technological change and prolonged deterioration, the machine becomes commercially unusable and its productive value reaches zero. The machine is not automatically treated as extinct value. It may initially enter: ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ because restoration potential remains. The organization may investigate repair, modernization, conversion, replacement components, new production methods, or other ReMonet™ pathways. If a viable pathway exists, the productive value may eventually be restored. If, however, the underlying capability necessary to recover that same productive value has been irreversibly lost and the legitimate restoration space has ended, VXSS provides the governance basis for distinguishing: Zero but Recoverable Value from Extinguished Productive Value. The physical machine may still possess scrap, component, historical, or another form of value. Extinction of productive value does not mean extinction of every possible value associated with the machine. Use Case 2 — Historical Data and Future Technology An organization possesses a historical dataset that currently provides no usable economic or analytical value. The dataset becomes dormant and may effectively enter a zero-value condition because existing technology cannot extract useful information from it. VXSS prevents the organization from automatically declaring the informational value extinct merely because current analytical capability cannot recover it. Future AI, reconstruction methods, data integration, or other technologies may restore previously inaccessible informational value. If restoration potential remains, the dataset may remain within the recoverable lifecycle and later enter ReMonet™. However, if the information necessary to reconstruct the original informational relationship has been irreversibly destroyed, the original value may legitimately become extinct. If future AI later discovers an entirely different use for the remaining data, that does not necessarily reverse the extinction. It may represent: New Value Emergence from the same Value Object. This allows VFM® to distinguish between: recovering value that previously existed and creating a new value relationship that did not previously exist. Enterprise Value VXSS gives organizations a governed way to answer a difficult lifecycle question: When should we continue treating lost or zero value as recoverable, and when has that value lifecycle legitimately ended? This distinction can improve asset lifecycle governance, technology portfolios, data governance, capital allocation, restoration decisions, legacy-system management, intellectual-property portfolios, infrastructure planning, and other environments where value can disappear, return, transform, or permanently cease to be recoverable. Declaring extinction too early may destroy legitimate restoration opportunities. Refusing to recognize extinction indefinitely may preserve fictional restoration potential and distort decisions. VXSS governs the boundary between those two errors. Foundational Principle Value reaches extinction not when it merely reaches zero, but when the same governed value can no longer legitimately return within its lifecycle.
