title: Value Extinction Record Module (VXRM)
text: Value Extinction Record Module (VXRM) Value Extinction Record Module (VXRM) Value Extinction Record Module (VXRM) Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture Parent Standard: Value Extinction Standard (VXSS) Module: VXRM — Value Extinction Record Module Operational Layer: Value Extinction Record Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Value Extinction Record Origin ID: VFM-VXSS-VXRM-011.5 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 28 August 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Value Extinction Record Module (VXRM) is the fifth and final Core Module of the Value Extinction Standard (VXSS) within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture. VXRM governs the creation, structuring, preservation, linkage, and lifecycle positioning of the authoritative governance record produced when previously existing value has legitimately reached Value Extinction and, where applicable, Value Finality. Its purpose is to ensure that terminal value outcomes do not disappear into undocumented organizational decisions, accounting actions, asset disposal processes, system changes, or historical ambiguity. VXRM establishes a persistent methodological record of: what governed value became extinct; which Value Object or relationship carried that value; which Value Context applied; which value dimension was affected; what extinction boundary applied; what extinction determination was reached; whether Value Finality was established; what residual values remained; what lifecycle pathways were closed; what lifecycle history preceded extinction; and what distinction must be preserved between the extinguished value and any future new value. The Module therefore ensures: Value Extinction becomes a governed lifecycle fact rather than an undocumented terminal assumption. Architectural Position VXRM is the final Core Module of VXSS and the terminal recording point of the VFM® Value Lifecycle. The VXSS module sequence is: VXCM — Value Extinction Conditions Module → VXTM — Value Extinction Threshold Module → VXDM — Value Extinction Determination Module → VXFM — Value Finality Module → VXRM — Value Extinction Record Module VXFM establishes: Value Finality. VXRM preserves: the governed record of how that terminal lifecycle state was reached and what exactly it means. Therefore: Value Finality ≠ Value Extinction Record. Internal Flow Value Extinction Determination → Value Finality Status where applicable → Governed Value Identification → Extinction Scope Capture → Extinction Basis Capture → Lifecycle History Linkage → Residual Value Separation Capture → Finality Boundary Capture → Terminal Status Capture → Record Integrity Requirements → Value Extinction Record Creation → Record Preservation → Terminal VFM® Lifecycle Record Operational Space VXRM governs the recording space associated with terminal Value Lifecycle outcomes. Its operational space includes: extinction record creation; terminal value identification; lifecycle linkage; Value Context linkage; Value Object linkage; value-dimension identification; extinction-scope recording; extinction-basis recording; threshold-reference recording; extinction-determination recording; finality-status recording; residual-value recording; restoration-pathway closure recording; lifecycle chronology; terminal-state provenance; record status; record correction; record supersession; future Value Emergence separation; cross-system referenceability. Operational Scope VXRM does not determine whether value is extinct. It does not determine whether the extinction threshold was reached. It does not establish Value Finality. It records the governed results produced through the preceding VXSS lifecycle. Therefore: Record Creation ≠ Extinction Determination. Record Creation ≠ Value Finality. VXRM preserves governance outcomes; it does not manufacture them. Value Extinction Record Principle A Value Extinction Record is the structured governance representation of the terminal lifecycle outcome of a defined governed value. The record should make it possible to determine: What value existed? What happened to it? Which lifecycle boundary was crossed? What exactly became extinct? Was extinction partial, dimensional, contextual, or complete within the defined scope? Was Value Finality established? What remained outside the extinction boundary? What lifecycle history supports the terminal status? The record therefore preserves the meaning of extinction beyond the moment when the determination occurred. Extinction Record ≠ Value Object Record VXRM records the extinction of governed value. It does not automatically become the master record of the underlying Value Object. An object may continue to exist after one of its values becomes extinct. Therefore: Value Object Record ≠ Value Extinction Record. The two may be linked, but they remain methodologically distinct. Extinction Record ≠ Deletion Record Value Extinction does not require deletion of the object, data, evidence, or lifecycle history. Likewise, the Value Extinction Record is not a deletion instruction. Therefore: Value Extinction Record ≠ Data Deletion Record. Record retention and data deletion may be governed by separate legal, operational, security, privacy, or information- governance requirements. Record Identity Each governed Value Extinction Record should possess a distinguishable record identity sufficient to prevent confusion between: different Value Objects; different values associated with the same object; different value dimensions; different Value Contexts; different lifecycle instances; repeated extinction assessments; corrected determinations; superseded records; future newly emerged value. Record identity must preserve the distinction between: the object and the value whose lifecycle ended. Governed Value Identification VXRM should identify the value to which the extinction record applies. The identification should be sufficiently precise to distinguish: Extinguished Value A from: Remaining Value B and: Future New Value C. This prevents terminal records from being interpreted as universal statements about all possible value associated with the underlying object. Value Object Linkage Where the extinguished value is associated with a Value Object, the record should maintain a governed reference to that object. However: Object Linkage ≠ Value Identity. The same Value Object may support multiple values and multiple value lifecycles. The extinction of one does not automatically terminate the others. Value Context Capture Because value is contextual, VXRM should preserve the Value Context within which extinction was determined. This may include relevant: operational context; economic context; technological context; temporal context; organizational context; relational context; jurisdictional context; strategic context; where those dimensions materially define the governed value. Therefore: Extinction Without Context May Become Semantically Ambiguous. Value Dimension Capture Where extinction applies only to a particular value dimension, that dimension must remain explicit. Examples may include: productive value; operational value; informational value; strategic value; economic value; functional value; temporal value; relational value. The record must prevent: Dimensional Extinction from being interpreted as: Universal Value Extinction. Extinction Scope Capture VXRM should preserve the exact scope of the extinction determination. The scope may be: total within the governed value lifecycle; partial; dimensional; contextual; relational; temporal; capability-specific. Therefore: Extinction Record Scope must not exceed Extinction Determination Scope. Extinction Basis Capture The record should preserve the governed basis on which extinction was determined. This may include references to: extinction conditions; threshold satisfaction; recoverability findings; restoration limitations; relevant Value States; prior ReMonet™ attempts where applicable; material dependencies; relevant external determinations; final extinction determination. VXRM does not independently validate these inputs. It preserves their relationship to the terminal lifecycle conclusion. Threshold Reference Where an extinction threshold was used, VXRM should preserve sufficient reference to establish: which threshold applied; which governed value it applied to; which context applied; when the threshold was considered satisfied; which determination relied upon it. This creates continuity between: Threshold and Terminal Lifecycle Outcome. Determination Capture The Value Extinction Record should preserve the actual extinction determination. The record should distinguish among outcomes such as: extinction not established; extinction indeterminate; partial extinction; dimensional extinction; contextual extinction; Value Extinction established. Only a legitimately established terminal outcome should be represented as final extinction. Finality Status Capture Where VXFM has established Value Finality, VXRM should preserve that status separately from the extinction determination. This maintains the distinction: Value Extinct from: Value Final. The record should therefore be capable of representing an extinction determination before finality where the architecture requires an intermediate governance state. Finality Boundary Capture Where Value Finality applies, VXRM should preserve its exact boundary. This may include: value identity; lifecycle identity; value dimension; Value Context; affected relationship; effective point; excluded residual values; same-value restoration closure. This ensures that Finality remains bounded rather than becoming an uncontrolled universal conclusion. Residual Value Record VXRM must preserve material residual value where it exists. For example: Productive Value → Extinct and Final may coexist with: Material Value → Active Historical Value → Active Informational Value → Active The terminal record should therefore distinguish: what ended from: what remained. Residual Value ≠ Exception to Extinction The presence of another surviving value does not invalidate extinction of the governed value. A machine may permanently lose its original production value while retaining scrap value. Therefore: Residual Value ≠ Persistence of the Extinguished Value. Lifecycle History Linkage VXRM should maintain sufficient linkage to the preceding VFM® lifecycle so that terminal status is not isolated from its methodological history. The lifecycle may include: Value Context → Value Origin → Value Emergence → Value Recognition → Value State → Value Change → Value Development / Value Degradation → Value Nullification where applicable → ZVA™ where applicable → Value Restoration where applicable → Value Extinction → Value Finality → Value Extinction Record Not every lifecycle must pass through every optional branch. The record should preserve the actual governed pathway. Lifecycle Record ≠ Lifecycle Reconstruction VXRM should not invent missing historical states merely to produce a complete-looking record. Where lifecycle information is unavailable, the record should preserve that limitation. Therefore: Unknown Lifecycle History ≠ Assumed Lifecycle History. Chronology Integrity VXRM should preserve the temporal ordering of relevant lifecycle events. Important distinctions may include: degradation date; zero-value date; restoration attempt date; extinction-threshold date; extinction-determination date; finality effective date; record creation date; correction date. These dates must not be collapsed into a single terminal timestamp where doing so would distort lifecycle reality. Record Creation Time ≠ Extinction Time The record may be created after the value actually became extinct. Therefore: Record Creation Date ≠ Value Extinction Effective Date by Default. Both should remain separately identifiable where known. Terminal Status VXRM should establish a record status indicating the governance position of the terminal record. Possible statuses may include: 1. Draft Extinction Record Terminal information is being assembled. 2. Pending Extinction Record Required terminal governance inputs remain incomplete. 3. Active Extinction Record A governed extinction determination has been recorded. 4. Final Extinction Record Value Finality has been established and terminal lifecycle recording is complete. 5. Record Under Review Material information challenges the existing record. 6. Corrected Extinction Record The record has been formally corrected while preserving prior history. 7. Superseded Extinction Record A later governed record replaces the current authoritative representation without erasing the earlier record. These are VFM® governance statuses rather than accounting, legal, archival, or regulatory classifications. Record Finality ≠ Immutability A final record should be stable. However, stability does not mean that factual or governance errors must remain permanently uncorrectable. Therefore: Record Finality ≠ Absolute Immutability. A governed correction pathway should remain available where legitimate evidence demonstrates that the record is inaccurate. Correction Principle Where a Value Extinction Record is incorrect, VXRM should permit controlled correction. A correction should preserve: the original record; the corrected information; the reason for correction; the relationship between versions; the effective status of the correction. The architecture should avoid silent replacement of terminal lifecycle history. Therefore: Correction ≠ Historical Erasure. Supersession Principle Where a new authoritative record supersedes an earlier record, the relationship should remain visible. The earlier record should not silently disappear. This enables reconstruction of: what was previously believed versus: what is currently governed as authoritative. New Evidence After Finality New evidence may emerge after a terminal record has been created. VXRM should distinguish two fundamentally different situations: Situation A — Prior Determination Was Wrong Evidence demonstrates that the value was not legitimately extinct. The appropriate pathway is: Review → Correction → Lifecycle Repositioning Situation B — Genuine New Value Appears The original value was legitimately extinct, but new circumstances create a different value. The appropriate pathway is: New Value Emergence → New Value Lifecycle Therefore: New Evidence ≠ Automatic Restoration. Future Value Separation The extinction record should provide sufficient semantic separation to prevent future new value from being confused with the extinguished value. This is particularly important where the same Value Object later acquires: new technological use; new economic relevance; new cultural significance; new strategic importance; new informational value; new relational value. The future value may share the same object. It does not necessarily share the same Value Lifecycle. Record Continuity VXRM should preserve continuity between the terminal record and the lifecycle that produced it. Continuity may include references to: value identity; Value Object; Value Context; prior Value States; relevant Value Changes; DeMonet™ where applicable; ZVA™ where applicable; ReMonet™ where applicable; extinction conditions; extinction threshold; extinction determination; finality status. The purpose is not to duplicate every prior record. The purpose is to make the terminal outcome traceable to its governed lifecycle. Record Integrity VXRM requires that the Value Extinction Record remain sufficiently reliable for its governance purpose. This includes preservation of: completeness appropriate to scope; internal consistency; lifecycle linkage; version relationships; correction history; finality status; record identity. However, broader integrity governance belongs to INTEGROS®. Therefore: VXRM defines what the Value Extinction Record must represent. INTEGROS® may govern the integrity of that representation. Auditability Boundary VXRM establishes the terminal value record. It does not replace independent auditability or evidence governance. Where auditability is required: ADIT® may govern the evidence and audit trail supporting the record. Therefore: Value Extinction Record ≠ Independent Audit Evidence. Validation Boundary VXRM may reference validated inputs. It does not independently validate the truth of every external claim used in the extinction process. Where formal validation is required: VALIDOS® governs the validation process. Therefore: Recorded Claim ≠ Validated Claim by Default. Identity Boundary VXRM may link the terminal record to a Value Object. The authoritative identity, provenance, ownership, or origin of that object may be governed through OBIDENITY®. Therefore: Value Extinction Record ≠ Object Identity Governance. Record Retention Boundary VXRM establishes the methodological requirement to preserve terminal lifecycle meaning. It does not prescribe universal legal retention periods. Retention duration may depend on: law; regulation; contractual obligations; industry requirements; organizational policy; evidence requirements; operational needs. Therefore: Methodological Preservation Requirement ≠ Universal Retention Period. Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum VXRM implementation should establish: 1. Record Identity Assign a distinguishable identity to the Value Extinction Record. 2. Governed Value Identification Identify the specific value whose lifecycle reached extinction. 3. Value Object Linkage Link the record to the relevant Value Object or relationship where applicable. 4. Value Context Capture Preserve the context within which extinction was determined. 5. Extinction Scope Record whether extinction is total, partial, dimensional, contextual, temporal, or otherwise bounded. 6. Extinction Basis Reference the governed basis supporting the extinction determination. 7. Extinction Determination Capture the authoritative determination produced by VXDM. 8. Finality Status Capture the Value Finality status produced by VXFM where applicable. 9. Residual Value Separation Record material values remaining outside the extinction boundary. 10. Lifecycle Linkage Maintain traceability to relevant preceding VFM® lifecycle stages. 11. Chronology Preserve material lifecycle and terminal timestamps separately. 12. Record Status Assign the appropriate terminal record status. 13. Correction Governance Provide a controlled pathway for review, correction, and supersession. 14. Future Value Separation Prevent future new Value Emergence from being misrepresented as restoration of legitimately extinguished value. 15. Preservation Maintain the terminal record for the period and governance purpose required by applicable systems. Governance Outputs VXRM may produce: Value Extinction Record Terminal Value Identification Record Value Extinction Scope Record Value Extinction Basis Record Extinction Threshold Reference Value Extinction Determination Record Value Finality Status Record Value Finality Boundary Record Residual Value Record Restoration Pathway Closure Reference Value Lifecycle History Reference Terminal Lifecycle Chronology Value Extinction Effective Point Record Status Record Review Notice Value Extinction Record Correction Supersession Record Future Value Separation Reference Terminal VFM® Lifecycle Record Enterprise Application VXRM provides organizations with a structured terminal record for values that have legitimately completed the VFM® lifecycle. This is particularly useful where organizations manage: industrial assets; infrastructure; technology portfolios; legacy systems; digital assets; data; intellectual property; product portfolios; research programs; organizational capabilities; strategic resources; long-lived operational assets. Without a governed terminal record, organizations may lose the distinction between: value that is currently zero and value that has actually become extinct. They may also lose the distinction between: an extinguished value and new value that later emerges from the same object. VXRM preserves these distinctions across time. Use Case 1 — Industrial Asset Extinction Record A production machine has permanently lost its original specialized productive value. The preceding VXSS modules establish: Extinction Conditions Satisfied → Extinction Threshold Reached → Productive Value Extinct → Productive Value Final However, the physical machine remains. It retains: Material Value and potentially: Historical Value. VXRM creates a terminal record specifying: Governed Value: Original Specialized Productive Value Extinction Scope: Productive Value Dimension Finality: Established ReMonet™ Pathway: Closed for Original Productive Value Residual Value: Material Value retained Object Status: Object continues to exist Years later, the machine becomes historically significant. That new historical value can enter a new or continuing applicable Value Lifecycle without rewriting the extinction record of the original productive value. Use Case 2 — Extinction Record for Irrecoverable Digital Information An organization possesses fragments of a legacy dataset. The original contextual structure required to interpret the information has been irreversibly lost. Following governed assessment: Original Informational Value → Extinct and: Original Informational Value → Final. VXRM records: Value Object: Surviving Data Fragments Governed Value: Original Contextual Informational Value Extinction Scope: Original Informational Relationship Extinction Basis: Irrecoverable loss of required contextual structure Finality: Established Residual Value: Raw data fragments remain Lifecycle Status: Closed for Original Informational Value Several years later, a new analytical technology discovers a different use for the fragments. The original extinction record remains valid. The newly created analytical usefulness is governed as: New Value Emergence rather than: restoration of the original extinguished informational value. Foundational Principles Value Extinction Record ≠ Value Extinction Determination. Value Extinction Record ≠ Value Finality. Value Extinction Record ≠ Value Object Record. Value Extinction Record ≠ Data Deletion Record. Value Extinction Record ≠ Independent Audit Evidence. Recorded Claim ≠ Validated Claim by Default. Record Creation Date ≠ Extinction Effective Date by Default. Record Scope Must Not Exceed Extinction Scope. Dimensional Extinction Must Remain Dimensionally Recorded. Contextual Extinction Must Remain Contextually Recorded. Residual Value ≠ Persistence of the Extinguished Value. Lifecycle Closure ≠ Lifecycle Erasure. Unknown Lifecycle History ≠ Assumed Lifecycle History. Record Finality ≠ Absolute Immutability. Correction ≠ Historical Erasure. Supersession ≠ Silent Replacement. Future New Value ≠ Restoration of Extinguished Value by Default. The same Value Object may support a new Value Lifecycle after another value associated with it has legitimately ended. A terminal value record must preserve what ended without falsely declaring that everything associated with the object ended. Canonical Closing Statement Value Extinction Record Module establishes the terminal recording layer of the Value Extinction Standard by preserving the governed identity, context, scope, basis, determination, finality, chronology, residual value, and lifecycle history of value that has legitimately reached extinction. VXRM ensures that terminal value outcomes remain distinguishable from object destruction, accounting write-offs, data deletion, temporary zero value, dormancy, failed restoration, and future new Value Emergence. Through explicit record identity, lifecycle linkage, bounded extinction scope, residual-value separation, correction governance, supersession continuity, and terminal-state preservation, the Module converts Value Extinction from a transient organizational conclusion into a persistent and interpretable governance record. The VFM® Value Lifecycle therefore ends not by erasing value history, but by preserving exactly what value existed, how its governed lifecycle ended, what remained, and where any future value must begin anew. Governed Links → Value Extinction Standard (VXSS) → VFM® Architecture Map → Previous: Value Finality Module (VXFM)

title: Value Extinction Threshold Module (VXTM)
text: Value Extinction Threshold Module (VXTM) Value Extinction Threshold Module (VXTM) Value Extinction Threshold Module (VXTM) Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture Parent Standard: Value Extinction Standard (VXSS) Module: VXTM — Value Extinction Threshold Module Operational Layer: Value Extinction Threshold Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Value Extinction Threshold Origin ID: VFM-VXSS-VXTM-011.2 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 28 August 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Value Extinction Threshold Module (VXTM) is the second Core Module of the Value Extinction Standard (VXSS) within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture. VXTM governs the definition, application, testing, and documentation of the threshold separating value that remains legitimately recoverable from value whose recoverability has become sufficiently exhausted, unavailable, or terminated to justify formal Value Extinction determination. The Module receives qualified extinction conditions from VXCM — Value Extinction Conditions Module and evaluates whether those conditions collectively reach the governed boundary beyond which restoration of the same relevant value can no longer be treated as a legitimate continuation pathway within the defined value lifecycle. Its operational purpose is: to establish whether the governed boundary between recoverable value loss and potential terminal non- recoverability has been reached before any formal Value Extinction determination is made. Architectural Position VXTM occupies the critical boundary between: Extinction Conditions and Extinction Determination. Its architectural position is: VXCM — Value Extinction Conditions Module → VXTM — Value Extinction Threshold Module → VXDM — Value Extinction Determination Module VXCM establishes which conditions are materially relevant. VXTM establishes whether those conditions reach the required terminal boundary. VXDM subsequently determines whether the relevant value is legitimately extinct. Therefore: Condition ≠ Threshold. Threshold ≠ Determination. Internal Flow Governed Extinction Conditions → Relevant Value Boundary Confirmation → Recoverability Criteria Definition → Restoration Boundary Definition → Threshold Criteria Definition → Threshold Evidence Association → Alternative Recovery Pathway Test → Residual Recoverability Test → Threshold Satisfaction Assessment → Threshold Status → Governed Extinction Threshold Result → VXDM — Value Extinction Determination Module Operational Space VXTM governs the space between: material conditions threatening recoverability and formal determination that the relevant value has become extinct. Its operational space includes: recoverability criteria; restoration boundaries; extinction-threshold criteria; threshold evidence; threshold dependencies; threshold satisfaction; residual recoverability; alternative recovery pathways; partial threshold satisfaction; dimensional thresholds; contextual thresholds; temporal thresholds; compound thresholds; uncertainty; threshold reassessment; threshold status. VXTM does not itself declare Value Extinction. It establishes whether the required boundary for such a determination has been reached. The Extinction Threshold The Value Extinction Threshold is the governed boundary separating: value that remains recoverable within its defined lifecycle from value for which legitimate recoverability has been sufficiently exhausted to permit formal extinction determination. The threshold must be connected to: the specific governed value; the relevant Value Object; the relevant value dimension; the relevant Value Context; the defined lifecycle; the restoration boundary; the available recovery pathways; the applicable recoverability criteria. An extinction threshold cannot be meaningfully governed in abstraction from the value to which it applies. Threshold ≠ Zero The extinction threshold is not automatically reached when value reaches zero. A value may enter: ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ while retaining significant restoration potential. Therefore: Zero Value ≠ Extinction Threshold. The zero-value condition describes the present Value State. The extinction threshold addresses whether the pathway for recovery of that same value has reached its terminal boundary. Threshold ≠ Nullification DeMonet™ may move positive value into a zero-value condition. That transition does not establish that the value is unrecoverable. The architecture therefore preserves: Positive Value → DeMonet™ → ZVA™ → Recoverability Remains → ReMonet™ remains possible and separately: ZVA™ → Extinction Conditions → Extinction Threshold Reached → Extinction Determination Therefore: Value Nullification ≠ Value Extinction Threshold. Recoverability Criteria Before an extinction threshold can be applied, the meaning of recoverability must be sufficiently defined. Recoverability criteria may include, where relevant: technical recoverability; functional recoverability; informational recoverability; operational recoverability; relational recoverability; contextual recoverability; temporal recoverability; legal or rights-dependent recoverability; economic recoverability; structural recoverability. Not every criterion must apply to every value. The applicable criteria must derive from the nature of the governed value and its defined restoration boundary. Recoverability Is Value-Specific A Value Object may contain multiple forms or dimensions of value. The extinction threshold must therefore apply to the relevant value rather than automatically to the entire object. For example, a production machine may permanently lose: productive value while retaining: material value component value historical value or informational value. Therefore: Threshold Reached for One Value Dimension ≠ Threshold Reached for Every Value Dimension. Restoration Boundary VXTM requires a defined restoration boundary. The restoration boundary identifies the legitimate space within which recovery of the same value may still be treated as Value Restoration rather than creation of a different value. This distinction is essential. Without it, almost any future value associated with an object could incorrectly be interpreted as restoration of the original value. The restoration boundary may include: identity of the prior value; value dimension; value relationship; relevant context; functional continuity; temporal continuity; permissible transformation; restoration mechanism; required dependencies; acceptable discontinuities. Same Value Test VXTM must distinguish recovery of the same relevant value from creation of another value. For example: A destroyed industrial machine is replaced by a new machine. Production capability returns. But the new machine's productive value may represent: New Value Emergence rather than: restoration of the extinguished productive value of the original machine. Therefore: Replacement Value ≠ Restored Value. The extinction threshold concerns recoverability of: the same governed value not whether some substitute value can eventually perform a similar function. Alternative Recovery Pathway Test Before the extinction threshold is treated as satisfied, materially credible alternative restoration pathways should be considered. Potential pathways may include: repair; reconstruction; remanufacturing; technological conversion; data recovery; reconstruction from secondary sources; reactivation; rights recovery; contextual transfer; dependency replacement; controlled substitution where continuity of the same value remains legitimate. The existence of one failed pathway does not establish threshold satisfaction. Failed Recovery Pathway ≠ Exhausted Recoverability. Residual Recoverability Recoverability does not need to be complete to remain material. A value may retain: partial recoverability; conditional recoverability; dimensional recoverability; contextual recoverability; delayed recoverability; uncertain but credible recoverability. Where such recoverability remains legitimately material: the extinction threshold may not yet be satisfied. Restoration Potential ≠ Restoration Certainty A value does not need to be easily recoverable to remain below the extinction threshold. The architecture distinguishes: Restoration Potential from Restoration Certainty. A difficult, expensive, technically complex, or uncertain restoration pathway may still represent legitimate recoverability. Therefore: Low Probability of Restoration ≠ Automatic Extinction Threshold. Economic Threshold Principle Current restoration cost may exceed current economic value. That fact may influence organizational decisions. But it does not universally establish Value Extinction. For example: Restoration Cost > Current Economic Return may justify: Do Not Restore without establishing: Cannot Be Restored as the Same Value. Therefore: Economic Non-Viability ≠ Universal Non-Recoverability. Where economic recoverability is itself the governed value dimension, however, economic criteria may legitimately form part of the extinction threshold. Technical Possibility ≠ Unlimited Recoverability The opposite error must also be avoided. The mere theoretical possibility that some future technology might recover value does not require VFM® to preserve the lifecycle indefinitely. VXTM operates within a governed restoration boundary. Recoverability should therefore be evaluated against: established capabilities; reasonably identifiable pathways; materially credible dependencies; applicable governance criteria; known constraints; defined lifecycle assumptions. Therefore: Theoretical Future Possibility ≠ Established Restoration Pathway. Threshold Criteria A Value Extinction Threshold may require one or more criteria to be satisfied. Examples may include: essential value basis irreversibly lost; required value relationship permanently terminated; critical information irrecoverably unavailable; required capability no longer reconstructable; all legitimate restoration pathways exhausted; necessary dependencies permanently unavailable; restoration would create fundamentally new value rather than recover the prior value; contextual conditions permanently eliminate the relevant value relationship; temporal boundary permanently passed; required continuity irreversibly broken. The applicable threshold must remain specific to the governed value. Single-Criterion Threshold Certain value relationships may depend upon one indispensable condition. If that condition is irreversibly lost, a single criterion may be sufficient to satisfy the extinction threshold. For example: A unique cryptographic key may be indispensable to a particular access value. If the key is irretrievably lost and no legitimate recovery or reconstruction pathway exists, the loss of that single dependency may be sufficient to reach the threshold for that specific access value. Compound Threshold Many extinction cases require multiple criteria. A Compound Extinction Threshold exists where several conditions collectively establish terminal non-recoverability. For example: Critical Component Loss Source Documentation Loss Control-System Incompatibility No Reconstruction Capability No Alternative Restoration Pathway may collectively satisfy the threshold even where no single condition would independently be terminal. Necessary and Sufficient Criteria VXTM may distinguish: Necessary Criteria from Sufficient Criteria. A necessary criterion must be present before the threshold can be reached. A sufficient criterion, where legitimately defined, may independently establish threshold satisfaction. Compound thresholds may require: Criterion A + Criterion B + Criterion C before terminal-boundary satisfaction occurs. This structure prevents arbitrary threshold interpretation. Threshold Materiality Threshold criteria must be materially connected to recoverability. A condition should not contribute to threshold satisfaction merely because it is negative, inconvenient, costly, or undesirable. The relevant question remains: Does this criterion materially affect whether the same governed value can legitimately be recovered? Threshold Satisfaction States VXTM may recognize: 1. Threshold Not Reached Material recoverability remains. 2. Threshold Approaching Extinction conditions are materially reducing recoverability, but the terminal boundary has not been reached. 3. Threshold Conditionally Reached The threshold is satisfied only under defined contextual, temporal, or dependency conditions. 4. Threshold Partially Reached The threshold is satisfied for one value dimension or portion of the governed value but not others. 5. Threshold Reached Applicable extinction-threshold criteria have been satisfied sufficiently to permit formal Value Extinction determination. 6. Threshold Indeterminate Available information is insufficient to establish whether the threshold has been reached. These states preserve uncertainty and prevent binary conclusions where evidence does not support them. Threshold Reached ≠ Value Extinct This is the central governance boundary of VXTM. Reaching the threshold means: the case is eligible for formal Value Extinction determination. It does not mean: Value Extinction has already been formally determined. Therefore: Threshold Reached ≠ Extinction Determined. The formal determination belongs to: VXDM — Value Extinction Determination Module. Partial Threshold Satisfaction A Value Object may cross the extinction threshold for only part of its value. For example: An industrial system may permanently lose its original production capability while retaining valuable materials and technical documentation. VXTM may therefore establish: Productive Value → Threshold Reached while: Material Value → Threshold Not Reached and: Informational Value → Recoverability Retained. Contextual Threshold The threshold may be reached within one context without being reached universally. A technology may become permanently unusable under one regulatory, technical, or operational environment while remaining usable elsewhere. Therefore: Contextual Threshold Reached ≠ Universal Value Extinction. The context must remain explicit. Temporal Threshold Certain value depends upon a time-bound opportunity. Where the relevant temporal boundary passes irreversibly, the associated value may become unrecoverable. However, VXTM must distinguish: loss of a specific historical opportunity from loss of every future value associated with the underlying object. The expired opportunity may cross its extinction threshold while other value persists. Threshold Uncertainty Where material uncertainty remains concerning: alternative restoration pathways; condition reversibility; missing evidence; technological recoverability; dependency reconstruction; continuity of the same value; VXTM should preserve that uncertainty. A threshold should not be declared reached merely because recovery has not yet been demonstrated. Absence of Demonstrated Recovery ≠ Demonstration of Non-Recoverability. Threshold Reassessment Material new information may justify reassessment before formal extinction determination. Examples include: discovery of backup data; identification of an alternative repair pathway; recovery of missing documentation; discovery of a previously unknown dependency; new evidence that a condition is reversible; discovery that the relevant value dimension was incorrectly defined. VXTM therefore permits threshold reassessment while the lifecycle remains open. Boundary with VXCM VXCM asks: What conditions materially threaten recoverability? VXTM asks: Have those conditions reached the governed terminal boundary? Therefore: Extinction Conditions ≠ Extinction Threshold. Boundary with VRSS VRSS governs the pathway through which previously existing value may be restored. VXTM governs whether legitimate restoration potential has become sufficiently exhausted to permit extinction determination. The architecture therefore creates a decisive branch: Recoverability Retained → VRSS — Value Restoration Standard Recoverability Terminally Exhausted → VXSS — Value Extinction Pathway Boundary with VNS VNS governs the transition to zero value. VXTM governs whether recoverability of that zero value has reached its terminal boundary. Therefore: ZVA™ may remain below the extinction threshold. Boundary with VXDM VXTM determines threshold status. VXDM determines extinction status. Therefore: Threshold Assessment ≠ Extinction Determination. Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum VXTM implementation should establish: 1. Governed Value Boundary Confirm the exact value, dimension, context, and lifecycle under assessment. 2. Extinction Condition Input Receive qualified Extinction Conditions from VXCM. 3. Recoverability Criteria Define what constitutes legitimate recovery of the same value. 4. Restoration Boundary Define the boundary separating restoration from replacement, substitution, or New Value Emergence. 5. Threshold Criteria Define necessary, sufficient, compound, contextual, dimensional, or temporal threshold criteria. 6. Alternative Pathway Test Assess materially credible restoration pathways. 7. Residual Recoverability Test Determine whether partial, conditional, contextual, or other material recoverability remains. 8. Threshold Satisfaction Assessment Evaluate the governed conditions against the applicable threshold. 9. Threshold Status Assign the appropriate threshold state. 10. Determination Transfer Transfer the governed threshold result to VXDM for formal Value Extinction determination. Governance Outputs VXTM may produce: Value Recoverability Criteria Record Value Restoration Boundary Value Extinction Threshold Definition Threshold Criteria Record Alternative Recovery Pathway Assessment Residual Recoverability Assessment Compound Threshold Assessment Dimensional Threshold Record Contextual Threshold Record Temporal Threshold Record Threshold Uncertainty Record Threshold Satisfaction Assessment Value Extinction Threshold Status Governed Extinction Threshold Result Enterprise Application VXTM provides organizations with a governed boundary for deciding when impaired, dormant, inaccessible, zero-value, or failed-restoration assets should move from recovery governance into formal extinction consideration. This is especially relevant to: industrial asset portfolios; legacy infrastructure; distressed investments; intellectual property portfolios; abandoned technologies; obsolete platforms; digital assets; historical data; discontinued products; stranded assets; long-term research programs; organizational capabilities. Without such a threshold, organizations may make two opposite errors: Premature Extinction — abandoning recoverable value. or Artificial Recoverability — indefinitely treating terminally lost value as recoverable. VXTM creates the governance boundary between those two states. Use Case 1 — Specialized Industrial Asset A specialized industrial machine has reached ZVA™ after severe degradation. The manufacturer no longer exists, essential components are unavailable, original control software has been lost, and two restoration attempts have failed. VXCM has already established material Extinction Conditions. VXTM now tests: ZVA™ → Recoverability Criteria → Restoration Boundary → Component Reconstruction Possibility → Software Reconstruction Possibility → Alternative Modernization Pathway → Residual Productive Value Recoverability → Threshold Assessment If a legitimate modernization pathway can restore the same productive value relationship, the threshold remains unreached. If every legitimate pathway has been exhausted and any replacement would constitute New Value rather than restoration of the machine's prior productive value: Productive Value Extinction Threshold → Reached The machine may still retain material or historical value. Use Case 2 — Irretrievably Lost Digital Access Value A digital asset depends upon a unique cryptographic credential. The credential has been permanently lost. No backup exists. No recovery key exists. No reconstruction pathway exists. The underlying system remains operational, but the specific access relationship represented by the credential cannot be recreated as the same governed access value. VXTM evaluates: Credential Loss → Recoverability Criteria → Alternative Recovery Pathways → Dependency Reconstruction Test → Same Value Test → Residual Recoverability Test → Threshold Satisfaction If a replacement credential would establish a fundamentally new access relationship rather than restore the prior one: Original Access Value Extinction Threshold → Reached This permits the case to proceed to formal extinction determination without incorrectly declaring every other value associated with the digital asset extinct. Foundational Principles Zero Value ≠ Value Extinction Threshold. Value Nullification ≠ Value Extinction Threshold. Extinction Condition ≠ Extinction Threshold. Extinction Threshold ≠ Extinction Determination. Threshold Reached ≠ Value Extinct. Failed ReMonet™ ≠ Extinction Threshold Reached. Failed Recovery Pathway ≠ Exhausted Recoverability. Low Restoration Probability ≠ Automatic Extinction. Economic Non-Viability ≠ Universal Non-Recoverability. Theoretical Future Possibility ≠ Established Restoration Pathway. Replacement Value ≠ Restored Value. Residual Recoverability must be tested before terminal threshold satisfaction. Thresholds apply to specific value dimensions, contexts, relationships, and lifecycles. A threshold may be reached for one value dimension while other value persists. Absence of demonstrated recovery is not proof of non-recoverability. The extinction threshold exists to determine when formal extinction determination becomes legitimate—not to make that determination itself. Canonical Closing Statement Value Extinction Threshold Module establishes the governed boundary between recoverable value loss and potential terminal non-recoverability within VFM®. Through explicit recoverability criteria, restoration boundaries, threshold criteria, alternative recovery pathway testing, residual recoverability assessment, dimensional and contextual boundaries, uncertainty preservation, and formal threshold status, VXTM prevents zero value, failed restoration, obsolescence, economic non-viability, or severe impairment from being automatically interpreted as Value Extinction. The Module determines when the governed basis for formal extinction determination has been reached while preserving the architectural distinction between Value Nullification, Value Restoration, and Value Extinction. Value crosses the extinction threshold not merely because recovery is difficult or absent today, but because the legitimate pathway for recovery of that same governed value has reached its defined terminal boundary. title: Value Extinction Standard (VXSS)
text: Value Extinction Standard (VXSS) Value Extinction Standard (VXSS) Value Extinction Standard (VXSS) Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture Parent Standard: Value Extinction Standard (VXSS) Operational Layer: Value Extinction Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Type: Parent Standard Governed Space: Value Extinction Origin ID: VFM-VXSS-011 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 28 August 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Value Extinction Standard (VXSS) is the Parent Standard within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture that governs the terminal lifecycle condition in which previously existing value ceases to exist as recoverable value within the governed lifecycle. VXSS establishes the methodological boundary between zero value and extinguished value by determining when a value condition has moved beyond degradation, dormancy, impairment, loss, nullification, or recoverable zero value into a state in which restoration of the relevant value is no longer legitimately available within the same governed lifecycle. The Standard does not define every physical, economic, technological, legal, organizational, market, environmental, or operational event capable of causing extinction. Its task is narrower: to determine when the value consequence of those events has crossed the governed boundary from recoverable value into terminal value finality. Core Question When does value cease to exist as recoverable value within the governed lifecycle? Architectural Position VXSS occupies the eleventh and final governed space of the VFM® value lifecycle. It follows: Value Restoration Standard (VRSS). The preceding standards govern value as it: emerges → is identified → is attributed → enters a governed state → changes → develops → degrades → reaches zero where applicable → may be restored where recoverability remains. VXSS governs the final question: When is restoration no longer a legitimate continuation of the same value lifecycle? This makes Value Extinction the terminal lifecycle boundary of VFM®. Governance Flow Position Existing Value → Value Development / Value Change → Value Degradation → Value Nullification where applicable → ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ where applicable → Restoration Potential Assessment → Value Extinction Conditions → Value Extinction Threshold → Value Extinction Determination → Value Finality → Value Extinction Record The critical architectural boundary is: Zero Value ≠ Value Extinction. Operational Space VXSS governs the space between: value that remains recoverable and value that has ceased to exist as recoverable value within the governed lifecycle. Its operational space includes: extinction-condition identification; recoverability assessment; restoration-potential exhaustion; extinction-threshold definition; threshold satisfaction; irreversible value loss; lifecycle termination; value identity discontinuity; terminal impairment; terminal obsolescence; terminal loss of utility; terminal loss of capability; terminal loss of relevance; terminal loss of rights where value-dependent; terminal loss of recoverable economic function; extinction determination; value finality; terminal-state recording; distinction between extinction and temporary zero value; distinction between extinction and dormancy; distinction between extinction and degradation; distinction between extinction and new Value Emergence. Operational Scope VXSS may apply to value associated with: physical assets; industrial assets; infrastructure; digital assets; data; intellectual property; technologies; products; services; productive capabilities; operational capabilities; contractual or economic rights; organizational capabilities; financial or economic assets; information; knowledge structures; platforms; systems; market relationships; other governable Value Objects. Value Extinction does not require destruction of the underlying object. An object may continue to exist while a particular value associated with it becomes extinct. Value Object ≠ Value VXSS preserves a fundamental distinction: Object Existence ≠ Value Existence. A machine may physically remain after its productive value becomes extinct. A dataset may remain stored after its relevant informational value becomes extinct. A technology may remain technically functional after its commercial value becomes extinct. An intellectual property right may remain legally registered after a particular economic value becomes extinct. The continued existence of the object therefore does not prove continued recoverability of the governed value. Zero Value ≠ Value Extinction This is the foundational distinction of VXSS. A value may reach: zero without becoming extinct. A ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ may retain: restoration potential; dormant utility; technological recoverability; economic recoverability; informational recoverability; functional recoverability; strategic recoverability; rights-based recoverability; future relevance. Therefore: Zero Value may be a state. Value Extinction is a terminal lifecycle determination. ZVA™ and Extinction A ZVA™ may remain within the active governed lifecycle because ReMonet™ may still restore previously existing value. The lifecycle may therefore legitimately contain: Positive Value → DeMonet™ → ZVA™ → ReMonet™ → Restored Value. VXSS applies when that restoration pathway is no longer legitimately available for the relevant value within the same governed lifecycle. Therefore: ZVA™ ≠ Extinguished Value. Value Extinction Principle Value Extinction occurs only when sufficient governed conditions establish that the relevant previously existing value no longer remains recoverable within the governed lifecycle. The determination must relate to a defined value. It must not be inferred merely because: current value is zero; an asset is unused; an asset is obsolete; a market temporarily disappeared; restoration is expensive; restoration has not yet been attempted; one restoration attempt failed; current technology cannot restore the value; an organization no longer wants the asset; a business model has temporarily failed. Extinction requires a stronger governed basis. Recoverability Principle Recoverability is the central boundary variable of VXSS. The relevant question is not merely: Does the value exist now? It is: Does the previously existing value remain legitimately recoverable within the governed lifecycle? Recoverability may depend upon: physical possibility; technical possibility; informational continuity; legal continuity; identity continuity; economic viability where materially relevant; functional continuity; restoration mechanism availability; remaining asset capability; preservation of the underlying value basis; temporal conditions; contextual conditions. Recoverability ≠ Immediate Restorability A value does not need to be immediately restorable in order to remain recoverable. Restoration may require: new technology; capital; time; infrastructure; regulatory change; reconstruction; market recovery; technical intervention; data reconstruction; new operational capability. Therefore: Not Currently Restorable ≠ Extinct. VXSS must avoid premature extinction determinations based solely on current limitations. Restoration Cost ≠ Extinction A value may be economically irrational to restore while still technically recoverable. Conversely, unlimited expenditure does not guarantee that extinct value can be restored. VXSS therefore separates: Restoration Economics from Value Existence. High restoration cost may influence organizational decisions. It does not automatically establish Value Extinction. Failed Restoration ≠ Extinction A failed ReMonet™ process does not automatically prove extinction. Failure may result from: incorrect restoration method; insufficient resources; incomplete intervention; technical execution failure; incorrect assumptions; missing capabilities; premature intervention; temporary external conditions. VXSS requires the failure of a particular restoration attempt to remain distinct from the broader determination that the relevant value itself is no longer recoverable. Therefore: Failed ReMonet™ ≠ Value Extinction. Extinction Conditions VXSS requires explicit conditions capable of supporting an extinction determination. Depending upon the governed value, conditions may include: destruction of the underlying value basis; irreversible loss of required information; irreversible loss of identity continuity; permanent loss of necessary rights; irreversible functional destruction; permanent technological incompatibility; irreversible disappearance of the relevant utility; loss of the conditions necessary for restoration; permanent elimination of the relevant economic relationship; irreversible environmental change; terminal structural deterioration; exhaustion of all legitimate restoration pathways; another defined terminal condition. No single universal condition applies to every value class. Extinction Threshold Value Extinction requires a threshold separating: recoverable impairment from terminal value loss. The threshold may be: physical; functional; informational; technological; legal; economic; operational; temporal; contextual; composite. The threshold must correspond to the governed value relationship. VXSS does not require one universal numerical extinction threshold. Threshold Crossing ≠ Automatic Determination Even where an extinction threshold appears to have been crossed, the lifecycle should not automatically terminate without a governed determination. The threshold provides the basis for evaluation. The extinction determination establishes the terminal state. Therefore: Threshold Crossing ≠ Extinction Determination. Extinction Determination A Value Extinction Determination establishes that: the relevant previously existing value no longer remains recoverable within the governed lifecycle. The determination should identify: the Value Object; the relevant value; prior Value State; applicable extinction conditions; extinction threshold; recoverability basis; restoration pathways considered; material uncertainty; determination basis; effective extinction point; finality consequences. Extinction Uncertainty Value Extinction should not be declared where material uncertainty prevents a legitimate terminal determination. Where recoverability cannot currently be established or excluded, the appropriate state may remain: Indeterminate rather than: Extinct. This is especially important for: emerging technologies; inaccessible data; future reconstruction capability; uncertain rights; unresolved ownership; rapidly changing markets; evolving scientific capability. VXSS must not transform uncertainty into finality. Temporary Impossibility ≠ Extinction A value may temporarily be impossible to restore because of: unavailable technology; regulatory restriction; inaccessible infrastructure; temporary market conditions; missing resources; geopolitical conditions; temporary legal barriers. If the underlying value remains recoverable when those conditions change, extinction has not necessarily occurred. Dormancy ≠ Extinction Dormant value may remain recoverable even where it has not produced active utility for a long period. Examples include: dormant intellectual property; archived data; inactive infrastructure; unused productive capacity; inactive rights; temporarily irrelevant technology. Time alone does not establish extinction. Obsolescence ≠ Automatic Extinction Obsolescence may contribute to Value Degradation or Value Nullification. It does not automatically establish extinction. An obsolete technology may: regain historical value; gain collector value; become strategically relevant; be repurposed; be modernized; regain functionality; support another value relationship. VXSS therefore requires the specific governed value to be evaluated rather than treating the label obsolete as a terminal determination. Extinction of One Value ≠ Extinction of All Value A single Value Object may support multiple value relationships. For example, an industrial machine may lose: productive manufacturing value while retaining: scrap value historical value training value or component value. VXSS may therefore determine extinction of one governed value without declaring the entire object valueless. This distinction prevents Value Extinction from becoming an object-destruction classification. Value Identity Continuity Restoration requires continuity between: the value that previously existed and the value claimed to have returned. Where that continuity is permanently lost, restoration may no longer be a legitimate description. This creates an important extinction boundary. If a later value appears but represents a materially different value relationship, it may constitute: new Value Emergence rather than restoration of the extinguished value. Extinction ≠ New Emergence Prohibition Value Extinction terminates a particular governed value lifecycle. It does not mean the Value Object can never possess value again. A new value may later emerge through: new technology; new use; new market; new rights; new information; new functionality; new context; new demand; new strategic relevance. Where the later value does not represent recovery of the extinguished value, it should enter governance as: new Value Emergence. Therefore: Value Extinction ≠ Permanent Prohibition of Future Value. Value Finality Once Value Extinction has been legitimately determined, VXSS establishes Value Finality for the relevant value lifecycle. Value Finality means that the extinguished value is no longer treated as: degraded value; dormant value; zero value awaiting restoration; a ReMonet™ candidate; pending restored value. The lifecycle has reached its terminal condition. Finality ≠ Erasure Value Finality does not erase the previous value lifecycle. The governed record should preserve: Value Emergence → Value States → Value Changes → Value Development → Value Degradation → Value Nullification where applicable → Restoration history where applicable → Value Extinction → Value Finality. Extinction ends the lifecycle. It does not delete it. Finality Reopening A legitimate extinction determination should not be casually reversed. Where new evidence later demonstrates that the extinction determination itself was incorrect, the organization may require: Determination Review rather than treating the value as having been restored. This distinction is important. If the value was never actually extinct, correcting the record is: Extinction Determination Correction not ReMonet™. Value Extinction States VXSS may recognize minimum governance states such as: 1. Extinction Not Established Available evidence does not establish that the value has ceased to be recoverable. 2. Extinction Indeterminate Available evidence is insufficient to determine whether recoverability remains. 3. Extinction Threshold Approaching Material conditions indicate proximity to a defined extinction threshold, but terminal loss has not yet been established. 4. Extinction Threshold Reached The defined threshold has been reached, requiring formal extinction determination. 5. Value Extinct The relevant value has been determined to no longer exist as recoverable value within the governed lifecycle. 6. Value Final The extinction determination has entered final lifecycle status and the value is no longer eligible for restoration governance within that lifecycle. These are governance states and should be adapted to the relevant implementation context. VXSS Boundary with Value Degradation Standard VDGS governs declining value while value continues to exist. VXSS governs the terminal condition where recoverable value no longer exists. Therefore: Declining Value ≠ Extinguished Value. VXSS Boundary with Value Nullification Standard VNS governs the transition from positive value into a zero-value condition. VXSS governs whether recoverability itself has ended. Therefore: Zero Value ≠ Value Extinction. A ZVA™ may remain recoverable. An extinguished value does not. VXSS Boundary with Value Restoration Standard VRSS governs recovery of previously impaired, degraded, dormant, lost, inaccessible, or zero value where restoration remains legitimate. VXSS establishes the boundary beyond which restoration no longer represents continuation of the same value lifecycle. Therefore: Recoverable Value → VRSS Non-Recoverable Value → VXSS VXSS Boundary with Value State Standard VSS determines the current governed state of value. VXSS determines terminal lifecycle extinction and finality. A zero Value State under VSS must not automatically be interpreted as Value Extinction. VXSS Boundary with Value Change Standard Value Change governs what materially happened to value. Value Extinction governs whether the consequence has become terminal. A material change may contribute to extinction without itself constituting an extinction determination. VXSS Boundary with Value Emergence Once a value has legitimately reached Value Finality, later value cannot automatically be classified as restoration. The architecture must first determine whether the later value represents: correction of an incorrect extinction determination or new Value Emergence. This protects the semantic integrity of the lifecycle. Foundational Principles Zero Value is not Value Extinction. ZVA™ may retain restoration potential. Value Extinction requires loss of recoverability, not merely absence of current value. Object existence does not prove value existence. Object destruction is not required for Value Extinction. Not currently restorable does not mean extinct. Restoration cost does not determine whether value exists. Failed restoration does not automatically establish extinction. Dormancy is not extinction. Obsolescence is not automatically extinction. Extinction of one value does not extinguish every value associated with the same object. Threshold crossing is not itself an Extinction Determination. Uncertainty must not be converted into finality. Value Finality ends a governed value lifecycle; it does not erase its history. An extinguished value cannot legitimately enter ReMonet™ within the same governed lifecycle. Future value may emerge after extinction, but new Value Emergence must remain distinct from restoration of extinguished value. Canonical Closing Statement Value Extinction Standard establishes the terminal governance layer of VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture by determining when previously existing value ceases to remain recoverable within its governed lifecycle. Through governance of extinction conditions, recoverability, restoration potential, extinction thresholds, terminal uncertainty, extinction determination, Value Finality, value identity continuity, historical preservation, and terminal lifecycle records, VXSS establishes the critical distinction between zero value and extinguished value. The Standard prevents temporary impairment, dormancy, obsolescence, failed restoration, high restoration cost, or a ZVA™ — Zero Value Asset™ from being prematurely interpreted as terminal value loss while also providing a formal point at which a value that can no longer legitimately be recovered ceases to remain within restoration governance. By preserving the distinction between Value Extinction, Value Nullification, Value Restoration, and future Value Emergence, VXSS closes the governed value lifecycle without preventing new value from later emerging from the same underlying object. Value Extinction therefore represents not the moment when value merely reaches zero, but the moment when the governed lifecycle can no longer legitimately support the proposition that the same value can return. Mahlad Value Extinction Standard (VXSS) Architecture: VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Value Lifecycle Governance Canonical Definition: Value Extinction Standard governs the terminal lifecycle condition in which previously existing value ceases to remain recoverable within the governed lifecycle and establishes the methodological boundary between recoverable zero value and legitimate Value Finality. Governed Space: Value Extinction Value becomes legitimately extinct only when its recoverability as the same governed value has ended within the defined lifecycle; zero value, dormancy, obsolescence, failed restoration, or temporary impossibility do not by themselves establish extinction. → View Standard Avout standard Module Architecture → Value Extinction Conditions Module (VXCM) → Value Extinction Threshold Module (VXTM) → Value Extinction Determination Module (VXDM) → Value Finality Module (VXFM) → Value Extinction Record Module (VXRM) Related Documents → About Value Extinction Standard (VXSS) → VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture

title: About OOF® Global Interest Heat Map™
text: About OOF® Global Interest Heat Map™ About OOF® Global Interest Heat Map™ The OOF® Global Interest Heat Map™ shows where around the world people are engaging with OOF® governance methodologies, architectures, standards, maps, and related methodological resources. The map is updated automatically every 24 hours and presents interest at the country level. It is designed to answer one simple question: Where in the world is interest in governance methodology developing? How It Works OOF® uses aggregated country-level interaction signals from its public methodological infrastructure. The map does not require cookies, visitor profiles, or individual tracking. It measures geographic patterns rather than people. No cookies. No visitor profiles. No individual tracking. Country activity is evaluated comparatively, with population differences and data reliability taken into account so that the map is not simply a ranking of website traffic. No individual visitor data or raw traffic numbers are displayed. Reading the Map Countries are represented by simple interest states: 🟢 High Interest — strong relative interest in OOF® governance methodology. 🔵 Moderate Interest — meaningful and established interest. 🟡 Emerging Interest — interest is beginning to develop. ⚪ Insufficient Signal — there is not yet enough information for a reliable classification. Insufficient Signal does not mean Low Interest. Where sufficient information exists, the map may also indicate whether interest is rising, stable, or declining. Why the Map Exists Governance challenges are global. The OOF® Global Interest Heat Map™ makes the geographic development of interest in governance methodology visible. It allows researchers, organizations, institutions, developers, policymakers, students, and other observers to see where methodological attention is forming and how that pattern changes over time. A country seeing strong interest elsewhere may begin exploring the same governance questions, architectures, and standards. The map therefore serves not only as an observation tool, but also as an invitation to explore. See where governance methodology is being studied. See where interest is emerging. Then explore the methodologies behind it. Global Methodological Interest The map does not claim that a country, government, institution, or population endorses OOF®. It shows a geographic signal of engagement with OOF® methodological infrastructure. As OOF® reaches new countries, the map evolves with that interest. The OOF® Global Interest Heat Map™ makes global methodological attention visible — one country at a time.

title: OOF™ About Tax-Relevant Event Boundary Standard - (TREBS)
text: OOF™ About Tax-Relevant Event Boundary Standard - (TREBS) About Tax-Relevant Event Boundary Standard - (TREBS) Architecture: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Standard Type: Parent Standard Governed Space: Tax-Relevant Event Boundary ------------------------------ Understanding the Tax-Relevant Event Boundary Standard Real-world and digital activity rarely arrives as perfectly separated events. A commercial transaction may contain multiple operational steps. A digital service may involve several systems, settlements, infrastructure operations, and machine-generated actions. An autonomous process may execute hundreds or thousands of technical operations while contributing to only one or several meaningful governed events. Before such activity can progress through tax-relevant event governance, the system must establish where one governed event ends, what belongs within it, what remains outside it, and where separation from surrounding activity is required. The Tax-Relevant Event Boundary Standard (TREBS) establishes the governance layer for making that distinction. TREBS does not determine whether the event is taxable. It determines the legitimate structural extent of the governed event that may later be evaluated by taxation systems. ------------------------------ What Is the Tax-Relevant Event Boundary Standard? TREBS is the fourth Parent Standard within TREGA™. It receives a sufficiently formed event from the Tax-Relevant Event Formation Standard (TREFS) and governs the establishment of its structural boundary. Its purpose is to prevent operational systems, transaction identifiers, database structures, platform conventions, machine processes, or technical workflows from automatically defining what constitutes the governed extent of an event. TREBS therefore addresses a fundamental question: What actually belongs to this governed event, and what does not? This distinction becomes increasingly important when economic activity spans multiple organizations, platforms, systems, jurisdictions, digital environments, autonomous agents, or machine operations. ------------------------------ Canonical Definition The Tax-Relevant Event Boundary Standard governs how a sufficiently formed real-world, economic, operational, transactional, digital, autonomous, machine-generated, or value-affecting event is bounded as a distinct governed event by establishing its legitimate structural extent, including what belongs within the event, what remains outside it, and where separation from adjacent or overlapping activity is required. TREBS preserves the distinction between Event Formation, Event Boundary, Event Timing, Event Location, Event Participation, Event Relationships, Event Determination, and jurisdiction-specific taxation. Event Formation ≠ Event Boundary. A structurally formed event does not automatically possess a legitimate final boundary. ------------------------------ Why TREBS Exists Operational reality does not naturally divide itself according to database rows, invoice numbers, transaction IDs, API calls, machine instructions, accounting records, or tax categories. The same underlying activity may appear differently across different systems. A marketplace may organize activity around an order. A payment provider may organize it around settlements. A logistics system may organize it around shipments. An ERP system may organize it around invoices. An autonomous system may organize it around objectives, tasks, executions, or machine actions. None of those representations should automatically determine the governed Event Boundary. Without explicit Event Boundary governance, the same operational reality can be artificially aggregated into one oversized event or fragmented into numerous artificial events. TREBS provides the methodology for preventing both conditions. ------------------------------ TREGA™ Architecture Governance Flow TREGA™ governs the Tax-Relevant Event lifecycle through twelve sequential Parent Standards. 1. TRECS — Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard Event Context ↓ 2. TRERS — Tax-Relevant Event Recognition Standard Event Recognition ↓ 3. TREFS — Tax-Relevant Event Formation Standard Event Formation & Root Association ↓ ↓ 4. TREBS — Tax-Relevant Event Boundary Standard ←Event Boundary — CURRENT STANDARD ↓ 5. TRETS — Tax-Relevant Event Timing Standard Event Timing ↓ 6. TRELS — Tax-Relevant Event Location Standard Event Location ↓ 7. TREPS — Tax-Relevant Event Participation Standard Event Participation ↓ 8. TRVAS — Tax-Relevant Value Association Standard Event-to-Value Association ↓ 9. TRERLS — Tax-Relevant Event Relationship Standard Event Relationships ↓ 10. TREDS — Tax-Relevant Event Determination Standard Governed Event Determination ↓ 11. TREGS — Tax-Relevant Event Record Governance Standard Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record ↓ 12. TRECLS — Tax-Relevant Event Lifecycle & Continuity Standard Event Lifecycle & Continuity ↓ Jurisdiction-Ready Tax-Relevant Event ↓ Jurisdictional Tax Rules / Tax Engine ↓ Tax Determination ↓ Reporting / Compliance TREBS Position Event Formation ↓ EVENT BOUNDARY ↓ Event Timing TREBS therefore occupies the governance layer immediately after an event has been structurally formed and before its governed temporal position is established. ------------------------------ What TREBS Governs TREBS governs the structural extent of a formed event. This includes governance of: Event Boundary identification Event Boundary scope inclusion within the governed event exclusion from the governed event separation from adjacent activity separation of potentially independent event structures overlapping boundary conditions boundary ambiguity boundary revision prevention of artificial event aggregation prevention of artificial event fragmentation traceability of boundary decisions The result is a Governed Bounded Event capable of progressing into Event Timing governance. ------------------------------ What TREBS Does Not Determine TREBS does not determine: whether the event is legally taxable which jurisdiction may tax the event when a legal tax point occurs the applicable tax period who is legally the taxpayer the applicable tax base tax rate exemptions or deductions reporting obligations payment obligations tax liability enforcement consequences It also does not replace the responsibilities of later TREGA™ Parent Standards. TREBS establishes the event boundary. It does not determine the legal tax consequence of that boundary. ------------------------------ Why the Distinction Matters A boundary is a representation of the governed event. It is not a tax conclusion. For example, an activity may span Switzerland, Germany, and France and still require one coherent governed event representation. Conversely, a single commercial contract or platform order may contain several operationally distinct events that should not automatically be collapsed into one governed event. TREBS must therefore establish the event structure independently of the tax interpretation subsequently applied. This supports the broader TREGA™ principle: One Event ↓ One Governed Event Layer ↓ Multiple Jurisdictional Evaluations The governed event should remain stable even when different jurisdictions interpret its tax consequences differently. ------------------------------ Event Inclusion and Exclusion A boundary becomes meaningful only when the system can distinguish between what belongs to the event and what does not. TREBS therefore requires a governed basis for inclusion and exclusion. An operational action should not become part of an event merely because it: occurred in the same system shares a transaction identifier belongs to the same customer account occurred within the same workflow was executed by the same machine belongs to the same commercial contract occurred within the same accounting period Each relationship must be evaluated according to the governed structure of the event. Technical Association ≠ Event Membership. ------------------------------ Event Separation TREBS also governs when activity must remain structurally separated. Two occurrences may be closely connected while still representing distinct governed events.
