Real-System Use Case 1 — Cross-Border Digital Marketplace Transaction A customer places an order through a global marketplace at 23:58. The platform confirms the transaction at 00:01. Payment authorization occurs at 00:03. The merchant accepts the order several hours later. Goods are shipped the following day. Delivery occurs three days later. Financial settlement occurs another two days afterward. Different systems therefore contain several potentially relevant timestamps. If one system timestamp were automatically treated as the event time, the underlying operational event could be represented differently depending on which database, platform, accounting system, or jurisdiction examines it. TRETS governs the event's temporal structure independently. It identifies and preserves relevant temporal signals, establishes Event Start, Event Completion, Duration, and Temporal Order, and produces a traceable Governed Temporally Situated Event. Only afterward may different jurisdictions determine which legally defined moment constitutes their applicable tax point or tax period. The operational timeline is governed once; its legal tax interpretation may differ by jurisdiction. Real-System Use Case 2 — Autonomous Machine-to-Machine Economy An autonomous industrial AI system detects demand, schedules production, activates robotic equipment, purchases machine capacity, consumes digital services, coordinates logistics, and automatically initiates settlement. Thousands of machine actions occur across distributed systems. Individual machines generate timestamps in milliseconds. Cloud services record different processing times. The payment infrastructure records authorization and settlement separately. No human presses a button that naturally defines when the economic event occurred. Treating every machine timestamp as an independent event time would create artificial fragmentation. Treating the entire autonomous workflow as occurring at one timestamp would destroy important temporal structure. TRETS establishes a governed temporal representation capable of distinguishing operationally relevant timing from technical execution noise. The resulting event can then proceed through the TREGA™ lifecycle and ultimately be evaluated by jurisdiction-specific taxation systems. Machine execution time does not automatically define the governed time of the event. Canonical Boundary TRETS governs the operational temporal representation of a sufficiently bounded event, including Event Time identification, Event Start, Event Completion, Event Duration, Event Temporal Order, temporal ambiguity, competing temporal signals, distributed timing, machine-generated timing, and temporal traceability. TRETS does not govern Event Formation, Event Boundary, Event Location, Tax Jurisdiction, Event Participation, taxpayer determination, value lifecycle, Event-to-Value Association, Event Relationships, final Event Determination, Legal Tax Point, Tax Period Determination, legal taxability, tax base, tax rate, exemptions, deductions, tax liability, reporting obligations, payment, collection, or enforcement. TRETS begins with a Governed Bounded Event and ends with a Governed Temporally Situated Event. Canonical Closing Statement TRETS establishes the governed temporal reality of an event before jurisdiction-specific taxation systems interpret that reality under law. It prevents database timestamps, accounting dates, platform records, payment timestamps, machine clocks, autonomous execution sequences, and downstream taxation assumptions from silently becoming authoritative representations of when the event occurred. TRETS governs when the event occurred operationally — not when tax law decides the event becomes legally relevant. TREGA™ governs the event. The jurisdiction governs the tax.

title: OOF™ About Tax-Relevant Value Association Standard - (TRVAS)
text: OOF™ About Tax-Relevant Value Association Standard - (TRVAS) About Tax-Relevant Value Association Standard - (TRVAS) Architecture: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Standard: TRVAS — Tax-Relevant Value Association Standard Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Governed Space: Tax-Relevant Value Association What Is TRVAS? The Tax-Relevant Value Association Standard (TRVAS) is the TREGA™ Parent Standard that governs how value is connected to a governed Tax-Relevant Event. Its purpose is not to calculate tax. Its purpose is to establish something that must exist before reliable tax analysis can occur: Which governed value results actually belong to this event? A real-world or digital event may involve money, goods, services, digital assets, rights, resources, energy, computational capacity, economic benefits, losses, or multiple forms of value simultaneously. TRVAS provides a structured method for associating those value results with the correct governed event. It creates the value-association layer between operational reality and later jurisdiction-specific taxation. Why Does TRVAS Exist? Modern economic systems generate enormous quantities of value-related information. Banks record payments. ERP systems record invoices and accounting entries. Marketplaces record prices, commissions, fees, refunds, and settlements. Blockchain networks record transfers of digital assets. Industrial systems record resource consumption and production. AI agents may initiate transactions or allocate resources. Autonomous machines may consume energy, request services, exchange information, or trigger economic activity. But the existence of a number, payment, asset transfer, or accounting entry does not automatically explain what value belongs to the underlying event. For example: Payment ≠ Complete Event Value Invoice Amount ≠ Taxable Value Asset Transfer ≠ Ownership Determination Recorded Amount ≠ Governed Value by Default Before a taxation system can legitimately interpret value, the relationship between the value and the event must first be understood. TRVAS governs that relationship. The Problem TRVAS Solves Traditional systems often begin taxation analysis from transaction records. This works reasonably well when the economic structure is simple: Seller ↓ Product ↓ Buyer ↓ Payment Modern economic activity can be substantially more complex. A single event may involve: several participants; multiple payments; multiple currencies; digital assets; service components; platform fees; automated settlement; rebates or refunds; non-monetary value; machine-generated activity; autonomous agents; distributed infrastructure; and several jurisdictions. In these environments, asking only: “What amount was recorded?” is no longer sufficient. The more fundamental governance question is: “Which value results materially belong to which event?” TRVAS provides the methodology for answering that question before jurisdiction-specific tax rules are applied. What TRVAS Governs TRVAS governs the relationship between a Tax-Relevant Event and the value associated with that event. It establishes a framework for determining: which governed value information is relevant to the event; which value references belong to the event; which governed Value States are associated with the event; which governed Value Changes are associated with the event; whether multiple values belong to the same event; whether a value relationship is direct or indirect; whether the association is sufficiently supported; whether uncertainty exists; whether conflicting value associations exist; and whether the relationship remains sufficiently traceable. The result is a: Governed Value-Associated Event This becomes the input for subsequent TREGA™ governance. What TRVAS Does Not Govern TRVAS deliberately stops before several other governance and legal questions. It does not determine: who legally owns the value; where value originated; the complete Value Lifecycle; who is entitled to the value; whether the value is taxable; which jurisdiction may tax it; the applicable Tax Base; taxable income; taxable gain; customs value; transfer-pricing value; deductions; exemptions; tax rates; or Tax Liability. These questions belong to other governance architectures or jurisdiction-specific taxation systems. The central distinction is: Governed Event Value ≠ Taxable Value TRVAS prepares the event-value relationship. The jurisdiction later determines its legal tax meaning. Why Value Association Is Different from Value Governance TRVAS does not replace VFM® — Value Flow Mechanism. VFM® governs what happens to value throughout its lifecycle. Its governance may establish how value originates, emerges, changes, develops, degrades, becomes nullified, is restored, or ultimately becomes extinct. TRVAS asks a different question: Which of those governed value results belong to this particular event? The architectural separation is therefore: VFM® governs what happened to value.TRVAS governs which governed value result belongs to the event. This prevents TREGA™ from becoming a second Value Lifecycle architecture. Why a Payment Is Not Enough A payment is an operational fact. It may be highly relevant. But it does not necessarily represent the complete value structure of the event. A payment may include: several goods; several services; platform charges; commissions; taxes; discounts; refunds; financing components; deposits; bundled consideration; or amounts associated with several events. Likewise, an event may have value even when no conventional payment occurs. Therefore: Payment ≠ Complete Event Value TRVAS allows systems to represent the actual event-value structure rather than assuming that one payment field explains the entire economic event. Monetary and Non-Monetary Value TRVAS is designed for economic environments where value cannot always be reduced immediately to money. Value associated with an event may include: currency; digital assets; goods; services; rights; access; data-related value; computational capacity; energy; productive resources; economic benefits; or other governed forms of value. This becomes increasingly important as digital and autonomous economies develop. TRVAS therefore does not begin with the assumption: Value = Currency Instead, it allows governed value information to exist first and jurisdiction-specific valuation to occur later. Why TRVAS Matters for Banks Banks operate at one of the most important intersections between events and value. They observe: payments; settlements; transfers; account movements; merchant transactions; financing; digital payments; cross-border flows; and increasingly tokenized or programmable financial assets. But a bank transaction record does not necessarily contain the complete economic event. TRVAS provides a methodology for connecting financial value information to a governed event structure. Instead of seeing only: Account A ↓ CHF 10,000 ↓ Account B a governed infrastructure can potentially understand: Event ↓ Participants ↓ Value Association ↓ Related Events ↓ Tax-Relevant Event Record This creates richer structured information for downstream compliance, reporting, audit, risk, and tax systems without requiring the bank itself to determine the tax consequence. Why TRVAS Matters for Blockchain and Digital Assets Blockchain networks provide strong transaction records, but transaction visibility alone does not explain economic meaning. A token movement may represent: payment; collateral; transfer between wallets controlled by the same actor; exchange; staking; settlement; asset migration; protocol interaction; liquidity movement; or another operational event. Therefore: On-Chain Transfer ≠ Taxable Event by Default TRVAS can associate governed digital-asset value results with the correct event while preserving the distinction between operational reality and legal taxation. This is especially important where one blockchain transaction contains several economically relevant actions or where one economic event spans several on-chain and off-chain operations. Why TRVAS Matters for Businesses and ERP Systems Businesses already possess large amounts of value information. It exists across: ERP; accounting; procurement; invoicing; inventory; payments; logistics; CRM; marketplaces; and operational systems. The problem is often not absence of data. The problem is that the data describes different fragments of the same economic reality. TRVAS provides a common governance layer for connecting governed value information to the correct event. For businesses, this can support: cleaner event records; stronger auditability; better data interoperability; reduced ambiguity; clearer cross-border analysis; more structured tax-engine inputs; and better readiness for automated compliance. The business value comes from improving the quality of the information entering downstream decision systems. Why TRVAS Matters for Digital Platforms A platform may participate in millions of economically relevant events involving customers, merchants, payment providers, logistics providers, advertisers, service providers, and digital infrastructure. One platform event may contain: Product Value + Service Value + Platform Fee + Payment Fee + Discount + Refund + Digital Benefit Treating this as one undifferentiated transaction amount can hide the underlying event-value structure. TRVAS provides a method for preserving materially distinct Value Associations while keeping them connected to the same governed event where appropriate. This becomes particularly valuable for platforms operating across multiple jurisdictions. Why TRVAS Matters for AI Agents and Autonomous Systems Economic activity will increasingly be initiated and executed by software. An AI agent may select a supplier. Another agent may negotiate a service. A machine may automatically request maintenance. An autonomous system may allocate computational resources. Machines may exchange services or resources without contemporaneous human action. These activities may create or affect value even where there is no traditional invoice at the moment the event occurs. TRVAS allows those value relationships to be governed without forcing them prematurely into traditional transaction assumptions. The principle is: No Human Transaction ≠ No Value Association This makes TRVAS suitable not only for today's economy but also for emerging machine and autonomous economic environments. Multi-Jurisdiction Value Governance One of the strongest reasons for separating Value Association from tax determination is cross-border activity. The same governed event and the same governed value structure may be evaluated differently by different jurisdictions. TRVAS supports: One Governed Event → One Governed Value Association Structure → Multiple Jurisdictional Evaluations Jurisdiction A may interpret the value one way. Jurisdiction B may apply another legal classification. Jurisdiction C may determine that only part of the associated value is relevant. TREGA™ does not need to rewrite operational reality for each jurisdiction. It provides a stable governed event layer that different jurisdictional systems can consume. Position Within TREGA™ TRVAS is Parent Standard 8 of the 12-standard TREGA™ architecture. The complete Governance Flow is: 1. TRECS — Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard → 2. TRERS — Tax-Relevant Event Recognition Standard → 3. TREFS — Tax-Relevant Event Formation Standard → 4. TREBS — Tax-Relevant Event Boundary Standard → 5. TRETS — Tax-Relevant Event Timing Standard → 6. TRELS — Tax-Relevant Event Location Standard → 7. TREPS — Tax-Relevant Event Participation Standard → 8. TRVAS — Tax-Relevant Value Association Standard ← CURRENT → 9. TRERLS — Tax-Relevant Event Relationship Standard → 10. TREDS — Tax-Relevant Event Determination Standard → 11. TREGS — Tax-Relevant Event Record Governance Standard → 12. TRECLS — Tax-Relevant Event Lifecycle & Continuity Standard Its immediate position is: Event Participation ↓ Value Association ↓ Event Relationships TREPS establishes who or what materially participated. TRVAS establishes which governed value results materially belong to the event. TRERLS then establishes how that value-associated event relates to other events. How TRVAS Works at a High Level TRVAS is operationalized through five Core Modules: VAIM — Value Association Identification Module Identifies value information that may materially belong to the event. VARM — Value Reference Module Establishes stable references between the event and governed value results. VACM — Value Change Association Module Associates governed Value Changes with the event. VASM — Value State Association Module Associates relevant governed Value States with the event. VATM — Value Association Traceability Module Preserves the reconstructability, qualification, uncertainty, and traceability of the association structure. Together they transform: Governed Participatory Event + Governed Value Results into: Governed Value-Associated EventWhat Organizations Gain from TRVAS TRVAS provides a common methodological layer for organizations that must understand economic activity across fragmented systems. The principal benefit is not another tax calculation. It is better structured input before tax calculation begins. Organizations can gain: clearer relationships between events and value; separation of operational value from legal tax valuation; improved interoperability between operational and tax systems; better treatment of multi-value events; stronger traceability; preservation of uncertainty instead of artificial certainty; better cross-border event representation; compatibility with machine-generated economic activity; stronger inputs for audit and compliance; and reduced dependence on transaction records that contain only partial economic context. TRVAS is therefore particularly relevant to: banks, payment infrastructure, ERP providers, accounting platforms, marketplaces, blockchain systems, digital-asset platforms, multinational businesses, tax technology providers, AI-agent platforms, autonomous-system operators, auditors, compliance infrastructures, and public tax administrations. Use Case 1 — Global Digital Commerce Infrastructure A customer purchases a bundled digital and physical service through a global marketplace. The event involves a merchant, marketplace, payment provider, logistics provider, cloud infrastructure, and customer. Operational systems contain: product value; digital-service value; platform commission; payment-processing fee; delivery charge; promotional discount; currency conversion; and later a partial refund. A conventional system may see several independent records or reduce everything to a single invoice total. TRVAS allows the governed event to preserve the materially relevant value relationships without deciding which amount is legally taxable. The resulting Governed Value-Associated Event can subsequently be evaluated by different jurisdictional tax systems according to their own laws. The same operational event therefore remains stable while its legal tax interpretation may differ across jurisdictions. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Digital-Asset and Machine Economy An autonomous industrial system detects excess production capacity. An AI agent allocates that capacity to another organization through a digital marketplace. A second autonomous agent negotiates the resource allocation. The service consumes energy and computational resources, produces operational value, and settlement occurs through a digital asset. Several governed value results may therefore exist: computational capacity; energy consumption; operational service value; digital-asset transfer; and associated value changes. TRVAS can associate these governed value results with the event without assuming that the blockchain transfer alone represents the complete economic event. It also does not determine whether the AI agent, machine owner, operating company, platform, or another actor is legally taxable. The resulting event-value structure provides downstream tax systems with a governed representation of what occurred before jurisdiction-specific law determines what is taxable and by whom. Canonical Boundary TRVAS governs the relationship between governed value results and a Tax-Relevant Event. It does not govern the complete Value Lifecycle, determine ownership or entitlement, replace VFM®, determine Event Participation, establish accountability or liability, or calculate jurisdiction-specific taxable value, Tax Base, Tax Liability, rates, exemptions, deductions, reporting obligations, collection, payment, or enforcement. Its purpose is to make the value dimension of an event sufficiently structured, distinguishable, traceable, and jurisdiction-neutral for subsequent governance and taxation analysis. Canonical Closing Statement TRVAS creates the governed bridge between value reality and event reality before tax law interprets either. A payment is not necessarily the complete value of an event. A blockchain transfer is not necessarily the economic event. A participant is not necessarily the owner of the associated value. And a governed value associated with an event is not automatically taxable value. VFM® governs what happened to value. TREGA™ governs which governed value result belongs to the event.Governed Event Value ≠ Taxable Value. TREGA™ governs the event. The jurisdiction governs the tax.

title: OOF™ About TREGA™

text: OOF™ About TREGA™ About TREGA™ Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture Economic activity is increasingly digital. Transactions cross systems before they cross borders. Digital services may involve participants operating from multiple locations. AI agents may initiate, negotiate, execute, or support transactions. Autonomous machines may exchange services, resources, information, and Value without continuous human intervention. Distributed systems may create economically relevant activity across infrastructures that do not correspond neatly to traditional transactional boundaries. Taxation systems increasingly need to understand Events that are more complex than a single invoice, payment, contract, location, or technical transaction. TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ was created to provide a stable governance architecture for this expanding Tax-Relevant Event domain. TREGA™ does not define tax laws, tax rates, tax jurisdictions, taxpayer status, tax nexus, tax periods, tax bases, filing obligations, payment systems, or enforcement mechanisms. TREGA™ governs the event. The jurisdiction governs the tax. Why TREGA™ Exists Tax systems process enormous amounts of transactional and economic information. But the existence of transaction data does not itself answer fundamental governance questions: What actually constitutes the Event? Within what context does the Event exist? When should an occurrence become a governed Tax-Relevant Event? Where does the Event begin and end? When did it occur? Where did it occur? Who or what materially participated? Which governed Value belongs to the Event? How is the Event related to other Events? When is the Event sufficiently governed to become tax-relevant? How should the Event remain reconstructable when information changes? TREGA™ addresses these questions by defining the governable spaces that exist throughout the complete Tax-Relevant Event lifecycle. Rather than standardizing one taxation technology, TREGA™ standardizes the governance conditions under which occurrences can be contextualized, recognized, formed, bounded, timed, located, associated with participants and Value, related to other Events, determined as tax-relevant, recorded, maintained, and made Jurisdiction-Ready. The Event Before the Tax The objective of TREGA™ is not to prescribe how a jurisdiction must tax an Event. The objective is to define how the Event must remain governable before jurisdiction-specific taxation begins. Every Event exists within a context. Relevant occurrences must be recognized. Recognized occurrences must be formed into governed Events. Every Event requires a boundary. Every Event exists in time. Every Event exists somewhere physically, digitally, operationally, or across distributed environments. Events involve participants. Tax-relevant Events may involve Value. Events may depend upon, precede, follow, group with, merge with, or split from other Events. An Event must be sufficiently governed before it can receive a Tax-Relevant Event Determination. A Determined Tax-Relevant Event requires a governed Record. That Event may later require Amendment, Correction, Supersession, Closure, or reopening. TREGA™ therefore treats the Tax-Relevant Event as an independent governance domain between Operational Reality and jurisdiction-specific taxation. The Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture TREGA™ consists of twelve independent Tax-Relevant Event Governance spaces. Each space answers one architectural question. Each space governs one distinct part of the Event lifecycle. Each space has a defined beginning, operational purpose, and governance boundary. Each space begins where the preceding Event Governance requirement has been sufficiently established. Together, these spaces form the complete Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture. The architecture progresses through: Real-World / Digital Event ↓ Event Context ↓ Event Recognition ↓ Event Formation & Root Association ↓ Event Boundary ↓ Event Timing ↓ Event Location ↓ Event Participation ↓ Value Association ↓ Event Relationships ↓ Event Determination ↓ Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record ↓ Event Continuity & Lifecycle ↓ Jurisdiction-Ready Tax-Relevant Event This progression represents the governance journey from identifying the context in which something happened to determining whether the resulting governed Event is sufficiently structured, reconstructable, and lifecycle-governed to enter jurisdiction-specific taxation analysis. Event Spaces Rather Than Tax-System Components TREGA™ does not organize Tax-Relevant Event Governance around tax engines, accounting platforms, ERP systems, payment processors, jurisdictions, tax authorities, vendors, departments, or technical components. Instead, it organizes governance around distinct Tax-Relevant Event Governance spaces. Each space represents an independent governance responsibility that exists regardless of the taxation technology or jurisdiction ultimately consuming the Event. A physical sale, digital subscription, financial transaction, cross-border service, platform transaction, digital-asset Event, AI-agent transaction, autonomous machine exchange, or future machine-economy Event may be operationally very different. Yet each may still require governance of: context ↓ recognition ↓ formation ↓ boundary ↓ timing ↓ location ↓ participation ↓ Value Association ↓ Event relationships ↓ determination ↓ record ↓ lifecycle. Because these spaces are technology-neutral and jurisdiction-neutral, TREGA™ can remain applicable while taxation technologies, digital economies, autonomous systems, and legal tax frameworks continue to evolve. A Methodology Rather Than a Tax Implementation TREGA™ is a governance methodology. It is not a tax calculation framework. The architecture defines which Event Governance conditions must exist, how they relate to one another, where their boundaries lie, and what must remain explicit before an Event becomes suitable for jurisdiction-specific taxation analysis. Organizations and jurisdictions remain free to select their own: - tax engines, - ERP systems, - accounting platforms, - transaction systems, - payment infrastructure, - reporting systems, - tax calculation methodologies, - jurisdictional rules, - legal classifications, - compliance processes, - data infrastructure. TREGA™ governs the methodological Event structure surrounding those implementations rather than replacing them. This separation allows the architecture to remain stable while taxation systems and technologies change. From Operational Occurrence to Jurisdiction-Ready Event A Tax-Relevant Event cannot be governed as a single transaction-data object. Before an occurrence can be recognized, its Context must be understood. Before an Event can be bounded, it must be formed. Before participants and Value can be associated, the Event must be sufficiently identifiable in time and location. Before Event Determination, materially relevant relationships between Events must be governed. Before a Determined Tax-Relevant Event can be consumed downstream, it must become an identifiable, structured, linked, traceable, and interoperable governed Record. And before that Event can remain reliable through time, its Continuity, Amendment, Correction, Supersession, and Closure states must remain governable. TREGA™ transforms these dependencies into a structured and navigable Tax-Relevant Event lifecycle. Tax-Relevant Is Not Legally Taxable One of the most important distinctions within TREGA™ is: Tax-Relevant Event ≠ Legally Taxable Event An Event may be economically significant. It may involve Value. It may involve several participants. It may cross physical or digital boundaries. It may be relevant to multiple jurisdictions. None of these facts alone determines whether a jurisdiction legally taxes the Event. TREGA™ therefore preserves the distinction between: Tax-Relevant Event and Legally Taxable Event. Tax relevance means that the Event is sufficiently relevant and governed to enter taxation analysis. Legal taxability remains a determination of the applicable jurisdiction. Event Location Is Not Tax Jurisdiction TREGA™ also establishes another fundamental distinction: Event Location ≠ Tax Jurisdiction A digital Event may involve: - a user in one country, - a platform in another, - infrastructure in another, - a service provider elsewhere, - payment processing in another location, - autonomous computation distributed across multiple systems. TREGA™ governs the Event Locations relevant to understanding what occurred. It does not decide which country, state, canton, municipality, or other jurisdiction possesses legal taxing authority. This creates a methodological boundary between: where the Event occurred and which jurisdiction may legally tax the Event. Event Participation Is Not Taxpayer Determination TREGA™ deliberately separates Event Participation from taxpayer determination. TREGA™ determines whether and how an actor materially participates in a governed Event. Jurisdiction-specific taxation systems determine whether that participant, another actor, or another legally defined person becomes the taxpayer or otherwise acquires a tax obligation. An Event Participant may be: - a human, - an organization, - a platform, - a digital service, - an AI agent, - an autonomous machine, - or another governable actor. Participation establishes an Event relationship. It does not automatically establish legal tax status. Participant ≠ Taxpayer. The Event-to-Jurisdiction Boundary The transition from governed Event to jurisdiction-specific taxation is one of the most consequential points in the architecture. A cross-border digital service may involve multiple Locations. An autonomous transaction may involve several machine and organizational participants. A distributed platform Event may contain multiple technical operations. A Value change may span several systems. These facts matter. But the governance question is not simply: Which tax applies? The earlier question is: What Event has actually been established for the taxation system to evaluate? TREGA™ therefore treats the transition from Jurisdiction-Ready Tax-Relevant Event to Jurisdictional Tax Rules as an explicit architectural boundary rather than allowing jurisdiction-specific interpretation to redefine the underlying Event. Lifecycle Governance and Event Continuity Tax-Relevant Event Governance does not end when an Event Record is created. Information changes. New participants may become known. Location information may be corrected. Value Associations may be refined. Event Relationships may be discovered. A Determination may require reconsideration. A corrected state may supersede a previous state. An Event may close. A Closed Event may later require reopening. A material transformation may mean that the original Event can no longer legitimately continue. TREGA™ therefore extends governance beyond Event Determination and Record creation into Tax-Relevant Event Lifecycle & Continuity. Where material change affects the Event basis, the architecture supports governed re-entry into the earliest materially affected Event Governance space. The result is not uncontrolled reconstruction of the complete Event. It is targeted governed Event lifecycle re-entry. Who May Benefit TREGA™ may support: - tax authorities, - public institutions, - tax technology providers, - ERP providers, - accounting platforms, - financial institutions, - banks, - payment infrastructures, - digital platforms, - marketplaces, - digital-service providers, - multinational organizations, - cross-border commerce environments, - digital-asset infrastructures, - AI developers and operators, - autonomous-system operators, - machine-to-machine platforms, - compliance organizations, - audit and assurance organizations, - organizations processing complex Tax-Relevant Events. Relationship to Other OOF® Architectures TREGA™ governs Tax-Relevant Events. It operates alongside complementary OOF® architectures. GOA™ — Governance Architecture governs governance structure, authority, scope, delegation, accountability, continuity, and interoperability. ORA™ — Operational Reality Architecture governs Operational Reality and provides the methodological distinction between what actually occurs and how that occurrence subsequently becomes a governed Tax-Relevant Event. OBIDENITY® — Origin-Bound Identity Governance Architecture® governs origin, identity, ownership, authority, permission, responsibility, provenance, transfer, continuity, and auditability. VFM® — Value Flow Mechanism governs what happens to Value throughout its lifecycle, while TREGA™ associates governed Value results with specific Events. CLA® — Classification Architecture governs classification across governed objects and states. VALIDOS™ — Validation Governance Architecture governs validation purpose, criteria, methods, evidence fitness, determination, Validation States, reliance, and revalidation. INTEGROS® — Integrity Governance Architecture governs integrity across the complete integrity lifecycle. AGA™ — Accountability Governance Architecture governs accountability, responsibility, attribution, delegation, and accountable relationships. HALIA™ — Harm & Liability Architecture governs the lifecycle of harm and liability. AIG® — AI Governance Architecture governs AI behavior. ASGA™ — Autonomous Systems Governance Architecture governs autonomous systems, autonomous agents, authority, constraints, execution, and operational autonomy. ADIT® — Audit in Real Time Architecture governs continuous auditability, evidential observation, preservation, verification, and traceability across operational lifecycles. Together, these architectures allow Tax-Relevant Event Governance to interact with Operational Reality, identity, Value, classification, validation, integrity, accountability, liability, AI, autonomy, and auditability without collapsing those independent governance domains into one architecture. Use Case 1 — Cross-Border Digital Service Event A digital platform provides a service involving: - a customer in one country, - a service provider in another, - platform infrastructure distributed across several locations, - payment processing through another system, - and Value exchanged across multiple technical steps. A conventional tax system may begin with transaction records and immediately attempt to apply jurisdiction-specific rules. TREGA™ asks an earlier set of questions. What occurrence constitutes the Event? Within what Context does it exist? Where does the Event begin and end? When did it occur? Which physical, digital, and distributed Locations belong to it? Which actors materially participated? Which governed Value result belongs to the Event? Are the payment, platform, service, and infrastructure operations separate Events or related components of one governed Event? Is the Event sufficiently governed to become tax-relevant? The result is: One Governed Tax-Relevant Event ↓ Multiple Jurisdictional Evaluations Each jurisdiction may then independently determine tax nexus, legal taxability, taxpayer status, Tax Base, Tax Rate, reporting obligations, and other legal consequences. TREGA™ does not decide which jurisdiction wins. It establishes the Event that each jurisdiction is evaluating. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Machine-to-Machine Economic Event An autonomous industrial machine identifies a required resource, communicates with another machine or digital service, initiates a transaction, receives the resource or service, generates a Value change, and records the interaction without direct human execution. Several technical messages may exist. Several AI or machine actors may participate. The transaction may cross organizational and national infrastructure. TREGA™ provides the governance structure for establishing: what occurrence constitutes the Event; within what Context it exists; how the Event is formed and bounded; when and where it occurs; which machine, platform, organizational, or human actors materially participate; which governed Value result belongs to the Event; how the Event relates to preceding or subsequent machine Events; whether the Event is sufficiently governed to become tax-relevant; how it becomes a governed Event Record; and how its lifecycle remains reconstructable if information later changes. The resulting Event may then be evaluated independently by applicable jurisdiction-specific taxation systems. The autonomous machine does not need to become a taxpayer merely because it participated in the Event. Machine Participation may become part of Event Reality—but legal taxpayer status remains a jurisdictional determination. The Long-Term Vision Economic activity is moving from human-readable transactions toward increasingly distributed, automated, autonomous, and machine-generated Events. AI agents may negotiate and execute transactions. Machines may purchase resources from other machines. Digital services may operate continuously across jurisdictions. Value may emerge, change, move, degrade, or disappear across systems that do not correspond neatly to traditional invoices or contracts. One economic activity may contain thousands of technical operations. One technical operation may participate in several economically relevant relationships. As this transition accelerates, the central question will no longer be only whether taxation systems can process more transaction data. It will also be: How can taxation systems know what Event they are actually taxing? The long-term objective of TREGA™ is to provide a common Tax-Relevant Event Governance language through which organizations, platforms, machines, public institutions, and taxation infrastructures can identify, structure, compare, govern, reconstruct, exchange, and evaluate Events without confusing operational occurrence with legal tax consequence. TREGA™ is intended to make Tax-Relevant Events governable before tax determination, across digital and physical environments, across organizational and national boundaries, throughout lifecycle change, and at the boundary between Event Reality and jurisdiction-specific tax law. Canonical Principle Economic systems, digital platforms, AI agents, autonomous machines, taxation technologies, and jurisdiction-specific tax laws will continue to change. Tax-Relevant Event Governance must remain stable. TREGA™ therefore governs the methodological conditions that determine what Event exists, within what Context it exists, how it is recognized, formed and bounded, when and where it occurs, who or what materially participates, which governed Value belongs to it, how it relates to other Events, when it becomes tax-relevant, how it remains represented and reconstructable throughout its lifecycle, and when it becomes sufficiently governed to enter jurisdiction-specific taxation analysis. Canonical Closing Statement TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ provides the governance foundation through which real-world, economic, operational, digital, transactional, machine-generated, autonomous, and value-affecting occurrences can be contextualized, recognized, formed into governed Events, bounded, temporally and spatially situated, associated with participants and Value, related to other Events, formally determined as tax-relevant, represented as governed Event Records, and continuously maintained through Event Continuity, Amendment, Correction, Supersession, Closure, and lifecycle re-entry. By defining the independent governable spaces of the complete Tax-Relevant Event lifecycle, TREGA™ establishes a technology-neutral and jurisdiction-neutral methodology for ensuring that taxation systems can consume governed Events without being required to reconstruct operational reality independently or allowing jurisdiction-specific tax interpretation to redefine what originally occurred. TREGA™ therefore establishes the methodological Event layer between Operational Reality and jurisdiction-specific taxation systems, enabling one governed Event to remain structurally coherent, historically reconstructable, interoperable, and Jurisdiction-Ready while multiple jurisdictions independently determine what that Event legally means under their respective tax laws. TREGA™ governs the event. The jurisdiction governs the tax.

title: OOF™ The Event Amendment Module (EADM) governs how a continuing Tax-Relevant
text: OOF™ The Event Amendment Module (EADM) governs how a continuing Tax-Relevant The Event Amendment Module (EADM) governs how a continuing Tax-Relevant OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: TRECLS — Tax-Relevant Event Lifecycle & Continuity Standard Module: EADM — Event Amendment Module Operational Layer: Event Amendment Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Event Amendment Primary Governed Object: Governed Event Amendment State Origin ID: TREGA-TRECLS-EADM-002 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 3 September 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language Canonical Definition The Event Amendment Module (EADM) governs how a continuing Tax-Relevant Event may receive materially relevant additions, refinements, or modifications without treating every legitimate lifecycle update as a Correction or New Event Formation. Its principal transition is: Governed Event Continuity State ↓ Event Amendment Governance ↓ Governed Event Amendment State EADM governs amendments that update the governed Event while preserving legitimate Event Continuity. Its foundational distinction is: Amendment ≠ Correction. And: Amendment ≠ New Event by default. Operational Role After ECOM establishes that the same Event may legitimately continue, new information may need to be incorporated into the governed Event state. That information may not correct an error. It may simply add, refine, or extend what is known. EADM answers: How can new materially relevant information be incorporated into the continuing Event without erasing prior state, misclassifying the change as a correction, or creating a new Event unnecessarily? EADM prevents: silent Event modification; uncontrolled data enrichment; loss of prior Event state; amendment/correction confusion; over-expansion of Event scope; amendment without continuity basis; amendment without materiality assessment; and amendment that improperly overrides upstream governance. Internal Module Flow TRECLS operates through: ECOM — Event Continuity ↓ EADM — Event Amendment ↓ ECRTM — Event Correction ↓ ESPM — Event Supersession ↓ ECLM — Event Closure ↓ Jurisdiction-Ready Tax-Relevant Event EADM receives: Governed Event Continuity State and produces: Governed Event Amendment State for subsequent lifecycle governance. Operational Transition The canonical transition is: Governed Event Continuity State ↓ Amendment Trigger ↓ Amendment Scope ↓ Amendment Assessment ↓ Amendment Integration ↓ Governed Event Amendment State Operational Space EADM governs: Amendment Trigger identification; Amendment eligibility; Amendment scope; Amendment materiality; amendment content; prior-state preservation; current-state update; amendment qualification; Event component refinement; supporting-information addition; Event Context amendment; Participation amendment; Timing amendment reference; Location amendment reference; Value Association amendment reference; Relationship amendment reference; Determination-impact reference; amendment conflict; amendment ambiguity; amendment withdrawal; amendment replacement; amendment continuity; and amendment handoff. Operational Scope EADM may govern amendments within: physical transactions; digital services; commercial transactions; financial activity; platform Events; AI-agent Events; machine-to-machine Events; autonomous systems; distributed environments; digital assets; smart contracts; industrial systems; cross-border activity; multi-party Events; long-running Events; and future machine economies. The module remains technology-neutral and jurisdiction-neutral. Amendment Object The Amendment Object is the materially relevant new or refined information proposed for incorporation into an existing continuing Event. The Amendment Object may modify the governed Event state without asserting that the prior state was wrong. New Information ≠ Prior Error by default. Amendment Trigger An Amendment Trigger may arise from: newly available information; newly identified participant involvement; additional supporting records; refined Event Context; new Location information; expanded Timing information; updated Value Association; new relationship information; later operational development; improved machine-generated information; new cross-system representation; or previously unavailable governed reference. Not every new data point requires formal amendment. Amendment Eligibility An amendment is eligible where: Event Continuity remains valid or sufficiently qualified; the new information belongs to the same governed Event; the change is not primarily the correction of known error; the amendment does not illegitimately redefine Event Formation or Boundary; and the information is materially relevant to Event governance or downstream reliance. Available Information ≠ Eligible Amendment by default. Amendment vs Correction The principal distinction is: Amendment adds or refines legitimate Event information. Correction replaces or rectifies information that was materially wrong or improperly represented. For example: A newly identified supporting participant may require Amendment. A participant that was incorrectly identified may require Correction. Additional Information ≠ Correction by default. Amendment vs New Event An amendment remains within the same Event only while Continuity remains legitimate. Where the proposed change materially alters Event Formation, Event Boundary, or the underlying occurrence, the change may no longer qualify as an Amendment. It may require upstream reassessment or New Event Formation. Amendment Scope EADM shall define which governed part of the Event is being amended. Possible scopes include: Context; Timing; Location; Participation; Value Association; Event Relationships; supporting references; Determination-related qualification; lifecycle metadata. Scope should remain explicit. Amending One Event Component ≠ Reopening the Entire Event by default. Amendment Materiality Amendments should be governed according to materiality. A material amendment may affect: interpretation of Event state; downstream tax evaluation; Continuity; Determination; Event Relationships; Value Association; traceability; jurisdiction readiness. A non-material amendment may only improve metadata or operational clarity. Non-Material Amendment Examples may include: additional internal reference; technical documentation enrichment; supplementary supporting information; non-substantive descriptive clarification. Such amendments should not create unnecessary lifecycle complexity. Material Amendment A Material Amendment changes information sufficiently to affect governed understanding or downstream reliance while still preserving legitimate Event Continuity. Material amendments should remain traceable and clearly distinguishable from prior Event state. Prior-State Preservation Every materially relevant Amendment shall preserve access to the prior governed Event state. The canonical pattern is: Prior Event State ↓ Amendment ↓ Amended Event State not: Prior Event State ↓ Silent Replacement Current Effective State Once validly integrated, the amended state may become the current effective Event state. The prior state remains historically reconstructable. Current Amended State ≠ Only Event State That Ever Existed. Amendment Addition An amendment may add information that was previously unknown. Examples include: additional Event participant; newly identified operational Location; additional Event relationship; supplementary Value reference; new supporting Record. Addition does not automatically imply the earlier Event state was defective. Amendment Refinement An amendment may improve precision. Examples include: more precise Location; better Timing granularity; richer Participant Role information; refined Context; more specific Value reference. Refinement may preserve both Event identity and earlier historical state. Amendment Extension An amendment may extend governed information where the Event is still active or continuing. This is common in long-running digital or machine Events. Extension must not be used to absorb a substantively separate occurrence. Extension ≠ Unlimited Event Expansion. Event Context Amendment TRECS owns Event Context. EADM may incorporate an amended Context result where new context becomes legitimately relevant during Event lifecycle. EADM does not redefine Context independently. Timing Amendment Additional Timing information may become available. Where the prior Timing was not wrong but incomplete, Amendment may be appropriate. If the prior Timing was materially incorrect, ECRTM may instead be required. TRETS remains authoritative. Location Amendment A new operational Location may legitimately be added without correcting an earlier Location. For example, a distributed Event may later involve another valid operational node. Additional Location ≠ Location Correction by default. TRELS remains authoritative over Location. Participation Amendment A continuing Event may acquire additional participants or participant roles. EADM may govern the lifecycle incorporation of those results after TREPS governance. New Participant ≠ New Event by default. Where participant change materially alters Event Formation, ECOM continuity reassessment may be required. Value Association Amendment An additional governed Value Association may be incorporated where the Event remains the same Event. TRVAS owns the Value Association result. VFM® owns the Value lifecycle itself. Event Relationship Amendment A new Event Relationship may become known after the initial Event Record was established. TRERLS governs the relationship. EADM governs the lifecycle incorporation of the resulting relationship information. Supporting Reference Amendment New supporting records may be added to the Event without redefining the Event. Examples include: later invoice; additional settlement record; supporting technical log; contract reference; machine-state record. New Supporting Record ≠ New Event. Determination Impact An Amendment may affect the basis on which TREDS previously determined the Event as tax-relevant. Where material, EADM should trigger or reference TREDS reconsideration. EADM does not independently modify Determination. Amendment Impact ≠ Determination Authority. Amendment Qualification An Amendment may be incorporated with qualification where: supporting information remains incomplete; the amendment scope remains bounded; downstream reliance should be limited; one upstream governance result remains unresolved. Qualification shall remain visible. Amendment Ambiguity Amendment Ambiguity exists where it is unclear: whether new information belongs to the same Event; whether it is amendment or correction; whether the change is material; whether upstream reassessment is required. The amendment shall remain unresolved until sufficient governance exists. Amendment Conflict Conflict exists where materially authoritative governance information supports incompatible amendment outcomes. Examples include: one source supports adding a Participant; another establishes that the actor did not participate; one system extends Event Timing; another authoritative result establishes Event completion earlier. Conflict shall remain explicit. Amendment Rejection A proposed Amendment may be rejected where: the information does not belong to the Event; continuity is invalid; the amendment attempts to overwrite a Correction; it would materially redefine Event Formation or Boundary; governance basis is insufficient; or the amendment would import downstream tax conclusions into canonical Event governance. Amendment Withdrawal A proposed Amendment may be withdrawn before becoming effective. Withdrawal should preserve relevant governance history where material. Withdrawn Amendment ≠ Never-Proposed Amendment. Amendment Replacement A proposed Amendment may be replaced by a more complete or authoritative Amendment before final integration. Replacement should not silently erase earlier materially relevant lifecycle state. Amendment Sequence An Event may undergo multiple amendments: Original State ↓ Amendment A ↓ Amendment B ↓ Amendment C Each materially relevant Amendment should remain reconstructable. Multiple amendments do not automatically create multiple Events. Amendment Continuity Where an Amendment materially changes the Event enough to call Continuity into question, EADM shall return the case to ECOM. Valid Prior Continuity ≠ Permanent Continuity Guarantee. Cross-System Amendment An amendment may originate in a different system from the one holding the canonical Event Record. The amendment should be associated with the same governed Event identity. Different systems do not create different amendment realities by default. Cross-Organization Amendment Different organizations may contribute legitimate Event updates. EADM shall preserve the distinction between: amendment source; amendment authority; canonical Event state. External Contribution ≠ Automatic Canonical Amendment. Cross-Border Amendment New cross-border information may amend the Event. For example: new operational Location; new Participant; new Value Association; new Event Relationship. The amendment itself remains jurisdiction-neutral. Cross-Border Amendment ≠ Tax Jurisdiction Determination. Machine-Generated Amendment Autonomous systems may propose amendments automatically. Examples include: additional machine participant; refined sensor-derived Timing; new supporting transaction reference; newly correlated Value information. Automated generation does not eliminate governance requirements. Machine-Generated Update ≠ Governed Amendment by default. Amendment Frequency High-frequency systems may generate many candidate amendments. Formal lifecycle governance should apply only where changes are materially relevant. More Updates ≠ More Amendments by default. Amendment and Historical Reconstruction Amendments should preserve sufficient information to reconstruct: prior Event state; amendment trigger; amendment scope; amendment basis; amended state; current effective state. ERTM remains authoritative for Record Traceability. Amendment and Record Governance TREGS owns Record identity, structure, linkage, traceability, and interoperability. EADM governs the Event lifecycle effect of amendment. The Event Record may then need to be updated through TREGS-compatible mechanisms. Event Amendment ≠ Record Mutation by default. Amendment and Tax Law A jurisdiction may react to an Amendment by: reassessing tax; requiring new filing; changing Tax Base; changing legal treatment. Those are downstream outcomes. Event Amendment ≠ Tax Reassessment Decision. Governance States EADM may represent: Amendment Governance Not Initiated Amendment Trigger Identified Amendment Candidate Identified Amendment Eligibility Under Review Amendment Eligible Amendment Scope Defined Amendment Non-Material Amendment Material Amendment Under Review Amendment Qualified Amendment Ambiguous Amendment Conflicted Upstream Review Required Continuity Reassessment Required Amendment Rejected Amendment Withdrawn Amendment Integrated Governed Event Amendment State Established Ready for Correction Governance Governance Requirements EADM implementations shall ensure that: a valid Governed Event Continuity State exists; the proposed change belongs to the continuing Event; Amendment remains distinct from Correction; Amendment remains distinct from New Event Formation; amendment scope is explicit where material; amendment materiality is assessed; materially relevant prior Event state remains reconstructable; current amended state remains distinguishable from prior state; additional information is not automatically treated as prior error; amendment does not independently redefine upstream TREGA™ results; Context, Timing, Location, Participation, Value Association, and Relationship amendments use authoritative upstream governance where required; Determination impact is referred to TREDS where material; qualified amendments remain explicit; ambiguity and conflict remain visible; rejected or withdrawn material amendments remain reconstructable where necessary; amendments do not silently absorb substantively separate occurrences; continuity is reassessed where amendment materiality challenges same-Event identity; machine-generated changes are not automatically accepted; high-frequency update volume does not determine amendment count; downstream tax conclusions remain outside amendment governance; and the resulting Event state is suitable for subsequent TRECLS lifecycle governance. Governance Logic IF no valid Governed Event Continuity State exists, THEN EADM shall not establish a canonical Event Amendment. IF new information does not belong to the same governed Event, THEN it shall not be integrated as an Amendment. IF the change primarily rectifies materially incorrect information, THEN the change shall be referred to ECRTM rather than treated as Amendment. IF the change adds or refines materially relevant information while Event Continuity remains valid, THEN Amendment Governance may proceed. IF amendment scope materially changes Event Formation or Boundary, THEN continuity shall be reassessed before integration. IF a material Amendment affects Event Determination, THEN TREDS reconsideration shall be triggered or referenced. IF Amendment information is materially ambiguous or conflicted, THEN it shall remain qualified or unresolved rather than silently integrated. IF the proposed Amendment contains downstream legal tax conclusions, THEN those conclusions shall remain outside canonical Event Amendment. IF a proposed Amendment is withdrawn or rejected, THEN it shall not become the current effective Event state. IF the Amendment is validly governed and integrated, THEN the amended Event state may become the current effective state while the prior state remains historically reconstructable. Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum EADM implementation should support: Amendment Governance ID A stable identifier for the EADM governance process. Canonical Event Reference The Event being amended. Governed Event Continuity State Reference The applicable ECOM output. Prior Event State Reference The state existing before Amendment. Amendment Trigger Type New Information, Additional Participant, Context Refinement, Timing Extension, Location Addition, Value Association Addition, Relationship Addition, Supporting Reference Addition, or other governed trigger. Amendment Candidate Reference The proposed amendment information. Amendment Scope The Event component or governance area affected. Amendment Type Addition, Refinement, Extension, Supporting Reference, Qualification Update, or other governed type. Amendment Materiality State Non-Material, Material, Critical, Unresolved. Amendment Eligibility State Eligible, Qualified, Ineligible, Unresolved. Amendment Basis Reference The governance or information basis for the Amendment. Context Amendment Reference Any TRECS-related amendment. Timing Amendment Reference Any TRETS-related amendment. Location Amendment Reference Any TRELS-related amendment. Participation Amendment Reference Any TREPS-related amendment. Value Association Amendment Reference Any TRVAS-related amendment. Relationship Amendment Reference Any TRERLS-related amendment. Determination Impact State None, Potential, Material, Reconsideration Required. Determination Reconsideration Reference Any TREDS reconsideration reference. Amendment Qualification Any limitations attached to the Amendment. Amendment Ambiguity State Whether amendment meaning or eligibility remains uncertain. Amendment Conflict State Whether materially incompatible amendment conclusions exist. Continuity Reassessment State Whether ECOM reassessment is required. Amendment Withdrawal State Whether the proposed Amendment was withdrawn. Amendment Replacement Reference Any superseding Amendment candidate. Current Effective Event State Reference The Event state after valid Amendment integration. Historical Amendment Reference Prior materially relevant Amendment state. Governance State The current EADM governance state. Amendment Outcome Integrated, Qualified, Rejected, Withdrawn, or Unresolved. Handoff State Whether the Event is ready for subsequent TRECLS lifecycle governance. Governance Outputs EADM may produce: Amendment Trigger State; Amendment Candidate; Amendment Eligibility State; Amendment Scope; Amendment Type; Amendment Materiality State; Amendment Basis Reference; Amendment Qualification; Amendment Ambiguity State; Amendment Conflict State; Context Amendment Reference; Timing Amendment Reference; Location Amendment Reference; Participation Amendment Reference; Value Association Amendment Reference; Relationship Amendment Reference; Determination Impact State; Continuity Reassessment State; Amendment Withdrawal State; Amendment Replacement Reference; Current Effective Event State; and the principal output: Governed Event Amendment State. Critical Distinctions Amendment ≠ Correction. Amendment ≠ New Event by default. New Information ≠ Prior Error by default. Available Information ≠ Eligible Amendment by default. Additional Information ≠ Correction by default. Amending One Event Component ≠ Reopening the Entire Event by default. Current Amended State ≠ Only Event State That Ever Existed. Extension ≠ Unlimited Event Expansion. Additional Location ≠ Location Correction by default. New Participant ≠ New Event by default. New Supporting Record ≠ New Event. Amendment Impact ≠ Determination Authority. Withdrawn Amendment ≠ Never-Proposed Amendment. Valid Prior Continuity ≠ Permanent Continuity Guarantee. External Contribution ≠ Automatic Canonical Amendment. Cross-Border Amendment ≠ Tax Jurisdiction Determination. Machine-Generated Update ≠ Governed Amendment by default. More Updates ≠ More Amendments by default. Event Amendment ≠ Record Mutation by default. Event Amendment ≠ Tax Reassessment Decision. Enterprise Application EADM provides the controlled update layer that allows a governed Event to absorb legitimate new information without destabilizing Event identity. The operational pattern is: Governed Event Continuity State → New Information → Amendment Eligibility → Amendment Scope & Materiality → Amendment Integration → Governed Event Amendment State Where the proposed change is actually an error correction: Amendment Candidate ↓ ECRTM — Event Correction Governance Where the proposed change threatens continuity: Amendment Candidate ↓ ECOM — Continuity Reassessment This prevents ordinary lifecycle updates from becoming either uncontrolled Record edits or unnecessary New Event Formation. Use Case 1 — New Participant Added to a Continuing Digital Service Event A cross-border digital service Event has already been governed and remains active. After the original Record was created, another platform is identified as having materially participated in execution. The original Event was not wrong when first governed; the additional participation information simply was not previously available. TREPS establishes the new Participation result. EADM governs its lifecycle incorporation: Existing Event State ↓ New Participation Information ↓ Amendment Eligible ↓ Amended Event State The Event remains continuous. The prior Event state remains historically reconstructable. No Correction or New Event Formation is required solely because another legitimate participant became known. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Event Receives Additional Value Association An autonomous machine Event has already been governed. Later, a newly completed operational stage creates an additional Value Association that belongs to the same continuing Event. TRVAS governs the Value Association. ECOM confirms Event Continuity. EADM integrates the additional Value Association into the current Event state. The lifecycle becomes: Prior Event State ↓ Additional Governed Value Association ↓ Material Amendment ↓ Amended Current Event State If the new Value relationship had instead represented a substantively separate occurrence, ECOM would require continuity reassessment rather than allowing EADM to expand the original Event indefinitely. Canonical Boundary EADM owns the governance of Event Amendment eligibility, Amendment Triggers, Amendment scope, Amendment type, Amendment materiality, incorporation of legitimate new or refined information, prior-state preservation, current amended state, amendment qualification, ambiguity, conflict, withdrawal, replacement, continuity reassessment triggers, and establishment of the Governed Event Amendment State. EADM does not determine whether the Event remains continuous; ECOM owns Event Continuity. It does not govern correction of materially wrong information; ECRTM owns Event Correction. It does not govern Event Supersession or Closure. It does not independently redefine Event Context, Formation, Boundary, Timing, Location, Participation, Value Association, Event Relationships, or Event Determination. It does not determine legal Taxability, Tax Jurisdiction, taxpayer status, Tax Base, Tax Rate, legal tax point, Tax Period, Tax Liability, reassessment obligations, filing requirements, or other jurisdiction-specific tax consequences. Its governance begins with a valid: Governed Event Continuity State and a proposed or required Event Amendment. Its governance ends with: Governed Event Amendment State or with referral to: ECOM for Continuity Reassessment or: ECRTM where Correction Governance is required. Canonical Handoff ECOM — Governed Event Continuity State ↓ EADM — Governed Event Amendment State ↓ ECRTM — Event Correction Governance Where continuity becomes materially uncertain: EADM ↓ ECOM — Continuity Reassessment Canonical Closing Statement EADM allows a governed Event to learn more about itself without pretending that every new fact corrects an error or creates a new Event. Amendment preserves legitimate Event evolution while keeping prior state, continuity, and upstream governance boundaries intact. Amendment ≠ Correction. Amendment ≠ New Event by default. New Information ≠ Prior Error.

title: OOF™ Event Boundary Exclusion Module (EBEM)
text: OOF™ Event Boundary Exclusion Module (EBEM) Event Boundary Exclusion Module (EBEM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: Tax-Relevant Event Boundary Standard (TREBS) Module: EBEM — Event Boundary Exclusion Module Operational Layer: Event Boundary Exclusion Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Event Boundary Exclusion Origin ID: TREGA-TREBS-EBEM-003 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 30 August 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English ------------------------------ Canonical Definition The Event Boundary Exclusion Module (EBEM) governs how elements provisionally associated with or contained within a Governed Event Boundary Scope are evaluated and, where materially justified, excluded from the governed Event Boundary because they represent surrounding activity, dependencies, contextual conditions, technical artifacts, supporting infrastructure, independent operational structures, or other non-member elements. EBEM establishes the negative side of Event Boundary governance: what must not remain inside the event merely because it is related, connected, proximate, technically linked, or operationally supportive. Its specific task is: to establish a governed Event Boundary Exclusion Structure that removes materially unjustified scope elements while preserving their relevant external relationships, traceability, and downstream governance significance. EBEM governs what must remain outside the event. It does not yet determine whether excluded or adjacent structures constitute separate governed events or how multiple events must be separated from one another. ------------------------------ Operational Role EBSCM establishes: what provisionally belongs within the Event Boundary Scope. EBEM asks: which of those provisionally associated elements must not remain inside the governed Event Boundary? This distinction is essential. Positive scope governance identifies a sufficiently coherent candidate extent. Exclusion governance then tests that scope for elements that are materially relevant but do not legitimately belong to the event itself. Therefore: Scope Membership Candidate ≠ Final Boundary Membership. And: Operational Relevance ≠ Event Membership. EBEM protects the boundary from uncontrolled expansion through related, dependent, supporting, contextual, or technically adjacent activity. ------------------------------ Internal Flow Governed Event Boundary Scope ↓ Exclusion Candidate Identification ↓ Exclusion Basis Assessment ↓ Membership Reassessment ↓ External Relevance Preservation ↓ Exclusion Conflict / Uncertainty Handling ↓ Governed Event Boundary Exclusion Structure ↓ EBSM — Event Boundary Separation Module ------------------------------ Operational Space EBEM operates within the governance space where potentially included elements must be tested for legitimate exclusion from the Event Boundary. Its Operational Space includes: Exclusion Candidate identification exclusion basis assessment surrounding-activity exclusion dependency exclusion context-only exclusion technical-artifact exclusion duplicate-representation exclusion supporting-infrastructure exclusion non-member participant activity exclusion non-member machine activity exclusion external value-related activity exclusion external process-stage exclusion external relationship preservation exclusion ambiguity exclusion conflict exclusion uncertainty exclusion qualification exclusion traceability EBEM governs boundary exclusion. It does not own Event Separation between distinct governed event candidates. ------------------------------ Operational Scope EBEM may govern exclusions involving: commercial activity financial activity digital services platform operations distributed systems autonomous systems AI agents robotic operations machine-to-machine interactions payments logistics production infrastructure digital assets service execution enterprise workflows hybrid physical-digital activity future machine economies The module remains actor-neutral, technology-neutral, organization-neutral, and jurisdiction-neutral. An element may be excluded regardless of whether it was created by a human, enterprise, machine, autonomous system, API, robot, platform, or distributed infrastructure. ------------------------------ Exclusion Principle A valid Event Boundary must not absorb every element that helps explain, enable, evidence, support, or relate to the event. Many operational structures can be relevant without being members of the event. Therefore: Relevant ≠ Included. And more specifically: Related Activity ≠ Event Membership. EBEM exists to make this distinction explicit. ------------------------------ Exclusion Candidate An Exclusion Candidate is an element currently associated with the Governed Event Boundary Scope whose continued inclusion requires reassessment. Possible Exclusion Candidates may include: background activity contextual information supporting infrastructure prior dependencies later dependencies technical copies duplicate representations monitoring records authentication events administrative records accounting representations platform-management operations unrelated machine actions shared resource operations surrounding contractual structures Candidate status does not establish exclusion. Therefore: Exclusion Candidate ≠ Excluded Element. ------------------------------ Exclusion Basis An element should be excluded only where a governed basis demonstrates that it does not legitimately form part of the event's structural extent. Possible exclusion bases may include: the element is merely contextual the element is a dependency rather than event membership the element is technical representation only the element duplicates another governed representation the element is background infrastructure the element belongs to a surrounding process the element is operationally related but structurally independent the element supports several unrelated events the element belongs to another formation candidate inclusion would materially distort the event inclusion would cause uncontrolled event expansion Exclusion must remain reasoned and traceable. Exclusion Convenience ≠ Exclusion Legitimacy. ------------------------------ Dependency Exclusion Formation Dependencies are a major source of Event Boundary over-expansion. A formed event may depend on prior authorization, infrastructure, delegated authority, an account relationship, a platform relationship, or a prior operational state. Those dependencies may remain relevant. They do not automatically belong inside the Event Boundary. Therefore: Qualified Formation Dependency ≠ Event Membership. EBEM may explicitly exclude such dependencies while preserving their association with the event. This maintains the distinction established earlier by EFDM. ------------------------------ Context Exclusion TRECS may establish extensive context around the occurrence. That context can remain important throughout the TREGA™ lifecycle. But contextual relevance does not mean boundary inclusion. Examples may include: market conditions organizational environment infrastructure state prior contractual framework system configuration broader business process surrounding supply-chain activity Therefore: Context Relevance ≠ Event Membership. EBEM may exclude context-only elements while preserving their contextual references. ------------------------------ Technical Artifact Exclusion Operational systems frequently produce records that appear closely attached to the event but represent only technical implementation. Examples include: API retries synchronization messages database replication telemetry logging system-status messages internal reconciliation records cache operations monitoring records duplicated ledger views Such elements may be useful for evidence, auditability, or technical reconstruction. They do not automatically belong to the governed event. Therefore: Technical Trace ≠ Event Membership. ------------------------------ Shared Infrastructure Exclusion An event may rely on infrastructure used by many unrelated activities. Examples include: cloud infrastructure payment networks energy grids identity services shared production lines network infrastructure distributed ledgers warehouse systems Use of the same infrastructure does not make that infrastructure part of each event. Therefore: Shared Infrastructure ≠ Shared Event Membership. EBEM must prevent infrastructure dependency from becoming unlimited event scope. ------------------------------ Shared Participant Activity The same participant may perform multiple activities around one event. Not all of those activities must belong inside the Event Boundary. For example, a provider may: authenticate a customer perform the service issue an invoice provide unrelated support process a later complaint The shared participant does not collapse these activities into one event. Therefore: Same Participant ≠ Same Event Membership. Participation itself is later governed by TREPS. ------------------------------ Temporal Proximity Activity occurring shortly before or after an event may appear to belong within it. Temporal closeness may provide useful information. It does not independently determine Event Boundary membership. Therefore: Temporal Proximity ≠ Event Membership. Event Timing is governed later by TRETS. EBEM must not convert time proximity into automatic inclusion or exclusion. ------------------------------ Spatial and Digital Proximity Activities may occur: at the same physical location within the same data center within the same platform inside the same digital environment through the same API ecosystem This proximity may be operationally relevant. It does not establish Event Membership. Therefore: Shared Location ≠ Shared Event Boundary. And: Shared Digital Environment ≠ Shared Event Membership. Event Location belongs later to TRELS. ------------------------------ Contractual Relationship A contract may govern numerous operational events over time. Conversely, one event may involve several contractual structures. Therefore: Same Contract ≠ Same Event Boundary. EBEM must prevent contractual packaging from automatically becoming event membership logic. ------------------------------ Accounting Relationship Accounting systems may group several activities under: one ledger entry one invoice one settlement one accounting period one cost center one journal reference Such grouping may be useful for financial reporting. It does not automatically govern Event Membership. Therefore: Accounting Grouping ≠ Event Boundary Membership. ------------------------------ Commercial Relationship Long-running commercial relationships may generate many events. A customer, provider, marketplace, or supplier relationship can continue for years. The existence of that relationship does not make the whole relationship one event. Therefore: Commercial Relationship ≠ Event Membership. EBEM excludes relationship-level structures where they do not legitimately belong inside the event. ------------------------------ Excluded ≠ Irrelevant Exclusion is not equivalent to deletion, rejection, or irrelevance.
