An excluded element may remain important for: context dependencies evidence event relationships validation auditability accountability later legal analysis tax analysis operational reconstruction Therefore: Excluded from Event Boundary ≠ Removed from Governance. This is a foundational EBEM principle. ------------------------------ External Relationship Preservation When an element is excluded, EBEM should preserve relevant association with the event. Possible external associations may include: dependency reference contextual reference supporting-system reference prior-event reference subsequent-event reference evidential reference participant reference infrastructure reference This prevents exclusion from destroying operational understanding. ------------------------------ Exclusion and Event Separation Some Exclusion Candidates may appear to represent independent event structures. EBEM must not decide whether they constitute separate events. That belongs to: EBSM — Event Boundary Separation Module. EBEM may identify: Potential Independent Structure or Separation Review Required but must not complete the separation itself. Therefore: Boundary Exclusion ≠ Event Separation. ------------------------------ Exclusion Ambiguity In some cases, it may remain unclear whether an element belongs within or outside the Event Boundary. Possible exclusion states include: Exclusion Candidate Excluded Retained in Scope Exclusion Qualified Exclusion Conflict Exclusion Unresolved EBEM must preserve uncertainty where the governance basis remains insufficient. Uncertain Membership ≠ Automatic Exclusion. Likewise: Uncertain Membership ≠ Automatic Inclusion. ------------------------------ Exclusion Conflict Different systems may support different membership conclusions. For example: the ERP may treat a payment settlement as part of the commercial transaction. The marketplace may treat it as a separate financial operation. The payment system may represent it independently. EBEM must not silently privilege one system. Where the conflict cannot yet be resolved, it must remain governed. System Ownership ≠ Boundary Authority. ------------------------------ Exclusion Traceability Every material exclusion should remain reconstructable. Traceability may preserve: excluded element prior scope status exclusion basis supporting information external relationship retained uncertainty or conflict decision state downstream separation flag later reconsideration reference This ensures that exclusion does not become unexplained disappearance. ------------------------------ Machine and Autonomous Exclusion Machine systems may generate large amounts of supporting activity that should remain outside the Event Boundary. Examples include: sensor activity internal optimization resource monitoring load balancing machine-health checks technical retries background model inference orchestration messages These operations may surround an economically meaningful machine-generated event. They should not automatically become event members. Therefore: Machine Support Activity ≠ Event Membership by Default. Similarly: Autonomous Internal Decision ≠ Event Membership by Default. Only materially relevant event structure should remain inside the boundary. ------------------------------ Distributed Systems A distributed event may involve many technical systems. Some systems may contribute materially to the event. Others may only host, transmit, replicate, monitor, or support the activity. EBEM must distinguish the two. Therefore: Distributed Presence ≠ Boundary Membership. An element may exist across the infrastructure without forming part of the governed event itself. ------------------------------ Governance Requirements EBEM requires that: 1. Exclusion governance begins from a Governed Event Boundary Scope. 2. Exclusion Candidates are explicitly identified. 3. exclusion is supported by a governed basis. 4. operational relevance is distinguished from Event Membership. 5. context does not automatically become Event Membership. 6. dependencies do not automatically become Event Membership. 7. technical artifacts do not automatically become Event Membership. 8. shared infrastructure does not automatically become Event Membership. 9. same participant does not automatically establish common Event Membership. 10. temporal proximity does not automatically establish Event Membership. 11. spatial or digital proximity does not automatically establish Event Membership. 12. contractual grouping does not automatically establish Event Membership. 13. accounting grouping does not automatically establish Event Membership. 14. commercial relationship does not automatically establish Event Membership. 15. excluded elements retain relevant external associations where materially necessary. 16. exclusion does not erase traceability. 17. uncertain membership remains explicitly governed. 18. potential independent event structures are transferred to EBSM rather than separated within EBEM. 19. EBEM remains independent of Tax Jurisdiction and legal taxability. ------------------------------ Governance Logic EBEM applies the following logic: Does this provisionally scoped element materially belong inside the Event Boundary itself? If yes: → retain the element within Event Boundary Scope. If the element is relevant but structurally external: → exclude it while preserving its external association. If the element is a dependency: → preserve the dependency relationship without automatic Event Membership. If the element is a technical artifact or duplicate representation: → exclude it from boundary membership while preserving evidential or technical traceability where relevant. If the element may represent an independent event structure: → flag it for EBSM. If the membership basis remains materially uncertain: → preserve the unresolved state. The transformation is: Governed Event Boundary Scope → Exclusion Candidates → Exclusion Basis → Membership Reassessment → Governed Exclusions → Governed Event Boundary Exclusion Structure ------------------------------ Minimum Implementation Framework A conforming implementation of EBEM must be capable of: 1. receiving the Governed Event Boundary Scope from EBSCM 2. identifying Exclusion Candidates 3. assessing exclusion basis 4. distinguishing structural membership from contextual relevance 5. distinguishing structural membership from dependency 6. identifying technical-only and duplicate representations 7. identifying supporting infrastructure that should remain external 8. preserving external associations after exclusion 9. representing retained, excluded, qualified, conflicting, and unresolved membership states 10. preserving exclusion traceability 11. identifying potential independent event structures requiring EBSM review 12. producing a Governed Event Boundary Exclusion Structure 13. transferring that structure to EBSM 14. preventing exclusion governance from becoming Event Separation, Event Relationship, Tax Jurisdiction, or taxability determination ------------------------------ Governance Outputs EBEM may produce: Governed Event Boundary Exclusion Structure Excluded Boundary Element Retained Boundary Element Exclusion Candidate Record Exclusion Basis Record External Relationship Reference Dependency-Preserved Exclusion Technical Artifact Exclusion Duplicate Representation Exclusion Exclusion Conflict Indicator Exclusion Uncertainty Indicator Separation Review Required Indicator Exclusion Traceability Record Its principal governed output is: Governed Event Boundary Exclusion Structure This output proceeds to: EBSM — Event Boundary Separation Module ------------------------------ Critical Distinctions Relevant ≠ Included Related Activity ≠ Event Membership Scope Membership Candidate ≠ Final Boundary Membership Exclusion Candidate ≠ Excluded Element Exclusion Convenience ≠ Exclusion Legitimacy Qualified Formation Dependency ≠ Event Membership Context Relevance ≠ Event Membership Technical Trace ≠ Event Membership Shared Infrastructure ≠ Shared Event Membership Same Participant ≠ Same Event Membership Temporal Proximity ≠ Event Membership Shared Location ≠ Shared Event Boundary Shared Digital Environment ≠ Shared Event Membership Same Contract ≠ Same Event Boundary Accounting Grouping ≠ Event Boundary Membership Commercial Relationship ≠ Event Membership Excluded from Event Boundary ≠ Removed from Governance Boundary Exclusion ≠ Event Separation Uncertain Membership ≠ Automatic Exclusion Uncertain Membership ≠ Automatic Inclusion System Ownership ≠ Boundary Authority Machine Support Activity ≠ Event Membership by Default Distributed Presence ≠ Boundary Membership Event Boundary Exclusion ≠ Tax Jurisdiction Event Boundary Exclusion ≠ Taxability Determination ------------------------------ Enterprise Application Enterprise systems routinely carry far more information around an event than should belong inside the event itself. A commercial transaction may be surrounded by: Account Data ↓ Authentication ↓ Contract Framework ↓ Platform Operations ↓ Payment Infrastructure ↓ Logistics Infrastructure ↓ ERP Processing ↓ Reporting Systems All of those structures may be relevant. None should automatically become part of the Event Boundary. Without EBEM, event records may expand until they effectively represent the entire enterprise process or system environment. EBEM creates the governed exclusion layer that keeps the event structurally bounded while preserving important external relationships. ------------------------------ Use Case 1 — Global Marketplace Event Absorbs Too Much Supporting Activity A global marketplace processes one governed transaction. The Event Boundary Scope currently contains: customer order seller acceptance fulfilment activity payment execution customer authentication seller onboarding record marketplace account relationship payment-network infrastructure warehouse platform activity historical supplier agreement All of these structures are operationally related. But several do not legitimately belong inside the event. EBEM may exclude: prior customer authentication as supporting context seller onboarding as prior activity the marketplace account relationship as background relationship payment-network infrastructure as shared infrastructure the historical supplier agreement as external contractual context while preserving their relationships to the event. The result is a narrower, more coherent event representation. Relevant commercial infrastructure remains visible without becoming event membership. ------------------------------ Use Case 2 — Autonomous Factory Event Is Surrounded by Thousands of Machine Operations An autonomous production system executes a governed manufacturing event. Its Event Boundary Scope contains material production actions but also thousands of: sensor checks predictive-maintenance calculations background AI inference energy-balancing operations internal machine synchronization network messages shared robotic calibration actions plant-wide infrastructure monitoring These operations are related to the production environment. Many may be necessary for safe or efficient execution. But they do not automatically belong inside the governed event. EBEM excludes structurally external machine-support activity while preserving relevant technical, evidential, dependency, or infrastructure references. The result prevents the manufacturing event from expanding into the entire factory operating system. Operational support does not become Event Membership merely because the event depended upon it. ------------------------------ Canonical Boundary EBEM governs the identification, assessment, exclusion, retention, external-association preservation, ambiguity, conflict, uncertainty, and traceability of elements that should remain outside a Governed Event Boundary despite being related to, supportive of, dependent upon, proximate to, or technically associated with the event. It does not define the original Candidate Event Boundary, establish the positive Event Boundary Scope, determine whether excluded structures constitute separate governed events, perform Event Boundary Separation, revise previously established Event Boundaries, determine Event Timing, Event Location, Event Participation, Event Relationships, Tax Jurisdiction, legal taxability, or jurisdiction-specific tax consequences. ------------------------------ Module Handoff EBSCM — Governed Event Boundary Scope ↓ EBEM — Governed Event Boundary Exclusion Structure ↓ EBSM — Event Boundary Separation Module ------------------------------ Canonical Closing Statement The Event Boundary Exclusion Module establishes the governed negative perimeter of the event by determining what must remain outside the Event Boundary even when that activity remains operationally relevant, technically connected, contextually important, or materially supportive. EBEM prevents dependencies, context, infrastructure, technical artifacts, shared participants, contractual structures, accounting representations, and machine-support activity from causing uncontrolled expansion of the event. It preserves excluded elements as governed external relationships rather than deleting them from the event's broader governance environment. EBEM determines what must remain outside the event — while EBSM subsequently determines whether any excluded or adjacent structure must be governed as a separate event.

title: OOF™ Event Boundary Identification Module (EBIM)
text: OOF™ Event Boundary Identification Module (EBIM) Event Boundary Identification Module (EBIM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: Tax-Relevant Event Boundary Standard (TREBS) Module: EBIM — Event Boundary Identification Module Operational Layer: Event Boundary Identification Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Event Boundary Identification Origin ID: TREGA-TREBS-EBIM-001 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 30 August 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English ------------------------------ Canonical Definition The Event Boundary Identification Module (EBIM) governs how the potential structural perimeter of a sufficiently formed event is identified before its detailed scope, exclusions, separation conditions, or subsequent boundary revisions are established. EBIM receives a Governed Formed Event from the Tax-Relevant Event Formation Standard (TREFS) and identifies the materially relevant structural limits that may define where the event begins, where it ends, and where surrounding operational activity may require distinction. Its specific task is: to establish an evidence-linked Candidate Event Boundary that can legitimately proceed into Event Boundary Scope governance without treating technical, commercial, organizational, platform, or machine structures as authoritative Event Boundaries by default. EBIM identifies the candidate boundary. It does not finalize the complete Event Boundary. ------------------------------ Operational Role Event Formation establishes what has been structurally formed as an event. EBIM establishes where the potential structural perimeter of that formed event appears to lie. This distinction is fundamental. A formed event may contain a coherent internal structure while its precise perimeter relative to surrounding activity remains unresolved. Therefore: Formed Event ≠ Bounded Event. And: Candidate Event Boundary ≠ Final Event Boundary. EBIM provides the first governed transition from Event Formation into Event Boundary governance. ------------------------------ Internal Flow Governed Formed Event ↓ Boundary Signal Identification ↓ Candidate Boundary Element Identification ↓ Boundary Anchor Assessment ↓ Boundary Perimeter Construction ↓ Boundary Ambiguity Detection ↓ Candidate Event Boundary ↓ EBSCM — Event Boundary Scope Module ------------------------------ Operational Space EBIM operates within the governance space where a formed event must be distinguished from surrounding operational reality. Its Operational Space includes: identification of potential Event Boundary signals identification of candidate boundary elements recognition of possible beginning and ending limits identification of structural perimeter indicators assessment of potential boundary anchors detection of competing boundary representations detection of incomplete boundary information detection of ambiguous boundary conditions identification of technical structures incorrectly presenting themselves as boundaries identification of commercial structures incorrectly presenting themselves as boundaries identification of machine or autonomous execution structures incorrectly presenting themselves as boundaries traceability of the basis used to identify the Candidate Event Boundary EBIM governs boundary identification, not complete boundary adjudication. ------------------------------ Operational Scope EBIM applies to formed events arising from: commercial transactions financial operations contractual activity digital services platform activity distributed systems autonomous agents AI systems robotic operations machine-to-machine activity infrastructure operations digital assets value-affecting processes mixed physical-digital activity future machine economies The module is actor-neutral and technology-neutral. The same governance logic applies whether the underlying activity was performed by humans, organizations, software, autonomous systems, machines, or combinations of them. ------------------------------ Boundary Signals A Candidate Event Boundary may be indicated by multiple forms of operational information. Potential Boundary Signals may include: initiation or termination of a materially coherent activity transition between materially distinct operational structures completion of a defined operational objective change in the governed formation structure emergence of an independent operational result separation between coordinated but distinguishable activities discontinuity in operational execution transition between materially different participant structures transition between materially different value-affecting structures separation between independently reconstructable operational occurrences No individual signal automatically establishes the Event Boundary. Boundary Signal ≠ Event Boundary. Boundary Signals provide governed inputs for identification. ------------------------------ Candidate Boundary Elements EBIM identifies the elements that may contribute to the structural perimeter of the event. A Candidate Boundary Element may represent: a beginning indicator an ending indicator a structural transition an operational separation point an interface with surrounding activity a transition into another formed event a discontinuity requiring further boundary analysis Candidate Boundary Elements must remain traceable to the underlying Governed Formed Event and supporting operational information. Candidate Boundary Element ≠ Confirmed Boundary Element. Confirmation of what belongs within the Event Boundary is handled through subsequent Boundary Scope governance. ------------------------------ Boundary Anchors Operational systems frequently contain apparent boundary anchors. These may include: order IDs invoice numbers payment IDs settlement records shipment numbers contract identifiers workflow instances API sessions database transactions machine jobs robotic tasks autonomous objectives blockchain transactions accounting entries Such anchors may provide useful evidence. They must not become authoritative Event Boundaries merely because they exist. Therefore: Technical Identifier ≠ Event Boundary. Commercial Identifier ≠ Event Boundary. Workflow Boundary ≠ Governed Event Boundary by Default. Machine Task Boundary ≠ Governed Event Boundary by Default. EBIM evaluates these structures as possible boundary evidence rather than accepting them as boundary truth. ------------------------------ Multiple Boundary Representations The same formed event may be represented differently across systems. For example: Marketplace ↓ Order Bank ↓ Settlement ERP ↓ Invoice Logistics Platform ↓ Shipment Machine System ↓ Execution Objective These representations may describe different aspects of the same operational reality. EBIM must therefore allow multiple Candidate Boundary representations to coexist where the available information does not yet justify one dominant interpretation. Multiple Representations ≠ Multiple Events by Default. Likewise: One Shared Representation ≠ One Event by Default. ------------------------------ Boundary Ambiguity A Candidate Event Boundary may remain ambiguous. Ambiguity may arise where: beginning or ending indicators conflict different systems represent different perimeters formation structures overlap operational activity is continuous distributed systems lack a single termination point autonomous systems execute continuously commercial and operational structures diverge available evidence does not sufficiently distinguish surrounding activity EBIM must preserve such ambiguity rather than forcing artificial precision. Possible identification states include: Boundary Candidate Identified Boundary Candidate Ambiguous Multiple Boundary Candidates Boundary Candidate Insufficient Boundary Identification Unresolved Uncertainty must remain visible for downstream governance. ------------------------------ Continuous and Distributed Activity Some events do not contain obvious physical or technical start and end points. Examples include: continuous cloud services streaming digital services autonomous infrastructure distributed compute operations algorithmic trading systems machine networks continuous manufacturing subscription-based digital activity persistent AI-agent operations EBIM must therefore support boundary identification without requiring a single transaction record or discrete technical execution. Continuous Operation ≠ Boundaryless Event. Where operational reality is continuous, the Candidate Event Boundary must be identified from materially meaningful structural distinctions rather than arbitrary technical segmentation. ------------------------------ Autonomous and Machine-Generated Events Machine systems can generate extremely large numbers of operational actions. EBIM must prevent those actions from automatically becoming independent Event Boundaries. A robot movement, API request, model invocation, machine instruction, sensor event, compute allocation, or automated payment step may contribute to a larger event without defining its perimeter. Likewise, one autonomous objective may generate multiple materially distinguishable events. Therefore: Machine Action ≠ Event Boundary by Default. Autonomous Objective ≠ Single Event Boundary by Default. The governed boundary must follow operational structure rather than machine execution granularity. ------------------------------ Governance Requirements EBIM requires that: 1. Boundary identification begins from a Governed Formed Event. 2. Potential Boundary Signals are identified before a Candidate Event Boundary is established. 3. Technical identifiers are treated as evidence rather than authoritative boundaries. 4. Commercial identifiers do not automatically determine Event Boundaries. 5. Workflow structures do not automatically determine Event Boundaries. 6. Machine and autonomous execution structures remain subject to the same governed boundary logic as human activity. 7. Competing Candidate Boundaries remain visible where unresolved. 8. Boundary ambiguity is preserved rather than artificially resolved. 9. Boundary identification remains traceable to supporting operational information. 10. Event Boundary identification remains independent of jurisdiction-specific tax consequences. 11. EBIM does not determine detailed Boundary Scope. 12. EBIM does not perform Event Boundary exclusion or separation governance. 13. EBIM does not determine legal taxability. ------------------------------ Governance Logic EBIM follows the following governance logic: If a Governed Formed Event exists, its potential structural perimeter must be identifiable before detailed Boundary Scope can be governed. If sufficient Boundary Signals exist: → establish a Candidate Event Boundary. If several legitimate Candidate Boundaries exist: → preserve the alternatives for subsequent governance. If Boundary Signals conflict: → classify the boundary identification as ambiguous or unresolved. If technical or commercial structures are the only available basis: → retain them as provisional boundary evidence rather than automatically accepting them as the governed boundary. If the available information cannot support meaningful boundary identification: → the event must not be represented as boundary-ready. ------------------------------ Minimum Implementation Framework A conforming implementation of EBIM must be capable of: 1. receiving the Governed Formed Event from TREFS 2. identifying materially relevant Boundary Signals 3. identifying Candidate Boundary Elements 4. distinguishing operational boundary evidence from technical segmentation 5. evaluating potential Boundary Anchors 6. constructing at least one Candidate Event Boundary where sufficient information exists 7. representing multiple Candidate Boundaries where necessary 8. detecting boundary ambiguity 9. detecting insufficient boundary information 10. preserving traceability between the Candidate Event Boundary and its supporting basis 11. assigning a governed boundary-identification state 12. transferring the Candidate Event Boundary to EBSCM 13. preventing boundary identification from becoming tax determination EBIM does not prescribe a specific database model, event-stream architecture, graph representation, ERP structure, AI model, workflow system, blockchain architecture, or tax engine. ------------------------------ Governance Outputs EBIM may produce: Candidate Event Boundary Boundary Signal Record Candidate Boundary Element Set Boundary Anchor Record Boundary Identification State Boundary Ambiguity Indicator Multiple Boundary Candidate Record Boundary Insufficiency Indicator Boundary Identification Traceability Record Its principal governed output is: Candidate Event Boundary This output proceeds to: EBSCM — Event Boundary Scope Module ------------------------------ Critical Distinctions Event Formation ≠ Event Boundary Formed Event ≠ Bounded Event Boundary Signal ≠ Event Boundary Candidate Event Boundary ≠ Final Event Boundary Candidate Boundary Element ≠ Confirmed Boundary Element Technical Identifier ≠ Event Boundary Commercial Identifier ≠ Event Boundary Workflow Boundary ≠ Governed Event Boundary by Default Machine Task Boundary ≠ Governed Event Boundary by Default Multiple Records ≠ Multiple Event Boundaries Multiple Representations ≠ Multiple Events by Default One Shared Identifier ≠ One Event by Default Continuous Operation ≠ Boundaryless Event Machine Action ≠ Event Boundary by Default Autonomous Objective ≠ Single Event Boundary by Default Event Boundary Identification ≠ Event Boundary Scope Event Boundary ≠ Tax Jurisdiction Candidate Event Boundary ≠ Legal Tax Point Boundary Identification ≠ Taxability Determination ------------------------------ Enterprise Application Enterprise systems rarely agree on where an event begins and ends. The same activity may be represented as: CRM Opportunity ↓ Commerce Order ↓ ERP Invoice ↓ Bank Settlement ↓ Logistics Shipment ↓ Accounting Entry Each system creates boundaries appropriate to its own operational purpose. Those boundaries are not necessarily the boundaries required for a governed Tax-Relevant Event. EBIM creates a neutral governance layer above those representations. It allows organizations to identify Candidate Event Boundaries without allowing one internal system, commercial identifier, or technical architecture to become the authoritative definition of operational reality. This is particularly important where governed event information must later be consumed by multiple tax systems or jurisdictions. ------------------------------ Use Case 1 — One Marketplace Order Across Multiple Operational Structures A customer places one marketplace order containing products from three merchants. The platform creates one order ID. The merchants generate three invoices. Two logistics providers create four shipments. The payment provider performs two settlements. One item is subsequently refunded. Each system presents a different apparent boundary. EBIM does not automatically accept the order ID, invoice, shipment, settlement, or refund record as the Event Boundary. Instead, it identifies the materially relevant Boundary Signals and constructs one or more Candidate Event Boundaries for subsequent scope governance. This prevents the platform's technical architecture from deciding the governed structure of the event. The order identifier is boundary evidence — not boundary authority. ------------------------------ Use Case 2 — Continuous Autonomous Cloud Infrastructure An autonomous AI infrastructure platform continuously allocates compute, storage, networking, model execution, and settlement resources across multiple data centers. Millions of technical actions occur every day. There is no single transaction record representing the complete operational activity. Treating every machine action as an Event Boundary would produce artificial fragmentation. Treating the entire continuous platform operation as one permanent event would produce artificial aggregation. EBIM identifies materially meaningful Boundary Signals within the continuous operational structure and establishes Candidate Event Boundaries capable of progressing into Boundary Scope governance. Continuous machine execution does not eliminate the need for governed Event Boundaries. ------------------------------ Canonical Boundary EBIM governs the identification of the potential structural perimeter of a Governed Formed Event and the establishment of a traceable Candidate Event Boundary. It does not determine detailed Event Boundary Scope, exclusions, separation between finalized event structures, Boundary Revision, Event Timing, Event Location, Event Participation, Event Relationships, Event Determination, Tax Jurisdiction, legal taxability, or jurisdiction-specific tax consequences. ------------------------------ Module Handoff TREFS — Governed Formed Event ↓ EBIM — Candidate Event Boundary ↓ EBSCM — Event Boundary Scope Module ------------------------------ Canonical Closing Statement The Event Boundary Identification Module establishes the first governed representation of where a formed event may structurally begin and end. It prevents transaction identifiers, database structures, commercial labels, workflows, platform representations, autonomous objectives, and machine execution granularity from becoming accidental Event Boundaries. EBIM preserves ambiguity where necessary and produces a traceable Candidate Event Boundary for subsequent Boundary Scope governance. EBIM identifies the candidate perimeter of the event — it does not yet decide everything that belongs inside it.

title: OOF™ Event Boundary Revision Module (EBRM)
text: OOF™ Event Boundary Revision Module (EBRM) Event Boundary Revision Module (EBRM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: Tax-Relevant Event Boundary Standard (TREBS) Module: EBRM — Event Boundary Revision Module Operational Layer: Event Boundary Revision Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Event Boundary Revision Origin ID: TREGA-TREBS-EBRM-005 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 30 August 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English ------------------------------ Canonical Definition The Event Boundary Revision Module (EBRM) governs how an established or developing Event Boundary is reconsidered, revised, confirmed, or preserved when new information, corrected information, structural change, resolved uncertainty, separation results, conflicting representations, or other materially relevant boundary evidence affects the legitimacy of the existing boundary structure. EBRM establishes the governance conditions under which Event Boundary revision may occur while preserving traceability between the previous boundary state and the revised boundary state. Its specific task is: to ensure that an Event Boundary can change when materially justified without allowing revision to become uncontrolled reconstruction, retrospective convenience, historical erasure, or downstream tax-driven redefinition of the event. EBRM is the final Core Module of the Tax-Relevant Event Boundary Standard. It converts the boundary structures established through EBIM, EBSCM, EBEM, and EBSM into a sufficiently governed and revision-controlled Event Boundary capable of proceeding into Event Timing governance. ------------------------------ Operational Role The preceding TREBS modules establish: EBIM — where a candidate Event Boundary may exist. EBSCM — what belongs within its provisional scope. EBEM — what must remain outside that scope. EBSM — whether materially distinct event structures must be separated. EBRM asks: Does the resulting Event Boundary remain legitimate in light of the complete governed boundary structure, and how must any justified change to that boundary be controlled and preserved? EBRM therefore governs the transition: Developing Event Boundary ↓ Revision-Controlled Event Boundary ↓ Governed Bounded Event Its narrow task is: to govern material revision, confirmation, preservation, and traceability of the Event Boundary before the event proceeds into subsequent TREGA™ lifecycle stages. ------------------------------ Internal Flow Governed Event Boundary Separation Structure ↓ Boundary Revision Readiness ↓ Revision Trigger Identification ↓ Materiality Assessment ↓ Affected Boundary Element Identification ↓ Revision / Preservation Determination ↓ Revised Boundary Construction ↓ Boundary Consistency & Traceability Control ↓ Boundary Confirmation ↓ Governed Bounded Event ↓ TRETS — Tax-Relevant Event Timing Standard ------------------------------ Operational Space EBRM operates within Event Boundary Revision. Its Operational Space includes: Boundary Revision readiness revision trigger identification revision materiality affected boundary identification inclusion revision exclusion revision separation revision boundary expansion boundary contraction boundary restructuring boundary preservation boundary confirmation revision conflict revision uncertainty revision traceability previous-boundary preservation revised-boundary linkage boundary version continuity downstream boundary impact signalling final Event Boundary readiness EBRM owns controlled revision of the Event Boundary. It does not reopen the entire event lifecycle by default. ------------------------------ Operational Scope EBRM may govern boundary revision across: commercial transactions digital transactions financial operations logistics manufacturing marketplaces platform activity subscriptions digital services banking distributed systems autonomous systems AI-agent activity machine-to-machine operations robotic operations digital assets infrastructure operations hybrid physical-digital events future machine economies The revision logic remains technology-neutral, actor-neutral, organization-neutral, and jurisdiction-neutral. ------------------------------ Boundary Revision Principle An Event Boundary must not be treated as permanently immutable merely because it was previously established. Operational reality may later become clearer. New information may reveal that: relevant activity was omitted, external activity was incorrectly included, one event was incorrectly aggregated, one event was incorrectly fragmented, an assumed separation was unsupported, an unresolved boundary condition has become resolvable, a source representation was incorrect, or a material structural change occurred. A governed architecture must therefore support revision. However: Revisability ≠ Arbitrary Mutability. Boundary revision requires a governed basis. ------------------------------ Revision Readiness Before revision begins, EBRM must establish whether sufficient reason exists to reopen the current Event Boundary. A boundary may be: Revision Not Indicated Revision Candidate Revision Required Revision Unresolved Revision readiness prevents every new technical record or minor informational difference from reopening an otherwise legitimate Event Boundary. Therefore: New Information ≠ Revision Requirement by Default. ------------------------------ Revision Trigger A Revision Trigger is a materially relevant condition that creates a legitimate basis for reconsidering an existing Event Boundary. Potential triggers may include: newly discovered operational information corrected source information previously unavailable evidence resolved boundary uncertainty resolved boundary conflict incorrect inclusion incorrect exclusion incorrect separation newly established event distinctness newly established event unity structural transformation system reconciliation material inconsistency downstream discovery of a boundary defect autonomous-system correction machine-generated correction prior governance error A trigger initiates reconsideration. It does not predetermine the result. Therefore: Revision Trigger ≠ Boundary Change. ------------------------------ Revision Materiality Not every difference justifies revision. EBRM must determine whether the identified issue is materially capable of affecting the governed Event Boundary. A difference may be: Non-Material Potentially Material Material Materiality Unresolved Non-material differences may be recorded without changing the Event Boundary. Material differences require governed reconsideration. This prevents unnecessary boundary instability. ------------------------------ Affected Boundary Elements Where revision is justified, EBRM must identify which part of the Event Boundary is affected. Affected elements may include: included activity excluded activity separation structure overlapping structure nested structure composite structure distributed structure machine-generated structure autonomous structure boundary qualification unresolved boundary condition Revision should remain proportionate to the affected boundary element. Therefore: Local Boundary Defect ≠ Full Event Reconstruction by Default. ------------------------------ Boundary Preservation EBRM must explicitly allow the existing Event Boundary to remain unchanged where reconsideration does not establish a material reason for revision. Possible outcome: Boundary Reviewed — Existing Boundary Preserved This is important because revision governance is not a mechanism for producing change. It is a mechanism for governing whether change is legitimate. Therefore: Boundary Review ≠ Boundary Revision. ------------------------------ Boundary Expansion A boundary may require expansion when materially relevant activity was incorrectly excluded or previously unavailable information establishes legitimate inclusion. Boundary expansion must identify: what is being added, why it is being added, the prior state, the revised state, supporting basis, downstream implications. However: Additional Related Activity ≠ Automatic Boundary Expansion. The activity must satisfy the governed boundary basis. ------------------------------ Boundary Contraction A boundary may require contraction where activity previously included is later established as outside the legitimate structural extent of the event. Boundary contraction must preserve the historical fact that the activity was previously included. Therefore: Boundary Contraction ≠ Historical Deletion. The previous boundary state remains reconstructable. ------------------------------ Boundary Restructuring Some revisions cannot be represented merely as expansion or contraction. New information may establish that: one boundary should become multiple boundaries, multiple boundaries should be consolidated, overlapping structures require reorganization, nested structures were incorrectly represented, separation logic must be reconsidered. Such cases may require Boundary Restructuring. Where restructuring creates materially distinct event structures, EBRM must preserve linkage to the EBSM separation basis. EBRM must not independently absorb EBSM's separation function. ------------------------------ Revision of Inclusion Where previous inclusion becomes materially questionable, EBRM may reopen the relevant inclusion result established through EBSCM. The revision record must identify: previous inclusion state, reason for reconsideration, new information, revised state, resulting boundary effect. EBRM governs the revision. It does not replace EBSCM's underlying scope methodology. ------------------------------ Revision of Exclusion Where previous exclusion becomes materially questionable, EBRM may reopen the relevant exclusion result established through EBEM. The revision must preserve: previous exclusion basis, revision trigger, revised determination, resulting Event Boundary impact. Therefore: Previously Excluded ≠ Permanently Excluded. But equally: New Association ≠ Automatic Inclusion. ------------------------------ Revision of Separation Where later information materially challenges an existing separation structure, EBRM may trigger reconsideration of the EBSM result. Possible outcomes include: separation preserved, separation modified, separation removed, additional separation required, separation remains unresolved. EBRM governs revision control. EBSM remains the owner of separation logic. ------------------------------ Boundary Version Continuity Every material Event Boundary revision must preserve continuity between boundary states. A conceptual version sequence may be represented as: Boundary State B1 ↓ Revision Trigger ↓ Boundary Review ↓ Boundary State B2 ↓ Subsequent Revision ↓ Boundary State B3 Each state must remain distinguishable and traceable. Therefore: Current Boundary ≠ Only Boundary State That Matters. ------------------------------ Historical Preservation Revision must never silently overwrite prior governed reality. The architecture must preserve: previous Event Boundary previous governance basis revision trigger changed elements unchanged elements revision rationale revised Event Boundary time of governance revision linkage between states This supports later reconstruction of what the system knew and how the Event Boundary evolved. Therefore: Event Boundary Revision ≠ Historical Erasure. ------------------------------ Correction ≠ Revision A purely technical correction may not materially change the Event Boundary. For example: spelling correction identifier formatting correction duplicate metadata removal non-material system-field correction Such corrections should not automatically create a new material boundary version. Therefore: Technical Correction ≠ Material Boundary Revision by Default. Materiality governs whether EBRM revision logic is required. ------------------------------ New Event ≠ Boundary Revision Not every later development should modify an existing Event Boundary. New operational activity may represent a new event rather than an extension of the existing event. Therefore: New Activity ≠ Existing Boundary Expansion by Default. Where the later activity represents a materially new occurrence, it may require new TREGA™ Event Recognition and Event Formation rather than revision of the previous boundary. EBRM must prevent revision from becoming unlimited event absorption. ------------------------------ Material Transformation In exceptional cases, new information may establish that the event has transformed so materially that revision of the existing boundary would no longer preserve event identity coherently. Such a condition may require escalation back into appropriate TREGA™ lifecycle governance. Therefore: Material Event Transformation may require New Event Formation. EBRM must not force continuity where operational continuity no longer exists. ------------------------------ Boundary Revision and Event Timing The time at which a boundary is revised is not necessarily the operational time of the event. Likewise, discovering an omitted component later does not mean that component occurred at the time of revision. Therefore: Boundary Revision Time ≠ Event Time. Final Event Timing belongs to: TRETS — Tax-Relevant Event Timing Standard. ------------------------------ Boundary Revision and Tax Rules Tax law may change after an Event Boundary has already been governed. A jurisdiction may later classify or tax the event differently. This does not automatically justify reconstructing the Event Boundary. Therefore: Tax Rule Change ≠ Event Boundary Change by Default. TREGA™ must preserve operational event representation independently of downstream tax-rule evolution. ------------------------------ Boundary Revision and Tax Outcome A tax authority, tax engine, or compliance system may identify that a different Event Boundary would produce a different tax result. That fact alone does not authorize TREGA™ to revise operational reality. Therefore: Different Tax Outcome ≠ Boundary Revision Basis by Default. Revision must remain grounded in governed event structure. ------------------------------ Boundary Revision and Jurisdiction A jurisdiction may legally aggregate or divide operational events differently for taxation. Such legal treatment does not automatically alter TREGA's governed Event Boundary. Therefore: Jurisdictional Aggregation ≠ Operational Event Aggregation. Jurisdictional Separation ≠ Operational Event Separation. The same governed event layer may support multiple jurisdictional evaluations. ------------------------------ Autonomous Boundary Revision Autonomous systems may discover inconsistencies or new information without direct human intervention. Examples include: reconciliation agents machine monitoring distributed ledgers automated settlement systems AI anomaly detection autonomous logistics systems An autonomous system may generate a Revision Trigger. It must not silently rewrite the Event Boundary. Therefore: Autonomous Detection ≠ Autonomous Authority to Rewrite Governed Event History. The same governed revision requirements apply regardless of whether the trigger originates from a human, organization, machine, or autonomous agent. ------------------------------ Revision Conflict Different sources may propose incompatible boundary revisions. For example: one system indicates expansion, another indicates contraction, one participant disputes separation, an autonomous system detects conflicting structure, later records contradict earlier operational representations. EBRM must preserve the conflict. It must not select a revision merely because one source has technical priority. Possible state: Boundary Revision Conflict The boundary may remain qualified or unresolved until sufficient governance basis exists. ------------------------------ Revision Uncertainty A Revision Trigger may be legitimate while the correct revised boundary remains uncertain. EBRM must distinguish: Reason to Reconsider from Sufficient Basis to Change Therefore: Revision Readiness ≠ Revision Determination. Where uncertainty remains material, EBRM preserves: Boundary Revision Unresolved rather than creating artificial certainty. ------------------------------ Boundary Confirmation Once revision analysis is complete, EBRM must establish whether the resulting Event Boundary is sufficiently governed to proceed. Boundary Confirmation may result from: preservation of the existing boundary, legitimate expansion, legitimate contraction, legitimate restructuring, resolution of separation, qualified acceptance of non-material uncertainty. The confirmation does not establish taxability. It establishes only that the structural Event Boundary is sufficiently governed for subsequent TREGA™ lifecycle stages. ------------------------------ Governed Bounded Event The principal final output of EBRM and TREBS is: Governed Bounded Event A Governed Bounded Event is an event whose structural extent has been sufficiently: identified, scoped, excluded, separated where necessary, revised where materially justified, preserved where revision was not justified, traceably maintained, and confirmed for progression. It does not yet establish final Event Timing, Event Location, Event Participation, Event-to-Value Association, Event Relationships, Event Determination, or legal taxability. Therefore: Governed Bounded Event ≠ Determined Tax-Relevant Event. ------------------------------ Governance Requirements EBRM requires that: 1. revision begins from a governed Event Boundary structure. 2. a legitimate Revision Trigger is identified before material revision occurs. 3. Revision Trigger and revision outcome remain distinct. 4. revision materiality is evaluated. 5. non-material differences do not automatically reopen the Event Boundary. 6. affected boundary elements are explicitly identified. 7. revision remains proportionate to the affected boundary condition. 8. preservation of the existing boundary remains a legitimate outcome. 9. expansion requires a governed inclusion basis. 10. contraction preserves historical inclusion state. 11. restructuring preserves linkage to prior boundary states. 12. inclusion revision remains traceable to EBSCM. 13. exclusion revision remains traceable to EBEM. 14. separation revision remains traceable to EBSM. 15. previous Event Boundary states remain reconstructable. 16. material revisions maintain Boundary Version Continuity. 17. technical corrections do not automatically become material revisions. 18. new activity is not automatically absorbed into an existing Event Boundary. 19. material transformation may require new Event Formation rather than boundary revision. 20. revision time remains distinct from Event Timing. 21. tax-rule change does not automatically alter Event Boundary. 22. tax outcome does not determine revision legitimacy. 23. jurisdictional aggregation or separation does not redefine operational Event Boundary. 24. autonomous systems may identify revision triggers but may not silently rewrite governed history. 25. revision conflict and uncertainty remain explicit. 26. confirmed Event Boundary is sufficiently governed before transfer to TRETS. ------------------------------ Governance Logic EBRM applies the following logic: Has a legitimate Boundary Revision Trigger been identified? If no: → preserve the existing Event Boundary. If yes: → assess materiality. Is the identified difference materially relevant to the Event Boundary? If no: → record the information and preserve the boundary. If yes: → identify affected boundary elements. Does the new governance basis support a boundary change? If no: → preserve the existing boundary and record the review. If yes: → determine whether expansion, contraction, restructuring, or reconsideration of prior scope, exclusion, or separation is required. Would the proposed change destroy coherent continuity with the existing event? If yes: → evaluate whether the condition requires new Event Formation rather than Event Boundary revision. If no: → construct the revised boundary. Can the previous and revised states remain reconstructable and traceably linked? If no: → Boundary Revision Unresolved. If yes: → preserve Boundary Version Continuity. Is the resulting Event Boundary sufficiently governed for subsequent lifecycle processing? If yes: → confirm Governed Bounded Event. If no: → preserve qualified, conflicting, or unresolved state. ------------------------------ Minimum Implementation Framework A conforming implementation of EBRM must be capable of: 1. receiving the Governed Event Boundary Separation Structure from EBSM 2. determining Boundary Revision readiness 3. identifying Revision Triggers 4. evaluating revision materiality 5. identifying affected boundary elements 6. distinguishing material revision from technical correction 7. governing boundary preservation 8. governing boundary expansion 9. governing boundary contraction 10. governing boundary restructuring 11. reconnecting revision to relevant EBSCM, EBEM, or EBSM governance where necessary 12. preserving previous Event Boundary states 13. establishing Boundary Version Continuity 14. maintaining revision traceability 15. identifying Revision Conflict 16. representing Revision Uncertainty 17. preventing tax-driven boundary rewriting 18. preventing jurisdictional rules from silently redefining operational Event Boundary 19. preventing autonomous systems from silently overwriting governed event history 20. distinguishing boundary revision from new Event Formation 21. confirming the resulting Event Boundary 22. producing a Governed Bounded Event 23. transferring the Governed Bounded Event to TRETS ------------------------------ Governance Outputs EBRM may produce: Boundary Revision Readiness Record Boundary Revision Trigger Record Revision Materiality State Affected Boundary Element Record Boundary Preservation Decision Boundary Expansion Record Boundary Contraction Record Boundary Restructuring Record Boundary Revision Conflict Boundary Revision Uncertainty Boundary Version Record Previous-to-Revised Boundary Linkage Boundary Revision Traceability Record Boundary Confirmation Record New Event Formation Referral Governed Bounded Event Its principal output is: Governed Bounded Event This proceeds to: TRETS — Tax-Relevant Event Timing Standard ------------------------------ Critical Distinctions Revisability ≠ Arbitrary Mutability New Information ≠ Revision Requirement by Default Revision Trigger ≠ Boundary Change Local Boundary Defect ≠ Full Event Reconstruction by Default Boundary Review ≠ Boundary Revision Additional Related Activity ≠ Automatic Boundary Expansion Boundary Contraction ≠ Historical Deletion Previously Excluded ≠ Permanently Excluded New Association ≠ Automatic Inclusion Current Boundary ≠ Only Boundary State That Matters Event Boundary Revision ≠ Historical Erasure Technical Correction ≠ Material Boundary Revision by Default New Activity ≠ Existing Boundary Expansion by Default Boundary Revision Time ≠ Event Time Tax Rule Change ≠ Event Boundary Change by Default Different Tax Outcome ≠ Boundary Revision Basis by Default Jurisdictional Aggregation ≠ Operational Event Aggregation Jurisdictional Separation ≠ Operational Event Separation Autonomous Detection ≠ Autonomous Authority to Rewrite Governed Event History Revision Readiness ≠ Revision Determination Governed Bounded Event ≠ Determined Tax-Relevant Event ------------------------------ Enterprise Application Enterprise event records evolve. Initial representations are frequently incomplete because information arrives asynchronously from: commerce systems payment systems logistics platforms banks suppliers customers autonomous systems distributed infrastructure reconciliation processes Without controlled revision governance, organizations commonly face two bad options: freeze an incorrect historical event representation or silently overwrite the original representation whenever new information appears. EBRM provides a third model: governed event evolution with preserved historical continuity. A boundary may legitimately change while every material state remains reconstructable. This enables ERP systems, digital platforms, tax infrastructure, AI systems, auditors, regulators, and downstream jurisdictional engines to understand not only the current Event Boundary, but also how and why that boundary became legitimate. ------------------------------ Use Case 1 — Cross-Border Marketplace Event Changes After Partial Refund and Fulfilment Reconciliation A marketplace initially records one customer order containing products from several sellers. TREBS establishes several governed Event Boundaries based on the operational structures available at the time. Weeks later, reconciliation reveals that: one shipment never occurred, one product was fulfilled by a different seller, one settlement was incorrectly associated with the original fulfilment, and a partial refund relates only to one previously bounded event. The platform cannot simply overwrite the original Event Boundaries. EBRM identifies the new reconciliation information as potential Revision Triggers. It evaluates materiality and determines which Event Boundaries are affected. One boundary is preserved. Another is contracted. A third requires reconsideration of its separation structure. Every previous boundary state remains linked to the revised state. The resulting Governed Bounded Events can then proceed through Event Timing and later TREGA™ governance. The tax engines of different jurisdictions may subsequently interpret the events differently, but those tax interpretations do not rewrite the underlying operational boundary history. ------------------------------ Use Case 2 — Autonomous Industrial Network Discovers That Previously Unified Machine Activity Contained a Distinct Event An autonomous manufacturing network coordinates robots, procurement agents, inventory systems, production equipment, and settlement services. Initial operational information indicates that thousands of machine actions belong to one governed production event. After reconciliation, an autonomous monitoring system discovers that part of the resource consumption and machine execution was independently initiated by another production objective. The new information creates a legitimate Revision Trigger. EBSM separation logic is reconsidered through the governed revision process. The previously unified boundary is restructured into two materially distinct event structures. EBRM preserves: the original Event Boundary, the new information, the revision trigger, the separation reconsideration, the revised Event Boundaries, and the linkage between all boundary states. The autonomous monitoring system therefore contributes new information without gaining uncontrolled authority to rewrite historical event reality. Machine-discovered reality can change a governed Event Boundary — but only through governed, traceable revision. ------------------------------ Canonical Boundary EBRM governs the readiness, triggering, materiality, reconsideration, preservation, expansion, contraction, restructuring, version continuity, conflict, uncertainty, traceability, and confirmation of Event Boundary revisions. It does not perform original Event Boundary Identification, original Event Boundary Scope determination, original Event Boundary Exclusion, original Event Boundary Separation, Event Timing, Event Location, Event Participation, Event-to-Value Association, Event Relationship determination, final Event Determination, legal taxability determination, Tax Jurisdiction determination, taxpayer determination, tax-base calculation, tax-rate application, exemptions, deductions, tax liability, reporting obligations, payment, collection, or enforcement. EBRM begins with the: Governed Event Boundary Separation Structure and ends with the: Governed Bounded Event ------------------------------ Module Handoff EBSM — Governed Event Boundary Separation Structure ↓ EBRM — Event Boundary Revision Governance ↓ Governed Bounded Event ↓ TRETS — Tax-Relevant Event Timing Standard ------------------------------ Canonical Closing Statement The Event Boundary Revision Module ensures that a governed Event Boundary can respond to better information without losing methodological control over its history. It allows legitimate correction of the governed structural extent of an event while preserving previous boundary states, revision reasons, material changes, unresolved conditions, and continuity between representations. It prevents both rigid preservation of a materially incorrect boundary and uncontrolled rewriting of operational reality. An Event Boundary may change when reality justifies the change — but governed history must never disappear merely because the current representation has changed.

title: OOF™ Event Boundary Scope Module (EBSCM)
text: OOF™ Event Boundary Scope Module (EBSCM) Event Boundary Scope Module (EBSCM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: Tax-Relevant Event Boundary Standard (TREBS) Module: EBSCM — Event Boundary Scope Module Operational Layer: Event Boundary Scope Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Event Boundary Scope Origin ID: TREGA-TREBS-EBSCM-002 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 30 August 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English ------------------------------ Canonical Definition The Event Boundary Scope Module (EBSCM) governs how a Candidate Event Boundary is translated into a defined Event Boundary Scope by determining which materially relevant structures, components, relationships, operational states, and supporting elements fall within the governed perimeter under examination. EBSCM establishes the positive scope of the Event Boundary: what is provisionally governed as belonging within the event perimeter for subsequent Boundary Exclusion and Boundary Separation governance. Its specific task is: to establish a coherent, traceable, and operationally justified Event Boundary Scope without treating technical grouping, commercial packaging, organizational structure, shared identifiers, or jurisdiction-specific tax treatment as authoritative scope criteria. EBSCM governs what falls within the candidate event perimeter. It does not yet determine formal exclusions, separation into distinct event structures, or later Boundary Revision. ------------------------------ Operational Role EBIM identifies where the potential Event Boundary appears to lie. EBSCM determines what the identified boundary is intended to contain. This creates the transition: Candidate Event Boundary ↓ Governed Event Boundary Scope A Candidate Event Boundary may appear structurally plausible while still leaving uncertainty about which surrounding elements properly belong within its scope. Therefore: Candidate Event Boundary ≠ Governed Event Boundary Scope. And: Structural Proximity ≠ Scope Membership by Default. EBSCM converts boundary identification into an explicit positive scope that can be tested by the subsequent Boundary Exclusion and Boundary Separation modules. ------------------------------ Internal Flow Candidate Event Boundary ↓ Scope Candidate Identification ↓ Scope Relevance Assessment ↓ Scope Membership Assessment ↓ Scope Coherence Assessment ↓ Scope Ambiguity / Conflict Handling ↓ Governed Event Boundary Scope ↓ EBEM — Event Boundary Exclusion Module ------------------------------ Operational Space EBSCM operates within the governance space where the content of an identified Candidate Event Boundary must be explicitly defined. Its Operational Space includes: identification of Candidate Scope Elements assessment of material relevance to the Event Boundary assessment of provisional scope membership structural coherence of included elements treatment of shared operational structures treatment of supporting activities treatment of composite event structures treatment of distributed event structures treatment of machine-generated and autonomous structures treatment of overlapping Candidate Scope Elements detection of over-inclusive scope detection of under-inclusive scope representation of scope ambiguity representation of scope conflict preservation of scope traceability EBSCM owns the positive definition of Event Boundary Scope. It does not own formal exclusion decisions or separation of distinct event structures. ------------------------------ Operational Scope EBSCM applies wherever a Candidate Event Boundary must be converted into an explicit governed scope across: physical operations commercial transactions financial activity digital services platform operations distributed systems autonomous agents AI systems robotic operations machine-to-machine activity infrastructure operations digital assets value-affecting activity composite physical-digital events cross-organizational activity future machine economies The module remains actor-neutral, technology-neutral, and jurisdiction-neutral. Scope membership must follow the governed operational structure of the event rather than the architecture of the system recording it. ------------------------------ Candidate Scope Elements A Candidate Event Boundary may contain many structures that appear potentially relevant. These become Candidate Scope Elements. They may include: qualified Event Formation Components materially connected operational actions materially connected states materially connected transitions supporting operational structures distributed execution elements machine-generated activity autonomous execution structures value-affecting operational elements operational interfaces structurally connected records or representations Candidate Scope Elements must be assessed before being treated as part of the governed scope. Candidate Scope Element ≠ Scope Member. ------------------------------ Scope Membership EBSCM determines whether a Candidate Scope Element has sufficient structural relevance to be provisionally included within the Event Boundary Scope. Scope membership may be supported where an element: forms part of the governed event structure materially contributes to the operational coherence of that structure represents a materially relevant state or transition within the candidate perimeter is necessary to represent the event without material structural distortion belongs to a distributed but coherent execution structure cannot be removed from the represented scope without materially changing what the formed event represents Scope membership must not be established merely because an element: shares an identifier appears in the same database belongs to the same workflow occurs under the same contract belongs to the same customer order was executed by the same machine or agent belongs to the same organization occurs close in time occurs close in physical or digital space is processed under the same accounting structure Therefore: Association ≠ Scope Membership. ------------------------------ Positive Scope Governance EBSCM establishes the positive representation of what belongs within the Event Boundary Scope. This is distinct from exclusion governance. The module asks: What is sufficiently justified to remain within the governed scope at this stage? It does not yet ask: What must formally be excluded from that scope? That distinction preserves the separation between EBSCM and the subsequent Event Boundary Exclusion Module (EBEM). Therefore: Scope Definition ≠ Exclusion Determination. An element may remain provisionally within scope while requiring later exclusion analysis. ------------------------------ Scope Coherence The Event Boundary Scope must remain structurally coherent. A scope is not coherent merely because all included elements are individually relevant. The combined scope must represent a meaningful operational event structure. EBSCM therefore evaluates whether included elements collectively produce: sufficient structural unity meaningful operational coherence proportionate representation continuity with the Governed Formed Event consistency with the Candidate Event Boundary sufficient differentiation from surrounding activity A scope that combines unrelated structures may be over-inclusive. A scope that omits materially necessary structures may be under-inclusive. Relevant Elements ≠ Coherent Scope by Default. ------------------------------ Over-Inclusive Scope Over-inclusion occurs where the Event Boundary Scope absorbs surrounding activity beyond what is materially necessary to represent the formed event. Potential causes include: shared commercial identifiers shared contracts common workflows common organizational ownership continuous technical execution broad autonomous objectives shared infrastructure platform-level aggregation common accounting treatment EBSCM must detect potential over-inclusion before the scope progresses further. Shared Operational Environment ≠ Shared Event Scope by Default. ------------------------------ Under-Inclusive Scope Under-inclusion occurs where materially necessary structures are omitted from the Event Boundary Scope. This may happen where systems artificially fragment operational reality into: separate technical records separate platform operations separate machine instructions separate database transactions separate payment steps separate system instances Technical fragmentation must not produce artificial event fragmentation. Technical Separation ≠ Scope Separation by Default. ------------------------------ Composite and Distributed Scope A governed Event Boundary Scope may legitimately span: multiple systems multiple organizations multiple technical processes multiple machines multiple autonomous agents physical and digital environments distributed infrastructure multiple operational stages Distributed execution does not automatically require distributed Event Boundaries. Likewise, operational distribution does not justify unlimited scope expansion. EBSCM must preserve the materially coherent scope without allowing technical distribution to determine the event structure. Distributed Execution ≠ Distributed Event Scope by Default. ------------------------------ Autonomous and Machine Scope Autonomous systems may create particularly difficult scope conditions. One autonomous objective may generate: thousands of API calls multiple model executions resource allocations robotic actions financial operations external service interactions settlement operations EBSCM must determine which of those structures materially belong within the Event Boundary Scope. Neither extreme is acceptable by default: One Autonomous Objective ≠ One Unlimited Event Scope. One Machine Action ≠ One Independent Event Scope. The scope must follow material operational coherence. ------------------------------ Scope Ambiguity and Conflict The appropriate Event Boundary Scope may remain uncertain. Potential states include: Scope Candidate Scope Established Scope Ambiguous Scope Conflict Scope Insufficient Scope Unresolved Ambiguity may arise where different systems, evidence sources, or operational representations support competing scope structures. EBSCM must preserve that ambiguity rather than silently selecting the most convenient system representation. System Preference ≠ Governed Scope Resolution. ------------------------------ Governance Requirements EBSCM requires that: 1. Scope governance begins from a Candidate Event Boundary established through EBIM. 2. Candidate Scope Elements are explicitly identified. 3. Scope membership is based on material operational relevance and structural coherence. 4. Shared identifiers do not automatically establish common scope. 5. Shared contracts do not automatically establish common scope. 6. Common workflows do not automatically establish common scope. 7. Common organizational ownership does not automatically establish common scope. 8. Technical fragmentation does not automatically create separate scopes. 9. Distributed execution does not automatically create separate scopes. 10. Autonomous objectives do not automatically create unlimited Event Scope. 11. Machine actions do not automatically create independent Event Scope. 12. Over-inclusive and under-inclusive scope conditions are detectable. 13. Scope ambiguity and conflict remain visible. 14. Scope decisions remain traceable to their operational basis. 15. Scope governance remains independent of jurisdiction-specific tax treatment. 16. Formal exclusions remain governed by EBEM. 17. Separation between distinct event structures remains governed by EBSM. ------------------------------ Governance Logic EBSCM applies the following logic: If a Candidate Event Boundary exists, the materially relevant structures potentially belonging within that perimeter must be assessed before the boundary can progress toward exclusion and separation governance. If an element is materially necessary to represent the event coherently: → retain it within the Governed Event Boundary Scope. If its membership remains uncertain: → preserve it as an unresolved Scope Candidate. If inclusion would materially over-expand the event: → flag potential over-inclusion for further governance. If omission would materially distort the event: → flag potential under-inclusion. If competing scope structures remain legitimate: → preserve the competing representations. EBSCM must not force scope certainty where operational reality does not support it. ------------------------------ Minimum Implementation Framework A conforming implementation of EBSCM must be capable of: 1. receiving the Candidate Event Boundary from EBIM 2. identifying Candidate Scope Elements 3. assessing material scope relevance 4. assessing provisional scope membership 5. distinguishing association from scope membership 6. evaluating structural coherence 7. detecting potential over-inclusion 8. detecting potential under-inclusion 9. supporting composite and distributed scope structures 10. supporting autonomous and machine-generated structures 11. representing scope ambiguity and conflict 12. maintaining traceability of scope decisions 13. assigning a governed scope state 14. producing a Governed Event Boundary Scope 15. transferring that scope to EBEM 16. preventing Event Boundary Scope governance from becoming Event Exclusion, Event Separation, Tax Jurisdiction, or taxability determination ------------------------------ Governance Outputs EBSCM may produce: Governed Event Boundary Scope Candidate Scope Element Set Scope Membership Record Scope Coherence Record Scope Ambiguity Indicator Scope Conflict Indicator Potential Over-Inclusion Indicator Potential Under-Inclusion Indicator Distributed Scope Representation Scope Traceability Record Its principal governed output is: Governed Event Boundary Scope This output proceeds to: EBEM — Event Boundary Exclusion Module ------------------------------ Critical Distinctions Candidate Event Boundary ≠ Governed Event Boundary Scope Candidate Scope Element ≠ Scope Member Association ≠ Scope Membership Operational Relevance ≠ Scope Membership by Default Relevant Elements ≠ Coherent Scope by Default Scope Definition ≠ Exclusion Determination Shared Identifier ≠ Shared Event Scope Shared Contract ≠ Shared Event Scope Shared Workflow ≠ Shared Event Scope Shared Organization ≠ Shared Event Scope Technical Separation ≠ Scope Separation by Default Distributed Execution ≠ Distributed Event Scope by Default One Autonomous Objective ≠ One Unlimited Event Scope One Machine Action ≠ One Independent Event Scope System Preference ≠ Governed Scope Resolution Event Boundary Scope ≠ Event Boundary Exclusion Event Boundary Scope ≠ Event Separation Event Boundary Scope ≠ Tax Jurisdiction Event Boundary Scope ≠ Taxability Determination ------------------------------ Enterprise Application Modern enterprise activity is rarely represented consistently across systems. One economically coherent activity may appear as multiple objects across: CRM ↓ Commerce Platform ↓ ERP ↓ Payment Infrastructure ↓ Logistics ↓ Accounting ↓ Tax Systems Each system may define its own internal scope. EBSCM prevents those internal scopes from automatically becoming the governed Event Boundary Scope. Instead, the module establishes a neutral operational scope capable of being consumed by downstream governance and, eventually, multiple jurisdiction-specific taxation systems. This reduces dependence on system-specific interpretations of what constitutes the event. ------------------------------ Use Case 1 — Global SaaS Service Across Multiple Technical Systems A multinational SaaS provider receives one enterprise subscription agreement. Provisioning occurs across several cloud regions. Authentication is handled by another system. Usage is continuously measured. Billing is monthly. Payments may be split across several corporate entities. Support services operate separately. A contract-centric model may place the entire relationship inside one enormous event scope. A technical model may fragment the same relationship into millions of infrastructure operations. EBSCM evaluates which operational structures materially belong within the Candidate Event Boundary and establishes a coherent Event Boundary Scope without allowing either contractual aggregation or technical fragmentation to dictate the result. The governed scope follows operational coherence — not the architecture of the systems recording it. ------------------------------ Use Case 2 — Autonomous Manufacturing Network Across Multiple Machines An autonomous manufacturing system receives a production objective. The objective triggers material allocation, robotic handling, machining, welding, inspection, internal transport, packaging, inventory updates, and automated settlement actions. Thousands of machine operations are generated. Some operations directly contribute to the formed event. Others are shared infrastructure activities supporting many unrelated production cycles. EBSCM determines which structures provisionally belong within the Event Boundary Scope and which merely surround or support it. The module prevents both unlimited expansion into the entire factory environment and artificial fragmentation into thousands of machine-defined scopes. Operational participation in the same infrastructure does not automatically create common Event Scope. ------------------------------ Canonical Boundary EBSCM governs the identification, assessment, positive inclusion, structural coherence, ambiguity, conflict, and traceability of the materially relevant structures provisionally contained within a Candidate Event Boundary. It does not perform formal Event Boundary exclusions, separate distinct event structures, revise previously established boundaries, determine Event Timing, Event Location, Event Participation, Event Relationships, Tax Jurisdiction, legal taxability, or jurisdiction-specific tax consequences. ------------------------------ Module Handoff EBIM — Candidate Event Boundary ↓ EBSCM — Governed Event Boundary Scope ↓ EBEM — Event Boundary Exclusion Module ------------------------------ Canonical Closing Statement The Event Boundary Scope Module establishes what a Candidate Event Boundary is intended to contain. It prevents shared identifiers, contracts, workflows, organizations, platforms, machines, autonomous objectives, and technical system structures from becoming automatic rules of Event Scope. EBSCM produces a coherent and traceable positive scope while preserving uncertainty where operational reality remains unresolved. EBSCM determines what provisionally belongs within the event perimeter — before subsequent governance determines what must be excluded or separated.
