title: OOF™ Event Boundary Separation Module (EBSM)
text: OOF™ Event Boundary Separation Module (EBSM) Event Boundary Separation Module (EBSM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: Tax-Relevant Event Boundary Standard (TREBS) Module: EBSM — Event Boundary Separation Module Operational Layer: Event Boundary Separation Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Event Boundary Separation Origin ID: TREGA-TREBS-EBSM-004 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 30 August 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English ------------------------------ Canonical Definition The Event Boundary Separation Module (EBSM) governs how materially distinct event structures that are adjacent, overlapping, interconnected, technically combined, operationally continuous, commercially grouped, or otherwise at risk of being represented as one event are identified and separated into distinguishable governed Event Boundary structures. EBSM establishes whether activity surrounding or intersecting a developing Event Boundary represents: part of the same governed event, structurally external activity, a materially distinct event candidate, multiple event candidates requiring separation, or an unresolved separation condition. Its specific task is: to prevent materially distinct events from being incorrectly collapsed into one Event Boundary while also preventing one coherent event from being artificially fragmented into multiple event structures. EBSM governs event separation at the boundary level. It does not determine the later semantic, economic, causal, contractual, tax, or other governed relationships among separated events. ------------------------------ Operational Role EBIM identifies where the Event Boundary may exist. EBSCM establishes what provisionally belongs within its scope. EBEM determines what should remain outside that scope. EBSM asks: Does the resulting boundary structure still contain, overlap with, or become conflated with materially distinct event structures that must be separated? The governing problem is two-sided: Over-Aggregation Risk and Over-Fragmentation Risk Over-aggregation combines materially distinct events into one governed event. Over-fragmentation divides one coherent event into artificial event units. Therefore: Operational Connection ≠ Same Event. And: Technical Separation ≠ Separate Event. EBSM must govern both errors. ------------------------------ Internal Flow Governed Event Boundary Exclusion Structure ↓ Separation Candidate Identification ↓ Distinctness Assessment ↓ Overlap / Conflation Assessment ↓ Over-Aggregation / Over-Fragmentation Assessment ↓ Separation Structure Determination ↓ Separation Conflict / Uncertainty Handling ↓ Governed Event Boundary Separation Structure ↓ EBRM — Event Boundary Revision Module ------------------------------ Operational Space EBSM operates where one developing Event Boundary may intersect with, contain, overlap, obscure, or become confused with other materially distinct event structures. Its Operational Space includes: Separation Candidate identification event distinctness assessment adjacent-event separation overlapping-event separation nested-event assessment composite-structure separation distributed-event separation repeated-event separation process-stage separation technical-fragment consolidation assessment over-aggregation detection over-fragmentation detection separation ambiguity separation conflict separation uncertainty separation traceability machine-generated event separation autonomous event separation cross-system event separation EBSM owns whether materially distinct event structures must be separated at the Event Boundary level. It does not own the later relationship governance among those events. ------------------------------ Operational Scope EBSM may operate across: commercial transactions financial operations digital services platform activity logistics manufacturing supply chains subscription environments marketplaces banking distributed systems digital assets autonomous systems AI-agent activity robotic operations machine-to-machine transactions infrastructure operations hybrid physical-digital activity future machine economies The separation logic remains actor-neutral, technology-neutral, organization-neutral, and jurisdiction-neutral. ------------------------------ Separation Candidate A Separation Candidate is a structure whose relationship to the developing Event Boundary creates a legitimate possibility that materially distinct event structures have been combined or insufficiently distinguished. A Separation Candidate may arise from: excluded structures identified by EBEM, internal scope analysis, overlapping operational activity, repeated activities, composite processes, multiple settlements, multiple deliveries, multiple executions, distributed technical operations, autonomous sub-operations, competing system representations, new information. Candidate status does not mean that a separate event exists. Therefore: Separation Candidate ≠ Separate Event. ------------------------------ Material Event Distinctness Separation must depend upon material structural distinctness rather than superficial technical difference. Potential distinctness indicators may include: independently coherent operational structure materially independent execution independent operational objective separately reconstructable occurrence independently meaningful completion materially independent value-affecting consequence distinct participant configuration distinct operational root structural independence from the candidate event ability to exist without destroying the coherence of the other event No single indicator automatically establishes separation. EBSM evaluates the structure as a whole. ------------------------------ Same Process ≠ Same Event A single business or operational process may contain multiple governed events. Examples may include: Order ↓ Fulfilment ↓ Delivery ↓ Settlement ↓ Refund The entire chain may belong to one commercial process. That does not mean the chain must be represented as one event. Therefore: One Process ≠ One Event by Default. EBSM prevents process-level aggregation from automatically becoming Event Boundary logic. ------------------------------ Multiple Process Steps ≠ Multiple Events The opposite error must also be prevented. One event may require many technical or operational steps. Therefore: Multiple Process Steps ≠ Multiple Events by Default. A manufacturing event may involve hundreds of machine actions. A digital-service event may involve thousands of API calls. A payment may involve multiple technical processing stages. Technical multiplicity does not independently establish event multiplicity. ------------------------------ Shared Identifier Operational systems frequently group activity under: order ID transaction ID contract ID customer ID project ID batch ID invoice ID workflow ID Such identifiers may help locate related activity. They do not govern Event Boundary separation. Therefore: Shared Identifier ≠ Same Event Boundary. Likewise: Different Identifier ≠ Separate Event by Default. ------------------------------ Adjacent Events Two events may occur directly beside one another within the same operational process. For example: a sale may be followed immediately by a separate service. A delivery may be followed by a return. A resource allocation may be followed by an independently initiated reallocation. Temporal or process adjacency does not collapse those structures. Therefore: Event Adjacency ≠ Event Unity. EBSM determines whether structural separation is required. ------------------------------ Overlapping Events Event structures may overlap operationally. They may share: participants infrastructure records assets technical systems contractual environments operational stages Shared elements do not automatically mean the events are identical. Therefore: Operational Overlap ≠ Same Event. EBSM may preserve overlapping references while maintaining distinct Event Boundaries where materially justified. ------------------------------ Nested Event Structures Some operational environments may contain event structures within larger activity structures. A nested structure may represent: a component of the same event, a supporting operation, or an independently governable event. The mere existence of a smaller coherent structure does not automatically establish a separate event. Therefore: Nested Structure ≠ Separate Event by Default. EBSM must determine whether separation is structurally justified. ------------------------------ Composite Activity Composite commercial or operational arrangements may combine several activities. Examples include: bundled services marketplace transactions multimodal logistics integrated manufacturing cloud-service packages autonomous resource orchestration A composite commercial presentation does not automatically establish one Event Boundary. Therefore: Commercial Bundle ≠ Single Event by Default. Conversely, a composite operational structure should not be fragmented merely because several technical systems participated. ------------------------------ Repeated Activity Repeated activity presents another boundary problem. Examples include: recurring service delivery repeated machine execution subscription consumption periodic resource allocation continuous platform operations repeated digital transactions Repeated activity may represent: repeated independent events, one continuing event, or another governed structure requiring further analysis. Therefore: Repeated Activity ≠ Repeated Event by Default. EBSM governs the structural separation question without determining later timing or tax-period treatment. ------------------------------ Distributed Systems One event may be represented across many systems. Multiple systems may also collectively represent several distinct events. Therefore: Multiple System Representations ≠ Multiple Events. And: One Distributed Workflow ≠ One Event by Default. EBSM evaluates governed operational structure rather than system topology. ------------------------------ Machine and Autonomous Systems Autonomous systems can create extreme event-granularity problems. A single autonomous objective may generate: planning operations model inference API requests resource reservations execution actions payment operations settlement operations corrective actions EBSM must prevent two opposite distortions: every machine action becoming a separate event and every action generated under one autonomous objective becoming one giant event. Therefore: Machine Action ≠ Independent Event by Default. And: Autonomous Objective ≠ Single Event by Default. Event separation must remain grounded in material operational structure. ------------------------------ Over-Aggregation Over-Aggregation occurs when materially distinct event structures are incorrectly combined within one Event Boundary. Possible indicators include: independently coherent substructures unrelated operational objectives materially distinct executions independently meaningful outcomes independent operational roots artificial grouping through system identifiers commercial packaging masking distinct activity process-level aggregation Over-aggregation can make downstream governance unable to distinguish what actually happened. EBSM must identify and correct this risk. ------------------------------ Over-Fragmentation Over-Fragmentation occurs when one coherent event structure is artificially divided into multiple event candidates. Possible causes include: system boundaries database records API calls technical processing stages machine actions accounting entries infrastructure layers organizational departments Therefore: Technical Granularity ≠ Event Granularity. EBSM must preserve coherent events even when their technical implementation is highly fragmented. ------------------------------ Separation Structure Where separation is justified, EBSM establishes distinguishable Event Boundary structures. This may result in: Single Event Structure Confirmed Multiple Event Structures Identified Partial Separation Required Separation Qualified Separation Conflict Separation Unresolved The output must preserve traceability to the original boundary analysis. ------------------------------ Separation Does Not Determine Event Relationships Separated events may later prove to be: sequential dependent grouped economically related causally connected part of a larger activity chain Those relationships are not governed by EBSM. They belong later to: TRERLS — Tax-Relevant Event Relationship Standard. Therefore: Event Separation ≠ Event Relationship Determination. EBSM answers: Are these materially distinct event structures? TRERLS later answers: How are governed events related? ------------------------------ Separation Does Not Determine Event Timing Temporal information may support separation analysis. However, EBSM does not establish final Event Timing. That belongs to: TRETS — Tax-Relevant Event Timing Standard. Therefore: Temporal Separation Evidence ≠ Event Timing Determination. ------------------------------ Separation Does Not Determine Event Location Spatial or digital differences may support separation analysis. But EBSM does not determine final Event Location. That belongs to: TRELS — Tax-Relevant Event Location Standard. Therefore: Location Difference ≠ Separate Event by Default. ------------------------------ Separation Does Not Determine Tax Treatment A jurisdiction may later: aggregate events, treat them separately, apply special transaction rules, apply tax-period rules, apply nexus rules, apply exemptions, treat multiple events as one taxable supply, treat one operational structure as multiple taxable consequences. Those are downstream legal questions. EBSM must remain independent. Therefore: Governed Event Separation ≠ Tax Separation. And: Separate Governed Events ≠ Separate Tax Liabilities by Default. ------------------------------ Separation Conflict Different systems or stakeholders may represent event multiplicity differently. For example: the commerce platform may represent one transaction. The logistics platform may represent three deliveries. The payment system may represent two settlements. The accounting system may represent one invoice. No system representation automatically governs the Event Boundary. Therefore: System Representation ≠ Event Reality by Default. Conflicting representations must remain explicit until a governed separation determination can be supported. ------------------------------ Separation Uncertainty Where material distinctness cannot yet be established, EBSM must preserve uncertainty. It must not force separation merely because downstream systems require a discrete record. Therefore: Data Model Requirement ≠ Event Separation Authority. Likewise, it must not suppress legitimate separation because one source system cannot represent multiple events. ------------------------------ Separation Traceability Every material separation determination should preserve: original boundary structure Separation Candidates separation basis retained common elements separated elements unresolved overlaps supporting information qualification conflict uncertainty resulting boundary structures downstream revision requirements This allows the separation decision to remain reconstructable. ------------------------------ Governance Requirements EBSM requires that: 1. separation begins from a governed Event Boundary Exclusion Structure. 2. Separation Candidates are explicitly identified. 3. material structural distinctness is evaluated before separation. 4. shared process membership does not automatically establish one event. 5. multiple process steps do not automatically establish multiple events. 6. shared identifiers do not automatically establish one Event Boundary. 7. different identifiers do not automatically establish separate events. 8. adjacency does not automatically establish unity. 9. operational overlap does not automatically establish unity. 10. nested structures do not automatically establish separate events. 11. commercial bundling does not automatically establish one event. 12. repeated activity does not automatically establish repeated events. 13. technical system topology does not determine event multiplicity. 14. machine actions do not automatically become independent events. 15. autonomous objectives do not automatically become single events. 16. both over-aggregation and over-fragmentation are governed. 17. separation conflict and uncertainty remain explicit. 18. separation decisions remain traceable. 19. EBSM does not determine relationships among separated events. 20. EBSM does not determine Tax Jurisdiction, taxability, taxpayer status, tax base, tax rate, or tax liability. ------------------------------ Governance Logic EBSM applies the following logic: Does the current Event Boundary contain or intersect with a materially distinct event structure? If no: → confirm the single-event separation structure. If yes: → establish distinguishable Event Boundary structures. If technical fragmentation exists but material event distinctness does not: → preserve the coherent event and reject artificial fragmentation. If operational aggregation exists but materially independent event structures can be established: → separate those structures. If substantial overlap exists: → preserve shared references while establishing distinct boundaries where justified. If the separation basis conflicts: → record Separation Conflict. If material distinctness remains unresolved: → preserve Separation Unresolved. If separation materially changes the developing Event Boundary: → transfer the resulting structure to EBRM for final boundary revision and confirmation. ------------------------------ Minimum Implementation Framework A conforming implementation of EBSM must be capable of: 1. receiving the Governed Event Boundary Exclusion Structure from EBEM 2. identifying Separation Candidates 3. assessing material event distinctness 4. detecting over-aggregation 5. detecting over-fragmentation 6. evaluating adjacent and overlapping event structures 7. evaluating nested and composite structures 8. handling repeated activity 9. handling distributed system representations 10. handling machine-generated and autonomous event structures 11. preserving common references across separated structures 12. representing separation conflict and uncertainty 13. preserving separation traceability 14. distinguishing Event Separation from Event Relationship governance 15. producing a Governed Event Boundary Separation Structure 16. transferring the result to EBRM 17. preventing downstream tax rules from determining operational event separation ------------------------------ Governance Outputs EBSM may produce: Governed Event Boundary Separation Structure Separation Candidate Record Single Event Structure Confirmation Multiple Event Structure Determination Partial Separation Structure Over-Aggregation Indicator Over-Fragmentation Indicator Overlap Record Shared Element Reference Separation Qualification Separation Conflict Indicator Separation Uncertainty Indicator Separation Traceability Record Boundary Revision Required Indicator Its principal output is: Governed Event Boundary Separation Structure This proceeds to: EBRM — Event Boundary Revision Module ------------------------------ Critical Distinctions Separation Candidate ≠ Separate Event Operational Connection ≠ Same Event Technical Separation ≠ Separate Event One Process ≠ One Event by Default Multiple Process Steps ≠ Multiple Events by Default Shared Identifier ≠ Same Event Boundary Different Identifier ≠ Separate Event by Default Event Adjacency ≠ Event Unity Operational Overlap ≠ Same Event Nested Structure ≠ Separate Event by Default Commercial Bundle ≠ Single Event by Default Repeated Activity ≠ Repeated Event by Default Multiple System Representations ≠ Multiple Events Machine Action ≠ Independent Event by Default Autonomous Objective ≠ Single Event by Default Technical Granularity ≠ Event Granularity Event Separation ≠ Event Relationship Determination Temporal Separation Evidence ≠ Event Timing Determination Location Difference ≠ Separate Event by Default Governed Event Separation ≠ Tax Separation Separate Governed Events ≠ Separate Tax Liabilities by Default System Representation ≠ Event Reality by Default Data Model Requirement ≠ Event Separation Authority ------------------------------ Enterprise Application Modern enterprise systems rarely agree on what constitutes one event. A single operational reality may appear as: 1 order in Commerce 3 shipments in Logistics 2 settlements in Payments 1 invoice in ERP 14 technical transactions in Infrastructure hundreds of API operations in Platform Systems Without governed separation logic, organizations may either collapse materially different events into one record or treat every technical operation as an independent event. EBSM creates a system-independent event separation layer. It allows downstream systems to consume event structures grounded in governed operational reality rather than database architecture, application boundaries, commercial packaging, or tax-specific assumptions. ------------------------------ Use Case 1 — One Marketplace Order Produces Multiple Operationally Distinct Outcomes A marketplace receives one customer order containing goods from three independent sellers. The platform assigns: one customer order ID, three seller fulfilments, three shipments, two payment settlements, one later refund. The commerce system represents the activity as one order. The logistics system represents three delivery structures. The payment system represents multiple financial operations. The existence of one order ID cannot decide whether one or several governed events exist. EBSM evaluates the operational structures independently of those system representations. Where materially distinct event structures are established, it separates their Event Boundaries while preserving the common order reference. The result avoids both: one oversized event created by the commercial order ID and dozens of artificial events created by technical system records. The downstream tax system can subsequently evaluate the separated governed events under applicable law without TREGA™ deciding their tax treatment. ------------------------------ Use Case 2 — Autonomous Cloud Agent Executes One Objective Through Multiple Independent Operations An autonomous AI agent receives a high-level objective: Acquire and deploy computational resources required to complete a complex workload. The agent independently: purchases compute capacity, reserves storage, acquires specialized model access, initiates network resources, executes workloads across multiple providers, releases unused capacity, performs settlement operations. Thousands of API calls occur. One interpretation would treat the entire autonomous objective as one event. Another would treat every API operation as a separate event. Both may distort operational reality. EBSM evaluates whether materially independent event structures exist within the autonomous activity. It may distinguish independently coherent resource acquisitions and executions while preserving technical sub-operations as components or supporting activity rather than artificial independent events. Autonomous complexity is therefore converted into governable event structure without allowing machine granularity to dictate event granularity. ------------------------------ Canonical Boundary EBSM governs the identification, assessment, differentiation, separation, consolidation protection, overlap handling, over-aggregation control, over-fragmentation control, conflict, uncertainty, and traceability of materially distinct event structures at the Event Boundary level. It does not identify the original Candidate Event Boundary, establish the initial Event Boundary Scope, perform Boundary Exclusion, determine semantic or economic relationships among separated events, establish final Event Timing, determine Event Location, govern Event Participation, determine Event-to-Value Association, determine legal taxability, identify the taxpayer, determine Tax Jurisdiction, establish legal tax point, calculate tax, or determine jurisdiction-specific tax consequences. ------------------------------ Module Handoff EBEM — Governed Event Boundary Exclusion Structure ↓ EBSM — Governed Event Boundary Separation Structure ↓ EBRM — Event Boundary Revision Module ------------------------------ Canonical Closing Statement The Event Boundary Separation Module prevents operational reality from being distorted by either excessive aggregation or excessive fragmentation. It separates materially distinct event structures where justified while preserving a coherent event where differences arise only from technical systems, records, infrastructure, or implementation granularity. EBSM does not determine what separated events legally mean or how they are taxed. EBSM determines when operationally connected activity must remain structurally distinguishable as separate governed events — without allowing systems, identifiers, commercial packaging, or tax rules to define event reality.

title: OOF™ Event Context Change Module (ECCHM)
text: OOF™ Event Context Change Module (ECCHM) Event Context Change Module (ECCHM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard (TRECS) Module: ECCHM — Event Context Change Module Operational Layer: Event Context Change Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Event Context Change Origin ID: TREGA-TRECS-ECCHM-004 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 29 August 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Event Context Change Module (ECCHM) is the Core Module within Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard (TRECS) that governs the identification, qualification, assessment, and representation of material changes affecting the governed context surrounding an occurrence throughout tax-relevant event governance. ECCHM establishes whether previously governed contextual conditions remain valid, have changed, require revision, or have been superseded, while preserving the historical contextual state against which the occurrence was originally understood. Its task is specific: to govern material change in Event Context without automatically converting contextual change into a new event, rewriting historical context, or determining a new legal tax consequence. Operational Role Context is not necessarily static. Between occurrence, recognition, event formation, determination, recording, and later review, relevant contextual conditions may change. An organization may restructure. A platform relationship may change. A machine may move between operational environments. A service may migrate between infrastructures. A business process may be modified. A digital asset may enter another operating environment. Previously unavailable contextual information may become known. ECCHM determines whether such changes materially affect the governed Event Context. The governing question is: Has the context materially changed, and if so, what part of the governed contextual representation must change with it? Internal Flow Governed Context State ↓ Context Change Detection ↓ Change Relevance Assessment ↓ Change Materiality Assessment ↓ Context Impact Determination ↓ Context Revision / Preservation / Supersession ↓ Governed Context Change Result The principal output is: Governed Context Change Result Operational Space ECCHM governs the space between: an established Event Context and a materially changed contextual condition requiring governed treatment. Its operational space includes: context change detection; contextual change identification; change relevance; change materiality; changed contextual relationships; scope-impacting changes; organizational changes; operational changes; transactional changes; digital and platform changes; technological changes; infrastructure changes; autonomous-system changes; value-related contextual changes; newly discovered context; contextual correction; contextual supersession; historical contextual preservation. ECCHM governs change to Event Context. It does not govern the complete lifecycle continuity of that context. Operational Scope ECCHM determines whether a detected contextual change materially affects the governed representation required to understand the occurrence. A contextual change may: have no material effect; modify an existing contextual element; introduce a new contextual element; remove the relevance of an existing element; alter a contextual relationship; require Context Scope reconsideration; or supersede a previously governed contextual state. Not every system update, organizational change, data correction, technical migration, or newly available record requires a material change to Event Context. ECCHM governs only changes capable of materially affecting contextual understanding. Context Change Principle The foundational rule is: Context must be capable of changing without allowing the past to be silently rewritten. A governed occurrence must remain interpretable against the context legitimately associated with it at the relevant time. Later reality may differ. That later reality does not automatically replace historical reality. Therefore: Current Context ≠ Historical Context. Change Detection ECCHM requires mechanisms capable of identifying materially relevant changes affecting previously governed context. A change may originate from: new operational information; organizational restructuring; participant environment changes; platform migration; system migration; infrastructure relocation; process modification; new contextual relationships; terminated contextual relationships; corrected source information; previously unavailable evidence; autonomous-system reconfiguration; material changes in surrounding value conditions. Detection alone does not establish materiality. Change Materiality A detected change becomes materially relevant where it can reasonably affect the interpretation or subsequent governance of the occurrence. ECCHM therefore distinguishes: Detected Change from Material Context Change. A software version update may be operationally visible but irrelevant to Event Context. A change in the economic role of a platform may materially alter contextual interpretation. A cloud migration may be irrelevant in one case but material in another. Materiality depends upon the relationship between the change and the governed occurrence. Context Change ≠ New Event One of the most important ECCHM boundaries is: Context Change ≠ New Event by Default. A contextual change does not automatically mean that a new Tax-Relevant Event exists. For example: an organization changes its internal structure; a platform changes infrastructure provider; a service migrates to another system; a machine changes operating location; additional contextual evidence becomes available. These changes may require contextual revision without creating a new governed event. Whether a materially transformed reality requires new Event Recognition or Event Formation belongs to later TREGA™ governance. Context Change Impact A material contextual change may affect: Context Elements — an existing contextual element changes. Context Scope — previously included or excluded elements require reconsideration. Context Relationships — relationships among contextual elements change. Context Interpretation — the same occurrence requires a revised contextual understanding. Context Status — the previous contextual state becomes superseded. ECCHM must identify which layer has been affected rather than treating every change as a complete reconstruction of context. Context Correction Not every difference between two contextual states represents a real-world change. Sometimes the underlying reality did not change. The earlier contextual representation was simply wrong or incomplete. ECCHM therefore distinguishes: Context Change — surrounding reality changed. from Context Correction — representation of surrounding reality was corrected. This distinction is critical for historical reconstruction. Context Correction ≠ Historical Erasure When an earlier contextual representation is corrected, the previous governed representation should not simply disappear where traceability is materially required. The architecture should be capable of distinguishing: what was previously represented, what was later corrected, and why the correction occurred. Therefore: Context Correction ≠ Historical Erasure. New Information ≠ New Reality A later-discovered fact may describe a condition that already existed when the occurrence happened. Its discovery is new. The underlying reality may not be. ECCHM must therefore distinguish: New Contextual Information from New Contextual Condition. This prevents the date on which information becomes available from being confused with the date on which the underlying contextual reality changed. Context Supersession Where a contextual state is materially replaced by a later governed state, ECCHM may establish contextual supersession. Supersession means that a newer contextual representation becomes applicable for the relevant subsequent governance purpose. It does not mean the previous state never existed. Therefore: Superseded Context ≠ Deleted Context. Temporal Integrity of Context ECCHM must preserve the ability to answer: What context was applicable when the occurrence happened? and separately: What context became applicable later? This distinction is essential where tax-relevant events are reconstructed months or years after operational activity occurred. A current system state must not automatically be projected backward onto historical occurrences. Change Uncertainty A suspected contextual change may not always be sufficiently established. ECCHM should permit states such as: Change Not Established Change Detected Change Under Assessment Material Change Established Context Corrected Context Superseded where appropriate to the implementation. Uncertainty should remain governed rather than converted into an assumed change. Governance Requirements ECCHM requires that: contextual change be distinguishable from ordinary system activity; detected change be evaluated for materiality; change be associated with the contextual element or relationship affected; current context remain distinguishable from historical context; real-world change be distinguishable from information correction; newly discovered information not automatically become a newly occurring condition; scope-impacting changes be capable of returning to appropriate TRECS governance; relationship changes be capable of updating the governed relationship structure; superseded context remain historically traceable where required; Context Change not automatically create a new Tax-Relevant Event; contextual change not determine legal tax consequences. Governance Logic ECCHM applies four principal questions: What changed? Did reality change, or did our representation of reality change? Is the change materially relevant to Event Context? What part of the governed contextual representation must now be revised, preserved, or superseded? The governing transformation is: Existing Governed Context → Detected Difference → Qualified Material Change → Governed Context Change Result A change that is not materially relevant should not destabilize the governed context. A material change should not silently overwrite it. Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum ECCHM implementation must be capable of: 1. referencing an established governed Context State; 2. detecting potentially relevant contextual changes; 3. distinguishing change from correction where reasonably possible; 4. assessing contextual change materiality; 5. identifying affected contextual elements, scope, or relationships; 6. recording the effective contextual change where materially relevant; 7. preserving prior contextual states where traceability requires it; 8. representing uncertainty where change cannot yet be established; 9. producing a Governed Context Change Result; 10. transferring continuity requirements to ECCM. No particular change-detection technology, database, ledger, ERP platform, AI model, event-stream architecture, or tax system is required. Governance Outputs ECCHM may produce: Governed Context Change Result — the qualified representation of a material contextual change. Context Change Record — identification of what changed. Change Materiality Result — determination of whether the change materially affects Event Context. Affected Context Reference — identification of affected contextual elements, scope, or relationships. Context Correction Record — where the representation rather than underlying reality was corrected. Context Supersession Reference — identification of a previous contextual state replaced for subsequent governance purposes. Change Uncertainty Indicator — unresolved contextual change conditions. Historical Context Reference — linkage preserving the previous governed contextual state. Critical Distinctions Context Change ≠ New Event. A changed environment does not automatically create another Tax-Relevant Event. Context Change ≠ Context Correction. Reality changing is different from correcting how reality was represented. New Information ≠ New Reality. Later discovery does not establish that the underlying condition began when it was discovered. Current Context ≠ Historical Context. Current conditions must not automatically redefine the environment surrounding a historical occurrence. Context Correction ≠ Historical Erasure. Correction should preserve material governance history. Context Supersession ≠ Context Deletion. A superseded contextual state may remain essential for reconstruction and auditability. Context Change ≠ Tax Consequence Change. A material contextual change does not itself determine that taxation treatment has changed. Context Change ≠ Context Continuity. ECCHM determines and governs change. ECCM governs continuity across contextual states and changes. Enterprise Application ECCHM becomes particularly important where tax-relevant activity is reconstructed from systems that continuously evolve. A modern enterprise may change: ERP systems ↓ corporate structures ↓ cloud providers ↓ payment providers ↓ platform configurations ↓ logistics systems ↓ autonomous workflows while the underlying tax-relevant records remain subject to later reporting, audit, dispute, or regulatory review. Without governed Context Change, a system may reconstruct an old occurrence using today's configuration. That can produce a representation of reality that never existed when the occurrence happened. ECCHM enables organizations and downstream public-sector systems to distinguish: historical context from later contextual change and from later correction of historical information. Use CasesUse Case 1 — Historical Cross-Border Transaction After Corporate Restructuring A multinational digital business completes large volumes of cross-border transactions. Two years later, the group restructures its entities, migrates customer contracts, changes payment providers, modifies platform responsibilities, and relocates parts of its infrastructure. A later tax review reconstructs transactions from current enterprise systems. Without governed Context Change, the current organizational and platform structure may be incorrectly projected backward, making historical transactions appear to have occurred within relationships that did not exist at the time. ECCHM separates the historical Event Context from later organizational, platform, and infrastructure changes. Where newly discovered information corrects the historical representation, it records the correction without pretending that the underlying historical reality changed at the date of discovery. The result preserves a fundamental requirement for reliable taxation infrastructure: a historical event must be evaluated against its historical context, not automatically against the organization that exists today. Use Case 2 — Autonomous System Changes During Continuous Machine Commerce An autonomous procurement system continuously purchases computing capacity, digital services, machine components, and operational resources from multiple providers. During operation, the system is reconfigured, authority pathways change, infrastructure is relocated, supplier relationships are modified, and parts of the autonomous workflow are transferred to another platform. Millions of machine records continue to be generated throughout the transition. A conventional transaction system may have difficulty determining which contextual configuration applied to which activity. ECCHM identifies material contextual changes and separates them from ordinary technical updates. It preserves the contextual states necessary to determine which operational environment surrounded an occurrence at the relevant time without declaring that every system reconfiguration created a new Tax-Relevant Event. This provides a governed method for handling a future problem of autonomous economies: the systems generating economic activity may change faster than the taxation systems evaluating that activity. Canonical Boundary ECCHM governs material change to Event Context. It does not govern continuity of the contextual identity across the complete lifecycle, determine whether contextual transformation creates a new Tax-Relevant Event, or determine the tax consequence of the change. The TRECS internal progression remains: ECIM — What contextual elements may matter? → ECSM — Which contextual elements belong within the relevant Context Scope? → ECRM — How are those contextual elements materially related? → ECCHM — What has materially changed in that governed context? → ECCM — How is contextual continuity preserved across those changes? Canonical Closing Statement Event Context Change Module establishes the contextual change governance capability of the Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard by determining when the economic, operational, organizational, transactional, digital, technological, infrastructural, autonomous, machine-generated, value-related, or relational conditions surrounding an occurrence have materially changed and how those changes must be represented without rewriting the contextual reality that previously existed. Through governance of change detection, materiality, affected context, correction, supersession, uncertainty, historical preservation, and temporal contextual integrity, ECCHM prevents current system states, later organizational structures, newly discovered information, technical migrations, or autonomous-system reconfigurations from silently redefining the context of historical activity. The Module preserves the critical distinctions between Context Change and Context Correction, new information and new reality, current context and historical context, contextual supersession and deletion, and contextual change and new Event Formation. ECCHM therefore allows Event Context to evolve while ensuring that the governed representation of what surrounded an occurrence remains reconstructable according to the reality that existed when that context was relevant. Model 5 Jasné. Module 5 — ECCM uzatvára TRECS. Jeho úloha je zásadná: po identifikácii, scope, vzťahoch a zmenách musí zabezpečiť, že kontext zostáva rekonštruovateľný ako ten istý governed contextual chain, aj keď sa jeho jednotlivé stavy menia.

title: OOF™ Event Context Continuity Module (ECCM)
text: OOF™ Event Context Continuity Module (ECCM) Event Context Continuity Module (ECCM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard (TRECS) Module: ECCM — Event Context Continuity Module Operational Layer: Event Context Continuity Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Event Context Continuity Origin ID: TREGA-TRECS-ECCM-005 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 29 August 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Event Context Continuity Module (ECCM) is the Core Module within Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard (TRECS) that governs the preservation, linkage, traceability, and reconstructability of Event Context across contextual states, material changes, corrections, system transitions, and subsequent stages of the TREGA™ lifecycle. ECCM establishes how the contextual representation surrounding an occurrence remains governably connected to its preceding and succeeding contextual states without requiring those states to remain unchanged. Its task is specific: to preserve the continuity and reconstructability of governed Event Context across change without freezing context, erasing historical states, or treating every contextual modification as a new event or new contextual identity. Operational Role Context may evolve after its initial establishment. ECIM identifies contextual elements. ECSM determines their legitimate scope. ECRM establishes their material relationships. ECCHM governs material changes. ECCM ensures that these states do not become disconnected fragments. Its operational question is: Can the governed contextual history surrounding an occurrence still be reconstructed and understood after the context has changed? ECCM therefore provides the continuity layer through which TRECS can preserve: original contextual states; subsequent contextual states; contextual revisions; contextual corrections; contextual supersessions; relationships between contextual states; historical applicability; continuity across system transitions; continuity across organizational change; continuity across long-running event governance. Internal Flow Governed Context State ↓ Continuity Reference Establishment ↓ Context State Linkage ↓ Change / Correction Association ↓ Historical State Preservation ↓ Continuity Verification ↓ Governed Context Continuity The principal governed output is: Governed Context Continuity Record This output preserves the contextual chain required for subsequent TREGA™ governance and later reconstruction. Operational Space ECCM governs the space between: separate governed contextual states and a continuous, traceable, and reconstructable contextual history associated with the same occurrence or developing event-governance process. Its operational space includes: contextual state linkage; historical contextual preservation; continuity references; contextual version relationships; correction continuity; supersession continuity; contextual lineage; temporal contextual traceability; continuity across system migration; continuity across organizational change; continuity across distributed environments; continuity uncertainty; contextual reconstruction. ECCM governs continuity of Event Context. It does not govern the complete lifecycle of the Tax-Relevant Event itself. Operational Scope ECCM applies where more than one contextual state, representation, version, correction, or materially relevant contextual configuration exists. The module ensures that later context can remain connected to earlier context without collapsing the two into one representation. A continuity relationship may be required where: contextual information is updated; material context changes; an earlier contextual representation is corrected; context is superseded; systems are migrated; organizations restructure; platforms change; contextual information is reconstructed later; historical occurrences are reviewed; multiple systems retain different portions of contextual history. ECCM must preserve sufficient continuity to determine which contextual state applied, when it applied, and how it relates to other governed contextual states. Continuity Principle Continuity does not require immutability. A context can change while remaining part of the same governed contextual history. Therefore: Context Continuity ≠ Context Permanence. The purpose of ECCM is not to prevent change. Its purpose is to ensure that change does not destroy the ability to understand the contextual chain. Continuity Across Change Where ECCHM establishes a material Context Change, ECCM preserves the relationship between: Previous Context State ↓ Context Change ↓ Subsequent Context State This allows downstream systems to distinguish evolution from replacement. A new contextual state should not automatically become disconnected from the state from which it developed. At the same time, continuity must not be artificially maintained where the contextual relationship has genuinely ended. Historical Context Preservation Historical contextual states may remain materially important long after they cease to represent current conditions. ECCM preserves the ability to answer: What context surrounded the occurrence at the relevant time? This is essential where tax-relevant activity is: reported later; audited later; disputed later; reconstructed from archived systems; re-evaluated after legal changes; examined by another jurisdiction; transferred between enterprise systems. Therefore: Historical Context ≠ Obsolete Context. A contextual state can cease to be current while remaining essential governance information. Continuity Across Correction A corrected contextual record should remain connected to the representation it corrected. ECCM preserves: Original Representation ↓ Correction ↓ Corrected Representation where traceability is materially required. This enables later governance to distinguish what was originally known from what was subsequently established. Therefore: Correction Continuity ≠ Preservation of Error as Current Truth. The earlier representation may remain historically visible without remaining operationally authoritative. Continuity Across Supersession Where one contextual state supersedes another, ECCM establishes the continuity relationship between them. Supersession must not silently destroy the previous contextual state. The architecture should be capable of representing: Context State A ↓ Superseded By ↓ Context State B while preserving the period or governance purpose for which Context State A remained applicable. Therefore: Supersession ≠ Historical Deletion. Continuity Across System Migration Enterprise and public-sector systems change. ERP platforms are replaced. Databases are migrated. Cloud providers change. Platform identifiers are regenerated. Legacy systems are retired. Data structures evolve. ECCM requires that a technical migration does not automatically break the governed contextual chain. Therefore: System Continuity ≠ Context Continuity. The technical system may change completely while the governed contextual history remains continuous. Conversely, technical persistence of the same database record does not by itself prove contextual continuity. Continuity Across Organizational Change Companies merge. Business units are transferred. Legal entities are reorganized. Operational responsibilities change. Platforms are acquired. Service providers are replaced. ECCM preserves contextual continuity where the surrounding governed context remains legitimately related across those changes. However: Organizational Continuity ≠ Event Context Continuity by Default. The existence of a corporate successor does not automatically prove continuity of every historical contextual relationship. Continuity must remain governable. Distributed Context Continuity A governed contextual history may be distributed across several systems. For example: Commerce Platform ↓ Payment Infrastructure ↓ ERP ↓ Logistics ↓ Archive No single system may retain the complete contextual chain. ECCM permits continuity to be established through governed references across distributed environments. This allows contextual reconstruction without requiring all underlying information to reside in one database or platform. Continuity Break Continuity should not be assumed indefinitely. Where a contextual relationship can no longer legitimately be maintained, ECCM must permit a: Context Continuity Break A continuity break indicates that two contextual states cannot legitimately be represented as part of the same continuous contextual chain without additional governance. This prevents forced continuity. Therefore: Similarity ≠ Continuity. Two contextual states may look similar without being demonstrably continuous. Continuity Uncertainty Where continuity cannot be sufficiently established, ECCM must preserve uncertainty rather than manufacture linkage. Possible governance conditions may include: Continuity Established Continuity Partially Established Continuity Uncertain Continuity Interrupted Continuity Re-established where appropriate to implementation. The existence of missing records does not automatically prove discontinuity. Equally, apparent similarity does not automatically prove continuity. Context Reconstruction A central capability of ECCM is reconstruction. A governed system should be capable, where sufficient information exists, of reconstructing: the relevant contextual state, the changes affecting it, the corrections applied to it, the states that superseded it, and the continuity relationships connecting those states. This capability becomes particularly important when the same governed occurrence is evaluated years later or by several downstream jurisdictions. Governance Requirements ECCM requires that: materially distinct contextual states remain distinguishable; continuity relationships are explicitly governable; historical context remains reconstructable where required; corrections remain linked to the states they correct; superseded states are not silently deleted; system migration does not automatically break contextual continuity; organizational succession does not automatically prove contextual continuity; continuity uncertainty remains explicit; continuity breaks can be represented; contextual history remains separable from current contextual state; continuity does not itself establish Event Continuity; continuity does not determine legal tax consequences. Governance Logic ECCM applies four principal questions: Which contextual state is being continued? What relationship connects the previous and subsequent contextual states? Has continuity remained sufficiently established across change, correction, migration, or supersession? Can the relevant contextual history still be reconstructed without rewriting previous states? The core transformation is: Separate Context States → Governed State Relationships → Traceable Context Chain → Reconstructable Event Context Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum ECCM implementation must be capable of: 1. identifying materially distinct contextual states; 2. linking related contextual states; 3. preserving previous contextual states where required; 4. associating changes, corrections, and supersessions with affected states; 5. representing contextual continuity and continuity breaks; 6. preserving uncertainty where continuity cannot be sufficiently established; 7. supporting contextual reconstruction; 8. maintaining continuity across technical system changes where legitimate; 9. distinguishing Context Continuity from Event Continuity; 10. producing a Governed Context Continuity Record suitable for subsequent TREGA™ processing. ECCM does not prescribe a blockchain, ledger, event-sourcing architecture, database, knowledge graph, ERP platform, AI model, archival technology, or tax infrastructure. Governance Outputs ECCM may produce: Governed Context Continuity Record — the governed representation of contextual continuity across relevant states. Context State Chain — the ordered or relational sequence of governed contextual states. Historical Context Reference — preserved reference to a previous applicable contextual state. Context Change Linkage — relationship between contextual states affected by material change. Context Correction Linkage — relationship between an original representation and its corrected representation. Context Supersession Linkage — relationship between superseded and succeeding contextual states. Continuity Status — governed representation of whether continuity is established, uncertain, interrupted, or re-established. Continuity Break Record — explicit representation of a material break in contextual continuity. Context Reconstruction Reference — information necessary to reconstruct the relevant contextual chain. Critical Distinctions Context Continuity ≠ Context Permanence. Continuity permits change. Context Continuity ≠ Event Continuity. ECCM preserves continuity of contextual representation. TRECLS — Tax-Relevant Event Lifecycle & Continuity Standard later governs continuity of the Tax-Relevant Event itself. Current Context ≠ Historical Context. Both may legitimately exist within the same contextual chain. Supersession ≠ Historical Deletion. A superseded context may remain essential evidence of historical reality. Correction ≠ New Context by Default. Correcting an earlier representation does not necessarily establish a new underlying contextual reality. System Continuity ≠ Context Continuity. A persistent technical identifier does not prove governed contextual continuity. System Migration ≠ Context Discontinuity. Changing technology does not automatically terminate the governed contextual chain. Similarity ≠ Continuity. Two similar contextual states are not necessarily the same continuous context. Context Continuity ≠ Tax Obligation Continuity. ECCM does not determine whether a tax obligation continues, changes, transfers, or ends. Enterprise Application ECCM addresses a structural problem in long-lived taxation and enterprise information environments: operational systems change faster than the lifecycle of the records that governments, organizations, auditors, and tax systems may later need to evaluate. An event recorded today may be reviewed years later after: ERP replacement ↓ cloud migration ↓ corporate restructuring ↓ platform migration ↓ identifier changes ↓ archive transfer ↓ tax-system modernization. Without contextual continuity governance, each migration may progressively disconnect the record from the reality in which it originally existed. ECCM provides a technology-neutral mechanism for maintaining the governed contextual chain independently of the systems that happen to store individual parts of that chain. This allows downstream tax infrastructure to consume historical context without requiring historical technology to remain operational forever. Use CasesUse Case 1 — Tax Audit Years After Enterprise Systems Have Been Replaced A multinational enterprise completes millions of transactions across ERP, payment, logistics, and digital commerce systems. Over the following six years, the company replaces its ERP, migrates cloud infrastructure, restructures several business units, changes internal identifiers, and archives portions of the original operational data. A tax authority later examines a historical cross-border transaction. The current systems contain the transaction, but the organizational and operational context surrounding the original activity has materially changed. Without governed continuity, the historical record may be interpreted using relationships, identifiers, system structures, or organizational conditions that did not exist when the occurrence took place. ECCM preserves the chain between the original Event Context, subsequent contextual changes, corrections, system migrations, and current representations. The historical occurrence can therefore be reconstructed against its historically applicable context rather than being silently reinterpreted through the enterprise environment that exists years later. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Economy Without Stable Technical Infrastructure An autonomous commercial agent operates continuously for several years, purchasing services, allocating computing resources, interacting with marketplaces, coordinating machines, and initiating machine-to-machine transactions. During that period its underlying models are replaced, APIs change, infrastructure migrates, platform accounts are transferred, identifiers evolve, and operational components are distributed across new providers. The economic activity continues even though much of the technical infrastructure that originally generated its records no longer exists. ECCM preserves governed contextual continuity across these transitions without assuming that identical technology, identifiers, or infrastructure must remain in place. Where continuity cannot legitimately be established, the module records the break rather than manufacturing an artificial chain. This addresses a fundamental problem of future machine economies: economic activity may remain continuous even when the technical systems producing it are repeatedly replaced. Canonical Boundary ECCM governs continuity of Event Context across contextual states. It does not govern continuity of the Tax-Relevant Event itself, continuity of legal tax obligations, identity continuity, value continuity, or jurisdictional tax treatment. The complete TRECS internal progression is therefore: ECIM — What contextual elements may matter? → ECSM — Which contextual elements belong within the relevant Context Scope? → ECRM — How are those contextual elements materially related? → ECCHM — What has materially changed in that governed context? → ECCM — How is the governed contextual chain preserved across those changes? The final TRECS result can then support: Governed Event Context ↓ TRERS — Tax-Relevant Event Recognition Standard Canonical Closing Statement Event Context Continuity Module establishes the continuity and reconstructability layer of the Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard by preserving the governed relationships among historical, current, corrected, changed, and superseded contextual states surrounding an occurrence. Through governance of contextual state linkage, historical preservation, correction continuity, supersession, continuity status, continuity breaks, distributed reconstruction, organizational transition, and system migration, ECCM prevents evolving technologies, changing enterprise structures, disappearing platforms, modified identifiers, later corrections, or current operational conditions from severing or silently rewriting the contextual history required to understand earlier activity. The Module preserves the distinction between continuity and permanence, similarity and continuity, Context Continuity and Event Continuity, and contextual history and current state. ECCM therefore ensures that Event Context can evolve across systems, organizations, technologies, and time while remaining sufficiently traceable and reconstructable for subsequent TREGA™ governance without allowing contextual continuity itself to determine event identity, legal taxability, tax jurisdiction, or tax consequence.

title: OOF™ Event Context Identification Module (ECIM)
text: OOF™ Event Context Identification Module (ECIM) Event Context Identification Module (ECIM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard (TRECS) Module: ECIM — Event Context Identification Module Operational Layer: Event Context Identification Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Event Context Identification Origin ID: TREGA-TRECS-ECIM-001 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 29 August 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Event Context Identification Module (ECIM) is the Core Module within Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard (TRECS) that governs the identification of materially relevant contextual elements surrounding an observed occurrence entering the TREGA™ lifecycle. ECIM establishes which economic, operational, organizational, transactional, digital, technological, infrastructural, autonomous, machine-generated, value-related, or other contextual conditions are potentially relevant to understanding the occurrence before Context Scope, contextual relationships, contextual change, and contextual continuity are governed. Its task is specific: to identify the contextual elements that may be necessary to understand an occurrence without determining what ultimately belongs within the governed Context Scope or whether a Tax-Relevant Event exists. Operational Role ECIM is the entry module of TRECS. An observed occurrence may arrive from an ERP system, transaction platform, financial infrastructure, industrial process, autonomous system, digital service, machine network, API, marketplace, or another operational environment. The occurrence alone may not contain enough information to establish its meaning. ECIM identifies the surrounding contextual elements that should become candidates for further context governance. These may include: economic environment; operational process; organizational setting; transaction structure; digital environment; technological system; platform environment; infrastructure; autonomous-system conditions; machine-execution environment; value-related conditions; relevant process or activity; distributed operational environment; potentially relevant cross-border circumstances. ECIM identifies context. It does not yet decide the complete governed extent of that context. Internal Flow Observed Occurrence ↓ Context Signal Detection ↓ Context Element Identification ↓ Relevance Screening ↓ Context Element Qualification ↓ Identified Context Set The governed output is: Identified Context Set This output provides the contextual candidates required by the next TRECS governance stages. Governance Requirements ECIM requires that contextual identification: begins from an identifiable occurrence; distinguishes the occurrence from its surrounding context; identifies materially plausible contextual elements; permits multiple context types where required; does not assume that one technical record represents one economic event; preserves uncertainty where contextual meaning remains unresolved; distinguishes identified context from confirmed Event Recognition; avoids treating tax rules as the primary constructor of operational context; permits machine-generated and autonomous contexts; preserves references to upstream governed information where available; produces an identifiable contextual result suitable for subsequent governance. Identification must remain proportionate. ECIM should not collect unrelated surrounding information merely because that information is technically available. Governance Logic ECIM applies a simple methodological question: What surrounding conditions may materially affect how this occurrence should be understood within subsequent tax-relevant event governance? A contextual element may be identified where it has a plausible material relationship to: the operational meaning of the occurrence; its economic environment; its transaction structure; the process in which it occurred; its organizational environment; its digital or technological environment; autonomous or machine execution; relevant value conditions; subsequent Event Recognition or Event Formation. ECIM does not require that every identified element ultimately remain within the governed context. Identification precedes scope determination. Therefore: Potential Context Relevance ↓ Identification does not mean: Potential Context Relevance ↓ Final Context Inclusion. That later determination belongs to ECSM — Event Context Scope Module. Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum implementation of ECIM must be capable of: 1. receiving or referencing an observed occurrence; 2. identifying available surrounding contextual signals; 3. distinguishing contextual information from the occurrence itself; 4. identifying one or more potentially relevant context types; 5. recording the basis for material contextual relevance where necessary; 6. representing uncertainty or missing context; 7. preserving references to upstream governed sources where available; 8. producing an Identified Context Set for subsequent TRECS processing. The implementation may operate through human governance, structured workflows, enterprise systems, rule-based systems, automated processes, AI-assisted systems, or combinations of these approaches. ECIM does not prescribe a particular database, ontology, AI model, ERP platform, tax engine, or technical implementation. Governance Outputs ECIM may produce: Identified Context Set — the governed collection of contextual elements identified around the occurrence. Context Type References — identification of relevant economic, operational, organizational, transactional, digital, technological, autonomous, value-related, or other context types. Context Element References — references to individual contextual elements requiring subsequent governance. Context Relevance Basis — the governed reason an element has been identified as potentially material. Context Uncertainty Indicator — identification of missing, ambiguous, or unresolved contextual information. Upstream Governance References — references to relevant governed results supplied by other systems or OOF® architectures where available. These outputs provide input to ECSM — Event Context Scope Module and other subsequent TRECS modules. Critical Distinctions Occurrence ≠ Context. The occurrence is the observed action, condition, transaction, signal, or operation. Context describes the environment necessary to understand it. Context Identification ≠ Context Scope. ECIM identifies potentially relevant contextual elements. ECSM subsequently determines the governed extent of context. Identified Context ≠ Tax-Relevant Event. Identification of relevant context does not establish that a Tax-Relevant Event exists. Context Relevance ≠ Taxability. A contextual element may be important for downstream taxation analysis without itself establishing any legal tax consequence. Cross-Border Context ≠ Tax Jurisdiction. Identifying several geographic or operational environments does not determine taxation rights. Actor Context ≠ Taxpayer Determination. Identifying a person, organization, machine, platform, or autonomous agent within context does not establish taxpayer status. Enterprise Application ECIM can operate as the first contextual identification layer between heterogeneous enterprise systems and the broader TREGA™ event lifecycle. Potential environments include: ERP ↓ ECIM Commerce Platform ↓ ECIM Banking Infrastructure ↓ ECIM Industrial System ↓ ECIM Digital Platform ↓ ECIM AI Agent ↓ ECIM Machine Network ↓ ECIM Distributed Infrastructure ↓ ECIM The module allows these environments to provide different technical records while applying a common methodological question: What contextual information must be identified before this occurrence can be interpreted coherently? This is particularly useful where one economic activity produces multiple technical records or where machine-generated activity crosses organizational, technological, or geographic boundaries. Use CasesUse Case 1 — Autonomous Digital Purchase An autonomous agent purchases a digital service through a platform using an automated payment infrastructure. The transaction produces records from the agent, platform, API, payment system, and service provider. ECIM identifies the potentially relevant agent environment, platform context, service context, payment context, operational relationships, and distributed infrastructure surrounding the occurrence. It does not determine whether these elements constitute one event or several events, which jurisdiction may tax the activity, or whether tax is legally due. Its output is an Identified Context Set ready for Context Scope governance. Use Case 2 — Automated Industrial Movement An automated manufacturing system transfers a component between production, internal storage, and logistics systems. Several systems record the movement differently. ECIM identifies the relevant production process, internal organizational environment, inventory context, logistics environment, system relationships, and associated operational circumstances. The module does not assume that every system record represents a separate economic event. It identifies the contextual elements required before subsequent TREGA™ governance determines how the occurrence should be interpreted. Canonical Closing Statement Event Context Identification Module establishes the entry-level contextual identification capability of the Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard by determining which economic, operational, organizational, transactional, digital, technological, infrastructural, autonomous, machine-generated, value-related, and other surrounding conditions may be materially relevant to understanding an observed occurrence. Through governed identification of context signals, context types, contextual elements, relevance bases, uncertainty, and upstream governance references, ECIM prevents isolated records from entering the TREGA™ lifecycle without their potentially material surrounding reality while preserving the boundaries between Context Identification, Context Scope, Event Recognition, and legal taxation determination. ECIM therefore does not determine what the final event is or what tax consequence follows; it establishes the contextual elements from which those later governance processes can legitimately begin.

title: OOF™ The Event Closure Module (ECLM) governs how a Tax-Relevant Event reaches
text: OOF™ The Event Closure Module (ECLM) governs how a Tax-Relevant Event reaches The Event Closure Module (ECLM) governs how a Tax-Relevant Event reaches OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: TRECLS — Tax-Relevant Event Lifecycle & Continuity Standard Module: ECLM — Event Closure Module Operational Layer: Event Closure Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Event Closure Primary Governed Object: Governed Event Closure State Origin ID: TREGA-TRECLS-ECLM-005 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 3 September 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language Canonical Definition The Event Closure Module (ECLM) governs how a Tax-Relevant Event reaches a methodologically governed lifecycle endpoint after its continuity, amendment, correction, and supersession states have been sufficiently established. Its principal transition is: Governed Event Supersession State / Current Effective Event State ↓ Event Closure Governance ↓ Governed Event Closure State ↓ Jurisdiction-Ready Tax-Relevant Event ECLM establishes whether ordinary TREGA™ lifecycle development for the Event can be considered complete, while preserving the Event’s current effective state, materially relevant historical states, unresolved qualifications, reopening conditions, and downstream jurisdiction-neutral readiness. Its foundational distinction is: Event Closure ≠ Tax Obligation Closure. Operational Role A governed Event cannot remain indefinitely open merely because it may later be consumed by tax systems, reporting systems, auditors, courts, or other downstream environments. At some point, TREGA™ must be able to establish that the Event itself has reached a sufficiently governed lifecycle state for downstream jurisdiction-specific analysis. ECLM answers: Has the Tax-Relevant Event reached a sufficiently stable and reconstructable governed state to close its ordinary lifecycle and become Jurisdiction-Ready? Closure does not mean that nothing can ever happen again. It means that no further ordinary TREGA™ lifecycle processing is presently required. Internal Module Flow TRECLS operates through: ECOM — Event Continuity ↓ EADM — Event Amendment ↓ ECRTM — Event Correction ↓ ESPM — Event Supersession ↓ ECLM — Event Closure ↓ Jurisdiction-Ready Tax-Relevant Event ECLM is the fifth and final Core Module. It receives: Governed Event Supersession State / Current Effective Event State and produces: Governed Event Closure State followed by the final TREGA™ lifecycle output: Jurisdiction-Ready Tax-Relevant Event Operational Transition The canonical transition is: Current Effective Event State ↓ Closure Trigger ↓ Closure Readiness Assessment ↓ Unresolved-State Review ↓ Closure Determination ↓ Governed Event Closure State ↓ Jurisdiction-Ready Tax-Relevant Event Operational Space ECLM governs: Closure Trigger identification; Closure eligibility; Closure readiness; current effective Event state confirmation; historical-state sufficiency; continuity-state sufficiency; amendment-state sufficiency; correction-state sufficiency; supersession-state sufficiency; unresolved-state review; lifecycle qualification; Closure qualification; Closure ambiguity; Closure conflict; Closure deferral; Closure rejection; Event reopening references; reopening eligibility; Closure history; jurisdiction-readiness; and final TREGA™ lifecycle handoff. Operational Scope ECLM may govern Closure for: physical transactions; digital Events; commercial Events; financial Events; platform Events; AI-agent activity; autonomous systems; machine-to-machine Events; distributed Events; digital assets; industrial activity; cross-border Events; multi-party Events; long-running Events; and future machine economies. The module remains technology-neutral and jurisdiction-neutral. Closure Object The Closure Object is the current governed Tax-Relevant Event lifecycle state proposed for closure. Closure applies to the Event lifecycle, not automatically to: every Record; every technical process; every accounting period; every filing; every tax assessment; every payment obligation; or every downstream legal process. Closure Trigger A Closure Trigger may arise when: the governed occurrence has operationally completed; no further ordinary Event development is expected; a final current effective state has been established; amendment and correction processes are complete; supersession state is clear; Event relationships relevant to closure are sufficiently governed; a long-running Event reaches a defined endpoint; a prior Event is replaced by a materially different new Event; or lifecycle governance authority initiates closure review.
