Closure Eligibility An Event may be eligible for Closure where: a valid current effective Event state exists; continuity is sufficiently governed; materially relevant amendments are resolved or qualified; materially relevant corrections are resolved or qualified; supersession state is sufficiently clear; materially relevant historical states remain reconstructable; unresolved matters do not prevent downstream use; and Event lifecycle governance can produce a Jurisdiction-Ready state. Closure Readiness Closure Readiness asks whether the Event lifecycle is sufficiently complete for ordinary TREGA™ governance to stop. It does not require absolute informational perfection. Closure Readiness ≠ Absence of All Uncertainty. A qualified Event may still be closable where uncertainty is explicit and does not prevent legitimate downstream analysis. Current Effective State Confirmation Before Closure, ECLM shall establish which Event state is currently effective. This prevents: superseded states from being closed as current; obsolete states from being exported downstream; multiple competing current states; ambiguity about which Event representation is authoritative. ESPM provides the principal supersession state. Historical-State Sufficiency Closure requires enough historical state to reconstruct materially relevant lifecycle transitions. This may include: prior Event states; Amendments; Corrections; Supersessions; Continuity reassessments; prior Closure or reopening states. Closed Event ≠ History-Free Event. Continuity Sufficiency ECLM should not close an Event as one continuous lifecycle where ECOM has established unresolved material Continuity Conflict. Where continuity is materially unresolved, Closure may be: deferred; qualified; or referred upstream. Amendment Sufficiency Pending material Amendments should be reviewed before Closure. A non-material or explicitly deferred update may not prevent Closure. A material Amendment capable of changing the current Event state may prevent unqualified Closure. Correction Sufficiency Known material errors should not be ignored merely to achieve Closure. Where correction remains materially unresolved, Closure may require qualification or deferral. Closure ≠ Permission to Freeze Known Error. Supersession Sufficiency The current effective state should be identifiable before Closure. If competing successor states remain unresolved, Closure should not silently select one. Closure Materiality Not every open technical issue prevents Event Closure. ECLM should distinguish: material lifecycle issue; non-material technical issue; unresolved but bounded qualification; downstream legal issue outside TREGA™. Closure decisions should reflect governed Event materiality. Qualified Closure Qualified Closure may be appropriate where the Event is sufficiently governed for downstream use but one or more bounded uncertainties remain. Examples include: unresolved minor supporting reference; qualified distributed Location; limited Participation uncertainty; bounded Value Association uncertainty. The qualification must remain visible. Qualified Closure ≠ Failed Closure. Unqualified Closure Unqualified Closure may be established where all materially relevant TREGA™ lifecycle states are sufficiently governed without material unresolved qualification. Closure Ambiguity Closure Ambiguity exists where it is unclear whether: the Event has operationally ended; additional lifecycle development belongs to the same Event; unresolved information is material; Closure or continuation is appropriate. The Event should remain under review rather than being arbitrarily closed. Closure Conflict Closure Conflict exists where materially authoritative governance states support incompatible closure outcomes. For example: operational data indicates Event completion; participation governance indicates continuing material activity. Conflict shall remain explicit. Closure Deferral Closure may be deferred where: material Amendment remains pending; material Correction remains pending; Supersession remains unresolved; Continuity remains materially uncertain; Event Relationships remain materially unresolved; upstream governance is required. Closure Deferral ≠ Closure Failure. Closure Rejection A proposed Closure may be rejected where the Event remains materially active or incomplete. Rejection does not prevent future Closure. Closure State A valid Closure State should establish: Event identity; current effective state; Closure basis; Closure effective state; lifecycle qualification; historical-state references; reopening conditions or references; jurisdiction-readiness state. Closure Effective Time Where materially relevant, the system may distinguish: operational Event completion; Closure review initiation; Closure decision; Closure governance effective time. These governance timestamps do not establish a jurisdiction-specific legal tax point. Operational Completion vs Governance Closure The underlying activity may operationally complete before TREGA™ Closure. Conversely, some lifecycle governance may complete after operational activity ends. Operational Completion ≠ Event Closure by default. ORA™ remains relevant to operational reality. TREGA™ governs the Event lifecycle. Technical Process Completion A technical workflow ending does not necessarily mean that the governed Event is ready to close. Likewise, a technical process may remain active after the Event itself is already complete. Technical Process End ≠ Event Closure. Long-Running Event Closure A long-running Event may require an explicit governed endpoint. This may depend on: completion state; contractual or operational transition; defined Event Boundary; cessation of material activity; replacement by a new Event. ECLM does not artificially close Events merely because a reporting period ended. Recurring Activity Boundary Recurring activity may involve: repeated separate Events; one continuing Event; one Event followed by successor Events. ECLM consumes prior Formation, Boundary, and Continuity governance rather than deciding recurrence structure independently. Event Closure and New Event Formation A materially transformed occurrence may require Closure of the prior Event and formation of a new Event. The pattern may be: Event A ↓ Material Transformation ↓ Continuity Broken ↓ Event A Closure ↓ TREFS Review ↓ Event B ECLM closes Event A. TREFS governs Event B Formation. Event Closure and Amendment An Amendment may occur before Closure. A material Amendment after Closure may require reopening. EADM owns Amendment Governance. Event Closure and Correction A Correction may occur before Closure. A material Correction discovered after Closure may require reopening or another governed lifecycle path. ECRTM owns Correction Governance. Event Closure and Supersession ESPM determines which state is current. ECLM closes the current governed lifecycle state. Superseded State ≠ Closure Target by default. Event Closure and Record Governance A closed Event may continue to have active Records for: storage; interoperability; audit; reporting; downstream tax processing. Event Closure ≠ Record Deletion. TREGS remains authoritative over Record Governance. Closure and Reopening Closure does not make an Event permanently immutable. A closed Event may be reopened where materially relevant new information emerges. Possible triggers include: material Correction; material Amendment; newly discovered Participation; new Event Relationship; corrected Location; reconsidered Determination; evidence affecting prior governed state. Reopening Eligibility Reopening is appropriate only where new information materially affects the same Event lifecycle. If the new occurrence is separate, New Event Formation may be required instead. New Information After Closure ≠ Automatic Reopening. Reopening State Where reopening is valid, the lifecycle may become: Closed ↓ Reopening Review ↓ Reopened ↓ Lifecycle Governance ↓ Reclosed The prior Closure remains historical. Reopening vs New Event ECLM shall preserve the distinction between: Same Event Reopened and: New Event Formed ECOM governs Continuity. TREFS governs New Event Formation. Closure Reversal A Closure may be reversed where governance establishes that closure was invalid or premature. The reversal shall remain historically reconstructable. Closure Reversal ≠ Historical Erasure. Repeated Closure An Event may be: Closed ↓ Reopened ↓ Closed Again Each materially relevant Closure state should remain traceable. Cross-System Closure Different systems may independently mark records as closed. That does not automatically establish canonical TREGA™ Event Closure. Local System Closed ≠ Canonical Event Closed. Cross-Organization Closure One organization may consider its involvement complete while the Event remains active elsewhere. Organizational Completion ≠ Event Closure. Canonical Event Closure depends on the governed Event, not one participant's internal workflow. Cross-Border Closure A Tax-Relevant Event may be closed within TREGA™ while different jurisdictions continue their own tax processing. TREGA™ Event Closure ≠ Jurisdictional Tax Case Closure. Multi-Jurisdiction Closure The canonical Event lifecycle should remain one lifecycle even when multiple tax authorities or tax engines process it independently. One Event ↓ One Governed Closure State ↓ Multiple Downstream Legal Lifecycles Tax Obligation Boundary A tax obligation may: arise after Event Closure; continue long after Event Closure; be disputed after Event Closure; be reassessed after Event Closure; remain unpaid after Event Closure; be appealed after Event Closure. None of those states redefines TREGA™ Event Closure automatically. Tax Assessment Boundary A jurisdiction may issue or amend a tax assessment after the Event has closed. Tax Assessment Open ≠ Event Open. Likewise: Tax Assessment Closed ≠ Event Closure Determination. Tax Period Boundary A reporting or tax period ending does not automatically close the Event. Tax Period End ≠ Event Closure. Machine and Autonomous Event Closure Autonomous systems may continue generating technical messages after the governed Event has substantively completed. ECLM focuses on Event lifecycle reality rather than telemetry volume. Machine Activity Continuation ≠ Event Continuation by default. Machine-Generated Closure Proposal An AI agent or autonomous system may propose Event Closure automatically. The proposal must still satisfy governance conditions. Automated Closure Proposal ≠ Governed Closure. Jurisdiction Readiness A closed Event becomes Jurisdiction-Ready where its current state and materially relevant lifecycle history are sufficiently governed for downstream tax-rule application. Jurisdiction Readiness may require: canonical Event identity; current effective state; relevant prior state; lifecycle transitions; qualifications; Continuity state; Closure state; Record traceability; sufficient interoperability. Jurisdiction-Ready Tax-Relevant Event The principal final output of TRECLS is: Jurisdiction-Ready Tax-Relevant Event This means the Event is methodologically prepared for jurisdiction-specific taxation analysis. It does not mean: taxable; located in a specific Tax Jurisdiction; assigned to a taxpayer; subject to a particular Tax Rate; associated with a legal Tax Period; or legally due. Jurisdiction-Ready ≠ Jurisdiction-Determined. Final TREGA™ Handoff The final architecture transition is: Jurisdiction-Ready Tax-Relevant Event ↓ Jurisdictional Tax Rules / Tax Engine ↓ Tax Determination ↓ Reporting / Compliance TREGA™ ends before jurisdiction-specific legal tax determination begins. Closure and Downstream Reuse A closed Event may be reused by: multiple tax engines; audit systems; accounting systems; reporting systems; analytical systems; AI systems; future regulatory infrastructures. Downstream reuse does not reopen the Event by itself. Downstream Consumption ≠ Event Reopening. Closure and Historical Reconstruction A closed Event should remain capable of reconstruction from: current effective state; prior materially relevant states; Amendment history; Correction history; Supersession history; Continuity history; Closure history. Closure finalizes ordinary lifecycle governance; it does not destroy it. Closure Authority Closure should occur under identifiable governance authority or authorized system logic. Automated Closure may be permitted where governance conditions are satisfied. Automation does not remove traceability or accountability requirements. Closure Reassessment A prior Closure state may be reassessed when new materially relevant information appears. Reassessment shall preserve the prior Closure decision as historical state. Governance States ECLM may represent: Closure Governance Not Initiated Closure Trigger Identified Closure Readiness Under Assessment Closure Not Ready Closure Deferred Closure Eligible Closure Qualified Closure Ambiguous Closure Conflicted Upstream Review Required Continuity Reassessment Required Amendment Resolution Required Correction Resolution Required Supersession Resolution Required Closure Rejected Closure Pending Closed Closed — Qualified Reopening Under Review Reopening Eligible Reopening Rejected Reopened Reclosure Pending Governed Event Closure State Established Jurisdiction-Ready Governance Requirements ECLM implementations shall ensure that: a valid current effective Event state exists; Event Continuity is sufficiently governed; materially relevant Amendment states are resolved or qualified; materially relevant Correction states are resolved or qualified; Supersession state is sufficiently clear; materially relevant historical states remain reconstructable; Closure Readiness is explicitly assessed; unresolved material issues prevent unqualified Closure where appropriate; qualified Closure remains distinguishable from unqualified Closure; Closure remains distinct from operational completion; Closure remains distinct from Record deletion; Closure remains distinct from tax-obligation closure; Closure remains distinct from tax-assessment closure; Tax Period end does not automatically close the Event; material post-Closure information may trigger reopening review; reopening remains distinct from New Event Formation; prior Closure history remains preserved after reopening; machine activity volume does not determine Closure; automated Closure proposals remain governed; local system closure does not automatically establish canonical Event Closure; downstream jurisdictional activity does not redefine canonical Closure; jurisdiction-readiness remains distinct from jurisdiction determination; and the final Event state is suitable for downstream jurisdiction-specific tax evaluation. Governance Logic IF no valid current effective Event state exists, THEN ECLM shall not establish canonical Event Closure. IF material Continuity Conflict remains unresolved, THEN Closure shall be deferred or qualified. IF a material Amendment capable of changing the current Event state remains pending, THEN unqualified Closure shall not proceed. IF a known material Correction remains unresolved, THEN Closure shall not be used to freeze the known error. IF Supersession state does not clearly identify the current effective state, THEN Closure shall remain pending or conflicted. IF remaining uncertainty is bounded, explicitly qualified, and does not prevent legitimate downstream analysis, THEN Qualified Closure may be established. IF ordinary Event lifecycle development is sufficiently complete and the current and historical states are reconstructable, THEN Closure may be established. IF materially relevant new information emerges after Closure and belongs to the same Event, THEN reopening review shall be initiated. IF post-Closure information represents a substantively new occurrence, THEN New Event Formation shall be considered instead of reopening. IF the Event is validly closed and sufficiently governed for downstream taxation analysis, THEN the Event shall enter the Jurisdiction-Ready state. Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum ECLM implementation should support: Closure Governance ID Stable identifier for the ECLM governance process. Canonical Event Reference The Event under Closure Governance. Current Effective Event State Reference The state proposed for Closure. Governed Supersession State Reference The applicable ESPM output where relevant. Closure Trigger Type Operational Completion, Lifecycle Completion, Continuity Break, Event Replacement, Long-Running Event Endpoint, Governance Review, or other governed trigger. Closure Eligibility State Eligible, Qualified, Ineligible, Unresolved. Closure Readiness State Ready, Qualified Ready, Not Ready, Unresolved. Continuity State Reference The relevant ECOM outcome. Amendment State Reference The relevant EADM outcome. Correction State Reference The relevant ECRTM outcome. Supersession State Reference The relevant ESPM outcome. Pending Material Issue State Whether material unresolved issues remain. Historical-State Sufficiency State Sufficient, Qualified, Insufficient, Unresolved. Closure Scope The governed Event lifecycle being closed. Closure Basis Reference The governance basis for Closure. Closure Qualification Any limitations attached to Closure. Closure Ambiguity State Whether Closure appropriateness remains uncertain. Closure Conflict State Whether materially incompatible Closure conclusions exist. Closure Deferral State Whether Closure is deferred. Closure Effective Time Reference Where materially relevant. Closure History Reference Any prior Closure states. Reopening Eligibility State Not Applicable, Under Review, Eligible, Ineligible. Reopening Trigger Reference Any material post-Closure development. Reopening State Not Initiated, Under Review, Reopened, Rejected. Continuity Reassessment Reference Where reopening or post-Closure change affects continuity. New Event Formation Referral State Where post-Closure development represents a new occurrence. Jurisdiction-Readiness State Not Ready, Qualified, Ready. Governance State The current ECLM governance state. Closure Outcome Closed, Closed — Qualified, Deferred, Rejected, Reopened, or Unresolved. Final Handoff State Whether the Event is ready for jurisdiction-specific tax-rule application. Governance Outputs ECLM may produce: Closure Trigger State; Closure Eligibility State; Closure Readiness State; Current Effective Event State; Historical-State Sufficiency State; Closure Basis; Closure Qualification; Closure Ambiguity State; Closure Conflict State; Closure Deferral State; Closure Effective State; Closure History; Reopening Eligibility State; Reopening State; Continuity Reassessment Reference; New Event Formation Referral; Jurisdiction-Readiness State; Governed Event Closure State; and the principal final output: Jurisdiction-Ready Tax-Relevant Event . Critical Distinctions Event Closure ≠ Tax Obligation Closure. Closure Readiness ≠ Absence of All Uncertainty. Closed Event ≠ History-Free Event. Closure ≠ Permission to Freeze Known Error. Qualified Closure ≠ Failed Closure. Closure Deferral ≠ Closure Failure. Operational Completion ≠ Event Closure by default. Technical Process End ≠ Event Closure. Superseded State ≠ Closure Target by default. Event Closure ≠ Record Deletion. New Information After Closure ≠ Automatic Reopening. Closure Reversal ≠ Historical Erasure. Local System Closed ≠ Canonical Event Closed. Organizational Completion ≠ Event Closure. TREGA™ Event Closure ≠ Jurisdictional Tax Case Closure. Tax Assessment Open ≠ Event Open. Tax Assessment Closed ≠ Event Closure Determination. Tax Period End ≠ Event Closure. Machine Activity Continuation ≠ Event Continuation by default. Automated Closure Proposal ≠ Governed Closure. Jurisdiction-Ready ≠ Jurisdiction-Determined. Downstream Consumption ≠ Event Reopening. Enterprise Application ECLM provides the final lifecycle-control layer that converts a governed Event into a stable jurisdiction-ready object. The operational pattern is: Current Effective Event State → Closure Readiness Assessment → Material Lifecycle Issues Resolved / Qualified → Event Closure → Historical States Preserved → Jurisdiction-Ready Tax-Relevant Event The downstream transition becomes: Jurisdiction-Ready Tax-Relevant Event → Country A Tax Engine → Country B Tax Engine → Country C Tax Engine The Event remains one governed Event. Each jurisdiction may independently determine its legal tax consequence. Use Case 1 — Cross-Border Digital Service Reaches Governed Closure A global digital service Event has completed its operational activity. During its lifecycle: one participant was added through Amendment; one Location was corrected; a corrected Event state superseded the prior state. ECLM confirms that: Event Continuity is valid; the Amendment is resolved; the Correction is governed; the current effective state is clear; prior materially relevant states remain reconstructable. ECLM establishes: Closed ↓ Jurisdiction-Ready Tax-Relevant Event The Event is then supplied to several jurisdiction-specific tax engines. Each jurisdiction determines its own legal result. Closure of TREGA™ Event governance does not mean any jurisdiction's tax obligation has also closed. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Event Reopens After Material Post-Closure Information An autonomous machine transaction has been closed and made Jurisdiction-Ready. Later, authoritative machine-control information establishes that a material participant relationship was previously unavailable. ECLM initiates: Closed ↓ Reopening Review ECOM confirms that the new information belongs to the same Event. TREPS governs the additional Participation result. EADM or ECRTM governs the appropriate lifecycle update depending on whether the prior state was incomplete or incorrect. The Event then proceeds through Supersession where required and returns to ECLM for: Reopened ↓ Updated Governed State ↓ Reclosed The original Closure remains part of Event history. If the new machine activity had instead constituted a substantively separate occurrence, the case would be referred for New Event Formation rather than reopening the existing Event. Canonical Boundary ECLM owns the governance of Event Closure eligibility, Closure Readiness, current effective-state confirmation for Closure, historical-state sufficiency, unresolved lifecycle-state review, Closure qualification, ambiguity, conflict, deferral, rejection, Closure state, reopening references, reopening eligibility, Closure history, jurisdiction-readiness, and the final transition from governed Event lifecycle to Jurisdiction-Ready Tax-Relevant Event. ECLM does not own Event Continuity; ECOM does. It does not own Amendment; EADM does. It does not own Correction; ECRTM does. It does not own Supersession; ESPM does. It does not independently recreate Event Context, Recognition, Formation, Boundary, Timing, Location, Participation, Value Association, Relationships, Determination, or Record Governance. It does not create a New Event; TREFS owns Event Formation. It does not determine legal Taxability, Tax Jurisdiction, taxpayer status, tax nexus, legal tax point, Tax Period, Tax Base, Tax Rate, exemption, deduction, Tax Liability, filing obligations, tax reassessment, payment, collection, enforcement, limitation periods, appeal, or legal closure of a tax obligation. Its governance begins with a sufficiently governed: Current Effective Tax-Relevant Event State and ends with: Governed Event Closure State ↓ Jurisdiction-Ready Tax-Relevant Event Canonical Handoff ESPM — Governed Event Supersession State ↓ ECLM — Governed Event Closure State ↓ Jurisdiction-Ready Tax-Relevant Event ↓ Jurisdictional Tax Rules / Tax Engine ↓ Tax Determination ↓ Reporting / Compliance Where material post-Closure information arises: ECLM — Reopening Review ↓ ECOM / Relevant TREGA™ Governance ↓ Updated Event Lifecycle ↓ ECLM Reclosure Where a substantively different occurrence exists: ECLM / ECOM ↓ TREFS — New Event Formation Review Canonical Closing Statement ECLM establishes when a governed Tax-Relevant Event has reached a sufficiently stable lifecycle state to leave TREGA™ and enter jurisdiction-specific taxation analysis. Closure does not erase history, prevent legitimate reopening, or decide whether tax is legally due. It establishes that the Event itself is sufficiently governed for the next system to decide what the law makes of it. Event Closure ≠ Tax Obligation Closure. Closed Event ≠ History-Free Event. Jurisdiction-Ready ≠ Jurisdiction-Determined. TREGA™ governs the event. The jurisdiction governs the tax.

title: OOF™ The Event Continuity Module (ECOM) governs whether and how a Governed
text: OOF™ The Event Continuity Module (ECOM) governs whether and how a Governed The Event Continuity Module (ECOM) governs whether and how a Governed OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: TRECLS — Tax-Relevant Event Lifecycle & Continuity Standard Module: ECOM — Event Continuity Module Operational Layer: Event Continuity Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Event Continuity Primary Governed Object: Governed Event Continuity State Origin ID: TREGA-TRECLS-ECOM-001 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 3 September 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language Canonical Definition The Event Continuity Module (ECOM) governs whether and how a Governed Tax-Relevant Event remains the same governed Event as information, representations, operational conditions, supporting records, or lifecycle states change over time. ECOM establishes the methodological continuity relationship between the Event's prior governed state and its current or proposed state. Its principal transition is: Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record ↓ Event Continuity Governance ↓ Governed Event Continuity State ECOM determines whether change can legitimately remain within the existing Event lifecycle or whether the change is sufficiently material to require qualification, upstream reassessment, or referral for New Event Formation. Its foundational distinction is: Change ≠ New Event by default. Equally: Continuity ≠ Unlimited Permission to Modify the Same Event. Operational Role After TREGS has established a Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record, subsequent information may affect the Event. Before amendment, correction, supersession, or closure can be governed, the system must understand whether the same Event still exists as the continuing governance object. ECOM answers: Does the changed state still represent the same governed Tax-Relevant Event? It prevents two opposite governance failures: unnecessary creation of new Events for ordinary lifecycle changes; and indefinite extension of one Event identity across materially different operational realities. Internal Module Flow TRECLS operates through: ECOM — Event Continuity ↓ EADM — Event Amendment ↓ ECRTM — Event Correction ↓ ESPM — Event Supersession ↓ ECLM — Event Closure ↓ Jurisdiction-Ready Tax-Relevant Event ECOM is the first Core Module. It receives: Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record and produces: Governed Event Continuity State for subsequent lifecycle governance. Operational Transition The canonical ECOM transition is: Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record ↓ Continuity Trigger ↓ Prior/Current State Comparison ↓ Material Change Assessment ↓ Continuity Determination ↓ Governed Event Continuity State Operational Space ECOM governs: Continuity Trigger identification; prior Event state identification; proposed or changed Event state identification; Event identity continuity; Formation continuity; Boundary continuity; temporal continuity; Location continuity relevance; Participation continuity relevance; Value Association continuity relevance; Event Relationship continuity relevance; Determination continuity relevance; material-change assessment; continuity qualification; continuity ambiguity; continuity conflict; continuity break; upstream reassessment referral; New Event Formation referral; continuity state; and continuity handoff. Operational Scope ECOM may govern continuity across: physical transactions; digital services; commercial transactions; financial activity; platform activity; distributed transactions; digital assets; AI-agent operations; autonomous systems; machine-to-machine interactions; industrial processes; smart-contract environments; cross-border activities; multi-party Events; long-running Events; and future machine economies. The continuity logic remains technology-neutral and jurisdiction-neutral. Continuity Object The Continuity Object is the governed relationship between: Prior Governed Event State and: Current or Proposed Event State ECOM does not ask merely whether data changed. It asks whether the governed occurrence represented by those states remains methodologically the same Event. Data Continuity ≠ Event Continuity. Continuity Trigger A Continuity Trigger is a materially relevant development that creates a legitimate need to evaluate whether the Event remains continuous. Triggers may include: new information; proposed Amendment; identified error; proposed Correction; Record Supersession; Determination reconsideration; Event Relationship change; Merge/Split result; material operational development; changed participant information; changed Value Association; changed Timing or Location information; reopening; or preparation for Closure. Any Data Change ≠ Continuity Trigger by default. Prior Governed State ECOM shall identify the applicable prior governed Event state against which continuity is evaluated. The prior state should be sufficiently reconstructable through TREGS and relevant TREGA™ references. Continuity cannot be meaningfully determined where the system cannot identify what is supposedly continuing. Current or Proposed State The current or proposed state represents the Event after the relevant lifecycle development. It may represent: additional information; changed information; corrected information; revised governance result; updated representation; or changed operational condition. ECOM compares this state against the prior governed Event state. Continuity Anchor The Continuity Anchor is the combination of governed characteristics necessary to preserve the identity of the same Event through change. Depending on the Event, relevant anchors may include: Event Formation; Event Root association; Event Boundary; core operational occurrence; materially relevant participants; temporal relationship; Location relationship; Value relationship; Event Relationships. Not every characteristic must remain technically identical. The question is whether the governed Event remains substantively continuous. Event Identity Continuity Event identity should remain stable where the underlying governed occurrence remains the same Event. A change to Record representation, technical identifier, storage location, or downstream use does not by itself change Event identity. Technical Change ≠ Event Identity Change. Formation Continuity TREFS establishes how the Event is formed. ECOM evaluates whether later change remains compatible with that Formation. If the components or root association change so materially that the original Event Formation no longer describes the occurrence, continuity may fail. ECOM does not reform the Event. It refers the issue to TREFS. Boundary Continuity TREBS establishes Event Boundary. Changes inside an existing Boundary may remain compatible with Event Continuity. Where the Event Boundary must be materially redrawn to represent a substantively different occurrence, continuity requires reassessment. Boundary Adjustment ≠ Continuity Break by default. But: Material Boundary Replacement May Require New Event Formation. Temporal Continuity Changes or corrections to Event Timing do not automatically create a new Event. ECOM evaluates whether the temporal relationship still represents the same underlying occurrence. Timing Change ≠ New Event by default. TRETS remains authoritative over Event Timing. Location Continuity Location information may change or be corrected while the Event remains continuous. For distributed or digital Events, multiple operational Locations may be associated with one Event. Location Change ≠ New Event by default. TRELS remains authoritative over Event Location. Participation Continuity Participants may: be added; be removed; be corrected; change role; become newly identifiable. These changes do not automatically create a new Event. The question is whether the same underlying Event remains governed. Where participant change materially transforms the operational occurrence, continuity may require reassessment. TREPS remains authoritative over Participation. Machine and Autonomous Actor Continuity An autonomous agent or machine may be replaced, upgraded, delegated, or technically re-instantiated during a long-running process. Such technical actor changes do not automatically create new Events. ECOM evaluates whether the governed operational occurrence remains continuous. Identity and authority questions remain outside ECOM. Value Association Continuity Value information may change through correction, refinement, or additional governed Value Association. The Event may remain continuous where the same underlying Value relationship is being more accurately represented. Where a materially different Value relationship emerges as a new occurrence, continuity may require reassessment. TRVAS remains authoritative over Value Association. VFM® remains authoritative over the Value lifecycle itself. Relationship Continuity Changes to Event Relationships may affect continuity. A new dependency or grouping does not automatically create a new Event. A valid Merge or Split, however, may materially alter Event identity and lifecycle. TRERLS owns Event Relationship Governance. ECOM governs the resulting continuity consequence. Determination Continuity A TREDS Determination may be reconsidered while the underlying Event remains the same Event. Determination Change ≠ New Event by default. ECOM preserves Event Continuity where appropriate while TREDS remains authoritative for Determination. Record Continuity Boundary A Record may change while the Event remains continuous. Likewise, Record identity continuity does not prove Event Continuity. Therefore: Record Continuity ≠ Event Continuity. TREGS owns Record Governance. ECOM owns Event Continuity. Technical Representation Continuity The Event Record may migrate between: databases; schemas; APIs; platforms; organizations; storage models; technical identifiers. These transformations do not create new Events where governed Event meaning remains continuous. Representation Change ≠ New Event. Operational Continuity Operational activity may develop over time while remaining one governed Event. The relevant test is whether the development remains part of the originally governed occurrence rather than constituting a substantively separate occurrence. Continuous Events Some Events may extend over meaningful periods. Examples include: long-running digital services; continuous infrastructure activity; subscription-related activity; distributed machine operations; autonomous service execution. ECOM does not force such Events into artificial fragmentation merely because technical operations occur repeatedly. Continuous Operation ≠ Multiple Events by default. Recurring Activity Boundary Recurring activities may represent: one continuing Event; repeated Events; or a combination of both. ECOM does not determine this solely from recurrence frequency. Formation and Boundary governance remain authoritative. Material Change Material Change is a change sufficiently significant to affect whether the same Event can legitimately continue. Materiality may depend on impact upon: Event Formation; Event Boundary; core operational substance; participant configuration; Value relationship; Event Relationship structure; Determination basis; or reconstructability. More Changed Fields ≠ Greater Event Change by default. Non-Material Change A Non-Material Change does not alter the Event sufficiently to challenge continuity. Examples may include: formatting changes; local identifier updates; schema migration; non-material metadata updates; additional supporting references; technical storage changes. Such changes should not trigger unnecessary Event proliferation. Material Transformation Material Transformation exists where the changed occurrence can no longer legitimately be represented by the existing Event Formation and Boundary. This may indicate: Continuity Broken ↓ Upstream Reassessment ↓ New Event Formation Potentially Required ECOM identifies the continuity condition. TREFS owns any New Event Formation. Continuity Preservation Where change remains compatible with the same Event, ECOM establishes Continuity Preservation. The canonical pattern is: Prior Governed Event State ↓ Legitimate Lifecycle Change ↓ Same Event Identity ↓ New Governed State Continuity Confirmation Continuity may be confirmed where: the same Event remains identifiable; Formation remains materially compatible; Boundary remains materially compatible; change does not create a substantively separate occurrence; materially relevant historical state remains reconstructable. Continuity Qualification Continuity may remain legitimate but qualified. Examples include: unresolved participant role; uncertain temporal extent; unresolved distributed Location; incomplete Value information; pending upstream reconsideration. Qualified Continuity ≠ Failed Continuity. Continuity Ambiguity Continuity Ambiguity exists where available governed information does not sufficiently establish whether the same Event continues. The Event should not be arbitrarily forced into either continuity or New Event Formation. Possible outcome: Continuity Under Review Continuity Conflict Continuity Conflict exists where materially authoritative governance results support incompatible conclusions. For example: Formation indicates continuity; Boundary indicates a substantively new occurrence. Conflict shall remain explicit until resolved or appropriately qualified. Continuity Break Continuity Break exists where the changed occurrence can no longer legitimately remain under the same Event lifecycle. A Continuity Break may require: closure of the prior Event; New Event Formation; Merge/Split governance; upstream reassessment; new Determination; new Record Governance. Continuity Break ≠ Automatic New Event Creation. New Event Formation Referral Where continuity fails because the changed occurrence appears materially different, ECOM shall refer the occurrence to TREFS. The canonical transition is: Existing Event ↓ Material Transformation ↓ Continuity Broken ↓ TREFS New Event Formation Review ECOM does not assign the new Event identity. Upstream Governance Referral Continuity may require reassessment by: TREFS — Formation; TREBS — Boundary; TRETS — Timing; TRELS — Location; TREPS — Participation; TRVAS — Value Association; TRERLS — Relationships; TREDS — Determination; TREGS — Record Governance. ECOM coordinates continuity implications without taking ownership of those spaces. Merge Continuity Where TRERLS establishes a Merge, ECOM evaluates continuity consequences. Possible outcomes include: one Event continues; prior Events terminate and a merged Event requires Formation; continuity remains qualified pending Formation review. Merge Result ≠ Automatic Continuity Outcome. Split Continuity Where TRERLS establishes a Split, ECOM evaluates whether: original Event continues alongside successors; original Event closes; resulting occurrences require new Event Formation. Split Result ≠ Automatic Event Identity Replication. Reopening Continuity Where a closed Event is proposed for reopening, ECOM evaluates whether the new development belongs to the same Event. Prior Closure ≠ Automatic Continuity Break. But: Reopening ≠ Automatic Same-Event Continuity. Cross-System Continuity A Record moving across systems shall not create new Event identities merely because local systems use different identifiers or schemas. ERINM governs interoperability. ECOM governs whether the Event remains the same Event. Cross-Organization Continuity The same Event may remain continuous across organizational handoffs. A new custodian, processor, platform, or data owner does not automatically create a new Event. Organizational Change ≠ New Event by default. Cross-Border Continuity A Tax-Relevant Event may enter multiple jurisdictional environments while remaining one Event. Jurisdictional Entry ≠ New Event Formation. Different legal tax treatments do not change canonical Event identity. Multi-Jurisdiction Continuity The canonical model is: One Governed Event ↓ One Lifecycle ↓ Multiple Jurisdictional Evaluations not: One Jurisdiction ↓ One New Event Tax Outcome Boundary A jurisdiction may later determine that an Event is: taxable; non-taxable; exempt; outside scope; subject to reassessment. These legal outcomes do not independently determine TREGA™ Event Continuity. Tax Outcome Change ≠ Event Continuity Change by default. Tax Period Boundary An Event may cross multiple tax periods. Tax-period treatment does not automatically split the Event. Multiple Tax Periods ≠ Multiple Events by default. TRETS governs operational Timing. Jurisdictions govern tax periods. Lifecycle Continuity and Legal Change Tax law may change while the Event remains continuous. TREGA™ Event Continuity shall not be rewritten merely because downstream law changed. Legal Rule Change ≠ Event Reality Change. Machine-Economy Continuity Machine environments may produce enormous numbers of: logs; messages; state changes; API calls; automated decisions; settlement records. ECOM focuses on governed Event continuity rather than raw technical activity. Technical State Change ≠ Event Lifecycle Change by default. Continuity Confidence Where useful, implementations may express the degree to which continuity is sufficiently supported. Confidence does not replace governance determination. High Continuity Confidence ≠ Automatic Continuity Determination. Continuity Authority Continuity determination shall occur under an identifiable governance authority, process, or authorized system. Automated continuity decisions may be permitted where governance conditions are satisfied. Automation does not eliminate accountability or traceability requirements. Continuity Reassessment A previously established continuity state may require reassessment where materially relevant new information appears. Reassessment does not erase the prior continuity decision. Continuity State History Material continuity states should remain reconstructable. A lifecycle may therefore preserve: Continuity Confirmed ↓ Continuity Under Review ↓ Continuity Qualified ↓ Continuity Confirmed or: Continuity Confirmed ↓ Material Transformation ↓ Continuity Broken Governance States ECOM may represent: Continuity Governance Not Initiated Continuity Trigger Identified Prior Event State Identified Current / Proposed State Identified Continuity Under Assessment Non-Material Change Material Change Identified Continuity Confirmed Continuity Qualified Continuity Ambiguous Continuity Conflicted Upstream Review Required Continuity Broken New Event Formation Referral Required Governed Event Continuity State Established Ready for Amendment Governance Governance Requirements ECOM implementations shall ensure that: a valid Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record exists; a materially relevant Continuity Trigger is identifiable; prior Event state is reconstructable; current or proposed Event state is identifiable; data change remains distinct from Event change; Event identity continuity is evaluated independently of technical identifiers; Formation continuity is considered where material; Boundary continuity is considered where material; Timing and Location changes do not automatically create new Events; Participation changes do not automatically create new Events; Value Association changes do not automatically create new Events; Determination changes do not automatically create new Events; Record continuity remains distinct from Event Continuity; technical representation changes do not automatically create new Events; materiality is assessed according to governed Event meaning rather than field count; qualified continuity remains distinguishable from confirmed continuity; ambiguity and conflict remain explicit; Continuity Break does not automatically create a new Event; New Event Formation is referred to TREFS; Merge/Split continuity consequences remain distinct from Event Relationship governance; reopening requires continuity evaluation where material; jurisdictional tax outcomes remain outside Event Continuity governance; machine activity volume does not determine Event count; material continuity decisions remain reconstructable; and the resulting continuity state is suitable for subsequent TRECLS lifecycle governance. Governance Logic IF no valid Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record exists, THEN ECOM shall not establish canonical Event Continuity. IF no materially relevant change exists, THEN Event Continuity may remain unchanged without unnecessary lifecycle transition. IF change affects only technical representation and governed Event meaning remains unchanged, THEN Event Continuity shall normally remain preserved. IF Timing, Location, Participation, Value Association, or supporting information changes without materially changing the underlying occurrence, THEN the Event may remain continuous. IF change materially affects Formation or Boundary, THEN upstream reassessment shall be required before Continuity is confirmed. IF available information supports continuity but material uncertainty remains, THEN Continuity may be Qualified. IF materially authoritative governance information supports incompatible continuity conclusions, THEN Continuity Conflict shall be established. IF continuity cannot be sufficiently established, THEN the Event shall remain Under Review rather than being arbitrarily continued or replaced. IF the changed occurrence can no longer legitimately be represented by the existing Event Formation and Boundary, THEN Continuity Broken shall be established. IF Continuity is Broken, THEN ECOM may require New Event Formation Referral without itself creating the new Event. IF the same governed Event remains materially identifiable through the change, THEN ECOM shall establish the Governed Event Continuity State. Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum ECOM implementation should support: Continuity Governance ID A stable identifier for the ECOM governance process. Canonical Event Reference The Event whose continuity is under governance. Governed Event Record Reference The applicable TREGS Record. Prior Event State Reference The prior governed Event state. Current / Proposed Event State Reference The state being evaluated. Continuity Trigger Type Amendment, Correction, Supersession, Reconsideration, Merge/Split, New Information, Reopening, Closure Review, or other governed trigger. Trigger Reference The source or governance reference initiating continuity review. Formation Continuity State Preserved, Qualified, Materially Changed, Unresolved. Boundary Continuity State Preserved, Qualified, Materially Changed, Unresolved. Timing Continuity State Preserved, Changed, Qualified, Unresolved. Location Continuity State Preserved, Changed, Qualified, Unresolved. Participation Continuity State Preserved, Changed, Qualified, Unresolved. Value Association Continuity State Preserved, Changed, Qualified, Unresolved. Relationship Continuity State Preserved, Changed, Qualified, Unresolved. Determination Continuity State Preserved, Reconsidered, Qualified, Unresolved. Record Continuity Reference The relevant TREGS continuity information. Change Materiality State Non-Material, Material, Critical, Unresolved. Continuity Qualification Any limitation attached to the continuity outcome. Continuity Ambiguity State Whether same-Event continuity remains uncertain. Continuity Conflict State Whether materially incompatible conclusions exist. Upstream Review Reference Any referral to an authoritative TREGA™ layer. New Event Formation Referral State Not Required, Under Review, Required. Prior Continuity State Reference Any earlier materially relevant continuity determination. Continuity Reassessment State Whether reassessment is active or required. Governance State The current ECOM governance state. Continuity Outcome Confirmed, Qualified, Broken, or Unresolved. Handoff State Whether the Event is ready for subsequent TRECLS lifecycle governance. Governance Outputs ECOM may produce: Continuity Trigger State; Prior Event State Reference; Current / Proposed Event State Reference; Formation Continuity State; Boundary Continuity State; Timing Continuity State; Location Continuity State; Participation Continuity State; Value Association Continuity State; Relationship Continuity State; Determination Continuity State; Change Materiality State; Continuity Qualification; Continuity Ambiguity State; Continuity Conflict State; Upstream Review Referral; New Event Formation Referral; Continuity Reassessment State; and the principal output: Governed Event Continuity State. Critical Distinctions Change ≠ New Event by default. Continuity ≠ Unlimited Permission to Modify the Same Event. Data Continuity ≠ Event Continuity. Any Data Change ≠ Continuity Trigger by default. Technical Change ≠ Event Identity Change. Boundary Adjustment ≠ Continuity Break by default. Material Boundary Replacement May Require New Event Formation. Timing Change ≠ New Event by default. Location Change ≠ New Event by default. Determination Change ≠ New Event by default. Record Continuity ≠ Event Continuity. Representation Change ≠ New Event. Continuous Operation ≠ Multiple Events by default. More Changed Fields ≠ Greater Event Change by default. Qualified Continuity ≠ Failed Continuity. Continuity Break ≠ Automatic New Event Creation. Merge Result ≠ Automatic Continuity Outcome. Split Result ≠ Automatic Event Identity Replication. Prior Closure ≠ Automatic Continuity Break. Reopening ≠ Automatic Same-Event Continuity. Organizational Change ≠ New Event by default. Jurisdictional Entry ≠ New Event Formation. Tax Outcome Change ≠ Event Continuity Change by default. Multiple Tax Periods ≠ Multiple Events by default. Legal Rule Change ≠ Event Reality Change. Technical State Change ≠ Event Lifecycle Change by default. High Continuity Confidence ≠ Automatic Continuity Determination. Enterprise Application ECOM provides the identity-continuity control required before later lifecycle changes are accepted into the canonical Event. The operational pattern is: Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record → Change Detected → Continuity Assessment → Same Event / Qualified Same Event / Continuity Broken If continuity remains legitimate: Governed Event Continuity State ↓ EADM / Subsequent TRECLS Governance If continuity fails: Continuity Broken ↓ Appropriate Upstream Governance ↓ Potential New Event Formation This prevents both Event fragmentation and Event overextension. Use Case 1 — Digital Service Event Receives Corrected Location Information A cross-border digital service has already become a Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record. New operational information shows that one Location attribute was incorrectly represented. The service, participants, core operational occurrence, Event Formation, and Boundary remain materially unchanged. ECOM evaluates the change and establishes: Location Changed ↓ Event Formation Preserved ↓ Event Boundary Preserved ↓ Continuity Confirmed The Event proceeds to Correction Governance under ECRTM. A new Event is not created merely because Location information changed. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Transaction Changes Beyond Its Original Event Boundary An autonomous machine-to-machine service begins as one governed Event. During execution, the original service terminates and the autonomous systems initiate a substantively different transaction involving a different operational objective, materially different Value relationship, and a new Event Boundary. Although the technical process remains continuously active, ECOM determines that the changed occurrence can no longer legitimately remain inside the original Event. The outcome becomes: Material Transformation ↓ Continuity Broken ↓ New Event Formation Referral Required The original Event remains historically governed. The new occurrence is referred to TREFS. Technical process continuity does not override governed Event Reality. Canonical Boundary ECOM owns the governance of Event Continuity assessment, Continuity Triggers, prior-versus-current Event state comparison, Event identity continuity, Formation and Boundary continuity implications, material-change assessment, Continuity Confirmation, qualification, ambiguity, conflict, Continuity Break, upstream reassessment referral, New Event Formation referral, and establishment of the Governed Event Continuity State. ECOM does not recognize or form the Event. It does not redefine Event Boundary, Timing, Location, Participation, Value Association, Event Relationships, or Event Determination. It does not establish Record identity, structure, linkage, traceability, or interoperability. It does not execute Amendment, Correction, Supersession, or Closure governance. It does not determine legal Taxability, Tax Jurisdiction, taxpayer status, Tax Base, Tax Rate, legal tax point, Tax Period, Tax Liability, or other jurisdiction-specific tax consequences. Its governance begins with a valid: Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record and a materially relevant Continuity Trigger. Its governance ends with: Governed Event Continuity State or, where continuity fails: Continuity Broken ↓ Upstream Review / New Event Formation Referral Canonical Handoff Where continuity remains valid: TREGS — Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record ↓ ECOM — Governed Event Continuity State ↓ EADM — Event Amendment Governance Where continuity fails: ECOM — Continuity Broken ↓ Appropriate Upstream TREGA™ Governance ↓ TREFS where New Event Formation is required Canonical Closing Statement ECOM establishes whether change belongs to the lifecycle of the same governed Event or marks the point at which that Event can no longer legitimately contain what happened next. Continuity protects Event identity from unnecessary fragmentation, but it must never be used to force materially different operational realities into one Event. Change ≠ New Event by default. Continuity ≠ Unlimited Permission to Modify the Same Event. Material Transformation May Require New Event Formation.

title: OOF™ Event Context Relationship Module (ECRM)
text: OOF™ Event Context Relationship Module (ECRM) Event Context Relationship Module (ECRM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard (TRECS) Module: ECRM — Event Context Relationship Module Operational Layer: Event Context Relationship Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Event Context Relationships Origin ID: TREGA-TRECS-ECRM-003 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 29 August 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Event Context Relationship Module (ECRM) is the Core Module within Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard (TRECS) that governs the establishment and representation of materially relevant relationships among contextual elements surrounding an occurrence entering the TREGA™ lifecycle. ECRM transforms a scoped collection of contextual elements into a relational contextual structure by establishing how relevant economic, operational, organizational, transactional, digital, technological, infrastructural, autonomous, machine-generated, value-related, and other contextual elements relate to one another. Its task is specific: to establish how governed contextual elements are connected without determining causal responsibility, Event Relationships, legal tax relationships, or tax consequences. Operational Role A list of contextual elements does not necessarily explain an occurrence. For example, a governed context may identify: AI Agent · Platform · API · Payment System · Service Provider · Customer · Digital Service but this alone does not explain how those elements relate. ECRM establishes the relevant contextual structure between them. Relationships may include: operational relationships; organizational relationships; transactional relationships; process relationships; system relationships; platform relationships; infrastructure relationships; service relationships; economic relationships; execution relationships; dependencies; contextual sequences; hierarchical relationships; distributed-system relationships; value-related contextual relationships. The result is not merely a set of contextual facts. It is a Governed Context Relationship Structure. Internal Flow Governed Context Scope ↓ Relationship Candidate Identification ↓ Relationship Relevance Assessment ↓ Relationship Type Establishment ↓ Relationship Qualification ↓ Relationship Consistency Check ↓ Governed Context Relationship Structure The principal governed output is: Governed Context Relationship Structure Operational Space ECRM governs the space between: a sufficiently scoped collection of contextual elements and a structured representation of the materially relevant relationships among those elements. Its operational space includes: relationship identification; relationship relevance; relationship type; relationship direction where relevant; contextual dependency; contextual sequence; contextual hierarchy; multi-party contextual relationships; system-to-system relationships; platform relationships; machine-to-system relationships; organizational relationships; distributed relationships; relationship uncertainty; relationship consistency. ECRM governs relationships within Event Context. It does not govern formal relationships among already formed Tax-Relevant Events. Operational Scope ECRM establishes relationships where understanding the connection between contextual elements materially improves interpretation of the occurrence. For example: Customer ↓ Platform ↓ Service Provider may describe a service environment. Machine ↓ Production System ↓ Warehouse System may describe an operational environment. AI Agent ↓ API ↓ Digital Service may describe an autonomous execution environment. Order ↓ Fulfilment Process ↓ Payment Infrastructure may describe a transactional environment. ECRM may preserve multiple simultaneous relationship structures where reality requires them. It must not force complex activity into a single artificial linear chain. Relationship Relevance Principle The presence of two elements within the same Context Scope does not automatically establish a meaningful relationship between them. ECRM requires a legitimate basis for representing the relationship. Therefore: Context Coexistence ≠ Context Relationship. Two systems may appear in the same environment without directly interacting. Two organizations may participate in the same commercial ecosystem without having the same operational relationship to the occurrence. Two technical records may share a timestamp without representing a meaningful contextual relationship. Relationship governance must therefore remain evidence-sensitive and structurally justified. Relationship Type Where materially necessary, ECRM should distinguish the nature of a contextual relationship. A relationship may be: Operational Organizational Transactional Technical Digital Infrastructural Process-Based Economic Service-Based Execution-Based Dependency-Based Hierarchical Sequential Value-Related Distributed Multiple relationship types may coexist between the same contextual elements. A platform and service provider, for example, may have both a technical and an economic relationship. ECRM should preserve materially relevant distinctions rather than collapsing them into a generic concept of connection. Relationship Direction Some contextual relationships are directional. For example: Instruction ↓ Execution Request ↓ Service System A ↓ Data Transfer ↓ System B Agent ↓ API Invocation ↓ Platform Other relationships may be non-directional or reciprocal. ECRM should represent direction only where it materially contributes to understanding the occurrence. Direction must not be invented merely because a technical representation requires it. Context Dependency One contextual element may depend upon another. A machine operation may depend upon: software authorization ↓ infrastructure availability ↓ operational instruction. A digital service may depend upon: platform access ↓ API execution ↓ external service capability. ECRM may govern those dependencies where they materially contribute to contextual understanding. However: Dependency ≠ Causality. A dependency relationship does not by itself establish that one contextual element legally or operationally caused another. Context Sequence Contextual relationships may have an ordered structure. For example: Order ↓ Authorization ↓ Execution ↓ Delivery ↓ Settlement ECRM may preserve this sequence as contextual structure. This does not determine the formal timing of the Tax-Relevant Event. That governance belongs to TRETS — Tax-Relevant Event Timing Standard. Therefore: Context Sequence ≠ Event Timing Determination. Relationship Uncertainty The relationship between contextual elements may not always be known. For example: two platform records may appear connected but lack a reliable common reference; an autonomous agent may invoke several services without a clear dependency chain; several corporate entities may appear in a transaction environment while their operational roles remain unclear; machine records may show temporal correlation without establishing functional relationship. ECRM must allow such relationships to remain: Confirmed Probable Unresolved or another appropriately governed state. The architecture must not convert incomplete information into artificial relational certainty. Correlation ≠ Causation This distinction is especially important in large digital and machine environments. Systems may generate enormous numbers of temporally or technically correlated signals. ECRM must not treat correlation alone as proof that: one action caused another; one participant controlled another; one system initiated another; one economic relationship existed; one event produced another; legal responsibility exists. Therefore: Correlation ≠ Causation. Relationship Aggregation Risk Large enterprise and platform systems frequently connect records through shared identifiers, accounts, customers, devices, contracts, sessions, or infrastructure. A shared reference can be useful. It can also create false aggregation. For example: Same Customer ≠ Same Event. Same Account ≠ Same Transaction. Same Device ≠ Same Economic Activity. Same Platform Session ≠ Same Tax-Relevant Event. ECRM must preserve these distinctions before later event formation and relationship governance occur. Governance Requirements ECRM requires that: relationships are established only among contextual elements within the relevant governed context; materially relevant relationship types remain distinguishable; relationship direction is represented where necessary; dependency is distinguished from causality; correlation is distinguished from governed relationship; uncertainty remains explicit where relationships cannot be sufficiently established; multiple simultaneous relationships may coexist; relationship structures remain traceable where materially necessary; contextual relationships do not silently become Event Relationships; contextual relationships do not determine legal tax consequences. Governance Logic ECRM applies three principal questions: Are these contextual elements materially related? What is the nature of that relationship? Is the relationship sufficiently established to be represented as governed context? Where the relationship is sufficiently established, ECRM creates a governed relationship representation. Where evidence is insufficient, the relationship remains unresolved or qualified. Where no material relationship exists, contextual coexistence alone does not create one. The methodological transformation is: Scoped Context Elements → Qualified Relationships → Structured Context Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum implementation of ECRM must be capable of: 1. receiving the Governed Context Scope from ECSM; 2. identifying candidate relationships among contextual elements; 3. determining whether those relationships are materially relevant; 4. distinguishing relevant relationship types; 5. representing direction or dependency where necessary; 6. preserving relationship uncertainty; 7. preventing correlation from automatically becoming causation; 8. maintaining separation between Context Relationships and Event Relationships; 9. producing a Governed Context Relationship Structure for subsequent TRECS processing. The module does not prescribe a graph database, knowledge graph, ontology, AI model, relational database, ERP structure, or other specific technical implementation. Governance Outputs ECRM may produce: Governed Context Relationship Structure — the canonical relational representation of materially relevant contextual elements. Context Relationship Set — identified and qualified relationships within the governed context. Relationship Type References — governed characterization of relationship types. Relationship Direction References — directionality where materially relevant. Context Dependency References — identified dependencies among contextual elements. Relationship Uncertainty Indicators — unresolved or insufficiently established relationships. Relationship Consistency Result — identification of materially inconsistent or conflicting contextual relationships requiring further governance. These outputs support subsequent Context Change and Context Continuity governance and provide structured contextual input to later TREGA™ Parent Standards. Critical Distinctions Context Coexistence ≠ Context Relationship. Being present within the same contextual environment does not establish a material relationship. Context Relationship ≠ Event Relationship. ECRM governs relationships among contextual elements. TRERLS — Tax-Relevant Event Relationship Standard governs relationships among governed Tax-Relevant Events. Dependency ≠ Causality. Operational dependence does not itself prove causal responsibility. Correlation ≠ Causation. Technical or temporal correlation does not automatically establish a governed causal relationship. Context Sequence ≠ Event Timing. A contextual sequence does not determine the formal temporal position of the governed event. Relationship ≠ Accountability. A contextual relationship does not determine who is accountable. Relationship ≠ Tax Relationship. ECRM does not determine legal tax relationships between participants, organizations, transactions, or jurisdictions. Enterprise Application ECRM is particularly valuable in environments where one economic activity crosses many systems and where technical connectivity can easily be mistaken for economic structure. Typical environments include: ERP ↔ Commerce Platform ↔ Payment Infrastructure ↔ Logistics AI Agent ↔ API ↔ Platform ↔ External Service Industrial Machine ↔ Production System ↔ Warehouse ↔ ERP Banking System ↔ Payment Network ↔ Merchant Platform ↔ Customer Account ECRM creates a governed relational layer across these heterogeneous systems without requiring them to use identical technologies or data models. This allows downstream systems to distinguish: records that merely coexist from contextual elements that are materially related. Use CasesUse Case 1 — Platform Economy: One Payment, Multiple Parties, Multiple Relationships A global marketplace processes a customer payment associated with a merchant, marketplace operator, payment provider, logistics provider, advertising service, platform fee, and automated settlement system. All parties may appear within the same technical transaction environment. A conventional system may incorrectly infer that every participant has the same relationship to the underlying economic activity simply because all are linked to the same transaction identifier. ECRM separates the contextual relationships. It may establish that: Customer ↓ Merchant represents one contextual relationship, Merchant ↓ Platform another, Platform ↓ Payment Provider another, and Merchant ↓ Logistics Provider another. ECRM does not determine which relationship creates a taxable supply, who is the taxpayer, whether VAT or another tax applies, or which jurisdiction has taxation rights. It prevents a technically shared transaction structure from being mistaken for a single undifferentiated economic relationship. Use Case 2 — AI Agent Chain with Hidden Economic Dependencies An autonomous procurement agent receives an operational objective and independently interacts with several APIs, compares suppliers, reserves cloud capacity, purchases a digital component, triggers payment, and initiates another autonomous service. Hundreds of system calls may occur within seconds. Technical logs can establish chronology but may not clearly show which actions were dependencies of the same economic activity and which were unrelated background operations. ECRM establishes the materially relevant contextual relationships among the agent, APIs, services, payment infrastructure, platform operations, and dependent executions. It distinguishes: technical correlation from governed contextual dependency. This allows TREGA™ to preserve the structure of autonomous economic activity without treating every API call as an independent Tax-Relevant Event or assuming that technical execution order itself determines legal tax consequences. Canonical Boundary ECRM governs relationships among contextual elements surrounding an occurrence. It does not govern relationships among Tax-Relevant Events. The TRECS sequence remains: ECIM — What contextual elements may matter? → ECSM — Which contextual elements belong within the relevant Context Scope? → ECRM — How are those contextual elements materially related? → ECCHM — What happens when that governed context materially changes? → ECCM — How is contextual continuity maintained across the lifecycle? The later architectural boundary is: Context Relationship ↓ ECRM Event Relationship ↓ TRERLS Canonical Closing Statement Event Context Relationship Module establishes the relational governance capability of the Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard by transforming a sufficiently scoped collection of economic, operational, organizational, transactional, digital, technological, infrastructural, autonomous, machine-generated, and value-related contextual elements into a structured representation of how those elements materially relate. Through governance of relationship relevance, type, direction, dependency, sequence, uncertainty, consistency, correlation, and distributed contextual structures, ECRM prevents shared identifiers, technical proximity, temporal correlation, platform connectivity, or machine interaction from being automatically interpreted as causal, economic, event-level, accountable, or legally taxable relationships. The Module therefore establishes how the context surrounding an occurrence is structurally connected while preserving the critical boundary between Context Relationships and the formal relationships among Tax-Relevant Events governed later in TREGA™.

title: OOF™ The Event Correction Module (ECRTM) governs how materially incorrect,
text: OOF™ The Event Correction Module (ECRTM) governs how materially incorrect, The Event Correction Module (ECRTM) governs how materially incorrect, OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: TRECLS — Tax-Relevant Event Lifecycle & Continuity Standard Module: ECRTM — Event Correction Module Operational Layer: Event Correction Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Event Correction Primary Governed Object: Governed Event Correction State Origin ID: TREGA-TRECLS-ECRTM-003 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 3 September 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language Canonical Definition The Event Correction Module (ECRTM) governs how materially incorrect, incomplete, inconsistent, or improperly represented information associated with a continuing Tax-Relevant Event is corrected while preserving the Event’s prior materially relevant state, correction basis, current effective state, and historical reconstructability. Its principal transition is: Governed Event Amendment State / Governed Event Continuity State ↓ Event Correction Governance ↓ Governed Event Correction State ECRTM distinguishes legitimate correction from amendment, silent overwrite, Record-only correction, and New Event Formation. Its foundational principle is: Correction ≠ Historical Erasure. Operational Role A governed Event may later be found to contain information that was materially wrong. The problem may concern: Context; Timing; Location; Participation; Value Association; Event Relationships; Determination; or the Event’s governed representation. Correction must restore the current Event state without creating the false impression that the earlier governed state never existed. ECRTM answers: How can a materially incorrect Event state be corrected while preserving what was previously governed, why it changed, and which state is now effective? Internal Module Flow TRECLS operates through: ECOM — Event Continuity ↓ EADM — Event Amendment ↓ ECRTM — Event Correction ↓ ESPM — Event Supersession ↓ ECLM — Event Closure ↓ Jurisdiction-Ready Tax-Relevant Event ECRTM receives the applicable continuing or amended Event state and produces: Governed Event Correction State for subsequent lifecycle governance. Operational Transition The canonical transition is: Current Governed Event State ↓ Correction Trigger ↓ Error Characterization ↓ Correction Scope ↓ Corrected State Establishment ↓ Historical Preservation ↓ Governed Event Correction State Operational Space ECRTM governs: Correction Trigger identification; error identification; error characterization; Correction eligibility; Correction scope; Correction materiality; prior-state preservation; corrected-state establishment; correction basis; correction qualification; correction ambiguity; correction conflict; Event-level vs Record-level correction distinction; upstream reassessment; Determination impact; continuity reassessment; effective-state transition; correction withdrawal; replacement correction; correction history; and correction handoff. Operational Scope ECRTM may govern corrections involving: physical Events; digital Events; commercial transactions; financial activity; platform Events; distributed systems; AI-agent activity; autonomous systems; machine-to-machine Events; digital assets; industrial Events; cross-border Events; multi-party Events; long-running Events; and future machine economies. The module remains technology-neutral and jurisdiction-neutral. Correction Object The Correction Object is the materially inaccurate, incomplete, inconsistent, or improperly represented governed information requiring rectification. The Correction Object is not automatically the whole Event. Incorrect Event Component ≠ Entire Event Invalid by default. Correction Trigger A Correction Trigger may arise from: newly verified contradictory information; discovered data error; incorrect participant association; incorrect Timing; incorrect Location; incorrect Value Association; incorrect relationship representation; incorrect Determination input; technical transformation error; duplicate or misapplied Record information; upstream governance revision; validation result; evidence review; or system reconciliation. Correction Eligibility Correction is appropriate where: a prior governed state exists; a materially relevant part of that state was wrong, incomplete, inconsistent, or improperly represented; the Event remains continuous or sufficiently governed for correction; the issue is not merely new information suitable for Amendment; and the change does not itself require New Event Formation. Correction vs Amendment Correction addresses prior information that was materially wrong or improperly represented. Amendment adds or refines information without necessarily establishing prior error. Correction ≠ Amendment. New Information ≠ Correction by default. Correction vs New Event Formation A Correction remains within the same Event where the corrected occurrence is still legitimately the same Event. Where the correction reveals that the original Formation or Boundary was fundamentally wrong, continuity may fail and upstream New Event Formation may be required. Correction ≠ Permission to Preserve Invalid Event Identity. Error Characterization ECRTM shall characterize the nature of the error. Possible categories include: factual error; omission; misassociation; misclassification within TREGA™ event data; temporal error; Location error; Participation error; Value Association error; Relationship error; Determination-input error; representation error; transformation error; duplicate attribution; state-transition error. Material Error A Material Error is an error capable of changing governed understanding, continuity, Determination, downstream reliance, or jurisdiction readiness. Material errors require formal Correction Governance. Non-Material Error A Non-Material Error does not materially affect governed Event meaning. Examples may include: typographical metadata error; non-substantive formatting issue; technical label defect; redundant non-governance field. Such changes may not require full canonical Correction Governance. Correction Scope Correction scope shall identify the specific governed component affected. Possible scopes include: Context; Timing; Location; Participation; Value Association; Event Relationship; Determination-related input; lifecycle state; Record representation. Correction Scope ≠ Permission to Reopen All Event Governance. Prior-State Preservation The materially relevant prior state shall remain reconstructable after Correction. The canonical pattern is: Prior State ↓ Correction Basis ↓ Corrected State not: Prior State ↓ Overwrite ↓ No Recoverable History Current Corrected State Once correction is validly established, the corrected state may become the current effective Event state. The prior state remains historical. Current Corrected State ≠ Only State That Ever Existed. Historical Error Preservation Historical preservation does not mean the erroneous state remains currently valid.
