It means the system can reconstruct: what was previously represented; why it was considered incorrect; what replaced it; and which state is now effective. Correction Basis A material Correction should possess an identifiable governance basis. The basis may reference: upstream governance result; validated information; evidence; reconciliation result; authoritative operational update; system defect; prior transformation error. ECRTM does not itself own evidence validation. Correction Effective Time Where materially relevant, the governance system should distinguish: when the original state was established; when the error was discovered; when the Correction was governed; when the corrected state became effective. This governance timing is not the legal tax point. Event-Level Correction Event-Level Correction exists where a substantively governed Event attribute was wrong. Examples include: wrong Event Location; wrong participant role; wrong Event Timing; wrong Value Association; wrong Event Relationship. The relevant upstream TREGA™ standard remains authoritative for the corrected substantive result. ECRTM governs the lifecycle correction transition. Record-Level Correction Record-Level Correction exists where the underlying Event was correct but its TREGS representation was wrong. Examples include: incorrect field mapping; wrong local identifier; failed schema transformation; omitted canonical reference; technical duplication. Record Correction ≠ Event Correction by default. TREGS owns the Record correction mechanism; ECRTM governs only where the Event lifecycle state is affected. Upstream Correction Referral Where the substantive error belongs to an upstream TREGA™ governed space, ECRTM shall consume the corrected upstream result rather than independently recreate it. Examples: TRECS for Context; TRETS for Timing; TRELS for Location; TREPS for Participation; TRVAS for Value Association; TRERLS for Event Relationships; TREDS for Event Determination. Formation Error Boundary Where correction reveals that Event Formation itself was materially invalid, the issue returns to TREFS. ECRTM shall not preserve Event identity merely for continuity convenience. Boundary Error Boundary Where correction reveals that Event Boundary was materially invalid, TREBS remains authoritative. The correction may trigger ECOM continuity reassessment. Determination Correction Impact A corrected Event state may alter the basis of TREDS Determination. Where material, TREDS reconsideration shall be triggered or referenced. Correction Impact ≠ Determination Authority. Continuity Reassessment A Correction may preserve the same Event. But where the correction materially changes Formation, Boundary, core operational substance, or Event identity basis, ECOM shall reassess Continuity. Valid Correction ≠ Automatic Continuity Preservation. Correction Qualification A Correction may be qualified where: the corrected value is known only within a range; one source remains unresolved; part of the prior state is corrected while another part remains uncertain; downstream use must remain restricted. Qualification shall remain visible. Partial Correction Partial Correction exists where only part of the identified error can currently be resolved. The unresolved component shall remain explicit. Partial Correction ≠ Complete Correction. Correction Ambiguity Correction Ambiguity exists where: the prior state appears wrong but the corrected state is not sufficiently established; multiple plausible corrected values exist; scope remains uncertain; Event-level vs Record-level error is unresolved. The Event shall not be silently rewritten. Correction Conflict Correction Conflict exists where materially authoritative sources or governance states support incompatible corrected outcomes. Conflict shall remain explicit until resolved or qualified. Correction Rejection A proposed Correction may be rejected where: the prior state is not established as materially wrong; evidence or governance basis is insufficient; the proposed state belongs to a different Event; the change is actually an Amendment; or the correction attempts to import jurisdiction-specific tax conclusions into the canonical Event. Correction Withdrawal A proposed Correction may be withdrawn before becoming effective. Materially relevant withdrawal history should remain reconstructable. Replacement Correction A proposed or completed Correction may itself require later correction. The lifecycle may therefore contain: State A ↓ Correction 1 ↓ State B ↓ Correction 2 ↓ State C Each materially relevant transition remains reconstructable. Correction Chain Multiple Corrections may occur over time. The current effective Event state should remain clearly identifiable. Multiple Corrections ≠ Multiple Events by default. Correction and Supersession A corrected state may supersede the prior effective state. ECRTM governs the correction. ESPM governs formal Supersession where required. Correction ≠ Supersession by default. Correction and Closure An Event may require Correction before Closure. A previously Closed Event may also require reopening if material correction information appears. ECLM governs Closure. Cross-System Correction An error may originate in one system but affect a canonical Event consumed by many systems. Correction should preserve one canonical corrected Event state and propagate through governed Record interoperability. Cross-Organization Correction Different organizations may identify conflicting corrections. Contribution does not equal canonical authority. Correction Proposal ≠ Canonical Correction. Cross-Border Correction A canonical Event Correction remains jurisdiction-neutral. Downstream jurisdictions may react differently to the corrected state. Event Correction ≠ Jurisdictional Tax Reassessment Decision. Machine-Generated Correction AI systems, autonomous platforms, and machine processes may detect or propose corrections automatically. Automated detection does not eliminate governance requirements. Machine-Detected Error ≠ Automatically Governed Correction. Correction at Scale High-volume environments may identify many technical inconsistencies. ECRTM should distinguish material Event Corrections from low-value technical noise. More Detected Errors ≠ More Material Corrections. Correction Traceability A material Correction should remain traceable to: Event; prior state; error characterization; correction basis; corrected state; effective transition; qualification; downstream references where appropriate. ERTM owns Record Traceability. Correction and Interoperability Corrected Event meaning should propagate without semantic drift across downstream systems. ERINM owns Record Interoperability. ECRTM establishes which Event state is current. Correction and Tax Law A jurisdiction may respond to a Correction by changing: Taxability; Tax Base; filing; assessment; payment; legal treatment. Those consequences remain outside ECRTM. Corrected Event ≠ Corrected Tax Assessment by default. Governance States ECRTM may represent: Correction Governance Not Initiated Correction Trigger Identified Potential Error Identified Error Under Assessment Error Non-Material Error Material Correction Eligible Correction Scope Defined Correction Under Governance Correction Qualified Correction Partial Correction Ambiguous Correction Conflicted Upstream Correction Required Continuity Reassessment Required Correction Rejected Correction Withdrawn Corrected State Established Historical State Preserved Governed Event Correction State Established Ready for Supersession Governance Governance Requirements ECRTM implementations shall ensure that: a valid continuing governed Event state exists; the suspected error is identifiable; Correction remains distinct from Amendment; Correction remains distinct from New Event Formation; Event-level and Record-level errors remain distinguishable; correction scope is explicit where material; error materiality is assessed; materially relevant prior state remains reconstructable; corrected current state remains distinguishable from prior state; Correction basis remains identifiable; upstream TREGA™ ownership is preserved; TREFS is re-engaged where Formation was materially invalid; TREBS is re-engaged where Boundary was materially invalid; TREDS reconsideration is triggered where Determination basis materially changes; ECOM reassesses Continuity where correction challenges same-Event identity; Partial Correction remains distinguishable from complete Correction; ambiguity and conflict remain explicit; rejected and withdrawn material correction proposals remain reconstructable where necessary; automated correction proposals are not accepted solely because they are machine-generated; downstream tax effects remain outside Event Correction governance; and the resulting corrected Event state is suitable for subsequent TRECLS lifecycle governance. Governance Logic IF no governed Event state exists, THEN ECRTM shall not establish canonical Event Correction. IF new information does not establish that prior information was materially wrong or improperly represented, THEN the change should not be treated as Correction by default. IF the change merely adds or refines legitimate information, THEN EADM may be the appropriate governance path. IF the error exists only in technical Record representation while underlying Event governance remains correct, THEN the issue shall remain primarily within TREGS Record Governance. IF a substantive Event attribute was materially wrong, THEN the relevant upstream TREGA™ authority shall establish or support the corrected result. IF correction materially changes Formation or Boundary, THEN Continuity reassessment shall be required. IF correction materially affects Event Determination, THEN TREDS reconsideration shall be triggered or referenced. IF the corrected state is only partially established, THEN the Correction shall remain Partial or Qualified. IF competing materially authoritative corrected states exist, THEN Correction Conflict shall be established. IF the prior state is not sufficiently shown to be wrong, THEN a proposed Correction shall not silently replace it. IF a valid Correction is established, THEN the corrected state may become current while the prior materially relevant state remains historically reconstructable. Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum ECRTM implementation should support: Correction Governance ID Stable identifier for the correction process. Canonical Event Reference The Event under Correction Governance. Prior Event State Reference The state believed to contain the error. Correction Trigger Type Error Discovery, Reconciliation, Upstream Revision, Validation Result, Evidence Result, Technical Defect, Transformation Error, or other governed trigger. Potential Error Reference The identified issue. Error Type Factual, Omission, Misassociation, Timing, Location, Participation, Value, Relationship, Determination Input, Representation, Transformation, Duplicate Attribution, or other. Error Materiality State Non-Material, Material, Critical, Unresolved. Correction Scope The governed Event component affected. Correction Level Event-Level, Record-Level, Mixed, Unresolved. Correction Eligibility State Eligible, Qualified, Ineligible, Unresolved. Correction Basis Reference The governance basis supporting the correction. Corrected Upstream Result Reference Where applicable. Prior State Preservation State Whether the previous materially relevant state remains reconstructable. Corrected Event State Reference The corrected governed state. Current Effective State Reference The state currently effective after correction. Correction Effective Time Reference Where materially relevant. Correction Qualification Any limitation attached to the corrected state. Partial Correction State Whether only part of the error has been resolved. Correction Ambiguity State Whether the corrected outcome remains uncertain. Correction Conflict State Whether materially incompatible correction outcomes exist. Determination Impact State None, Potential, Material, Reconsideration Required. TREDS Reconsideration Reference Where applicable. Continuity Reassessment State Whether ECOM reassessment is required. Correction Withdrawal State Whether a proposed Correction was withdrawn. Replacement Correction Reference Any subsequent correction replacing the current correction result. Historical Correction Chain Reference Prior materially relevant correction states. Governance State The current ECRTM governance state. Correction Outcome Corrected, Qualified, Partial, Rejected, Withdrawn, or Unresolved. Handoff State Whether the Event is ready for Supersession Governance. Governance Outputs ECRTM may produce: Correction Trigger State; Error Characterization; Error Materiality State; Correction Scope; Correction Level; Correction Eligibility State; Correction Basis Reference; Upstream Correction Reference; Corrected Event State; Current Effective State; Prior-State Preservation State; Correction Qualification; Partial Correction State; Correction Ambiguity State; Correction Conflict State; Determination Impact State; Continuity Reassessment State; Historical Correction Chain; and the principal output: Governed Event Correction State. Critical Distinctions Correction ≠ Historical Erasure. Incorrect Event Component ≠ Entire Event Invalid by default. Correction ≠ Amendment. New Information ≠ Correction by default. Correction ≠ Permission to Preserve Invalid Event Identity. Correction Scope ≠ Permission to Reopen All Event Governance. Current Corrected State ≠ Only State That Ever Existed. Record Correction ≠ Event Correction by default. Correction Impact ≠ Determination Authority. Valid Correction ≠ Automatic Continuity Preservation. Partial Correction ≠ Complete Correction. Correction Proposal ≠ Canonical Correction. Multiple Corrections ≠ Multiple Events by default. Correction ≠ Supersession by default. Event Correction ≠ Jurisdictional Tax Reassessment Decision. Machine-Detected Error ≠ Automatically Governed Correction. More Detected Errors ≠ More Material Corrections. Corrected Event ≠ Corrected Tax Assessment by default. Enterprise Application ECRTM provides the controlled repair layer for governed Event Reality. The operational pattern is: Governed Event State → Material Error Detected → Error Characterization → Upstream Correction Where Required → Corrected Event State → Prior State Preserved → Governed Event Correction State Where the issue is merely new legitimate information: Correction Candidate ↓ EADM Where correction threatens Event identity: Correction Candidate ↓ ECOM Continuity Reassessment Where the corrected state replaces a prior effective state: Governed Event Correction State ↓ ESPM — Supersession Governance This keeps correction precise without allowing systems to rewrite history. Use Case 1 — Incorrect Event Location Discovered After Multi-Jurisdiction Use A Governed Tax-Relevant Event has already been distributed to multiple downstream tax environments. Later, authoritative operational information establishes that one previously governed Location was materially incorrect. TRELS establishes the corrected Location. ECRTM governs the lifecycle transition: Prior Location State ↓ Correction Basis ↓ Corrected Location State ↓ Historical State Preserved The Event remains the same Event after ECOM confirms Continuity. The corrected state becomes current. Each jurisdiction may decide independently whether the correction changes tax treatment. ECRTM does not determine that legal consequence. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Platform Corrects a Wrong Participant Association An autonomous transaction Record associates Machine Agent A as a material Event participant. Subsequent governed information establishes that Agent A only transmitted a message and did not materially participate; Agent B performed the governed activity. TREPS establishes the corrected Participation result. ECRTM preserves the prior Participant state, records the correction basis, establishes the corrected Participant state, and triggers TREDS reconsideration if Participation was material to Event Determination. The Event remains one Event if ECOM confirms Continuity. Correcting who participated does not require pretending that the earlier governed state never existed. Canonical Boundary ECRTM owns the governance of Event Correction Triggers, error characterization, Correction eligibility, Correction scope, Correction materiality, Event-level versus Record-level correction distinction, correction basis, prior-state preservation, corrected-state establishment, current effective state, qualification, Partial Correction, ambiguity, conflict, withdrawal, replacement correction, correction history, Determination-impact referral, Continuity-reassessment trigger, and establishment of the Governed Event Correction State. ECRTM does not own Event Continuity; ECOM does. It does not own Amendment; EADM does. It does not own formal Supersession; ESPM does. It does not own Closure; ECLM does. It does not independently recreate Context, Formation, Boundary, Timing, Location, Participation, Value Association, Event Relationships, Determination, or Record Governance. It does not validate evidence or determine general integrity. It does not determine legal Taxability, Tax Jurisdiction, taxpayer status, legal tax point, Tax Period, Tax Base, Tax Rate, exemptions, deductions, Tax Liability, filing, reassessment, payment, collection, or enforcement. Its governance begins when a materially relevant potential error exists within a continuing governed Event. Its governance ends with: Governed Event Correction State or with referral to the appropriate upstream governance layer where substantive correction or New Event Formation is required. Canonical Handoff EADM / Current Governed Event State ↓ ECRTM — Governed Event Correction State ↓ ESPM — Event Supersession Governance Where Continuity is materially affected: ECRTM ↓ ECOM — Continuity Reassessment Where substantive upstream governance is required: ECRTM ↓ Relevant TREGA™ Parent Standard ↓ Corrected Governed Result ↓ ECRTM Canonical Closing Statement ECRTM allows a governed Event to become more correct without allowing the governance system to become less truthful about its own history. A corrected state may replace the prior state as current, but it must not make the prior governed state disappear from reconstructable reality. Correction ≠ Historical Erasure. Record Correction ≠ Event Correction by default. Current Corrected State ≠ Only State That Ever Existed.

title: OOF™ Event Context Scope Module (ECSM)
text: OOF™ Event Context Scope Module (ECSM) Event Context Scope Module (ECSM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard (TRECS) Module: ECSM — Event Context Scope Module Operational Layer: Event Context Scope Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Event Context Scope Origin ID: TREGA-TRECS-ECSM-002 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 29 August 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Event Context Scope Module (ECSM) is the Core Module within Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard (TRECS) that governs the determination of how much of the contextual environment identified around an observed occurrence is materially relevant and legitimately necessary for subsequent tax-relevant event governance. ECSM establishes the governed scope of Event Context by determining which identified contextual elements remain inside the relevant contextual representation, which remain outside it, and where contextual expansion must stop. Its task is specific: to establish a sufficient and proportionate contextual scope around an occurrence without defining the boundary of the Tax-Relevant Event itself. ECSM therefore prevents two opposite governance failures: Context Under-Scope — material surrounding conditions are excluded. Context Over-Scope — unrelated or unnecessarily remote conditions are absorbed into Event Context. Operational Role ECIM identifies potentially relevant contextual elements. ECSM determines the legitimate extent of that context. Its operational question is: How much surrounding context is necessary to understand this occurrence sufficiently for subsequent TREGA™ governance? The module may scope relevant: economic context; operational context; organizational context; transactional context; digital and platform context; technological context; infrastructural context; autonomous-system context; value-related context; process context; distributed-system context; cross-border operational context. ECSM does not seek maximum context. It seeks sufficient context. Internal Flow Identified Context Set ↓ Context Relevance Assessment ↓ Materiality Assessment ↓ Scope Inclusion / Exclusion ↓ Scope Sufficiency Check ↓ Governed Context Scope The principal output is: Governed Context Scope This becomes the bounded contextual environment used by subsequent TRECS governance. Operational Space ECSM governs the space between: potentially relevant contextual elements identified around an occurrence and the sufficiently bounded contextual representation legitimately required for subsequent event governance. Its operational space includes: context inclusion; context exclusion; contextual materiality; contextual proximity; contextual depth; contextual breadth; multi-system context; distributed context; contextual sufficiency; scope uncertainty; scope expansion; scope contraction; proportionality of context. ECSM governs the boundary of relevant context, not the boundary of the event. Operational Scope ECSM determines whether identified contextual elements should remain within the governed Event Context because they materially contribute to understanding the occurrence. An element may remain in scope where its exclusion could materially impair: interpretation of the occurrence; understanding of the operational process; understanding of the economic environment; recognition of relevant dependencies; subsequent Event Recognition; subsequent Event Formation; interpretation of distributed activity; reconstruction of the occurrence; understanding of machine or autonomous execution; legitimate downstream event governance. Information should remain outside scope where it is materially unrelated, unnecessarily remote, duplicative without governance value, or included solely because it is technically available. Context Scope Principle The governing principle of ECSM is: Context should be as broad as necessary to understand the occurrence, but no broader than materially justified. Too narrow a scope can distort reality. Too broad a scope can bury the occurrence inside irrelevant information. Therefore: Context Sufficiency ≠ Maximum Context. Context Materiality Context inclusion requires more than simple association. A contextual element should have a material relationship to understanding the occurrence or enabling its subsequent governance. Materiality may arise from: operational dependency; economic relevance; transactional relevance; organizational relationship; system dependency; technological dependency; process relationship; autonomous execution conditions; value-related relevance; distributed operational relevance. The existence of a data connection alone does not establish material contextual relevance. Therefore: Data Availability ≠ Context Materiality. Context Inclusion and Exclusion ECSM must support explicit inclusion and exclusion. A governed scope should be capable of establishing: Included Context — materially relevant contextual elements retained for subsequent governance. Excluded Context — identified elements determined not to be necessary within the governed contextual representation. Where exclusion is materially significant, the basis should remain governable. This prevents silent disappearance of context that may later affect event interpretation. Context Depth Some occurrences require examination beyond the immediately surrounding transaction or system record. For example: API Call ↓ Platform Operation ↓ Service Execution ↓ Economic Activity The API call alone may be insufficient to understand what happened. ECSM may therefore extend contextual depth where the surrounding layers materially affect interpretation. However, contextual expansion must stop when additional layers cease to provide material governance value. Distributed Context Modern activity may span several systems, organizations, platforms, infrastructures, or countries. ECSM must permit a governed Context Scope to cross technical or organizational boundaries where those environments materially contribute to understanding the same occurrence. This is particularly important where no single system contains a complete representation of the activity. But: Distributed Context ≠ Tax Jurisdiction Determination. Scope Sufficiency A Governed Context Scope becomes sufficient when excluding additional surrounding information would not reasonably prevent the next TREGA™ stage from performing its governance role. Sufficiency does not mean certainty. Material uncertainty may remain explicitly represented. Therefore: Scope Sufficient ≠ Context Certain. Scope Revision Context Scope may require later expansion or contraction when: new contextual information becomes available; an earlier assumption is corrected; previously unknown system relationships are discovered; distributed activity becomes visible; contextual relevance changes; later governance exposes a material contextual gap. A revised scope must remain distinguishable from the previous governed scope where historical traceability matters. Governance Requirements ECSM requires that: scope begins from identified contextual elements; inclusion has a material governance basis; exclusion does not remove context necessary for legitimate downstream interpretation; scope remains proportionate to the occurrence; multiple context types may coexist; distributed context may cross system boundaries; uncertainty may remain explicit; scope may be revised when justified; scope decisions remain distinguishable from Event Boundary decisions; tax rules do not automatically define the upstream Event Context Scope. Governance Logic ECSM evaluates each identified contextual element against a central test: Would inclusion or exclusion of this element materially affect the legitimate understanding or subsequent governance of the occurrence? Where yes, the element may remain within scope. Where no, it may remain outside the governed Context Scope. Where the answer cannot yet be established, the element may remain: Scope-Uncertain rather than being automatically included or excluded. This prevents uncertainty from being converted into arbitrary scope decisions. Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum ECSM implementation must be capable of: 1. receiving the Identified Context Set from ECIM; 2. evaluating contextual relevance and materiality; 3. determining contextual inclusion and exclusion; 4. representing scope uncertainty; 5. evaluating Context Scope sufficiency; 6. supporting justified scope revision; 7. preserving the distinction between Context Scope and Event Boundary; 8. producing a Governed Context Scope usable by subsequent TRECS governance. No particular software architecture, AI model, database, ERP, tax engine, ontology, or jurisdiction is required. Governance Outputs ECSM may produce: Governed Context Scope — the established extent of relevant context surrounding the occurrence. Included Context Set — contextual elements retained within scope. Excluded Context Set — identified elements determined to remain outside scope. Scope Materiality Basis — the governance basis supporting material inclusion or exclusion. Scope Uncertainty Indicator — unresolved scope conditions requiring preservation or further governance. Context Sufficiency Status — whether the contextual representation is sufficiently scoped for subsequent processing. Scope Revision Record — where applicable, a traceable record of material scope expansion or contraction. Critical Distinctions Context Identification ≠ Context Scope. ECIM identifies what may matter. ECSM determines how much of it legitimately belongs within the relevant contextual representation. Context Scope ≠ Event Boundary. Context may extend beyond the eventual governed Tax-Relevant Event. Context Inclusion ≠ Event Inclusion. An element may be necessary to understand an event without becoming part of the event itself. Context Materiality ≠ Tax Materiality. ECSM determines materiality for contextual governance, not legal materiality under tax law. Cross-Border Scope ≠ Tax Jurisdiction. Several countries may legitimately appear inside Event Context without TREGA™ deciding which country has taxation rights. Enterprise Application ECSM is particularly valuable where organizations must reconstruct economic activity from fragmented systems. A single activity may appear across: ERP ↓ CRM ↓ Payment System ↓ Platform ↓ Logistics ↓ Cloud Infrastructure ↓ External Provider without any system holding the complete contextual picture. ECSM provides a common methodological mechanism for determining which parts of that distributed environment are necessary for event understanding without requiring every available record to enter the final contextual representation. This allows enterprise and public-sector tax infrastructures to consume governed, proportionate context rather than uncontrolled volumes of operational data. Use CasesUse Case 1 — Cross-Border Digital Platform with Fragmented Transaction Reality A digital platform facilitates a service involving a customer in one country, a service provider established in another, payment infrastructure in a third, cloud execution distributed across several regions, and automated platform functions operating globally. The technical environment may contain thousands of records associated with one commercial activity. Using every record creates excessive contextual noise. Using only the payment record may remove essential operational meaning. ECSM determines which platform, service, payment, organizational, operational, and distributed-system conditions are materially necessary to create a sufficient Event Context. It deliberately does not decide which country may tax the activity. The result is a Governed Context Scope capable of supporting subsequent TREGA™ processing without allowing either technical complexity or jurisdictional assumptions to define the event prematurely. Use Case 2 — One Economic Activity Producing Thousands of Machine Records A highly automated factory executes a production and delivery process involving robots, sensors, inventory systems, autonomous transport, ERP records, internal transfers, energy systems, quality systems, and logistics infrastructure. Thousands of machine events may be generated around a single economically meaningful activity. Treating every technical record as equally relevant could create thousands of artificial event candidates. Restricting analysis to the final invoice could hide the operational reality necessary to understand what occurred. ECSM establishes the appropriate contextual depth and breadth required to understand the occurrence while excluding machine telemetry and technical records that do not materially contribute to tax-relevant event governance. The module therefore addresses a fundamental problem of increasingly automated economies: machine systems can generate vastly more technical events than economically meaningful events. Canonical Boundary ECSM governs the extent of Event Context. It does not govern the extent of the Tax-Relevant Event itself. The handoff is explicit: ECIM — What contextual elements may matter? → ECSM — Which contextual elements belong within the relevant Context Scope? → ECRM — How are those contextual elements related? The later TREBS — Tax-Relevant Event Boundary Standard answers a fundamentally different question: What belongs to the governed event itself? Canonical Closing Statement Event Context Scope Module establishes the contextual scoping capability of the Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard by determining how much of the economic, operational, organizational, transactional, digital, technological, infrastructural, autonomous, machine-generated, value-related, and distributed environment surrounding an occurrence is materially necessary for legitimate downstream event governance. Through governance of contextual inclusion, exclusion, materiality, depth, breadth, sufficiency, uncertainty, distributed context, and justified scope revision, ECSM prevents both incomplete contextual representations and uncontrolled expansion of surrounding information while preserving the critical distinction between the context required to understand an occurrence and the boundary of the Tax-Relevant Event itself. ECSM therefore establishes not the largest possible contextual representation, but the smallest sufficiently governed context capable of supporting the next stage of TREGA™ without distorting the reality it is intended to represent.

title: OOF™ The Event Determination Conditions Module (EDCM) governs the conditions
text: OOF™ The Event Determination Conditions Module (EDCM) governs the conditions The Event Determination Conditions Module (EDCM) governs the conditions OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: TREDS — Tax-Relevant Event Determination Standard Module: EDCM — Event Determination Conditions Module Operational Layer: Event Determination Conditions Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Event Determination Conditions Origin ID: TREGA-TREDS-EDCM-002 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 2 September 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language Canonical Definition The Event Determination Conditions Module (EDCM) governs the conditions that a determination-ready Event must satisfy before a formal Tax-Relevant Event Determination Decision can be made. EDCM transforms readiness into an explicit, reviewable set of determination conditions and evaluates whether those conditions are satisfied, conditionally satisfied, unsatisfied, conflicted, or unresolved. Its principal transition is: Governed Determination Readiness State ↓ Determination Conditions Governance ↓ Governed Determination Condition State EDCM does not decide whether the Event is ultimately determined as Tax-Relevant. That decision belongs to EDDM. Its foundational distinction is: Determination Condition Satisfaction ≠ Determination Decision. Operational Role An Event may be ready for determination while still failing one or more conditions necessary for a defensible final decision. Readiness asks: Can formal determination begin? EDCM asks: What must be true for this Event to support a formal Determination Decision, and are those conditions satisfied? This distinction prevents readiness from being treated as automatic approval. EDCM provides the formal condition layer between EDRDM and EDDM. Internal Module Flow TREDS operates through: EDRDM — Event Determination Readiness ↓ EDCM — Event Determination Conditions ↓ EDDM — Event Determination Decision ↓ EDUM — Event Determination Uncertainty ↓ EDREM — Event Determination Reconsideration ↓ Determined Tax-Relevant Event EDCM receives the Governed Determination Readiness State from EDRDM. Its principal output is passed to EDDM. Operational Transition The canonical transition is: Governed Determination Readiness State + Governed Event Structure ↓ Condition Identification ↓ Condition Evaluation ↓ Governed Determination Condition State Possible condition states include: Satisfied; Conditionally Satisfied; Partially Satisfied; Unsatisfied; Ambiguous; Conflicted; Unresolved; Not Applicable. Operational Space EDCM governs: condition identification; condition applicability; condition materiality; condition sufficiency; condition dependency; condition qualification; condition satisfaction; partial satisfaction; conditional satisfaction; unsatisfied conditions; condition exceptions where methodologically valid; condition conflicts; condition ambiguity; unresolved conditions; condition evidence references; condition coherence; condition interaction; condition traceability; condition reassessment; and determination-condition handoff. Operational Scope EDCM may govern Determination Conditions for events arising from: commerce; marketplaces; banking; payments; ERP; accounting; logistics; supply chains; digital platforms; blockchain systems; smart contracts; digital assets; AI agents; autonomous machines; industrial systems; energy systems; distributed infrastructure; cross-border activity; machine-to-machine environments; and future machine economies. The same methodological logic applies regardless of technical source. Determination Condition A Determination Condition is a governed requirement that must be evaluated before EDDM can issue a formal Determination Decision. A condition may relate to: Event Identity; Event Formation; Event Boundary; Event Timing; Event Location; Event Participation; Value Association; Event Relationships; coherence; stability; traceability; or another materially necessary aspect of the governed Event. Determination Condition ≠ Tax Rule. EDCM conditions govern Event sufficiency, not legal tax consequence. Condition Identification EDCM shall identify the materially relevant conditions for the Event under review. Conditions shall be derived from the Event structure and upstream governance state. They shall not be invented merely to increase process complexity. Possible Condition ≠ Required Condition by default. Condition Applicability Not every condition applies equally to every Event. For example: Location may be materially central for one Event; less material for another; machine Participation may be critical in autonomous systems; Value Association may be central in one Event and limited in another. EDCM shall distinguish applicable from non-applicable conditions. Universal Condition Template ≠ Universal Condition Applicability. Condition Materiality A condition is material where failure to satisfy it could materially affect the validity, interpretability, or downstream usability of the Event Determination. EDCM shall distinguish: materially required; materially relevant but qualified; non-material; not applicable. Condition Presence ≠ Condition Materiality. Condition Sufficiency A condition is sufficiently satisfied where the available governed information supports the condition to the level needed for a defensible Determination Decision. This does not require absolute certainty. Condition Sufficiency ≠ Absolute Certainty. Condition Satisfaction A condition may be considered Satisfied where materially necessary governance supports it without unresolved issue sufficient to undermine the Determination Decision. The state shall remain traceable. Conditional Satisfaction A condition may be Conditionally Satisfied where a bounded limitation remains but does not necessarily prevent downstream decision-making. The condition shall explicitly preserve the limitation. Conditional Satisfaction ≠ Full Satisfaction. Partial Satisfaction A condition may be only partially satisfied. Partial satisfaction shall not be generalized into complete satisfaction. Partial Satisfaction ≠ Satisfied by default. Unsatisfied Condition A condition is Unsatisfied where materially necessary governance does not support it sufficiently. An Unsatisfied material condition may prevent a positive Determination Decision. Unsatisfied Condition ≠ Negative Tax Conclusion. It is an Event-governance state. Not Applicable Condition A condition may be Not Applicable where the governed Event does not require it for Determination. This state shall be distinguished from Missing or Unsatisfied. Not Applicable ≠ Missing. Condition Dependency Some conditions may depend on other conditions. For example: Value Association condition may depend on stable Event Identity; Participation condition may depend on Event Boundary; Relationship condition may depend on correctly formed Events. EDCM may preserve these dependencies. Condition Dependency ≠ Event Dependency. ERLDM remains authoritative for Event-to-Event dependency. Condition Sequence Some conditions may need to be evaluated in a logical order. For example: Formation Integrity ↓ Boundary Sufficiency ↓ Participation Sufficiency ↓ Value Association Sufficiency This sequence is methodological. It is not Event Sequence. Condition Sequence ≠ Event Sequence. Condition Coherence Satisfied conditions must also remain mutually coherent. An Event may have individually satisfied fields that together contradict one another. Examples include: valid Participant reference outside the governed Event Boundary; valid Value Association tied to another Event; valid Timing record inconsistent with Event Formation. Individually Satisfied Conditions ≠ Coherent Determination Conditions by default. Condition Interaction EDCM shall evaluate materially relevant interactions among conditions. One weak condition may become material because it affects another. For example: uncertain Boundary may undermine Participation; uncertain Event Identity may undermine Relationship structure; incomplete Formation may undermine Value Association. Condition evaluation shall therefore not be purely isolated. Formation Condition The Event must have sufficiently governed Formation where material. EDCM does not recreate Formation. TREFS remains authoritative. Formation Condition ≠ Formation Governance. Boundary Condition The Event Boundary shall be sufficient for Determination where material. EDCM assesses condition satisfaction, not the Boundary itself. Boundary Condition ≠ Boundary Determination. Timing Condition Event Timing may need to be sufficiently governed where materially relevant. EDCM does not establish legal tax timing. Timing Condition ≠ Legal Tax Point Condition. Location Condition Location may need to be sufficiently governed to support downstream evaluation. EDCM does not determine jurisdiction. Location Condition ≠ Tax Jurisdiction Condition. Participation Condition The materially relevant participant structure may need to be sufficiently governed. EDCM does not determine taxpayer status. Participation Condition ≠ Taxpayer Condition. Value Association Condition Material Value Associations may need to be sufficiently established. EDCM does not determine taxable value or Tax Base. Value Association Condition ≠ Tax Base Condition. Relationship Condition Material Event Relationships may need to be sufficiently governed. EDCM does not recreate relationship structure. Relationship Condition ≠ Relationship Governance. Identity Coherence Condition The Event reference used across upstream outputs should resolve to a coherent governed Event Identity. Broken identity continuity may prevent condition satisfaction. Record Similarity ≠ Event Identity Coherence. Traceability Condition The basis for materially important conditions should be reconstructable. A condition that appears satisfied but cannot be linked to its governance basis may require qualification. Apparent Satisfaction ≠ Traceable Satisfaction. Stability Condition Where the Event structure remains under material reconsideration, condition satisfaction may be qualified. Condition Satisfaction ≠ Structural Finality. Uncertainty Condition Bounded uncertainty may be tolerated where it does not materially undermine the condition. Material unresolved uncertainty may prevent satisfaction. Uncertainty ≠ Automatic Condition Failure. Conflict Condition Where materially conflicting upstream governance exists, EDCM shall preserve the conflict. Conflict ≠ Permission to Select the Convenient Condition State. Condition Exception A methodological exception may exist where a generally expected condition is legitimately inapplicable to the specific Event. Any exception shall be explicit, bounded, and justified. Exception ≠ Silent Waiver. Condition Waiver Boundary EDCM shall not permit material Event-governance conditions to be waived solely for: processing speed; system convenience; tax outcome; reporting convenience; missing data; automation pressure; commercial preference. Operational Convenience ≠ Condition Waiver Basis. Condition Qualification A condition may carry qualification where its satisfaction is bounded by: scope; confidence; time; system coverage; participant coverage; Value scope; or another materially relevant limitation. The qualification shall remain visible downstream. Condition Threshold EDCM may establish a methodological threshold for determining when a condition is sufficiently satisfied. Thresholds shall reflect Event-governance sufficiency rather than arbitrary scoring. Numeric Score ≠ Condition Satisfaction by default. Composite Condition State The Event may receive an overall Determination Condition State based on the set of applicable conditions. Possible composite states include: Conditions Satisfied; Conditions Conditionally Satisfied; Conditions Partially Satisfied; Conditions Unsatisfied; Conditions Ambiguous; Conditions Conflicted; Conditions Unresolved. The composite state shall not replace the visibility of individual material conditions. Condition Conflict Across Systems Different systems may indicate different condition states. For example: ERP shows Participant A; marketplace shows Participant B; payment system references Participant C. EDCM shall preserve materially relevant conflict rather than collapsing it prematurely. Cross-Organization Conditions Required conditions may rely on governance from several organizations. EDCM may evaluate sufficiency across organizational boundaries without assigning accountability or legal responsibility. Cross-Border Conditions Cross-border Events may require stronger Location, Participation, and Relationship condition governance. This does not transform EDCM into Tax Jurisdiction governance. Cross-Border Condition Complexity ≠ Tax Jurisdiction Determination. Blockchain Conditions On-chain information may satisfy some conditions strongly while leaving others unresolved. For example: transaction order may be clear; participant legal identity may not be; off-chain service Formation may remain uncertain. On-Chain Completeness ≠ Determination Condition Completeness. Smart-Contract Conditions Smart-contract execution may support Event Timing, execution, or relationship conditions. It does not automatically satisfy Formation, Participation, Value, or legal conditions. Smart-Contract Execution ≠ Determination Condition Satisfaction. AI-Agent Conditions Machine-generated Event structures remain subject to the same Determination Conditions. An AI agent's internal classification cannot substitute for governed condition evaluation. Agent Confidence ≠ Condition Satisfaction. Autonomous-System Conditions Autonomous execution may require materially sufficient governance concerning: machine participant association; execution relationship; Value Association; Event Boundary; and system-to-system traceability. The absence of a human actor does not invalidate Event Determination. Condition Automation EDCM may be implemented through automated rules, AI systems, or hybrid governance. Automation shall preserve: condition identity; applicability; state; basis; qualification; uncertainty; conflict; traceability. Automated Condition Check ≠ Governed Condition State by default. Condition Reassessment Conditions may require reassessment where upstream Event governance changes. Examples include: corrected Boundary; revised Participant; new Value Association; changed Event Relationship; Merge or Split; corrected Timing. Prior condition states shall remain traceable. Condition Reassessment ≠ Historical Erasure. Condition Invalidation A previously satisfied condition may become invalid where materially relevant governance changes. Prior Satisfaction ≠ Permanent Satisfaction. The Event may need renewed EDDM evaluation. Condition Supersession A new condition state may supersede an earlier state. Supersession shall preserve the earlier governance history. Superseded Condition State ≠ Deleted Condition State. Condition and Determination Decision EDCM does not issue the final Determination Decision. It establishes the condition state that EDDM consumes. Therefore: Conditions Satisfied ≠ Tax-Relevant Event Determined. EDDM remains authoritative for the final Determination Decision. Condition and Determination Uncertainty EDCM may identify uncertainty affecting specific conditions. EDUM governs Determination-level uncertainty after or around the decision layer. The two functions shall remain distinct. Condition Uncertainty ≠ Determination Uncertainty by default. Condition and Reconsideration EDCM may reassess conditions. EDREM governs broader Determination reconsideration once a prior Determination has been issued. Condition Reassessment ≠ Determination Reconsideration. Condition and Taxability EDCM does not evaluate tax-law requirements. A legal jurisdiction may impose its own separate legal conditions downstream. Event Determination Condition ≠ Taxability Condition. Condition and Tax Jurisdiction Location sufficiency may be a TREDS condition. Tax jurisdiction remains downstream. Location Condition Satisfaction ≠ Tax Jurisdiction Determination. Condition and Taxpayer Participation sufficiency may be a condition. Taxpayer identity remains downstream. Participation Condition Satisfaction ≠ Taxpayer Determination. Condition and Tax Base Value Association sufficiency may be a condition. Tax Base remains downstream. Value Condition Satisfaction ≠ Tax Base Determination. Governance States EDCM may represent: Condition Governance Not Initiated Applicable Conditions Identified Condition Evaluation Underway Condition Satisfied Condition Conditionally Satisfied Condition Partially Satisfied Condition Unsatisfied Condition Not Applicable Condition Ambiguous Condition Conflicted Condition Unresolved Condition Reassessment Required Conditions Satisfied Conditions Conditionally Satisfied Conditions Partially Satisfied Conditions Unsatisfied Conditions Conflicted Governed Determination Condition State Established Governance Requirements EDCM implementations shall ensure that: conditions are evaluated only after a valid readiness state; applicable conditions are distinguishable from non-applicable conditions; condition materiality is explicit; condition satisfaction remains distinct from final Determination Decision; conditions remain based on Event governance rather than tax-law interpretation; materially necessary Formation conditions are traceable to TREFS; Boundary conditions remain traceable to TREBS; Timing conditions remain distinct from legal tax point; Location conditions remain distinct from Tax Jurisdiction; Participation conditions remain distinct from taxpayer status; Value conditions remain distinct from Tax Base; Relationship conditions remain traceable to TRERLS; conditional satisfaction remains distinguishable from full satisfaction; partial satisfaction is not silently treated as complete; Not Applicable remains distinct from Missing; material conflicts remain visible; material uncertainty remains visible; condition exceptions are explicit and justified; operational convenience does not waive material conditions; condition interaction can be represented; cross-system contradictions can be represented; automation does not erase governance basis; reassessment preserves historical states; prior satisfaction is not treated as permanent where upstream governance changes; and the resulting condition state is suitable for EDDM. Governance Logic IF the Event does not possess a valid Governed Determination Readiness State, THEN EDCM shall not proceed to full condition evaluation. IF a potential condition is not materially relevant to the Event, THEN it may be classified Not Applicable rather than Unsatisfied. IF a materially required condition is sufficiently supported by governed upstream information, THEN it may be classified Satisfied. IF a materially required condition is sufficiently supported but retains a bounded limitation, THEN it may be classified Conditionally Satisfied. IF only part of a materially required condition is supported, THEN the condition shall remain Partially Satisfied rather than being generalized to Satisfied. IF materially necessary governance is insufficient, THEN the condition shall remain Unsatisfied or Unresolved according to the nature of the deficiency. IF materially conflicting governance affects a condition, THEN the condition shall remain Conflicted until sufficiently resolved or qualified. IF multiple individually satisfied conditions materially contradict one another, THEN the composite condition state shall not be treated as fully Satisfied. IF a condition failure belongs to an upstream governance layer, THEN EDCM shall preserve the failure and refer the substantive issue to the appropriate Parent Standard. IF a material condition is proposed for waiver solely because of tax outcome, processing pressure, automation, or system convenience, THEN the waiver shall be rejected. IF all materially applicable conditions are sufficiently governed, THEN EDCM shall establish a Governed Determination Condition State for EDDM. IF upstream governance changes materially after condition evaluation, THEN relevant conditions shall be reassessed. Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum EDCM implementation should support: Condition Evaluation Identifier A stable identifier for the condition-governance process. Governed Event Reference The Event whose Determination Conditions are being evaluated. Readiness State Reference The EDRDM output authorizing entry into condition governance. Condition Identifier A stable identifier for each Determination Condition. Condition Type Formation, Boundary, Timing, Location, Participation, Value Association, Relationship, Coherence, Stability, Traceability, or other governed condition type. Condition Description The precise governance requirement being evaluated. Condition Applicability State Applicable, Not Applicable, or Applicability Unresolved. Condition Materiality State Material, Qualified Material, Non-Material, or Unresolved. Condition Basis Reference The upstream governance output supporting evaluation. Condition Dependency Reference Any material dependency on another Determination Condition. Condition Satisfaction State Satisfied, Conditionally Satisfied, Partially Satisfied, Unsatisfied, Ambiguous, Conflicted, or Unresolved. Condition Qualification Any bounded limitation attached to satisfaction. Condition Evidence / Governance Reference Traceable basis supporting the condition state. Condition Uncertainty State Any material uncertainty affecting the condition. Condition Conflict State Any materially conflicting governance information. Condition Exception Reference Where a legitimate methodological exception applies. Coherence Interaction Reference Material interaction with other conditions. Prior Condition State Any earlier governed condition state. Condition Reassessment Reference Any later reassessment. Condition Supersession Reference Where a new state supersedes an earlier one. Composite Condition State The overall Event-level Determination Condition State. Condition Traceability Reference Information required to reconstruct the evaluation. Governance State The current EDCM governance state. Handoff State Whether the Event is ready to proceed to EDDM. Governance Outputs EDCM may produce: Applicable Condition Set; Condition Materiality State; Condition Satisfaction State; Conditional Satisfaction State; Partial Satisfaction State; Unsatisfied Condition State; Not Applicable Condition State; Condition Ambiguity State; Condition Conflict State; Condition Exception Record; Condition Dependency Record; Condition Coherence Record; Condition Interaction Record; Condition Qualification; Condition Reassessment Record; Condition Supersession Record; Composite Determination Condition State; Condition Traceability Record; and the principal output: Governed Determination Condition State. Critical Distinctions Determination Condition Satisfaction ≠ Determination Decision. Determination Condition ≠ Tax Rule. Possible Condition ≠ Required Condition by default. Universal Condition Template ≠ Universal Condition Applicability. Condition Presence ≠ Condition Materiality. Condition Sufficiency ≠ Absolute Certainty. Conditional Satisfaction ≠ Full Satisfaction. Partial Satisfaction ≠ Satisfied by default. Unsatisfied Condition ≠ Negative Tax Conclusion. Not Applicable ≠ Missing. Condition Dependency ≠ Event Dependency. Condition Sequence ≠ Event Sequence. Individually Satisfied Conditions ≠ Coherent Determination Conditions by default. Formation Condition ≠ Formation Governance. Boundary Condition ≠ Boundary Determination. Timing Condition ≠ Legal Tax Point Condition. Location Condition ≠ Tax Jurisdiction Condition. Participation Condition ≠ Taxpayer Condition. Value Association Condition ≠ Tax Base Condition. Relationship Condition ≠ Relationship Governance. Record Similarity ≠ Event Identity Coherence. Apparent Satisfaction ≠ Traceable Satisfaction. Condition Satisfaction ≠ Structural Finality. Uncertainty ≠ Automatic Condition Failure. Conflict ≠ Permission to Select the Convenient Condition State. Exception ≠ Silent Waiver. Operational Convenience ≠ Condition Waiver Basis. Numeric Score ≠ Condition Satisfaction by default. On-Chain Completeness ≠ Determination Condition Completeness. Smart-Contract Execution ≠ Determination Condition Satisfaction. Agent Confidence ≠ Condition Satisfaction. Automated Condition Check ≠ Governed Condition State by default. Condition Reassessment ≠ Historical Erasure. Prior Satisfaction ≠ Permanent Satisfaction. Superseded Condition State ≠ Deleted Condition State. Conditions Satisfied ≠ Tax-Relevant Event Determined. Condition Uncertainty ≠ Determination Uncertainty by default. Condition Reassessment ≠ Determination Reconsideration. Event Determination Condition ≠ Taxability Condition. Enterprise Application EDCM creates the formal conditions layer between readiness and decision. A typical operational path is: TRERLS — Governed Event Relationship Structure → EDRDM — Governed Determination Readiness State → EDCM — Governed Determination Condition State → EDDM — Event Determination Decision This allows enterprises to make visible exactly which Event-governance conditions support or prevent a formal Determination Decision, instead of relying on opaque yes/no system logic. Use Case 1 — Marketplace Event with Conditionally Satisfied Location Condition A marketplace Event is determined Ready by EDRDM. Formation, Boundary, Participation, Value Association, and Event Relationships are sufficiently governed. The Event Location is distributed across digital infrastructure and remains bounded but not fully precise. EDCM determines that Location is materially relevant but that the available governance is sufficient for controlled downstream analysis. The Location Condition is therefore classified Conditionally Satisfied, while the remaining material conditions are Satisfied. EDCM passes the qualified composite condition state to EDDM. It does not determine Tax Jurisdiction. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Settlement Event with Conflicting Participation Condition An autonomous settlement Event has stable Formation, Boundary, Timing, Value Association, and Relationship governance. However, two systems provide materially incompatible representations of which autonomous entity performed the settlement role. EDCM identifies Participation as a material condition and classifies it Conflicted. The composite Determination Condition State remains Conflicted and is passed to EDDM. The module preserves the conflict and routes the substantive Participation issue to TREPS rather than selecting the participant that produces the most convenient downstream result. Canonical Boundary EDCM owns the governance of Determination Condition identification, applicability, materiality, sufficiency, dependency, qualification, satisfaction, partial satisfaction, conditional satisfaction, unsatisfied states, legitimate exceptions, condition interaction, coherence, ambiguity, conflict, reassessment, supersession, and establishment of the Governed Determination Condition State. EDCM does not own upstream Event Formation, Boundary, Timing, Location, Participation, Value Association, or Event Relationship governance. It does not issue the final Tax-Relevant Event Determination Decision and does not determine legal taxability, Tax Jurisdiction, taxpayer status, Tax Base, Tax Rate, Tax Liability, legal tax point, exemption, deduction, filing obligation, or any other jurisdiction-specific tax consequence. Its governance begins when EDRDM establishes a suitable Determination Readiness State. Its governance ends when the Event possesses a sufficiently governed Determination Condition State for handoff to EDDM. Canonical Handoff EDRDM — Governed Determination Readiness State ↓ EDCM — Governed Determination Condition State ↓ EDDM — Event Determination Decision Governance Canonical Closing Statement EDCM turns readiness into explicit governance conditions so that a Determination Decision can be based on what is materially satisfied, qualified, unresolved, or conflicted rather than on assumption or system convenience. A condition can support a decision without becoming the decision itself. Determination Condition Satisfaction ≠ Determination Decision. Event Determination Condition ≠ Taxability Condition.

title: OOF™ The Event Determination Decision Module (EDDM) governs how the results of
text: OOF™ The Event Determination Decision Module (EDDM) governs how the results of The Event Determination Decision Module (EDDM) governs how the results of OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: TREDS — Tax-Relevant Event Determination Standard Module: EDDM — Event Determination Decision Module Operational Layer: Event Determination Decision Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Event Determination Decision Origin ID: TREGA-TREDS-EDDM-003 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 2 September 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language Canonical Definition The Event Determination Decision Module (EDDM) governs how the results of Determination Readiness and Determination Conditions governance are converted into a formal Tax-Relevant Event Determination Decision. EDDM determines the governed Event status that follows from the available readiness, condition, qualification, coherence, uncertainty, and conflict information at the point of decision. Its principal transition is: Governed Determination Condition State ↓ Determination Decision Governance ↓ Governed Event Determination Decision EDDM does not determine legal taxability. It does not determine tax jurisdiction, taxpayer status, taxable value, Tax Base, Tax Rate, legal tax point, Tax Liability, exemption, deduction, filing obligation, collection, enforcement, or any other jurisdiction-specific tax consequence. Its foundational distinction is: Event Determination Decision ≠ Tax Decision. Operational Role EDDM is the formal decision layer of TREDS. EDRDM determines whether the Event is ready for formal Determination. EDCM determines whether the applicable Determination Conditions are satisfied. EDDM then answers: What formal TREGA™ Determination state should this Event receive? The Decision may be: Positive; Conditional; Deferred; Rejected; Ambiguous; Conflicted; or otherwise qualified. EDDM transforms prior governance into an explicit and traceable Determination outcome. Internal Module Flow TREDS operates through: EDRDM — Event Determination Readiness ↓ EDCM — Event Determination Conditions ↓ EDDM — Event Determination Decision ↓ EDUM — Event Determination Uncertainty ↓ EDREM — Event Determination Reconsideration ↓ Determined Tax-Relevant Event EDDM is the third Core Module. Its output is passed to EDUM for Determination-level uncertainty governance where required. Operational Transition The canonical transition is: Governed Determination Condition State + Readiness State + Relevant Qualifications ↓ Decision Evaluation ↓ Governed Event Determination Decision Possible outputs include: Tax-Relevant Event Determined Conditionally Determined Determination Deferred Determination Rejected Determination Ambiguous Determination Conflicted Determination Escalation Required Determination Reconsideration Flagged The Decision shall always be explicit. Operational Space EDDM governs: decision initiation; decision basis; decision eligibility; decision state selection; positive determination; conditional determination; deferred determination; rejected determination; ambiguous determination; conflicted determination; decision qualification; decision rationale; decision consistency; decision provenance; decision traceability; decision authority reference; decision timing; decision finalization; decision handoff; and decision-level governance control. Operational Scope EDDM may govern Event Determination Decisions arising from: commerce; marketplaces; banking; payments; accounting; ERP; logistics; supply chains; digital platforms; digital assets; blockchain systems; smart contracts; AI agents; autonomous systems; industrial systems; energy systems; distributed infrastructure; cross-border operations; machine-to-machine activity; and future machine economies. The decision logic remains technology-neutral and jurisdiction-neutral. Decision Object The Decision Object is the governed Event represented through: the EDRDM Readiness State; the EDCM Condition State; relevant upstream governance references; material qualifications; uncertainty indicators; and conflict indicators. EDDM decides the TREGA™ status of this governed Event. It does not decide the legal tax status. Decision Initiation Decision governance begins when EDCM establishes a sufficiently governed Determination Condition State. EDDM shall not begin a formal Decision process where required condition governance remains absent. Decision Initiation ≠ Positive Determination. Decision Eligibility An Event is decision-eligible where the relevant Readiness and Condition governance provides enough basis for EDDM to issue a formal status. Decision eligibility does not require that the result will be positive. A Decision may still be: Deferred; Rejected; Conflicted; or Conditional. Decision Eligible ≠ Determination Positive. Decision Basis Every Determination Decision shall be linked to its governance basis. The Decision basis may include: Readiness State; Condition State; material qualifications; unresolved issues; conflict state; uncertainty state; upstream referrals; governance traceability. A Decision without a reconstructable basis shall not qualify as a governed Decision. Decision Output Without Decision Basis ≠ Governed Decision. Positive Determination A Positive Determination means that the Event is sufficiently governed to be formally recognized within TREGA™ as a Tax-Relevant Event. It means: The Event is eligible for downstream jurisdiction-specific taxation analysis. It does not mean: Tax is legally due. Therefore: Positive Event Determination ≠ Positive Tax Determination. Conditional Determination A Conditional Determination may be issued where the Event is sufficiently governed for controlled downstream use but one or more bounded qualifications remain. These qualifications shall be explicit. Conditional Determination ≠ Unqualified Determination. The downstream system shall be able to identify the conditions attached to the Decision. Deferred Determination A Deferred Determination means that the Event cannot yet receive a final Determination state because materially necessary governance remains unresolved. Deferral may result from: unresolved condition; material uncertainty; material conflict; unstable Event structure; unresolved upstream referral; or pending structural reconsideration. Deferred Determination ≠ Rejected Determination. Rejected Determination A Rejected Determination means that the governed Event structure does not support establishment of a Tax-Relevant Event under TREGA™ at that time. Rejection may occur where the apparent Event fails a foundational governance requirement. Examples may include: invalid Event Formation; non-establishable Event Boundary; duplicate technical artifact; purely technical operation incorrectly treated as an Event; or materially incoherent Event structure. Rejected Determination ≠ Legal Non-Taxability. Ambiguous Determination A Determination may remain Ambiguous where more than one materially plausible Event interpretation remains and the available governance does not support a single stable Decision. Ambiguity shall remain visible. Ambiguity ≠ Permission to Choose the Convenient Decision. Conflicted Determination A Determination may be Conflicted where materially authoritative governance inputs support incompatible outcomes. The Decision shall preserve the conflict rather than collapse it artificially. Decision Conflict ≠ Decision Discretion without Governance Basis. Decision Qualification A Decision may contain a qualification. Qualification may relate to: bounded uncertainty; incomplete geographic precision; limited participant certainty; partial Value Association; conditional Relationship structure; provisional source availability; or another materially relevant limitation. The qualification shall not disappear when the Event moves downstream. Decision Finality EDDM may establish operational finality sufficient for downstream processing. This does not mean absolute or legal finality. A later correction or reconsideration may change the Decision. Operational Decision Finality ≠ Legal Finality. Decision Consistency EDDM shall apply consistent decision logic across materially comparable Events. Consistency does not require identical outcomes where Event circumstances differ. Decision Consistency ≠ Mechanical Uniformity. The governing principle is methodological consistency. Decision Rationale A formal Decision shall be accompanied by sufficient rationale to reconstruct why the Decision state was selected. The rationale should identify: the Event under review; the Readiness State; the relevant Condition State; material satisfied conditions; material unsatisfied or qualified conditions; material uncertainty; material conflict; and the reason for the resulting Decision. Decision Provenance The Decision shall preserve provenance to the governance information from which it arose. This may include references to: upstream Parent Standards; EDRDM readiness evaluation; EDCM condition evaluation; relevant system or governance-source identifiers; previous Decision states. Decision Provenance ≠ Identity Provenance. OBIDENITY® remains authoritative for broader identity and origin governance. Decision Traceability The Determination Decision shall remain reconstructable. A reviewer should be able to identify: what was decided; why; on what governance basis; under which qualifications; with what uncertainty; and whether the Decision later changed. EDDM owns Decision traceability. ADIT® may govern broader evidential or audit requirements. Decision Authority The Decision process may be: automated; human; hybrid; delegated; rules-based; AI-assisted. EDDM requires the Decision authority or process reference to remain identifiable. It does not assign organizational accountability. AGA™ remains authoritative for accountability governance. Decision Timing The time at which the Determination Decision was made should be captured separately from the Event Timing itself. Decision Time ≠ Event Time. and: Decision Time ≠ Legal Tax Point. Decision Sequence Where repeated Decision processes occur, Decision sequence may be preserved. For example: Initial Decision ↓ Qualification ↓ Correction ↓ Reconsideration This does not alter the underlying Event Sequence governed by TRERLS. Decision Sequence ≠ Event Sequence. Positive Decision Threshold A Positive Determination should require that: the Event is sufficiently ready; materially required conditions are sufficiently satisfied; remaining qualifications are compatible with downstream use; no unresolved issue fundamentally undermines Event Identity or structure; and the Decision basis is reconstructable. The threshold is methodological sufficiency. It is not a jurisdiction-specific tax threshold. Conditional Decision Threshold A Conditional Determination may be appropriate where: Event identity is stable; material Event structure is sufficient; remaining limitations are bounded; downstream interpretation remains possible; the qualification is explicit. Conditional Determination shall not be used to hide a fundamentally unresolved Event. Deferred Decision Threshold Deferral is appropriate where material issues remain unresolved but the Event may become determinable later. Deferral should preserve: reason; required follow-up; affected governance layer; and current Decision state. Rejected Decision Threshold Rejection should require a sufficiently governed basis showing that the apparent Event does not qualify as a governed Tax-Relevant Event. Rejection shall not be based merely on: low tax value; no expected Tax Liability; jurisdictional exemption; or reporting convenience. Low Tax Relevance under Law ≠ TREGA™ Rejection Criterion. Decision and Readiness EDDM consumes the Readiness State. It does not reperform readiness governance. Decision ≠ Readiness Assessment. If Readiness becomes invalid, the matter should be referred back to EDRDM. Decision and Conditions EDDM consumes the Condition State. It does not reperform condition governance. Decision ≠ Condition Evaluation. If the Condition basis materially changes, EDCM remains authoritative. Decision and Uncertainty EDDM may identify uncertainty affecting the Decision. EDUM governs Determination-level uncertainty in greater detail. Therefore: Decision Uncertainty Recognition ≠ Full Uncertainty Governance. Decision and Reconsideration EDDM may flag that reconsideration is required. EDREM owns the reconsideration process. Decision Change ≠ Determination Reconsideration by default. Decision and Event Recognition TRERS decides whether an occurrence should enter Event governance. EDDM decides the formal Determination state after the Event has passed through the necessary governance layers. Recognition Decision ≠ Determination Decision. Decision and Event Formation EDDM cannot use a positive Decision to override defective Formation. Positive Decision ≠ Formation Authority. TREFS remains authoritative. Decision and Event Boundary EDDM cannot redefine Event Boundary. Decision ≠ Boundary Redetermination. TREBS remains authoritative. Decision and Event Timing EDDM cannot determine legal tax timing. Event Determination Decision ≠ Legal Tax Point Determination. TRETS remains authoritative for Event Timing. Decision and Event Location EDDM may rely on governed Location information. It does not determine the taxing jurisdiction. Positive Determination ≠ Tax Jurisdiction Determination. Decision and Participation EDDM may rely on governed Participant structure. It does not determine who is legally the taxpayer. Positive Determination ≠ Taxpayer Determination. Decision and Value EDDM may rely on governed Value Association. It does not determine taxable amount. Positive Determination ≠ Tax Base Determination. Decision and Relationships EDDM may rely on a Governed Event Relationship Structure. It does not merge, split, group, sequence, or otherwise recreate relationships. Decision ≠ Relationship Governance. Decision after Merge Where ERLMM has governed a Merge and the resulting Event has completed relevant upstream governance, EDDM may issue a Decision for the resulting Event. The resulting Event shall not inherit the prior Decision automatically. Merged Event ≠ Automatically Determined Event. Decision after Split Each resulting Event after a governed Split may require its own Determination Decision. Split Event ≠ Automatically Determined Event. Decision after Correction Where an upstream correction materially changes the Event structure, the existing Decision may become invalid or require reconsideration. EDDM may identify the Decision impact. EDREM governs broader reconsideration. Technical Record Decisions A system may label a transaction as: taxable; non-taxable; completed; posted; settled; final; reconciled. These labels do not constitute TREGA™ Determination Decisions. System Status ≠ Governed Event Determination Decision. Accounting Decisions Accounting classification may inform Event governance but does not replace EDDM. Accounting Classification ≠ Event Determination Decision. Invoice Decisions An invoice-status engine cannot determine by itself whether the underlying activity is a governed Tax-Relevant Event. Invoice Status ≠ Event Determination Decision. Payment Decisions Payment completion does not establish Event Determination. Payment Completion ≠ Event Determination Decision. Blockchain Finality Blockchain finality establishes technical ledger state. It does not establish Tax-Relevant Event Determination. Blockchain Finality ≠ Event Determination Decision. Smart-Contract Completion Smart-contract completion does not establish Determination. Smart-Contract Completion ≠ Event Determination Decision. AI Classification An AI system may propose a Decision state. That proposal remains subject to EDDM governance. AI Classification ≠ Governed Determination Decision. AI Confidence Model confidence may support the Decision process. It cannot substitute for the Decision itself. Model Confidence ≠ Decision. Autonomous Decisioning EDDM supports autonomous Determination processes where governance requirements are satisfied. Autonomy does not remove: Decision basis; Decision rationale; qualification; traceability; or authority reference. Automated Decision ≠ Ungoverned Decision. Cross-System Decision The same governed Event may appear in multiple systems. EDDM shall seek one governed Determination Decision for the governed Event rather than one Decision per technical record. Multiple Records ≠ Multiple Determination Decisions by default. Cross-Organization Decision The Event may involve several organizations. Different organizations may hold separate records or internal classifications. EDDM governs the TREGA™ Event Decision, not organizational tax positions. Multiple Organizational Views ≠ Multiple Event Realities. Cross-Border Decision A cross-border Event may receive a Positive Determination while Tax Jurisdiction remains unresolved downstream.
