text: OOF™ The Event Determination Uncertainty Module (EDUM) governs how uncertainty The Event Determination Uncertainty Module (EDUM) governs how uncertainty OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: TREDS — Tax-Relevant Event Determination Standard Module: EDUM — Event Determination Uncertainty Module Operational Layer: Event Determination Uncertainty Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Event Determination Uncertainty Origin ID: TREGA-TREDS-EDUM-004 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 2 September 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language Canonical Definition The Event Determination Uncertainty Module (EDUM) governs how uncertainty affecting a Governed Event Determination Decision is identified, classified, bounded, assessed for materiality, represented, qualified, escalated, monitored, and resolved or preserved before the Event proceeds to final Determination completion or reconsideration. Its principal transition is: Governed Event Determination Decision + Determination Uncertainty Indicators ↓ Determination Uncertainty Governance ↓ Governed Determination Uncertainty State EDUM does not recreate Event Readiness, Determination Conditions, or the Determination Decision itself. It governs what uncertainty means for that Decision. Its foundational distinction is: Determination Uncertainty ≠ Determination Failure. Operational Role A Determination Decision may be methodologically valid even where some uncertainty remains. The critical governance question is not whether uncertainty exists. It is: Does the uncertainty materially undermine the Event Determination, and if so, how must that uncertainty affect the governed Decision state? EDUM prevents two opposite failures: treating every uncertainty as fatal; ignoring material uncertainty merely to produce a definitive result. Its role is to preserve a usable but honest Determination state. Internal Module Flow TREDS operates through: EDRDM — Event Determination Readiness ↓ EDCM — Event Determination Conditions ↓ EDDM — Event Determination Decision ↓ EDUM — Event Determination Uncertainty ↓ EDREM — Event Determination Reconsideration ↓ Determined Tax-Relevant Event EDUM receives the Governed Event Determination Decision from EDDM. Its principal output is passed to EDREM where reconsideration becomes necessary. Operational Transition The canonical transition is: Governed Event Determination Decision + Relevant Uncertainty Indicators ↓ Uncertainty Identification ↓ Classification ↓ Materiality Assessment ↓ Qualification / Escalation ↓ Governed Determination Uncertainty State Possible outcomes include: No Material Uncertainty Bounded Uncertainty Qualified Uncertainty Material Uncertainty Critical Uncertainty Conflicted Uncertainty Unresolved Uncertainty Reconsideration Required Operational Space EDUM governs: uncertainty identification; uncertainty source; uncertainty type; uncertainty scope; uncertainty materiality; uncertainty severity; bounded uncertainty; residual uncertainty; structural uncertainty; factual uncertainty; relationship uncertainty; participation uncertainty; value uncertainty; location uncertainty; timing uncertainty; uncertainty interaction; uncertainty accumulation; uncertainty conflict; uncertainty qualification; uncertainty escalation; uncertainty tolerance; uncertainty threshold; uncertainty traceability; uncertainty reassessment; uncertainty persistence; and uncertainty handoff. Operational Scope EDUM may govern uncertainty affecting Events arising from: commerce; marketplaces; banking; payments; ERP environments; digital platforms; blockchain systems; smart contracts; AI agents; autonomous systems; industrial systems; energy infrastructure; distributed systems; machine-to-machine environments; cross-border activity; multi-party economic structures; and future machine economies. The uncertainty-governance logic remains technology-neutral and jurisdiction-neutral. Determination Uncertainty Determination Uncertainty is uncertainty that may affect the reliability, qualification, interpretation, or continued validity of the Event Determination Decision. It may arise from: incomplete upstream information; conflicting sources; bounded measurement limitations; unstable Event structure; ambiguous Participation; uncertain Value Association; uncertain Event Relationships; incomplete Location precision; timing ambiguity; or subsequent information. Uncertainty Indicator ≠ Material Determination Uncertainty. Uncertainty Identification EDUM shall identify uncertainty that remains materially relevant after EDDM has issued or proposed a Determination Decision. Uncertainty shall be distinguishable from: missing data; conflict; error; unresolved governance; condition failure; or mere lack of precision. These states may overlap, but they are not identical. Uncertainty Source The source of uncertainty should be identifiable where possible. Sources may include: Event Context; Event Formation; Event Boundary; Event Timing; Event Location; Event Participation; Value Association; Event Relationships; system interoperability; incomplete records; distributed execution; machine inference; model estimation; or contradictory operational sources. EDUM governs the uncertainty impact. It does not seize ownership of the underlying governed space. Uncertainty Type EDUM may classify uncertainty as: Factual Uncertainty Uncertainty over what happened. Structural Uncertainty Uncertainty over the constitution or structure of the Event. Identity Uncertainty Uncertainty over which governed Event is under consideration. Boundary Uncertainty Uncertainty over Event scope. Temporal Uncertainty Uncertainty over Event timing. Location Uncertainty Uncertainty over Event location. Participation Uncertainty Uncertainty over actor participation. Value Uncertainty Uncertainty over Event–Value Association. Relationship Uncertainty Uncertainty over relationships among Events. Decision Uncertainty Uncertainty affecting the validity or qualification of the Determination Decision itself. Uncertainty Scope Uncertainty shall be bounded wherever possible. EDUM should identify whether uncertainty affects: one attribute; one participant; one relationship; one Event segment; one Value Association; the entire Event; or the Determination Decision as a whole. Local Uncertainty ≠ Global Event Uncertainty by default. Uncertainty Materiality The central EDUM question is whether uncertainty is materially significant to Event Determination. Uncertainty is material where it could materially change: Event Identity; Event Formation; Event Boundary; Determination status; Event count; participant structure; Value Association; relationship structure; or downstream interpretability. Uncertainty Presence ≠ Material Uncertainty. Immaterial Uncertainty Immaterial uncertainty may remain without invalidating the Decision. For example, minor imprecision in a non-material technical attribute may not affect Event Determination. EDUM shall avoid transforming trivial imperfection into unnecessary governance failure. Imprecision ≠ Material Uncertainty by default. Bounded Uncertainty Bounded Uncertainty exists where uncertainty remains but its scope and potential impact are sufficiently understood. A bounded uncertainty may be compatible with a Positive or Conditional Determination. Bounded Uncertainty ≠ Ungoverned Uncertainty. Residual Uncertainty Residual Uncertainty is uncertainty that remains after reasonable governance has been completed. Its existence may be acceptable where: it is known; bounded; materially limited; traceable; and does not invalidate the Event structure. Residual Uncertainty ≠ Governance Failure. Material Uncertainty Material Uncertainty exists where the uncertainty could materially alter the meaning or validity of the Event Determination. This may require: Decision qualification; Decision deferral; escalation; upstream referral; or reconsideration. Critical Uncertainty Critical Uncertainty exists where Event Determination cannot be responsibly relied upon without further governance. Examples may include uncertainty over: whether the Event exists; whether one or several Events exist; which Event Boundary applies; whether the principal participant is correctly associated; or whether the Value Association belongs to another Event. Critical Uncertainty ≠ Permission to Maintain an Unqualified Decision. Uncertainty Severity EDUM may govern uncertainty severity through states such as: Low Moderate Material High Critical Severity shall reflect governance impact rather than arbitrary scoring. Higher Score ≠ Greater Materiality by default. Uncertainty Confidence Confidence may be recorded as supporting information. However: Confidence ≠ Certainty. and: Confidence Score ≠ Determination Validity. A high-confidence model output may still be methodologically unsupported. Uncertainty Qualification Where uncertainty does not invalidate the Decision but materially limits its interpretation, EDUM may attach an explicit qualification. Qualification may specify: affected governance dimension; uncertainty scope; known limitation; potential Decision impact; required downstream caution; reassessment condition. Qualification ≠ Concealment of Uncertainty. Uncertainty Interaction Multiple small uncertainties may interact and create material combined impact. For example: moderate Location uncertainty; moderate Participation uncertainty; moderate Value uncertainty may together undermine downstream interpretability. EDUM shall therefore consider cumulative impact where material. Several Immaterial Uncertainties ≠ Automatically Immaterial in Combination. Uncertainty Accumulation Uncertainty may accumulate across Event governance layers. EDUM shall identify whether cumulative uncertainty has reached a threshold where the Determination Decision requires qualification or reconsideration. Uncertainty and Conflict Uncertainty and conflict shall remain distinct. Uncertainty means the correct state is not fully known. Conflict means materially relevant sources support incompatible states. Uncertainty ≠ Conflict. A Determination may contain both. Conflicted Uncertainty Where uncertainty exists because authoritative inputs conflict, EDUM may establish a Conflicted Uncertainty state. It shall preserve: competing positions; source references; material effect; unresolved status. Conflict Resolution by Convenience ≠ Governed Uncertainty Resolution. Uncertainty Tolerance A governed system may define tolerance for bounded uncertainty. Tolerance shall be based on Event-governance materiality. It shall not be determined solely by: commercial pressure; reporting deadlines; tax advantage; processing cost; system limitations. Operational Pressure ≠ Uncertainty Tolerance Criterion. Uncertainty Threshold EDUM may establish thresholds determining when uncertainty requires: qualification; escalation; Decision deferral; upstream referral; or reconsideration. Thresholds shall remain methodological rather than jurisdiction-specific tax thresholds. Uncertainty Escalation Escalation may be required where: uncertainty is critical; uncertainty cannot be bounded; material conflict remains unresolved; automated evaluation cannot reliably classify impact; or downstream reliance would be unsafe. Escalation does not itself resolve the uncertainty. Upstream Referral Where uncertainty originates in an upstream governed space, EDUM may route the substantive issue to the authoritative Parent Standard. Typical routing includes: Context ↓ TRECS Recognition ↓ TRERS Formation ↓ TREFS Boundary ↓ TREBS Timing ↓ TRETS Location ↓ TRELS Participation ↓ TREPS Value Association ↓ TRVAS Event Relationships ↓ TRERLS EDUM governs the Determination impact of the uncertainty. The authoritative upstream layer governs the underlying issue. Uncertainty and Readiness EDRDM may already identify uncertainty affecting Readiness. EDUM does not repeat that function. At EDUM level, the question is whether uncertainty affects an existing Determination Decision. Readiness Uncertainty ≠ Determination Uncertainty. Uncertainty and Conditions EDCM may identify uncertainty attached to individual Determination Conditions. EDUM evaluates the consolidated impact on the Determination Decision. Condition Uncertainty ≠ Determination-Level Uncertainty by default. Uncertainty and Decision EDDM establishes the Decision. EDUM governs how uncertainty qualifies, constrains, destabilizes, or preserves that Decision. Uncertainty Governance ≠ Decision Issuance. Uncertainty and Reconsideration EDUM may conclude that uncertainty is significant enough to trigger reconsideration. EDREM owns the reconsideration process. Reconsideration Trigger ≠ Reconsideration Decision. Uncertainty and Correction An uncertainty is not automatically an error. Correction is appropriate where a governed state is known to be wrong. Uncertainty exists where the correct state remains insufficiently established. Uncertainty ≠ Error. Uncertainty Persistence Some uncertainty may persist legitimately over time. Persistent uncertainty shall remain governed, visible, and traceable. Persistent Uncertainty ≠ Permission to Ignore Uncertainty. Uncertainty Resolution Uncertainty may be resolved through: additional governance; better source information; corrected Event structure; participant clarification; Value reassociation; Event Relationship correction; reconciliation of conflicting sources; or later evidence. Resolution shall preserve prior uncertainty history where material. Uncertainty Reassessment EDUM shall support reassessment when: new information appears; upstream governance changes; the Event is corrected; Merge or Split occurs; a conflict is resolved; or downstream reliance reveals material inconsistency. Uncertainty Reassessment ≠ Historical Erasure. Uncertainty State Supersession A later uncertainty state may supersede an earlier one. Historical states shall remain traceable. Resolved Uncertainty ≠ Never-Existing Uncertainty. Machine-Generated Uncertainty Machine-generated Events may carry uncertainty resulting from: probabilistic classification; incomplete sensor data; inferred participation; distributed execution; asynchronous systems; model estimation. Machine processing does not reduce the requirement for explicit uncertainty governance. Machine Confidence ≠ Governed Certainty. AI-Generated Uncertainty AI systems may propose: Event classification; Event association; participant mapping; relationship interpretation; Value mapping. Where such conclusions are probabilistic, EDUM shall preserve relevant uncertainty rather than convert probability into certainty automatically. AI Probability ≠ Governed Determination Certainty. Blockchain Uncertainty Blockchain infrastructure may provide strong certainty about ledger state while leaving uncertainty about: off-chain Event Formation; participant role; Value meaning; legal or operational context; Event Relationship. Therefore: Ledger Certainty ≠ Event Determination Certainty. Distributed-System Uncertainty Distributed systems may contain: asynchronous timestamps; replicated records; delayed updates; differing system states; partial visibility. EDUM shall evaluate their effect on the governed Decision rather than assuming technical inconsistency equals Event failure. Cross-System Uncertainty The same Event may appear differently across systems. EDUM may classify whether those differences are: harmless representation differences; bounded uncertainty; material uncertainty; or conflict. Representation Difference ≠ Event Uncertainty by default. Cross-Organization Uncertainty Different organizations may possess incomplete or inconsistent views of the same Event. EDUM may govern the resulting Determination uncertainty without assigning accountability. Cross-Border Uncertainty Cross-border Events may contain uncertain operational location, participant roles, or distributed execution. These uncertainties may affect Event governance. They do not authorize EDUM to determine Tax Jurisdiction. Cross-Border Uncertainty ≠ Tax Jurisdiction Determination. Multi-Jurisdiction Neutrality EDUM shall preserve uncertainty in jurisdiction-neutral Event terms. A jurisdiction may later interpret the same uncertainty differently under law. Determination Uncertainty ≠ Jurisdictional Tax Uncertainty. Uncertainty and Taxability EDUM does not govern uncertainty over legal tax interpretation. It governs uncertainty over the Tax-Relevant Event Determination. Event Determination Uncertainty ≠ Taxability Uncertainty. Uncertainty and Taxpayer Participant uncertainty may affect Event Determination. EDUM does not determine taxpayer status. Participant Uncertainty ≠ Taxpayer Determination. Uncertainty and Tax Base Value uncertainty may affect Event Determination. EDUM does not calculate Tax Base. Value Uncertainty ≠ Tax Base Determination. Uncertainty and Legal Tax Point Timing uncertainty may affect Event representation. EDUM does not determine legal tax timing. Temporal Uncertainty ≠ Legal Tax Point Determination. Governance States EDUM may represent: Uncertainty Governance Not Initiated Uncertainty Indicator Identified Uncertainty Under Evaluation No Material Uncertainty Immaterial Uncertainty Bounded Uncertainty Residual Uncertainty Qualified Uncertainty Material Uncertainty Critical Uncertainty Ambiguous Uncertainty Conflicted Uncertainty Unresolved Uncertainty Uncertainty Escalation Required Upstream Referral Required Uncertainty Reassessment Required Reconsideration Required Uncertainty Resolved Governed Determination Uncertainty State Established Governance Requirements EDUM implementations shall ensure that: uncertainty remains distinct from Determination failure; uncertainty indicators remain distinct from material uncertainty; uncertainty source is identifiable where possible; uncertainty type is distinguishable; uncertainty scope can be bounded where possible; materiality is explicitly assessed; immaterial uncertainty does not automatically invalidate the Decision; bounded uncertainty may be preserved without forcing false certainty; residual uncertainty remains visible; critical uncertainty cannot support an unqualified Decision; uncertainty severity reflects governance impact; confidence scores do not replace uncertainty governance; qualifications remain visible downstream; interacting uncertainties are evaluated where materially relevant; cumulative uncertainty can be represented; uncertainty remains distinguishable from conflict; conflicted uncertainty preserves competing governance states; operational pressure does not determine uncertainty tolerance; escalation remains available; upstream issues are referred to the authoritative governance layer; uncertainty does not recreate Readiness, Conditions, or Decision governance; reconsideration triggers remain distinct from reconsideration itself; uncertainty remains distinct from known error; persistent uncertainty remains governed; resolution preserves historical traceability; AI or machine probability does not become certainty automatically; blockchain finality does not eliminate off-chain Event uncertainty; cross-border uncertainty does not determine Tax Jurisdiction; and the resulting uncertainty state is suitable for EDREM or final TREDS completion. Governance Logic IF an uncertainty indicator exists, THEN EDUM shall evaluate its scope and materiality before modifying the Determination state. IF uncertainty is immaterial to Event Identity, structure, or downstream interpretability, THEN the Determination Decision may remain unchanged. IF uncertainty is bounded and materially limited, THEN the Decision may remain valid with an explicit uncertainty qualification. IF several individually limited uncertainties combine into a material Determination risk, THEN EDUM shall govern their cumulative effect rather than evaluate them only in isolation. IF uncertainty materially undermines Event Identity, Formation, Boundary, Participation, Value Association, or Event Relationships, THEN the Decision shall be qualified, escalated, deferred, or referred for reconsideration as appropriate. IF uncertainty results from conflicting materially relevant sources, THEN EDUM shall preserve the conflict rather than select the most convenient representation. IF the underlying uncertainty belongs to an upstream TREGA™ governed space, THEN EDUM shall preserve Determination impact and refer the substantive issue to the authoritative layer. IF uncertainty cannot be sufficiently bounded and downstream reliance would be materially unsafe, THEN Reconsideration Required shall be established. IF new information resolves the uncertainty, THEN the new uncertainty state shall supersede the prior state without erasing historical uncertainty. IF the Determination Decision remains sufficiently reliable after uncertainty governance, THEN EDUM shall establish the Governed Determination Uncertainty State for downstream TREDS processing. Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum EDUM implementation should support: Uncertainty Governance Identifier A stable identifier for the uncertainty-governance process. Governed Event Reference The Event affected by uncertainty. Determination Decision Reference The EDDM Decision under uncertainty governance. Uncertainty Identifier A stable identifier for each uncertainty. Uncertainty Source The governance layer, system, record, process, or condition from which uncertainty arises. Uncertainty Type Factual, Structural, Identity, Boundary, Temporal, Location, Participation, Value, Relationship, Decision, or other governed type. Uncertainty Scope The part of the Event or Decision affected. Uncertainty Materiality State Immaterial, Bounded, Material, Critical, or Unresolved. Uncertainty Severity State The relative governance impact. Uncertainty Confidence Reference Any supporting confidence or probability measure where used. Affected Governance Dimension The Event governance area influenced by the uncertainty. Decision Impact State No Impact, Qualification Required, Escalation Required, Deferral Required, or Reconsideration Required. Uncertainty Qualification Any explicit limitation attached to the Determination Decision. Cumulative Uncertainty Reference Any interaction with other uncertainty states. Conflict Reference Any materially conflicting governance source. Upstream Referral Reference Any referral to another TREGA™ Parent Standard. Uncertainty Tolerance State Whether the uncertainty remains within an acceptable governance tolerance. Uncertainty Resolution State Unresolved, Partially Resolved, Resolved, or Persistent. Resolution Basis Reference The basis for any uncertainty resolution. Prior Uncertainty State Any earlier governed uncertainty state. Reassessment Reference Any later uncertainty reassessment. Reconsideration Trigger State Whether EDREM review is required. Uncertainty Traceability Reference Information required to reconstruct the uncertainty assessment. Governance State The current EDUM governance state. Handoff State Whether the Event may proceed to EDREM or final TREDS completion. Governance Outputs EDUM may produce: Uncertainty Identification Record; Uncertainty Source Record; Uncertainty Classification; Uncertainty Scope; Materiality State; Severity State; Bounded Uncertainty State; Residual Uncertainty State; Material Uncertainty State; Critical Uncertainty State; Conflicted Uncertainty State; Uncertainty Qualification; Cumulative Uncertainty State; Decision Impact State; Upstream Referral; Uncertainty Escalation; Uncertainty Reassessment Record; Uncertainty Resolution Record; Reconsideration Trigger; Uncertainty Traceability Record; and the principal output: Governed Determination Uncertainty State. Critical Distinctions Determination Uncertainty ≠ Determination Failure. Uncertainty Indicator ≠ Material Determination Uncertainty. Local Uncertainty ≠ Global Event Uncertainty by default. Uncertainty Presence ≠ Material Uncertainty. Imprecision ≠ Material Uncertainty by default. Bounded Uncertainty ≠ Ungoverned Uncertainty. Residual Uncertainty ≠ Governance Failure. Critical Uncertainty ≠ Permission to Maintain an Unqualified Decision. Confidence ≠ Certainty. Confidence Score ≠ Determination Validity. Qualification ≠ Concealment of Uncertainty. Several Immaterial Uncertainties ≠ Automatically Immaterial in Combination. Uncertainty ≠ Conflict. Conflict Resolution by Convenience ≠ Governed Uncertainty Resolution. Operational Pressure ≠ Uncertainty Tolerance Criterion. Readiness Uncertainty ≠ Determination Uncertainty. Condition Uncertainty ≠ Determination-Level Uncertainty by default. Uncertainty Governance ≠ Decision Issuance. Reconsideration Trigger ≠ Reconsideration Decision. Uncertainty ≠ Error. Persistent Uncertainty ≠ Permission to Ignore Uncertainty. Uncertainty Reassessment ≠ Historical Erasure. Resolved Uncertainty ≠ Never-Existing Uncertainty. Machine Confidence ≠ Governed Certainty. AI Probability ≠ Governed Determination Certainty. Ledger Certainty ≠ Event Determination Certainty. Representation Difference ≠ Event Uncertainty by default. Cross-Border Uncertainty ≠ Tax Jurisdiction Determination. Determination Uncertainty ≠ Jurisdictional Tax Uncertainty. Event Determination Uncertainty ≠ Taxability Uncertainty. Enterprise Application EDUM provides the uncertainty-control layer between formal Event Determination and later reconsideration or final downstream use. A canonical enterprise path is: EDCM — Governed Determination Condition State → EDDM — Governed Event Determination Decision → EDUM — Governed Determination Uncertainty State → EDREM — Event Determination Reconsideration Governance → Determined Tax-Relevant Event This enables systems to preserve usable Determination results while exposing the exact uncertainty that remains rather than forcing every Event into a misleading binary state. Use Case 1 — Distributed Digital Service with Bounded Location Uncertainty A distributed digital service has stable Formation, Boundary, Participation, Value Association, and Event Relationship governance. EDDM issues a Positive Determination. However, infrastructure execution occurred across several geographically distributed systems and the exact operational Location of one component cannot be established with full precision. EDUM determines that the Location uncertainty is bounded and does not alter Event Identity or prevent downstream jurisdiction-specific analysis. The Determination remains valid with an explicit Bounded Location Uncertainty qualification. EDUM does not determine which jurisdiction may tax the Event. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Settlement with Material Participation Uncertainty An autonomous settlement Event receives a provisional Determination Decision. Two materially authoritative systems disagree over which autonomous participant executed the decisive settlement function. The uncertainty could materially change the governed Participation structure and downstream interpretation. EDUM classifies the uncertainty as Material and Conflicted, preserves both participant representations, refers the substantive Participation issue to TREPS, and establishes Reconsideration Required. The module does not select the participant that produces the preferred tax result. Canonical Boundary EDUM owns the governance of Determination-level uncertainty identification, source, classification, scope, materiality, severity, bounded uncertainty, residual uncertainty, cumulative uncertainty, conflict interaction, qualification, tolerance, escalation, persistence, reassessment, resolution, traceability, and Determination-level reconsideration triggers. EDUM does not perform Event Readiness governance, Determination Condition governance, Determination Decision issuance, or Determination Reconsideration itself. It does not recreate Event Context, Recognition, Formation, Boundary, Timing, Location, Participation, Value Association, or Event Relationships. It does not determine legal taxability, Tax Jurisdiction, taxpayer status, legal tax point, Tax Period, Tax Base, Tax Rate, Tax Liability, exemption, deduction, filing obligation, or any other jurisdiction-specific tax consequence. Its governance begins when a Governed Event Determination Decision contains or encounters materially relevant uncertainty. Its governance ends when uncertainty has been sufficiently governed for continued reliance, qualification, escalation, or handoff to EDREM. Canonical Handoff EDDM — Governed Event Determination Decision ↓ EDUM — Governed Determination Uncertainty State ↓ EDREM — Event Determination Reconsideration Governance Canonical Closing Statement EDUM ensures that uncertainty is governed according to its material impact rather than hidden, exaggerated, or converted into false certainty. A Determination may remain valid while uncertainty exists, but only when that uncertainty is understood, bounded, visible, and compatible with continued reliance. Determination Uncertainty ≠ Determination Failure. Uncertainty ≠ Error.

title: OOF™ Event Formation Assembly Module (EFAM)
text: OOF™ Event Formation Assembly Module (EFAM) Event Formation Assembly Module (EFAM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: Tax-Relevant Event Formation Standard (TREFS) Module: EFAM — Event Formation Assembly Module Operational Layer: Event Formation Assembly Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Event Formation Assembly Origin ID: TREGA-TREFS-EFAM-002 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 30 August 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Event Formation Assembly Module (EFAM) governs how qualified Event Formation Components are structurally organized, related, grouped, ordered, and assembled into a coherent Event Formation Candidate. EFAM determines whether qualified components can legitimately operate together as one structurally meaningful formation, whether alternative assembly structures must remain visible, and whether the available component set supports coherent progression through TREFS. Its task is specific: to assemble qualified Event Formation Components into a governed event structure without determining final Event Boundary, Formation Dependencies, Event Formation Root, Formation Integrity, or legal tax consequences. Operational Role EFCM establishes: which elements qualify as Event Formation Components. EFAM then determines: how those qualified components fit together structurally. This distinction is necessary because a valid component set does not automatically produce a valid event structure. Several legitimate components may: belong to one coherent formation; belong to different formation candidates; represent parallel parts of one activity; represent sequential stages; represent alternative structural interpretations; require further differentiation before assembly. Therefore: Qualified Components ≠ Coherent Event Structure by Default. EFAM creates the governed structural arrangement required before Formation Dependencies and the Event Formation Root can be established. Internal Flow Governed Event Formation Component Set ↓ Assembly Relationship Identification ↓ Structural Grouping ↓ Assembly Pattern Determination ↓ Assembly Coherence Assessment ↓ Alternative / Conflicting Assembly Handling ↓ Governed Event Formation Assembly The principal output is: Governed Event Formation Assembly This output proceeds to: EFDM — Event Formation Dependency Module Operational Space EFAM governs the space between: a governed set of qualified Event Formation Components and a coherent structural assembly capable of supporting further Event Formation governance. Its operational space includes: component relationship identification; structural grouping; ordering where materially relevant; parallel assembly; sequential assembly; composite assembly; distributed assembly; autonomous assembly; machine-generated assembly; assembly coherence; assembly ambiguity; assembly conflict; alternative formation structures; over-aggregation risk; over-fragmentation risk; assembly traceability. EFAM governs how qualified components are structurally brought together. It does not determine whether every surrounding dependency belongs to the event. Operational Scope EFAM may assemble formation components originating from: commercial transactions; financial operations; payments; transfers; production; fulfilment; logistics; service delivery; platform activity; digital services; enterprise systems; banking infrastructure; software systems; APIs; autonomous agents; AI systems; robots; machine-to-machine exchanges; automated marketplaces; distributed systems; hybrid physical-digital activity. The assembly may involve: human actions; organizational actions; digital actions; machine actions; autonomous actions; distributed actions. EFAM remains actor-neutral and technology-neutral. Assembly Relationship Qualified components require a legitimate structural basis for being assembled together. Possible assembly relationships may include: sequential; parallel; conditional; composite; coordinated; distributed; hierarchical; mutually supporting. These relationships describe structural formation. They do not yet establish the broader relationship between separate governed events. Therefore: Assembly Relationship ≠ Event Relationship Governance. Relationships among governed events are later governed by TRERLS — Tax-Relevant Event Relationship Standard. Structural Grouping EFAM may group components where their combined structure materially represents one formation candidate. Grouping should be based on governed structural relevance. Components should not be grouped solely because they: share an identifier; appear in the same ERP workflow; involve the same participant; occur close together in time; are processed by the same platform; share a payment reference; belong to the same database record. Therefore: Technical Grouping ≠ Event Assembly. Shared Identifier ≠ One Assembly by Default A shared identifier can support assembly analysis. It cannot determine assembly by itself. One order identifier may include: several deliveries; several settlements; several service executions; several reversals; several materially distinct operational actions. Conversely, one event formation may span several identifiers across different systems. Therefore: Shared Identifier ≠ Common Event Assembly by Default. Assembly Coherence A governed assembly should represent a structurally understandable event candidate. Assembly coherence may consider whether: components materially relate to the same formation; their arrangement is structurally consistent; no material contradiction prevents assembly; the assembly does not depend only on technical proximity; the structure does not artificially collapse distinct activity; the structure does not unnecessarily fragment one coherent activity. EFAM must protect against both over-aggregation and over-fragmentation. Over-Aggregation Risk Over-aggregation occurs when distinct activity is incorrectly combined into one Event Formation Assembly. For example: a marketplace may place: Order + Refund + Later Replacement Order under one customer reference. That does not establish that all three belong to one formation. Therefore: Common Process ≠ One Assembly by Default. Over-Fragmentation Risk Over-fragmentation occurs when one coherent event structure is divided merely because several technical systems or operational records are involved. For example: Authorization ↓ Activation ↓ Delivery ↓ Settlement may be represented across four systems. The existence of four system records does not itself justify four formation assemblies. Therefore: Multiple Systems ≠ Multiple Assemblies by Default. Sequential Assembly Some Event Formation Components may form a meaningful sequence. For example: Commitment ↓ Execution ↓ Fulfilment The sequence may support structural understanding. However: Assembly Sequence ≠ Event Timing Determination. EFAM may represent structural order without determining the legally or operationally definitive Event Time. Event Timing belongs to TRETS. Parallel Assembly Some components may occur in parallel while contributing to the same event formation. For example: an autonomous platform may simultaneously allocate: computing capacity; energy; storage; network resources. Parallel execution does not automatically imply separate events. EFAM determines whether these components can legitimately participate in one formation candidate. Composite Assembly A composite assembly may contain several materially different components that collectively form one coherent structure. For example: Service Activation + Resource Allocation + Delivery Confirmation may participate in one formation candidate. But: Composite Assembly ≠ Final Event Boundary. TREBS later determines the final extent of the event. Distributed Assembly An event structure may need to be assembled from components held across several systems. For example: Marketplace Component → Payment Component → Service Provider Component → Enterprise Component EFAM permits distributed assembly where sufficient governed linkage exists. Therefore: Distributed Components ≠ Separate Assemblies by Default. Machine and Autonomous Assembly Autonomous systems may generate complex chains of qualified components. EFAM must assemble those components according to structural reality rather than machine-process topology. For example, one autonomous objective may produce: Negotiation ↓ Reservation ↓ Allocation ↓ Consumption ↓ Settlement Some elements may form one structure. Others may later become separate formations. Therefore: One Autonomous Objective ≠ One Assembly by Default. And: Many Machine Actions ≠ Many Assemblies by Default. Assembly Ambiguity The same qualified component set may support more than one plausible assembly. For example: three related service actions may represent: one composite formation; two connected formations; three independent formations. Where the available information does not justify one structure, EFAM must preserve assembly ambiguity. Possible states may include: Assembly Candidate Assembly Established Assembly Ambiguous Assembly Conflict Assembly Unresolved Alternative Assembly Structures EFAM may preserve several alternative assembly candidates where each has material support. The system should not select one simply because it is operationally convenient. Alternative assemblies may later be clarified through: additional dependency analysis; root analysis; integrity assessment; new evidence; later boundary governance. Therefore: Preferred System Structure ≠ Governed Assembly by Default. Assembly Conflict An Assembly Conflict exists where qualified components support materially incompatible formation structures. For example: one system indicates one composite event; another indicates two materially separate operational outcomes. EFAM should preserve the conflict rather than silently resolving it through system precedence. Assembly Traceability A Governed Event Formation Assembly should remain traceable to: the component set received from EFCM; the structural relationship basis; grouping decisions; exclusions from a particular assembly; alternative assembly structures; unresolved ambiguity; material assembly revisions. This permits later modules to understand how the formation structure was constructed. Governance Requirements EFAM requires that: only governed Event Formation Components enter assembly; structural relationships are identified before grouping; assembly is not determined by technical records alone; shared identifiers do not automatically create one assembly; multiple systems do not automatically create multiple assemblies; over-aggregation risk is controlled; over-fragmentation risk is controlled; distributed components may be assembled where justified; autonomous and machine-generated structures remain actor-neutral; assembly ambiguity remains visible; conflicting structures are preserved where unresolved; assembly decisions remain traceable; EFAM does not determine final Event Boundary; EFAM does not determine Formation Dependencies; EFAM does not determine Event Formation Root; EFAM does not determine legal taxability. Governance Logic EFAM applies a focused structural logic: How do the qualified Event Formation Components materially relate to one another? Which components can legitimately be grouped within the same formation structure? Does the proposed assembly avoid both artificial aggregation and artificial fragmentation? Are alternative or conflicting assembly structures materially plausible? What Governed Event Formation Assembly can legitimately proceed into dependency governance? The transformation is: Governed Component Set → Structural Relationships → Grouping → Assembly → Coherence Assessment → Governed Event Formation Assembly Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum EFAM implementation must be capable of: 1. receiving the Governed Event Formation Component Set from EFCM; 2. identifying material structural relationships among qualified components; 3. grouping components on a governed basis; 4. representing sequential, parallel, composite, or distributed assembly where relevant; 5. preventing technical identifiers from automatically defining assembly; 6. detecting over-aggregation risk; 7. detecting over-fragmentation risk; 8. preserving alternative assembly candidates where materially justified; 9. representing Assembly Ambiguity or Assembly Conflict; 10. preserving assembly traceability; 11. producing a Governed Event Formation Assembly; 12. transferring that assembly to EFDM for Formation Dependency governance; 13. preventing assembly from determining Event Boundary or jurisdiction-specific tax consequences. EFAM does not prescribe a specific graph model, workflow engine, ERP structure, event-stream format, database schema, AI model, tax engine, or transaction architecture. Governance Outputs EFAM may produce: Governed Event Formation Assembly — the principal Module output. Assembly Relationship Structure — governed representation of how components relate structurally. Component Grouping Result — the governed grouping used in formation. Composite Assembly Candidate — a multi-component formation structure. Alternative Assembly Candidate — a materially plausible alternative structure. Assembly Ambiguity Indicator — unresolved uncertainty concerning assembly. Assembly Conflict Record — materially incompatible assembly structures. Over-Aggregation Indicator — risk that distinct activity has been combined. Over-Fragmentation Indicator — risk that one coherent activity has been unnecessarily divided. Assembly Traceability Record — the basis through which the assembly was established. Critical Distinctions Qualified Components ≠ Coherent Event Structure by Default. Component qualification does not determine assembly. Technical Grouping ≠ Event Assembly. System structure does not establish governed event structure. Shared Identifier ≠ Common Event Assembly by Default. Technical identifiers are supporting signals, not structural proof. Multiple Systems ≠ Multiple Assemblies by Default. Distributed representation does not establish event multiplicity. Common Process ≠ One Assembly by Default. One operational workflow may contain several event formations. Assembly Relationship ≠ Event Relationship Governance. TRERLS later governs relationships among formed events. Assembly Sequence ≠ Event Timing Determination. TRETS owns Event Timing. Composite Assembly ≠ Final Event Boundary. TREBS owns final event extent. One Autonomous Objective ≠ One Assembly by Default. Autonomous purpose does not establish event granularity. Assembly Conflict ≠ Assembly Failure. Conflicting structures may remain governed and unresolved. Preferred System Structure ≠ Governed Assembly by Default. Operational convenience does not establish methodological legitimacy. Event Assembly ≠ Taxability Determination. EFAM does not determine tax law. Enterprise Application EFAM addresses a common problem in complex systems: different systems group the same operational reality differently. A marketplace may group activity by order. A bank may group by settlement. An ERP may group by invoice. A logistics system may group by shipment. An autonomous platform may group by machine objective. Each grouping may be valid internally. None automatically defines the governed Event Formation Assembly. EFAM creates a neutral structural layer capable of assembling qualified components according to event formation logic rather than the data model of any single system. Use CasesUse Case 1 — One Marketplace Order Contains Three Deliveries, Two Settlements, and a Partial Refund A global marketplace uses one order identifier for a customer purchase. The order results in: three separate deliveries; two payment settlements; one partial refund; multiple ERP records; several provider fulfilment actions. EFCM has already qualified the relevant formation components. If EFAM simply groups everything under the order identifier, the architecture may create one oversized formation that hides materially distinct activity. If every delivery and settlement is separated automatically, the architecture may create unnecessary fragmentation. EFAM evaluates the structural relationships among the qualified components and creates one or more legitimate Assembly Candidates while preserving ambiguity where required. The key principle is: the commercial identifier must not decide the event structure. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Cloud Marketplace Executes One Objective Across Hundreds of Parallel Resource Operations An AI agent purchases computing capacity for a complex workload. The workload is distributed across multiple providers and creates hundreds of qualified operational components involving: compute allocation; storage allocation; network reservation; execution; release; settlement. The underlying autonomous objective is one workload, but the operational components may support several event structures. EFAM determines whether particular components form coherent composite assemblies, whether separate provider operations require distinct assembly candidates, and whether any structure remains ambiguous. It prevents both extremes: one autonomous objective becoming one artificial mega-event and every machine-level resource allocation becoming a separate event formation. Canonical Boundary EFAM governs the structural relationship, grouping, arrangement, ambiguity, conflict, and coherent assembly of qualified Event Formation Components into a Governed Event Formation Assembly. It does not identify the original components, determine Formation Dependencies, establish the Event Formation Root, assess complete Formation Integrity, determine the final Event Boundary, govern relationships among completed events, or determine any jurisdiction-specific tax consequence. The handoff is: EFCM — Governed Event Formation Component Set → EFAM — Governed Event Formation Assembly → EFDM — Event Formation Dependency Module Canonical Closing Statement Event Formation Assembly Module establishes the structural assembly layer of Tax-Relevant Event Formation by determining how qualified formation components can legitimately operate together as a coherent Event Formation Assembly. By separating governed structural relationships from technical grouping, shared identifiers, system workflows, platform representations, machine topology, and operational convenience, EFAM prevents both artificial aggregation and artificial fragmentation of recognized economic activity. The Module preserves alternative and conflicting formation structures where necessary and produces a traceable assembly ready for Formation Dependency governance without prematurely determining Event Boundary, Event Timing, relationships among completed events, or jurisdiction-specific tax consequences.

title: OOF™ Event Formation Component Module (EFCM)
text: OOF™ Event Formation Component Module (EFCM) Event Formation Component Module (EFCM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: Tax-Relevant Event Formation Standard (TREFS) Module: EFCM — Event Formation Component Module Operational Layer: Event Formation Component Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Event Formation Components Origin ID: TREGA-TREFS-EFCM-001 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 30 August 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Event Formation Component Module (EFCM) governs how materially relevant elements of a Governed Recognized Occurrence are identified, differentiated, qualified, and prepared as legitimate components for subsequent Event Formation. EFCM determines which observable or governed elements may participate in the formation of the event structure and which elements should remain outside the formation-component set because they represent technical noise, duplicate representation, background activity, contextual information, or non-forming dependencies. Its task is specific: to establish the governed set of materially relevant Event Formation Components without assembling those components into the final event structure or determining the Event Boundary. Operational Role TREFS begins after TRERS has established that an occurrence legitimately warrants Event Formation. But a recognized occurrence may still contain many different elements: operational actions; transaction stages; technical records; system messages; machine operations; value-affecting actions; supporting activities; duplicated representations; contextual information; dependencies. EFCM separates the elements that may legitimately participate in Event Formation from those that should not automatically become formation components. It therefore creates the first structural input to TREFS. The distinction is fundamental: Recognized Information ≠ Formation Component by Default. Internal Flow Governed Recognized Occurrence ↓ Candidate Formation Element Identification ↓ Element Differentiation ↓ Formation Relevance Assessment ↓ Component Qualification / Exclusion ↓ Duplicate and Technical-Noise Screening ↓ Governed Event Formation Component Set The principal output is: Governed Event Formation Component Set This output proceeds to: EFAM — Event Formation Assembly Module Operational Space EFCM governs the space between: a recognized occurrence containing potentially relevant structural elements and a governed set of qualified Event Formation Components ready for assembly. Its operational space includes: candidate component identification; component differentiation; structural relevance; formation materiality; component qualification; component exclusion; duplicate component risk; technical-record filtering; machine-operation filtering; distributed component identification; autonomous activity component identification; component uncertainty; component traceability. EFCM governs what may become part of Event Formation. It does not govern how those components are assembled. Operational Scope EFCM may identify formation components originating from: commercial transactions; financial operations; payments; transfers; production; fulfilment; delivery; service execution; platform activity; digital services; software systems; APIs; banking infrastructure; enterprise systems; digital assets; AI agents; autonomous systems; robots; machine-to-machine activity; automated marketplaces; distributed systems; hybrid physical-digital processes. A formation component may represent a human, organizational, digital, machine-generated, or autonomous operational element. EFCM remains actor-neutral and technology-neutral. Candidate Formation Elements A recognized occurrence may contain more observable information than Event Formation requires. Candidate elements may include: initiating actions; operational state changes; transfer actions; fulfilment actions; service executions; resource consumption; resource provision; machine instructions with material operational significance; settlement actions; digital activations; delivery actions; materially relevant autonomous actions. Candidate status means only that the element requires formation assessment. Therefore: Candidate Element ≠ Qualified Formation Component. Formation Relevance An element should become a formation component only where it materially contributes to the structure of the event being formed. Formation relevance may arise where the element helps establish: what operational action occurred; what materially changed; what was executed; what was transferred; what was delivered; what service was performed; what operational stage is structurally necessary; what activity materially contributes to event formation. An element should not become a formation component merely because it exists in the technical record. Technical Record ≠ Formation Component Modern systems may produce many records for the same underlying activity. Examples include: synchronization records; API retries; database replication; monitoring messages; internal status updates; duplicate ledger representations; audit logs; telemetry. These records may be useful evidence or context. They do not automatically become Event Formation Components. Therefore: Technical Record ≠ Formation Component by Default. This distinction prevents system architecture from defining event architecture. Component ≠ Independent Event A qualified formation component may be materially important without independently constituting a separate event. For example: Authorization Service Activation Delivery Settlement may each contribute to a broader event formation. Whether any of these should later become separate events is not determined by EFCM. Therefore: Formation Component ≠ Independent Event by Default. Component Materiality EFCM should apply a materiality principle. A component is materially relevant where removing it would materially weaken, distort, or misrepresent the structural understanding of the event formation. Materiality should not be confused with legal tax materiality. Therefore: Formation Materiality ≠ Tax Materiality. EFCM asks whether the element matters to event structure. It does not determine whether the element affects tax liability. Duplicate Component Risk One operational action may appear several times across systems. For example: Payment Gateway Record → Bank Record → ERP Record → Reporting Database These may represent one underlying operational element. EFCM must avoid treating each representation as a separate formation component merely because each exists independently in a system. Therefore: Multiple Records ≠ Multiple Formation Components. At the same time: Shared Identifier ≠ Same Component by Default. Distinct actions may legitimately share identifiers. Distributed Formation Components A legitimate component may be visible only through distributed information. For example: one system may record authorization; another execution; another confirmation. EFCM may use governed distributed information to establish a component where no single system contains a complete representation. Therefore: Distributed Evidence ≠ Multiple Components by Default. Machine-Generated Components Machine environments create a particular risk of structural over-fragmentation. An automated process may generate thousands of instructions while only a few materially contribute to Event Formation. EFCM must distinguish: technical execution from structurally relevant operational action. Therefore: Machine Instruction ≠ Formation Component by Default. Only machine activity materially contributing to the event structure should enter the component set. Autonomous Components Autonomous agents may create legitimate Event Formation Components without direct human initiation. For example, an AI agent may: commit to a service; initiate a transfer; allocate a resource; activate a contractually governed service; trigger settlement; release an asset. EFCM may qualify those actions where structurally relevant. It does not determine legal personhood, responsibility, taxpayer status, authority, or liability of the autonomous actor. Component Uncertainty Where it is unclear whether an element materially belongs in Event Formation, EFCM should preserve the uncertainty. Possible states may include: Component Candidate Component Qualified Component Excluded Component Unresolved A component should not be included solely because the system requires a binary decision. Component Traceability A qualified component should remain traceable to the basis on which it entered Event Formation. Where materially required, traceability may preserve: source reference; recognized occurrence reference; component type; qualification basis; materiality basis; duplicate-resolution basis; uncertainty state; exclusion reason where relevant. This allows EFAM and later TREGA™ stages to understand why the element entered the formation structure. Governance Requirements EFCM requires that: components originate from a Governed Recognized Occurrence; technical records do not automatically become components; candidate elements are differentiated before qualification; structural relevance is established; formation materiality is considered; duplicate representations are controlled; distributed information may support component identification; machine activity is filtered for structural relevance; autonomous activity may qualify without human initiation; component uncertainty remains visible; component qualification remains traceable; component status does not determine independent event status; component inclusion does not determine the final Event Boundary; component qualification does not determine taxability. Governance Logic EFCM applies a simple structural logic: What materially relevant elements are present within the Governed Recognized Occurrence? Which of those elements contribute to Event Formation rather than merely represent technical, contextual, duplicate, or background information? Which elements can be qualified as legitimate Event Formation Components? Which elements must be excluded or remain unresolved? The transformation is: Recognized Occurrence → Candidate Elements → Formation Relevance → Qualification / Exclusion → Governed Event Formation Component Set Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum EFCM implementation must be capable of: 1. receiving the Governed Recognized Occurrence from TRERS; 2. identifying candidate formation elements; 3. distinguishing operational elements from technical representations; 4. assessing structural formation relevance; 5. applying formation materiality; 6. identifying and controlling duplicate component representations; 7. qualifying legitimate Event Formation Components; 8. excluding non-forming technical or background elements; 9. representing unresolved component status where necessary; 10. preserving source and qualification traceability; 11. producing a Governed Event Formation Component Set; 12. transferring that set to EFAM for Event Formation Assembly; 13. preventing component qualification from becoming Event Boundary or tax determination. EFCM does not prescribe a specific ERP schema, transaction model, data format, AI model, rules engine, database, event-stream implementation, or tax platform. Governance Outputs EFCM may produce: Governed Event Formation Component Set — the principal output of the Module. Qualified Formation Component — an element accepted for subsequent assembly. Excluded Formation Element — an element determined not to participate in Event Formation. Unresolved Formation Component Candidate — an element whose formation relevance remains unresolved. Component Qualification Record — the basis for inclusion or exclusion. Duplicate Component Indicator — indication that several records may represent one underlying component. Component Traceability Reference — linkage between the component and its governed basis. Critical Distinctions Recognized Information ≠ Formation Component by Default. Recognition does not automatically establish event structure. Candidate Element ≠ Qualified Formation Component. Identification precedes qualification. Technical Record ≠ Formation Component by Default. System observability does not define structural relevance. Formation Component ≠ Independent Event by Default. Event multiplicity is not determined by component count. Formation Materiality ≠ Tax Materiality. Structural relevance is not tax-law significance. Multiple Records ≠ Multiple Formation Components. Duplicate representation must not create artificial structure. Shared Identifier ≠ Same Component by Default. Technical linking is not proof of structural identity. Machine Instruction ≠ Formation Component by Default. Technical granularity must not become event granularity. Component Qualification ≠ Event Assembly. EFAM owns assembly. Component Inclusion ≠ Event Boundary. TREBS later determines final event extent. Component Qualification ≠ Taxability Determination. EFCM does not apply tax law. Enterprise Application EFCM addresses a common structural problem in enterprise and public-sector systems: the data available for an event is usually much larger than the event structure itself. A modern platform may expose: Order Record ↓ API Records ↓ Payment Records ↓ ERP Records ↓ Fulfilment Records ↓ Analytics Records ↓ Tax Interface Records Without EFCM, every technically available record may be carried forward as if it contributes equally to formation. This produces oversized, duplicated, and unstable event structures. EFCM creates the first structural filter inside TREFS. It identifies the operational elements that genuinely matter to Event Formation and separates them from technical representation. Use CasesUse Case 1 — One Global Transaction Produces Twenty Records Across Six Systems A multinational digital platform processes one service transaction. The activity produces: an order record; three API messages; a payment authorization; a payment confirmation; two ERP postings; a service activation; a usage record; an invoice; reporting copies; replicated warehouse records; tax-interface records. TRERS has already recognized the underlying occurrence. Without EFCM, all records could be forwarded into Event Formation and treated as structural elements. EFCM identifies which records represent materially relevant operational elements and which are duplicates, technical copies, or supporting records. The resulting component set may contain only: Order Commitment Service Activation Service Delivery Settlement while preserving traceability to the broader evidence base. This prevents the event structure from being defined by system record volume. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Factory Generates 50,000 Machine Actions Around One Commercial Production Cycle An autonomous factory executes a customer production order. Robots, sensors, production software, inventory systems, autonomous transport, and energy-management systems generate more than 50,000 technical actions. TRERS recognizes the economically relevant production occurrence. EFCM then determines which actions materially contribute to Event Formation. Machine telemetry, synchronization signals, internal retries, and control-loop instructions remain outside the formation component set. Material production completion, resource transformation, transfer to finished inventory, and delivery release may qualify as formation components. The key result is: machine execution volume no longer determines event structure. Canonical Boundary EFCM governs the identification, differentiation, qualification, exclusion, uncertainty, and traceability of materially relevant Event Formation Components within a Governed Recognized Occurrence. It does not assemble those components into the event structure, determine formation dependencies, establish the Event Formation Root, assess complete Formation Integrity, determine the final Event Boundary, or determine any jurisdiction-specific tax consequence. The handoff is: Governed Recognized Occurrence → EFCM — Governed Event Formation Component Set → EFAM — Event Formation Assembly Module Canonical Closing Statement Event Formation Component Module establishes the first structural layer of Tax-Relevant Event Formation by determining which materially relevant elements of a Governed Recognized Occurrence may legitimately participate in the formation of the event. By separating operationally meaningful components from technical records, duplicate representations, machine noise, background activity, and unresolved elements, EFCM prevents system granularity from becoming event granularity and ensures that subsequent Event Formation begins from a governed component set rather than an uncontrolled collection of data. EFCM therefore establishes what may enter Event Formation while preserving the boundaries between component qualification, Event Assembly, Event Boundary, and jurisdiction-specific tax determination.

title: OOF™ Event Formation Dependency Module (EFDM)
text: OOF™ Event Formation Dependency Module (EFDM) Event Formation Dependency Module (EFDM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: Tax-Relevant Event Formation Standard (TREFS) Module: EFDM — Event Formation Dependency Module Operational Layer: Event Formation Dependency Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Event Formation Dependencies Origin ID: TREGA-TREFS-EFDM-003 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 30 August 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Event Formation Dependency Module (EFDM) governs how material dependencies supporting, enabling, conditioning, constraining, or otherwise affecting a Governed Event Formation Assembly are identified, differentiated, qualified, related, and preserved without automatically incorporating those dependencies into the formed event itself. EFDM determines which external or surrounding conditions, actions, structures, systems, permissions, resources, prior activities, or operational states are materially necessary to understand how the event formation became possible or structurally coherent. Its task is specific: to establish the governed dependency structure supporting Event Formation without treating dependency as automatic Event Membership, legal causality, Event Root, or final Event Boundary. Operational Role EFCM establishes: which elements qualify as Event Formation Components. EFAM establishes: how those components are assembled into a coherent formation structure. EFDM then determines: what that formation materially depends upon. This distinction is necessary because an event may depend on surrounding activity that does not belong inside the event itself. For example: a payment may depend on an existing account. A digital service may depend on prior authentication. An autonomous transaction may depend on delegated authority. A production event may depend on infrastructure availability. A machine-to-machine exchange may depend on a previously established protocol or resource allocation. Those conditions may be essential to understanding Event Formation. They do not automatically become Event Formation Components. Therefore: Formation Dependency ≠ Formation Component. And more importantly: Formation Dependency ≠ Event Membership. Internal Flow Governed Event Formation Assembly ↓ Dependency Candidate Identification ↓ Dependency Relevance Assessment ↓ Dependency Type Differentiation ↓ Dependency Qualification / Exclusion ↓ Dependency Relationship Establishment ↓ Dependency Conflict / Uncertainty Handling ↓ Governed Event Formation Dependency Structure The principal output is: Governed Event Formation Dependency Structure This output proceeds to: EFRM — Event Formation Root Module Operational Space EFDM governs the space between: a Governed Event Formation Assembly and a formation structure whose material dependencies are sufficiently identified and governed for Event Formation Root analysis. Its operational space includes: dependency candidate identification; dependency relevance; enabling dependencies; conditional dependencies; structural dependencies; resource dependencies; system dependencies; authorization-related dependencies; prior-activity dependencies; infrastructure dependencies; distributed dependencies; machine dependencies; autonomous-system dependencies; dependency qualification; dependency exclusion; dependency relationships; dependency chains; dependency uncertainty; dependency conflict; dependency traceability. EFDM governs what the Event Formation materially depends upon. It does not determine the operational root of the event or whether a dependency ultimately belongs inside the final Event Boundary. Operational Scope EFDM may govern dependencies associated with: commercial transactions; financial operations; payments; transfers; production; supply chains; fulfilment; logistics; service delivery; digital platforms; marketplaces; banking infrastructure; enterprise systems; APIs; software services; digital assets; infrastructure; AI agents; autonomous systems; robots; machine-to-machine exchanges; automated marketplaces; distributed systems; hybrid physical-digital environments. Dependencies may originate from human, organizational, contractual, digital, infrastructural, machine-generated, or autonomous environments. EFDM remains actor-neutral and technology-neutral. Formation Dependency Principle An event does not exist in isolation. Its formation may rely on surrounding conditions or prior activity. But dependency must remain distinct from structural membership. For example: Account Creation ↓ Payment The payment may depend on the account. That does not mean account creation becomes part of every later payment event. Similarly: Delegated Authority ↓ Autonomous Purchase The purchase may depend on valid delegation. That does not automatically make the delegation itself part of the purchase event. Therefore: Necessary for Formation ≠ Part of the Event by Default. Dependency Candidate A Dependency Candidate is an element that may materially support, enable, condition, constrain, or explain the Event Formation Assembly. Possible candidates may include: prior authorization; existing contractual state; account status; infrastructure availability; prior resource allocation; system permission; operational prerequisite; platform access; prior transfer; machine configuration; delegated authority; external service availability; prerequisite production state. Candidate status does not establish a dependency. Therefore: Dependency Candidate ≠ Qualified Formation Dependency. Dependency Relevance A dependency should be qualified only where it materially affects the formation or structural understanding of the event. A dependency may be relevant because the event: could not have occurred without it; could not have formed in the observed manner without it; requires it to explain a material structural relationship; relies on it for execution; relies on it for access or authorization; relies on a prior operational state; relies on external infrastructure or resources. Minor background conditions should not automatically become governed dependencies. Otherwise, dependency chains could expand indefinitely. Background Condition ≠ Formation Dependency Every event ultimately depends on countless background conditions. A digital payment depends on electricity. Electricity depends on infrastructure. Infrastructure depends on other systems. Those facts do not mean every background condition must enter Event Formation governance. EFDM therefore requires material dependency relevance. Background Condition ≠ Formation Dependency by Default. Only dependencies materially necessary to understand the formation should be governed within EFDM. Enabling Dependency An Enabling Dependency makes the formation operationally possible. Examples may include: activated service access; available payment infrastructure; valid system access; available production capability; machine availability; resource allocation. The enabling condition supports formation. It does not automatically belong to the event. Conditional Dependency A Conditional Dependency exists where Event Formation depends upon a particular condition being satisfied. For example: Approval ↓ Release Authorization ↓ Execution Inventory Availability ↓ Fulfilment The condition may be structurally relevant even where it represents a separate operational occurrence. Therefore: Conditional Dependency ≠ Event Component by Default. Prior-Activity Dependency A current formation may depend on earlier activity. For example: a refund may depend on a previous purchase. A subscription renewal may depend on an existing subscription. A machine settlement may depend on earlier resource consumption. A later delivery may depend on a prior production action. EFDM may preserve that dependency. It does not automatically merge the earlier activity into the current event. Therefore: Prior Event Dependency ≠ Same Event. Dependency Chain Some formations rely on several dependencies. For example: Delegation ↓ Agent Authorization ↓ Resource Reservation ↓ Service Execution EFDM may represent a dependency chain where materially necessary. However, dependency chains must remain proportionate. The existence of a chain does not require every historical prerequisite to become part of the governed formation. Therefore: Dependency Chain ≠ Event Expansion. Dependency ≠ Legal Causality EFDM governs structural and operational dependency. It does not determine legal causation. For example, establishing that one operational condition enabled another action does not establish: legal responsibility; contractual causation; tax liability; damages; fault; legal attribution. Therefore: Formation Dependency ≠ Legal Causality. Where accountability or liability must be determined, other governance or legal systems own those questions. Dependency ≠ Authority An autonomous action may depend on delegated authority. EFDM may record that the formation relies upon an authority-related condition. It does not determine whether the authority was legally valid or who owns that authority relationship. Therefore: Authority Dependency ≠ Authority Governance. Where available, EFDM may consume governed authority information from OBIDENITY®, ASGA™, or other relevant architecture. Dependency ≠ Identity An event may depend on an existing account, actor relationship, device, organization, or autonomous agent. That does not make identity itself part of Event Formation Dependency governance. Therefore: Identity Reference ≠ Identity Governance. EFDM may consume identity references. It does not establish identity origin, ownership, continuity, or provenance. Distributed Dependencies A formation may depend on several systems or organizations. For example: Marketplace ↓ Identity Service ↓ Payment Network ↓ Cloud Infrastructure ↓ Service Provider No single system may contain the complete dependency representation. EFDM must permit distributed dependencies to be represented where materially relevant. Therefore: Distributed Dependency ≠ Multiple Events by Default. Machine Dependencies Machine-generated events may depend on: software state; resource availability; sensor state; machine permission; automated authorization; infrastructure capacity; prior machine execution. EFDM must distinguish dependencies that materially affect formation from ordinary machine operating conditions. Therefore: Machine Prerequisite ≠ Formation Dependency by Default. Autonomous Dependencies Autonomous systems may rely on complex chains of permissions, delegated objectives, resource conditions, or other agents. EFDM may govern these dependencies where they materially affect Event Formation. However: Autonomous Dependency ≠ Autonomous Responsibility. The existence of a dependency does not determine who is accountable for the resulting event. Dependency Conflict Different systems may provide incompatible representations of the dependencies supporting the same formation. For example: a platform may state that authorization preceded execution; another system may indicate that execution occurred before final authorization. EFDM must preserve material dependency conflict rather than silently selecting one representation. Possible states may include: Dependency Candidate Dependency Qualified Dependency Excluded Dependency Conflict Dependency Unresolved Dependency Uncertainty Where a material dependency cannot be sufficiently established, EFDM must preserve uncertainty. The system should not invent a dependency merely because one would make the event structure easier to explain. Therefore: Expected Dependency ≠ Established Dependency. Dependency Traceability A qualified Formation Dependency should remain traceable to its governed basis. Where materially required, traceability may preserve: dependency reference; dependency type; related formation or component; qualification basis; source reference; dependency relationship; uncertainty; conflict; revision history. This allows subsequent modules to distinguish the event structure from the conditions upon which that structure depends. Dependency Independence from Event Boundary EFDM identifies dependencies before TREBS establishes the final Event Boundary. This means a qualified dependency may later: remain outside the Event Boundary; contribute to Boundary analysis; relate the event to another event; become relevant to Event Relationships; require separate governance. Therefore: Qualified Dependency ≠ Boundary Inclusion. TREBS later determines final event extent.
