Governance Requirements EFDM requires that: dependencies are assessed against a Governed Event Formation Assembly; dependency candidates are distinguished from qualified dependencies; dependency relevance is materially established; background conditions do not automatically become dependencies; dependencies remain distinct from Event Formation Components; dependencies remain distinct from Event Membership; prior activity is not automatically merged into the current event; dependency chains remain proportionate; structural dependency remains distinct from legal causality; identity and authority dependencies do not absorb identity or authority governance; distributed dependencies may be represented; machine prerequisites are filtered for material relevance; dependency conflicts remain visible; unresolved dependencies remain explicitly unresolved; dependency decisions remain traceable; dependency qualification does not determine Event Boundary; dependency qualification does not determine legal taxability. Governance Logic EFDM applies a focused dependency logic: What surrounding condition, action, structure, system, resource, or prior activity materially supports this Event Formation Assembly? Is the relationship sufficiently material to qualify as a Formation Dependency? Is the dependency part of the formation structure, or merely a condition upon which that structure relies? Are dependency relationships conflicting or unresolved? What dependency structure must remain visible before Event Formation Root analysis begins? The transformation is: Governed Event Formation Assembly → Dependency Candidates → Dependency Relevance → Qualification / Exclusion → Dependency Relationships → Governed Event Formation Dependency Structure Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum EFDM implementation must be capable of: 1. receiving the Governed Event Formation Assembly from EFAM; 2. identifying candidate Formation Dependencies; 3. assessing material dependency relevance; 4. distinguishing dependencies from Event Formation Components; 5. distinguishing dependencies from ordinary background conditions; 6. qualifying or excluding dependency candidates; 7. representing enabling, conditional, prior-activity, infrastructural, distributed, machine, or autonomous dependencies where relevant; 8. representing material dependency chains without uncontrolled expansion; 9. identifying Dependency Conflict or Dependency Uncertainty; 10. preserving dependency traceability; 11. preventing dependency from automatically becoming Event Membership; 12. producing a Governed Event Formation Dependency Structure; 13. transferring the governed formation and dependency structure to EFRM for Event Formation Root governance; 14. preventing dependency analysis from becoming Event Boundary, legal causality, responsibility, or jurisdiction-specific tax determination. EFDM does not prescribe a specific dependency graph, ERP model, workflow system, database schema, AI model, transaction architecture, tax engine, identity system, or legal causality model. Governance Outputs EFDM may produce: Governed Event Formation Dependency Structure — the principal Module output. Qualified Formation Dependency — a materially established dependency supporting Event Formation. Excluded Dependency Candidate — a candidate determined not to require dependency governance. Unresolved Formation Dependency — a materially relevant dependency whose status remains unresolved. Dependency Relationship Record — the governed relationship between a dependency and the formation. Dependency Chain Reference — representation of materially relevant connected dependencies. Dependency Conflict Indicator — indication of materially incompatible dependency representations. Dependency Qualification Record — the basis for dependency qualification or exclusion. Dependency Traceability Reference — linkage between the dependency and its governed basis. Critical Distinctions Formation Dependency ≠ Formation Component. A dependency may support formation without becoming a component. Formation Dependency ≠ Event Membership. Dependency does not determine final inclusion. Necessary for Formation ≠ Part of the Event by Default. Operational necessity and structural membership are different questions. Dependency Candidate ≠ Qualified Formation Dependency. Identification precedes qualification. Background Condition ≠ Formation Dependency by Default. Dependency governance must remain materially bounded. Conditional Dependency ≠ Event Component by Default. A condition may remain external to the formed event. Prior Event Dependency ≠ Same Event. Dependency does not merge separate activity. Dependency Chain ≠ Event Expansion. Historical prerequisites must not create unlimited event structures. Formation Dependency ≠ Legal Causality. EFDM does not determine legal consequence. Authority Dependency ≠ Authority Governance. Authority remains governed by the architecture owning that space. Identity Reference ≠ Identity Governance. EFDM may reference identity without governing identity. Machine Prerequisite ≠ Formation Dependency by Default. Ordinary machine operation does not automatically become governed dependency. Autonomous Dependency ≠ Autonomous Responsibility. Dependency does not determine accountability. Expected Dependency ≠ Established Dependency. Structural assumptions require governed support. Qualified Dependency ≠ Boundary Inclusion. TREBS owns final Event Boundary. Formation Dependency ≠ Taxability Determination. EFDM does not determine tax law. Enterprise Application EFDM addresses a major structural problem in complex enterprise and digital systems: systems frequently confuse what an event depends on with what the event actually is. A payment may depend on an account. A delivery may depend on a warehouse release. A digital service may depend on authentication. An autonomous transaction may depend on delegated authority. A production action may depend on resource allocation. If every prerequisite is absorbed into the event, the event can expand indefinitely. If dependencies are ignored entirely, the event loses the structural conditions necessary to understand how it formed. EFDM creates the governed middle layer: the dependency remains visible without automatically becoming part of the event. Use CasesUse Case 1 — Global Digital Service Depends on Multiple Prior Activities Across Different Companies A customer purchases a cloud-based enterprise service through a global marketplace. The Event Formation Assembly includes: service commitment; activation; service execution; settlement. However, the formation also relies on: prior customer account creation; platform authentication; an existing provider agreement; payment authorization infrastructure; previously allocated cloud capacity. Without EFDM, a system may either ignore these dependencies completely or absorb them all into one oversized event. EFDM determines which dependencies materially support the formation and preserves their relationship without automatically treating them as Event Formation Components. The customer account does not become part of every service event. The provider agreement does not become part of every execution. The cloud infrastructure does not become the event merely because execution depends on it. The result is a governed dependency structure that explains how the formation became possible without redefining what the formation is. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Industrial Network Creates a Deep Chain of Machine Dependencies An AI-controlled manufacturing network autonomously accepts a production requirement and coordinates: production capacity; energy allocation; robotic equipment; material availability; autonomous transport; machine authorization; digital settlement. The resulting Event Formation Assembly depends on several prior machine and infrastructure states. If every dependency is recursively absorbed, the event could expand from one production formation into the entire factory, energy grid, software stack, and historical authorization chain. If dependencies are ignored, critical structural relationships disappear. EFDM identifies only the dependencies materially necessary to understand the formation. It may preserve: Production Formation → depends on Material Availability → depends on Production Capacity Allocation → depends on Authorized Machine Execution without converting every underlying technical prerequisite into an Event Formation Component. The key result is: dependency remains governable without allowing the event to expand indefinitely through the systems that made it possible. Canonical Boundary EFDM governs the identification, differentiation, qualification, relationship, uncertainty, conflict, and traceability of material dependencies supporting a Governed Event Formation Assembly. It does not identify original Event Formation Components, assemble those components, establish the Event Formation Root, determine complete Formation Integrity, determine final Event Boundary, establish legal causality, govern identity or authority, determine accountability, or determine any jurisdiction-specific tax consequence. The handoff is: EFAM — Governed Event Formation Assembly → EFDM — Governed Event Formation Dependency Structure → EFRM — Event Formation Root Module Canonical Closing Statement Event Formation Dependency Module establishes the dependency governance layer of Tax-Relevant Event Formation by determining what conditions, actions, structures, resources, systems, or prior activities materially support a Governed Event Formation Assembly without automatically incorporating those dependencies into the event itself. By separating dependency from Formation Components, Event Membership, identity, authority, legal causality, responsibility, and final Event Boundary, EFDM preserves the operational conditions necessary to understand how an event formation became possible while preventing unlimited structural expansion through every prerequisite on which the event ultimately relies. The Module therefore produces a bounded, traceable Event Formation Dependency Structure ready for Event Formation Root governance without allowing dependency analysis to redefine the event or determine jurisdiction-specific tax consequences.

title: OOF™ Event Formation Integrity Module (EFIM)
text: OOF™ Event Formation Integrity Module (EFIM) Event Formation Integrity Module (EFIM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: Tax-Relevant Event Formation Standard (TREFS) Module: EFIM — Event Formation Integrity Module Operational Layer: Event Formation Integrity Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Event Formation Integrity Origin ID: TREGA-TREFS-EFIM-005 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 30 August 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Event Formation Integrity Module (EFIM) governs whether a developing Event Formation is sufficiently coherent, structurally complete, internally consistent, traceable, and formation-ready to legitimately exit Tax-Relevant Event Formation governance and proceed into Event Boundary governance. EFIM evaluates the governed formation produced through the preceding TREFS modules as an integrated structural whole, including its qualified Formation Components, Formation Assembly, material Formation Dependencies, and Event Formation Root Association. Its task is specific: to determine whether the governed Event Formation possesses sufficient formation integrity to proceed into Event Boundary governance without treating formation integrity as validation, audit determination, evidence sufficiency, legal taxability, or final Event Determination. EFIM therefore governs the final structural integrity gate of TREFS. Operational Role The preceding TREFS modules establish different structural dimensions of Event Formation: EFCM — Event Formation Component Module establishes the qualified components required for formation. EFAM — Event Formation Assembly Module establishes how those components form a coherent structural assembly. EFDM — Event Formation Dependency Module establishes the material dependencies supporting or constraining the formation. EFRM — Event Formation Root Module establishes the operational root association anchoring the formation. EFIM then asks: Does the resulting formation, considered as a governed structural whole, possess sufficient integrity to proceed into Event Boundary governance? EFIM does not recreate the work of the preceding modules. It evaluates whether their governed outputs collectively support a sufficiently coherent Event Formation. The principal transition is: Developing Governed Event Formation ↓ Formation Integrity Assessment ↓ Governed Formed Event Internal Flow Qualified Event Formation Components + Governed Event Formation Assembly + Governed Event Formation Dependency Structure + Governed Event Formation Root Association → Formation Integrity Readiness Assessment → Structural Completeness Assessment → Formation Coherence Assessment → Internal Consistency Assessment → Formation Traceability Assessment → Conflict / Gap / Uncertainty Assessment → Formation Integrity Determination → Integrity-Sufficient / Integrity-Insufficient / Integrity-Unresolved Formation → Governed Formed Event The principal successful output is: Governed Formed Event This output proceeds to: TREBS — Tax-Relevant Event Boundary Standard Operational Space EFIM governs the space between: a structurally developed Event Formation produced through EFCM, EFAM, EFDM, and EFRM and a Governed Formed Event sufficiently coherent to enter Event Boundary governance. Its operational space includes: formation integrity readiness; structural completeness; component-to-assembly consistency; dependency consistency; root consistency; cross-formation coherence; internal contradiction detection; structural gap identification; formation conflict identification; formation uncertainty; formation traceability; formation integrity states; integrity insufficiency; integrity reconsideration; formation readiness for Event Boundary governance. EFIM governs integrity of formation as formation. It does not govern universal system integrity, legal integrity, evidence validity, audit conclusions, validation status, Event Boundary, or taxation. Operational Scope EFIM may govern Event Formation Integrity across: commercial transactions; financial activity; payments; transfers; production; manufacturing; supply chains; logistics; service delivery; digital services; subscriptions; platforms; marketplaces; banking; enterprise systems; APIs; software interactions; digital assets; automated infrastructure; AI systems; autonomous agents; robots; machine-to-machine transactions; automated marketplaces; distributed systems; hybrid physical-digital environments; future machine economies. EFIM is actor-neutral, system-neutral, technology-neutral, and jurisdiction-neutral. The formation may originate through human, organizational, digital, machine-generated, autonomous, or mixed activity. Formation Integrity Principle A collection of individually governed formation elements does not automatically constitute an integrity-sufficient Event Formation. Qualified components may exist. A formation assembly may exist. Dependencies may be established. A root may be associated. Yet contradictions, structural gaps, incompatible relationships, unresolved dependencies, or material uncertainty may prevent the resulting formation from legitimately proceeding. Therefore: Governed Formation Elements ≠ Formation Integrity by Default. Formation integrity must be assessed at the level of the formation as a whole. Formation Integrity Readiness Before substantive integrity assessment occurs, EFIM determines whether the formation contains sufficient governed structure to undergo integrity evaluation. Formation Integrity Readiness may require the availability of materially necessary outputs from preceding TREFS modules. However, readiness does not require artificial completeness. A legitimate unresolved or qualified condition may remain represented where it does not prevent meaningful integrity assessment. Therefore: Formation Integrity Ready ≠ Formation Integrity Sufficient. Readiness permits assessment. It does not predetermine its result. Structural Completeness EFIM assesses whether the Event Formation contains the materially necessary structural dimensions required to function as a coherent formation. Structural completeness does not mean that every possible data field is populated. It means that no materially necessary formation element is absent in a manner that prevents the formation from being meaningfully governed. Therefore: Data Completeness ≠ Structural Completeness. A formation containing thousands of records may remain structurally incomplete. A formation containing relatively few records may nevertheless be structurally sufficient. The relevant question is: Does the formation contain what is materially necessary to represent its governed structure? Formation Coherence EFIM evaluates whether the formation makes structural sense as a unified governed representation. Formation Components, Assembly, Dependencies, and Root Association should collectively describe a formation that can be understood without relying on materially incompatible structural assumptions. Coherence may require that: qualified components can legitimately coexist within the formation; assembly relationships remain intelligible; dependencies do not contradict the assembled structure; the Event Formation Root remains compatible with the formation; material structural relationships remain explainable; unresolved conditions remain visible; no hidden assumption is required to make the formation appear coherent. Therefore: Structural Presence ≠ Structural Coherence. Internal Consistency EFIM evaluates whether governed formation outputs materially contradict one another. Possible inconsistencies may include: a component classified as materially necessary but absent from the assembly; an assembly relationship incompatible with a governed dependency; a dependency contradicting the proposed operational root; two components represented as mutually exclusive while simultaneously required within the same formation; materially incompatible root representations; formation logic requiring mutually contradictory structural states. EFIM must not silently normalize material contradictions. Therefore: Resolvable Difference ≠ Material Inconsistency. But: Material Contradiction Must Remain Governed. Formation Traceability A formation should remain sufficiently traceable to understand how its structure was established. EFIM may assess whether the formation preserves traceable relationships to: the Governed Recognized Occurrence; qualified Formation Components; component qualification decisions; Formation Assembly; material Formation Dependencies; Event Formation Root Association; unresolved formation questions; reconsiderations; structural changes; formation integrity decisions. Traceability does not require EFIM to conduct an audit. Therefore: Formation Traceability ≠ Audit Determination. Formation Gap A Formation Gap exists where a materially necessary structural element, relationship, dependency, root association, or governance basis is absent or insufficiently established. Not every missing field creates a Formation Gap. Not every Formation Gap prevents progression. EFIM must assess materiality within the formation. Possible states include: Non-Material Gap Material Resolvable Gap Material Blocking Gap Unresolved Gap Therefore: Missing Information ≠ Formation Failure by Default. Formation Conflict A Formation Conflict exists where materially incompatible formation representations cannot simultaneously remain valid without qualification. Conflicts may arise between: components; assembly structures; dependencies; root associations; source representations; distributed-system records; machine-generated representations; human and automated interpretations. EFIM must preserve material conflict rather than forcing artificial consistency. Therefore: Conflict Visibility Is Part of Formation Integrity. A formation that openly represents a governed unresolved conflict may possess greater methodological integrity than one that hides the conflict. Formation Uncertainty Formation integrity does not require false certainty. Where uncertainty remains materially relevant, EFIM must determine whether it: can coexist with progression; requires qualification; requires reconsideration by an earlier TREFS module; prevents formation integrity from being established. Possible treatment includes: Integrity Sufficient with Qualified Uncertainty or: Formation Integrity Unresolved Therefore: Uncertainty ≠ Integrity Failure by Default. But uncertainty must never be silently converted into certainty. Formation Integrity States EFIM may establish the following governed states: 1. Formation Integrity Assessment Ready The formation contains sufficient governed structure for integrity assessment. 2. Formation Integrity Under Assessment Integrity evaluation is actively occurring. 3. Formation Integrity Sufficient The formation possesses sufficient structural integrity to proceed. 4. Formation Integrity Sufficient with Qualification The formation may proceed while explicitly preserving non-blocking uncertainty, limitation, or qualification. 5. Formation Integrity Insufficient Material structural deficiencies prevent legitimate progression. 6. Formation Integrity Unresolved Available governance basis does not permit a legitimate sufficient/insufficient determination. 7. Formation Integrity Reconsideration Required A material issue requires governed reconsideration of one or more preceding formation dimensions. 8. Governed Formed Event The formation has successfully completed the TREFS formation layer and is ready to enter Event Boundary governance. Integrity Insufficiency Formation Integrity may be insufficient where material structural problems prevent the formation from legitimately representing a coherent formed event. Possible causes include: materially missing Formation Components; materially incoherent Assembly; unresolved blocking dependencies; materially incompatible root association; structural contradictions; untraceable material formation decisions; unresolved blocking conflicts; formation fragmentation; unsupported structural assumptions. An integrity-insufficient formation should not be artificially promoted merely because downstream systems require an event record. Therefore: Downstream Processing Requirement ≠ Formation Integrity. Return to Earlier Formation Governance EFIM is not required to repair every detected formation problem itself. Where a material integrity problem belongs to an earlier formation dimension, EFIM should return or route the issue to the appropriate TREFS module. Examples: component deficiency ↓ EFCM assembly deficiency ↓ EFAM dependency deficiency ↓ EFDM root deficiency ↓ EFRM This preserves module ownership. Therefore: Integrity Assessment ≠ Formation Reconstruction. EFIM identifies whether formation integrity exists. The relevant module governs correction of its own formation dimension. Formation Integrity Reconsideration New information may materially affect an earlier Formation Integrity determination. EFIM must support governed reconsideration. Reconsideration should preserve: previous integrity state; previous assessment basis; reason for reconsideration; new or changed information; affected formation dimensions; revised integrity state; progression or return decision. Therefore: Integrity Reconsideration ≠ Historical Erasure. Formation Integrity ≠ Validation EFIM does not validate the event in the broader methodological sense. Within the OOF® architecture ecosystem, validation belongs to VALIDOS™ where applicable. EFIM asks: Is this Event Formation structurally coherent and sufficiently governed as a formation? It does not ask: Has the event been independently validated under a broader validation methodology? Therefore: Formation Integrity ≠ Validation. Formation Integrity ≠ General Integrity Governance EFIM governs a narrow integrity question within TREFS. It does not replace broader integrity governance. Where broader system, information, process, or methodological integrity must be governed, INTEGROS® may own the relevant architecture space. Therefore: Event Formation Integrity ≠ General Integrity Governance. Formation Integrity ≠ Evidence Sufficiency EFIM may consume evidence references or traceable source information. It does not determine general evidential sufficiency or auditability. Those governance spaces may belong to ADIT® where applicable. Therefore: Formation Integrity ≠ Evidence Sufficiency. Formation Traceability ≠ Evidence Validation. Formation Integrity ≠ Event Boundary A formation may possess sufficient integrity while its final extent remains undetermined. That is intentional. TREFS establishes what coherent event structure has been formed. TREBS subsequently governs what belongs inside, outside, separated from, or associated with the Event Boundary. Therefore: Formation Integrity Sufficient ≠ Event Boundary Determined. EFIM must not solve Event Boundary questions merely to make the formation appear complete. Formation Integrity ≠ Event Determination A successfully formed event is not yet a formally determined Tax-Relevant Event. TREDS later determines whether the governed event is sufficiently structured and governed to constitute a Tax-Relevant Event for downstream taxation analysis. Therefore: Governed Formed Event ≠ Determined Tax-Relevant Event. Formation Integrity ≠ Legal Taxability EFIM must remain independent of jurisdiction-specific taxation rules. A structurally coherent event may ultimately: be taxable; be non-taxable; be exempt; fall outside a jurisdiction; be evaluated differently by multiple jurisdictions; require additional legal analysis. None of these outcomes alters the purpose of EFIM. Therefore: Formation Integrity ≠ Legal Taxability. Tax Rule Independence Formation integrity should describe the governed event structure rather than the tax rule subsequently applied to it. A tax-law change should therefore not automatically alter the historical Formation Integrity state where the underlying operational formation has not changed. Therefore: Tax Rule Change ≠ Formation Integrity Change by Default. This supports the TREGA™ principle: One Event ↓ One Governed Event Layer ↓ Multiple Jurisdictional Evaluations. Machine and Autonomous Formation Integrity Machine-generated and autonomous events may contain structures that differ significantly from traditional human transactions. They may involve: high-frequency actions; distributed execution; autonomous decisions; machine-generated dependencies; API chains; microtransactions; dynamic resource allocation; autonomous settlement; machine-to-machine interaction. EFIM must evaluate the integrity of the governed formation rather than assume that every technical action represents a separate event. Therefore: Technical Complexity ≠ Formation Integrity Failure. And: Machine Granularity ≠ Event Granularity. Distributed Formation Integrity A governed formation may span multiple systems, entities, infrastructures, or technical environments. No single system must necessarily contain the entire formation. EFIM may assess structural integrity across distributed representations where sufficient governed relationships exist. Therefore: Distributed Representation ≠ Fragmented Event by Default. However, distributed representations must not be artificially combined where structural coherence cannot be established. Governance Requirements EFIM requires that: the formation be assessed as an integrated governed structure; integrity readiness be established before substantive integrity determination; structural completeness be distinguished from raw data completeness; Formation Components remain consistent with Formation Assembly; material Formation Dependencies remain structurally compatible; Event Formation Root Association remain compatible with the formation; material contradictions remain visible; material Formation Gaps be identified; Formation Conflicts be governed; uncertainty not be converted into false certainty; formation traceability be sufficiently preserved; blocking and non-blocking deficiencies be differentiated; qualified progression remain possible where uncertainty is non-blocking; integrity-insufficient formations not be artificially promoted; deficiencies belonging to earlier modules be returned to the appropriate module; reconsideration preserve historical integrity states; Formation Integrity remain distinct from validation; Formation Integrity remain distinct from general integrity governance; Formation Integrity remain distinct from audit and evidence sufficiency; Formation Integrity not determine Event Boundary; Formation Integrity not determine Event Timing, Event Location, Event Participation, or Event-to-Value Association; Formation Integrity not determine legal taxability; Formation Integrity not determine Tax Jurisdiction; successful completion produce a Governed Formed Event suitable for TREBS. Governance Logic EFIM applies the following core logic: Is the formation sufficiently complete at the structural level? Do its components, assembly, dependencies, and root association remain materially coherent with one another? Are material contradictions, gaps, conflicts, and uncertainties visible and governed? Does any unresolved condition prevent legitimate progression? Does the formation require reconsideration by EFCM, EFAM, EFDM, or EFRM? Can the formation legitimately exit TREFS and enter Event Boundary governance? The transformation is: Developed Event Formation → Integrity Readiness → Completeness + Coherence + Consistency + Traceability → Gap / Conflict / Uncertainty Governance → Formation Integrity Determination → Governed Formed Event Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum EFIM implementation must be capable of: 1. receiving governed outputs from EFCM, EFAM, EFDM, and EFRM; 2. determining Formation Integrity Readiness; 3. assessing structural completeness; 4. assessing Formation Coherence; 5. assessing internal structural consistency; 6. assessing material Formation Traceability; 7. identifying material Formation Gaps; 8. identifying Formation Conflicts; 9. identifying and preserving Formation Uncertainty; 10. differentiating blocking and non-blocking integrity conditions; 11. supporting qualified progression where justified; 12. establishing governed Formation Integrity States; 13. identifying which preceding TREFS module owns remediation of a detected structural deficiency; 14. supporting governed Formation Integrity reconsideration; 15. preserving prior integrity states and decisions; 16. preventing integrity assessment from becoming validation, audit, evidence determination, Event Boundary determination, or tax determination; 17. producing a Governed Formed Event where Formation Integrity is sufficient; 18. transferring that Governed Formed Event to TREBS. EFIM does not prescribe a specific database, event schema, ERP platform, accounting model, tax engine, AI model, validation framework, evidence methodology, distributed ledger, autonomous-system architecture, or jurisdiction-specific taxation methodology. Governance Outputs EFIM may produce: Formation Integrity Assessment Record — governed record of the integrity assessment. Formation Integrity State — current governed integrity status. Formation Gap Record — identified material structural gap. Formation Conflict Record — identified material structural incompatibility. Formation Uncertainty Record — preserved material uncertainty. Formation Integrity Qualification — explicit non-blocking limitation attached to progression. Formation Reconsideration Requirement — governed requirement for reconsideration by a preceding TREFS module. Formation Integrity Insufficiency Record — basis on which progression is prevented. Governed Formed Event — principal successful output of EFIM and final output of TREFS. Critical Distinctions Governed Formation Elements ≠ Formation Integrity by Default. Individual governed outputs must still form a coherent whole. Formation Integrity Ready ≠ Formation Integrity Sufficient. Readiness enables assessment. Data Completeness ≠ Structural Completeness. More data does not automatically create better formation. Structural Presence ≠ Structural Coherence. Existing components may still form an incoherent structure. Resolvable Difference ≠ Material Inconsistency. Not every difference blocks formation. Missing Information ≠ Formation Failure by Default. Materiality governs the consequence. Conflict Visibility Is Part of Formation Integrity. Hiding conflict does not create integrity. Uncertainty ≠ Integrity Failure by Default. Governed uncertainty may remain legitimate. Downstream Processing Requirement ≠ Formation Integrity. System pressure cannot manufacture methodological sufficiency. Integrity Assessment ≠ Formation Reconstruction. Earlier modules retain ownership of their formation dimensions. Integrity Reconsideration ≠ Historical Erasure. Previous states remain traceable. Formation Integrity ≠ Validation. VALIDOS™ owns broader validation governance where applicable. Event Formation Integrity ≠ General Integrity Governance. INTEGROS® owns broader integrity governance where applicable. Formation Integrity ≠ Evidence Sufficiency. ADIT® owns applicable evidence and auditability governance. Formation Integrity Sufficient ≠ Event Boundary Determined. TREBS owns Event Boundary. Governed Formed Event ≠ Determined Tax-Relevant Event. TREDS owns Event Determination. Formation Integrity ≠ Legal Taxability. Jurisdictional law determines taxation. Tax Rule Change ≠ Formation Integrity Change by Default. Operational formation remains independently governed. Machine Granularity ≠ Event Granularity. Technical actions do not automatically define governed events. Distributed Representation ≠ Fragmented Event by Default. Distribution alone does not determine event structure. Enterprise Application Modern enterprise and digital systems frequently create event representations independently. An ERP may create one record. A payment processor may create several. A marketplace may create another. An autonomous agent may create dozens of machine actions. A logistics platform may represent the same operational activity differently. A tax engine may subsequently consume only a subset. The existence of these records does not establish that a coherent governed event has been formed. EFIM provides a structural integrity gate before the event enters later governance. Instead of asking: “Do we have enough system records to create a tax record?” EFIM asks: “Is the underlying Event Formation structurally coherent enough to become a Governed Formed Event?” This creates a stable governance layer between fragmented operational representations and downstream Event Boundary and taxation analysis. Use CasesUse Case 1 — Cross-Border Marketplace Produces Conflicting Event Structures A global marketplace processes a transaction involving: customer order placement; payment authorization; third-party seller confirmation; automated fulfilment; cross-border shipment; digital invoicing; payment settlement. The marketplace represents the activity as one transaction. The payment system represents it as authorization plus settlement. The logistics system represents several operational movements. The seller ERP creates an order, invoice, receivable, and fulfilment record. A downstream tax system requires an event representation. The existence of all these records does not establish a coherent Event Formation. EFCM identifies materially relevant components. EFAM establishes their formation assembly. EFDM governs material dependencies. EFRM establishes the operational root association. EFIM then evaluates whether these outputs collectively represent a structurally coherent formation. If the payment settlement is incorrectly represented as the root while the formation structure demonstrates that service fulfilment is operationally central, EFIM may identify a material inconsistency and route the root question back to EFRM. If a material seller confirmation is missing from the assembly, EFIM may identify a Formation Gap and route the issue to EFCM or EFAM. Only after the resulting formation becomes sufficiently coherent does EFIM produce: Governed Formed Event The event may then proceed to TREBS, where its final Event Boundary is governed. No tax jurisdiction, taxpayer, tax point, or tax liability has yet been determined. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Machine Economy Generates Thousands of Technical Actions An autonomous industrial system dynamically purchases energy, computing capacity, maintenance services, and replacement components. During one operational cycle, interconnected agents and machines generate thousands of: sensor signals; API calls; pricing requests; autonomous decisions; resource reservations; machine commands; payment messages; settlement records. Technical systems initially produce several competing event formations. One model treats every API interaction as an independent event. Another aggregates the entire operational cycle into one event. A third groups activity by settlement. TREFS forms the relevant structural candidates through its preceding modules. EFIM evaluates whether each proposed formation possesses sufficient structural integrity. It may determine that a formation based purely on API-call granularity lacks coherence because technical granularity does not correspond to materially distinct operational formation. It may also determine that aggregating the entire cycle into one formation hides materially independent operational structures. The integrity process therefore prevents both artificial fragmentation and artificial aggregation. The resulting Governed Formed Events can subsequently enter TREBS for explicit Event Boundary governance and later TREGA stages. Machine complexity is preserved without allowing technical system structure to dictate economic event reality. Canonical Boundary EFIM governs the final structural integrity assessment of Event Formation, including formation readiness, structural completeness, coherence, internal consistency, material gaps, conflicts, uncertainty, traceability, integrity states, qualification, insufficiency, reconsideration, and readiness for Event Boundary governance. It does not independently identify Formation Components, reconstruct Formation Assembly, establish Formation Dependencies, establish Event Formation Root, determine Event Boundary, determine Event Timing, Event Location, Event Participation, Event-to-Value Association, validate the event, perform audit determination, establish general evidential sufficiency, determine a Tax-Relevant Event, identify the taxpayer, determine Tax Jurisdiction, establish legal tax point, calculate tax, or determine jurisdiction-specific tax consequences. The final TREFS handoff is: EFCM — Event Formation Components → EFAM — Event Formation Assembly → EFDM — Event Formation Dependencies → EFRM — Event Formation Root → EFIM — Event Formation Integrity → Governed Formed Event → TREBS — Tax-Relevant Event Boundary Standard Canonical Closing Statement Event Formation Integrity Module establishes the final governance gate of Tax-Relevant Event Formation by determining whether qualified components, assembly, dependencies, and operational root collectively constitute a sufficiently coherent, complete, consistent, traceable, and governable Event Formation. EFIM preserves gaps, conflicts, uncertainty, qualification, and reconsideration rather than manufacturing structural certainty for downstream systems. It separates Formation Integrity from validation, general integrity governance, evidence sufficiency, Event Boundary, Event Determination, and legal taxability, allowing TREFS to produce a stable Governed Formed Event without crossing into jurisdiction-specific taxation. With EFIM complete, TREFS transforms a Governed Recognized Occurrence into a Governed Formed Event ready for Event Boundary governance — while preserving the foundational TREGA™ principle: TREGA™ governs the event. The jurisdiction governs the tax.

title: OOF™ Event Formation Root Module (EFRM)
text: OOF™ Event Formation Root Module (EFRM) Event Formation Root Module (EFRM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: Tax-Relevant Event Formation Standard (TREFS) Module: EFRM — Event Formation Root Module Operational Layer: Event Formation Root Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Event Formation Root Association Origin ID: TREGA-TREFS-EFRM-004 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 30 August 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Event Formation Root Module (EFRM) governs how the operational root association of a developing Event Formation is identified, differentiated, qualified, related, and preserved so that the formation can be anchored to the materially relevant operational basis from which its structure originates or becomes meaningfully organized. EFRM establishes the governed relationship between a formed event structure and the operational occurrence, condition, transition, action, interaction, or state change that provides the most relevant structural anchor for understanding how that formation came into being. Its task is specific: to establish the governed operational root association of Event Formation without converting that root into identity origin, provenance, legal causality, legal tax point, Event Boundary, or jurisdiction-specific tax determination. Operational Role EFCM establishes: which elements qualify as Event Formation Components. EFAM establishes: how those components are assembled into a coherent formation structure. EFDM establishes: what that formation materially depends upon. EFRM then determines: what operational basis most appropriately anchors the formation as its Event Formation Root. This distinction is necessary because a formation may contain multiple components and depend on multiple prior conditions while still requiring a coherent operational anchor. For example: a payment formation may be rooted in execution of a transfer instruction. A service formation may be rooted in commencement or activation of the governed service interaction. A production formation may be rooted in a materially relevant production initiation. An autonomous transaction may be rooted in an autonomous execution action. A machine-to-machine formation may be rooted in a governed machine interaction or operational state transition. The Event Formation Root provides structural orientation. It does not determine legal origin, ownership, identity provenance, responsibility, or taxation. Therefore: Event Formation Root ≠ Identity Origin. Event Formation Root ≠ Legal Tax Point. Internal Flow Governed Event Formation Assembly + Governed Event Formation Dependency Structure ↓ Root Candidate Identification ↓ Operational Root Relevance Assessment ↓ Root Candidate Differentiation ↓ Root Qualification / Exclusion ↓ Root Association Establishment ↓ Root Conflict / Uncertainty Handling ↓ Governed Event Formation Root Association The principal output is: Governed Event Formation Root Association This output proceeds to: EFIM — Event Formation Integrity Module Operational Space EFRM governs the space between: an assembled Event Formation with governed material dependencies and an Event Formation whose operational root association is sufficiently established for Formation Integrity governance. Its operational space includes: root candidate identification; operational root relevance; root differentiation; root qualification; root exclusion; direct root association; indirect root association; composite root association; distributed root association; machine-generated roots; autonomous roots; root ambiguity; root conflict; root uncertainty; root traceability; root reconsideration. EFRM governs the operational anchor of Event Formation. It does not determine who originally created an identity, who owns an asset, who possesses authority, who is responsible, where legal causation begins, when tax legally arises, or what belongs inside the final Event Boundary. Operational Scope EFRM may govern Event Formation Roots associated with: commercial transactions; payments; financial operations; transfers; production; supply chains; fulfilment; logistics; service delivery; digital services; subscriptions; platforms; marketplaces; banking systems; enterprise systems; APIs; software interactions; digital assets; infrastructure operations; AI agents; autonomous systems; robots; machine-to-machine transactions; automated marketplaces; distributed systems; hybrid physical-digital environments; future machine economies. An Event Formation Root may arise from human, organizational, transactional, digital, operational, machine-generated, or autonomous activity. EFRM remains actor-neutral and technology-neutral. Event Formation Root Principle Complex formations frequently contain many plausible starting points. The first technical record is not necessarily the operational root. The earliest timestamp is not necessarily the operational root. The first participant action is not necessarily the operational root. The oldest dependency is not necessarily the operational root. The Event Formation Root must instead represent the operational basis that materially anchors the formation being governed. Therefore: Earliest Record ≠ Event Formation Root by Default. First Technical Action ≠ Event Formation Root by Default. Oldest Dependency ≠ Event Formation Root by Default. Root Candidate A Root Candidate is an operational occurrence, action, interaction, transition, or state that may provide the materially relevant structural anchor for Event Formation. Possible Root Candidates may include: transaction initiation; execution instruction; service activation; resource commitment; production initiation; asset transfer initiation; machine execution; autonomous action; platform interaction; state transition; governed system trigger; coordinated multi-system initiation. Candidate status does not establish the root. Therefore: Root Candidate ≠ Qualified Event Formation Root. Operational Root Relevance A Root Candidate should be qualified only where it materially explains the structural emergence or organization of the formation. Relevant considerations may include whether the candidate: materially initiates the formation; creates the operational condition around which components assemble; establishes the principal structural transition represented by the formation; provides a coherent anchor for associated components; distinguishes the formation from surrounding activity; remains consistent with governed dependencies; can be sufficiently traced to the recognized occurrence. Root qualification must not be based solely on technical convenience. Technical Origin ≠ Operational Root Digital and enterprise systems often create several technical origins for the same activity. A transaction may produce: API requests; database entries; message-queue events; accounting records; audit logs; settlement instructions; system notifications. The earliest technical artifact does not automatically define the Event Formation Root. Therefore: Technical Origin ≠ Operational Root. EFRM must preserve the distinction between the system artifact that first records activity and the operational basis that materially anchors the event formation. Dependency ≠ Root EFDM may establish several material dependencies supporting the formation. EFRM must not automatically select one of those dependencies as the Event Formation Root. For example: an autonomous purchase may depend on prior delegation. The delegation may be essential. But the purchase formation may be operationally rooted in the autonomous execution of the purchase rather than the earlier delegation. Therefore: Formation Dependency ≠ Event Formation Root by Default. Trigger ≠ Root A technical or operational trigger may initiate a process without constituting the Event Formation Root. For example: a scheduled timer may trigger an autonomous system. A sensor may trigger a machine workflow. A notification may trigger an API call. A price threshold may trigger an algorithm. The trigger may explain why execution began. The root must explain what operational basis anchors the formation itself. Therefore: Trigger ≠ Event Formation Root by Default. Event Root ≠ Identity Origin EFRM does not determine where an actor, organization, machine, account, asset, agent, or digital identity originated. Identity origin belongs to the architecture governing identity and origin. Within the OOF architecture ecosystem, this space is governed principally through OBIDENITY® where applicable. EFRM may consume identity references where necessary. It does not redefine them. Therefore: Event Root ≠ Identity Origin. Root Association ≠ Provenance Governance. Event Root ≠ Ownership Origin The operational root of an event does not determine ownership. A transfer formation may be rooted in execution of a transfer. That does not determine who legally owned the transferred object before or after that execution. Therefore: Event Formation Root ≠ Ownership Determination. Event Root ≠ Authority Origin An event may be executed under delegated or inherited authority. The existence of that authority may be a dependency. The operational root may nevertheless be the execution itself. EFRM does not determine where the authority originated or whether it was legally valid. Therefore: Event Formation Root ≠ Authority Origin. Event Root ≠ Legal Causality The operational root provides a structural anchor. It does not establish legal causation. The operational point from which an event formation is organized may differ from the point considered legally causal under contract, tort, regulatory, tax, or other law. Therefore: Operational Root ≠ Legal Cause. Event Formation Root ≠ Legal Tax Point A particularly important TREGA™ boundary concerns taxation. EFRM may determine that a particular operational action or transition provides the most appropriate root for Event Formation. It must not determine that tax legally arises at that point. Tax legislation may establish a legally relevant tax point using rules concerning: supply; delivery; invoicing; payment; transfer; realization; recognition; residence; permanent establishment; jurisdiction-specific timing rules. Those determinations remain outside EFRM. Therefore: Event Formation Root ≠ Legal Tax Point. Root ≠ Event Start Time The Event Formation Root may be associated with a particular operational moment. That does not make EFRM the owner of Event Timing. TRETS later governs Event Timing. Therefore: Event Formation Root ≠ Event Start Time Determination. EFRM may preserve relevant temporal references without determining the governed Event Start, Completion, Duration, or Temporal Order. Root ≠ Event Location An operational root may occur through a particular system, facility, machine, platform, or geographic environment. EFRM does not determine governed Event Location. TRELS owns that space. Therefore: Root Association ≠ Event Location Determination. Single Root Formation Some formations have one sufficiently clear operational root. For example: Transfer Execution ↓ Governed Transfer Formation Where evidence and structure support one materially dominant operational anchor, EFRM may establish a Single Root Association. However, a single root should not be imposed merely for simplicity. Composite Root Formation Some event formations may emerge from several operational actions that jointly provide the structural basis of the formation. EFRM must therefore permit Composite Root Association where no single operational element legitimately represents the formation. Therefore: Multiple Root Elements ≠ Multiple Events by Default. A composite root does not itself determine whether one or multiple final events exist. Distributed Root Formation In distributed systems, no single technical system may contain the complete operational root. A cross-platform transaction may emerge through coordinated actions across: marketplace; payment network; service provider; autonomous agent; infrastructure; distributed ledger; external API. EFRM must permit a root to be represented across multiple operational sources where necessary. Therefore: Distributed Root Representation ≠ Multiple Event Roots by Default. Machine-Generated Root A machine-generated formation may possess a legitimate operational root even where no human initiates the immediate action. Possible examples include: automated resource purchase; machine-triggered replenishment; algorithmic settlement; robotic service execution; autonomous infrastructure allocation. Therefore: Human Initiation Is Not Required for Event Formation Root. However: Machine Execution ≠ Independent Event Root by Default. Material operational relevance remains required. Autonomous Event Formation Root Autonomous agents may create formations through independently executed operational decisions. EFRM may establish an autonomous execution as the Event Formation Root where it materially anchors the formation. This does not establish: autonomous legal personality; taxpayer status; legal responsibility; ownership; authority; tax liability. Therefore: Autonomous Event Root ≠ Autonomous Legal Responsibility. Root Conflict Different systems or evidence sources may identify different plausible operational roots. For example: a marketplace may identify order acceptance as the root. A payment system may identify payment authorization. A supplier system may identify service activation. EFRM must not silently collapse materially different representations. Possible states may include: Root Candidate Root Qualified Root Excluded Composite Root Root Conflict Root Unresolved Root Uncertainty Where the operational root cannot be sufficiently established, EFRM must preserve uncertainty. A root must not be invented merely because downstream systems require one. Therefore: Required Data Field ≠ Legitimately Established Root. Where necessary, the formation may remain: Root Unresolved until sufficient governance basis becomes available. Root Reconsideration New information may materially alter the basis on which the Event Formation Root was established. EFRM must permit governed reconsideration. Reconsideration must preserve: previous root association; previous basis; reason for reconsideration; new information; revised root association; temporal sequence of changes. Therefore: Root Reconsideration ≠ Historical Erasure. Root Traceability A governed Event Formation Root should remain traceable to its basis. Where materially required, traceability may preserve: root identifier; root candidate references; qualification basis; associated formation; relevant dependencies; source references; uncertainty; conflict; composite-root structure; revision history; reconsideration history. Traceability enables subsequent governance to understand why a particular operational root was associated with the formation. Root Independence from Event Boundary EFRM operates before TREBS determines final Event Boundary. The operational root may help subsequent Boundary governance understand the formation. It does not establish which elements ultimately belong inside or outside the event. Therefore: Event Formation Root ≠ Event Boundary. A root may anchor an event without defining its complete extent. Root Independence from Event Determination EFRM does not determine that a Tax-Relevant Event formally exists. TREDS later owns Governed Event Determination. EFRM establishes only one structural dimension required for formation. Therefore: Root Established ≠ Event Determined. Root Independence from Tax Rules Event Formation Root should remain governed independently of jurisdiction-specific tax interpretation. A subsequent change in tax law should not automatically require the operational root of the historical event to be rewritten. Therefore: Tax Rule Change ≠ Event Root Change by Default. The same governed Event Formation Root may support multiple downstream jurisdictional evaluations. Governance Requirements EFRM requires that: Root Candidates are evaluated against the governed Event Formation; root qualification is based on material operational relevance; the earliest record is not automatically treated as the root; technical origin is distinguished from operational root; dependencies are not automatically converted into roots; triggers are not automatically converted into roots; Event Root remains distinct from Identity Origin; Root Association remains distinct from provenance; Event Root remains distinct from ownership and authority origin; Event Root remains distinct from legal causality; Event Root remains distinct from legal tax point; Event Root does not determine Event Timing; Event Root does not determine Event Location; single, composite, and distributed roots may be represented where appropriate; machine and autonomous roots may be governed without requiring human initiation; root conflict remains visible; unresolved roots remain explicitly unresolved; root reconsideration preserves history; root decisions remain traceable; root establishment does not determine Event Boundary; root establishment does not determine legal taxability. Governance Logic EFRM applies focused root-association logic: What operational occurrence, action, interaction, transition, or state most materially anchors this Event Formation? Is the candidate an operational root or merely a dependency, trigger, technical record, or surrounding condition? Can one root be legitimately established, or is a composite or distributed root required? Are competing root representations materially conflicting? Is the root sufficiently established to proceed into Formation Integrity governance? The transformation is: Governed Event Formation + Governed Dependency Structure → Root Candidates → Operational Relevance → Root Qualification / Exclusion → Root Association → Governed Event Formation Root Association Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum EFRM implementation must be capable of: 1. receiving the Governed Event Formation Assembly and Governed Event Formation Dependency Structure; 2. identifying Root Candidates; 3. assessing operational root relevance; 4. distinguishing Root Candidates from dependencies; 5. distinguishing operational roots from technical origins and triggers; 6. qualifying or excluding Root Candidates; 7. establishing Single, Composite, or Distributed Root Associations where justified; 8. supporting machine-generated and autonomous Event Formation Roots; 9. identifying Root Conflict and Root Uncertainty; 10. preserving unresolved root states; 11. preserving root traceability; 12. supporting governed root reconsideration; 13. preventing root association from becoming Identity Origin, provenance, ownership, authority, legal causality, Event Timing, Event Location, Event Boundary, or legal tax point determination; 14. producing a Governed Event Formation Root Association; 15. transferring the governed formation, dependencies, and root association to EFIM for Event Formation Integrity governance. EFRM does not prescribe a particular transaction model, event schema, database structure, ERP architecture, AI model, distributed ledger, autonomous-system design, identity system, tax engine, legal causality model, or jurisdiction-specific taxation methodology. Governance Outputs EFRM may produce: Governed Event Formation Root Association — the principal Module output. Qualified Event Formation Root — a sufficiently established operational root. Excluded Root Candidate — a candidate determined not to represent the operational root. Composite Root Association — multiple operational elements jointly establishing the root. Distributed Root Association — a root represented across multiple operational sources or systems. Unresolved Event Formation Root — a materially relevant root question that remains unresolved. Root Conflict Indicator — materially incompatible root representations. Root Qualification Record — the governed basis for qualification or exclusion. Root Reconsideration Record — preserved history of a materially revised root. Root Traceability Reference — linkage between the root association and its governed basis. Critical Distinctions Root Candidate ≠ Qualified Event Formation Root. Candidate identification precedes qualification. Earliest Record ≠ Event Formation Root by Default. Chronological precedence does not establish operational root. Technical Origin ≠ Operational Root. System representation and operational formation are different layers. Formation Dependency ≠ Event Formation Root by Default. What an event depends upon is not necessarily where its formation is rooted. Trigger ≠ Event Formation Root by Default. A trigger may initiate execution without structurally anchoring the event. Event Root ≠ Identity Origin. EFRM does not govern identity origin. Root Association ≠ Provenance Governance. Operational association does not replace provenance governance. Event Formation Root ≠ Ownership Determination. Operational root does not determine ownership. Event Formation Root ≠ Authority Origin. Operational root does not determine authority. Operational Root ≠ Legal Cause. EFRM does not determine legal causality. Event Formation Root ≠ Legal Tax Point. Tax law owns legal tax timing. Event Formation Root ≠ Event Start Time Determination. TRETS owns Event Timing. Root Association ≠ Event Location Determination. TRELS owns Event Location. Multiple Root Elements ≠ Multiple Events by Default. Composite formation may still represent one event. Distributed Root Representation ≠ Multiple Event Roots by Default. Distributed technical representation does not determine event multiplicity. Human Initiation Is Not Required for Event Formation Root. Machine economies remain governable. Autonomous Event Root ≠ Autonomous Legal Responsibility. Operational autonomy does not determine legal status. Required Data Field ≠ Legitimately Established Root. System requirements cannot manufacture governance certainty. Root Reconsideration ≠ Historical Erasure. Governance history must remain preserved. Event Formation Root ≠ Event Boundary. TREBS owns final Event Boundary. Root Established ≠ Event Determined. TREDS owns Governed Event Determination. Tax Rule Change ≠ Event Root Change by Default. Operational reality remains independently governed. Enterprise Application EFRM addresses a recurring problem in enterprise, platform, financial, autonomous, and distributed systems: different systems often define the “origin” of the same event according to whichever technical record they control. A marketplace may use order creation. A payment system may use authorization. An ERP may use invoice creation. A logistics system may use dispatch. A cloud platform may use service activation. An autonomous system may use machine execution. A tax engine may later use a legally defined tax point. These are not automatically the same thing. EFRM establishes a separate governed concept: the Event Formation Root. This creates an operational anchor that can remain stable even when different systems, jurisdictions, accounting methods, or tax rules subsequently interpret the event differently. Use CasesUse Case 1 — Cross-Border Digital Transaction Has Five Competing “Origins” A global digital platform provides a service involving: customer order creation in Country A; payment authorization through infrastructure in Country B; automated service activation in Country C; cloud execution across several regions; invoicing from an entity in Country D. Each system records a different apparent starting point. A tax engine may additionally apply jurisdiction-specific rules to determine a legally relevant tax point. Without EFRM, the operational event may be reconstructed differently depending on which system or jurisdiction examines it. EFRM evaluates the formation independently of those downstream legal rules. It may determine that service activation provides the materially relevant operational root for the governed Event Formation while preserving order creation and payment authorization as separate components or dependencies where appropriate. That determination does not establish: tax jurisdiction; tax point; taxpayer; tax liability. The result is one stable operational Event Formation Root that multiple jurisdictional systems may subsequently evaluate under their own laws. One Governed Operational Root ↓ Multiple Possible Jurisdictional Interpretations. Use Case 2 — Autonomous AI Agent Creates Transaction Without Direct Human Initiation An enterprise AI agent continuously manages computational infrastructure. Based on operational demand, it autonomously: detects additional capacity requirements; selects a provider; negotiates within delegated parameters; reserves resources; activates infrastructure; initiates machine settlement. Multiple possible roots exist: the original human delegation; the AI's capacity decision; the provider selection; the reservation; infrastructure activation; settlement initiation. EFDM may identify the earlier delegation as a material dependency. EFRM must determine what operationally anchors the specific infrastructure acquisition formation. It may establish the autonomous resource commitment or infrastructure activation as the Event Formation Root without converting the earlier human delegation into the root merely because the autonomous action depended upon it. The result preserves a critical distinction: the authority that enabled autonomous action is not automatically the operational root of every event the agent subsequently creates. EFRM establishes the operational root. OBIDENITY® / ASGA™ may govern authority and autonomous execution. AGA™ may govern accountability. TRETS later governs timing. TRELS later governs location. Jurisdiction-specific tax systems determine legal tax consequences. Canonical Boundary EFRM governs the identification, differentiation, qualification, association, uncertainty, conflict, reconsideration, and traceability of the operational root of Event Formation. It does not identify original Formation Components, assemble those components, establish Formation Dependencies, determine complete Formation Integrity, determine Event Boundary, govern Identity Origin, provenance, ownership, authority, legal causality, Event Timing, Event Location, accountability, legal tax point, taxpayer status, Tax Jurisdiction, or jurisdiction-specific tax consequences. The handoff is: EFDM — Governed Event Formation Dependency Structure → EFRM — Governed Event Formation Root Association → EFIM — Event Formation Integrity Module Canonical Closing Statement Event Formation Root Module establishes the operational anchor of Tax-Relevant Event Formation by determining what occurrence, action, interaction, transition, or state materially roots a governed formation without confusing that root with technical origin, dependency, trigger, Identity Origin, provenance, ownership, authority, legal causality, Event Timing, Event Location, Event Boundary, or legal tax point. By permitting single, composite, distributed, machine-generated, and autonomous root associations while preserving conflict, uncertainty, traceability, and reconsideration, EFRM creates a stable operational reference for complex event formations before Formation Integrity is assessed. The Module therefore anchors what the event formation operationally grows from while preserving the foundational TREGA™ boundary: the operational root explains the formation — it does not determine the tax.

title: OOF™ The Event Location Correlation Module (ELCM) governs how the physical,
text: OOF™ The Event Location Correlation Module (ELCM) governs how the physical, The Event Location Correlation Module (ELCM) governs how the physical, OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: Tax-Relevant Event Location Standard (TRELS) Module: ELCM — Event Location Correlation Module Operational Layer: Event Location Correlation Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Event Location Correlation Origin ID: TREGA-TRELS-ELCM-005 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 31 August 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language Canonical Definition The Event Location Correlation Module (ELCM) governs how the physical, digital, distributed, temporal, and supporting spatial representations of a Tax-Relevant Event are correlated into a coherent, traceable, and jurisdiction-neutral final location representation of the governed event. ELCM operates after the relevant Event Location signals have been identified through ELIM, Physical Event Location has been governed through ELPM, Digital Event Location has been governed through ELDM, and Distributed Event Location has been governed through ELDSM. Its canonical task is: to correlate the legitimate spatial representations of the governed event into a coherent Governed Event Location without collapsing distinct physical, digital, distributed, or temporally changing locations into an artificial single point and without converting operational location correlation into Tax Jurisdiction determination. ELCM completes the spatial governance of the Tax-Relevant Event. The principal transition is: Governed Event Physical Location + Governed Event Digital Location + Governed Event Distributed Location + Governed Event Timing ↓ Governed Event Location Correlation ↓ Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event The resulting event is sufficiently governed in operational time and operational space to proceed to: TREPS — Tax-Relevant Event Participation Standard Operational Role An event may contain several legitimate spatial representations. It may possess: one or more physical locations; one or more digital locations; distributed locations; changing locations; simultaneous locations; sequential locations; machine locations; autonomous-system locations; infrastructure locations; and location signals with different levels of precision, confidence, and evidential strength. These locations may describe different spatial dimensions of the same event. Without correlation, downstream systems may incorrectly: select one location and discard others; treat different spatial dimensions as contradictions; confuse infrastructure location with Event Location; confuse participant location with Event Location; interpret distributed execution as multiple events; infer Tax Jurisdiction directly from operational geography; or convert uncertain spatial evidence into false geographic certainty. ELCM establishes the final governance layer that determines how already-governed location components relate to the same Tax-Relevant Event. Location Correlation ≠ Location Simplification. Its purpose is not to make complex spatial reality appear simple. Its purpose is to make complex spatial reality governable. Internal Flow Within TRELS, ELCM occupies the fifth and final operational position: ELIM — What spatial information legitimately belongs to the event? ↓ ELPM — What physical location materially belongs to the event? ↓ ELDM — What digital location materially belongs to the event? ↓ ELDSM — How is a genuinely distributed event spatially represented? ↓ ELCM — How are the legitimate event locations correlated into a coherent governed spatial representation? ↓ Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event ELCM receives: Governed Event Physical Location Governed Event Digital Location Governed Event Distributed Location together with relevant governed temporal information from TRETS. It produces: Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event This output completes TRELS and becomes the governed input to TREPS. Operational Space ELCM governs the final correlation of Event Location information. Its operational space includes: physical-digital location correlation; distributed-location correlation; temporal-spatial correlation; multi-location correlation; location-role correlation; location-type differentiation; location consistency; location coexistence; location hierarchy; location equivalence; location divergence; location conflict; location uncertainty; location precision; location confidence; location transitions; simultaneous location; sequential location; hybrid location; dynamic location; machine and autonomous location correlation; spatial evidence correlation; location correction; location continuity; location traceability; final Event Location representation; and readiness for Event Participation governance. Operational Scope ELCM shall support final spatial correlation for events involving: physical commerce; digital commerce; cross-border transactions; cloud services; digital platforms; financial infrastructure; payment systems; distributed computing; AI systems; AI agents; autonomous systems; robotics; machine-to-machine activity; IoT systems; telecommunications; industrial automation; logistics; supply chains; manufacturing; digital assets; distributed ledgers; infrastructure networks; hybrid physical-digital services; and future decentralized or machine-mediated economic environments. 1. Location Correlation Readiness ELCM shall determine whether sufficient governed spatial information exists to begin final location correlation. Correlation readiness may include: Governed Event Physical Location; Governed Event Digital Location; Governed Event Distributed Location; relevant Event Timing; Event Boundary; spatial evidence; spatial precision; uncertainty states; conflict states; and traceability references. Not every event requires every location type. Therefore: Missing Location Type ≠ Correlation Failure by Default. A purely physical event may legitimately possess no Digital Event Location. A purely digital event may possess no meaningful Physical Event Location. A distributed event may require several spatial components. ELCM shall correlate only spatial dimensions legitimately belonging to the event. 2. Location Component Identification ELCM shall identify the governed spatial components requiring correlation. Each component shall remain distinguishable by type and operational role. Possible components include: physical; digital; distributed; hybrid; sequential; simultaneous; dynamic; machine; autonomous; infrastructural; or qualified spatial representations. Correlation ≠ Erasure of Spatial Type. Physical and digital locations shall not lose their governance meaning merely because they are incorporated into a final Event Location representation. 3. Physical-Digital Correlation Where both physical and digital locations materially belong to the event, ELCM shall establish their operational relationship. For example: Physical Machine Location ↔ Edge Environment ↔ Cloud Execution Environment or: Physical Service Delivery Location ↔ Digital Platform Environment The resulting representation may legitimately contain both dimensions. Physical Location ≠ Digital Location. Physical-Digital Correlation ≠ Requirement to Select One. 4. Distributed Location Correlation Where ELDSM establishes a Governed Event Distributed Location, ELCM shall correlate its constitutive spatial components into the final Event Location representation. ELCM shall preserve: distributed structure; component roles; temporal association; supported precision; uncertainty; conflict; and traceability. Distributed Location Correlation ≠ Geographic Consolidation by Default. A distributed event shall remain distributed where that is the legitimate operational representation. 5. Temporal-Spatial Correlation Event Location may change throughout the governed Event Timing. ELCM shall support correlation such as: T1 ↓ Location A T2 ↓ Location B T3 ↓ Location B + Digital Environment C T4 ↓ Distributed Locations D/E/F Temporal-spatial correlation shall preserve the relationship between when and where without changing ownership boundaries. TRETS owns Event Timing. TRELS owns Event Location. ELCM correlates governed spatial representation with the temporal structure necessary to represent location correctly. Temporal-Spatial Correlation ≠ Event Relationship Determination. 6. Sequential Location Correlation Where an event moves through several locations sequentially, ELCM shall preserve that sequence. For example: Location A ↓ Location B ↓ Location C ELCM shall not automatically select the first, last, longest, or commercially preferred location as the definitive Event Location. First Location ≠ Primary Event Location by Default. Final Location ≠ Primary Event Location by Default. Longest-Duration Location ≠ Primary Event Location by Default. 7. Simultaneous Location Correlation An event may legitimately occur across several locations simultaneously. ELCM shall represent simultaneous spatial states without treating them as contradictory. Different Concurrent Locations ≠ Location Conflict by Default. Simultaneous distributed activity can be a legitimate property of one bounded event. 8. Dynamic Location Correlation Events involving mobile machines, vehicles, devices, autonomous systems, migrating workloads, or changing infrastructure may possess dynamic spatial states. ELCM shall preserve materially relevant changes without forcing every movement into a separate event. Dynamic Location ≠ Unstable Governance. Location Change ≠ New Event by Default. 9. Location Role Correlation Different locations may perform different operational roles. ELCM may classify location roles such as: constitutive; execution; physical performance; digital execution; coordination; processing; transitional; supporting; infrastructure; storage; observation; recording; or other justified operational roles. Role classification shall prevent unlike locations from being treated as equivalent merely because all are associated with the event. Location Association ≠ Location Equivalence. 10. Constitutive and Supporting Location Correlation ELCM shall preserve the distinction between locations constituting the event and locations merely supporting it. A supporting data center, payment processor, logging environment, corporate office, or routing node may be spatially relevant without constituting Event Location. Supporting Location ≠ Constitutive Event Location. A supporting location shall not be elevated to constitutive status merely because it is easier to identify. 11.
