Location Hierarchy Spatial information may exist at several levels: Coordinates ↓ Facility ↓ City ↓ Region ↓ Country or: Execution Instance ↓ Availability Zone ↓ Cloud Region ↓ Distributed Cloud Environment ELCM shall preserve legitimate hierarchical relationships where relevant. However: Higher Geographic Level ≠ More Authoritative Location. Country-Level Classification ≠ Complete Event Location by Default. The final representation shall preserve the precision justified by operational evidence. 12. Location Equivalence Different location records may refer to the same operational place. For example: coordinates and facility address; facility identifier and industrial site; cloud-region code and named cloud region; machine identifier and known machine installation location. ELCM may establish operational equivalence where supported. Different Location Representations ≠ Different Locations by Default. Equivalence shall be evidence-based and traceable. 13. Location Divergence Two legitimate locations may differ because they describe different spatial dimensions of the same event. For example: Physical execution: Switzerland Digital execution: Germany This is not necessarily a conflict. Location Divergence ≠ Location Conflict by Default. ELCM shall preserve legitimate divergence where operational reality supports it. 14. Location Conflict Location Conflict exists where two or more location claims purport to describe the same spatial property of the event but cannot be reconciled under available evidence. Examples may include: incompatible physical-location evidence; conflicting device-location records; contradictory infrastructure-location records; inconsistent geolocation sources; or incompatible event-location claims. ELCM shall distinguish conflict from legitimate multi-location reality. Multiple Locations ≠ Conflict by Default. Contradictory Claims About the Same Location Property = Potential Location Conflict. 15. Conflict Isolation A conflict affecting one spatial component shall not automatically invalidate the entire Event Location representation. For example: Physical Location may be established; Digital Location may be established; one cloud-region component may remain conflicted. ELCM shall isolate the unresolved component. Partial Spatial Conflict ≠ Total Spatial Invalidity. 16. Location Uncertainty ELCM shall preserve uncertainty where available evidence does not support exact spatial determination. Possible representations include: exact; bounded; approximate; regional; multi-region; distributed; inferred; qualified; partially known; conflicted; or unresolved. Location Uncertainty ≠ Permission to Manufacture Geographic Certainty. Where the event can only legitimately be situated at regional level, ELCM shall not create artificial city-level or facility-level precision. 17. Location Precision ELCM shall maintain the highest spatial precision legitimately supported by evidence and operational relevance. However: Technical Location Precision ≠ Governance Accuracy. Exact GPS coordinates can be irrelevant or misleading. A broad cloud region may be the most legitimate representation of a digital component. Precision shall therefore be governed, not merely inherited from source systems. 18. Location Confidence ELCM may associate confidence with spatial components where useful. Confidence shall reflect governance quality of the location representation, not the convenience of the source. A highly precise but weakly supported signal may legitimately receive lower confidence than a broader but strongly evidenced location. Precision ≠ Confidence. Confidence ≠ Legal Certainty. 19. Spatial Evidence Correlation ELCM shall preserve the evidence supporting each material spatial conclusion. Evidence may include: operational system records; machine records; infrastructure records; device data; network information; physical records; transaction data; platform records; cloud metadata; logistics records; or other governed evidence sources. ADIT® governs evidence and auditability. ELCM governs how legitimate spatial evidence supports Event Location correlation. 20. Infrastructure Location Correlation Infrastructure locations may support an event without defining it. ELCM shall distinguish: Infrastructure Location from: Event Location Examples include: server facilities; cloud regions; network nodes; storage facilities; payment infrastructure; data centers; telecommunications infrastructure; or replicated systems. Infrastructure Location ≠ Event Location by Default. 21. Server Location Correlation A server may process part of an event. That does not automatically make server geography the definitive location of the event. Server Location ≠ Event Location by Default. Where server execution is materially constitutive, it may form one component of Digital or Distributed Event Location. It shall not automatically displace other legitimate locations. 22. IP Location Correlation IP-based geolocation may provide useful spatial evidence. However: IP Address Location ≠ Event Location by Default. IP Geolocation ≠ Participant Residence. IP Geolocation ≠ Tax Jurisdiction. ELCM may use IP-derived information only at the level of confidence and precision justified by the evidence. 23. Device Location Correlation Device location may contribute to Event Location where the device materially participates in the event. However: Device Location ≠ Event Location by Default. A device may be remote from: service execution; value creation; physical performance; participant residence; organizational location; or other event components. ELCM shall preserve these distinctions. 24. Participant Location Correlation Event participants may have locations relevant to downstream analysis. However, Participant Location is not automatically Event Location. TREPS governs Event Participation. OBIDENITY® governs origin-bound identity. Therefore: Participant Location ≠ Event Location by Default. Participant Residence ≠ Event Location. Event Location ≠ Taxpayer Residence. ELCM shall not determine participant identity, residence, taxpayer status, or legal presence. 25. Corporate Location Correlation Corporate headquarters, registered offices, operational offices, subsidiaries, branches, or management locations may be associated with an event. Their existence does not automatically establish Event Location. Corporate Headquarters ≠ Event Location by Default. Registered Office ≠ Event Location by Default. Corporate Presence ≠ Event Location by Default. Legal consequences associated with corporate presence remain outside TREGA™. 26. Autonomous-System Location Correlation Autonomous systems may operate across: physical machines; edge infrastructure; cloud services; external APIs; distributed databases; other autonomous agents; and digital platforms. ELCM shall correlate materially constitutive spatial components without attempting to create a fictional legal residence for the autonomous system. Autonomous System Location ≠ Legal Residence. Autonomous Execution Geography ≠ Tax Residence. 27. AI Agent Location Correlation AI-agent activity may have no meaningful single physical location. The agent may operate through a distributed orchestration environment while invoking models, tools, services, databases, and physical systems in different places. ELCM shall permit: Distributed Agent Operational Location where that representation best reflects the event. AI Agent Location ≠ Owner Location. AI Agent Location ≠ Developer Location. AI Agent Location ≠ Tax Jurisdiction. 28. Machine-to-Machine Location Correlation Machine-to-machine events may involve several physical machines and multiple digital environments. ELCM shall correlate these spatial components without requiring human geography to define the event. For example: Machine A — Physical Location A Machine B — Physical Location B Edge Controller — Digital Environment C Cloud Orchestrator — Digital Environment D may jointly form the governed spatial representation. Machine Event Geography ≠ Human Participant Geography. 29. Platform Location Correlation A digital platform may operate globally while an individual event uses only a limited subset of its infrastructure. ELCM shall correlate event-specific locations rather than the entire geographic footprint of the platform. Platform Presence ≠ Event Presence. Global Platform Infrastructure ≠ Global Event Location. 30. Distributed Ledger Location Correlation Distributed ledger infrastructure may contain nodes across many jurisdictions. ELCM shall not treat every node maintaining, validating, observing, or replicating ledger state as a constitutive location of every event. Ledger Distribution ≠ Event Distribution by Default. Only operationally material spatial components shall enter the final Event Location representation. 31. Location Correlation and Event Boundary ELCM shall remain within the Event Boundary established under TREBS. It shall not expand the event merely because additional spatial information exists. Spatial Association ≠ Event Inclusion by Default. A location outside the governed Event Boundary shall not become part of Event Location merely through technical, commercial, or organizational association. 32. Location Correlation and Event Timing TRETS provides the temporal structure necessary to determine when particular spatial states belong to the event. ELCM may correlate those spatial states with time. It shall not redefine Event Start, Event Completion, Event Duration, or Event Temporal Order. Location Correlation ≠ Timing Governance. TRETS governs when. TRELS governs where. 33. Location Correlation and Event Participation The next Parent Standard, TREPS, determines who or what participated in the event and in what governed role. ELCM shall therefore preserve spatial information without prematurely converting location into participation. Presence at Event Location ≠ Event Participation by Default. Event Participation ≠ Taxpayer Determination. 34. Location Correlation and Value Association TRVAS subsequently governs which governed value result belongs to the event. ELCM shall not infer value ownership, value origin, value state, value movement, value recognition, or value allocation from location alone. Value at a Location ≠ Event Value Association by Default. VFM® governs what happened to value. TREGA™ later governs which governed value result belongs to the event. 35. Location Correlation and Event Relationships Spatial proximity or shared location may indicate that events warrant further relationship analysis. It does not establish the relationship. Same Location ≠ Same Event. Same Location ≠ Event Relationship by Default. Spatial Proximity ≠ Causation. TRERLS governs Event Relationships. 36. Location Correlation and Event Determination ELCM prepares spatially governed information for later TREGA stages. It does not determine whether the event is legally taxable. Governed Event Location ≠ Taxability Determination. Spatial Completeness ≠ Legal Taxability. TREDS governs Tax-Relevant Event Determination. Jurisdiction-specific systems subsequently govern legal tax consequences. 37. Event Location Correction Final Event Location correlation may require correction as evidence improves or errors are identified. ELCM shall preserve: previous spatial state; corrected spatial state; correction reason; supporting evidence; timestamp; governance authority; and traceability. Event Location Correction ≠ Historical Erasure. 38. Event Location Continuity ELCM shall preserve continuity of spatial representation across material location changes. A governed event may move from: Location State 1 ↓ Location State 2 ↓ Location State 3 without losing its Event Identity. Location Continuity ≠ Spatial Immutability. The location representation may change while the same bounded event continues. 39. Final Event Location Representation ELCM shall construct the final operational location representation appropriate to the event. Possible representations include: Single Physical Location Single Digital Location Physical + Digital Location Sequential Multi-Location Simultaneous Multi-Location Distributed Physical Location Distributed Digital Location Hybrid Distributed Location Dynamic Location Qualified Location Partially Resolved Location No Legitimate Single Primary Location The final representation shall reflect operational reality rather than downstream schema convenience. 40. Single-Location Reduction Control ELCM shall prevent unjustified reduction of a complex event into a single location. A downstream system may require a country code or one location field. Such technical requirements shall not redefine the governed event. Single Database Location Field ≠ Single Event Location Reality. Where necessary, downstream mappings may derive jurisdiction-specific representations from the governed event layer while the canonical TREGA™ record preserves the richer operational reality. 41. Location Correlation and Tax Jurisdiction ELCM shall maintain a strict boundary between operational Event Location and legal Tax Jurisdiction. ELCM does not determine: Tax Jurisdiction; tax nexus; residence; permanent establishment; significant economic presence; source jurisdiction; place of supply; legal situs; customs origin; taxable presence; taxing rights; profit allocation; revenue allocation; tax-base allocation; transfer-pricing treatment; Legal Tax Point; Tax Period; Tax Liability; or jurisdiction-specific reporting obligations. The foundational distinction is: Event Location ≠ Tax Jurisdiction. Related distinctions include: Operational Location ≠ Legal Tax Situs. Digital Location ≠ Legal Place of Supply. Server Location ≠ Tax Nexus. Data Center Location ≠ Permanent Establishment by Default. Participant Location ≠ Taxpayer Residence. Distributed Location ≠ Distributed Taxing Rights. Location Correlation ≠ Jurisdiction Determination. 42. Jurisdiction-Ready Spatial Representation The output of ELCM shall be capable of supporting multiple downstream jurisdictional evaluations without being rewritten for each jurisdiction. The canonical model is: One Governed Event ↓ One Governed Temporal-Spatial Reality ↓ Multiple Jurisdictional Evaluations Jurisdiction A may evaluate the physical component. Jurisdiction B may apply digital-service rules. Jurisdiction C may apply participant, source, nexus, residence, or place-of-supply rules. These legal evaluations may differ. The underlying governed event should not. Jurisdiction-Ready ≠ Jurisdiction-Determined. 43. Governance States ELCM may assign states including: Correlation Ready Required governed spatial inputs are sufficiently available. Correlation Under Governance Spatial components are being correlated. Correlation Established Material spatial components are coherently correlated. Correlation Single-Location One location legitimately represents the event. Correlation Multi-Location Several locations legitimately represent the event. Correlation Distributed Distributed representation is required. Correlation Hybrid Physical and digital spatial dimensions jointly represent the event. Correlation Dynamic The event's legitimate spatial state changes materially over time. Correlation Partial A legitimate spatial representation exists but some components remain unresolved. Correlation Qualified The representation requires explicit qualification. Correlation Conflicted Material spatial evidence remains conflicting. Correlation Unresolved Available evidence cannot support a legitimate final correlation. Spatially Situated The event has achieved sufficient location governance to proceed to Event Participation governance. 44. Governance Requirements ELCM implementations shall: consume governed spatial outputs from ELIM, ELPM, ELDM, and ELDSM as applicable; consume relevant governed Event Timing from TRETS; identify spatial components requiring correlation; preserve location types; preserve physical-digital distinctions; preserve distributed spatial structure; support temporal-spatial correlation; support sequential location; support simultaneous location; support dynamic location; distinguish constitutive from supporting locations; distinguish divergence from conflict; support location hierarchy; support location equivalence; preserve spatial precision; preserve uncertainty; preserve confidence; isolate conflicts; preserve evidence references; preserve correction history; preserve location continuity; preserve Event Boundary; prevent artificial single-location reduction; prevent participant location from becoming Event Location by default; prevent infrastructure location from becoming Event Location by default; prevent Event Location from becoming Tax Jurisdiction; maintain jurisdiction neutrality; produce a traceable final Event Location representation; and produce a Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event suitable for TREPS. 45. Governance Logic ELCM follows the canonical logic: Governed Physical Location + Governed Digital Location + Governed Distributed Location + Governed Event Timing ↓ identify legitimate spatial components ↓ correlate physical, digital, distributed, sequential, simultaneous, hybrid, and dynamic spatial states ↓ distinguish coexistence, equivalence, divergence, and conflict ↓ preserve precision, uncertainty, confidence, continuity, correction, and traceability ↓ establish final Governed Event Location ↓ produce Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event. The governing rule is: Preserve spatial reality first. Permit legal interpretation later. 46. Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum ELCM implementation should support: Governed Event Reference Reference to the bounded Tax-Relevant Event. Location Correlation Identifier Unique identifier for the final location-correlation record. Physical Location Reference Governed ELPM output where applicable. Digital Location Reference Governed ELDM output where applicable. Distributed Location Reference Governed ELDSM output where applicable. Temporal Reference Relevant governed TRETS information. Location Components Material spatial components belonging to the event. Location Type Physical, digital, distributed, hybrid, dynamic, or other legitimate type. Location Role Operational role of each spatial component. Constitutive State Whether the location materially constitutes the event. Temporal Association Relevant time or interval associated with each location. Location Relationship Operational spatial relationship among components. Location Equivalence State Whether different records describe the same operational place. Location Divergence State Whether legitimate spatial dimensions differ. Location Conflict State Whether incompatible claims remain. Location Precision Supported geographic or digital precision. Location Uncertainty Known spatial uncertainty. Location Confidence Governance confidence where applicable. Primary Location State Primary, non-primary, no-primary, or unresolved where relevant. Evidence References Evidence supporting correlation. Correction History Material corrections. Traceability Reference Governance history. Jurisdiction-Neutrality State Confirmation that no jurisdiction-specific tax conclusion has been embedded. Governance State Current ELCM state. Handoff State Readiness for TREPS. 47. Governance Outputs ELCM may produce: Location Correlation Readiness Record; Spatial Component Register; Physical-Digital Correlation Record; Distributed Location Correlation Record; Temporal-Spatial Correlation Record; Sequential Location Record; Simultaneous Location Record; Dynamic Location Record; Location Role Record; Constitutive Location Record; Supporting Location Record; Location Hierarchy Record; Location Equivalence Record; Location Divergence Record; Location Conflict Record; Location Uncertainty Record; Location Precision Record; Location Confidence Record; Spatial Evidence Correlation Record; Location Correction Record; Location Continuity Record; Final Event Location Representation; Jurisdiction-Neutrality Record; and the principal TRELS output: Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event This output becomes the governed input to: TREPS — Tax-Relevant Event Participation Standard48. Critical Distinctions Location Correlation ≠ Location Simplification Missing Location Type ≠ Correlation Failure Correlation ≠ Erasure of Spatial Type Physical Location ≠ Digital Location Physical-Digital Correlation ≠ Requirement to Select One Distributed Location Correlation ≠ Geographic Consolidation Temporal-Spatial Correlation ≠ Event Relationship Determination First Location ≠ Primary Event Location Final Location ≠ Primary Event Location Longest-Duration Location ≠ Primary Event Location Different Concurrent Locations ≠ Location Conflict Dynamic Location ≠ Unstable Governance Location Change ≠ New Event Location Association ≠ Location Equivalence Supporting Location ≠ Constitutive Event Location Higher Geographic Level ≠ More Authoritative Location Country-Level Classification ≠ Complete Event Location Different Location Representations ≠ Different Locations Location Divergence ≠ Location Conflict Multiple Locations ≠ Conflict Partial Spatial Conflict ≠ Total Spatial Invalidity Location Uncertainty ≠ Permission to Manufacture Geographic Certainty Technical Location Precision ≠ Governance Accuracy Precision ≠ Confidence Confidence ≠ Legal Certainty Infrastructure Location ≠ Event Location Server Location ≠ Event Location IP Address Location ≠ Event Location IP Geolocation ≠ Participant Residence Device Location ≠ Event Location Participant Location ≠ Event Location Participant Residence ≠ Event Location Event Location ≠ Taxpayer Residence Corporate Headquarters ≠ Event Location Registered Office ≠ Event Location Autonomous System Location ≠ Legal Residence AI Agent Location ≠ Owner Location AI Agent Location ≠ Developer Location Machine Event Geography ≠ Human Participant Geography Platform Presence ≠ Event Presence Global Platform Infrastructure ≠ Global Event Location Ledger Distribution ≠ Event Distribution Spatial Association ≠ Event Inclusion Location Correlation ≠ Timing Governance Presence at Event Location ≠ Event Participation Value at a Location ≠ Event Value Association Same Location ≠ Same Event Spatial Proximity ≠ Causation Governed Event Location ≠ Taxability Determination Spatial Completeness ≠ Legal Taxability Event Location Correction ≠ Historical Erasure Location Continuity ≠ Spatial Immutability Single Database Location Field ≠ Single Event Location Reality Event Location ≠ Tax Jurisdiction Operational Location ≠ Legal Tax Situs Digital Location ≠ Legal Place of Supply Server Location ≠ Tax Nexus Data Center Location ≠ Permanent Establishment by Default Distributed Location ≠ Distributed Taxing Rights Location Correlation ≠ Jurisdiction Determination Jurisdiction-Ready ≠ Jurisdiction-Determined 49. Enterprise Application ELCM provides the final spatial-governance layer between complex operational reality and jurisdiction-specific taxation infrastructure. A generalized enterprise implementation may operate as: ERP + Commerce + Banking + Digital Platform + Cloud Infrastructure + AI Agents + Autonomous Machines + Operational Systems ↓ TREGA™ Event Layer ↓ TRETS Governed Event Timing ↓ TRELS Governed Event Location ↓ ELCM Location Correlation ↓ Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event ↓ TREPS Event Participation ↓ Subsequent TREGA Governance ↓ Jurisdiction-Specific Tax Engines This allows organizations to maintain one governed operational representation of the event while multiple jurisdictions independently evaluate its legal tax implications. The operational record therefore does not need to be reconstructed differently for every tax regime. One governed event reality can support multiple legitimate legal interpretations without allowing those interpretations to rewrite the event itself. 50. Use Case 1 — Global Cloud and AI Service Event A corporate customer initiates a complex AI service from Switzerland. The service is orchestrated through a European cloud region. Model inference is executed through several computational environments. A specialist external API processes part of the workload in another region. Data is retrieved from distributed infrastructure. An autonomous agent coordinates the workflow. The final digital output is delivered to a business system operating from Switzerland. ELPM may identify relevant physical components. ELDM establishes materially relevant digital environments. ELDSM determines that the event possesses a legitimate distributed digital structure. ELCM correlates these spatial components with the governed Event Timing. It does not force the event into: customer location; cloud-provider headquarters; one server location; billing address; model-provider country; or one arbitrary country code. The result is a Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event preserving the actual operational geography. Different jurisdictions may subsequently evaluate place of supply, nexus, source, residence, or other tax rules independently. ELCM preserves one governed operational reality even where several tax systems may later interpret that reality differently. 51. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Machine-to-Machine Economic Event An autonomous industrial machine in Country A detects that a component is required. An AI agent operating through distributed infrastructure identifies a supplier. A machine in Country B manufactures the component. Payment authorization occurs through infrastructure in Country C. An autonomous logistics system transports the component. Final installation occurs at an industrial site in Country A. The event contains physical, digital, machine, autonomous, distributed, and changing spatial components. Selecting the buyer machine, seller machine, payment infrastructure, AI execution environment, logistics location, or corporate headquarters as the sole Event Location would materially distort the event. ELCM correlates the legitimate spatial components and their temporal associations into one governed representation. The resulting event can subsequently be evaluated by the relevant jurisdiction-specific tax systems. ELCM itself does not decide: which jurisdiction taxes the event; whether a permanent establishment exists; where legal place of supply lies; which participant is a taxpayer; how tax base is allocated; or whether tax is legally due. The machine economy may be spatially distributed while the governed event remains methodologically coherent. 52. Canonical Boundary ELCM owns the final correlation of governed Event Location information within TRELS, including physical-digital correlation, distributed-location correlation, temporal-spatial correlation, sequential and simultaneous location, dynamic location, location roles, constitutive/supporting distinctions, location hierarchy, equivalence, divergence, conflict, uncertainty, precision, confidence, evidence correlation, correction, continuity, final Event Location representation, and construction of the Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event. ELCM does not own Event Location Signal Identification, which belongs to ELIM. It does not own Physical Event Location, which belongs to ELPM. It does not own Digital Event Location, which belongs to ELDM. It does not own Distributed Event Location, which belongs to ELDSM. It does not own Event Timing, which belongs to TRETS. It does not own Event Participation, which belongs to TREPS. It does not own origin-bound identity, which belongs to OBIDENITY®. It does not own Value Lifecycle governance, which belongs to VFM®. It does not own semantic Event Relationships, which belong to TRERLS. It does not own Tax-Relevant Event Determination, which belongs to TREDS. It does not determine Tax Jurisdiction, tax nexus, permanent establishment, significant economic presence, tax residence, source jurisdiction, place of supply, legal situs, customs origin, taxable presence, taxing rights, profit allocation, revenue allocation, tax-base allocation, transfer-pricing treatment, Legal Tax Point, Tax Period, taxability, Tax Liability, tax rate, reporting obligation, or any jurisdiction-specific tax consequence. The complete TRELS internal handoff is: ELIM — Governed Event Location Signal Set ↓ ELPM — Governed Event Physical Location ↓ ELDM — Governed Event Digital Location ↓ ELDSM — Governed Event Distributed Location ↓ ELCM — Governed Event Location Correlation ↓ Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event ↓ TREPS — Tax-Relevant Event Participation Standard Canonical Closing Statement ELCM completes the spatial governance of the Tax-Relevant Event by correlating its legitimate physical, digital, distributed, dynamic, and temporally associated locations into one coherent representation without erasing the complexity of operational reality. A governed event does not require one location. It requires a spatial representation that truthfully reflects where the event occurred. ELCM determines how the locations of the event fit together — not which jurisdiction acquires the legal right to tax it. TRELS governs where the event occurred as governed operational reality — not where tax law decides that the event is taxable. TREGA™ governs the event. The jurisdiction governs the tax.

title: OOF™ The Event Digital Location Module (ELDM) governs how materially relevant
text: OOF™ The Event Digital Location Module (ELDM) governs how materially relevant The Event Digital Location Module (ELDM) governs how materially relevant OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: Tax-Relevant Event Location Standard (TRELS) Module: ELDM — Event Digital Location Module Operational Layer: Event Digital Location Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Event Digital Location Origin ID: TREGA-TRELS-ELDM-003 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 31 August 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language Canonical Definition The Event Digital Location Module (ELDM) governs how materially relevant digital spatial signals associated with a Tax-Relevant Event are identified, differentiated, evaluated, qualified, and assembled into a governed representation of where the event digitally occurs, is executed, is instantiated, is processed, or materially manifests within digital operational environments. ELDM operates on the Governed Event Location Signal Set established by ELIM and alongside the Governed Event Physical Location established by ELPM. Its canonical task is: to establish a coherent, traceable, and operationally justified Governed Event Digital Location without allowing IP addresses, server positions, cloud regions, user-device locations, platform registrations, network routes, corporate addresses, or jurisdiction-specific legal rules to become the digital location of the event merely because they contain geographic information. The principal transition is: Governed Event Location Signal Set + Governed Event Physical Location ↓ Governed Event Digital Location ELDM governs digital Event Location. It does not determine Tax Jurisdiction, digital tax nexus, legal place of supply, or any jurisdiction-specific tax consequence. Operational Role Digital events frequently have no single obvious geographic position. A transaction may be initiated from a device in one country, authenticated by infrastructure in another, processed across several cloud regions, executed through a platform operated from another jurisdiction, recorded in distributed databases, and consumed by a user located elsewhere. An AI agent may initiate and complete an economic operation without a human being physically present at the location where computational execution occurs. A machine may act physically in one country while its decision logic, orchestration, data processing, and supporting services operate across globally distributed digital infrastructure. Traditional information systems frequently represent such events through whichever geographic field is easiest to obtain: IP address; billing country; user profile country; server region; platform registration; device location; merchant address; or infrastructure location. ELDM prevents these signals from being treated as authoritative by default. Its purpose is to govern the digital spatial reality of the event. Internal Flow Within TRELS, ELDM occupies the third operational position: ELIM — What spatial information legitimately belongs to the event? ↓ ELPM — What physical location materially belongs to the event? ↓ ELDM — What digital location materially belongs to the event? ↓ ELDSM — How is a genuinely distributed event spatially represented? ↓ ELCM — How are relevant event locations correlated into a governed spatial representation? ↓ Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event ELDM receives: Governed Event Location Signal Set + Governed Event Physical Location and produces: Governed Event Digital Location for subsequent distributed-location governance. Operational Space ELDM governs the digital spatial representation of the Tax-Relevant Event. Its operational space includes: digital execution environments; platform environments; application environments; cloud environments; cloud regions; cloud availability zones; edge environments; network environments; API environments; digital service environments; virtualized infrastructure; distributed computing environments; digital transaction environments; machine-to-machine environments; AI-agent environments; autonomous-system environments; device-associated digital locations; server-associated locations; infrastructure-associated locations; network-associated locations; digital endpoint locations; digital resource locations; logical locations; digital-location transitions; digital-location precision; digital-location uncertainty; digital-location conflict; digital-location continuity; and digital-location traceability. ELDM governs digital location only to the extent required to represent the operational digital reality of the event. Operational Scope ELDM shall support digital-location governance for: e-commerce; digital marketplaces; cloud services; SaaS; digital content; streaming; financial technology; digital payments; banking systems; API transactions; telecommunications; online platforms; distributed applications; AI services; AI agents; autonomous systems; machine-to-machine transactions; robotics; IoT; edge computing; digital assets; virtualized infrastructure; hybrid physical-digital systems; and future machine economies. ELDM shall support both digitally centralized and digitally distributed events. 1. Digital Location Candidate Identification ELDM shall identify digital-location candidates from the Governed Event Location Signal Set. Candidates may include: server location; cloud region; availability zone; edge node; network endpoint; API endpoint; device location; IP-derived location; application environment; platform environment; execution environment; processing environment; storage environment; digital resource location; logical service location; or other materially relevant digital spatial references. A candidate shall not become Governed Event Digital Location merely because it is technically observable. Digital Location Candidate ≠ Governed Event Digital Location. 2. Constitutive Digital Location ELDM shall determine whether a digital environment materially participates in the constitution of the governed event. A Constitutive Digital Location is a digital environment in which activity forming part of the event itself is executed, instantiated, processed, or materially realized. This distinction prevents infrastructure merely supporting the event from being mistaken for the digital location of the event. Supporting Digital Infrastructure ≠ Constitutive Digital Location by Default. 3. Digital Execution Location Where an event involves computational execution, ELDM shall govern the digital environment in which material event execution occurs. Execution may occur through: application servers; cloud workloads; edge systems; platform services; distributed applications; AI inference systems; autonomous agents; smart-contract environments; machine controllers; or other computational environments. Digital execution shall be governed according to its role in the event rather than the geographic location of infrastructure alone. Infrastructure Geography ≠ Digital Event Location by Default. 4. Server Location A server may participate in the event, support the event, store event data, authenticate participants, or merely route information. ELDM shall determine the operational significance of the server before its location is attributed to the event. Server Location ≠ Event Digital Location by Default. A server physically located in a country does not, by itself, establish that the digital event operationally occurred in that country. Nor does it establish taxation authority. 5. Cloud Region Location Cloud platforms frequently distribute workloads across regions, availability zones, and dynamic infrastructure. A cloud region may be materially relevant where event execution is deliberately or operationally bound to that region. However: Cloud Region ≠ Event Digital Location by Default. Cloud Region ≠ Tax Jurisdiction. Infrastructure allocation decisions made by a cloud provider shall not automatically redefine the operational spatial identity of the event. 6. Availability Zone and Infrastructure Instance Location Cloud workloads may migrate between availability zones, physical hosts, containers, virtual machines, or other infrastructure components. ELDM shall distinguish the operational digital environment from transient infrastructure implementation. Infrastructure Instance Location ≠ Event Location by Default. The movement of a workload between infrastructure instances shall not automatically constitute a change in the governed digital location of the event. 7. Edge Computing Location Edge systems may perform material event processing near devices, machines, users, infrastructure, or physical operations. Where edge execution forms a constitutive part of the event, ELDM may govern the edge environment as a relevant Digital Event Location. However: Edge Node Location ≠ Complete Event Digital Location by Default. An edge node may represent one component of a broader distributed digital event. 8. User Device Location A user's device may provide relevant spatial information. However, the device may be: mobile; remotely controlled; connected through VPN; using roaming services; operating through proxies; shared; automated; or physically separated from the event's principal digital execution. Therefore: User Device Location ≠ Event Digital Location by Default. The operational role of the device shall be established before its location is attributed to the event. 9. IP Address Location IP addresses may provide evidence about network connectivity. They shall not be treated as definitive Event Location. IP geolocation may be affected by: VPNs; proxies; corporate networks; carrier routing; mobile networks; cloud gateways; content-delivery networks; network address translation; satellite connectivity; privacy services; and inaccurate geolocation databases. Therefore: IP Address ≠ Event Location. IP Geolocation ≠ Governed Digital Location by Default. IP-derived information may remain a governed signal with explicit confidence and provenance. 10. Network Route Location Digital communications may traverse infrastructure across many countries. Network routing can change dynamically without changing the governed event itself. Therefore: Network Transit Location ≠ Event Digital Location by Default. Packet Route ≠ Event Location. Transit infrastructure may be recorded where operationally material but shall not automatically become part of the constitutive Digital Event Location. 11. API Location An event may be initiated, mediated, executed, or completed through APIs. An API may possess: logical endpoint; domain; gateway; service region; execution region; provider infrastructure; and downstream service dependencies. ELDM shall determine which of these are materially relevant to the event. API Endpoint ≠ Geographic Event Location by Default. API Provider Location ≠ Event Digital Location by Default. 12. Platform Location Digital marketplaces and platforms may operate across many jurisdictions simultaneously. A platform may have: legal headquarters; regional offices; infrastructure regions; user markets; seller markets; payment entities; data centers; operational subsidiaries; and globally distributed services. ELDM shall not reduce these structures to a single platform location unless operational evidence supports such representation for the governed event. Platform Headquarters ≠ Event Digital Location. Platform Registration Country ≠ Event Digital Location. 13. Digital Service Location Digital services may be provided through distributed infrastructure without a clear physical point of delivery. ELDM shall govern the operational digital environment through which the event is materially performed. This representation may be: centralized; multi-region; distributed; logical; hybrid; or qualified as unresolved. Digital Service Delivery ≠ Single Geographic Location by Default. 14. Data Storage Location Event-related data may be stored separately from where the event is executed. Data may also be replicated across multiple regions. Therefore: Data Storage Location ≠ Event Digital Location by Default. Database Location ≠ Event Execution Location by Default. Storage location may remain a relevant digital spatial signal but requires independent operational qualification. 15. Processing Location Data processing may constitute part of the event or merely support it. ELDM shall determine whether processing activity belongs to the governed Event Boundary. Where processing is constitutive, its digital environment may form part of the Governed Event Digital Location. Where processing is ancillary: Processing Location ≠ Constitutive Event Location by Default. 16. Digital Resource Location Digital assets, records, files, models, tokens, software components, or other digital resources may be associated with an event. Their technical storage or registration position shall not automatically establish the location of the event. Digital Resource Location ≠ Event Digital Location by Default. The resource's operational role must first be established. 17. Logical Digital Location Some digital environments are better represented through logical rather than physical geography. Examples include: platform tenancy; virtual network; distributed ledger environment; application namespace; service domain; computational cluster; autonomous-agent environment; or governed digital operational space. ELDM shall support logical location where geographic representation would distort operational reality. Digital Location ≠ Geographic Coordinate by Default. 18. AI Agent Location AI agents may operate across distributed computational environments and interact with platforms, APIs, machines, digital assets, and other agents. An AI agent may possess no stable physical location. ELDM shall therefore distinguish: agent execution environment; orchestration environment; model execution environment; tool environment; external service environment; and physical infrastructure. AI Agent Location ≠ Server Location by Default. AI Agent Location ≠ Owner Location. AI Agent Location ≠ User Location. Agent identity, authority, and responsibility remain outside ELDM. 19. Autonomous-System Digital Location Autonomous systems may continuously migrate workloads, invoke external services, distribute processing, and coordinate with other systems. ELDM shall preserve the actual digital execution structure without artificially assigning the event to the corporate or physical location of a supervising human. Autonomous Execution ≠ Human Supervisor Location. Autonomous System Location ≠ Operator Residence. 20. Machine-to-Machine Event Location Machine-to-machine events may involve: physical machines; embedded controllers; edge systems; cloud services; APIs; payment systems; AI agents; and distributed infrastructure. ELDM governs the digital dimension of such events independently from the physical location governed by ELPM. A machine-to-machine event may legitimately possess both: Governed Event Physical Location + Governed Event Digital Location without requiring those locations to coincide. 21. Digital Location Transition The digital location of an event may change during its lifecycle. Workloads may migrate. Agents may invoke services in different environments. Processing may move between edge and cloud systems. Transactions may pass through sequential digital execution stages. ELDM shall preserve materially relevant transitions where they form part of the bounded event. Digital Location Change ≠ New Event by Default. 22. Digital Location and Event Timing Digital location may vary over the duration of an event. ELDM shall support temporal association where required. For example: Time T1 ↓ Edge Environment A Time T2 ↓ Cloud Environment B Time T3 ↓ Platform Environment C TRETS remains authoritative for Event Timing. ELDM governs only the spatial association. 23. Digital Location Precision Digital spatial representation shall use only the precision supported by evidence and operational relevance. Possible representations may include: specific execution instance; service; cluster; availability zone; cloud region; platform environment; logical environment; distributed environment; or qualified unknown digital location. Technical Infrastructure Precision ≠ Governed Event Location Precision. Greater technical detail does not automatically produce better governance. 24. Digital Location Uncertainty Digital environments may obscure or dynamically change infrastructure location. ELDM shall preserve uncertainty where the digital spatial reality cannot legitimately be reduced further. Permissible states may include: exact; logical; regional; multi-region; distributed; dynamic; approximate; qualified; conflicted; partially established; or unresolved. Unknown Infrastructure Geography ≠ Unknown Digital Event Location by Default. A logical or distributed location may still be governed even where exact physical infrastructure geography is unavailable. 25. Digital Location Conflict ELDM shall govern conflicts among digital-location signals. Examples include: IP geolocation indicating one country; cloud execution indicating another; device location indicating another; platform profile indicating another; network routing indicating another; and user billing information indicating another. Such differences do not necessarily represent evidence conflict. They may represent different legitimate spatial dimensions. Different Digital Location Signals ≠ Location Conflict by Default. Conflict exists only where signals make incompatible claims about the same governed spatial dimension. 26. Digital Location Continuity ELDM shall preserve continuity of Digital Event Location across changes in infrastructure where the event itself remains continuous. Container migration, load balancing, failover, scaling, routing changes, or infrastructure replacement shall not automatically create a new event or new digital location identity. Infrastructure Change ≠ Event Change by Default. Failover ≠ New Event by Default. 27. Physical and Digital Location Separation ELDM shall preserve the distinction established with ELPM. A physical event may be digitally coordinated elsewhere. A digital event may trigger physical execution elsewhere. A machine may operate physically in one country while its digital control environment spans several others. Therefore: Physical Event Location ≠ Digital Event Location. Neither dimension automatically overrides the other. Their relationship is governed later within TRELS. 28. Digital Location and Participant Location Participant location shall not automatically establish Digital Event Location. A participant may connect remotely to an event executed elsewhere. A customer may travel. A seller may operate through a platform. An AI agent may act on behalf of an organization. A machine may transact without contemporaneous human participation. Therefore: Participant Location ≠ Digital Event Location by Default. TREPS governs participation. OBIDENITY® governs origin-bound identity, ownership, and authority where applicable. 29. Digital Location and Corporate Location Corporate headquarters, incorporation country, registered office, business establishment, billing entity, and contractual entity may be relevant downstream. They do not automatically establish Digital Event Location. Corporate Location ≠ Digital Event Location. Company Registration ≠ Digital Execution Location. Contracting Entity Location ≠ Event Digital Location by Default. 30. Digital Location and Tax Jurisdiction ELDM shall maintain a strict boundary between operational digital location and jurisdiction-specific taxation. Governed Event Digital Location may become an input to downstream tax analysis. It does not itself determine: Tax Jurisdiction; digital tax nexus; permanent establishment; significant economic presence; tax residence; source jurisdiction; place of supply; place of effective management; customer location under tax law; supplier establishment; marketplace tax responsibility; legal situs; or any other jurisdiction-specific taxation criterion. Digital Event Location ≠ Tax Jurisdiction. Server Location ≠ Tax Nexus. Cloud Region ≠ Permanent Establishment. IP Geolocation ≠ Legal Place of Supply. Digital Execution Location ≠ Tax Residence. These determinations belong to jurisdiction-specific tax systems. 31. Multi-Jurisdiction Readiness ELDM shall preserve digital operational reality independently from jurisdiction-specific interpretation. Canonical logic: One Governed Digital Event Reality ↓ Multiple Possible Jurisdictional Evaluations The same governed digital event may legitimately be evaluated differently by multiple jurisdictions. TREGA™ therefore establishes the event representation once. Jurisdictions subsequently apply their own legal rules. 32. Governance States ELDM may assign states including: Digital Location Ready Relevant digital spatial signals are available. Digital Location Under Governance Candidate environments are being evaluated. Digital Location Established A sufficient digital spatial representation has been established. Digital Location Logical The event is legitimately represented through a logical digital environment. Digital Location Multi-Region Material execution spans multiple regions. Digital Location Dynamic Material digital location changes during the event. Digital Location Distributed The digital event cannot legitimately be reduced to one execution location. Digital Location Qualified The location is established subject to explicit qualification. Digital Location Conflicted Material evidence concerning the same digital dimension conflicts. Digital Location Unresolved Available evidence is insufficient for legitimate determination. 33. Governance Requirements ELDM implementations shall: consume the Governed Event Location Signal Set established by ELIM; preserve the Governed Event Physical Location established by ELPM; identify materially relevant digital-location candidates; distinguish constitutive digital environments from supporting infrastructure; differentiate execution, processing, storage, routing, platform, device, and resource locations; support logical digital location; support cloud, edge, API, platform, AI-agent, autonomous-system, and machine-to-machine environments; support centralized, dynamic, multi-region, and distributed digital events; preserve digital-location transitions where materially relevant; preserve supported precision; preserve uncertainty and conflict; prevent infrastructure convenience from becoming location authority; maintain physical/digital separation; prevent jurisdiction-specific rules from redefining operational digital reality; maintain traceability; and produce a Governed Event Digital Location suitable for subsequent TRELS processing. 34. Governance Logic ELDM follows the canonical logic: Governed Event Location Signal Set ↓ identify digital-location candidates ↓ determine their operational roles ↓ distinguish constitutive execution from supporting infrastructure ↓ evaluate logical, platform, cloud, edge, device, network, and distributed dimensions ↓ govern precision, uncertainty, continuity, and conflict ↓ establish Governed Event Digital Location. Digital infrastructure shall describe operational reality. It shall not silently determine legal geography. 35. Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum ELDM implementation should support: Governed Event Reference Reference to the event under digital-location governance. Digital Location Identifier Unique reference for each governed digital location. Digital Location Type Execution environment, platform, cloud region, edge environment, API environment, logical environment, network environment, device-associated environment, or other legitimate type. Operational Role Constitutive, supporting, contextual, transitional, or other governed role. Digital Environment Reference Relevant service, platform, cluster, region, logical environment, or infrastructure reference. Physical Infrastructure Association Physical infrastructure relationship where known and materially relevant. Temporal Association Relationship to governed Event Timing. Execution State Whether material event execution occurs within the environment. Distribution State Centralized, multi-region, dynamic, or distributed. Precision State Supported digital-location precision. Uncertainty State Known uncertainty. Conflict State Known evidence conflict. Evidence Reference Supporting operational evidence. Traceability Reference Governance history enabling reconstruction. Governance State Current ELDM determination state. Handoff State Readiness for distributed-location governance. 36. Governance Outputs ELDM may produce: Digital Location Candidate Register; Constitutive Digital Location Record; Digital Execution Location Record; Cloud Environment Record; Edge Environment Record; API Location Record; Platform Location Record; Device Location Association; Network Location Association; Logical Digital Location Record; AI Agent Execution Location Record; Machine-to-Machine Digital Location Record; Digital Location Transition Record; Digital Location Precision Record; Digital Location Uncertainty Record; Digital Location Conflict Record; Digital Location Traceability Record; and the principal output: Governed Event Digital Location This output becomes an input to ELDSM. 37. Critical Distinctions Digital Location Signal ≠ Governed Event Digital Location Digital Location Candidate ≠ Governed Event Digital Location Supporting Digital Infrastructure ≠ Constitutive Digital Location Infrastructure Geography ≠ Digital Event Location Server Location ≠ Event Digital Location Cloud Region ≠ Event Digital Location Infrastructure Instance Location ≠ Event Location Edge Node Location ≠ Complete Event Digital Location User Device Location ≠ Event Digital Location IP Address ≠ Event Location IP Geolocation ≠ Governed Digital Location Network Transit Location ≠ Event Digital Location Packet Route ≠ Event Location API Endpoint ≠ Geographic Event Location API Provider Location ≠ Event Digital Location Platform Headquarters ≠ Event Digital Location Platform Registration Country ≠ Event Digital Location Data Storage Location ≠ Event Digital Location Database Location ≠ Event Execution Location Digital Resource Location ≠ Event Digital Location AI Agent Location ≠ Server Location AI Agent Location ≠ Owner Location AI Agent Location ≠ User Location Autonomous Execution ≠ Human Supervisor Location Participant Location ≠ Digital Event Location Corporate Location ≠ Digital Event Location Physical Event Location ≠ Digital Event Location Digital Location Change ≠ New Event Infrastructure Change ≠ Event Change Digital Event Location ≠ Tax Jurisdiction Server Location ≠ Tax Nexus Cloud Region ≠ Permanent Establishment IP Geolocation ≠ Legal Place of Supply Digital Execution Location ≠ Tax Residence Operational Digital Reality ≠ Jurisdictional Tax Determination 38. Enterprise Application ELDM can operate as the digital spatial-governance layer between modern computational systems and downstream taxation infrastructure. A generalized implementation pattern is: Digital Platform / Cloud Service / API / AI Agent / Autonomous System / Machine Network ↓ ELIM ↓ ELPM ↓ ELDM ↓ Governed Event Digital Location ↓ ELDSM ↓ ELCM ↓ Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event ↓ Jurisdiction-Specific Tax Engines This allows tax infrastructure to consume a governed representation of digital reality without forcing the event itself to adopt the assumptions of one tax regime. 39. Use Case 1 — Global AI Agent Transaction An autonomous AI procurement agent operating for an enterprise identifies a supplier, negotiates through APIs, obtains authorization, initiates a digital purchase, and coordinates fulfillment. The agent's orchestration service operates through a European cloud region. Model inference may occur in another region. The supplier platform operates globally. Payment authorization passes through infrastructure in additional countries. The purchasing organization is headquartered elsewhere. The human who configured the agent is not involved when the transaction occurs. ELDM distinguishes the digital environments materially constituting the event from infrastructure that merely supports, routes, stores, or observes it. It does not select the company's headquarters, server country, user location, IP geolocation, or cloud region as the legal location of the transaction. The result is a governed digital spatial representation capable of being consumed by multiple jurisdictional tax systems. Autonomous digital execution requires governed location before legal jurisdiction can legitimately interpret that location. 40. Use Case 2 — Multi-Region Digital Service A customer accesses a digital service through a mobile device while traveling. The account was created in another country. The billing address belongs to another jurisdiction. The service platform dynamically routes the session through edge infrastructure. Application processing occurs across two cloud regions. Data is replicated globally. Payment is handled by a separate provider. A conventional system may derive location from the IP address, billing country, server region, or customer profile depending on which field is available. ELDM instead governs each signal according to its operational role. It establishes the digital spatial structure of the event without allowing any single technical or administrative signal to become authoritative by default. The digital event is governed as it actually operates before any jurisdiction determines what that operational reality means under tax law. 41. Canonical Boundary ELDM owns the governance of the digital spatial manifestation of the Tax-Relevant Event, including constitutive digital environments, digital execution locations, cloud and edge environments, API environments, platform environments, device-associated locations, network-associated locations, logical digital locations, AI-agent execution environments, autonomous-system digital environments, machine-to-machine digital locations, digital-location transitions, digital-location precision, uncertainty, conflict, continuity, and traceability. ELDM does not own final Distributed Event Location or final Event Location Correlation. It does not redefine Event Context, Event Recognition, Event Formation, Event Boundary, Event Timing, Physical Event Location, Event Participation, Participant Identity, Value Association, Event Relationships, Event Determination, or Event Record Governance. It does not determine Tax Jurisdiction, digital tax nexus, permanent establishment, significant economic presence, tax residence, source jurisdiction, place of supply, customer location under tax law, supplier establishment, marketplace tax responsibility, Legal Tax Point, Tax Period, taxability, Tax Liability, tax rate, reporting obligation, or any jurisdiction-specific tax consequence. The canonical handoff is: ELIM — Governed Event Location Signal Set ↓ ELPM — Governed Event Physical Location ↓ ELDM — Governed Event Digital Location ↓ ELDSM — Event Distributed Location Governance Canonical Closing Statement ELDM establishes where the governed event materially exists and operates within digital environments without allowing servers, IP addresses, cloud regions, devices, platforms, network routes, or corporate locations to become authoritative merely because they can be geographically identified. Digital infrastructure can reveal where parts of an event operate. It cannot, by itself, determine where the event legally belongs. ELDM governs where the event occurs digitally — not which jurisdiction may tax the digital activity. TREGA™ governs the event. The jurisdiction governs the tax.

title: OOF™ The Event Distributed Location Module (ELDSM) governs how a Tax-Relevant
text: OOF™ The Event Distributed Location Module (ELDSM) governs how a Tax-Relevant The Event Distributed Location Module (ELDSM) governs how a Tax-Relevant OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: Tax-Relevant Event Location Standard (TRELS) Module: ELDSM — Event Distributed Location Module Operational Layer: Event Distributed Location Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Event Distributed Location Origin ID: TREGA-TRELS-ELDSM-004 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 31 August 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language Canonical Definition The Event Distributed Location Module (ELDSM) governs how a Tax-Relevant Event is spatially represented when its materially constitutive activity occurs across multiple physical, digital, hybrid, machine, autonomous, or infrastructural locations and cannot legitimately be reduced to one operational location without distorting the reality of the event. ELDSM operates on the Governed Event Physical Location established by ELPM and the Governed Event Digital Location established by ELDM. Its canonical task is: to establish a coherent, traceable, and operationally justified Governed Event Distributed Location where multiple locations materially constitute the same governed event, without forcing that event into an artificial single-location representation or converting distributed operational reality into jurisdiction-specific tax allocation. The principal transition is: Governed Event Physical Location + Governed Event Digital Location ↓ Governed Event Distributed Location ELDSM governs spatial distribution of the event. It does not determine how taxation rights, tax bases, revenues, profits, obligations, or liabilities are allocated among jurisdictions. Operational Role Modern economic activity increasingly occurs across distributed operational environments. A single governed event may involve: physical activity in several places; digital execution across several cloud regions; edge and central infrastructure; machines operating at different sites; autonomous agents invoking services across multiple systems; platform activity spanning several operational environments; distributed ledger infrastructure; cross-border logistics; remote control and physical execution; or simultaneous physical and digital activity. Traditional systems often attempt to reduce such events to one location. They may select: customer country; seller country; server country; billing address; headquarters; IP location; transaction-processing location; device location; or another convenient geographic proxy. Such reduction may simplify downstream processing while materially misrepresenting the event. ELDSM exists to prevent that distortion. Where the event is genuinely distributed, its governed location may also be distributed. Distributed Operational Reality ≠ Governance Failure. A legitimate governance result does not require artificial spatial simplicity. Internal Flow Within TRELS, ELDSM occupies the fourth operational position: ELIM — What spatial information legitimately belongs to the event? ↓ ELPM — What physical location materially belongs to the event? ↓ ELDM — What digital location materially belongs to the event? ↓ ELDSM — How is a genuinely distributed event spatially represented? ↓ ELCM — How are relevant event locations correlated into a governed spatial representation? ↓ Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event ELDSM receives: Governed Event Physical Location + Governed Event Digital Location and produces: Governed Event Distributed Location for final location correlation by ELCM. Operational Space ELDSM governs distributed spatial representation of Tax-Relevant Events. Its operational space includes: multi-location events; cross-border operational events; distributed physical events; distributed digital events; hybrid physical-digital events; multi-site operations; multi-region digital execution; edge-cloud distribution; machine-to-machine distribution; autonomous-system distribution; AI-agent distributed execution; distributed infrastructure; distributed platform operations; multi-node events; distributed transaction execution; distributed service delivery; distributed production; distributed logistics; distributed financial operations; location transitions; simultaneous multi-location activity; sequential multi-location activity; location contribution; location dependency; distributed-location continuity; distributed-location precision; distributed-location uncertainty; distributed-location conflict; and distributed-location traceability. Operational Scope ELDSM shall support distributed-location governance for: international commerce; digital marketplaces; cloud computing; distributed applications; AI services; AI agents; autonomous systems; machine economies; robotics; industrial automation; IoT networks; telecommunications; banking; financial infrastructure; payment networks; logistics; manufacturing; supply chains; digital assets; distributed ledgers; remote services; cross-border professional services; platform economies; infrastructure operations; and future decentralized or machine-mediated economic systems. 1. Distributed Location Candidate Identification ELDSM shall identify whether the governed physical and digital locations indicate that materially constitutive parts of the same event occur across more than one location. A Distributed Location Candidate exists where multiple locations may legitimately belong to the same governed event. However: Multiple Location Signals ≠ Distributed Event by Default. The locations must materially relate to the bounded event itself. 2. Constitutive Location Assessment ELDSM shall distinguish locations constituting the event from locations that merely support, observe, record, route, finance, administer, or provide infrastructure to it. A location may be relevant without being constitutive. Therefore: Relevant Location ≠ Constitutive Event Location by Default. Only locations with a materially justified operational relationship to the event shall form the Governed Event Distributed Location. 3. Distributed Event Determination ELDSM shall determine whether the event is legitimately represented as distributed. A distributed representation is appropriate where: no single location sufficiently represents the event; multiple locations contain constitutive activity; the event exists through coordinated activity across locations; physical and digital components materially interact across locations; execution migrates between locations; or simultaneous distributed execution forms part of the event. Multiple Locations ≠ Multiple Events by Default. The Event Boundary remains governed by TREBS. ELDSM shall not fragment one bounded event merely because its spatial reality is complex. 4. Physical Distribution An event may contain constitutive physical activity across multiple locations. Examples include: goods moving through multiple operational stages; coordinated manufacturing across facilities; infrastructure operations across sites; distributed energy systems; multi-site industrial processes; logistics networks; or machines performing coordinated operations in different locations. ELDSM shall preserve those locations where they materially form part of the same event. Multiple Physical Locations ≠ Multiple Events by Default. 5. Digital Distribution Digital events may execute across multiple computational environments. Relevant locations may include: cloud regions; edge nodes; execution clusters; platform environments; API services; autonomous-agent environments; distributed databases; or networked machine systems. Where these environments materially constitute the event: Distributed Digital Execution ≠ Single Digital Location by Default. ELDSM shall preserve the distributed structure rather than selecting one infrastructure component as the authoritative location. 6. Hybrid Physical-Digital Distribution Many modern events combine physical and digital activity. For example: Physical Machine ↓ Edge Controller ↓ Cloud AI Service ↓ External API ↓ Machine Execution The event may therefore possess both physical and digital spatial dimensions. ELDSM shall permit a hybrid distributed representation. Physical Location + Digital Location ≠ Requirement to Select One Dominant Location. Both may legitimately belong to the governed event. 7. Simultaneous Distribution Constitutive activity may occur in several locations at the same time. ELDSM shall support simultaneous multi-location representation. Examples include: distributed computing; synchronized industrial systems; multi-node autonomous operations; replicated digital execution; coordinated machine networks; or concurrent platform processes. Simultaneous Multi-Location Activity ≠ Spatial Conflict. Several locations can legitimately describe one event simultaneously. 8. Sequential Distribution An event may move through locations over time. For example: Location A ↓ Location B ↓ Location C ELDSM shall preserve this spatial progression where all stages remain within the same governed Event Boundary. Location Transition ≠ New Event by Default. TRETS governs the temporal structure. ELDSM governs the spatial progression. 9. Dynamic Location Some events possess locations that change dynamically. Examples include: mobile machines; vehicles; aircraft; vessels; mobile devices; migrating cloud workloads; autonomous robots; mobile edge systems; or dynamic digital services. ELDSM shall support dynamic location without requiring every location change to create a new event. Changing Location ≠ Changing Event Identity by Default. 10. Location Contribution Not every constitutive location contributes equally to the event. ELDSM may represent the operational contribution of locations where supported by evidence. Possible states may include: primary constitutive; secondary constitutive; supporting constitutive; transitional; simultaneous; sequential; conditional; or indeterminate. However: Operational Location Contribution ≠ Tax Allocation Weight. A location's operational significance shall not automatically become a percentage of taxation rights, profit allocation, or tax base. 11. Primary Location Some distributed events may possess an operationally dominant location. ELDSM may identify such a location where evidence supports it. However: Primary Operational Location ≠ Exclusive Event Location. Primary Operational Location ≠ Primary Tax Jurisdiction. Dominance shall not erase other constitutive locations. 12. No Primary Location A distributed event may legitimately have no single primary location. This is a valid governance outcome. No Single Primary Location ≠ Unresolved Event Location. Where operational reality is genuinely distributed, the correct representation may be: Governed Distributed Location — No Single Dominant Location rather than an artificial geographic assignment. 13. Distributed Cloud Execution Cloud services may distribute event execution dynamically across multiple regions. ELDSM shall distinguish: deliberate multi-region execution; dynamic workload migration; redundancy; replication; failover; storage distribution; and constitutive processing. Only materially constitutive locations shall form the distributed event representation. Cloud Replication ≠ Distributed Event Execution by Default. Redundant Infrastructure ≠ Constitutive Event Location by Default. 14. Edge-Cloud Distribution An event may begin at an edge device, undergo local processing, invoke cloud services, and return a result to physical infrastructure. ELDSM shall preserve this structure where the components form one bounded event. Edge Location ≠ Complete Event Location. Cloud Location ≠ Complete Event Location. The legitimate governed representation may be their operationally justified combination. 15. AI Agent Distributed Location AI agents may operate through: orchestration environments; model providers; external tools; APIs; databases; payment systems; digital platforms; physical machines; and other agents. The agent's activity may therefore have no stable single digital location. ELDSM shall govern the distributed operational environments materially constituting the event. AI Agent Distributed Execution ≠ Agent Legal Residence. AI Agent Execution Geography ≠ Owner Tax Residence. AI Agent Infrastructure Distribution ≠ Tax Jurisdiction Allocation. 16. Autonomous-System Distribution Autonomous systems may coordinate decisions and actions across multiple physical and digital locations without contemporaneous human control. ELDSM shall preserve this spatial reality independently from the location of: system owner; operator; developer; supervising organization; manufacturer; or human beneficiary. Autonomous Event Location ≠ Human Controller Location by Default. 17. Machine-to-Machine Distribution Machine-to-machine events may involve machines physically located in different places while their communications and decision processes operate through distributed digital infrastructure. ELDSM shall support representation such as: Machine A Physical Location + Machine B Physical Location + Edge Environment + Cloud Execution Environment ↓ Governed Event Distributed Location without prematurely assigning the event to one jurisdiction. 18. Platform Distribution Platforms may coordinate events across: buyers; sellers; service providers; infrastructure; payment systems; logistics providers; and digital services. ELDSM shall govern only locations materially constituting the bounded event. Platform Global Presence ≠ Event Distributed Location by Default. A platform's worldwide infrastructure shall not automatically become the spatial footprint of every event processed through it. 19. Distributed Ledger Environments Events involving distributed ledgers may be technically replicated across many nodes. Node distribution alone shall not establish the distributed location of the event. Ledger Node Distribution ≠ Event Location Distribution by Default. ELDSM shall determine whether specific distributed components materially constitute the governed event rather than merely maintaining replicated infrastructure. 20. Network Distribution Network traffic may traverse numerous jurisdictions. Transit does not automatically constitute event distribution. Network Path ≠ Distributed Event Location by Default. Routing infrastructure shall be included only where its operational role materially forms part of the event. 21. Data Distribution Event-related data may be stored or replicated globally. Such distribution shall not automatically create distributed Event Location. Distributed Data Storage ≠ Distributed Event Location by Default. Storage becomes spatially constitutive only where its role forms part of the governed event itself. 22. Distributed Service Delivery Services may be delivered through multiple locations. For example, a digital service may involve: customer interaction in one place; computational execution elsewhere; specialized processing elsewhere; and physical fulfillment elsewhere. ELDSM shall preserve materially constitutive locations without forcing them into one geographic point. Distributed Service Delivery ≠ Single Place of Supply by Default. Legal place-of-supply determination remains outside TREGA™. 23. Distributed Production Production may occur across several facilities or machine environments while remaining part of one governed event. ELDSM shall preserve the spatial structure established by operational evidence. It shall not infer: origin law; customs origin; tax situs; permanent establishment; transfer-pricing allocation; or taxation rights. Operational Production Location ≠ Legal Origin Determination. 24. Distributed Logistics Logistics events may involve movement through many locations. ELDSM shall distinguish spatial progression belonging to one event from separate events formed under TREFS and bounded under TREBS. Route Complexity ≠ Event Multiplicity by Default. A multi-location journey can remain one governed event where its Event Boundary supports that representation. 25. Cross-Border Distribution A Tax-Relevant Event may operationally cross national borders. ELDSM shall record such distribution where materially relevant. However: Cross-Border Event ≠ Multi-Jurisdiction Tax Liability by Default. Operational border crossing may become an input to jurisdiction-specific tax or customs analysis. It is not itself a legal conclusion. 26. Distribution and Event Boundary ELDSM shall not redefine the Event Boundary merely because the event spans multiple locations. TREBS remains authoritative for Event Boundary. Spatial Distribution ≠ Boundary Expansion by Default. A location belongs to the distributed representation only where the activity at that location is already legitimately associated with the bounded event. 27. Distribution and Event Timing Distributed locations may correspond to different points or intervals in Event Timing. ELDSM shall support temporal-spatial association such as: T1 ↓ Physical Location A T2 ↓ Digital Environment B T3 ↓ Physical Location C + Cloud Environment D T4 ↓ Distributed Execution E/F/G TRETS owns Event Timing. ELDSM owns distributed spatial representation. 28. Distribution and Participation Participants may operate from locations different from the locations constituting the event. Therefore: Participant Distribution ≠ Event Location Distribution by Default. TREPS governs Event Participation. ELDSM shall not infer taxpayer status, participant legal residence, identity, authority, or responsibility from spatial distribution. 29. Distribution and Value Value may originate, move, change state, develop, degrade, or be recognized across different locations. VFM® governs the Value Lifecycle.
