ELDSM may associate governed spatial information with an event involving value. It shall not determine value ownership or value lifecycle state. Distributed Value Activity ≠ Distributed Event Location by Default. 30. Distribution and Event Relationships Multiple events may occur in different locations and remain related. Conversely, one event may occur across multiple locations. These are distinct governance questions. Multiple Locations Within One Event ≠ Multiple Related Events. Multiple Related Events ≠ One Distributed Event. TRERLS governs Event Relationships. ELDSM governs spatial distribution within the bounded event. 31. Distribution Precision ELDSM shall represent distributed locations only at precision supported by evidence and operational relevance. Possible levels may include: exact point; facility; city; region; country; cloud region; logical digital environment; multi-region environment; network zone; distributed physical network; distributed digital environment; or qualified unknown location. More Location Data ≠ Greater Governance Precision by Default. 32. Distribution Uncertainty Some constitutive locations may be known while others remain uncertain. ELDSM shall permit partial spatial governance. For example: Location A — Established Location B — Established Location C — Regional Only Digital Environment D — Distributed / Exact Infrastructure Unknown The event may still possess a legitimate Governed Event Distributed Location. Partial Location Uncertainty ≠ Total Location Failure. 33. Distribution Conflict Conflicting evidence concerning one spatial component shall not invalidate correctly established components. ELDSM shall isolate the conflict. One Conflicted Location ≠ Entire Distributed Location Invalid. Likewise: Multiple Different Locations ≠ Conflict by Default. Different locations may all legitimately constitute the event. 34. Distribution Continuity Distributed spatial representation shall preserve continuity as locations enter, leave, migrate, fail, recover, or change during the event. A constitutive location may cease participation while the event continues elsewhere. Location Departure ≠ Event Completion. Location Addition ≠ New Event by Default. Infrastructure Failover ≠ Event Replacement by Default. 35. Distributed Location Traceability Every constitutive location shall remain traceable to: source evidence; operational role; Event Boundary; relevant Event Timing; location type; confidence; uncertainty; conflicts; corrections; and governance decisions. A downstream system shall be able to reconstruct why a location was included in or excluded from the distributed representation. 36. Distributed Location Correction Distributed Event Location may require correction when evidence changes. Corrections shall preserve governance history. Location Correction ≠ Historical Erasure. A corrected location record shall preserve the previous state, reason for correction, supporting evidence, and resulting state where required. 37. Distributed Location and Tax Jurisdiction ELDSM shall maintain a strict separation between distributed operational reality and legal jurisdiction allocation. It shall not determine: Tax Jurisdiction; tax nexus; permanent establishment; significant economic presence; place of supply; source jurisdiction; residence; legal situs; customs origin; taxable presence; taxing rights; tax-base allocation; profit allocation; revenue allocation; transfer-pricing outcome; or jurisdiction-specific tax liability. Distributed Event Location ≠ Distributed Tax Liability. Multiple Event Locations ≠ Multiple Tax Jurisdictions by Default. Operational Location Contribution ≠ Taxing Rights Allocation. Cross-Border Distribution ≠ Legal Nexus Determination. Distributed Digital Infrastructure ≠ Permanent Establishment by Default. 38. Jurisdiction-Neutral Representation ELDSM shall preserve the event independently from the legal rules of any single jurisdiction. The canonical logic is: One Distributed Operational Event ↓ One Governed Distributed Event Representation ↓ Multiple Possible Jurisdictional Evaluations Jurisdiction A may legally interpret the event differently from Jurisdiction B. Jurisdiction C may apply another nexus, source, place-of-supply, residence, or allocation rule. TREGA™ shall not alter the underlying governed event to satisfy any one of them. 39. Governance States ELDSM may assign states including: Distribution Ready Sufficient physical and digital location inputs exist. Distribution Under Governance Potential constitutive locations are being assessed. Distribution Not Required A distributed representation is not operationally justified. Distribution Established Multiple constitutive locations are sufficiently governed. Distribution Sequential The event progresses through multiple locations. Distribution Simultaneous Constitutive activity occurs in multiple locations concurrently. Distribution Hybrid Physical and digital locations jointly constitute the event. Distribution Dynamic Constitutive locations materially change during the event. Distribution Partial Some spatial components are established while others remain unresolved. Distribution Qualified The representation is subject to explicit qualifications. Distribution Conflicted Material evidence concerning one or more spatial components conflicts. Distribution Unresolved Available evidence cannot support a legitimate distributed representation. 40. Governance Requirements ELDSM implementations shall: consume Governed Event Physical Location from ELPM; consume Governed Event Digital Location from ELDM; determine whether distributed spatial representation is operationally justified; distinguish multiple location signals from genuine event distribution; identify constitutive locations; distinguish constitutive from supporting locations; support physical distribution; support digital distribution; support hybrid physical-digital distribution; support simultaneous distribution; support sequential distribution; support dynamic location; support AI-agent, autonomous-system, and machine-to-machine distribution; preserve Event Boundary; preserve temporal-spatial association; preserve supported precision; preserve uncertainty; isolate location conflicts; preserve continuity; preserve corrections; maintain traceability; prevent artificial single-location reduction; prevent operational distribution from becoming legal jurisdiction allocation; and produce a Governed Event Distributed Location suitable for ELCM. 41. Governance Logic ELDSM follows the canonical logic: Governed Physical Location + Governed Digital Location ↓ identify potential spatial distribution ↓ determine which locations materially constitute the same bounded event ↓ classify physical, digital, hybrid, simultaneous, sequential, and dynamic distribution ↓ preserve temporal association, precision, uncertainty, conflict, continuity, and traceability ↓ establish Governed Event Distributed Location. Where one location legitimately represents the event, ELDSM shall not manufacture complexity. Where several locations legitimately constitute the event, ELDSM shall not manufacture simplicity. 42. Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum ELDSM implementation should support: Governed Event Reference Reference to the bounded event. Distributed Location Identifier Unique identifier for the governed distributed-location structure. Constitutive Location References Locations forming the distributed event representation. Location Type Physical, digital, or hybrid. Distribution Type Sequential, simultaneous, dynamic, hybrid, or other legitimate form. Operational Role Role of each location in the event. Contribution State Operational significance where legitimately established. Temporal Association Relevant governed Event Timing for each spatial component. Primary Location State Primary, non-primary, no-primary, or unresolved. Distribution Precision Supported spatial precision. Distribution Uncertainty Known uncertainty. Distribution Conflict Known evidence conflict. Evidence References Evidence supporting inclusion or exclusion. Continuity State Location continuity through the event. Correction History Material spatial corrections. Traceability Reference Governance history. Governance State Current ELDSM state. Handoff State Readiness for Event Location Correlation. 43. Governance Outputs ELDSM may produce: Distributed Location Candidate Register; Constitutive Location Register; Physical Distribution Record; Digital Distribution Record; Hybrid Distribution Record; Sequential Location Record; Simultaneous Location Record; Dynamic Location Record; Location Contribution Record; Primary Location Assessment; No-Primary-Location Determination; Temporal-Spatial Association Record; Distribution Precision Record; Distribution Uncertainty Record; Distribution Conflict Record; Distribution Continuity Record; Distribution Correction Record; Distribution Traceability Record; and the principal output: Governed Event Distributed Location This output becomes an input to ELCM. 44. Critical Distinctions Multiple Location Signals ≠ Distributed Event Relevant Location ≠ Constitutive Event Location Multiple Locations ≠ Multiple Events Multiple Physical Locations ≠ Multiple Events Distributed Digital Execution ≠ Single Digital Location Physical Location + Digital Location ≠ Requirement to Select One Dominant Location Simultaneous Multi-Location Activity ≠ Spatial Conflict Location Transition ≠ New Event Changing Location ≠ Changing Event Identity Operational Location Contribution ≠ Tax Allocation Weight Primary Operational Location ≠ Exclusive Event Location Primary Operational Location ≠ Primary Tax Jurisdiction No Single Primary Location ≠ Unresolved Event Location Cloud Replication ≠ Distributed Event Execution Redundant Infrastructure ≠ Constitutive Event Location Edge Location ≠ Complete Event Location Cloud Location ≠ Complete Event Location AI Agent Distributed Execution ≠ Agent Legal Residence AI Agent Execution Geography ≠ Owner Tax Residence Autonomous Event Location ≠ Human Controller Location Platform Global Presence ≠ Event Distributed Location Ledger Node Distribution ≠ Event Location Distribution Network Path ≠ Distributed Event Location Distributed Data Storage ≠ Distributed Event Location Distributed Service Delivery ≠ Single Place of Supply Operational Production Location ≠ Legal Origin Determination Route Complexity ≠ Event Multiplicity Cross-Border Event ≠ Multi-Jurisdiction Tax Liability Spatial Distribution ≠ Boundary Expansion Participant Distribution ≠ Event Location Distribution Multiple Locations Within One Event ≠ Multiple Related Events Multiple Related Events ≠ One Distributed Event Partial Location Uncertainty ≠ Total Location Failure One Conflicted Location ≠ Entire Distributed Location Invalid Location Correction ≠ Historical Erasure Distributed Event Location ≠ Distributed Tax Liability Multiple Event Locations ≠ Multiple Tax Jurisdictions Operational Location Contribution ≠ Taxing Rights Allocation Cross-Border Distribution ≠ Legal Nexus Determination Distributed Digital Infrastructure ≠ Permanent Establishment 45. Enterprise Application ELDSM can operate as the distributed spatial-governance layer between modern operational systems and downstream jurisdiction-specific taxation infrastructure. A generalized implementation pattern is: Physical Operations + Digital Platforms + Cloud Infrastructure + Edge Systems + AI Agents + Autonomous Machines ↓ ELIM ↓ ELPM ↓ ELDM ↓ ELDSM ↓ Governed Event Distributed Location ↓ ELCM ↓ Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event ↓ Jurisdiction-Specific Tax Engines This allows the same governed event to remain operationally coherent even when several jurisdictions later evaluate it differently. 46. Use Case 1 — Autonomous Cross-Border Manufacturing Network A multinational industrial network uses autonomous production systems across several facilities. A machine in one country identifies a production requirement. An AI orchestration service running through distributed cloud infrastructure generates a production plan. A specialized component is manufactured at a second facility. An autonomous logistics system transfers the component to a third facility. Final machine processing occurs there. Digital coordination continues across edge systems, cloud services, APIs, and machine controllers throughout the process. If TREBS establishes that the relevant activity forms one bounded Tax-Relevant Event, ELDSM does not force that event into the country containing the first machine, the AI server, corporate headquarters, or final facility. It governs the materially constitutive spatial structure of the event. The output may legitimately contain multiple physical and digital locations. It does not decide which country possesses taxation rights. The event may be operationally distributed before any jurisdiction decides how that distribution matters under law. 47. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Global Digital Service An AI agent autonomously acquires and coordinates a digital service. The agent executes through one cloud environment. Model inference occurs through an external provider in another region. Data processing occurs across several regions. A specialized API is invoked through another provider. Payment infrastructure operates elsewhere. The service is delivered to a machine-controlled system in another country. No single technical location adequately represents the event. Selecting the server location, customer device, corporate headquarters, billing country, or one cloud region would erase material parts of the operational reality. ELDSM establishes a Governed Event Distributed Location containing only those physical and digital environments that materially constitute the event. Downstream jurisdictions may then independently apply their own nexus, place-of-supply, source, residence, or other tax rules. Distributed digital reality is governed once; legal jurisdictional interpretation may occur many times. 48. Canonical Boundary ELDSM owns the governance of distributed spatial representation within the bounded Tax-Relevant Event, including physical distribution, digital distribution, hybrid distribution, simultaneous distribution, sequential distribution, dynamic location, constitutive-location assessment, operational location contribution, primary/no-primary location states, temporal-spatial association, distributed-location precision, uncertainty, conflict, continuity, correction, and traceability. ELDSM does not own Event Location Signal Identification, which belongs to ELIM. It does not own Physical Event Location, which belongs to ELPM. It does not own Digital Event Location, which belongs to ELDM. It does not own final Event Location Correlation, which belongs to ELCM. It does not redefine Event Context, Event Recognition, Event Formation, Event Boundary, Event Timing, Event Participation, Participant Identity, Value Association, Event Relationships, Event Determination, or Event Record Governance. It does not determine Tax Jurisdiction, tax nexus, permanent establishment, significant economic presence, tax residence, source jurisdiction, place of supply, legal situs, customs origin, taxable presence, taxing rights, tax-base allocation, revenue allocation, profit allocation, transfer-pricing outcome, Legal Tax Point, Tax Period, taxability, Tax Liability, tax rate, reporting obligation, or any jurisdiction-specific tax consequence. The canonical handoff is: ELIM — Governed Event Location Signal Set ↓ ELPM — Governed Event Physical Location ↓ ELDM — Governed Event Digital Location ↓ ELDSM — Governed Event Distributed Location ↓ ELCM — Event Location Correlation Canonical Closing Statement ELDSM preserves the spatial reality of events that genuinely exist across multiple physical, digital, machine, autonomous, or infrastructural locations without forcing operational complexity into an artificial single-location model. A distributed event does not become geographically simple merely because a downstream system requires one country field. ELDSM governs where the event is distributed — not how taxation rights are distributed among jurisdictions. TREGA™ governs the event. The jurisdiction governs the tax.

title: OOF™ The Event Location Identification Module (ELIM) governs how spatial
text: OOF™ The Event Location Identification Module (ELIM) governs how spatial The Event Location Identification Module (ELIM) governs how spatial OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: Tax-Relevant Event Location Standard (TRELS) Module: ELIM — Event Location Identification Module Operational Layer: Event Location Identification Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Event Location Identification Origin ID: TREGA-TRELS-ELIM-001 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 31 August 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition The Event Location Identification Module (ELIM) governs how spatial information potentially associated with a Governed Temporally Situated Event is discovered, identified, contextualized, differentiated, correlated, and qualified before any specific physical, digital, distributed, or composite Event Location is established. ELIM creates the governed spatial-input layer required for subsequent Event Location governance. Its canonical task is: to establish a coherent and traceable Governed Event Location Signal Set representing the materially relevant spatial signals associated with the governed event without prematurely determining Physical Event Location, Digital Event Location, Distributed Event Location, Tax Jurisdiction, tax nexus, place of supply, source jurisdiction, or any other jurisdiction-specific tax consequence. ELIM therefore answers: What location information legitimately belongs to the event? It does not yet answer: What is the final governed location of the event? And it never answers: Which jurisdiction has authority to tax the event? Operational Role A modern event may generate numerous location-bearing signals. These may originate from physical facilities, devices, users, machines, networks, servers, cloud regions, delivery points, payment infrastructure, operational systems, autonomous agents, transaction records, digital platforms, sensors, logistics systems, or other sources. The existence of such information does not automatically establish Event Location. ELIM determines which spatial signals are materially associated with the bounded event and creates the governed location evidence structure that subsequent TRELS modules can evaluate. Its operational transition is: Governed Temporally Situated Event ↓ Governed Event Location Signal Set The module prevents downstream systems from selecting the easiest, earliest, most commercially convenient, or legally advantageous location signal and treating it as operational truth. Internal Flow Within TRELS, ELIM occupies the first operational position: ELIM — What spatial information legitimately belongs to the event? ↓ ELPM — What physical location materially belongs to the event? ↓ ELDM — What digital location materially belongs to the event? ↓ ELDSM — How is a genuinely distributed event spatially represented? ↓ ELCM — How are relevant event locations correlated into a governed spatial representation? ↓ Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event ELIM therefore establishes the spatial signal foundation. It does not perform the downstream determinations owned by ELPM, ELDM, ELDSM, or ELCM. Operational Space ELIM governs the identification layer between an event that has already been bounded and temporally situated and the subsequent determination of its operational spatial characteristics. Its operational space includes: physical location signals; digital location signals; infrastructure location signals; device-derived location signals; machine-generated location signals; platform-recorded location signals; network-derived location signals; transaction-associated location signals; service-execution location signals; delivery and fulfillment location signals; participant-associated spatial signals where materially relevant to the event; distributed-system location signals; autonomous-system location signals; spatial metadata; location-source relationships; location-signal relevance; location-signal precision; location-signal uncertainty; location-signal ambiguity; conflicting location signals; spatial traceability. The module governs these signals as potential descriptors of operational reality. It does not assume that any one signal represents the Event Location. Operational Scope ELIM shall support the identification and governance of spatial signals associated with physical, digital, hybrid, distributed, transactional, service-based, machine-generated, autonomous, and value-affecting events. The module shall be capable of distinguishing between: where an actor is located; where an object is located; where infrastructure is located; where a device is located; where a system records an event; where computation occurs; where a service executes; where goods move; where goods are delivered; where instructions originate; where an autonomous action executes; where payment processing occurs; where records are stored; and where the governed event itself may operationally occur. These locations may coincide. They must not be assumed to coincide. 1. Spatial Signal Discovery ELIM shall identify available spatial signals materially associated with the Governed Temporally Situated Event. A spatial signal may include a coordinate, address, facility identifier, device position, infrastructure region, network-derived location, system location attribute, delivery point, service execution environment, machine location, or another spatial descriptor. Signal discovery shall not itself establish Event Location. Available Location Data ≠ Governed Event Location. The purpose of discovery is to identify the spatial evidence environment surrounding the event. 2. Spatial Signal Identification Each materially relevant spatial signal shall be identifiable as a distinct governed object within the location-identification process. Where feasible, the signal shall retain information concerning: source; type; spatial representation; associated event component; temporal relevance; precision; acquisition method; confidence or qualification state; transformation history; and traceability reference. Spatial signals shall not be collapsed merely because they appear to reference the same geographic area. Two signals may describe different operational dimensions of the same event. 3. Spatial Signal Source Governance ELIM shall distinguish the source of location information from the operational meaning of that information. Potential sources include: human-provided information; organizational records; sensors; mobile devices; machines; autonomous systems; platform records; logistics systems; payment systems; network infrastructure; cloud infrastructure; geolocation services; digital identity systems; transaction systems; or external evidence sources. A source may provide useful spatial information without possessing authority to define Event Location. Location Source ≠ Event-Location Authority by Default. 4. Physical and Digital Signal Differentiation ELIM shall preserve the distinction between physical and digital spatial signals. Physical signals may describe facilities, devices, machines, persons, goods, infrastructure, delivery destinations, or other physically situated components. Digital signals may describe logical infrastructure, service execution environments, cloud regions, network endpoints, platform environments, or other digitally represented operational spaces. The presence of a digital signal shall not automatically establish physical location. The presence of a physical signal shall not automatically establish the location of a digital operation. Digital Location Signal ≠ Physical Event Location. Physical Location Signal ≠ Digital Event Location. Final governance of these dimensions belongs to subsequent TRELS modules. 5. Participant-Associated Location Signals Participants may produce location information materially relevant to an event. Examples include customer location, provider location, employee location, machine operator location, autonomous-agent infrastructure location, organization address, or recipient location. ELIM may identify these signals where they materially describe the event environment. It shall not infer that Participant Location is automatically Event Location. Participant Location ≠ Event Location by Default. Participant identity and participation governance remain outside ELIM. 6. Infrastructure Location Signals Digital and machine-mediated events may rely upon infrastructure distributed across multiple places. ELIM may identify locations associated with: servers; data centers; cloud regions; edge infrastructure; telecommunications infrastructure; payment infrastructure; machine controllers; industrial facilities; storage infrastructure; or computational environments. Infrastructure location may be operationally relevant. It shall not automatically define the location of the event. Infrastructure Location ≠ Event Location by Default. 7. Device and Machine Location Signals Devices, robots, industrial machines, vehicles, sensors, autonomous systems, and connected equipment may generate precise spatial information. ELIM shall distinguish the location of the device or machine from the spatial meaning of the event. A machine may participate in an event without its physical location being sufficient to represent the complete event. Similarly, a mobile device may generate geolocation data without proving that the relevant economic or operational event occurred at that exact position. Device Location ≠ Event Location by Default. Machine Location ≠ Event Location by Default. 8. Network-Derived Location Signals IP addresses, network endpoints, routing information, telecommunications records, and similar technical signals may provide spatial indicators. ELIM may identify these signals where materially relevant. Network-derived location shall be qualified according to its evidential characteristics and operational meaning. IP Location ≠ Event Location by Default. Technical geolocation may contribute to Event Location governance without becoming operational truth merely because it is machine-readable. 9. Transaction and Payment Location Signals Transaction systems may associate events with merchant locations, terminal locations, bank locations, payment-processor locations, account addresses, settlement locations, or other spatial attributes. ELIM shall distinguish such signals from the location of the underlying governed event. Payment Processing Location ≠ Event Location by Default. Settlement Location ≠ Event Location by Default. Financial infrastructure may describe part of the event environment without defining where the event itself occurred. 10. Delivery and Fulfillment Location Signals Events involving physical goods may contain origin, dispatch, transit, warehouse, transfer, delivery, collection, and destination locations. ELIM shall identify materially relevant signals without assuming that any one logistics point constitutes the Event Location. The meaning of each location depends upon the bounded event under governance. Delivery Location ≠ Complete Event Location by Default. 11. Service Execution Location Signals A service may involve several operational locations. The customer, service provider, personnel, platform, infrastructure, data processing, and actual service execution may all be spatially separated. ELIM shall identify the relevant signals while preserving their distinct operational meanings. For digital services, a server or cloud region shall not automatically become the service's governed Event Location. For human-delivered services, corporate registration address shall not automatically become the operational location of service performance. 12. Distributed Location Signal Sets An event may legitimately contain materially relevant spatial signals from several locations. ELIM shall not treat multiplicity as an error requiring artificial reduction. Multiple Location Signals ≠ Location Conflict by Default. Several signals may accurately describe different spatial dimensions of one governed event. Determining whether the event is genuinely distributed belongs downstream within TRELS. 13. Spatial Signal Correlation ELIM shall establish relevant associations between identified spatial signals and the bounded event. Correlation may consider: event component; activity; object; infrastructure; participant role; machine action; transaction stage; service stage; temporal position; or other legitimate event relationships. Correlation shall preserve distinctions among signals. Spatial Correlation ≠ Spatial Equivalence. Two signals associated with the same event need not describe the same location function. 14. Spatial Relevance Assessment Not every location appearing in surrounding systems materially describes the governed event. ELIM shall support differentiation among: materially relevant location signals; contextual location signals; supporting location signals; technically generated but operationally weak signals; administratively associated signals; redundant signals; and unrelated spatial information. The purpose is not to eliminate complexity but to prevent irrelevant location data from acquiring false governance significance. 15. Location Precision Spatial signals may exist at different levels of precision. Examples include: exact coordinates; facility; building; site; municipality; region; country; infrastructure zone; cloud region; network region; or unknown / qualified spatial range. ELIM shall preserve the precision legitimately supported by the underlying information. Recorded Spatial Precision ≠ Proven Spatial Accuracy. A coordinate with many decimal places is not automatically more operationally reliable than a qualified facility-level location. 16. Spatial Ambiguity Where available information supports more than one legitimate spatial interpretation, ELIM shall preserve that ambiguity. Systems shall not manufacture false precision solely because downstream data structures require a single location field. A governed result may legitimately indicate: approximate location; bounded location; multiple candidate locations; distributed spatial signals; conflicting location information; or unresolved location. Required Location Field ≠ Permission to Invent Location Certainty. 17. Conflicting Location Signals Conflicting signals shall be identifiable and traceable. Conflict may arise because: systems use different location sources; devices report inconsistent positions; network-derived location differs from physical location; participant information is outdated; infrastructure is distributed; timestamps correspond to different operational stages; records were transformed; or systems apply different location conventions. ELIM shall not resolve such conflict by arbitrary source preference. System Preference ≠ Governed Spatial Resolution. 18. Machine and Autonomous Event Environments Autonomous systems may generate large volumes of location-bearing information. An autonomous economic event may involve: an AI agent operating through one infrastructure environment; a robot acting in another location; a cloud service executing elsewhere; a payment system in another region; and a recipient in another location. ELIM shall identify the materially relevant spatial signals without equating infrastructure topology with Event Location. Machine Location Data Volume ≠ Event Spatial Granularity. One Machine Location ≠ One Event Location. 19. Location Normalization Spatial data may require normalization for interoperability. Normalization may include standardized coordinates, address structures, facility identifiers, region identifiers, or other spatial representations. The original location information shall remain traceable where material. Normalized Location ≠ Original Location Evidence. Normalization shall improve interoperability without rewriting the spatial evidence history of the event. 20. Location Signal Correction Where a spatial signal is later shown to be incorrect, incomplete, or improperly associated, correction shall remain traceable. Correction shall not silently erase the previous state where historical reconstruction is required. Location Correction ≠ Historical Erasure. Correction of a signal also does not automatically change the Event Boundary or create a new event. 21. Governance Requirements ELIM implementations shall: identify materially relevant spatial signals; preserve signal-source traceability; distinguish signal type from Event Location; distinguish physical, digital, infrastructure, participant, device, machine, transaction, and other location dimensions; preserve legitimate spatial multiplicity; identify ambiguity and conflict; maintain appropriate spatial precision; avoid false geographic certainty; preserve original spatial evidence where normalization occurs; support distributed and autonomous environments; prevent downstream legal assumptions from redefining operational spatial information; and produce a governed location signal set suitable for subsequent TRELS processing. No individual spatial signal shall become authoritative Event Location solely because it is technically available, commercially convenient, administratively preferred, or required by a downstream tax system. 22. Governance Logic ELIM follows the canonical logic: Location information exists ↓ identify its source ↓ determine its relationship to the governed event ↓ classify its spatial function ↓ assess material relevance ↓ preserve precision ↓ identify ambiguity or conflict ↓ correlate legitimate signals ↓ establish Governed Event Location Signal Set. The module deliberately stops before final Event Location determination. 23. Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum ELIM implementation should support: Governed Event Reference Reference to the event received from TRETS. Spatial Signal Identifier Unique reference for each materially relevant spatial signal. Spatial Signal Type Physical, digital, infrastructure, device, machine, participant-associated, network-derived, transactional, logistics, service-execution, or other legitimate category. Spatial Signal Source System, device, actor, infrastructure, record, or evidence source producing the signal. Spatial Representation The location information itself at the legitimately supported precision. Event Association Relationship between the signal and the governed event. Operational Function The spatial role represented by the signal. Temporal Association Relevant relationship between the location signal and governed Event Timing where necessary. Precision State Level of spatial precision legitimately supported. Relevance State Material, contextual, supporting, weak, redundant, excluded, or unresolved. Ambiguity State Known ambiguity associated with the signal. Conflict State Known conflict with other spatial signals. Traceability Reference Evidence or governance reference supporting reconstruction. Governance State Current state of the signal within ELIM. Handoff State Readiness for downstream Physical, Digital, Distributed, and Correlation governance. 24. Governance Outputs ELIM may produce: Spatial Signal Register; Spatial Source Map; Spatial Relevance Assessment; Physical Signal Set; Digital Signal Set; Infrastructure Signal Set; Machine / Autonomous Spatial Signal Set; Spatial Precision Record; Spatial Ambiguity Record; Spatial Conflict Record; Spatial Correlation Map; Spatial Traceability Record; and the principal output: Governed Event Location Signal Set This output becomes the spatial governance input for ELPM. 25. Critical Distinctions Location Data ≠ Event Location Location Signal ≠ Governed Event Location Location Source ≠ Event-Location Authority Participant Location ≠ Event Location Organization Address ≠ Event Location Device Location ≠ Event Location Machine Location ≠ Event Location Server Location ≠ Event Location Cloud Region ≠ Event Location IP Location ≠ Event Location Payment Processing Location ≠ Event Location Settlement Location ≠ Event Location Delivery Location ≠ Complete Event Location Digital Location Signal ≠ Physical Event Location Physical Location Signal ≠ Digital Event Location Multiple Location Signals ≠ Location Conflict Spatial Correlation ≠ Spatial Equivalence Recorded Precision ≠ Proven Accuracy Required Location Field ≠ Governed Location Certainty Normalized Location ≠ Original Location Evidence Location Correction ≠ Historical Erasure Event Location ≠ Tax Jurisdiction Operational Spatial Reality ≠ Jurisdictional Tax Determination 26. Enterprise Application ELIM can operate as the spatial-input governance layer between operational systems and downstream taxation infrastructure. A generalized implementation pattern is: ERP / Commerce / Banking / Digital Platform / Logistics / Cloud / AI Agent / Machine System ↓ Spatial Signal Discovery ↓ ELIM ↓ Governed Event Location Signal Set ↓ TRELS Location Modules ↓ Governed Event Location ↓ TREGA™ Event Layer ↓ Jurisdiction-Specific Tax Engines This allows organizations to preserve one governed operational representation of spatial reality while enabling multiple downstream legal systems to interpret that reality independently. 27. Use Case 1 — Distributed Digital Marketplace A customer initiates a digital purchase from a mobile device in Country A. The platform operator is established in Country B. Authentication infrastructure operates in Country C. The application executes through cloud regions in Countries D and E. Payment authorization is processed through Country F. The customer's account contains an address in Country G. The platform therefore contains several technically valid location signals. A conventional implementation may select the customer's IP address, billing address, merchant address, or server region and immediately treat it as transaction location. ELIM instead identifies each materially relevant spatial signal, records its source and operational function, preserves its precision, and establishes its relationship to the governed event. It does not decide which location is the final Event Location. It does not decide which country may tax the transaction. The output is a Governed Event Location Signal Set that subsequent TRELS modules can evaluate. Complex spatial reality must be governed before it is compressed into a legal jurisdictional conclusion. 28. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Industrial Event An AI-controlled production network receives a manufacturing requirement. Planning occurs through cloud infrastructure in one country. A robotic production cell operates in another. Components arrive from a separate facility. Machine coordination uses edge infrastructure in another region. Quality verification occurs through remote computational infrastructure. The finished component is transferred to an autonomous logistics system serving another country. Thousands of machine, sensor, infrastructure, network, and logistics records contain location information. ELIM identifies which spatial signals materially belong to the governed event and distinguishes machine location, infrastructure location, computational location, logistics location, and other relevant spatial dimensions. It does not allow the physical position of the AI infrastructure, the robot, or a server to become Event Location automatically. The location of the machine performing an action is evidence about the event — not automatically the complete spatial identity of the event. 29. Canonical Boundary ELIM owns the identification, contextualization, differentiation, relevance assessment, correlation, precision qualification, ambiguity recognition, conflict recognition, normalization traceability, and governance of spatial signals materially associated with the Tax-Relevant Event. ELIM does not determine final Physical Event Location, Digital Event Location, Distributed Event Location, or final Event Location Correlation. It does not redefine Event Context, Event Recognition, Event Formation, Event Boundary, Event Timing, Event Participation, Participant Identity, Value Association, Event Relationships, Event Determination, or Event Record Governance. It does not determine Tax Jurisdiction, tax nexus, tax residence, permanent establishment, place of supply, source jurisdiction, customs jurisdiction, taxpayer status, legal taxability, Tax Liability, Tax Period, Legal Tax Point, tax rate, tax calculation, filing obligation, or any other jurisdiction-specific tax consequence. The canonical handoff is: TRETS — Governed Temporally Situated Event ↓ ELIM — Governed Event Location Signal Set ↓ ELPM — Event Physical Location Governance Canonical Closing Statement ELIM establishes which spatial signals legitimately describe the governed event before any individual address, device, machine, server, infrastructure region, or participant location is permitted to define where that event occurred. ELIM identifies the locations that may describe the event — it does not yet decide the final Event Location, and it never decides the Tax Jurisdiction.

title: OOF™ The Event Physical Location Module (ELPM) governs how materially relevant
text: OOF™ The Event Physical Location Module (ELPM) governs how materially relevant The Event Physical Location Module (ELPM) governs how materially relevant OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: Tax-Relevant Event Location Standard (TRELS) Module: ELPM — Event Physical Location Module Operational Layer: Event Physical Location Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Event Physical Location Origin ID: TREGA-TRELS-ELPM-002 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 31 August 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language Canonical Definition The Event Physical Location Module (ELPM) governs how materially relevant physical spatial signals associated with a Tax-Relevant Event are evaluated, differentiated, qualified, and assembled into a governed representation of where the event physically occurred, was performed, manifested, or materially interacted with operational reality. ELPM operates on the Governed Event Location Signal Set established by ELIM and determines the physical spatial characteristics legitimately attributable to the event. Its canonical task is: to establish a coherent, traceable, and operationally justified Governed Event Physical Location without allowing participant addresses, device coordinates, infrastructure positions, contractual locations, administrative records, or jurisdiction-specific tax rules to redefine the physical location of the governed event. The principal transition is: Governed Event Location Signal Set ↓ Governed Event Physical Location ELPM determines physical Event Location. It does not determine Tax Jurisdiction. Operational Role Physical events frequently involve more than one location. Goods may be produced in one facility, inspected in another, transferred through several logistics nodes, and delivered elsewhere. A service may involve a provider, customer, equipment, and operational object situated in different places. An autonomous machine may act physically in one country while being controlled through infrastructure located elsewhere. A transaction may contain addresses belonging to participants, payment systems, warehouses, corporate entities, and delivery destinations without any one of those addresses fully representing where the governed event physically occurred. ELPM establishes which physical locations materially constitute, host, contain, support, or otherwise describe the physical manifestation of the event. Its purpose is not to find a convenient geographic field. Its purpose is to govern physical spatial reality. Internal Flow Within TRELS, ELPM occupies the second operational position: ELIM — What spatial information legitimately belongs to the event? ↓ ELPM — What physical location materially belongs to the event? ↓ ELDM — What digital location materially belongs to the event? ↓ ELDSM — How is a genuinely distributed event spatially represented? ↓ ELCM — How are relevant event locations correlated into a governed spatial representation? ↓ Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event ELPM receives: Governed Event Location Signal Set and produces: Governed Event Physical Location for subsequent integration with digital and distributed location governance. Operational Space ELPM governs the physical spatial representation of the Tax-Relevant Event. Its operational space includes: physical event sites; facilities; buildings; production locations; service-performance locations; machine operating locations; equipment locations; goods locations; object locations; transfer locations; delivery locations; collection locations; storage locations; logistics locations; physical interaction points; mobile-event locations; multi-site events; physically distributed events; physical-location precision; physical-location uncertainty; physical-location conflict; physical-location transitions; physical-location traceability; and physical spatial continuity. ELPM governs physical location only to the extent required to represent the operational spatial reality of the event. Operational Scope ELPM shall support physical-location governance for: manufacturing; logistics; transportation; construction; physical services; retail; warehousing; infrastructure operations; energy systems; healthcare operations; automated facilities; robotics; autonomous vehicles; IoT environments; machine-to-machine operations; hybrid physical-digital events; and other events possessing a material physical spatial dimension. The module shall support both stationary and mobile events. It shall also support events whose physical manifestation spans more than one location. 1. Physical Location Candidate Identification ELPM shall identify physical-location candidates from the Governed Event Location Signal Set produced by ELIM. Candidates may include: coordinates; addresses; facilities; operational sites; warehouses; factories; stores; terminals; construction sites; machines; vehicles; delivery points; collection points; physical infrastructure; or other materially relevant spatial references. A physical-location candidate shall not become Governed Event Physical Location merely because it is available. Physical Location Candidate ≠ Governed Event Physical Location. 2. Constitutive Physical Location ELPM shall determine whether a physical location materially participates in the constitution of the event. A constitutive physical location is one at which activity forming part of the governed event actually occurs or materially manifests. This distinction prevents surrounding locations from being mistaken for the physical location of the event. For example, the registered office of a company may be associated with the event while no constitutive event activity occurs there. Associated Physical Location ≠ Constitutive Physical Location. 3. Physical Performance Location Where an event involves physical performance, ELPM shall govern the location at which that performance occurs. Examples may include: manufacturing; assembly; repair; installation; inspection; construction; physical service delivery; machine operation; loading; unloading; or other material activity. The physical performance location shall be established from operational evidence rather than administrative convention. Registered Address ≠ Physical Performance Location by Default. 4. Object Location Where a physical object materially participates in the event, ELPM may govern the object's location as a relevant spatial dimension. Objects may include: goods; machinery; equipment; components; vehicles; infrastructure assets; physical documents; commodities; or other tangible objects. Object Location shall not automatically become complete Event Location. Object Location ≠ Complete Event Location by Default. Its significance depends upon the governed Event Boundary and the object's operational role. 5. Goods Location Events involving goods may include several legitimate physical locations. Goods may be: produced; stored; transferred; transported; inspected; modified; delivered; returned; or destroyed at different places. ELPM shall preserve these distinctions where they materially describe the event. Location of Goods at One Stage ≠ Location of the Entire Event by Default. 6. Machine and Equipment Location Where machines, robots, industrial equipment, autonomous vehicles, or other physical systems participate in the event, their physical position may form a material component of Event Location. ELPM shall determine the operational significance of that position. A machine's physical location may represent: the place of execution; one component location; a supporting location; a mobile location; or merely the position of equipment associated with a larger event. Machine Location ≠ Complete Event Location by Default. The location of computational infrastructure controlling the machine is governed separately as appropriate. 7. Human Physical Presence Human presence may be materially relevant to the physical event. ELPM may govern the physical location of persons where their presence forms part of the event's operational spatial reality. However: Human Presence Location ≠ Event Location by Default. A customer may be physically located in one place while a service is performed elsewhere. An operator may control machinery remotely. An employee's location may differ from the location of the operational object. Participant role governance remains with TREPS. 8. Facility Location Facilities may provide strong physical anchors for an event. Examples include factories, warehouses, offices, hospitals, stores, laboratories, terminals, data facilities, construction sites, and energy installations. ELPM shall distinguish between: facility where constitutive event activity occurs; facility supporting the event; facility merely associated with a participant; facility appearing only in administrative records; and facility unrelated to the bounded event. Facility Association ≠ Event Location by Default. 9. Delivery and Collection Location Delivery or collection may form a constitutive part of some events. Where so bounded, ELPM shall govern the relevant physical location. However: Delivery Location ≠ Complete Event Location by Default. Collection Location ≠ Complete Event Location by Default. The significance of delivery or collection depends upon the event under governance rather than downstream legal preference. 10. Mobile Event Location Some events move through physical space. Examples include: transportation; logistics; autonomous vehicle operations; maritime operations; aviation; mobile services; infrastructure inspection; robotics; and moving industrial processes. ELPM shall not force such events into a single static coordinate where the operational reality is spatially mobile. A mobile event may require: origin location; destination location; route; relevant intermediate locations; spatial intervals; or a governed spatial trajectory. Mobile Event ≠ Single Static Location by Default. 11. Multi-Site Physical Events One governed event may legitimately span several physical sites. ELPM shall preserve multi-site physical reality where supported by the Event Boundary. Examples include distributed manufacturing, coordinated construction, multi-facility processing, supply-chain operations, and infrastructure events. Multiple Physical Locations ≠ Multiple Events by Default. Conversely: One Commercial Transaction ≠ One Physical Location by Default. Whether multiple activities belong to one event is governed upstream through Event Formation and Event Boundary. 12. Physical Location Transition Where the physical position of the event or a constitutive event object changes over time, ELPM shall preserve materially relevant location transitions. This may require correlation with the governed Event Timing established under TRETS. The representation may include: Location A ↓ Location B ↓ Location C without implying that each transition constitutes a new event. Location Change ≠ New Event by Default. 13. Physical Location and Event Timing Physical location may change throughout the duration of an event. ELPM shall therefore support temporal association of location where necessary. A location record may specify that a physical location applies: at Event Start; during a defined interval; during a particular event phase; at Event Completion; or across the full governed duration. ELPM does not redefine Event Timing. TRETS remains authoritative for temporal governance. 14. Physical Location Precision Physical Event Location shall be represented only at the precision legitimately supported by evidence. Possible representations include: exact coordinate; machine position; room; building; facility; site; municipality; region; corridor; route; bounded geographic area; or qualified unknown location. Technical Coordinate Precision ≠ Operational Location Certainty. An exact GPS coordinate with uncertain provenance may be less governance-reliable than a verified facility-level location. 15. Physical Location Uncertainty Where physical location cannot be established with full certainty, ELPM shall preserve the uncertainty. Permissible states may include: exact; bounded; approximate; multi-candidate; mobile; distributed; conflicted; partially established; or unresolved. Downstream requirements for a single country or address shall not override operational uncertainty. Required Geographic Field ≠ Permission for False Location Certainty. 16. Conflicting Physical Locations ELPM shall govern conflicts among physical-location signals. Conflicts may arise from: inconsistent sensor data; inaccurate addresses; stale records; mobile devices; machine movement; participant movement; delayed system updates; incorrect geocoding; inconsistent facility identifiers; or conflicting operational records. Resolution shall be evidence-based and traceable. Administrative Preference ≠ Governed Physical Location. 17. Physical Location Continuity Where an event persists across time, ELPM shall support continuity of its physical spatial representation. Continuity may be: stationary; mobile; sequential; multi-site; interrupted; or distributed. Physical continuity shall be evaluated against the existing Event Boundary. A spatial transition alone shall not automatically split the event. 18. Physical and Digital Separation ELPM shall preserve a strict distinction between physical and digital location. A physical operation may depend upon digital infrastructure elsewhere. A digital transaction may interact with physical goods or devices. Neither dimension shall automatically redefine the other. Physical Event Location ≠ Digital Event Location. Digital location governance belongs to ELDM. 19. Physical Location and Participant Location A participant may be physically situated somewhere relevant to the event without that location representing the physical event itself. Examples include: remote employee; remote machine operator; customer placing an order while traveling; corporate headquarters; beneficial owner; platform administrator; or service recipient. ELPM shall not derive Event Physical Location solely from Participant Location. Participant Location ≠ Physical Event Location by Default. 20. Physical Location and Organizational Address Registered office, headquarters, billing address, correspondence address, branch address, or contractual address may provide useful contextual information. They do not automatically establish where the event physically occurred. Legal Address ≠ Operational Physical Location. Billing Address ≠ Physical Event Location. Corporate Residence ≠ Physical Event Location. 21. Physical Location and Tax Jurisdiction ELPM shall maintain a strict boundary between operational physical location and jurisdiction-specific taxation. Physical Event Location may become an input to downstream jurisdictional analysis. It does not itself establish: tax jurisdiction; tax nexus; permanent establishment; tax residence; source jurisdiction; place of supply; place of performance under tax law; customs jurisdiction; legal situs; or taxing authority. Physical Event Location ≠ Tax Jurisdiction. A physical event may occur in one or several places while different legal systems legitimately apply different tax rules to that same governed spatial reality. 22. Multi-Jurisdiction Readiness ELPM shall preserve operational spatial reality in a form capable of supporting multiple downstream jurisdictional evaluations. Canonical logic: One Governed Physical Reality ↓ Multiple Possible Jurisdictional Evaluations The physical event representation shall therefore remain independent from any single jurisdiction's legal interpretation. This enables TREGA™ to maintain a stable governed event layer while tax rules change across countries and over time. 23. Governance States ELPM may assign states including: Physical Location Ready Relevant physical signals are available for governance. Physical Location Under Governance Candidate locations are being evaluated. Physical Location Established A sufficient physical representation has been established. Physical Location Multi-Site The event legitimately spans multiple physical sites. Physical Location Mobile The event materially moves through physical space. Physical Location Qualified The location is established subject to explicit qualification. Physical Location Conflicted Material physical-location evidence conflicts. Physical Location Unresolved Available evidence is insufficient for legitimate determination. These states shall remain traceable. 24. Governance Requirements ELPM implementations shall: consume the Governed Event Location Signal Set produced by ELIM; identify materially relevant physical-location candidates; distinguish constitutive from contextual physical locations; govern physical performance location where relevant; preserve object, goods, machine, facility, participant-associated, and logistics location distinctions; support stationary, mobile, multi-site, and physically distributed events; preserve temporal association where location changes during the event; maintain evidence-supported spatial precision; preserve uncertainty and conflict; avoid artificial single-location reduction; maintain physical/digital separation; prevent legal or tax classifications from redefining operational physical reality; preserve traceability; and produce a Governed Event Physical Location suitable for subsequent TRELS processing. 25. Governance Logic ELPM follows the canonical logic: Governed Event Location Signal Set ↓ identify physical-location candidates ↓ determine their operational roles ↓ distinguish constitutive from contextual locations ↓ assess physical performance and manifestation ↓ evaluate mobility and multi-site structure ↓ govern precision, uncertainty, and conflict ↓ establish Governed Event Physical Location. No downstream legal tax rule may substitute for this operational determination. 26. Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum ELPM implementation should support: Governed Event Reference Reference to the event under location governance. Physical Location Identifier Unique reference for each governed physical location. Physical Location Type Facility, coordinate, site, route, machine location, object location, delivery point, mobile position, or other legitimate type. Operational Role Constitutive, supporting, contextual, transitional, or other governed role. Spatial Representation Physical location at the legitimately supported precision. Temporal Association Relevant relationship to Event Timing. Physical Object Association Object, goods, machine, infrastructure, or other physical component where relevant. Mobility State Stationary, mobile, transitional, or mixed. Multi-Site State Whether the event materially spans multiple sites. Precision State Supported spatial precision. Uncertainty State Known uncertainty. Conflict State Known evidence conflict. Evidence Reference Supporting operational evidence. Traceability Reference Governance history enabling reconstruction. Governance State Current ELPM determination state. Handoff State Readiness for subsequent digital and distributed location governance. 27. Governance Outputs ELPM may produce: Physical Location Candidate Register; Constitutive Physical Location Map; Physical Performance Location Record; Object Location Record; Goods Location Record; Machine Location Record; Facility Location Record; Mobile Event Location Map; Multi-Site Event Map; Physical Location Transition Record; Physical Location Precision Record; Physical Location Uncertainty Record; Physical Location Conflict Record; Physical Location Traceability Record; and the principal output: Governed Event Physical Location This output becomes an input to subsequent TRELS modules. 28. Critical Distinctions Physical Location Signal ≠ Governed Event Physical Location Physical Location Candidate ≠ Governed Event Physical Location Associated Physical Location ≠ Constitutive Physical Location Registered Address ≠ Physical Performance Location Object Location ≠ Complete Event Location Goods Location ≠ Complete Event Location Machine Location ≠ Complete Event Location Human Presence Location ≠ Event Location Facility Association ≠ Event Location Delivery Location ≠ Complete Event Location Collection Location ≠ Complete Event Location Mobile Event ≠ Single Static Location Multiple Physical Locations ≠ Multiple Events Location Change ≠ New Event Technical Coordinate Precision ≠ Operational Location Certainty Administrative Preference ≠ Governed Physical Location Participant Location ≠ Physical Event Location Legal Address ≠ Operational Physical Location Billing Address ≠ Physical Event Location Physical Event Location ≠ Digital Event Location Physical Event Location ≠ Tax Jurisdiction Physical Event Location ≠ Tax Nexus Physical Event Location ≠ Permanent Establishment Physical Event Location ≠ Tax Residence Physical Event Location ≠ Legal Place of Supply Physical Event Location ≠ Source Jurisdiction Operational Physical Reality ≠ Jurisdictional Tax Determination 29. Enterprise Application ELPM can operate as the physical spatial-governance layer between operational systems and downstream taxation infrastructure. A generalized implementation pattern is: ERP / Manufacturing / Logistics / Commerce / IoT / Robotics / Infrastructure System ↓ ELIM Governed Event Location Signal Set ↓ ELPM ↓ Governed Event Physical Location ↓ Remaining TRELS Modules ↓ Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event ↓ Jurisdiction-Specific Tax Engines This allows operational systems to preserve physical reality independently from the legal rules later applied to that reality. 30. Use Case 1 — Cross-Border Manufacturing and Logistics Event A component is manufactured at Facility A in Country A. It is transferred to Facility B in Country B for specialized processing. Quality verification occurs at Facility C. The component is then transported through several logistics nodes before delivery to a customer in Country D. Operational systems contain the manufacturer's registered address, production coordinates, warehouse addresses, transport locations, customs facilities, customer address, and delivery location. A conventional system may select one of these locations because a downstream tax field requires a country. ELPM instead determines which physical locations materially constitute the bounded event. It preserves the event's multi-site physical structure where required and distinguishes production, processing, inspection, transit, and delivery locations. It does not determine which country has taxation authority. A cross-border event may possess one governed physical reality and still support several legitimate jurisdictional interpretations. 31. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Mobile Industrial Operation An autonomous industrial vehicle receives instructions through cloud infrastructure and performs inspection and repair operations across a large energy facility. The vehicle moves through multiple physical zones. Its onboard systems record coordinates continuously. Remote AI infrastructure analyzes sensor information from another country. Human supervisors may monitor the operation from additional locations. ELPM governs the physical spatial reality of the event by identifying where the autonomous vehicle materially performs the bounded operation, preserving relevant movement, operational zones, and spatial transitions. It does not treat the cloud infrastructure location, supervisor location, company headquarters, or every individual GPS coordinate as the complete Event Physical Location. Where the operation is genuinely mobile, ELPM preserves that mobility. A moving event must be governed as a moving event rather than forced into a static location merely because downstream systems expect one address. 32. Canonical Boundary ELPM owns the governance of the physical spatial manifestation of the Tax-Relevant Event, including constitutive physical locations, physical performance locations, object and goods locations, machine and equipment locations, facility locations, relevant physical presence, mobile locations, multi-site structures, physical-location transitions, physical-location precision, uncertainty, conflict, continuity, and traceability. ELPM does not own final Digital Event Location, Distributed Event Location, or final cross-dimensional Event Location Correlation. It does not redefine Event Context, Event Recognition, Event Formation, Event Boundary, Event Timing, Event Participation, Participant Identity, Value Association, Event Relationships, Event Determination, or Event Record Governance. It does not determine Tax Jurisdiction, tax nexus, tax residence, permanent establishment, place of supply, source jurisdiction, legal situs, customs jurisdiction, taxpayer status, Legal Tax Point, Tax Period, taxability, Tax Liability, tax rate, filing obligation, or any jurisdiction-specific tax consequence. The canonical handoff is: ELIM — Governed Event Location Signal Set ↓ ELPM — Governed Event Physical Location ↓ ELDM — Event Digital Location Governance Canonical Closing Statement ELPM establishes where the governed event materially manifests in physical reality without allowing addresses, facilities, devices, machines, logistics points, or administrative conventions to become authoritative merely because they contain geographic information. ELPM governs where the event physically occurred — not which jurisdiction may tax what occurred there. TREGA™ governs the event. The jurisdiction governs the tax. Moful3

title: OOF™ The Event Actor Association Module (EPAM) governs how identified
text: OOF™ The Event Actor Association Module (EPAM) governs how identified The Event Actor Association Module (EPAM) governs how identified OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: TREPS — Tax-Relevant Event Participation Standard Module: EPAM — Event Actor Association Module Operational Layer: Event Actor Association Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Event Actor Association Origin ID: TREGA-TREPS-EPAM-003 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 1 September 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language Canonical Definition The Event Actor Association Module (EPAM) governs how identified Participant Candidates and their governed operational roles are materially associated with a specific Tax-Relevant Event. EPAM determines whether the available actor, role, event, temporal, spatial, and operational information is sufficient to establish that an actor materially participates in the governed event. Its principal transition is: Governed Participant Candidate + Governed Participation Role ↓ Governed Actor–Event Association EPAM does not identify the actor. EPIM owns Participant Identification. EPAM does not establish the actor's operational role. EPRM owns Participation Role governance. EPAM establishes the governed relationship between the actor and the specific event. The foundational distinction is: Actor Association ≠ Event Participation by Default An actor becomes a Governed Event Participant only when its association with the event is sufficiently supported and materially relevant. Operational Role Modern event records may contain many identifiable actors and many technically plausible relationships. An actor may appear because it: owns infrastructure; appears in a contract; operates a platform; holds an account; processes information; provides connectivity; owns a machine; receives a notification; appears in a payment record; is geographically nearby; or belongs to the same corporate structure as another actor. None of these conditions alone necessarily establishes material participation. EPAM exists to determine whether the relationship between an identified actor, its governed operational role, and the specific event is sufficient to establish Event Participation. Internal Module Flow TREPS operates through: EPIM — Participant Identification → EPRM — Participation Role → EPAM — Actor Association → EPMAM — Machine & Autonomous Actor Governance → EPCM — Participation Continuity → Governed Participatory Event EPAM receives: Governed Participant Candidate Set and: Governed Participant Role Set and establishes: Governed Actor–Event Association SetOperational Transition The canonical EPAM transition is: Governed Participant Candidate + Governed Participation Role + Governed Event → Actor–Event Association Governance → Governed Actor–Event Association Where multiple actors are involved: Governed Event ↓ Multiple Governed Actor–Event Associations The existence of multiple associations does not create multiple events by default. Operational Space EPAM governs: actor-event linkage; association materiality; association basis; direct participation; indirect participation; supporting association; multi-actor association; role-event alignment; temporal association; spatial association; operational association; association strength; association uncertainty; association conflict; association change; and association traceability. EPAM governs whether an actor's relationship to the event constitutes material Event Participation. Operational Scope EPAM may operate across: commercial transactions; services; manufacturing; logistics; banking; digital platforms; marketplaces; infrastructure operations; AI-mediated events; autonomous transactions; machine-to-machine operations; robotic systems; distributed systems; hybrid physical-digital events; and other governable operational events. The association logic remains jurisdiction-neutral and technology-neutral. Association Basis A Governed Actor–Event Association requires an operationally justified basis. Association may be supported by information showing that an actor materially: initiated; executed; provided; received; transferred; processed; authorized; coordinated; facilitated; controlled; operated; delivered; consumed; or otherwise performed a governed operational role within the event. The existence of actor information alone is insufficient. Actor Record Presence ≠ Actor–Event Association. Material Association EPAM shall distinguish materially relevant participation from incidental or background association. An actor may be connected to an event without materially participating in it. Therefore: Event Connection ≠ Material Event Participation. A material association exists only where the actor's governed operational relationship is sufficiently relevant to the event being governed. Materiality shall be determined according to operational reality rather than downstream tax convenience. Direct and Indirect Association Participation may occur through direct or indirect operational relationships. A direct association may exist where an actor directly performs a material function within the event. An indirect association may exist where an actor materially contributes through an intermediate operational structure. EPAM shall preserve this distinction where it materially improves the event representation. However: Indirect Association ≠ Non-Participation by Default. Likewise: Direct Technical Connection ≠ Material Participation by Default. The operational function and event relationship remain decisive. Supporting Association Some actors or systems may support an event without becoming material Event Participants. Examples may include generic infrastructure, background communications, passive hosting, administrative systems, or other supporting resources. EPAM shall permit supporting association to remain distinguishable from material participation. Supporting Association ≠ Governed Event Participation by Default. This prevents every technical dependency from becoming a participant. Role–Event Alignment A Governed Participation Role must relate materially to the specific event before it can support Event Participation. An actor may perform the same general role across many activities without participating in every event occurring within that environment. Therefore: Governed Role ≠ Event Participation by Default. EPAM establishes whether the governed role is actually exercised in relation to the specific event. Temporal Association Actor participation shall be compatible with the governed temporal structure of the event. An actor appearing in records before or after an event does not automatically establish participation during that event. EPAM may use TRETS-governed temporal information to evaluate association. However: Temporal Proximity ≠ Event Participation by Default. EPAM does not redefine Event Timing. TRETS remains authoritative for the event's temporal structure. Spatial Association An actor may be physically or digitally located at, near, or within an Event Location without materially participating. Likewise, an actor may participate remotely. Therefore: Spatial Presence ≠ Event Participation by Default. Remote Actor ≠ Non-Participant by Default. EPAM may consume TRELS-governed location information when evaluating Actor–Event Association but shall not redefine Event Location. Transactional Association An actor may appear within a transaction record without being materially involved in the underlying governed event. Likewise, an actor may materially participate even where a conventional transaction record does not explicitly name it. Therefore: Transaction Record Presence ≠ Event Participation by Default. Transaction Record Absence ≠ Non-Participation by Default. EPAM governs operational association rather than database visibility alone. Contractual Association Contracts may provide important evidence of actor relationships. They do not automatically establish what operationally occurred. Therefore: Contractual Party ≠ Event Participant by Default. Conversely: Non-Contractual Actor ≠ Non-Participant by Default. EPAM preserves the distinction between contractual representation and operational participation. Ownership Association Ownership may connect an actor to assets, machines, infrastructure, organizations, or systems involved in an event. Ownership alone does not establish participation. Therefore: Owner ≠ Event Participant by Default. Ownership governance remains outside EPAM. Where necessary, governed ownership information may be consumed from OBIDENITY®. Organizational Association Corporate groups may contain parent companies, subsidiaries, branches, operating entities, service companies, and other related organizations. EPAM shall not transfer participation automatically across organizational relationships. Corporate Relationship ≠ Shared Event Participation. Parent Company Participation ≠ Subsidiary Participation by Default. Subsidiary Participation ≠ Parent Company Participation by Default. Each Actor–Event Association requires its own sufficient operational basis. Platform Association A digital platform may host, facilitate, coordinate, execute, intermediate, or merely technically support an event. EPAM shall determine whether the platform's governed operational role creates a material Actor–Event Association in the specific event. Platform Presence ≠ Event Participation by Default. Platform participation shall be based on operational function rather than platform category alone. Machine and Autonomous Association Machines, AI agents, robots, and autonomous systems may possess material Actor–Event Associations independently from humans or organizations connected to them. EPAM may establish such associations where operational evidence supports them. However, specialized governance of machine and autonomous participation belongs to: EPMAM — Event Machine & Autonomous Actor Module EPAM therefore establishes the association while EPMAM governs the specific characteristics of non-human participation. Machine Association ≠ Owner Association. AI Agent Association ≠ Developer Association. Multiple Actor Associations One governed event may legitimately contain multiple Actor–Event Associations. The canonical model is: One Governed Event → Actor A Association → Actor B Association → Actor C Association → Actor N Association These associations may differ in role, materiality, timing, location, directness, and operational significance. Multiple Actor Associations ≠ Equal Participation. Association Strength Actor–Event Associations may possess different levels of operational support. EPAM shall permit association strength or confidence to be qualified where required. An association may be: Established Qualified Partial Ambiguous Conflicted Unresolved Qualification shall reflect available operational support rather than desired downstream legal outcomes. Association Uncertainty Where available evidence does not sufficiently establish or reject participation, uncertainty shall remain visible. Association Uncertainty ≠ Permission to Assume Participation. Likewise: Association Uncertainty ≠ Permission to Exclude Participation Arbitrarily. The event representation shall preserve uncertainty where legitimate resolution is not available. Association Conflict Different sources may provide incompatible representations of an actor's relationship to the event. EPAM shall preserve material conflicts until sufficient governance supports resolution. Association Conflict ≠ Permission for Convenient Participant Selection. Original materially relevant representations shall remain traceable. Association Change An actor's relationship to an event may evolve. A supporting actor may become materially active.
