A direct participant may cease involvement. An intermediary may assume execution. A machine may replace a human process. EPAM shall preserve materially relevant association changes. However: Association Change ≠ New Event by Default. Participation Continuity is governed subsequently by EPCM. Association and Identity EPAM does not determine who an actor fundamentally is. EPIM provides the Participant Candidate reference, while OBIDENITY® may provide deeper governed identity structures. EPAM governs the relationship: Actor ↔ Specific Governed Event Therefore: Actor–Event Association ≠ Identity Governance. Association and Participation Role EPRM determines the operational role. EPAM determines whether that role materially connects the actor to the specific event. The distinction is: EPRM: What operational function may the actor perform? EPAM: Does that governed function materially associate this actor with this event? Therefore: Participation Role ≠ Actor–Event Association. Association and Accountability Material participation does not automatically establish responsibility or accountability. Therefore: Governed Actor–Event Association ≠ Accountability. Governed Event Participant ≠ Responsible Party by Default. AGA™ remains authoritative for accountability governance where applicable. Association and Liability Actor–Event Association does not establish liability. An actor may materially participate without being legally liable for the event or its consequences. Therefore: Event Participation ≠ Liability. HALIA™ governs the lifecycle of harm and liability where applicable. Association and Value Material participation does not determine which value belongs to an actor or which value result belongs to the event. Therefore: Actor–Event Association ≠ Value Association. Event Participant ≠ Value Owner by Default. TRVAS subsequently governs Value Association. VFM® governs the Value Lifecycle itself. Association and Tax Status EPAM shall not transform Event Participation into a jurisdiction-specific legal classification. A Governed Event Participant is not automatically: a taxpayer; taxable person; supplier; customer; employer; employee; principal; legal agent; marketplace facilitator; withholding party; permanent establishment; beneficial owner; liable party; or reporting party. Therefore: Governed Event Participant ≠ Taxpayer A jurisdiction may subsequently interpret the participation according to its own law. EPAM preserves the operational participation reality on which such interpretation can operate. Multi-Jurisdiction Readiness The same Actor–Event Association may support different legal conclusions across jurisdictions. The canonical model is: One Governed Actor–Event Association ↓ Multiple Jurisdictional Evaluations EPAM shall therefore avoid embedding one jurisdiction's legal assumptions into the governed participation structure. Governance States EPAM may represent: Association Ready Association Under Governance Association Established Association Qualified Association Supporting Association Partial Association Ambiguous Association Conflicted Association Unresolved Governed Event Participant Established These states govern Actor–Event Association only. They do not determine legal or tax status. Governance Requirements EPAM implementations shall ensure that: associations refer to governed Participant Candidates; relevant Participation Roles are preserved; association with the specific event is operationally justified; material participation is distinguished from incidental connection; direct and indirect associations can be differentiated where relevant; supporting relationships do not automatically become material participation; role existence does not automatically establish Event Participation; temporal proximity does not automatically establish participation; spatial presence does not automatically establish participation; transaction-record presence does not automatically establish participation; contractual status does not automatically establish participation; ownership does not automatically establish participation; corporate relationships do not automatically transfer participation; machine and autonomous actors can possess independent associations; multiple actor associations can coexist; uncertainty remains visible; conflicts remain visible; material association changes remain traceable; identity governance remains separate; accountability and liability remain separate; Value Association remains separate; and legal tax status remains downstream. Governance Logic IF a Governed Participant Candidate and a Governed Participation Role exist, THEN their relationship to the specific governed event may be evaluated. IF the actor's governed role is materially exercised in relation to the event, THEN a Governed Actor–Event Association may be established. IF the relationship is merely incidental, technical, administrative, or insufficiently material, THEN it shall not automatically establish Event Participation. IF participation evidence is uncertain, THEN the association shall remain qualified or unresolved. IF materially conflicting representations exist, THEN the conflict shall remain visible until legitimately resolved. IF the Actor–Event Association is sufficiently governed, THEN the actor may be represented as a Governed Event Participant. EPAM SHALL NOT convert Event Participation into taxpayer status, accountability, liability, or another jurisdiction-specific legal conclusion. Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum EPAM implementation should support: Governed Event Reference The specific governed event to which association is evaluated. Participant Candidate Reference The EPIM-governed actor. Participation Role Reference The EPRM-governed operational role. Association Identifier The stable reference for the Actor–Event Association. Association Type The operational nature of the association. Association Basis The basis supporting material association. Association Materiality Whether the relationship is materially relevant to Event Participation. Association Directness Whether the relationship is direct, indirect, supporting, or otherwise qualified. Temporal Association The relationship between participation and governed Event Timing. Spatial Association The relationship between participation and governed Event Location where relevant. Association Confidence The qualified confidence attached to the association. Association Ambiguity State Whether participation remains materially ambiguous. Association Conflict State Whether material association conflicts exist. Association Change State Whether the Actor–Event relationship materially changes. Evidence / Traceability Reference The information required to reconstruct the association result. Governance State The current EPAM state. Handoff State Whether the association is sufficiently governed for subsequent TREPS processing. Governance Outputs EPAM may produce: Governed Actor–Event Association; Governed Event Participant; Association Type; Association Materiality State; Direct Association Representation; Indirect Association Representation; Supporting Association Representation; Temporal Association Record; Spatial Association Record; Association Confidence State; Association Ambiguity State; Association Conflict State; Association Change Record; Association Traceability Record; and the principal output: Governed Actor–Event Association Set This output represents actors whose relationships to the specific event have been sufficiently governed. Critical Distinctions Actor Association ≠ Event Participation by Default Actor Record Presence ≠ Actor–Event Association Event Connection ≠ Material Event Participation Indirect Association ≠ Non-Participation by Default Direct Technical Connection ≠ Material Participation by Default Supporting Association ≠ Governed Event Participation by Default Governed Role ≠ Event Participation by Default Temporal Proximity ≠ Event Participation by Default Spatial Presence ≠ Event Participation by Default Remote Actor ≠ Non-Participant by Default Transaction Record Presence ≠ Event Participation by Default Transaction Record Absence ≠ Non-Participation by Default Contractual Party ≠ Event Participant by Default Non-Contractual Actor ≠ Non-Participant by Default Owner ≠ Event Participant by Default Corporate Relationship ≠ Shared Event Participation Platform Presence ≠ Event Participation by Default Machine Association ≠ Owner Association AI Agent Association ≠ Developer Association Multiple Actor Associations ≠ Equal Participation Actor–Event Association ≠ Identity Governance Participation Role ≠ Actor–Event Association Governed Actor–Event Association ≠ Accountability Event Participation ≠ Liability Actor–Event Association ≠ Value Association Event Participant ≠ Value Owner by Default Governed Event Participant ≠ Taxpayer Enterprise Application EPAM establishes the material connection between governed actors and the specific event: ERP / Commerce / Banking / Platform / AI Agent / Machine System → EPIM — Governed Participant Candidate Set → EPRM — Governed Participant Role Set → EPAM — Governed Actor–Event Association Set → EPMAM — Machine & Autonomous Actor Governance → EPCM — Participation Continuity → Governed Participatory Event This prevents downstream tax and compliance systems from treating every actor appearing in operational data as an Event Participant. Use Case 1 — Global Digital Commerce Event A digital purchase contains records relating to a customer, merchant, marketplace, payment processor, cloud provider, analytics provider, logistics company, and several technical services. EPIM identifies the relevant Participant Candidates and EPRM establishes their possible operational roles. EPAM then determines which of those actors possess a materially relevant relationship to the specific governed event. A cloud provider appearing in infrastructure records or an analytics service receiving technical data does not automatically become a Governed Event Participant. The resulting Actor–Event Association structure provides downstream tax systems with a governed representation of actual operational participation rather than an unfiltered list of technically connected entities. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Industrial Procurement Event An AI agent detects a production requirement, evaluates suppliers, initiates procurement, and communicates with an autonomous logistics system. A manufacturing robot later receives and uses the component. The AI developer, robot manufacturer, equipment owner, cloud provider, operating company, supplier, and monitoring systems may all appear in available records. EPAM determines which governed roles materially associate which actors with the specific event. Ownership, development, technical hosting, or monitoring alone does not automatically establish Event Participation. The resulting associations can proceed to specialized machine and autonomous participation governance without prematurely determining responsibility, liability, taxpayer status, or another legal consequence. Canonical Boundary EPAM owns the governance of the material relationship between governed Participant Candidates, their governed operational roles, and a specific Tax-Relevant Event, including association basis, materiality, directness, supporting association, temporal and spatial relevance, uncertainty, conflict, change, and traceability. EPAM does not own Participant Identification, Participation Role definition, complete identity governance, specialized Machine & Autonomous Actor governance, Participation Continuity, Event Timing, Event Location, Value Association, Event Relationships, accountability, responsibility, liability, ownership, authority, taxpayer status, Tax Jurisdiction, tax nexus, permanent establishment, place of supply, taxability, Tax Liability, or another jurisdiction-specific legal conclusion. Its governance ends when the Actor–Event relationship is sufficiently established for subsequent TREPS governance. Canonical Handoff EPIM — Governed Participant Candidate Set → EPRM — Governed Participant Role Set → EPAM — Governed Actor–Event Association Set → EPMAM — Event Machine & Autonomous Actor Governance Canonical Closing Statement EPAM establishes whether an identified actor and its governed operational role materially belong to the specific event — not what legal consequence follows from that participation. Being connected to an event is not the same as participating in it. Being a participant is not the same as being legally responsible or taxable. Governed Event Participant ≠ Taxpayer.

title: OOF™ The Event Participation Continuity Module (EPCM) governs how
text: OOF™ The Event Participation Continuity Module (EPCM) governs how The Event Participation Continuity Module (EPCM) governs how OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: TREPS — Tax-Relevant Event Participation Standard Module: EPCM — Event Participation Continuity Module Operational Layer: Event Participation Continuity Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Event Participation Continuity Origin ID: TREGA-TREPS-EPCM-005 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 1 September 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language Canonical Definition The Event Participation Continuity Module (EPCM) governs how participation in a Tax-Relevant Event is preserved, updated, qualified, and traced when participants, roles, associations, machine or autonomous actors, or participation states change during the lifecycle of the same governed event. EPCM determines whether changes in participation represent continuity within the same event or indicate a material transformation that must be referred back to the appropriate upstream TREGA™ governance layer. Its principal task is: Governed Participation Structure ↓ Governed Participation Continuity EPCM does not identify participants. EPIM owns Participant Identification. EPCM does not determine Participation Roles. EPRM owns Participation Role governance. EPCM does not establish the original Actor–Event Association. EPAM owns Actor–Event Association. EPCM does not establish specialized machine or autonomous participation. EPMAM owns that governance. EPCM governs what happens after participation has already been established and subsequently changes. The foundational distinction is: Participation Change ≠ New Event by DefaultOperational Role Participation in real-world and digital events is not always static. A participant may: enter the event; leave the event; pause participation; resume participation; change role; be replaced; act through another system; transfer execution; become inactive; re-enter later; move from human to machine execution; or participate only during one stage of the event. Without continuity governance, systems may incorrectly: create duplicate participants; erase historical participation; merge distinct actors; treat every role change as a new event; lose the sequence of participation; or rewrite prior participation states. EPCM preserves participation as a governed lifecycle structure. Internal Module Flow TREPS operates through: EPIM — Participant Identification → EPRM — Participation Role → EPAM — Actor Association → EPMAM — Machine & Autonomous Actor Governance → EPCM — Participation Continuity → Governed Participatory Event EPCM is the final Core Module within TREPS. It receives the governed participation structures produced by the preceding modules and establishes whether participation remains coherent across change. Operational Transition The canonical EPCM transition is: Governed Participant References + Governed Participation Roles + Governed Actor–Event Associations + Governed Machine / Autonomous Participation → Participation Continuity Governance → Governed Participation Continuity Structure → Governed Participatory EventOperational Space EPCM governs: participant entry; participant exit; participation pause; participation resumption; role change; participant replacement; actor substitution; participation transfer; sequential participation; overlapping participation; participation interruption; participation reactivation; participation-state change; participation-history preservation; machine/human participation transitions; continuity uncertainty; continuity conflict; and continuity traceability. EPCM governs these mechanisms only within the already governed event boundary. Operational Scope EPCM may operate across: commercial events; digital transactions; manufacturing; logistics; banking; marketplaces; platform operations; distributed services; AI-agent workflows; autonomous systems; robotic operations; machine-to-machine events; multi-stage processes; cross-border operations; and other events in which participation changes while the event continues. Participation Continuity Participation Continuity means that changes in the participant structure remain linked to the same governed event where the event itself has not materially transformed into a different event. The continuity question is therefore: Does the participation change represent evolution within the same event, or does it require upstream event re-evaluation? EPCM governs the participation side of this question. It does not independently redefine Event Formation or Event Boundary. Participant Entry A participant may become materially involved after the event has already begun. EPCM shall support legitimate participant entry without forcing the creation of a new event. Therefore: Participant Entry ≠ New Event by Default. The new participant must still satisfy the relevant TREPS governance requirements. Participant Exit A participant may cease material involvement before the event ends. EPCM shall preserve both: the fact that the actor participated; and the point at which participation ended where materially relevant. Therefore: Participant Exit ≠ Historical Non-Participation. Past governed participation shall not be erased merely because an actor later exits. Participation Pause and Resumption Participation may temporarily stop and later resume. EPCM shall distinguish temporary interruption from permanent exit where operational reality supports that distinction. Participation Pause ≠ Participant Exit by Default. Likewise: Participation Resumption ≠ New Participant by Default. Role Change A participant may change operational role while remaining part of the same event. EPCM shall preserve the transition between governed roles. For example: Initiator ↓ Coordinator Processor ↓ Transfer Actor Human Operator ↓ Supervisor Autonomous Agent ↓ Escalated Human Control Such change shall remain traceable. Role Change ≠ New Participant by Default. Role Change ≠ New Event by Default. EPRM remains authoritative for the actual role definitions. EPCM governs continuity across the change. Participant Replacement One actor may replace another during an event. Replacement does not mean the actors are the same actor. Therefore: Participant Replacement ≠ Actor Identity Continuity. EPCM shall preserve: outgoing participant; incoming participant; transition relationship; participation interval where relevant; and historical traceability. Actor Substitution An operational process may substitute one actor for another. Examples may include: employee replacement; service-provider replacement; machine replacement; agent handoff; system failover; or autonomous actor substitution. EPCM shall not overwrite the original participant merely because another actor assumes the same role. Same Role ≠ Same Participant. Participation Transfer An actor may transfer an operational function to another actor. Where this occurs within the same governed event, EPCM shall preserve the transfer relationship without automatically treating the entire event as newly formed. Participation Transfer ≠ Event Transfer. Authority or legal delegation related to that transfer remains outside EPCM. Sequential Participation Actors may participate one after another. EPCM shall support sequence where materially relevant. For example: Actor A ↓ Actor B ↓ Actor C may all legitimately belong to the same governed event. Therefore: Sequential Participants ≠ Sequential Events by Default. Event Relationships remain governed by TRERLS where separate events exist. Overlapping Participation Two or more participants may be active during overlapping periods. EPCM shall preserve overlap without forcing artificial exclusivity. Overlapping Participation ≠ Shared Identity. Overlapping Participation ≠ Equal Role. Participation Interruption Operational disruptions may temporarily alter participation. A network outage may remove one system. A machine may fail. A human may intervene. A backup provider may take over. EPCM shall preserve the participation history through such interruptions where the event remains the same governed event. Human-to-Machine Transition An event may begin with human execution and later continue through automated or autonomous systems. EPCM shall preserve the transition rather than rewriting the entire event under one actor type. Example: Human Operator ↓ Automated System ↓ Autonomous Agent may remain one participation-continuity structure. Human-to-Machine Transition ≠ New Event by Default. Machine-to-Human Transition The opposite may also occur. An autonomous system may escalate control to a human. EPCM shall preserve both participation states. Machine-to-Human Escalation ≠ Erasure of Prior Machine Participation. This is particularly important for auditability and later legal analysis. Machine Replacement A machine may be replaced by another machine during the event. Where the event itself continues, EPCM shall preserve both machine participants and their participation periods or transitions. Replacement Machine ≠ Original Machine. Machine Replacement ≠ New Event by Default. Autonomous Actor Replacement One AI agent or autonomous system may transfer activity to another. EPCM shall preserve actor continuity without assuming that two autonomous instances represent the same governed actor. EPIM and EPMAM remain authoritative for actor identity and non-human participation classification. Participation State Participation may occupy different operational states. EPCM may represent states such as: Active Inactive Paused Resumed Transferred Replaced Exited Completed Qualified Unresolved These states describe participation continuity only. Historical Preservation A current participation state shall not overwrite materially relevant historical states. The canonical rule is: Current Participation State ≠ Complete Participation History EPCM shall preserve reconstructability of prior participation states where materially relevant. Correction Versus Historical Erasure An earlier participation record may later be found incorrect. A legitimate correction may amend the governed participation history. However: Participation Correction ≠ Historical Erasure. The original state and correction should remain traceable where governance requires reconstruction. Continuity and Actor Identity Participation continuity does not prove identity continuity. The same role may pass between different actors. The same actor may appear through changing references. Therefore: Participation Continuity ≠ Actor Identity Continuity. EPIM and OBIDENITY® remain authoritative for actor identification and deeper identity governance. Continuity and Event Boundary EPCM operates inside the existing governed Event Boundary. If a participation change appears to fundamentally alter what constitutes the event, EPCM shall not independently redefine that event. Instead, the issue must be referred to the relevant upstream TREGA™ layer. Therefore: Participation Change ≠ Permission to Redefine Event Boundary. TREBS remains authoritative for Event Boundary. Continuity and Event Formation Some changes may be so material that they indicate the formation of another event. EPCM shall support escalation where this possibility exists. However: Material Participation Change ≠ New Event Automatically. TREFS and TREBS determine whether a new event actually exists. Continuity and Timing Participation continuity may use governed Event Timing to establish entry, exit, sequence, overlap, pause, or resumption. EPCM does not redefine Event Timing. Therefore: Participation Interval ≠ Event Timing Governance. TRETS remains authoritative for the temporal structure of the event. Continuity and Location A participant may change location while participation continues. Likewise, the event itself may move across operational locations. EPCM shall not treat participant movement as automatic participation discontinuity. Participant Location Change ≠ Participation Break by Default. TRELS remains authoritative for Event Location. Continuity and Role EPCM consumes roles governed under EPRM. It does not redefine role meaning. Its responsibility is to preserve how those roles change over time. Therefore: Role Governance ≠ Role Continuity Governance. Continuity and Machine / Autonomous Participation EPCM consumes non-human participation structures from EPMAM. It governs how they persist or change across the event. Examples may include: autonomous execution becoming supervised; one agent replacing another; machine failover; human escalation; autonomous delegation; or return from human intervention to autonomous execution. EPCM preserves continuity while EPMAM remains authoritative for machine/autonomous participation characteristics. Continuity and Value Participation changes do not automatically determine changes in value ownership, value entitlement, benefit, cost, revenue, or Tax Base. Therefore: Participation Continuity ≠ Value Continuity. TRVAS governs Value Association. VFM® governs the Value Lifecycle. Continuity and Accountability A participant entering, leaving, or changing role does not automatically determine accountability. Therefore: Participation Continuity ≠ Accountability Continuity. AGA™ governs accountability where applicable. Continuity and Liability Historical participation may become relevant to later liability analysis. EPCM preserves the facts necessary for such analysis but does not determine liability. Therefore: Participation History ≠ Liability Determination. HALIA™ governs harm and liability lifecycle where applicable. Continuity and Tax Status A participant may change role or involvement while a jurisdiction later assigns different legal significance to different parts of that participation. EPCM does not determine such tax consequences. Therefore: Participation State Change ≠ Tax Status Change by Default. Participant Exit ≠ End of Tax Obligation by Default. Participant Entry ≠ Creation of Tax Liability by Default. These are jurisdiction-specific determinations. Continuity Uncertainty It may be unclear whether participation genuinely continued, ceased, resumed, transferred, or was replaced. EPCM shall preserve uncertainty where available information cannot legitimately resolve the state. Continuity Uncertainty ≠ Permission to Invent Continuous Participation. Continuity Conflict Different records may present conflicting participation histories. One source may indicate continuous activity. Another may indicate termination and later re-entry. EPCM shall preserve materially relevant conflict until sufficiently resolved. Continuity Conflict ≠ Permission to Select the Most Convenient Timeline. Continuity Traceability A governed participation structure shall remain reconstructable across change. The record should permit determination of: who participated; when participation began; what role was held; when role changed; whether participation paused; whether participation resumed; whether another actor replaced the participant; whether machine/human control changed; when participation ended; what uncertainty existed; and what corrections were later made. This traceability supports downstream governance without converting participation history into legal conclusions. Governance States EPCM may represent continuity states including: Continuity Ready Continuity Under Governance Continuous Participation Interrupted Participation Paused Participation Resumed Participation Transferred Participation Replaced Participation Participation Exited Participation Completed Continuity Qualified Continuity Conflicted Continuity Unresolved Participation Continuity Established Governance Requirements EPCM implementations shall ensure that: participation changes remain linked to the governed event; participant entry can be represented; participant exit does not erase historical participation; pause and resumption can be distinguished; role changes remain traceable; participant replacement does not merge identities; actor substitution preserves outgoing and incoming actors; participation transfer can be represented; sequential participants can belong to one event where legitimate; overlapping participation can be represented; human-to-machine transitions can be preserved; machine-to-human transitions can be preserved; machine and autonomous replacement can be represented; historical participation states remain reconstructable; corrections do not erase prior governance history; participant-location changes do not automatically break continuity; participation changes do not automatically redefine Event Formation or Event Boundary; uncertainty remains visible; conflicts remain visible; Value Association remains separate; accountability and liability remain separate; and tax status remains downstream. Governance Logic IF a Governed Event Participant already exists and its participation changes, THEN EPCM shall determine whether the change can remain within the same governed participation lifecycle. IF a participant enters or exits while the governed event remains the same, THEN participation history shall be updated without automatic event reformation. IF a participant changes role, THEN the role transition shall remain traceable without automatically creating a new participant. IF one actor replaces another, THEN both actors shall remain separately attributable. IF human and machine execution transition during the event, THEN both participation states shall remain preserved where materially relevant. IF participation change may indicate a fundamentally different event, THEN EPCM shall escalate the issue to the relevant upstream TREGA™ governance layer rather than redefining the event independently. IF continuity remains uncertain or conflicted, THEN the uncertainty or conflict shall remain visible. IF participation continuity is sufficiently governed, THEN TREPS may produce a Governed Participatory Event. Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum EPCM implementation should support: Governed Event Reference The event whose participation continuity is being governed. Participant Reference The governed participant whose continuity is being evaluated. Participation Continuity Identifier The stable reference for the continuity record. Prior Participation State The immediately preceding governed participation state. Current Participation State The current governed participation state. Role Reference The governed role applicable to the participation state. State Effective Point The governed temporal reference associated with the state change. Entry State Whether the actor enters participation. Exit State Whether the actor exits participation. Pause / Resume State Whether participation temporarily stops or resumes. Replacement Reference The outgoing or incoming actor where replacement occurs. Transfer Reference The relationship representing transfer of participation. Human / Machine Transition State Whether execution transitions between human and non-human actors. Continuity Confidence The qualified confidence attached to the continuity representation. Ambiguity State Whether continuity remains materially ambiguous. Conflict State Whether materially conflicting histories exist. Correction Reference Any governed correction affecting participation history. Traceability Reference The information required to reconstruct participation continuity. Governance State The current EPCM state. Handoff State Whether TREPS participation governance is complete. Governance Outputs EPCM may produce: Governed Participation Continuity Record; Participant Entry Record; Participant Exit Record; Participation Pause Record; Participation Resumption Record; Participation Role Transition Record; Participant Replacement Record; Participation Transfer Record; Sequential Participation Structure; Overlapping Participation Structure; Human–Machine Transition Record; Machine–Human Transition Record; Participation History; Participation Continuity Confidence State; Participation Continuity Ambiguity State; Participation Continuity Conflict State; Participation Correction Record; and the principal output: Governed Participation Continuity Structure When combined with the preceding TREPS outputs, this enables the Parent Standard to produce: Governed Participatory EventCritical Distinctions Participation Change ≠ New Event by Default Participant Entry ≠ New Event by Default Participant Exit ≠ Historical Non-Participation Participation Pause ≠ Participant Exit by Default Participation Resumption ≠ New Participant by Default Role Change ≠ New Participant by Default Role Change ≠ New Event by Default Participant Replacement ≠ Actor Identity Continuity Same Role ≠ Same Participant Participation Transfer ≠ Event Transfer Sequential Participants ≠ Sequential Events by Default Overlapping Participation ≠ Shared Identity Human-to-Machine Transition ≠ New Event by Default Machine-to-Human Escalation ≠ Erasure of Prior Machine Participation Machine Replacement ≠ New Event by Default Current Participation State ≠ Complete Participation History Participation Correction ≠ Historical Erasure Participation Continuity ≠ Actor Identity Continuity Participation Change ≠ Permission to Redefine Event Boundary Material Participation Change ≠ New Event Automatically Participation Interval ≠ Event Timing Governance Participant Location Change ≠ Participation Break by Default Role Governance ≠ Role Continuity Governance Participation Continuity ≠ Value Continuity Participation History ≠ Liability Determination Participation State Change ≠ Tax Status Change by Default Participant Exit ≠ End of Tax Obligation by Default Participant Entry ≠ Creation of Tax Liability by Default Enterprise Application EPCM completes the TREPS participation-governance chain: ERP / Commerce / Banking / Platform / AI Agent / Machine System → EPIM — Governed Participant Candidate Set → EPRM — Governed Participant Role Set → EPAM — Governed Actor–Event Association Set → EPMAM — Governed Machine & Autonomous Participation Set → EPCM — Governed Participation Continuity Structure → Governed Participatory Event → TRVAS — Tax-Relevant Value Association Standard This allows downstream systems to consume a stable participation history rather than only a snapshot of who appears to participate at one moment. Use Case 1 — Multi-Stage Cross-Border Service Event A service begins with one operating entity and one specialist. During execution, the specialist is replaced, another organization performs a later stage, and a digital platform takes over part of the coordination. The customer remains the same, while participation roles change over time. EPCM preserves the original participant, replacement actor, role transitions, entry and exit points, and overlapping periods without automatically creating a new event for every participation change. The resulting Governed Participatory Event allows downstream tax systems to evaluate the complete participation history rather than a misleading final-state participant list. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Industrial Operation with Human Escalation An autonomous machine begins an industrial operation under normal autonomous control. An AI agent coordinates the process until an anomaly is detected. A human operator temporarily takes control, performs corrective action, and then returns execution to the autonomous system. EPCM preserves the sequence: Autonomous Machine Participation ↓ AI-Agent Coordination ↓ Human Intervention ↓ Return to Autonomous Execution without erasing the original non-human participation or treating every control transition as a separate event. The complete governed participation history can later support jurisdiction-specific evaluation, accountability analysis, audit, or liability governance without EPCM itself determining any of those legal conclusions. Canonical Boundary EPCM owns the governance of continuity, change, entry, exit, pause, resumption, role transition, replacement, substitution, transfer, sequence, overlap, human-machine transition, history preservation, correction, uncertainty, conflict, and traceability of already-governed Event Participation. EPCM does not own Participant Identification, Participation Role definition, original Actor–Event Association, specialized Machine & Autonomous Actor qualification, Event Formation, Event Boundary, Event Timing, Event Location, identity, ownership, authority, Value Association, Event Relationships, accountability, responsibility, liability, taxpayer status, Tax Jurisdiction, tax nexus, permanent establishment, place of supply, taxability, Tax Liability, filing, reporting, collection, payment, or enforcement. Its governance ends when participation throughout the event is sufficiently coherent, historically reconstructable, and ready to become part of the final TREPS output. Canonical Handoff EPAM — Governed Actor–Event Association Set EPMAM — Governed Machine & Autonomous Participation Set → EPCM — Governed Participation Continuity Structure → TREPS — Governed Participatory Event → TRVAS — Tax-Relevant Value Association Standard Canonical Closing Statement EPCM preserves who or what participated as participation changes over time without allowing every entry, exit, role change, replacement, or human-machine transition to redefine the event itself. Participation may change while the governed event remains continuous. Participation Change ≠ New Event by Default.

title: OOF™ The Event Participant Identification Module (EPIM) governs how actors
text: OOF™ The Event Participant Identification Module (EPIM) governs how actors The Event Participant Identification Module (EPIM) governs how actors OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: TREPS — Tax-Relevant Event Participation Standard Module: EPIM — Event Participant Identification Module Operational Layer: Event Participant Identification Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Event Participant Identification Origin ID: TREGA-TREPS-EPIM-001 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 1 September 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language Canonical Definition The Event Participant Identification Module (EPIM) governs how actors potentially relevant to a Tax-Relevant Event are identified, distinguished, referenced, and maintained as stable Participant Candidates for subsequent participation governance. EPIM establishes whether available actor information is sufficient to distinguish one actor from another within the context of the governed event. Its purpose is not to determine whether an identified actor materially participated in the event. Its purpose is to establish which actor is under participation governance. The principal distinction is: Identified Actor ≠ Governed Event Participant An actor may be identifiable without materially participating in the event. Participation role, actor-event association, machine and autonomous participation, and participation continuity are governed by subsequent TREPS modules. Operational Role Modern operational events may contain references to many actors. These may include humans, organizations, platforms, software systems, machines, AI agents, autonomous systems, infrastructure providers, intermediaries, accounts, devices, or other operational entities. The same actor may also appear differently across multiple systems. A company name may vary. A person may appear through different account identifiers. A machine may be represented through a device ID, asset record, serial number, or system identifier. An AI agent may operate through multiple sessions or technical instances. A platform may appear through several legal, commercial, or technical references. EPIM establishes sufficient actor differentiation so that subsequent TREPS governance does not confuse different actors or incorrectly treat multiple references to the same actor as multiple participants. Internal Module Flow TREPS is operationalized through the following internal flow: EPIM — Participant Identification → EPRM — Participation Role → EPAM — Actor Association → EPMAM — Machine & Autonomous Actor Governance → EPCM — Participation Continuity → Governed Participatory Event EPIM is the first module. It establishes the actor reference upon which subsequent participation governance can operate. Operational Transition EPIM receives actor-related information associated with the: Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event and produces: Governed Participant Candidate Set The canonical transition is: Actor Information Associated with the Governed Event ↓ EPIM ↓ Governed Participant Candidate Set A Participant Candidate is an actor sufficiently identified for participation governance. It is not yet a confirmed Governed Event Participant. Operational Space EPIM governs participant-identification operations including: actor discovery; actor differentiation; actor reference establishment; duplicate actor detection; ambiguous actor handling; conflicting actor identification; human actor references; organizational actor references; digital actor references; machine actor references; autonomous actor references; cross-system actor references; identification confidence; identification traceability; and participant-candidate formation. EPIM governs these mechanisms only to the extent necessary to establish stable actor references for TREPS. It does not replace comprehensive identity governance. Operational Scope EPIM may operate across events involving: individuals; companies; institutions; marketplaces; platforms; software services; accounts; AI agents; autonomous systems; robots; machines; devices; infrastructure systems; machine-to-machine environments; and other distinguishable operational actors. EPIM remains neutral to whether an actor is human, organizational, digital, or autonomous. Actor Identification EPIM shall establish whether an actor can be sufficiently distinguished from other actors relevant to participation governance. Identification may rely on one or more available references. These may include, where appropriate: governed identity references; organizational identifiers; account identifiers; platform identifiers; system identifiers; machine identifiers; device identifiers; transaction-associated actor references; operational records; external governed references; or combinations of relevant identification information. No single identifier type is universally authoritative. Identifier Availability ≠ Actor Identification Sufficiency. Identification must be adequate for the operational purpose of TREPS. Participant Candidate Where an actor is sufficiently distinguishable for subsequent participation governance, EPIM may establish that actor as a: Participant Candidate Participant Candidate means: an identified actor whose possible participation in the governed event requires subsequent TREPS governance. This state deliberately precedes confirmed Event Participation. Therefore: Participant Candidate ≠ Governed Event Participant EPRM and EPAM subsequently determine the relevant participation structure. Actor Reference Stability A governed participant candidate requires a sufficiently stable reference. The reference must allow subsequent TREPS modules to determine that they are operating on the same actor. A stable reference does not require every underlying source system to use the same identifier. Instead, EPIM shall preserve sufficient linkage to distinguish: Same Actor / Multiple References from: Different Actors / Similar References This prevents fragmented source data from unnecessarily fragmenting the participation structure. Multiple References to the Same Actor One actor may appear through multiple records. For example: Company Name + Platform Account + Merchant ID + Payment Account may represent the same underlying organization. Likewise: Machine Serial Number + Asset ID + Device ID + Network Identifier may refer to the same machine. EPIM shall permit multiple references to be associated with one Participant Candidate where sufficient governance supports that association. However: Multiple Actor References ≠ Multiple Actors by Default. Similar References to Different Actors The opposite problem must also be governed. Different actors may share: similar names; shared addresses; shared infrastructure; group-level identifiers; platform accounts; devices; corporate branding; or organizational relationships. EPIM shall not merge actors merely because available records appear similar. Reference Similarity ≠ Actor Equivalence. Human Actor Identification Where the potential participant is human, EPIM shall establish only the degree of identification required for participation governance. EPIM shall not unnecessarily reconstruct or govern the person's complete identity. Where authoritative identity governance is required, governed identity information may be consumed from OBIDENITY® or another legitimate identity source. Participant Identification ≠ Complete Human Identity Governance. Organizational Actor Identification Organizations may appear under: legal names; trading names; subsidiaries; branches; business units; platform accounts; group structures; or technical system references. EPIM shall distinguish the actor actually under participation governance from related organizations where available evidence permits. Corporate Relationship ≠ Actor Equivalence. A parent company, subsidiary, branch, platform operator, and merchant shall not automatically be treated as the same actor. Digital Actor Identification Digital environments may contain actors represented primarily through technical references. EPIM shall permit digital actors to be identified where they can be sufficiently distinguished for participation governance. A technical identifier may support identification without establishing participation. Therefore: Digital Identifier ≠ Event Participation. Machine and Autonomous Actor Identification Machines, robots, AI agents, and autonomous systems may require identification independently from their owners, developers, operators, or supervising organizations. EPIM shall support such actors as distinct Participant Candidates where operational reality requires it. Therefore: Machine Identity Reference ≠ Owner Identity. AI Agent Reference ≠ Developer Identity. Autonomous System Reference ≠ Human Operator Identity. Whether these actors materially participate is governed subsequently within TREPS. Identification Source Governance Actor identification may originate from multiple sources. EPIM shall preserve the distinction between the actor and the source describing the actor. Identification Source ≠ Identified Actor. A source may be incomplete, outdated, ambiguous, conflicting, or technically generated. EPIM shall therefore preserve sufficient source traceability to support later review. Identification Confidence Not every actor can be identified with equal certainty. EPIM shall allow identification confidence to be qualified where required. Possible conditions may include: Established Qualified Ambiguous Conflicted Unresolved An actor shall not be assigned artificial certainty merely because downstream systems require a participant field. Required Participant Field ≠ Permission to Invent Actor Certainty. Ambiguous Actor Identification Where available information may correspond to more than one actor, EPIM shall preserve that ambiguity until sufficient information supports differentiation. Ambiguity shall not be resolved through convenience alone. Actor Ambiguity ≠ Permission for Arbitrary Actor Selection. Conflicting Actor Identification Different sources may provide materially incompatible identification information. EPIM shall preserve material conflicts and prevent silent replacement of one actor reference by another. Where conflict cannot legitimately be resolved, the Participant Candidate may remain qualified or unresolved. Identification Conflict ≠ Permission for Convenient Identity Selection. Duplicate Identification EPIM shall reduce the risk that the same actor becomes represented as several independent Participant Candidates merely because different systems use different identifiers. Duplicate resolution shall remain traceable. The objective is: One Governed Actor Reference where evidence supports one actor. However, consolidation shall not occur where actor equivalence remains materially uncertain. Identification Change Actor information may change while the governed event remains the same. Examples include changes to: names; account identifiers; system references; organizational labels; machine identifiers; or platform representations. EPIM shall preserve materially relevant identification changes without automatically creating a new actor. Identification Change ≠ New Actor by Default. Historical references required for traceability shall remain reconstructable. Cross-System Identification The same actor may appear across ERP, commerce, banking, logistics, platform, machine, or autonomous-system records. EPIM shall support governed linkage across these systems where sufficient evidence establishes that the references concern the same actor. Cross-system linkage must remain traceable. Cross-System Match ≠ Actor Equivalence Without Sufficient Support. Relationship to OBIDENITY® EPIM does not own comprehensive identity governance. OBIDENITY® governs origin-bound identity structures including identity, origin, ownership, authority, permission, provenance, transfer, continuity, and auditability where applicable. EPIM consumes only the actor-identification information necessary for Event Participation governance. The boundary is: OBIDENITY® governs who the actor is as a governed identity. EPIM governs whether that actor can be sufficiently distinguished as a Participant Candidate within the TREPS process. Therefore: Actor Identity ≠ Participant Identification and: Participant Identification ≠ Event Participation Relationship to Event Location An actor may be identified through location-associated records. Location alone does not establish actor identity or participation. Therefore: Location Reference ≠ Actor Identification by Default. Actor Location ≠ Event Participation. TRELS remains authoritative for Event Location. Relationship to Participation Role EPIM does not determine what operational role an identified actor performs. That belongs to: EPRM — Event Participation Role Module Therefore: Participant Identification ≠ Participation Role. EPIM answers: Which actor is under participation governance? EPRM answers: What operational participation role does that actor perform? Relationship to Actor–Event Association EPIM does not establish that a Participant Candidate materially participates in the governed event. That relationship is governed subsequently through EPAM. Therefore: Identified Actor ≠ Actor–Event Association and: Participant Candidate ≠ Governed Event Participant. This separation prevents the existence of an actor in a record from becoming automatic proof of participation. Governance States EPIM may assign identification states including: Actor Reference Detected Identification Under Governance Actor Distinguished Actor Qualified Actor Ambiguous Actor Conflicted Actor Unresolved Participant Candidate Established These states describe identification governance only. They do not establish Event Participation. Governance Requirements EPIM implementations shall ensure that: actor references relevant to participation governance can be identified; materially different actors remain distinguishable; multiple references to the same actor can be governed; similar references are not automatically merged; human, organizational, digital, machine, and autonomous actors can be represented; identification sources remain traceable; identification uncertainty remains visible; material identification conflicts remain visible; duplicate actor representations can be governed; identification changes remain traceable; cross-system references can be linked where sufficiently supported; complete identity governance is not duplicated; participation roles are not prematurely assigned; actor-event participation is not prematurely established; and taxpayer or other legal status is not inferred from identification. Governance Logic IF actor-related information is materially relevant to participation governance, THEN EPIM shall evaluate whether the actor can be sufficiently distinguished. IF sufficient identification exists, THEN a stable Participant Candidate reference may be established. IF multiple references sufficiently correspond to the same actor, THEN they may be governed under one Participant Candidate while preserving source traceability. IF actor equivalence remains uncertain, THEN separate or qualified references shall be preserved. IF identification is ambiguous or conflicted, THEN uncertainty shall remain visible. IF a Participant Candidate is established, THEN the actor may proceed to subsequent TREPS governance. EPIM SHALL NOT treat identification alone as proof of Event Participation. Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum EPIM implementation should support: Governed Event Reference The event within which participant identification is being performed. Participant Candidate Identifier The stable reference created for the identified actor. Actor Type The governed actor category relevant to participation processing. Source Actor Reference The original actor reference supplied by a source system or governed source. Identification Source The source from which identification information originates. Reference Linkage The relationship between multiple references believed to concern the same actor. Differentiation State Whether the actor is sufficiently distinguishable from other actors. Duplicate State Whether multiple references may represent the same actor. Identification Confidence The qualified confidence attached to the identification. Ambiguity State Whether actor identity remains materially ambiguous. Conflict State Whether identification sources materially conflict. Traceability Reference The information required to reconstruct the identification decision. Governance State The current EPIM identification state. Handoff State Whether the Participant Candidate is sufficiently governed to proceed to EPRM. Governance Outputs EPIM may produce: Governed Actor Reference; Participant Candidate Identifier; Actor Type Representation; Actor Reference Linkage; Duplicate Actor Resolution; Identification Confidence State; Actor Ambiguity State; Actor Conflict State; Identification Traceability Record; Participant Candidate Governance State; and the principal output: Governed Participant Candidate Set The output represents actors sufficiently identified for subsequent participation governance. It does not represent confirmed Event Participants. Critical Distinctions Identified Actor ≠ Governed Event Participant Participant Candidate ≠ Governed Event Participant Participant Identification ≠ Event Participation Actor Identity ≠ Participant Identification Participant Identification ≠ Complete Identity Governance Identifier Availability ≠ Actor Identification Sufficiency Multiple Actor References ≠ Multiple Actors by Default Reference Similarity ≠ Actor Equivalence Corporate Relationship ≠ Actor Equivalence Digital Identifier ≠ Event Participation Machine Identity Reference ≠ Owner Identity AI Agent Reference ≠ Developer Identity Autonomous System Reference ≠ Human Operator Identity Identification Source ≠ Identified Actor Required Participant Field ≠ Permission to Invent Actor Certainty Actor Ambiguity ≠ Permission for Arbitrary Actor Selection Identification Change ≠ New Actor by Default Participant Identification ≠ Participation Role Identified Actor ≠ Actor–Event Association Participant Identification ≠ Taxpayer Identification Enterprise Application EPIM can operate between operational systems and the remaining TREPS participation-governance process: ERP / Commerce / Banking / Platform / AI Agent / Machine System → Actor-Related Event Information → EPIM → Governed Participant Candidate Set → EPRM — Participation Role Governance → Remaining TREPS Modules → Governed Participatory Event This provides downstream systems with stable actor references without prematurely assigning participation, legal identity, or tax status. Use Case 1 — Multi-Platform Commercial Event A commercial event contains a merchant name, marketplace seller ID, payment-account reference, logistics customer number, and corporate identifier. Several references may describe the same organization, while another similarly named company belongs to the same corporate group. EPIM governs the references, distinguishes the relevant actors, prevents unsupported merging, and establishes a stable Participant Candidate for subsequent participation governance. It does not yet determine whether the merchant, marketplace, payment provider, or logistics provider materially participated in the event or what legal tax status any actor possesses. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Industrial Event An autonomous production event contains references to an industrial robot, machine controller, AI optimization agent, equipment owner, software provider, operating company, and remote monitoring system. EPIM distinguishes the machine and autonomous actors from the organizations and humans associated with them and establishes stable Participant Candidates where sufficient identification exists. It does not assume that the machine owner is the machine participant, that the AI developer is the AI participant, or that every identifiable actor materially participated in the event. Those questions proceed through subsequent TREPS governance. Canonical Boundary EPIM owns the identification, differentiation, stable referencing, duplicate governance, ambiguity governance, conflict preservation, cross-system linkage, and identification traceability required to establish Participant Candidates for TREPS. EPIM does not own complete identity, origin, ownership, authority, permission, or provenance governance. It does not determine Participation Role, final Actor–Event Association, machine/autonomous participation status, Participation Continuity, Event Location, Value Association, accountability, responsibility, liability, taxpayer status, Tax Jurisdiction, tax nexus, permanent establishment, legal taxability, Tax Liability, or another jurisdiction-specific legal conclusion. Its governance ends when actors are sufficiently identified and represented as Participant Candidates for subsequent TREPS processing. Canonical Handoff Governed Temporally and Spatially Situated Event + Actor Information → EPIM — Governed Participant Candidate Set → EPRM — Event Participation Role Governance Canonical Closing Statement EPIM establishes which actor is sufficiently identifiable to enter participation governance without treating identification itself as proof of participation. Knowing who an actor is does not establish whether or how that actor participated in the event. Identified Actor ≠ Governed Event Participant.

title: OOF™ The Event Machine & Autonomous Actor Module (EPMAM) governs how machines,
text: OOF™ The Event Machine & Autonomous Actor Module (EPMAM) governs how machines, The Event Machine & Autonomous Actor Module (EPMAM) governs how machines, OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: TREPS — Tax-Relevant Event Participation Standard Module: EPMAM — Event Machine & Autonomous Actor Module Operational Layer: Machine & Autonomous Event Participation Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Machine & Autonomous Event Participation Origin ID: TREGA-TREPS-EPMAM-004 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 1 September 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language Canonical Definition The Event Machine & Autonomous Actor Module (EPMAM) governs how machines, software agents, AI agents, robots, autonomous systems, machine-to-machine actors, and other non-human operational actors are represented as participants in a Tax-Relevant Event once their Actor–Event Association has been sufficiently established. EPMAM governs the specific conditions under which non-human participation can be represented independently from the identities, ownership, authority, supervision, development, operation, or legal status of humans and organizations associated with the machine or autonomous actor. Its principal task is: Governed Actor–Event Association ↓ Governed Machine / Autonomous Participation EPMAM does not establish general Actor–Event Association. EPAM owns that governance. EPMAM governs the additional participation characteristics that arise when the actor itself is machine-based, software-based, autonomous, or capable of materially acting without contemporaneous human execution. The foundational distinction is: Machine Participant ≠ Machine Owner and: Autonomous Participant ≠ Human Operator by DefaultOperational Role Traditional event models often assume that economically relevant action is performed directly by a human or organization. That assumption is increasingly insufficient. A machine may: detect a requirement; select an action; initiate a workflow; place an order; receive a service; transfer information; operate equipment; allocate resources; trigger payment; negotiate with another system; coordinate another machine; or execute economically relevant activity. An AI agent may perform similar functions without a human selecting each individual action. EPMAM ensures that operational reality can represent these actors directly where they materially participate. It prevents non-human participation from being automatically rewritten as human participation merely because legal responsibility must eventually attach somewhere. Internal Module Flow TREPS operates through: EPIM — Participant Identification → EPRM — Participation Role → EPAM — Actor Association → EPMAM — Machine & Autonomous Actor Governance → EPCM — Participation Continuity → Governed Participatory Event EPMAM receives machine or autonomous Actor–Event Associations already established through EPAM. It qualifies those associations for the specific characteristics of non-human participation. Operational Transition The canonical EPMAM transition is: Governed Machine / Autonomous Actor–Event Association → Machine & Autonomous Participation Governance → Governed Machine / Autonomous Event Participation Where human and non-human actors participate together, EPMAM preserves their distinct participation structures. Operational Space EPMAM governs: machine participation; AI-agent participation; software-agent participation; robotic participation; autonomous-system participation; machine-to-machine participation; autonomous action state; execution independence; human-supervision relationship; ownership separation; operator separation; developer separation; delegated machine action; system-mediated participation; multi-agent participation; autonomous coordination; machine-participation uncertainty; and non-human participation traceability. It does not determine legal personality or legal capacity. Operational Scope EPMAM may operate across: autonomous procurement; robotic manufacturing; machine-to-machine commerce; automated logistics; AI-agent transactions; autonomous financial operations; smart infrastructure; distributed industrial systems; automated marketplaces; IoT ecosystems; software-agent workflows; autonomous service delivery; and future machine economies. The module remains neutral to the technology used. Machine Actor A Machine Actor is a non-human operational actor capable of performing a materially relevant function within the governed event. Its existence as equipment or infrastructure does not automatically make it a participant. Therefore: Machine Presence ≠ Machine Participation by Default. The machine must possess a governed Actor–Event Association and materially perform a participation role. Autonomous Actor An Autonomous Actor is an operational actor capable of selecting, initiating, adapting, coordinating, or executing materially relevant activity with a degree of operational independence. Autonomy may exist at different levels. EPMAM does not require complete independence from human design, configuration, ownership, or supervision. However: Human Supervision ≠ Human Execution by Default. A supervised autonomous system may still be the actor that operationally performs the governed function. Automation Versus Autonomy EPMAM shall distinguish where materially relevant between automated execution and autonomous action. Automation may execute predetermined logic. Autonomy may include decision selection, adaptation, goal-directed behavior, or independent operational choice. The distinction shall reflect actual system behavior rather than marketing terminology. Automated System ≠ Autonomous System by Default. Likewise: AI Label ≠ Autonomous Participation by Default. Actor Versus Tool A machine or software system may function merely as a tool used by another participant. In other cases, it may itself perform a materially distinct operational role. EPMAM shall preserve this distinction. Tool Use ≠ Independent Machine Participation by Default. A calculator, passive database, or static software component does not become an independent participant merely because it contributes technically to an event. Execution Actor Where a machine or autonomous system directly executes a materially relevant event function, EPMAM may represent that system as an Execution Actor. However: Execution Actor ≠ Legal Responsible Party. The fact that a system executed an action does not determine who legally authorized, owns, controls, benefits from, or bears responsibility for that action. Decision Actor An AI agent or autonomous system may materially select among alternatives. Where such decision activity forms part of the governed event, EPMAM may preserve the system's operational decision role. However: Operational Decision Actor ≠ Legal Decision-Maker. Questions of authority, permission, accountability, and legal responsibility remain separate. Machine Ownership Separation The owner of a machine may be relevant to downstream governance. Ownership does not determine who operationally participated in the event. Therefore: Machine Participant ≠ Machine Owner Machine Ownership ≠ Machine Participation OBIDENITY® governs ownership where applicable. EPMAM consumes ownership information only where it is relevant to representing the participation structure. Operator Separation A machine may be operated directly by a person or organization. It may also act with substantial operational independence. EPMAM shall not automatically collapse machine participation into operator participation. Therefore: Machine Participant ≠ Machine Operator by Default. Likewise, the operator's existence does not remove the machine's own materially relevant role from the event representation. Developer Separation Software developers, AI-model developers, system integrators, and equipment manufacturers may be identifiable and operationally relevant in some contexts. Their development relationship does not automatically establish Event Participation. Therefore: AI Agent Participant ≠ AI Developer Autonomous System Participant ≠ System Developer Machine Participant ≠ Manufacturer by Default Development provenance and operational participation are separate governance questions. Controller and Supervisor Separation A supervising or controlling actor may coexist with a machine participant. EPMAM shall permit both to remain distinct where operational reality supports both associations. Therefore: Supervisory Relationship ≠ Participation Equivalence. Control Capability ≠ Execution by Default. The system that acts and the actor with control authority may be different participants. Delegated Machine Action A human or organization may delegate operational authority to a machine or software agent. EPMAM may represent the machine as the executing participant while preserving the existence of delegation where relevant. However: Delegation ≠ Identity Transfer. Delegated Execution ≠ Delegator Execution by Default. Authority and delegation governance remain outside EPMAM. Machine-to-Machine Participation A governed event may contain no contemporaneous human action. For example: Machine A ↓ Service Request ↓ Machine B ↓ Resource Transfer or: AI Agent A ↓ Autonomous Marketplace ↓ AI Agent B EPMAM shall support such participation structures without forcing a human actor into the event record merely to satisfy a traditional transaction model. Machine-to-Machine Event ≠ Human-to-Human Event by Default. Multi-Agent Participation Multiple autonomous systems may participate in the same event. They may: collaborate; compete; negotiate; delegate; coordinate; sequence actions; exchange information; or perform complementary functions. EPMAM shall support distinct non-human Actor–Event Associations without merging them into a generic “system” participant. Multiple Autonomous Actors ≠ One Autonomous Participant by Default. Agent Instance Versus Persistent Actor An autonomous actor may operate through multiple sessions, runtime instances, devices, or execution environments. EPMAM shall distinguish the technical instance from the governed actor where necessary. Therefore: Agent Instance ≠ Autonomous Actor by Default. Likewise: New Runtime Instance ≠ New Participant by Default. Actor continuity across instances may require governed references from EPIM and continuity governance from EPCM. Model Versus Agent A model may support an AI agent without itself constituting the operational participant. EPMAM shall distinguish where relevant between: model; agent; application; orchestration layer; execution environment; and autonomous actor. Therefore: AI Model ≠ AI Agent by Default. Model Invocation ≠ Independent Event Participation by Default. Infrastructure Versus Actor Cloud infrastructure, compute resources, networks, databases, and communication layers may enable autonomous action without becoming Event Participants. Therefore: Infrastructure Execution ≠ Infrastructure Participation by Default. The operational role and material Actor–Event Association remain decisive. Autonomy State EPMAM may preserve the degree or state of autonomy relevant to the event. The purpose is not to create a universal technical autonomy scale. The purpose is to record whether the actor's participation was, for example: directly controlled; automated; delegated; semi-autonomous; autonomous; or otherwise qualified where materially relevant. Autonomy State ≠ Legal Capacity. Human Intervention Human intervention may occur before, during, or after autonomous participation. EPMAM shall preserve materially relevant intervention without automatically treating the human as the executing participant. Possible intervention may include: configuration; approval; supervision; override; correction; escalation; or post-event review. Therefore: Human Intervention ≠ Human Participation in Every Operational Step. Override An autonomous actor may operate subject to human or system override. The existence of override capability does not prove that the override was exercised. Therefore: Override Capability ≠ Override Execution. Likewise, override capability does not eliminate autonomous participation. Autonomous Coordination One autonomous actor may instruct, trigger, coordinate, or delegate to another. EPMAM shall preserve materially relevant distinctions among the actors involved. However: Autonomous Coordination ≠ Actor Identity Merger. Each governed actor remains separately attributable where operationally justified. Machine Participation and Event Location A machine's physical or digital location may be relevant to participation. It does not automatically determine Event Location. Therefore: Machine Location ≠ Event Location by Default. Execution Node Location ≠ Tax Jurisdiction. TRELS remains authoritative for Event Location. Machine Participation and Timing Machine activity may generate highly granular timestamps. These do not redefine Event Timing. Therefore: Machine Timestamp ≠ Governed Event Time by Default. TRETS remains authoritative for Event Timing. Machine Participation and Identity EPMAM does not establish comprehensive machine or autonomous identity. EPIM establishes the governed Participant Candidate. OBIDENITY® may govern deeper identity, origin, ownership, authority, permission, and provenance. Therefore: Machine Identity ≠ Machine Participation. Autonomous Identity ≠ Autonomous Participation. EPMAM governs the participation characteristics of already associated machine or autonomous actors. Machine Participation and Authority A machine may operationally execute an action without having legally valid authority to do so. Therefore: Machine Participation ≠ Authority. Autonomous Execution ≠ Legal Authorization. Authority and permission remain separate governance spaces. Machine Participation and Accountability Non-human participation does not itself determine accountability. Therefore: Machine Participant ≠ Accountable Party by Default. Autonomous Participant ≠ Responsible Party by Default. AGA™ governs accountability where applicable. Machine Participation and Liability A machine or AI agent may participate operationally without possessing legal liability. Likewise, its participation does not automatically assign liability to the owner, developer, operator, or supervisor. Therefore: Machine Participation ≠ Legal Liability. Autonomous Participation ≠ Owner Liability by Default. HALIA™ governs the lifecycle of harm and liability where applicable. Machine Participation and Value A machine may create, consume, transfer, transform, or interact with value. Its participation does not by itself determine value ownership or entitlement. Therefore: Machine Participation ≠ Value Ownership. Autonomous Participation ≠ Value Entitlement. TRVAS governs Value Association. VFM® governs the Value Lifecycle. Machine Participation and Tax Status EPMAM does not determine whether a machine or autonomous actor can legally possess taxpayer status or another tax-law status in any jurisdiction. Nor does it automatically transfer such status to an associated human or organization. Therefore: Machine Participant ≠ Taxpayer and: Autonomous Participant ≠ Taxpayer Jurisdictions may later determine how non-human operational participation is legally attributed. EPMAM preserves the governed operational facts required for that analysis. Participation Uncertainty It may be unclear whether a system acted independently, merely executed instructions, or functioned only as technical infrastructure. EPMAM shall preserve such uncertainty. Autonomy Uncertainty ≠ Permission to Assume Human or Machine Participation. Where the participation mode cannot be sufficiently established, qualification shall remain visible. Participation Conflict Different systems may describe the same actor differently. One record may identify autonomous execution while another describes manual control. EPMAM shall preserve materially relevant conflicts until they can be legitimately resolved. Machine Participation Conflict ≠ Permission for Convenient Attribution. Governance States EPMAM may represent states including: Machine Participation Ready Machine Participation Under Governance Machine Participation Established Autonomous Participation Established Machine-to-Machine Participation Multi-Agent Participation Human-Supervised Autonomous Participation Delegated Machine Participation Participation Qualified Participation Ambiguous Participation Conflicted Participation Unresolved These states describe operational machine/autonomous participation only. They do not establish legal status. Governance Requirements EPMAM implementations shall ensure that: machine and autonomous actors can be represented independently; non-human actors are linked to governed Actor–Event Associations; tools are distinguished from independent participants; automated execution can be distinguished from autonomy where materially relevant; machine execution is not automatically attributed to the owner; autonomous action is not automatically attributed to the developer; operator, controller, supervisor, owner, and machine can remain distinct actors; delegated execution can be represented; machine-to-machine events can be governed without artificial human insertion; multi-agent participation can be represented; technical instances are not automatically treated as separate actors; AI models are distinguished from autonomous agents where relevant; infrastructure does not automatically become a participant; autonomy state can be qualified; human intervention and override can be preserved; machine location does not determine Event Location; machine timestamps do not redefine Event Timing; identity, authority, accountability, liability, and value governance remain separate; uncertainty remains visible; conflicts remain visible; and machine participation does not determine taxpayer status or another legal tax conclusion. Governance Logic IF EPAM establishes an Actor–Event Association for a machine, software agent, AI agent, robot, autonomous system, or other non-human actor, THEN EPMAM shall evaluate the specific participation characteristics of that actor. IF the actor materially performs an operational function, THEN non-human participation may be represented independently from associated humans or organizations. IF the actor merely serves as a passive tool or infrastructure component, THEN independent machine participation shall not be established by default. IF autonomous execution occurs under supervision, THEN the autonomous actor and supervisor may remain distinct participants where operational reality supports both. IF machine-to-machine participation occurs, THEN human participation shall not be invented solely to fit a traditional transaction model. IF autonomy or machine participation remains uncertain or conflicted, THEN the state shall remain qualified.
