Dependency Extent Dependency may apply to: the whole event; part of the event; one Value Association; one participant relationship; one operational component; one execution phase. Dependency of Part ≠ Dependency of Whole by default. Dependency Qualification Dependency may require qualification. Examples include: direct; indirect; partial; conditional; deferred; provisional; uncertain. Qualification shall remain explicit. Qualified Dependency ≠ Defective Dependency. Dependency Uncertainty Available information may indicate that dependency exists without establishing its exact form. ERLDM shall preserve uncertainty. Dependency Uncertainty ≠ Permission to Assume Independence. Dependency Conflict Different systems may describe dependency differently. For example: ERP says Event B depends on Event A; payment system says Event B depends on Event C; marketplace data suggests both A and C. ERLDM shall preserve the conflict. Dependency Conflict ≠ Permission for Convenient Dependency Selection. Dependency Reconsideration New information may justify reconsidering an earlier Dependency determination. ERLDM shall support reconsideration while preserving prior history. Dependency Reconsideration ≠ Historical Erasure. Dependency Stability Once dependency is established, it should remain stable unless materially relevant information changes. Technical migrations or identifier changes should not alter dependency by themselves. System Change ≠ Dependency Change by default. Dependency and Sequence Dependency and sequence are related but distinct. An event may depend on another event without necessarily following it in a simple linear time sequence. Likewise, one event may follow another without depending on it. Therefore: Dependency ≠ Sequence. ERLSM governs sequence. Dependency and Causation Dependency may suggest causal relevance. However: Dependency ≠ Causation by default. ERLDM does not establish full causal responsibility. Dependency and Event Formation ERLDM does not form new events. Dependency Discovery ≠ New Event Formation. TREFS remains authoritative. Dependency and Event Boundary Strong dependency does not remove Event Boundary. Dependency ≠ Shared Event Boundary. TREBS remains authoritative. Dependency and Participation A shared participant may contribute to dependency, but shared participation does not establish dependency by itself. Shared Participant ≠ Dependency. TREPS remains authoritative. Dependency and Value Association Value relationships may support dependency. However: Shared Value ≠ Dependency by default. TRVAS remains authoritative for Value Association. Dependency and Grouping Several dependent events may later form an Event Group or Event Network. ERLDM does not establish that grouping. Dependency Structure ≠ Event Group. ERLGM governs grouping. Dependency and Merge / Split Strong dependency may reveal potential formation or boundary issues. It does not authorize merge or split. Dependency ≠ Merge Criterion by itself. Dependency ≠ Split Criterion by itself. ERLMM, together with upstream TREFS and TREBS governance, remains authoritative. Dependency and Taxation Dependency may later be legally relevant for tax analysis. However: Governed Event Dependency ≠ Tax Dependency Determination. ERLDM does not determine: taxable supply chains; tax aggregation; taxable series; Tax Base; tax jurisdiction; Tax Liability; related-party rules; withholding; deductibility; or another jurisdiction-specific legal consequence. Cross-Border Dependency Events in different jurisdictions may be dependent. For example: order in one country; production in another; settlement in another; delivery elsewhere. ERLDM preserves the dependency structure. It does not determine taxing rights. Cross-Border Dependency ≠ Tax Jurisdiction. Blockchain Dependency Blockchain activity may include dependencies among: smart-contract calls; bridge transactions; settlement transactions; token transfers; protocol states; off-chain events. Technical execution dependency may be relevant. However: Blockchain Execution Dependency ≠ Tax-Relevant Event Dependency by default. The governed Event structure remains decisive. AI-Agent Dependency Autonomous agents may create complex dependency graphs. One agent may request activity. Another may execute it. A machine may provide resources. A separate agent may settle value. ERLDM shall support these relationships. Agent Coordination ≠ Same Event. Machine Dependency Machine-generated events may depend on: prior instructions; system states; resource allocations; sensor conditions; other machine events. ERLDM may represent these dependencies without requiring human involvement. Machine Dependency ≠ Ungoverned Dependency. Dependency Traceability Dependency decisions shall remain reconstructable. Traceability may include: candidate relationship; dependency indicators; direction; conditions; qualification; extent; confidence; ambiguity; conflict; correction; and reconsideration. Dependency Traceability ≠ Event Record Governance. TREGS remains authoritative for the complete Event Record. Governance States ERLDM may represent: Dependency Governance Ready Dependency Under Governance No Material Dependency Established Direct Dependency Indirect Dependency Unidirectional Dependency Mutual Dependency Conditional Dependency Partial Dependency Structural Dependency Operational Dependency Value-Related Dependency Execution Dependency Settlement Dependency Dependency Qualified Dependency Ambiguous Dependency Conflicted Dependency Unresolved Governed Event Dependency Established Governance Requirements ERLDM implementations shall ensure that: dependency is governed only after Event Relationship candidacy is established; dependency remains distinct from Event Identity; dependency direction is explicit; unidirectional and mutual dependency can be represented; conditional dependency can be represented; partial dependency can be represented; structural and operational dependency remain distinguishable; value-related dependency does not replace TRVAS governance; one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-one, and many-to-many dependencies can be represented; direct and indirect dependencies remain distinguishable; dependency strength and extent can be qualified; dependency uncertainty remains visible; dependency conflict remains visible; dependency reconsideration remains traceable; system changes do not automatically change dependency; dependency remains distinct from sequence; dependency does not establish causation by default; Event Formation remains under TREFS; Event Boundary remains under TREBS; Event Participation remains under TREPS; Value Association remains under TRVAS; grouping remains under ERLGM; merge and split remain under ERLMM; and jurisdiction-specific tax interpretation remains downstream. Governance Logic IF ERLIM establishes a valid Relationship Candidate, THEN ERLDM shall evaluate whether a material dependency exists among the involved events. IF Event B materially relies on Event A, THEN a dependency may be established with explicit direction. IF dependency operates in both directions, THEN mutual dependency may be represented without merging the events. IF dependency exists only under a condition, THEN the condition shall remain explicit. IF dependency applies only to part of an event, THEN partial dependency shall be preserved rather than generalized to the entire event. IF multiple events contribute to one dependent event, THEN many-to-one dependency may be represented without merging the source events. IF one event creates dependencies for several events, THEN one-to-many dependency may be represented without creating one combined event. IF dependency is uncertain or conflicted, THEN the applicable governance state shall remain visible. IF dependency information suggests a potential Event Formation or Boundary problem, THEN the issue shall be referred to the appropriate upstream governance layer rather than resolved inside ERLDM. IF the dependency structure is sufficiently governed, THEN it shall proceed to ERLSM for Event Relationship Sequence governance. Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum ERLDM implementation should support: Relationship Candidate Reference The ERLIM candidate under dependency governance. Primary Event Reference The first governed event involved. Dependent Event Reference The event potentially dependent on another event. Dependency Identifier A stable identifier for the dependency relationship. Dependency Direction The directional structure of dependency. Dependency Type Direct, indirect, conditional, partial, structural, operational, value-related, or other governed type. Dependency Basis The governed information supporting dependency. Dependency Condition Any condition required for the dependency to operate. Dependency Trigger Reference Where a trigger contributes materially to dependency. Dependency Extent Whole-event or partial-event dependency. Dependency Cardinality One-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-one, or many-to-many. Dependency Strength The qualified strength of dependency. Dependency Confidence Confidence in the dependency determination. Ambiguity State Whether material uncertainty remains. Conflict State Whether materially conflicting dependency information exists. Prior Dependency Reference Where dependency has been reconsidered or corrected. Correction / Reconsideration Reference The relevant governance history. Traceability Reference Information required to reconstruct the dependency decision. Governance State The current ERLDM state. Handoff State Whether the dependency structure is ready for ERLSM. Governance Outputs ERLDM may produce: Governed Event Dependency; Unidirectional Dependency; Mutual Dependency; Conditional Dependency; Partial Dependency; Structural Dependency; Operational Dependency; Value-Related Dependency; Execution Dependency; Fulfillment Dependency; Settlement Dependency; Refund Dependency; Reversal Dependency; Replacement Dependency; Continuation Dependency; Parent–Child Dependency; One-to-One Dependency; One-to-Many Dependency; Many-to-One Dependency; Many-to-Many Dependency; Dependency Direction Record; Dependency Condition Record; Dependency Extent Record; Dependency Strength State; Dependency Confidence State; Dependency Ambiguity State; Dependency Conflict State; Dependency Traceability Record; and the principal output: Governed Event Dependency Structure. Critical Distinctions Event Dependency ≠ Event Identity. Relationship Candidate ≠ Dependency by default. A ↓ B ≠ B ↓ A. Mutual Dependency ≠ Single Event by default. Conditional Dependency ≠ Authority Governance. Partial Dependency ≠ Full Event Dependency. Structural Dependency ≠ Same Event Structure. Operational Dependency ≠ Legal Dependency. Value Dependency ≠ Value Ownership. Settlement Dependency ≠ Event Merge. Refund Dependency ≠ Tax Adjustment Determination. Reversal Dependency ≠ Original Event Erasure. Continuation Dependency ≠ Same Event Continuity by default. Parent–Child Dependency ≠ Event Ownership. One Source Event ≠ One Dependent Event. Many Dependencies ≠ Event Merge by default. Indirect Dependency ≠ Irrelevant Dependency. Immediate Dependency ≠ Temporal Immediacy. Dependency Condition ≠ Event Identity. Strong Dependency ≠ Event Merger. Essential Dependency ≠ Same Event. Dependency of Part ≠ Dependency of Whole by default. Qualified Dependency ≠ Defective Dependency. Dependency Uncertainty ≠ Permission to Assume Independence. Dependency Conflict ≠ Permission for Convenient Dependency Selection. System Change ≠ Dependency Change by default. Dependency ≠ Sequence. Dependency ≠ Causation by default. Dependency Discovery ≠ New Event Formation. Dependency ≠ Shared Event Boundary. Shared Participant ≠ Dependency. Shared Value ≠ Dependency by default. Dependency Structure ≠ Event Group. Dependency ≠ Merge Criterion by itself. Governed Event Dependency ≠ Tax Dependency Determination. Cross-Border Dependency ≠ Tax Jurisdiction. Blockchain Execution Dependency ≠ Tax-Relevant Event Dependency by default. Agent Coordination ≠ Same Event. Dependency Traceability ≠ Event Record Governance. Enterprise Application ERLDM provides a governed dependency layer for systems in which one event relies materially on another event but must remain independently identifiable. A typical path is: ERLIM — Governed Event Relationship Candidate Set → ERLDM — Governed Event Dependency Structure → ERLSM — Event Relationship Sequence → ERLGM — Event Relationship Grouping → ERLMM — Merge & Split Governance → Governed Event Relationship Structure This enables enterprises, platforms, banks, autonomous systems, and tax infrastructure to distinguish between events that merely occur near each other and events that are operationally dependent. Use Case 1 — Settlement Dependent on Multiple Commercial Events A payment platform creates one merchant settlement covering hundreds of earlier sales events. The settlement event cannot be understood independently from those earlier events, but the sales remain separate governed events. ERLDM establishes a many-to-one dependency structure between the sales and the settlement. The dependency can remain explicit without merging the sales into one event or treating the settlement as identical to any one purchase. The resulting dependency structure can then move to ERLSM for sequence governance and later to grouping where appropriate. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Resource Execution Dependency An AI agent requests additional computational capacity. A resource-allocation event occurs only after the request is accepted. A machine-execution event then depends on that allocation. Digital settlement depends on measured resource consumption. ERLDM governs the dependencies among these independently formed events: Request ↓ Allocation ↓ Execution ↓ Settlement It does not determine their final sequence, grouping, tax treatment, or whether some technical operations belong to the same event. The result is a governed dependency structure suitable for subsequent TRERLS processing. Canonical Boundary ERLDM owns the establishment, direction, qualification, extent, cardinality, conditionality, uncertainty, conflict, reconsideration, continuity, and dependency-specific traceability of dependencies among Event Relationship Candidates admitted by ERLIM. ERLDM does not identify initial Relationship Candidates, govern Event Sequence, create Event Groups or Event Networks, merge or split events, form new events, redefine Event Boundaries, determine Event Timing, Event Location, Event Participation, Value Association, accountability, liability, tax aggregation, Tax Base, Tax Liability, or another jurisdiction-specific legal conclusion. Its governance ends when material Event Dependencies are sufficiently represented for downstream Event Relationship Sequence governance under ERLSM. Canonical Handoff ERLIM — Governed Event Relationship Candidate Set ↓ ERLDM — Governed Event Dependency Structure ↓ ERLSM — Event Relationship Sequence Governance Canonical Closing Statement ERLDM governs how events rely on one another without allowing dependency to erase their independent Event Identity. An event may depend completely on another event and still remain a distinct governed event. Event Dependency ≠ Event Identity. Dependency ≠ Sequence.

title: OOF™ The Event Relationship Grouping Module (ERLGM) governs how
text: OOF™ The Event Relationship Grouping Module (ERLGM) governs how The Event Relationship Grouping Module (ERLGM) governs how OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: TRERLS — Tax-Relevant Event Relationship Standard Module: ERLGM — Event Relationship Grouping Module Operational Layer: Event Relationship Grouping Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Event Relationship Grouping Origin ID: TREGA-TRERLS-ERLGM-004 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 1 September 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language Canonical Definition The Event Relationship Grouping Module (ERLGM) governs how already-related, dependency-qualified, and sequence-governed Tax-Relevant Events are organized into coherent multi-event structures without destroying their individual Event Identity. ERLGM establishes when related events may legitimately be represented as an Event Group, Event Chain, Event Network, parent–child structure, component structure, parallel structure, or other governed multi-event configuration. Its principal transition is: Governed Event Sequence Structure ↓ Event Grouping Governance ↓ Governed Event Group Structure ERLGM does not merge events into one Event Identity, split events, form new events, redefine Event Boundaries, or determine tax aggregation. The foundational distinction is: Event Group ≠ Single Event. Operational Role Complex economic activity rarely produces isolated Event Relationships. A marketplace transaction may involve purchase, payment, delivery, settlement, commission, refund, and reversal events. A machine economy may generate resource requests, allocations, executions, measurements, settlements, and later corrective events. A supply chain may contain dozens of related events distributed across multiple organizations and countries. ERLGM provides the governance layer that allows these events to be represented together as coherent structures while preserving the independence of each governed event. Grouping therefore solves a different problem from Event Formation or Event Merge. Grouping organizes events. It does not redefine what the events are. Internal Module Flow TRERLS operates through: ERLIM — Event Relationship Identification ↓ ERLDM — Event Relationship Dependency ↓ ERLSM — Event Relationship Sequence ↓ ERLGM — Event Relationship Grouping ↓ ERLMM — Event Relationship Merge & Split ↓ Governed Event Relationship Structure ERLGM receives the Governed Event Sequence Structure from ERLSM. Its output is passed to ERLMM. Operational Transition The canonical transition is: Governed Event Sequence Structure + Governed Relationship Information ↓ Grouping Governance ↓ Governed Event Group Structure ERLGM uses already-governed: Event Relationships; dependencies; sequences; participants; contexts; Value Associations; and other relevant governed information. It does not recreate those upstream determinations. Operational Space ERLGM governs: Event Group identification; Event Group qualification; Event Group membership; Event Group boundary; group entry; group exit; group membership change; group identifier; group purpose; group basis; Event Chain formation; Event Network formation; parent–child grouping; component grouping; parallel-event grouping; branching structures; converging structures; cross-system grouping; cross-organization grouping; cross-border grouping; multi-jurisdiction-ready grouping; machine-generated grouping; autonomous-system grouping; group uncertainty; group conflict; group reconsideration; group continuity; and grouping-specific traceability. Operational Scope ERLGM may govern event structures across: commerce; marketplaces; banking; payment systems; ERP; accounting; logistics; supply chains; digital platforms; blockchain ecosystems; smart-contract systems; digital assets; AI agents; autonomous systems; industrial environments; energy infrastructure; distributed systems; machine-to-machine activity; cross-border operations; and future machine economies. Event Group An Event Group is a governed representation of several distinct Tax-Relevant Events that possess sufficient material relationship to be represented together for downstream governance. The events remain independently identifiable. Therefore: Event Group ≠ Single Event. An Event Group is a relationship structure, not a replacement Event Identity. Group Membership Each event included in an Event Group shall retain its own governed Event Reference. Membership indicates that the event belongs to the governed multi-event structure. It does not transfer the identity of the event to the group. Group Membership ≠ Event Identity Transfer. Group Membership Basis Membership shall be supported by materially relevant relationship information. Possible bases may include: dependency; sequence; shared economic activity; shared operational process; shared settlement structure; shared contractual arrangement; shared Value Relationship; parent–child structure; component structure; reversal relationship; or another governed basis. Shared Attribute Alone ≠ Group Membership by default. Group Purpose An Event Group shall have a governable purpose. Examples may include representing: one broader commercial activity; a settlement structure; a fulfillment structure; a supply-chain segment; a refund and reversal structure; an autonomous workflow; a machine-service process; or a distributed Event Network. The group purpose shall describe why the events are represented together. Group Identifier A group may receive a stable identifier. However: Group Identifier ≠ Event Identifier. The group identifier references the multi-event structure. Each event retains its own Event Identifier. Group Boundary An Event Group requires a defined membership boundary. The boundary determines which events belong to the group and which do not. This is not the same as TREBS Event Boundary governance. Event Group Boundary ≠ Event Boundary. TREBS governs the boundary of an individual event. ERLGM governs the membership boundary of a multi-event structure. Group Entry An event may enter a group when sufficient governed relationship information supports membership. Entry shall remain traceable. Group Entry ≠ New Event Formation. Group Exit An event may be removed from a group where later governance establishes that membership was incorrect or no longer valid. Removal from the group does not erase the event. Group Exit ≠ Event Deletion. Group Membership Change Group membership may evolve when: new events occur; new relationships are discovered; prior relationships are corrected; an event is superseded; a reversal occurs; new evidence becomes available. Membership changes shall remain historically reconstructable. Group Membership Change ≠ Event Lifecycle Change by default. Event Chain An Event Chain is a governed multi-event structure in which events form a materially relevant progression. Example: Event A ↓ Event B ↓ Event C ↓ Event D The chain may incorporate dependency and sequence. However: Event Chain ≠ Single Event Lifecycle by default. Several independently governed events may form one chain. Linear Event Chain A simple Event Chain may contain one primary progression path. Example: Order ↓ Payment ↓ Delivery ↓ Settlement Each event remains distinct. Branching Event Chain A chain may branch. Example: Order ↓ Payment and: Order ↓ Fulfillment Those branches may later converge. ERLGM may preserve the branching structure. Converging Event Chain Multiple event paths may converge into a later event. Example: Sale A + Sale B + Sale C ↓ Settlement This does not merge the source events. Chain Convergence ≠ Event Merge. Event Network An Event Network is a multi-event relationship structure containing more complex connections than a simple chain. A network may contain: several branches; multiple convergence points; parallel paths; direct and indirect dependencies; reversals; replacement relationships; multiple participants; multiple value flows. Event Network ≠ Single Event. Network Node Each governed event may function as a node within an Event Network. Node status does not alter Event Identity. Network Node ≠ Sub-Event by default. Network Edge A governed Event Relationship may function as an edge connecting events. The edge may represent: dependency; sequence; reversal; continuation; settlement linkage; or another governed relationship. Relationship Edge ≠ Event. Parent–Child Group Structure Some events may be represented hierarchically. A Parent Event may be related to several Child Events. However: Parent Event ≠ Owner of Child Event. and: Child Event ≠ Component of Parent Event by default. The relationship structure must remain explicit. Component Event Structure Several distinct events may constitute components within a broader Event Group. Component grouping does not mean they should be merged into one event. Event Component Relationship ≠ Event Merge by default. Parallel Event Group Several events may proceed in parallel while belonging to the same broader activity. ERLGM may represent that structure. Parallel Events ≠ Same Event. Shared Participant Grouping Events may share one or more participants. This may support grouping. However: Same Participant ≠ Same Event Group by default. Shared participation must be materially relevant to the group purpose. Shared Value Grouping Events may share or reference the same governed value. This may support grouping. However: Shared Value Reference ≠ Event Group by default. TRVAS remains authoritative for Value Association. Shared Context Grouping Events may occur within the same governed context. This may support grouping. However: Shared Context ≠ Event Group by default. TRECS remains authoritative for Event Context. Shared Contract Grouping Several events may arise under the same contract. This may support grouping but does not automatically require it. One Contract ≠ One Event Group by default. A contract may govern thousands of unrelated or only loosely related events. Shared Invoice Grouping Events appearing on one invoice may be grouped where relationship governance supports it. However: One Invoice ≠ One Event Group by default. Shared Payment Grouping A single payment may reference several events. This may create a legitimate group structure. However: One Payment ≠ One Event Group by default. The payment relationship must remain governed. Settlement Grouping Settlement processes frequently bring many earlier events together. ERLGM may establish a settlement-related Event Group where appropriate. The underlying events remain independent. Settlement Group ≠ Merged Event. Refund and Reversal Grouping An original event, refund event, and reversal event may belong to one governed group. Grouping preserves their relationship without erasing historical Event Identity. Refund Grouping ≠ Original Event Cancellation. Reversal Grouping ≠ Historical Erasure. One Economic Activity and Event Grouping One economic activity may justify representing several events together. However: One Economic Activity ≠ One Event. ERLGM provides a way to represent common economic structure without forcing Event Identity collapse. Multiple Technical Operations Multiple technical operations may relate to one event, several events, or a broader Event Group. The number of technical records does not determine the number of group members. More Technical Operations ≠ Larger Event Group by default. Cross-System Grouping Events belonging to one relationship structure may reside in different systems. ERLGM shall support grouping across: ERP; payment systems; banking; marketplaces; logistics; blockchain; autonomous systems; and other operational infrastructure. System Boundary ≠ Event Group Boundary. Cross-Organization Grouping One Event Group may span several organizations. For example: Marketplace ↓ Merchant ↓ Bank ↓ Logistics Provider ERLGM may represent the broader relationship while preserving each organization's event references. Organization Boundary ≠ Event Group Boundary by default. Cross-Border Grouping Related events may belong to one Event Group even when they occur in several countries. This does not determine tax jurisdiction. Cross-Border Event Group ≠ Tax Jurisdiction. Multi-Jurisdiction Readiness A Governed Event Group may later be evaluated differently by different jurisdictions. The underlying group structure remains jurisdiction-neutral. The canonical principle is: One Governed Event Group ↓ Multiple Jurisdictional Evaluations ERLGM does not determine how a jurisdiction legally aggregates the events. Blockchain Event Grouping Blockchain systems may generate multiple on-chain operations associated with a broader governed activity. ERLGM may group independently governed Tax-Relevant Events where relationship governance supports it. However: One Smart Contract ≠ One Event Group by default. One Wallet ≠ One Event Group by default. One Block ≠ One Event Group. Technical ledger architecture does not determine economic grouping. AI-Agent Event Grouping One autonomous agent may coordinate numerous events. Those events may form one group, several groups, or remain independent. Therefore: One Agent Workflow ≠ One Event Group by default. Grouping depends on governed Event Relationships. Multi-Agent Event Networks Several agents may create distributed Event Networks. ERLGM may represent the resulting multi-event structure across agents without assigning identity, authority, or accountability. Those domains remain under their respective architectures. Machine-to-Machine Grouping Machine-generated events may be grouped where they belong to a common governed operational or economic structure. Machine Correlation ≠ Event Group by default. Technical coordination alone is insufficient. Group Cardinality An Event Group may contain any number of governed events necessary to represent the materially relevant relationship structure. Cardinality shall not determine Event Identity. Group Size ≠ Economic Importance. Nested Group Structures Where necessary, an Event Group may participate in a broader grouping structure. For example: Local Fulfillment Group ↓ Regional Settlement Group ↓ Global Commercial Event Network Nested grouping shall preserve the identity of underlying events. Nested Group ≠ Event Merge. Overlapping Groups An event may legitimately belong to more than one relationship group where the groups represent different governed purposes. For example, one payment event may belong to: a customer purchase group; and a merchant settlement group. ERLGM may support such overlap where explicit. Multiple Group Membership ≠ Multiple Event Identity. Group Independence Two Event Groups may remain independent even where some attributes are similar. Similar Groups ≠ Same Group. Group Identity requires governed relationship basis, not superficial similarity. Group Qualification A group may be qualified according to its structure or purpose. Examples include: commercial; payment; settlement; fulfillment; reversal; autonomous workflow; machine-service; distributed; cross-border; multi-system. Qualification provides structure but does not determine tax treatment. Group Confidence Group membership may carry a governance confidence state where uncertainty remains. Possible states may include: Confirmed · Qualified · Limited · Ambiguous · Conflicted · Unresolved Confidence shall not substitute for evidence or validation. Group Ambiguity Available information may establish that events belong to a broader relationship structure without identifying the exact membership boundary. ERLGM shall preserve that uncertainty. Group Ambiguity ≠ Permission for Convenient Membership Selection. Group Conflict Different systems may represent group structure differently. For example: ERP groups A, B, C; payment system groups B, C, D; marketplace records indicate A, B, C, D. ERLGM shall preserve the conflict until sufficient governance resolves it. Group Conflict ≠ Permission for Selective Aggregation. Group Reconsideration New information may justify group reconsideration. Events may be: added; removed; reclassified; moved to another group; linked across groups. Previous group states shall remain traceable. Group Reconsideration ≠ Historical Erasure. Group Stability A governed Event Group should remain stable unless materially relevant information changes. System migration, database consolidation, or platform replacement shall not automatically alter group structure. System Change ≠ Event Group Change by default. Grouping and Event Identity Grouping does not redefine the events. Each member remains independently governed. Grouped Events ≠ Same Event. Grouping and Event Formation ERLGM does not form events. Grouping Discovery ≠ New Event Formation. TREFS remains authoritative. Grouping and Event Boundary ERLGM does not redefine individual Event Boundaries. Group Boundary ≠ Individual Event Boundary. TREBS remains authoritative. Grouping and Dependency Dependency may contribute to group structure. ERLGM does not redetermine dependency. Group Membership ≠ Dependency by default. ERLDM remains authoritative. Grouping and Sequence Sequence may contribute to Event Chain or Event Network structure. ERLGM does not redetermine sequence. Group Membership ≠ Sequence Relationship by default. ERLSM remains authoritative. Grouping and Merge Grouping is not merge. This is a critical distinction. Event Group ≠ Merged Event. Grouping preserves separate Event Identities. Merge governance may determine that two or more event representations should instead constitute one event, but that belongs to ERLMM together with upstream Event Formation and Boundary authority. Grouping and Split A complex Event Group does not automatically mean an underlying event should be split. Group Complexity ≠ Event Split Criterion. ERLMM remains authoritative. Grouping and Tax Aggregation A tax jurisdiction may later decide to aggregate several related events for legal purposes. That decision does not alter the underlying TREGA™ Event Group. Therefore: Governed Event Group ≠ Tax Aggregation Determination. Grouping and Taxpayer Determination A group may contain events involving several participants. Group membership does not establish taxpayer status. Event Group Participant Set ≠ Taxpayer Set. Grouping and Tax Jurisdiction A cross-border Event Group may span several jurisdictions. ERLGM does not determine which country has taxing rights. Event Group Geography ≠ Tax Jurisdiction Determination. Grouping and Tax Base Values associated with events within a group shall not automatically be aggregated into one taxable amount. Grouped Value ≠ Tax Base. TRVAS governs Value Association; jurisdiction-specific tax systems determine legal Tax Base. Governance States ERLGM may represent: Grouping Governance Ready Grouping Under Governance Group Candidate Group Membership Qualified Event Group Established Linear Event Chain Branching Event Chain Converging Event Chain Parallel Event Structure Parent–Child Event Structure Component Event Structure Event Network Nested Event Group Overlapping Group Membership Cross-System Event Group Cross-Organization Event Group Cross-Border Event Group Autonomous Event Group Group Ambiguous Group Conflicted Group Under Reconsideration Group Superseded Governed Event Group Structure Established Governance Requirements ERLGM implementations shall ensure that: grouping operates only on already-governed Event Relationships; each group member retains independent Event Identity; group membership has an explicit governance basis; Event Group purpose is identifiable; Event Group identifiers remain distinct from Event Identifiers; group membership boundaries can be represented; group entry and exit remain traceable; group membership change remains historically reconstructable; Event Chains can be represented; Event Networks can be represented; branching and converging structures can be represented; parent–child and component structures can be represented; overlapping group membership can be supported where justified; nested group structures can be represented where materially necessary; shared context, participants, value, contracts, invoices, or payments do not automatically establish group membership; cross-system grouping can be represented; cross-organization grouping can be represented; cross-border grouping does not determine tax jurisdiction; blockchain and autonomous-system groups remain independent of technical architecture; ambiguity remains visible; conflict remains visible; reconsideration remains traceable; Event Formation remains under TREFS; Event Boundary remains under TREBS; dependency remains under ERLDM; sequence remains under ERLSM; Merge & Split remains under ERLMM; and tax aggregation remains jurisdiction-specific. Governance Logic IF several governed related events possess a materially coherent common relationship structure, THEN ERLGM may establish an Event Group. IF events belong to the same group, THEN their independent Event Identities shall remain preserved. IF one event progresses into several related branches, THEN a branching Event Chain or Event Network may be represented. IF several event paths converge into one later event, THEN convergence may be represented without merging the source events. IF an event belongs legitimately to more than one group for different governed purposes, THEN overlapping membership may be represented explicitly. IF group membership becomes ambiguous or conflicted, THEN the applicable governance state shall remain visible. IF new materially relevant information changes group membership, THEN the group may be reconsidered while preserving prior history. IF group structure suggests that existing Event Identity or Event Boundary may be incorrect, THEN the issue shall proceed to ERLMM and, where necessary, upstream TREFS or TREBS rather than being silently resolved through grouping. IF the group structure is sufficiently governed, THEN it shall proceed to ERLMM for Merge & Split governance. Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum ERLGM implementation should support: Sequence Structure Reference The ERLSM output entering grouping governance. Event Group Identifier A stable identifier for the governed multi-event structure. Group Purpose The governed reason the events are represented together. Group Basis The materially relevant Relationship information supporting grouping. Group Type Event Group, Event Chain, Event Network, parent–child structure, component structure, parallel structure, or another governed form. Group Member Event References The individual governed events included in the structure. Group Membership State The governance state of each event's membership. Group Entry Reference Where and why an event entered the group. Group Exit Reference Where and why an event was removed. Group Membership Boundary The governed membership boundary of the group. Parent Event Reference Where a parent–child structure exists. Child Event References Where child relationships exist. Component Event References Where component structure is governed. Event Chain Reference Where a linear or branching chain exists. Event Network Reference Where a broader network exists. Branch References Where group structure branches. Convergence References Where event paths converge. Nested Group Reference Where the group belongs to a broader grouping structure. Overlapping Group Reference Where an event belongs to another legitimate group. Group Qualification The applicable structural or operational qualification. Group Confidence The qualified confidence in the grouping decision. Ambiguity State Whether group membership or structure remains uncertain. Conflict State Whether materially conflicting grouping information exists. Prior Group State Reference The preceding group state where reconsideration has occurred. Correction / Reconsideration Reference The relevant change history. Grouping Traceability Reference Information required to reconstruct the grouping decision. Governance State The current ERLGM governance state. Handoff State Whether the group structure is ready for ERLMM. Governance Outputs ERLGM may produce: Governed Event Group; Event Group Identifier; Event Group Membership Record; Event Group Boundary Record; Event Chain; Linear Event Chain; Branching Event Chain; Converging Event Chain; Event Network; Parent–Child Event Structure; Component Event Structure; Parallel Event Structure; Nested Event Group; Overlapping Event Group Membership; Cross-System Event Group; Cross-Organization Event Group; Cross-Border Event Group; Autonomous Event Group; Group Qualification State; Group Confidence State; Group Ambiguity State; Group Conflict State; Group Reconsideration Record; Group Traceability Record; and the principal output: Governed Event Group Structure. Critical Distinctions Event Group ≠ Single Event. Grouping Organizes Events ≠ Redefining Events. Group Membership ≠ Event Identity Transfer. Shared Attribute Alone ≠ Group Membership by default. Group Identifier ≠ Event Identifier. Event Group Boundary ≠ Event Boundary. Group Entry ≠ New Event Formation. Group Exit ≠ Event Deletion. Group Membership Change ≠ Event Lifecycle Change by default. Event Chain ≠ Single Event Lifecycle by default. Chain Convergence ≠ Event Merge. Event Network ≠ Single Event. Network Node ≠ Sub-Event by default. Relationship Edge ≠ Event. Parent Event ≠ Owner of Child Event. Event Component Relationship ≠ Event Merge by default. Parallel Events ≠ Same Event. Same Participant ≠ Same Event Group by default. Shared Value Reference ≠ Event Group by default. Shared Context ≠ Event Group by default. One Contract ≠ One Event Group by default. One Invoice ≠ One Event Group by default. One Payment ≠ One Event Group by default. Settlement Group ≠ Merged Event. Refund Grouping ≠ Original Event Cancellation. One Economic Activity ≠ One Event. More Technical Operations ≠ Larger Event Group by default. System Boundary ≠ Event Group Boundary. Cross-Border Event Group ≠ Tax Jurisdiction. One Smart Contract ≠ One Event Group by default. One Agent Workflow ≠ One Event Group by default. Machine Correlation ≠ Event Group by default. Nested Group ≠ Event Merge. Multiple Group Membership ≠ Multiple Event Identity. Group Ambiguity ≠ Permission for Convenient Membership Selection. Group Conflict ≠ Permission for Selective Aggregation. Group Reconsideration ≠ Historical Erasure. System Change ≠ Event Group Change by default. Grouped Events ≠ Same Event. Grouping Discovery ≠ New Event Formation. Group Boundary ≠ Individual Event Boundary. Group Membership ≠ Dependency by default. Group Membership ≠ Sequence Relationship by default. Event Group ≠ Merged Event. Group Complexity ≠ Event Split Criterion. Governed Event Group ≠ Tax Aggregation Determination. Event Group Participant Set ≠ Taxpayer Set. Event Group Geography ≠ Tax Jurisdiction Determination. Grouped Value ≠ Tax Base. Enterprise Application ERLGM provides the organizational layer required to represent large multi-event structures without destroying the identity of their component events. A typical path is: ERLIM — Governed Event Relationship Candidate Set → ERLDM — Governed Event Dependency Structure → ERLSM — Governed Event Sequence Structure → ERLGM — Governed Event Group Structure → ERLMM — Event Relationship Merge & Split Governance → Governed Event Relationship Structure This makes it possible for enterprises, platforms, banks, distributed systems, and autonomous infrastructures to represent broad economic activities as coherent multi-event structures without prematurely treating those structures as one event. Use Case 1 — Marketplace Purchase, Settlement, and Refund Network A marketplace processes hundreds of customer purchases. Each purchase may generate payment, fulfillment, delivery, platform-fee, settlement, refund, and reversal events. Several sales are later combined into one merchant settlement while individual refunds remain linked to particular purchases. ERLGM can establish purchase-related Event Groups while also representing broader settlement Event Groups. One settlement event may therefore legitimately participate in a settlement structure involving several purchase groups. The underlying purchases remain independently governed. This creates a coherent Event Network without collapsing hundreds of events into a single “transaction.” Use Case 2 — Autonomous Industrial Service Network An industrial AI system coordinates multiple machines to provide a continuously delivered service. Resource-request events, machine allocations, execution events, energy-consumption events, measurement events, digital settlements, and later corrections occur across several systems. ERLGM groups the events into appropriate service, execution, and settlement structures while preserving individual Event Identities. Events may participate in overlapping structures where operational reality requires it. The resulting Governed Event Group Structure provides ERLMM with the organized relationship context required to determine whether any Event Formation or Boundary representation requires Merge or Split governance. Canonical Boundary ERLGM owns the formation and governance of multi-event relationship structures, including Event Groups, Event Chains, Event Networks, group membership, membership boundaries, parent–child structures, component structures, parallel structures, nested groups, overlapping groups, cross-system groups, cross-organization groups, cross-border groups, qualification, uncertainty, conflict, reconsideration, and grouping-specific traceability. ERLGM does not create new events, redefine individual Event Boundaries, determine Event Timing, establish Event Participation or Value Association, redetermine dependency or sequence, merge or split Event Identities, determine taxpayer status, aggregate taxable value, determine tax jurisdiction, Tax Base, Tax Liability, or another jurisdiction-specific legal consequence. Its governance ends when the multi-event structure is sufficiently represented for downstream Event Relationship Merge & Split governance under ERLMM. Canonical Handoff ERLSM — Governed Event Sequence Structure ↓ ERLGM — Governed Event Group Structure ↓ ERLMM — Event Relationship Merge & Split Governance Canonical Closing Statement ERLGM organizes related events into coherent structures without allowing the convenience of grouping to erase the identity of the events themselves. A group can explain how many events belong together without claiming that those events are one event. Event Group ≠ Single Event. Governed Event Group ≠ Tax Aggregation Determination.

title: OOF™ The Event Relationship Identification Module (ERLIM) governs how
text: OOF™ The Event Relationship Identification Module (ERLIM) governs how The Event Relationship Identification Module (ERLIM) governs how OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: TRERLS — Tax-Relevant Event Relationship Standard Module: ERLIM — Event Relationship Identification Module Operational Layer: Event Relationship Identification Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Event Relationship Identification Origin ID: TREGA-TRERLS-ERLIM-001 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 1 September 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language Canonical Definition The Event Relationship Identification Module (ERLIM) governs how materially relevant relationships among already-governed Tax-Relevant Events are discovered, screened, distinguished, qualified, and admitted into Event Relationship governance. ERLIM determines whether sufficient indications exist that two or more governed events may possess a relationship requiring further governance under TRERLS. Its principal transition is: Governed Value-Associated Events ↓ Event Relationship Identification ↓ Governed Event Relationship Candidate Set ERLIM does not determine the final type, dependency structure, sequence, grouping, merge, or split of the relationship. It identifies which events require relationship governance. The foundational distinction is: Relationship Indicator ≠ Established Event Relationship. Operational Role Modern systems may contain thousands or millions of governed events. It is neither methodologically valid nor operationally efficient to assume that every event relates to every other event. At the same time, important relationships may be missed when systems consider events only as isolated records. ERLIM provides the entry mechanism into TRERLS. It identifies potentially meaningful Event Relationships based on governed information such as: shared context; shared participants; shared value; operational linkage; temporal proximity; common source structures; contractual association; technical references; settlement linkage; reversal references; machine-generated relationships; or other materially relevant indicators. These indicators initiate relationship governance. They do not complete it. Relationship Discovery ≠ Relationship Determination. Internal Module Flow TRERLS operates through: ERLIM — Event Relationship Identification ↓ ERLDM — Event Relationship Dependency ↓ ERLSM — Event Relationship Sequence ↓ ERLGM — Event Relationship Grouping ↓ ERLMM — Event Relationship Merge & Split ↓ Governed Event Relationship Structure ERLIM is the entry point. Its output becomes the governed candidate structure consumed by ERLDM and subsequent TRERLS modules. Operational Transition The canonical ERLIM transition is: One or More Governed Value-Associated Events + Relationship Indicators ↓ Relationship Identification Governance ↓ Governed Event Relationship Candidate Set The output establishes that relationship governance is warranted. It does not establish the final relationship structure. Operational Space ERLIM governs: relationship candidate discovery; event-pair identification; multi-event candidate identification; relationship-indicator identification; indicator differentiation; shared-context screening; shared-participant screening; shared-value screening; temporal-proximity screening; operational-linkage screening; technical-reference screening; contractual-link screening; settlement-link screening; reversal and correction reference screening; cross-system relationship discovery; cross-organization relationship discovery; machine-generated relationship discovery; duplicate candidate detection; candidate inclusion; candidate exclusion; candidate qualification; candidate uncertainty; candidate conflict; and relationship-governance readiness. Operational Scope ERLIM may identify potential Event Relationships across: commerce; banking; payments; ERP systems; accounting infrastructure; marketplaces; logistics; supply chains; digital platforms; blockchain systems; smart contracts; digital assets; industrial infrastructure; energy systems; AI agents; autonomous systems; machine-to-machine environments; cross-border operations; and other governed economic or operational systems. The technology generating the event does not determine whether a relationship exists. Relationship Candidate A Relationship Candidate is a governed indication that two or more events may possess a materially relevant relationship requiring further TRERLS governance. A candidate may be created because one or more relationship indicators are present. However: Relationship Candidate ≠ Established Event Relationship. Candidate status means the relationship deserves governance. It does not mean the relationship has already been proven. Eligible Events ERLIM operates on already-governed events. An occurrence that has not entered sufficient TREGA™ governance shall not become an Event Relationship merely because another record refers to it. Referenced Occurrence ≠ Governed Related Event by default. Where ERLIM discovers information indicating a possible ungoverned event, that issue should be referred to the relevant upstream TREGA™ governance layer. Event Pair Identification The simplest relationship candidate involves two events. The structure is: Event A ↔ Event B ERLIM identifies whether sufficient indicators exist to place the pair under relationship governance. It does not determine the final direction or type of relationship. Multi-Event Candidate Identification Relationships may involve more than two events. ERLIM shall support candidate structures such as: Event A ↔ Event B ↔ Event C or broader multi-event candidate sets. Relationship Identification ≠ Pairwise-Only Governance. Complex activity may require several events to enter governance together. Relationship Indicator A Relationship Indicator is information suggesting that events may possess a meaningful relationship. Indicators may include: common participants; common value; common context; temporal proximity; shared source references; operational dependencies; process linkage; contractual linkage; common settlement; reversal references; replacement references; machine instructions; smart-contract references; or other governed information. Indicator Presence ≠ Relationship Proof. Multiple Indicators Several indicators may support the same Relationship Candidate. For example: Shared Participant + Shared Value + Temporal Proximity + Common Order Reference may provide stronger reason for relationship governance than any single indicator. However: More Indicators ≠ Established Relationship by default. Indicator quantity and indicator quality are separate considerations. Shared Context Screening Events occurring within the same governed Event Context may warrant relationship evaluation. However: Shared Event Context ≠ Established Event Relationship. Thousands of independent events may occur within the same commercial or operational context. TRECS remains authoritative for Event Context. Shared Participant Screening Events involving the same participant may warrant relationship evaluation. Examples may include the same: customer; supplier; platform; bank; AI agent; autonomous machine; organization; or service provider. However: Same Participant ≠ Related Event by default. TREPS remains authoritative for Event Participation. Shared Value Screening Events associated with the same governed value, Value Reference, Value Change, or Value State may warrant relationship evaluation. For example, one payment may relate to several purchases. A refund may reference value associated with an earlier event. An asset may participate in several events. However: Shared Value ≠ Established Event Relationship by default. TRVAS remains authoritative for Value Association. Temporal Proximity Screening Events occurring close together in time may warrant relationship evaluation. However: Temporal Proximity ≠ Event Relationship. Two independent events may occur simultaneously. Two strongly related events may occur months apart. TRETS remains authoritative for Event Timing. Shared Location Screening Events occurring at the same physical, digital, or distributed location may warrant relationship evaluation. However: Same Location ≠ Event Relationship. TRELS remains authoritative for Event Location. Operational Linkage Screening Operational systems may explicitly link events. For example: an order references fulfillment; a refund references purchase; settlement references payment; machine execution references instruction; delivery references shipment; resource consumption references allocation. These links may provide strong Relationship Indicators. However: Operational Link ≠ Governed Event Relationship by default. The operational system may contain incomplete, incorrect, or technically convenient linkage. Technical Reference Screening Events may share technical identifiers. Examples include: transaction IDs; session IDs; order IDs; invoice references; settlement IDs; API correlation IDs; ledger references; blockchain hashes; smart-contract identifiers; machine-job identifiers. These references may support candidate identification. However: Shared Technical Reference ≠ Same Event. and: Shared Technical Reference ≠ Established Event Relationship by default. Contractual Link Screening Events may arise under the same contract or commercial arrangement. This may be relevant to relationship identification. However: Same Contract ≠ Same Event. and: Same Contract ≠ Established Event Relationship by default. A long-term agreement may produce thousands of independent events. Invoice Link Screening Several events may appear on one invoice. One event may also appear across several invoice records. Therefore: Same Invoice ≠ Same Event. Invoice linkage may become a Relationship Indicator but not a final Event Relationship determination. Payment Link Screening A payment may provide an important relationship indicator. However: one payment may settle several events; several payments may settle one event; a payment may be unrelated to a nearby event; a later payment may settle an earlier activity. Therefore: Same Payment ≠ Same Event. and: Payment Link ≠ Established Event Relationship by default. Settlement Link Screening Settlement systems frequently aggregate multiple underlying activities. A settlement reference may therefore identify a multi-event candidate structure. One Settlement ≠ One Event by default. ERLIM may admit the relevant events into relationship governance without deciding their eventual relationship structure. Refund Reference Screening A refund may explicitly refer to an earlier transaction. This is a strong relationship indicator. However, ERLIM does not determine whether the refund is: part of the original event; a separate related event; a reversal event; or another relationship structure. That determination belongs downstream. Refund Reference ≠ Relationship Type Determination. Reversal Reference Screening A reversal may explicitly reference an earlier event. ERLIM may identify the two events as Relationship Candidates. It does not determine the full reversal structure. Reversal Reference ≠ Established Reversal Relationship. Correction Reference Screening A later event may refer to an earlier event as part of a correction. ERLIM may admit that relationship into governance. It does not determine whether the later activity represents correction, replacement, continuation, or another relationship type. Common Source Screening Two or more events may originate from a common operational source. For example, one customer request may produce several events. A machine instruction may generate several operational events. A smart contract may trigger several executions. A common source can therefore be relevant. However: Common Source ≠ Same Event by default. Common Destination Screening Several events may converge on the same operational destination. For example, several commercial events may settle into one payment or resource pool. This may create a Relationship Candidate. Common Destination ≠ Event Merger. Cross-System Relationship Discovery Related events may exist in different systems. For example: Commerce Event ↓ Payment Event ↓ Banking Event ↓ Logistics Event ERLIM shall support discovery across system boundaries. Different Systems ≠ Independent Events by default. Likewise: Same System ≠ Related Events by default. System architecture and Event Relationship architecture are separate. Cross-Organization Relationship Discovery Related events may be distributed across several organizations. One organization may hold only part of the relationship information. ERLIM may therefore use governed cross-organizational references where available. Different Organizations ≠ Unrelated Events by default. Cross-Border Relationship Discovery Potentially related events may occur across different countries. Geographic separation does not invalidate relationship candidacy. Likewise, shared geography does not prove relationship. Different Countries ≠ Unrelated Events. Same Country ≠ Related Events by default. ERLIM does not determine tax jurisdiction. Blockchain Relationship Discovery Blockchain systems may contain technical relationships through: transaction references; wallet interactions; smart-contract calls; token movements; bridge operations; settlement structures; or protocol execution. ERLIM may use these as Relationship Indicators. However: On-Chain Link ≠ Governed Event Relationship by default. and: One Blockchain Transaction ≠ One Tax-Relevant Event by default. Off-chain information may also be necessary. AI-Agent Relationship Discovery AI agents may initiate, coordinate, or respond to multiple governed events. Agent-generated references may identify potential relationships. For example: Agent Instruction ↓ Resource Allocation Event ↓ Service Event ↓ Settlement Event ERLIM may identify these as Relationship Candidates. It does not determine dependency, sequence, or grouping. Machine-to-Machine Relationship Discovery Autonomous machines may exchange instructions, resources, services, energy, or value. Machine-generated correlation data may support relationship discovery. Machine Correlation ≠ Governed Event Relationship by default. Machine-generated activity remains subject to the same governance requirements as human-mediated activity. Direct Relationship Indicator Some indicators explicitly connect two events. Examples include: refund-of reference; correction-of reference; replacement-of reference; settlement-of reference. These may constitute Direct Relationship Indicators. However: Direct Indicator ≠ Final Relationship Determination. Indirect Relationship Indicator Some relationships become visible only through intermediate information. For example: Event A ↓ Shared Value Reference ↓ Settlement Record ↓ Event B ERLIM may identify an indirect candidate relationship. Indirect Indicator ≠ Weak Relationship by default. The quality of the relationship depends on the governed information, not merely on whether the indicator is direct. Candidate Relevance Not every detectable connection deserves continued governance. ERLIM shall evaluate whether the potential relationship is materially relevant to Tax-Relevant Event governance. A technically detectable but economically or operationally meaningless correlation may be excluded. Detectable Connection ≠ Material Relationship Candidate. Candidate Inclusion A Relationship Candidate may be included where sufficient materially relevant indicators justify further TRERLS governance. Inclusion means: Further Relationship Governance Required. It does not mean: Relationship Established. Candidate Exclusion A potential relationship may be excluded where available information does not support material relevance. Exclusion should remain traceable where materially important. Candidate Exclusion ≠ Proof of Permanent Unrelatedness. New information may justify reconsideration. Duplicate Relationship Candidates Multiple systems may independently identify the same potential relationship. ERLIM shall support duplicate detection. Multiple Candidate Records ≠ Multiple Relationships by default. Duplicate consolidation shall preserve source traceability. Candidate Overlap Several Relationship Candidates may partially overlap. For example: Candidate 1: Events A and B; Candidate 2: Events B and C; Candidate 3: Events A, B, and C. ERLIM shall preserve these structures without prematurely deciding whether they form one group or network. Grouping belongs to ERLGM. Candidate Confidence ERLIM may qualify confidence that further relationship governance is warranted. Possible states may include: High · Qualified · Limited · Ambiguous · Conflicted · Unresolved Confidence applies to candidacy. It does not represent final Relationship Confidence. Candidate Ambiguity Information may indicate that a relationship exists while leaving uncertainty about which events are involved. For example, a payment may clearly settle one of several earlier events but available records may not identify which one. ERLIM shall preserve that ambiguity. Candidate Ambiguity ≠ Permission to Select a Convenient Event. Candidate Conflict Different systems may identify incompatible Relationship Candidates. For example: ERP links settlement to Event A; bank metadata links it to Event B; marketplace records link it to Events A and B. ERLIM shall preserve the conflict. Candidate Conflict ≠ Permission for Convenient Relationship Selection. Missing Relationship Information Absence of an explicit relationship reference does not prove that events are unrelated. No Explicit Link ≠ No Event Relationship. ERLIM may use other governed indicators where appropriate. Excessive Relationship Generation Systems may generate large numbers of weak correlations. ERLIM shall prevent indiscriminate admission of every detectable connection. Correlation ≠ Relationship. This is particularly important for large-scale AI, graph, banking, marketplace, and machine systems. Relationship Identification and Event Formation ERLIM identifies potential relationships among already-governed events. It does not form new events. Relationship Discovery ≠ New Event Formation. Where relationship analysis reveals a possible previously unrecognized event, the matter shall be referred to TREFS and relevant upstream governance. Relationship Identification and Event Boundary ERLIM shall not alter Event Boundaries merely because two events appear strongly related. Strong Relationship Indicator ≠ Shared Event Boundary. TREBS remains authoritative. Relationship Identification and Dependency ERLIM may detect information suggesting dependency. It does not govern dependency. Dependency Indicator ≠ Governed Event Dependency. ERLDM owns dependency governance. Relationship Identification and Sequence ERLIM may detect temporal or operational ordering. It does not establish governed sequence. Sequence Indicator ≠ Governed Event Sequence. ERLSM owns sequence governance. Relationship Identification and Grouping ERLIM may identify several events that appear structurally connected. It does not create an Event Group. Multi-Event Candidate ≠ Event Group. ERLGM owns grouping governance. Relationship Identification and Merge / Split ERLIM may detect indications that event structure requires reconsideration. It does not merge or split events. Merge Indicator ≠ Governed Event Merge. Split Indicator ≠ Governed Event Split. ERLMM owns Merge & Split governance while respecting TREFS and TREBS boundaries. Relationship Identification and Taxation ERLIM shall not identify relationships based solely on a desired tax result. A relationship must arise from governed operational or economic information. Desired Tax Outcome ≠ Relationship Indicator. ERLIM does not determine whether related events should be legally aggregated. Relationship Candidate ≠ Tax Aggregation Candidate by default. Governance States ERLIM may represent: Relationship Screening Ready Relationship Screening Active Potential Relationship Detected Direct Relationship Indicator Detected Indirect Relationship Indicator Detected Multi-Event Candidate Detected Relationship Candidate Qualified Relationship Candidate Included Relationship Candidate Excluded Duplicate Relationship Candidate Relationship Candidate Ambiguous Relationship Candidate Conflicted Relationship Candidate Unresolved Governed Event Relationship Candidate Established Governance Requirements ERLIM implementations shall ensure that: relationship identification operates on governed event references; Relationship Indicators remain distinct from established Event Relationships; event pairs and multi-event candidates can be represented; shared context can be screened without establishing Event Identity; shared participants can be screened without establishing Event Identity; shared value can be screened without establishing Event Identity; temporal proximity can be considered without being treated as proof; shared location can be considered without being treated as proof; operational and technical references can support candidacy; contractual, invoice, payment, and settlement links remain indicators rather than automatic conclusions; refund, reversal, and correction references can initiate governance; cross-system relationships can be discovered; cross-organization relationships can be discovered; cross-border relationships can be discovered; blockchain and machine-generated indicators can be consumed; direct and indirect indicators remain distinguishable; materially irrelevant correlations can be excluded; candidate inclusion and exclusion remain governable; duplicate candidates can be identified; candidate overlap can remain visible; ambiguity remains visible; conflict remains visible; missing explicit linkage does not automatically establish unrelatedness; Event Formation remains under TREFS; Event Boundary remains under TREBS; dependency remains under ERLDM; sequence remains under ERLSM; grouping remains under ERLGM; Merge & Split remains under ERLMM; and jurisdiction-specific tax interpretation remains downstream. Governance Logic IF two or more governed events possess one or more materially relevant Relationship Indicators, THEN ERLIM shall evaluate whether a Relationship Candidate should be established. IF an indicator is merely technical and lacks material relationship relevance, THEN the candidate may be excluded. IF multiple indicators support the same potential relationship, THEN those indicators may strengthen candidacy without establishing the final relationship. IF multiple systems produce duplicate candidates, THEN duplication shall be identified without creating multiple Event Relationships. IF the candidate remains ambiguous or conflicted, THEN the corresponding governance state shall remain visible. IF relationship discovery suggests an ungoverned event may exist, THEN the matter shall be referred to appropriate upstream Event governance rather than creating the event within ERLIM. IF indicators suggest dependency, sequence, grouping, merge, or split, THEN ERLIM shall preserve those indications for the appropriate downstream TRERLS module without determining them. IF the candidate possesses sufficient material relevance, THEN it shall enter the Governed Event Relationship Candidate Set for downstream Relationship governance. Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum ERLIM implementation should support: Primary Governed Event Reference The governed event from which relationship screening is performed. Related Event Candidate Reference The other governed event potentially involved. Relationship Candidate Identifier A stable identifier for the candidate relationship. Candidate Cardinality Whether the candidate contains two or multiple events. Relationship Indicator Type The category of information suggesting the relationship. Relationship Indicator Reference The underlying governed reference supporting candidacy. Indicator Source The system or governance source from which the indicator originates. Indicator Directness Direct or indirect. Shared Context Reference Where Event Context contributes to candidacy. Shared Participant Reference Where Event Participation contributes to candidacy. Shared Value Reference Where governed value contributes to candidacy. Temporal Relationship Indicator Where Event Timing contributes to candidacy. Location Relationship Indicator Where Event Location contributes to candidacy. Operational Link Reference Where operational systems explicitly connect the events. Technical Link Reference Where technical identifiers contribute to candidacy. Candidate Material Relevance State Whether the potential relationship warrants further governance. Duplicate State Whether the candidate duplicates another Relationship Candidate. Candidate Confidence The qualified confidence that further relationship governance is warranted. Ambiguity State Whether candidate membership or relevance remains ambiguous. Conflict State Whether materially conflicting candidate information exists. Inclusion / Exclusion State Whether the candidate enters further TRERLS governance. Traceability Reference Information required to reconstruct the identification decision. Governance State The current ERLIM state. Handoff State Whether the candidate is ready for ERLDM. Governance Outputs ERLIM may produce: Event Pair Candidate; Multi-Event Relationship Candidate; Direct Relationship Indicator; Indirect Relationship Indicator; Shared Context Relationship Indicator; Shared Participant Relationship Indicator; Shared Value Relationship Indicator; Temporal Relationship Indicator; Operational Relationship Indicator; Technical Relationship Indicator; Cross-System Relationship Candidate; Cross-Organization Relationship Candidate; Machine-Generated Relationship Candidate; Candidate Inclusion Record; Candidate Exclusion Record; Duplicate Candidate Record; Candidate Confidence State; Candidate Ambiguity State; Candidate Conflict State; Relationship Identification Traceability Record; and the principal output: Governed Event Relationship Candidate Set. Critical Distinctions Relationship Indicator ≠ Established Event Relationship. Relationship Discovery ≠ Relationship Determination. Relationship Candidate ≠ Established Event Relationship. Referenced Occurrence ≠ Governed Related Event by default. Relationship Identification ≠ Pairwise-Only Governance. Indicator Presence ≠ Relationship Proof. More Indicators ≠ Established Relationship by default. Shared Event Context ≠ Established Event Relationship. Same Participant ≠ Related Event by default. Shared Value ≠ Established Event Relationship by default. Temporal Proximity ≠ Event Relationship. Same Location ≠ Event Relationship. Operational Link ≠ Governed Event Relationship by default. Shared Technical Reference ≠ Same Event. Same Contract ≠ Same Event. Same Invoice ≠ Same Event. Same Payment ≠ Same Event. One Settlement ≠ One Event by default. Refund Reference ≠ Relationship Type Determination. Reversal Reference ≠ Established Reversal Relationship. Common Source ≠ Same Event by default. Common Destination ≠ Event Merger. Different Systems ≠ Independent Events by default. On-Chain Link ≠ Governed Event Relationship by default. Machine Correlation ≠ Governed Event Relationship by default. Detectable Connection ≠ Material Relationship Candidate. Candidate Exclusion ≠ Proof of Permanent Unrelatedness. Multiple Candidate Records ≠ Multiple Relationships by default. Candidate Ambiguity ≠ Permission to Select a Convenient Event. No Explicit Link ≠ No Event Relationship. Correlation ≠ Relationship. Relationship Discovery ≠ New Event Formation. Dependency Indicator ≠ Governed Event Dependency. Sequence Indicator ≠ Governed Event Sequence. Multi-Event Candidate ≠ Event Group. Merge Indicator ≠ Governed Event Merge. Split Indicator ≠ Governed Event Split. Desired Tax Outcome ≠ Relationship Indicator. Relationship Candidate ≠ Tax Aggregation Candidate by default. Enterprise Application ERLIM provides the discovery layer required to identify meaningful Event Relationships across fragmented enterprise and digital infrastructures. A typical operational path is: ERP / Marketplace / Bank / Payment Network / Blockchain / AI Agent / Machine Systems → Governed Value-Associated Events → ERLIM — Relationship Identification → Governed Event Relationship Candidate Set → ERLDM — Relationship Dependency Governance → ERLSM — Relationship Sequence Governance → ERLGM — Relationship Grouping Governance → ERLMM — Merge & Split Governance → Governed Event Relationship Structure This enables large systems to identify which events require relationship governance without assuming that every technical correlation represents an economically meaningful relationship. Use Case 1 — Multi-System Commerce Relationship Discovery A marketplace processes thousands of purchases, payments, settlements, deliveries, returns, and refunds each day. The events exist across several independent systems and use different identifiers. A later settlement covers multiple merchant transactions, while several refunds refer to earlier purchases through different technical references. ERLIM uses governed indicators such as shared Value References, participant information, order references, payment records, settlement identifiers, and refund references to identify which events should enter Relationship governance. It does not decide whether those events are dependent, sequential, grouped, merged, or split. The output is a Governed Event Relationship Candidate Set for further TRERLS processing. Use Case 2 — Autonomous and Blockchain Relationship Discovery An AI agent initiates a resource request that causes machine allocation, energy consumption, digital service execution, smart-contract activity, and several blockchain transfers. The infrastructure produces numerous governed events and many more technical records. ERLIM identifies materially relevant relationship candidates using agent references, resource identifiers, machine execution records, Value References, smart-contract links, and settlement information. It filters technical correlations that do not justify further Event Relationship governance while preserving ambiguous or conflicting candidates. The result allows subsequent TRERLS modules to determine the actual dependency, sequence, grouping, and structural relationships without treating every autonomous or blockchain operation as an independent economic event. Canonical Boundary ERLIM owns the discovery, screening, differentiation, qualification, inclusion, exclusion, duplication control, uncertainty, conflict, and identification-level traceability of potential relationships among already-governed Tax-Relevant Events. ERLIM does not establish final Event Relationships, govern dependency, determine sequence, create Event Groups, determine Event Chains or Networks, merge events, split events, form new events, redefine Event Boundaries, determine Event Timing, Event Location, Event Participation, Value Association, Event Determination, tax aggregation, Tax Liability, or another jurisdiction-specific legal conclusion. Its governance ends when materially relevant Event Relationship Candidates are sufficiently identified for downstream Relationship Dependency governance under ERLDM. Canonical Handoff Governed Value-Associated Events ↓ ERLIM — Governed Event Relationship Candidate Set ↓ ERLDM — Event Relationship Dependency Governance Canonical Closing Statement ERLIM determines which governed events require relationship governance without treating every shared record, technical correlation, common participant, or nearby occurrence as proof that a relationship has already been established. The discovery of a possible relationship and the governance of that relationship are separate operations. Relationship Indicator ≠ Established Event Relationship. Correlation ≠ Relationship.

title: OOF™ The Event Record Linkage Module (ERLKM) governs how a structurally
