Governance State The current ERLSM governance state. Handoff State Whether the sequence structure is ready for ERLGM. Governance Outputs ERLSM may produce: Governed Event Sequence; Predecessor Relationship; Successor Relationship; Immediate Sequence; Deferred Sequence; Concurrent Sequence; Parallel Sequence; Branching Sequence; Converging Sequence; Conditional Sequence; Interrupted Sequence; Resumed Sequence; Reversal Sequence; Refund Sequence; Replacement Sequence; Correction Sequence; Sequence Direction Record; Sequence Cardinality Record; Sequence Confidence State; Sequence Ambiguity State; Sequence Conflict State; Sequence Traceability Record; and the principal output: Governed Event Sequence Structure. Critical Distinctions Event Sequence ≠ Event Identity. Sequence Object ≠ Event Timing Record. Earlier Event ≠ Sequence Relationship by default. Predecessor ≠ Cause by default. Successor ≠ Dependent Event by default. Immediate Sequence ≠ Same Event. Time Distance ≠ Sequence Absence. Concurrent Events ≠ Same Event. Parallel Sequence ≠ Event Group by default. Sequence Branching ≠ Event Fragmentation. Sequence Convergence ≠ Event Merge. Conditional Sequence ≠ Permission Governance. Sequence ≠ Dependency. Event Sequence ≠ Event Timing Determination. System Timestamp Order ≠ Operational Sequence by default. Before ≠ Because Of. Event Sequence ≠ Causation. Interrupted Sequence ≠ Broken Event Relationship by default. Sequence Resumption ≠ Same Event Continuity. Reversal Sequence ≠ Historical Erasure. Refund Sequence ≠ Tax Adjustment Determination. Replacement Sequence ≠ Original Event Invalidity by default. Correction Sequence ≠ Earlier Event Erasure. System Timestamp ≠ Governed Sequence by default. Record Order ≠ Event Sequence by default. Cross-Border Sequence ≠ Tax Period Determination. Blockchain Order ≠ Complete Economic Event Sequence by default. Smart-Contract Execution Order ≠ Tax-Relevant Event Sequence by default. Agent Action Order ≠ Event Identity. Qualified Sequence ≠ Invalid Sequence. Unknown Order ≠ Unrelated Events. Sequence Conflict ≠ Permission to Select the Most Convenient Order. System Change ≠ Sequence Change by default. Sequence Structure ≠ Event Group. Sequential Proximity ≠ Merge Criterion. Governed Event Sequence ≠ Tax Timing Determination. Enterprise Application ERLSM provides the sequencing layer needed to reconstruct how related events progress across fragmented systems. A typical path is: ERLIM — Governed Event Relationship Candidate Set → ERLDM — Governed Event Dependency Structure → ERLSM — Governed Event Sequence Structure → ERLGM — Event Relationship Grouping → ERLMM — Merge & Split Governance → Governed Event Relationship Structure This allows systems to preserve operational progression without confusing timestamps, dependencies, or technical processing order with legal tax timing. Use Case 1 — Cross-System Commerce Sequence A global commerce transaction generates an order event, payment authorization, fulfillment event, shipment event, settlement event, and later refund event. Different systems record these events at different times and in different technical orders. ERLSM uses governed Event Timing and operational relationships to establish the actual Event Sequence while preserving concurrency, delays, and later reversal activity. It does not determine the legal tax point or tax period. The resulting Governed Event Sequence Structure can then proceed to ERLGM for grouping. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Parallel Event Sequence An AI agent initiates a resource request. One branch performs machine allocation and execution. Another branch performs pricing and settlement preparation. The branches later converge when consumption data is finalized and settlement occurs. ERLSM represents the parallel, branching, and converging sequence without collapsing the autonomous workflow into one event or forcing a false linear order. The sequence remains jurisdiction-neutral and suitable for subsequent Event Grouping governance. Canonical Boundary ERLSM owns the governance of relative order, predecessor–successor relationships, concurrency, parallel progression, branching, convergence, conditional sequence, interruption, resumption, sequence qualification, uncertainty, conflict, reconsideration, and sequence-specific traceability among governed related events. ERLSM does not determine Event Timing itself, establish dependency, create Event Groups, determine Event Networks, merge or split events, form new events, redefine Event Boundaries, determine participation, Value Association, causation, accountability, liability, legal tax point, tax period, Tax Base, Tax Liability, or another jurisdiction-specific legal conclusion. Its governance ends when the relevant Event Sequence is sufficiently represented for downstream Event Relationship Grouping governance under ERLGM. Canonical Handoff ERLDM — Governed Event Dependency Structure ↓ ERLSM — Governed Event Sequence Structure ↓ ERLGM — Event Relationship Grouping Governance Canonical Closing Statement ERLSM governs how related events progress without allowing chronology to become Event Identity, dependency, causation, or legal tax timing. The fact that one event happens before another explains order. It does not, by itself, explain why the event happened or what tax law should do with it. Event Sequence ≠ Event Identity. Event Sequence ≠ Tax Timing Determination.

title: OOF™ Event Recognition Rule Module (ERRM)
text: OOF™ Event Recognition Rule Module (ERRM) Event Recognition Rule Module (ERRM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: Tax-Relevant Event Recognition Standard (TRERS) Module: ERRM — Event Recognition Rule Module Operational Layer: Event Recognition Rule Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Event Recognition Rules Origin ID: TREGA-TRERS-ERRM-003 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 29 August 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Event Recognition Rule Module (ERRM) is the Core Module within Tax-Relevant Event Recognition Standard (TRERS) that governs the criteria, logic, conditions, rule structures, decision pathways, exceptions, and traceable recognition mechanisms used to determine whether a relevance-screened occurrence should be formally recognized for continued progression through the TREGA™ event-governance lifecycle. ERRM receives an occurrence that has passed or remained eligible after Event Relevance Screening and establishes the governed recognition logic through which the occurrence can be advanced, withheld, rejected, conditionally recognized, or referred for further recognition governance. Its task is specific: to govern how recognition decisions are made without converting recognition logic into jurisdiction-specific tax law, taxability rules, or legal tax determinations. Operational Role ORIM determines whether a distinguishable occurrence exists. ERSM determines whether that occurrence has sufficient potential relevance to remain within tax-event governance. ERRM answers the next question: What governed rules determine whether this relevance-screened occurrence should be formally recognized? The distinction is critical. Potential relevance alone should not automatically create recognition. At the same time, recognition should not depend on undocumented, inconsistent, or opaque logic. ERRM therefore establishes the rule-governance layer between: potential relevance and formal Event Recognition. Internal Flow Relevance-Screened Occurrence ↓ Applicable Recognition Rule Identification ↓ Recognition Condition Evaluation ↓ Rule Interaction / Priority Resolution ↓ Exception and Uncertainty Handling ↓ Recognition Rule Result ↓ Recognition Decision Candidate The principal output is: Governed Recognition Rule Result This output proceeds to ERCM — Event Recognition Confidence Module for assessment of the strength and reliability of the recognition basis. Operational Space ERRM governs the space between: an occurrence that has sufficient potential relevance and a governed rule-based basis for formal recognition. Its operational space includes: recognition rule identification; recognition criteria; recognition conditions; recognition thresholds where appropriate; rule applicability; rule precedence; rule combinations; exception handling; conflict resolution; deterministic recognition logic; probabilistic recognition logic; AI-assisted recognition logic; hybrid recognition logic; manual recognition logic; rule versioning; rule traceability; recognition-rule change; recognition-rule uncertainty; rule-based rejection; rule-based conditional recognition. ERRM governs the mechanism by which recognition logic is applied. It does not determine whether those rules represent legal tax obligations. Operational Scope ERRM may support recognition methods implemented through: deterministic rules; decision trees; policy logic; threshold logic; pattern-based rules; statistical criteria; AI-assisted classification; machine-learning outputs; human review rules; hybrid human-machine processes; rule engines; workflow systems; enterprise event processors; public-sector tax infrastructure. The implementation technology may vary. The governance requirement remains the same: the basis for recognition must remain explicit, traceable, bounded, and separable from jurisdiction-specific tax determination. Recognition Rule Principle ERRM establishes a foundational distinction: Recognition Rule ≠ Tax Rule. A Recognition Rule determines whether an occurrence should continue through TREGA™ event governance. A Tax Rule determines legal consequences under a jurisdiction. A Recognition Rule may ask: Does this occurrence satisfy sufficient conditions to be formally recognized for Event Formation? A Tax Rule may later ask: Does this governed event create a taxable obligation under applicable law? These are different questions and must remain architecturally separated. Rule Applicability Not every Recognition Rule applies to every occurrence. Rule applicability may depend on governed characteristics such as: occurrence type; operational environment; economic characteristics; transaction characteristics; machine or autonomous execution; value-related attributes; distributed-system characteristics; available context; evidence availability; relevance domain. ERRM must establish which Recognition Rules are applicable before those rules are evaluated. Therefore: Rule Availability ≠ Rule Applicability. Recognition Conditions A Recognition Rule may contain one or more conditions that must be evaluated. Conditions may examine whether: the occurrence is sufficiently distinguishable; the occurrence passed relevance screening; required contextual elements exist; material relationships are available; duplicate occurrence risk is sufficiently controlled; minimum evidence conditions are satisfied; unresolved contradictions remain within acceptable limits; required governance references exist. These conditions remain methodological recognition conditions. They are not statutory taxation conditions. Recognition Thresholds Some implementations may use thresholds. For example, a threshold may determine whether: sufficient information exists; a probabilistic model has adequate support; duplicate risk is below an acceptable governance level; contextual coverage is sufficient; rule confidence is adequate for automatic progression. ERRM allows such thresholds where appropriate. However: Recognition Threshold ≠ Statutory Threshold. A governance threshold should not be confused with a monetary tax threshold, filing threshold, exemption threshold, or other legal threshold. Rule Interaction Several Recognition Rules may apply to the same occurrence. ERRM must govern their interaction. Rules may be: complementary; cumulative; alternative; conditional; hierarchical; mutually exclusive; conflicting. The existence of several applicable rules must not automatically create several recognition decisions. ERRM requires a governed method for resolving rule interaction. Rule Priority Where multiple rules conflict, precedence must not be arbitrary. Rule priority may be established through: architecture-defined precedence; implementation policy; rule specificity; evidence quality; system authority; approved governance hierarchy. ERRM must preserve the reason why one rule prevailed over another where the decision is materially significant. Therefore: Rule Priority ≠ Hidden System Preference. Rule Conflict Recognition rules may produce contradictory results. For example: one rule may support recognition; another may reject; a probabilistic model may indicate uncertainty; a human-review rule may require escalation. ERRM must represent the conflict rather than suppress it. Possible outcomes may include: Recognition Rule Conflict Conditional Recognition Recognition Withheld Escalation Required Rule conflict is a governance state, not a system failure. Deterministic Recognition Rules A deterministic rule produces a defined outcome where its conditions are satisfied. Example logic may take the form: If Condition A + Condition B + Condition C are established ↓ Recognition Rule Satisfied. Deterministic logic can improve consistency. But deterministic logic does not guarantee correctness if its inputs, scope, or assumptions are wrong. Therefore: Deterministic Rule ≠ Correct Recognition by Default. Probabilistic Recognition Rules Some occurrence types may require probabilistic assessment. Examples may include: pattern recognition; transaction clustering; machine-generated activity classification; distributed occurrence association; anomaly-driven recognition. ERRM permits probabilistic methods where governed. However: Model Probability ≠ Recognition Truth. A probability score must remain distinct from the final recognition outcome. Its use must be subject to governed confidence, uncertainty, and escalation mechanisms. AI-Assisted Recognition AI systems may assist in determining whether an occurrence satisfies Recognition Rules. They may: classify occurrences; detect patterns; identify duplicates; assess rule applicability; surface missing information; detect contradictions; recommend recognition outcomes. But AI output cannot become an ungoverned substitute for Recognition Rules. Therefore: AI Recommendation ≠ Governed Recognition Decision. Where AI participates, ERRM requires the applicable rule basis to remain sufficiently interpretable and governable for the implementation context. Human Recognition Manual review may also form part of recognition governance. Human reviewers may resolve: unusual activity; incomplete evidence; rule conflicts; novel machine-generated occurrences; exceptional economic arrangements. But manual involvement does not remove the need for governance. Therefore: Human Decision ≠ Governed Decision by Default. The decision basis must remain traceable where materially required. Hybrid Recognition Many operational systems will combine: Automated Rules + AI Analysis + Human Escalation ERRM supports hybrid recognition where the division of responsibilities remains explicit. For example: Rule Engine ↓ AI-Assisted Assessment ↓ Confidence Evaluation ↓ Human Escalation The architecture remains technology-neutral. Recognition Rule Versioning Recognition Rules may evolve. Operational systems change. New activity types emerge. AI and machine economies create new patterns. Governance methodologies improve. ERRM therefore requires that materially relevant rule changes remain distinguishable. A historical occurrence should not silently be represented as if a Recognition Rule created years later had been applied originally. Therefore: Current Recognition Rule ≠ Historical Recognition Rule. Rule Change ≠ Occurrence Change A Recognition Rule may change while the underlying occurrence remains identical. This is especially important where organizations reprocess historical data. A newly revised Recognition Rule may lead to a different governance result. But: Rule Change ≠ Change in Operational Reality. The historical occurrence must remain separable from the recognition logic later applied to it. Recognition Rule Independence from Tax-Law Change Jurisdiction-specific tax laws may change frequently. TREGA™ Recognition Rules should not need to be reconstructed solely because a tax rate, exemption, legal test, or filing obligation changes downstream. Where a legal change alters what occurrences need to reach tax systems, implementation-level recognition rules may be updated. But the architecture itself preserves the separation: Tax-Law Change ≠ Recognition Rule Change by Default. Rule Transparency A Recognition Rule should be sufficiently explainable to establish: what rule applied; why it applied; what conditions were evaluated; what result it produced; what exceptions or conflicts occurred; what version was used. Transparency does not require disclosure of every implementation detail to every actor. It requires enough governance traceability to reconstruct materially important recognition decisions. Rule Traceability Where materially required, ERRM should preserve: Occurrence Reference ↓ Applied Rule ↓ Rule Version ↓ Evaluated Conditions ↓ Rule Result This creates a traceable bridge between potential event relevance and formal recognition. Recognition Exceptions Some occurrences may fall outside ordinary rule logic. Exceptions may arise where: a novel economic model appears; autonomous agents create unfamiliar activity; existing rules do not cover a new platform structure; available information is incomplete; a transaction structure is materially unusual. ERRM must allow exceptions to be governed rather than forcing them into inappropriate rule categories. Possible handling includes: Exception Review Conditional Recognition Recognition Withheld Escalation Recognition Rule Failure A Recognition Rule may fail because: required inputs are unavailable; conditions cannot be evaluated; the rule conflicts with another rule; the rule is technically unavailable; the occurrence falls outside the rule's valid scope. Such failure should not automatically become rejection. Therefore: Rule Failure ≠ Occurrence Rejection. The appropriate result may instead be unresolved recognition or escalation. Rule Coverage A governance system should understand whether the relevant occurrence is covered by available Recognition Rules. Possible states may include: Rule Coverage Established Partial Rule Coverage Rule Coverage Gap Rule Applicability Unresolved A coverage gap is important in new economic environments. It may reveal that the methodology does not yet adequately govern a type of occurrence. Governance Requirements ERRM requires that: Recognition Rules remain distinct from Tax Rules; rule applicability is established; rule conditions are explicit; rule outputs are governable; rule conflicts can be represented; rule precedence is governed; thresholds remain distinguishable from legal thresholds; deterministic outputs are not treated as truth by default; probabilistic outputs remain distinguishable from recognition outcomes; AI-assisted recommendations remain governed; manual decisions remain traceable where materially required; rule versions are distinguishable; historical recognition remains reconstructable; rule failure does not automatically become occurrence rejection; exceptions can be governed; rule coverage gaps remain visible; recognition logic does not establish legal taxability. Governance Logic ERRM applies five principal questions: Which Recognition Rule or Rules legitimately apply to this occurrence? What recognition conditions must be evaluated? What happens if several rules interact or conflict? What governed result does the applicable rule logic produce? Is the resulting rule basis suitable for confidence assessment or must it remain unresolved? The transformation is: Relevant Occurrence → Applicable Recognition Rules → Condition Evaluation → Rule Resolution → Governed Recognition Rule Result Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum ERRM implementation must be capable of: 1. receiving a relevance-screened occurrence from ERSM; 2. identifying applicable Recognition Rules; 3. evaluating Recognition Conditions; 4. representing rule applicability; 5. resolving or representing multiple-rule interactions; 6. preserving rule conflicts; 7. distinguishing governance thresholds from statutory thresholds; 8. recording rule versions where materially required; 9. representing exceptions and rule failures; 10. producing a Governed Recognition Rule Result for ERCM; 11. preserving enough traceability to reconstruct the recognition logic; 12. preventing Recognition Rules from becoming jurisdiction-specific Tax Determinations. ERRM does not prescribe a specific rules engine, programming language, machine-learning model, AI system, tax platform, or workflow technology. Governance Outputs ERRM may produce: Governed Recognition Rule Result — the result produced by applicable recognition logic. Applicable Recognition Rule Set — the rules determined to apply to the occurrence. Recognition Condition Result — the outcome of individual or combined rule conditions. Recognition Rule Conflict Record — representation of contradictory rule outcomes. Recognition Exception Record — representation of an occurrence requiring exception handling. Recognition Rule Version Reference — identification of the rule version used. Rule Coverage Status — whether adequate recognition-rule coverage exists. Rule Failure Indicator — representation of a recognition rule that could not be legitimately executed. Recognition Decision Candidate — the rule-supported candidate result transferred to confidence assessment. Critical Distinctions Recognition Rule ≠ Tax Rule. Recognition governs architecture progression. Tax law governs legal consequence. Rule Availability ≠ Rule Applicability. A rule existing in the system does not mean it applies to the occurrence. Recognition Threshold ≠ Statutory Threshold. Governance thresholds must not become legal tax thresholds. Deterministic Rule ≠ Correct Recognition by Default. Predictability of logic is not proof of validity. Model Probability ≠ Recognition Truth. A probability score is an input, not a legal or governance fact. AI Recommendation ≠ Governed Recognition Decision. AI assistance remains subject to rule governance. Human Decision ≠ Governed Decision by Default. Human review also requires a legitimate basis. Rule Priority ≠ Hidden System Preference. Precedence must remain governed. Rule Conflict ≠ Recognition Failure. Conflict may legitimately require additional governance. Rule Failure ≠ Occurrence Rejection. Failure of logic execution does not prove non-relevance. Current Recognition Rule ≠ Historical Recognition Rule. Rule evolution must not rewrite past governance. Rule Change ≠ Occurrence Change. Methodology may evolve while operational reality remains the same. Recognition Rule Result ≠ Recognition Confidence. ERRM determines what the rule logic says. ERCM determines how strong the basis for relying on that result is. Recognition Rule Result ≠ Taxability Determination. No recognition rule establishes that tax is legally due. Enterprise Application ERRM addresses a major governance weakness in large transaction-processing environments: recognition logic often exists, but is fragmented across systems, undocumented, embedded in code, mixed with tax logic, or changed without preserving historical meaning. A multinational enterprise may process the same activity through: Commerce Rules ↓ Payment Rules ↓ ERP Logic ↓ Tax Engine Filters ↓ Reporting Rules while an autonomous platform may add: AI Classification ↓ Machine Rules ↓ Dynamic Policies ↓ Human Exception Review. Without ERRM, different systems can decide independently what counts as an event candidate. The result may be inconsistent recognition across systems, duplication, missing events, non-reconstructable historical logic, and premature legal assumptions. ERRM creates a governed recognition-rule layer that can sit before jurisdiction-specific Tax Engines. Use CasesUse Case 1 — Historical Tax Review After Recognition Logic Has Changed Repeatedly A multinational digital platform processes hundreds of millions of transactions each year. Over six years, it changes: payment infrastructure; transaction classification logic; ERP workflows; event filters; AI models; tax engines; internal recognition thresholds. A tax authority later asks why a particular historical transaction entered one reporting pathway while another apparently similar transaction did not. The current recognition logic cannot answer the question because the rules have changed several times. ERRM preserves the applicable Recognition Rule, rule version, conditions, exceptions, and resulting rule outcome associated with the historical occurrence. The organization can reconstruct: what recognition logic existed when the decision was made without pretending that today's rules governed yesterday's activity. This preserves a critical institutional distinction: historical economic reality and historical recognition methodology must remain independently reconstructable. Use Case 2 — AI Recognition System Changes Behavior Across a Machine-to-Machine Marketplace A machine-to-machine marketplace processes continuous exchanges of computing capacity, energy, digital services, data access, and autonomous resource reservations. An AI model assists in identifying which occurrences should enter full Event Formation. As the marketplace evolves, the model is retrained and begins treating certain resource reservations differently. Two operationally similar machine interactions processed six months apart now produce different recognition recommendations. Without governed Recognition Rules, the organization may be unable to explain whether the difference resulted from: changed economic activity; changed model behavior; changed thresholds; changed policy; changed evidence; or genuine methodological improvement. ERRM separates the underlying occurrence from the recognition logic applied to it. AI output becomes one governed input within a traceable Recognition Rule structure rather than the invisible definition of what constitutes a Tax-Relevant Event candidate. This allows machine-scale recognition to evolve without surrendering methodological control to the model producing the recommendation. Canonical Boundary ERRM governs the criteria, rules, conditions, logic, interactions, exceptions, and traceable mechanisms through which a relevance-screened occurrence receives a governed recognition-rule result. It does not determine the confidence that should be placed in that result, resolve unresolved recognition through escalation, form the Tax-Relevant Event, or determine legal taxability. The TRERS internal progression remains: ORIM — Did a distinguishable occurrence occur? → ERSM — Does it possess sufficient potential relevance? → ERRM — What governed Recognition Rules apply and what result do they produce? → ERCM — How strong and reliable is the recognition basis? → EREM — Does unresolved recognition require escalation? Canonical Closing Statement Event Recognition Rule Module establishes the rule-governance layer of Tax-Relevant Event Recognition by ensuring that progression from relevance-screened occurrence to formal recognition is governed through explicit, applicable, traceable, and bounded recognition logic rather than through undocumented system behavior, hidden AI outputs, arbitrary thresholds, or jurisdiction-specific tax conclusions. Through governance of rule applicability, conditions, thresholds, rule interaction, precedence, conflict, deterministic and probabilistic logic, AI-assisted and human decisions, exceptions, rule failure, versioning, coverage, and traceability, ERRM enables recognition methodology to evolve without rewriting the operational reality to which that methodology is applied. The Module preserves the distinctions between Recognition Rules and Tax Rules, governance thresholds and statutory thresholds, model probability and recognition truth, rule change and occurrence change, and rule result and Recognition Confidence. ERRM therefore establishes not whether tax is legally due and not yet how confidently an occurrence should be recognized, but the governed methodological basis upon which that recognition decision can legitimately be assessed.

title: OOF™ Event Relevance Screening Module (ERSM)
text: OOF™ Event Relevance Screening Module (ERSM) Event Relevance Screening Module (ERSM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: Tax-Relevant Event Recognition Standard (TRERS) Module: ERSM — Event Relevance Screening Module Operational Layer: Event Relevance Screening Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Event Relevance Screening Origin ID: TREGA-TRERS-ERSM-002 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 29 August 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Event Relevance Screening Module (ERSM) is the Core Module within Tax-Relevant Event Recognition Standard (TRERS) that governs whether a sufficiently distinguishable occurrence possesses enough plausible economic, operational, transactional, digital, autonomous, machine-generated, value-related, or other tax-event relevance to justify continued progression through the TREGA™ recognition process. ERSM receives a Recognized Occurrence from ORIM and determines whether that occurrence should remain within the candidate population for potential Tax-Relevant Event Formation. Its task is specific: to screen recognized occurrences for legitimate potential relevance to tax-event governance without determining legal taxability, tax jurisdiction, tax liability, or the final structure of the Tax-Relevant Event. Operational Role ORIM answers: Did a sufficiently distinguishable occurrence occur? ERSM asks the next question: Does that occurrence have enough potential relevance to justify further tax-relevant event governance? This distinction prevents TREGA™ from processing every recognized occurrence through the complete event lifecycle. Many genuine occurrences may have no material relationship to taxation analysis. For example: a machine performs routine internal diagnostics; a software service updates a configuration; a warehouse sensor records temperature; an employee opens an internal application; an autonomous system performs non-economic optimization; a platform generates technical housekeeping operations. These may be real occurrences. They do not automatically require Tax-Relevant Event Formation. ERSM acts as the relevance gateway. Internal Flow Recognized Occurrence ↓ Potential Relevance Signal Identification ↓ Relevance Domain Screening ↓ Material Relevance Assessment ↓ Relevance Sufficiency Determination ↓ Relevant / Non-Relevant / Unresolved Screening Result The principal output is: Event Relevance Screening Result Where relevance is sufficiently established, the occurrence proceeds toward governed Recognition Rules. Operational Space ERSM governs the space between: a recognized occurrence and an occurrence sufficiently relevant to remain within the TRERS recognition process. Its operational space includes: relevance-signal identification; economic relevance; transactional relevance; operational relevance; digital economic relevance; autonomous-system relevance; value-related relevance; transfer relevance; exchange relevance; service relevance; resource relevance; distributed activity relevance; machine-generated economic relevance; relevance materiality; relevance uncertainty; non-relevance determination. ERSM governs potential relevance to event governance. It does not govern legal relevance under any particular tax code. Operational Scope ERSM may identify plausible relevance where an occurrence is materially associated with activity such as: provision of goods; provision of services; payments; transfers; exchanges; production; consumption; resource allocation; asset movement; value creation; value change; value transfer; value extinguishment; ownership-related activity; commercial execution; financial activity; digital-service activity; platform-mediated activity; autonomous purchasing; machine-to-machine exchange; distributed economic activity; other activity capable of requiring downstream taxation evaluation. This list is not itself a legal tax rule. It defines a broad governance screening space. Potential Relevance Principle ERSM deliberately operates on potential relevance, not legal taxability. This is essential. A transaction may later be exempt. A transfer may later fall outside a particular tax. A service may not create nexus. A value movement may be legally neutral. A machine-generated action may have no independent tax consequence. Those questions belong downstream. ERSM asks only: Is there a sufficient governance basis to keep this occurrence within the tax-event analysis lifecycle? Therefore: Potential Tax Relevance ≠ Legal Taxability. Relevance Signal A relevance signal is any governed characteristic indicating that the occurrence may materially matter to downstream taxation analysis. Possible signals include: exchange of value; transfer of an asset or resource; provision or receipt of a service; economic benefit; economic sacrifice; commercial commitment; payment; settlement; ownership-related change; operational production; consumption; resource allocation; cross-border economic activity; platform-mediated exchange; autonomous commercial action; machine-to-machine economic execution. A single relevance signal may be sufficient in some contexts. In others, several signals may need to be considered together. Relevance Signal ≠ Taxable Trigger ERSM must preserve a strict distinction: Relevance Signal ≠ Taxable Trigger. A payment may indicate relevance. It does not prove tax liability. A transfer may indicate relevance. It does not prove a taxable disposition. A service activation may indicate relevance. It does not establish a jurisdictional tax point. Recognition infrastructure must not smuggle legal tax conclusions into the relevance-screening stage. Economic Relevance ERSM may identify economic relevance where the occurrence materially affects, represents, enables, transfers, consumes, generates, allocates, or relates to economic value or resources. However: Economic Relevance ≠ Taxability. Economic meaning is a reason for further governance, not a legal conclusion. Operational Relevance An occurrence may be operationally significant without appearing immediately as a conventional transaction. For example: production completion; delivery; automated resource consumption; asset deployment; machine execution; platform fulfilment. Such activity may require downstream event governance even where no payment occurs at the same moment. Therefore: Payment ≠ Required Condition for Relevance. Transactional Relevance A transaction record may provide a strong relevance signal. But ERSM must not assume that: Transaction Record = Tax-Relevant Event. A transaction record may represent: initiation; authorization; partial execution; reversal; synchronization; settlement; internal technical posting. Its actual event structure belongs to later governance. Value-Related Relevance Where governed value information is available, ERSM may consume it as a relevance signal. For example, a governed representation may indicate: Value Emergence; Value Change; Value Development; Value Degradation; Value Nullification; Value Restoration; Value Extinction. But TREGA™ does not recreate Value Governance. Therefore: VFM® governs what happened to value. TREGA™ governs whether the governed value result is relevant to event construction. Cross-Border Relevance An occurrence spanning multiple locations, organizations, platforms, or infrastructures may justify continued governance because different taxation systems may later require evaluation. However: Cross-Border Relevance ≠ Tax Jurisdiction. ERSM does not decide which jurisdiction has taxation rights. It preserves the occurrence for later jurisdiction-specific evaluation where appropriate. Machine and Autonomous Relevance Autonomous systems create a major relevance-screening challenge. An AI agent may: reserve capacity; compare prices; negotiate; acquire digital resources; release reservations; initiate payment; terminate services; transfer machine resources. Some actions may have economic significance. Others may be purely technical. ERSM distinguishes plausible tax-event relevance from ordinary machine activity. Therefore: Autonomous Activity ≠ Economic Relevance by Default. and: Economic Relevance ≠ Legal Taxability. Relevance Materiality ERSM should prevent insignificant technical or operational activity from advancing unnecessarily through the architecture. Material relevance may depend upon whether an occurrence could reasonably affect: economic interpretation; transaction interpretation; value association; participant relationships; resource transfer; service provision; downstream Event Formation; later jurisdictional taxation evaluation. Materiality at this stage remains governance materiality. It is not a statutory threshold. Therefore: Governance Materiality ≠ Legal Tax Materiality. Relevance Sufficiency An occurrence becomes relevance-sufficient when enough governed information exists to justify continued recognition processing. This does not require every downstream fact to be known. ERSM may legitimately advance an occurrence while uncertainty remains regarding: Event Boundary; Event Timing; Event Location; participants; value; jurisdiction; tax treatment. Those questions belong later in TREGA™. Non-Relevance ERSM must permit a recognized occurrence to exit the recognition pathway where no sufficient potential relevance exists. Examples may include: purely technical system housekeeping; duplicated internal processing; non-economic diagnostic activity; irrelevant sensor activity; routine state synchronization; machine operations with no material relationship to economic activity. A non-relevant result means: the recognized occurrence does not currently justify further TREGA™ recognition processing. It does not mean: the occurrence has been legally determined non-taxable. Relevance Uncertainty Some occurrences cannot be confidently screened. For example: an autonomous agent action may have unclear economic purpose; a platform transfer may lack sufficient business context; a machine resource movement may or may not be internal; a digital-asset movement may have ambiguous operational meaning. ERSM must preserve an unresolved condition rather than forcing a binary result. Possible outcomes may include: Relevant Not Relevant Relevance Unresolved Further Context Required This allows uncertainty to remain visible and governable. False Positive and False Negative Risk Relevance screening must control two opposing risks. False Positive An occurrence proceeds through expensive governance even though it has no plausible tax-event relevance. False Negative A potentially important occurrence is filtered out prematurely. Both matter. In machine-scale economies, false positives can create massive processing volumes. In fragmented or novel economic environments, false negatives can remove activity that should have proceeded to Event Formation. ERSM therefore seeks proportionate relevance screening, not maximum exclusion. Governance Requirements ERSM requires that: screening begins from a Recognized Occurrence; relevance remains distinct from occurrence existence; economic, operational, transactional, digital, autonomous, and value-related signals may be evaluated; relevance criteria remain jurisdiction-neutral at the architecture layer; potential relevance remain distinct from legal taxability; legal tax rules do not become mandatory upstream recognition rules; non-relevance can be governed explicitly; uncertainty can remain unresolved; machine-generated activity is not assumed economically relevant; lack of payment does not automatically eliminate relevance; cross-border characteristics do not determine Tax Jurisdiction; relevance decisions remain traceable where materially required. Governance Logic ERSM applies four principal questions: What characteristics of this occurrence may make it relevant to downstream tax-event governance? Are those characteristics materially meaningful rather than purely technical? Is the relevance basis sufficient to justify continued TREGA™ processing? If relevance cannot yet be established, should the occurrence be preserved as unresolved rather than rejected? The transformation is: Recognized Occurrence → Potential Relevance Signals → Material Relevance Assessment → Event Relevance Screening Result Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum ERSM implementation must be capable of: 1. receiving a Recognized Occurrence from ORIM; 2. identifying potential relevance signals; 3. evaluating one or more relevant governance domains; 4. distinguishing technical significance from potential economic or tax-event relevance; 5. assessing governance materiality; 6. determining relevance sufficiency; 7. representing non-relevance; 8. preserving unresolved relevance; 9. recording the screening basis where materially required; 10. transferring relevance-positive occurrences to ERRM. ERSM does not prescribe jurisdiction-specific tax logic, statutory classifications, legal thresholds, AI models, rules engines, ERP platforms, or tax software. Governance Outputs ERSM may produce: Event Relevance Screening Result — the governed outcome of relevance screening. Relevant Occurrence — an occurrence sufficiently relevant to continue through TRERS. Non-Relevant Occurrence Result — a recognized occurrence that does not currently justify further event-recognition governance. Relevance Signal Set — the materially relevant characteristics supporting screening. Relevance Domain References — economic, operational, transactional, digital, autonomous, value-related, or other relevant domains. Relevance Materiality Result — the governed assessment of whether identified relevance is sufficient. Relevance Uncertainty Indicator — unresolved conditions affecting the screening outcome. Further Context Requirement — identification of material contextual information required before screening can be completed. Critical Distinctions Occurrence Recognition ≠ Event Relevance Screening. ORIM establishes that something sufficiently distinguishable occurred. ERSM determines whether that occurrence plausibly matters to downstream tax-event governance. Occurrence ≠ Relevant Occurrence. Not every genuine occurrence requires TREGA™ progression. Potential Relevance ≠ Legal Taxability. Relevance keeps an occurrence in governance. It does not create tax liability. Relevance Signal ≠ Taxable Trigger. Operational or economic characteristics cannot replace legal tax analysis. Economic Relevance ≠ Tax Liability. Economic significance does not establish a legal obligation. Payment ≠ Required Condition for Relevance. Economically meaningful activity may exist before or without payment. Transaction Record ≠ Tax-Relevant Event. A record remains a representation, not a final event determination. Governance Materiality ≠ Statutory Materiality. ERSM does not establish legal thresholds. Cross-Border Relevance ≠ Tax Jurisdiction. Several jurisdictions may later evaluate the same occurrence. Non-Relevant ≠ Legally Non-Taxable. ERSM's negative result is methodological, not legal. Enterprise Application ERSM provides an important scaling mechanism for enterprises and tax infrastructures processing very high volumes of operational data. Without relevance screening, every recognized occurrence could proceed through: Formation ↓ Boundary ↓ Timing ↓ Location ↓ Participation ↓ Value Association ↓ Relationships ↓ Determination even where most occurrences have no plausible need for taxation analysis. In a machine-intensive environment this becomes operationally unrealistic. ERSM creates a governed filtering layer between occurrence recognition and full event construction. This allows high-volume platforms, banks, industrial systems, autonomous systems, and digital infrastructures to focus deeper TREGA™ governance on occurrences with a legitimate relevance basis while preserving unresolved cases that should not yet be discarded. Use CasesUse Case 1 — Global Cloud Platform Generating Billions of Operational Occurrences A global cloud provider operates millions of servers and automated services across many regions. Its systems generate enormous volumes of recognizable occurrences: resource allocation, container creation, internal network routing, temporary storage allocation, service activation, resource release, customer consumption, billing events, machine balancing, and technical maintenance. If every recognizable occurrence proceeds into full tax-event formation, the governance system becomes dominated by infrastructure activity rather than economically meaningful operations. ERSM screens these occurrences. Internal load balancing and technical maintenance may be recognized as genuine occurrences but screened as non-relevant to further tax-event governance. Customer resource consumption, service provision, billable allocation, or economically meaningful transfers may remain relevant and proceed. ERSM therefore separates: what genuinely happens inside a digital economy from what legitimately requires deeper tax-event governance. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Marketplace Where Machines Trade Resources Continuously An automated marketplace allows autonomous agents and machines to purchase computing capacity, energy, data access, transport capacity, and digital services from one another. Millions of machine interactions occur every hour. Some are quotations. Some are rejected offers. Some reserve capacity temporarily. Some change resource availability. Some create actual exchanges. Some trigger settlements. Some are merely technical negotiation messages. A conventional system may either treat all interactions as transactions or apply rigid rules that discard novel forms of machine commerce. ERSM evaluates recognized occurrences for plausible economic, transactional, resource, and value-related relevance before deeper Event Formation begins. It does not determine whether a reservation, resource transfer, machine exchange, or settlement is legally taxable. Instead it ensures that potentially meaningful machine-economic activity survives the recognition gateway while technical negotiation noise does not automatically flood the downstream tax architecture. This establishes a crucial capability for future tax infrastructure: the system can scale with machine economies without equating computational activity with taxable economic activity. Canonical Boundary ERSM governs whether a Recognized Occurrence possesses sufficient potential relevance to remain within Tax-Relevant Event Recognition. It does not determine the rules by which formal recognition is made, the confidence of that recognition, whether escalation is required, how the event is formed, or whether any jurisdiction legally taxes it. The TRERS internal progression remains: ORIM — Did a distinguishable occurrence occur? → ERSM — Does the occurrence have sufficient potential relevance to tax-event governance? → ERRM — What governed Recognition Rules determine progression? → ERCM — How strong is the recognition basis? → EREM — Does unresolved recognition require escalation? Canonical Closing Statement Event Relevance Screening Module establishes the relevance-gating capability of the Tax-Relevant Event Recognition Standard by determining which sufficiently distinguishable occurrences possess enough plausible economic, operational, transactional, digital, autonomous, machine-generated, value-related, or other material relevance to justify continued progression through TREGA™ recognition governance. Through governance of relevance signals, relevance domains, materiality, sufficiency, non-relevance, uncertainty, cross-border characteristics, machine activity, and false-positive and false-negative screening risk, ERSM prevents every genuine technical or operational occurrence from automatically entering full Tax-Relevant Event Formation while preserving potentially meaningful activity that should not be discarded merely because its eventual legal treatment remains unknown. The Module preserves the boundaries between occurrence existence and relevance, governance materiality and statutory materiality, relevance signals and taxable triggers, potential tax relevance and legal taxability, and cross-border significance and Tax Jurisdiction. ERSM therefore establishes not whether an occurrence is taxable, but whether it matters enough for TREGA™ to continue asking what governed Tax-Relevant Event, if any, should ultimately be formed from it.

title: OOF™ The Event Record Structure Module (ERSTM) governs how an identified
text: OOF™ The Event Record Structure Module (ERSTM) governs how an identified The Event Record Structure Module (ERSTM) governs how an identified OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: TREGS — Tax-Relevant Event Record Governance Standard Module: ERSTM — Event Record Structure Module Operational Layer: Event Record Structure Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Event Record Structure Primary Governed Object: Governed Event Record Structure Origin ID: TREGA-TREGS-ERSTM-002 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 3 September 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language Canonical Definition The Event Record Structure Module (ERSTM) governs how an identified Tax-Relevant Event Record is structured so that the materially relevant meaning of the Determined Tax-Relevant Event can be represented in a sufficiently complete, coherent, bounded, and machine-readable form. Its principal transition is: Governed Event Record Identity ↓ Event Record Structure Governance ↓ Governed Event Record Structure ERSTM determines what structural elements a governed Record must contain or reference in order to preserve the Event meaning established by preceding TREGA™ governance layers. It does not recreate those upstream governance results. Its foundational distinction is: Record Structure ≠ Event Structure. Operational Role ERIDM establishes which governed Record represents the Event. ERSTM determines how that Record must be structurally represented. Its core function is to ensure that the Record does not become: too sparse to preserve Event meaning; too fragmented to be reconstructable; overloaded with unnecessary data; detached from its Determination state; structurally inconsistent; or dependent on one proprietary technical schema. The module answers: What structure must the governed Event Record possess so that the Determined Tax-Relevant Event remains meaningfully represented? Internal Module Flow TREGS operates through: ERIDM — Event Record Identification ↓ ERSTM — Event Record Structure ↓ ERLKM — Event Record Linkage ↓ ERTM — Event Record Traceability ↓ ERINM — Event Record Interoperability ↓ Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record ERSTM receives: Governed Event Record Identity and produces: Governed Event Record Structure for ERLKM. Operational Transition The canonical transition is: Governed Event Record Identity ↓ Structural Requirement Identification ↓ Component Structuring ↓ Sufficiency Assessment ↓ Structural State ↓ Governed Event Record Structure Operational Space ERSTM governs: Record component identification; structural requirement definition; mandatory and conditional components; Record composition; field grouping; governed references; representational sufficiency; structural completeness; structural coherence; structural consistency; structural modularity; representation boundaries; qualification representation; uncertainty representation; Determination-state representation; relationship-reference capacity; lifecycle-reference capacity; structural extensibility; and structure handoff. Operational Scope ERSTM may govern Event Record structures used across: ERP systems; commerce systems; banking infrastructure; accounting platforms; marketplaces; tax platforms; payment systems; distributed systems; blockchain environments; smart contracts; AI agents; autonomous systems; industrial systems; machine-to-machine infrastructure; cross-border platforms; and future machine economies. The structural logic remains technology-neutral and jurisdiction-neutral. Structural Object The structural object is the identified Governed Event Record whose canonical representation must be defined. ERSTM structures the Record. It does not redefine the underlying Event. Structural Object ≠ Underlying Event. Structural Requirement Identification ERSTM shall identify which information categories are materially necessary for the Record to perform its TREGS function. Requirements may include direct values or governed references. The module should avoid indiscriminate data replication. More Fields ≠ Better Record Structure by default. Mandatory Components Every governed Event Record should contain or reference, where applicable: Canonical Record Identifier; underlying Event Reference; Determination Reference; current Record State; governance-state references necessary to preserve meaning; relevant qualification state; relevant uncertainty state; and structural governance status. These form the minimum structural foundation. Conditional Components Some components are required only where materially relevant. Examples include: Location representation; Participation representation; Value Association; Event Relationship references; Merge/Split references; reconsideration references; cross-system references; or jurisdiction-neutral processing metadata. Conditional Component ≠ Optional Irrelevance. A component may be conditionally required where its absence would materially distort the Event. Reference Versus Replication ERSTM shall distinguish between: information that should be represented directly; and information that may be referenced from another governed source. The standard does not require all upstream TREGA™ data to be copied into the Record. Governed Reference ≠ Missing Information. Structural Completeness A Record is structurally complete when all materially required components are either: represented directly; or reliably referenced. Structural completeness is determined by governance sufficiency, not by maximum field population. Structural Completeness ≠ Every Field Populated. Structural Sufficiency Structural Sufficiency exists where the Record structure is sufficient to preserve the meaning and downstream usability of the governed Event. A Record may be structurally sufficient even where non-material detail is absent. Structural Coherence Record components shall not materially contradict each other. For example, a Record should not simultaneously represent: incompatible Determination states; contradictory Event references; incompatible Record states; or mutually exclusive qualification states without explicitly governing that conflict. Data Presence ≠ Structural Coherence. Structural Consistency The Record should apply the same structural meaning consistently across equivalent representations. Consistency includes: field semantics; state semantics; identifier usage; component relationships; and reference logic. Record Composition The Record may be composed of: core components; conditional components; embedded substructures; external references; state objects; and governed metadata. ERSTM governs their canonical function, not their physical storage implementation. Core Record Component A Core Record Component is structurally necessary for the Record to remain identifiable and interpretable. Core components should not be removable without materially affecting the Record's governance function. Supporting Record Component Supporting components provide additional governed context without defining the Record identity itself. They may include: technical references; implementation metadata; supporting source references; processing metadata; or non-material extensions. Structural Modularity ERSTM may permit modular Record structures where different Event classes require different component sets. Modularity shall preserve a common canonical core. Modular Structure ≠ Fragmented Governance. Event Reference Structure The Record shall structurally preserve the association with the Determined Tax-Relevant Event. The Event Reference should be distinguishable from: Record ID; transaction ID; document ID; external tax ID. Event Reference ≠ Record Identifier. Determination Reference Structure The Record shall contain or reference the applicable TREDS Determination state. This may include: final Decision state; qualification; uncertainty; reconsideration result. ERSTM represents the Determination state structurally. It does not govern that Determination. Qualification Structure Where TREDS produces a qualification, ERSTM shall preserve a structural location for that qualification. The Record shall not collapse: Conditional Determination ↓ Unqualified Record through omission. Structural Omission ≠ Qualification Removal. Uncertainty Structure Where material uncertainty remains, the Record should preserve an explicit structural representation or reference. The uncertainty shall not disappear merely because the Record is finalized. Record Finalization ≠ Uncertainty Elimination. Participation Representation Where Participation is materially relevant to downstream interpretation, the Record should contain or reference the governed Participation result. ERSTM does not determine participant identity or taxpayer status. Timing Representation The Record may structurally preserve: Event Start; Event Completion; Event Duration; Temporal Order; or relevant Event Time references. These remain operational Event times. Record Time Field ≠ Legal Tax Point. Location Representation The Record may preserve governed physical, digital, or distributed Location results. This does not establish Tax Jurisdiction. Location Component ≠ Jurisdiction Component. Value Representation The Record may preserve the governed Value Association established by TRVAS. ERSTM does not calculate: Tax Base; taxable amount; valuation under tax law. Value Representation ≠ Tax Base Representation. Relationship Representation Capacity The Record structure should support references to Event Relationships governed by TRERLS. ERSTM provides the structural capacity. ERLKM later governs actual Record linkage. Relationship Capacity ≠ Relationship Linkage. Merge and Split Representation Where Events have been merged or split, the Record structure should support the resulting governance references. ERSTM does not govern the Merge or Split decision. Reconsideration Representation Where EDREM has changed the effective Determination state, the Record structure should support representation of: current state; prior state reference; reconsideration reference; supersession relationship where relevant. Detailed traceability belongs to ERTM. Record State Representation The structure shall support clear representation of Record state. Possible Record states may include: Draft; Structurally Incomplete; Structurally Sufficient; Qualified; Active; Superseded; Archived; Ready for Lifecycle Governance. These states shall remain distinguishable from Event Determination states. Record State ≠ Determination State. State Separation Different governance dimensions shall not be collapsed into one generic status field where that would create ambiguity. For example: Record State; Determination State; Uncertainty State; Lifecycle State should remain conceptually distinguishable. One Status Field ≠ Complete Governance State by default. Structural Boundaries The Record should have a clear structural boundary defining which components belong to the canonical governed Record and which are external references. This prevents uncontrolled technical metadata from becoming part of the canonical Event representation. Structural Extensibility The Record should support extensions without destabilizing its canonical meaning. Extensions may support: sector-specific needs; implementation-specific fields; jurisdiction-specific downstream references; future technologies. Extensions shall not redefine the canonical TREGA™ Event. Extension ≠ Canonical Redefinition. Jurisdiction-Specific Extension Boundary A jurisdiction may append: tax classification; tax codes; filing references; tax base; rate; exemption; legal treatment. These fields remain downstream extensions. They should not become part of the canonical jurisdiction-neutral TREGS Record structure by default. Schema Independence ERSTM does not require one universal technical schema. The governed structure may be implemented through: relational databases; JSON; XML; graph structures; event streams; distributed ledgers; object stores; semantic models; or future data systems. Canonical Structure ≠ Mandatory Technical Schema. Schema Mapping Boundary Mapping the canonical structure into specific system schemas may be necessary. ERSTM defines the structural meaning. ERINM governs broader interoperability. Data-Type Flexibility Different technical implementations may represent the same governed concept using different data types. ERSTM requires semantic preservation rather than identical physical encoding. Record Granularity The Record structure shall correspond to the governed Event granularity. It shall not fragment or aggregate Events merely because a system prefers a particular storage model. Storage Granularity ≠ Event Granularity. Nested Records Some complex Events may require nested structural representations. Nested structures may be used where they preserve: Event hierarchy; components; relationship references; or conditional data. Nested technical structures do not automatically create separate governed Events. Distributed Record Structure A governed Event Record may be physically distributed across multiple systems. ERSTM permits distributed representation where: canonical identity remains stable; required structural components remain reconstructable; and governance meaning remains coherent. Distributed Storage ≠ Distributed Record Identity. Record Compression Systems may compress or abstract data. Compression shall not remove materially necessary governance meaning. Compact Representation ≠ Incomplete Representation. Structural Versioning Record structure may evolve over time. Versioning shall preserve: semantic continuity; interpretability; canonical identity association; and historical reconstruction. Schema Version Change ≠ New Governed Event. Backward Compatibility Where structure versions change, older Record representations should remain interpretable where material to historical continuity. ERSTM does not require indefinite technical compatibility, but it does require governance interpretability. Forward Extensibility Future components may be added where new system types or governance requirements emerge. Extensions should not invalidate the canonical core. Structural Validation Boundary ERSTM may assess structural sufficiency and coherence. It does not perform general validation governance. VALIDOS™ remains authoritative for validation. Structural Sufficiency ≠ Validation. Structural Integrity Boundary ERSTM requires internally coherent representation. Broader integrity governance belongs to INTEGROS®. Structural Coherence ≠ General Integrity Certification. Traceability Boundary ERSTM provides fields or references necessary for later traceability. ERTM governs the actual Record Traceability space. Traceability Capacity ≠ Traceability Governance. Linkage Boundary ERSTM provides structural slots for links. ERLKM governs the creation and governance of those links. Link Field ≠ Governed Linkage. Interoperability Boundary ERSTM establishes canonical structural meaning. ERINM governs preservation of that meaning across systems and organizations. Canonical Structure ≠ Interoperability Completion. Governance States ERSTM may represent: Structure Governance Not Initiated Structural Requirements Identified Core Components Defined Conditional Components Identified Structure Under Construction Structure Incomplete Structure Ambiguous Structure Conflicted Structure Coherent Structure Sufficient Structure Qualified Structure Ready for Linkage Governance Governed Event Record Structure Established Governance Requirements ERSTM implementations shall ensure that: a valid Governed Event Record Identity exists; Record Structure remains distinct from Event Structure; structurally required components are identified; mandatory and conditional components remain distinguishable; material components are represented or reliably referenced; Record completeness does not require indiscriminate data replication; Event Reference remains structurally distinguishable from Record Identifier; Determination state is structurally preserved; qualifications are not removed through omission; material uncertainty remains representable; Participation, Timing, Location, Value, and Relationship information is represented only where materially required; tax-law conclusions remain downstream extensions; Record State remains distinct from Determination State; state dimensions are not collapsed where this creates ambiguity; canonical structure remains technology-neutral; schema differences do not automatically create governance differences; structure can support extension without redefining the canonical Event; record granularity follows governed Event granularity; distributed representation remains reconstructable; structural versioning preserves semantic continuity; structural sufficiency remains distinct from validation; structural coherence remains distinct from general integrity governance; linkage, traceability, and interoperability remain delegated to their respective modules; and the resulting Governed Event Record Structure is suitable for ERLKM. Governance Logic IF no valid Governed Event Record Identity exists, THEN ERSTM shall not establish a canonical Record Structure. IF a materially necessary component is neither represented nor reliably referenced, THEN the Record Structure shall remain incomplete. IF a component is not materially required, THEN its absence shall not automatically make the Record incomplete. IF upstream governance information can be reliably referenced, THEN ERSTM shall not require unnecessary duplication. IF structural components materially contradict each other, THEN the structure shall not be considered coherent until the conflict is governed. IF a Determination qualification exists, THEN the Record Structure shall preserve that qualification explicitly or by reliable reference. IF material uncertainty exists, THEN the Record Structure shall provide a governed representation or reference for it. IF a jurisdiction-specific tax field is added, THEN it shall remain distinguishable from the canonical jurisdiction-neutral Record structure. IF system schema changes while the governed Event meaning remains stable, THEN Record Structure continuity may remain intact. IF the structure preserves the materially necessary Event meaning and supports downstream linkage, traceability, and interoperability, THEN ERSTM shall establish the Governed Event Record Structure. Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum ERSTM implementation should support: Record Structure Governance ID A stable identifier for the ERSTM governance process. Canonical Record Identifier The ERIDM-established Record identity. Determined Event Reference The underlying governed Event. Structural Version The active canonical Record structure version. Core Component Set The structurally mandatory Record components. Conditional Component Set Components required only under specified governance conditions. Event Reference Component The canonical reference to the underlying Event. Determination Reference Component The applicable TREDS Determination state. Record State Component The current TREGS Record state. Qualification Component Any material Determination qualification. Uncertainty Component Any material governed uncertainty or reference. Timing Representation Relevant Event Timing reference where required. Location Representation Relevant Event Location reference where required. Participation Representation Relevant governed Participation reference where required. Value Association Representation Relevant TRVAS output where required. Relationship Representation Capacity Structural capability to support ERLKM linkage. Reconsideration Reference Relevant EDREM state where applicable. Prior Structure Version Reference The previous structural version where applicable. Extension Reference Any implementation or sector-specific extensions. Jurisdiction-Specific Extension State Whether downstream jurisdictional fields are attached separately. Structural Completeness State Incomplete, Partial, Complete, or Qualified. Structural Coherence State Coherent, Ambiguous, Conflicted, or Unresolved. Structural Sufficiency State Insufficient, Conditionally Sufficient, or Sufficient. Governance State The current ERSTM governance state. Handoff State Whether the Record is ready for ERLKM. Governance Outputs ERSTM may produce: Structural Requirement Set; Core Component Set; Conditional Component Set; Event Reference Structure; Determination Representation; Qualification Representation; Uncertainty Representation; Record State Representation; Value Representation; Participation Representation; Timing Representation; Location Representation; Relationship Representation Capacity; Structural Completeness State; Structural Coherence State; Structural Sufficiency State; Structural Version Reference; Extension State; and the principal output: Governed Event Record Structure. Critical Distinctions Record Structure ≠ Event Structure. Structural Object ≠ Underlying Event. More Fields ≠ Better Record Structure by default. Conditional Component ≠ Optional Irrelevance. Governed Reference ≠ Missing Information. Structural Completeness ≠ Every Field Populated. Data Presence ≠ Structural Coherence. Modular Structure ≠ Fragmented Governance. Event Reference ≠ Record Identifier. Structural Omission ≠ Qualification Removal. Record Finalization ≠ Uncertainty Elimination. Record Time Field ≠ Legal Tax Point. Location Component ≠ Jurisdiction Component. Value Representation ≠ Tax Base Representation. Relationship Capacity ≠ Relationship Linkage. Record State ≠ Determination State. One Status Field ≠ Complete Governance State by default. Extension ≠ Canonical Redefinition. Canonical Structure ≠ Mandatory Technical Schema. Storage Granularity ≠ Event Granularity. Distributed Storage ≠ Distributed Record Identity. Compact Representation ≠ Incomplete Representation. Schema Version Change ≠ New Governed Event. Structural Sufficiency ≠ Validation. Structural Coherence ≠ General Integrity Certification. Traceability Capacity ≠ Traceability Governance. Link Field ≠ Governed Linkage. Canonical Structure ≠ Interoperability Completion. Enterprise Application ERSTM provides the structural layer that converts an identified Record into a governed representation capable of being linked, traced, exchanged, and later maintained. The canonical enterprise path is: ERIDM — Governed Event Record Identity → ERSTM — Governed Event Record Structure → ERLKM — Governed Event Record Linkage → ERTM — Governed Event Record Traceability → ERINM — Governed Event Record Interoperability → Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record This allows organizations to use different technologies while preserving one canonical Event meaning. Use Case 1 — Cross-Border Marketplace Record with Conditional Location Data A marketplace Event has completed TREDS and ERIDM has established the canonical Record identity. The Event contains fully governed: Formation; Participation; Value Association; and Determination. Its distributed digital Location remains qualified. ERSTM creates the governed Record structure with: Record Identifier; Event Reference; Determination Reference; Participation reference; Value Association reference; Location qualification; and current Record State. The Record does not duplicate all TREGA™ data and does not remove the Location qualification. It remains structurally sufficient for downstream Record Linkage and later jurisdiction-specific evaluation. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Machine Event Across Heterogeneous Systems An autonomous industrial Event is represented across an ERP platform, machine-control system, payment infrastructure, and AI-agent environment. Each system uses a different schema. ERIDM has already established one canonical Record identity. ERSTM defines the canonical structural meaning required across those representations, including: Event Reference; Determination state; relevant Participation; Value Association; material machine context; and Record State. Each system may implement the structure differently. The underlying governed meaning remains consistent. Different Schemas ↓ One Governed Record Structure. Canonical Boundary ERSTM owns the governance of Record structural requirements, mandatory and conditional components, Record composition, material representation, structural completeness, sufficiency, coherence, consistency, modularity, Event and Determination representation, qualification and uncertainty representation, state separation, structural extensibility, schema independence, structural versioning, and establishment of the Governed Event Record Structure. ERSTM does not establish canonical Record identity; ERIDM owns that function. It does not govern actual Record links; ERLKM owns linkage. It does not govern complete Record lineage; ERTM owns traceability. It does not govern cross-system semantic exchange; ERINM owns interoperability. It does not recreate upstream TREGA™ Event governance and does not determine legal tax consequences. Its governance begins when a valid Governed Event Record Identity exists. Its governance ends when a sufficiently coherent and complete Governed Event Record Structure is established for Record Linkage Governance. Canonical Handoff ERIDM — Governed Event Record Identity ↓ ERSTM — Governed Event Record Structure ↓ ERLKM — Event Record Linkage Governance Canonical Closing Statement ERSTM ensures that a governed Event Record contains enough structure to preserve what the Event means without forcing every system to store the Event in the same way. The structure must be complete enough to govern the Record, but never so rigid that the technical schema becomes the Event itself. Record Structure ≠ Event Structure. Canonical Structure ≠ Mandatory Technical Schema.

title: OOF™ The Event Record Traceability Module (ERTM) governs how a linked
text: OOF™ The Event Record Traceability Module (ERTM) governs how a linked The Event Record Traceability Module (ERTM) governs how a linked OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: TREGS — Tax-Relevant Event Record Governance Standard Module: ERTM — Event Record Traceability Module Operational Layer: Event Record Traceability Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Event Record Traceability Primary Governed Object: Governed Event Record Traceability State Origin ID: TREGA-TREGS-ERTM-004 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 3 September 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language Canonical Definition The Event Record Traceability Module (ERTM) governs how a linked Tax-Relevant Event Record remains reconstructable across its materially relevant governance lineage, source references, state transitions, corrections, reconsiderations, transformations, and downstream representations. Its principal transition is: Governed Event Record Linkage State ↓ Event Record Traceability Governance ↓ Governed Event Record Traceability State ERTM establishes whether the Record's governed history can be reconstructed sufficiently to determine: what Record is being examined; which Event it represents; which Determination applies; which material governance states contributed to it; what changed; why a materially relevant change occurred; and which Record state is currently effective. Its foundational distinction is: Traceability ≠ Audit. Operational Role A Record may be correctly identified, structurally complete, and richly linked while still being difficult to reconstruct over time. ERTM addresses this problem. It answers: Can the governed Record and its materially relevant history be reconstructed from its present state back through the governance states and transitions that produced it? ERTM prevents: orphaned Record states; undocumented Record transformation; loss of prior material states; broken Determination lineage; invisible correction; silent supersession; unexplained Record changes; and historical state collapse. Internal Module Flow TREGS operates through: ERIDM — Event Record Identification ↓ ERSTM — Event Record Structure ↓ ERLKM — Event Record Linkage ↓ ERTM — Event Record Traceability ↓ ERINM — Event Record Interoperability ↓ Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record ERTM receives: Governed Event Record Linkage State and produces: Governed Event Record Traceability State for ERINM. Operational Transition The canonical transition is: Governed Event Record Linkage State ↓ Trace Scope Identification ↓ Lineage Construction ↓ State Transition Reconstruction ↓ Traceability Sufficiency Assessment ↓ Governed Event Record Traceability State Operational Space ERTM governs: trace scope; Record lineage; Event-to-Record lineage; Determination lineage; governance-state lineage; source-reference lineage; state-transition traceability; qualification traceability; uncertainty traceability; reconsideration traceability; correction traceability; supersession traceability; transformation traceability; version lineage; cross-system trace references; trace continuity; trace gaps; trace ambiguity; trace conflict; reconstruction sufficiency; and traceability handoff. Operational Scope ERTM may govern Record Traceability across: ERP systems; digital commerce; financial systems; tax infrastructure; payment systems; marketplaces; distributed systems; blockchain environments; smart contracts; AI systems; autonomous systems; industrial environments; machine-to-machine infrastructure; cross-border systems; and future machine economies.
