The module remains technology-neutral and jurisdiction-neutral. Traceability Object The traceability object is the governed lineage through which the Event Record and its materially relevant states can be reconstructed. Traceability is not merely the presence of links. It is the governed ability to reconstruct meaningful sequence and state history. Link Network ≠ Traceability by itself. Trace Scope ERTM shall define the materially required scope of reconstruction. Trace scope may include: Record identity; underlying Event; TREDS Determination; material upstream governance states; Record structure state; Record linkage state; material qualifications; uncertainty; reconsideration; corrections; supersession; transformations; current effective Record state. Traceability should remain proportional. Maximum Historical Data ≠ Optimal Traceability. Canonical Trace Path The canonical TREGS trace path is: Determined Tax-Relevant Event ↓ Governed Record Identity ↓ Governed Record Structure ↓ Governed Record Linkage ↓ Governed Record Traceability State Where deeper reconstruction is required, the Record may reference upstream TREGA™ governance. Event-to-Record Lineage ERTM shall preserve sufficient lineage to establish how the Event became represented by the Record. The reconstructable path should answer: Which Determined Event does this Record represent, and how can that association be verified through governed references? Determination Lineage The Record shall remain traceable to the applicable TREDS Determination state. Where the Determination was reconsidered, traceability should distinguish: prior Determination; reconsideration trigger; reconsideration outcome; current effective Determination. Current Determination ≠ Only Relevant Determination History. Governance-State Lineage Where material to interpretation, ERTM may preserve lineage to earlier TREGA™ governance outputs. This can include: Context; Recognition; Formation; Boundary; Timing; Location; Participation; Value Association; Event Relationships; Determination. ERTM does not reopen these governance processes. State Transition Traceability Material transitions in Record state should be reconstructable. Possible transitions include: Draft ↓ Structurally Sufficient Structurally Sufficient ↓ Linked Linked ↓ Traceable Active ↓ Corrected Active ↓ Superseded Qualified ↓ Unqualified after valid resolution Each material transition should preserve sufficient basis. Transition Basis A materially relevant state transition should possess a traceable reason or governance reference. Examples include: upstream correction; new supporting information; Determination reconsideration; Record correction; superseding representation; Merge/Split outcome; identity resolution; link correction. State Change ≠ Self-Explanatory Change. Prior-State Preservation Where a material Record state changes, ERTM shall preserve sufficient reference to the prior state. Current State ≠ Historical Replacement. Historical Reconstruction ERTM should support reconstruction of materially relevant historical Record states without requiring historical states to remain operationally active. The objective is to answer: What did the governed Record state mean at that time? Effective-State Traceability ERTM shall distinguish: historical Record state; superseded Record state; current effective Record state. Historical State ≠ Current Effective State. Qualification Traceability Where a qualification appears, changes, or is removed through legitimate governance, ERTM should preserve: prior qualification; reason for change; resulting qualification state. Qualification Removal ≠ Qualification Never Existed. Uncertainty Traceability Where material uncertainty affects Record use, ERTM should preserve the transition from: Uncertainty Identified ↓ Uncertainty Governed ↓ Uncertainty Resolved / Reduced / Persisting ERTM does not govern the uncertainty itself. EDUM remains authoritative for determination uncertainty. Reconsideration Traceability Where EDREM reopens a Determination, ERTM shall support reconstruction of: Prior Determination ↓ Reconsideration Trigger ↓ Reconsideration Process Reference ↓ New Effective Determination Reconsideration ≠ Historical Reset. Correction Traceability A Record correction should preserve enough information to determine: what was corrected; why; when; what prior state existed; what current state became effective. Correction ≠ Historical Erasure. Representational Correction Where only Record representation changes, traceability should preserve that representational correction without falsely implying a new Event. Record Correction ≠ New Event by default. Event-Level Correction Boundary If the underlying Event Reality changes, ERTM records the resulting governance transition. It does not decide the Event correction. That function belongs to the authoritative TREGA™ governance layer or TRECLS where applicable. Supersession Traceability Where one Record supersedes another, ERTM should preserve: superseded Record reference; successor Record reference; supersession basis; effective transition state; relevant continuity references. Supersession ≠ Deletion. Version Traceability Technical or structural versions may change while canonical Record identity remains continuous. ERTM should distinguish: Version Change ↓ Same Canonical Record from: New Governed Record Identity where applicable. Version History ≠ Event History by default. Transformation Traceability A Record may be transformed between: schemas; platforms; storage environments; organizations; formats; APIs. ERTM should preserve enough lineage to determine whether the transformed Record remains the same canonical governed Record. Format Transformation ≠ Governance Break by default. Cross-System Traceability Where the same Record appears across multiple systems, ERTM may preserve: Canonical Record ↓ System A Representation ↓ System B Representation ↓ System C Representation This helps reconstruct how the Record moved through infrastructure. Cross-Organization Traceability Where organizations exchange the Record, traceability may preserve materially relevant handoff references without making TREGS responsible for contractual or legal accountability. Record Handoff Trace ≠ Accountability Assignment. Cross-Border Traceability A Governed Event Record may enter several jurisdictional tax environments. ERTM may preserve downstream references such as: evaluation ID; filing reference; assessment reference; processing reference. These remain downstream tax objects. Tax Evaluation Trace ≠ Tax Determination Governance. Traceability and Jurisdictional Divergence Different jurisdictions may reach different tax conclusions from the same governed Event Record. ERTM should preserve the association of those downstream outcomes with the same Record without merging them into one canonical tax result. Source Reference Traceability ERTM may preserve references to source records or source systems where materially required for reconstruction. It does not own broader evidence governance. Source Reference ≠ Evidence Validation. Technical Log Boundary System logs may contribute trace information. They do not automatically constitute governed traceability. Logging ≠ Traceability. Blockchain Boundary An immutable blockchain ledger may provide strong technical chronology. It does not automatically establish complete Event Record Traceability. Immutability ≠ Complete Traceability. Timestamp Boundary Timestamp presence alone does not make a Record traceable. Traceability requires meaningful state and transition reconstruction. Timestamp ≠ Traceability. Audit Trail Boundary A technical audit trail may support ERTM. ERTM itself does not become a complete audit function. ADIT® remains authoritative for evidence and auditability governance. Audit Trail ≠ Governance Audit. Traceability Depth Traceability depth should reflect: Event complexity; downstream reliance; materiality; system distribution; change frequency; multi-jurisdiction use; uncertainty; correction history. A simple Event may require shallow traceability. A distributed autonomous Event may require deep lineage. Traceability Granularity Traceability may apply at: Record level; component level; state level; link level; transition level. Granularity should be sufficient to reconstruct materially relevant changes. Traceability Continuity Traceability should survive: system migration; schema change; technical identifier change; Record correction; Record supersession; organizational handoff; infrastructure replacement. Infrastructure Change ≠ Traceability Loss by default. Trace Gap A Trace Gap exists where a materially necessary part of Record history cannot be reconstructed. Possible causes include: missing prior state; broken link; unknown transformation; deleted technical source; identifier loss; incomplete migration; unresolved lineage. Trace Gap Materiality Not every missing historical detail is material. ERTM shall evaluate whether the gap affects: Record interpretation; Determination reliance; lifecycle continuity; downstream use; reconstruction. Missing Data ≠ Material Trace Gap by default. Trace Ambiguity Trace ambiguity exists where multiple plausible histories exist and one cannot be sufficiently established. Ambiguity should remain explicit. Plausible History ≠ Established Trace. Trace Conflict Trace conflict exists where material sources support incompatible Record histories. Conflict may involve: inconsistent state sequence; incompatible Determination references; contradictory correction histories; competing supersession paths. ERTM should not silently select one history without governance basis. Trace Reconstruction Sufficiency A Record is sufficiently traceable where materially relevant lineage can be reconstructed with sufficient confidence and governance clarity for its intended downstream use. Complete reproduction of every technical interaction is not required. Machine-Generated Traceability Autonomous systems may produce massive logs and event streams. ERTM governs the meaningful lineage of the Record rather than preserving every machine action indiscriminately. Machine Log Volume ≠ Traceability Quality. AI-Generated Record Changes Where AI or agents modify Record representations, ERTM should preserve materially relevant change lineage. The use of automated systems does not reduce traceability requirements. Automated Change ≠ Untraceable Change. Traceability Authority ERTM requires an identifiable governance basis for accepting the Record lineage as sufficiently reconstructable. Traceability authority does not establish legal truth or tax authority. Traceability Acceptance ≠ Legal Determination. Traceability and Record Identity ERIDM establishes identity. ERTM reconstructs identity continuity over time. Identity Continuity Trace ≠ Identity Establishment. Traceability and Record Structure ERSTM establishes structure. ERTM reconstructs materially relevant structural state changes. Structure History ≠ Structure Governance. Traceability and Linkage ERLKM establishes links. ERTM uses materially relevant links to reconstruct lineage. Linkage ≠ Traceability. Traceability and Interoperability ERTM establishes reconstructable lineage. ERINM governs whether Record meaning survives system exchange. Traceability ≠ Interoperability. Traceability and Lifecycle TRECLS governs broader Event lifecycle amendment, correction, supersession, and closure. ERTM supports reconstruction of Record-level history but does not own the entire Event lifecycle. Record Traceability ≠ Event Lifecycle Governance. Governance States ERTM may represent: Traceability Governance Not Initiated Trace Scope Defined Lineage Under Construction Event Lineage Established Determination Lineage Established State Transition Lineage Established Trace Gap Detected Trace Gap Material Trace Ambiguous Trace Conflicted Trace Qualified Trace Continuity Established Historical Reconstruction Sufficient Current Effective State Reconstructable Traceability Sufficient Governed Event Record Traceability State Established Ready for Interoperability Governance Governance Requirements ERTM implementations shall ensure that: a valid Governed Event Record Linkage State exists; materially required trace scope is defined; Record identity lineage remains reconstructable; Event-to-Record association remains traceable; Determination lineage remains reconstructable; materially relevant governance-state references are preservable; material state transitions remain traceable; transition basis is recorded or referenced where necessary; prior material states are not silently erased; current effective state remains distinguishable from historical state; qualification history remains reconstructable where material; uncertainty history remains traceable where relevant; reconsideration does not erase prior Determination history; corrections preserve materially relevant prior states; supersession preserves predecessor/successor lineage; technical version history remains distinguishable from Event history; transformations remain traceable where they could affect meaning; cross-system representations can be associated where material; technical logs are not treated as sufficient traceability by default; immutable records are not treated as complete traceability by default; trace gaps are assessed for materiality; ambiguity and conflict remain visible; machine-generated changes remain traceable; Record Traceability remains distinct from Audit, Linkage, Interoperability, and Event Lifecycle Governance; and the resulting Traceability State is suitable for ERINM. Governance Logic IF no valid Governed Event Record Linkage State exists, THEN ERTM shall not establish complete Record Traceability. IF a materially relevant Record state changed, THEN sufficient transition basis shall be preserved or referenced. IF a prior Record state materially affects interpretation of the current Record, THEN that state shall remain reconstructable. IF a Determination was reconsidered, THEN prior and current effective Determination states shall remain distinguishable. IF a Record was corrected, THEN the correction shall not silently erase materially relevant prior representation. IF a Record was superseded, THEN predecessor and successor lineage shall remain reconstructable. IF technical transformation occurs while canonical Record identity remains continuous, THEN transformation lineage should preserve that continuity. IF a trace gap exists but does not materially affect reconstruction, THEN the Record may remain traceable with appropriate qualification. IF a material trace gap, ambiguity, or conflict prevents reliable reconstruction, THEN Traceability shall remain qualified or insufficient. IF materially relevant Record lineage can be reconstructed sufficiently, THEN ERTM shall establish the Governed Event Record Traceability State and hand it to ERINM. Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum ERTM implementation should support: Traceability Governance ID A stable identifier for the ERTM governance process. Canonical Record Identifier The ERIDM-established Record identity. Record Structure Reference The ERSTM-governed structure. Record Linkage Reference The ERLKM-governed Linkage State. Underlying Event Reference The Determined Tax-Relevant Event represented by the Record. Determination Reference The applicable TREDS Determination. Prior Determination Reference Any materially relevant prior Determination. Reconsideration Reference Any relevant EDREM process or outcome. Trace Scope The required depth and granularity of reconstruction. Trace Entry Identifier A stable identifier for materially relevant trace entries. Trace Entry Type Identity, Structure, Linkage, Determination, Qualification, Uncertainty, Correction, Supersession, Transformation, Handoff, or other governed type. Prior State Reference The previous materially relevant Record state. Current State Reference The resulting Record state. Transition Type The nature of the state transition. Transition Basis Reference Why the transition occurred. Transition Time Reference The applicable time reference where material. Qualification Trace Reference Any relevant qualification history. Uncertainty Trace Reference Any relevant uncertainty history. Correction Trace Reference Any Record correction lineage. Supersession Trace Reference Any predecessor/successor lineage. Transformation Trace Reference Any schema, platform, or system transformation. Cross-System Trace Reference Representations across technical environments. Cross-Organization Trace Reference Relevant organizational handoffs. Jurisdictional Evaluation Reference Any downstream jurisdiction-specific evaluation reference where appropriate. Trace Gap State None, Non-Material, Material, Critical, or Unresolved. Trace Ambiguity State Whether multiple plausible histories remain. Trace Conflict State Whether incompatible histories exist. Historical Reconstruction State Incomplete, Partial, Qualified, or Sufficient. Current Effective State Reference The presently effective governed Record state. Trace Continuity State Whether materially relevant lineage remains continuous. Governance State The current ERTM governance state. Handoff State Whether the Record is ready for ERINM. Governance Outputs ERTM may produce: Trace Scope; Event-to-Record Lineage; Determination Lineage; Governance-State Lineage; Record State Transition History; Qualification Trace; Uncertainty Trace; Reconsideration Trace; Correction Trace; Supersession Trace; Transformation Trace; Version Lineage; Cross-System Trace; Cross-Organization Trace; Trace Gap State; Trace Ambiguity State; Trace Conflict State; Historical Reconstruction State; Current Effective State Reference; Trace Continuity State; and the principal output: Governed Event Record Traceability State. Critical Distinctions Traceability ≠ Audit. Link Network ≠ Traceability by itself. Maximum Historical Data ≠ Optimal Traceability. Current Determination ≠ Only Relevant Determination History. State Change ≠ Self-Explanatory Change. Current State ≠ Historical Replacement. Historical State ≠ Current Effective State. Qualification Removal ≠ Qualification Never Existed. Reconsideration ≠ Historical Reset. Correction ≠ Historical Erasure. Record Correction ≠ New Event by default. Supersession ≠ Deletion. Version History ≠ Event History by default. Format Transformation ≠ Governance Break by default. Record Handoff Trace ≠ Accountability Assignment. Tax Evaluation Trace ≠ Tax Determination Governance. Source Reference ≠ Evidence Validation. Logging ≠ Traceability. Immutability ≠ Complete Traceability. Timestamp ≠ Traceability. Audit Trail ≠ Governance Audit. Infrastructure Change ≠ Traceability Loss by default. Missing Data ≠ Material Trace Gap by default. Plausible History ≠ Established Trace. Machine Log Volume ≠ Traceability Quality. Automated Change ≠ Untraceable Change. Traceability Acceptance ≠ Legal Determination. Identity Continuity Trace ≠ Identity Establishment. Structure History ≠ Structure Governance. Linkage ≠ Traceability. Traceability ≠ Interoperability. Record Traceability ≠ Event Lifecycle Governance. Enterprise Application ERTM provides the reconstructability layer required before a governed Event Record can be safely exchanged across systems and organizations. The canonical enterprise path is: ERIDM — Governed Event Record Identity → ERSTM — Governed Event Record Structure → ERLKM — Governed Event Record Linkage State → ERTM — Governed Event Record Traceability State → ERINM — Governed Event Record Interoperability → Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record This allows organizations to determine not only what the current Record says, but how that governed Record reached its present state. Use Case 1 — Record Reconsidered After New Participation Information A cross-border digital Event has already produced a Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record. Later, new governed Participation information causes TREDS to reconsider the original Determination. EDREM produces a new effective Determination. ERTM preserves: original Determination; reconsideration reference; prior Record state; resulting Determination; updated Record state; and the transition basis. A downstream tax engine can consume the current state without losing the history of how that state was reached. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Platform Migrated Across Three Technical Systems An autonomous platform creates one governed Event Record. Over several years, the Record is migrated from: System A ↓ System B ↓ System C The technical schema, local identifiers, and storage model change. The canonical Record identity remains continuous. ERTM preserves the relevant transformation lineage and allows the Record to be reconstructed across all three environments. The system can therefore demonstrate that the current Record is the continued governed representation of the original Determined Event rather than an unrelated new Event. Canonical Boundary ERTM owns the governance of Record lineage, Event-to-Record lineage, Determination lineage, governance-state lineage, materially relevant state transitions, prior-state preservation, historical reconstruction, qualification/uncertainty/reconsideration/correction/supersession traceability, transformation lineage, version lineage, trace gaps, ambiguity, conflict, trace continuity, reconstruction sufficiency, and establishment of the Governed Event Record Traceability State. ERTM does not establish Record identity; ERIDM owns identification. It does not define Record Structure; ERSTM owns structure. It does not establish material Record links; ERLKM owns linkage. It does not govern semantic preservation across systems; ERINM owns interoperability. It does not perform general evidence or audit governance; ADIT® remains authoritative. It does not govern the substantive Event lifecycle; TRECLS owns lifecycle and continuity governance. It does not determine legal taxability, Tax Jurisdiction, taxpayer status, Tax Base, Tax Rate, legal tax point, Tax Period, Tax Liability, filing obligation, or other jurisdiction-specific tax consequences. Its governance begins when a valid Governed Event Record Linkage State exists. Its governance ends when the materially relevant history and present state of the Record are sufficiently reconstructable and the Governed Event Record Traceability State is ready for Interoperability Governance. Canonical Handoff ERLKM — Governed Event Record Linkage State ↓ ERTM — Governed Event Record Traceability State ↓ ERINM — Event Record Interoperability Governance Canonical Closing Statement ERTM ensures that a governed Event Record can change without losing the history required to understand what it was, what changed, why it changed, and which state is now effective. Traceability preserves governed continuity through change without turning historical data into an audit conclusion. Traceability ≠ Audit. Current State ≠ Historical Replacement. modul5

title: OOF™ The Event Supersession Module (ESPM) governs how a prior governed
text: OOF™ The Event Supersession Module (ESPM) governs how a prior governed The Event Supersession Module (ESPM) governs how a prior governed OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: TRECLS — Tax-Relevant Event Lifecycle & Continuity Standard Module: ESPM — Event Supersession Module Operational Layer: Event Supersession Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Event Supersession Primary Governed Object: Governed Event Supersession State Origin ID: TREGA-TRECLS-ESPM-004 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 3 September 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language Canonical Definition The Event Supersession Module (ESPM) governs how a prior governed Tax-Relevant Event state or Event Record representation is replaced as the current effective state by a later governed state while preserving historical continuity, predecessor-successor relationships, prior-state reconstructability, and the distinction between Event Supersession and New Event Formation. Its principal transition is: Governed Event Correction State / Current Governed Event State ↓ Event Supersession Governance ↓ Governed Event Supersession State ESPM establishes which governed state is currently effective without deleting the state that preceded it. Its foundational distinction is: Supersession ≠ Historical Deletion. Operational Role A Tax-Relevant Event may accumulate multiple governed states over time. A later state may need to become authoritative for current lifecycle use because of: Amendment; Correction; reconsideration; Record replacement; Merge/Split consequences; schema or representation change; improved governance state; or another legitimate lifecycle transition. ESPM answers: Which governed Event state now replaces the prior effective state, what exactly was superseded, why, and what historical relationship must remain preserved? Its purpose is to prevent: competing current states; silent replacement; historical erasure; ambiguous predecessor-successor chains; accidental creation of new Events; and confusion between Record replacement and Event replacement. Internal Module Flow TRECLS operates through: ECOM — Event Continuity ↓ EADM — Event Amendment ↓ ECRTM — Event Correction ↓ ESPM — Event Supersession ↓ ECLM — Event Closure ↓ Jurisdiction-Ready Tax-Relevant Event ESPM receives the applicable current governed Event state and produces: Governed Event Supersession State for Closure Governance. Operational Transition The canonical transition is: Current Governed Event State ↓ Supersession Trigger ↓ Predecessor Identification ↓ Successor Identification ↓ Supersession Basis ↓ Effective-State Transition ↓ Governed Event Supersession State Operational Space ESPM governs: Supersession Trigger identification; predecessor-state identification; successor-state identification; supersession eligibility; supersession scope; supersession basis; Event-state supersession; Record-state supersession; effective-state transition; predecessor-successor relationship; supersession materiality; partial supersession; full supersession; supersession qualification; supersession ambiguity; supersession conflict; supersession chain; supersession reversal; supersession withdrawal; continuity impact; upstream reassessment; historical-state preservation; and supersession handoff. Operational Scope ESPM may govern supersession in: physical Events; digital transactions; commercial Events; financial Events; platform activity; AI-agent Events; autonomous systems; machine-to-machine Events; distributed systems; digital assets; industrial activity; cross-border Events; multi-party Events; long-running Events; and future machine economies. The module remains technology-neutral and jurisdiction-neutral. Supersession Object The Supersession Object is the prior governed Event state or governed Event Record representation that is proposed to be replaced as the current effective state. The object being superseded may be: Event state; lifecycle state; corrected state; amended state; Record representation; Determination-linked state; qualified state. Superseded State ≠ Deleted State. Supersession Trigger A Supersession Trigger may arise from: validated Amendment; established Correction; revised Determination; successor Record creation; schema migration; representation replacement; Merge/Split result; continuity decision; governance reconciliation; reopening; or other lifecycle transition. Not every change requires formal Supersession. Supersession Eligibility A state is eligible for Supersession where: a valid predecessor state exists; a valid successor state exists or is being established; the successor legitimately replaces the predecessor for current use; the predecessor remains reconstructable; continuity remains valid or appropriately governed; and the transition does not improperly conceal New Event Formation. Predecessor State The Predecessor State is the governed state that was current or materially effective before Supersession. It must remain identifiable. A system should be able to answer: what the predecessor was; when it was effective; why it ceased to be current; and what replaced it. Successor State The Successor State is the governed state that becomes current after valid Supersession. It may result from: Amendment; Correction; reconsideration; Record replacement; or other lifecycle governance. Successor State ≠ New Event by default. Effective-State Transition Supersession governs the transition: Prior Effective State ↓ Supersession ↓ New Effective State The transition shall preserve both lifecycle meaning and historical reconstructability. Event-State Supersession Event-State Supersession occurs where a later governed state of the same Event replaces an earlier state as current. Examples include: corrected Location state; revised Participation state; amended Value Association; reconsidered Determination-linked lifecycle state. The Event may remain the same Event. Record-State Supersession A Record representation may be superseded while the Event remains unchanged. Examples include: schema replacement; canonical Record version replacement; corrected Record structure; migrated Record representation. Record Supersession ≠ Event Supersession by default. TREGS remains authoritative over Record Governance. Event Supersession vs New Event Formation Supersession must not be used to hide a genuinely new Event. If the successor represents a materially different operational occurrence, Continuity must be reassessed. Supersession ≠ Permission to Replace One Event with Another Under the Same Identity. Full Supersession Full Supersession occurs where the prior governed state is no longer current in its entirety. The prior state remains historical. Partial Supersession Partial Supersession occurs where only part of the prior state is replaced. The remaining unaffected components may continue as current. Partial Supersession ≠ Full State Replacement. Supersession Scope The supersession scope should identify exactly what is being replaced. Possible scopes include: full Event state; one Event component; one lifecycle state; one Record representation; one Determination-linked state; one downstream representation reference. Supersession Basis A valid Supersession should possess an identifiable basis. Examples include: Correction result; Amendment result; TREDS reconsideration result; Record Governance outcome; upstream governance revision; Merge/Split consequence; continuity decision. The basis should remain reconstructable. Supersession Effective Time Where materially relevant, the system should distinguish: predecessor effective period; successor establishment time; supersession decision time; successor effective time. These governance timestamps do not establish legal tax timing. Current Effective State After valid Supersession, the successor becomes the current effective state. The predecessor remains historical. Current Effective State ≠ Only Historically Valid State. Historical Preservation ESPM shall preserve materially relevant predecessor states. The canonical principle is: Supersession Replaces Current Effect — Not Historical Existence. Supersession Chain An Event may undergo multiple Supersessions: State A ↓ State B ↓ State C ↓ State D The chain should remain reconstructable. The system should identify: immediate predecessor; immediate successor; current state; historical supersession path. Broken Supersession Chain A Broken Supersession Chain exists where one or more predecessor-successor relationships cannot be reconstructed. A materially broken chain may prevent reliable lifecycle closure or jurisdiction readiness. Supersession Conflict Conflict exists where multiple successor states claim to supersede the same predecessor without clear governance priority. Examples include: two corrected states; competing jurisdiction-neutral Record versions; incompatible upstream governance results. Conflict shall remain explicit. Supersession Ambiguity Ambiguity exists where it is unclear: whether Supersession occurred; which state was superseded; which successor is current; whether replacement is partial or full; whether continuity remains valid. Supersession Qualification A Supersession may be qualified where: some predecessor information remains partially current; successor state remains incomplete; one upstream governance issue is unresolved; downstream use requires limitation. Qualification shall remain visible. Supersession Reversal A Supersession may later be reversed where the successor is invalidated and a prior state becomes current again or another successor is established. Reversal shall not erase the intermediate state. A valid pattern may be: State A ↓ State B ↓ Reversal ↓ State A Reinstated or: State A ↓ State B ↓ State C State Reinstatement A prior state may be reinstated where governance establishes it as current again. Reinstatement does not mean the intervening lifecycle history never occurred. Reinstatement ≠ Historical Reset. Supersession Withdrawal A proposed Supersession may be withdrawn before becoming effective. Materially relevant withdrawal history should remain reconstructable. Supersession Replacement A pending Supersession may itself be replaced by a superior successor decision. The latest valid governance result should remain clearly distinguishable. Supersession and Amendment An Amendment may create a new current Event state. ESPM may then govern its replacement relationship to the prior state. Amendment ≠ Supersession by default. Supersession and Correction A Correction may create a corrected successor state. ESPM may establish that corrected state as the current effective state. Correction ≠ Supersession by default. The mechanisms remain distinct. Supersession and Continuity Supersession assumes that Event Continuity remains valid unless explicitly broken. Where successor state materially challenges Event identity, ECOM must reassess Continuity. Valid Successor State ≠ Automatic Same-Event Continuity. Supersession and Closure Before an Event is closed, ECLM should be able to identify which state is currently effective. ESPM provides that effective-state clarity. A Superseded state should not be mistaken for the state being closed. Supersession and Reopening A reopened Event may create a successor to the previously Closed state. The prior Closure remains historically reconstructable. Supersession and Event Relationships TRERLS owns Merge and Split. ESPM governs whether valid Merge/Split results supersede prior lifecycle states or require predecessor-successor relationships. Merge Supersession A Merge may cause prior Event states to cease being current in favor of a merged successor Event. Where that successor is a new Event, Formation remains upstream. Merge Supersession ≠ Merge Formation. Split Supersession A Split may supersede one prior Event state with multiple successor Event states. Event identity implications require ECOM and TREFS where appropriate. Cross-System Supersession Different systems may hold different versions of one Event Record. ESPM helps establish which canonical state is current. Most Recent Technical Record ≠ Current Governed State by default. Cross-Organization Supersession Organizations may independently produce successor candidates. Canonical Supersession requires governed authority and basis. Later External Record ≠ Canonical Successor by default. Cross-Border Supersession Different jurisdictions may maintain different tax assessments based on different Event Record versions. Those legal states do not determine canonical TREGA™ Supersession. Jurisdictional Tax Replacement ≠ Event Supersession. Machine-Generated Supersession Autonomous systems may continuously emit newer state representations. A later timestamp or version number does not automatically make a state the governed successor. Newest Machine State ≠ Canonical Successor by default. High-Frequency Supersession In high-volume systems, frequent technical state replacement should not generate unnecessary canonical Supersession events. Formal Supersession is required only where current governed Event meaning materially changes. Version Supersession A newer technical Record version may supersede an older version. Version Supersession remains distinct from Event Supersession. Record Version Change ≠ Event State Change by default. Semantic Supersession Where a successor materially changes the canonical meaning of the Event state, the change should be governed substantively rather than treated as simple version replacement. Supersession and Traceability Material Supersession shall remain traceable through predecessor-successor relationships. ERTM owns Record Traceability. ESPM owns lifecycle supersession meaning. Supersession and Interoperability The current effective state should propagate across systems without semantic drift. ERINM owns Interoperability. ESPM identifies which governed state should be treated as current. Supersession and Tax Law A successor Event state may produce a new downstream tax outcome. ESPM does not determine: reassessment; amended filing; tax adjustment; refund; additional Tax Liability. These remain jurisdiction-specific. Event Supersession ≠ Tax Assessment Supersession. Governance States ESPM may represent: Supersession Governance Not Initiated Supersession Trigger Identified Predecessor State Identified Successor Candidate Identified Supersession Eligibility Under Review Supersession Eligible Supersession Scope Defined Partial Supersession Full Supersession Supersession Under Governance Supersession Qualified Supersession Ambiguous Supersession Conflicted Continuity Reassessment Required Upstream Review Required Supersession Rejected Supersession Withdrawn Successor State Established Predecessor State Preserved Current Effective State Established Governed Event Supersession State Established Ready for Closure Governance Governance Requirements ESPM implementations shall ensure that: a valid current governed Event state exists; predecessor state is identifiable; successor state is identifiable or governably proposed; Supersession remains distinct from Amendment and Correction; Record Supersession remains distinct from Event Supersession; Supersession does not conceal New Event Formation; supersession scope is explicit; partial and full Supersession remain distinguishable; predecessor state remains reconstructable; successor state becomes current only through valid governance; supersession basis is identifiable; predecessor-successor relationship remains traceable; current effective state is unambiguous where possible; Supersession Conflict remains explicit; Supersession Ambiguity remains explicit; qualified Supersession remains distinguishable from complete Supersession; reversal and reinstatement preserve lifecycle history; Merge/Split ownership remains with TRERLS; Continuity is reassessed where Event identity is materially challenged; technical recency is not treated as canonical authority; downstream tax replacement remains outside ESPM; and the resulting state is suitable for Event Closure Governance. Governance Logic IF no valid predecessor state exists, THEN ESPM shall not establish canonical Supersession. IF no valid successor state exists, THEN Supersession shall remain pending or unresolved. IF a successor merely adds information without replacing the current state, THEN EADM may remain the relevant mechanism. IF the successor primarily corrects error, THEN ECRTM shall establish the corrected state before ESPM establishes Supersession where needed. IF the replacement affects only technical Record representation, THEN Event Supersession shall not be assumed. IF successor and predecessor represent the same Event and continuity remains valid, THEN Supersession may proceed. IF successor state materially represents a different occurrence, THEN ECOM Continuity reassessment and potentially TREFS New Event Formation shall be required. IF multiple successor candidates conflict, THEN no single current state shall be silently selected without governance basis. IF the Supersession is partial, THEN unaffected predecessor components may remain current. IF a valid successor is established, THEN the predecessor shall cease to be current but remain historically reconstructable. IF a later valid governance result reverses Supersession, THEN the reversal shall preserve the supersession history. IF the current effective state is clear, historically reconstructable, and continuity remains governed, THEN ESPM shall establish the Governed Event Supersession State. Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum ESPM implementation should support: Supersession Governance ID Stable identifier for the ESPM governance process. Canonical Event Reference The Event under Supersession Governance. Current Governed Event State Reference The state existing before Supersession. Supersession Trigger Type Amendment, Correction, Reconsideration, Record Replacement, Merge/Split, Reopening, Technical Migration, or other governed trigger. Predecessor State Reference The state proposed to be superseded. Successor State Reference The proposed or established successor. Supersession Scope Full Event State, Partial Event State, Record State, Lifecycle State, or other governed scope. Supersession Type Full, Partial, Record-Level, Event-Level, Qualified, Reversal, Reinstatement. Supersession Basis Reference The governance result supporting replacement. Supersession Materiality State Non-Material, Material, Critical, Unresolved. Supersession Eligibility State Eligible, Qualified, Ineligible, Unresolved. Predecessor Effective State The prior effective status. Successor Effective State The new effective status. Supersession Effective Time Reference Where materially relevant. Predecessor Preservation State Whether prior state remains reconstructable. Predecessor-Successor Link Reference The governed relationship between states. Supersession Qualification Any limitation attached to replacement. Supersession Ambiguity State Whether the replacement remains uncertain. Supersession Conflict State Whether competing successors exist. Continuity Reassessment State Whether ECOM reassessment is required. Upstream Review Reference Any referral to another TREGA™ Parent Standard. Supersession Withdrawal State Whether proposed Supersession was withdrawn. Supersession Reversal Reference Any later reversal. Reinstatement Reference Any prior state restored as current. Historical Supersession Chain Reference The sequence of materially relevant predecessor-successor states. Current Effective State Reference The state current after Supersession. Governance State The current ESPM governance state. Supersession Outcome Superseded, Partial, Qualified, Rejected, Withdrawn, Reversed, or Unresolved. Handoff State Whether the Event is ready for ECLM Closure Governance. Governance Outputs ESPM may produce: Supersession Trigger State; Predecessor State; Successor State; Supersession Scope; Supersession Type; Supersession Basis; Supersession Materiality State; Supersession Eligibility State; Partial Supersession State; Full Supersession State; Predecessor-Successor Relationship; Predecessor Preservation State; Current Effective State; Supersession Qualification; Supersession Ambiguity State; Supersession Conflict State; Continuity Reassessment State; Supersession Reversal State; Reinstatement State; Historical Supersession Chain; and the principal output: Governed Event Supersession State. Critical Distinctions Supersession ≠ Historical Deletion. Superseded State ≠ Deleted State. Successor State ≠ New Event by default. Record Supersession ≠ Event Supersession by default. Supersession ≠ Permission to Replace One Event with Another Under the Same Identity. Partial Supersession ≠ Full State Replacement. Current Effective State ≠ Only Historically Valid State. Supersession Replaces Current Effect — Not Historical Existence. Reinstatement ≠ Historical Reset. Amendment ≠ Supersession by default. Correction ≠ Supersession by default. Valid Successor State ≠ Automatic Same-Event Continuity. Merge Supersession ≠ Merge Formation. Most Recent Technical Record ≠ Current Governed State by default. Later External Record ≠ Canonical Successor by default. Jurisdictional Tax Replacement ≠ Event Supersession. Newest Machine State ≠ Canonical Successor by default. Record Version Change ≠ Event State Change by default. Event Supersession ≠ Tax Assessment Supersession. Enterprise Application ESPM gives organizations a controlled way to determine which Event state is current when several valid historical states exist. The operational pattern is: Prior Governed Event State → Amendment / Correction / Reconsideration / Replacement → Successor Candidate → Supersession Governance → Current Effective State → Historical Predecessor Preserved → Governed Event Supersession State This enables downstream systems to consume one clear current Event state without losing the Event’s lifecycle history. Use Case 1 — Corrected Event State Replaces Prior State Across Multiple Tax Systems A cross-border Event has been consumed by several downstream systems. Later, ECRTM establishes a valid corrected Location and Participation state. ESPM identifies: the prior effective Event state; the corrected successor state; the correction basis; the predecessor-successor relationship. The corrected state becomes current. The earlier state remains reconstructable as superseded. Downstream jurisdictions may reassess their own tax outcomes independently. TREGA™ maintains one Event lifecycle. One current state replaces another without rewriting Event history. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Platform Generates New Record Version After System Migration An autonomous platform migrates its canonical Event Records into a new infrastructure. A new Record version is created with different schema, local identifiers, and storage architecture. The underlying Event remains unchanged. TREGS establishes valid Record Governance and interoperability. ESPM determines that the new Record representation supersedes the prior technical representation for current use while the Event itself remains continuous. The result is: Prior Record Representation ↓ Successor Record Representation ↓ Record Supersession ↓ Same Governed Event The technical successor does not become a new Tax-Relevant Event. Canonical Boundary ESPM owns the governance of Event and Record Supersession state, predecessor identification, successor identification, Supersession eligibility, scope, basis, full and Partial Supersession, current effective-state transition, predecessor-successor relationships, historical preservation, Supersession qualification, ambiguity, conflict, reversal, reinstatement, withdrawal, Supersession chains, Continuity-reassessment triggers, and establishment of the Governed Event Supersession State. ESPM does not own Event Continuity; ECOM does. It does not own Amendment; EADM does. It does not own Correction; ECRTM does. It does not own Closure; ECLM does. It does not independently govern Merge or Split; TRERLS does. It does not create New Events; TREFS governs Event Formation. It does not determine Event Record identity, structure, linkage, traceability, or interoperability; TREGS governs those spaces. It does not determine legal Taxability, Tax Jurisdiction, taxpayer status, tax nexus, legal tax point, Tax Period, Tax Base, Tax Rate, exemption, deduction, Tax Liability, filing, reassessment, payment, collection, or enforcement. Its governance begins when a valid predecessor state and a legitimate successor candidate exist. Its governance ends with: Governed Event Supersession State and a clearly identifiable: Current Effective Event State ready for Event Closure Governance. Canonical Handoff ECRTM / Current Governed Event State ↓ ESPM — Governed Event Supersession State ↓ ECLM — Event Closure Governance Where Event identity becomes materially uncertain: ESPM ↓ ECOM — Continuity Reassessment Where a materially different occurrence is identified: ESPM ↓ ECOM ↓ TREFS — New Event Formation Review Canonical Closing Statement ESPM establishes which governed Event state is current without allowing the state it replaces to disappear from history. Supersession gives lifecycle governance a clear present while preserving a reconstructable past. Supersession ≠ Historical Deletion. Successor State ≠ New Event by default. Current Effective State ≠ Only Historically Valid State.

title: OOF™ Event Completion Module (ETCM)
text: OOF™ Event Completion Module (ETCM) Event Completion Module (ETCM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: Tax-Relevant Event Timing Standard (TRETS) Module: ETCM — Event Completion Module Operational Layer: Event Completion Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Event Completion Origin ID: TREGA-TRETS-ETCM-003 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 31 August 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English ------------------------------ Canonical Definition The Event Completion Module (ETCM) governs how the operational completion of a Governed Bounded Event is determined after its Governed Event Start has been established, by identifying, evaluating, qualifying, and establishing the temporal condition at which the governed event has sufficiently completed as the event under examination. ETCM distinguishes operational Event Completion from later settlement, confirmation, invoicing, reconciliation, reporting, warranty, monitoring, archival activity, accounting closure, contractual closure, legal finality, and jurisdiction-specific taxation points that may occur after the event has operationally completed. Its specific task is: to establish a coherent, traceable, and operationally justified Governed Event Completion without allowing technical workflow closure, administrative processing, commercial settlement, accounting recognition, contractual conventions, or jurisdiction-specific tax rules to redefine when the governed event itself operationally completes. ETCM governs when the bounded event has completed as an operational event. It does not determine when that event is legally completed, recognized, reportable, taxable, or settled under a jurisdiction-specific framework. ------------------------------ 1. Operational Role ETSM establishes when the Governed Bounded Event begins. ETCM determines when that same governed event has sufficiently completed. The transition governed by ETCM is: Governed Event Start ↓ Governed Event Completion The module must distinguish completion of the governed event from activities that merely follow it. An event may operationally complete before: payment settlement, invoice issuance, system confirmation, reconciliation, accounting posting, reporting, administrative closure, contractual closure, legal acceptance, tax recognition. Likewise, the last available timestamp in a technical workflow may represent downstream processing rather than Event Completion. Latest Timestamp ≠ Event Completion by Default. ------------------------------ 2. Internal Flow The TRETS Internal Module Flow is: Governed Bounded Event ↓ ETIM — Event Time Identification ↓ ETSM — Event Start ↓ ETCM — Event Completion ↓ ETDM — Event Duration ↓ ETOM — Event Temporal Order ↓ Governed Temporally Situated Event ETCM governs: Governed Event Start ↓ Completion Candidate Identification ↓ Completion Condition Assessment ↓ Constitutive Activity Completion Assessment ↓ Post-Event Activity Differentiation ↓ Completion Qualification ↓ Completion Ambiguity / Conflict Handling ↓ Governed Event Completion ↓ ETDM ETCM may consume relevant temporal signals identified by ETIM but does not recreate the temporal signal inventory. It establishes the legitimate operational completion of the same event whose start was governed by ETSM. ------------------------------ 3. Operational Space ETCM governs the operational space in which the completion of the bounded event must be distinguished from surrounding or subsequent temporal activity. This space includes: completion candidates, completion signals, completion conditions, final constitutive activity, operational fulfillment, physical completion, digital completion, transactional completion, service completion, transfer completion, machine execution completion, autonomous operation completion, distributed completion, phased completion, conditional completion, partial completion, failed completion, interrupted completion, post-event activity, delayed confirmation, delayed settlement, completion ambiguity, completion conflict, completion precision, completion traceability. The continued existence of related processes after operational completion does not automatically extend the Event Completion point. ------------------------------ 4. Operational Scope ETCM governs: 1. identification of candidate Event Completion signals; 2. assessment of candidate completion conditions; 3. determination of final constitutive event activity; 4. distinction between Event Completion and post-event activity; 5. assessment of physical, digital, transactional, service, distributed, machine-generated, and autonomous completion; 6. treatment of partial completion; 7. treatment of interrupted or failed event execution; 8. treatment of conditional completion; 9. treatment of phased or distributed completion; 10. detection of completion ambiguity; 11. detection of conflicting completion representations; 12. establishment of supported completion precision; 13. preservation of completion uncertainty; 14. maintenance of traceability to relevant temporal signals; 15. production of Governed Event Completion for ETDM. ETCM does not calculate Event Duration, determine final Temporal Order, establish Event Location, determine legal taxability, or establish a Legal Tax Point. ------------------------------ 5. Event Completion Candidate Identification ETCM identifies temporal signals or conditions that could plausibly establish Event Completion. Potential candidates may include: final material operational action, completion of physical transformation, completion of transfer, final delivery, service fulfillment, digital execution completion, final constitutive machine action, autonomous objective execution completion, completion of required event components, final governed state transition, operational release of the completed result. A candidate is not automatically authoritative. Completion Candidate ≠ Governed Event Completion. ------------------------------ 6. Constitutive Event Completion A legitimate Event Completion should represent the point or condition at which the materially constitutive activity belonging to the governed event has sufficiently concluded. ETCM therefore asks: When did the governed event finish occurring as the event under examination? This differs from asking: When did all activity associated with the event stop? Supporting, administrative, technical, financial, monitoring, or reporting processes may continue after the event itself has completed. End of Constitutive Activity ≠ End of All Related Activity. ------------------------------ 7. Post-Event Activity Differentiation Events commonly generate activity after operational completion. Examples include: confirmation messages, invoice generation, payment settlement, reconciliation, bookkeeping, reporting, quality review, monitoring, warranty processing, customer feedback, data synchronization, audit logging, archival activity. Such activities may remain materially related to the event while occurring outside its operational completion. ETCM must prevent downstream activity from silently extending the governed event. Post-Event Relevance ≠ Event Continuation. ------------------------------ 8. Completion vs. Confirmation A system may confirm an event after the event has already operationally completed. Examples include: delivery confirmation after physical delivery, transaction confirmation after execution, machine completion signal after physical operation, cloud-service acknowledgement after processing, settlement confirmation after transfer execution. Confirmation can provide evidence of completion without necessarily constituting completion itself. Completion Confirmation ≠ Event Completion by Default. ------------------------------ 9. Completion vs. Settlement Financial and commercial settlement frequently occurs after the underlying operational event. A service may be delivered today and paid later. Goods may be transferred before final settlement. A digital transaction may execute before financial reconciliation. ETCM preserves these distinctions. Settlement Time ≠ Event Completion by Default. Settlement may constitute Event Completion only where settlement itself belongs to the governed event structure established by TREBS. ------------------------------ 10. Completion vs. Administrative Closure Administrative systems often maintain workflow states such as: completed, closed, archived, reconciled, posted, approved, finalized. These labels do not automatically define operational Event Completion. A workflow may remain technically open after the event has completed, or may be administratively closed before all constitutive activity has finished. Workflow Closure ≠ Event Completion by Default. ------------------------------ 11. Physical Event Completion Physical events may complete when the material physical activity constituting the event has concluded. Examples include: completion of manufacturing transformation, physical delivery, unloading completion, construction-stage completion, transfer of a physical object, completion of machine operation. Later inspection, documentation, invoicing, or payment does not automatically extend Event Completion. Physical Process End ≠ Administrative Process End. ------------------------------ 12. Digital Event Completion Digital events may complete through conditions such as: processing completion, digital delivery, successful execution, completed data transfer, completed deployment, access provision, final governed state transition. Digital systems frequently generate additional logs and synchronization events afterward. ETCM must distinguish these downstream technical traces from the completion of the governed digital event. Last System Timestamp ≠ Digital Event Completion by Default. ------------------------------ 13. Transactional Event Completion Transactional processes may contain multiple possible completion points. For example: Execution ↓ Confirmation ↓ Clearing ↓ Settlement ↓ Reconciliation ↓ Accounting Posting ETCM does not impose a universal completion point. It determines completion according to the Governed Bounded Event. If the event represents execution, later settlement may remain downstream. If the governed event legitimately includes settlement, completion may occur later. Transaction Completion Depends on Governed Event Structure — Not System Convention Alone. ------------------------------ 14. Service Event Completion Service events may complete: at delivery, at fulfillment of a defined operational objective, after a period of continuous performance, after completion of required service components, upon legitimate operational termination. A contract end date or billing date does not automatically determine service completion. For continuing services, ETCM must avoid manufacturing a completion point where the governed event remains operationally active. Billing Boundary ≠ Service Completion by Default. ------------------------------ 15. Machine and Autonomous Event Completion Autonomous and machine-mediated events may produce large numbers of internal operations before the governed event completes. A machine may: execute, verify, adjust, communicate, self-check, release resources, generate logs. An autonomous agent may continue monitoring or reporting after its primary governed operation has completed. ETCM determines which operational condition represents completion of the governed event rather than simply selecting the final machine-generated timestamp. Last Machine Action ≠ Event Completion by Default. Autonomous Reporting ≠ Autonomous Event Continuation by Default. ------------------------------ 16. Distributed Event Completion Distributed events may complete across multiple systems, participants, machines, or locations. Different components may finish at different times. ETCM must determine whether: one component establishes completion, all required components must complete, a defined completion threshold must be satisfied, a bounded completion interval is required, completion remains unresolved. The methodology must reflect the governed event structure rather than impose artificial simultaneity. Distributed Completion ≠ Single-System Closure. ------------------------------ 17. Phased Event Completion Some events complete through multiple operational phases. Where the event remains one coherent Governed Bounded Event, completion occurs only when the required constitutive phases have sufficiently concluded. However, ETCM must not absorb Event Boundary governance by deciding that phases are actually separate events. If evidence indicates a potential boundary problem, the issue should be routed to appropriate boundary governance rather than silently resolved inside ETCM. Event Phase ≠ Separate Event by Default. ------------------------------ 18. Partial Completion An event may begin and progress without reaching complete fulfillment. Examples include: partial delivery, partially completed manufacturing, interrupted data transfer, partially executed service, incomplete autonomous operation. ETCM must distinguish partial progress from legitimate Event Completion. Possible representations may include: Completion Pending Partial Completion Completion Qualified Completion Failed Completion Unresolved Partial Performance ≠ Full Event Completion. ------------------------------ 19. Failed or Interrupted Events An event that does not reach its intended operational outcome may still constitute a governed event. Failure does not automatically erase the event. ETCM must determine whether: the event completed unsuccessfully, the event terminated before completion, the event remains suspended, the event was aborted, the completion state is unresolved. The module must not equate successful outcome with event existence. Event Failure ≠ Event Non-Existence. Likewise: Termination ≠ Successful Completion. ------------------------------ 20. Conditional Completion Some events complete only when defined operational conditions are satisfied. For example: required delivery elements are fulfilled, required data reaches the destination, specified transformation finishes, required machine state is achieved, required service result is delivered. A timestamp may record when the condition was detected, but the underlying condition governs operational completion. Completion Timestamp ≠ Completion Condition by Default. ------------------------------ 21. Completion Ambiguity Completion ambiguity exists when more than one plausible completion representation remains and available information does not sufficiently establish which one represents operational completion. Possible causes include: asynchronous systems, incomplete logs, delayed observations, unclear completion criteria, conflicting operational records, distributed execution, uncertain final activity. ETCM must preserve ambiguity rather than fabricate certainty. Required Completion Field ≠ Completion Certainty. ------------------------------ 22. Completion Conflict Completion conflict exists when materially relevant information supports incompatible completion determinations. Examples include: machine logs show completion before ERP closure; physical delivery records conflict with platform records; autonomous-system logs disagree across nodes; service records show performance continuing after administrative closure. ETCM must identify and preserve such conflict until sufficient governance can resolve it. Preferred System Timestamp ≠ Authoritative Event Completion by Default. ------------------------------ 23. Event Completion Precision Governed Event Completion may be represented as: exact timestamp, second, minute, hour, date, bounded interval, approximate period, condition-relative completion. The selected precision must not exceed the temporal support available. Recorded Precision ≠ Evidential Precision. Where only a bounded interval can legitimately be established, ETCM should preserve the interval. ------------------------------ 24. Event Completion States ETCM may represent Event Completion through states such as: Completion Candidate A signal or condition may represent operational completion. Completion Qualified The candidate is sufficiently supported. Completion Established Operational completion is sufficiently established. Completion Approximate Completion is established without exact temporal precision. Partial Completion Only part of the required event structure has completed. Completion Pending The governed event remains active. Completion Interrupted Execution has stopped without normal completion. Completion Failed The event reached a governed unsuccessful termination condition. Completion Ambiguous Multiple plausible completion representations remain. Completion Conflicted Materially incompatible completion evidence exists. Completion Insufficient Available information cannot support reliable determination. Completion Unresolved Further governance is required. Completion Established ≠ Legal Completion Established. ------------------------------ 25. Governance Requirements A conforming ETCM implementation should: 1. consume the Governed Event Start from ETSM; 2. maintain reference to relevant ETIM temporal signals; 3. identify plausible Event Completion candidates; 4. assess candidates against the Governed Bounded Event; 5. identify final constitutive event activity or completion condition; 6. distinguish Event Completion from post-event activity; 7. distinguish completion from confirmation; 8. distinguish completion from settlement; 9. distinguish completion from administrative closure; 10. support physical, digital, transactional, service, distributed, machine-generated, and autonomous events; 11. support partial, failed, interrupted, conditional, and approximate completion; 12. preserve ambiguity and conflict; 13. avoid artificial temporal precision; 14. maintain completion traceability; 15. avoid jurisdiction-specific taxation assumptions; 16. produce a Governed Event Completion suitable for ETDM. ------------------------------ 26. Governance Logic The minimum ETCM governance logic is: IF one or more temporal signals plausibly represent completion, THEN they must be evaluated as Completion Candidates. IF materially constitutive event activity remains incomplete, THEN normal Event Completion must not be established. IF later activity is merely administrative, financial, technical, reporting, monitoring, or archival, THEN that activity must not automatically extend Event Completion. IF confirmation occurs after operational completion, THEN confirmation may support completion without redefining it. IF settlement occurs after operational completion, THEN settlement must remain distinct unless settlement belongs to the Governed Bounded Event itself. IF an event terminates unsuccessfully, THEN its termination state must be represented without treating the event as nonexistent. IF completion is distributed, THEN the completion representation must reflect the required distributed event structure. IF multiple completion candidates materially conflict, THEN the conflict must remain explicit. IF exact completion cannot be legitimately established, THEN supported approximation or interval representation should be used. IF jurisdiction-specific law assigns another legal point, THEN that determination must remain outside ETCM. ------------------------------ 27. Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum ETCM implementation should support: 1. Governed Event Reference Reference to the Governed Bounded Event. 2. Governed Event Start Reference Reference to ETSM output. 3. Temporal Signal Reference Reference to relevant ETIM signals. 4. Completion Candidate Identifier Unique reference for each candidate completion condition. 5. Completion Candidate Type Physical, digital, transactional, service, machine, autonomous, distributed, conditional, or other. 6. Completion Condition The operational condition potentially establishing completion. 7. Constitutive Completion Assessment Whether required event activity has sufficiently concluded. 8. Post-Event Activity Indicator Whether later related activity remains outside Event Completion. 9. Completion Type Normal, partial, interrupted, failed, conditional, approximate, or unresolved. 10. Completion Precision Supported temporal precision. 11. Completion Traceability Reference Links to relevant temporal and operational records. 12. Ambiguity / Conflict State Representation of unresolved completion issues. 13. Completion Governance State Candidate, qualified, established, approximate, partial, pending, interrupted, failed, ambiguous, conflicted, insufficient, or unresolved. 14. Governed Event Completion The established operational completion representation. 15. Handoff State Readiness for ETDM. ------------------------------ 28. Governance Outputs ETCM may produce: Governed Event Completion Event Completion Candidate Set Completion Condition Record Constitutive Completion Assessment Post-Event Activity Record Completion Qualification Record Partial Completion Indicator Completion Pending Indicator Interrupted Completion Record Failed Completion Record Completion Precision Record Completion Ambiguity Indicator Completion Conflict Indicator Completion Insufficiency Indicator Distributed Completion Representation Machine / Autonomous Completion Representation Event Completion Traceability Record Event Duration Governance Readiness State The principal output is: Governed Event Completion This output proceeds to: ETDM — Event Duration Module ------------------------------ 29. Critical Distinctions Completion Candidate ≠ Governed Event Completion Latest Timestamp ≠ Event Completion by Default End of Constitutive Activity ≠ End of All Related Activity Post-Event Relevance ≠ Event Continuation Completion Confirmation ≠ Event Completion by Default Settlement Time ≠ Event Completion by Default Workflow Closure ≠ Event Completion by Default Physical Process End ≠ Administrative Process End Last System Timestamp ≠ Digital Event Completion by Default Billing Boundary ≠ Service Completion by Default Last Machine Action ≠ Event Completion by Default Autonomous Reporting ≠ Autonomous Event Continuation by Default Distributed Completion ≠ Single-System Closure Event Phase ≠ Separate Event by Default Partial Performance ≠ Full Event Completion Event Failure ≠ Event Non-Existence Termination ≠ Successful Completion Completion Timestamp ≠ Completion Condition by Default Recorded Precision ≠ Evidential Precision Event Completion ≠ Event Duration Event Completion ≠ Final Temporal Order Event Completion ≠ Accounting Closure Event Completion ≠ Contractual Closure Operational Event Completion ≠ Legal Tax Point Event Completion ≠ Tax Period Determination Event Completion ≠ Tax Liability Determination ------------------------------ 30. Enterprise Application ETCM can support Event Completion governance across: ERP systems, banking infrastructure, payment systems, digital marketplaces, e-commerce platforms, logistics networks, SaaS environments, manufacturing systems, industrial automation, robotics, autonomous agents, IoT infrastructure, machine-to-machine systems, distributed computing, digital-asset infrastructure, cross-border commerce, automated accounting infrastructure, tax technology platforms. ETCM enables these systems to maintain a governed operational completion representation independently of how downstream systems subsequently interpret settlement, accounting recognition, legal completion, reporting obligations, or taxation. ------------------------------ 31. Real-System Use Case 1 — Marketplace Delivery, Confirmation, and Settlement Occur at Different Times A marketplace transaction generates the following timeline: 10:03 — Order accepted 10:08 — Payment authorized 13:42 — Seller dispatches goods Next day 11:16 — Goods physically delivered 11:31 — Carrier system uploads delivery confirmation 12:05 — Marketplace marks order “completed” Following day — Merchant settlement occurs Three days later — Accounting reconciliation closes Multiple systems therefore contain different plausible “completion” timestamps. ETCM does not automatically accept the marketplace's completed status, carrier confirmation, payment settlement, or accounting closure. It evaluates the Governed Bounded Event and determines when its constitutive operational activity actually completed. If the bounded event concerns fulfillment and delivery, physical delivery may establish the Governed Event Completion even though platform confirmation, settlement, and reconciliation occur later. Those later activities remain traceably associated without silently extending the event. The resulting completion record can subsequently be consumed by taxation systems without TREGA™ deciding which jurisdiction-specific legal tax point applies. The event can operationally finish before the systems surrounding it finish processing it. ------------------------------ 32. Real-System Use Case 2 — Autonomous Manufacturing Event Continues After Human Systems Think It Is Finished An autonomous manufacturing system begins material transformation at 08:04. Primary machining finishes at 08:47. The production management system automatically marks the job “complete” at 08:48. However, the governed manufacturing operation requires an autonomous finishing stage. A robotic finishing unit continues processing until 08:55. Machine verification occurs at 08:56. Quality telemetry is uploaded until 08:59. Administrative production records are closed at 09:12. An accounting entry is generated later. ETCM determines whether the 08:48 system status legitimately represents completion of the Governed Bounded Event. Because required constitutive manufacturing activity continues until the finishing stage concludes, the administrative “complete” flag cannot independently establish Event Completion. At the same time, telemetry upload and administrative closure after operational completion do not automatically extend the event. ETCM therefore establishes the supported operational completion condition while preserving all later signals as associated temporal information. A system may declare an event finished before operational reality has actually finished — or continue processing it long after operational reality has ended. ------------------------------ 33. Canonical Boundary ETCM governs the identification, assessment, qualification, establishment, precision, ambiguity, conflict, partial completion, interruption, failure, and traceability of the operational completion of the Governed Bounded Event after its Governed Event Start has been established. It does not redefine the Governed Event Start, calculate Event Duration, determine final Event Temporal Order, redefine Event Boundary, determine Event Location, govern Event Participation, determine Event-to-Value Association, establish Event Relationships, perform Event Determination, determine Legal Tax Point, establish Tax Period, determine Tax Jurisdiction, identify the taxpayer, determine legal taxability, calculate tax, or establish jurisdiction-specific tax consequences. ETCM receives: ETSM — Governed Event Start ETCM produces: Governed Event Completion The output is handed to: ETDM — Event Duration Module The canonical handoff is: ETSM — Governed Event Start ↓ ETCM — Governed Event Completion ↓ ETDM — Event Duration Module ------------------------------ 34. Canonical Closing Statement ETCM establishes when the governed event has finished occurring in operational reality without allowing the administrative, financial, technical, or legal processes surrounding that event to redefine its operational end. ETCM determines when the event completes — not when a system closes it, a payment settles, or a jurisdiction decides that a legal tax point has occurred.

title: OOF™ Event Duration Module (ETDM)
text: OOF™ Event Duration Module (ETDM) Event Duration Module (ETDM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: Tax-Relevant Event Timing Standard (TRETS) Module: ETDM — Event Duration Module Operational Layer: Event Duration Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Event Duration Origin ID: TREGA-TRETS-ETDM-004 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 31 August 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language ------------------------------ Canonical Definition The Event Duration Module (ETDM) governs how the temporal extent of a Tax-Relevant Event is established from its governed temporal structure, including its Governed Event Start, Governed Event Completion, intermediate temporal conditions, interruptions, suspensions, phases, distributed execution, and supported temporal precision. ETDM determines how long the governed event persisted as operational reality without converting that duration into a jurisdiction-specific tax period, accounting period, reporting period, contractual period, billing period, or legal duration. Its specific task is: to establish a coherent, traceable, and operationally justified representation of the temporal extent occupied by the governed event between its legitimate operational start and completion. ETDM governs how long the event existed or persisted as the governed event . It does not determine the period in which a jurisdiction recognizes, reports, assesses, or taxes that event. ------------------------------ 1. Operational Role ETSM establishes the Governed Event Start. ETCM establishes the Governed Event Completion. ETDM governs the temporal extent between and across those governed temporal conditions. The primary transition is: Governed Event Start + Governed Event Completion ↓ Governed Event Duration Duration may appear mathematically simple, but governed duration cannot always be reduced to: Completion Timestamp − Start Timestamp Events may contain: pauses, suspensions, inactive intervals, phased execution, asynchronous components, distributed operations, partial completion, uncertain temporal boundaries, approximate timestamps, open-ended activity, machine execution cycles, autonomous continuation. ETDM therefore governs the meaning and representation of duration rather than merely calculating elapsed clock time.
