ETOM normalizes and qualifies the available temporal information while preserving the original timestamps and synchronization uncertainty. Where evidence supports only: Machine A Event ↓ Agent Processing ↓ Machine B Response within bounded temporal ranges, ETOM records that governed sequence. Where exact micro-ordering remains unsupported, it remains unresolved. ETOM does not infer responsibility, causation, authority, or liability from the sequence. The resulting structure can be consumed by downstream governance architectures without corrupting operational reality through misleading timestamp precision. In distributed autonomous systems, the earliest timestamp is not necessarily the earliest event. ------------------------------ 39. Canonical Boundary ETOM governs the temporal ordering of the Tax-Relevant Event relative to relevant governed temporal references after Event Time Identification, Event Start, Event Completion, and Event Duration have been established through TRETS. It owns: temporal comparison, temporal precedence, temporal succession, simultaneity, concurrency, overlap, temporal containment, partial ordering, distributed ordering, machine ordering, autonomous ordering, temporal-order precision, temporal-order uncertainty, temporal-order conflict, temporal-order correction, temporal-order traceability, construction of the Governed Temporally Situated Event. ETOM does not own Event Context, Event Recognition, Event Formation, Event Boundary, Event Location, Event Participation, Value Association, semantic Event Relationships, causation, dependency, attribution, responsibility, accountability, legal priority, Tax Jurisdiction, Taxpayer determination, Legal Tax Point, Tax Period, taxability, tax liability, tax rate, reporting obligation, or jurisdiction-specific tax consequence. ETOM receives: ETDM — Governed Event Duration together with the governed temporal structure produced by: ETIM ↓ ETSM ↓ ETCM ↓ ETDM ETOM produces: Governed Event Temporal Order and completes the Parent Standard output: Governed Temporally Situated Event The canonical handoff is: ETIM — Event Time Identification ↓ ETSM — Event Start ↓ ETCM — Event Completion ↓ ETDM — Event Duration ↓ ETOM — Event Temporal Order ↓ Governed Temporally Situated Event ↓ TRELS — Tax-Relevant Event Location Standard ------------------------------ 40. Canonical Closing Statement ETOM completes the temporal governance of the Tax-Relevant Event by establishing where the event stands in operational time relative to relevant events and temporal references while preserving uncertainty, concurrency, distributed timing, and the boundary between sequence and meaning. Temporal order can establish what came before, after, during, or alongside an event. It cannot, by itself, establish why it happened, what caused it, or what legal consequence follows. TRETS governs when the event occurred as governed operational reality — not when tax law decides that the event becomes taxable. TREGA™ governs the event. The jurisdiction governs the tax.

title: OOF™ Event Start Module (ETSM)
text: OOF™ Event Start Module (ETSM) Event Start Module (ETSM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: Tax-Relevant Event Timing Standard (TRETS) Module: ETSM — Event Start Module Operational Layer: Event Start Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Event Start Origin ID: TREGA-TRETS-ETSM-002 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 31 August 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English ------------------------------ Canonical Definition The Event Start Module (ETSM) governs how the operational beginning of a Governed Bounded Event is determined from the Governed Event Time Signal Set by identifying, evaluating, qualifying, and establishing the temporal condition at which the governed event legitimately begins as the event under examination. ETSM distinguishes the operational beginning of the governed event from earlier preparatory activity, system initialization, authorization, scheduling, communication, recording, technical activation, contractual milestones, accounting recognition, and jurisdiction-specific legal or taxation points that may occur before, at, or after the event begins. Its specific task is: to establish a coherent, traceable, and operationally justified Governed Event Start without allowing technical timestamps, administrative conventions, contractual dates, accounting treatment, or jurisdiction-specific tax rules to redefine the operational beginning of the governed event. ETSM governs when the bounded event begins as an operational event. It does not determine when that event is legally recognized for taxation. ------------------------------ 1. Operational Role ETIM identifies and structures the materially relevant temporal signals associated with the Governed Bounded Event. ETSM determines which temporal condition legitimately establishes the beginning of that event. The transition governed by ETSM is: Governed Event Time Signal Set ↓ Governed Event Start This requires more than selecting the earliest available timestamp. The earliest recorded activity may represent: preparation, authorization, scheduling, system initialization, resource reservation, communication, preliminary machine activity, data creation, contractual formation, administrative processing. None necessarily establishes that the governed event itself has begun. ETSM therefore determines the operational threshold separating activity preceding the event from activity constituting the event. Earliest Timestamp ≠ Event Start by Default. ------------------------------ 2. Internal Flow The TRETS Internal Module Flow is: Governed Bounded Event ↓ ETIM — Event Time Identification ↓ ETSM — Event Start ↓ ETCM — Event Completion ↓ ETDM — Event Duration ↓ ETOM — Event Temporal Order ↓ Governed Temporally Situated Event ETSM governs: Governed Event Time Signal Set ↓ Start Candidate Identification ↓ Start Condition Assessment ↓ Pre-Event Activity Differentiation ↓ Start Qualification ↓ Start Ambiguity / Conflict Handling ↓ Governed Event Start ↓ ETCM ETSM receives temporal evidence from ETIM. It does not recreate the temporal signal inventory. It determines which governed temporal condition establishes Event Start. ------------------------------ 3. Operational Space ETSM governs the operational space in which the beginning of the bounded event must be distinguished from surrounding temporal activity. This space includes: candidate start signals, candidate start conditions, operational initiation, first constitutive event activity, preparatory activity, authorization activity, scheduling, resource allocation, system initialization, machine activation, autonomous-system initiation, transaction initiation, service activation, physical commencement, digital commencement, distributed commencement, conditional commencement, phased commencement, approximate start conditions, conflicting start signals, start uncertainty, start traceability. The presence of earlier activity does not automatically extend the governed event backward to that activity. ------------------------------ 4. Operational Scope ETSM governs: 1. identification of candidate Event Start signals; 2. assessment of candidate start conditions; 3. distinction between pre-event activity and constitutive event activity; 4. determination of the operational commencement threshold; 5. evaluation of physical, digital, transactional, distributed, machine-generated, and autonomous starts; 6. treatment of multiple possible start signals; 7. treatment of phased or distributed commencement; 8. detection of start ambiguity; 9. detection of conflicting start representations; 10. preservation of start uncertainty where necessary; 11. establishment of Event Start precision; 12. maintenance of traceability to ETIM temporal signals; 13. production of the Governed Event Start for ETCM. ETSM does not determine Event Completion, Event Duration, final Event Temporal Order, Legal Tax Point, Tax Period, or jurisdiction-specific tax consequences. ------------------------------ 5. Event Start Candidate Identification ETSM begins by identifying temporal signals that could plausibly establish Event Start. Candidate signals may include: first material operational action, physical commencement, transaction execution, service activation, transfer initiation, machine execution, autonomous execution, first constitutive state transition, digital process commencement, first material performance, first governed event component entering execution. Candidate identification does not establish Event Start. Each candidate must be evaluated against the governed structure of the bounded event. Start Candidate ≠ Governed Event Start. ------------------------------ 6. Constitutive Event Activity A legitimate Event Start should correspond to a temporal condition at which the governed event begins to exist operationally as the event defined by its governed structure. ETSM therefore distinguishes constitutive activity from activity merely associated with the event. Constitutive activity materially participates in the event's operational realization. Associated activity may support, prepare, authorize, document, or anticipate the event without itself constituting commencement. The relevant question is not: What happened first? The relevant question is: When did the governed event begin to occur as the event under examination? First Related Activity ≠ First Constitutive Event Activity. ------------------------------ 7. Pre-Event Activity Differentiation Many operational processes contain substantial activity before the governed event begins. Examples include: quotation, negotiation, scheduling, reservation, planning, approval, authorization, resource allocation, software initialization, machine warm-up, preliminary data exchange, contract preparation, risk screening. ETSM must prevent such activity from automatically extending Event Start backward. However, activity that appears preparatory in one event model may be constitutive in another. The determination must therefore remain tied to the Governed Bounded Event received from TREBS. Event Association ≠ Event Commencement. ------------------------------ 8. Authorization vs. Execution Authorization frequently occurs before operational execution. A payment may be authorized before settlement. A machine may receive authorization before physical operation. An autonomous agent may receive permission before executing an action. A service may be approved before activation. ETSM preserves this distinction. Authorization may constitute Event Start only where the governed event itself is legitimately defined around the authorization activity. Otherwise: Authorization Time ≠ Event Start by Default. Likewise: Permission ≠ Execution. ------------------------------ 9. System Activation vs. Event Start Technical systems often activate before the governed event begins. Examples include: application session creation, API authentication, device wake-up, machine initialization, database transaction creation, cloud resource provisioning, workflow initialization. Such timestamps may be operationally relevant without constituting Event Start. ETSM must prevent technical architecture from redefining event reality. System Activation ≠ Event Start by Default. ------------------------------ 10. Transactional Event Start Transactional environments may contain several plausible commencement signals. For example: Order Creation ↓ Order Submission ↓ Merchant Acceptance ↓ Payment Authorization ↓ Execution ↓ Confirmation The correct operational start depends on the structure of the Governed Bounded Event. ETSM does not impose a universal rule that every transaction begins with order creation, acceptance, payment, or settlement. Instead, it determines the start condition from the governed event itself. Transaction Record Creation ≠ Transaction Event Start by Default. ------------------------------ 11. Physical Event Start Physical events may begin through observable operational activity. Examples include: movement, production commencement, loading, construction activity, physical transfer, machine execution, delivery commencement, resource transformation. Where physical commencement is relevant, ETSM must associate the start determination with sufficient supporting temporal signals. Physical events may nevertheless contain preparatory physical activity that does not belong to the governed event. Physical Activity ≠ Event Start by Default. ------------------------------ 12. Digital Event Start Digital events may begin without a physical action. Potential start conditions include: execution of a digital service, transfer initiation, access activation, processing commencement, digital delivery, deployment, state transition, autonomous instruction execution. ETSM evaluates when the governed digital event actually begins rather than automatically using the first timestamp generated by the technical system. First Digital Timestamp ≠ Digital Event Start by Default. ------------------------------ 13. Distributed Event Start A governed event may begin across multiple systems or locations. There may therefore be no single perfectly synchronized timestamp representing commencement. ETSM may need to establish: one sufficiently supported start timestamp, a bounded start interval, a start condition represented across multiple correlated signals, an approximate operational start, a distributed commencement state. The methodology must preserve the temporal precision actually supported by the evidence. Distributed Commencement ≠ Artificial Single-Time Precision. ------------------------------ 14. Machine and Autonomous Event Start Autonomous systems introduce additional complexity because planning, decision, authorization, communication, and execution may occur without direct human intervention. A sequence may be: Objective Received ↓ Autonomous Analysis ↓ Decision ↓ Resource Reservation ↓ Command ↓ Machine Execution The first autonomous computation does not necessarily constitute Event Start. Nor does the first machine-generated timestamp. ETSM identifies the point at which the governed autonomous or machine-mediated event begins operationally. Autonomous Decision ≠ Event Start by Default. Machine Command ≠ Machine Execution. ------------------------------ 15. Conditional Event Start Some events begin only when specified operational conditions become true. A process may be initialized earlier but remain inactive until: acceptance occurs, resources become available, required input arrives, physical execution begins, threshold conditions are reached, service activation occurs. ETSM may therefore represent Event Start through a governed condition rather than merely selecting a pre-existing timestamp field. Process Creation ≠ Operational Commencement. ------------------------------ 16. Phased Event Start Some bounded events begin through several tightly connected actions rather than one instantaneous transition. Where operational reality does not support a single precise start moment, ETSM may represent commencement as a governed temporal interval or composite start condition. This should occur only when supported by the event structure and temporal evidence. ETSM must not manufacture precision where operational reality is genuinely gradual. Temporal Precision Requirement ≠ Operational Reality. ------------------------------ 17. Start Ambiguity Start ambiguity exists where available governed information supports more than one plausible Event Start and available evidence does not sufficiently justify selection. ETSM should preserve such ambiguity explicitly. Possible causes include: incomplete logs, contradictory records, uncertain event formation, asynchronous systems, delayed recording, approximate physical observations, insufficient machine telemetry, competing operational interpretations. An unresolved start should not be silently converted into an exact timestamp. Required Start Field ≠ Governed Start Certainty. ------------------------------ 18. Start Conflict Start conflict exists when materially relevant temporal evidence supports incompatible commencement representations. ETSM must identify and preserve the conflict until sufficient governance can establish a legitimate resolution. Resolution should be based on operational event structure and evidence rather than system hierarchy alone. A preferred ERP timestamp does not automatically override contradictory physical or digital evidence. System Authority ≠ Event-Time Authority by Default. ------------------------------ 19. Event Start Precision Event Start may legitimately be represented at different precision levels. Examples include: exact timestamp, second, minute, hour, date, bounded interval, approximate period, sequence-relative start. The selected precision must not exceed what the governed temporal evidence supports. Timestamp Precision ≠ Temporal Certainty. ------------------------------ 20. Event Start States ETSM may represent Event Start governance through states such as: Start Candidate A temporal signal or condition may represent Event Start. Start Qualified The candidate is sufficiently supported as constitutive commencement. Start Established A legitimate operational Event Start has been established. Start Approximate Commencement is sufficiently known but not precisely timestamped. Start Ambiguous Multiple plausible commencement representations remain. Start Conflicted Material evidence supports incompatible start determinations. Start Insufficient Available information is inadequate for reliable determination. Start Unresolved Further governance or evidence is required. Start Established ≠ Legal Tax Point Established. ------------------------------ 21. Governance Requirements A conforming ETSM implementation should: 1. consume the Governed Event Time Signal Set from ETIM; 2. identify plausible Event Start candidates; 3. evaluate start candidates against the Governed Bounded Event; 4. distinguish preparatory activity from constitutive event activity; 5. distinguish authorization from execution where relevant; 6. distinguish technical activation from operational commencement; 7. support physical, digital, distributed, transactional, machine-generated, and autonomous events; 8. preserve ambiguity and conflict; 9. prevent artificial temporal precision; 10. maintain traceability to supporting temporal signals; 11. avoid jurisdiction-specific tax assumptions; 12. avoid treating accounting, contractual, technical, or administrative dates as authoritative by default; 13. establish a Governed Event Start suitable for Event Completion governance. ------------------------------ 22. Governance Logic The minimum ETSM governance logic is: IF one or more temporal signals plausibly represent commencement, THEN they must be evaluated as Event Start candidates. IF a signal represents only preparatory or supporting activity, THEN it must not establish Event Start unless that activity is constitutive of the Governed Bounded Event. IF authorization precedes execution, THEN authorization must not automatically establish Event Start. IF system initialization precedes operational commencement, THEN initialization must remain distinct from Event Start. IF multiple start candidates are compatible, THEN they may support one governed commencement representation. IF multiple start candidates materially conflict, THEN the conflict must remain explicit until sufficiently resolved. IF precise commencement cannot be legitimately established, THEN an approximate time or bounded interval must be preserved where appropriate. IF a jurisdiction-specific tax rule uses a different legal date, THEN that legal date must not retroactively redefine the operational Event Start governed by ETSM. ------------------------------ 23. Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum ETSM implementation should support: 1. Governed Event Reference Reference to the Governed Bounded Event. 2. Temporal Signal Set Reference Reference to ETIM output. 3. Start Candidate Identifier Unique reference for each candidate commencement signal or condition. 4. Start Candidate Type Physical, digital, transactional, machine, autonomous, conditional, distributed, or other. 5. Start Condition Operational condition represented by the candidate. 6. Constitutive Activity Assessment Whether the candidate represents actual commencement of the governed event. 7. Pre-Event Activity Indicator Whether preceding activity remains outside Event Start. 8. Start Precision Supported temporal precision. 9. Start Evidence / Traceability Reference Links to supporting temporal signals and operational records. 10. Ambiguity / Conflict State Explicit representation of unresolved start issues. 11. Start Governance State Candidate, qualified, established, approximate, ambiguous, conflicted, insufficient, or unresolved. 12. Governed Event Start The established operational commencement representation. 13. Handoff State Readiness for ETCM. ------------------------------ 24. Governance Outputs ETSM may produce: Governed Event Start Event Start Candidate Set Start Condition Record Constitutive Activity Assessment Pre-Event Activity Record Start Qualification Record Start Precision Record Start Ambiguity Indicator Start Conflict Indicator Start Insufficiency Indicator Distributed Start Representation Machine / Autonomous Start Representation Event Start Traceability Record Event Completion Governance Readiness State The principal output is: Governed Event Start This output proceeds to: ETCM — Event Completion Module ------------------------------ 25. Critical Distinctions Temporal Signal ≠ Event Start Start Candidate ≠ Governed Event Start Earliest Timestamp ≠ Event Start by Default First Related Activity ≠ First Constitutive Event Activity Event Association ≠ Event Commencement Preparation ≠ Event Start Authorization Time ≠ Event Start by Default Permission ≠ Execution System Activation ≠ Event Start by Default Transaction Record Creation ≠ Transaction Event Start by Default Physical Activity ≠ Event Start by Default First Digital Timestamp ≠ Digital Event Start by Default Autonomous Decision ≠ Event Start by Default Machine Command ≠ Machine Execution Process Creation ≠ Operational Commencement Distributed Commencement ≠ Artificial Single-Time Precision Timestamp Precision ≠ Temporal Certainty Required Start Field ≠ Governed Start Certainty System Authority ≠ Event-Time Authority by Default Event Start ≠ Event Completion Event Start ≠ Event Duration Event Start ≠ Final Temporal Order Operational Event Start ≠ Legal Tax Point Event Start ≠ Tax Period Determination Event Start ≠ Tax Liability Determination ------------------------------ 26. Enterprise Application ETSM can support operational event governance across: ERP systems, banking infrastructure, payment systems, digital marketplaces, e-commerce platforms, SaaS environments, logistics networks, manufacturing systems, IoT infrastructure, autonomous agents, robotics, machine-to-machine systems, distributed computing environments, digital-asset infrastructure, cross-border transaction platforms, automated accounting and tax infrastructure. ETSM enables these systems to preserve one governed operational Event Start independently of how downstream accounting, regulatory, contractual, or jurisdiction-specific taxation systems subsequently interpret the event. ------------------------------ 27. Real-System Use Case 1 — Cross-Border Digital Service A business customer requests a cloud service at 23:56. The platform records the order at 23:57. Payment authorization occurs at 23:59. The provider accepts the request at 00:01. Cloud resources are provisioned at 00:03. The service becomes operationally available at 00:04. The invoice is generated at 00:06. Payment settles the following day. Several systems could independently claim that their timestamp represents the beginning of the transaction. ETSM does not automatically choose the earliest timestamp, invoice date, payment authorization, or settlement date. It evaluates the Governed Bounded Event and the temporal signals produced by ETIM to determine which condition represents the actual commencement of the event under governance. Where the governed event concerns operational delivery of the digital service, service activation may provide the constitutive commencement condition even though multiple related activities occurred earlier. The resulting Governed Event Start remains distinct from any jurisdiction-specific rule determining when a taxable supply legally occurs. Operational commencement must be established from the event itself — not inherited from whichever downstream system needs a date. ------------------------------ 28. Real-System Use Case 2 — Autonomous Manufacturing Operation An AI production controller receives an objective at 07:52. It begins planning at 07:53. Resources are reserved at 07:56. Production authorization is issued at 08:00. A robotic handling system moves raw material at 08:02. The production machine begins material transformation at 08:04. Quality sensors and supporting robots subsequently perform thousands of machine operations. A naive implementation could define Event Start using the objective receipt, AI planning, authorization, first robotic movement, or first machine-control timestamp. ETSM evaluates which activity constitutes commencement of the Governed Bounded Event. If the bounded event represents the manufacturing transformation itself, preliminary AI planning and resource allocation remain pre-event activities, while commencement of material transformation may establish the legitimate operational start. ETSM records that determination without asserting when any jurisdiction considers the resulting activity legally taxable. Autonomous preparation can precede the event without becoming the event. ------------------------------ 29. Canonical Boundary ETSM governs the identification, assessment, qualification, establishment, precision, ambiguity, conflict, and traceability of the operational commencement of a Governed Bounded Event using the Governed Event Time Signal Set produced by ETIM. It does not determine Event Completion, Event Duration, final Event Temporal Order, Event Location, Event Participation, Event-to-Value Association, Event Relationships, Event Determination, Legal Tax Point, Tax Period, Tax Jurisdiction, legal taxability, tax liability, or jurisdiction-specific tax consequences. ETSM receives: ETIM — Governed Event Time Signal Set ETSM produces: Governed Event Start The output is handed to: ETCM — Event Completion Module The canonical handoff is: ETIM — Governed Event Time Signal Set ↓ ETSM — Governed Event Start ↓ ETCM — Event Completion Module ------------------------------ 30. Canonical Closing Statement ETSM establishes when the governed event begins in operational reality before accounting systems, legal frameworks, or taxation regimes determine what that beginning means for their own purposes. ETSM determines when the event begins — not when a jurisdiction decides that tax begins.

title: OOF™ Governance Architecture Implementation
text: OOF™ Governance Architecture Implementation Governance Architecture Implementation Implementing OOF® Architectures Across AI, Software and Enterprise Systems OOF® governance architectures can be translated from methodological structures into operational capabilities that integrate with existing AI, software, data, and enterprise environments. Organizations do not need to replace their existing systems. OOF® architectures can operate as a methodological governance layer that structures how operational data is identified, evaluated, validated, connected, and transformed into governed outputs. Enterprise Systems / AI / Operational Data ↓ OOF® Governance Architecture Layer ↓ Selected Governance Architectures ↓ Governance Standards & Modules ↓ Governed Analysis ↓ Operational Output From Architecture to Operational Capability An OOF® architecture defines a distinct governable space. For implementation, relevant architectures can be selected and composed according to the operational problem being addressed. This allows organizations to implement specific governance capabilities without requiring every OOF® architecture to be deployed. Operational Problem ↓ Required Governance Capabilities ↓ Relevant OOF® Architectures ↓ Software Integration ↓ Governed Operational Output The architecture provides the methodological structure. The organization's existing systems provide operational data. AI and software can perform analysis within that governed structure. Six Architecture Implementation Use Cases The following examples illustrate how the same OOF® methodological infrastructure can support distinct economic and organizational decisions without reducing value to a single financial number. 1. Insurance → Insurable Value Reality An insurer may need to understand whether the value presented by an organization corresponds to its actual operational capability, evidence, dependencies, and current value state. A governance implementation could combine relevant OOF® architectures to examine: Declared Organizational Value ↓ Value Origin & Identity ↓ Operational Reality ↓ Current Value State ↓ Evidence ↓ Critical Dependencies ↓ Value Degradation Exposure ↓ Restoration Capacity ↓ Validation ↓ Insurable Value Reality The resulting output can provide a structured view of: Declared Value Operationally Supported Value Active Value Value at Risk Critical Dependencies Evidence State Restoration Capacity Validation State This does not replace actuarial valuation, underwriting judgment, or regulated insurance processes. It provides an additional methodological governance layer for understanding the operational reality supporting the value being assessed. 2. Investor → Investment Value Reality Financial statements and management presentations can describe what an organization reports. Investors may additionally need to understand what the organization can actually sustain operationally. OOF® architectures can structure that assessment across: Reported Enterprise Value ↓ Value Origin ↓ Operational Capability ↓ Actual Performance ↓ Evidence ↓ Dependencies ↓ Value Sustainability ↓ Degradation Exposure ↓ Scenario Simulation ↓ Investment Value Reality The assessment can distinguish between: Reported Performance Operational Performance Evidence-Supported Capability Dependency-Concentrated Value Sustainable Value Value at Risk Potential Value Degradation Restoration Potential Alternative operational conditions can then be evaluated through governed simulation. Examples may include: Loss of a Critical Customer Production Capacity Reduction Supply-Chain Disruption Loss of Critical Infrastructure Automation Investment AI Deployment Rapid Expansion Operational Recovery The objective is not to replace conventional financial valuation. The objective is to provide a structured methodology for determining what operational reality exists beneath the reported value and performance of an organization. 3. Bank → Lending Value & Continuity A bank evaluating a company may need to understand more than historical financial statements, collateral values, and projected cash flows. It may also need a structured view of whether the operational capabilities supporting repayment can continue under changing conditions. Borrower Profile ↓ Value-Producing Capabilities ↓ Operational Performance ↓ Critical Dependencies ↓ Continuity Capacity ↓ Degradation Exposure ↓ Evidence & Validation ↓ Lending Value & Continuity The governed output can support a structured view of operationally supported value, dependency concentration, continuity exposure, evidence strength, recovery capacity, and material conditions that could affect the organization's ability to sustain performance. This capability complements conventional credit analysis rather than replacing regulated lending decisions or financial risk models. 4. M&A → Acquisition Value Reality An acquisition target may contain value that is visible in financial reporting but dependent on capabilities, people, customers, infrastructure, intellectual assets, relationships, or operational conditions that may change after ownership transfers. Reported Acquisition Value ↓ Value Origin & Identity ↓ Operationally Supported Value ↓ Critical Dependencies ↓ Transferability ↓ Post-Acquisition Continuity ↓ Scenario Simulation ↓ Acquisition Value Reality This can help distinguish value that is owned, transferable and sustainable from value that depends heavily on specific employees, customers, suppliers, infrastructure, permissions, relationships, or operating conditions. The objective is to provide an additional methodological layer for due diligence and post-acquisition value continuity analysis. 5. Management → Enterprise Value Intelligence Management may need to understand where value actually exists across the organization, what produces it, what sustains it, what is degrading, and where future value could emerge. Organization ↓ Value Objects & Capabilities ↓ Value Origin ↓ Operational Contribution ↓ Current Value State ↓ Dependencies & Degradation Signals ↓ Development / Restoration Potential ↓ Enterprise Value Intelligence This creates a governed view across physical assets, digital assets, organizational capabilities, processes, relationships, knowledge, infrastructure, and other identifiable sources of enterprise value. Management can use this layer to understand not merely how much the organization reports, but where operational value is produced, how it changes, and what threatens or strengthens it. 6. Organization → Workforce Value Intelligence Employees are not interchangeable cost units. Different roles and individuals can contribute different forms of operational value through capability, knowledge, productivity, quality, continuity, problem solving, relationships, specialization, and organizational dependency. OOF® architectures can support a governed assessment of role and workforce contribution without reducing a person to a monetary score. Role & Responsibility ↓ Capability & Competence ↓ Operational Contribution ↓ Performance Evidence ↓ Knowledge & Dependency ↓ Cost of Capability ↓ Replacement / Transition Exposure ↓ Continuity Impact ↓ Workforce Value Intelligence The resulting view could identify dimensions such as operational contribution, capability scarcity, knowledge concentration, replacement difficulty, transition time, continuity impact, development potential, and the organizational cost of losing or replacing a capability. For example, replacing an experienced specialist may involve recruitment cost, onboarding time, training, certification, temporary productivity loss, knowledge transfer, quality exposure, and operational disruption. These effects can be evaluated as separate governed dimensions rather than collapsed into an unsupported estimate of a person's monetary value. The purpose is not to assign a financial price to a human being or automate employment decisions. It is to help organizations understand the operational value, dependencies, continuity requirements, and development potential associated with their workforce capabilities. Integration Model OOF® architectures are designed to complement existing technology environments. ERP / Financial Systems / Operational Systems / Data Platforms / AI ↓ OOF® Governance Layer ↓ Architecture Composition ↓ Governed Analysis ↓ Customer Application / Dashboard / Decision System This creates a pathway from governance architecture to practical software capability without requiring the underlying enterprise infrastructure to be replaced. One Infrastructure — Multiple Applications The same methodological infrastructure can support different operational objectives. Insurance Insurable Value Reality Investment Investment Value Reality Banking Lending Value & Continuity M&A Acquisition Value Reality Enterprise Management Enterprise Value Intelligence Workforce & Organization Workforce Value Intelligence AI Systems Governed Decision & Operational Reality Analysis The application changes. The underlying principle remains: Identify the relevant governance space, apply the appropriate architecture, evaluate the operational reality, and produce a governed output. Architecture on Demand Where an existing OOF® architecture can address the required governance problem, it can provide the methodological foundation for implementation. Where the operational environment requires a different governance configuration, Architecture on Demand can determine the appropriate architecture composition for the required capability. Governance Architecture Implementation connects methodological architecture with operational use — enabling OOF® architectures to move from reference structures toward practical governance capabilities across AI, software, and enterprise systems.

title: OOF™ Occurrence Recognition Module (ORIM)
text: OOF™ Occurrence Recognition Module (ORIM) Occurrence Recognition Module (ORIM) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: Tax-Relevant Event Recognition Standard (TRERS) Module: ORIM — Occurrence Recognition Module Operational Layer: Occurrence Recognition Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Core Module Governed Space: Occurrence Recognition Origin ID: TREGA-TRERS-ORIM-001 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 29 August 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Occurrence Recognition Module (ORIM) is the Core Module within Tax-Relevant Event Recognition Standard (TRERS) that governs the identification and establishment of a distinguishable occurrence from the signals, records, messages, state changes, transactions, instructions, observations, or other representations through which real-world, digital, operational, or machine activity becomes observable. ORIM determines whether available observations provide a sufficient basis to establish that an occurrence exists as a distinct governance object for subsequent recognition processing. Its task is specific: to distinguish a governable occurrence from the technical signals and records through which it is observed without determining whether that occurrence is tax-relevant, how it should be formed into an event, or whether any tax is legally due. Operational Role Modern systems rarely present economic reality as clean, pre-defined events. They produce records. A payment system produces authorization and settlement messages. An ERP creates transaction entries. A marketplace creates orders and status changes. An API produces requests and responses. A robot generates commands and execution records. A sensor generates observations. An autonomous agent may create hundreds of machine interactions while pursuing one operational objective. Before TREGA™ can ask whether any of this activity may be relevant to taxation analysis, it requires a more basic determination: What occurrence can legitimately be distinguished from these observations? ORIM performs this first recognition function. Internal Flow Governed Context + Observable Signals / Records ↓ Observation Qualification ↓ Occurrence Candidate Identification ↓ Signal Association / Differentiation ↓ Duplicate and Noise Screening ↓ Occurrence Distinguishability Assessment ↓ Recognized Occurrence The principal output is: Recognized Occurrence This output proceeds to ERSM — Event Relevance Screening Module. Operational Space ORIM governs the space between: observable operational or digital representations and a sufficiently distinguishable occurrence capable of entering further TRERS governance. Its operational space includes: observation qualification; signal interpretation; record association; occurrence candidate identification; occurrence differentiation; duplicate signal screening; technical-noise separation; repeated observation handling; distributed observation association; machine-generated occurrence identification; occurrence distinguishability; occurrence uncertainty. ORIM governs whether a distinguishable occurrence can be established. It does not govern whether the occurrence has sufficient potential tax relevance. Operational Scope ORIM may process observations originating from: transactions; payments; orders; invoices; ERP records; banking systems; logistics systems; production systems; digital platforms; marketplaces; APIs; software services; digital assets; sensors; machines; robots; autonomous agents; AI systems; machine-to-machine systems; distributed infrastructure; automated workflows; hybrid physical-digital systems. Multiple observations may support one occurrence. One observation may also contain evidence relevant to more than one occurrence. ORIM must therefore avoid assuming a fixed relationship between record count and occurrence count. Signal ≠ Occurrence This is the foundational distinction of ORIM. A signal indicates that a system observed, recorded, transmitted, or represented something. An occurrence represents something sufficiently distinguishable as having happened. For example: Payment Authorization Message ≠ New Economic Occurrence by Default. API Retry ≠ New Occurrence by Default. Database Replication ≠ New Occurrence by Default. Sensor Update ≠ New Occurrence by Default. ERP Synchronization ≠ New Occurrence by Default. ORIM prevents the technical architecture producing the data from automatically defining the governance architecture of reality. Record ≠ Reality Operational systems represent reality according to their own technical purposes. A warehouse system may represent a movement. A payment system may represent a settlement. A marketplace may represent an order. An accounting system may represent a posting. These records can describe different aspects of the same underlying activity. Therefore: Record ≠ Occurrence by Default. ORIM must be capable of looking across available representations rather than assuming that each database object is an independent governance object. Occurrence Candidate Identification ORIM may initially establish one or more Occurrence Candidates from available observations. A candidate may be created where the observations provide a plausible basis for believing that a distinguishable action, transition, condition, exchange, execution, transfer, or other occurrence took place. Candidate identification does not yet mean that occurrence recognition is complete. Where distinguishability remains unresolved, the candidate must remain qualified accordingly. Observation Association Several signals may relate to the same occurrence. For example: Order Creation Payment Authorization Payment Confirmation ERP Posting Invoice Generation may all relate to one broader commercial activity. ORIM may associate observations where a legitimate governance basis exists. Possible association indicators may include: shared references; temporal relationships; operational relationships; system relationships; process relationships; participant references; contextual relationships; upstream governed context. But no single indicator should automatically establish occurrence identity. Shared Identifier ≠ Same Occurrence Two records containing the same transaction number, account, customer, device, session, asset, or system identifier may still represent distinct occurrences. Conversely, records with different identifiers may describe the same underlying occurrence. Therefore: Identifier Equality ≠ Occurrence Identity. Technical identifiers may support recognition. They must not replace governance reasoning. Duplicate Observation One occurrence may be recorded repeatedly. Duplicates may arise through: system synchronization; retries; replicated databases; mirrored infrastructure; multiple reporting systems; platform integrations; archival processes; redundant sensors; distributed ledgers; downstream accounting systems. ORIM must prevent duplicated representations from automatically generating duplicated occurrences. Therefore: Duplicate Record ≠ Duplicate Occurrence. Technical Noise Some observations do not represent materially distinguishable real-world or economic occurrences. Examples may include: health-check signals; heartbeat messages; failed API retries; synchronization traffic; caching operations; internal logging; monitoring events; non-material state refreshes; technical acknowledgements. ORIM may classify such observations as non-occurrence technical activity where sufficient governance basis exists. This prevents technical system complexity from artificially expanding the number of occurrences entering TREGA™. Distributed Occurrence A distinguishable occurrence may be visible only through several systems. For example: Marketplace Record ↓ Payment Record ↓ Service Activation Record ↓ Provider Record No individual record may establish the complete occurrence. ORIM must permit distributed observations to contribute to one occurrence-recognition process. Therefore: Distributed Observation ≠ Distributed Occurrence by Default. The number of systems observing activity does not determine the number of occurrences. Machine-Generated Occurrence ORIM is actor-neutral. An occurrence may arise from: human action; organizational process; software execution; AI agent activity; autonomous-system operation; robot action; machine-to-machine interaction. However: Machine Execution ≠ Distinct Occurrence by Default. A machine may perform thousands of technical operations in executing one higher-level action. ORIM determines which activity can legitimately be distinguished as an occurrence before any assessment of potential tax relevance begins. Occurrence Distinguishability A Recognized Occurrence should be sufficiently distinguishable from surrounding activity. Distinguishability may depend upon: observable change; operational separation; contextual separation; identifiable execution; transaction separation; process transition; value-related change; sufficient evidential support; reliable association of observations. The required degree of distinguishability should remain proportionate to the governance purpose. ORIM does not require absolute knowledge of every aspect of the occurrence. Occurrence Uncertainty Some observations may indicate that something happened without allowing the occurrence to be sufficiently distinguished. ORIM must preserve this uncertainty. Possible conditions may include: Occurrence Candidate Occurrence Unresolved Occurrence Recognized Observation Rejected as Noise Potential Duplicate This prevents incomplete information from becoming false occurrence certainty. Governance Requirements ORIM requires that: occurrence recognition begins from observable information and governed context; signals remain distinguishable from occurrences; technical records do not automatically define occurrence identity; multiple observations may support one occurrence; one observation may require further decomposition where justified; duplicate observations are considered; technical noise can be excluded; distributed observations can be associated where legitimately supported; machine-generated activity is treated actor-neutrally; occurrence uncertainty remains explicit; recognized occurrences remain traceable to supporting observations where materially required; occurrence recognition does not determine tax relevance or legal taxability. Governance Logic ORIM applies four principal questions: What has actually been observed? Do the observations indicate that a distinguishable occurrence exists? Do multiple observations represent the same occurrence, separate occurrences, or an unresolved relationship? Is the occurrence sufficiently distinguishable to proceed to relevance screening? The transformation is: Signals / Records → Qualified Observations → Occurrence Candidate → Recognized Occurrence Only after this transformation should the next module ask whether the occurrence has potential relevance to tax-event governance. Minimum Implementation Framework A minimum ORIM implementation must be capable of: 1. receiving governed contextual information and observable records or signals; 2. qualifying observations; 3. identifying occurrence candidates; 4. associating potentially related observations; 5. distinguishing duplicate representations; 6. identifying technical noise where sufficiently established; 7. assessing occurrence distinguishability; 8. preserving unresolved occurrence conditions; 9. producing a Recognized Occurrence; 10. transferring the recognized occurrence to ERSM for relevance screening. ORIM does not prescribe a particular database, event-stream system, ERP, AI model, knowledge graph, ledger, sensor architecture, or tax platform. Governance Outputs ORIM may produce: Recognized Occurrence — a sufficiently distinguishable occurrence eligible for further TRERS governance. Occurrence Reference — a governed reference enabling subsequent processing. Supporting Observation Set — the records, signals, or observations associated with the recognized occurrence. Occurrence Association Result — the governed relationship between multiple observations and the occurrence. Duplicate Observation Indicator — identification of potentially duplicated representations. Technical Noise Classification — observations excluded from occurrence recognition where sufficiently justified. Occurrence Uncertainty Indicator — unresolved conditions affecting occurrence distinguishability. Occurrence Recognition Basis — the governance basis supporting recognition. Critical Distinctions Signal ≠ Occurrence. A technical observation does not automatically establish something independently happened. Record ≠ Reality. The representation produced by a system is not identical to the reality it represents. Record ≠ Occurrence by Default. A database entry is not automatically a governance object. Multiple Records ≠ Multiple Occurrences. One activity may produce many technical representations. Duplicate Record ≠ Duplicate Occurrence. Replication of information does not replicate reality. Shared Identifier ≠ Same Occurrence. Technical identifiers support governance but do not determine occurrence identity. Machine Execution ≠ Distinct Occurrence by Default. Technical execution granularity must not automatically become economic-event granularity. Occurrence Recognition ≠ Event Relevance Screening. ORIM establishes that a distinguishable occurrence exists. ERSM determines whether it has sufficient potential relevance to proceed further. Occurrence Recognition ≠ Event Formation. Recognition does not construct the governed Tax-Relevant Event. Occurrence Recognition ≠ Taxability Determination. Nothing in ORIM establishes that tax is legally due. Enterprise Application ORIM addresses a major structural problem in modern enterprise and public-sector data environments: the number of records generated by systems is increasingly disconnected from the number of meaningful occurrences in the underlying economy. A single commercial activity may appear across: Commerce Platform ↓ Payment Gateway ↓ Bank ↓ ERP ↓ Warehouse ↓ Logistics ↓ Accounting while an autonomous workflow may generate thousands of additional machine-level records. Without occurrence recognition governance, downstream systems may either: over-fragment reality by treating every record as a separate occurrence, or over-aggregate reality by assuming records sharing an identifier represent one occurrence. ORIM establishes a common governance layer capable of distinguishing occurrences independently of the technical systems that record them. Use CasesUse Case 1 — Duplicate Transaction Explosion Across Government and Enterprise Systems A cross-border seller completes one commercial activity. The marketplace creates an order record. The payment provider creates authorization and settlement records. The bank creates transaction records. The ERP creates sales and accounting records. The logistics provider creates shipment and delivery records. Several systems subsequently replicate these records into reporting and compliance environments. A downstream tax-data platform may receive dozens of records associated with the same underlying activity. Without ORIM, each technical representation risks becoming an independent event candidate, producing duplicate analysis, inconsistent reporting, and artificial transaction volumes. ORIM associates the relevant observations and determines which distinguishable occurrences can legitimately be established. It does not yet determine which occurrences are tax-relevant. It prevents the architecture of the IT systems from becoming the architecture of economic reality. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Agent Producing Thousands of Operations for One Commercial Objective An autonomous procurement agent receives an objective to acquire computing capacity at an acceptable price. It queries hundreds of providers, invokes APIs, performs availability checks, compares offers, requests quotations, retries failed connections, reserves temporary capacity, releases unsuitable reservations, selects a provider, executes a purchase, and initiates payment. Thousands of machine records may be generated. A system that treats every technically observable action as an independent occurrence could create thousands of potential tax-event candidates from one autonomous commercial process. ORIM distinguishes technical signals, retries, observations, and machine execution from sufficiently distinguishable occurrences. The resulting Recognized Occurrence or Occurrences can then proceed to ERSM for tax-relevance screening. This establishes a critical governance capability for machine economies: machine execution can scale almost without limit, but governed occurrence recognition must remain tied to distinguishishable reality rather than computational activity volume. Canonical Boundary ORIM governs whether a distinguishable occurrence can be established from observable activity. It does not determine whether that occurrence has sufficient potential tax relevance, how it becomes a formed Tax-Relevant Event, or whether any legal tax consequence exists. The TRERS internal progression begins: ORIM — Did a distinguishable occurrence occur? → ERSM — Does that occurrence have sufficient potential relevance to tax-event governance? → ERRM — What governed recognition rules apply? → ERCM — How strong is the recognition basis? → EREM — Does unresolved recognition require escalation? This preserves the critical sequence: Observable Signal ↓ Recognized Occurrence ↓ Relevance Screening ↓ Governed Recognition Canonical Closing Statement Occurrence Recognition Module establishes the occurrence-identification layer of the Tax-Relevant Event Recognition Standard by transforming observable signals, records, messages, state changes, machine operations, and distributed system representations into sufficiently distinguishable occurrences capable of entering further TREGA™ governance. Through governance of observation qualification, occurrence candidate identification, signal association, duplicate detection, technical-noise separation, distributed observation, machine-generated activity, distinguishability, and uncertainty, ORIM prevents database entries, API calls, replicated records, system retries, sensor messages, or autonomous execution steps from automatically becoming independent representations of economic reality. The Module preserves the distinctions between Signal and Occurrence, Record and Reality, technical representation and occurrence identity, Occurrence Recognition and Event Relevance Screening, and occurrence existence and legal taxability. ORIM therefore establishes not whether an occurrence is tax-relevant, but whether something sufficiently distinguishable has happened for TREGA™ to legitimately ask that question.

title: OOF™ Tax-Relevant Event Boundary Standard - (TREBS)
text: OOF™ Tax-Relevant Event Boundary Standard - (TREBS) Tax-Relevant Event Boundary Standard - (TREBS) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: Tax-Relevant Event Boundary Standard (TREBS) Operational Layer: Tax-Relevant Event Boundary Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Parent Standard Governed Space: Tax-Relevant Event Boundary Origin ID: TREGA-TREBS-004 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 30 August 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Tax-Relevant Event Boundary Standard (TREBS) governs how a sufficiently formed real-world, economic, operational, transactional, digital, autonomous, machine-generated, or value-affecting event is bounded as a distinct governed event by establishing what belongs within its governed extent, what remains outside it, where separation from adjacent or overlapping activity is required, and when an established Event Boundary must be reconsidered or revised. TREBS receives a Governed Formed Event from the Tax-Relevant Event Formation Standard (TREFS) and establishes the governed boundary necessary for that event to proceed through subsequent TREGA™ lifecycle stages without allowing Event Boundary governance to determine Event Timing, Event Location, Event Participation, Event-to-Value Association, Event Relationships, legal taxability, Tax Jurisdiction, taxpayer status, tax liability, or jurisdiction-specific tax consequences. The principal transition is: Governed Formed Event → Governed Bounded Event TREBS governs where the governed event begins and ends as an event structure — not where taxation begins or ends under law. Operational Role TREBS occupies the fourth governance stage of TREGA™. TREFS establishes: What coherent governed event structure has been formed? TREBS establishes: What belongs within that event, what remains outside it, and where must its governed structural extent be drawn? Its narrow architectural task is: to establish a sufficiently explicit, coherent, traceable, and revisable Event Boundary around a Governed Formed Event so that subsequent TREGA™ governance can operate on a distinguishable event without allowing technical, organizational, accounting, contractual, geographic, or taxation boundaries to automatically define the event itself. TREBS therefore converts: Governed Formed Event into: Governed Bounded Event Governance Flow Governed Formed Event → Event Boundary Identification → Event Boundary Scope → Event Boundary Exclusion → Event Boundary Separation → Event Boundary Revision Governance → Governed Bounded Event The Governance Flow establishes the Parent Standard-level progression through Event Boundary governance. Detailed operational mechanics remain governed by the individual TREBS Core Modules. Governed Space TREBS governs the methodological space through which the structural extent of a formed event becomes explicitly governable. This includes: Event Boundary readiness; Event Boundary identification; Event Boundary basis; Event Boundary scope; inclusion within the Event Boundary; exclusion from the Event Boundary; separation of adjacent activity; separation of overlapping activity; distinction between event structure and surrounding process structure; distinction between technical boundaries and Event Boundaries; distinction between organizational boundaries and Event Boundaries; distinction between contractual boundaries and Event Boundaries; distinction between accounting boundaries and Event Boundaries; composite Event Boundaries; distributed Event Boundaries; machine-generated Event Boundaries; autonomous Event Boundaries; overlapping Event Boundaries; nested event structures; Event Boundary ambiguity; Event Boundary conflict; Event Boundary uncertainty; Event Boundary insufficiency; Event Boundary revision; Event Boundary traceability; readiness for subsequent Event Timing governance. TREBS governs the structural extent of the event. It does not govern the legal extent of taxation. Operational Scope TREBS may govern Event Boundaries across: commercial transactions; financial activity; payments; transfers; production; manufacturing; procurement; supply chains; logistics; service delivery; digital services; subscriptions; platforms; marketplaces; banking; enterprise systems; APIs; software systems; digital assets; automated infrastructure; AI systems; autonomous agents; robots; machine-to-machine transactions; automated marketplaces; distributed systems; cross-border operations; hybrid physical-digital environments; future machine economies. TREBS is actor-neutral, technology-neutral, system-neutral, sector-neutral, and jurisdiction-neutral. An Event Boundary may govern activity involving humans, organizations, software, autonomous systems, machines, infrastructure, digital assets, or combinations thereof. Event Boundary Principle A formed event requires a governable extent. Without a governed boundary, surrounding processes, technical operations, records, actors, systems, contracts, or economic activity may become incorrectly absorbed into the event or incorrectly separated from it. TREBS therefore establishes: Event Formation ≠ Event Boundary. Formation establishes the coherent structure from which the event emerges. Boundary establishes the governed extent of that structure. A formed event may exist before its final governed boundary is sufficiently established. Therefore: Governed Formed Event ≠ Governed Bounded Event. Boundary Is a Governance Construct An Event Boundary must not be assumed merely because a technical or administrative system already contains a boundary. Examples of pre-existing boundaries may include: database records; transaction IDs; invoices; contracts; payment sessions; API sessions; accounting periods; workflow instances; organizational departments; platform accounts; system processes; physical sites; legal entities. These boundaries may provide relevant information. They do not automatically constitute the governed Event Boundary. Therefore: System Boundary ≠ Event Boundary. Record Boundary ≠ Event Boundary. Contract Boundary ≠ Event Boundary. Accounting Boundary ≠ Event Boundary. Organizational Boundary ≠ Event Boundary. Boundary Readiness A Governed Formed Event must contain sufficient structural formation to permit meaningful Event Boundary governance. TREBS must not manufacture a boundary around an event whose formation remains materially insufficient. Where a blocking formation problem exists, the event may require reconsideration within TREFS. Therefore: Boundary-Ready ≠ Boundary-Determined. Boundary readiness establishes that meaningful boundary governance can begin. It does not establish the boundary itself. Boundary Basis An Event Boundary should be supported by a governed basis rather than convenience alone. Relevant boundary considerations may arise from: operational coherence; material event components; event formation structure; material dependencies; operational root association; distinguishable operational outcomes; separation from adjacent activity; relationship to surrounding processes; continuity of the formed event; material structural differences; distributed representations; machine or autonomous execution patterns. No single consideration must automatically dominate every event. TREBS must preserve the distinction between evidence relevant to boundary governance and the Event Boundary determination itself. Boundary Inclusion An Event Boundary must support a governed understanding of what belongs within the event. Inclusion should reflect the event's legitimate structural extent rather than merely the availability of associated information. An element should not automatically fall within an Event Boundary solely because it: shares a transaction identifier; involves the same participant; occurs within the same system; occurs within the same workflow; occurs within the same accounting process; occurs within the same contract; occurs close in time; occurs at the same location; contributes to the same commercial relationship. Therefore: Association ≠ Boundary Inclusion by Default. Boundary Exclusion Governance of an Event Boundary requires the ability to establish what does not belong within the event. Relevant but external activity may remain associated with the event without becoming part of its governed extent. TREBS must therefore preserve: Related Activity ≠ Event Membership. An excluded element may remain important for: context; relationships; evidence; operational understanding; later tax analysis; accountability; validation; auditability. Exclusion from the Event Boundary does not mean irrelevance. It means that the element does not form part of the governed structural extent of that event. Boundary Separation Modern economic activity frequently contains multiple events within a common process, transaction chain, system workflow, contract, platform interaction, or economic objective. TREBS must allow legitimate separation where structurally distinct events exist. Therefore: One Process ≠ One Event by Default. One Contract ≠ One Event by Default. One Workflow ≠ One Event by Default. One Economic Objective ≠ One Event by Default. Conversely: Multiple Technical Operations ≠ Multiple Events by Default. Event separation must follow governed Event Boundary logic rather than raw technical granularity. Boundary and Event Multiplicity TREBS must support the possibility that a formed structure contains: one governed event; multiple distinguishable governed events; a composite event; nested event structures; overlapping event structures; unresolved event multiplicity. Neither aggregation nor fragmentation should be assumed. Therefore: Aggregation ≠ Boundary Integrity by Default. Fragmentation ≠ Boundary Precision by Default. The objective is not to create the smallest or largest possible event. The objective is to establish the most methodologically legitimate governed event extent. Composite Event Boundaries Some operational structures may legitimately require composite Event Boundaries. A composite event may contain multiple materially connected structural elements that cannot be meaningfully governed as entirely independent events without losing the operational reality of the activity. Composite representation must not become a mechanism for hiding materially independent events. Therefore: Composite Structure ≠ Single Event by Default. TREBS must preserve sufficient structural transparency for later Event Relationship governance to determine relationships between governed events. Nested Event Structures An event may exist within a broader operational structure while remaining independently governable. TREBS may therefore support nested structural representations where necessary. A nested event must not automatically inherit every characteristic of its surrounding event or process. Therefore: Contained Activity ≠ Identical Event Identity. And: Parent Process ≠ Parent Event by Default. Overlapping Event Boundaries Complex systems may produce legitimate situations in which governed events share certain operational elements, resources, infrastructure, participants, or contextual conditions. Shared elements do not automatically require merger into a single event. Nor do they automatically require complete separation. TREBS must preserve overlapping structures where operational reality requires them and where the overlap remains explicit and governable. Therefore: Shared Element ≠ Shared Event Boundary by Default. Distributed Event Boundaries A single event may extend across multiple technical systems, infrastructures, organizations, or operational environments. No single technical system must necessarily contain the complete Event Boundary. Therefore: Distributed System Boundary ≠ Event Boundary. And: Multiple System Representations ≠ Multiple Events by Default. TREBS must permit a governed Event Boundary to extend across distributed representations where the underlying event structure supports such treatment. Machine-Generated Event Boundaries Machine environments may generate extremely granular operational records. A machine may create thousands or millions of signals, commands, state transitions, API calls, resource allocations, or settlement messages. Technical granularity must not automatically determine Event Boundary granularity. Therefore: Machine Action Boundary ≠ Event Boundary by Default. API Call Boundary ≠ Event Boundary by Default. System State Change ≠ Independent Event Boundary by Default. TREBS must govern the event at the appropriate operational structural level. Autonomous Event Boundaries Autonomous agents and systems may initiate, modify, execute, coordinate, or complete operational activity without direct human intervention. Their internal decision cycles must not automatically define Event Boundaries. Likewise, a single autonomous objective may generate multiple legitimate events. Therefore: Autonomous Decision Cycle ≠ Event Boundary by Default. One Autonomous Objective ≠ One Event by Default. TREBS governs the structural event extent. ASGA™ governs autonomous-system operation and execution where applicable. Event Boundary Ambiguity Some Event Boundaries cannot initially be established with sufficient certainty. TREBS must preserve ambiguity where multiple plausible boundaries remain methodologically defensible. It must not force a false boundary merely because a downstream system requires a single event representation. Possible outcomes may include: Boundary Qualified Boundary Unresolved Boundary Reconsideration Required Therefore: Boundary Ambiguity ≠ Governance Failure. Explicitly governed ambiguity is preferable to artificially precise event boundaries. Event Boundary Conflict Different systems, actors, records, methodologies, or operational representations may support conflicting Event Boundaries. TREBS must govern such conflict without automatically privileging: the tax engine; the ERP; the payment system; the invoice; the contract; the platform; the accounting record; the machine-generated record; a single participant's representation. No downstream representation should silently redefine operational event reality. Therefore: Existing System Representation ≠ Authoritative Event Boundary by Default. Event Boundary Uncertainty Uncertainty may remain even after substantial boundary governance. TREBS must determine whether remaining uncertainty: is immaterial; may remain as a qualification; requires additional governance; requires reconsideration; prevents legitimate progression. Therefore: Boundary Uncertainty ≠ Boundary Failure by Default. But: Uncertainty Must Remain Visible. Event Boundary States TREBS may recognize governance states including: 1. Boundary Ready The Governed Formed Event is sufficiently structured for Event Boundary governance. 2. Boundary Under Governance The Event Boundary is being established. 3. Boundary Qualified A usable boundary exists subject to explicit non-blocking qualification. 4. Boundary Unresolved Available governance basis does not support a sufficiently legitimate boundary. 5. Boundary Established The governed structural extent of the event has been sufficiently established. 6. Boundary Revision Required Material new information or structural change requires reconsideration of an established Event Boundary. 7. Governed Bounded Event The event has successfully completed Event Boundary governance and may proceed into Event Timing governance. Boundary Revision Principle An Event Boundary must remain governable when materially relevant information changes. New operational information may demonstrate that: an included element should have been excluded; an excluded element belongs within the event; one event should be separated into multiple events; previously separated structures should be reconsidered; an overlapping structure exists; the original boundary basis was materially incomplete. TREBS must therefore support governed revision without erasing historical states. Event Boundary Revision ≠ Historical Erasure. A revised boundary should preserve the previous boundary, revision basis, affected elements, decision path, and resulting boundary state. Boundary Stability Revision capability does not mean that Event Boundaries should change whenever downstream interpretation changes. The governed Event Boundary represents operational event structure. A later tax-law change, tax classification change, rate change, exemption change, reporting rule change, or jurisdictional interpretation should not automatically reconstruct the underlying Event Boundary. Therefore: Tax Rule Change ≠ Event Boundary Change by Default. This separation enables stable governed event representations across changing taxation regimes. Event Boundary and Event Timing TREBS precedes the Tax-Relevant Event Timing Standard (TRETS). TREBS establishes: What is the governed structural extent of the event? TRETS subsequently establishes: When does that governed event occur, begin, complete, persist, and relate temporally to other governed activity? Temporal proximity may inform Event Boundary governance, but TREBS must not determine legal tax points or tax periods. Therefore: Event Boundary ≠ Event Timing. Event Boundary ≠ Legal Tax Point. Event Boundary ≠ Tax Period Determination. Event Boundary and Event Location An event may cross physical, digital, organizational, infrastructural, or national boundaries. Its structural Event Boundary does not determine its governed location. Location is governed later by TRELS. Therefore: Event Boundary ≠ Event Location. And critically: Event Boundary ≠ Tax Jurisdiction. A cross-border Event Boundary does not itself establish which jurisdiction may tax the event. Event Boundary and Participation The inclusion of activity within an Event Boundary does not establish the legal or tax status of actors associated with that activity. Participation is governed later by TREPS. Therefore: Event Boundary Inclusion ≠ Participant Determination. Event Boundary Inclusion ≠ Taxpayer Determination. Event Boundary and Value TREBS may encounter value-related information when establishing structural extent. It does not govern the lifecycle of value or final Event-to-Value Association. VFM® governs the value lifecycle where applicable. TRVAS later governs which governed value result belongs to the event. Therefore: Event Boundary ≠ Value Governance. Boundary Inclusion ≠ Event-to-Value Association by Default. Event Boundary and Event Relationships TREBS may separate events from one another. It does not govern the full relationship structure between those events. TRERLS later governs Event Relationships. Therefore: Event Separation ≠ Event Relationship Determination. Two events may be structurally separate while remaining strongly related. Event Boundary and Event Determination A Governed Bounded Event is not yet a formally determined Tax-Relevant Event. TREDS later governs Event Determination. Therefore: Governed Bounded Event ≠ Determined Tax-Relevant Event. And: Event Boundary Established ≠ Legal Taxability Established. Jurisdiction-Neutral Event Boundary TREBS must establish Event Boundaries independently of the legal taxation rule that may later consume the governed event. A jurisdiction may subsequently interpret the same event differently for taxation purposes. That does not require the underlying governed event to be reconstructed for each jurisdiction. TREGA™ therefore preserves: One Event ↓ One Governed Event Layer ↓ Multiple Jurisdictional Evaluations TREBS contributes the governed structural boundary within that common event layer. Cross-Architecture Boundary TREBS operates within a wider OOF® architecture ecosystem. Where applicable: ORA™ governs what actually occurred in operational reality. ASGA™ governs autonomous-system operation and execution. OBIDENITY® governs identity, origin, ownership, authority, permission, responsibility, and provenance. VFM® governs the value lifecycle. CLA® governs classification. INTEGROS® governs broader integrity questions. ADIT® governs evidence and auditability. VALIDOS™ governs validation. AGA™ governs accountability. TREGA™, through TREBS, governs the structural Event Boundary of the tax-relevant event lifecycle. TREBS must consume relevant governed outputs without absorbing their architecture ownership. Governance Requirements TREBS requires that: Event Boundary governance begin from a sufficiently governed Formed Event; Event Formation remain distinct from Event Boundary; the Event Boundary possess an explicit governed basis; inclusion and exclusion remain distinguishable; related activity not automatically become event membership; technical boundaries not automatically become Event Boundaries; contractual boundaries not automatically become Event Boundaries; accounting boundaries not automatically become Event Boundaries; organizational boundaries not automatically become Event Boundaries; event aggregation not be assumed; event fragmentation not be assumed; composite and nested structures remain governable where required; overlapping structures remain explicit where legitimate; distributed representations not automatically create separate events; machine granularity not determine Event Boundary granularity; autonomous decision cycles not automatically determine Event Boundaries; material ambiguity, conflict, and uncertainty remain visible; Event Boundary revisions preserve prior states; tax-rule changes not automatically redefine Event Boundaries; Event Boundary remain distinct from Event Timing; Event Boundary remain distinct from Event Location; Event Boundary remain distinct from Event Participation; Event Boundary remain distinct from Event-to-Value Association; Event Boundary remain distinct from Event Relationships; Event Boundary remain distinct from Event Determination; Event Boundary not determine Tax Jurisdiction; Event Boundary not determine legal taxability; successful Event Boundary governance produce a Governed Bounded Event suitable for TRETS. Governance Logic TREBS applies the following Parent Standard-level logic: Is the Governed Formed Event sufficiently ready for Event Boundary governance? What structural extent can legitimately be attributed to the event? What belongs within that extent? What must remain outside it? Does adjacent or overlapping activity require explicit separation? Are technical, contractual, accounting, organizational, or system boundaries being incorrectly substituted for the Event Boundary? Does ambiguity, conflict, or uncertainty prevent a legitimate boundary from being established? Has material new information made revision necessary? Is the resulting boundary sufficiently governed for progression into Event Timing governance? The transformation is: Governed Formed Event → Governed Event Boundary → Governed Bounded Event Core Modules TREBS is operationalized through five Core Modules: 1.
