title: OOF™ Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard - (TRECS)
text: OOF™ Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard - (TRECS) Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard - (TRECS) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard (TRECS) Operational Layer: Tax-Relevant Event Context Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Parent Standard Governed Space: Tax-Relevant Event Context Origin ID: TREGA-TRECS-001 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 29 August 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard (TRECS) is the Parent Standard within TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ that governs the contextual environment within which an observed real-world, economic, operational, transactional, digital, autonomous, machine-generated, or value-affecting occurrence is situated before and throughout its progression into tax-relevant event governance. TRECS establishes how economic, operational, organizational, transactional, technological, digital, infrastructural, autonomous, value-related, and other materially relevant contextual conditions are identified, scoped, related, maintained, and revised so that an occurrence can be interpreted within a sufficiently governed environment rather than as an isolated signal. The Standard establishes the methodological distinction between: what happened around an occurrence and what TREGA™ subsequently determines the occurrence to represent as a governed event. TRECS does not determine whether an occurrence has been sufficiently recognized as a candidate tax-relevant event, how that event is formally assembled, where its event boundary lies, whether it is legally taxable, which jurisdiction may tax it, whether nexus exists, who is a taxpayer, what tax base applies, or what legal consequence follows. Its task is narrower: to establish the governed contextual basis necessary for subsequent tax-relevant event governance without allowing context itself to become a tax determination. Core Question What context must be sufficiently governed before an observed occurrence can be meaningfully evaluated and represented within the tax-relevant event lifecycle? Architectural Position TRECS occupies the first governed space of TREGA™. It sits between: Observed Real-World / Digital Occurrence and Tax-Relevant Event Recognition. TRECS therefore operates before TRERS — Tax-Relevant Event Recognition Standard determines whether an observed occurrence is sufficiently established as a candidate tax-relevant event. Its position is foundational because occurrences rarely possess sufficient meaning in isolation. The same technical action, transaction, transfer, machine operation, digital instruction, platform interaction, asset movement, contractual action, or value change may have materially different significance depending upon the environment within which it occurs. TRECS establishes that environment without predetermining the event itself. The architectural sequence is therefore: Occurrence enters TREGA™ → Context is governed → Recognition becomes possible → Event Formation may subsequently occur → Tax-Relevant Event governance continues. TRECS must remain distinct from recognition because: Context establishes the environment in which an occurrence can be interpreted. Recognition determines whether the occurrence should proceed as a candidate tax-relevant event. Governance Flow Position Real-World / Digital Occurrence ↓ Event Context ↓ Event Recognition ↓ Event Formation & Root Association ↓ Event Boundary ↓ Event Timing ↓ Event Location ↓ Event Participation ↓ Value Association ↓ Event Relationships ↓ Event Determination ↓ Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record ↓ Event Lifecycle & Continuity ↓ Jurisdiction-Ready Tax-Relevant Event TRECS governs: Real-World / Digital Occurrence ↓ Event Context and establishes the contextual basis consumed by: TRERS — Tax-Relevant Event Recognition Standard. The critical architectural boundary is: Event Context ≠ Event Recognition. Operational Space TRECS governs the space between: an occurrence observed without sufficiently governed surrounding meaning and an occurrence situated within a sufficiently structured contextual environment for subsequent TREGA™ governance. Its operational space may include: economic context; operational context; organizational context; transactional context; commercial context; digital context; technological context; platform context; infrastructural context; system context; autonomous-system context; machine-generated context; value-related context; contractual context where operationally relevant; process context; activity context; business-model context; service context; production context; supply-chain context; marketplace context; distributed-system context; cross-border operational context; contextual dependencies; contextual relationships; contextual scope; contextual relevance; contextual uncertainty; contextual change; contextual continuity; historical context; multi-context occurrences; contextual information necessary for subsequent event governance. TRECS does not require every possible contextual fact surrounding an occurrence to enter governance. It requires the context that is materially relevant to the governed interpretation and subsequent processing of that occurrence within TREGA™. Operational Scope TRECS may apply to occurrences arising from: human activity; organizational activity; commercial transactions; financial operations; physical asset movements; digital transactions; digital services; software operations; platform interactions; APIs; automated workflows; AI systems; autonomous agents; robots; machine-to-machine interactions; distributed systems; digital assets; automated marketplaces; infrastructure operations; industrial systems; supply chains; service delivery; data-driven economic activity; hybrid physical-digital operations; future machine economies; other governable activity capable of entering TREGA™. TRECS is actor-neutral, technology-neutral, and jurisdiction-neutral. The Standard does not assume that an occurrence must originate from a conventional transaction between two human or corporate parties. Occurrence ≠ Context TRECS preserves a foundational distinction: The occurrence is what is observed. The context is the governed environment necessary to interpret that occurrence. An occurrence may be: a transfer; an execution; a delivery; a payment; an instruction; a machine action; an asset movement; a platform interaction; a service activation; a digital exchange; a value-affecting operation. Its context may include the surrounding economic activity, operational process, organizational environment, digital infrastructure, contractual arrangement, platform structure, system state, value relationship, or other materially relevant conditions. Therefore: Occurrence ≠ Event Context. TRECS governs the latter. Context ≠ Event A sufficiently governed context does not itself establish a tax-relevant event. TRECS may establish: “This occurrence took place within this governed contextual environment.” It may not establish merely from that contextual determination: “A Tax-Relevant Event exists.” That determination belongs later in the TREGA™ lifecycle. Therefore: Governed Context ≠ Governed Tax-Relevant Event. Context Relevance Principle Not every surrounding fact belongs to the governed Event Context. Context must have a legitimate relationship to the occurrence or to its subsequent governance. Potential relevance may arise because a contextual element affects: interpretation of the occurrence; relationship between actions; operational meaning; transaction structure; event recognition; subsequent event formation; event separation; temporal interpretation; location interpretation; participant association; value association; relationship with other events; reconstructability; continuity. TRECS must avoid both: context under-specification and context over-collection. Insufficient context may produce a misleading event representation. Unbounded context may make event governance unnecessarily ambiguous, intrusive, or operationally unusable. Context Scope Every governed Event Context requires an appropriate scope. Context Scope determines which surrounding conditions are materially relevant to interpreting the occurrence and which remain outside the contextual representation. Scope may be: operational; economic; organizational; transactional; technological; infrastructural; digital; process-based; activity-based; system-based; value-related; temporal where contextual history is relevant; geographically distributed where operational circumstances require it; composite. Context Scope does not establish the final Event Boundary. This distinction is critical. Context Scope asks what surrounding information is relevant to understanding the occurrence. Event Boundary asks what belongs to the governed event itself. Therefore: Context Scope ≠ Event Boundary. Context Sufficiency TRECS requires sufficient context, not unlimited context. A contextual representation becomes sufficiently governed when the material conditions necessary for subsequent TREGA™ processing are established to an appropriate degree. Context Sufficiency may depend upon: identification of the relevant operational environment; identification of the relevant economic environment; availability of materially relevant relationships; contextual coherence; contextual traceability; known dependencies; known limitations; treatment of material uncertainty; ability to distinguish relevant context from unrelated surrounding information; preservation of contextual continuity where required. Sufficiency is therefore purpose-dependent within the architecture. TRECS does not require exhaustive knowledge of reality. It requires a sufficiently governed representation of the relevant reality surrounding the occurrence. Context Completeness ≠ Reality Completeness No governed system can be assumed to contain every fact existing around an occurrence. TRECS therefore distinguishes: Context Sufficiency from Absolute Context Completeness. A contextual representation may legitimately support downstream governance even though irrelevant or immaterial facts remain unknown. Conversely, a large quantity of contextual information does not prove contextual sufficiency. Therefore: More Context ≠ Better Governed Context. Context Relationship Principle Contextual elements rarely exist independently. TRECS governs relationships among materially relevant contextual conditions so that the occurrence is not represented through disconnected facts. Relevant relationships may include: operational relationships; organizational relationships; transaction relationships; process relationships; system relationships; platform relationships; infrastructure relationships; service relationships; activity relationships; economic relationships; value-related relationships; dependencies; triggering conditions; contextual sequences; contextual hierarchies. The existence of a contextual relationship does not automatically establish causality. Therefore: Contextual Relationship ≠ Causal Determination. Multi-Context Occurrences A single occurrence may exist simultaneously within multiple legitimate contexts. For example, the same machine-generated operation may belong to: an industrial context a platform context a contractual context a digital-service context a value-related context a cross-border operational context. TRECS must permit multiple contexts where they materially contribute to understanding the occurrence. It must not force complex activity into one artificial contextual category merely for administrative convenience. Therefore: One Occurrence may have Multiple Governed Contexts. Multiple Contexts ≠ Multiple Events The presence of several contextual environments does not establish that several tax-relevant events exist. A single occurrence may require several contextual perspectives while later TREGA™ governance determines that only one governed event exists. Conversely, one shared contextual environment may contain multiple distinct occurrences that later form separate events. Therefore: Multiple Contexts ≠ Multiple Events. Shared Context ≠ Single Event. Event formation and event separation remain governed elsewhere in TREGA™. Economic Context TRECS may govern economic context necessary to understand the environment surrounding an occurrence. Economic context may include, where materially relevant: exchange relationships; commercial purpose; service relationships; production relationships; marketplace structures; economic dependencies; business-model structures; value exchanges; resource use; economically relevant operational relationships. Economic Context does not determine: taxable income; tax base; deductible cost; taxable value; transfer-pricing result; tax liability; legal characterization under tax law. Therefore: Economic Context ≠ Tax Determination. Operational Context Operational Context establishes how an occurrence sits within the actual operation, process, system, service, transaction chain, workflow, production environment, or other real activity from which it arose. Operational Context may be essential where identical technical records can represent materially different real-world activity. TRECS may consume governed operational-reality results from ORA™ — Operational Reality Architecture where available. TRECS does not independently redefine operational reality where that governance has already been established. Therefore: ORA™ establishes what actually happened operationally. TRECS establishes which operational context is relevant to the occurrence entering TREGA™. Digital Context Digital activity may produce occurrences whose meaning cannot be established solely through conventional physical or documentary context. TRECS may therefore govern context involving: software environments; platform structures; digital-service environments; API interactions; execution environments; distributed infrastructure; digital asset environments; automated marketplaces; system-to-system interaction; machine-readable instructions; computational workflows; virtual operational environments. A digital signal does not automatically represent an economically independent event. Therefore: Digital Operation ≠ Tax-Relevant Event by Default. Autonomous and Machine Context TRECS must support occurrences produced without direct human initiation at the moment of execution. These may arise from: autonomous agents; AI systems; robots; algorithmic systems; automated trading or marketplace systems; machine-to-machine transactions; autonomous infrastructure; automated service execution; self-triggering software processes. The absence of immediate human action does not remove the need for contextual governance. Where autonomous-system operation itself requires governance, TRECS may consume relevant governed results from ASGA™ — Autonomous Systems Governance Architecture. TRECS does not determine autonomous-system authority, permission, execution legitimacy, or control. It governs the contextual relevance of those results to the occurrence. Machine Execution Context ≠ Actor Identity A machine, agent, API, platform, or system may participate in the circumstances surrounding an occurrence. Its presence in context does not itself determine: legal personhood; taxpayer status; ownership; authority; responsibility; beneficial ownership; legal attribution. Where origin-bound identity, ownership, authority, permission, or provenance must be governed, those spaces remain with OBIDENITY®. Therefore: Contextual Actor Reference ≠ Identity Governance. Value Context An occurrence may exist within a materially relevant value environment. TRECS may identify that value-related context is relevant. It does not independently determine: Value Origin; Value Emergence; Value Recognition; Value State; Value Change; Value Development; Value Degradation; Value Nullification; Value Restoration; Value Extinction. Those governed spaces remain with VFM®. Where VFM® results exist, TRECS may use them as contextual references. Later, TRVAS — Tax-Relevant Value Association Standard governs the formal association between governed event structures and governed value results. Therefore: Value Context ≠ Value Governance. Transactional Context ≠ Transaction Taxability TRECS may establish that an occurrence exists within a transactional environment. It may identify relationships such as: request ↓ execution ↓ delivery ↓ settlement or another operational transaction structure. This does not establish whether any component represents a taxable supply, taxable disposal, taxable transfer, taxable income, taxable service, or another legally defined taxable event. Therefore: Transactional Context ≠ Taxable Transaction. Cross-Border Context Modern occurrences may span several countries, infrastructures, platforms, organizations, systems, or operational environments. TRECS may preserve contextual facts indicating that activity is distributed across multiple locations or environments. This may be essential for later event governance. However: Cross-Border Context ≠ Tax Jurisdiction. The presence of multiple countries, systems, locations, participants, infrastructures, or economic relationships does not authorize TRECS to determine taxation rights. Jurisdiction-specific rules remain downstream. Jurisdictional Information ≠ Jurisdiction Determination Jurisdiction-related facts may legitimately form part of context. Examples may include: location references; organizational establishment references; infrastructure locations; participant locations; operational locations; delivery locations; digital infrastructure locations; contractual environment references. TRECS may preserve such contextual information where relevant. It must not transform those references into: tax jurisdiction tax nexus permanent establishment residence source determination or another legal taxation conclusion. Therefore: Jurisdiction-Relevant Context ≠ Jurisdiction Determination. Context Change Context may change before, during, or after an occurrence progresses through TREGA™. Relevant changes may include: organizational restructuring; platform migration; system change; contractual change; operational reconfiguration; infrastructure change; participant-environment change; business-model change; technological change; value-environment change; process change; distribution change. TRECS requires material contextual changes to remain governable rather than allowing an earlier contextual representation to persist indefinitely after reality has changed. Context Change ≠ New Event by Default A change in context does not automatically create a new event. The change may: modify interpretation; require contextual amendment; affect later recognition; affect event formation; affect event boundary; create a new occurrence; contribute to a later event. Whether a new event exists is determined through subsequent TREGA™ governance. Therefore: Context Change ≠ New Event by Default. Context Continuity TRECS governs continuity between contextual states so that downstream systems can understand not only the current context but, where necessary, how the relevant contextual environment evolved. Context Continuity may preserve: Initial Context → Material Context Change → Revised Context → Current Context. Continuity is especially important where an event develops across: long-running transactions; distributed processes; multi-stage services; autonomous operations; changing organizational structures; cross-border activity; evolving platform environments. Current Context ≠ Historical Context A current contextual state must not automatically overwrite the context under which an earlier occurrence took place. Where historical context materially affects interpretation, TRECS must preserve the relevant prior contextual state. Otherwise, an event may later be reconstructed using conditions that did not exist when the occurrence happened. Therefore: Current Context must not rewrite Historical Context. Context Correction ≠ Historical Erasure Incorrect contextual information may require correction. Correction must preserve sufficient traceability to distinguish: what was previously represented from what is now established as the corrected contextual representation. TRECS must therefore prevent contextual maintenance from silently rewriting the historical basis used by downstream governance. Context Uncertainty Context may contain unresolved uncertainty. Examples include: incomplete operational information; unknown system relationships; ambiguous organizational relationships; uncertain transactional purpose; incomplete digital traces; unavailable historical records; unresolved participant relationships; unclear machine execution conditions; inconsistent contextual sources. TRECS must permit uncertainty to remain explicitly governed. It must not require unsupported certainty merely to move an occurrence through an automated process. Therefore: Unknown Context ≠ Assumed Context. Context Ambiguity More than one contextual interpretation may remain plausible. Where competing interpretations materially affect subsequent event governance, TRECS should preserve that ambiguity until sufficient basis exists to resolve it or downstream governance explicitly handles it. The Standard must not force a single contextual interpretation merely because a system architecture requires one field to contain one value. Data Model Simplicity ≠ Reality Simplicity. Context Evidence ≠ Context Truth by Default Documents, system records, platform logs, contractual records, machine logs, transaction records, organizational data, and other information may support contextual governance. Their existence alone does not establish their integrity, validity, evidential fitness, or truth. Where those questions require dedicated governance: INTEGROS® governs integrity. ADIT® governs audit and evidence. VALIDOS™ governs validation. TRECS consumes sufficiently governed results where available rather than silently absorbing those functions. Source Quantity ≠ Context Reliability Multiple contextual sources do not automatically establish reliable context. Ten records derived from one incorrect source may provide less governance confidence than one properly validated independent record. TRECS therefore separates: Context Information Volume from Context Governance Quality. Context Classification Contextual information may require classification to support coherent governance. Where formal classification governance is required, CLA® owns the classification space. TRECS may consume classification results but does not redefine the classification architecture within tax-relevant event governance. Therefore: Context Use ≠ Classification Ownership. Context Attribution ≠ Accountability TRECS may establish that a contextual element is associated with a participant, organization, system, process, or operational environment. This does not determine who is accountable for the occurrence or its consequences. Where accountability must be governed, that space remains with AGA™. Therefore: Context Association ≠ Accountability Determination. Context Granularity Context must be represented at a level of granularity appropriate to the occurrence and its subsequent governance. Too little granularity may hide material differences. Too much granularity may fragment coherent reality into unusable contextual noise. TRECS therefore requires granularity to remain proportionate to the governance purpose. The appropriate unit of context may differ between: a retail transaction; an industrial operation; a financial transfer; a digital service; an autonomous-agent interaction; a distributed infrastructure process; a machine-to-machine exchange. There is no universal contextual granularity suitable for every event class. Context Normalization Different operational systems may describe equivalent contextual conditions using different data models, terminology, schemas, identifiers, or technical structures. TRECS permits contextual representations to be normalized where necessary for TREGA™ interoperability. Normalization must not erase material differences. Therefore: Normalized Context ≠ Artificially Uniform Reality. Context Interoperability TREGA™ is intended to operate above heterogeneous operational environments. TRECS must therefore allow contextual representations originating from different systems to become sufficiently coherent for subsequent event governance without requiring those systems to become technically identical. Potential upstream environments may include: ERP Commerce Banking Digital Platforms Industrial Systems AI Agents Autonomous Systems Machine Networks Distributed Infrastructure. The methodological objective is: heterogeneous operational context ↓ governed contextual representation ↓ consistent downstream event governance. Context Independence from Tax Rule Changes The contextual representation of what surrounded an occurrence should not need to be reconstructed merely because a downstream jurisdiction changes: tax rates; exemptions; deductions; tax classifications; reporting rules; nexus rules; filing requirements; legal interpretations. TRECS therefore supports separation between: governed contextual reality and subsequent legal interpretation of that reality. This is fundamental to TREGA™. Tax Rule ≠ Context Constructor A downstream tax rule may require particular contextual facts. It should not retroactively redefine the underlying operational context merely to produce a desired tax result. TRECS therefore establishes the principle: Tax rules may consume governed context; they should not reconstruct operational reality by default. Jurisdiction-Neutral Context TRECS is jurisdiction-neutral. This does not mean that jurisdiction-related information is excluded. It means the Standard does not embed the legal tax interpretation of a particular jurisdiction into the canonical definition of Event Context. The same governed context may therefore support different downstream evaluations. For example: Governed Context → Jurisdiction A Evaluation → Jurisdiction B Evaluation → Jurisdiction C Evaluation. The context may remain methodologically consistent even where legal conclusions differ. Context Readiness An occurrence becomes context-ready for subsequent TREGA™ governance when the contextual conditions materially necessary for its next governance stage are sufficiently: identified; scoped; related; represented; traceable where required; qualified for material uncertainty; maintainable through relevant change; distinguishable from unrelated surrounding information. Context Readiness does not establish Event Recognition. It establishes readiness for recognition. Therefore: Context-Ready ≠ Event-Recognized. Context Governance States TRECS may recognize minimum governance states such as: 1. Context Unidentified The occurrence has entered TREGA™ but the materially relevant contextual environment has not yet been sufficiently identified. 2. Context Partially Established Relevant contextual elements have been identified, but material gaps remain. 3. Context Ambiguous Multiple materially different contextual interpretations remain unresolved. 4. Context Sufficiently Established The contextual environment is sufficiently governed to support the next relevant TREGA™ stage. 5. Context Changed A material change has occurred requiring contextual reassessment or revision. 6. Context Superseded A previous contextual representation has been replaced by a newer governed representation while historical traceability is preserved. These are governance states and may be adapted to the relevant implementation environment without changing the architectural boundary of TRECS. TRECS Boundary with TRERS — Tax-Relevant Event Recognition Standard TRECS establishes the governed context surrounding an occurrence. TRERS determines whether that occurrence is sufficiently established as a candidate tax-relevant event. Therefore: TRECS ↓ What contextual environment surrounds the occurrence? TRERS ↓ Should the occurrence proceed as a candidate Tax-Relevant Event? The boundary is: Event Context ≠ Event Recognition. TRECS Boundary with TREFS — Tax-Relevant Event Formation Standard TRECS establishes contextual conditions. TREFS governs how eligible facts, actions, transactions, operations, system occurrences, autonomous actions, value effects, and related components are assembled into a coherent governed event. Context may inform formation. It does not perform formation. Therefore: Contextual Relationship ≠ Event Component Assembly. TRECS Boundary with TREBS — Tax-Relevant Event Boundary Standard TRECS determines the scope of context relevant to understanding the occurrence. TREBS determines what belongs inside the governed event and what remains outside it. Therefore: Context Scope ≠ Event Boundary. Context may legitimately extend beyond the final governed event. TRECS Boundary with TRETS — Tax-Relevant Event Timing Standard TRECS may preserve temporal context where relevant. TRETS owns formal governance of the operational temporal position, beginning, completion, duration, and ordering of the governed event. Therefore: Temporal Context ≠ Event Timing Determination. TRECS Boundary with TRELS — Tax-Relevant Event Location Standard TRECS may identify that physical, digital, operational, virtual, infrastructural, or distributed location information forms part of the relevant context. TRELS governs formal association of location with the tax-relevant event. Therefore: Location Context ≠ Governed Event Location. And: Neither determines Tax Jurisdiction. TRECS Boundary with TREPS — Tax-Relevant Event Participation Standard TRECS may identify actors, systems, organizations, machines, platforms, or other entities present in the contextual environment. TREPS governs their formal association and participation role within the event. Therefore: Actor in Context ≠ Event Participant Determination. TRECS Boundary with TRVAS — Tax-Relevant Value Association Standard TRECS may identify that value conditions are contextually relevant. TRVAS governs the formal association of governed value results with the tax-relevant event. Therefore: Value Context ≠ Event-to-Value Association. TRECS Boundary with TRERLS — Tax-Relevant Event Relationship Standard TRECS may identify contextual relationships among surrounding activities and conditions. TRERLS governs formal relationships among governed tax-relevant events. Therefore: Context Relationship ≠ Event Relationship. TRECS Boundary with TREDS — Tax-Relevant Event Determination Standard TRECS establishes context readiness. TREDS determines whether sufficient governed event structure exists for formal determination that a Tax-Relevant Event exists for downstream taxation evaluation. Therefore: Context Sufficiency ≠ Event Determination. TRECS Boundary with Jurisdiction-Specific Tax Systems TRECS may provide governed contextual information to downstream systems. It does not determine: legal taxability; tax jurisdiction; tax nexus; taxpayer status; permanent establishment; tax residence; tax source; tax base; valuation under tax law; tax rate; exemption; deduction; allowance; liability; filing obligation; payment obligation; enforcement consequence. The boundary is absolute within TREGA™: TREGA™ governs the event. The jurisdiction governs the tax. Cross-Architecture Boundary TRECS may interact with other OOF® architectures without absorbing their governed spaces. ORA™ — Operational Reality Architecture Establishes what actually happened operationally. TRECS determines which governed operational conditions are contextually relevant to the occurrence entering TREGA™. ASGA™ — Autonomous Systems Governance Architecture Governs autonomous-system operation and execution. TRECS may consume relevant autonomous-operation results as Event Context. OBIDENITY® — Origin-Bound Identity Governance Architecture® Governs identity, origin, ownership, authority, permission, and provenance. TRECS may reference those governed results without redefining them. VFM® — Value Flow Mechanism Governs what happens to value throughout its lifecycle. TRECS may identify value-related context without governing value itself. CLA® Governs classification where formal classification is required. TRECS may consume classification results. INTEGROS® Governs integrity. TRECS does not independently establish the integrity of every contextual source. ADIT® Governs audit and evidence. TRECS does not replace evidence governance. VALIDOS™ Governs validation. TRECS may consume validated contextual results where required. AGA™ Governs accountability. Contextual association does not determine accountability. The architectural principle is: TRECS consumes governed reality where available; it does not recreate every governance architecture inside Event Context. Foundational Principles An occurrence should not enter event governance as an isolated signal when material context determines its meaning. Occurrence ≠ Context. Context ≠ Event. Governed Context ≠ Governed Tax-Relevant Event. Event Context ≠ Event Recognition. Context Scope ≠ Event Boundary. Context Sufficiency ≠ Absolute Reality Completeness. More Context ≠ Better Governed Context. Contextual Relationship ≠ Causal Determination. Multiple Contexts ≠ Multiple Events. Shared Context ≠ Single Event. Economic Context ≠ Tax Determination. Transactional Context ≠ Taxable Transaction. Digital Operation ≠ Tax-Relevant Event by Default. Machine Execution Context ≠ Actor Identity. Value Context ≠ Value Governance. Cross-Border Context ≠ Tax Jurisdiction. Jurisdiction-Relevant Context ≠ Jurisdiction Determination. Context Change ≠ New Event by Default. Current Context must not rewrite Historical Context. Context Correction ≠ Historical Erasure. Unknown Context ≠ Assumed Context. Data Model Simplicity ≠ Reality Simplicity. Context Information Volume ≠ Context Governance Quality. Context Association ≠ Accountability Determination. Context-Ready ≠ Event-Recognized. Tax rules may consume governed context; they should not redefine operational reality. The same governed context may support multiple legitimate jurisdictional evaluations without TRECS deciding which evaluation is legally correct. Canonical Closing Statement Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard establishes the foundational contextual governance layer of TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ by determining how the economic, operational, organizational, transactional, technological, digital, infrastructural, autonomous, machine-generated, and value-related environment surrounding an observed occurrence becomes sufficiently identified, scoped, related, maintained, and qualified for subsequent event governance. Through governance of contextual relevance, scope, sufficiency, relationships, granularity, uncertainty, ambiguity, change, continuity, historical context, multi-context activity, cross-border environments, digital operations, autonomous-system context, and contextual interoperability, TRECS prevents isolated signals, incomplete surrounding information, excessive context, current-state assumptions, or jurisdiction-specific tax rules from prematurely defining what an occurrence represents. The Standard preserves the critical distinctions between occurrence and context, context and event, Context Scope and Event Boundary, contextual actors and governed participants, Value Context and Value Governance, Cross-Border Context and Tax Jurisdiction, and Context Readiness and Event Recognition. By establishing a governed contextual basis that can remain methodologically consistent while downstream tax laws, jurisdictions, tax rates, reporting requirements, and legal interpretations differ, TRECS creates the first governed layer through which real-world and digital occurrences can enter TREGA™ without allowing the taxation system to redefine the reality it is subsequently required to evaluate. TRECS therefore establishes not whether an occurrence is taxable, nor even whether it has yet become a Tax-Relevant Event, but the governed contextual environment required before that question can legitimately proceed to the next stage of the architecture. Module Architecture → Event Context Identification Module (ECIM) → Event Context Scope Module (ECSM) → Event Context Relationship Module (ECRM) → Event Context Change Module (ECCHM) → Event Context Continuity Module (ECCM) Related Documents → About Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard (TRECS)

title: OOF™ Tax-Relevant Event Determination Standard - (TREDS)
text: OOF™ Tax-Relevant Event Determination Standard - (TREDS) Tax-Relevant Event Determination Standard - (TREDS) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: TREDS — Tax-Relevant Event Determination Standard Operational Layer: Tax-Relevant Event Determination Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Parent Standard Governed Space: Tax-Relevant Event Determination Primary Governed Object: Tax-Relevant Event Determination Origin ID: TREGA-TREDS-010 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 2 September 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language Canonical Definition The Tax-Relevant Event Determination Standard (TREDS) governs how an event that has passed through the preceding TREGA™ governance layers is formally evaluated and determined to constitute a sufficiently governed Tax-Relevant Event for downstream record governance and jurisdiction-specific taxation analysis. TREDS establishes whether the governed Event structure is sufficiently complete, coherent, attributable, bounded, temporally and spatially situated, participatory, value-associated, relationship-aware, and methodologically reliable to become a formal Tax-Relevant Event within TREGA™. Its principal transition is: Governed Event Relationship Structure ↓ Tax-Relevant Event Determination ↓ Determined Tax-Relevant Event TREDS does not determine whether tax is legally due. It does not determine the applicable jurisdiction, taxpayer, tax base, tax rate, exemption, deduction, tax point, filing obligation, or legal tax consequence. Its foundational distinction is: Event Determination ≠ Taxability Determination. Purpose The purpose of TREDS is to create a formal governance threshold between: an event that has been progressively structured by TREGA™ and: an event that is sufficiently governed to be treated as Tax-Relevant for downstream taxation analysis. Without this threshold, downstream systems may consume: incomplete events; unresolved events; contradictory events; technically generated records; improperly bounded activities; uncertain participant structures; unresolved Value Associations; or unstable Event Relationships as though they were fully governed taxation inputs. TREDS prevents that failure. It establishes a formal determination layer before the event becomes a governed tax-relevant record. Core Question Has the event been governed sufficiently across the TREGA™ lifecycle to become a formal Tax-Relevant Event suitable for downstream jurisdiction-specific taxation analysis without determining the tax itself? Architecture Position TREDS is Parent Standard 10 of 12 within TREGA™. Its immediate position is: Event Relationships ↓ Event Determination ↓ Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record TREDS consumes the governed structures produced by the first nine Parent Standards and determines whether the event is ready to become a formal governed Tax-Relevant Event. Complete TREGA™ Governance Flow 1. TRECS — Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard → 2. TRERS — Tax-Relevant Event Recognition Standard → 3. TREFS — Tax-Relevant Event Formation Standard → 4. TREBS — Tax-Relevant Event Boundary Standard → 5. TRETS — Tax-Relevant Event Timing Standard → 6. TRELS — Tax-Relevant Event Location Standard → 7. TREPS — Tax-Relevant Event Participation Standard → 8. TRVAS — Tax-Relevant Value Association Standard → 9. TRERLS — Tax-Relevant Event Relationship Standard → 10. TREDS — Tax-Relevant Event Determination Standard ← CURRENT → 11. TREGS — Tax-Relevant Event Record Governance Standard → 12. TRECLS — Tax-Relevant Event Lifecycle & Continuity Standard The complete system position remains: Real-World / Digital Event ↓ TREGA™ ↓ Governed Tax-Relevant Event ↓ Jurisdictional Tax Rules ↓ Tax Determination ↓ Reporting / Compliance Governed Input TREDS consumes the governed outputs produced by preceding TREGA™ layers. These may include: Governed Event Context; Governed Event Recognition; Governed Event Formation; Governed Event Boundary; Governed Event Timing; Governed Event Location; Governed Event Participation; Governed Value Association; Governed Event Relationship Structure; associated uncertainty states; conflict states; correction history; and relevant governance traceability. TREDS does not recreate those determinations. It evaluates whether, taken together, they are sufficient for formal Event Determination. Principal Governance Transition The canonical transition is: Governed Event Relationship Structure + Upstream Governance State ↓ Determination Readiness ↓ Determination Conditions ↓ Determination Decision ↓ Determination Uncertainty / Reconsideration ↓ Determined Tax-Relevant Event The result may be: Tax-Relevant Event Determined; Determination Deferred; Determination Conditional; Determination Uncertain; Determination Conflicted; Determination Rejected; or Determination Reconsideration Required. Tax-Relevant Event Determination Tax-Relevant Event Determination is the formal TREGA™ governance decision that an event has been sufficiently governed to proceed as a Tax-Relevant Event. It answers: Is this event sufficiently governed for taxation systems to evaluate it? It does not answer: Is this event legally taxable? That distinction is fundamental. Tax-Relevant Event ≠ Legally Taxable Event. Determination Readiness An event shall not enter formal Determination merely because it exists in an operational system. TREDS shall first establish whether the event is ready for determination. Readiness may require that all materially necessary upstream governance areas are sufficiently established. These include, where applicable: Context; Recognition; Formation; Boundary; Timing; Location; Participation; Value Association; Event Relationships. Event Presence ≠ Determination Readiness. Readiness Completeness Determination readiness requires sufficient completeness for the specific event. This does not require infinite or total information. It requires sufficient governed information to support a defensible determination. Determination Completeness ≠ Total Data Capture. Missing immaterial information shall not automatically block determination. Missing materially necessary information shall. Readiness Coherence Upstream governance outputs shall be sufficiently coherent. For example: Event Boundary should not contradict Formation; Timing should not contradict the governed Event structure; Participant structure should fit the Event; Value Association should refer to the governed Event; Event Relationships should not conflict with Event Identity. Material contradictions may prevent determination. Data Availability ≠ Governance Coherence. Readiness Stability The event should be sufficiently stable to support formal determination. A structure undergoing unresolved Formation, Boundary, Participation, Value, or Relationship reconsideration may not yet be ready. However, perfect permanence is not required. Governance Stability ≠ Immutability. Determination Conditions TREDS shall govern the conditions that must be satisfied before a Tax-Relevant Event can be formally determined. Conditions may include: Event Identity sufficiently established; Event Formation sufficiently governed; Event Boundary sufficiently governed; Event Timing sufficiently established; Event Location sufficiently represented where material; Event Participation sufficiently represented; material Value Association sufficiently governed; material Event Relationships sufficiently governed; material conflicts sufficiently resolved or explicitly qualified; material uncertainty sufficiently controlled; and sufficient traceability for downstream reconstruction. The conditions may vary according to event complexity. The standard governs sufficiency, not identical data volume for every event. Material Sufficiency TREDS operates on material sufficiency. The relevant question is not whether every possible data field exists. The question is whether the governed Event representation is sufficient for downstream taxation evaluation without requiring the tax system to reconstruct Event Reality itself. More Data ≠ Greater Determination Quality by default. Event Integrity at Determination TREDS shall evaluate whether the event remains internally coherent across its governed layers. An event should not be formally determined where: Event Identity is unresolved; Boundary materially conflicts with Formation; Value Association materially contradicts Event structure; Participant structure is fundamentally uncertain; or material relationships remain incompatible with the event representation. Determination is therefore a governance synthesis point. It is not merely another classification label. Determination Decision The Determination Decision establishes the formal status of the governed Event. Possible decisions include: Tax-Relevant Event Determined Determination Conditional Determination Deferred Determination Rejected Determination Uncertain Determination Conflicted Determination Reconsideration Required The decision shall be explicit. Silence shall not be interpreted as determination. No Decision ≠ Positive Determination. Positive Determination A positive determination means that the event is sufficiently governed to become a formal Tax-Relevant Event. It means: Eligible for downstream jurisdiction-specific taxation analysis. It does not mean: Tax legally due. Therefore: Positive Event Determination ≠ Positive Tax Determination. Conditional Determination An event may be sufficiently governed for downstream processing while one or more explicitly bounded conditions remain. Conditional determination may be appropriate where uncertainty is controlled and does not invalidate the Event structure. The condition shall remain visible. Conditional Determination ≠ Unqualified Determination. Deferred Determination Determination shall be deferred where materially necessary upstream governance remains incomplete. Examples may include unresolved: Event Boundary; Event Participation; Value Association; Event Relationship; or material Event Identity questions. Deferred Determination ≠ Rejected Event. The event may become determinable after additional governance. Rejected Determination TREDS may reject formal Tax-Relevant Event Determination where the available governed structure does not support the existence of a sufficiently constituted Tax-Relevant Event. Rejection may result where: Recognition was incorrect; Formation fails; Event Boundary cannot be established; the apparent event is merely a technical artifact; or another fundamental governance failure exists. Determination Rejection ≠ Legal Non-Taxability. It means the event does not currently satisfy TREGA™ requirements for a governed Tax-Relevant Event. Determination Uncertainty Uncertainty does not automatically invalidate an event. TREDS shall distinguish between: immaterial uncertainty; bounded uncertainty; material uncertainty; unresolved uncertainty. The effect on determination shall depend on whether the uncertainty prevents reliable downstream taxation analysis. Uncertainty ≠ Automatic Determination Failure. Material Uncertainty Uncertainty becomes material where it could materially change the governed identity or structure of the Event. Examples may include uncertainty over: whether one or several events exist; which participant materially participated; which governed Value Result belongs to the event; which Event Boundary applies; or which relationship structure is valid. Material uncertainty may require deferral or conditional determination. Determination Conflict Conflicting upstream governance outputs may prevent reliable determination. For example: one system represents one event; another represents two events; one source identifies Participant A; another identifies Participant B; one Value Association conflicts with another. TREDS shall preserve material conflict. Conflict ≠ Permission to Select the Convenient Result. Conflict Resolution Boundary TREDS may evaluate whether a conflict prevents determination. It does not necessarily resolve the underlying subject matter itself. Where the conflict belongs to: Formation ↓ TREFS; Boundary ↓ TREBS; Timing ↓ TRETS; Location ↓ TRELS; Participation ↓ TREPS; Value Association ↓ TRVAS; Event Relationships ↓ TRERLS, the issue shall be referred to the authoritative upstream layer. TREDS governs determination impact, not ownership of every upstream issue. Determination Confidence TREDS may qualify confidence in the determination where useful. Possible states may include: High; Qualified; Limited; Conditional; Ambiguous; Conflicted; Unresolved. Confidence shall not replace the determination decision. Confidence Score ≠ Determination Decision. Determination Reasoning A formal Determination shall be supported by reconstructable governance reasoning. The reasoning should show: which event is being determined; which upstream governed outputs were relied upon; what material conditions were satisfied; what uncertainties remained; whether conflicts existed; and why the resulting determination state was reached. Determination Result Without Governance Basis ≠ Governed Determination. Determination Traceability The determination shall remain traceable to its upstream governance lineage. This allows downstream systems to understand not only that a Tax-Relevant Event exists, but how that conclusion was reached. Traceability supports: review; audit; correction; reconsideration; cross-system interoperability; and multi-jurisdiction evaluation. TREDS does not replace TREGS Event Record Governance. It establishes the determination information that TREGS will formally structure into the governed Event Record. Event Determination and Recognition Recognition identifies that an occurrence may require TREGA™ governance. Determination decides whether the fully governed Event is ready to become a Tax-Relevant Event. Therefore: Event Recognition ≠ Event Determination. TRERS is the entry recognition layer. TREDS is the formal downstream determination layer. Event Determination and Formation Formation establishes what constitutes the event. Determination evaluates whether that formed and subsequently governed event is sufficiently complete. Event Formation ≠ Event Determination. TREDS cannot compensate for defective Formation by declaring the event determined. Event Determination and Boundary Boundary establishes where the event begins and ends conceptually. TREDS consumes that result. Event Determination ≠ Event Boundary Determination. Event Determination and Timing TREDS does not determine Event Time. It evaluates whether the governed timing information is sufficient where timing is material. Event Determination ≠ Event Timing Determination. and: Event Determination ≠ Legal Tax Point Determination. Event Determination and Location TREDS may require sufficient Event Location information where material. However: Event Determination ≠ Tax Jurisdiction Determination. Event Location remains operationally governed by TRELS. Jurisdictional tax nexus remains downstream. Event Determination and Participation TREDS consumes the governed participation structure. It does not determine taxpayer status. Event Participant ≠ Taxpayer. and: Event Determination ≠ Taxpayer Determination. Event Determination and Value TREDS may require sufficient Value Association where materially relevant. It does not determine taxable value. Governed Value Association ≠ Taxable Value. and: Event Determination ≠ Tax Base Determination. Event Determination and Event Relationships TREDS consumes the Governed Event Relationship Structure from TRERLS. It evaluates whether relationship ambiguity or structural conflict prevents determination. It does not recreate the Event Relationship structure. Event Determination ≠ Event Relationship Redetermination. Determination of Independent Events Several strongly related events may each receive independent Tax-Relevant Event Determination. Relationship strength does not eliminate Event Identity. Related Events ≠ One Determined Event by default. Determination of Event Groups Events belonging to one Event Group may still require individual Event Determination where they retain separate Event Identities. Event Group ≠ Determination Unit by default. The governed Event Identity remains primary. Determination after Merge Where ERLMM establishes a governed Merge and Formation/Boundary governance support the resulting event, TREDS shall determine the resulting governed Event representation. Prior Event representations remain traceable. Merged Representation ≠ Historical Erasure. Determination after Split Where an event has been legitimately split, each resulting independently governed Event may require separate Determination. Split Result ≠ Automatic Positive Determination. Each resulting event must satisfy applicable TREDS conditions. Determination and Technical Records A technical record, transaction record, log entry, blockchain transaction, API call, database object, invoice line, or accounting entry is not automatically a determined Tax-Relevant Event. Technical Record ≠ Determined Tax-Relevant Event. TREDS evaluates the governed Event, not the technical artifact. Determination and Payments A payment may constitute an independently governed event, form part of another Event structure, or relate to several events. TREDS does not assume: Payment = Tax-Relevant Event without preceding TREGA™ governance. Determination and Invoices An invoice may provide evidence or operational structure. It does not itself establish Event Determination. Invoice ≠ Tax-Relevant Event by default. Determination and Contracts A contract may contextualize one or many events. It does not itself establish a determined event. Contract ≠ Tax-Relevant Event by default. Determination and Blockchain Transactions A blockchain transaction may correspond to: one event; part of one event; several event relationships; or a purely technical operation. Therefore: Blockchain Transaction ≠ Determined Tax-Relevant Event by default. TREDS relies on the complete governed Event structure. Determination and Smart Contracts Smart-contract execution does not automatically create one Tax-Relevant Event per call or transaction. Smart-Contract Execution ≠ Tax-Relevant Event Determination. Determination and AI Agents AI agents may initiate or execute large numbers of activities. TREDS determines governed Tax-Relevant Events rather than counting Agent Actions. Agent Action ≠ Tax-Relevant Event by default. Determination and Machine Activity Machines may generate millions of technical operations. Only those operational structures that pass TREGA™ governance may become determined Tax-Relevant Events. Machine Operation Count ≠ Tax-Relevant Event Count. Determination and Automation Automated classification or detection systems may propose a determination. They shall not substitute for the governance conditions of TREDS. Automated Classification ≠ Governed Event Determination. Determination and AI Confidence Scores AI systems may assign confidence or probability to a candidate Event. Such scores may inform governance. They do not constitute the Determination itself. Model Confidence ≠ Governance Determination. Cross-System Determination One event may be represented across several systems. TREDS shall determine the governed Event representation rather than treating each system record as a separate Event. System Record Count ≠ Event Count. Cross-Organization Determination The same broader Event may involve several organizations. TREDS may consume governed cross-organizational information without deciding ownership, accountability, or tax liability. Multiple Organizations ≠ Multiple Events by default. Cross-Border Determination An event may span several physical or digital locations. TREDS may still determine the event as Tax-Relevant without deciding which jurisdiction may tax it. Cross-Border Tax-Relevant Event ≠ Tax Jurisdiction Determination. Multi-Jurisdiction Readiness A central purpose of TREDS is to produce an event representation that can support more than one legitimate downstream jurisdictional evaluation. The canonical model is: One Determined Tax-Relevant Event ↓ Multiple Jurisdictional Tax Evaluations TREDS therefore seeks to preserve the governed Event Reality independently of later legal interpretation. Jurisdiction-Neutral Determination Determination conditions shall not be rewritten merely to fit one jurisdiction's tax law where the event is intended for jurisdiction-neutral TREGA™ governance. Legal rules may later consume the event differently. TREGA™ does not permit downstream law to retroactively redefine Event Reality. Jurisdictional Interpretation ≠ Event Determination Authority. Tax-Relevant ≠ Taxable This is the central boundary of TREDS. An event becomes Tax-Relevant when it is sufficiently governed for taxation analysis. It becomes legally taxable only if the applicable jurisdictional rules establish that legal consequence. The architecture therefore preserves: Tax-Relevant Event ↓ Jurisdictional Tax Evaluation ↓ Legal Tax Determination not: Tax-Relevant Event = Taxable Event Taxability Boundary TREDS shall never determine: whether a supply is taxable; whether income is taxable; whether a transfer is taxable; whether VAT is due; whether withholding applies; whether capital gains arise; whether an exemption applies; or whether any other legal tax consequence exists. These belong downstream. Tax Jurisdiction Boundary TREDS may determine that Location governance is sufficient for downstream evaluation. It does not select the taxing jurisdiction. Jurisdiction-Ready ≠ Jurisdiction-Determined. Taxpayer Boundary TREDS may consume governed Event Participation. It does not determine which participant is legally the taxpayer. Participant ≠ Taxpayer. Tax Base Boundary TREDS may require that material Event–Value relationships are governed. It does not convert governed value into legal Tax Base. Value Association ≠ Tax Base. Tax Rate Boundary No TREDS Determination contains a tax rate. Determined Tax-Relevant Event ≠ Tax Rate Determination. Tax Period Boundary Event Timing may be available. TREDS does not translate operational timing into a jurisdiction-specific taxable period. Operational Event Time ≠ Legal Tax Period. Legal Characterization Boundary Tax law may later characterize the event as: sale; service; transfer; income; disposal; import; export; remuneration; royalty; taxable benefit; or another legal category. TREDS does not make that legal characterization unless such terminology merely reflects an upstream governed operational description. Governed Event Determination ≠ Legal Tax Characterization. Determination Readiness Across Different Event Types TREDS shall remain adaptable to different Event structures. A simple event may require relatively little information. A distributed autonomous transaction may require significantly more governance. A multi-party cross-border event may require stronger Location, Participation, Value, and Relationship representation. The determination threshold shall therefore be materially sufficient, not mechanically identical. Proportional Governance Determination governance should be proportionate to: Event complexity; Event materiality; number of participants; distributed nature; value complexity; relationship complexity; uncertainty; cross-system fragmentation; and downstream reliance. More Complex Event ↓ Greater Governance Demand does not mean: More Complex Event ↓ Different Canonical Principle. The same governance boundary remains. Determination Reliance Once an event is positively determined, downstream systems may rely on that determination as confirmation that the Event has passed the required TREGA™ determination threshold. This reliance shall remain bounded. Downstream systems may rely on: the governed Event representation but not assume that TREDS has already made the legal tax decision. Downstream Tax Engine Consumption A downstream tax engine may consume a Determined Tax-Relevant Event and apply jurisdiction-specific rules. The canonical handoff is: Determined Tax-Relevant Event ↓ Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record ↓ Jurisdiction-Ready Tax-Relevant Event ↓ Tax Engine The tax engine should not need to reconstruct basic Event Reality from raw operational records. That is one of the principal infrastructure purposes of TREGA™. Determination Reconsideration A prior Event Determination may require reconsideration where materially relevant governance changes. Examples include: corrected Event Boundary; corrected Participant; revised Value Association; newly discovered Event Relationship; Merge or Split; newly available operational information; or correction of material upstream error. TREDS shall preserve both the prior and reconsidered determination states. Reconsideration ≠ Historical Erasure. Determination Supersession A new Determination may supersede an earlier one. Supersession shall not erase the historical record. Superseded Determination ≠ Deleted Determination. TRECLS will govern longer-term lifecycle continuity. Determination Correction Where a determination contains an error that does not require complete reconsideration of Event structure, a governed correction may be issued. Correction shall remain traceable. Correction ≠ Silent Replacement. Determination Finality TREDS may establish operational finality sufficient for downstream use. This does not imply absolute legal finality. Future corrections, evidence, or upstream governance changes may justify reconsideration. Governance Finality ≠ Legal Finality. Determination Interoperability A Determined Tax-Relevant Event should be representable across systems without losing its core governance meaning. Interoperability requires preservation of: Event identity; determination status; relevant upstream governance references; uncertainty; conflicts; and determination lineage. Formal record structure belongs to TREGS. Determination Auditability A determination should be reviewable. The relevant reviewer should be able to establish: what event was determined; on what governed basis; what conditions were satisfied; what uncertainty remained; who or what governance process produced the result; and whether the determination was later corrected or reconsidered. ADIT® may govern broader audit and evidential requirements. TREDS owns the determination governance itself. Determination Validation Boundary VALIDOS™ may validate a methodology, system, evidence structure, or determination process. TREDS does not replace validation architecture. Event Determination ≠ Validation. Determination Integrity Boundary INTEGROS® may govern broader integrity requirements. TREDS requires sufficient determination integrity but does not absorb the full integrity architecture. Determination Accountability Boundary AGA™ may govern accountability for decisions, roles, and failures. TREDS determines Event status, not accountability. Determination Authority ≠ Accountability Assignment. Cross-Architecture Governance Boundary TREDS shall preserve the following ownership structure: ORA™ Governs what occurred operationally. TREFS Governs Event Formation. TREBS Governs Event Boundary. TRETS Governs Event Timing. TRELS Governs Event Location. TREPS Governs Event Participation. TRVAS Governs Event–Value Association. TRERLS Governs relationships among Events. TREDS Governs whether the resulting Event is sufficiently governed to become a formal Tax-Relevant Event. TREGS Governs the resulting Event Record. TRECLS Governs Event lifecycle and continuity. OBIDENITY® Governs identity, origin, ownership, authority, permission, and provenance. VFM® — Value Flow Mechanism Governs what happened to value throughout its lifecycle. ADIT® Governs evidence and auditability. VALIDOS™ Governs validation. AGA™ Governs accountability. Jurisdiction-Specific Tax System Determines legal tax consequences. Governance States TREDS may represent: Determination Not Ready Determination Readiness Under Review Determination Ready Determination Conditions Incomplete Determination Conditions Satisfied Determination Conditional Determination Deferred Determination Rejected Determination Uncertain Determination Ambiguous Determination Conflicted Determination Under Reconsideration Determination Corrected Determination Superseded Tax-Relevant Event Determined Determined Tax-Relevant Event Ready for Record Governance Governance Requirements TREDS shall require that: Event Determination occurs only after materially necessary upstream TREGA™ governance; Event Determination remains distinct from Event Recognition; Event Determination remains distinct from Event Formation; Event Determination remains distinct from Taxability Determination; Determination Readiness is explicit; material determination conditions are identifiable; completeness is assessed according to material sufficiency rather than total data capture; materially contradictory upstream governance is not silently ignored; determination uncertainty remains visible; determination conflict remains visible; positive, conditional, deferred, rejected, and reconsidered determination states remain distinguishable; positive Event Determination does not imply positive Tax Determination; tax jurisdiction remains downstream; taxpayer status remains downstream; Tax Base remains downstream; Tax Rate remains downstream; tax period remains downstream; legal tax characterization remains downstream; downstream systems can identify the governance basis for the determination; determination reasoning remains reconstructable; determination corrections remain traceable; determination reconsideration preserves prior history; supersession does not erase prior determination states; cross-system representation does not create duplicate Event Determinations; cross-border Event Determination remains jurisdiction-neutral; AI-generated or automated determinations remain subject to TREDS governance; and the resulting Determined Tax-Relevant Event is suitable for TREGS Record Governance. Governance Logic IF the governed Event has not completed materially necessary upstream TREGA™ governance, THEN formal Tax-Relevant Event Determination shall not occur. IF materially necessary Event Context, Formation, Boundary, Timing, Location, Participation, Value Association, or Event Relationship governance remains unresolved, THEN Determination shall be deferred, conditioned, or otherwise qualified according to material impact. IF the governed Event structure is sufficiently complete, coherent, stable, and reconstructable for downstream taxation analysis, THEN a positive Tax-Relevant Event Determination may be issued. IF uncertainty remains but does not materially undermine Event Identity or downstream interpretability, THEN Conditional or Qualified Determination may be permitted. IF material uncertainty prevents reliable Event interpretation, THEN Determination shall remain deferred, uncertain, or unresolved. IF upstream governance outputs materially conflict, THEN the conflict shall remain visible and the authoritative upstream layer shall be invoked where required. IF the apparent Event is only a technical artifact and does not satisfy Event Formation or Boundary governance, THEN Determination shall be rejected. IF Merge or Split has changed the governed Event structure, THEN the resulting Event representation shall undergo appropriate Determination rather than inheriting positive Determination automatically. IF an automated system proposes a determination, THEN that proposal shall remain subject to the same TREDS conditions as a human-generated determination. IF a positive Determination is established, THEN the resulting Determined Tax-Relevant Event shall proceed to TREGS for Governed Event Record construction. IF later materially relevant information changes the Event structure, THEN the Determination may be reconsidered without erasing its prior governance history. Governance Outputs TREDS may produce: Determination Readiness State; Determination Condition Set; Determination Sufficiency State; Determination Coherence State; Determination Stability State; Determination Decision; Positive Determination; Conditional Determination; Deferred Determination; Rejected Determination; Determination Uncertainty State; Determination Conflict State; Determination Confidence State; Determination Reasoning Record; Determination Traceability Reference; Determination Correction; Determination Reconsideration Record; Determination Supersession Record; Jurisdiction-Ready Evaluation Indicator; and the principal output: Determined Tax-Relevant Event. Critical Distinctions Event Determination ≠ Taxability Determination. Tax-Relevant Event ≠ Legally Taxable Event. Event Presence ≠ Determination Readiness. Determination Completeness ≠ Total Data Capture. Data Availability ≠ Governance Coherence. Governance Stability ≠ Immutability. More Data ≠ Greater Determination Quality by default. No Decision ≠ Positive Determination. Positive Event Determination ≠ Positive Tax Determination. Conditional Determination ≠ Unqualified Determination. Deferred Determination ≠ Rejected Event. Determination Rejection ≠ Legal Non-Taxability. Uncertainty ≠ Automatic Determination Failure. Conflict ≠ Permission to Select the Convenient Result. Confidence Score ≠ Determination Decision. Determination Result Without Governance Basis ≠ Governed Determination. Event Recognition ≠ Event Determination. Event Formation ≠ Event Determination. Event Determination ≠ Event Boundary Determination. Event Determination ≠ Event Timing Determination. Event Determination ≠ Legal Tax Point Determination. Event Determination ≠ Tax Jurisdiction Determination. Event Determination ≠ Taxpayer Determination. Governed Value Association ≠ Taxable Value. Event Determination ≠ Tax Base Determination. Event Determination ≠ Event Relationship Redetermination. Related Events ≠ One Determined Event by default. Event Group ≠ Determination Unit by default. Merged Representation ≠ Historical Erasure. Split Result ≠ Automatic Positive Determination. Technical Record ≠ Determined Tax-Relevant Event. Invoice ≠ Tax-Relevant Event by default. Contract ≠ Tax-Relevant Event by default. Blockchain Transaction ≠ Determined Tax-Relevant Event by default. Smart-Contract Execution ≠ Tax-Relevant Event Determination. Agent Action ≠ Tax-Relevant Event by default. Machine Operation Count ≠ Tax-Relevant Event Count. Automated Classification ≠ Governed Event Determination. Model Confidence ≠ Governance Determination. System Record Count ≠ Event Count. Cross-Border Tax-Relevant Event ≠ Tax Jurisdiction Determination. Jurisdictional Interpretation ≠ Event Determination Authority. Jurisdiction-Ready ≠ Jurisdiction-Determined. Participant ≠ Taxpayer. Value Association ≠ Tax Base. Operational Event Time ≠ Legal Tax Period. Governed Event Determination ≠ Legal Tax Characterization. Governance Finality ≠ Legal Finality. Event Determination ≠ Validation. Determination Authority ≠ Accountability Assignment. Enterprise Application TREDS establishes the decision threshold between governed Event construction and downstream tax infrastructure. A canonical enterprise path is: ERP / Commerce / Banking / Marketplace / Blockchain / AI Agent / Machine System → TREGA™ Event Governance → Governed Event Relationship Structure → TREDS — Tax-Relevant Event Determination → Determined Tax-Relevant Event → TREGS — Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record → TRECLS — Jurisdiction-Ready Event Lifecycle → Country / Jurisdiction Tax Engine → Legal Tax Determination This separation allows organizations to construct one governed Event Reality layer that can be consumed by multiple tax systems without forcing each tax engine to independently reconstruct what happened. Operational Value TREDS provides a practical control point for organizations managing complex economic activity. It prevents: raw system records entering tax engines as if they were governed events; inconsistent Event representations across systems; unresolved Event Boundaries entering legal tax determination; unknown participants being silently treated as taxpayers; Value Associations being treated automatically as Tax Base; technical blockchain operations being counted automatically as taxable events; AI-agent actions becoming tax events merely because they were machine-generated; and jurisdiction-specific interpretations from rewriting the underlying Event Reality. The result is a reusable, jurisdiction-neutral Event Determination layer. Canonical Boundary TREDS owns the governance of Determination Readiness, Determination Conditions, Determination Sufficiency, Determination Decision, Determination Uncertainty, Determination Conflict, Determination Qualification, Determination Reasoning, Determination Reconsideration, Determination Correction, Determination Supersession, and the formal establishment of a Determined Tax-Relevant Event. TREDS does not own Event Context, Recognition, Formation, Boundary, Timing, Location, Participation, Value lifecycle, Value Association, Event Relationship construction, Event Record structure, Event lifecycle continuity, identity, ownership, provenance, accountability, liability, tax jurisdiction, taxpayer status, legal tax point, taxable value, Tax Base, Tax Rate, exemption, deduction, Tax Liability, reporting obligation, collection, enforcement, or any other jurisdiction-specific legal tax consequence. Its governance begins when the Event Relationship structure and materially necessary upstream TREGA™ outputs are available for formal Determination. Its governance ends when the event has received a sufficiently governed Determination state for downstream Event Record Governance under TREGS. Canonical Handoff TRERLS — Governed Event Relationship Structure ↓ TREDS — Determined Tax-Relevant Event ↓ TREGS — Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record Canonical Closing Statement TREDS establishes the point at which a governed event becomes sufficiently complete, coherent, and reconstructable to enter taxation infrastructure without allowing event governance to become tax law. Its purpose is not to decide whether tax is due. Its purpose is to ensure that when a jurisdiction asks what happened, the event presented to that jurisdiction has already been methodologically governed. Tax-Relevant Event ≠ Legally Taxable Event. Event Determination ≠ Taxability Determination. Jurisdiction-Ready ≠ Jurisdiction-Determined. TREGA™ governs the event. The jurisdiction governs the tax.
