title: OOF™ Tax-Relevant Event Formation Standard - (TREFS)
text: OOF™ Tax-Relevant Event Formation Standard - (TREFS) Tax-Relevant Event Formation Standard - (TREFS) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: Tax-Relevant Event Formation Standard (TREFS) Operational Layer: Tax-Relevant Event Formation Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Parent Standard Governed Space: Tax-Relevant Event Formation Origin ID: TREGA-TREFS-003 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 30 August 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Tax-Relevant Event Formation Standard (TREFS) governs how a sufficiently recognized real-world, economic, operational, transactional, digital, autonomous, machine-generated, or value-affecting occurrence is transformed into a coherent governed event structure capable of progressing through the subsequent stages of the TREGA™ lifecycle. TREFS establishes the governance conditions through which recognized occurrence elements are structurally organized into an Event Formation, including the identification of materially relevant formation components, their assembly, material formation dependencies, operational root association, and the integrity of the resulting formation. The Standard establishes the transition from: Recognized Occurrence → Governed Formed Event without determining the final Event Boundary, Event Timing, Event Location, Event Participation, Event-to-Value Association, relationships among governed events, legal taxability, Tax Jurisdiction, or any jurisdiction-specific tax consequence. TREFS therefore governs how the event is formed, not how the event is legally taxed. Operational Role TREGA™ must distinguish between recognizing that an occurrence warrants further governance and establishing what governed event can legitimately be formed from that occurrence. Recognition alone does not create a sufficiently structured event. A recognized occurrence may involve: multiple operational actions; several technical records; distributed system representations; machine-generated operations; autonomous execution; several transaction stages; related value-affecting actions; dependencies on other activity; multiple possible structural interpretations. TREFS establishes the formation layer through which these recognized elements become a coherent governed event structure. Its narrow task is: to establish whether and how a recognized occurrence can be structurally formed into a governed event suitable for subsequent Event Boundary governance. Governance Flow Governed Recognized Occurrence → Formation Component Identification → Formation Assembly → Formation Dependency Establishment → Formation Root Association → Formation Integrity → Governed Formed Event TREFS begins with the governed output of TRERS — Tax-Relevant Event Recognition Standard. It ends when a sufficiently coherent Governed Formed Event exists for progression into TREBS — Tax-Relevant Event Boundary Standard. Governed Space TREFS governs Tax-Relevant Event Formation, including: formation readiness; event-forming component identification; formation component qualification; formation component differentiation; event assembly; formation coherence; formation dependency identification; formation dependency qualification; operational formation root association; distributed event formation; machine-generated event formation; autonomous event formation; composite formation; formation ambiguity; formation conflict; formation uncertainty; formation integrity; formation insufficiency; formation reconsideration; formation traceability. TREFS establishes whether a recognized occurrence can legitimately become a Governed Formed Event capable of entering Event Boundary governance. Operational Scope TREFS may apply to recognized occurrences originating from: commercial transactions; financial activity; payments; transfers; production processes; supply chains; service delivery; digital platforms; marketplaces; APIs; software systems; digital assets; banking infrastructure; enterprise systems; autonomous agents; AI systems; robots; machine-to-machine activity; automated marketplaces; distributed systems; infrastructure operations; hybrid physical-digital environments; future machine economies. TREFS remains actor-neutral and technology-neutral. A formed event does not require a human initiator. Nor does the number of machine actions, technical records, accounting entries, or system messages determine the number or structure of formed events. Event Formation Principle Recognition establishes that an occurrence warrants further governance. Formation establishes what governed event structure can legitimately be constructed from it. Therefore: Recognition ≠ Formation. TRERS may establish: this occurrence should proceed into Event Formation. TREFS must then establish: what governed event structure can legitimately be formed from this recognized occurrence? This distinction prevents recognition decisions from prematurely defining the structure of the event. Recognized Occurrence ≠ Formed Event A recognized occurrence is an occurrence that has passed the recognition governance layer. It has not yet necessarily acquired sufficient internal structure to function as a governed event. Therefore: Recognized Occurrence ↓ Eligible for Event Formation not: Recognized Occurrence ↓ Event Structure Automatically Established. TREFS creates the governed transition between these states. Formation Readiness A recognized occurrence becomes formation-ready when sufficient governed information exists to begin structural Event Formation. Formation readiness may depend on whether: the occurrence is sufficiently recognized; materially relevant occurrence information is available; candidate formation elements can be identified; material structural ambiguity is visible; distributed representations can be sufficiently related; formation can proceed without inventing unsupported event structure. Formation readiness does not mean that formation has already been completed. Therefore: Formation-Ready ≠ Formed. Event Formation Components A recognized occurrence may contain several materially relevant elements that contribute to formation of the governed event. These may arise from: operational actions; transactions; transfers; service execution; production; delivery; settlement; resource allocation; digital operations; autonomous actions; machine execution; state changes; other materially relevant occurrence elements. TREFS requires those elements to be governed as part of Event Formation rather than allowing technical system structure to define the event automatically. Therefore: Recorded Element ≠ Event Formation Component by Default. And: Event Formation Component ≠ Independent Event by Default. Formation Assembly Identified formation elements must be capable of being organized into a coherent event structure. The existence of several related records does not itself establish how those records should be assembled. Records may represent: different views of the same activity; different stages of one occurrence; dependencies; duplicate representations; separate operational actions; components of a larger event structure. TREFS therefore requires governed assembly rather than automatic aggregation. Technical Association ≠ Event Formation. Similarly: Shared Identifier ≠ Common Event Structure by Default. Formation Dependencies Event Formation may depend on activity, conditions, or structures that support the occurrence without necessarily becoming part of the formed event itself. A service may depend on prior authorization. A payment may depend on an account relationship. An autonomous execution may depend on prior delegation. A machine transaction may depend on infrastructure activation. TREFS must preserve the distinction between what is structurally necessary to understand formation and what ultimately belongs inside the event. Therefore: Formation Dependency ≠ Event Membership. The final extent of the event belongs to subsequent Event Boundary governance. Event Formation Root A formed event must remain capable of being associated with the operational occurrence from which its formation originates. TREFS therefore governs association with an Event Formation Root sufficient to anchor the event structure within the recognized operational reality. The Event Formation Root is an operational formation concept. It is not an identity-origin concept. Therefore: Event Root ≠ Identity Origin. Likewise: Root Association ≠ Provenance Governance. Identity origin, ownership, authority, permission, and provenance remain governed by the architectures that own those spaces. Operational Root ≠ Legal Tax Point The operational root of Event Formation does not establish when tax legally arises. The operational action that anchors an event may differ from: invoice date; payment date; delivery date; accounting date; statutory tax point; reporting period. Therefore: Event Formation Root ≠ Legal Tax Point. TREFS establishes structural origin within Event Formation. It does not establish jurisdiction-specific tax timing. Formation Coherence A formed event must represent a coherent structure rather than an arbitrary collection of related data. Formation coherence requires that materially included elements possess a legitimate structural relationship to the recognized occurrence. TREFS must prevent event formation based solely on: database proximity; shared identifiers; common accounts; common participants; similar timestamps; common infrastructure; common software processes; technical workflow membership. These characteristics may support formation analysis. They do not independently establish Event Formation. One Process ≠ One Event One operational or commercial process may generate several events. Likewise, several operational steps may collectively contribute to one event. For example: Order ↓ Authorization ↓ Production ↓ Delivery ↓ Settlement may represent several system stages around one broader activity. TREGA™ must not assume that each stage is an independent event. Nor may it assume that the entire process necessarily forms one event. Therefore: One Process ≠ One Event by Default. and: Multiple Process Steps ≠ Multiple Events by Default. Distributed Event Formation A recognized occurrence may be represented across multiple systems. For example: Platform A ↓ Payment Infrastructure B ↓ Service Provider C ↓ Enterprise System D Each system may contain only part of the operational representation. TREFS must permit a governed event to be formed from distributed occurrence information where the structural basis is sufficiently established. Therefore: Distributed Records ≠ Distributed Events by Default. and: Multiple System Representations ≠ Multiple Formed Events. Machine-Generated Event Formation Machine environments can produce extremely large numbers of recognized actions. An autonomous system may perform: API operations; resource reservations; machine instructions; service invocations; transfers; allocations; settlements; releases; automated purchases. TREFS must prevent the technical granularity of machine execution from becoming the granularity of Event Formation. Therefore: Machine Operation ≠ Independent Formed Event by Default. A machine-generated event must be formed according to governed structural reality rather than computational activity volume. Autonomous Event Formation A formed event may originate from activity performed without immediate human initiation. TREFS therefore supports event formation involving: autonomous agents; AI systems; robots; automated marketplaces; autonomous infrastructure; machine coordination systems. TREFS does not determine legal personhood, responsibility, taxpayer status, ownership, authority, or liability of autonomous actors. Its responsibility remains structural Event Formation. Therefore: Autonomous Formation ≠ Autonomous Tax Liability. Composite Event Formation Some recognized occurrences may contain multiple materially connected elements that collectively support one event formation. TREFS must permit such composite structures where a legitimate formation basis exists. However, the existence of a composite formation does not predetermine the final Event Boundary or later relationships among events. Therefore: Composite Formation ≠ Final Event Boundary. Formation Ambiguity The same recognized occurrence may sometimes support more than one plausible formation structure. For example: a distributed service may appear as: one composite occurrence; several sequential operational occurrences; several technically independent but economically connected actions. TREFS must preserve material formation ambiguity where available information cannot yet justify one structure. It must not select a formation merely because one structure is easier for the implementing system to process. Formation Uncertainty Where the available information is insufficient to establish a legitimate formation structure, TREFS must preserve uncertainty. A formation may remain: Formation Unresolved where the architecture cannot legitimately establish a sufficiently coherent formed event. This prevents structural uncertainty from becoming artificial event certainty. Formation States A TREGA™ implementation may represent formation through governance states such as: 1. Formation Ready 2. Formation Under Construction 3. Formation Unresolved 4. Formation Structurally Established 5. Formation Integrity Insufficient 6. Governed Formed Event 7. Formation Reconsidered These states represent Event Formation governance status. They do not represent legal tax status. Formation Integrity A formed event must possess sufficient structural integrity to proceed into Event Boundary governance. Formation Integrity concerns whether the resulting formation is sufficiently coherent as an event structure. It does not determine whether every underlying claim has been independently validated or audited. Therefore: Formation Integrity ≠ Validation. and: Formation Integrity ≠ Audit Determination. Where appropriate, TREFS may consume governed integrity, evidence, audit, or validation outputs from architectures that own those spaces. Formation Insufficiency TREFS must permit formation to remain insufficient where a recognized occurrence cannot yet be legitimately transformed into a coherent event structure. Possible causes may include: missing material formation elements; unresolved structural contradictions; unresolved component relationships; insufficient root association; distributed information that cannot yet be reconciled; materially incompatible formation interpretations. Formation insufficiency prevents premature progression. However: Formation Insufficiency ≠ Recognition Rejection. The occurrence may have been legitimately recognized while still lacking sufficient information for Event Formation. Formation Reconsideration A formed event may later require reconsideration where: new structural information becomes available; previously unknown components are discovered; a dependency was incorrectly represented; the operational root was materially misidentified; distributed records reveal a different formation structure; the original formation basis is shown to be materially incorrect. Reconsideration must remain traceable. Therefore: Formation Reconsideration ≠ Historical Erasure. A revised formation should not silently remove the earlier governed state. Formation Traceability A Governed Formed Event should remain traceable to the recognition and formation basis from which it emerged. Where materially required, the system should preserve: the recognized occurrence reference; relevant formation inputs; formation basis; materially relevant formation components; structural assembly basis; material dependencies; root association; formation uncertainty; formation integrity state; formation reconsideration. This allows subsequent TREGA™ stages to understand: how the recognized occurrence became the formed event presented for Event Boundary governance. Formation Independence from Tax Rules TREFS must remain capable of forming the operational event independently of the jurisdiction-specific tax rule eventually applied to it. This is essential because the same Governed Formed Event may later be evaluated by several taxation systems. The event should not need to be structurally reconstructed merely because tax law changes. Therefore: Tax Rule Change ≠ Event Reformation by Default. Jurisdiction-Neutral Formation A formed event may contain operational characteristics relevant to several jurisdictions. TREFS may preserve those characteristics. It does not determine which jurisdiction has legal authority to tax the event. Therefore: Cross-Border Event Formation ≠ Tax Jurisdiction Determination. The same Governed Formed Event may later support multiple legitimate jurisdictional evaluations. This preserves the TREGA™ model: One Event ↓ One Governed Event Layer ↓ Multiple Jurisdictional Evaluations. Formation Readiness for Event Boundary A formation becomes ready for Event Boundary governance when sufficient structural information exists to determine what should ultimately fall inside or outside the governed event. This does not mean that the final boundary has already been established. Therefore: Formation Complete ≠ Boundary Determined. Similarly: Boundary Determined ≠ Taxable. These distinctions preserve the sequential integrity of TREGA™. Governance Boundary with TRERS TRERS — Tax-Relevant Event Recognition Standard governs whether a contextualized occurrence legitimately warrants further tax-relevant event governance. TREFS consumes the Governed Recognized Occurrence produced by TRERS. TRERS asks: Should this occurrence proceed into Event Formation? TREFS asks: What governed event structure can legitimately be formed from this recognized occurrence? Therefore: Event Recognition ≠ Event Formation. Governance Boundary with TREBS TREBS — Tax-Relevant Event Boundary Standard begins after sufficient Event Formation. TREFS establishes the structural event candidate. TREBS determines the governed extent of that event — what belongs inside the Event Boundary, what remains outside it, and how the event is separated from surrounding activity. Therefore: Event Formation ≠ Event Boundary. TREFS does not determine the final inclusion or exclusion boundary merely because an element contributed to formation. Governance Boundary with TREDS TREDS — Tax-Relevant Event Determination Standard later determines whether the fully governed event structure is sufficiently established as a Tax-Relevant Event suitable for downstream taxation analysis. TREFS performs a much earlier structural function. Therefore: Event Formation ≠ Event Determination. Formation may establish: a coherent governed event structure has been formed. Determination may later establish: a sufficiently governed Tax-Relevant Event exists. Neither statement means: tax is legally due. Cross-Architecture Boundary TREFS may consume governed results from other OOF® architectures where available. ORA™ may establish what actually occurred operationally. ASGA™ may govern autonomous-system operation and execution. OBIDENITY® may govern identity, origin, ownership, authority, permission, responsibility, and provenance. VFM® may govern what happened to value. CLA® may provide governed classification. INTEGROS® may govern integrity. ADIT® may govern evidence and auditability. VALIDOS™ may validate relevant claims, methods, or results. AGA™ may govern accountability. TREFS does not absorb these governed spaces. Its responsibility remains: structural formation of the recognized occurrence into a Governed Formed Event within TREGA™. Foundational Principles Recognized Occurrence ≠ Formed Event. Recognition ≠ Formation. Formation-Ready ≠ Formed. Recorded Element ≠ Formation Component by Default. Formation Component ≠ Independent Event by Default. Technical Association ≠ Event Formation. Shared Identifier ≠ Common Event Structure by Default. Formation Dependency ≠ Event Membership. Event Root ≠ Identity Origin. Root Association ≠ Provenance Governance. Event Formation Root ≠ Legal Tax Point. One Process ≠ One Event by Default. Multiple Process Steps ≠ Multiple Events by Default. Distributed Records ≠ Distributed Events by Default. Multiple System Representations ≠ Multiple Formed Events. Machine Operation ≠ Independent Formed Event by Default. Autonomous Formation ≠ Autonomous Tax Liability. Composite Formation ≠ Final Event Boundary. Formation Integrity ≠ Validation. Formation Insufficiency ≠ Recognition Rejection. Formation Reconsideration ≠ Historical Erasure. Tax Rule Change ≠ Event Reformation by Default. Cross-Border Event Formation ≠ Tax Jurisdiction Determination. Formation Complete ≠ Boundary Determined. Event Formation ≠ Event Determination. Formed Event ≠ Legally Taxable Event. TREGA™ governs the event. The jurisdiction governs the tax. Canonical Closing Statement Tax-Relevant Event Formation Standard establishes the structural formation governance layer of TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ by determining how a sufficiently recognized real-world, economic, operational, transactional, digital, autonomous, machine-generated, or value-affecting occurrence legitimately becomes a coherent Governed Formed Event capable of progressing into Event Boundary governance. Through governance of formation readiness, event-forming elements, structural assembly, material formation dependencies, operational root association, distributed and autonomous formation, formation ambiguity, uncertainty, integrity, insufficiency, reconsideration, and traceability, TREFS prevents technical records, system structures, shared identifiers, machine operations, accounting representations, or jurisdiction-specific tax assumptions from automatically defining the structure of the event. The Standard preserves the architectural distinctions between Recognition and Formation, formation components and independent events, formation dependencies and event membership, Event Root and Identity Origin, Formation and Event Boundary, Formation and Event Determination, and operational event structure and legal taxability. By creating a jurisdiction-neutral structural layer between Event Recognition and Event Boundary governance, TREFS enables human, enterprise, digital, distributed, and autonomous economic activity to acquire a coherent governed event representation without allowing Event Formation itself to determine whether tax is legally due. title: OOF™ Tax-Relevant Event Lifecycle & Continuity Standard - (TRECLS)
text: OOF™ Tax-Relevant Event Lifecycle & Continuity Standard - (TRECLS) Tax-Relevant Event Lifecycle & Continuity Standard - (TRECLS) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: TRECLS — Tax-Relevant Event Lifecycle & Continuity Standard Operational Layer: Tax-Relevant Event Lifecycle & Continuity Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Parent Standard Governed Space: Tax-Relevant Event Lifecycle & Continuity Primary Governed Object: Governed Tax-Relevant Event Lifecycle State Origin ID: TREGA-TRECLS-012 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 3 September 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language Canonical Definition The Tax-Relevant Event Lifecycle & Continuity Standard (TRECLS) governs how a Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record remains methodologically continuous, historically reconstructable, and governably current as the underlying Event representation is amended, corrected, superseded, maintained, or closed over time. TRECLS establishes the final lifecycle governance layer of TREGA™. It ensures that a governed Event does not lose continuity merely because new information appears, an earlier representation is corrected, a Record is superseded, or the Event reaches an operational endpoint. Its principal transition is: Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record ↓ Event Lifecycle & Continuity Governance ↓ Jurisdiction-Ready Tax-Relevant Event TRECLS does not govern the legal lifecycle of a tax obligation. It governs the lifecycle and continuity of the Tax-Relevant Event itself as a governed object. Its foundational distinction is: Event Continuity ≠ Tax Obligation Lifecycle. Core Question How can a governed Tax-Relevant Event remain continuous, reconstructable, correctable, and jurisdiction-ready throughout change without erasing historical reality or converting Event lifecycle governance into tax-law administration? Governance Purpose TRECLS exists because governed Events do not remain static. After a Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record has been established, later developments may reveal: corrected operational information; additional Event evidence; revised Event attributes; changed participation information; corrected timing or location; amended value association; corrected record representation; reconsidered Event Determination; Record supersession; Event closure; or circumstances suggesting that the original governed Event should no longer continue in its prior state. Without explicit lifecycle governance, systems may: overwrite prior Event states; lose historical reconstruction; treat every correction as a new Event; treat every amendment as continuation; confuse Record change with Event change; preserve obsolete states as current; or silently convert tax-system outcomes into canonical Event history. TRECLS governs these transitions. Architecture Position TRECLS is the twelfth and final Parent Standard in TREGA™. The complete TREGA™ Parent Standard Governance Flow is: TRECS — Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard → TRERS — Tax-Relevant Event Recognition Standard → TREFS — Tax-Relevant Event Formation Standard → TREBS — Tax-Relevant Event Boundary Standard → TRETS — Tax-Relevant Event Timing Standard → TRELS — Tax-Relevant Event Location Standard → TREPS — Tax-Relevant Event Participation Standard → TRVAS — Tax-Relevant Value Association Standard → TRERLS — Tax-Relevant Event Relationship Standard → TREDS — Tax-Relevant Event Determination Standard → TREGS — Tax-Relevant Event Record Governance Standard → TRECLS — Tax-Relevant Event Lifecycle & Continuity Standard ← CURRENT TRECLS closes the canonical TREGA™ governance lifecycle. Immediate Governance Position The immediate transition is: Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record ↓ Event Lifecycle & Continuity Governance ↓ Jurisdiction-Ready Tax-Relevant Event This is the point at which the governed Event becomes maintainable across time and suitable for continued downstream jurisdiction-specific evaluation. Governed Input TRECLS receives the final TREGS output: Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record The governed Record may contain or reference: canonical Event identity; canonical Record identity; Event Context; Recognition; Formation; Boundary; Timing; Location; Participation; Value Association; Event Relationships; Event Determination; qualification; uncertainty; reconsideration history; Record Structure; Record Linkage; Record Traceability; Record Interoperability state; and existing lifecycle references. TRECLS consumes these governed results. It does not recreate them. Primary Governed Output The principal TRECLS output is: Jurisdiction-Ready Tax-Relevant Event A Jurisdiction-Ready Tax-Relevant Event is a governed Event whose current state, prior materially relevant states, lifecycle transitions, continuity relationships, and closure status are sufficiently governed for downstream jurisdiction-specific taxation analysis. Jurisdiction-Ready ≠ Jurisdiction-Determined. Lifecycle Governance Principle A governed Event may change while remaining the same Event. A governed Event may also change so materially that continuation is no longer methodologically justified. TRECLS therefore governs the distinction between: Continuity and: New Event Formation This distinction is fundamental. Event Continuity Event Continuity exists where the same governed Event remains methodologically continuous despite changes to its representation, supporting information, state, or lifecycle position. Continuity shall preserve: Event identity; historical state; current effective state; relevant prior governance; material transition basis; and reconstructability. Change ≠ New Event by default. Continuity Qualification Continuity may be qualified where uncertainty remains about whether an Event should continue under the same governed identity. A qualified continuity state may require: further upstream review; Event Formation reassessment; Event Boundary reassessment; Event Relationship review; Determination reconsideration; or escalation. Continuity Break A Continuity Break occurs where the governed Event can no longer legitimately be treated as the same Event. A Continuity Break may arise where: Event Formation materially changes; Event Boundary materially changes; the original Event is replaced by a substantively different occurrence; Merge/Split creates a new Event object; corrected information invalidates the previous Event identity; or the Event has undergone material transformation requiring new Formation. A Continuity Break does not itself create the new Event. It triggers the appropriate upstream governance process. New Event Formation Boundary Where change exceeds legitimate continuity, the Event should return to appropriate upstream governance rather than be forced into the existing Event lifecycle. The canonical principle is: Material Transformation May Require New Event Formation. TRECLS may identify this condition. TREFS owns Event Formation. Amendment Governance An Amendment changes a governed Event representation without necessarily correcting an error. Amendments may add: newly available information; additional context; supplementary participation information; updated supporting references; clarified value association; lifecycle-relevant metadata. An Amendment does not automatically create a new Event. Amendment ≠ New Event by default. Amendment Boundary An amendment remains within the same Event only where the new information does not materially invalidate the Event's governed identity, Formation, or Boundary. Where it does, upstream reassessment may be required. Correction Governance A Correction addresses information that was materially wrong, incomplete, or improperly represented. Correction may apply to: Event Context; Event Formation representation; Timing; Location; Participation; Value Association; Event Relationship references; Determination; Record representation; or lifecycle state. Correction shall preserve the prior materially relevant state. Correction ≠ Historical Erasure. Correction and Historical Reality TRECLS shall not permit corrected data to overwrite history in a way that makes it impossible to reconstruct what the governed system previously represented. The canonical pattern is: Prior State ↓ Correction ↓ Corrected Current State not: Prior State ↓ Deletion ↓ Artificially Timeless Current State Correction Effective State The corrected state may become the current effective Event state. The prior state remains historically reconstructable. Current Corrected State ≠ Only State That Ever Existed. Representation Correction A Record may be technically incorrect while the underlying Event remains correct. Examples include: wrong field encoding; incorrect local identifier; schema mapping error; accidental omission; format conversion problem. A representation correction does not automatically require Event-level correction. Record Correction ≠ Event Correction by default. Event-Level Correction Where the actual governed Event state was wrong, the relevant upstream governance layer remains authoritative. TRECLS governs continuity and lifecycle effect of the corrected result. It does not independently re-govern the substantive Event component. Supersession Governance Supersession occurs where one governed Event representation or lifecycle state replaces another as the effective state. Supersession shall preserve: prior state; superseding state; effective relationship; reason reference; continuity state. Supersession ≠ Historical Deletion. Record Supersession A new Record may supersede an earlier Record. Record Supersession does not automatically mean the underlying Event became a new Event. New Record ≠ New Event by default. Event Supersession An Event state may be superseded by a later governed state while Event identity remains continuous. Where the replacement reflects material new Event Formation, however, a new Event may be required. Supersession and Traceability Superseded states shall remain reconstructable through TREGS traceability and TRECLS lifecycle references. TRECLS governs lifecycle meaning. ERTM governs Record Traceability. Lifecycle State TRECLS may assign explicit lifecycle states to the governed Event. Possible canonical states include: Active; Active — Qualified; Under Amendment; Amended; Under Correction; Corrected; Under Reconsideration; Superseded; Continuity Under Review; Continuity Confirmed; Continuity Broken; Closure Pending; Closed; Closed — Qualified; Reopened where permitted by governance; Referred for New Event Formation. Active State An Event is Active where it remains a current governed object requiring continued lifecycle maintenance or downstream use. Active does not mean legally taxable. Qualified Active State An Event may remain Active while material lifecycle uncertainty or qualification exists. Qualification shall remain explicit. Closure Governance Closure establishes that the governed Event lifecycle has reached a state where no further ordinary lifecycle development is currently required. Closure may occur because: the Event is operationally complete; lifecycle amendments have been resolved; relevant corrections are complete; no further Event continuation is expected; or governance policy establishes closure conditions. Event Closure ≠ Tax Obligation Closure. Closure Preconditions Closure should require that: current effective Event state is identifiable; material amendments are resolved or qualified; material corrections are resolved or qualified; supersession state is clear; material continuity conflicts are resolved or qualified; historical state remains reconstructable; closure basis is documented or referenced. Closure Qualification An Event may be closed with qualification where some uncertainty remains but does not justify continued active lifecycle governance. The qualification shall remain visible. Closure and Reopening A closed Event may require reopening where materially relevant new information appears. Reopening shall not erase the prior closure. The lifecycle should preserve: Closed ↓ Reopened ↓ New Effective State where legitimate. Reopening Boundary Reopening does not automatically preserve Event continuity. The new information may instead require New Event Formation. TRECLS shall distinguish these cases. Lifecycle Continuity Through System Change Event continuity shall survive: system migration; data transformation; Record schema changes; organizational transfer; Record identifier mapping; archive transition; interoperability transformation. Technical Migration ≠ Event Lifecycle Reset. Lifecycle Continuity Through Organizational Change A governed Event may move between organizations or operating entities while retaining its canonical Event identity where governance continuity remains valid. Organizational ownership changes do not automatically create new Events. Lifecycle Continuity Through Cross-Border Use The same governed Event may remain continuous while entering multiple tax jurisdictions. Different jurisdictions may evaluate the Event at different times and under different legal rules. These downstream evaluations do not alter the canonical Event lifecycle. Multiple Jurisdictional Evaluations ≠ Multiple Event Lifecycles. Lifecycle Continuity in Autonomous Systems Autonomous systems may continuously update Event-related data. TRECLS shall prevent every machine-generated update from being interpreted as a new Event. The relevant question is whether the underlying governed Event remains continuous. Machine Update ≠ New Event by default. High-Frequency Event Environments In high-frequency machine economies, thousands of technical updates may occur during the lifecycle of one governed Event. TRECLS governs meaningful lifecycle transitions rather than raw message frequency. Technical Update Count ≠ Event Lifecycle Count. Lifecycle State and Event Identity Lifecycle state shall remain distinct from Event identity. The same Event identity may pass through multiple lifecycle states. Lifecycle State Change ≠ Event Identity Change by default. Lifecycle State and Record State Record State and Event Lifecycle State shall remain distinguishable. A Record may be archived while the Event remains relevant downstream. A Record may be superseded while the Event identity continues. Record State ≠ Event Lifecycle State. Lifecycle State and Determination State TREDS determines whether the Event is sufficiently governed to constitute a Tax-Relevant Event. TRECLS governs how that Event continues after Determination. Lifecycle Governance ≠ Event Determination. Lifecycle State and Tax State A tax system may assign statuses such as: Taxable; Exempt; Filed; Assessed; Paid; Under Appeal; Closed. These are downstream tax-law states. They are not TRECLS lifecycle states. Event Lifecycle State ≠ Tax Obligation State. Lifecycle Amendment and Tax Reassessment An Event amendment may cause a jurisdiction to reassess tax. TRECLS governs the changed Event state. The jurisdiction determines whether reassessment is required. Event Amendment ≠ Tax Reassessment Decision. Lifecycle Correction and Tax Consequence A corrected Event may produce a different downstream tax result. TRECLS does not calculate or determine that result. It makes the corrected Event state available. Lifecycle Supersession and Tax Filing A superseded Event Record may require amended tax filings in some jurisdictions. That filing decision remains downstream. Record Supersession ≠ Filing Amendment Requirement. Lifecycle Closure and Statutory Periods TRECLS Event Closure does not determine: limitation periods; retention periods under tax law; appeal periods; filing deadlines; audit periods; reassessment windows. These remain jurisdiction-specific. Historical State Preservation TRECLS requires materially relevant historical Event states to remain reconstructable. Historical preservation should include, where applicable: prior Event state; current Event state; amendment reference; correction reference; supersession reference; closure reference; reopening reference; continuity decision. Historical State Authority Historical state preservation does not mean every prior state remains valid for current downstream use. The lifecycle shall distinguish: historical; superseded; corrected; current effective. Lifecycle Sequence The lifecycle may follow simple or complex patterns. Examples include: Active ↓ Amended ↓ Active Active ↓ Corrected ↓ Active Active ↓ Superseded ↓ Closed Closed ↓ Reopened ↓ Corrected ↓ Closed Active ↓ Continuity Broken ↓ New Event Formation Referral TRECLS does not require one universal linear lifecycle. Lifecycle Branching Complex Events may create branching lifecycle paths. Branching should remain governable without collapsing distinct Event identities. Where branches become independent Events, upstream Formation governance may be required. Lifecycle Merge Boundary Event Merge belongs to TRERLS. TRECLS governs lifecycle consequences after a valid Merge result. Lifecycle Consequence of Merge ≠ Merge Governance. Lifecycle Split Boundary Event Split belongs to TRERLS. TRECLS governs continuity consequences after a Split. A Split may terminate continuity of the original Event and create multiple successor Events. Lifecycle and Event Boundary TREBS owns Event Boundary. TRECLS may identify that lifecycle changes call the continuing Boundary into question. It does not independently redraw the Boundary. Lifecycle and Event Formation TREFS owns Event Formation. TRECLS may refer a materially transformed Event for re-Formation. It does not create the new Event directly. Lifecycle and Event Relationships TRERLS owns Event Relationships. TRECLS consumes Merge, Split, dependency, sequence, or grouping results where they affect lifecycle continuity. Lifecycle and Event Determination TREDS owns Event Determination. Where lifecycle change materially affects the Determination basis, TRECLS may trigger or reference reconsideration. TREDS remains authoritative for the Determination result. Lifecycle and Record Governance TREGS owns Governed Event Record identity, structure, linkage, traceability, and interoperability. TRECLS operates on the governed Record after TREGS completion. It does not recreate TREGS mechanics. Lifecycle and Identity Governance OBIDENITY® owns origin-bound identity, ownership, authority, and provenance. TRECLS governs continuity of the Event lifecycle, not identity governance of participants. Lifecycle and Value Governance VFM® owns the lifecycle of Value. TRECLS may consume updated Value states or Value Associations where they materially affect the Event lifecycle. It does not govern Value itself. Lifecycle and Operational Reality ORA™ governs what actually happened operationally. Where new operational reality invalidates the governed Event state, TRECLS consumes the resulting authoritative Event updates. Lifecycle and Evidence ADIT® owns evidence and auditability governance. TRECLS may require supporting references for lifecycle changes but does not perform evidence audit. Lifecycle and Validation VALIDOS™ owns validation governance. TRECLS may require validated lifecycle states where applicable but does not itself become the validation architecture. Lifecycle and Integrity INTEGROS® owns broader integrity governance. TRECLS governs methodological continuity of the Event lifecycle. Lifecycle and Accountability AGA™ governs accountability. TRECLS does not determine who is responsible for Event changes. Lifecycle and Harm or Liability HALIA™ governs harm and liability lifecycle. TRECLS does not determine liability arising from the Event. Lifecycle Stability Principle A governed lifecycle should remain stable enough that downstream systems can rely on a clearly identifiable current state. Frequent technical changes shall not produce unnecessary lifecycle state churn. More Lifecycle Transitions ≠ Better Governance. Materiality Principle Only changes materially affecting Event representation, continuity, reconstructability, or downstream reliance require formal lifecycle governance. Minor technical metadata changes may remain outside canonical lifecycle transitions. Lifecycle Trigger A lifecycle transition may be triggered by: new governed information; correction request; upstream governance change; Determination reconsideration; Record supersession; Event Merge/Split; closure condition; reopening condition; material continuity concern. Triggers should remain identifiable. Lifecycle Decision TRECLS may determine governance outcomes such as: Continue Event; Continue with Qualification; Amend Event State; Correct Event State; Supersede Prior State; Close Event; Reopen Event; Refer for Upstream Review; Refer for New Event Formation. These are lifecycle governance decisions, not tax decisions. Lifecycle Decision Basis Lifecycle decisions should be based on the governed Event state and materially relevant lifecycle information. The basis should remain reconstructable. Lifecycle Conflict Lifecycle Conflict exists where materially authoritative governance information supports incompatible lifecycle outcomes. Examples include: continuity vs New Event Formation; closure vs continued active state; competing corrected states; incompatible supersession chains. Conflict shall remain explicit until resolved or qualified. Lifecycle Ambiguity Lifecycle Ambiguity exists where the correct Event continuity or state cannot yet be determined sufficiently. Ambiguity shall not be hidden through arbitrary status assignment. Lifecycle Escalation Material ambiguity or conflict may require escalation to: upstream Event Formation; Event Boundary; Event Relationships; Event Determination; identity governance; validation; evidence governance; or another authoritative architecture. Lifecycle Governance States TRECLS may represent: Lifecycle Governance Not Initiated Active Active — Qualified Amendment Pending Amended Correction Pending Corrected Reconsideration Pending Supersession Pending Superseded Continuity Under Review Continuity Confirmed Continuity Qualified Continuity Broken Closure Pending Closed Closed — Qualified Reopening Under Review Reopened Upstream Review Required New Event Formation Referral Required Jurisdiction-Ready Governance Requirements TRECLS implementations shall ensure that: a valid Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record exists before lifecycle governance begins; current Event state remains distinguishable from historical Event state; Event continuity remains distinct from Record continuity; lifecycle change does not automatically create a new Event; material transformation may trigger New Event Formation; Amendments preserve Event identity only where continuity remains valid; Corrections do not erase materially relevant prior states; corrected current state remains distinguishable from historical state; Record correction is not automatically treated as Event correction; Supersession preserves prior materially relevant Event states; New Record creation does not automatically create a new Event; closure does not erase historical Event state; closure remains distinct from tax obligation closure; reopening preserves prior closure history; system migration does not reset Event lifecycle; organizational transfer does not automatically create new Event lifecycle; multiple jurisdictional evaluations remain downstream; machine-generated update volume does not determine Event count; lifecycle state remains distinct from Record State, Determination State, and Tax State; material lifecycle changes remain traceable; lifecycle transitions possess identifiable governance basis; ambiguity and conflict remain explicit; upstream governance is re-engaged where continuity can no longer be legitimately preserved; tax-law outcomes remain outside TRECLS; and the resulting Event is sufficiently current and reconstructable to become a Jurisdiction-Ready Tax-Relevant Event. Governance Logic IF a Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record does not exist, THEN TRECLS shall not establish complete Event Lifecycle Governance. IF new information changes the Event representation without materially changing Event identity, Formation, or Boundary, THEN the Event may remain continuous through Amendment or Correction Governance. IF materially incorrect Event information is corrected, THEN the prior materially relevant state shall remain reconstructable. IF only Record representation changes while Event Reality remains unchanged, THEN the change shall not automatically become an Event-level correction. IF a new Record supersedes a prior Record while the same Event continues, THEN Event identity may remain continuous. IF a lifecycle change materially invalidates Event Formation or Event Boundary, THEN TRECLS shall refer the case to the appropriate upstream governance layer. IF material transformation means the occurrence can no longer legitimately remain the same Event, THEN Continuity Break shall be established and New Event Formation may be required. IF the Event reaches a stable lifecycle endpoint and materially relevant lifecycle issues are resolved or qualified, THEN Event Closure may be established. IF materially relevant information emerges after closure, THEN reopening or New Event Formation shall be considered according to continuity. IF multiple jurisdictions produce different legal tax outcomes, THEN those outcomes shall not independently modify the canonical TREGA™ lifecycle. IF the current Event state, historical continuity, lifecycle transitions, and closure status are sufficiently governed, THEN TRECLS shall establish the Jurisdiction-Ready Tax-Relevant Event. Governance Outputs TRECLS may produce: Event Lifecycle State; Event Continuity State; Continuity Qualification; Continuity Break State; Amendment State; Correction State; Supersession State; Reconsideration Reference; Historical State Reference; Current Effective Event State; Closure State; Reopening State; New Event Formation Referral; Upstream Governance Referral; Lifecycle Conflict State; Lifecycle Ambiguity State; Lifecycle Escalation State; Jurisdiction-Readiness State; and the principal output: Jurisdiction-Ready Tax-Relevant Event. Internal Module Architecture TRECLS operationalizes its governed space through five Core Modules: 1. ECOM — Event Continuity Module 2. EADM — Event Amendment Module 3. ECRTM — Event Correction Module 4. ESPM — Event Supersession Module 5. ECLM — Event Closure Module The Internal Module Flow is: ECOM — Event Continuity ↓ EADM — Event Amendment ↓ ECRTM — Event Correction ↓ ESPM — Event Supersession ↓ ECLM — Event Closure ↓ Jurisdiction-Ready Tax-Relevant Event Each module governs one distinct lifecycle mechanism. Module Governance Boundaries ECOM — Event Continuity Module Governs whether and how the same Tax-Relevant Event remains continuous through lifecycle change. EADM — Event Amendment Module Governs legitimate additions or modifications that update the Event state without necessarily correcting an error. ECRTM — Event Correction Module Governs correction of materially inaccurate or improper Event state while preserving historical reconstructability. ESPM — Event Supersession Module Governs replacement of prior effective Event or Record states by later governed states without historical erasure. ECLM — Event Closure Module Governs transition of the Event into a closed lifecycle state and, where necessary, subsequent reopening references. Critical Distinctions Event Continuity ≠ Tax Obligation Lifecycle. Jurisdiction-Ready ≠ Jurisdiction-Determined. Change ≠ New Event by default. Material Transformation May Require New Event Formation. Amendment ≠ New Event by default. Correction ≠ Historical Erasure. Current Corrected State ≠ Only State That Ever Existed. Record Correction ≠ Event Correction by default. Supersession ≠ Historical Deletion. New Record ≠ New Event by default. Event Closure ≠ Tax Obligation Closure. Technical Migration ≠ Event Lifecycle Reset. Multiple Jurisdictional Evaluations ≠ Multiple Event Lifecycles. Machine Update ≠ New Event by default. Technical Update Count ≠ Event Lifecycle Count. Lifecycle State Change ≠ Event Identity Change by default. Record State ≠ Event Lifecycle State. Lifecycle Governance ≠ Event Determination. Event Lifecycle State ≠ Tax Obligation State. Event Amendment ≠ Tax Reassessment Decision. Record Supersession ≠ Filing Amendment Requirement. Lifecycle Consequence of Merge ≠ Merge Governance. More Lifecycle Transitions ≠ Better Governance. Cross-Architecture Boundary TRECLS operates only within the Tax-Relevant Event lifecycle space. Its relationship to other OOF® architectures is: ORA™ governs operational reality. OBIDENITY® governs identity, origin, ownership, authority, and provenance. VFM® governs the lifecycle of Value. CLA® governs classification. INTEGROS® governs integrity. ADIT® governs evidence and auditability. VALIDOS™ governs validation. AGA™ governs accountability. HALIA™ governs harm and liability lifecycle. TREGA™ / TRECLS governs continuity, amendment, correction, supersession, and closure of the Tax-Relevant Event. Jurisdiction-Specific Tax Systems govern the legal tax consequence and subsequent tax obligation lifecycle. Enterprise Application TRECLS enables long-lived Event governance across complex enterprise and machine environments. A canonical infrastructure pattern is: Operational / Digital Event → TREGA™ Event Governance → Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record → TRECLS Lifecycle & Continuity → Jurisdiction-Ready Tax-Relevant Event → Jurisdiction A Tax Engine → Jurisdiction B Tax Engine → Jurisdiction C Tax Engine This enables one governed Event to remain stable and reconstructable even where downstream tax rules, systems, and legal conclusions change. Use Case 1 — Cross-Border Digital Service Corrected After New Location Information A digital-service Event has completed TREGS and is consumed by tax systems in several jurisdictions. Later, materially improved operational information shows that one distributed Location reference was incorrectly represented. The underlying service Event remains the same Event. TRECLS governs the correction lifecycle: Prior Event State ↓ Location Correction Reference ↓ Corrected Event State ↓ Continuity Confirmed The historical prior state remains reconstructable. The corrected state becomes current. Each jurisdiction may independently decide whether the corrected Location changes legal tax consequences. TRECLS does not make that tax decision. Correction changes the governed Event state without rewriting the fact that an earlier governed state existed. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Machine Event Materially Transforms into a New Event An autonomous industrial system begins one governed Event involving a specific machine-to-machine service execution. During operation, the execution changes materially: the original operational Boundary, participants, and Value relationship cease, and a substantively different autonomous transaction begins. TRECLS evaluates continuity and determines that the original Event cannot legitimately absorb the transformation. The lifecycle state becomes: Continuity Broken ↓ New Event Formation Referral Required The original Event remains historically governed and may later be closed. The materially different occurrence is referred back to TREFS for New Event Formation. This prevents a system from stretching one Event identity indefinitely across economically and operationally distinct occurrences. Canonical Boundary TRECLS owns the governance of Tax-Relevant Event continuity, lifecycle state, amendment, correction, supersession, closure, reopening references, current-vs-historical state distinction, continuity qualification, continuity break, lifecycle ambiguity, lifecycle conflict, lifecycle escalation, and the transition from Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record to Jurisdiction-Ready Tax-Relevant Event. TRECLS does not recreate Event Context, Recognition, Formation, Boundary, Timing, Location, Participation, Value Association, Event Relationships, Event Determination, or Event Record Governance. It may refer an Event back to those authoritative layers where lifecycle change materially affects their governed result. TRECLS does not determine: legal taxability; Tax Jurisdiction; taxpayer status; tax nexus; legal tax point; Tax Period; Tax Base; Tax Rate; exemption; deduction; Tax Liability; filing obligation; reassessment obligation; payment; collection; enforcement; statutory limitation; appeal rights; or closure of a legal tax obligation. Its governance begins with a valid: Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record and ends with a sufficiently current, continuous, reconstructable, and lifecycle-governed: Jurisdiction-Ready Tax-Relevant Event Canonical Handoff TREGS — Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record ↓ TRECLS — Tax-Relevant Event Lifecycle & Continuity Governance ↓ Jurisdiction-Ready Tax-Relevant Event ↓ Jurisdictional Tax Rules / Tax Engine ↓ Tax Determination ↓ Reporting / Compliance Canonical Closing Statement TRECLS ensures that a Tax-Relevant Event can change through time without losing the distinction between what happened, what was previously recorded, what has been corrected, what remains current, and when the same Event can no longer legitimately continue. Lifecycle governance preserves continuity where continuity is justified and forces new Event Formation where continuity would distort operational reality. Correction ≠ Historical Erasure. Amendment ≠ New Event by default. Material Transformation May Require New Event Formation. Event Continuity ≠ Tax Obligation Lifecycle. Jurisdiction-Ready ≠ Jurisdiction-Determined. TREGA™ governs the event. The jurisdiction governs the tax.
