Canonical Record ≠ Identical Database Schema. Record Structure TREGS governs the requirement that the Event Record possess sufficient structure to represent the materially relevant governed Event. The record may reference, rather than duplicate, governed upstream structures. Its structure should support the representation of: Event reference; Event Determination state; relevant governance-state references; Event relationships; qualifications; uncertainty where material; record status; traceability; and lifecycle linkage. Detailed field-level implementation belongs to the Core Modules. Material Representation The Event Record shall represent information that is materially necessary to preserve the governed meaning of the Event. TREGS does not require indiscriminate duplication of every upstream data point. Governed Record Completeness ≠ Total Data Replication. Record Sufficiency A record is sufficiently governed where it can reliably support its intended downstream governance role without materially distorting the Event it represents. Record sufficiency may require: stable identification; sufficient structural representation; Event association; relevant linkage; traceability; and interoperability. Record Integrity Boundary TREGS requires the Event Record to preserve the governed Event meaning received from upstream TREGA™ layers. It does not independently validate evidential truth or perform general integrity governance. Where broader integrity governance is required, INTEGROS® remains authoritative. Where validation is required, VALIDOS™ remains authoritative. Where audit/evidence governance is required, ADIT® remains authoritative. Record Linkage A Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record may require links to: its underlying Event; related Event Records; predecessor or successor representations; upstream governance states; supporting system references; superseding records; correction records; downstream consumption references. TREGS governs the existence and governance meaning of these links. It does not recreate Event Relationships governed by TRERLS. Record Linkage ≠ Event Relationship Governance. Relationship Preservation Where TRERLS establishes relationships among governed Events, TREGS shall preserve sufficient references for those relationships to remain reconstructable at the record layer. TREGS shall not reinterpret: dependency; sequence; grouping; Merge; or Split. Representing a Relationship ≠ Governing the Relationship. Determination Preservation The Event Record shall preserve the applicable TREDS Determination state. This may include: Positive Determination; Conditional Determination; relevant qualification; uncertainty state; reconsidered Determination; final effective TREDS state. TREGS does not issue or modify the Determination. Recording a Determination ≠ Making a Determination. Qualification Preservation Material qualifications attached to the Determination shall remain visible where necessary for downstream reliance. A record shall not convert a Conditional Determination into an apparently unqualified Event merely through representation. Record Simplification ≠ Qualification Removal. Uncertainty Preservation Where EDUM establishes material uncertainty relevant to continued downstream use, TREGS shall preserve sufficient reference to that uncertainty. Record Finalization ≠ Elimination of Uncertainty. Reconsideration Preservation Where EDREM has reconsidered a prior Determination, the Event Record shall represent the current effective Determination while preserving sufficient traceability to prior materially relevant states. Current Record State ≠ Erasure of Prior Determination History. Record State TREGS may govern record states such as: Record Not Initiated; Record Under Formation; Record Identified; Record Structurally Incomplete; Record Structurally Sufficient; Record Linked; Record Traceable; Record Interoperable; Record Qualified; Record Active; Record Superseded; Record Ready for Lifecycle Governance. These are record-governance states. They are not tax states. Record Version and State Distinction A technical system may maintain several versions of a record. TREGS shall distinguish technical versioning from governed Event state where material. Record Version ≠ New Event. and: Record Update ≠ Event Change by default. Record Traceability A Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record shall support reconstruction of its governance lineage. A downstream reviewer or system should be able to establish, where relevant: Event ↓ Upstream Governance ↓ Determination ↓ Record Traceability should preserve sufficient references without requiring unnecessary duplication of all underlying information. Traceability Depth The required depth of traceability may vary according to Event complexity, downstream reliance, and governance materiality. TREGS applies proportional governance. A simple Event may require limited linkage. A complex distributed or autonomous Event may require significantly deeper traceability. More Traceability Data ≠ Better Governance by default. Record Provenance Boundary TREGS may preserve references to the origin of record information. It does not own origin-bound identity or provenance governance. OBIDENITY® remains authoritative for identity, origin, ownership, authority, permission, responsibility, provenance, transfer, continuity, and auditability within its governed space. Record Provenance Reference ≠ Provenance Governance. Record Interoperability A governed Event Record should be capable of moving across systems without losing its canonical Event meaning. Interoperability may require preservation of: stable Event reference; stable Record reference; semantic meaning; governance state; Determination state; material qualification; relationship references; traceability; and lifecycle state. Semantic Interoperability Technical transfer alone does not establish interoperability. Two systems may successfully exchange data while interpreting the Event differently. Therefore: Data Transfer ≠ Semantic Interoperability. TREGS requires the governed meaning of the Event to remain sufficiently stable across representations. Structural Interoperability Different systems may use different schemas while preserving the same governed Event meaning. TREGS therefore distinguishes: Structural Difference ≠ Governance Incompatibility by default. Interoperability is achieved when the governed Event can remain identifiable and interpretable across the transformation. Cross-System Record Governance TREGS supports Event Records spanning: ERP; CRM; accounting; banking; payment; marketplace; logistics; tax; reporting; audit; AI; and machine systems. A system-specific record may remain a local representation while the Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record acts as the canonical governance reference. Cross-Organization Record Governance Events may cross organizational boundaries. TREGS supports exchange of governed Event representations without requiring each organization to redefine the Event independently. Organizations may retain different internal records while referencing the same governed Event Reality. Different Organizational Records ≠ Different Event Reality by default. Cross-Border Record Governance A Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record may be consumed by multiple jurisdiction-specific systems. TREGS shall preserve the jurisdiction-neutral Event layer. The record shall not embed one jurisdiction's legal interpretation as the canonical Event Reality. Cross-Border Event Record ≠ Jurisdictional Tax Record by default. Multi-Jurisdiction Reuse A principal TREGA™ infrastructure pattern is: One Determined Tax-Relevant Event ↓ One Governed Event Layer ↓ Multiple Jurisdictional Evaluations TREGS operationalizes the record layer necessary to support this pattern. A single Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record may therefore support: Governed Event Record ↓ Jurisdiction A Tax Evaluation Governed Event Record ↓ Jurisdiction B Tax Evaluation Governed Event Record ↓ Jurisdiction C Tax Evaluation without allowing any one evaluation to redefine the underlying Event Record. Jurisdiction-Specific Extensions A downstream jurisdiction may append: tax classification; tax nexus; taxpayer determination; tax point; Tax Base; Tax Rate; exemption; Tax Liability; reporting treatment. These outputs shall remain downstream jurisdiction-specific layers. They shall not silently overwrite the canonical TREGA™ Event Record. Jurisdictional Tax Extension ≠ Canonical Event Record. Tax Engine Consumption TREGS enables tax engines to consume a governed Event rather than reconstruct operational reality independently. The preferred model is: Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record ↓ Jurisdictional Tax Rules / Tax Engine ↓ Tax Determination This reduces repeated Event reconstruction across downstream systems. Record and Taxability The presence of a Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record means that a sufficiently governed Tax-Relevant Event exists. It does not mean the Event is legally taxable. Governed Event Record ≠ Evidence That Tax Is Due. Record and Tax Jurisdiction The record may contain governed Location information. It does not establish Tax Jurisdiction. Event Location Record ≠ Tax Jurisdiction Determination. Record and Taxpayer The record may preserve governed Participation. It does not establish taxpayer status. Participant Record ≠ Taxpayer Determination. Record and Tax Base The record may preserve governed Value Association. It does not establish Tax Base. Value Association Record ≠ Tax Base Determination. Record and Legal Tax Point The record may preserve Event Timing. It does not establish legal tax timing. Event Time Record ≠ Legal Tax Point. Record and Tax Liability The record does not calculate, establish, or enforce Tax Liability. Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record ≠ Tax Liability Record. Record and Reporting A TREGS record may serve as an input to reporting systems. It is not itself a jurisdiction-specific tax return, declaration, invoice obligation, or regulatory filing. Event Record ≠ Tax Filing. Technical Record Boundary A database row, message, transaction ID, invoice, accounting entry, blockchain transaction, smart-contract log, sensor event, or machine record may contribute to a TREGS record. None qualifies automatically as the Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record. Technical Record ≠ Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record. Invoice Boundary An invoice may reference an Event. It does not define the Event. Invoice ≠ Governed Event Record by default. Accounting Boundary An accounting entry may represent a financial consequence of an Event. It does not necessarily represent the Event itself. Accounting Entry ≠ Governed Event Record. Payment Boundary A payment record may relate to a governed Event. Payment and Event remain distinct. Payment Record ≠ Event Record by default. Blockchain Boundary A blockchain transaction may be immutable and uniquely identified while still representing only part of the governed Event Reality. Blockchain Record ≠ Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record by default. Smart-Contract Boundary A smart-contract execution log may contribute to Event representation. It does not automatically capture: Event Context; complete Participation; off-chain Value; Event Boundary; or Event Relationships. Smart-Contract Log ≠ Governed Event Record by default. AI and Agent Record Governance AI agents and autonomous systems may generate Event Records automatically. TREGS requires such records to preserve the same governance principles as human-generated records. Machine-Generated Record ≠ Governed Record by default. Machine-to-Machine Record Governance A machine economy may generate extremely large numbers of technical interactions. TREGS prevents technical record volume from becoming Event count automatically. Machine Record Count ≠ Tax-Relevant Event Count. Only governed Events that have passed TREGA™ Determination should become canonical TREGS Event Records. Record Granularity Record granularity shall reflect the governed Event Boundary and Event Formation. TREGS shall not arbitrarily aggregate or fragment Events for storage convenience. Database Granularity ≠ Event Granularity. Record Duplication Duplicate technical representations shall not automatically create duplicate Governed Event Records. TREGS should support detection and preservation of canonical association where multiple technical records refer to the same Event. Duplicate Record ≠ Duplicate Event by default. Record Transformation A record may be transformed between: formats; schemas; systems; organizations; APIs; data models. Transformation shall preserve the governed Event meaning. Record Transformation ≠ Event Transformation. Record Compression and Abstraction Systems may reduce or abstract record information for operational purposes. Such abstraction shall not remove materially necessary governance meaning. Data Reduction ≠ Permission to Remove Material Governance State. Record Persistence The Governed Event Record should remain available for the period required by its governance lifecycle and downstream reliance context. TREGS establishes the requirement for persistence capability. TRECLS governs the broader lifecycle and continuity of the Event after record establishment. Record Supersession Boundary TREGS may represent that one record supersedes another. It does not govern the broader Event supersession lifecycle. TRECLS remains authoritative for lifecycle supersession. Record Supersession ≠ Event Supersession by default. Record Correction Boundary A technical or representational error in the Event Record may require correction. If the underlying Event Reality changes, the matter may require upstream or TRECLS governance rather than simple record correction. Record Correction ≠ Event Correction by default. Record Lifecycle Handoff Once a sufficiently governed Event Record exists, the Event enters TRECLS for lifecycle and continuity governance. The canonical handoff is: Determined Tax-Relevant Event ↓ Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record ↓ Event Continuity & Lifecycle Governance TREGS therefore establishes the persistent governed representation upon which TRECLS can operate. Core Modules TREGS is operationalized through five Core Modules: 1. ERIDM — Event Record Identification Module Governs stable identification of the Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record and its association with the underlying Determined Tax-Relevant Event. 2. ERSTM — Event Record Structure Module Governs the canonical structural representation required to preserve the materially relevant governed Event. 3. ERLKM — Event Record Linkage Module Governs record-level links to underlying Events, related Event Records, governance states, predecessor/successor representations, and other materially necessary references. 4. ERTM — Event Record Traceability Module Governs reconstruction of the Event Record's governance lineage, state transitions, and material references. 5. ERINM — Event Record Interoperability Module Governs preservation of Event identity, meaning, state, qualification, linkage, and traceability across system and organizational boundaries. Internal Module Flow The TREGS Internal Module Flow is: ERIDM — Event Record Identification ↓ ERSTM — Event Record Structure ↓ ERLKM — Event Record Linkage ↓ ERTM — Event Record Traceability ↓ ERINM — Event Record Interoperability ↓ Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record Each module governs a distinct operational part of Record Governance. Governance States TREGS may recognize: Determined Event Received Record Governance Initiated Record Identity Established Record Structure Under Governance Record Structurally Sufficient Record Linkage Established Record Traceability Established Record Interoperability Established Record Qualified Record Active Record Supersession Referenced Record Ready for Lifecycle Governance Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record Established These states shall remain distinct from jurisdiction-specific tax states. Governance Requirements TREGS implementations shall ensure that: only a sufficiently Determined Tax-Relevant Event enters canonical Record Governance; the Event remains distinguishable from its Record; Record creation does not create a new Event by default; stable Record identity can be established; Record identity remains distinguishable from Event identity; the Record remains associated with its underlying Event; multiple technical representations do not create multiple Events by default; Record structure preserves materially necessary Event meaning; Record completeness does not require indiscriminate data replication; Determination state is preserved; material qualifications remain visible; material uncertainty remains representable; reconsideration history remains traceable where required; Record linkage does not recreate Event Relationship governance; Record traceability supports reconstruction of governance lineage; interoperability preserves Event meaning rather than merely transporting data; structural differences across systems do not automatically create governance incompatibility; jurisdiction-specific tax conclusions remain downstream; jurisdictional outputs do not overwrite the canonical Event Record; technical records do not automatically become governed Event Records; record granularity follows governed Event structure rather than database convenience; duplicate representations do not automatically create duplicate Events; record transformation preserves Event meaning; record correction remains distinguishable from Event correction; record supersession remains distinguishable from Event lifecycle supersession; and the resulting Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record is suitable for TRECLS. Governance Logic IF no valid Determined Tax-Relevant Event exists, THEN TREGS shall not establish a canonical Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record. IF a technical record exists without sufficient association to a Determined Tax-Relevant Event, THEN that technical record shall not qualify as the canonical TREGS output. IF multiple technical records represent the same governed Event, THEN they shall not automatically create multiple governed Events or multiple canonical Event Records. IF materially necessary Event meaning would be lost through record abstraction, transformation, or compression, THEN the resulting representation shall not be considered sufficiently governed. IF a Determination contains material qualification or uncertainty, THEN the Event Record shall preserve sufficient reference to that state for downstream reliance. IF a record transformation preserves Event identity, governed meaning, state, and required traceability, THEN structural differences may remain interoperable. IF a jurisdiction-specific tax system adds legal tax conclusions, THEN those conclusions shall remain downstream extensions and shall not redefine the canonical TREGA™ Event Record. IF a technical correction affects only representation, THEN the Record may be corrected without automatically reopening Event governance. IF the correction changes the underlying governed Event Reality, THEN the issue shall be routed to the authoritative TREGA™ governance layer rather than treated as a record-only correction. IF Record Governance is sufficiently complete, THEN TREGS shall establish the Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record and hand it to TRECLS. Governance Outputs TREGS may produce: Governed Event Record Identifier; Event-to-Record Association; Canonical Record State; Record Structure State; Record Sufficiency State; Record Linkage State; Determination Reference; Qualification Reference; Uncertainty Reference; Reconsideration Reference; Relationship Representation Reference; Record Traceability State; Record Provenance Reference; Record Interoperability State; Cross-System Record Reference; Cross-Organization Record Reference; Multi-Jurisdiction Reuse State; Record Supersession Reference; Lifecycle Handoff State; and the principal output: Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record. Critical Distinctions Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record ≠ Tax Assessment. Event ≠ Event Record. Record Creation ≠ Event Creation. Record Identity ≠ Event Identity. Multiple Technical Records ≠ Multiple Tax-Relevant Events. Canonical Record ≠ Identical Database Schema. Governed Record Completeness ≠ Total Data Replication. Record Linkage ≠ Event Relationship Governance. Representing a Relationship ≠ Governing the Relationship. Recording a Determination ≠ Making a Determination. Record Simplification ≠ Qualification Removal. Record Finalization ≠ Elimination of Uncertainty. Current Record State ≠ Erasure of Prior Determination History. Record Version ≠ New Event. Record Update ≠ Event Change by default. More Traceability Data ≠ Better Governance by default. Record Provenance Reference ≠ Provenance Governance. Data Transfer ≠ Semantic Interoperability. Structural Difference ≠ Governance Incompatibility by default. Different Organizational Records ≠ Different Event Reality by default. Cross-Border Event Record ≠ Jurisdictional Tax Record by default. Jurisdictional Tax Extension ≠ Canonical Event Record. Governed Event Record ≠ Evidence That Tax Is Due. Event Location Record ≠ Tax Jurisdiction Determination. Participant Record ≠ Taxpayer Determination. Value Association Record ≠ Tax Base Determination. Event Time Record ≠ Legal Tax Point. Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record ≠ Tax Liability Record. Event Record ≠ Tax Filing. Technical Record ≠ Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record. Invoice ≠ Governed Event Record by default. Accounting Entry ≠ Governed Event Record. Payment Record ≠ Event Record by default. Blockchain Record ≠ Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record by default. Smart-Contract Log ≠ Governed Event Record by default. Machine-Generated Record ≠ Governed Record by default. Machine Record Count ≠ Tax-Relevant Event Count. Database Granularity ≠ Event Granularity. Duplicate Record ≠ Duplicate Event by default. Record Transformation ≠ Event Transformation. Data Reduction ≠ Permission to Remove Material Governance State. Record Supersession ≠ Event Supersession by default. Record Correction ≠ Event Correction by default. Cross-Architecture Boundaries ORA™ governs what actually happened operationally. TREGS represents the already-governed Tax-Relevant Event; it does not reconstruct operational reality. OBIDENITY® governs identity, origin, ownership, authority, permission, responsibility, provenance, transfer, continuity, and auditability within its governed space. TREGS may reference those outputs but does not recreate them. VFM® — Value Flow Mechanism governs what happens to Value throughout its lifecycle. TREGS may preserve the governed Value Association established through TRVAS. INTEGROS® governs integrity. TREGS requires preservation of Event meaning but does not replace general integrity governance. ADIT® governs evidence and auditability within its governed space. TREGS preserves traceability references but does not become the audit architecture. VALIDOS™ governs validation. TREGS does not validate the Event merely by recording it. AGA™ governs accountability. TREGS does not assign accountability merely because an actor appears in a Record. TREDS owns Tax-Relevant Event Determination. TREGS records the resulting Determination but does not recreate it. TRECLS owns subsequent Tax-Relevant Event Lifecycle & Continuity governance. TREGS establishes the governed Record on which that lifecycle operates. Downstream Boundary TREGS ends before jurisdiction-specific taxation logic begins. The canonical downstream architecture remains: Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record ↓ Jurisdictional Tax Rules / Tax Engine ↓ Tax Determination ↓ Reporting / Compliance TREGS does not own any of the downstream legal tax conclusions. Canonical Boundary TREGS owns the governance of the persistent canonical representation of a Determined Tax-Relevant Event, including Event Record identification, structural sufficiency, Event-to-Record association, record-level linkage, Determination preservation, qualification preservation, uncertainty reference, traceability, cross-system representation, semantic interoperability, and establishment of the Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record. TREGS does not determine whether an Event exists, recognize the Event, form the Event, define its Boundary, establish its Timing or Location, determine Participation, govern Value, establish Event Relationships, or issue the Tax-Relevant Event Determination. It does not own broader Event lifecycle amendment, correction, supersession, or closure after Record Governance; those functions belong to TRECLS. It does not determine legal taxability, Tax Jurisdiction, taxpayer status, Tax Base, Tax Rate, legal tax point, Tax Period, exemption, deduction, Tax Liability, filing obligation, collection, enforcement, or any other jurisdiction-specific tax consequence. Its governance begins when TREDS produces a Determined Tax-Relevant Event. Its governance ends when a sufficiently governed Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record is established for lifecycle governance and downstream consumption. Canonical Handoff TREDS — Determined Tax-Relevant Event ↓ TREGS — Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record ↓ TRECLS — Tax-Relevant Event Lifecycle & Continuity Governance Canonical Closing Statement TREGS ensures that a Determined Tax-Relevant Event does not lose its governed meaning when it becomes data. The Event Record exists to preserve and transport governed Event Reality — not to recreate the Event, reinterpret it, or decide its tax consequence. Event ≠ Event Record. Governed Tax-Relevant Event Record ≠ Tax Assessment. One governed Event can support many downstream tax evaluations without becoming many different Event realities. TREGA™ governs the event. The jurisdiction governs the tax. Module Architecture → Event Record Identification Module (ERIDM) → Event Record Structure Module (ERSTM) → Event Record Linkage Module (ERLKM) → Event Record Traceability Module (ERTM) → Event Record Interoperability Module (ERINM) Related Documents → About Tax-Relevant Event Record Governance Standard (TREGS)

title: OOF™ Tax-Relevant Event Relationship Standard - (TRERLS)
text: OOF™ Tax-Relevant Event Relationship Standard - (TRERLS) Tax-Relevant Event Relationship Standard - (TRERLS) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: TRERLS — Tax-Relevant Event Relationship Standard Operational Layer: Tax-Relevant Event Relationship Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Parent Standard Governed Space: Tax-Relevant Event Relationships Origin ID: TREGA-TRERLS-009 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 1 September 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: UCL — Universal Canonical Language Canonical Definition The Tax-Relevant Event Relationship Standard (TRERLS) governs how two or more Governed Tax-Relevant Events are related, distinguished, sequenced, dependent, grouped, linked, merged, split, or otherwise structurally associated before final Tax-Relevant Event Determination occurs. TRERLS establishes the governance conditions under which relationships among events can be represented without collapsing distinct events into one, fragmenting one event into artificial sub-events, or converting technical process structure directly into economic or tax-event structure. Its principal governed transition is: Governed Value-Associated Events ↓ Governed Event Relationship Structure TRERLS does not create Event Context, recognize occurrences, form events, establish Event Boundaries, determine Event Timing, determine Event Location, establish Event Participation, or govern Value Association. It consumes those governed results and determines how already-governed events relate to one another. The foundational principle is: Event Relationship ≠ Event Identity. Purpose Modern economic and digital activity rarely occurs as isolated transactions. One business activity may produce: an order; reservation; authorization; payment; shipment; delivery; settlement; refund; reversal; return; service execution; resource allocation; machine instruction; smart-contract interaction; or several related technical operations. Some of these may belong to one governed event. Others may constitute separate but related governed events. Still others may represent later events that depend upon, modify, reverse, continue, supersede, or economically relate to an earlier event. TRERLS exists to prevent two opposite governance failures: Fragmentation — treating every technical operation as an independent Tax-Relevant Event. Collapse — treating several materially distinct events as one event merely because they belong to one commercial activity. TRERLS provides the governance layer required to preserve the actual relationship structure between events. Core Question How should multiple governed Tax-Relevant Events be related, distinguished, sequenced, grouped, dependent, merged, or split without allowing technical workflow structure, operational proximity, or later tax interpretation to redefine the events themselves? Governance Objective TRERLS ensures that Tax-Relevant Event governance can represent economic and operational structures where: one activity produces multiple events; one event contains multiple technical operations; later events depend on earlier events; several events occur in sequence; events form a meaningful group; one event replaces or reverses another; previously treated events require governed merge; one previously treated event requires governed split; several jurisdictions evaluate related events differently; and autonomous or distributed systems produce complex event networks. Its objective is not simplification at any cost. Its objective is correct relationship representation. Complete TREGA™ Governance Flow 1. TRECS — Tax-Relevant Event Context Standard → 2. TRERS — Tax-Relevant Event Recognition Standard → 3. TREFS — Tax-Relevant Event Formation Standard → 4. TREBS — Tax-Relevant Event Boundary Standard → 5. TRETS — Tax-Relevant Event Timing Standard → 6. TRELS — Tax-Relevant Event Location Standard → 7. TREPS — Tax-Relevant Event Participation Standard → 8. TRVAS — Tax-Relevant Value Association Standard → 9. TRERLS — Tax-Relevant Event Relationship Standard ← CURRENT → 10. TREDS — Tax-Relevant Event Determination Standard → 11. TREGS — Tax-Relevant Event Record Governance Standard → 12. TRECLS — Tax-Relevant Event Lifecycle & Continuity Standard The immediate governance position is: Value Association ↓ Event Relationships ↓ Event Determination TRVAS establishes which governed value results belong to the event. TRERLS determines how that governed event relates to other governed events. TREDS subsequently determines whether the resulting governed event structure is sufficiently complete and coherent to become a formally determined Tax-Relevant Event. Governed Input TRERLS consumes already-governed events that may contain: Event Context; Event Recognition; Event Formation; Event Boundary; Event Timing; Event Location; Event Participation; and Value Association. Its canonical input is: One or More Governed Value-Associated Events Governed Output TRERLS produces: Governed Event Relationship Structure This structure preserves the relationship between events without deciding their jurisdiction-specific tax consequences. The output proceeds to TREDS. Event Relationship An Event Relationship is a governed association between two or more events that preserves how those events interact without necessarily changing the identity, validity, or independence of each event. Relationships may include: dependency; sequence; grouping; continuation; reversal; replacement; parent–child relationship; component relationship; parallel relationship; conditional relationship; merge; split; or another sufficiently governed structural relationship. Related Events ≠ Same Event by default. Relationship Identification TRERLS shall determine whether a meaningful relationship exists among governed events. Possible indicators may include: shared participants; shared Value References; temporal sequence; operational dependency; contractual connection; shared Event Context; shared process; common technical execution; common settlement; common source transaction; machine-generated linkage; or another materially relevant association. No single indicator automatically proves a specific relationship. Shared Attribute ≠ Event Relationship Determination by default. Event Independence Two events may be related while remaining independently governed. For example, a sale and later refund may have a strong relationship but remain distinct events. TRERLS shall preserve event independence where formation and boundary governance support it. Strong Relationship ≠ Event Identity. Event Dependency One event may depend on another event. Examples include: fulfillment depending on an order; settlement depending on a payment instruction; refund depending on an earlier purchase; resource consumption depending on prior allocation; autonomous execution depending on a machine instruction. TRERLS may establish dependency without declaring the dependent event part of the same event. Event Dependency ≠ Event Merger. Unidirectional Dependency A relationship may operate in one direction. For example: Event B depends on Event A does not necessarily mean: Event A depends on Event B. TRERLS shall preserve directional relationships where relevant. A ↓ B ≠ B ↓ A. Mutual Dependency Some events may be mutually dependent. Where neither event can be coherently represented without the other, TRERLS may establish mutual dependency. However: Mutual Dependency ≠ Single Event by default. The Event Boundary remains decisive. Event Sequence Events may occur in governed sequence. Examples include: Order ↓ Payment ↓ Delivery or: Reservation ↓ Execution ↓ Settlement Sequence explains temporal or operational ordering. It does not establish that the events are one event. Sequence ≠ Event Identity. Temporal Sequence One event occurring before another may be relevant. However: Earlier Event ≠ Causal Event by default. and: Temporal Proximity ≠ Event Relationship by default. TRETS governs Event Timing. TRERLS consumes timing information only to represent relationships. Operational Sequence Events may be connected by process order even where their exact timestamps overlap or differ across systems. TRERLS may preserve operational sequence independently from legal interpretation. Operational Sequence ≠ Tax Sequence. Conditional Relationship An event may occur only if another event satisfies a particular condition. For example: release follows approval; refund follows return; payment follows service completion; autonomous execution follows authorization. TRERLS may represent the conditional relationship without governing the authority or permission itself. Conditional Event Relationship ≠ Authority Governance. Parent–Child Event Relationship One event may generate or contain relationships to subordinate events while the events remain independently identifiable. TRERLS may establish Parent–Child Event Relationships where governance supports such structure. However: Parent Event ≠ Owner of Child Event. and: Child Event ≠ Event Component by default. The relationship describes structure, not ownership. Component Event Relationship A wider activity may contain several independently governed events that function as components of a larger economic or operational structure. TRERLS may preserve these relationships while preventing their automatic collapse. Event Component Relationship ≠ Event Merge by default. Parallel Events Two or more events may occur simultaneously or independently within the same broader process. For example, a marketplace may trigger payment processing and logistics activity in parallel. TRERLS shall support parallel relationship structures. Parallel Events ≠ Same Event. Shared Participant Relationship Two events may share one or more participants. This may support relationship identification. It does not establish event identity. Same Participant ≠ Same Event. TREPS remains authoritative for Event Participation. Shared Value Relationship Two events may refer to the same governed value or Value Change. This may establish an important relationship. However: Shared Value Reference ≠ Same Event. A single payment may settle several events. A single asset may participate in several events. A refund may refer to value associated with an earlier event. TRVAS remains authoritative for Value Association. Shared Location Events may occur at the same physical, digital, or distributed location. This does not establish relationship by itself. Same Location ≠ Related Event by default. TRELS remains authoritative for Event Location. Shared Timing Events may happen at the same time. This does not establish that they belong together. Same Time ≠ Same Event. Shared Context Events may occur within the same Event Context. TRERLS may consume that relationship information. However: Shared Context ≠ Same Event. TRECS remains authoritative for Event Context. Economic Activity and Event Structure One economic activity may contain one event or many governed events. Therefore: One Economic Activity ≠ One Event by default. Likewise: Multiple Technical Operations ≠ Multiple Economically Independent Events by default. TRERLS preserves the distinction between technical operation count and governed event structure. Technical Operations Modern systems frequently generate multiple technical records for one event. For example: API calls; database updates; ledger entries; token movements; smart-contract executions; machine commands; authorization requests; settlement messages. TRERLS shall not convert each technical operation into a separate Tax-Relevant Event merely because a record exists. Technical Operation ≠ Tax-Relevant Event by default. Distributed Event Structure One operational or economic event may span distributed systems. For example: AI Agent ↓ Marketplace ↓ Payment Network ↓ Blockchain ↓ Logistics System The systems may create many technical records. TRERLS may preserve one event where Event Formation and Boundary governance support that conclusion, while separately representing genuinely distinct related events. Event Grouping TRERLS may group several events where they share a meaningful structural relationship. Grouping can support: navigation; reconstruction; analysis; reporting; economic activity representation; or later jurisdictional evaluation. However: Event Group ≠ Single Event. Grouping shall not erase the independent identities of the grouped events. Group Membership An event may belong to one or more legitimate groups. For example, an event may belong simultaneously to: a commercial transaction group; a settlement group; a supply-chain group; a contractual group; or a machine-operation group. Multiple Group Memberships ≠ Multiple Event Identities. Group Identifier TRERLS may establish a governed group reference. The group identifier supports relationship governance. It does not replace the individual Event Identifiers. Group Identifier ≠ Event Identifier. Event Chain A sequence of related events may form an Event Chain. For example: Order Event ↓ Fulfillment Event ↓ Payment Event ↓ Refund Event An Event Chain preserves relationship structure across the lifecycle of economic activity. Event Chain ≠ Single Event Lifecycle by default. TRECLS governs lifecycle and continuity of individual governed events. Event Network Complex systems may produce event structures that cannot be represented as a simple linear chain. One event may lead to multiple subsequent events. Multiple earlier events may converge into one later event. TRERLS shall support Event Networks. The relationship model may therefore include: One-to-One One-to-Many Many-to-One Many-to-Many relationships. One-to-Many Relationship One governed event may trigger several related events. Example: one purchase event may later generate: shipment; payment settlement; loyalty allocation; platform commission; and reporting-related operational events. One Source Event ≠ One Resulting Event by default. Many-to-One Relationship Several events may converge into one later event. For example, several invoices may be settled by one payment event. TRERLS shall support convergence without treating the earlier events as one event. One Settlement ≠ One Prior Event by default. Many-to-Many Relationship Distributed business systems may create multiple interconnected events on both sides of a relationship. TRERLS shall support such structures without requiring artificial simplification. Event Merge Governance Two or more previously distinguished governed events may later be shown to constitute one event under the applicable event-governance criteria. TRERLS may govern the structural merge relationship where sufficient basis exists. However: Relationship Convenience ≠ Permission to Merge Events. A merge must not be used merely because downstream taxation, reporting, or system design becomes easier. Merge Conditions A governed merge may become appropriate where evidence shows that events previously treated separately do not possess sufficient independent Event Formation or Boundary. TRERLS does not independently recreate those earlier governance decisions. Where necessary, the relevant issue shall be referred to TREFS or TREBS. Event Merge ≠ Silent Event Deletion. The prior governance history must remain traceable. Merged Event History Where a governed merge occurs, historical event identities and the reason for merge should remain reconstructable. Merged ≠ Never Previously Separate. Event Split Governance A previously governed event may later be shown to contain multiple materially distinct events. TRERLS may govern the structural split relationship. However: Additional Technical Detail ≠ Permission to Split Event by default. A split requires sufficiently supported Event Formation or Boundary differentiation. Split Conditions A split may become appropriate where later information establishes: independent Event Roots; materially separate Event Boundaries; separate participants or value structures; independent operational purposes; or another material governance basis. TRERLS shall refer formation or boundary redetermination to the appropriate upstream Parent Standard where required. Split Event History Where a governed split occurs, the original representation must remain reconstructable. Event Split ≠ Historical Erasure. The relationship between the original representation and successor events shall be preserved. Merge and Split Neutrality Merge and split governance shall not be driven by a desired tax outcome. Therefore: Tax Advantage ≠ Event Merge Criterion. Tax Exposure ≠ Event Split Criterion. Event structure must remain grounded in governed operational reality. Reversal Relationship A later event may reverse some or all effects of an earlier event. Examples include: payment reversal; asset return; service cancellation; transaction reversal; resource release. TRERLS may establish a reversal relationship. Reversal Event ≠ Original Event Erasure. The original event remains part of governed history. Refund Relationship A refund event may relate to an earlier purchase or service event. TRERLS governs the event relationship. It does not determine whether the refund is legally deductible or modifies Tax Liability. Refund Relationship ≠ Tax Adjustment Determination. Replacement Relationship One event may replace another operationally. For example, a failed fulfillment event may be replaced by another fulfillment event. TRERLS may preserve the relationship without erasing the replaced event. Replacement Event ≠ Original Event Nonexistence. Supersession Relationship A later event may supersede an earlier operational event. Supersession indicates that later activity replaces the earlier event for some future operational purpose. It does not erase the historical event. Event Supersession ≠ Historical Erasure. Continuation Relationship A later event may continue activity initiated by an earlier event while remaining independently governed. TRERLS may establish continuation where appropriate. Event Continuation Relationship ≠ Same Event Continuity by default. TRECLS remains authoritative for the lifecycle continuity of one event. Correction Relationship A later event may exist specifically to correct consequences or records associated with an earlier event. TRERLS may represent that relationship. Correction Event ≠ Corrected Event Erasure. Causation Event relationship governance may preserve indications of causal structure where available. However, TRERLS does not automatically convert dependency, sequence, or proximity into causal proof. Event Sequence ≠ Causation. Event Dependency ≠ Universal Causation. Where causal determination belongs to another architecture or case-specific process, TRERLS shall preserve the boundary. Relationship Direction Relationships may be: directional; reciprocal; symmetric; asymmetric; conditional; hierarchical; sequential; or networked. TRERLS shall preserve the applicable relationship direction where material. Relationship Cardinality TRERLS shall permit relationship cardinalities including: one-to-one; one-to-many; many-to-one; many-to-many. Cardinality represents event structure. It does not determine tax aggregation. Relationship Cardinality ≠ Tax Aggregation Rule. Relationship Strength Relationships may possess different degrees of support. TRERLS may qualify relationships as: established; qualified; partial; probable; ambiguous; conflicted; unresolved. A weak relationship should not be presented as equivalent to a strongly governed relationship. Relationship Uncertainty Available information may show that events are related without establishing the exact relationship type. TRERLS shall preserve this uncertainty. Known Relationship ≠ Known Relationship Type by default. Relationship Conflict Different sources may describe event relationships differently. For example, one system may treat a payment as settlement of Event A, while another links it to Events A and B. TRERLS shall preserve materially relevant conflict. Relationship Conflict ≠ Permission for Convenient Event Mapping. Relationship Reconsideration New evidence may justify reconsideration of a relationship. TRERLS shall support governed reconsideration while preserving previous relationship history. Relationship Reconsideration ≠ Historical Erasure. Relationship Stability A relationship should remain stable unless materially relevant information changes. Changes in technical identifiers, storage systems, or reporting formats shall not automatically create new Event Relationships. System Change ≠ Relationship Change by default. Cross-System Event Relationships Related events may exist across multiple systems. TRERLS shall support relationships between events generated in: ERP; payment systems; banking systems; blockchains; marketplaces; logistics; AI-agent platforms; autonomous machines; industrial systems; or other infrastructures. System boundaries do not automatically equal Event Boundaries. System Boundary ≠ Event Boundary. Cross-Organization Relationships Events may span several organizations. For example: Buyer Event ↔ Marketplace Event ↔ Seller Event ↔ Payment Event ↔ Logistics Event TRERLS may preserve relationships among those events without requiring all organizations to represent them identically. Cross-Border Event Relationships Several related events may occur across multiple countries. TRERLS preserves the jurisdiction-neutral relationship structure. It does not decide: tax jurisdiction; source jurisdiction; residence jurisdiction; permanent establishment; place of supply; customs jurisdiction; or taxing rights. Cross-Border Event Relationship ≠ Tax Jurisdiction Determination. Multi-Jurisdiction Evaluation The same governed relationship structure may be evaluated differently by multiple jurisdictions. The model is: One Governed Event Relationship Structure ↓ Multiple Jurisdictional Evaluations Jurisdiction A may legally aggregate related events. Jurisdiction B may treat them separately. Jurisdiction C may apply anti-avoidance or other jurisdiction-specific doctrines. TREGA™ preserves the underlying governed event structure. Jurisdictions remain free to determine their legal tax treatment. Artificial Fragmentation Protection TRERLS shall protect against artificial fragmentation of one governed event into several events where no legitimate Event Formation or Boundary basis supports separation. More Records ≠ More Events. More Systems ≠ More Events. More Participants ≠ More Events. More Payments ≠ More Events. Artificial Aggregation Protection TRERLS shall equally protect against artificial aggregation. Several distinct events must not be collapsed merely because they: involve the same participants; occur under one contract; use one invoice; settle through one payment; occur on the same day; or belong to one commercial program. One Contract ≠ One Event by default. One Invoice ≠ One Event by default. One Payment ≠ One Event by default. Machine and Autonomous Event Relationships Autonomous economic systems may generate event networks without conventional human transaction boundaries. One AI agent may initiate an event. Another machine may execute a service. A smart contract may trigger settlement. A robot may deliver physical output. A later machine process may correct or reverse the operation. TRERLS shall support these event relationships without assuming that one machine workflow equals one event. One Autonomous Workflow ≠ One Tax-Relevant Event by default. Likewise: Multiple Agent Actions ≠ Multiple Tax-Relevant Events by default. Blockchain Event Relationships One economic activity may produce several blockchain transactions. One blockchain transaction may contain several operational actions. An on-chain operation may also depend on off-chain events. Therefore: One Blockchain Transaction ≠ One Tax-Relevant Event by default. and: Multiple Blockchain Transactions ≠ Multiple Tax-Relevant Events by default. TRERLS preserves the relationship between technical ledger events and governed Tax-Relevant Events. Event Relationship and Event Formation TREFS determines whether a valid event has been formed. TRERLS does not independently create event identity. Relationship Discovery ≠ New Event Formation. Where relationship analysis suggests that an additional event may exist, the issue shall be referred to TREFS. Event Relationship and Event Boundary TREBS governs where one event ends and another begins. TRERLS consumes those boundaries. It does not independently override them. Event Relationship ≠ Event Boundary Redetermination. Potential boundary problems shall be referred to TREBS. Event Relationship and Event Timing TRETS governs Event Timing. TRERLS may use temporal order as relationship information. It does not redefine Event Timing. Relationship Sequence ≠ Event Timing Determination. Event Relationship and Event Location TRELS governs Event Location. Shared or differing locations may inform event relationships. TRERLS does not determine location itself. Event Relationship and Participation TREPS governs Event Participation. Shared participants may contribute to relationship analysis. TRERLS shall not convert shared participation into Event Identity. Event Relationship and Value Association TRVAS governs which governed value results belong to each event. TRERLS may use shared or related Value Associations to establish event relationships. However: Shared Value ≠ Shared Event Identity. Event Relationship and Accountability TRERLS does not determine who is accountable for relationships among events. AGA™ remains authoritative for accountability governance. Event Relationship ≠ Accountability Relationship. Event Relationship and Liability A relationship between events may be relevant to downstream liability analysis. TRERLS does not determine liability. HALIA™ remains authoritative for the lifecycle of harm and liability. Related Events ≠ Shared Liability by default. Event Relationship and Taxation TRERLS does not determine: whether related events should be legally aggregated; whether several events constitute one taxable supply; whether transactions are linked for anti-avoidance purposes; whether an event series creates Tax Liability; whether consideration should be combined; whether a series forms one tax period; or another jurisdiction-specific tax conclusion. Therefore: Governed Event Relationship ≠ Tax Aggregation Determination. Tax law may later consume TRERLS output and reach jurisdiction-specific conclusions. Governance States TRERLS may establish architecture-level states including: Relationship Ready Relationship Under Governance Independent Events Related Events Dependent Events Sequential Events Parallel Events Grouped Events Parent–Child Events Composite Event Structure Event Chain Event Network Merge Candidate Merge Governed Split Candidate Split Governed Reversal Relationship Replacement Relationship Continuation Relationship Relationship Qualified Relationship Ambiguous Relationship Conflicted Relationship Unresolved Governed Event Relationship Structure Established These states govern relationship structure. They do not determine Tax-Relevant Event Determination under TREDS. Governance Principles TRERLS shall operate according to the following principles: Event identity must remain distinct from Event Relationship. Technical operation count must not determine Event count. Economic activity count must not automatically determine Event count. Related events may remain independent. Independent events may remain strongly related. Sequence does not prove identity or causation. Shared participants do not prove Event Identity. Shared value does not prove Event Identity. Grouping does not merge events. Merge and split must remain evidence-based. Tax outcome must not determine event structure. Historical relationship states must remain reconstructable. Jurisdiction-specific interpretation must remain downstream. Governance Requirements A conforming TRERLS implementation shall ensure that: relationships are established only among sufficiently governed events; event identity remains distinct from relationship identity; dependency can be represented; relationship direction can be preserved; sequence can be represented without implying event identity; parallel events can remain distinct; parent–child and component relationships can be represented; shared participants do not automatically merge events; shared Value References do not automatically merge events; common timing does not automatically merge events; common location does not automatically merge events; shared Event Context does not automatically merge events; technical operations are not automatically treated as independent events; one economic activity is not automatically treated as one event; event grouping preserves individual Event Identity; Event Chains and Event Networks can be represented; one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-one, and many-to-many relationships are supported; merge and split governance remains traceable; reversal does not erase the original event; replacement does not erase the replaced event; corrections do not erase event history; uncertainty remains visible; conflict remains visible; relationship reconsideration remains traceable; system migration does not automatically change relationships; cross-system and cross-organization relationships can be represented; autonomous and blockchain event structures can be governed; TREFS ownership of Event Formation remains preserved; TREBS ownership of Event Boundary remains preserved; TRETS ownership of Event Timing remains preserved; TRELS ownership of Event Location remains preserved; TREPS ownership of Event Participation remains preserved; TRVAS ownership of Value Association remains preserved; and tax aggregation or other jurisdiction-specific legal interpretation remains downstream. Governance Logic IF two or more Governed Value-Associated Events possess a materially relevant structural connection, THEN TRERLS shall evaluate the Event Relationship. IF events are related but independently formed and bounded, THEN their individual Event Identities shall remain preserved. IF Event B depends on Event A, THEN dependency may be established without merging the events. IF events occur in sequence, THEN sequence may be governed without assuming causation or Event Identity. IF several events share one economic activity, THEN neither automatic grouping nor automatic merger shall occur without sufficient governance basis. IF multiple technical operations belong to one already-governed event, THEN technical record multiplicity shall not create additional events. IF multiple governed events require grouping, THEN group membership shall preserve individual Event Identity. IF available evidence suggests that previously separate events should be merged, THEN relevant Formation and Boundary governance shall be respected and the historical relationship shall remain traceable. IF available evidence suggests that one event should be split, THEN relevant Formation and Boundary governance shall be respected and the original representation shall remain reconstructable. IF relationship uncertainty or conflict remains material, THEN it shall remain explicitly represented. IF the Event Relationship Structure is sufficiently governed, THEN the result shall proceed to TREDS for Tax-Relevant Event Determination. Governance Outputs TRERLS may produce: Governed Event Relationship; Event Dependency Relationship; Directed Event Relationship; Mutual Event Dependency; Event Sequence; Parallel Event Relationship; Conditional Event Relationship; Parent–Child Event Relationship; Component Event Relationship; Shared Value Event Relationship; Event Group; Event Chain; Event Network; One-to-Many Event Structure; Many-to-One Event Structure; Many-to-Many Event Structure; Event Merge Relationship; Event Split Relationship; Event Reversal Relationship; Event Refund Relationship; Event Replacement Relationship; Event Supersession Relationship; Event Continuation Relationship; Event Correction Relationship; Relationship Confidence State; Relationship Ambiguity State; Relationship Conflict State; Relationship Traceability Record; and the principal output: Governed Event Relationship Structure. Internal Module Architecture TRERLS is operationalized through five Core Modules: 1. ERLIM — Event Relationship Identification Module Identifies materially relevant relationships among already-governed events. 2. ERLDM — Event Relationship Dependency Module Governs dependency, direction, conditionality, and structural dependence among events. 3. ERLSM — Event Relationship Sequence Module Governs temporal and operational sequence among related events without converting sequence into identity or causation. 4. ERLGM — Event Relationship Grouping Module Governs Event Groups, chains, networks, parent–child structures, and other multi-event group structures while preserving individual Event Identity. 5. ERLMM — Event Relationship Merge & Split Module Governs justified merge and split relationships where event structure must be revised while preserving traceability and upstream governance boundaries. The Internal Module Flow is: ERLIM — Relationship Identification ↓ ERLDM — Relationship Dependency ↓ ERLSM — Relationship Sequence ↓ ERLGM — Relationship Grouping ↓ ERLMM — Merge & Split Governance ↓ Governed Event Relationship Structure Cross-Architecture Boundaries ORA™ — Operational Reality Architecture governs what actually happened operationally. TREFS governs Event Formation. TREBS governs Event Boundary. TRETS governs Event Timing. TRELS governs Event Location. TREPS governs Event Participation. TRVAS governs Event–Value Association. TRERLS governs relationships among already-governed events. OBIDENITY® governs origin-bound identity, ownership, authority, permission, and provenance. VFM® — Value Flow Mechanism governs the lifecycle of value. AGA™ governs accountability. HALIA™ governs the lifecycle of harm and liability. ADIT® governs auditability and relevant evidence structures. VALIDOS™ governs validation. Jurisdiction-specific taxation systems remain authoritative for the legal tax consequences of related events. Critical Distinctions Event Relationship ≠ Event Identity. Related Events ≠ Same Event by default. Shared Attribute ≠ Event Relationship Determination by default. Strong Relationship ≠ Event Identity. Event Dependency ≠ Event Merger. Mutual Dependency ≠ Single Event by default. Sequence ≠ Event Identity. Temporal Proximity ≠ Event Relationship by default. Operational Sequence ≠ Tax Sequence. Conditional Event Relationship ≠ Authority Governance. Event Component Relationship ≠ Event Merge by default. Parallel Events ≠ Same Event. Same Participant ≠ Same Event. Shared Value Reference ≠ Same Event. Same Location ≠ Related Event by default. Same Time ≠ Same Event. Shared Context ≠ Same Event. One Economic Activity ≠ One Event by default. Multiple Technical Operations ≠ Multiple Economically Independent Events by default. Technical Operation ≠ Tax-Relevant Event by default. Event Group ≠ Single Event. Group Identifier ≠ Event Identifier. Event Chain ≠ Single Event Lifecycle by default. Relationship Convenience ≠ Permission to Merge Events. Event Merge ≠ Silent Event Deletion. Additional Technical Detail ≠ Permission to Split Event by default. Event Split ≠ Historical Erasure. Tax Advantage ≠ Event Merge Criterion. Tax Exposure ≠ Event Split Criterion. Reversal Event ≠ Original Event Erasure. Replacement Event ≠ Original Event Nonexistence. Event Supersession ≠ Historical Erasure. Event Sequence ≠ Causation. Relationship Cardinality ≠ Tax Aggregation Rule. Relationship Conflict ≠ Permission for Convenient Event Mapping. System Change ≠ Relationship Change by default. System Boundary ≠ Event Boundary. Cross-Border Event Relationship ≠ Tax Jurisdiction Determination. More Records ≠ More Events. One Contract ≠ One Event by default. One Invoice ≠ One Event by default. One Payment ≠ One Event by default. One Autonomous Workflow ≠ One Tax-Relevant Event by default. One Blockchain Transaction ≠ One Tax-Relevant Event by default. Relationship Discovery ≠ New Event Formation. Event Relationship ≠ Event Boundary Redetermination. Shared Value ≠ Shared Event Identity. Event Relationship ≠ Accountability Relationship. Related Events ≠ Shared Liability by default. Governed Event Relationship ≠ Tax Aggregation Determination. Enterprise Application TRERLS provides a governed relationship layer for systems where economic activity spans multiple technical, operational, organizational, or digital events. A typical enterprise path is: ERP / Banking / Marketplace / Blockchain / AI Agent / Machine Infrastructure → Multiple Governed Tax-Relevant Events → TRERLS — Relationship Governance → Governed Event Relationship Structure → TREDS — Tax-Relevant Event Determination → Jurisdiction-Specific Tax Engine This allows organizations to preserve the actual event structure before tax law decides whether related events should be legally aggregated, separated, recharacterized, or treated differently. Canonical Boundary TRERLS owns the governance of relationships among already-governed Tax-Relevant Events, including relationship identification, dependency, direction, sequence, parallelism, conditionality, grouping, Event Chains, Event Networks, parent–child relationships, component relationships, convergence, divergence, reversal, replacement, continuation, merge, split, qualification, uncertainty, conflict, reconsideration, and relationship-level traceability. TRERLS does not create Event Context, recognize occurrences, form new events, independently redefine Event Boundaries, determine Event Timing, determine Event Location, establish Event Participation, govern the Value Lifecycle, establish Event–Value Association, determine Event Readiness or final Tax-Relevant Event status, determine Event Record structure, govern Event Lifecycle continuity, establish identity, ownership, accountability, liability, taxable value, Tax Base, Tax Liability, tax jurisdiction, or another jurisdiction-specific legal consequence. Its governance ends when the relationships among the relevant governed events are sufficiently represented for formal Tax-Relevant Event Determination under TREDS. Canonical Handoff TRVAS — Governed Value-Associated Event ↓ TRERLS — Governed Event Relationship Structure ↓ TREDS — Tax-Relevant Event Determination Canonical Closing Statement TRERLS preserves the structure between events without allowing technical workflows, shared records, common participants, or desired tax outcomes to redefine what the events are. One economic activity may contain several events, and several technical operations may belong to one event. Relationship governance exists precisely because those are not the same question. Event Relationship ≠ Event Identity. Multiple Technical Operations ≠ Multiple Economically Independent Events by default. Governed Event Relationship ≠ Tax Aggregation Determination. TREGA™ governs the event. The jurisdiction governs the tax. title: OOF™ Tax-Relevant Event Timing Standard - (TRETS)
text: OOF™ Tax-Relevant Event Timing Standard - (TRETS) Tax-Relevant Event Timing Standard - (TRETS) OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: TREGA™ — Tax-Relevant Event Governance Architecture™ Parent Standard: Tax-Relevant Event Timing Standard (TRETS) Operational Layer: Tax-Relevant Event Timing Governance Layer Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Tax-Relevant Event Governance Type: Parent Standard Governed Space: Tax-Relevant Event Timing Origin ID: TREGA-TRETS-005 Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 31 August 2026 AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodology Intellectual Property Protection Canonical Language: English ------------------------------ Canonical Definition The Tax-Relevant Event Timing Standard (TRETS) governs how a sufficiently bounded real-world, economic, operational, transactional, digital, autonomous, machine-generated, or value-affecting event is temporally situated through governed identification of its operational time, start, completion, duration, and temporal order. TRETS establishes the governance conditions through which a Governed Bounded Event becomes a Governed Temporally Situated Event capable of progressing through subsequent TREGA™ lifecycle stages. It governs the temporal representation of what happened operationally without determining the legal tax point, tax period, filing period, recognition date under tax law, legal timing of tax liability, or any other jurisdiction-specific taxation consequence. The principal transition governed by TRETS is: Governed Bounded Event → Governed Temporally Situated Event TRETS governs when the event occurred as governed operational reality — not when a jurisdiction decides that the event becomes relevant for taxation under law. ------------------------------ Operational Role TREBS establishes: What belongs within the governed event and where its structural Event Boundary lies. TRETS establishes: When that bounded event occurred, began, completed, persisted, and how it is temporally ordered relative to other relevant events. Its narrow task is: to establish a sufficiently explicit, coherent, traceable, and jurisdiction-neutral temporal representation of a Governed Bounded Event so that subsequent TREGA™ governance can operate on an event whose operational temporal position is known without allowing Event Timing itself to determine a legal tax point or tax period. TRETS therefore creates the governed temporal layer between Event Boundary and Event Location. ------------------------------ Core Question When did a Governed Bounded Event occur operationally, and how can its temporal position be governed without converting operational time into a jurisdiction-specific legal tax point? ------------------------------ Governance Flow Governed Bounded Event ↓ Event Time Identification ↓ Event Start Governance ↓ Event Completion Governance ↓ Event Duration Governance ↓ Event Temporal Order Governance ↓ Governed Temporally Situated Event ↓ TRELS — Tax-Relevant Event Location Standard ------------------------------ Governed Space TRETS governs: Tax-Relevant Event Timing This governed space includes the temporal structures necessary to situate an already bounded event within operational reality. TRETS governs: Event Time identification temporal signal differentiation temporal source association Event Start Event Completion Event Duration temporal sequence temporal order temporal uncertainty temporal conflict temporal qualification distributed event timing machine-generated timing autonomous event timing multi-stage event timing temporal continuity temporal traceability readiness for Event Location governance TRETS does not determine the legal taxation consequence of any temporal state. ------------------------------ Event Timing Principle Operational events require temporal representation. However, different systems may record different times for the same underlying activity. Examples may include: order creation authorization execution shipment delivery acceptance settlement invoice creation database entry ledger posting API execution machine initiation machine completion system synchronization human confirmation These timestamps do not automatically represent the governed Event Time. Therefore: Recorded Timestamp ≠ Governed Event Time by Default. TRETS determines which temporal information legitimately represents the operational event within the governed event lifecycle. ------------------------------ Operational Event Time An Operational Event Time represents the governed temporal position of an event within operational reality. Depending on the event structure, this may require: a single temporal point, multiple temporal points, a start and completion, an interval, a duration, an ordered sequence, or a qualified temporal representation. TRETS must preserve the temporal structure actually required by the event rather than forcing every event into a single timestamp. Therefore: Event Time ≠ Single Timestamp by Default. ------------------------------ Temporal Source Principle Temporal information may originate from multiple sources. These may include: physical observations enterprise systems transaction systems payment infrastructure distributed systems digital platforms sensors machines autonomous agents human records external systems synchronized clocks asynchronous logs A temporal source may provide evidence about Event Timing. It does not automatically determine Event Timing. Therefore: Source Timestamp ≠ Authoritative Event Time by Default. ------------------------------ Event Time Identification Before Start, Completion, Duration, or Temporal Order can be governed, the relevant temporal representation of the event must be identified. This requires distinguishing temporal signals associated with the event from timestamps that merely describe: system processing, record creation, synchronization, reporting, later correction, downstream settlement, unrelated activity. Detailed Event Time Identification belongs to: ETIM — Event Time Identification Module. ------------------------------ Event Start Where the event has a meaningful operational beginning, TRETS must govern the Event Start. Event Start must be grounded in the event's operational structure. It must not be inferred automatically from: earliest database record, earliest technical log, first associated communication, contract creation, first payment record, or earliest dependency. Therefore: Earliest Timestamp ≠ Event Start by Default. Detailed Event Start governance belongs to: ETSM — Event Start Module. ------------------------------ Event Completion Where the event has a meaningful operational completion, TRETS must establish when the event became operationally complete. Completion may differ from: payment, invoicing, accounting posting, system closure, reporting, legal acceptance, tax recognition. Therefore: Operational Completion ≠ Legal Tax Recognition. Detailed Event Completion governance belongs to: ETCM — Event Completion Module. ------------------------------ Event Duration Some events cannot be represented legitimately by a single temporal point. They may persist across: seconds, hours, days, months, continuous service periods, production cycles, distributed operations, autonomous execution periods. TRETS must therefore support governed Event Duration where duration is structurally relevant. Therefore: Event Duration ≠ Tax Period. Detailed Event Duration governance belongs to: ETDM — Event Duration Module. ------------------------------ Temporal Order Events may exist within chains, sequences, dependencies, or broader operational structures. TRETS must support governed temporal ordering where relative order matters. Examples may include: Event A ↓ Event B ↓ Event C or: Event A ∥ Event B ↓ Event C Temporal order must distinguish chronological relationship from other relationships. Therefore: Temporal Order ≠ Causal Relationship by Default. Detailed Temporal Order governance belongs to: ETOM — Event Temporal Order Module. ------------------------------ Point Events Some events may legitimately be represented by a sufficiently precise operational temporal point. TRETS permits point representation where the underlying event structure supports it. However: Technical Timestamp Precision ≠ Operational Temporal Precision. A system capable of recording microseconds does not establish that the event itself can legitimately be governed at microsecond precision. ------------------------------ Interval Events Some events have a meaningful start and completion and must therefore be represented as temporal intervals. Conceptually: Event Start ↓ Event Activity ↓ Event Completion The interval belongs to the operational event representation. It must not automatically be converted into a jurisdiction-specific taxation period. ------------------------------ Open Events An event may begin without having reached operational completion. Such an event may remain: Temporally Open until sufficient operational conditions establish completion. TRETS must not manufacture a completion point merely because downstream systems require one. Therefore: Missing Completion ≠ Permission to Invent Completion. ------------------------------ Continuous Events Certain governed events may represent continuous operational activity rather than discrete instantaneous occurrence. Examples may include: continuing digital services infrastructure operation continuous machine activity ongoing resource provision autonomous service execution TRETS must preserve legitimate temporal continuity without automatically dividing the event according to accounting or tax periods. Therefore: Continuous Operational Event ≠ Periodic Tax Event by Default. ------------------------------ Multi-Stage Events A bounded event may contain multiple operational stages. For example: Initiation ↓ Processing ↓ Fulfilment ↓ Completion The existence of multiple temporal stages does not automatically create multiple governed events. That distinction belongs to prior Event Boundary governance. Therefore: Multiple Temporal Stages ≠ Multiple Events by Default. ------------------------------ Distributed Event Timing A distributed event may occur across systems operating: asynchronously, in different time zones, with different clock precision, with synchronization delays, across multiple infrastructure layers. TRETS must allow these temporal representations to be reconciled without assuming that one system clock defines the event. Therefore: System Clock ≠ Event Clock by Default. ------------------------------ Machine-Generated Event Timing Machines may produce extremely granular timestamp streams. One autonomous industrial event may generate thousands or millions of machine timestamps. TRETS must distinguish machine telemetry from governed Event Timing. Therefore: Machine Timestamp ≠ Independent Event Time by Default. ------------------------------ Autonomous Event Timing Autonomous systems may initiate, execute, modify, and complete activities without direct human temporal intervention. TRETS applies the same governance principle: the temporal structure must represent the governed operational event rather than merely the internal execution cycle of the autonomous system. Therefore: Autonomous Execution Cycle ≠ Governed Event Timing by Default. ------------------------------ Time-Zone Governance Operational events may involve systems and participants operating across different time zones. TRETS must preserve sufficient information to distinguish: recorded local time, normalized time, source time zone, temporal conversion, operational temporal context. Time-zone normalization must not destroy the original temporal representation. Therefore: Normalized Time ≠ Original Recorded Time. Both may need to remain reconstructable. ------------------------------ Temporal Precision Event Timing must be represented only at a precision legitimately supported by the governed information. Possible precision may include: date hour minute second sub-second bounded interval approximate interval qualified temporal range TRETS must not manufacture false temporal precision. Therefore: Available Clock Precision ≠ Justified Event-Time Precision. ------------------------------ Temporal Ambiguity Multiple plausible temporal interpretations may exist. TRETS must represent temporal ambiguity explicitly where the available governed information does not support one legitimate interpretation. Therefore: Temporal Ambiguity ≠ Permission for Arbitrary Timestamp Selection. ------------------------------ Temporal Conflict Sources may disagree. For example: payment system says 23:59, marketplace says 00:01, logistics system says 00:04, autonomous agent log says 23:58. TRETS must preserve material temporal conflict rather than silently selecting the timestamp most convenient for downstream taxation. Possible state: Temporal Conflict ------------------------------ Temporal Uncertainty Event Timing may be known only within a range. For example: 14:00–14:10 may be more legitimate than an unsupported claim of: 14:03:27 Therefore: Qualified Temporal Range > False Temporal Precision. TRETS permits explicit temporal uncertainty where operational reality requires it. ------------------------------ Temporal Correction Later information may establish that a temporal representation was incorrect. Correction must preserve traceability between previous and corrected temporal states. Therefore: Event Time Correction ≠ Historical Erasure. Temporal correction must not silently rewrite the governed event history. ------------------------------ Event Timing and Event Boundary TRETS receives a Governed Bounded Event. It does not use timing information to silently redefine Event Boundary. If temporal information reveals a material structural problem in the existing boundary, the issue may require governed reconsideration through TREBS. Therefore: Event Timing ≠ Event Boundary Governance. ------------------------------ Event Timing and Event Location Knowing when an event occurred does not establish where it occurred.
